[Col. 0009]

## Dedicatory Letter to John V, King of Portugal

[Col. 0009A] Before you, great John, stand the four most holy Gospels of Jesus Christ, arranged in four parallel columns after the model of the remarkable *Tetrapla* of Origen Adamantius. I am not deterred, in approaching the royal throne by letter, by my uncultivated manner of writing; for, just as those who dare to speak before you according to their rank do not know your greatness, so those who do not dare in any fashion do not know your humanity.

From the most ancient times it has been customary to commit memorials of memorable deeds to writing, compile them into books, and offer them to princely men; because nothing is begun unless, after God, the emperor has given it his favor—as Flavius Vegetius Renatus once said when he addressed the Emperor Valentinian II and offered him his *Commentaries*. And since among human things nothing is more illustrious than to deserve well of the commonwealth, it will be reckoned a great glory to you that you have received my labors into royal protection—labors that will bring some usefulness.

For they present that common Latin Italian version, hitherto unpublished, [Col. 0009B] which, wisely composed at the beginning of the nascent Church by some unknown contemporary of the apostles, prevailed in the churches first of Italy, then of Africa and Gaul, before the divine library of blessed Jerome. Its passages are found, seen, and shine forth in the holy Fathers of the earliest centuries, especially in Cyprian of Carthage, Hilary of Poitiers, Lucifer of Cagliari, Zeno of Verona, Gaudentius of Brescia, Victor the African, Ambrose of Milan, Jerome of Stridon, Leo, and Gregory the Great.

Saint Augustine esteemed the Italian version so highly that he preferred it to the others because of its close adherence to the wording together with its clarity of meaning. What better witness can we seek, to make manifest to all how much power and usefulness are found in its reading?

This treasure lay hidden until the present day in the chests and archives of certain distinguished cathedral churches. From these I either first unearthed it, or received it through the hands of friends most learned in these matters. Now, emerging into the light under your royal auspices, it brings forth both new things and old: namely, manuscripts—who would believe it?—most splendidly written in gold and silver pigment, at the expense of munificent kings, upon purple parchment which the remotest antiquity, indeed of fourteen centuries, has consecrated.

[Col. 0009C] That distant age will possess its immovable certainty through specimens of the characters, reproduced with their native features in engraved plates, so that they may be witnesses of the times and messengers of truth, and may point out the ages of copyists, as though they were a chronological era.

These magnificent volumes of the divine Scriptures, written in gold and silver, do not seem to have been in use in the first or second century of Christ, while the Church still held fast to apostolic [Col. 0010A] poverty. When peace had been restored under Constantine and wealth had increased, the example of the great emperor—who commanded that sacred books be copied and adorned by most skillful scribes, as Eusebius records in his *Life*—led other Christian kings and princes to enrich the manuscript repositories of royal basilicas with costly copies, especially of the Gospels.

Therefore immortal thanks are due from us to Desiderius, Charlemagne, Berengar, and other princely men, through whose munificent care and expenditure books have reached us which I am the first to publish, so that they may be handled by all and henceforth perish only with letters themselves. And since so many illustrious kings seem, as it were by joining their right hands and services, to have conspired in offering you a gift worthy of a king, I hope that your sacred Majesty will most graciously receive my labors into protection.

If you do so, yours will be the highest greatness in this benefaction, and mine the greatest glory; and future ages will owe to these most beautiful monuments [Col. 0010B] the light and permanence prepared under the most fortunate auspices of King John.

Alcuin, the most learned man of all produced by that age, dedicated to the most excellent king, Charlemagne—who ought himself to stand in the place of very many men—a volume of the sacred Bible in Jerome’s edition, containing both Testaments. This autograph exemplar, of a thousand years’ age, exists in the library of our Congregation of the Roman Oratory. That library acquired so great a treasure through the gift of the most distinguished Portuguese Achille Statius, by means of Cardinal Cesare Baronius, the immortal glory and ornament of the same congregation.

A complete description of this manuscript also, and likewise of another Carolingian manuscript, which the monastery of Saint Paul Outside the Walls guards with the utmost reverence, will be available in the continuation of this work, O pious, fortunate, august King of Portugal, with you as patron and protector. For it has been corrected and most carefully emended, and surpasses the others in this respect: the supreme pontiffs caused the Vulgate edition of the sacred Bible to be restored according to its standard and rule.

[Col. 0010C] Our forefathers quite rightly judged that Jerome’s version—contained in Alcuin’s volume—ought to be preferred to the others; yet they did not reject the Italian version. Rather, their policy was to take both into account. For the sake of preserving the authority and memory of both, Saint Gregory the Great ordered the New and Old Versions to be written down, included them in his commentaries, and set them before the churches, so that the faithful might have the opportunity of recognizing the excellence of each. We too still employ the reading of both today. For the two, joined together, produced the present Vulgate. This is why, in the end, the name and recognition of the Italian version disappeared in the latter age.

Thus certain most distinguished men, illustrious in this literary age by the highest abilities and most refined learning, [Col. 0011A] as soon as they learned that by the singular benefit of God, best and greatest, I had discovered the Italian version, urged me with prayers to publish as soon as possible a monument of such venerable antiquity, which had slipped from human memory through the long passage of time and been wholly effaced.

It was fitting for a generous man to comply with their wish, particularly because the remarkable work of the Italian version, from which our Vulgate is derived as streams from a fountain, wonderfully illuminates the holy Fathers of the first four centuries. There was also this consideration: God chose to inaugurate my first entry into the inner sanctuaries of Scripture with an autograph manuscript of Saint Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli and venerable martyr, for which no like or equal exists in the world.

The authenticity of this manuscript is established by all antiquity, and the published acts of that most holy bishop testify that the tradition of the Church of Vercelli is neither uncertain nor interrupted. The notable testimony of King Berengar, who visited that same church, is added to it, and I gladly produce it. He did not wish that a manuscript so ancient, written by the martyr’s own hand and already decaying at that time—namely, around the year of Christ 888, when Berengar was chosen king of Italy—should be ever more consumed by the injury of time and the envious tooth of the ages.

[Col. 0011B] Therefore, to preserve it unharmed for the future, he arranged for the book to be protected with silver plates interwoven with gold and gems. The verses proclaim this; he ordered them to be inscribed beneath the image of the most holy Eusebius placed in the manuscript itself. They read:

> This bishop Eusebius wrote it, and antiquity dissolved it;  
> But King Berengar restored the same.  
> After drawing forth silver and bright gold,  
> He himself offered it, O Bishop, to your church.

What King Berengar rendered to the martyr, I, devoted to your name and Majesty, O most powerful king, give, bestow, and dedicate to you together with the other venerable manuscripts of that same ancient Italian version.

[Col. 0011C] The subject of the work, the merits of the most holy Eusebius, and the concern of so many kings and queens—to whom this edition owes the reception of nearly all its manuscripts—give me the surest hope that you too will prove its most munificent patron and singular protector.

Moreover, no greater gift could be brought to a great king than the evangelical covenant, by which kingship is reconciled with priesthood and majesty with religion, and by the reading and use of which all royal virtues have been acquired, perfected, and adorned. God, best and greatest, has poured these gifts upon you so abundantly that you have attained the summit of piety, which has won for you an eternal name.

Happy Portugal, which under you as governor and prince enjoys tranquillity and peace amid the assaults of wars raging on every side. Happier still [Col. 0012A] because, with you as father of the country, it knows that evils are removed and guarded against lest they return, while benefits are supplied and brought about lest they prove transitory. Most happy because, while you are safe, the kingdom is safe, and all things succeed according to desire.

And since Saint Augustine calls Christian kings blessed when they rule justly and make their power a servant of God’s Majesty, chiefly for the widest possible extension of his worship, here is the ground of your blessedness and felicity, which no adversity will ever disturb. Justice, piety, and religion hold the kingdom in astonishment; and all call you father and look upon you as their brightest ray of light. For, most illustrious king, you at once diffuse virtue through all things; like the sun, you make yourself wholly, not merely in some part, common not to one or another but to all subject to you.

Your devotion to letters makes you common to them, a devotion which you have devoted to restoring a magnificent printing house. In this your generosity has so poured itself out that it may serve as a standard and example to other kings. Certainly this further distinction had to be added to your most illustrious [Col. 0012B] praises—a distinction than which, in my judgment, none is more useful to posterity and none more glorious.

Accordingly, by the judgment and common agreement of all Portugal, you are rightly and deservedly called, named, and are the Father of Letters. For they see, with the altered face of affairs, letters flourishing in the kingdom; they see seminaries, schools, and academies founded, established, and endowed with stipends worthy of you alone and comparable to no one else. Finally, they see your distinguished royal library, enlarged by so many additions that it seems almost to obscure the memory of the Ptolemaic and Attalid libraries.

Since the example which proceeds from a most wise king carries enormous weight, there is hope that, under you as author and leader, all liberal disciplines and the silent arts will gain ever greater growth and new splendor. But your Majesty compels me to make an end of writing. Though I see you only from afar, I, a humble priest, commend you daily in my sacrifices to God, to the Blessed Virgin Mary, and to Saint Anthony Thaumaturgus, [Col. 0012C] mindful of the great benefits which you, most munificent king, have conferred upon Bishop Francesco Blanchini, my uncle, and upon Gaspare Blanchini, my brother, your Knight of Christ.

In beloved Rome there is one prayer: that God, best and greatest, may continue to bless you, best of kings, with perfect health and uninterrupted successes. The commonwealth of letters, stretching its hands to heaven, repeats the same prayer; so does the Christian world. The voice of all is the voice of God; it gives hope for a long life to King John and for the public prosperity of Portugal.

From the Vallicellian residence of the Congregation of the Roman Oratory, on the Ides of January, in the year of the Lord 1744.

[Col. 0011D]

## Letter of Philip Garbelli to Blanchini: On the Brescia Manuscript

Philip Garbelli sends greetings in the Lord to the most distinguished Joseph Blanchini.

Your most gracious attentions recalled me, when I was thinking of no such thing, to studies which I had often laid aside and often resumed, but had now at last entirely postponed because other matters called me away. For when you had resolved to publish the copy of the ancient translator which was preserved in the archive of the chief church of your city, you found among the papers of your uncle Francesco, a man of the highest distinction, a specimen of our silver manuscript which he had once received from me.

[Col. 0012D] You then wrote to ask me to extract its readings that depart from the Vulgate; and, if I thought anything else might be useful to you, not to refuse to bring that very thing, or contribution, to this feast. I did so gladly. For what would not be demanded of me by your undertaking? Not long ago it so occupied men of great reputation that they thought matters would have gone excellently for themselves and the entire Christian world if, just as Martianay in Gaul published an ancient copy of Matthew, so others who possessed these sacred monuments had labored with equal fidelity and diligence in bringing the remainder to light.

Certainly no one can fail to see that your plan, worthy of you, worthy of Italy, and worthy also of the memory of your uncle, in whose footsteps you continue to tread with such distinction, will be welcomed and approved by all learned men. But while I was revisiting and comparing the variant readings which I had formerly set aside in my notebooks—all from Matthew’s text, and some from Luke and John—lest any errors perhaps introduced while I was reading or copying should be imposed upon posterity, behold, I received another of your most affectionate letters, in which you indicate that you are considering publishing the text of the complete manuscript.

[Col. 0013A] I praised this proposal, which seemed likely to satisfy those occupied with sacred matters far more fully than mere extracts could. For although, in distinguishing what the ancients derived from sources and what from the storehouse of memory; what form texts took in public church manuscripts and what in private ones; and what was read in the earlier and later centuries, such matters are of great value, nevertheless nothing is equally useful and pleasing as to examine and publish, in these very ancient copies, the very sequence, character, genius, and finally the minutest features, as it were, of the entire body.

For this reason Bentley once pressed John Mill to publish the Alexandrian, Cambridge, Oxford, and finally French manuscripts, in such a manner that the edition should follow accurately and scrupulously every letter and stroke of the exemplars, even where scribes had erred (*Letter to Mill*, in Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Graeca*). Later, however, occupied with his celebrated edition of the Greek New Testament, he was soon snatched away by premature death, leaving this Sparta to be adorned by others.

Indeed, since in the age of our forefathers—and far more in our own—love of antiquity has been great, and since men have devoted themselves to searching out the many things that lay hidden and still lie hidden, among both sacred and profane monuments of antiquity, in order to bring them into public light, [Col. 0013B] it may accordingly seem surprising that no one has yet published in full the version of the earliest translator as it existed before Jerome.

For apart from the remarkable agreement of so many centuries in setting forth the Gospel history, this also might perhaps have become clear: many who suppose that there were formerly numerous Latin versions of the New Testament in the Church do not press Jerome’s and Augustine’s authority with sufficient attention. The older manuscripts differ from one another to such a degree only in a few places, and indeed only verbally, except for one or two which private license, ignorance, and sometimes even misguided piety have interpolated in astonishing ways.

Add that no safer provision can be made for these treasures, lest they perish through age, than that they should be printed and handled by everyone, thereafter to perish only with letters themselves. For however carefully the very characters may be preserved in private chests or in princely libraries, they nevertheless disappear through damp, moths, dust, and above all the devouring power of time. Thus it happens that what could be read fairly conveniently one or two centuries ago can now scarcely, indeed not even scarcely, be distinguished as its strokes fade away.

[Col. 0013D] I have no doubt that this will someday happen to our manuscript. For in some places, especially in Luke, the purple has turned into a dark blue; and as the silver adhesive with which the characters were coated has here and there fallen away, it is difficult to ascertain what is written except in very strong light.

Therefore I arranged for a copyist to take down the complete text of the four evangelists as I read it aloud before him. You know what indulgence must be granted in such a matter, as do all who devote themselves to studies of this kind. Not thinking this sufficient proof of my good faith, after everything had been carried through to the end, I compared it again with the original, except Matthew, which I had sent to you earlier when a convenient opportunity presented itself. My eyes, weak by nature, had at last grown weary through that unremitting exertion so that I could not proceed further. Yet I came through and delivered the work complete.

You now have what I think more probable concerning the character of that manuscript; what I have conjectured concerning its age; and what I had formerly observed in haste, now somewhat enlarged by further examination, considered, and arranged as best I could. [Col. 0014B] If anything in these reflections of mine seems useful to you, use it as though it were your own; for we have arranged it solely for your sake. If not, suppress it in silence. I shall gladly agree, knowing that in a field so trodden and dust so thoroughly stirred up there is scarcely room for new footprints, and that our age, fortunate only in rare and exquisite talents, looks for such things from great minds—things which we certainly can neither expect for ourselves amid our very slender resources nor, much less, offer to others. But let us now proceed to the matters proposed.

Among the most celebrated monasteries not only of Italy but of all Europe, there always was, and still is, that which Desiderius, king of the Lombards, raised from its foundations in our city; its church was dedicated to the Savior. Although later, when this church had not indeed been wholly abandoned but had been set aside for private devotions because of its narrowness and, I suppose, excessive darkness, the noble virgins built another more suitable for sacred rites and dedicated it to Saint Julia.

[Col. 0014C] The liberality and favor both of that king and of the emperors who, after overthrowing the Lombard empire, came into possession of affairs had raised this place, if any other, to such wealth that it possessed extensive estates, rights, fiefs, churches, and their priesthoods in several provinces of Italy. Yet the greater part of these, as is the condition of human affairs, soon passed to one owner after another, leaving the old masters only titles and documents.

For besides copies of Desiderius and Adelchis, there still survive the very autograph diplomas of ancient emperors, by which they bestowed immense benefactions upon granddaughters, daughters, and sisters consecrated there to God. There are also rescripts of subsequent emperors, including the invincible Emperor Charles VI, and of the kings of Spain, by which the privileges of these women are confirmed in the Milanese dominion. For our prince’s Majesty has most graciously received all the remaining matters into protection.

Moreover, there is a great abundance of ancient parchments, containing private donations, emphyteutic leases, purchases, sales, and, finally, all other matters relating to the administration of this most extensive establishment; also material capable of greatly enlarging our knowledge of the customs, deeds, laws, and judgments of those times, and especially the glossaries of barbarous Latin.

[Col. 0015A] And would that the passage of so many centuries, the difficulty of the writing, ignorance of the subjects, occasional neglect, and above all the ravings of idle hands had not prevented other documents which ought to have remained there from still living and flourishing. But the deed is done, and it is no longer permitted to stir those ashes.

I had copied not a few of them with my own hand into notebooks, lest they suffer the same fate, intending some day to publish them if life and strength remained. But later other concerns, new studies, and health increasingly impaired—which forbids me to entertain long hopes—overturned my earlier plans and shook them from my hands.

But to return to our matter: among the aforementioned monuments lay a silver manuscript of the Gospels, which those virgins used to call the breviary of Queen Ansa. When it was offered to me by my cousin, then abbess, and I had only seen it and greeted it at the threshold while occupied with other manuscripts, I subsequently obtained it. This was first so that I might send the aforesaid specimen to your uncle, who had shown the marks of purple parchment to the most eminent Giovanni Francesco Barbarigo and, together with us—who had been given him as companions of honor by that most gracious prince—had examined it and attempted to copy its characters. It was also so that on the same occasion I might inspect it more carefully and at the same time extract the variants, which I did not doubt would someday be useful to me, though this has now in fact occurred to a degree even greater than I had promised myself.

[Col. 0015C] For to those labors I owe both your friendship and the light and permanence, prepared under happier auspices, for a monument far more beautiful than it might perhaps still have awaited from me.

That this manuscript remained unseen by every sacred critic until these times, and certainly was used in study by none of them, may be demonstrated by this: among all the other manuscripts they mention as sources for their variants, you will not find even one who has produced a reading from it. So far as I know, only Paul Galleardus, my distinguished fellow citizen, has presented us with one or two readings in his very elegant edition of the works of Gaudentius. He would certainly have given us an edition much enlarged and more excellent, had he not been obliged to proceed according to another’s judgment and to hasten, rather than to publish the outstanding work by his own decision.

Mabillon himself, when he visited Brescia during his journey through Italy, passed over all these relics of ancient times in silence, since no one among us held a torch before him. I often complained of this among friends: that he had not commended these too to posterity in immortal writings, together with those of so many most famous cities.

[Col. 0015D] But now at last I see that matters have been excellently arranged for us, so that we need not owe every memory of our antiquities to foreign talents; and so that Italy, the mother of letters and arts, may someday repay to Gaul, and indeed with interest, the favor which we once received from it in the text of Matthew alone.

The manuscript is oblong in shape, so that its length exceeds its width by nearly a quarter. Although its parchments were dyed purple, most of them now display a bluish appearance through the antiquity of time. The characters, as also that fourfold table visible in the outer margin of each page, are coated with a certain silver pigment. Yet in many places its faded color resembles gold and deceives the eye unless closely inspected. For this reason we once called it the golden manuscript.

That pigment is sometimes smooth, at other times thick and rough, whether owing to the different hands of illuminators, the material itself, or finally the brushes. Although the above-mentioned Mabillon seems to suggest that such golden and silver manuscripts were written with bird feathers (*Supplement to De re diplomatica*, p. 51), I think this must be understood of the first hand, so to speak. For it is certain that the characters were first drawn by scribes in ink and afterward adorned by illuminators with that mixture of gold or silver, which assuredly could not have been applied with feathers.

[Col. 0016B] In places it is so thick and projects so far from the parchments—especially in Mark—that we even found a fly, still whole, coated and trapped in that adhesive. From this I once conjectured that the manuscript was completed in summer. At that time, because the paint dried more readily, when the workers had finished the front page they could begin the reverse not much later.

I said that the characters were originally drawn in plain ink; this can be established most clearly in several places, especially at the beginning of Luke and John, where that pigment has fallen away.

At the beginning of each Gospel, the first lines are covered with gold leaf, which remains even now brilliant and untouched. All the lines were ruled with a stylus for the copyist to follow in writing. The characters are equal in size, except that larger ones are used for more notable pericopes, to which a lection is generally added in the left margin. Conversely, if something remained to be added at the end of a line, the scribe supplied it in smaller letters. As to their arrangement, I shall add nothing for the present, since the specimen itself sets before the eyes the continuous sequence and structure used by the ancients.

[Col. 0016C] In some places, though rarely, two letters are fused into one, but always at the end of a line. The scribe does this only by adding a long stroke above an *N* or *V*, so as to express a *T* in one and the same stroke. Stone-cutters employed this joining of letters much more freely in ancient inscriptions. For one can see them doing the same not only at the end of lines but also in their middle, and not merely once.

Nothing, however, is more frequent in this manuscript than the interchange of letters: *O* for *V*, *T* for *D*, but above all *B* for *V* and conversely. This might sometimes set an insoluble difficulty before those unskilled in such matters, since not infrequently the very sense of the words seems to be reversed, as the past tense passes into the future and the future into the past. But we are dealing with learned persons, to whom nothing is better known in these ancient monuments.

I have also found, though sparingly, in Matthew and John, *V* used for *Y* and conversely: namely, *murram* for *myrram* (“myrrh”), and *verbym* for *verbum* (“word”). Whether all this is attributed to the fault of readers or copyists, or more truly to the idioms of those times, it is certain that it has affected almost all manuscript exemplars, as well as ancient stone inscriptions and coins.

[Col. 0017A] We once observed that Jerome called copies written in uncial letters “burdens” rather than books (*Preface to Job*, end); and that Alcuin afterward imitated this, calling books difficult to carry “weights,” and therefore heavy for readers’ hands (*Preface to Questions on Genesis*). We decided to weigh this manuscript in a scale: it was found to weigh fourteen pounds.

It is also clear from the mentioned passage of Jerome that, already in his time, copies written on purple parchment in golden and silver letters were in use, both for the use of churches, which he had previously mentioned, and for private persons, whom he rebukes in the same place. He objected to them the magnificence of manuscripts which nevertheless were less accurate. Perhaps copyists sinned more in sumptuous copies of this kind than in others, because weariness and fatigue followed the painstaking slowness of the work, and then haste and carelessness followed; particularly because errors were more difficult to correct, owing to the beauty of the characters and of the parchment, whose appearance, unlike plain parchment, could scarcely bear erasure and the sponge.

[Col. 0017B] Yet even long before Jerome’s time these laborious copies were in use, as Capitolinus testifies in his account of Maximinus II. Among the omens of that man’s future empire, he says, this happened: when, as a boy, he was given to a grammarian, all the books of Homer, written on purple parchment in gold letters, were first presented to him.

There is no doubt that this custom flowed from pagan copyists to our own. At what time is uncertain. Yet I think it was not in the first, perhaps not even in the middle of the second, century, while the Church was still poor and retained its ancient simplicity. Rather, it arose when the Church had spread far and wide and began to abound as not only the people but also men and women of rank flocked to her bosom. It did so far more abundantly after peace was restored under Constantine and wealth increased. Then, following his own example—for, as we shall shortly see, he ordered sacred books to be copied and adorned by the most skillful scribes—private persons, as often happens, imitated the prince’s care and soon increased it still further.

[Col. 0017C] The Canons of Eusebius are prefixed to the Gospels. Of these, however, the first four, the seventh entire, and the greater part of the eighth have perished. The form and sequence of the letters are almost the same as in the Gospels, except that they are smaller, crude, unpolished, uneven, and in many places worn down by dirt and age. It is apparent that they were once illuminated with silver; for the slight coating has mostly disappeared, leaving only the rusty ink visible.

The parchments themselves are mutilated, decayed, and disfigured by a violet but darker color. It is therefore easy to conjecture that these Canons, once attached to an old and worn-out manuscript, were afterward added to this one through someone’s intervention. This becomes much more evident from the signature of the quires. Since the Canons occupy seven quires, if they had originally been copied together with this manuscript, the first quire of Matthew ought already to have been the eighth.

[Col. 0018A] In arranging these Canons, the copyist seems to have followed not the order of Eusebius but that of the manuscripts before him. For in Canon X, in which Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John occur in Eusebius, John follows Matthew here, then Luke, and afterward Mark. At the end of each is added the heading: “Canon X of Matthew ends; Canon X of John begins”; “Canon X of John ends; Canon X of Luke begins”; “Canon X of Luke ends; Canon X of Mark begins.”

At the end of the eighth Canon, in which Matthew and John are otherwise lacking, the copyist did not follow the sequence of Ammonius and Eusebius; for under section 339 he presents what in them, and in the manuscript, occurs under 340. Nor does he carry Mark’s pericopes beyond the thirty-fourth after the two hundredth. Whether this agrees with the manuscript is uncertain, since the end of Mark has perished.

A kind of preface follows the Canons and fills one or two pages. Here it is for you; for perhaps scholars will find grains of gold even in this sand.

> Saint Peter the apostle, disciple of our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior, instructing the faithful, warns all, because of the diversity of the assertion of languages, as it is written in the eighth book of Clement, teaching thus:
>
> “Listen to me, beloved fellow servants. It is good that each one of you, according to his ability, should benefit those approaching the faith of our religion. Therefore do not be reluctant, according to the wisdom bestowed upon you by divine providence, to teach by discourse, and to instruct the ignorant; yet in such a way that to those things which you have heard from me and which have been handed down to you, you add only the eloquence of your own speech, and do not utter anything of your own which has not been handed down to you, even if it seems plausible to you. But, as I have said, continue to transmit what I myself received from the true Prophet and handed down to you, even if it seems to be expressed less fully.
>
> [Col. 0018C] “And therefore, lest in interpretations of languages, according to what is shown in the inner part of the book, it should seem to the reader that one thing has been designated and written in the Greek language, another in Latin or Gothic, let him observe this: although linguistic instruction displays a difference, it nevertheless converges upon one intention. Therefore no one ought to waver because the authority itself makes clear that, according to the intention of the language, the inflections and sounds of the voice have been established by careful understanding, as is read in the writings that follow.
>
> “This matter has made it advisable to publish these things because of certain persons who, by a false assertion, according to their own will placed lies in the Law or in the Gospels through their own interpretation. Therefore, rejecting those things, these have been set forth which are found in the antiquity of the Law to be contained in the sayings of the Greeks; and the very etymologies of the languages, written in agreement with one another, are shown to converge upon one sense.
>
> [Col. 0018D] “For it is also fitting to indicate that, because ‘*in vult habere*’ has been done, an annotation is indicated in the Latin language. Therefore it may be recognized where the letters ‘Gr.’ are found above ‘*vult habere*’: the reader should know that in that very ‘*vult habere*’ it is written according to what the Greek contains. But where the letters ‘Lat.’ are found above ‘*vult habere*,’ it is shown in the Latin language according to ‘*in vult habere*.’ And therefore this instruction has been provided, lest readers fail to understand the very *vult haberes*, for which reason they have been placed; but because . . . . .”

The characters of this mutilated rhapsody, produced by a barbarous and unhappy age, resemble neither those in which the Canons were written nor those represented in the codex. For that wretched scribe—whoever he finally was—used letters smaller than those of the Canons and somewhat larger than those represented in the codex. The lines of the pages were indeed ruled with a stylus, but not deeply as in the text, and more closely joined. Hence, although only twenty lines were drawn on each side, just as in the Gospels, the head, sides, and margins extend more broadly.

The membrane has been sewn in here by a later-period patcher, who repaired the decaying codex; both the parchment and its position sufficiently prove this. For it is sewn between two other purple leaves, indeed, but their colour, though fresh and therefore vivid, is thin and diluted, unlike that in the codex. Moreover, they are blank and have not been ruled for use. On the first of them, which that cutter arranged upside-down, are read the following words, in letters larger than those in the little preface and fashioned after the appearance of the codex: “May the reader be willing to see [and] recite.” On the latter, however, although traces of letters can somehow be seen, he has so erased them with a sponge that nothing at all can be recovered. But for what purpose, or whence this scrap crept in here, let those determine who have leisure.

This is noteworthy: the Gothic version of Wulfila was already in use at that time—the half-destroyed remains of whose New Testament Francis Junius published, to the great benefit of posterity—if indeed this patcher is speaking of it.

[Col. 0019C]

What we noted above—that is, that the parchments on which the Canons are written were divided into quires of four sheets—the scribe did likewise in the Gospels, of which we shall speak shortly. There is the mark placed at the foot of the verso of every eighth page, Q. I., Q. II., and so forth, which Valesius says was customary in the most ancient codices and which he himself observed in a manuscript copy of Gregory of Tours about nine hundred years old.

That those ancient copies consisted not only of quires of four sheets but also, from time to time, of mixed quires of three sheets is indicated by a passage of Eusebius (*Life of Constantine*, IV.37), in which he says that Constantine instructed him to arrange for fifty copies of the divine Scriptures to be written on finely prepared parchment by highly skilled copyists, and to send them to him at once, accompanied by a deacon. He immediately adds:

> Αὐτίκα δ` ἔργον ἐπηκολούθει τῷ λόγῳ, ἐν πολυτελῶς ἠσκημένοις τεύχεσι τρισσὰ καὶ τετρασσὰ διαπεμψάντων ἡμῶν.

“Immediately the deed followed the command, when we sent [them] in threes and fours in elaborately adorned volumes.”

That is, the emperor’s commands were at once taken in hand; and he sent quires of three and four sheets in carefully finished volumes. In these words of the historian, a most learned man thinks there is an enallage, and therefore that it ought to have read *τεύχη ἐν τετρασσοῖς* (“volumes in fours”), rather than *τετρασσὰ ἐν τεύχεσι* (“fours in volumes”). But, unless I am mistaken, Eusebius’s cited words are correct. For those carefully finished and decorated *τεύχη* were plainly nothing other than the coverings of the codices. After the copyists had arranged the books in ternions and quaternions, the bookbinders, after the boards had been cut, covered and bound them, usually in leather, sometimes also in silk ornamented with gold and gems. Both the text itself and the words *πολυτελῶς ἠσκημένα* (“elaborately adorned”), which could not apply to ternions, seem to require that Eusebius’s words be understood in this way.

At the head of each Gospel is read, in small characters, the author’s name. This was retained not only at the beginning, but throughout the text on alternate pages, so that on every page—verso and recto alike—the reader encounters part of the title, with the added heading: “According to Matthew,” “According to John,” and so forth.

What we observed in the Canons sewn into the codex—namely, that the Gospels were arranged differently from the Eusebian order—may also be seen in the text itself.

[Col. 0020B]

Matthew comes first, then John, then Luke, and finally Mark. Since this is a remarkable matter and, so far as I know, not yet sufficiently investigated, we shall discuss it later in a somewhat fuller special observation.

It is clear to readers that the copyist by whom this our exemplar was written was not merely careless, but unskilled and utterly unlearned. A most defective punctuation has furthermore been added. I therefore judge that it was written about the time when, after the Roman Empire of the West had been overthrown amid so many invasions of foreign peoples, learning itself had been reduced to squalor and ruin, from which, after so many centuries, it finally emerged through the brilliance of Italian minds.

What formerly happened to codices—that unskilled critics corrected them wrongly—also happened in many places to this one.

[Col. 0020C]

Not indeed because that corrector, whoever he was, added anything or altered anything. But, by erasing what he judged faulty, he repeatedly distorted what was correct, while carelessly passing over what was erroneous. Everywhere there remain traces of letters from which we can discern the original writing. That he was also deficient in Latin may be illustrated, among other things, by this single example occurring at Luke 10:40. There Martha, complaining of her sister because she did not assist her with domestic service, says: “Lord, is it not a concern to you that my sister has left me to serve alone?” In this passage, fearing the solecism if *curae* were left, he rubbed out the final *e*. Yet that he looked to Jerome’s Vulgate when he laid his bold hands upon the codex is proved, among other things, by the famous passage Matthew 2:1, “When Jesus therefore had been born in Bethlehem of Judaea,” and again verse 5, “But they said to him, In Bethlehem of Judaea.” Jerome, judging these forms corrupt in the copies of his time, had restored *Juda*. For that corrupter, in order to bring the reading into conformity with the Vulgate, scraped away the second diphthong in both places.

[Col. 0020D]

But the errors which he passed over are so numerous that I am reluctant to list them—especially since not one of these blemishes of the very beautiful body is absent from the transcript which we sent you.

As for the Latin style, scholars capable of judging such matters will perceive that in the spelling of words there are scattered forms which display the age and simplicity of the primitive translator.

[Col. 0021A]

There is no need to adduce extracts from it.

Both the appearance of the manuscript and several passages that we shall later examine most clearly prove that this our exemplar derived from those copies which preceded not only Jerome’s time but that of Hilary of Poitiers.

I once conjectured, in writing to your uncle, that it was brought here in the declining eighth century or at the beginning of the next; and I still think so. Perhaps it was a gift of princes who betrothed their daughters and granddaughters to God Most High in that celebrated place; or perhaps one of the noblest virgins brought it with her. Unless, more probably, it was drawn from the treasures of Desiderius and Ansa and entrusted to their daughter’s piety.

[Col. 0021B]

Among the other ornaments of spiritual marriage, she deposited it in the royal house for the use of herself and of the others who were betrothed with her. No one versed in these antiquities can be unaware that gifts of this kind were commonly presented to sacred places. Such costly and magnificent codices, moreover, were usually prepared only for the wealthy or for churches; the expense exceeded the means of private persons, for whom the poor “sheets,” as Jerome called them, would otherwise have been more than sufficient.

That several sacred codices were preserved in the royal monastery while Desiderius and Adelgis were still alive is clear from a parchment copy of a certain bull issued by Sigoald, Patriarch of Aquileia, to Anseberga. We copied it elsewhere and entered it in our *Adversaria*. It reads as follows:

[Col. 0021C]

“Sigoald, servant of the servants of the Lord, Patriarch. When our humble person, together with our colleagues, the most religious and holy bishops, had come before the most fortunate princes Desiderius and Adelgis concerning the condition of the whole orthodox Church, and, with God’s help, had more carefully refined each superfluous matter, your most blessed reverence, Anseberga, abbess, requested of us through Prandulus, chamberlain of the sacred palace and provost of your monastery, that the same venerable monastery of yours, situated in the city called Brescia and known to have been built in honour of the Lord Saviour, might enjoy the distinctions of a privilege from our authority. Thus, with the agreement of our most reverend bishops and by common consent, the firmness of our written instrument might bestow perpetual force upon the aforesaid oracle.

[Col. 0021D]

And since those things which have been sought through useful refinements ought always to be granted, it pleased us in every way that the entreaty of pious devotion should be moderated by the assent of a salutary intervention. Since, therefore, your religious devotion has beneficially sought to obtain from us that the aforesaid monastery, with all the basilicas belonging to it, which is known to have been built by right of the most pious and most serene Queen Ansa, should be adorned with the privileges of our holy see of Aquileia, which, by God’s aid, we serve: favouring your pious desires, by this our authority we command that what is rightly sought be carried into effect.

“And therefore we prohibit every priest of any church from having any … occasion [*occasione*, supplied].

“Unless invited by the abbess of the monastery, let no one presume in any way to celebrate there the solemnity of Masses.

[Col. 0022A]

“Let the sisters dwelling there be free to observe inviolably the regular rule. Let priestly orders be conferred without reproach by whatever bishop and from whatever city the abbess shall choose. But whenever, as are the accidents of human life, the abbess should die, let the most religious nuns elect a successor in the place of the deceased abbess, not from elsewhere but from the same community. Adding, moreover, that whatever things have been brought there in due order by any bishop or by any person [the text is defective; supply: *Episcopo aut qualibet*], or shall be brought in future times, whether from our jurisdiction or from that of our bishops, may remain entirely unimpaired in every respect.

[Col. 0022B]

“Nor do we pass over this point: that no abbess, whenever she may be, be granted permission in any time to give away or alienate in any manner codices, sacred vessels, or any treasure of the Church. If anyone, with rash boldness, attempts to act against this our most serene ordinance, we decree that he is to be punished with eternal anathema.

“The tenor of this privilege was written in the sixteenth and fourteenth years of the invincible princes Desiderius and Adelgis, in the eleventh indiction. Given at Ticinum, in the royal city, on the third Ides of October.

“Sigoald, Patriarch by the grace of God: beneath this text of privilege, beneficially refined by us, I have written with my own hand. Apollinaris, through Christ’s mercy unworthy humble bishop: beneath this text of privilege I have subscribed with my own hand. Otto, bishop in God’s name: beneath this text of privilege I have subscribed with my own hand. Julian, humble bishop, in this text of privilege, with my own hand, subscribed. Felix, humble bishop, in this text of privilege, with my own hand, subscribed. Felix, sinner and bishop, in this text of privilege, made his mark and subscribed.”

[Col. 0022C]

You see that the most ancient practice of the Churches, by which they entered these codices among the sacred treasury, no differently from the remaining furnishings dedicated to God, endured down to Sigoald’s age. Would that the excessive laxity of succeeding times, struck by that anathema, had kept its most free hands not only from these but from the other gifts of kings and princes as well. What an abundance of ancient monuments of the Church might perhaps still survive here; what religious devotion might remain! In their place, however, nothing has passed down to posterity except the memory of an ill-considered generosity—or rather, extravagance.

[Col. 0022D]

Whether the monuments that still survive can undergo or evade the same hazard of fortune is uncertain. Both the vicissitudes of time and past events make me fear it, and especially the memorable occurrence which I received from those virgins:

“When so great a store of parchments lay wholly neglected and confused, at the advice of a nobleman, keen enough in other judgments but ignorant of these antiquities, a certain notary was summoned to inspect and put them in order. Having laid down his terms, he undertook the work. When he came upon original documents written by Lombard notaries in that barbarous deformation of Latin script, he judged that no one would understand them and threw them away as the refuse of an archive.

[Col. 0023A]

The copies of those documents, which were together in one place, assisted this destruction, he thinking it more than enough if they were preserved.”

Thus those original documents, scattered and dispersed, perished. Only one survives, whose inscription added to the parchment rolled up in a circle is certainly worthy of being committed to writing, as a monument remarkable above all others no less for that man’s ignorance than for his impudence.

“It was issued at Ticinum, in the third and first years of the reign of Desiderius and Adelgis, 17 September, indiction XIII; containing the bequest of one Gisulf, a royal groom, who had left his wife Radoara usufructuary from a half-share, and then, upon her death, ordered the bishop of Lodi, after selling the property, to distribute the proceeds to the poor. After Gisulf’s death, his above-mentioned wife, in a rare example of piety, petitioned the king that her husband’s will should immediately be fulfilled, so that”—these are the words of the document—“without any hindrance, that alms of his might more swiftly bring rest or refreshment to his soul.” She obtained this. Accordingly, after the property had been sold, the bishop distributed to the poor the price of 2,850 gold coins paid by one Gaider, procurator of the royal monastery, and subscribed this charter together with Radoara and the other witnesses named there. His chirograph reads as follows:

[Col. 0023B]

“I, Hippolytus, though unworthy bishop by the grace of God, at the petition of Radoara, dedicated to God, by royal authority, concerning the sale of the little estate which her husband granted to her after his death, have written with my own hand, together with faithful priests; and I received the price, three thousand eight hundred and fifty, and distributed it for the soul of Gisulf the groom.”

This document, which concerns the acquisition of properties that they still possess, together with others, in the district of Cremona, the most illustrious virgins had once asked the consuls of our city, as the thirteenth century was declining, to have transcribed by public notaries so that it should not perish through the passage of time. A copy made by these same notaries survives together with the original, but in many places it is by no means faithful to the truth of the original. Here is the chirograph of the above-mentioned Hippolytus as they transcribed it:

[Col. 0023C]

“I, Hippolytus Zolentinus, worthy bishop by the grace of God, at the petition of Sadoara, dedicated to God, made [this] and protested concerning the sale of the estate,” etc., down to the final words, “Gisulf the *rorator*.”

That wretched scribe who arranged the parchments, unable to make sense of the original, cast his eyes upon the copy and carved from it this heading, which was intended to hold out to posterity a light for understanding the document:

> 1299, 26 November. Hippolytus Lolentinus, bishop of Sadovara, concerning the bequest of Ghisolfo Roratore.

[Col. 0023D]

You see with what sort of man those unfortunate charters had to deal. Yet it is remarkable that he did not touch other diplomas. Nor, however, were they granted to escape other hands: the seals of many were removed, seals in which were preserved the images and names of emperors.

Moved by these misfortunes, and because it was reported that everything was again in confusion, I urged the most distinguished virgins to select a man of proven integrity and trustworthiness, fit to complete the work, who would carefully inspect all the parchments and arrange them in a more commendable sequence, and, if they wished it to endure longer, establish an archive. This was done. Our friend John Andrew Astezatus, a Cassinese monk, learned and most eager for these antiquities, pressed forward with the work. By unwearied and persevering effort—being, as he is, wonderfully patient in work once undertaken—he finally put the finishing hand to it.

[Col. 0024A]

But to return again to our exemplar: we said that the copyist had prefixed the author’s name to each Gospel, plainly so that readers, by looking at the titles at first sight, might identify whichever Evangelist they wished.

Yet Millius asserts that this was done only after the Canon had been established (*Prolegomena*, no. 347, edition of the New Testament from Kuster’s recension).

[Col. 0024B]

Before that, he says, the Gospels circulated without authors’ names prefixed, no differently from other *διηγήσεις*—“narratives”—of unknown writers, so that by the addition of titles these alone might be recognized as true and authentic evangelical records. Hence, he says, Tertullian reproached Marcion because he had assigned no author to his Gospel “in imitation of the ancient Church.”

But that most learned man, writing this and hastening to other matters, did not sufficiently guard against having this conjecture of his clearly refuted by Tertullian himself, whom he cites. Tertullian diminishes the credibility of Marcion’s Gospel precisely because it lacks a title:

> “And here I might already take my stand, maintaining that a work ought not to be acknowledged which does not raise its head, which displays no constancy, which promises no credibility from the fullness of its title and the due declaration of its author.”  
> —Tertullian, *Against Marcion* IV.2

Therefore, even before Marcion’s time, and indeed in the ancient Church, the Gospels bore their own names. Why else would Tertullian have objected to him this bareness of title, against which the Marcionites could have defended themselves by the antiquity of the period and the practice of the Churches? According to Millius’s own reckoning, for at least thirty years before the evangelical Canon was established by the bishops of Asia, as he supposes, the Gospels of Luke and Mark, and Matthew’s for far longer, would have existed without titles.

[Col. 0024C]

As for his statement that the makers of the Canon ordained the authors’ inscriptions so that the true Gospels might be recognized, even by this means they would not have sufficiently safeguarded the credibility of those Gospels. For Marcion, having corrupted the Luke he used, and any others who laid adulterating hands upon Matthew, Mark, or John, could equally impose the same title upon readers. There is therefore no room for doubt that already at that time copyists followed in sacred books the same practice as in secular ones: namely, that they should display the names of their authors.

It remains now to inquire into the particular ordering of the Canon in certain codices, preserved also in ours, and into the origin of such diversity.

Richard Simon, after examining the Cambridge codex, in which the Gospels are arranged in the same order as in ours, observes that this arrangement is not peculiar to it, both from a very ancient catalogue of the Saint-Germain exemplar in which the Gospels are listed in the same sequence,

[Col. 0025A]

and from a passage of Druthmar, which we shall consider later. He adds that this practice seems to have been introduced by Latin scribes who copied Greek exemplars for their own use. But that man, otherwise long and deeply occupied in these matters, and destined to gain still greater praise from them had he not yielded to preconceived opinions, did not observe that the Latins would not have introduced this order into the Canon unless copies preceding them had supplied the pattern. Why would they have put Luke before Mark, or John before both, rather than the reverse, when either order could equally conveniently have been adapted to their use? Nor could he draw anything more from Druthmar’s passage than that, in the codex attributed at that time to Hilary, Matthew and John preceded the rest.

Millius thus decides concerning this arrangement of the Canon in the above-mentioned exemplar (*Prolegomena*, no. 1269): it was done by the compiler’s design. For at the end of Matthew is written:

> Εὐαγγέλιον κατὰ Ματθαῖον ἐτελέθη. ἄρχεται Εὐαγγέλιον κατὰ Ἰωάννην.

“The Gospel according to Matthew is completed. The Gospel according to John begins.”

Then Luke, and finally Mark, follow under the same heading. Thus, he says, these books were arranged so that the Gospels of apostles should be placed before the Gospels of apostolic men, just as Tertullian calls Mark and Luke companions of apostles (*Against Marcion* IV.2).

[Col. 0025B]

What Millius means in the cited words by saying that this order prevailed through the compiler’s design, I frankly do not understand. Nor, I think, did he rightly infer from the cited heading that the copyist had done this from his own invention. That note was added by scribes so that the order of the books might not mislead the workmen later when binding the codices. Moreover, this order of the Canon that we are now discussing was far older than the barbarous and miserably unlearned scribe—as I use Millius’s own words—who wrote that transcript. Millius himself had seen this from Nazianzen’s poem (*Notes at the end of the Gospel of Matthew*).

Therefore he must have meant, unless I am mistaken, that the copyist did not place the Gospels in his transcript spontaneously or by chance, but followed the copies of earlier times and arranged them as they had been arranged in those exemplars. Millius rightly conjectured that those among whom this sequence was first used intended to grant this precedence to the dignity of the apostles—for another explanation must be sought for why Luke preceded Mark.

[Col. 0025C]

Yet he could have illuminated the matter at issue from other passages of the same writer, if he had had leisure, rather than from the cited and insufficiently clear passage of Tertullian. Since these passages are notable and have been passed over both by Millius himself and by learned men in notes upon him, I think it worthwhile to examine them briefly.

This writer, having first established that the authors of the evangelical record were apostles (*ibid.* IV.2), upon whom the Lord had imposed the office of preaching the Gospel, then says that there were also apostolic men, but “with the apostles,” as he says, and “after the apostles.” Luke, moreover, taught nothing but what the Churches had learned from the apostles; and because of this agreement in doctrine, Luke’s Gospel came to be received by the faithful as an apostolic monument, and always remained among them such as they defended it even in his own time. By the same reasoning he then establishes the authority of the Gospels of Matthew, John, and Mark: namely, because the Churches founded by the apostles, and then all others after their example, had always received them as genuine records of Christian faith.

Having thus laid down these points, he then presses that apostate, saying (*ch.* 4):

[Col. 0026A]

> “And so Marcion must also be required to explain why, passing over these, he has rather attached himself to Luke—as if these also had not existed in the Churches from the beginning. Indeed, it is more credible that these were from the beginning as the prior ones, because apostolic, and as having been dedicated with the Churches themselves. Therefore, since it is agreed that these too existed in the Churches, why did Marcion not attack these also—either to correct them if adulterated, or to acknowledge them if entire? For it is fitting that, if anyone perverted the Gospel, they should take more care to pervert those whose authority they knew to be more readily accepted.”

This passage of Tertullian is all the more notable because it is perplexed and needs some illumination if its force is to be properly established; and also because it seems to offer us some light for investigating what ordering of the Canon may formerly have prevailed in the African Church.

Thus, since there is scarcely room for doubt that from the very publication of the Gospels those Churches in whose bosom, so to speak, they were brought forth preserved them as authentic records of the new Law and made them known to the faithful, and that copies of them were immediately distributed to other places as well—whether the Churches sent copyists to have them transcribed for themselves, or whether the disciples of the apostles themselves, “striving eagerly to preach Christ,” as Eusebius says (*Ecclesiastical History* III.37), also handed down “the writing of the divine Gospels”:

> κηρύττειν τὸν Χριστὸν φιλοτιμουμένοις  
> “those eagerly desiring to preach Christ,”

> τὴν τῶν θείων Εὐαγγελίων παραδιδόναι γραφήν  
> “to hand down the writing of the divine Gospels”—

[Col. 0026B]

and thus excellently providing, as circumstances required, for the benefit of believers, so that, after the Gospel had already been proclaimed to them, they freely offered the faithful the opportunity of copying those sacred volumes: accordingly, copies of Matthew, which appeared first of all at Jerusalem or not far from it, were carried here and there by believers flocking thither from every direction as to the cradle of nascent Christianity. Then, in the passage of time, Mark and Luke, and finally John, occupied all the Churches everywhere.

But just as Churches were not established immediately everywhere among the nations, some provinces being called earlier and others later to the sacrament of faith, so certain Churches, according to place and time, acquired now this, now that Gospel and entered it in their codices; then they added the others as opportunity or means presented themselves.

[Col. 0026C]

Thus it is credible that no fixed and certain order was then observed, until, once all four Gospels had been published and widely distributed, some Churches, considering the time at which they had appeared, and others their authors, set them forth differently in their copies.

Origen seems to indicate that most Eastern Churches followed the chronological order. For, adhering to the ecclesiastical Canon, he lists the Gospels of Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John in such a way as also to state, on the basis of received tradition, which appeared earlier and which later (*in Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History* VI.25). Eusebius maintains the same sequence; and afterwards, when Jerome the Vulgate translator adopted it, it prevailed in Western Churches as well.

[Col. 0026D]

But that other Churches, considering not chronology but authorship, arranged apostles first and then apostolic men in their codices is most clearly demonstrated by our exemplar and the Cambridge manuscript, together with that formerly attributed, by report, to Hilary by Druthmar.

Indeed, the cited passages of Tertullian seem to prove that one of this twofold sequences of the Canon was preserved in the African Church. That is: the Gospel’s authors were apostles, and also apostolic men, but “with the apostles” and “after the apostles.” Then more clearly: “Indeed, it is more credible that these were from the beginning as the prior ones, because apostolic.” No sensible person will believe that Tertullian was speaking of the time when they appeared. Therefore he intended to indicate something different by this, so to speak, priority, by which he assigned the chief place to the Gospels of Matthew and John.

[Col. 0027A]

And this, unless I am mistaken, can mean nothing other than that in the Churches’ reckoning of the sacred books of the New Testament, those apostolic Gospels preceded the others. The following words seem to support this conjecture: “For it is fitting that, if anyone perverted the Gospel, they should take more care to pervert those whose authority they knew to be more readily accepted.”

By these words, I think he meant nothing other than that, although the Gospels of both apostles and apostolic men had the same authority in the Churches, nevertheless those of the former, in view of their apostolic office and teaching authority, had the stronger practical standing among them. For authority was more frequently drawn from them in preaching the divine word, and they were always read first before the apostolic Gospels in the assemblies.

Whatever may be the case here—for in such darkness of antiquity we seek to attain truth by conjectures—I would not dare positively to affirm that in Tertullian’s age the apostles were given the first place in the Canon in those Churches.

[Col. 0027B]

Yet, from the cited passages of this writer which we have examined above, I think this more probable. I said “in Tertullian’s age”; for later the same order prevailed as in Jerome’s recension, at least at Carthage, as is clear from the order of the Evangelists which Augustine writes was observed there (*Sermon* 144, *On Time*).

What we conjectured concerning the Churches of Africa in arranging the Canon, the above-mentioned codices allow us to affirm with no small appearance of truth concerning some Churches of Gaul. Although the Cambridge codex was not in use by any Church but by a private individual, who, retaining only the sequence of the Canon prevailing there, so freely mixed, inverted, and recast the rest—both in the Gospels and especially in the Acts of the Apostles—that, according to Millius, who examined it most carefully, it has proved the most interpolated of all that have reached our times.

[Col. 0027C]

For this reason one may rightly criticize Simon, who in his *Critical History of the New Testament* seems more than once, without sound judgment, to have believed that the Latin version was prepared from these corrupt sources. But since our concern is with these earlier copies, let us now examine the passage of Druthmar which we touched on above.

This writer (*Exposition on Matthew*, ch. 1), after comparing the four Evangelists with the four rivers that issued from the Paradise of Delight and then with the four elements, establishes a certain arrangement of the Gospels:

> “The order of the Gospels itself may perhaps be so arranged that one apostle is at the head, another at the end, and the two placed between them have their authority from those two. Yet I saw a Greek-written book of the Gospel which was said to have belonged to Hilary, in which Matthew and John were first, and the other two came later. I asked Euphemius the Greek why this was so. He said to me: ‘In imitation of the good farmer, who first yokes the oxen he has that are stronger.’”

[Col. 0028A]

There is nothing here from which Simon could assert that this order was introduced by Latins.

Cutantius, in the *Life of St Hilary* prefixed to his works—of which I acknowledge that I owe a copy of your most beautiful edition to your kindness and goodwill toward me—observes that Hilary spent time copying sacred books. He infers this from the will of St Perpetuus, bishop of Tours, in which he bequeathed to Euphronius of Autun a book of Gospels “which Hilary of Poitiers, formerly a priest, wrote”; and he believes that this is the very book still preserved at Tours in the church of St Gatianus.

[Col. 0028B]

From these words of the will he thinks the cited passage of Druthmar can be explained: namely, that the codex was called St Hilary’s because it was written in his own hand.

For my part, if it is permitted to make a comparison, although I do not altogether reject this conjecture of that most learned man, I would think that this codex was one of the Asiatic copies which Hilary employed in his studies while he was living in exile in Phrygia, and which, when he returned from exile, he brought back into his homeland. I confess that I am led to this conjecture all the more readily because it is quite plausible that the Churches of Asia Minor, in arranging the Canon, paid no attention to the chronological sequence in which the Gospels appeared but rather, in view of apostolic status, entered Matthew first—since it was found everywhere among the nations—and then John, by whom they had been founded and set right, in their codices.

[Col. 0028C]

Thus perhaps that custom was introduced into Gaul, unless it had already prevailed there. This would be clearer if, in the cited transcript of the Church of Tours, copied by Hilary before his exile, if that is so, the Canon followed the same sequence as in the examples mentioned above.

This would persuade me much more strongly if Cutantius’s view were true: that Hilary, immediately after his commentaries on Matthew, extended this care to John. For then he would seem to have followed the order of his exemplars.

[Col. 0028D] Whether, however, the distinguished editor rightly inferred from the cited passage of Druthmar that, in Hilary’s exemplar, after Matthew and John came the remaining two, Mark (as he says) and Luke, is wholly uncertain. Those in whose possession older manuscripts survive should therefore examine whether, in those in which Matthew and John stand first, Luke is always followed by Mark, as in our manuscript and the Cambridge one, or whether they follow in another order. For perhaps from their differing sequence one might discover both the practice of churches and of private persons in arranging the Canon, and also which of the Gospels of Luke and Mark they happened to obtain first. For although the first place in the Canon was assigned to apostles on account of their rank, it remains uncertain why Luke was placed before Mark. Was it because those using that order received a copy of Mark later, Luke having already been entered in their codices; or was there another reason? Perhaps they also assigned Luke the leading place after the apostles because he arranged the Gospel history much more fully than Mark, tracing events further back and carefully setting out the Savior’s genealogy according to the flesh. Certainly, that those among whom this canonical sequence prevailed took no account of chronological order is clear from the ancients, who believed that Mark committed his Gospel to writing before Luke, as we observed above from Origen—though Clement of Alexandria thought otherwise. According to Eusebius’ testimony (*Ecclesiastical History* VI.14), Clement “said that the Gospels containing the genealogies had been written first” (προγεγράφθαι ἔλεγεν τῶν Εὐαγγελίων τὰ περιέχοντα τὰς γενεαλογίας).

[Col. 0029B] Since the lineage of Christ according to the dispensation of the flesh seemed to be the source and foundation of Gospel history, Clement accordingly judged it more probable that, once the way had been prepared by Matthew and Luke and that which ought first of all to be known had been established, Mark then applied himself to his Gospel. I said “by Matthew and Luke,” although it is uncertain whether Clement believed that this one or that one had preceded the other. Yet perhaps he gave support to the view of those who suppose Luke to have been the first of all to write Gospel history. Among them are two eminent Protestant scholars, Basnage and Le Clerc. For the latter, commenting on a passage of Dodwell in which he had asserted that Matthew was the earliest Evangelist, says that he had nowhere seen this proved (*Dissertation III, On the Four Gospels*, at the end of the *Gospel Harmony*). Whatever later Greeks have conjectured about the age of the Gospels, he says, rests upon no foundation. But, I think, his memory failed him through prolonged concentration upon his work. For not much earlier he had said:

> Origen, most thoroughly acquainted not only with the doctrines of his age but also with ecclesiastical antiquities, speaks thus concerning the four Gospels in a fragment of Book I of his *Commentary on Matthew*, preserved by Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VI.25: “First was written that according to him who was once a tax collector, then an apostle of Jesus Christ, Matthew” (πρῶτον μὲν γέγραπται τὸ κατὰ τὸν ποτὲ τελώνην, ὕστερον δὲ Ἀπόστολον Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ Ματθαῖον). Moreover, if the later Greeks after Origen say that Matthew wrote before the rest, they rest upon a sufficiently solid foundation—namely, the authority of a man exceptionally well acquainted with ecclesiastical antiquities, who affirmed that the first of the Gospels was written by Matthew, formerly a tax collector and afterwards an apostle of Jesus Christ.

[Col. 0029D] But Basnage is much more unrestrained (*A.D. 60*). In order to make Luke earlier than Matthew, he did not hesitate, among other conjectures, to advance this: that matters would have been arranged more suitably in setting forth Christ’s genealogy if Luke’s order had first stood, and then Matthew’s. And consequently, because of this propriety, the narrative ought then to have begun where it ought to have begun: namely, with the angel’s mission to Elizabeth and Mary, and with Augustus’s decree, by which the Virgin was compelled to go to Bethlehem and there gave birth. Behold a man who, with the dangerous wisdom of the age, judges the writers of sacred history no differently from those of secular history, as though these men were not inspired by God (θεόπνευστοι), and as though the divine Spirit might permit those called to such an office to remain ignorant of what befitted it.

[Col. 0030A] It is indeed astonishing that this critic did not charge both Evangelists with failing to observe propriety because they did not, as John later did, begin the genealogy at a higher point—from the divine generation of the Word. Perhaps he would have summoned Eusebius to account, since Eusebius wrote that this task had been reserved for John by the Holy Spirit. For this certainly seemed necessary in view of the supreme matters of which they were later to treat. It would also have held a torch before distorted minds that were to represent Jesus Christ as a mere man, so that they might not most miserably dash themselves against those dreadful straits.

We have now observed, insofar as it has been possible for us to see through the mist of so many centuries, what order certain Eastern churches, and then churches of Africa and Gaul, employed in arranging the Gospel Canon. Yet we shall readily yield to those who, finding us wandering through these desert places, may lead us back into the path if we have not attained the truth, or at least what is perhaps more probable.

[Col. 0030B] As to what may readily be conjectured concerning Italy—especially concerning the Roman Church, foremost among all others—I confess that I do not know. For although in its Canon it may formerly have preferred Matthew and John to the other two, taking account of their apostolic office—and all the more because John was at Rome and, according to Tertullian, bore witness to his faith by being plunged into burning oil (the Vatican manuscript of Gregory of Nyssa, in the second encomium on Saint Stephen among the monuments of the Greek Church published by the distinguished Zacagni, wrongly reads εἰς ὕδωρ, “into water”) (*On the Prescription against Heretics*, ch. 38)—yet with regard to Luke and Mark there is room for doubt either way.

Indeed, believing that some assistance for this inquiry might be hoped for from the Vatican Library, I once asked the most eminent prince Angelo Maria Quirini, librarian of the Roman Church, to order the learned custodians of that library to inspect any manuscripts surviving there in which an order different from the Vulgate prevailed. Being a man distinguished not only by greatness of spirit, splendor of works, munificence, and liberality—qualities truly befitting a prince—but also by renown in learning, by fostering letters, and thereby advancing talents to the immortality of his name, he graciously acceded to my request and ordered those sacred records to be examined. But no light shone forth from them: all those inspected agreed with Jerome’s Canon.

[Col. 0030D] With regard to the other churches in Italy more distant from Rome, especially Cisalpine Gaul, it would be easy, for the question under discussion, to invent something from the much-debated passage of Epiphanius (*Heresy* LI) concerning Luke’s preaching in Italy and Gaul. But perhaps we have indulged our own conjectures and those of others more than is proper. Let us therefore at last leave these estuaries for solid ground and examine several more notable passages in this our manuscript.

I had said that it derived from those exemplars which were current before Hilary’s time. The blessed author supplied grounds for this assertion in Book X of *On the Trinity*, §41, where, speaking of the passage Luke 22:43–44—“And being in agony, he prayed more earnestly; and his sweat became like drops of blood running down to the ground”—which is absent from our codex, he says:

[Col. 0031A] “Nor should we be ignorant that in very many Greek and Latin codices nothing is found written either about the angel who appeared or about the sweat of blood. Thus, since there is doubt whether in various books this is absent or superfluous—for the diversity of books leaves this uncertain to us—certainly,” etc.

In what matter, or in what century, or by whom those words were expunged is obscure. Yet Grotius’s remarks on this passage (*Notes on Luke*) and on another passage of the same Evangelist deserve examination, lest the judgment of a most learned man mislead readers. Speaking of the angel’s appearance and the sweat, he says: “The superstition and rashness of those who deleted this passage and the following one about the sweat were equally blameworthy, and for no more serious a reason than that for which, as we said above, the passage concerning the weeping was deleted.” But on Luke 19:41 he had said that the passage about Christ’s weeping was retained by the Latin, Syriac, and Arabic translators, whereas Epiphanius testifies that in his own time it did not occur in publicly received exemplars; and that the words in the *Anchoratus* deserve notice, “if only,” he says, “that we may see how much the rulers of the churches allowed themselves.”

[Col. 0031B] Mill, however, supplied the words of Epiphanius omitted by Grotius, which had given him occasion to condemn the alleged license of church leaders. “Grotius,” Mill says (*Prolegomena*, §798), “is grievously mistaken in thinking thus of the rulers of the churches.” The words are: “The orthodox removed the saying, being afraid and not understanding its end and its strongest point” (Ὀρθόδοξοι δὲ ἀφειλοντο τὸ ῥητὸν φοβηθέντες, καὶ μὴ νοήσαντες αὐτοῦ τὸ τέλος, καὶ τὸ ἰσχυρότατον).

It is indeed surprising that a man of boundless reading and the keenest judgment should have understood “the orthodox,” who had deleted those words from an uncommendable fear that Christ’s weeping might seem unworthy of our Savior Jesus Christ, here to mean the rulers of churches. Still more surprising is it that, if uncorrected copies (ἀδιόρθωτα), to which Epiphanius appeals in the same place, still survived, these surely must have been copies preserved in churches more chastely and accurately than among private persons. Far from churchmen themselves or bishops having allowed themselves to remove anything from the original text.

Another passage is read by Hilary just as it stands in our codex, Matthew 26:53: “Do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he will presently furnish me with more than twelve thousand legions of angels?” Hilary, *On the Trinity* X.42: “No angel is sent to him, who, if he wished, could bring down twelve thousand legions from heaven.” And on Psalm 53: “because twelve thousand legions of angels could stand with the Lord at the time of his Passion.” Likewise again on Psalm 54: “But amid these things he possesses power to summon twelve thousand heavenly legions.”

[Col. 0031D] Mill, following Erasmus, thought that Hilary had suffered a lapse of memory when, in the passage on Psalm 54, he wrote “twelve thousand.” For, he says, in Canon 32 on Matthew Hilary reads as the printed editions do.
