Mill was evidently misled by one or two of the three cited passages, nor could he have seen what the most learned editor observed: namely, that in the better manuscripts Hilary consistently retains this reading everywhere.

From this consistency in citing passages of sacred books, diverse though they are in both place and subject, with no alteration of wording anywhere, we may certainly infer that the ancient writers of the Church quoted them not from the storehouse of memory, as they generally did, but faithfully from their codices; and we may infer this still more certainly when they repeatedly press such passages, exactly and clause by clause, to illuminate an argument. A further example will be supplied by a passage of Tertullian overlooked by Mill. It makes entirely clear that this writer once read thus in his exemplar, and it is no slight proof that our codex, which exhibits the same reading, was copied from transcripts collated with very ancient exemplars.

[Col. 0032B] Luke 15:8, Vulgate: “Or what woman, having ten drachmas, if she loses one drachma, does she not light a lamp, sweep the house, and search carefully until she finds it?” Our Silver Codex: “Does she not light a lamp, and clean the house with brooms, and search carefully,” etc.

Tertullian (*On Modesty*, ch. 9):

> But we do not invent subjects from parables; rather, we interpret parables from their subjects. Nor do we greatly labor to force every detail in the exposition, provided that we avoid contraries as well. Why a hundred sheep? Why specifically ten drachmas? And what are those brooms? It was necessary, if he wished to express that the salvation of one sinner is most pleasing to God, to name some quantity from which he might describe one as having perished. It was necessary that the manner of a woman seeking a drachma in the house should be fitted out with the aid both of brooms and of a lamp.

John 7:8, Vulgate: “Go up yourselves to this feast; but I do not go up to this feast, because my time has not yet been fulfilled.” Our codex: “But you go up to this feast; I do not yet go up to this feast,” etc., like almost all Greek manuscripts: ἐγὼ οὔπω ἀναβαίνω, “I do not yet go up”; though some have οὐκ ἀναβαίνω, “I do not go up.”

[Col. 0032C] Grotius, followed afterwards by Mill, says on this passage: “This was certainly the ancient reading. For if οὔπω had stood in Porphyry’s time, he would never have slandered Christ here as guilty of falsehood, since in the word οὔπω lay the solution of the difficulty. To escape it, some wrote οὔπω, others οὐκ ἀναβαίνω νῦν, ‘I do not go up now.’”

Le Clerc, in his letter to Optimianus prefixed to Mill’s Leipzig edition, likewise says: “It has been rightly observed from Grotius that the ancient reading was not οὔπω, ‘not yet,’ but οὐκ, ‘not.’” Yet it would have been better to cite Jerome himself, *Against the Pelagians* II, from whom Grotius derived this. Either Le Clerc had not read attentively Mill’s *Prolegomena* (§703), where he examines Porphyry’s passages, or his memory failed him; for he would have encountered the words of Jerome quoted there. In his *Gospel Harmony*, however, he retained the contested reading found in the Greek manuscripts, and in his historical commentary fully explained it as Christ’s response to the apostles: they could indeed go to Jerusalem in order to be present there at the beginning of the feast, but he himself would not yet go because the suitable time for his journey there had not yet arrived.

[Col. 0033A] Let the learned judge whether they rightly infer from Jerome’s passage that οὐκ, “not,” rather than οὔπω, “not yet,” was anciently read. His words are these (*Against the Pelagians* II, ch. 6):

> He denies to his brothers and relatives that he will go to the Feast of Tabernacles. And afterwards it is written: “But when his brothers had gone up, then he too went up to the feast, not openly but as it were in secret.” “He denied that he would go, and did what he had earlier denied,” barks Porphyry. He accuses him of inconsistency and change, not knowing that all stumbling-blocks are to be referred to the flesh.

Christ certainly denied that he would go up to the Feast of Tabernacles whether the particle used was οὔπω or οὐκ; we express denial in either way when we say, “I am not coming,” or “I am not yet coming.” Moreover, what ground did that little word οὐκ provide Porphyry for charging Christ with falsehood—unless that, to men excited and raging, whatever weapons present themselves are weapons? For the following words, “because my time is NOT YET fulfilled,” plainly enough indicate that he was waiting for the time and hour of going up. I for my part do not think that a mind otherwise perverse, but acute and vigorous, was so foolish as to wish to employ such a feeble argument.

[Col. 0033B] I therefore do not doubt that Porphyry, using an interpolated codex, read: ἐγὼ γὰρ οὐκ ἀναβήσομαι, “for I shall not go up”—a singular reading exhibited by Mill’s cited edition—unless that impostor had corrupted an ancient and genuine reading. For Jerome charged him with using interpolated copies (*Commentary on Matthew*, on Mark 12). Certainly, if the entire context of the cited passage is considered, it will be clear that Jerome attributes this reading to Porphyry, rendering his very words: “Porphyry barks, ‘He denied that he would go.’” We have drawn this out a little more fully in defense of the reading of the Silver Codex, which I think is more likely to be that of the earliest copies of the primitive translator before Jerome, rather than a later reading arising from Porphyry’s slander.

John 5:4: our codex lacks the entire passage about the angel descending from heaven at stated times, the stirring of the water, and so forth. Kuster says (*Preface to Mill’s edition of the New Testament*) that it may be inferred from ancient manuscripts—several of which he cites in succession, having consulted them in the Royal Library at Paris—that this passage was once judged doubtful by some. He then adds: “If that verse was absent from New Testament manuscripts at the beginning and only later crept into the text of John’s Gospel, this must have happened before Tertullian’s time, since in his work *On Baptism* he alludes to this passage, saying, ‘An angel intervening stirred the pool of Bethesda.’”

[Col. 0033D] It is rather harsh indeed that so learned a man should have doubted whether this passage was present in John’s autograph, when the sequence of the entire narrative suggests otherwise. What purpose otherwise would there be in the earlier statements about the Sheep Pool having five porticoes, and about the multitude of sick persons waiting there for the movement of the water? And what purpose in the subsequent account of that miserable man, infirm now for thirty-eight years, who, when Christ asked whether he wished to be healed, answered that he had no person to put him into the pool when the water had been stirred? These things surely imply that something is missing in which the stirring of the water was mentioned.

[Col. 0034A] Why then was that passage omitted? Was it because the angel’s descent seemed paradoxical (παράδοξον): occurring annually, only once, and benefiting only one out of so many sick persons? Or because Josephus makes no mention of so remarkable an event, one contributing to the glory of his nation? Or did Tertullian himself provide idle critics with an occasion for this gap? We shall supply the passage omitted by Kuster.

Tertullian says (*Against the Jews*, ch. 13): “Since the Jews still contend that their Christ has not yet come, whom we have shown in so many ways to have come, let the Jews recognize the end predicted for them after Christ’s advent, on account of the impiety by which they despised and killed him.” Then, after inserting other matters concerning the calling of the Gentiles and the cessation of heavenly benefits among that people, he adds: “And so, when the former gifts had been withdrawn, the Law and the Prophets were until John. And the pool of Bethesda was until Christ’s advent, curing the ailments of Israel; it ceased to benefit them when, in the persistence of their rage, the name of the Lord was blasphemed.” Whether, as we have said, the words “until Christ’s advent” could have deceived a reader not sufficiently attentive—the kind of reader this African writer certainly requires—into supposing that the miracle did not continue beyond that point, just as prophets did not exist among the Jews beyond John’s advent, we leave as a mere conjecture.

[Col. 0034C] But both this and every other such consideration, as well as Kuster’s doubt whether the history of the Sheep Pool was intruded into John’s Gospel, are completely refuted by the material preceding and following this disputed passage, as we have said. If anyone suspected that miracle, he would surely have had to delete all of these things as well.

Nothing, therefore, is more certain than that either someone copying his exemplar from an antigraph, or a reader guiding the copyist’s work, was deceived by his eyes as he passed from the third clause to the fifth, skipping the fourth; and that the same error afterwards passed into one transcript after another. For this very reason that passage was marked in some copies with critical signs or asterisks, and in others written either in the margin or at the top of the page in a different hand, according to Kuster: that is, private persons who found it omitted somewhere marked it in their transcript, as suspect, by this critical notation.

[Col. 0034D] But among the observations critics have made upon this passage of John, nothing is so astonishing as the invention of the learned Henry Hammond. While nevertheless retaining the entire context of the passage, he sought to transfer the healing power of the water, hitherto ascribed by everyone to divine power, to water medicated by the blood of animals slaughtered there in great number for sacrifices. Thus it was not an angel of the Lord, but some messenger sent by the priests, who stirred the water so that the medicinal power of the blood might be mixed throughout it. This notion about the messenger he borrowed from Grotius; see the latter on the cited passage of John.

And, surpassing belief, only one person each year, among so many sick persons awaiting that benefit there, entered the healing bath—as though it did not matter to provide for the others also, or as though the medicinal power would be sufficient for only one person. Moreover, by this remedy every disease was cured: lameness, wasting disease, blindness, and all others which must have existed among that multitude of sick persons—something unknown to all physicians until now.

[Col. 0035A] How many blind persons, not to mention other chronic illnesses which often baffle even most learned physicians, among the wealthiest families would have ordered one or two herds slaughtered if by that means they could return from darkness to their former light? It is indeed a striking example of how readily the lure of novelty can deceive a mind otherwise excellent. Certainly, whoever examines that commentary will, I think, agree with me. Yet Le Clerc, who illustrated so many other points in that work with critical notes (second Frankfurt edition, Thomas Fritsch), silently passed over Hammond’s paradox and the weak—if ever there were weak—arguments adduced to support it.

Among the blemishes of the Silver Codex is another notable one: the omission of the history of the adulterous woman in John 8. Yet this is common to it and to very many of the most ancient manuscripts. In this subject, already exhausted by learned men, we shall merely add a few observations made elsewhere.

I pass over Grotius’s view (*Notes on John*, at this passage): namely, that the story was not written by John, but was often related orally by him and the other apostles; that it was later attached to John’s Gospel by Papias and other disciples of John; and that it was approved by the Church because it was sufficiently established by testimony that it had been handed down by the apostles. For this conjecture rests on no foundation whatsoever, and it is also fraught with danger if we believe that anything could once have been added by private persons to the Evangelists’ history as canonical.

[Col. 0035C] Mill, in commenting on this passage, says through a lapse of memory that this story appeared in the Gospel according to the Hebrews and was thence sewn onto our Gospel by Papias, according to Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* III.39. Yet Eusebius says nothing of this attachment and, besides, mentions not an adulterous woman but another woman guilty of many sins.

Le Clerc wonders that Hammond, following Grotius’s conjectures, retained this story (*Notes on this passage*, edition cited above). Yet Le Clerc himself retained it in both texts of his *Gospel Harmony*, then expounded it at length in his historical commentary and later adduced it as an example in his Gospel canons. But all who read what Le Clerc there adduces on verse 6, where Jesus is said to have bent down and written with his finger upon the ground, will have still greater reason to wonder. His words are:

[Col. 0036A] “Those who think this history has been sewn on here may suppose that Papias, or someone else, borrowed this circumstance from what is reported of Menedemus, which Diogenes Laertius narrates thus in Book II, §127.” He here cites Laertius’s Greek, which we omit for brevity and give in Latin translation: “For he mocked and spoke freely; therefore, when a young man said something harsh to him, he gave no answer, but, taking up a straw, drew a figure of a man who submitted to sexual use, until the young man, understanding the insult while everyone looked on, went away.”

So great was Le Clerc’s regard for a scrap of learning—learning in which he was indeed powerful, varied, manifold, and, I would say, exceptionally exact in many matters—that he was not ashamed to introduce such filthy and, if anywhere, certainly in this context utterly disgraceful material into a most serious argument. And he represented Papias, an apostolic man, as having devoted himself to such nonsense! Yet he treated him more gently than when he did not hesitate to brand him both empty and an impostor.

> [Note: [Col. 0036A] *Dissertation on the Authors of the Gospels*, at the end of the *Gospel Harmony*; *Observations on Herodotus*, Book I; *Chronology*, at the end of Volume III.]

Add also the conspicuous chronological error: if Diogenes Laertius lived after Marcus Antoninus, as Palmerius thinks, or rather flourished about A.D. 210, in the seventeenth or eighteenth year of Severus, as Tillemont says; see also Ménage, Preface to Laertius. For on this reckoning Papias died at least fifty years before Laertius.

[Col. 0036B] Other things also are absent from the codex which are read in the Vulgate. Thus Matthew 27:8: “For this reason that field was called Haceldama, that is, the field of blood”; the codex, omitting the word *Haceldama*, reads: “that field was called the field of blood.” So too in Matthew 27:35, the entire passage, “that what was spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled: They divided among themselves,” etc. Likewise Matthew 8:9, “for I too am a man set under authority”: our codex omits “set under authority,” as does the Gothic translation. But these omissions, most of which are very ancient, as well as others, will at once be apparent to the learned reader; so too will the addition in Luke 11:36 and 13:17, and other such things.

I shall add a reading peculiar to the Silver Codex, Luke 21:25. Vulgate: “And upon earth distress of nations, because of the confusion caused by the roaring of the sea and the movement of waves.” Our text: “And upon earth the encounter of nations in anxiety, like the roaring of the sea and the movement of waves.” I once thought this had been fashioned from a passage of Tertullian (*Against Marcion* IV.39), where he says: “Having then shown the time of destruction, when Jerusalem had begun to be surrounded by armies, he recounts signs of the final end—the portents of sun, moon, and stars—and upon earth the straits of nations astounded, **as if by the sound of a surging sea**, in expectation of impending evils.”

[Col. 0036D] But whatever its ultimate source, the reading is vigorous, and wonderfully expresses the murmur of that immense multitude rushing against one another in anxiety over impending ruin, like the sound of a surging sea.

Here is another notable passage of the excellent writer, which he presses against Marcion (*Against Marcion* IV.26) for the sake of argument; and therefore it is evident that it was so read in the copies of his time. For he would not have urged a reading departing from the archetypes, especially in Luke, whom that apostate had chosen above the other Evangelists and knew through long, though perverse, use.

The passage is Luke 11:13, where the Vulgate reads: “How much more will your Father from heaven give the GOOD Spirit to those who ask him?” Our codex reads, “the HOLY Spirit,” as do almost all Greek manuscripts: Πνεῦμα ἅγιον, “Holy Spirit.” Tertullian says:

[Col. 0037A] “Recognize therefore the Father whom you also call the Creator. He is the one who knows what his children ask. For to those asking for bread he gave manna from heaven, and to those desiring flesh he sent forth quail; not a serpent for a fish, nor a scorpion for an egg. It belongs to him, whose are both, not to give evil in place of good. But Marcion’s god, since he did not possess a scorpion, could not say that he would not give what he did not possess; whereas he who has a scorpion does not give it. Therefore he will also give the HOLY Spirit, with whom is also the non-HOLY spirit.”

[Col. 0037B] I shall here examine another reading of the Silver Codex, Luke 9:54, and whether Tertullian followed it is disputed. It is: “Lord, do you wish that we should say for fire to come down from heaven and consume them, **as Elijah also did**?” These final words are absent from Vulgate manuscripts.

Almost all Greek manuscript copies exhibit this reading, according to Mill on this passage, as do the Syriac, Arabic, Ethiopic, and Gothic translators; Erasmus himself retained it in his 1558 edition of the New Testament, published by Roville. Mill had thought that Tertullian read it thus. But when he finally came to the *Prolegomena*, he adopted an entirely different opinion (§4, 18). We give his words because they bear considerably upon the criterion for this passage:

> “The following words, ὡς καὶ Ἠλίας ἐποίησε, ‘as Elijah also did,’ which so remarkably illuminate the thought of James and John, were, as the matter itself cries out, written in the margin of a book by some student as a comment, and from there passed into the body of the text. For who in his right mind would have deleted such remarkable words? Rather, because they shed no little light upon the apostles’ thought, I do not doubt that they were seized upon and inserted into the text. But that Tertullian read them, which we once affirmed in our notes, is not so clear. It is more likely that the example of Elijah, noted by himself in Book IV, chapter 25 of *Against Marcion*, and by others on this passage, gave occasion for this interpolation.”

[Col. 0037D] It is indeed not sufficiently clear whether Tertullian read this in his copy of Luke or himself added the example of Elijah. His words are: “The Creator displays the plague of fire, at Elijah’s request, against that false prophet. Recognize the severity of the Judge. In contrast, recognize Christ’s gentleness in rebuking his disciples when they intended the same punishment against that Samaritan village.” Certainly, when in *On Patience* 3 he referred to the cited Lukan passage, he makes no mention of Elijah. We give the words overlooked by Mill: “Speaking of Christ, Tertullian says: ‘He did not despise sinners or tax collectors. He was not even angry with that city which had refused to receive him, though the disciples wished heavenly fires to be brought against so insulting a town.’”

But Mill’s assertion that those words, written by someone in the margin of his codex, passed thence into the text, and that their being noted on Luke’s passage by others, as previously by Tertullian, gave rise to this interpolation, is mere conjecture—and conjecture not always successful in matters of fact.

[Col. 0038A] For the principle that carries greatest weight in critical judgments when distinguishing genuine text from additions—namely, that where there was no reason to remove something from ancient writings, but a probable reason to add it, it is an addition—can often mislead. Many things may have been omitted here and there by careless copyists: some because their eyes were deceived as another’s dictation ran ahead; others because their ears were deceived. Readers of New Testament manuscripts encounter numerous examples of this, such as the notable John 5:4 which we observed a little before. Therefore it is wholly uncertain whether those words were deleted or omitted in the exemplars in which they are absent.

Another of Mill’s critical observations also stands against his conjecture: namely, that a reading found in few codices is more suspicious than one exhibited by many. For it is difficult to believe that so many copies, whether produced by copyists for public use or prepared by many private persons for themselves, all individually derived from some corrupted exemplar—which could very easily have happened to a few copies. It is likewise difficult to believe that the Syriac, Arabic, Ethiopic, and Gothic translators all employed interpolated exemplars at this point. Add that almost all Greek manuscripts, as Mill admits, read thus; few will persuade themselves that these words entered them from Tertullian’s annotations or those of others, or from Latin copies. For at that time the use among Easterners of the Latin language, and of that African writer or other authors of our language, was rare; that of the Vulgate translator was rarer still—or rather nonexistent, since they had no need of him.

[Col. 0038C] But what most leads me to believe that it was anciently read thus is the rarity and magnitude of the event itself: that the apostles wished to call down fire from heaven upon an insulting town, without any precedent being mentioned. Therefore it is highly probable that they cited to Christ the case of Elijah, so outstanding and well known among the Jews, in order that he might grant the apostles themselves that same power formerly given to the prophet.

What we said above, that various things could have been omitted by copyists here and there, is suggested to me by another passage, Luke 6:26. Where the Vulgate, with almost all Greek manuscripts, reads: “For according to these things their fathers did to the false prophets,” our exemplar reads: “their fathers did to the prophets.” Some codices before Jerome read likewise, according to Mill. Tertullian also read thus (*Against Marcion* IV), as Mill observes. His words are: “Woe when men bless you: according to these things their fathers did also to the prophets. The Creator likewise accuses through Isaiah those who seek human blessing and praise: ‘My people, those who call you blessed lead you astray and confuse the paths of your feet’ [Isaiah 3:12].”

[Col. 0038D] One should read what Mill adduces on this passage, as well as Erasmus’s judgment, who thought that this variation first crept into the manuscripts through some petty scholar. I do not doubt that whatever error occurred is to be attributed to a copyist who, having read exactly the same words in the preceding verse 23, either thought that they ought to be retained here too and thus skipped the first syllables of *pseudoprophetis* (“false prophets”), or, his eyes deceiving him, read that clause a second time in place of the other. Certainly our Savior appears to have referred to the cited passage in Isaiah. And just as in former times there were those false prophets who were said to see falsehood and prophesy lies to the people, so there would not be lacking those who, to harden the obstinate minds of the Jews, would not cease to heap good and favorable things upon them; and he therefore likened them to false prophets. Indeed, were it not for the agreement of all manuscripts hitherto, it would seem necessary to read: “For according to these things the false prophets did to their fathers.” But we offer this only as a simple conjecture.

[Col. 0039A] I should be too lengthy if I continued here to examine other readings peculiar to our codex which depart from the Vulgate, including some that learned men have needlessly troubled themselves over—especially since perhaps others, whose work we have not been able to inspect, have brought forward what we might offer. It will therefore be better to turn to such manuscripts and inquire, insofar as the obscurity of the times and the powers of our understanding permit, whence this diversity of readings finally arose, by whom, or when, it began to be introduced.

It is certain, as we said before, that the divine records of the apostles, as each came forth, were entered by the churches to which they first became known into their codices; that copies were then communicated to nearer churches, and these in turn to other believers, so that they might be readily available. They were certainly copied with that care which befitted the purity of the nascent Church and, at the same time, the reverence and dignity due to the writings: by men, as is reasonable to believe, selected for that office, whose fidelity and diligence could not in the least be doubted; [Col. 0039C] and thus, in the earlier centuries, they were kept with the utmost scruple in the sanctuaries of those churches, perhaps also among private persons who had not yet learned to be wiser than they ought.

And indeed, at that time it was not merely difficult but unsafe to introduce into copies anything differing from the archetypes, while these still remained in the principal churches, to which appeal might be made. Tertullian appears to have done this (*On the Prescription against Heretics*, XXXVI), and that too in open conflict with heretics; for, had he deceived them, they could either have laughed at him as credulous or denounced him as a liar. For he says:

> Come now, you who would better exercise your curiosity in the matter of your salvation, run through the apostolic churches, in which the very chairs of the apostles still preside in their own places, in which [Col. 0039D] their own AUTHENTIC letters are read aloud, sounding forth the voice and representing the face of each one. Is Achaia nearest to you? You have Corinth. If you are not far from Macedonia, you have Philippi; you have Thessalonica. If you can make your way into Asia, you have Ephesus. But if you are adjacent to Italy, you have Rome, whence authority is also at hand for us.

I am not unaware what Rigaultius wrote in his notes on this passage. These “authentic letters” to which Tertullian appeals were, of course, letters in the very language in which they had been written by the apostles.

Simon, following Rigaultius (*Critical History of the New Testament*, Part I, IV), says that, when Tertullian appealed to authentic exemplars, he understood nothing other than writings composed in Greek, [Col. 0040A] because in the African Church only Latin codices of the Gospels were read.

I confess that I do not understand why Rigaultius thought so, unless perhaps he believed it impossible for the apostles’ archetypes to have survived down to Tertullian’s time. For why else would this African have appealed only to those churches to which it is known that the Apostle had written? Were there not, in other places also, authentic copies of Paul’s Epistles, if they were written in Greek?

Simon, as in many passages of that history, insufficiently mindful and not very consistent with himself, having said with great confidence (*ibid.*, Part I, I) that in those earliest times of the Church it had been difficult to distinguish genuine books of the apostles or disciples from those which heretics inscribed with their forged names, [Col. 0040B] since there were no archives to which believers might appeal, shortly afterwards adds that, if ever some sectarian brought forward forged Gospels, the Fathers convicted him of falsity by appealing to the genuine ones preserved in the apostolic churches as though in archives: “They convicted him of the falsity of the documents which he produced by means of the TRUE ones, preserved in the apostolic churches and serving in place of archives.” What, then, did non-apostolic churches do when need arose? Again, because the Gospels read in the churches of Africa, Italy, Gaul, and other regions of the West had been translated into Latin, had they for that reason ceased to be true and authentic? Although Tertullian there speaks not of the Gospels but of Paul’s Epistles. [Col. 0040C]

Whether the Apostle’s autographs still survived in the churches mentioned in Tertullian’s own age or not, no prudent person can determine in a factual matter of this sort without suitable evidence. Yet nothing prevents their having been preserved. Indeed, that they were preserved is far more probable. For if so many copies survived, why not the archetypes from which they flowed? In them lay both the greatest glory of the churches to which those Epistles had been given, churches which rightly boasted of having been founded by the Apostle, and an authority always at hand against innovators if they attempted fraudulently to add, omit, or corrupt anything in the copies. Therefore Tertullian appealed to these churches not because the Epistles had been written in Greek there—for they were equally so in many others—but because Paul’s Epistles themselves, written by his own hand (*idiócheirai*), [Col. 0040D] still survived.

As to the Gospels, although Simon, in the passage praised above, seems to have thought their archetypes preserved in apostolic churches, no one, so far as I know, explicitly appealed to any one of them except Peter of Alexandria in a fragment on Easter, of which later.

But however difficult it may have been, precisely because the original records of the New Covenant were preserved in apostolic churches, to alter anything in their copies, still nothing at that time was so effective in preserving their integrity as the very care and reverence shown for the sacred codices, joined with the simplicity of believers. Thus, although some persons [Col. 0041A] may have dared to alter something in their own copies, I consider it exceedingly difficult that this could have been done in ecclesiastical copies. For they were read either privately only by ministers of sacred office, or publicly by readers, almost always in the bishops’ presence.

If any conjecture may be allowed, it was not in the first century but perhaps in the second that the appearance of Greek and Latin codices began to be tampered with by the scholia of a few persons—whether through presumption or credulity is uncertain. Soon, as the Church increased day by day in learning and wealth, a greater licence began to grow: cultivated Greek minds having become impatient with apostolic simplicity in writing, and Latin minds with that plainness (*idiōteuousin*, “writing in an unlearned/popular manner”) which the first translators had employed in translating for the people’s understanding. Yet, if I am not mistaken, this licence was still confined within the bounds of private persons, [Col. 0041B] while ecclesiastical exemplars remained untouched—until, as the morals both of people and bishops declined for the worse, that dreadful storm of persecutors descended, by God’s permission, upon His ungrateful vineyard, as Eusebius testifies (*Ecclesiastical History*, VIII.1; A.D. 303).

Then came the first, and indeed the more grievous, disaster of the sacred codices. Magistrates everywhere were ordered not only to destroy churches, but above all publicly to burn in the streets the divine books, zealously sought out from bishops themselves and their ministers. How many therefore perished in the ruins, having previously been concealed; how many were extorted by force and tortures; how many were betrayed by slaves, maidservants, and deserters; and finally how many were most miserably surrendered through fear by believers—indeed by the very heads of churches and their ministers, from which the designation *traditores* (“handers-over”) began to be used—let anyone who has seen that most sorrowful condition of the Church in the histories of the time consider. Hence it happened that, after churches had been destroyed and their copies either burned or otherwise consumed, when persecution finally ceased, private copies—most of which could more easily have been hidden or carried elsewhere—were meanwhile used by ecclesiastical scribes to replace the former copies; and then by copyists, to meet the piety of believers. Thus there was a departure from that primitive purity of the codices, with scholia admitted into the text, especially through the ignorance of scribes or through that impulse toward novelty which, as with other commodities, commonly increases the price of books.

I therefore think that the condition of Latin exemplars to which Jerome later referred [Col. 0041D] must be assigned to those times: he complained (*Letter to Damasus*) that in them many things had been badly rendered by faulty translators, corrected still more perversely by ignorant presumptuous persons, and either added or altered by drowsy copyists; that, in short, all things were confused throughout the sequence of the Gospels. He asserted that there were almost as many exemplars as codices. From this arose the opinion of several Latin versions of the New Testament. It was further promoted by another passage of Augustine (*On Christian Doctrine*, II), where he says that those who had translated the Scriptures from Hebrew into Greek could be counted, but Latin translators could not at all. For, in the earliest periods of the faith, whenever a Greek codex came into anyone’s hands and he seemed to himself to have some slight command of both languages, he had dared to translate it.

Yet, unless the words of the blessed writer are to be taken more broadly, it is not so easy to believe that there were everywhere so many private translators in those earliest times of the faith; and it is far more difficult if he meant translations of the Old Testament. The same, I think, must be said of translators of the New Testament, since those then called to the sacrament of faith were for the most part uneducated and from the common people. I therefore think that the cited passage of that most holy man should be understood, not of the first century and the following one, but of the times touched on above. The term “translators” too must be understood more broadly: not as though they produced complete translations, but rather as scholiasts, who were correctors or elucidators, as they thought, of certain passages. Often they were ignorant even of the Greek language, and therefore rendered what they had misunderstood still worse. A clear example will be supplied by the passage in the Silver Codex, where that private person, collating a Latin copy with a Greek exemplar, rendered Luke 2:4, “from the house and lineage of David” (*ex oíkou kaì tês patriâs Dauíd*), as “from the house and COUNTRY of David.”

But two considerations especially move me to believe that those several Latin versions were nothing other than additions made here and there in their codices by private persons, as we have said. First: in the very earliest periods of the faith, a translation prepared by translators of the Roman Church was available to Italy—and consequently to neighbouring Africa and the other churches of the West—as each sacred record issued from the hands of apostles or disciples, so that the piety of believers might be provided for. Secondly: copies drawn from the older exemplars that circulated before Jerome and Augustine, [Col. 0042C] in which those additions indeed appear, but the underlying basis and the popular idiom (*idiōtismos*) of the translation praised above are most manifest.

I said “translators.” For, as I once wrote to you, there was not one and the same translator throughout; this is shown both by the chronology, if one counts the years that elapsed from the first Gospel, Matthew’s, to the last, John’s, and especially by the diversity of style, as Mill observes (*Prolegomena* I, to his edition of Matthew’s Gospel). From this diversity Marzianaeus, insufficiently attentively, inferred several Latin versions, no differently than from the dissimilar form of sections and chapters in the codices. It is indeed more likely that in the Church which was chief among all the rest there flourished not merely one translator but several, so that, if [Col. 0042D] one upon whom the task of translating rested had been removed by circumstances, hindered by illness, or finally forestalled by death, another might be at hand to take care of the vacant charge. For what Walton asserted (*Prolegomena* X, §1)—namely, that the Latin Church could not have existed without a Latin version—I judge so evident that nothing could be more so. In what language, after all, could the reading of the sacred books have been made to the people in the liturgical assemblies, except in the people’s own language? Therefore Mill’s opinion, following Grotius, that Greek was then a familiar language at Rome and in Italy, seems to me a dream. Here are his words, by which he attempted to overturn Walton’s opinion:

[Col. 0043A] “For they have not observed,” he says (*Prolegomena*, no. 377), “that for nearly fifty years, from the founding of that Church until the establishment of the canon of the New Testament, there had not even been any thought of collecting the writings of evangelists and apostles into one body, much less of translating them into other languages; and that this nascent Church had no need at all of a Latin version. For the believers then dwelling at Rome—Jewish, Egyptian, and other eastern immigrants—were familiarly acquainted with Greek, which was plainly their vernacular. The same must be said of Christians in the provinces and in certain other regions of the world.”

The poet’s familiar saying is:

> “The whole world now possesses Greek Athens.”  
> > (Juvenal, *Satires*, XV)

Jerome too says concerning the eastern peoples even of his own age:

> “The whole East speaks in the Greek tongue.”

You know what I have thought about that establishment of the canon: I do not doubt that Mill, without any witness, postponed it later than he should have done. Now, as concerns our subject, who could ever believe that the nascent Roman Church consisted only of Jews, Egyptians, and other easterners? What are we to suppose Peter and Paul were doing there during those two years in which Paul remained in free custody, unless enlightening with evangelical teaching all who assembled to hear—Greeks and barbarians alike, to both of whom the Apostle confessed himself indebted? Add the disciples, and not only them, but recent converts from the Gentiles, striving, wherever opportunity offered, to sow that same teaching among household members, companions, and acquaintances, following the example of the apostles. [Col. 0043C] How many, therefore, not from the East alone, became partakers of heavenly gifts in that immense confluence of nations?

But the satirist wrote that Greek letters were spread throughout the world. Granted—even allowing poetic hyperbole. One might add another passage (*Satire* VI), in which he mocks certain affected women for spilling out *anima* and *vita*—*psychē* and *zōē* (“soul” and “life”)—as though these were native words, and wittily invents Greek-style intercourse from this. And indeed there were many grammarians at Rome who taught Greek literature. There were also men in the wealthy households of private citizens, many of whom knew Greek. Let us grant the same thing to the cities of Italy, to Gaul, and to Britain; if one wishes, let us grant it even to Africa. What follows? Just as we had to learn Latin not by household use but from teachers, so they had to learn Greek. Many examples of this could be supplied from antiquity, if needed. Must the same therefore be said of everyone else? What of that huge throng of slaves in the city, in the countryside, and throughout Italy? What of the shopkeepers, travelling merchants, butchers, craftsmen, fullers, shoemakers—would I not be ridiculous if I tried to call every trade and occupation to the roll? In a word, what of so vast a multitude of humbler persons at Rome, in colonies, in municipal towns, everywhere; and then of respectable people whose means at home were narrow? Had these too spent their days in school to learn to speak Greek? Yet the Church in those earliest times consisted chiefly of such persons, God choosing the weak things of the world in order to confound the wisdom of the age.

Hence Eusebius rightly said that the apostles used an unlearned tongue (*tēn glôttan idiōteúontes*) [Col. 0044A] (*Ecclesiastical History*, III.24), and that they neither knew nor attempted (*oúte ḗdesan, oúte enekheíroun*) to set forth their Master’s precepts in the ornaments of eloquence. For those who knew not how to preach Christ, and Him crucified, in persuasive words of human wisdom—by what rhetorical colours could they have undertaken it? And thus, Erasmus says (fifth edition of the New Testament, Froben and Episcopius), it was expedient for the apostles to use the speech which extended most widely and was understood alike by the learned and the unlearned. What he later affirms of the earliest translators is the same: namely, that the same judgment applies to their manner of expression as to apostolic speech, since the Roman tongue was still common to the mixed multitude. Therefore, in translating, they made many concessions to the mass of unlearned persons for whom these things were then written.

But what Mill adduced from Jerome as a concluding proof [Col. 0044B] had plainly fallen outside the scope of the inquiry in that great harvest of annotations which he had assembled with the utmost diligence from ecclesiastical writers, while his attention was absorbed amid such a mass of material. For the comparison there made between the East and the West could have no bearing upon this argument. Nor do the points he later added stand in the way: that translations of the Bible, or at least of certain books of the New Testament, for public use were not considered immediately upon acceptance of Christian faith, but only after an interval of several years; and that the Italic version, since it appeared among Italians and, as he thinks altogether credible, under the auspices of the Roman Church, can scarcely be reckoned to have been published before the time of Pope Pius, because he was then the first of the Latin popes and had administered the affairs of the Church for a somewhat longer period—namely fifteen years. [Col. 0044C] “For,” he says, “the other pontiffs up to that point had been almost Greeks.”

For two considerations especially weaken all this. First, he himself had asserted that no Latin version was needed, because Greek was already familiar at Rome and in the provinces—unless perhaps he supposed that it had disappeared in Pius’s time; but experience itself refutes that. The languages of peoples are all strengthened by long usage; they neither die, unless the whole political order is utterly overthrown, nor gradually become obsolete except through an influx of foreign nations. Neither occurred while the Empire, as it was, was flourishing. Secondly, he says that the popes were almost Greeks up to Pius, and that Pius was the first Latin. The most learned man had forgotten that Linus, the first after Peter, perhaps also Cletus after him, and certainly Clement, the third, were Latins. [Col. 0044D] Indeed, we learn from the ancients that Linus administered the affairs of the Church for twelve years. Why, then, should a translation of the sacred books of the New Testament have been prepared under Pius rather than under Linus, after so great an interval of time? Did the chief Church of all lack copies, as soon as they appeared, amid the very frequent arrivals at the City of people from the provinces of the Empire, so that the books could not conveniently be translated? Or perhaps, as the number of believers increased daily, was there no need for them to be translated? Neither, surely, if I am not mistaken.

All this has been said for the sake of this argument. Having formerly encountered it while observing Mill’s excellent *Prolegomena*, we first jotted down certain doubts on paper; now, reconsidering the same questions as circumstances arose, [Col. 0045A] we have developed them a little more fully. And since no monument survives from antiquity by which we might determine the date of that translation, we are trying the way by conjectures, as Mill himself did, to see whether some approach to truth may perhaps be found. Whether rightly or otherwise, let impartial judges of the matter decide.

Returning, therefore, to our purpose: we were saying that Jerome’s and Augustine’s words cited above confirmed for many the opinion that several versions existed in the Latin Church, although later, strengthened by supports sought elsewhere, it spread more widely. That is, the reading of the Fathers deceived most persons, even very learned ones. Seeing passages of the sacred text cited by them in different ways, and often even the same passages quoted differently by the same author, [Col. 0045B] they consequently supposed that the Fathers used different translations. “You will find,” says Huet (*On Distinguished Translators*), “that Tertullian, Cyprian, Ambrose, and the Latin Fathers followed editions various, indeed plainly different from one another, if you think it worth your while to investigate the matter.” Yet, though these versions sprang up suddenly, they vanished as suddenly after no long life, setting as it were at a sudden decline. In this, however, that most distinguished man was deceived by the first appearance of things that presented itself to his mind.

Pamelius maintained that Tertullian used a version of his own (*In the Life of Tertullian*, under A.D. 197), moved, I suppose, by Tertullian’s frequent Greek expressions, and also because he sometimes tests passages of the old translator against the Greek source—as clearly at Matthew 5:3 and John 1:1. Yet no writer was richer than Tertullian in citing divine authorities from the Old and New Testaments, and none freer in doing so: drawing them often from the ample storehouse of his memory, he cites the same texts now one way, now another; sometimes even taking the words of one writer for those of another, as is clear in the cited passage of Matthew. For since it is known that Marcion, rejecting the others, used only Luke’s Gospel, and that not even entire, Tertullian wished to confront him from that Gospel itself:

> I come now, he says, to his ordinary sayings, through which he introduces the characteristic feature of his doctrine into the proclamation, so to speak, of Christ: “Blessed are beggars”—for this is what the interpretation requires of the Greek word—“for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

Yet in this both Tertullian’s memory deceived him and Tertullian deceived Pamelius. For Pamelius says in his notes on this passage [Col. 0045D] that Luke has the Greek *ptōchoí*, which properly means “beggars.” But these are not Luke’s words but Matthew’s. In Matthew, as in Luke, the beginning of the clause is indeed the same—“Blessed are the poor” (*makárioi hoi ptōchoí*)—but what follows is not the same. Yet Tertullian elsewhere calls these *ptōchoí*, whom he wishes to translate there as “beggars,” *egenos*, “needy,” as Pamelius himself observed, citing a passage from *On Idolatry*, XII. He could have added another from the cited work *Against Marcion*, where Tertullian includes both beggars and poor persons under the name *egeni*, “needy.” We could produce more examples if the matter required it. But the evidence he brings from the *Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans*, formerly attributed to Ambrose, is wholly ambiguous and cannot in any way establish Tertullian’s alleged version.

[Col. 0046A] Another passage which Tertullian seems to test against the Greek original is that divine saying, “In the beginning was the Word” (*en archē ēn ho lógos*), which the old translator rendered: “In the beginning was the Word.” But Tertullian says (*Against Praxeas*, ch. 20): “And at the very outset, the preface itself of John the evangelist shows that he who was to become flesh had existed previously: ‘In the beginning was the discourse, and the discourse was with God, and God was the discourse.’”

Two passages above all indicate how the word *sermo* (“discourse”), which this African was the first among Latin writers to wish to use in this clause, was tested against the source. The first is in the *Apology* (ch. 21):

> We have already declared that God formed this universe by Word, reason, and power. Among your philosophers too it is agreed that the *Logos*, that is, DISCOURSE and Reason, is regarded as the artificer of the universe.

The other is in *Against Praxeas* (ch. 5), and is all the more notable because a man very celebrated in our own age employed it to support what he imagined about the meaning of the term *Logos* in the Evangelist:

> Before all things God was alone, Himself both world, place, and all things to Himself. Yet He was alone because there was nothing else external to Him. But even then He was not alone, for He had with Him that which He had in Himself—namely, His own REASON. God too is rational, and REASON was first in Him; and thus all things came from Him. That REASON is His own consciousness. THE GREEKS CALL THIS *LOGOS*, a word by which we also designate DISCOURSE. Hence it has already become customary among us, through the simplicity of translation, to say that DISCOURSE was with God. Yet it is more fitting that REASON be regarded as earlier, because God was not discursive from the beginning but RATIONAL even before the beginning; and because DISCOURSE ITSELF, CONSISTING OF REASON, shows that Reason, as its substance, is prior.

This same being, whom Tertullian called both Power and Reason and Spirit, he elsewhere calls Wisdom (*Against Hermogenes*, ch. 18): “But if WISDOM is the same as God’s DISCOURSE, and Wisdom in consciousness; and without whom nothing was made, just as nothing was arranged without WISDOM.” He had already gathered all these names in the *Apology* (ch. 23), asserting that Christ would come from heaven amid the convulsion of the whole world, the terror of the earth, and the mourning of all, except Christians, as the Power of God, the Spirit of God, Discourse, Wisdom, Reason, and the Son of God.

But was this innovator in terminology [Col. 0046D]—as Pamelius rightly calls him—consistent with himself when, setting aside the version of the primitive translator which he otherwise used, he preferred to render *Logos* as “Discourse” rather than “Word”? Hear him express it otherwise and more correctly (*On the Prescription against Heretics*, ch. 13):

> Now the rule of faith is this: from this point we declare what we defend—namely, that we believe in one God alone, and in no other besides the Maker of the world; and in His Son, so called, who created all things out of nothing through His WORD, first of all sent forth. This WORD we call His Son.

He uses the same term once and again in *On the Flesh of Christ* (chs. 12, 18), frequently calling Him WORD. There he represents the heretics of his time as using the old version, saying: “Because,” they say, “the WORD became FLESH.”

But nowhere did he express the force of the word *Logos* so explicitly as in the cited twenty-first chapter of the *Apology*, where, speaking of the Jews, he says:

> Therefore, since they had presumed Him to be merely a man because of His lowliness, it followed that they should judge Him a magician because of His power: since He expelled demons from men by a word, restored sight to the blind, made the paralysed whole, finally restored the dead to life by a word, made the very elements serve Him, calming storms and walking upon the seas—thus showing Himself to be the *Logos* of God, that is, the primordial, first-born WORD, accompanied by power and Reason and sustained by spirit.

From the matters which we have set forth at length and deliberately, it is sufficiently clear that Tertullian should be numbered not among translators who produced a complete version [Col. 0047B] but among those scholiasts of whom we spoke above, who tampered here and there with passages of the old translator. He did so for no advantage except novelty, which experience has often proved useless, and not infrequently dangerous, in matters of this kind. Add also that his use of *sermo* was not sufficiently suitable. For the meaning would then be not “the Word of God” but “the words of God.” Therefore, when in the cited passage against Praxeas he says that it had become customary among his people, through the simplicity of translation, to say that *sermo* was with God, Clericus rightly added—though for another purpose—“through ignorance.”

In the same class among Latin writers was Lactantius, no more consistent than his leader and no more accurate: he now calls the Son of God “Word,” now “Discourse” [Col. 0047C] (*On True Wisdom*, IV.8–9). Having said that discourse is spirit uttered with a voice signifying something, he nevertheless says that angelic spirits and that divine Discourse differ in this: spirit proceeds through the nostrils, discourse through the mouth. Angels, therefore, issued silently from God as spirits—well that he did not say “from God’s nostrils”—because they were created not to convey God’s teaching but for service. But he says that the other proceeded from God’s mouth with voice and sound, because God was to use His voice in addressing the people. He concludes this remarkable reasoning by saying: “Therefore Discourse and Word of God are rightly so called.”

Lactantius derived this vocal Discourse, like other matters that we shall subsequently mention, from Tertullian. For we have a very remarkable passage in Tertullian’s *Against Praxeas* (ch. 7):

> As soon as God willed to bring forth, into their own substances and forms, the things which He had arranged within Himself with Wisdom, Reason, and Discourse, He first brought forth Discourse itself, having within itself its inseparable Reason and Wisdom, so that through it all things might be made—through it by which they had been conceived and arranged, indeed already made, insofar as they existed in God’s consciousness. For this alone they lacked: that they should also be recognised and held forth visibly in their own forms and substances. Then, therefore, Discourse itself also takes its form and adornment—SOUND and VOICE—when God says, “Let there be light.” THIS IS THE PERFECT BIRTH OF DISCOURSE, when it proceeds from God: first formed by God for thought under the name of Wisdom, “The Lord created me as the beginning of His ways”; [Col. 0048A] then begotten for effect, “When He prepared the heavens, I was present with Him together.”

These things, like most other things in this writer, are clouded and still await light: namely, those two births of Discourse, first formed for thought and then begotten for effect. But from what he has set down beforehand and from what follows, we can readily correct and reduce them to clarity.

Before proceeding to other matters in Lactantius, it is worth observing what Hilary wrote (*On the Trinity*, X, p. 334, Verona edition): that certain heretics, wishing the Only-Begotten God—God the Word, who in the beginning was with God—not to be a substantial God but the discourse of an emitted voice, held that the Son was to God the Father what a speaker’s own word is to the speaker. Proceeding from this, they said that it was not God the Word who became man through birth from the Virgin, but that, as the spirit of prophecy was in the prophets, so the Word of God was in Jesus. Did these innovators fashion their “discourse of emitted voice” out of the vocal Discourse of Tertullian and Lactantius? Who can guess?

But to return to Lactantius: I said that he was no more consistent with himself than Tertullian. For, using “Word” and “Discourse” interchangeably, when he wished to cite John’s complete passage, he says: “John too handed it down thus: ‘In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word.’” But immediately—as though water drawn from a stream rather than a spring had less flavour—correcting both himself and his translator, he adds: “But the Greeks say *Logos* better than we say Discourse. [Col. 0048C] For *logos* signifies both DISCOURSE and REASON, because He is the voice and wisdom of God.”

To these ancient scholiasts must be added Jean Le Clerc, who, following both, chose in his additions to Henry Hammond’s New Testament (second Frankfurt edition, 1714, p. 391) to translate not “Word” or “Discourse,” but “Reason”:

> “In the beginning was REASON, and that REASON was with God, and God was that REASON.”

Why this undoubtedly learned but bold man, who very often indulged himself excessively, thought so, he himself explained in his second letter to the reader prefixed to his *Remarks on the First Eighteen Clauses of John’s Gospel*. There he nevertheless admits that there were persons who took it ill that he translated “Reason,” rather than “Discourse” or “Word.” [Col. 0048D]

Who these persons were, and whether they defended in their writings the most ancient version of the Latin Church, I candidly confess that I do not know. Therefore, if I should advance anything on this subject which they had previously published, I shall count it an honour to have agreed with learned men. If otherwise, whatever those arguments may be, they will be my own.

Le Clerc accordingly asserts that the word *Logos* is in itself ambiguous and can be translated “Reason” as well as “Word”; and immediately adds: “If the latter meaning prevailed in the West because of the incompetence of the old Latin translator—or, if you prefer, because of the poverty of the Latin language—the Greek Fathers everywhere show, when they deal with this subject, that they understood Reason no less than WORD.”

[Col. 0049A] If these things are true—as they are certainly most true—that *Logos* signifies Word equally with Reason, and that the Greek Fathers understood the latter no less than the former, what reason was there to tamper with the old translator? Was it his incompetence?—a word which, I do not doubt, slipped from Le Clerc. Certainly not: for he translated most correctly, if by Le Clerc’s own reckoning it could be translated that way. Was it the poverty of the Latin language? As if “Reason” and “Wisdom,” words constantly employed in divine matters by pagan writers, had been mysteries inaccessible to Christians of those times, so that oppressed by poverty of language he could produce nothing but “Word.”

He then continues: “The Latins themselves who considered the Greek term acknowledge that REASON rather than what is called WORD in Latin should be understood, since they said that they understood not the *lógos prophorikós*, ‘uttered word,’ but the *endiathetos*, ‘inherent’ or internal—not external—word. For what is an internal WORD except REASON, or a train of reasoning? Moreover, the whole Christian Church, Greek and Latin, combines *logos* with *sophía*, which is the same as REASON but wholly different from uttered word. Therefore, although I have departed somewhat from Latin usage as to sound, I have by no means departed from the thing itself.”

Who these Latin writers were who considered the Greek word *Logos* may readily be inferred from the authorities cited from Tertullian and Lactantius. Yet it may seem surprising that Le Clerc passed over Tertullian’s explicit passage which we have produced, while adducing other passages by the same writer from *On the Anger of God* and the *Divine Institutes*. Unless perhaps it was because Tertullian described less attentively the uttered Word (*verbum prophorikon*) as proceeding from God’s mouth with voice and sound, though he had previously said that it was conceived by God in His mind and therefore inherent (*endiatheton*).

But surely no one has ever doubted that both the Greek and Latin Church always understood, not an uttered word—or, in the phrase of the heretics mentioned by Hilary, the word which speakers possess—as being to God the Father what His Son is; but rather His only-begotten Word, inherent and unbegotten in God, and the Wisdom of the Father. But Le Clerc asks what an internal Word is. Rightly, since, after saying that it is Reason, he immediately recollects himself and adds, “or a train of reasoning.” For just as the inward reasoning of a human being is the word of the human mind, so too—since we wretched beings cannot measure those divine and incomprehensible realities except by human affections—so, I say, the eternal act of reasoning, coeternal with eternal Reason, is that primordial, first-born Word of Tertullian: the Spirit of God, the Power of God, Wisdom, and the Son of God.

Yet in those matters which Clericus brought forward as the conclusion of that letter—may the memory of a man from whom I admit having learned some things forgive me—you certainly miss a greater degree, not to say of humanity or modesty, but of restraint. For he continues:

> If anyone objects that the word *RATIO* denotes a quality rather than a thing, let him show that the word *VERBUM* is more suitable for signifying a substance, and I promise publicly to retract whatever I have said. Or if he thinks he may use an unsuitable word because of the usage of the LATINS, AND OF UNLEARNED LATINS, [Col. 0050A] let him allow me to employ one no less unsuitable because of the continual usage of the most learned Greek Fathers. Meanwhile let him permit me at once to signify by the word *RATIO* what he himself, when asked what he means by *VERBUM*, is finally compelled to call an internal DISCOURSE, that is, REASONING. Finally, let him hear Tertullian, who speaks thus against Praxeas in chapter 5, immediately adducing the passage which we reported above.

Clericus trifles with us when he forces upon us *Reason* and *Word* as bare words to be weighed, words which can signify many things apart from substance. Here we are dealing with divine things: namely, the divine Reason and the Word from Reason; the latter, being already eternal “in the beginning” (*ἐν ἀρχῇ*), is already substance from substance with Tertullian (*Against Praxeas*, ch. 7), substantive with Hilary, and consubstantial with the Church.

[Col. 0050B] Let learned persons judge whether the translator used an unsuitable term when he rendered *λόγον*, not as “Reason,” but as “Word.” Clericus acknowledged both that it could have been translated as “Reason” no less than as “Word,” and that the Greek Fathers understood the latter no less than the former; and therefore he admitted that he had departed somewhat from Latin usage in sound, though not from the thing itself.

As for his thereafter branding as unlearned all Latins up to the present who, following the translator, have said “the Word of God,” not “Reason,” I think he would not have written thus had the heat subsided and had he looked more attentively upon himself and, along with himself, upon so many of the most learned ancient and modern writers. I shall say only this: what is common to all who live this life happened also to Clericus—that he often suffered something merely human. But the Greek Fathers [Col. 0050C] always used the word *λόγος*. Remarkable indeed: in what language other than Greek, then, could they express “Word”? Yet it was too little for Clericus to expel “Word” from that clause unless he also disturbed the Evangelist’s meaning. Thus, after writing, “In the beginning was Reason,” he said that the words *ἐν ἀρχῇ* are not to be referred to the subject of that book, namely the Gospel. “All grammatical considerations,” he says, “advise that the force and sequence of the words immediately following should rather be considered.” But here *λόγος* follows; and the Evangelist says that all things were made through him, and that the world was made through him—showing that the subject is the BEGINNING of all things, or the creation of the world.

Grotius had supplied him with the foundation of this reasoning (*On John* 1:1), in these words: “*Ἐν ἀρχῇ* is taken from the Greek Genesis.” Then, after many learned observations, [Col. 0050D] he says: “A word drawn from a familiar passage of Scripture must be understood according to the sense of that passage. The sense of the passage of Moses is this: when God first created heaven and earth, the earth was,” etc. “Therefore *ἐν ἀρχῇ* means: when the universe first began to be created.”

Grotius is merely guessing when, with no adequate witness, he declares that the words *ἐν ἀρχῇ* are taken from Genesis—as though the Evangelist, wishing to show the eternal generation of the Word, needed borrowed words for this purpose. For what could be more direct, if he wished to say that it existed in the beginning, than to affirm that “being in the beginning” (*ἐν ἀρχῇ ὄντα*)? But that John is speaking there not of the creation of the world but of the generation of the Word is so evident that it may seem strange that a man learned in other respects should wander so far from the mark [Col. 0051A] in this place. For it was not enough for the divine writer to say that the Word was in the beginning, and was with God, and was God. Rather, he repeats emphatically: “This was in the beginning with God,” which he likewise repeats in 1 John 1:1: “That which was from the beginning” (*Ὃ ἦν ἀπ᾽ ἀρχῆς*). Consequently, what he proceeds to say—that all things were made through him, and that without him nothing of what exists was made—flows, like a stream from its source, from that first truth which he wished to establish.

Yet no one corrected this paradox of Grotius better than Grotius himself. For after noting many things with the refined learning customary to him on those opening words, “In the beginning was the Word” (*Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος*), he finally concludes: “Here John rejects the fiction of the Gnostics, who said that *Mind* (*νοῦς*) was born from the pre-beginning (*ἐκ τῆς προαρχῆς*) after many ages; then that the Only-begotten (*μονογενής*) was born from Mind, and the Word (*λόγος*) from him.” He equally felt the force of that truth [Col. 0051B] in the following clause, “This was in the beginning with God” (*οὗτος ἦν ἐν ἀρχῇ πρὸς τὸν Θεόν*). “He repeats this,” he says, “because he has already called him God; wishing it to be understood that he is God in such a way that this also remains, that he was with God.” That is, so that the Word is not all that God is. Origen and, after him, others called this a distinction of hypostases.

Had Clericus weighed these matters, he would have passed over the laws of grammar which he dragged, even against their will, into this passage. But he had resolved to represent the Evangelist as looking to the words of Philo and other Platonists. Whether under favorable auspices, let readers see. I shall add only this: in that translation of his Clericus rendered the distinction of hypostases entirely obscure and doubtful. Perhaps sensing this, when he wished to explain *VERBUM* by “Reason,” he expressed it by the term REASONING [*ratiocinatio*]. Indeed, in the second of his *Animadversions*, he confirms this very point by adducing a passage from Plato’s *Timaeus*, where that philosopher calls the Word (*Λόγος*) “the calculation/reasoning of God” (*τοῦ Θεοῦ λογισμόν*), which is the same thing, as we have said, as the WORD of the divine mind: in essence indeed REASON, but in hypostasis WORD.

It would therefore have been better for Clericus to follow the ancient translator along with all Latins than to translate the Evangelist’s passage in this fashion when its very sense requires otherwise.

But now, setting aside these commentators, whose work proved neither more exact in rendering the divine author’s words nor more useful, and returning to that numerous succession of translators which Huet thought he had found in ecclesiastical writers, I shall not hesitate to affirm that he would have judged differently [Col. 0051D] had he treated this subject more maturely. Certainly, when I had compared our Silver Codex with Tertullian and Cyprian—because among Latin writers they came closer to those ages of the Church in which purer copies of the ancient translators ought to have existed—and had carefully considered all the Gospel passages which they cited, I thought I had prepared some basis from which I might establish the readings of that codex by their authority. But when at length one day dawned upon another, I finally learned that I had been mistaken and had acquired no certain foundation for myself by that labor. For they express the same pericopes, as has been observed, not in the same words, and now with more, now with fewer words; so that one must say that they had before them not one or two [Col. 0052A] copies, but several, from which they drew an equal number of variants. Yet nothing is more certain than that the Fathers of the Church generally cited passages of the sacred books, especially of the New Testament, from the storehouse of memory, and sometimes even extemporaneously, as the matter itself or the time required—unless the exact authority of the sacred text was necessary to prove some assertion. For then they quoted exactly and section by section, as we observed in certain cited passages of Tertullian.

But even Latin copies, including the more ancient ones, differ in many respects. Granted. Are Greek copies free from such variations? Certainly not. Nor could it be otherwise, if, as Mill observes on the testimony of Clement of Alexandria (*Prolegomena*, no. 287), there were already persons “altering the things of the Gospels” (*τὰ τῶν Εὐαγγελίων μετατιθέντες*). Origen writes that this was done much more freely by many persons, in Homily VIII on Matthew—a passage supplied to us by Erasmus in the preface already cited to the fifth edition of the New Testament. His words are:

> For we find great differences among the copies, whether through the negligence of scribes, through the rashness of certain persons, through those who neglect to correct the Scriptures, or through those who, in the process of correction, either add or remove whatever seems right to them.

Hence it is no wonder that, when copies differed among themselves in a matter of some importance, the Greeks themselves were accustomed to appeal to the *ἀδιόρθωτα*—that is, copies which had not fallen into the hands of ill-qualified correctors. Yet Erasmus himself, deceived by memory, did not attend to this when in the same preface he says that he suspects that, if anything was changed in Greek [Col. 0052C] books, it proceeded from Latin copies after the Roman Church began to absorb Greece. Nothing could be more flimsy than this suspicion. Equally weak is what he there imagined concerning the ancient version, saying: “But the Roman Church accepted this.” Not even that is simply true. Let anyone observe what the Roman Church reads; he will find many discrepancies. “THIS APPEARS TO HAVE BEEN THE VERSION OF THE GAULS, which, when people had become weary of endless variation, came into use.”

It is indeed true that in the many New Testament copies which appeared after the invention of printing, very many things differ from one another. But he who published them repeatedly could himself have known the reason: namely, the diversity of manuscripts to which they were conformed. Their diversity, however, arose not from a variety of translators but from the causes which Origen and, after him, Jerome have recorded.

As for his statement that the version of which we speak appears to have belonged to the Gauls, I do not see what guarantors Erasmus would have produced to establish their possession of it. To the good fortune of Gaul we owe many monuments of antiquity, including copies of the New Testament that predate Jerome’s time; and we should owe more, had not, after that first disaster, a second, more grievous one destroyed so many other things that could have been preserved. Yet those which survive there underwent the same fate as the Italian copies: they are, namely, subject to variants. But all derive from the same source—namely, that primitive version of the Roman Church [Col. 0053A] which spread widely from the seat of empire and religion through the provinces of the West.

Why they differ from one another we have partly stated. We have plausibly inferred that this diversity is insufficient to establish so many separate versions. Greek texts of profound antiquity differ among themselves; no sane person would assert that several translations were therefore made from them in the Eastern Church. If some pure and untouched copy of the first translators were to present itself, we should more easily attain this truth by comparing the surviving witnesses with one another. But after the misfortune of those times which we have mentioned, a new disaster destroyed the purer copies: namely, the correction of the New Testament books undertaken by St Jerome at the urging of Damasus.

For as soon as that work began to circulate, Jerome’s name—already celebrated throughout the Christian world as that of a most eminent man, and thus attended by great expectation—together with the magnitude of the work and the attraction of novelty, always a lure for human minds, first recommended it and then caused it to be prized not merely by private persons but by the churches themselves. What followed is easy to guess. The new work began to be compared with old copies. Some eagerly seized upon it, extolled it with praise, and followed it. Others, clinging to the ancient custom, wondered at a man who first wished to return to the anvil and recast what had until then been read by all. Some even resisted, despised it, and disparaged its author. For Jerome did not lack detractors; nor will outstanding minds ever lack them—minds which burn with their splendor and outweigh the disciplines beneath them. [Col. 0053C] But the greater part, especially of the churches, pursued a middle course between the two parties—which in practical affairs is often useful, yet often dangerous and deceptive. They neither accepted the edition entire nor rejected it completely; rather, whatever it seemed to have supplied more purely, better, or finally more fully, they entered in their codices after displacing the words of the first translators.

Hence, after no long time, it became difficult to distinguish what the new and what the old edition contained; now it is altogether hopeless. Thus, while they thought they were giving novelty to old things, polish to obsolete things, and acceptability to all, that new and fermenting wine ruined the old skins into which they had poured it; for scribal workshops everywhere were busy so that they might have new copies ready for those who sought them. By the seventh century it had become generally established in the West; older copies had been set aside and then neglected, and later ages saw them, like so many other remnants of ancient monuments, serve the most ignorant bookbinders for making boards, strips, and wrappers for bound codices.

This was the end and fate of the Italian version—not through Jerome’s fault, but through that of the times. Let us spare great minds that were insufficiently provident and more accommodating than they ought to have been, which preferred new wares, admittedly of real value, to their inherited possessions, though they were by no means comparable with them. No one, I think, will deny what I have said: Jerome’s otherwise excellent work cannot be compared with the copies used by the translators of the Roman Church. For while translating, those men had before their eyes several autograph monuments of the New Testament and other copies faithfully transcribed directly from the autographs. But Jerome, when seeking the sources, was compelled, after more than three hundred years, to draw from their streams—indeed, streams not certainly pure in every respect—as they flowed from those sources; and he believed that he could thereby correct the Latin version more safely.

Could he have accomplished the same thing with equal security by using Western codices? Indeed, with greater security, as Mill thought (*Prolegomena*, no. 854 and following). For if truth was to be sought from several witnesses, why did he turn to Greek rather than Latin texts, which had emerged no less insufficiently corrected and wrongly revised than the Latin—whether through the liberty and rashness of presumptuous persons or through the carelessness of scribes and copyists? Jerome’s statement about Latin copies, that there were nearly as many texts as codices, was doubtless an exaggeration, as is often the case; and I do not doubt that it should be understood of the copies in common circulation. For one must judge otherwise concerning the more ancient copies that might still have survived in the archives of churches. From these, Mill says, after they had been carefully compared with one another, the Italian version could have been restored and brought back to its original integrity.

But the remainder of his words is so worth reading that we ought neither to reproduce it all here nor be reluctant to have those who have not read that excellent work weigh it. He continues:

> In short, the books current in that age, [Col. 0054C] even the best and those which were interpolated and mixed, not even the Origenian and other more approved copies, to which Jerome occasionally appeals, were free from additions and other faults. Only those which came directly from the autographs of the apostles were pure and unblemished; next to these, though not so pure, were those which happened to have been copied not long after the formation of the New Testament canon. The Italian version had been made from one of these. Therefore, in correcting it from the Greek, one ought to consult codices, if any existed, similar to those according to whose text it had been composed. But since scribes had increasingly interpolated these together with other copies of those times before Jerome’s century, it is vain to undertake a restoration of it to integrity from Greek manuscripts of later times. For since more recent books have often departed from the reading [Col. 0054D] represented by this version, the closer one approaches them in revising it, the more one will make the Italian version unlike its own original text; one will not reform it, but rather transform it into some new version entirely different from the genuine old Italian.

> At the very outset of his work, Jerome certainly perceived the great alteration of the Latin text which would result from a more exact recension according to his codices—an alteration by no means tolerable to Latin ears. Deterred by the magnitude and danger of the matter, he prudently drew back and adopted other, much sounder principles.
