Thus he says that, having corrected the Gospels, he restrained his pen so that, lest they differ too much from the customary Latin reading, only those things which appeared to change the meaning were corrected, while the rest were allowed to remain as they had been.

Although I cannot approve Mill’s judgment in every point—you know what I have thought about that formation of the canon—I nevertheless consider both correct and most lucid what he said about correcting the ancient version by Latin codices. “But to which codices,” you ask, “if, according to Augustine and Jerome, all were so interpolated and mixed?” I shall not repeat here what we have brought forward on this subject. Origen had already made the same complaint, and yet copies from preceding centuries were not lacking, by which he himself corrected his texts. The same must be said of the Latin copies. One ought to seek not those handled everywhere by everyone, but those preserved from private license, which ought to have been purer and closer to the sources. This would not have been difficult for the blessed author, had he wished, during the three years he remained at Rome, to inspect the ancient codices of the chief Church and others brought to light throughout Italy. For it is wholly incredible that none of the older copies had survived in their archives. Greek copies from earlier times had been preserved down to Origen’s age; why not Latin copies among us? Had our people perhaps less concern for sacred volumes than the Greeks? I do not think so. But the very archetypes had perished in the Church’s many calamities, though they ought surely to have been kept with greater care; how much more, then, copies of the first or second century—especially because things already worn and obsolete readily came to be cheapened and despised in comparison with the elegance of newer ones.

[Col. 0055C] That the autograph monuments of the apostles had perished before Jerome, or that their hiding places were unknown, seems proved by the fact that no ecclesiastical writer mentions them as still surviving and that no one appeals to them—except Tertullian, whom, when writing against Marcion at the beginning of the third century, we observed to have referred to Paul’s Epistles as though they still existed in the very churches to which they had been sent. Whether he knew this as fact, merely by report, or because he believed it to be so, is uncertain. Yet it is not implausible on other grounds that some, if not all, of them survived. Persecutors had not yet attacked the divine Scriptures as fiercely as they did later.

There is no record, except uncertain rumor, of where the divine authors left the Gospels—except in John’s case: because it was written at Ephesus, there is no doubt that it was preserved in that church also. But until when? Who can guess?

[Col. 0055D] Although Casaubon, having obtained from the Greek merchant Andreas Termarius a fragment on Easter attributed to Peter of Alexandria (*In Annals of Baronius*, Exercise XVI, §12), embraced it as a notable work of that famous bishop and martyr of the Church, and thus thought the Evangelist’s autograph was still surviving at Ephesus in the fourth century, the most learned man was nevertheless deceived by the author’s name, not having sufficiently considered the remaining facts. It was written by a certain Peter in the sixth or seventh century, as Tillemont observes (*Life of John*, art. 8), unless perhaps the writer himself or bookseller-scribes, employing a pseudepigraph, appropriated the illustrious name of Peter of Alexandria so that splendor and value might accrue to the merchandise.

Yet the author of the Alexandrian Chronicle reported both that it was preserved at Ephesus in the seventh century and held in veneration by the faithful. It is certainly strange that Jerome should not have known this, whether by report or through the customary knowledge of so many illustrious Greeks; for something known in the seventh century could scarcely have been unknown in the fourth. Besides, the story of the adulteress, omitted or marked with obeli in most ancient Greek and Latin codices—how easily could he both have brought this passage and others into conformity with the autograph? Yet among so many writers before and after him, no one did so.

Whatever the case in this matter, even if the archetypes had perished, there would be no reason for wonder. They were few, and in the hands of few. The more precious they were, the more likely, amid the afflictions of so many churches, they were moved from place to place; or, that they might be hidden more securely, concealed in more secret places and, when those who concealed them soon died or moved elsewhere, removed from human memory, and finally consumed by their condition and the passage of time.

The case of their copies was altogether different. They were very numerous and in the hands of many. Wherever there was a congregation of the faithful, there were divine Scriptures: in churches, private houses, cities, and countryside. Moreover, the heat of persecution that might consume them was not the same everywhere; it was not so intense in Italy as in Africa and the East, much less in Gaul, where Christianity was more peaceful under the most mild emperors Constantius and Constantine. From these places the earliest copies were to be sought; [Col. 0056C] they would certainly not have been lacking if diligently sought. A sufficiently clear proof is supplied by the very ancient codices still surviving, among which are our Silver Codex and others whose age amounts to more than nine hundred years. From this we may confidently infer that copies of the first and second centuries, transcribed by scribes with the utmost fidelity—as the Church’s care at that time required—could much more easily have survived to the end of the fourth century. With their help, not only could the original translation of the New Testament have been corrected in those places corrupted by scribal negligence and private license; Greek texts of that age also, no less than Latin, had departed from the sources and could have been corrected.

Add that this would have left no room at all for so many detractors unable to endure the novelty of a correction, once purer copies of the translators—neglected until then through their own indifference—were thrown in their faces, and Jerome had conformed his work to their authority.

[Col. 0056D] But this great man, either not attending to these considerations or setting them aside, was also influenced by the appearance of public codices. Thinking that all things were alike in every respect in all of them, and therefore considering it safer to return to the origin, he preferred to use the Greek copies available to him. The brevity of this course may be understood from the cited letter to Damasus: having corrected what seemed to have changed the meaning, he left the rest untouched. Nor could it have been otherwise with him. It was exceedingly difficult—indeed, impossible—to restore the condition of the ancient version to purity by the methods he adopted. This was not only because the Greek texts he used, separated from the sources by so great an interval of years, had contracted some impurity, as Mill thought; but also because neither the same syntax, nor simplicity, nor the idioms of earlier times, driven out by fastidious and presumptuous correctors, could be restored except by consulting Latin copies closer to the translators’ age.

Yet if we consider Jerome’s manner of life exactly, we shall admit that this task was neither convenient nor manageable for him at that time. He was Damasus’s secretary for ecclesiastical correspondence, entangled in frequent letters concerning a succession of most serious affairs. He had obligations of courtesy to discharge with many persons, now in person, now by letter. He was also occupied with his customary and continual studies, from which he could scarcely be torn away; and Damasus himself and others repeatedly asked him to illuminate obscure or explain difficult passages of the Old Testament. To this was added the instruction of many people attracted by his proven integrity of character, contempt for worldly things, love of poverty, self-denial, humility, chastity, and the knowledge of divine things, which seemed in some sense to shed its radiance upon his other virtues and in turn to borrow glory from them. Among these were noble virgins, married women, and widows from the leading families; all of them, by a most beautiful example of charity, were formed toward a more perfect state of Christian life through his counsel, exhortations, and instructions, both in person and in writing.

[Col. 0057C] Finally, the train of his cares was closed by the wit and license of the ever-free city—in which Augustus said that tongues ought to be free—since its corrupted morals could not endure a man rebuking its entrenched vices in return. Envy had long preceded this, which, as huge shadows follow tall trees, usually follows men distinguished either by fortune’s favor or by the splendor of their virtues; afterward it broke out into malice and hatred. Hence combinations against him, jests and insults directed at him secretly and openly, not only among the crowd but with vigorous activity from fellow initiates in the mysteries, who would have been better served by shame and silence, had they been capable of wisdom. Therefore the blessed author wished to commend them, as they surely deserved, to posterity through the immortal monuments of his genius.

[Col. 0057D] In that tumult of affairs and cares, with his mind tossed about and distracted, how could he undertake and complete a long, detailed, and even thankless work? Nor was he any longer free to delay amid the great expectation both of Damasus, who had imposed the work on him, and of many others accustomed to pluck the fruits of his most fertile mind almost as soon as they were sought. Thinking that the principal concern of both corrector and correction—that the truth should correspond to the words and the words in turn to the sense—could readily be achieved by the means he employed, just as by others, he therefore completed more quickly, through the shortcut of Greek codices, the path drawn out through so many windings of manuscripts, a path upon which one had repeatedly to halt and make rough ways passable. This was equally useful to readers, though not equally praised by all.

Would that it had not been completed too hastily—indeed, as we said, would that he had undertaken it using Latin copies descending from deeper antiquity. How much light, fidelity, and learning might have been expected for the Italian version had he wished to elucidate the obsolete modes and character of the translators?

Is restoration of the original version to integrity now wholly hopeless? The matter itself cries out that it is, once those aids have been removed by the long lapse of time, namely the copies by whose help we did not doubt this could once have been achieved, copies closer to the archetypes. Yet not a few older witnesses remain, whose age amounts to a thousand years and more. Granted; although I think one must observe above all not in what century they were written, but from copies of what period they were transcribed. But the farther these very witnesses are removed from the sources, the more they have suffered, more or less, either from scribes’ mistreatment or commentators’ license.

What then? Is there no benefit from them except perhaps that value which antiquity customarily lends to monuments of this kind? Indeed, there is something far more valuable. If we deem well bestowed the labor by which scholars endeavor, with the help of manuscript codices, to restore secular authors—mutilated and dislocated in many places through the injury of time or the negligence of antiquaries—to their former condition, how much more praiseworthy shall we think the labor by which the chief Italian version of the sacred books of the New Testament, using copies still extant, can conveniently be restored, if not completely, at least in large part to its native [Col. 0058C] simplicity and purity?

Did not those most learned men accomplish precisely this, who devoted all their care and industry to publishing our Vulgate as pure as could be done? Nothing else, certainly. Having diligently examined the oldest copies they could find and the passages of the holy Fathers, and then compared them with Greek copies of better quality, they attempted with utmost fidelity to present what seemed formerly to have been read in the churches of the earliest centuries. Mill therefore acknowledged (*Prolegomena*, no. 379) that no small portion of the genuine Italian version survives in this very Vulgate. Nor did he doubt that something more might someday be hoped for by employing the same means. After naming several codices preserved in Britain and Gaul, he says:

> The Vulgate itself, with the assistance of monuments of this kind, carefully compared with one another and with the Greek text, seems even now capable of restoring in great part this Italian version as the first translators gave it.

He then asserted that by this labor he had attained the genuine readings of the Italian version in most New Testament passages, and determined which Greek texts corresponded to this Latin version. What would he have said afterward had he been able to inspect the monuments which you will bring to public light, as well as those which perhaps still lie hidden unexplored or lie most miserably among piles of books in the possession of negligent owners of these antiquities? I indeed embrace this judgment of that illustrious writer, whose reading in these matters was infinite, so fully that I do not doubt in the least that learned men, if they should one day direct their studies to this task, will acknowledge from experience that he judged rightly.

Perhaps, however, there will not be lacking those who think such labors now useless in our times, since every church and private person has the New Testament version before their eyes in the Vulgate. They do not understand that this very Vulgate was prepared with similar care; and that, consequently, within so broad a harvest some room remains for gleaning. Nor are minds of later ages excluded from discovering in ancient codices something by which they may in some place illuminate that most beautiful work, and making their discoveries public.

In short: if, after all monuments now known and those now first brought from obscurity have been rigorously examined and carefully compared with one another, and after an appropriate selection has been made from each, an edition of the New Testament were prepared, I do not doubt that our Italian version, distinguished by its native colors, could be recognized very easily. It would not indeed possess exactly the same purity and chastity in which it once walked—for who could hope for that? Yet, if critical judgment wiped away the blemishes and stains which it has contracted in the long course of centuries, we should have it not ugly or sallow, but venerable in its very age and not unworthy of those primitive sources from which it flowed.

Meanwhile, my dear Blanchine, although later age has brought us to this banquet after our wishes, let us rejoice even in this: that we have come neither without a contribution nor shall return empty. For we have brought very rare dishes, made all the more precious because we have ensured that what would once have perished is now everlasting and can survive, together with letters themselves, even to the remotest descendants. We have also, I think, set before the gifted minds beyond the Alps a laudable example, that they too may strive toward the same end, drawing other dishes from their abundant and most ample storehouse, from which a far more splendid and richly adorned feast may be prepared for posterity.

What advantage awaits us as we leave the banquet, I shall say plainly: the most beautiful reward for honorable minds—good will joined with the consciousness of having acted rightly. That is ours. As for favor and esteem among fair judges of these matters, let each have them as he thinks fit. Farewell most heartily.

Pontivy, the fifth day before the Nones of September, in the year of the Lord 1739.

[Col. 0059D]

# DISSERTATION OF JEAN MARTIANAY ON THE ITALIAN VERSION OF THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW, TRANSCRIBED FROM THE CORBIE AND SAINT-GERMAIN CODICES AND PRINTED IN THIS EDITION AT THE FOOT OF EACH PAGE

## PREFACE

Among learned persons who devote some attention to the study of the divine Scriptures, there is frequent discussion of the ancient Vulgate and Italian translation; critics too, investigators of sacred literature, often mention this Italian version. Yet there is everywhere profound silence concerning its origin, its style, and additions or omissions in it through the carelessness of translator or scribes. Nor is it surprising that only the names of the ancient Vulgate and Italian version are heard among all who discuss Latin translations of Scripture, since no copy of this edition has yet appeared in print and no ancient writer has transmitted to posterity an adequately exact account of it.

To dispel such darkness, two most ancient copies are now at hand, preserved to the present day in our monasteries. With the help of these codices, scarcely anything concerning the ancient Italian translation of Matthew can remain unknown to us. For what may we not know when we become eyewitnesses of the very things and words? Yet so that the path toward comprehending whatever had previously been unknown concerning the ancient Italian [Col. 0060B] translation might be easier and more direct, we have willingly undertaken to furnish the reader with the *Prolegomena* as it were keys to the matter.

# CHAPTER ONE. ON THE ANCIENT VULGATE AND ITALIAN VERSION OF THE DIVINE SCRIPTURES

I. It bore many names among the ancient Fathers.  
II. The ancient Vulgate had not one author or translator, but as many as there were anonymous translators.  
III. Its copies were intermingled with many additions.

I. No one is unaware that the ancient Latin translation of the Holy Scriptures bore many and various names. Yet I long sought in vain, in Jerome’s *Commentary on Isaiah*, [Col. 0060C] chap. XLIX, the frequently cited testimony in which it is called the Vulgate edition; I had to supply it instead from the second book of his commentaries on Matthew, chap. XIII. For Jerome says there:

> I have read this in certain manuscripts, and the diligent reader may perhaps find the same thing: in the place where we have written, and where the Vulgate edition has, “that it might be fulfilled which was spoken through the prophet, saying,” there it is written, etc.

Jerome therefore calls the Vulgate edition of Matthew that Latin translation which, before his own age, possessed authority in the churches of Western Christians; and which, in the time of Gregory the Great, bore the name of the Old Translation, by comparison with the new edition which Jerome himself undertook to provide for the Church. Consult Gregory the Great’s letter to Leander, [Col. 0060D] chap. 5, prefixed to the *Moral Exposition on Job*.

Besides these names, Vulgate edition and Old Translation, blessed Augustine assigns it another—and indeed distinctive and special—name, in Book II of *On Christian Doctrine*, chap. 15:

> But among the translations themselves, let the Italian be preferred to the others; for it adheres more closely to the words while retaining clarity of meaning.

There was, then, among Latin speakers a translation called the Italian, close to the words and clear in meaning; and Augustine therefore judges it preferable to the rest. But we do not know with sufficient certainty why it was called Italian, although learned men wish it to have been distinguished by this name because Italian Fathers used it—I mean Ambrose, Gaudentius of Brescia, [Col. 0061A] Chromatius of Aquileia, Leo the Great, and many others who flourished in the churches of the Romans through learning and integrity of life. If this is so—as scarcely any learned person will deny to be highly probable—there remains no room for suspicion or doubt that our manuscript exemplars contain the genuine Italian version; for the Gospel text of our codices corresponds exactly to the passages of Scripture quoted by the aforesaid Italian Fathers. But of this below.

Moreover, lest ambiguity arise from the name “Vulgate,” the diligent reader should observe that there are two Vulgate Versions: namely, the ancient one, used before Jerome’s age; and our present one, received by use in the Catholic Church. The former had an anonymous author; the latter [Col. 0061B] and present version is the offspring of Jerome himself, according to the description of it which we have given in the prolegomena to the recently published Divine Library.

II. Yet no one should infer from this that the ancient Vulgate had a single author, just as the sole author of our present Vulgate is Jerome, apart from certain books. For the words written by St Augustine on the diverse kinds of translations oppose this opinion, Book II of *On Christian Doctrine*, chap. 11:

> Those who translated the Scriptures from Hebrew into Greek can be counted; Latin translators, however, cannot be counted at all. For in the earliest times of the faith, whenever a Greek codex came into anyone’s hands, and he thought himself to possess some ability in both languages, he dared to translate.

St Jerome acknowledges the same multitude of Latin translators in his preface to the Four Gospels:

> If faith is to be placed in Latin copies, let them answer which copies; for there are almost as many exemplars as codices. But if truth is to be sought from among many, why do we not return to the Greek original and correct those things which were badly produced by faulty translators, more perversely amended by unskilled presumptuous persons, or either added or altered by sleepy scribes?

So great a diversity of codices could by no means have arisen from one and the same translator. Therefore there must have been several authors of such translations as circulated among Latin speakers in the earliest ages of the Church. Jerome also expressly declared that there were many, when he said: “those things which were badly produced by faulty translators.” If [Col. 0061D] you sometimes read Jerome speaking as though of one Latin translator, do not immediately suppose that he is inconsistent with himself. For then he is not speaking generally of all Latin codices, but of a particular Latin edition approved by many—or by a few—Christian churches. Thus we may say of the Italian version that it alone enjoyed some esteem at Rome and in the other churches of Italy. This Italian edition, moreover, had one author, although very many variant readings were found in its exemplars, derived from sleepy scribes or unskilled presumptuous persons.

To confirm the same conclusion—that there were many Latin translators of the Scriptures of the Old and New Testament—the multiple systems of chapter-divisions and sections of the sacred text, which survive even today in different manuscript codices of the Bible, contribute no little. Nor is it credible that the same translator of Matthew, for example, should have left the sacred text divided in four or five different ways, and should at one time have wished it divided into twenty-eight sections, at another into eighty-eight, or into 117 parts. Therefore, just as the systems of ancient sections of the same sacred text differ, and the ancient chapters or summaries prefixed to manuscript exemplars of the Holy Scriptures are plainly different, so we must altogether concede that the earlier Latin translators were various and different.

Further, the style is not the same; indeed, wholly dissimilar turns of phrase are read in the text itself of the ancient Vulgate. [Col. 0062B] And sometimes its exemplars differ so greatly among themselves that entire chapters—that is, sections—are found in some which are absent from others. Two of our manuscript codices of the Italian version furnish examples of this diversity. The Corbie codex reads, for example, “Are you in any way the least?”; the Saint-Germain codex, however, “You are not the least.” Hardly a single page can be read in them without encountering dissimilar phrases and a different order of words. Moreover, the additions are neither the same in them nor found in the same places. In Matthew, chap. 20, the Corbie codex retains an interpolation from Luke’s Gospel which is absent from the Saint-Germain manuscript; and conversely, the Saint-Germain manuscript reports certain things concerning Christ’s baptism which are not read in the Corbie codex. These things surely indicate not one author, but plainly different Latin authors or translators of the Gospel according to Matthew. And what we say concerning the Gospel volume must also be understood concerning the other books, according to the rule transmitted above by Augustine, who held that Greek translators can be counted but Latin ones cannot.

III. We now say that this was common to the codices of the Old Translation: all circulated intermingled with additions from elsewhere. Jerome clearly stated the causes and origin of this disturbance and intermixture in the sacred text in his preface to Pope Damasus. By Damasus’s command, Jerome restored the Latin Gospel books to conformity with the Greek, and removed from them whatever had been wrongly added by translators or ancient scribes:

> A great error has indeed grown up in our codices: while one Evangelist said more about the same matter, they added it to another because they thought he had said less. Or, while one expressed the same sense differently, the person who had read one of the four judged that the others too should be corrected according to its exemplar. Hence it happened that among us everything is mixed together: in Mark, much from Luke and Matthew; again, in Matthew, much from John and Mark; and in the others there are found things belonging properly to the rest.

The holy Doctor removed the error of this confusion and restored to each Evangelist what belonged to him, when he inserted the Eusebian Canons into his Latin translation of the Gospels. Those who wish to know about this are directed to consult our edition of St Jerome’s Divine Library.

[Col. 0063A] Jerome thus testifies that everything among Latin copies had been intermixed; our two manuscript codices likewise testify to it, for in Matthew there are found several passages from Mark and Luke. To establish the matter by examples, we shall set forth certain mixed passages in our exemplars of the Italian version. In chap. IV, col. 162 of our edition, marginal note (e) indicates that a certain interpolation has been transferred from Luke, chap. 6, v. 26, into the Saint-Germain codex. For what Matthew had said less fully concerning the blessings of men, which were also bestowed upon false prophets, ancient scribes judged should be added from Luke. Thus they wished Matthew to read:

> For so they persecuted the prophets who were before you. Do not rejoice when all men bless you; for so their fathers did to the false prophets. You are the salt of the earth, etc.

Similar additions occur more often, especially taken from Mark, such as that in chap. XIV, p. CXVI of this Roman edition:

> For they had not understood, neither concerning the loaves; for their heart was dull.

This was transferred into Matthew’s text from Mark, chap. 6, v. 52, whether by ancient scribes or by other writers. Besides these things, the Corbie codex retained still more additions. But lest we linger too long in listing them, consult the following edition of St Matthew, col. 241, note (a), and col. 243, note (a), of our edition; and especially col. 277, note (a), where is read that famous interpolation borrowed from Luke which has wonderfully troubled the minds of learned men.

## CHAPTER II. ON THE CHAPTERS PREFIXED TO THE SACRED TEXT OF THE GOSPEL

[Col. 0063C]

I. These chapters are older than Jerome. II. Those prefixed in codices of Jerome’s version have been preserved from the ancient Vulgate and Italian translation. III. The usefulness of such chapter-divisions, or chapters.

I. We have rightly called these chapters older than Jerome. From Juvencus alone, a presbyter who flourished in the time of Constantine the Great, we may know that as many were placed in his exemplars of Matthew as are now read in the Corbie manuscript and in many other codices which, retaining the ancient [Col. 0063D] division of the sacred text, set out twenty-eight chapters at the head of the Gospel according to Matthew. The volumes of St Hilary’s commentaries on Matthew prove the same point: they are divided by canons or chapters, according as the Gospel text was then regarded as divided into several parts. Nor were those mistaken who thought that the titles prefixed to Matthew’s Gospel had already been marked in Gospel exemplars in Hilary’s time, and that he selected from them those whose explanation he deemed more useful.

Hilary wrote his commentaries on Matthew arranged by titles or chapters in the same way that Jerome testifies that Fortunatianus, bishop of Aquileia, wrote on the Gospels in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. “Fortunatianus,” he says, “an African by nation, bishop of Aquileia, under the emperor Constantine, wrote commentaries on the Gospels, arranged by titles, in a brief and rustic style.” Thus writers of commentaries carefully followed, in their expositions, the sequence of titles or ordered chapters prefixed to the sacred text, so that from the marked titles the reader might easily understand and find the passages elucidated by them. From this it is wholly clear that those diverse systems of chapter-divisions read at the head of manuscript copies of the Holy Scriptures are most ancient, and that already in Constantine the Great’s time many used them in copying the books of the Gospels. Hence is confirmed the truth of what Cassiodorus wrote in Book I of *Institutions of Divine Literature*, chap. 1: namely, that the titles in sacred books had been written in continuous order by our elders—by “our elders” meaning ecclesiastical authors celebrated in Christ’s Church some centuries before his own age.

II. Such was the force of use and established antiquity that, even after the old Latin translation had been set aside, the indexes of ancient titles and chapters were nonetheless retained in Jerome’s new edition of the Scriptures. We have discussed at sufficient length in the prolegomena placed at the beginning of St Jerome’s Divine Library the chapters or titles attached to the books of the Old Testament. Here it is incumbent upon me only briefly to discuss the titles marked at the beginning of the Gospel according to Matthew. To do this as readily as the matter requires, the diligent reader must remember that Jerome acknowledges in the Gospel text [Col. 0064C] issued by himself no division except that observed in the Eusebian Canons. Therefore all distinctions into chapters and all summaries in Jerome’s version which do not agree with the divisions of the Eusebian Canons must be judged foreign and spurious.

We have observed that none of the systems of ancient titles published by us agrees with those Eusebian divisions: not the first, which divides the whole text of Matthew into twenty-eight sections; not the second, which has only eighty-seven or eighty-eight chapters; nor finally the third, even though it counts 117 sections. For Jerome, following Eusebius of Caesarea, has different numbers and divisions of the sacred text different from those of the ancient translators. For whereas they divided it into 28, 88, or 117 chapters, Jerome, together with Eusebius, wished it divided into 355 canons, all confusion of error having been removed by this system of canonical divisions.

But to make it certain and settled among all learned persons that the chapters now published by us at the head of the Gospel according to Matthew were borrowed and preserved in Jerome’s version from another and older translation, which we call the Italian, it will suffice to point out one fact only: sometimes nothing is read in the text of Jerome’s translation corresponding to the prefixed chapters. For example, chapter XX in the first index, and chapter 75 in the third, is written “On the chief places at table, or the reclining places at supper.” Yet you will seek in vain in Jerome’s Gospel text of Matthew for what is said concerning those chief places at supper, since this parable was written and related by Luke alone. Hence arises an evident argument that the aforementioned chapters belonged properly to the ancient Vulgate and Italian version, which in Matthew retained certain passages from other Gospels, especially the parable of the guest invited to supper, from which we have taken this example. Let anyone who wishes compare Jerome’s text of Matthew with the chapters published by us: he will immediately discover many passages which do not agree with one another, though they do agree with the text of the Italian version. Nor is it surprising that they correspond perfectly with it, since the indexes of these chapters, of which we are speaking, were prepared from and for that translation.

[Col. 0065B] III. Now, although these chapters are foreign to Jerome’s Version and have been determined not to be genuine in relation to it, I nevertheless judge that they should by no means be despised or discarded. For they can assist in more than one way toward a complete knowledge of the ancient Latin Vulgate. Because these chapters were unknown to learned men, it happened that they followed every error when discussing additions in the old Latin translation. What usefulness those indexes of chapters possess for deciding such disputes among learned men will readily become clear from the example of a single chapter.

Among some writers of this age it is doubtful and contested whether, in the old Vulgate of St Matthew, chap. 20, there was read a certain interpolation borrowed from the Gospel of St Luke. Some affirm it; others deny it. But lest the controversy remain any longer undecided, let them consult the threefold index of chapters published by us. The first and third indexes will immediately declare that the aforesaid interpolation stood in many exemplars of the ancient Vulgate; whereas the second series of titles clearly demonstrates that not every sacred codex of St Matthew everywhere had a passage intermingled in its text, namely, a certain parable of St Luke concerning the avoidance of higher places at supper.

Thus, in the first index, Summary XX reads:

> On the first becoming last. The parable of labourers hired into the vineyard. On the request of the sons of Zebedee; and on the chief reclining places at supper.

In the third index, under no. 75, these words are read:

> And on the chief places at supper.

These would surely not be present unless, in some exemplars [Col. 0065D] of the ancient Vulgate, Luke’s parable concerning those invited to a wedding feast were read at this point in Matthew as a genuine part of the sacred text. I say that only some exemplars had this interpolation, because the second series of chapter-divisions certainly shows it to have been absent in other codices of the Italian version. For chapter-division LVIII makes no mention of this inserted parable:

> On the sons of Zebedee; and on the least becoming greater.

But why linger longer over listing these matters, when I have discussed the same subject more than sufficiently in my fuller notes written in French?

The learned presbyter Carus likewise discussed the usefulness of chapters prefixed to sacred books in the preface to his collection of ancient titles. [Col. 0066A] He says:

> Moreover, how much benefit will come to the reader himself if he runs through these titles of the divine books, by which—as I may speak with Cassiodorus—the sacred text is opened to us by a kind of abridgment; and if, having these summaries of the whole sequence of reading printed at the beginnings of the books, he is usefully instructed, made beneficially attentive, and readily finds every matter he seeks which he recognizes as briefly indicated for him.

Other benefits of no slight importance are added. For by these our titles or chapters—partly composed from that older Latin edition translated from the Seventy Interpreters—at least fragments of that edition are restored, of which no complete Latin exemplar survives today. And we are guided, as it were, by brief commentaries, especially in the prophets, toward the deeper sense of Scripture, while by almost a mere gesture of the finger we are beautifully instructed where to seek Christ, the Church, and the Sacraments of the New Law beneath some typical veil.

## CHAPTER III. ON THE USEFULNESS OF THE ANCIENT VULGATE EDITION, AND ON THE ANTIQUITY AND EXCELLENCE OF OUR MANUSCRIPT CODICES

I. It assists in understanding Scripture, confirming passages quoted by the Fathers, and making known the faith of the ancient Church. II. Our codices were written eight or nine hundred years ago and preserved in eminent monasteries.

I. St Augustine taught repeatedly that diverse translations of the same Scripture are useful, in *On Christian Doctrine*, Book II, chap. 12. After warning the reader concerning the multitude [Col. 0066C] of Latin translators, he immediately adds:

> This circumstance has assisted understanding more than it has hindered it, provided that readers are not negligent. For inspection of many codices has often clarified certain rather obscure statements, as when one translator says of the prophet Isaiah: “And do not despise the household members of your seed” [Isa. 58:7]; while another says: “And do not despise your flesh.” Each bears witness to the other. For one is explained by the other: “flesh” might be understood properly, so that each person should take himself to be admonished not to despise his own body; while “members of your seed” might be understood figuratively as Christians, spiritually born with us from the seed of the same word. But now, by comparing the translators’ meanings, the more probable interpretation emerges: the command concerns not despising one’s kindred in the proper sense, since, when “members of your seed” is referred to flesh, blood-relations occur most readily, etc.

What Augustine demonstrates by one sentence from Isaiah, we can establish by six hundred examples from the Italian version of Matthew. For nearly as many explanations of the sacred text are found as there are variant readings in the manuscript codices. Thus the saying of John the Baptist to the Jews, “And do not say within yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as father,’” stated more obscurely in the present Vulgate and in the Corbie codex of the Old Translation, is clearly explained by the variant reading in the Saint-Germain exemplar:

> And do not prefer yourselves, saying, “We have Abraham as father.”

The sense of the rebuke is therefore plain in the words “do not prefer yourselves”: John restrains only the arrogance of the Jews, not at all censuring descent from Abraham. The Saint-Germain codex also sheds light upon Matthew’s sentence, “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy,” where we read:

> Blessed are the merciful, for God will have mercy upon them.

For one may give the Vulgate reading the sense that other human beings will likewise pity someone established amid labours and miseries if he pities the sufferings of his fellow human beings. But another translator teaches that every merciful person may expect from his own mercy what he may without doubt expect: that God will finally have mercy upon him. Countless examples of similar variant readings are readily available to everyone in our ancient Vulgate of Matthew; therefore we shall add no others at present.

Our edition also greatly assists in confirming Scripture testimonies quoted by the Holy Fathers, which some critics perversely contend were often corrupt. I have heard people say that the early ecclesiastical doctors were careless: when quoting the words of Scripture from memory, they sometimes added, sometimes omitted, and sometimes followed a disordered sequence. They imply that it mattered nothing to them in what words the oracles of Christ and the prophets were uttered, provided their recital did no harm to the sense and understanding. But exemplars of the Italian version protest against suspicions of this kind, and clearly demonstrate that the Fathers were scrupulous in quoting the divine Scriptures.

Therefore, when you read in them many sentences not at all agreeing with the text of the present [Col. 0067C] Vulgate, do not at once cry out that their fidelity wavers, declaring that what your codices contain their exemplars often did not contain; or rather, that your codices do not contain what they commonly read. Thus Leo the Great, and before him Hilary and Ambrose, read:

> And you, Bethlehem of Judaea, are not the least among the rulers of Judah; for from you shall come forth a Ruler who will rule my people Israel.

Lucifer of Cagliari read:

> And do not prefer yourselves, saying, “We have Abraham as father.”

Chromatius of Aquileia:

> Blessed are you when they persecute and reproach you, and falsely say every evil thing against you for the sake of righteousness.

Finally Cyprian and others:

> I say to you that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not overcome it, etc.

But why do we idly recall these things, when they may be found adequately treated by us elsewhere? Let the curious reader, then, consult our fuller annotations, written in the vernacular, on the Italian version. He will immediately be compelled to confess the very great usefulness of the Italian edition, or ancient Vulgate, for defending the fidelity of the Holy Fathers in quoting Scripture passages from every unjust suspicion.

Another benefit, by no means slight, will come to us from the ancient Latin edition: from the chapters prefixed to it and from its very text, the faith of the ancient Church concerning the sacrament of the Eucharist becomes known. Nor may one doubt that the ancient Fathers and congregations of believers held firmly and certainly both the true substance of Christ’s body and its perfect offering in this [Col. 0068A] mystery. Chapter 106 of the third index indicates this not obscurely, being contained in these two words: “His offering.” Then, in the Corbie manuscript codex, after Christ’s words, “This is my body,” the following has been added: “which shall be delivered for you.” Hence it appears that the more ancient churches professed both a true Offering and Christ’s proper substance in the sacrament of the altar.

II. I shall now touch briefly upon the antiquity and excellence of our manuscript codices; for this matter is perceived and demonstrated more by eyewitnesses than by arguments. Would that as many learned and experienced men as there are in the Christian world were inspectors of our exemplars. I am mistaken if witnesses would not everywhere come forward to attest the antiquity displayed by the aforesaid codices. Let no one wonder at my confidence, for it arose in me from the judgments of learned men.

I shall produce one or two witnesses: the distinguished François Desmares, and above all Étienne Baluze, whose counsel and friendship I enjoy all the more happily because I have always found in him a most sincere heart, and at every time a person most ready to serve his friends. Having been trained by the use and continual handling of innumerable manuscript codices in the exceedingly rich Colbert Library, he granted me that our Corbie codex of Matthew was written eight hundred years ago. Nor without reason, since it is written upon ancient parchment in Saxon or Merovingian letters; for it has a mixed form of characters.

[Col. 0068C] Concerning the Saint-Germain exemplar, elegantly copied and written in an ancient hand, the judgment was the same among many diligent men curious about sacred matters and ancient monuments. Honoured by their conversations and friendship, I often showed them the manuscript codices of the Italian version for inspection and examination. I say nothing of my brethren and fellow-presbyter monks, although some among them are, without objection from anyone, regarded as exceptionally well informed in this kind of learning. But no one is accustomed to receive testimony from himself or from his own associates. In short, to finish in a word: our manuscripts are available for examination by every interested person who wishes to doubt their established antiquity.

I said that our most ancient manuscript codices of the Italian version were preserved in eminent monasteries. No one moderately versed in ecclesiastical and monastic history will deny that this is so. The celebrated monastery of ancient Corbie in France kept the first manuscript codex whole and unblemished. The most ancient library of the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés gave us the other surviving manuscript. Both are now preserved in the same library: the Corbie manuscript under shelfmark 21, the Saint-Germain manuscript under no. 15. But enough concerning the manuscript codices.

Moreover, I warn the reader that I have supplied in the margins of the pages certain things which were wrongly placed or [Col. 0069A] omitted, whether through the negligence of scribes or the incompetence of translators. I corrected many things in the second index of chapters because it displayed its ugliness to public readers through very many solecisms. In the third index I supplied ordinary numerals to distinguish each chapter. Use these things, then, kindly, and judge favourably this first edition of the Italian version, in which I fear that much has escaped me because nearly the whole work was written in haste. Yet since most of the learned persons who urgently pressed for the completion of the edition are responsible for the need to work quickly, let them themselves pardon its defects and its unpolished style, which I was not permitted to refine.

[Col. 0069A]

## LETTER OF RUGGERIUS OF NOVARA, CANON OF THE EUSEBIAN CATHEDRAL, TO BLANCHINI OF VERONA

[Col. 0069B] Description of the Vercelli Gospel Codex.

At last, the most ancient Eusebian Gospel codex, sought for many years by very many most wise men and learned writers, has enabled your wishes, most distinguished sir, to be fulfilled—not only that you might behold its antiquity, but even more that, for the confirmation of the Catholic faith, which is strengthened by the most holy Gospels as by the surest bulwarks, you might draw out the truth.

For it now comes to light. You possess it, not erased by oblivion through the long succession of ages, but preserved carefully, studiously, and with assiduous diligence; and now, with the help of God, the Best and Greatest, and by the arrangement of the most eminent and most reverend Lord Carlo Vincenzo Ferreri, of the Order of Preachers, [Col. 0069C] most vigilant bishop of this holy Church of Vercelli, with the assent of the dignitaries and canons of the Eusebian chapter, it has, through my assistance and labour, been faithfully and exactly transcribed from its exemplar.

Concerning the true owner of this sacred volume, besides the ancient and most constant veneration which the chapter and Church have always professed for it—preserving it in the very sacred repository of relics, where the bones of holy prophets, apostles, and very many martyrs are kept—there survive numerous documents of certain authority, recorded in public monuments. From these we learn that the book of the Four Gospels was rendered from Greek letters before St Jerome by our great holy father, bishop and martyr Eusebius.

Indeed, he possessed in Rome such perfection in reading and writing Greek that Pope Julius, successor of Mark, who invested Eusebius with the sacred rank of presbyter, judged that he ought not to devote himself to his own pursuits alone, but also to benefit the Christian commonwealth. This is contained in the most ancient records of this Church of Vercelli, in which it is handed down that the same Eusebius was appointed by the supreme pontiff as translator of the sacred volumes. For he had learned Greek letters for no other end than that he might more perfectly know the mysteries of the Sacred Scriptures.

At what time, in what place, and for what purpose he began, composed, and completed this work, I shall endeavour to disclose, not on my own authority, but by the testimony of the formerly most eminent bishop of this Church of Vercelli, Giovanni Stefano Ferreri, drawn from the *Life of Our Father, the Martyr and Bishop Eusebius* written by him. Thus on folio 16 of that *Life* one reads:

> Nor, while he was engaged in these and other matters, did he forget himself. Rather, constant tradition holds that, not only to remove the occasion by which the people, led astray through Arian hostility, might sin against him, but also from an ardent desire to devote himself to himself and to God, he withdrew at different times into the mountains of Oupa in the district of Biella, and beyond the Po to the castle of Credenzo—then in the diocese of Vercelli—so that he, who was occupied with so many cares for the sake of aiding others, might have a place where he could from time to time recollect himself, draw breath from heaven, and have greater strength available for advancing the glory of God.

It is also read in the same manuscript *Life* that, while Eusebius was staying in these religious and holy places, he wrote the four Gospels with his own hand, and that they have been preserved down to the present time. We have, indeed, in his *Life* the account that these holy Gospels were his cherished companions throughout the rest of his life. For Christians of those times customarily kept them continually with them and carried them about, as we know even women did. This is especially well established concerning St Cecilia, who, as her history relates, always carried Christ’s Gospels upon her breast.

Indeed, this was familiar to some even unto death, as to St Barnabas: on the breast of his dead body there was found the Gospel of St Matthew, copied in Barnabas’s own hand, when his body was discovered in the island of Cyprus under the emperor Zeno. For this reason I think it piously credible that Eusebius always kept this book at hand, no differently from Barnabas and Cecilia; that he regarded it as a treasure of his own; and that from it, as from an ocean of every kind of learning, virtue, and wonderful deed, there flowed both the streams and fountains of which Eusebius drank the holy waters. By them he cast out demons and the ministers of demons; he expelled and exterminated from the Church the foul monsters of vices, schisms, and heresies. Nor could any other fruits be expected either from the perfection and excellence of the instrument or from the consummate skill and expertise of the craftsman who used such an instrument.

It is indeed lamentable that this our treasure has in some part been consumed by the injury of time, although diligence to preserve it unspoiled and whole has more than once been exercised even by great kings, as by Berengar, who had the book covered with silver plates. The verses still proclaim this sufficiently; they are read beneath the image of most holy Eusebius, and are as follows:

> This bishop Eusebius wrote it, and antiquity dissolved it;  
> But King Berengar restored that same work.  
> After he brought forth silver together with gleaming gold,
of the Church, O bishop, he himself offered [it] to yours.

No less do I regret that I see one leaf of that sacred codex given to certain religious persons as a relic; as may be read in the below-written instrument [Col. 0071A] of Augustinus Ferrerius, then bishop of Vercelli and cousin of my grandfather. We shall therefore have that codex copied, before either the passage of time further damages it or any other part of it is lost, so that it may at least stand as the most reliable witness to a version older than the version of St Jerome which we use today. The instrument is as follows:

> “Augustinus Ferrerius, by the grace of God and of the Apostolic See bishop and count of Vercelli, to all Christ’s faithful who shall inspect these our present letters, everlasting greeting in the Lord. Be it known that lately, when Master Lord Jacobus of Circest and Petrus Ebult of Salus, of the diocese of Lausanne, ambassadors to our most excellent prince Charles, Duke of Savoy, for the general assembly of the Swiss, [Col. 0071B] had turned aside out of devotion to the Church of St Eusebius of Vercelli, they represented to us and to our venerable Chapter that there stands, within the bounds of Salus, at a place called Nieuchen, in the diocese of Lausanne, a church under the invocation of this holy Eusebius; and that the people and inhabitants of the said place venerate it with the greatest devotion and reverence, because of the exalted merit of the most holy bishop and martyr Eusebius. Therefore, if anything among the relics from his garment or personal effects were possessed by the aforesaid people, that same church would rejoice greatly in the Lord.
>
> “We therefore, desiring—as is fitting—that the aforesaid holy Eusebius, our patron, should everywhere and in all lands be exalted with devout praises and the highest veneration; considering the just devotion of those ambassadors, and likewise the singular goodwill towards the aforesaid ambassadors of our aforementioned prince and duke, [Col. 0071C] who wrote to us and our Chapter affectionately on their behalf and sent the magnificent Lord Stephen, lord of Mota in Savoy and captain of his Excellency; and since such a request redounds to the honour of Blessed Eusebius and to the devotion of the aforesaid people: with the consent of the venerable Chapter, we have bestowed upon those same ambassadors a portion of the stone by which Blessed Eusebius was stoned and delivered to death, and one leaf of the Gospels, written in the proper hand of the aforesaid St Eusebius one thousand one hundred and forty-four years ago, and extracted from the treasury of the aforesaid church with the reverence that was due.
>
> “Many miracles have been seen from this book of the Gospels, which no evasion can conceal; and we transmit all of them, preserved with the highest veneration in our aforesaid church, desiring that they be observed among them with equal veneration. We have granted these our letters, subscribed by our secretary at our command and strengthened by the affixing of our greater seal, as testimony to the foregoing. Given at Vercelli, in our episcopal palace, on 24 January 1515, in the presence there of Andrea Ferrerius, our uncle and general vicar, and Ludovico de Gromis, canon of Vercelli, witnesses summoned and requested for the foregoing. + In place of the sign. Jo. de Ferreriis.”

Finally, through this book God at times made known a certain special sanctity of the same saint, as the foregoing instrument itself also suggests. For it often happened that those who perjured themselves after touching it were either immediately [Col. 0072A] blinded or afflicted in another limb. But enough concerning this holy codex, so dear to us.

Thus far the aforesaid bishop Jo. Stephanus Ferrerius, who, although in his excellent description of this sacred codex he promised to commit it to posterity and everlasting remembrance in these words, “We shall therefore have it copied,” was nevertheless snatched away by death in 1610, before the life of St Eusebius collected by him could be published. By the supreme direction of providence, he left the task in these times to another bishop Ferrerius, adorned with the sacred purple of the cardinalate and endowed with incomparable solicitude for bringing the remarkable and venerable Eusebian codex again to present remembrance.

Another piece of evidence also occurs in the sermon of Atho, bishop of Vercelli in 752, which is enumerated among other sermons composed in praise of the holy martyr-bishop Eusebius by the holy Fathers and bishops Ambrose, Maximus, and Gregory of Tours. About the middle of that sermon, where mention is made of the council convened at Milan in 355—according to Cardinal Baronius’s annotation—by the emperor Constantius, the most destructive enemy and overthrower of the Catholic faith, we read:

> “Blessed Eusebius had delayed going to it, since he was by no means unaware what ought to be done.”

He then adds:

> “Nor could he restrain himself from going to the aforesaid council to contend for the faith, carrying with him the dear pledges of the holy Gospel.”

The Venerable Jo. Franciscus Bonomius, bishop of this church in 1554, likewise testifies to this. Among other materials concerning the arrangements for the planned translation [Col. 0072C] of the sacred body of St Eusebius, the martyr, he had excerpts of encomia from the writings of the holy Fathers, Greek as well as Latin, which were to be displayed in the Eusebian basilica, the episcopal court, upon arches, trophies, and public streets; Atho’s text was also among them. Finally, it is found in the printed Life of St Eusebius, no. XIV, fol. 138:

> “He kept the most holy Gospels, copied in his own hand, continually with him as his most faithful companions; and by using them he everywhere exterminated the foul monsters of vices, schisms, and heresies.”

But why do I linger over seeking proofs, when you, my Blanchini, know well how great is the dignity of this sacred codex, how certain its authorship, and how much credit, moreover, ought to be given to it? With this as your guide, endeavour to refute the errors of innovators, so that, just as [Col. 0072D] at the rising of the sun whatever remains of the night-time darkness of shadows swiftly vanishes, so, when this sacred volume is brought to light and disseminated not only in the republic of letters but throughout the whole world, the dim-sighted eyes of all heretics may be enlightened by the recognition of the Catholic faith.

May God grant that my wishes also be fulfilled: for a greater confirmation of the orthodox faith; for a greater increase in the glory of our most holy patron, the martyr-bishop Eusebius, and of the Chapter that serves him; and finally for a worthy commendation of your name. Receive therefore, most distinguished and ever most dear Blanchini, whatever my weakness has been able to select; I trust that all of it will be most pleasing to you. Live long, zealously defending the truth of the faith; and in the arduous and most important work you have undertaken, may God preserve you unharmed and finally bring you to the most blessed abode of eternal salvation. Farewell. Vercelli, 11 June, in the year of the Lord 1738.

[Col. 0075A]

## Blanchini of Verona’s Judgment concerning the Vercelli Codex

I shall celebrate the praises of the most illustrious Canon Ruggerius if he also composes a separate dissertation and publishes those monuments drawn from every period of antiquity which, as he seems to intimate in his letter, are preserved to this day in the archive of the distinguished Chapter, so that by their aid he may establish and vindicate for the most holy bishop and martyr Eusebius the celebrated codex of the Gospels. I repeatedly [Col. 0073B] urge him to carry this out, as he perceived from my letters to him how earnestly I desired it.

The Acts of St Eusebius, published by Ferdinandus Ughellius in volume IV of *Italia Sacra*, col. 1030 of the first edition, from what he calls a very ancient codex of saints’ lives from the monastery of Nonantola, teach us how much trust should be placed in the most ancient tradition of the Church of Vercelli. For there we read:

> “He—namely St Eusebius—was fighting against the most savage Arian beasts, who drove him from the city after stirring up the people’s persecution against him. But he, lest the people should sin against him—those whom he afterwards delighted to have as sons—knowing what was written, ‘If they persecute you in one city, flee to another,’ crossed beyond the river Po and, arriving at the fortress called that of the Credonenses, stayed there [Col. 0073C] for three months and built an oratory in honour of the Blessed Mother of God. Remaining there still longer, he WROTE the Gospel of Christ with his own hand. In the same codex of the four Gospels its miracle shines forth with such great power, not only through the words of Christ but also those of the same Father, that, if anyone deceived by the devil should swear a false oath upon it, a bodily affliction immediately appears upon him: so that he is either punished by death, or, losing his eyes, loses both spiritual and bodily light, or is made maimed or lame by the withering of his limbs, or is torn apart by demonic assault almost unto death.”

To these commendations and this witness Berengarius also joins himself, son of Eberhard, Duke of Friuli, who, still very young, was chosen king of Italy in 888, as is evident [Col. 0073D] from the wax seals of the diplomas which he issued in the first years of his reign. For there one sees the image of a beardless man with a youthful countenance, such as is not seen in diplomas of later years.

Guglielmus Godefridus Leibnitius, who furnished an edition and a brief chronology of the ancient panegyric poem on the praises of the Emperor Berengarius—first published by Hadrianus Valesius, historiographer to the Most Christian King of France—begins Berengarius’s reign in Italy in May 887. But this rests upon no sound foundations, as the most learned Abbot Ludovicus Muratorius says in part I, volume II of *Rerum Italicarum*, p. 373. Before him lay two diplomas of the Emperor Charles the Fat, issued in 887 on the third Ides of August at the royal estate of Lustonoa or Justonoa, concerning certain estates of the former Empress Angelberga, resident in Italy. From these it is clear that Berengarius had not yet had an opportunity in that year to seize the kingdom; this occurred only after Charles’s death in the following year, 888. Other, still unpublished diplomas of the same Berengarius establish the same point. One was issued in 889, on the fourth Ides of September, in the second year of his reign; another in 894, on the fourth Nones of September, in the seventh year of his reign—to omit others.

Berengarius’s age thus established, there now arises for me a new kind of proof in which I may almost rest. Yet because it cannot be explained without an inspection of the silver plates of the same Eusebian codex, covered in gold and silver by Berengarius and reverently offered by him to the chief church [Col. 0074B] of Vercelli, let the plates themselves be examined in Part II of this work, pp. DLXXIV and DLXXV. From them one may infer that, after he had plundered the rather extensive property of the bishop of Vercelli, he was inwardly touched by remorse and returned the Eusebian autograph with interest.

I recount the matter from Hadrianus Valesius, who says in chapter IV of his notes upon the aforesaid anonymous panegyric:

> “In 886 discord arose between Berengarius, duke of Friuli, and Luitward, bishop of Vercelli, the sole privy counsellor of the Emperor Charles. Berengarius entered Vercelli by force or intrigue, seized many of the bishop’s possessions as he pleased, and departed from the city laden with spoils, none preventing him. But in the following year, 887, he came to the emperor and, with great gifts, made satisfaction for the insult and injury done to the bishop, his enemy, as is found in the Bertinian Annals.”

For in 886, after Easter, they say, a general assembly having been held at Pavia, the emperor proceeded through Burgundy into Gaul to meet the Northmen, who were then at Paris. Henry, margrave of the Franks, who at that time held Neustria, having been killed there, the king, his affairs meeting with little success, returned to his own territories. Discord arose between Berengarius, the king’s kinsman, who possessed Friuli, and Liviward the bishop. Therefore Berengarius sent men to plunder the city of Vercelli; and, coming there himself, he seized many of the bishop’s goods as he pleased and returned. And in 887 the emperor was severely afflicted by a great illness. Afterwards, recovering a little, he set out for Alemannia; [Col. 0074D] turning toward the estate of Podona, he underwent an incision of the head for pain. After holy Easter Day had passed, a judicial assembly was held at Weibilinga. There, among other matters, Berengarius came to the emperor’s allegiance and, by a settlement accompanied by great gifts, discharged the offence which he had committed against Liviward in the preceding year.

The cover of the Eusebian codex, restored in silver and gold by King Berengarius, displays on one side an image of our Saviour, and on the other St Eusebius, inscribed `EUSEB. EPS.` At his feet are read the aforementioned verses:

> + This bishop Eusebius wrote [it], and age wore it away;  
> But King Berengarius restored the same.  
> After drawing out (read: adorning) silver with gleaming gold,  
> He himself offered it, O bishop, to your Church.

For the cover of this codex, to be pursued with every mark of honour and veneration, see the silver coverings engraved in copper in Part II of this work, pp. 574 and 575, which I have cited.

Therefore, from the epigram inscribed by Berengarius on the Vercelli codex, we have that the codex itself was written by St Eusebius; and this testimony, because it proceeds from that king, must be referred to the ninth century of Christ. Before taking our hand from the page, let us at least recount one passage of the celebrated codex, which the Arians removed with sacrilegious hand from the holy Gospel of John at the time when Auxentius occupied the Church of Milan with arms and an army, and Valens and Ursacius were attacking the Church of Sirmium: namely, verse 6 of chapter III. This outrage, since it was detected about the year [Col. 0075B] 357 of restored salvation, shows the extraordinary antiquity of the Eusebian codex and adds the greatest weight of authority to the inherited tradition.

In the aforesaid third chapter of John, verse 6, the reading was:

> “That which is born of flesh is flesh, because it is born of flesh; and that which is born of Spirit is spirit, because God is Spirit, and is born of God.”

This is still the reading in the Vercelli codex. But the impious men deceitfully and fraudulently erased from all sacred volumes the words “because God is Spirit,” as we learn from St Ambrose, who addresses the Arians thus in his book *On the Holy Spirit*:

> “Not only in this passage does Scripture plainly testify to the *theotēs* [θεότητα], that is, the Deity, of the Holy Spirit; but the Lord himself also said in the Gospel that God is Spirit. You Arians testify so expressly that this passage concerns the Spirit that you remove it from your own codices—and would that you removed it from yours alone, rather than also taking it from the codices of the Church!”

The Arians therefore deleted that passage not only from their own codices but also from those of the Church. And they successfully carried their crime through to completion, because very many of them, fraudulently concealing their heresy, long avoided openly withdrawing themselves from communion with the Catholic Church. Yet this perfidy of the Arians was discovered by the most vigilant pastors of the Church, as Ambrose himself relates; he also assigns the time:

> “For at the time when Auxentius, in impious unbelief, occupied the Church of Milan with arms and an army, or when the Church of Sirmium was attacked by Valens and Ursacius, who were changing its bishops, this falsehood and sacrilege of yours was discovered in ecclesiastical codices. And perhaps you did this in the East as well.”

Yet the most holy bishop of Milan affirms that the faith of the Church could neither be erased nor shaken by this great crime of the Arians:

> “You were indeed able,” he says, “to erase the letters, but you could not take away the faith. That erasure exposed you all the more; that erasure condemned you all the more. For you could not blot out the truth; rather, that erasure scraped your names out of the book of life.”

And indeed, says Germonius in his *On Ancient Heretics Who Corrupted Ecclesiastical Codices*, p. 116, it is evident to every reader that the passage “because God is Spirit” is no longer found in chapter three of the Gospel according to John; but that it existed in Latin codices, especially those of the metropolitan see of Milan—within whose territory Vercelli lay—written before the wicked times of the Arians, no one can doubt.

See also Tertullian in his book *On the Flesh of Christ*, which he wrote at Rome against Marcion, Apelles, and Valentinus. The first denied that Christ possessed true flesh; the second granted that he possessed true flesh but denied that he was truly born; the third, while admitting both that he possessed true flesh and that he was truly born, said that he was born through the Virgin and in the Virgin, but not from the Virgin. Against these heretics Tertullian cites this very passage of John:

> “The Lord himself,” he says, “has pronounced in a declarative and definitive manner that what is born in flesh is flesh, BECAUSE IT IS BORN OF FLESH. But if he said this only concerning man and not concerning himself, then certainly deny Christ and so maintain that it did not apply to him as well. Yet he adds: ‘and what is born of Spirit is spirit, BECAUSE GOD IS SPIRIT, AND IS BORN OF GOD.’ This surely bears upon him—or bears upon him all the more, if it also bears upon his believers. If therefore this too bears upon him, why not also what precedes?” Etc.

Tertullian did not read these words in John’s Gospel only at Rome, nor was he alone in doing so. Cyprian read them in Africa, as did with him very many bishops at the synod held at Carthage in 256, where the baptism of heretics was under discussion.

The most recent editor of St Ambrose judged the following worthy of observation concerning the Johannine passage quoted above from that celebrated doctor of the Church:

> “The following words,” he says, “*because it is born of flesh*, are absent from all Bibles in every language no less than the words under discussion here, *because God is Spirit*. Yet there can be no doubt that these latter words were erased from the register of the sacred pages by heretics.”

But perhaps this is why the Church did not restore that passage: it had not been sufficiently established whether it had truly existed in the most ancient and original copies of the Gospel. But enough on this matter.

It remains—and this seems the only remaining point—that those who refuse to recognize the age of St Eusebius in the Vercelli codex should carefully inspect the specimen of its characters printed in Part II, plate II, after p. 588. That Gospel-book must necessarily be of the most remote antiquity, since already in the very time of King Berengarius age had worn it out, and it required restoration, as is read in the silver epigram affixed to its cover:

> “And age wore it away;  
> But King Berengarius restored the same.”

Finally, I shall add a word concerning the image of St Eusebius, for it is too remarkable to pass over altogether in silence. Berengarius spent great sums on restoring the codex; he renewed and decorated the old icon and adorned it with gold. Yet he retained the original inscription, `EUSEBIUS EPISCOPUS`, without the addition “Saint,” adhering closely to venerable antiquity.

The most learned Mabillon, vol. I of his *Italian Journey*, p. 9, writes as follows concerning our Vercelli codex:

> “In the treasury of that same church—the cathedral of Vercelli—there is preserved a most ancient parchment codex containing the Gospels of St Matthew and St Mark [read: of SS. Matthew, John, Luke, and Mark]. It is believed to have been written by St Eusebius, that most noble bishop and martyr whom the Arians so grievously harassed, and given by him to this church. Certainly, the parchment is almost ruined by decay, its letters nearly faded and half-erased; they depart somewhat from Roman script. The letter A is shaped like the Greek lambda, Λ; the letter M, closed above, begins with a semicircle; the other letters are nearly similar to Roman ones. The cover of the codex, restored in silver by the Emperor Berengarius, displays on one side an image of the Saviour and on the other St Eusebius, at whose head the following verses are inscribed:
>
> ‘This bishop Eusebius wrote [it], and age wore it away;  
> But King Berengarius restored the same.’
>
> “At the lower part, at Eusebius’s feet:
>
> ‘After adorning silver with gleaming gold  
> [the Codex reads *deprompsit*, “brought forth”; read *decompsit*, “adorned”],  
> He himself offered it, O bishop, to your Church.’”

The most learned Montfaucon also went to Vercelli on 21 May and described the Eusebian codex as follows in his *Italian Diary*, ch. 28, p. 444:

> “We inspected there—namely, in the cathedral—a most ancient codex written on very thin parchment. They said that it had been copied in the hand of St Eusebius himself, who flourished in the fourth century, and that he had also made the translation from Greek into Latin. I read parts here and there and discovered that its version differs from our Vulgate as widely as heaven from earth. The codex is weakened and decayed in many places; they said that this had happened through an accident rather than through age, relating that it had long been submerged in a river.”

Montfaucon supplied an alphabet of it, corresponding to the earliest age, but it was inadequately reproduced by the engraver and differs greatly from the genuine form of the characters which I have presented in Part II, plate II, after p. 588. St Eusebius died in the year of Christ 371. Therefore this codex must be judged the most ancient of all Latin Bibles of the New Testament.

[Col. 0077D]

The first column of our four-column Gospel-book presents this Eusebian codex of which we speak. In order to produce a typographical representation of it with its natural features, I took pains to ensure that the edition should conform to this agreement and standard: namely, that the printed text should always have as many lines and as many line-endings as the manuscript book; and that the same spelling, errors, and frequent alterations of letters should be retained with the greatest scrupulousness. Thus whoever wishes to compare this edition with the autograph by careful collation may readily find every pericope expressed in the same number of lines and examine it by the standard of the most sacred Gospel-book of the Church of Vercelli.

Until now, no one has been allowed to use it. In 1726, when I was serving as a canon at Verona, I was, under the happy and favourable guidance of divine providence, informed by the most learned and renowned Scipione, Marquis Maffei—whose name will always be mentioned by me with exceptional and well-earned praise—that at Vercelli there existed a Gospel codex of such antiquity that it surpassed our Veronese one of twelve centuries. This latter codex, written on the thinnest parchment dyed purple in gold and silver characters, I had first copied in the chapter-house at Verona; from that time until 1732, when I came to Rome, I always kept it at home as my companion and, as it were, my tent-mate, because the most eminent Chapter of the most illustrious and reverend canons had granted to me alone the permission to publish it, as appears in the Chapter’s records.

Therefore, in the following year, 1727, I began by correspondence to entreat the aforesaid most illustrious Franciscus Hieronymus Ruggerius, eminent canon of the holy Church of Vercelli, that he would deign to devote every effort to copying that codex. At length he undertook the enormous labour and shared the copy with me in letters full of kindness, so that I might publish it and elucidate it with my observations.

While I write this, the distinguished Raphael Vernazza, doctor of philosophy and sacred theology and Greek-language scribe in the Vatican Library, while examining the codices of the Queen of Sweden, found one from the tenth century, marked no. 541. It contains nearly the same material as that quoted above from the millennium-old codex of the monastery of Nonantola on p. 61 of the Prolegomena, namely:

> “Knowing what was written, ‘If they persecute you in one city, flee to another,’ he crossed beyond the river Po. And arriving at the fortress called that of the Creudonenses, he built an oratory in honour of the Blessed Mary, Mother of God. Remaining there still longer, he wrote the Gospel of Christ in his own hand. In the same codex of the four Gospels its miracle very often shines forth with such power, not only through the words of Christ but also through those of the same Father, that if anyone deceived by the devil should swear a false oath upon it, a bodily punishment immediately appears, so that he is either punished by death, or, losing his eyes, loses spiritual and bodily light, or is made maimed or lame by the withering of his limbs, or is torn apart by demonic assault almost unto death. Meanwhile, while he was staying there in that fortress with his disciples, a council having been held,” etc.

Now, since I have already said much concerning this very ancient and venerable codex of the Gospels, marked with the name of Eusebius, most holy martyr and bishop of Vercelli, it will be worthwhile to show that it contains the *Itala*, which, as St Jerome says, strengthened the faith of the nascent Church and was used by the early Latin Fathers both to confirm the doctrines of faith and to impart moral precepts and heavenly instruction.

For after the apostles were sent to instruct the nations of the western regions in the Christian religion, a Latin translation of the New Testament immediately appeared which faithfully represented the autograph exemplar, so that those waters springing up into eternal life might flow also for the refreshment of Latin speakers. And although, as St Augustine testifies (*On Christian Doctrine*, II.2.16), those who translated the Scriptures from Hebrew into Greek can be counted, whereas Latin translators cannot be counted at all—for in the earliest times of faith, whenever anyone obtained a Greek codex and thought himself to have some competence in both languages, he ventured to translate—nevertheless, just as among the Greeks the authority of the Septuagint translation was pre-eminent, so among the Latins the *Itala* was preferred to all others. It was employed first by Italian Fathers and thereafter by other writers of the Latin Church—namely Tertullian, Cyprian, Ambrose, Augustine, and others—down to the time of Gregory the Great.

The distinguished Matth. Petitdier says in his tenth dissertation on Scripture: although in the passage of time nearly countless Latin versions appeared, nevertheless one among the others—the one Augustine calls the *Itala*, Jerome the *Vulgata*, and Gregory the *Old* version, and which we reasonably suspect to have been the very first—held the leading place. Many think, not without some basis, that it was prepared in the time of the apostles, lest the Latin Church should for so long be deprived of the treasure of the Scriptures.
