Yet by whom it was composed is unknown to us, although it could itself be distinguished from other translations by certain indications and marks. For St Augustine teaches us that among the various Latin versions the *Itala* was outstanding above the rest because it was clearer in meaning and more faithful to the wording:

> “Among the translations, let the ITALA be preferred to the others; for it adheres more closely to the words while retaining clarity of meaning.”

Accordingly, if I show that the Eusebian codex possesses this twofold excellence, it will be certain that it contains the *Itala* used in the Church. Moreover, the blemishes with which the *Itala* was marked still occur in the celebrated codex. Therefore it cannot in any way be doubted that it presents that very *Itala* to our eyes.

St Jerome must be heard, who by command of Pope St Damasus revised the Gospel codex of the *Itala*, or old translator, according to the Greek. Writing to Damasus, he says:

> “You compel me to make a new work out of an old one: after copies of the Scriptures have been dispersed throughout the whole world, I am to sit as a kind of arbiter and decide, since they differ among themselves, which are those that agree with the Greek truth. A pious labour, but a dangerous presumption.”
>
> And shortly afterwards:
>
> “For who, when he has taken a volume into his hands and finds that what he reads differs from the flavour once absorbed, will not immediately cry out, calling me a falsifier and sacrilegious because I dare to add, alter, or correct anything in the old books? Against this hostility I have a twofold consolation: first, that you, who are the chief priest, command it to be done; second, that what differs cannot be true, as is proved even by the testimony of detractors. For if faith is to be given to Latin copies, let them answer: to which ones? For there are almost as many copies as codices. But if truth must be sought from many copies, why, returning to the Greek original, should we not correct those things which have either been badly rendered by faulty translators, perversely revised by ignorant presumptuaries, or added or altered by sleepy scribes? …
>
> “This present preface promises only the four Gospels, corrected by comparison with Greek codices—but ancient ones. Lest they should differ too greatly from the customary Latin reading, we restrained our pen so that, correcting only those things which seemed to alter the sense, we allowed the rest to remain as they were. … A great error has become established in our codices: when one Evangelist said more about the same matter, they added it to another because they thought he had said less; or when one expressed the same sense differently, whoever had first read one of the four thought that the others too ought to be corrected after its model. Thus it has happened that among us everything is mixed together: in Mark are found many things from Luke and Matthew; again in Matthew, many things from John and Mark; and in the other Gospels are found matters peculiar to the rest.”

The most learned Petrus Sabatier, Benedictine monk of the Congregation of St Maur, says that several points in these words of the holy doctor deserve consideration. First, among the copies which differed from one another were some more genuine than others—such as the Eusebian Gospel codex. In Jerome’s judgment, those were more genuine than the others which agreed more closely with the Greek, as the holy doctor expressly indicates when he says that the task imposed upon him was to sit as an arbiter and determine, among discrepant copies of the Latin version of the Scriptures, which were those that agreed with Greek truth. But those copies of the Latin version which agree with Greek truth are precisely the copies that represent the pure and unmixed *Itala*, which Augustine declares ought to be preferred above the rest as more faithful to the words.

Next, in these different copies many things had indeed either been badly rendered by faulty translators, perversely revised by ignorant presumptuaries, or added or altered by sleepy scribes. Yet these blemishes, with which the old Gospel translation was marked in Jerome’s age, are not such an obstacle that it cannot be recognized in our own age; indeed, they contribute greatly to distinguishing it. Besides, one must not suppose that these blemishes were such that they entirely disfigured the old translation, since Jerome himself testifies that he left very many things untouched:

> “Lest they should differ too greatly from the customary Latin reading, we restrained our pen so that, correcting only those things which seemed to alter the sense, we allowed the rest to remain as they were.”

Therefore we ought to interpret more mildly both Jerome’s words in which he speaks of errors and blemishes and those in which he enlarges upon the number of Latin translations, rather than press them too severely.

Since the aforementioned very learned Sabatier adduces certain principal differences between the old and the new translations, let us try whether all those which he cites are such that the distinctive features of the *Itala* can of themselves be recognized in the Vercelli codex and in the other manuscripts presented in our four-column Gospel-book.

> **Note: [Col. 0081A] The following manuscript versions are printed in parallel in Migne.**

Matthew 1:23. In the modern Vulgate the reading is: “Behold, a virgin shall have in her womb”; but the ancients—Irenaeus, Cyprian, Ambrose, Augustine, Vigilius of Tapsus, Leo the Great, Maximus of Turin, and others—formerly read in the old version: “shall conceive in her womb,” or “shall receive [a child] in her womb.”

Matthew 2:5. The old translation read “in Bethlehem of Judaea,” from the Greek *tēs Ioudaias* [τῆς Ἰουδαίας], rather than “of Judah,” which is read in the modern Vulgate. Jerome likewise reads “in Bethlehem of Judaea” in his commentary on Matthew 2, vol. IV, col. 9; but here he warns that this is a scribal error:

> “For we think,” he says, “that the Evangelist first wrote, as we read in the Hebrew itself, ‘of Judah,’ not ‘of Judaea.’”

I agree with Jerome and concede that it is an error. Nevertheless, it is an error by which the old translation is recognized and shown to agree more closely with the Greek text.

Matthew 5:7. “Blessed are the merciful, for God will have mercy on them” is shown to derive from the *Itala* version by Hilary, Ambrose, Augustine, Chromatius of Aquileia, the author of the *Imperfect Work*, St Valerian, and others.

Matthew 5. Likewise in verse 22 of the same chapter: “Everyone who is angry with his brother without cause,” from the Greek *pas ho orgizomenos tō adelphō autou eikē* [Πᾶς ὁ ὀργιζόμενος τῷ ἀδελφῷ αὐτοῦ εἰκῇ]. For most ancient Fathers—namely Irenaeus, Cyprian, Hilary, Philastrius, Augustine, St Paulinus, the author of the *Imperfect Work*, and Gregory the Great—likewise add “without cause.”

Matthew, ch. VI, 4. “And your Father, who sees in secret,” or “in the hidden place, will repay you openly,” belongs to the same version, as Augustine testifies. In Book II of *The Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, he says: “Many Latin copies have it thus; but because,” he says, “we do not find ‘openly’ in the Greek copies, which are earlier, we did not think anything needed to be discussed here.” Yet the modern Greek has: ἀποδώσει σοι ἐν τῷ φανερῷ, “he will repay you openly.”

Matthew, ch. VI, 11. The old Vulgate read: “Give us this day our daily bread”; and Tertullian, Cyprian, Ambrose, Augustine, Chromatius, and Sedulius are known to have read it so. Besides these, Jerome, in Book II on the Epistle to Titus, expressly asserts that, according to the Latin interpreters, it was written, “Our daily bread”; but that the Greek has more correctly, “Our ἐπιούσιον bread,” that is, “our pre-eminent, excellent, peculiar bread.” And shortly afterward: “Some,” he says, “consider ἐπιούσιον to mean bread so called because it is above all οὐσίαι [substances/essences].” And in his Commentary on Matthew: “What we have rendered ‘supersubstantial,’ is in Greek ἐπιούσιον.”

Matthew, ch. XX, v. 28. After these words of verse 28, “Just as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many,” the following occurs in the Colbert manuscript, as also in other copies of the old translation:

> But you seek to grow from what is small and to become lesser (variant: lesser persons) from what is greater. And when you enter and are invited to supper, do not recline in the more eminent places, lest perhaps someone more distinguished than you arrive; and the person who invited you to supper come and say to you: “Move still lower down,” and you be put to shame. But if you recline in a lower place, and someone humbler than you arrives, the one who invited you to supper will say to you: “Come still higher up.” And it will be more advantageous to you.

These words are lacking in the present Vulgate text of the Gospel according to Matthew. But Juvencus, when he had before him a copy of Matthew according to the old translation for composing the Gospel history in verse, followed this copy and rendered in Latin verse whatever he read in the old translation as follows:

> Thus the Son of Man ministers in all things,  
> Alone performing holy offices by his own service,  
> And for many lays down his life with precious blood.  
> You desire to rise from the smallest fortunes,  
> And thus, fallen from the heights, you grasp the lowest places.  
> If anyone invites you to a banquet feast,  
> Let every prudent person avoid placing his limbs  
> Upon the highest couches; perhaps another of higher rank will come,  
> And he whom the swelling pride of an inflated heart had placed on high  
> Will shamefully be compelled to yield the distinguished place.  
> But if he is content to take the middling places at the feast,  
> And soon afterward, if a lower-ranking guest enters,  
> That guest will modestly move to the more honorable couch-coverings.

These verses of Juvencus ought certainly to be manifest proof that, in composing his Gospel history, the poet used a Latin copy very much like ours and one representing the old translation.

Mark, ch. III, 5. The ancient Latin Italic translation should be noted in these words of Mark’s Gospel:

> “And looking round at them with indignation, grieved at their deadened hearts, he said to the man: ‘Stretch out your hand.’ And he stretched it out, and his hand was restored to him, like the other.”

For this the Vulgate reads:

> “And looking round at them with anger, grieved at the blindness of their heart, he says to the man … and his hand was restored to him.”

The latter agrees more closely with the Greek, which reads:

> Καὶ περιβλεψάμενος αὐτοὺς μετ’ ὀργῆς, συλλυπούμενος ἐπὶ τῇ πωρώσει τῆς καρδίας αὐτῶν, λέγει τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ … καὶ ἀποκατεστάθη ἡ χεὶρ αὐτοῦ ὡς ἡ ἄλλη.  
> “And looking round at them with anger, grieving at the hardness of their heart, he says to the man … and his hand was restored, like the other.”

Mark, ch. X, 17. “A certain man kneeling down said,” which in our Vulgate is rendered: “A certain man, running up and bending the knee before him, asked him.”

Mark, ch. X, 38. Do you want another example from the New Testament making it plain that Irenaeus’s translator copied verses of Scripture from a Latin codex of the old translation? Irenaeus, Book I, ch. 21, no. 2, thus quotes the same verse, Mark 10:38:

> Δύνασθέ τε βάπτισμα βαπτισθῆναι, ὃ ἐγὼ μέλλω βαπτίζεσθαι;  
> “Are you able to be baptized with the baptism with which I am about to be baptized?”

His translator renders it:

> “Can you be baptized with the baptism which I have to be baptized with?”

The Colbert codex likewise indicates that these words came from the more ancient version:

> “Can you be baptized with the baptism which I have to be baptized with?”

Mark, ch. XII, 24. Where the Vulgate has, “One poor widow put in two small coins,” the old version read: “… put in two copper coins.”

Mark, ch. XIII, 15. “He who is in the upper rooms, let him not come down,” which our Vulgate expresses: “And he who is upon the roof, let him not come down.”

[Col. 0082A]

Matthew, ch. I, 23. Vercelli codex: “Behold … go in u … ro shall conceive.” Supply from the Verona and Corbie codices, which have: “Behold, a Virgin shall conceive in the womb.” So also Tertullian, *On the Flesh of Christ*, ch. 24. See Martianay, *Remarque sur la Version Italique de l’Evangile de S. Matthieu*, p. 118.

Matthew, ch. II, 5. Vercelli codex: “in Bethlehem of Judaea.” So also the Brixian and Saint-Germain codices. The Verona codex, however: “in the city of Bethlehem of Judaea.” St Hilary likewise, on Psalm 131, and St Ambrose, on Psalm 35, read: “in Bethlehem of Judaea.”

[Col. 0082B]

Matthew, ch. V, v. 7. Vercelli codex: “Blessed … mercif … God will … mercy.” Verona and Saint-Germain: “Blessed are the merciful, because [Saint-Germain: for] God will have mercy upon them.” See the cited Martianay, p. 12 of the same work.

Matthew, ch. V, 22. Vercelli codex: “Everyone who is angry with his brother without cause.” So also Verona, Brixia, and Corbie. St Augustine read this in Latin codices, but had not found it in the Greek, as he reports in Book I of the *Retractations*, ch. 19. St Jerome, on the contrary, in his Commentary on Matthew here, directs that τὸ “without cause” be removed from the Latin codices, into which it had crept, and that the true reading be retained, preserved in the best books. Cassian observes the same point in the *Institutes*, Book VIII, ch. 20.

[Col. 0082C]

Matthew, ch. VI, 4. Vercelli and Saint-Germain codices: “And your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you openly.” Verona: “And your Father, who sees you in secret, will repay you openly.” Brixia: “And your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you manifestly.”

Matthew, ch. VI, 11. Vercelli codex: “Give us this day our daily bread.” So also Verona, Brixia, and Corbie.

[Col. 0082D]

Matthew, ch. XX. The Vercelli codex adds after v. 28:

> “But you seek to grow from what is small, and to become lesser from what is greater. And when you enter and are invited to supper, do n… reclin… in the more eminent place… lest perhaps someone more distinguished than you arri…; and the person who invited you to supper come and say to you: ‘Move still lower …,’ and you be put to shame. But if you reclin… in a lower place, and someone humbler than you arrives, the one who invited you to supper will say to you: ‘Come still higher up.’ And this will be more advantageous to you.”

Verona:

> “But you seek to grow from what is small, and to become greater from what is lesser. And when you enter and are invited to supper, do not recline in the more eminent places, lest perhaps someone more distinguished than you arrive; and the person who invited you to supper come and say to you: ‘Move still lower down,’ and you be put to shame. But if you recline in a lower place, and someone humbler than you arrives, the one who invited you to supper will say to you: ‘Come still higher up.’ And this will be more advantageous to you.”

The Corbie, Saint-Germain, and another codex from the monastery of St Andrew near Avignon have similar readings. The same addition is also found in two Latin codices of the Bodleian Library and in certain old books of the Saxon version cited in Mill’s *Various Readings*; likewise in St Hilary here, no. 12, and in St Leo the Great’s letter to the Empress Pulcheria.

[Col. 0084B]

Mark, ch. III, 5. Vercelli codex:

> “And looking round at them with wrath, grieving over the blindness of their hearts, he said to the man: ‘Stretch out your hand.’ And he stretched it out; and his hand was restored, like the other.”

Verona:

> “And looking round at them with anger, indi… at the blindness of their hearts, he said to the man: ‘Stretch out your hand.’ And he stretched it out; and his hand was restored, like the other.”

Brixia:

> “And looking round at them with anger, he was grieved at the blindness of their heart; he said to the man: ‘Stretch out your hand.’ And he stretched it out; and his hand was restored.”

Vienna: “… with indignation, he was grieved over their deadened hearts … his hand was immediately restored.”

Corbie likewise has: “and his hand was immediately restored.” Gat.: “and his hand was restored to health, like the other.”

Mark, ch. X, 17. Vercelli codex: “one man, prostrate on his knees, asked him, saying.” Verona: “a certain man kneeling down, asking him and saying.” See the variant readings of the Greek text in Mill.

[Col. 0084D]

Mark, ch. X, 38. Vercelli codex: “Are you able … to be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?” So also Verona. The Vienna codex and Brixia: “Are you able … to baptize with the baptism with which I am baptized?”

Mark, ch. XII, 24. Vercelli codex: “one widow put in two small coins.” Vienna: “one widow put in two copper coins.” Verona: “one widow put in two copper [small] coins.”

Mark, ch. XIII, 15. Vercelli codex: “He who is upon the roof, let him not come down.” Corbie: “He who is in the upper rooms, let him not come down.” Verona and Brixia … [text incomplete].

[Col. 0085A]

In order that greater weight might attach to this unpolished judgment of mine, and that the character of the Italic version of the most sacred Vercelli codex might become known, I have brought forward all these passages of the Gospels which the most learned Lord Peter Sabatier cited in his general Preface from the earliest Fathers and from manuscripts of venerable antiquity, in order to present an image of the ancient Latin Italic translation. Nothing more learned or illuminating could have been accomplished by him in this field; for he does not touch lightly—still less rashly or from preconceived notions—upon the variant passages which he adduces. Rather, having examined and compared Greek copies, having also investigated the character of the Latin, and further having consulted the works of the older holy Fathers, he finally weighed with the utmost diligence each item that seemed capable of shedding any light upon such an inquiry.

Since he had been much engaged in this arena and consequently possessed secure knowledge of the striking testimonies he had produced, it is no wonder that this greatest of men never stumbled in adducing them. But because, through the many blemishes with which the Italic version is now sprinkled in its codices, it seems to some to have lost something like its ancient form, so that it can scarcely now be recognized, and they think that only some shadowy likeness has been sketched in the passages above and left to us, I shall seek its outstanding beauty again in the Fathers. After so great a man, I shall more carefully contemplate its native likeness in the original Greek text, so that no part of due diligence may be lacking on my part in illustrating the Vercelli Gospel codex. Here, then, is a forest of other parallel readings, which I have collected from the Fathers and commentators and which I gladly now bring forward.

John, ch. XIX, 31. Vercelli and Verona: *coena pura*, “pure supper.” Thus the old translator renders παρασκευή, *paraskeuē*, and quite rightly; for, Augustine says in Tractate 120 on John, the Jews call the *parasceve* “pure supper,” a term more usual among us in Latin. This name is also mentioned in Tertullian, Book V against Marcion, ch. 4.

John, ch. I, 29. Vercelli: “… sa au… when she saw … was moved.” Supply the lacuna from Verona and Brixia: “But she, when she saw him, was moved” (Brixia: “was troubled”). The Greek has: Ἥδε ἰδοῦσα διεταράχθη, that is, “but she, seeing, was troubled.”

Luke, ch. IX, 4. Vercelli: “and depart from there,” in conformity with the Greek, καὶ ἐκεῖθεν ἐξέρχεσθε, that is, “and depart from there.” Verona: “and set out from there,” as does the Corbie codex.

Luke, ch. XXIV, v. 43. In the Vercelli, Verona, Corbie, and Brixia codices the words “taking the remains, he gave them to them” are absent; nor do they occur in the Greek text.

Matthew, ch. VI, 14. The words “your trespasses” are absent from the Vercelli, Verona, and Brixia codices and from the Greek text.

[Col. 0086A]

Matthew, ch. VI, 18. In Vercelli, Verona, and Saint-Germain, “openly” is added, as in the Greek text.

Matthew, ch. X, 25. Vercelli, Corbie, and Brixia: “Beelzebul.” The Greek codices likewise read Βεελζεβούλ, which in Chaldaic means “god of filth.”

Matthew, ch. XXI, v. 31. Vercelli, Verona, and Corbie: “They say to him: ‘The latter.’” So some old Greek and Latin codices read here, namely the Greek-Latin Cambridge codex, Coptic, Armenian, Leicester, and Paris 6, in Mill. But books printed in Greek and Latin in our age read “the first.” This arises from a transposition of verses 29 and 30 in this manner:

> The father, approaching the first, said: “Son, go today, work in my vineyard.” But he replied: “I go, Lord”; and he did not go.  
> But approaching the other, he said likewise. He replied: “I will not.” Afterwards, moved by repentance, he went. Which of the two did the will of his father? They say to him: “The latter.”

This arrangement of the speech certainly requires this answer. Certain codices cited by Jerome, the Arabic and Saxon versions, Hilary, Augustine, the Codex of Constance used by Erasmus, and others retain the Vulgate order, yet read “the latter,” not “the first.” This arose because some persons, observing in the explanation of the parable that tax collectors and prostitutes—the classes of people indicated under the name of the other son—are preferred to those represented by the elder son, such as the Pharisees, judged that the text was corrupt and that “the latter,” namely the other son, ought to be read rather than “the first,” namely the elder son.

But the one whom the father approaches first is nowhere said to be the elder, nor is the one whom he approaches second said to be the younger. On the contrary, the order of the parable requires that the father first call the younger, the figure of sinful people, and then the elder, by whom the Pharisees were signified. So the distinguished Calmet in his Commentary on this passage.

Matthew, ch. XXII, v. 13. Vercelli: “… take him … feet and hands, and cast …” Supply the lacuna from Verona: “take him by the feet and hands, and cast him …,” etc. Corbie: “take him, with feet and hands bound, and cast him …,” etc. Brixia: “bind his feet and hands, take him, and cast him …,” etc. St Irenaeus: “take him by feet and hands and cast him …,” etc. So likewise Lucifer of Cagliari, in Book II for St Athanasius, though omitting the preposition *a*, “by.” St Ambrose agreed with him in the *Apology of David*, ch. IV, p. 699. But neither the Vulgate, nor the Coptic, Syriac, Arabic, and Ethiopic versions, nor St Augustine, read the words “take hold of him.” The Cambridge codex nevertheless has: “bind him by feet and hands.”

Matthew, ch. XXIII, 25. Vercelli: “They are full of robbery and intemperance.” Many Greek codices cited by Mill agree with the Vulgate; but printed editions read: Γέμουσιν ἐξ ἁρπαγῆς καὶ ἀκρασίας, that is, “you are full [perhaps: they are full] of robbery and intemperance,” as in Verona.

John, ch. VII, 23. Vercelli: “certain Jerusalemites.” Verona: “certain persons from among the Jerusalemites.” Brixia: “… from Jerusalemites”; and so the Greek text: ἐκ τῶν Ἱεροσολυμιτῶν.

John, ch. VII, 35. Vercelli and Verona: “Is he about to go into the dispersion of the Greeks” (Verona: “will he begin to go”) “and teach the Greeks?” The Greek text has:

> Εἰς τὴν διασπορὰν τῶν Ἑλλήνων μέλλει πορεύεσθαι, καὶ διδάσκειν τοὺς Ἕλληνας;  
> “Is he about to go into the dispersion of the Greeks and teach the Greeks?”

That is, the Gentiles or nations scattered and dispersed throughout the whole world. For most interpreters explain “dispersion” in this way. Yet some think that the Jews themselves are intended: those living outside Judaea and reckoned among the dispersed, since the regions in which they lived scattered abroad were also called “dispersions.” Thus διασπορὰ Πόντου, “the dispersion of Pontus,” denoted the region of Pontus in which Jews lived.

The word διασπορά, “dispersion,” is used in several Scriptural passages to signify the exile of Jews in various regions of the world, from which God was one day to recall them, as is foretold in Psalm 146, v. 2: τὰς διασπορὰς τοῦ Ἰσμαὴλ ἐπισκευάξει, “he will restore the dispersions of Ishmael” [perhaps an OCR error]. Therefore, they say, the dispersions of the Gentiles, who are sometimes denoted by the name “Greeks,” were the various regions of the world through which Jews were scattered, as Tobit 13:3 says, because God διέσπειρεν ἡμᾶς ἐν αὐτοῖς, “scattered us among them.” Therefore, according to this view, the Jews said: “Will he go to the Jews dispersed among the Gentiles, and teach the Greeks—that is, those who dwell among Gentiles?”

[Col. 0087C]

John, ch. X, 26. Vercelli, Verona, and Brixia add after “my sheep,” “as I said to you,” in accordance with the Greek text:

> Οὐ γὰρ ἐστε ἐκ τῶν προβάτων τῶν ἐμῶν, καθὼς εἶπον ὑμῖν.  
> “For you are not of my sheep, as I said to you.”

John, ch. XII, 20. Vercelli: “There were certain Greeks.” So likewise Verona and Corbie. These Gentiles, the Ἕλληνες, “Greeks,” were proselytes born not from Jews but from Gentiles. Jews called almost all peoples not of Israelite stock Ἕλληνες, “Greeks”; but they called Ἑλληνισταί, “Hellenists,” those Jews who read Greek Bibles in the synagogues. See nevertheless what we said shortly above on ch. VII, v. 35.

John, ch. XIV, 10. Vercelli: “But the Father who remains in me, he speaks, and the works which I do, he does.” Verona: “But the Father remaining in me, he speaks; and the works which I do, he does.” Corbie: “But the Father who remains in me, he speaks, and the works which I do, he does.” Brixia: “But the Father who remains in me himself does these works.” St Ambrose, Book III *On the Faith*, ch. 2, p. 513: “But the Father who remains in me, he himself does the works, and the works which I do, he himself does.” Likewise, Book IV, ch. 6, p. 533: “My Father, who remains in me, he himself speaks, and the works which I do, he himself does”; and so in Book V, p. 575, though omitting “my.” He has similar wording in *On the Sacrament of the Incarnation of the Lord*, ch. 8, p. 722.

John, ch. XIV, 30. Vercelli: “and in me he has nothing to find.” Brixia: “and in me he will find nothing.” Syriac, Gothic, Ethiopic, and Armenian versions; Sts Gregory of Nyssa, Athanasius, Basil, and other Greek Fathers; and the codices read:

> Καὶ ἐν ἐμοὶ οὐχ εὑρήσει οὐδέν.  
> “And in me he will find nothing.”

Some Latin Fathers, namely St Ambrose, Book II *On Flight from the World*, ch. 4, and St Gregory the Great, Homily 39 on the Gospels, have: “and in me he will find nothing.” But St Ambrose himself, in *On Tobit*, vol. I, p. 601, has: “and in me he finds nothing of his own.” He also explains this reading in the cited Book *On Flight from the World*, ch. 4, no. 24. St Augustine likewise, in Book II *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, vol. X, part 1, p. 307: “and in me he finds nothing.”

[Col. 0088B]

Luke, ch. III, 13. Vercelli: “Exact nothing more than what has been appointed for you.” Verona: “Exact nothing further than what has been appointed for you.” Gat. and Brixia: “Exact only what has been appointed for you.” The Greek reads:

> Μηδὲν πλέον παρὰ τὸ διατεταγμένον ὑμῖν πράσσετε.  
> “Exact nothing more than what has been appointed for you.”

For Greek πράσσω is often used in the sense “to exact”; πράσσετε means “exact.” This is indeed the meaning of the Greek word from which πράκτορες, “exactors,” derives. “The Greeks say,” says Aulus Gellius, Book XV, ch. 14, εἰσεπράξατό με ἀργύριον, “he exacted money from me.” And the Vulgate translator himself rendered πράκτορα as *exactorem*, “an exactor,” in Luke 12:58. Likewise, in ch. XIX, 23, he interprets σὺν τόκῳ ἂν ἔπραξα αὐτό as “I should certainly have exacted it with interest.”

Luke, ch. V, 14. Vercelli, with St Ambrose: “that this may be a testimony to you.” Verona: “that it may be a testimony … to you.” Corbie: “that this may be for testimonies to you.” Many Greek codices read: “that this may be a testimony to you,” Ἵνα ᾗ μαρτύριον τοῦτο ὑμῖν; and so do Marcion in St Epiphanius and Tertullian.

Luke, ch. IX, 54. Vercelli, Verona, and Brixia add at the end, “as Elijah did” (Brixia: “as Elijah also did”), as does the Greek text:

> Ὡς καὶ Ἡλίας ἐποίησε,  
> “as Elijah also did.”

The Arabic, Persian, Syriac, Ethiopic, and Gothic versions agree. Grotius fears that these words were removed by scribes because they were thought to favor the Marcionites. On this point see Tertullian, Book IV, p. 540, against Marcion.

Mark, ch. II, 14. Vercelli, Verona, and Corbie: “he saw James of Alphaeus,” as do most Greek books. But the Greek-Latin Cambridge codex, Leicester, Paris 6, and other codices, according to Victor of Antioch, read: “he saw James, son of Alphaeus.” Brixia, Gat., and the manuscripts: “Levi of Alphaeus.” Origen, Book I against Celsus, denies that this Levi was an apostle. Others read: “he saw Matthew the publican,” in place of what is read in the Vulgate and in most Greek codices, manuscript as well as printed: “Levi the publican.” Grotius, together with Origen, is mistaken in thinking that Levi may perhaps have been the tax-farmer himself and Matthew his deputy, and that the banquet mentioned by St Matthew was prepared not in Matthew’s house but in Levi’s.

[Col. 0089A]

Mark, ch. XIV, 61. In Vercelli, “God” is absent before “the Blessed,” as also in St Hilary, Book VI *On the Trinity*, vol. II, p. 170, and in the Greek text.

Matthew, ch. VIII, 31. In Vercelli, Verona, and Brixia, “from here” is absent, as also in the Greek text.

Matthew, ch. XIII, 50. In Vercelli, after the word “teeth,” “and he said” is added. In Brixia, however, it is “Jesus said to them,” in conformity with most Greek copies.

Matthew, ch. XVI, 18. Vercelli and Corbie: “And the gates of hell” (Corbie: “of the lower world”) “will not conquer it.” The Greek text has:

> καὶ πύλαι ᾅδου οὐ κατισχύσουσιν αὐτῆς.  
> “And the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.”

Matthew, ch. XVI, 20. In Vercelli, Verona, and Corbie, “Jesus” is omitted; nor is it read in many Greek and Latin codices reported by Mill in the *Various Readings*. Very many judge that the name is superfluous in the Vulgate.

[Col. 0089B]

Matthew, ch. XVIII, 19. Vercelli, Verona, Corbie, Saint-Germain, and Brixia: “Again, amen I say to you”; so also many Greek codices, almost thirty-four Latin manuscripts, and several editions cited in Mill.

Matthew, same chapter [apparently XVIII], Vercelli and Corbie: “if two agree.” Verona, Saint-Germain, and Brixia: “if two of you agree”; so also St Cyprian, p. 41 and Book III of the *Testimonies*, no. 3, and St Ambrose, *On the Institution of Virgins*, ch. 2, p. 252.

Matthew, ch. XIX, 1. Vercelli and Verona: “when Jesus had spoken.” Corbie likewise: “when Jesus had spoken”; so also St Hilary.

Matthew, same chapter, v. 10. Vercelli, Verona, and Saint-Germain: “the case of a husband”; so also St Ambrose, *On Virginity*, ch. 6, p. 220, and *Exhortation to Virginity*, ch. 3, p. 282.

[Col. 0089C]

Matthew, ch. XXVI, 11. Vercelli: “not … always shall you have …” Supply the lacuna from Verona, Corbie, and Brixia, which have: “you will not always have”; and so do two Greek copies, several manuscripts in Queen Christina of Sweden’s library, and the Sixtine edition.

Matthew, ch. XXVI, 61. Vercelli, Corbie, and Brixia: “to build,” as in the Greek text and in most manuscripts of St Augustine’s Book II *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*.

John, ch. I, 50. Vercelli, Verona, and Brixia: “greater things than these,” as in Greek μείζω τούτων, namely, “greater things than these.”

Matthew, ch. I, 16. Vercelli and Saint-Germain:

> “To whom the Virgin Mary, being betrothed, bore Jesus.”

Verona:

> “To whom the Virgin Mary had been betrothed. And the Virgin Mary bore Jesus.”

St Gaudentius, Sermon 8, p. 95: “To whom the Virgin Mary was betrothed, who bore Jesus.” The Verona codex places the Virgin Mary in the fourteenth group in the reckoning of generations, together with St Hilary; therefore no generation is missing.

[Col. 0089D]

Matthew, ch. III, 11. Vercelli: “but he who comes.” Verona, Saint-Germain, and Brixia: “but he who comes after me”; so also St Cyprian, Book I of the *Testimonies against the Jews to Quirinus*, ch. 12, p. 345; St Hilary, *Tractate on Psalm 118*, vol. I, p. 290; and St Ambrose, *Second Apology of David*, ch. 8, p. 722.

[Col. 0090A]

Matthew, ch. VI, 19 and 20. Vercelli, Verona, Corbie, Brixia, and Saint-Germain: “destroys”; so also St Cyprian, *On Works and Almsgiving*, p. 305, and Book III to Quirinus; St Ambrose, Book II *On the Holy Spirit*, p. 633; and St Augustine, Book II *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, vol. III, part II, p. 217.

Matthew, ch. VIII, 18. After “commanded,” Vercelli and Verona add “his disciples”; so also the Coptic version, St Hilary, and St Jerome. But the Saint-Germain codex has “to his disciples.”

Matthew, ch. X, 29. Vercelli, Verona, Corbie, and Brixia: “without the will of your Father”; so also the Arabic version, St Irenaeus, Book II against Heresies, vol. I, p. 154; Tertullian more than once; Novatian, *On the Trinity*, ch. 8; St Cyprian, Epistle 55 according to Pamelius (19, Oxford); St Hilary, Book IV *On the Trinity*, vol. II, p. 76; and others.

[Col. 0090B]

Matthew, ch. XIII, 15. Vercelli: “make heavy their ears and eyes.” Verona: “stop up their ears and make heavy their eyes.” St Irenaeus: “block their ears and blind their eyes.”

Matthew, ch. XIII, 47. Vercelli: “a net cast into the sea, which gathered from every kind of fish …” Supply the lacuna from Verona and Brixia: “a net cast into the sea, which gathered fish of every kind.” Saint-Germain: “a net cast into the sea, which gathered fish of every kind.” St Ambrose, *On Virginity*, ch. 19, p. 243: “a net cast into the sea,” etc.; and Book V of the *Hexaemeron*, ch. 6, p. 85: “a net cast into the sea, which gathered fish of every kind.”

[Col. 0090C]

Matthew, ch. XIII, 48. Vercelli: “when it was … full, they drew it to shore; and sitting, they chose the best fi… in their ves….” Verona: “when it was full, they drew it to shore; and sitting, they selected the best fish into their vessels.” Saint-Germain: “when it was full, they brought it to shore; and sitting, they selected the best into their vessels.” Brixia: “when it was full, they drew it to shore; and sitting, they selected the good fish into their vessels.” St Ambrose, Book V of the *Hexaemeron*, ch. 6, p. 85: “when it was full, they brought it to shore, and sitting, they selected the best into their vessels.”

Matthew, ch. XV, 26. Vercelli, Verona, and Corbie: “it is not permitted to take”; so also St Ambrose, *Exposition of Psalm 43*, p. 907. Brixia likewise has “to take.” The Persian version and St Hilary also read, “it is not permitted,” etc. Among Greek witnesses, St Basil of Seleucia has ἔξεστι, “it is permitted,” for ἔστι, “it is.”

[Col. 0090D]

John, ch. III, 16. Vercelli: “I shall baptize you with water unto repentance.” Verona: “I baptize you with water unto repentance.” Gat.: “in repentance.” Tertullian, p. 228: “I immerse you by repentance alone.”

John, ch. V, 44. Vercelli: “and do you not seek glory from the only one?” Verona: “and do you not seek the honor of him who is alone?” St Hilary: “and do you not seek the honor of him who alone is God?”

Luke, ch. X, 22. Vercelli: “and no one knows who the Father is except the Son,” etc. Verona: “and no one knows the Father except the Son, and wh… knows the Son … except the Father,” etc. St Irenaeus, Book II against Heresies, vol. I, p. 122: “no one knows the Father except the Son, nor the Son except the Father,” etc.

[Col. 0091A]

Matthew, ch. III, 9. Vercelli: “and do not suppose.” Verona and Brixia: “and do not put yourselves forward.” The royal Gallican codex cited in St Hilary’s tractate on Psalm 65, reported by the Maurist editors, vol. I, p. 201, likewise has “put yourselves forward,” etc.

Matthew, ch. V, 11. Vercelli: “when they curse you and persecute you and say every … righteousness.” Verona: “when they cur… you and persec… and say every evil against you because of righteousness.” Saint-Germain: “they will curse you and persecute you and say every evil against you because of righteousness”; so also St Ambrose, Book I *On the Duties of Ministers*, ch. 16, p. 17, and Book II, ch. 3, p. 73. Hilary the deacon, published under Ambrose’s name, in his Commentary on St Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, p. 52: “when they persecute you and say every evil against you because of righteousness.” Brixia likewise: “they will persecute.”

[Col. 0091B]

Matthew, ch. X, 10. Vercelli: “nor staffs”; so read Stephanus’s 10 codices, Bodleian 4, Vesulian 1, Huntington 1, Ussher 2, Laud 2, and very many other most ancient witnesses, concerning which Mill writes at length. Luke 9:5 likewise agrees with this reading.

Matthew, ch. X, 42. Vercelli: “his reward will perish.” Verona: “his own reward will perish.” The Italic Vulgate at first read “your reward will perish,” Mill says in the *Prolegomena*, p. 42, together with St Cyprian. The present reading appears to be from Mark, transferred here long ago.

[Col. 0091C]

Matthew, ch. XIII, 13. Vercelli: “so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not hear.” Verona and Saint-Germain: “so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may hear and not understand.” Corbie: “so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not hear nor understand.” St Irenaeus: “so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not hear; understanding, they may not understand.”

Matthew, ch. XVI, 22. Vercelli: “Merciful to you, Lord, this shall not be”; so also St Hilary, Book VI *On the Trinity*, vol. II, p. 162. Verona: “Far be it from you; be gracious, Lord; this shall not be.” Brixia: “Be gracious to yourself, Lord,” etc.; and so also St Hilary, in the cited passage, in a certain Vatican codex, as also in his Commentary on this passage of Matthew.

[Col. 0091D]

Matthew, ch. XVII, 20. Vercelli: “kind of demon.” Verona: “kind of demons.” St Ambrose likewise, in Epistle 42 of the first class, p. 969, and Epistle 63, p. 1026, adds “of demons.”

Matthew, ch. XXV, 41. Vercelli: “which my Father prepared.” Verona and Corbie: “whom my Father prepared.” St Irenaeus, Book III against Heresies, vol. I, p. 221, and Book IV, p. 273: “whom my Father prepared beforehand”; and this is likewise the reading of the ancient Italic translation published by the distinguished Father Martianay.

Matthew, ch. XXV, 29. Vercelli, Verona, and Corbie: “what he has shall be taken away”; so also St Hilary, Commentary on Matthew, ch. 27.

John, ch. II, 3. Vercelli: “and they did not have wine, because the wine of the wedding feast had been consumed”; so also St Gaudentius, Sermon VIII, pp. 88 and 97—consult the distinguished Galeardi edition. Verona: “and they did not have wine, because the wine of the wedding feast had run out.” Corbie: “and they did not have wine, because the wine of the wedding feast was consumed.”

[Col. 0092A]

John, ch. III, 36. Vercelli: “he who is disobedient to the word concerning the Son.” St Cyprian, Book II against the Jews, ch. 27, p. 361: “he who does not obey the word concerning the Son.” A manuscript codex of the same work of St Cyprian at the cited place has: “he who is disobedient to the word concerning the Son.” Verona, Corbie, and Brixia: “but he who does not believe the Son.” St Augustine, *Enchiridion on Faith, Hope, and Love*, vol. VI, p. 209: “but he who does not believe in the Son.”

[Col. 0092B]

John, ch. VI, 38. Vercelli: “… who sent me, of the Father.” Verona: “For I came down from heaven not to do my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me.” Ambrosiaster, on the Epistle to the Romans, ch. 14, p. 104: “For I came down from heaven not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me—the Father.”

John, ch. XII, 35. Vercelli, Verona, and Corbie: “Still a little time.” Brixia: “Still a little of time.” The Greek text also adds χρόνον, “time,” a word absent from the Vulgate and from certain other codices.

John, ch. XIV, 7. Vercelli: “If you knew me, you knew my Father also.” Verona and Corbie: “If you knew me, you knew my Father also.” St Augustine, on John 14, Tractates 71 and 72, vol. III, part 2, p. 683: “If you knew me, you certainly knew my Father also.” Erasmus’s and Gallican manuscripts, as well as St Irenaeus, Book IV against Heresies, have “if you knew me.” So too St Hilary, Book VII *On the Trinity*, vol. II, p. 202.

[Col. 0092C]

John, ch. XIV, 10. Vercelli, Verona, and Brixia: “Do you not believe?” So likewise St Hilary, Book VII *On the Trinity*, vol. II, p. 202; certain manuscript codices; and St Ambrose, Book I, *Exposition of the Gospel according to Luke*, p. 1267. St Augustine, however, in a sermon to catechumens, vol. IV, p. 559, has: “Do you not recognize?”

John, ch. XVI, 14. Vercelli: “he glorified”; so also St Hilary, Book III *On the Trinity*, vol. II, p. 47. Brixia: “he will glorify.”

[Col. 0092D]

John, ch. XX, 22. Verona: “this”; so also St Ambrose, Exposition of Psalm 118, p. 1092.

John, ch. XX, 23. Vercelli:

> “If you forgive anyone’s sins, they shall be forgiven him; if you retain anyone’s sins, they shall be retained.”

Verona:

> “And those whose sins you retain, they shall be retained.”

So likewise St Ambrose, *Exhortation to Virginity*, ch. 5, and Book I *On Repentance*, ch. 2, p. 391. Gat.: “… they shall be forgiven them; and those whose sins you retain, they are retained.” Brixia: “If you forgive anyone’s sins, they are forgiven him; if you retain anyone’s sins, they shall be retained.” St Cyprian, Epistle 75, p. 202: “If you forgive anyone’s sins, they shall be forgiven him; and if you retain anyone’s sins, they shall be retained.”

Luke, ch. I, 50. Vercelli: “unto ages of ages.” Verona: “unto the ages of ages.” Corbie and Brescia: [Col. 0093A] “unto generation and generation”; Gat.: “in generation and generations.” Two Latin manuscript Bibles of the Queen of Sweden: “unto generations and generations.”

Luke, ch. II, 33. Vercelli, Verona, Corbie, and Brescia have *Joseph* after the word “was,” in place of “his father.” The *Joseph* has slipped in from the margin, as Mill conjectures in the *Prolegomena*, p. 44.

Luke, ch. II, 34. Vercelli: “is contradicted”; and so certain manuscript codices and editions of St. Jerome, in Epistle 120 to Hedibia.

Luke, ch. IV, 1. Vercelli and Verona: “from the Jordan.” Brescia: “from Jordan”; and so St. Ambrose, *On the Holy Spirit*, book I, ch. 9, p. 618.

Luke, ch. V, 20. Vercelli, Verona, and Corbie: “have been forgiven.” Brescia: “have been dismissed”; and so St. Ambrose, *On Faith*, book III, [Col. 0093B] ch. 2, p. 499.

Luke, ch. IX, 22. Vercelli: “and after the third day”; and so Tertullian, p. 435. Verona: “and after three days.”

Mark, ch. VIII, 38. Vercelli, Verona, and Brescia: “will be ashamed of him”; and so St. Ambrose, *On Faith*, book III, ch. 13, vol. II, p. 516, and St. Augustine, *Mirror from the Gospel according to Mark*, vol. III, part 1, p. 764.

Mark, ch. XIV, 56. Vercelli: “their testimonies were not equal.” The Greek, *Καὶ ἴσαι αἱ μαρτυρίαι οὐκ ἦσαν*, literally reads: “and the testimonies were not equal.”

Luke, ch. II, 22. Vercelli: “and when they had been fulfilled.” St. Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book VII, vol. I, p. [Col. 0093C] 187: “when they had been completed.” St. Ambrose, *On Abraham*, book II, vol. I, p. 335: “when the forty days were being completed.”

Matthew, ch. V, 4. Vercelli: “they shall possess the earth by inheritance.” Brescia: “they shall inherit the earth”; and so St. Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book III, p. 210, and St. Cyprian, *Testimonies*, book III, ch. 5, p. 373.

Matthew, ch. V, 7. Vercelli: “. . . . . . . . . . God will show mercy.” The lacuna is supplied from Verona and Saint-Germain, which read: “God will show mercy to them”; and so St. Ambrose, *On the Duties of Ministers*, ch. 16, p. 17.

Matthew, ch. X, 23. Vercelli, Verona, and Corbie, after the words “flee into another,” have: “if in [Col. 0093D] another [Vercelli: ‘into the other’] they persecute you, flee into another [Corbie: ‘into the other’].” Some handwritten Greek codices, mentioned by Mill in the *Various Readings*, similarly add after “flee into another”: “if they have persecuted you in the other, flee into another.” St. Ambrose likewise, in *On Flight from the World*, ch. 4, p. 425: “if in another they persecute you, flee into another”; and so the Saxon version.

Matthew, ch. XXI, 37. Vercelli, Verona, and Corbie: “his only Son”; and so St. Irenaeus, St. Ambrose, and Lucifer of Cagliari. Brescia likewise has: “his only-begotten Son.”

Matthew, ch. XXI, 37. Vercelli and Verona: “he sent to them”; and so Lucifer of Cagliari, book II, *For St. Athanasius*. Likewise St. Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book IV, vol. I, p. 277, and St. Ambrose, *On Faith*, book V, ch. 7, p. 567: “he sent to them.”

Matthew, ch. XXIV, 36. Vercelli and Brescia have: “neither the angels of heaven, nor the Son.” Verona and Corbie: “neither the angels of heaven [Corbie: ‘but not,’ etc.] nor the Son,” from Mark, who in ch. XIII, 32 adds “nor the Son.” These words are found as transferred into Matthew in the Cambridge codex also, Paris Chrysostom codex 6, and certain others reported by Mill in the *Various Readings*. Saints Hilary, Ambrose, Augustine, and Theophylact interpret these same words here; nevertheless one cannot rightly infer from this that they had the same words in their books. For they borrowed them from Mark in order to answer the Arians. [Col. 0094B] St. Jerome observed that they were absent from the books of Origen and Pierius. They are nevertheless found in Martianay’s Old Vulgate. This passage was the seedbed of great disputes between Catholics and Arians, since the latter falsely inferred from it that Jesus was not God, because there was something whose knowledge escaped him. Answering this objection, St. Ambrose says in *On Faith*, book V, ch. 8: “The ancient Greek codices [of Mark] do not have, ‘which not even the Son knows’; but it is not surprising if those who have interpolated the divine Scriptures falsified this also.” Yet all Greek and Latin codices surviving in our age, both handwritten and printed, unanimously read these words in Mark, and many also in Matthew. The other Fathers acknowledge them besides.

John, ch. III, 6. Vercelli adds: “because what is born [Col. 0094C] of the flesh.” Verona: “because what is born of the flesh.” Tertullian, *On the Flesh of Christ*, ch. 18; Ambrose, *On the Holy Spirit*, book III, ch. 11; and a most ancient codex of the Gospels in the Bodleian Library likewise add: “because what is born of the flesh.”

John, ch. III, 6. Vercelli adds: “because God is spirit, and is born of God.” Corbie: “because God is Spirit.” St. Ambrose, *On the Holy Spirit*, book III, vol. II, p. 677, has: “because God is spirit.”

John, ch. VI, 57. Vercelli adds at the end of the verse: “if a man receives the body of the Son of Man, as the bread of life, he shall have life in him.” The ancient Greek-Latin Cambridge codex, the eighth of Henri Estienne, Victorinus of Africa, and other Fathers likewise read: [Col. 0094D] “as the Father is in me, and I in the Father. Amen, amen, I say to you: Unless you receive the body of the Son of Man as the bread of life, and unless you drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves. He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life.”

Mark, ch. VI, 11. Vercelli adds: “Amen, I say to you: it shall be more lenient for Sodom and Gomorrah on the day of judgment than for that city.” Brescia: “Amen, I say to you: it shall be more tolerable for Sodom or Gomorrah on the day of judgment than for that city”; and so at the end of this verse the Greek text adds: “Amen, I say to you: it shall be more tolerable for the land of the Sodomites and Gomorrheans on the day of judgment than for that city.” Yet these words are taken from Matthew, ch. X, 15, [Col. 0095A] and are not found in many of the best Greek codices.

Mark, ch. XV, 3. Vercelli adds at the end of the verse: “But he was answering nothing”; and so does a vast number of Greek books in this place: *Αὐτὸς δὲ οὐδὲν ἀπεκρίνατο*, that is, “But he answered nothing”; likewise the Complutensian, Vechelian, Armenian, Ethiopic, and many other books. The scribes seem to have added it.

Luke, ch. XXIV, 13. Vercelli: “whose name was Emmaus.” Verona: “named Cleophas, and Emmaus.” Corbie: “named Emmaus and Cleophas.” See St. Ambrose’s commentary on the Gospel of St. Luke at this point, where he mentions this very notable variant reading and adduces books favoring other readings against our codices.

Matthew, ch. VIII, 20. In Vercelli, Verona, and [Col. 0095B] Corbie, after “nests” is added: “where they may rest.” So also Ambrose, *Hexaemeron*, book VI, ch. 8, p. 131.

Matthew, ch. XVI, 13. Vercelli, Verona, Corbie, Saint-Germain, and Brescia: “Whom me”; and so St. Hilary, *Treatise on Psalm* CXIX, vol. I, p. 419, and St. Ambrose, *On the Mystery of the Incarnation of the Lord*, ch. 4, p. 709.

Matthew, ch. XXII, 4. Vercelli, Verona, and Brescia: “and the fattened animals have been killed”; and so Lucifer of Cagliari, book II, *For St. Athanasius*. Saint-Germain: “and my fattened animals have been killed,” etc.

Matthew, ch. XXII, 45. Vercelli, Verona, and Brescia add: “in the Spirit.” So St. Cyprian, p. 202, and St. Ambrose, *On Faith*, book V, ch. [Col. 0095C] 8, and *On the Holy Spirit*, book III, ch. 15, p. 687.

Matthew, ch. XXIV, 7. Vercelli and Verona: “in every place.” St. Cyprian: “in individual places.”

Matthew, ch. XXVI, 70. In Vercelli, after “you say,” is added: “nor do I know”; in Verona, “nor do I understand”; in St. Cyprian, p. 636, “nor do I know you.”

Matthew, ch. XXVII, 28. Vercelli: “and they clothed him in a purple tunic, and wrapped a scarlet cloak around him.” Verona: “and they clothed him in a purple tunic, and wrapped a scarlet cloak around him.” St. Ambrose, *Exposition of the Gospel according to Luke*, book X, vol. I, p. 1526: “but he is clothed by the soldiers in a scarlet cloak and a purple tunic.”

John, ch. XI, 39. Vercelli: “the sister of Lazarus,” omitting the words “who had died.” In Verona likewise “his sister, who had died” [Col. 0095D] is absent. So also Ambrose, *Exposition of Psalm* XXXVII, p. 841.

Luke, ch. VI, 21. Vercelli: “Blessed are you who now hunger and thirst,” etc. Verona: “Blessed are those who now hunger and thirst, for they shall be filled.” Corbie: “Blessed are those who now hunger and thirst, for they shall be filled”; and so St. Ambrose, *On the Duties of Ministers*, book II, ch. IV, p. 74, and *On Cain and Abel*, book I, ch. 5, p. 192.

Luke, ch. X, 7. Vercelli: “which are set before them.” St. Augustine, *On the Work of Monks*, vol. VI, p. 480: “which are from them.”

Mark, ch. I, 10. In Vercelli, after “descending” is added “upon him”; in Corbie, “over him”; [Col. 0096A] in Brescia, “upon him.” So also in certain manuscripts of the Holy Bible of St. Jerome.

Mark, ch. II, 17. Vercelli and the manuscripts: “but sinners unto repentance.” Many Greek codices add here “unto repentance”; but more do not. See Mill here. It is an addition taken from Matthew, ch. IX, 13.

Luke, ch. IX, 56. After “souls” is added “of men” in Vercelli, Verona, and Brescia; and so St. Cyprian, p. 211, and St. Ambrose, *On Penance*, book I, ch. 16.

Matthew, ch. V, 32. In Vercelli and Verona the words “and whoever marries the divorced woman commits adultery” are absent. St. Augustine observed, in Mill, that the words “and whoever marries the divorced woman commits adultery” are not read in certain Latin [Col. 0096B] codices. They are also absent from the ancient Greek-Latin Cambridge codex.

Matthew, ch. VI, 10. In Vercelli and Verona the word “as” is absent; and so in Tertullian, p. 131, and St. Augustine, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book IV, vol. X, part 1, p. 483.

Matthew, ch. XXIII, v. 14. Verse 14 is absent in Vercelli and Corbie; but in Brescia verse 13 is placed after verse 14. Ancient codices differ at this point. St. Chrysostom, Euthymius, Theophylact, the author of the *Incomplete Work on Matthew*, most Greek printed and handwritten codices, transpose verse 13 and place it after verse 14. Others place it before; others omit it entirely, such as the Greek-Latin Cambridge codex, Colbert 2, the Saxon version, Arabic manuscripts, and certain ancient [Col. 0096C] Latin codices cited by Martianay and Brugensis here. Origen and St. Jerome do not read it; and in Eusebius’s canon it is assigned to Luke, ch. XI, v. 52. Hence there is room for the conjecture that it was transferred from Luke into Matthew.

Matthew, ch. XXVI, v. 64. The word “God” is absent in Vercelli, Verona, Corbie, and Brescia; also in St. Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book I, vol. II, p. 20, and St. Ambrose, *On Faith*, book II, ch. 12, p. 490.

Matthew, ch. XXVII, v. 9. “Jeremiah” is absent in Vercelli and Verona. Lucas Brugensis, Jansen, Maldonatus, and Baronius say that the Evangelist here gave no prophet’s name, and that “Jeremiah” was supplied at a scribe’s discretion and thereafter retained out of deference to antiquity. Yet there are Greek, Syriac, Arabic, [Col. 0096D] and Persian codices in Mill’s *Various Readings*, likewise St. Augustine, *Harmony of the Gospels*, book III, ch. 7, and certain Latin codices in which it is not read at all—whether they were copied from more ancient exemplars in which it was absent, or whether the name was erased by them because it was inappropriate to the passage.

John, ch. VIII, v. 1. In the Vercelli and Brescia codices the first twelve verses of this chapter are absent. They are present in Corbie, Gat., and the manuscripts. In the Verona codex, however, the two pages containing them were erased; the margins still appear in the manuscript. Moreover, in very many Greek and Latin codices, even in St. Jerome’s age, they were absent, as he himself testifies in *Against the Pelagians*, book II, ch. 6, in these words: “In the Gospel according to John, in many Greek and Latin codices [Col. 0097A] the account of the adulterous woman is not found,” etc. Most Greek Fathers do not read these verses. Of the twenty-three interpreters collected in the Greek Catena, no one explained them. Origen, St. Chrysostom, Nonnus, and the rest omitted them. Maldonatus asserts that, among the Greek exemplars which he consulted, there was none in which this narrative was read except one only, containing the commentaries of Leontius; indeed, Leontius himself wholly passes it over in his commentaries, and the Greek text appended to such commentaries is marked with obeli at this point, so that one may understand the narrative to be apocryphal. Mill cites other codices lacking this narrative. The Armenians entirely removed it from their Bibles. The Syriac version in the Paris and London Polyglots, and Ulfilas’s ancient [Col. 0097B] Gothic version, do not contain it.

Certain ancient Greek codices do not have it in this place; others place it at the end of Luke, ch. XXI, such as the Leicester codex in Mill and Paris 6 in Kuster; others at the end of the Gospel, such as Royal codices 1879 and 1883. In some it is distinguished from the remaining text by special marks; in others it is read in the margin of the book or written in smaller letters. Euthymius, flourishing at the beginning of the twelfth century, explains it in his commentaries; but he asserts that it is absent from books of the best authority or marked with an obelus, and therefore, he says, it seems to have been written in or added. St. Chrysostom, whom the defenders of this narrative cite, does indeed mention the adulterous woman in the Latin translation of Homily LX on John, but by no means in the Greek, where he says only that the Pharisees [Col. 0097C] asked Jesus whether it was lawful to dismiss a wife for any cause.

Eusebius relates in *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, ch. 39, or the last chapter, that Papias, a disciple of John the Evangelist, collected many sayings and discourses from the mouths of the apostles which were not read in the books of the Gospels; and among the rest, the story of a woman accused before the Lord of many shameful acts. “This story,” Eusebius says, “is contained in the Gospel according to the Hebrews.” These words of Eusebius have raised a difficulty for certain learned men: whether the present narrative of the adulteress first came from John, or from Papias, a man of no intelligence, or finally from the Gospel of the Hebrews, which, it is established, contained many uncertain and apocryphal matters. An immense number of variant readings, more frequent in the first twelve verses of this chapter than elsewhere in this Gospel, likewise militates against its [Col. 0097D] authenticity, as may be seen in Sixtus of Siena, Grotius, Beza, Hammond, Jean Le Clerc, and Cajetan. Add to these the consensus of the Greek and Eastern churches, in many of whose books it is absent, as Selden testifies in *On Hebrew Wives*, book III, ch. 11. These are the objections advanced by the heretics of our age against the authenticity of this history.

We answer them by opposing codices to codices—Greek to Greek, Latin and Eastern to Latin and Eastern. Of the seventeen handwritten Greek books possessed by Theodore Beza, only one lacked this narrative. He had at hand the most celebrated and ancient Cambridge codex, in which it was formerly read. All the books used by Robert Estienne, no fewer than sixteen, all printed books, and innumerable handwritten ones—most of those seen by Mill—contained it. Of Latin codices in which it is absent, we know only Vercelli and Brescia. As to Syriac, Arabic, and Coptic copies, perhaps more contain it than omit it.

The Greek Fathers who interpreted John passed over this passage, either because it was clearer than [Col. 0098A] it needed explanation, or because it was absent from their books. Tatian, who flourished about A.D. 160, sixty years after the death of John the Evangelist, and Ammonius, writing about A.D. 220, 120 years after John, recognized the narrative as canonical and included it in the Gospel harmony composed by each, from which Eusebius drew the tables inserted into his canons. St. Jerome fully accepts it in *Against the Pelagians*, book II, since he turns it against the Pelagians themselves. St. Augustine uses it more than once in his books: here, in Tractate 32; in *On Adulterous Marriages*, book II, chs. 6 and 7; in *On True and False Penance*, ch. 13; in Epistle formerly 54, now 153; in *Harmony of the Evangelists*, ch. 10; and elsewhere. The ancient author of the Apostolic Constitutions, book II, ch. 24, mentions it; so also does the Synopsis attributed to St. Athanasius, as do St. Ambrose, *On the Holy Spirit*, book III, ch. [Col. 0098C] [uncertain omission in the source], book VII, Epistle 58, and book IX, Epistle 76, and the other Latin Fathers as occasion required. Finally, since the Council of Trent, session 4, *On the Canonical Scriptures*, pronounced all and each of the matters contained in copies of the Vulgate to be canonical, it admitted this passage along with the rest into the canon. Most learned critics, even heterodox ones—Calvin, Gomarus, Selden, *On Hebrew Wives*, book [III], ch. 11, Mill in his *Notes on the New Testament*, and others—also receive it as authentic, says Calmet on this passage.

Whence then is it that the ancient Vercelli and Brescia books, and others, especially Greek ones, do not contain this passage? St. Augustine, *On Adulterous Marriages*, book II, ch. 7, says that certain persons of little faith, or rather enemies of the true faith, fearing, I suppose, that impunity for sin might be granted [Col. 0098D] to their wives, removed from their codices what the Lord did in forgiving the adulteress—as if he who said, “From now on, do not sin,” had granted permission to sin. Others judged that it had migrated from the Gospel according to the Hebrews into John’s Gospel, either having been written by Papias in the margin of the book and then having slipped into the text. The words of Eusebius which we have cited gave occasion to these conjectures. But it is not sufficiently clear whether Eusebius there speaks of this adulterous woman, writing only that Papias had related the story of a woman accused before the Lord of many shameful acts, which story was contained in the Gospel according to the Hebrews. Eusebius does not mention a woman accused solely of adultery; nor do we learn from any evidence that this narrative was recounted in [Col. 0099A] the Gospel according to the Hebrews.

Grotius, who denies that it was first written by John, says that it was transmitted orally to the disciples by the apostles, but omitted from the Gospels because it might readily have given occasion for the slander of denouncing Christians before magistrates as persons overthrowing public judgments, upon which the safety of the commonwealth appears to depend. Mill, on the contrary, defends the position in *Prolegomena* 25, 252, 253, and 892 that the writer of the Gospel according to the Hebrews narrated it on the authority of those who had learned from the apostles, embellishing it with various additions, as commonly happens in such matters; that John then wrote it in his Gospel with the most exact truth, as he himself had been a witness of the event, wholly disregarding or being ignorant of the Gospel according to the Hebrews; [Col. 0099B] and that, afterward, when some superficial person had thought this narrative added to John’s Gospel from the Gospel according to the Hebrews, he marked it with an obelus as doubtful, and it was finally expunged by another person bolder still. Thus it gradually began to be absent from Greek codices; and, being regarded only as an apocryphal passage, it was corrupted by license freely exercised in many places and copied with less care and attention than the remaining parts of the Gospel. Hence arose the many variant readings found in this passage. Thus Calmet.

John, ch. XII, 47. At the first occurrence, “not” is absent in Vercelli, Verona, and Brescia; and so in St. Ambrose.

John, ch. XIII, 32. The words “if God has been glorified in him” are absent in Vercelli, Verona, and Corbie; and so in St. Ambrose, *On Faith*, book IV, ch. 10, p. 545, [Col. 0099C] and book V, p. 571, no. 113.

John, ch. XIV, 13. “The Father” is absent in Vercelli, Gat., the manuscripts, and Brescia. Verona has: “you shall ask of him”; and so St. Ambrose, *On Faith*, book V, ch. 5, p. 563.

John, ch. XVII, 18. Vercelli, Verona, and Brescia have, at both the first and second occurrence, “into this world”; and so St. Ambrose.

Luke, ch. III, 25. In Vercelli and Verona, “who was of Mattathias, who was of Amos” is absent. St. Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, ch. 33, p. 333, and the Verona codex acknowledge only seventy-two generations in the genealogy of the Lord according to Luke. Now seventy-six are counted. Thus some of these generations were then considered additional. Consult St. Ambrose, *Exposition of the Gospel according to Luke*, book III, no. 15, p. 1318, and likewise no. 16 of the Maurist edition, who likewise seems to favor the Verona codex.

Luke, ch. IV, 4. The words “onto a high mountain” are absent in Verona and in certain Greek copies, likewise in two manuscript Bibles of the Queen of Sweden reported in the Holy Bible of St. Jerome. They are also absent in Vercelli. But in their place it has: “Jerusalem, and set him upon the pinnacle of the temple.”

Luke, ch. VII, 31. The words “but the Lord said” are absent in Vercelli, Verona, Corbie, Gat., and the manuscripts; and so in certain Greek copies and in some manuscript copies of the Holy Bible of St. Jerome.

[Col. 0100A] Luke, ch. XXIV, 36. In Vercelli and Verona, “He says to them: Peace to you; it is I; do not be afraid” is absent. Moreover, the words “It is I; do not be afraid” are also absent in the Greek text. Yet they are read by the Coptic, Syriac, Persian, Arabic, Ethiopic, and Armenian versions, etc., and by Saints Ambrose and Augustine.

Matthew, ch. VII, v. 13. Vercelli and Verona: “how broad and spacious is the way.” St. Jerome, in Epistle 148, in one manuscript: “how broad and spacious the way is.” But in the Verona edition, vol. I, p. 1093: “how spacious the way.” St. Ambrose, *Exposition of the Gospel according to Luke*, book IV, p. 1344: “broad and spacious,” referring to the way. One manuscript of St. Augustine, *On the Sermon of the Lord*: “how broad the gate.”

Matthew, ch. VIII, 25. The words “his disciples” are absent in Vercelli and Corbie; and so in certain Latin manuscript [Col. 0100B] copies of the Holy Bible of the Queen of Sweden.

Matthew, ch. X, 19. In Vercelli and Verona the words “how” and “or” are omitted; and so in St. Cyprian’s Epistle 56 to the Thibaritans, *On Exhortation to Martyrdom*, p. 129.

Matthew, ch. XI, 2. Vercelli: “sending di . . . pul . . . his”; supply the lacuna from Verona and Brescia: “sending his disciples.” The Greek-Latin Cambridge codex has: “sending through his disciples.” The Gothic, Armenian, Persian, and Syriac versions agree. Juvencus, Ambrose, and Hilary, cited by Mill, *Prolegomena* 387, do not state the number of disciples sent by John.

Matthew, ch. XVI, 21. In Vercelli and Corbie, “scribes” is absent; and so in St. Irenaeus.

[Col. 0100C] Matthew, ch. XXIII, 4. In Vercelli and Verona the words “and unbearable” are absent; and so in the Syriac, Persian, Arabic, and Ethiopic versions and in Saints Irenaeus and Ambrose.

John, ch. I, v. 27. In Vercelli the second occurrence of “who” is absent; and so in the works of St. Cyprian. In Verona the words “who was made before me” are absent; and so in the Ethiopic and Coptic versions and other codices.

John, ch. V, 36. In Vercelli “which I do” is omitted; and so in the Vatican exemplar and St. Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book VI. In Verona only “I” is absent; and so in St. Hilary, vol. II, p. 152.

John, ch. XI, 37. “Born” is absent in Vercelli, Verona, and Brescia; and so in most Greek exemplars of better authority, as well as in certain manuscripts of the Holy Library of St. Jerome.

[Col. 0100D] John, ch. XVIII, 21. The second occurrence of “one” is absent in Vercelli and Verona, and likewise in St. Hilary’s manuscripts of *On the Trinity*, book VIII, vol. II, p. 217.

Luke, ch. IX, 23. Vercelli: “Let him deny himself and follow me,” omitting the words “and take up his cross daily.” Verona: “Let him deny himself, and, having taken up his cross, follow me.” Many ancient codices cited by Mill, *Various Readings*, do not have “daily.” Some also omit the entire clause, “let him take up his cross daily.” But the Syriac, Gothic, Vulgate versions and certain Latin copies contain it.

Luke, ch. XII, 27. In Vercelli, Verona, and Vienna, after “lilies” is added “of the field”; and so also certain editions of St. Augustine’s *Mirror from the Gospel according to Luke* read. [Col. 0101A]

Luke, ch. XII, 31. Before “kingdom,” “first” is absent in Vercelli, Verona, Corbie, the manuscripts, Gat., and Brescia; and so in other ancient Bibles, in the Greek text, and in St. Augustine’s *Mirror from the Gospel according to Luke*, vol. III, part 1, p. 771.

Luke, ch. XII, 31. The words “and his righteousness” are absent in Vercelli, Verona, Gat., Vienna, and Brescia; and so in the ancient Corbie Bibles, in the Greek text, and in the passage of St. Augustine just cited.

Luke, ch. XII, 35. Vercelli: “and let loins be,” etc. Verona, Corbie, Vienna, and Brescia: “but let loins be,” etc. St. Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book IV, vol. I, p. 278: “therefore let loins be,” etc.

Luke, ch. XXIV, 32. Omitting the words “as he spoke [Col. 0101B] on the way, and,” Vercelli has: “when he opened the Scriptures to us.” Verona: “when he opened the Scriptures to us”; and so St. Ambrose, *On the Institution of Virgins*, ch. 11, p. 266, and *Exposition of Psalm* XXXVIII, p. 849.

Luke, ch. XXIV, 46. The words “and thus it was necessary” are absent in Vercelli, Verona, Gat., and the manuscripts; and so in St. Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book III, vol. I, p. 206.

Mark, ch. XIV, 62. In Vercelli and Brescia, after “power,” “of God” is absent; and so in the Greek text, in ancient Corbie Bibles, in several manuscripts of the Holy Library of St. Jerome, and in St. Augustine, *Harmony of the Evangelists*, book III, vol. III, part 2, p. 114.

Matthew, ch. XXI, 31. Vercelli: “. . . . . . . . go before”; [Col. 0101C] supply the lacuna from Brescia, which has “go before”; and so St. Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book IV, vol. I, p. 257, and St. Zeno of Verona, book II, tract 14, *On Judas*, according to the reading of certain codices and editions.

Title of the Gospel of St. Luke. In Vercelli and Corbie: “The Gospel according to Lucanus”; Verona has: “The Gospel according to Lucan.” Gat.: “The Gospel *kata Lucam* [according to Luke].” Brescia: “The Gospel according to Lucan.” In the book of the Four Gospels, whose variant readings Calmet published at the end of his commentary on Revelation, he is likewise called Lucanus.

John, ch. XIV, 19. Vercelli, Verona, and Brescia: “you shall see me”; and so the Greek *θεωρεῖτε*, “you shall see,” if that word is understood in the second future: “because I live,” *ζῶ*—“I shall live, I shall rise from death. And you shall live: our enemies shall not kill you.”

Luke, ch. XV, 13. Vercelli: “living”; and so St. Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book IV, vol. I, p. 280.

Matthew, ch. VII, 2. Vercelli, Verona, and Saint-Germain: “it shall be judged concerning you”; and so Tertullian, p. 556.

Matthew, ch. VII, 12. Vercelli, Verona, and Saint-Germain add “good things”; and so St. Cyprian, p. 424. St. Augustine, *City of God*, book XIV, ch. 8, p. 356, omits “good things,” but adds: “Because of common usage, some translators added ‘good,’ and interpreted it thus: ‘Whatever good things you wish men to do to you,’ etc.; but in the Greek Gospel from which it was translated into Latin, ‘good’ is not read.”

John, ch. I, 3. Vercelli, Verona, Corbie, and Brescia read with this punctuation: “and without him was made nothing. That which was made,” etc.; and so St. Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book III, in certain manuscripts; Tertullian, *Against Hermogenes*; St. Cyprian, *Testimonies against the Jews to Quirinus*, book II, ch. 3, p. 352; St. Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book I, vol. II, p. 7, and book II, p. 37; and St. Ambrose, *On Faith*, book III, vol. II, p. 504.

John, ch. I, 26. Vercelli, Verona, and Brescia: “stands”; and so St. Cyprian, *Against the Jews*, book II, ch. 19, p. 359; St. Ambrose, *On Cain and Abel*, p. 198, and Epistle 33, first class, [Col. 0102B] p. 921.

Matthew, ch. IX, 2. Vercelli, Verona, Saint-Germain, and Brescia: “be of good courage”; and so St. Hilary and Orosius. But St. Cyprian, p. 644, has “be of good heart.”

John, ch. I, 27. Vercelli, Verona, and Brescia: “comes”; and so St. Ambrose, *On Faith*, book V, ch. 19, p. 593, and *On the Blessing of the Patriarchs*, ch. 4, p. 519. St. Cyprian has “coming.”

John, ch. VI, 5. Vercelli: “he says to Philip”; Verona: “Philip says”; Brescia: “he says,” etc. St. Augustine, Sermon 2, *On the Temptation of Abraham*, vol. V, part 1, p. 65: “for he says to Philip.”

John, ch. I, 14. Vercelli, Verona, Corbie, [Col. 0102C] and Brescia: “grace and truth”; and so St. Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book I, no. 10. The Greek text and St. Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book I, vol. I, p. 42, likewise have “truth.”

John, ch. II, 19. Vercelli: “Dissolve this temple, and in three days I shall raise it again.” Verona: “Dissolve this temple and in three days I shall raise it.” Brescia: “Destroy this temple,” etc. St. Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book IV, vol. I, p. 300: “Dissolve this temple, and in three days I shall raise it.” St. Cyprian, *On Mounts Sinai and Zion against the Jews*, p. 494: “Destroy,” etc.

John, ch. X, v. 36. Vercelli: “because he blasphemes”; Verona and the manuscripts: “because he blasphemes.” St. Cyprian has “because,” etc. In one manuscript of St. Cyprian “he blasphemes” [Col. 0102D] is read; in another, “he blasphemed.”

John, ch. X, 38. Vercelli: “because the Father is in me,” etc. Verona and Corbie: “because the Father is in me, and I in him.” Brescia: “because the Father is in me, and I into him.” St. Cyprian: “because the Father is in me, and I in him.”

John, ch. XI, 11. Vercelli: “I raise.” Verona, Corbie, and Brescia: “I may raise.” Gat.: “I may awaken”; and so two manuscripts of the Holy Library of St. Jerome. Observe, however, that one has “I may raise,” with the prefix *ex-* deleted upon later correction.

Luke, ch. I, 70. Vercelli: “through the mouth of the holy P . . . h . . . . . rum his . . .”; supply the lacuna from Brescia: “through the mouth of his holy prophets.” Verona: “through the mouth [Col. 0103A] of his holy prophets.” Corbie: “through the mouth of holy prophets.” Tertullian, pp. 187 and 188: “through the mouth of prophets.”

Luke, ch. II, 14. Vercelli: “in the high . . .”; supply the lacuna from Gat. and Brescia, which have “in the highest”; and so St. Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book III, vol. I, p. 186, and St. Jerome, *Commentaries on Isaiah*, book I, ch. 2, vol. IV, p. 34.

Luke, ch. II, 14. Vercelli: “upon earth”; and so one manuscript of St. Jerome’s *Commentaries on Isaiah*, book I, ch. 2.

[Col. 0103A]

## BLANCHINI’S LETTER TO JOSEPH, COUNT OF THE HOLY ROMAN EMPIRE OF THUN AND HOHENSTEIN, BISHOP OF GURK

Joseph Blanchini of Verona, priest of the Congregation of the Roman Oratory, wishes well-being to Joseph, Count of Thun and Hohenstein of the Holy Roman Empire, most excellent Bishop of Gurk. [Col. 0103B]

Some persons, most wise Prelate, are accustomed to press too strongly certain statements of the holy Fathers. They say that, as soon as the light of the Gospel shone upon the Gentiles, and Greeks, Latins, and barbarians alike had been instructed by the apostles in Christ’s teaching, almost countless versions of the divine Scriptures arose; under their guidance the health-giving waters of God’s utterances flowed out for all peoples to drink. Although the seeds of apostolic preaching, watered by those heavenly streams, nourished the unity of faith and the wisdom and knowledge of its mysteries like a grain of mustard seed when first sown among the Gentiles by those sowers of the Lord’s field, who were commanded, “Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature”; and although, already under Nero’s rule, the divine proclamation of the Law had penetrated almost to the furthest regions of the world, as Paul rejoiced in writing to the Romans (ch. I, v. 8)—yet I can scarcely, indeed not even scarcely, persuade myself that innumerable vernacular translations, even translations in nearly every nation’s own tongue, already existed at that time. Nor do I think that all those writers have grasped the mind of the holy Fathers who, in defense of their preconceived opinion, have brought forward certain testimonies from them which do nothing for the point at issue, or which require a non-hyperbolic interpretation. Here, most learned sir, I wish to adduce the principal passages [Col. 0103D] in which they suppose great force to reside, but which, in my judgment, prove nothing.

Eusebius Pamphilus, *Oration on the Praises of Constantine*, Mainz edition, 1672, p. 662, letters C–D.

> But that he promised, and spoke in word, and accomplished in deed, that they would become fishers of men; and that he bestowed upon them such excellence and power that they might compose writings and hand down books, and might prevail so greatly that, translated throughout the whole inhabited world into every language, both barbarian and Greek, they should be studied among all nations and believed to contain divine oracles—how greatly this serves as a clear demonstration of his divinity!

[Col. 0104A]

But what Christ promised them—that he would make the Apostles fishers of men—he not only said in words, but abundantly fulfilled in fact. He endowed them with such force and power that they wrote and published books; and these books had such authority that, translated into all the languages alike of Greeks and barbarians, they were eagerly learned by every nation everywhere, and the contents of them were believed to be divine oracles. How greatly this contributes to a clear declaration of his divinity!

The same Eusebius, in a fragment cited in Greek and Latin by John Grabe in his Notes on the *Spicilegium of the Fathers*, second century, p. 252.

> His name shines forth throughout the whole inhabited world, and his teaching illumines human souls through the Scripture of the Gospel which he delivered, translated into every language, Greek as well as barbarian, and preached each day so as to be heard by all nations.

Eusebius here speaks of John the son of Zebedee, whose name, he says, is celebrated throughout the whole world, and whose teaching enlightens human minds, through the Scripture of the Gospel delivered to them, which has been translated into every language, Greek and barbarian alike, and is preached daily so that all nations may hear it.

Saint John Chrysostom, Homily LXXX, or LXXXI in some editions, on Matthew, according to the Montfaucon edition, vol. VII, p. 767, letter B.

> That a prostitute woman poured out oil in the house of a certain leper, [Col. 0104C] while twelve men were present—this all men sing throughout the inhabited world; and so much time has passed, yet the memory of what occurred has not faded. Rather, Persians, Indians, Scythians, Thracians, Sauromatians, the race of the Moors, and those inhabiting the British islands, carry abroad the report of what happened secretly in a house in Judaea through a woman who had lived as a prostitute.

That a prostitute poured out oil in the house of a leper, with twelve men present, all people sing throughout the world; and after so long a time the memory of the deed has not diminished. Rather, Persians, Indians, Scythians, Thracians, Sauromatians, Moors, and those who inhabit the British islands proclaim what was done in Judaea, in a certain house and not publicly, by a prostitute.

[Col. 0104D] Saint John Chrysostom, Homily II—Homily I in some editions—on Saint John the Evangelist, according to the Montfaucon edition, vol. VIII, p. 10, letter B.

> Was it not reasonable that all those things should be extinguished and utterly vanish? Certainly: reasonably and as justice required. But not so the things belonging to that unlearned and illiterate man. Syrians, Indians, Persians, Ethiopians, and countless other nations, having translated into their own language the doctrines introduced by him, have learned, though barbarians, to philosophize.

After the same Saint John Chrysostom had spoken of Pythagorean and Platonic teachings, he adds:

> Was it not right that those things should be utterly extinguished and destroyed? Certainly, rightly and deservedly, as reason required. But not so the things belonging to that uneducated and illiterate man: [Col. 0105A] rather, Syrians, Egyptians, Indians, Persians, Ethiopians, and innumerable other nations, translating into their own tongue the doctrines introduced by him, have learned to philosophize, although they were barbarians.

Saint Jerome, in his Commentary on Psalm LXXXVI: “The Lord shall recount in the Scriptures of the peoples”—that is, in the Holy Scriptures. This Scripture is read to all peoples, so that all may understand.
