The same writer, in the Preface to the Four Gospels addressed to Damasus:

> I pass over, he says, those manuscripts which the perverse contention of a few persons claims are called after Lucian and Hesychius. Certainly they were permitted neither to amend anything in the whole Old Testament after the Seventy translators, nor did their amendment profit the New Testament; since Scripture, previously translated into the languages of many nations, teaches that the things added are false. [Col. 0105B]

Saint Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, book II, chapter 5, says:

> Thus it came about that even the divine Scripture, by which aid is given to such great diseases of human wills, having proceeded from one language, in which it could suitably be disseminated throughout the world, became widely known among the nations for salvation through the various languages of translators.

Blessed Theodoret, Sermon V, *On Human Nature*, p. 555, letters C–D, Paris, 1642.

> Who now leads the Stoic school? Who maintains the teaching of the Stagirite [Aristotle]? Who lives under Plato’s laws? Who has embraced the constitution written by him? Yet you will be unable to point out to us any teacher of these doctrines. But we clearly demonstrate the strength of apostolic and prophetic [Col. 0105C] doctrines; for the whole world beneath the sun is full of these teachings. And the language of the Hebrews has been translated not only into that of the Greeks, but also into those of the Romans, Egyptians, Persians, Indians, Armenians, Scythians, and Sauromatians—and, to say it briefly, into every language used continually by all nations.

Who today presides over the Stoic sect? Who upholds the teaching of the Stagirite? Where are those who govern states according to Plato’s laws, or who have embraced the constitution composed by him? Certainly you cannot show us a teacher of any of those doctrines. But we clearly show you the force and strength of **APOSTOLIC AND PROPHETIC DOCTRINE**. For the whole earth beneath [Col. 0105D] the sun is filled with these teachings. And the Hebrew language (*καὶ ἡ Ἑβραίων φωνή*, “and the language of the Hebrews”) has been rendered not merely into the language of the Greeks, but also into those of the Romans, Egyptians, Persians, Indians, Armenians, Scythians, and Sarmatians; indeed, to say it once for all, into every language used by nations to this day.

Saint Anastasius of Sinai, in the book entitled *Ὁδηγός* (*Guide*), chapter XXII.

> Christianity, then, is an uncomplicated faith, and one ought to receive and hear every Scripture—especially its doctrinal portions—in simplicity and uprightness of heart. For we know that the evangelical and apostolic writings are unadulterated. . . . Since the Gospel has been disseminated and written [Col. 0106A] in the letters of seventy-two languages and nations, it is impossible for it to suffer fraud, diminution, or addition. For even if someone attempted to adulterate the books in one or even two languages, this fraud would immediately be exposed by the other seventy languages.

Therefore the Christians’ faith is uncomplicated, accustomed to receive the whole divine Scripture in simplicity and uprightness of heart, but especially the teaching handed down by the Fathers. For we know that evangelical and apostolic sayings cannot in general be corrupted. . . . This is because the Gospel has been committed to writing in the letters of seventy-two languages and nations. Consequently, it cannot be corrupted by wicked men either through subtraction or addition. For although someone might attempt to falsify books in one language or another, [Col. 0106B] that wickedness would nevertheless be uncovered and refuted by the other seventy languages.

The Venerable Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, book I, chapter 1:

> Britain at present, according to the number of books in which the divine Law was written, searches out and confesses one and the same knowledge of the highest truth and true sublimity in the languages of five peoples: namely, those of the English, Britons, Scots, Picts, and Latins; the last of these, through the study of the Scriptures, has become common to all the rest.

“I confess,” says Henry Wharton, p. 466 of the *Auctarium on Vernacular Holy Scriptures*, “that no inference can be drawn from Bede’s cited words concerning the translation of Holy Scripture.”

Behold, most learned prelate, the principal testimonies which, wrongly understood or overstrained, are adduced by certain [Col. 0106C] modern writers to maintain that great multitude of versions among the nations—an assertion supported neither by the testimony of the ancients nor by examination of manuscripts. Since the sayings of the Fathers which I have cited are of three kinds, I assign to the first class, with the distinguished Father Le Long, the two passages from Saint John Chrysostom, the third from Theodoret, and the fourth from the Venerable Bede; these make no mention whatever even of a popular translation. To the second class I assign the other two passages from Saint Jerome and the third from Augustine. Some infer many translations from these. Let it be granted that in those times there existed a considerable number, whether Greek or Latin, and also Syriac, and so forth; nevertheless, in a far smaller number than these passages are made to imply. Finally, the last class consists of testimonies drawn from Eusebius of Caesarea [Col. 0106D] and Anastasius of Sinai. But these do not establish what those writers appear to wish, and what reason does not permit one to believe: namely, that no nation can be imagined which was imbued with Christian teachings and into whose idiom the sacred text had not been translated.

The author of the Preface to the Paris Polyglot Bible supposes that, even in Saint Jerome’s time, there existed some Arabic translation of certain books of Holy Scripture, especially the Book of Job. For he writes:

> Hence it derives its greatest commendation: that in the age of Saint Jerome certain writings from the Sacred Letters were found in this language, Arabic, with whose assistance he restored the Book of Job in nearly seven or eight hundred verses, as is evident from the preface prefixed to that book.

Here are Saint Jerome’s [Col. 0107A] words:

> This translation of ours follows none of the ancient translators; but from Hebrew, Arabic, and sometimes Syriac it will now reproduce words, now meanings, now both together.

But Walton aptly observes in Prolegomenon 14, §17:

> The Saint does not there speak of some Arabic version, although at first sight his words seem to suggest this. For, as is clear to anyone who considers his words more carefully, he speaks of his own Latin translation, which he had translated from Hebrew; and he means only that many Arabic words occur in the Hebrew Book of Job.

Many writers have likewise asserted that an Ethiopic version of the Bible—different from the present one—was prepared in apostolic times. Among them is Peter Victor Cajetan, *Paradigm of the Ethiopic Language*, [Col. 0107B] p. 160, where he says:

> First, there is no reason to doubt its antiquity, since from the very times of Christ and the apostles the sacred text of the prophecies, written in this Ethiopic idiom, was in the hands of the eunuch of royal Candace.

But in establishing this point Victor brings forward the authority of Palma, writing fifteen hundred years after these events are alleged to have occurred. How much that amounts to may be left to the judgment of the fair-minded reader. See John Mill, *Prolegomena*, p. 121, and Renaudot, chapter 11, *On the Perpetual Consent of the Church*, etc., p. 92.

Likewise, an Armenian version of the Bible is said to have been composed at the beginning of the Church’s infancy, from a Greek or Syriac translation.

> “It must by no means be omitted,” says John Mill, p. 152 of the Prolegomena to the Greek New Testament, [Col. 0107C] “that Louis Picques, Doctor of the Sorbonne, exceptionally versed in Armenian and indeed in all Oriental literature, informed us by letter: ‘The Armenian version is exceedingly ancient and is so Greek in its character (*ἑλληνίζει*) that it reproduces the Greek word for word; hence one may rightly restore from it the Greek original from which it flowed.’”

“But it is known,” says Gregory the Syrian Scholiast, cited by Walton, Prolegomenon 13, §15, “that although the Armenians translated their manuscripts from Greek, they afterwards compared their copy with the Syriac and made it agree with that in every passage.”

Whether, however, it flowed from a Greek or a Syriac exemplar, it is undoubtedly not of such antiquity as some suppose. Sixtus of Siena, *Sacred Library*, book VI, annotation 152, writes that Saint John [Col. 0107D] Chrysostom translated the New Testament and Davidic Psalms into Armenian. Yet no ancient writer reports this before George, Patriarch of Alexandria, who flourished in the year 620, in his *Life* of that most holy Doctor. “When Chrysostom,” says the cited George, “was exiled at Cucusus, a town of Armenia, he found, by God’s grant, certain persons who knew Greek; he caused them to translate the New Testament and the Psalter into their native language, so that they might gain knowledge of Holy Scripture.” Further, according to Photius, this writer seems to have related some things contrary to historical truth. It is also evident from Palladius’s dialogue on the life of Chrysostom that George largely copied Palladius, interweaving his own fables.

“What credit, then,” says the most learned [Col. 0108A] Le Long, chapter 2 of *Sacred Bibliography*, p. 137, “is to be given to an author of this kind, who, more than two hundred years after Chrysostom’s death, described deeds performed by him without any ancient record?”

Since others maintain that the books of the Old and New Testaments were translated from Greek into Armenian by Moses the Grammarian, David the philosopher, and Mampraeus, Armenians living about the time of the Emperor Arcadius, let us hear the authors of this opinion, whom Le Long himself cites:

> At this same time, namely under the Emperor Arcadius, there flourished in Armenia a celebrated hermit called Mesrob, a man thoroughly learned and of penetrating intellect. He was the first accurately to form the characters of both Armenian and Iberian letters, and left this singular benefit to posterity—a benefit of which [Col. 0108B] their ancestors had been deprived through so many preceding centuries. He therefore, together with Isaac, Patriarch of the Armenians, instructed many disciples in Armenia and sent them to Athens to acquire the Greek language and other disciplines. Among them three made the greatest progress: namely MOSES, surnamed the Grammarian; DAVID the philosopher; and MAMPRAEUS. By translating many books afterward, and especially the books of the Old and New Testament, from Greek into Armenian, they enriched their own language to a remarkable degree.

This is taken from the historical poem of Nierses Ghel, *On the Kings of Armenia*, no. 490, in Clement Galanus, historical part of the *Reconciliation of the Armenian Church with the Roman Church*, chapter 7, no. 12.

The writer of the *Life of Blessed Mesrop*, who [Col. 0108C] is called CORIUN in the title of that Life, relates the matter differently. Near its beginning we read:

> Mesrop determined to translate the twenty-two books of the Old Testament into Armenian, and his disciples John and Joseph assisted him in this. . . . At that time Theodosius the Younger was reigning.

He later relates that the two blessed men, Isaac, Patriarch of the Armenians, and Mesrop, resolved to enlarge the writing of their narrative and to increase the translations and writings according to God’s power. Therefore they sent two of their disciples, Eznac and Joseph, to the city of Edessa, in order that, translating the Holy Scriptures from the language of the Syrians into Armenian, they might commit the writings to their country. They went and carried out their instructions, and so forth. These matters are copied from an Armenian manuscript of the Royal Library, entitled *Sanctology*, [Col. 0108D] according to the translation made in 1669 by Oskan Vartabied, that is, an Armenian bishop.

Moses of Chorene relates almost the same thing, *History of Armenia*, book III, chapter 53, p. 430, Amsterdam edition of 1695, translated by Schroeter:

> Mesrop, having arranged the Armenian alphabet in accordance with the ease of Greek syllables, then set his hand to translation. Deliberately beginning with Proverbs, he completed them, and he and his disciples John of Ekel and Joseph of Baln transferred the twenty-two revealed books and the New Testament into the Haican—that is, ancient Armenian—language.

“Among these,” Schroeter continues, “Moses of Chorene himself must certainly be counted, being second to none among Mesrop’s disciples. [Col. 0109A] In the cited passage he withheld his own name out of modesty; but writing to Isaac Bagratides, he excuses himself (ibid., chapter 65, p. 446) for not having been able to furnish him with a fuller history of the Haican people, because he was old, infirm, and far from idle with translations and holier words.” This happened at the beginning of the fifth century, after Chrysostom’s death, around the year 410. Theodoret confirms this opinion, having asserted that the Armenian version was prepared in his own time; for he was ordained bishop in A.D. 423, and therefore that version has now survived for thirteen hundred years. So Schroeter.

There is certainly no passage in Theodoret to this effect, if these claims refer to what he wrote in Sermon 5, p. 555, of the *Cure of Greek Affections*, where he deals not with translations of Holy Scripture [Col. 0109B] but with the doctrines of the Christian religion.

A Punic version, too, is claimed to have been already in use among some African nations in the time of Saint Augustine. Many suppose its antiquity sufficiently established from a passage of the same holy Bishop of Hippo near the end of his exposition of Psalm CXVIII, where he says:

> We have been informed by those who know the Hebrew letters that all the groups of eight verses in the Hebrew manuscripts begin with the letter set before them; just as our people customarily compose, either in Latin or Punic, psalms which they call *abecedarian*.

But the holy Doctor is not there speaking of Davidic Psalms, but of abecedarian songs or chants. He himself mentions such a psalm, composed by himself against the Donatists, in *Retractations*, book II, [Col. 0109C] chapter 20. Moreover, if a Punic version had been customary among Africans in his day, he would not have omitted to mention it, since in his books *On Christian Doctrine* he expressly teaches what resources should be provided by one seeking to attain an understanding of Holy Scripture. Thus Gretser, *Defence of Bellarmine’s Controversies*, book II, chapter 15, p. 814.

Having therefore dismissed all these alleged translations into every language, which never arose in apostolic times, let us see, most learned prelate, whether those who suppose that innumerable Latin translations of both Testaments existed at the beginning of the nascent Church—intended for the use of the Church of the Gentiles which was to dominate the Roman Empire—do not strike against the same stone. Although, as Pliny says, book III, section VI, Italy, exalted by divine favor, gathered together scattered empires, softened their customs, and united [Col. 0109D] the discords of so many peoples and their savage languages through the intercourse of speech, I nevertheless hold it certain that the number of Latin translations of Holy Scripture serving the churches was not so immense.

Some persons, in order that all your effort in collating and publishing the ancient Latin Italic translation of the Viennese manuscript might be thought futile, produced certain statements of Saints Jerome and Augustine from which one might infer the existence of many private manuscripts like yours. They said that the supreme Doctor, in the Preface to the Four Gospels addressed to Pope Damasus, writes: “If faith is to be given to Latin copies, let them answer: to which? For there are almost as many exemplars as manuscripts.” They likewise cited [Col. 0110A] Saint Augustine, who, in book II, chapter 2 of *On Christian Doctrine*, mentions the infinite variety of Latin translators. And a little later, at section 16, he says:

> Those who translated the Scriptures from Hebrew into Greek can be counted; but Latin translators cannot be counted at all. For when, in the earliest times of the faith, a Greek manuscript came into anyone’s hands and he seemed to possess some slight ability in both languages, he dared to translate it.

I too say, and defend in my letter to the most learned Antonio Francesco Gori, that various Latin translations of the Holy Bible formerly existed. Yet the testimonies adduced from Saints Jerome and Augustine ought not to be pressed too strongly; nor should it be supposed that the various manuscripts of Holy Scripture extant at that time had all been written by various and different [Col. 0110B] translators. That diversity of which the Fathers spoke seems for the most part to have arisen from copyists and scribes, who, while transcribing one and the same version, individually dared to add, remove, or alter some things at their own discretion. For whenever an unknown word or obscure expression occurred to transcribers of Latin manuscripts, they themselves resorted to a Greek exemplar in the New Testament, even though they had little command of either language and lacked sufficient ability. The genuine sense of a corrupt expression or obscure word was to be obtained and recovered through diligent comparison with the original texts, as the Fathers taught.

Let Saint Augustine be heard. In book II, chapter 11, of *On Christian Doctrine*, he lays down these rules for Latin readers:

> Against unknown literal signs, [Col. 0110C] knowledge of languages is a great remedy. Those acquainted with Latin, whom we now undertake to instruct, need two other languages for knowledge of the divine Scriptures—namely Hebrew and Greek—so that they may have recourse to preceding exemplars if the infinite variety of Latin translators should raise any doubt. . . . For, because of the diversity of translators, as has been said, knowledge of those languages is necessary.

And in chapter 14 of the same book he says:

> For either an unknown word or an unknown expression causes the reader to hesitate. If these come from foreign languages, they must either be sought from persons who know those languages, or the languages themselves must be learned, if there is leisure and ability; or a comparison of several translators must be consulted, and so forth.

Here too the number of translators is of great assistance, once manuscripts have been compared, inspected, and [Col. 0110D] examined. Likewise, in the same work, chapter 13:

> Since even the meaning itself, which several translators each according to his own ability and judgment attempt to express, is not evident unless one examines the language which they translate, and since the translator very often strays from the author’s sense unless he is most learned, one must either seek knowledge of those languages from which Scripture has come into Latin, or possess translations by those who have bound themselves too closely to the words—not because these suffice, but so that from them the truth or error of others may be detected, who in translating have chosen to follow words no more closely than meanings.

Accordingly, recourse had to be made to the original text whenever translations, or manuscripts, disagreed with one another. Yet very many persons, [Col. 0111A] almost wholly ignorant of both languages and making no selection among translators or manuscripts, dared to correct, erase, or augment by additions the more difficult and obscure passages of the Italic version. And passages in the Gospels which could delay the reader they illustrated, as it were by making a certain Harmony, with the style and words of another Evangelist. From this arose diverse and discordant readings of one and the same ancient translator; these led Saints Jerome and Augustine alike to complain of so great a multitude of Latin translators.

For although, as the most learned Sabatier says in the General Preface, *On Ancient Latin Versions of the Holy Bible*, §2:

> The readings of the original text sometimes differ from each other and disagree in various words and even meanings, yet it is agreed that the original text is one and the [Col. 0111B] same. Why, then, should we not likewise say that the translation of Scripture was originally one and the same, although diverse discrepancies occur in manuscripts which appear to signify various translations produced by various translators? Surely those diverse discrepancies perhaps proceeded either from the negligent carelessness of inattentive scribes or from the rashness of presumptuous petty scholars. Some, by sleepily transcribing this translation, corrupted words and meanings; others altered according to their own judgment what they understood less well or thought faulty. Certainly, if this happened while transcribing the original text of Scripture, where it should have been unlawful to alter even a letter, [Col. 0111C] how much more could it have happened in transcribing a translation? Since the translation had not the same authority as the original text, it was copied with still less care and reverence by scribes and petty scholars, who did not regard it as wrong to alter, add, remove, or insert little glosses.

Moreover, there may be another origin of variant readings, one purer and more useful. For just as scribes and petty scholars sometimes corrupted the original translation through carelessness and rashness, so learned persons, whenever they recognized that the first translator had slipped—as can happen to anyone, since to err and be deceived is human and foreign to no one—corrected what had been translated less properly and cast light on obscure words or meanings. Hence what appear to be different translations of Scripture prepared [Col. 0111D] by different writers may perhaps be nothing else than various copies of one and the same translation, differing through the negligence, ignorance, and rashness of scribes, but also through the corrections of learned men.

This perhaps explains Jerome’s statement that there were almost as many exemplars as manuscripts, though it was somewhat exaggerated. Thus, when the same Jerome prepared a new translation of the New Testament and was criticized by many, the holy Doctor answered malevolent people who gnawed at and attacked him and his translation in words indicating not so much that he had produced a new translation of Scripture as that he had corrected an old one and cleansed it of the stains and corruptions under which it labored. [Col. 0112A] Thus, finally, Augustine—who writes nothing ineptly and nothing except rightly—may perhaps have been able to write that Latin translators could not be counted.

So the distinguished Sabatier, whose conjecture I shall press still further. I too have more than once maintained that various translations existed in the age of Saints Jerome and Augustine, in volume I of the *Defences of the Canonical Scriptures* and in this *Fourfold Gospel Book*, relying on the authority of the holy Fathers, especially Hilary, Jerome, and Augustine. In book II, chapter 14, of *On Christian Doctrine*, while laying down rules for correcting them, Augustine teaches that the greatest possible selection should be made of manuscripts derived from the same translator:

> For the correction of manuscripts, the diligence of those who desire to know the divine Scriptures must first be directed to ensuring that corrected copies yield precedence to uncorrected copies, provided they derive [Col. 0112B] from only **ONE KIND OF TRANSLATION**.

And in the same work, chapter 15, section 22:

> Among the translations themselves, the Italic should be preferred to the others; for it adheres more closely to the words while preserving clarity of meaning.

But when Saint Jerome sat as arbiter, by Blessed Damasus’s command, to decide—after copies of the New Testament Scriptures spread throughout the world had varied among themselves—which were those agreeing with the Greek truth, he said:

> Lest they should differ too much from the accustomed Latin reading, we so moderated the pen that, correcting only those things which seemed to alter the sense, we allowed the rest to remain as they were.

Accordingly, those exemplars which he says were nearly as numerous as manuscripts derived from only one kind of translation. For he would by no means have remedied the many remarkably corrupt copies of the Italic version [Col. 0112C] which he wished to cure, if they had been produced by different translators. Further, the discrepant Gospel readings which Jerome himself cites, especially in his Commentary on Matthew, do not indicate different translators but different copies of the same translator.

Finally, since the leading libraries have, with singular diligence down to this very day, preserved very many fragments of that most ancient translation which Augustine held in such high esteem and declared preferable to all others, why was the fate of all the other translations so utterly different and unlike? “They served private uses,” someone will say. But not all of them did. The Italic version indeed held preeminent authority among Latin readers; but there were nevertheless certain other versions which [Col. 0112D] some Fathers preferred to the Italic. Since these were few, they were first neglected in the pigeonholes of archives and then perished. But if they are supposed to have been nearly innumerable, how could all be said, and be, lost? This is no slight difficulty, nor is it an easy knot to untie for those who insist too strongly upon the statements of Saints Jerome and Augustine which I have cited. Yet this knot will be solved without difficulty if we believe that so many Latin translators never existed. But of this elsewhere.

So that no one may any longer entertain the thought—after so many highly learned men have written to me concerning the Viennese manuscript and its Italic version—that this exemplar belongs to an uncertain version, and that I have uselessly undertaken, with you as collator, to publish it, [Col. 0113A] let the rationale of my work be made known to all from the following presentation of parallel passages. Whoever considers these passages more attentively will both crown your labors with deserved glory and not begrudge my edition whatever praise of title it may deserve.

I owe much, indeed very much, to the distinguished Nicolaus Forlosiae, chief keeper of the Augustan Library, who with incomparable diligence not only collected Latin sacred manuscripts from the Viennese treasury, arranged the collected material in order in an index, and sent it to me, but also opened and transcribed the Gospel book of which we speak, adding a critical and historical judgment. Would that the entire manuscript, whose variant readings I publish, might someday be brought to light by you, most wise prelate. It is indeed an incomparable work [Col. 0113B] and worthy of immortality, but one to be handled only by persons who have made much progress in reading the early Latin Fathers—or rather, who have spent their lifetime upon it. Behold clearer evidence of the character of the Viennese manuscript.

Mark, chapter VIII, verse 10. The Viennese, Veronese, and Corbie manuscripts read *Magedam*. The Vulgate of Saint Mark here relates that Christ sailed over the Sea of Tiberias to Dalmanutha. Saint Matthew, however, chapter XV, verse 39, and several Latin manuscripts of Saint Mark, have that he came to Magedan. The Syriac and Arabic versions, and certain very ancient Greek exemplars, likewise read *Magedan*.

Luke, chapter XII, verse 35. The words “in your hands” are absent from the Viennese, Vercelli, Gatian, and Brixian manuscripts; likewise in the Greek text, in the ancient Corbie Bibles, in [Col. 0113C] certain other Latin manuscripts, in Saint Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book IV, vol. I, p. 278, and in Saint Cyprian, *On the Unity of the Catholic Church*, pp. 260 and 266.

Mark, chapter VIII, verse 15. For “of Herod,” the Viennese manuscript has “of the Herodians.” Some Greek manuscripts, to be consulted in Mill at this passage, read, instead of “the leaven of Herod,” *καὶ τῆς ζύμης Ἡρῳδιανῶν*, that is, “and the leaven of the Herodians”; nor is this reading to be despised.

Luke, chapter X, verse 15. The Viennese and Veronese manuscripts read, “what, unto heaven?”; the Brixian, “which, unto heaven?” In the present Greek text Matthew and Luke do not differ. Therefore the common translator read in the Greek version of Matthew *μὴ ἕως οὐρανοῦ*, “will you not [be exalted] unto heaven?”, as Beza testifies that he read in a certain exemplar.

[Col. 0113D] Luke, chapter XII, verse 8. The Viennese, Corbie, and “Mm.” manuscripts read “will confess in him”; and so, according to the Greek, does Saint Augustine in the *Mirror*, from the Gospel according to Luke, vol. III, part I, p. 770, and in Sermon 71, *On the Words of the Gospel*, Matthew 12, vol. V, part I, p. 401.

Luke, chapter XII, verse 43. The Viennese and Veronese manuscripts read “his lord.” Certain manuscript books of Saint Jerome’s Divine Library, according to the Greek, read “his own lord.”

Luke, chapter XII, verse 45. The Viennese, Veronese, Corbie, Gatian, and “Mm.” manuscripts have “boys” (*pueros*) instead of “servants”; and certain manuscript codices of Saint Jerome’s Divine Library likewise have this reading, closer to the Greek word.

Luke, chapter XII, verse 53. The Viennese and Veronese manuscripts read “mother-in-law against daughter-in-law,” etc. The Cantabrigiensis Greek manuscript has *διαμερισθήσονται* here; the Greek codex [Col. 0114A] has *ἐπὶ τὴν νύμφην*, which properly means “against the bride” or “daughter-in-law.”

Luke, chapter XVIII, verse 7. The Viennese, Vercelli, and Veronese manuscripts read “having patience.” In the present Greek text it is *καὶ μακροθυμῶν ἐπ’ αὐτοῖς*, “and having patience with them.” Formerly the Latin translator read *μακροθυμήσει*, “he will have patience with them.”

Luke, chapter XX, verse 35. The Viennese and Corbie manuscripts read “nor do they take wives”; the Brixian, “nor do they take wives [with the object preceding].” Certain manuscript copies in Saint Jerome’s Divine Library likewise read, according to the Greek, “nor do they take wives.”

Mark, chapter II, verse 19. The Viennese, Vercelli, and Brixian manuscripts read “sons of the bridegroom.” The Greek text has *τοῦ νυμφῶνος*, “of the bridal chamber.” So too Matthew, chapter IX, verse 15, and Luke, chapter V, verse 34.

[Col. 0114B] Mark, chapter VII, verse 3. The Viennese and Corbie manuscripts read “unless they have washed with the fist.” The Greek, instead of “unless they have washed their hands frequently,” reads: *Ἐὰν μὴ πυγμῇ νίψωνται τὰς χεῖρας, οὐκ ἐσθίουσι*, that is, “unless they wash [their hands] with the fist, they do not eat.”

Mark, chapter X, verse 40. In the Viennese, Vercelli, Corbie, and Veronese manuscripts, the word “to you” (*vobis*) is absent. Likewise, “to you” is absent from the Syriac and Greek codices.

Luke, chapter XII, verse 38. The Viennese reads, “If he comes in the evening-hour watch”; the Veronese, Corbie, and “Mm.”, “if he comes in the evening watch.” Some ancient manuscripts cited by Mill here read *Ἑσπερινῇ φυλακῇ*, that is, “in the evening watch,” instead of “the second watch.” Marcion too read thus, according to Epiphanius.

Luke, chapter XI, verse 13. The Viennese, Veronese, and Corbie manuscripts read “a good gift”; and so does the Cambridge manuscript. [Col. 0114C] Saint Ambrose, *On the Holy Spirit*, book I, chapter 5, p. 614, and certain manuscripts of the Gospel according to Luke, as Ambrose reports in that passage, together with “Mm.”, read “the good gift of the Spirit.” The Brixian reads “the Holy Spirit,” as does the Persian version. Didymus and the Syriac version read “the Spirit of holiness.” The Ethiopic, however, has “the good gift of the Holy Spirit.”

Luke, chapter XI, verse 50. The Viennese and Veronese manuscripts read “unto this generation”; likewise Lucifer of Cagliari. The Vercelli manuscript reads “unto this people.”

Luke, chapter XVIII, verse 14. The Viennese, Veronese, Brixian, Corbie, and Gatian manuscripts read “more than that Pharisee”; likewise the Syriac version and Saint Cyprian, *On the Lord’s Prayer*, p. 265. Saint Ambrose also, *On Cain and Abel*, book I, chapter IX, p. 199, reads “more than the Pharisee.” [Col. 0114D] “Mm.” reads “more than him.”

Mark, chapter VI, verse 3. The Viennese, Vercelli, Veronese, Gatian, and “Mm.” manuscripts read: “Is not this man”—the Gatian, “Mm.,” and Viennese have “this one”—“the son of a carpenter?” Some Greek manuscripts read *Οὐχ οὗτός ἐστι τοῦ τέκτονος*. Thus certain ancient codices, according to Erasmus, Colbert 8, Paris 6, Arabic, Ethiopic, and so forth. These words may be rendered in Latin, “Is not this the son of a carpenter or craftsman?” For the Greek term is generic and signifies any kind of artisan. Origen contends, in book VI *Against Celsus*, that nowhere in the Gospels received in the churches is Jesus recorded as a carpenter, although Joseph was a carpenter, saying: *Οὐδαμοῦ τῶν ἐν ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις φερομένων Εὐαγγελίων τέκτων αὐτὸς ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἀναγέγραπται*—“Nowhere in the Gospels current in the churches is Jesus himself recorded as a carpenter.” Yet the majority of handwritten manuscripts, all printed editions, Fathers, and translators unanimously teach that Jesus was a carpenter. Matthew, chapter XIII, verse 55, has: “Is not this the son of a carpenter?”

[Col. 0115A] Luke, chapter XII, verse 59. The Viennese, Gatian, “Mm.,” and Brixian manuscripts read “you pay the last quadrans”; the Veronese, “until you also pay the last quadrans”; the Corbie, “the last quadrans.” Saint Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book I, vol. I, p. 104, reads “until you pay the last quadrans.”

Luke, chapter XIII, verse 8. The Viennese reads “permit [it] . . . I shall put a basket of manure”; the Vercelli and Brixian, “. . . and I shall put a basket of manure”; the Veronese and Corbie, “forgive [it] . . . and I shall put a basket of manure.” So too Saint Paulinus, Saint Ambrose in *On Repentance*, book II, chapter 1, [Col. 0115B] p. 415, and in book I, *On Jacob and the Blessed Life*, chapter 1, p. 443, as well as Saint Augustine.

Luke, chapter XVII, verse 9. The Viennese and Veronese manuscripts read “the things commanded to him”; the Vercelli and Brixian, “the things commanded to him”; the Corbie, “to him.” Certain manuscript copies in Saint Jerome’s Divine Library likewise read thus. Saint Ambrose, in the *Exposition of Psalm CXVIII*, vol. I, p. 1179, has “what was commanded to him.”

Luke, chapter XVII, verse 18. The Viennese reads “there is not among them one who returned and gave thanks to God”; the Vercelli, “from these was not found,” etc.; the Veronese, “from them there is not one who returned and gave thanks to God”; the Corbie, “from them there was not one who returned and gave thanks to God.” Saint Ambrose, *On Cain and Abel*, book I, chapter 9, p. 199, reads: “There was not among them one who returned and gave thanks to God.”

[Col. 0115C] **Luke, ch. XIX, v. 8.** Vienna: “if I have taken anything from anyone by fraud”; Corbie and Brescia: “I have defrauded.” Saint Irenaeus has: “and if I have defrauded anyone of anything.” Saint Ambrose, *On Cain and Abel*, book II, ch. 4, p. 214: “if I have taken anything from anyone by fraud”; and so Chrysologus.

**Luke, ch. XXII, v. 31.** Vienna: “he demanded to sift you”; Corbie and Brescia: “he demanded to sift you,” etc. Verona: “. . . demanded, that . . . sift.” Saint Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book X, vol. II, p. 348: “he demanded to examine you”; but Saint Hilary’s Colbert manuscript, and others of no inferior authority, read “to sift you”; and so Saint Ambrose, *Interpellation of Job*, book III, ch. 5, p. 659; likewise Ambrosiaster, *Epistle to the Romans*, p. 77; Saint Cyprian, *On the Lord’s Prayer*, p. 271: “he demanded to harass you,” etc.

[Col. 0115D] **Luke, ch. XIII, v. 27.** Vienna: “I do not know whence you are”; Verona: “I do not know whence you are.” And so Saint Ambrose, *On Cain and Abel*, book I, ch. 5, p. 192.

**Luke, ch. XIV, v. 12.** Vienna and Corbie: “nor neighbours, nor the rich”; Vercelli: “neither your brothers, nor even neighbours, nor the rich, lest perhaps they too invite you”; Verona: “neither brothers, nor relatives, nor neighbours, nor the rich, lest perhaps they too invite you in return”; Brescia: “lest perhaps they too invite you in return.” Saint Cyprian, *Testimonies to Quirinus*, book III, ch. 2, p. 372: “neither brothers, nor neighbours, nor the rich, lest perhaps they too invite you in return.”

[Col. 0116A]

**Mark, ch. VIII, v. 39.** Vienna: “that there are some standing around”; Verona: “that there are some of those standing around with me”; Corbie: “there are some here among those standing around me.” Saint Ambrose, *On Faith*, book III, vol. II, ch. 12, p. 514: “that there are some among those standing around.”

**Luke, ch. XI, v. 2.** Vienna and Brescia: “May thy will be done” (Vienna: *volumptas*), “as in heaven, so on earth”; Vercelli: “May thy will be done”; Verona: “May thy will be done in heaven and on earth.” Very many Greek copies, both printed and handwritten, read: “May thy will be done, as in heaven, so on earth.” The Vulgate and very many manuscripts of excellent authority omit these words, as does Origen, *On Prayer*; on this see Mill, *Various Readings*, here, and Saint Augustine. The latter, in the *Enchiridion to Laurentius*, ch. 116, observes that the Lord’s Prayer in Luke contains only five petitions, but in Matthew seven.

[Col. 0116B] **Luke, ch. XI, v. 2.** In Vienna, after “Father,” is added “holy, who art in heaven”; in Vercelli and Corbie, “holy, who art in heaven”; in Verona and Brescia, “our [Father], who art in heaven” (in Gat.: “our”); and so in Saint Ambrose. In Mm.: “holy.” That the words “our [Father], who art in heaven” had already intruded before Origen’s time appears from his work *On Prayer* (*Περὶ Εὐχῆς*), p. 57.

**Luke, ch. XII, v. 11.** In Vienna, Vercelli, Verona, and Corbie, “and Hierico” is added; and so in Colb. 2, in Mill: *τὴν ἱερικώ* [a corrupt or uncertain reading, perhaps “the Hierico”].

**Luke, ch. X, v. 20.** Vienna: “are subject to you”; Verona: “evil spirits are subject to you”; Brescia: “demons are subject to you.” Ambrosiaster, *Epistle to the Corinthians*, I, ch. 12, p. 154: “demons are subject to you.”

[Col. 0116C] **Luke, ch. XIII, v. 25.** Vienna, Verona, and Brescia: “Lord, Lord.” The doubled “Lord” belongs to Matthew.

**Luke, ch. XXI, v. 17.** Vienna, Gat., and Brescia: “by all men.” And so Saint Ambrose, or Berengaudus, *Exposition on the Apocalypse*, on Vision IV, vol. II, p. 537.

**Luke, ch. X, v. 41.** In Vienna, Vercelli, Verona, and Corbie, the words “you are anxious and troubled about many things” are absent. So too Saint Ambrose, *Exposition on Psalm I*, p. 757; *Exposition on Psalm CXVIII*, p. 1107; and *Exposition of the Gospel according to Luke*, book I, p. 1268.

**Luke, ch. X, v. 42.** This verse is absent from Vienna, Vercelli, and Verona, and from Saint Ambrose.

[Col. 0116D] **Luke, ch. XIII, v. 35.** Vienna omits “desolate.” Moreover, many Greek manuscripts do not contain “desolate,” *ἔρημος*, nor does Saint Cyprian, nor the old Latin books, nor the Coptic and Armenian version. On this matter see Grotius, Brugensis, and Mill. It seems to have been added from v. 38 of ch. XXIII of Saint Matthew’s Gospel.

**Luke, ch. XVI, v. 21.** In Vienna, Vercelli, Verona, Gat., Mm., and Brescia, the words “and no one gave to him” are absent. So too in some manuscripts of the Royal Library of Saint Jerome, and in Saint Gaudentius, bishop of Brescia’s preface to Benivolus, as the learned Paul Galeardus observes, p. 10, no. 2; consult him. Not a few Greek manuscripts cited by Mill and Erasmus likewise lack “and no one gave to him,” as do very many Latin copies. These words are thought to have been added from ch. XV, v. 16 of this Gospel, where the subject is the Prodigal Son, who greatly desired to be filled with the husks of the swine, and no one gave to him.

[Col. 0117A] **Luke, ch. XVII, v. 29.** In Vienna and Corbie, “fire from heaven” is absent; and so in Saint Irenaeus. At Vercelli: “and destroyed all”; and so the same Saint Irenaeus.

**Luke, ch. XX, v. 36.** Vienna and Corbie: “for they are like the angels of God, because,” etc. Saint Jerome, *Against John of Jerusalem*, book II, p. 429: “but they shall be like the angels of God, because,” etc.

**Luke, ch. XXI, v. 15.** In Vienna, Vercelli, and Corbie, the words “and all [your adversaries] to contradict” are absent. So too in Saint Cyprian, *To Fortunatus, On the Exhortation to Martyrdom*, ch. 10, p. 333.

[Col. 0117B] **Luke, ch. XII, v. 7.** The words “but also” are absent in Vienna; and so in Saint Augustine, *City of God*, book XXII, vol. VII, p. 681.

**Luke, ch. XII, v. 42.** The word “thinkest thou” is omitted in Vienna, Verona, Corbie, and Brescia; and so in Saint Ambrose, *On Penance*, book I, ch. 9, p. 401.

**Luke, ch. XVII, v. 10.** “All” is absent in Vienna, Vercelli, and Verona; and so in Saint Cyprian, *Testimonies to Quirinus*, book III, ch. 51, p. 382.

**Luke, ch. XIX, v. 26.** The words “and he shall abound” are absent in Vienna, Vercelli, Corbie, and Brescia, likewise in the Greek text and in the older Latin Gospel manuscript of the Queen of Sweden.

[Col. 0117C] **Luke, ch. XIX, v. 8.** “Lord” is absent in Vienna; and so in Saint Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book IV, vol. I, p. 242, and Saint Cyprian, *On Works and Almsgiving*, p. 33.

**Luke, ch. XXII, v. 11.** In Vienna, Verona, and Corbie, “house” is absent; and so in Saint Ambrose.

**Mark, ch. V, v. 1.** After “strait,” “of the sea” is absent in Vienna, Verona, and Brescia; and so in the Greek-Latin Cambridge Codex.

**Mark, ch. V, v. 11.** “Great” is absent in Vienna and Verona, as in the Gothic, Coptic, and Persian versions.

**Mark, ch. XII, v. 30.** In Vienna “commandment” is absent; and so in certain manuscripts of Saint Cyprian’s *On the Lord’s Prayer*.

[Col. 0117D] **Luke, ch. XII, v. 50.** Vienna, Verona, Corbie, Gat., and Brescia: “baptism.” And so Saint Cyprian, p. 640.

**Mark, ch. XIII, v. 19.** Vienna and Gat.: “such tribulations”; and so two manuscripts of the Queen of Sweden in the Library of Saint Jerome.

**Luke, ch. XXII, v. 12.** Vienna, Verona, Corbie, and Brescia: “he will show you.” And so Saint Ambrose.

**Luke, ch. XIX, v. 12.** Vienna, Verona, and Brescia: “a certain . . . rich man.” And so Lucifer of Cagliari.

**Luke, ch. XXI, v. 15.** Vienna and Brescia: “they may not be able.” And so a certain manuscript of Saint Cyprian’s *To Fortunatus, On the Exhortation to Martyrdom*.

[Col. 0118A] **Mark, ch. VII.** Vienna, Corbie, Gat., and Brescia: “of the most high God.” And so certain manuscripts of the Library of Saint Jerome.

**Luke, ch. XI, v. 31.** Vienna and Gat.: “more than Solomon is here”; Brescia: “more-than-Solomon is here.” In some manuscripts of the Library of Saint Jerome occurs: “more than Solomon is here.”

**Luke, ch. XII, v. 58.** Vienna and Corbie: “to the magistrate.” And so Saint Ambrose, *On Tobias*, ch. 9, p. 601. Brescia: “to the judge.”

**Luke, ch. XIII, v. 34.** Vienna: “. . . hen [her] chicks beneath her wings”; Vercelli: “as a hen . . . beneath her wings”; Verona: “hen”; Brescia: “a hen [her] chicks.” Saint Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book IV, vol. I, p. 281: “. . . a hen [her] chicks beneath [her] wings.”

[Col. 0118B] **Luke, ch. XVIII, v. 30.** Vienna, Verona, and Corbie: “he may receive sevenfold.” And so Saint Cyprian and Saint Ambrose.

**Luke, ch. XIX, v. 9.** Vienna: “is a son.” Saint Cyprian has: “because this man too is a son of Abraham.”

**Luke, ch. XIX, v. 22.** Vienna, Vercelli, Verona, and Corbie: “I take . . . I reap.” And so Saint Ambrose, *On Tobias*, ch. 19, p. 613.

**Luke, ch. XIX, v. 23.** Vienna, Vercelli, Verona, and Brescia: “and I.” And so Saint Ambrose, *On the Orthodox Faith against the Arians*, vol. II, p. 357, and *On Tobias*, ch. 19, p. 613.

**Luke, ch. XXI, v. 10.** Vienna: “for [nation] shall rise”; Brescia: “shall rise up.” Saint Cyprian, *To Fortunatus, On the Exhortation to Martyrdom*, ch. 11, p. 334: “for nation shall rise up against nation, and kingdom against kingdom.”

[Col. 0118C] **Luke, ch. XXII, v. 3.** Vienna, Verona, Gat., Mm., and Brescia: “Scarioth.” And so certain manuscripts in the Library of Saint Jerome.

**Luke, ch. XXII, v. 2.** Vienna, Verona, and Brescia have “him” in place of “Jesus.” This is also found in certain Latin manuscripts in the Queen of Sweden’s library.

**Mark, ch. XII, v. 29.** Vienna: “your God”; Vercelli, Verona, and Corbie: “our God.” And so Saint Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book IX, vol. II, p. 276, and one manuscript of the Queen of Sweden in the Library of Saint Jerome.

**Mark, ch. XII, v. 32.** Vienna: “You have spoken well, Master, truly, that God is one and there is no other besides him.” And so Saint Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book XI, vol. II, p. 276.

[Col. 0118D] **Mark, ch. XIII, v. 32.** Vienna and Vercelli: “and the hour.” And so Saint Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book I, vol. II, p. 19.

But I have now expended enough words to show that the ancient Latin, or Italic, version is contained in the Vienna Gospel-book. I shall now append a complete description of that codex, drawn up by the learned Forlosia, together with the letters which you shared with me after receiving them from him. I publish them so that this edition may promise that I shall always remember your kindnesses. From these writings I recognized him as a man most devoted to you and most affectionate toward me.

**Description of the same Vienna codex, prepared by the learned Nicolaus Forlosia, chief keeper of the Imperial Library.**

[Col. 0119A]

This theological Latin manuscript codex is on purple parchment, written in square silver letters, and in folio. It presently consists of one hundred and forty-two leaves. Its dimensions are those of the copy which we had prepared as a specimen of the characters. The parchments are dyed red, although not all equally, but according to the hardness or thinness of each: most are so thin that one might think them not sheepskins but membranes of bladders. The leaves are written on both sides; each page contains fourteen lines, and each line approximately twenty letters. The letters are square in form, and all are in melted silver except those by which the name of God, Lord, or Jesus is written; these are in gold. According as the parchment is tougher or more yielding, it preserves more vividly the colour or the brilliance of the letters.

Besides these fourteen lines, at the top of the page, in letters likewise called square but smaller, “according to” is written on the left, while on the right, opposite it, stands the name of the Evangelist, “Luke” or “Mark,” around which several small lines are inscribed. That the name *Lucae* was mistakenly turned into *Lucanum*, after the form of a Latin patronymic, must be forgiven the copyist. That the codex was arranged in quires appears from such marks as Q. XLIII, etc.; these marks are seen at the foot of the page at the end of each quire.

[Col. 0119C]

The codex was brought here from Naples, and belonged to the library of the Augustinian Fathers of Saint John of Carbonaria. It had been bequeathed to that monastery by Cardinal Seripando, who served as legate of the Holy Roman Church at the Council of Trent. He had acquired many codices of the greatest value as a legacy from Janus Parrhasius. At the head of the first page, in the hand of Seripando or Parrhasius—which also appears elsewhere—there is an old inscription, “about one thousand years old”; so that even then it was considered to date from the fifth or sixth century.

At the beginning of every page a letter of larger size is painted in the outer margin, even where it happens to be in the middle of a word. Likewise the initial letters of each verse are larger.

[Col. 0119D]

At the ends of clauses or periods there are no marks of punctuation, save for a somewhat greater space, and not even that always. All letters are equally spaced from one another, with no separation of one word from another, except rarely. At the end of a period or verse no point is placed; only after a question is a single point added, and not always. These features appear to attest antiquity. Where divine names are written in gold, a gold point is added beside the last letter, for ornament. It is regrettable that the codex is defective at the beginning, the end, and also in leaves from the middle.

What remains, however, contains the two Gospels called those of Saints Luke and Mark, and precisely according to that edition which the Fathers called the Old Italic; its arrangement is as follows.

[Col. 0120A]

From the first leaf to leaf seventy-five is the Gospel according to Luke, whose name we always find transformed into *Lucanum*. It begins in the codex with the words of ch. X, v. 7: “but if it shall return to you,” etc. This beginning, perhaps because it had been erased, was afterwards incorrectly supplied by an unskilled person in this form: *Sinautemavos*, etc. It ends at ch. XXIII, v. 10, with the words: “steadfastly accusing him.”

From leaf seventy-six to the end follows the Gospel according to Mark, beginning with the words of ch. II, v. 17: “The healthy, [a] physician; but he who is ill,” etc. In our Vulgate it reads: “the healthy, [a] physician.” It ends at ch. XIV, v. 36 with the words: “Abba, Father, all things are possible to thee.”

To reproduce the form of the letters I employed one draftsman and another; but, since they did not execute the task at all as I wished, because they always rendered the letters in a more elegant form, I did not shrink from putting my own hand to this laborious work. I copied them upon transparent paper so that I seem almost to have touched the very original. The strokes of the letters are indeed thicker; but I think this resulted from the thickness of the molten silver, which does not permit itself to be drawn as the hand or mind of the scribe wishes.

[Col. 0120B]

The specimen of the manuscript codex displays the second page of the hundredth leaf, from the Gospel according to Mark, ch. VII, v. 4.

[Col. 0120C]

If this procedure satisfies the learned Mr Blanchini, it will be as welcome to me as anything could be.

Nicolaus Forlosia sends his most dutiful greetings from his heart to the Most Illustrious Prince of the Holy Roman Empire, Joseph Count Thun, Bishop of the Holy Church of Gurk.

Most gracious, as is your custom, most illustrious Prince, are you in reporting that the description of the Gospel codex was not unwelcome to the learned Mr Blanchini. It was indeed especially welcome, and I offer the thanks that are due; yet I would not have it credited to me as a favour that I have deservedly obeyed your commands and rendered him a service. I shall now, with no less eagerness of spirit, make it my concern, as you command, to search out whatever Latin manuscripts of Holy Scripture, written within the first ten centuries of the Christian religion, may be preserved in this Imperial Library.

[Col. 0120D]

I must ask only this one indulgence: that Blanchini may not think I can perform this so quickly. For, accustomed to Italy’s pleasant climate, unfamiliar with the cold of this region, and, most importantly, ignorant of our library, he will scarcely understand that it is as disagreeable and inhospitable to those who enter it in winter as it is pleasant in summer. Therefore, as soon as it can be done, I undertake to attend to this; and, if I discover anything useful for his purpose, it will be as gratifying to me to have obeyed you as anything could be. May God most good and great, most illustrious Prince, preserve you for the flourishing of your Church and grant your wishes. Farewell. Vienna, 23 March 1746.

Nicolaus Forlosia most dutifully sends greetings to the Most Illustrious Prince of the Holy Roman Empire, Joseph Thun, Bishop of Gurk.

As soon as the severe winter began to decline and spring to approach, I had nothing more urgent than to obey your commands, most illustrious Prince. I therefore surveyed the Latin manuscripts of the sacred books preserved in this Imperial Library; those which I found able to meet the wishes of the learned Blanchini I noted down and send to you, appended to this letter as an index. If this will be of any use to him, it will be most welcome to me; and if he wishes particular passages collated with the Clementine edition, I shall not refuse to do this at leisure. Let it therefore be his task to investigate, and yours to command.

[Col. 0121B]

May God preserve you unharmed for the good of your Church and for my protection. Farewell. Vienna, 23 April 1746.

**Manuscripts of the Sacred Bible in the Imperial Court Library at Vienna, arranged according to the order of the distinguished Gentleman Gentilotti.**

L. The fiftieth theological Latin codex is parchment, very ancient, written in rounded letters near the end of the eighth or beginning of the ninth century, at the expense of Radon, Abbot of Saint Vedast at Arras from A.D. 795 to A.D. 815. It was described by Lambecius, *Commentaries*, book II, p. 402 ff.; extracts from this description were reported by Jacques Le Long, *Bibliotheca Sacra*, vol. I, p. 536. It contains the Holy Bible of both Testaments. Gentilotti says that it is falsely called wholly ruined; yet he does not deny that this is not entirely untrue, for, if one strains one’s eyes, one may usually make out the letters that have faded in places.

[Col. 0121C]

LXIV. Parchment, A.D. 1341; and XCIV. Parchment, fourteenth century: both contain the Bible of the Old and New Testaments.

XCV. Parchment, tenth century: a defective codex containing the Prophets.

CL. Parchment, tenth century: contains the four Gospels.

CCLIX. Parchment, tenth century: contains the Acts of the Apostles, the Epistle of James, and the First Epistle of Peter.

CCLXXX. Parchment, eleventh century, defective: contains Solomon’s Proverbs and the Book of Wisdom.

[Col. 0121D]

CCCXLIII. Parchment, eleventh century: contains the four Gospels.

CCCLXXXI and CDLVIII. Parchment, fourteenth century: both contain the Bible of both Testaments.

CDLXXXV. Parchment, twelfth century: contains the Psalter of David with the Canticles of Isaiah and the rest.

DXC. Parchment, twelfth century: contains several books of the Old Testament and the four Gospels.

DCLXXXVII. Parchment, A.D. 1247: contains the Old and New Testament.

DCCLIX. Parchment, thirteenth century: contains the Old and New Testament.

DCCLXXVI. Parchment, fourteenth century: contains the New Testament.

[Col. 0122A]

Hohendorff. Parchment, twelfth century: contains the Old and New Testament.

Naples. Parchment, eleventh century; and Naples. Parchment, fourteenth century: contain the Old and New Testament.

The manuscripts of later centuries, of which there are very many, are not noted here.

Nicolaus Forlosia most dutifully sends greetings to the Most Illustrious Prince of the Holy Roman Empire, Joseph Thun, Bishop of Gurk.

Unless I trusted that my eagerness to obey you, most illustrious Prince, and my disposition for such labours as the learned Blanchini requests, had thus far been sufficiently proved to you, the last letter which I sent would readily demonstrate it.

[Col. 0122B]

For in it I did not without reason intimate that, should passages in the manuscripts need to be compared with the Vulgate edition, I would undertake this task. I certainly offered myself to you to the extent of my ability. But to begin such a labour, and continue for long at one requiring the eyes to be bent down, brought close, and fixed upon the work, is almost impossible for me, being nearly a myope (*μύωπι*), because of the weakness of my chest from which I suffer. Thus, if I undertook the burden of collating the sacred codices, I should necessarily fail to keep the promise which I cannot fulfil. But if perchance two ecclesiastics of your diocese are found here, to whose diligence you may entrust this work, I promise that I shall gladly assist them in catching the faded letters.

I refrain from saying more in my own excuse, lest I seem to distrust either your goodwill toward me or the authority you possess with Blanchini to persuade him. Indeed, I ask you also to persuade him that I cannot do what I would most gladly perform and what would best accord with my wishes, and that this is a matter of necessity.

[Col. 0122C]

May the Lord God Almighty preserve you long in health, most illustrious Prince. Farewell. Vienna, 8 June 1746.

These are the materials which you, most gracious Prince, shared with me from a librarian of the highest excellence and most seasoned by long experience in such matters, so that I might understand that I had gained the friendship of so great a man through your favour. I heard from eminent men, who could know this most easily, that in the Vienna treasury of manuscripts no other copy survives of that Italic version which was disseminated, as it were handed down from hand to hand, and retained with the greatest care in most Latin churches until the time of Saint Gregory the Great. That most sacred codex lay hidden on the shelves. But you were the first of all to labour in collating it, so that I, inserting the collated readings in this *Fourfold Gospel-book*, might share them with the Christian commonwealth.

[Col. 0122D]

Yet I should like the learned Forlosia to hear from you how conscious I am of, and openly acknowledge, my debt to him as well; and how happy I would count myself if I were given the means of returning thanks. I eagerly await your letters, most wise man; nothing could happen to me more agreeably than for you to command me to do something for your sake. I know how warmly you esteem me. Now, moreover, others too will understand from these writings how great is the union of purpose and scholarly zeal between us. Live long, most gracious bishop; live and grow old in your studies. While still young you have despised all those things which men commonly account of greatest importance even in old age. You think solely of God and your Church. You despise all else, because it is fleeting and perishable. All our brethren greet you. Greet Mr Forlosia there for me.

[Col. 0123A]

At present my occupations do not permit me to write to him; but I shall write shortly. Farewell; and do not cease to render the highest service to Holy Scripture, since this is permitted pre-eminently to you alone. The more zeal and diligence you devote to these matters, the more I shall know that you have bestowed yourself upon the Church of Gurk and upon the public good, whose welfare you have always endeavoured to promote. From the Vallicellian House, 5 April 1747.

[Col. 0123B]

## BLANCHINI’S LETTER TO MUSELLIUS

Joseph Blanchini of Verona, priest of the Congregation of the Oratory of Saint Philip Neri in the city, sends greeting and life to the most distinguished and highly deserving man Giovanni Francesco Muselli, canon and archpriest of the holy Church of Verona.

It is now the fifteenth year since, because of your singular zeal to deserve well of Sacred Scripture, you urged me to publish and elucidate that purple codex belonging to the celebrated library of the lords canons of the most distinguished chapter of Verona—of which I myself was once the lowest member, while you, most excellent Archpriest, are its supreme head and ornament—because it presents the ancient Latin, or Italic, translation, received into use from apostolic times [Col. 0123C] onward and preferred to others (on account of its fidelity to the words together with clarity of sense) almost down to the age of Saint Gregory the Great.

Therefore, since your wish ought to have with me the force of the highest law, because of your supreme authority and wisdom alike, I wish you to know that I am so disposed and so ready to comply with you in this matter, as in all others, that I do not decline to undertake, carry out, and complete the edition in whatever way I can. You know my respect for you, even since I left Verona to join this Congregation of Saint Philip Neri; for I have always obeyed you and remained united with you, at least through correspondence. In letters, indeed, I do not hear your voice, nor do you hear mine; but I nonetheless apprehend the thing that underlies the voice, just as I did when I served there as a canon. [Col. 0123D] The passage of so many years and the great distance between places have not at all altered my devotion to you; indeed, it grows daily and is brought to its height, thrice-venerable Archpriest.

Since, therefore, I have held nothing more important, expected nothing more eagerly, or observed more carefully than that the steadfast inclination of my mind to honour you should become evident through some public service, behold: I now gladly comply with your wish, which I have always valued so highly that I regard it as a command. I shall not, however, append here a description of the Veronese Gospel codex, written in the fifth or sixth century, because the book is in your possession and I have already done this in Part II of the present edition. Rather, in the interest of assisting posterity—as you have strongly and repeatedly urged me—I shall apply myself to the principal readings of the same Gospel-book which depart from our Vulgate edition. If this can in some measure be of service to the Catholic Church, as assuredly it can, I greatly hope that you will have no reason to regret either your duty in urging me on or the incomparable generosity of JOHN V, King of Portugal and the Algarves, in assisting me.

Here, then, is a florilegium of the chief passages, carefully excerpted from the works of the pre-Hieronymian Holy Fathers, which I now send you. Before I begin to set out their comparison, however, I want you to know that there have been some who, finding in the Veronese codex at John 1:13 the reading, “Who was born not [Col. 0124B] of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of a man, but of God,” have, through ignorance of the antiquity of this reading, supposed that our codex had been corrupted by heretics. I confess that this is a slippery defence. For all who know me know how highly I esteem them. Yet the matter itself compels me to say that they were somewhat more eager than was proper to criticize the most sacred codex. For if they had perhaps never read elsewhere, “was born,” they ought not immediately to have resorted to saying that all the Fathers read, “were born.” If they wish me to produce the testimony of some ancient writer in whom that reading is mentioned, they rightly demand it. For I assign very great authority to the Veronese codex, but not so great that “he himself said it” (*autos epha*) is sufficient.

I have weighty witnesses among the Fathers for that reading: Irenaeus, Tertullian, John Chrysostom, Augustine, Vigilius of Tapsus, and John of Damascus. I shall gladly produce the words of each.

Saint Irenaeus, clearly demonstrating in Book III Against Heresies that Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, is one and the same person, true God and true man, says in chapter XVI (p. 204, col. 2, no. 2, letter o):

> “Matthew could have said, ‘But the generation of Jesus was thus’; but the Holy Spirit, foreseeing corrupters and forearming us against their fraud, says through Matthew: ‘But the generation of Christ was thus’; and because he is Emmanuel, lest perhaps we should think him merely a man—for the Word was made flesh not by the will of the flesh, nor by the will of a man, but by the will [Col. 0124D] of God—nor suspect that one was Jesus and another Christ, but should know that he is one and the same.”

And in chapter XIX of the same book (p. 212, col. 2, no. 2, letter m), in order to prove from Scripture that the same Jesus Christ is truly the Son of God, begotten from God the Father, and truly the son of man, born from the Virgin, he adduces parallel passages from Isaiah (53:8) and Jeremiah (17:9), saying:

> “For this reason, who shall declare his generation? Since he is a man, who shall recognize him? But he recognizes him to whom the Father who is in heaven has revealed him: so that he may understand that he who was born, not by the will of the flesh nor by the will of a man, the Son of Man, is this Christ, the Son of the living God.”

Likewise, in chapter XXI (p. 217, col. 1, no. 5), intending to show that the Spirit of God announced through the apostles that Emmanuel was born of the Virgin, he recites Isaiah’s famous prophecy and refutes his opponents’ erroneous and heretical interpretation:

> “For this reason he promised a king also from the fruit of her womb, which belongs properly to a pregnant virgin; and not from the fruit of her loins, nor from the fruit of her kidneys, which belongs properly to a begetting man and to a woman conceiving from a man. Scripture therefore excluded the male organs from the promise; indeed, they are not even mentioned, because he who was being born was not from the will of a man.”

Then he explains the true meaning of the same prophet and confirms it with prophecies from Daniel and Isaiah, concluding thus (p. 217, col. 2, no. 7):

> “For this reason Daniel also, foreseeing his coming, signified that a stone cut out without hands had come into this world—for this is what ‘without hands’ means (Daniel 2:34)—because his coming into this world did not occur through human hands at work, that is, through those men who ordinarily cut stones; namely, Joseph did not act in this, but Mary alone cooperated in the dispensation. For this stone consists of earth through the power and art of God. Therefore Isaiah also says: ‘Thus says the Lord: Behold, I lay in the foundations of Zion a precious, chosen, chief cornerstone, honourable’; so that we may understand that his coming according to humanity was not by the will of a man but by the will of God.”

Finally, in Book V, chapter 1, he clearly shows that Valentinus and Ebion, who rejected the Incarnation of the Son of God from the Virgin Mary through the working of the Holy Spirit, remain under Adam’s old condemnation, and concludes:

> “For Adam never escaped the hands of God, to whom the Father, speaking, says: ‘Let us make man in our image and likeness.’ And therefore, at the end, not by the will of the flesh nor by the will of a man, but by the good pleasure of the Father, his hands made the living man perfect, so that Adam might be made according to the image and likeness of God.”

Consider, then, learned sir, whether those who think that the reading of the Veronese Gospel-book is supported by no ancient testimony do justice to truth. But I am pleased also to offer other testimonies, and first of all a notable passage of Tertullian, in which those who boast of being, as it were, physicians of ancient writers detect hidden ulcers—ulcers not appearing in the worst manuscripts. Thus in *On the Flesh of Christ*, chapter 19, where he argues against the Valentinians, we read:

> “What then is this: ‘He was born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of a man, but of God’? I shall rather make use of this passage once I have exposed its corrupters. For they maintain that it is written thus: ‘He was born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of that of a man, but of God.’ … We understand, then, that the Lord’s birth from sexual intercourse is denied, as is indicated by the will of man and flesh, not participation in the womb. And why indeed did he so emphatically insist that he was born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh or of a man, unless his flesh was from her who, no one could doubt, had herself been born through intercourse? Etc.”

Tertullian has similar words in the same work, *On the Flesh of Christ*, chapter 24, where he introduces the passage under discussion against Ebion:

> “Therefore also foreseeing Marcion, [the Holy Spirit says]: ‘I am God, and there is no other beside me.’ And when elsewhere he says the same thing in the same manner, he strikes at those genealogies, whatever they may be, of the Valentinian aeons. And, ‘He was born not of blood, nor of the will of flesh and man, but of God.’”

Saint John Chrysostom also seems to have had regard to the same reading of our Veronese Gospel-book—found and read, therefore, in some Greek copy—when he says:

> “For this reason the birth [of Christ] was twofold: both like ours and surpassing ours. To be born of a woman belongs to us; but to be born not of blood, nor of the will of man or flesh, but of the Holy Spirit, foreshadows the birth surpassing us and yet to come, which he was going to grant us from the Spirit.”

And lest these matters be thought lighter because they are less evident, the passage which I shall add can surely lend this letter some favour and give weight to the disputed reading even with fastidious critics. Saint Augustine therefore says in *Confessions*, Book VII, chapter 9:

> “And first, wishing to show me how you resist the proud but give grace to the humble, and how great was the mercy shown by you in the way of humility to humankind—because your Word was made flesh and dwelt among men—you procured for me, through a certain man swollen with monstrous pride, certain books of the Platonists translated from Greek into Latin. There I read, not indeed in these words, but with this same doctrine altogether commended by many and various arguments, that in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made. What was made in him is life, and life [Col. 0126D] was the light of men; and the light shines in darkness, and darkness did not comprehend it. And that the human soul, though it bears witness concerning the light, is not itself the light; but the Word of God, God, is the true light which enlightens every person coming into this world. And that he was in this world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him. But that he came to his own, and his own did not receive him, while to as many as received him he gave power to become children of God, believing in his name—I did not read this there. Likewise, there I read that God the Word was born not from flesh, not from blood, not from the will of man, nor from the will of flesh, but from God; but that the Word was made flesh [Col. 0127A] and dwelt among us, I did not read there.”

The author of the *Dialogues on the Holy Trinity*, thought to be Vigilius of Tapsus (as I demonstrated in the Pseudo-Athanasian Exposition of the Creed which I published at Verona), likewise brings forward one of the speakers, namely the Orthodox, as follows, to prove that the name of the eternal Father is in the Son and the Holy Spirit:

> “But John testifies that Christ was born of God: ‘He came unto his own, and his own did not receive him; but as many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God, believing in his name, who was born not of blood, nor of the will of flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.’”

Finally, Saint John of Damascus joins them. In vol. I, Book III of *On the Orthodox Faith*, chapter 7, p. 204, Paris edition of Father Michael Lequien, Order of Preachers, 1712, he says:

> “And the Word was immutably made flesh of the Holy Spirit and Mary, the holy ever-virgin and Mother of God; and he is the mediator of God and human beings, the only lover of humankind, conceived in the undefiled womb of the Virgin not by the will, desire, or union of a man, nor by a birth linked with pleasure, but by the Holy Spirit and that first creation of Adam.”

The learned editor just mentioned translated these Greek words into Latin thus:

> “Wherefore the Word was made flesh without any change, from the Holy Spirit and holy Mary, ever Virgin and Mother of God; and he exists as mediator of God and men, he alone most gracious toward humankind, conceived in the undefiled [Col. 0127C] womb of the Virgin not from the will, desire, or intercourse of a man, nor from generation joined with pleasure, but from the Holy Spirit and that first formation of Adam.”

Matthew 5:1: “Jesus” is absent in the Veronese and Brixian codices, and likewise in the Greek text and in most of the older Latin manuscripts of the Vatican Library.

Matthew 9:28: “to you” is absent in the Veronese codex, and likewise in a Greek copy and in some older Gospel books.

Matthew 21:4: It is wholly absent in the Veronese, Corbie, and Brixian codices, and likewise in Greek manuscripts of better authority and in the Latin manuscripts of Queen Christina of Sweden.

John 1:12: The Veronese has “believing,” in accordance with the Greek text, *tois pisteuousin* (“to those believing”).

John 6:58: The Veronese reads, “I live through the Father; and he himself lives through me.” The Greek has *dia ton patera*, “through the Father.”

[Col. 0127D] John 15:6: The Veronese and Corbie codices read, “and it withered,” closer to the Greek text.

Luke 2:34: The Veronese reads, “This one is set for a fall,” and so does the Greek text, *eis ptōsin*, that is, “for a fall.” “Fall” there denotes destruction, because one who has fallen is easily overcome by an enemy and is regarded as lost; likewise “resurrection” stands for salvation, because one who stands erect is deemed safe.

Luke 4:8: The Veronese reads, “Go behind me, Satan; for it is written: You shall worship the Lord your God.” The Greek reads, *Hypage opisō mou, Satana; gegraptai gar*, etc., that is, “Depart from me, Satan; for it is written,” etc. These words are taken from Matthew 4:10. A great number of manuscripts, however, do not have this addition.

Luke 6:35: The Veronese reads, “over the grateful and wicked.” This reading seems to relate to the codices Tertullian used in Book IV against Marcion, chapter 17, in which, after verse 36, there was this addition: “who rains upon the good and wicked and causes his sun to rise upon the righteous and unrighteous”; likewise the Greek copy used by the author of the Clementine Homilies, Homily 3, §57, had it.

Luke 10:15: The Veronese reads, “down to hell.” The same words occur in the Greek source, *heōs Hadou katabibasthēsē*, “down to hell.”

Luke 12:55: The Veronese reads, “and so it will be”; the Gat., Mm., Vindobonese, and Brixian codices read, “and so it is.” *To*, “so,” is also added [Col. 0128B] by some Greek manuscripts and by the Ethiopic version.

Mark 1:11: The Veronese reads, “in whom it pleased me well”; the Brixian, “you who have pleased me well.” Many printed and handwritten Greek codices, agreeing with Matthew, have “in whom I was pleased.” Luke and the greater number of books support the Vulgate.

Mark 6:33: The Veronese reads, “and they gathered there.” The Greek text also adds, “and they gathered to him.”

Matthew 12:31: The Veronese reads, “but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit, the sin shall not be forgiven him”; the Corbie codex, “but whoever blasphemes against the Spirit of God, it shall not be forgiven him”; the Brixian, “but blasphemy of the Spirit shall not be forgiven to men.” Saint Athanasius, in *On the Trinity*, vol. I, p. 981, reads, “but whoever blasphemes against [Col. 0128C] the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven”; and in the fragment on Matthew, vol. I, part II, p. 1169, “but blasphemy against the Spirit shall not be forgiven them.”

Luke 12:38: The Veronese reads, “and if he comes in the evening watch and finds them so, blessed are they; for he shall command them to recline, and shall minister to them.” The Corbie codex: “if he comes in the evening watch and finds them so, blessed are they, because he shall command them to recline, and shall pass by and minister to them; if in the second and if in the third [watch], blessed are they.” Mm.: “and if he comes in the evening watch and finds them so, blessed are those servants; because he shall command them to recline, and, coming by, shall minister to them; and if he comes in the second watch, and in the third, and finds them so, blessed,” etc. The Vindobonese: “and if he comes in the evening hour of the watch and finds them so, blessed are they … because he shall command them to recline, and shall pass by and minister to them; and if in the second, and if in the third, blessed are they.”

Also, in the Catholic codex used here by Marcion, before verse 38 the text was read as follows: *kai ean elthē en tē hesperinē phylakē kai heurē houtō, makarioi eisin hoti anaklinei autous, kai elthōn pan diakonēsei autois*: “And if he comes in the evening watch and finds [them] so, blessed are they, because he will cause them to recline and, having come, will minister everything to them.” Mill thinks this is not an addition but Luke’s genuine reading, p. 33 of the Prolegomena; for that reading is confirmed by the pre-Hieronymian Vulgate copy of Irenaeus’s translator, Ambrose’s Commentary on Luke, Book VII, chapter 2, and Methodius, *Oration 5, On the Banquet of Virgins*. Yet, since the opening words of this verse are the same as those of the verse immediately following, and likewise its final words are exactly the same as those of the verse immediately preceding, it seems very likely that through an easy error these words long ago fell out of the body of the text, both in Greek and in Latin manuscripts, in which the copyist omitted the whole of verse 38 in the Vulgate edition. Thus Mill.

Matthew 1:25: The Veronese, Corbie, and Brixian codices read, “and he did not know her”; likewise Saint Ambrose in *On the Institution of Virgins*, chapter 5, pp. 257–258, and in the *Exposition of the Gospel according to Luke*, p. 1284; also Saint Gregory the Great, *Morals on Blessed Job*, Book VIII, chapter 7, p. 286.

Matthew 3:3: The Veronese reads, “the paths of our God”; likewise Saint Irenaeus in Book III *Against Heresies*.

Matthew 4:13: The Veronese and Brixian codices read, “into maritime Capernaum”; likewise the Italic version, according to Mill, *Prolegomena to the New Testament*, p. 51.

Matthew 27:6: The Veronese reads, “into the treasury-box”; likewise [Col. 0129B] Saint Ambrose on Psalm 61, no. 13.

John 12:1: The Veronese reads, “Lazarus was, who was dead”; the Brixian, “Lazarus was, who had been dead.” The Greek, *Lazaros ho tethnēkōs*: “Lazarus, who had been dead.”

Luke 2:2: The Veronese, Vercelli, Corbie, and Gat. codices, after correction, read “registration” (*professio*). Mill, *Prolegomena*, p. 52, says that the Latin translator rendered Greek *apographesthai* not as “to be enrolled” but as “to make a declaration,” and *apographē* in verse 2 as “declaration”: words no longer in common use, but truly pertaining to the census, as learned men have observed, and almost technical terms. “Indeed,” says Boys, “it is more elegant to say ‘that they might make a declaration’ than ‘that they might be enrolled,’ especially in this passage, where *to apographesthai* refers not to those conducting the census but to those being assessed.” Thus *apographē*, referring to those assessed, properly means “declaration.”
