Luke 5:14: The Veronese reads, “offer a gift”; Tertullian, p. 420, “offer a gift”; Saint Augustine, Book VI *Against Faustus*, vol. VIII, p. 206, “offer your gift.”

Matthew 5:11: The Veronese and Brixian codices read, “you shall be”; likewise Tertullian, pp. 144 and 494; Saint Cyprian, *Letter* 26, p. 84; and Hilary the Deacon in the commentaries on Paul published under Ambrose’s name, *Letter to the Romans* 5, p. 52.

Matthew 5:23: The Veronese and Vercelli codices read, “you shall offer”; likewise most manuscript copies of Saint Augustine’s *Enchiridion on Faith, Hope, and Charity* and Book XXI *On the City of God*.

[Col. 0129D] Matthew 8:12: The Veronese, Vercelli, and Saint-Germain codices read, “they shall go”; likewise Saint Irenaeus, Book IV *Against Heresies*, vol. I, p. 281. Saint Cyprian, however, in Book I *Against the Jews, to Quirinus*, chapter 23, p. 348, has “they shall go out.”

Matthew 12:7: The Veronese, Corbie, and Brixian codices read, “than sacrifice”; likewise some manuscript copies of Irenaeus, Book IV *Against Heresies*.

Matthew 15:26: The Veronese and Vercelli codices read, “and to give [it] to the dogs”; likewise Saint Hilary in his commentary on this passage of Matthew, and Tertullian against Marcion, Book IV, chapter 7.

Matthew 15:32: The Veronese and Vercelli codices read, “and they have no food”; likewise Saint Ambrose.

[Col. 0130A] Matthew 16:19: The Veronese, Corbie, and Brixian codices read, “and whatever things … shall be bound … and whatever things … shall be loosed,” etc.; likewise Saint Ambrose, Book I *On Penance*, chapter 7, p. 399. Tertullian, *On Modesty*, chapter 21, reads “loosed.” Saint Cyprian: “and whatever things … shall be bound … and whatever things … shall be loosed,” etc. Pacian also, against the treatises of the Novatians, Letter 2, has “shall be loosed.”

Matthew 16:24: The Veronese and Saint-Germain codices read, “let him deny himself to himself.” Saint Irenaeus, Book III *Against Heresies*, vol. I, p. 210, has “let him deny himself.” Saint Hilary, in his commentary on this passage of Matthew, according to three manuscript codices, reads, “let him deny himself to himself,” and likewise Saint Ambrose, Letter LXIII, first class, p. 1040. In Book II *On Penance*, chapter 10, p. 437, however, he has, “let him deny his very self to himself.”

Matthew 21:9: The Vercelli codex reads, “Son of David”; likewise Saint Irenaeus.

Matthew 22:10: The Vercelli and Veronese codices read, “as many as they found”; likewise Saint Irenaeus and Lucifer of Cagliari, Book II *For Saint Athanasius*. The Corbie codex reads, “whomever they found.”

Matthew 22:30: The Veronese reads, “But in the resurrection they neither marry nor take wives.” Saint Cyprian likewise, p. 209, has “but.” Saint Ambrose, Book I *On Virgins*, chapter 8, p. 159: “but in the resurrection they shall neither marry nor take wives.” Saint Zeno of Verona, Book I, Treatise 5 *On Continence*, p. 49: “they neither marry.” The Greek text has, “they do not marry.”

John 13:18: The Veronese and Brixian codices read, “against me,” [Col. 0130C] and likewise Saint Ambrose in his exposition of Psalm 40, p. 876.

John 16:9: The Veronese and Corbie codices read, “they do not believe.” Some manuscripts in Saint Jerome’s library have, “they will not believe.”

John 16:12: In the Veronese, after “you are able,” *ea* (“these things”) is added; in the Vercelli codex, *illa* (“those things”). So too Saint Ambrose, Book III *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 14, p. 687.

Luke 1:39: The Veronese, Corbie, and Brixian codices read, “Judaea”; likewise Saint Ambrose, Book III *Exposition of the Gospel according to Luke*, p. 1315.

Luke 2:37: The Veronese and Vercelli codices read, “eighty-four years old”; Saint Ambrose, his sole book *On Widows*, chapter 4, p. 191, “of eighty-four years”; and in a first-class letter, p. 968, “eighty-four years of age.”

[Col. 0130D] Luke 3:1: The Veronese and Vercelli codices read, “Judaea”; likewise the old translator, according to Mill, *Prolegomena*, p. 52.

Luke 5:10: The Veronese, Vercelli, and Corbie codices read, “making alive”; likewise Saint Ambrose, Book VI *Hexaemeron*, chapter 8, p. 133.

Luke 7:42: The Veronese, Vercelli, Corbie, Gat., Mm., and Brixian codices read, “to be shaken by the wind?” One Vatican manuscript and two manuscripts of Queen Christina in Saint Jerome’s library read, “to be shaken by wind?”

Luke 16:6: The Veronese and Corbie codices read, “take your documents”; likewise Saint Gaudentius, Sermon XVIII, p. 202.

Mark 3:27: The Veronese, Mm., and Brixian codices read, “has bound”; likewise Saint Ambrose, *Exposition of the Gospel according to Luke*, Book II, p. 1307.

[Col. 0131A] Mark 3:35: After “sister,” “my” is absent in the Veronese and Brixian codices, and likewise in most Greek copies and in one manuscript of Queen Christina reported in Saint Jerome’s library.

Mark 10:17: The Veronese reads, “running ahead”; likewise Saint Augustine, *Mirror from the Gospel according to Mark*, vol. III, part I, p. 765.

Matthew 24:31: The Veronese adds to this verse: “But when these things begin to happen, look up and lift up your heads, because your redemption draws near.” Saint Luke, chapter 21, verse 28, and the ancient Greek-Latin Cambridge codex of Matthew reported by Mill likewise add here: “But when these things begin to happen, look up and lift up your heads, because your redemption draws near.”

[Col. 0131B] Matthew 26:27: The Veronese reads, “take and drink from this”; likewise Saint Ambrose, Book IV *On the Sacraments*, chapter 5, p. 371.

Matthew 26:53: The Veronese and Brixian codices read, “twelve thousand.” Saint Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 1, vol. X, p. 85, says: “You read also that twelve thousand legions of angels could have fought for Christ, lest he should suffer, if he had willed it; yet this did not happen.” Again, in chapter 35, p. 121, he says: “At the beginning of this discourse we set out certain things from the Gospel and the Law, such as the camel’s passing through the eye of a needle, and the twelve thousand legions of angels who could, if he had wished, have fought for Christ … all of which things did not happen.” See vol. X, Maurist edition, pp. 85 and 121.

Luke 1:3: The Veronese reads, “It seemed good also to me and to the Holy [Col. 0131C] Spirit.” Likewise certain ancient Greek books: *Edoxe kamoi kai tō Pneumati Hagiō*, that is, “it seemed good also to me and to the Holy Spirit.” Perhaps these words were expunged by the Marcionites, who admitted one part of Luke’s Gospel and rejected another. Saint Irenaeus argues against them in Book III, chapter 14.

Luke 1:34: The Veronese reads, “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it happen to me according to your word.” The Syriac, Arabic, Persian, and Ethiopic versions preserve the same order, as does Saint Ambrose in the *Exposition of the Gospel according to Luke*. The Corbie codex, in verse 38, has “let it happen to me”; likewise Saint Ambrose, first-class letter, p. 967.

Luke 10:1: The Veronese and Brixian codices read, “And he appointed seventy others.” A great many Greek copies, the Syriac, Coptic, and Arabic versions, Saint Irenaeus, Saint Ambrose, Tertullian, and many others read only “seventy,” not “seventy-two.” Yet those very writers who have “seventy” in their books acknowledge that there were seventy-two disciples, as may be seen in Mill’s *Various Readings* here, and in Maldonado, Grotius, and Selden, Book II *On Synedria*, chapter 9, article 8.

Luke 11:4: The Veronese and Corbie codices add, “but deliver us from evil.” The Vindobonese and Brixian: “but rescue us from evil” (*eripe*, Brixian; *erue*). Many Greek books, both printed and handwritten, likewise read, “but deliver us from evil.” The Vulgate, however, and most codices of the best authority omit these words; on this see Mill, *Various Readings*, here, and Saint Augustine.

Luke 12:9: The Veronese reads, “But whoever denies me before men, I too will deny him before my Father [Col. 0132A] who is in heaven.” Perhaps this addition was also present in Ambrose’s codices; for Saint Ambrose, explaining this passage of Matthew 10:33, says: “And thus it is written not only in the book of the Gospel of the Lord Jesus which is written according to Matthew, but it is also read in that which we find according to Luke; so that you may know that neither has inserted it without purpose.”

Matthew 10:29: The Veronese adds, “who is in heaven”; likewise Saint Irenaeus, Book V *Against Heresies*, chapter 22. The Corbie codex has, “who is in heaven.”

John 12:25: In the Veronese, after “his life,” “in this world” is first added. In Saint Cyprian, however, pp. 199, 337, 516, and 518, it is “in this age.”

Luke 7:11: In the Veronese, after “his,” “many” is added. The “many” seems to have intruded from verse 12. See Mill, *Prolegomena*, p. 44, col. 1.

Mark 9:40: In the Veronese, Gat., and Brixian codices, after “water,” “cold” is added. So too in some editions of Saint Augustine’s *Mirror from the Gospel according to Mark*.

Matthew 11:8: The Veronese and Brixian codices read, “clothed in soft garments?” Likewise Saint Ambrose, Book V *Hexaemeron*, chapter 23, p. 109.

Matthew 15:32: In the Veronese and Corbie codices, before “crowd,” but in the Brixian after it, “this” is added. In Saint Ambrose, Book V *Hexaemeron*, chapter 25, p. 114, “of this” is read.

Matthew 18:20: The Veronese and Vercelli codices read, “there also am I.” Likewise Saint Ambrose, *On the Mysteries*, chapter 5, p. 332, and Victor of Vita, *Vandal History*, Ruinart edition, p. 56. The Corbie codex reads, “there am I”; likewise Saint Ambrose, Book II *On Cain and Abel*, chapter 2, p. 208, [Col. 0132C] and first-class Letter 63, p. 1023. The Saint-Germain codex has, “there am I also.”

Matthew 20:23: In the Veronese, Vercelli, and Corbie codices, “Jesus” is added. Likewise Saint Ambrose, Book V *On Faith*, chapter 5, p. 562.

Matthew 5:48: In the Veronese and Saint-Germain codices, after “therefore,” “and” is added, as in Saint Ambrose, Book III *On the Duties of Ministers*, chapter 2, p. 110.

Matthew 7:15: The Veronese and Saint-Germain codices add “to yourselves” after “beware.” Likewise Tertullian, pp. 203, 217, and 218; Saint Ambrose, Book II *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 10, p. 655; and Book VI *Hexaemeron*, chapters 6 and 8, pp. 127 and 132.

Matthew 8:20: The Veronese, Vercelli, and Saint-Germain codices read, “its head.” Likewise Saint Ambrose, *Hexaemeron*, Book VI, chapter 8, p. 131.

Matthew 9:15: In the Veronese, Vercelli, and Saint-Germain codices, after “they shall fast,” “in those days” is added. Likewise Saint Ambrose, first-class Letter 32, p. 915.

Matthew 21:37: The Veronese reads, “perhaps they will reverence [him].” Likewise Saint Ambrose, Book II *On Penance*, chapter 5, p. 424. Saint Irenaeus has, “perhaps they will reverence [him].” The Corbie codex: “they will surely reverence [him].” The Brixian: “they will respect [him],” as do some Claromontane codices in the cited passage of Irenaeus.

John 3:36: The Veronese has “eternal life” in the second position. So do many editions of Saint Augustine.

John 16:33: The Veronese, Corbie, and Brixian codices read, “but in this world.” Saint Cyprian, *On the Benefit of Patience*, p. 316, has “but in the world.”

[Col. 0133A] Luke 7:44: In the Veronese and Brixian codices, after “tears,” “her own” is added; likewise Saint Ambrose, first-class Letter 42, p. 919.

Luke 22:6: In the Veronese and Vindobonese codices, “to them” is added; in the Corbie and Brixian, “to those [men].” It is an addition from Matthew 12:38.

Luke 13:10: The Veronese reads, “in one of the synagogues.” Mill considers the words “in one of the synagogues” a marginal gloss; but this seems less convincing to me, since it is found in all Greek codices. The Brixian reads, “in a certain synagogue.”

Luke 14:23: In the Veronese, Corbie, and Brixian codices, “around” is added before “hedges”; likewise Saint Ambrose, exposition of Psalm 40, p. 877.

Luke 16:9: After “tabernacles,” “their” is added [Col. 0133B] in the Veronese; likewise Saint Ambrose, Book III *On the Duties of Ministers*, chapter 22, p. 140, and Book I *On Abraham*, chapter 5, p. 295.

Luke 8:13: The Veronese and Corbie codices add, “Lord”; likewise Saint Ambrose, Book I *On Cain and Abel*, chapter 9, p. 199.

Mark 1:24: The Veronese, Corbie, Mm., and Brixian codices read, “I know you,” etc.; likewise Saint Ambrose, first-class letter, p. 880.

Matthew 1:25: In the Veronese and Saint-Germain codices, the words “her firstborn son” are absent, as in Saint Ambrose and Saint Gregory the Great.

John 7:53: It is absent in the Veronese and Brixian codices, as in a great many manuscript codices.

Matthew 4:4: The Veronese and Saint-Germain codices read, “word of God”; likewise Saint Ambrose, Book III *On Virgins*, chapter 4, p. 174; first-class Letter 63, p. 1026; and Book I *On Cain and Abel*, chapter 5, p. 191.

Matthew 6:33: “First” is absent in the Veronese; likewise Saint Ambrose, Book I *On Cain and Abel*, chapter 4, p. 188.

Matthew 8:29: “to you” is omitted in the Veronese and Saint-Germain codices; likewise Saint Ambrose’s exposition of Psalm 118, p. 1036, and *Exposition of the Gospel according to Luke*, p. 1283.

John 21:7: “Peter” is absent in the Veronese, and likewise in two manuscripts of Saint Jerome’s library.

John 21:15: The words “more than these” are omitted in the Veronese, Vercelli, and Corbie codices; likewise Saint Ambrose, *Apology of David*, chapter 9, p. 692.

John 21:15: The Veronese and Vercelli codices read, “certainly, Lord”; likewise Saint Ambrose in the cited passage.

John 21:16: The Veronese reads, “my little sheep”; likewise Saint Ambrose, preface to Book V *On Faith*, p. 551. But in Book II *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 13, p. 662, he has “my lambs.”

Luke 24:45: The words “on the third day” are absent in the Veronese codex and in Saint Irenaeus.

Mark 1:2: The words “before you” are omitted in the Veronese and Vercelli codices; likewise in some Greek copies, the Syriac, Coptic, Persian, and Ethiopic versions, Irenaeus, Origen, and some Latin manuscripts in Saint Jerome’s library.

Mark 10:6: “Of creation” is absent in the Veronese and Corbie codices; likewise in the Syriac and Persian. In the same passage, in the Veronese, Corbie, [Col. 0134A] and Brixian codices, “them” is absent before “God”; likewise in the Syriac and Persian.

Matthew 6:13: The Veronese, Vercelli, and Corbie codices omit “Amen”; likewise the ancient Cambridge book, many other Greek and Latin codices, two manuscripts in Saint Jerome’s library, Tertullian, Saint Cyprian, Saint Augustine, and the Syriac version. This word seems to have been added by another hand than Matthew’s after it began to be used at the end of the Lord’s Prayer in liturgical prayers.

Matthew 6:34: “Therefore” is absent in the Veronese and Vercelli codices; likewise Saint Cyprian, p. 221, and Saint Augustine, Book II *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, vol. II, part II, p. 222.

Matthew 7:27: In the Veronese and Saint-Germain codices, “and” is absent in the first, second, and third occurrences; likewise in Saint Cyprian.

Matthew 9:13: “For” is absent in the Veronese; likewise [Col. 0134B] Saint Ambrose, Book I *On Penance*, chapter 12, p. 405, and his exposition of Psalm 118, p. 1101.

Matthew 9:18: “Lord” is absent in the Veronese and Vercelli codices; likewise in some manuscripts of Queen Christina listed in Saint Jerome’s library.

Matthew 11:10: “For” is absent in the Veronese, Vercelli, and Saint-Germain codices; likewise in Saint Ambrose.

Matthew 13:37: “To them” is omitted in the Veronese, Vercelli, and Corbie codices; likewise in Greek manuscripts of better authority and in the royal Vatican Latin manuscripts of Saint Jerome’s library.

Matthew 16:11: “To you” is absent in the Veronese and Vercelli codices; likewise Saint Ambrose, Book I *On Penance*, chapter 15, p. 411.

Matthew 19:29: “Or wife” is absent in the Veronese, Vercelli, and Corbie codices; likewise Saint Ambrose, Book II *On the Duties of Ministers*, chapter 2, p. 71, and in his exposition of Psalm 118, p. 1059.

Matt. ch. XX, 4: in the Verona manuscript *meam* is absent; likewise in two manuscripts of the Queen of Sweden in the Divine Library of St. Jerome.

Matt. ch. XXI, 12: the Verona manuscript has *into the temple*, omitting *of God*; likewise everywhere in the New Testament and in Origen.

Matt. ch. XXII, 2: in the Verona, Corbie, and Brescia manuscripts *factum* (“made”) is absent; likewise in St. Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, bk. IV, vol. I, p. 279.

Matt. ch. XXII, 21: the Verona, Vercelli, and Corbie manuscripts have *render the things that...*, omitting *therefore*; likewise Tertullian, pp. 94, 97, 338, 339, 499, 522, and St. Ambrose, in the first class of his Letters, p. 872, as also in *On the Blessing of the Patriarchs*, ch. 8, p. 524.

Matt. ch. XXII, 30: the Verona and Brescia manuscripts have *angels*, omitting *of God*; likewise St. Zeno of Verona.

[Col. 0134D] Matt. ch. XXIV, 21: *then* is absent in the Verona manuscript; likewise in St. Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, bk. IV, vol. I, p. 274.

John ch. I, 21: in the Verona manuscript, before *Elijah*, *What then?* is absent; likewise in the Coptic version.

John ch. VI, 39: in the Verona and Brescia manuscripts *of the Father* is absent; likewise in St. Ambrose, bk. II, *On Faith in the Resurrection*, p. 1157.

John ch. VII, 37: *to me* is absent in the Verona manuscript; likewise in St. Cyprian, bk. I, *Against the Jews, to Quirinus*, ch. 22, p. 348.

John ch. X, 29: in the Verona and Vercelli manuscripts *my* is absent; likewise in St. Ambrose’s *Treatise on the Trinity*, p. 328; bk. V, *On Faith*, ch. 11, p. 576; bk. I, *On the Holy Spirit*, ch. 2, at the end, p. 607; and bk. III, ch. 16, p. 689.

[Col. 0135A] John ch. X, 37: *my* is absent in the Verona and Vercelli manuscripts; likewise in St. Cyprian.

John ch. XI, 45: *Jesus* is omitted in the Verona, Gatian, and Mm. manuscripts; likewise in certain Greek manuscripts, and also in some Latin manuscripts in the Divine Library of St. Jerome.

John ch. XII, 40: the Verona, Gatian, and Mm. manuscripts have *and understand with the heart*, omitting *not*. Thus also St. Ambrose, bk. III, *On the Holy Spirit*, ch. 22, p. 699, has *understand with the heart*, likewise omitting *not*.

John ch. XIII, 26: *I* is absent in the Verona manuscript; likewise in St. Ambrose, Sermon 27, p. 429.

John ch. XIV, 28: *indeed* is absent in the Verona, Vercelli, and Corbie manuscripts; likewise in St. Cyprian, pp. 161, 345, and 463.

John ch. XVII, 18: *you* is absent in the Verona and Vercelli manuscripts; likewise in Ambrosiaster, on First Corinthians [Col. 0135B] ch. 11, p. 147; on Second Corinthians ch. 11, p. 147; and on Second Corinthians, ch. 3, p. 175.

John ch. XX, 17: *my* is absent at its first occurrence in the Verona manuscript; likewise in St. Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, vol. I, p. 331.

Luke ch. II, 21: *the child* is absent in the Verona and Brescia manuscripts; likewise in Greek manuscripts of the better class, and in one manuscript of the Queen of Sweden cited in the Divine Library of St. Jerome; in another it was added on second consideration.

Luke ch. V, 7: *almost* is absent in the Verona, Vercelli, Corbie, Gatian, and Brescia manuscripts; likewise in certain manuscripts of the Queen of Sweden.

Luke ch. VI, 38: the Verona manuscript has *shaken together, overflowing*; likewise St. Ambrose, *On the Duties of Ministers*, ch. 31, p. 43, omitting *and* before *overflowing*; that conjunction is also absent from the Vercelli and Corbie manuscripts.

[Col. 0135C] Mark ch. II, 5: after *sins*, *your* is absent in the Verona manuscript; likewise in two manuscripts of the Queen of Sweden in the Divine Library of St. Jerome.

Mark ch. II, 23: *the Lord* is absent in the Verona, Vienna, and Brescia manuscripts; likewise in certain manuscripts cited in the Divine Library of St. Jerome. The Vercelli, Corbie, Gatian, and Mm. manuscripts have *him* in place of *the Lord*.

Mark ch. X, 6: the Verona and Corbie manuscripts read, “For from the beginning [the Corbie manuscript: *but*] God made male and female.” The Syriac, Persian, and Old Cambridge text alone read *ἀπὸ δὲ ἀρχῆς κτίσεως*, that is, “but from the beginning of creation God made male and female”; the other witnesses do not read *κτίσεως* (“of creation”).

Mark ch. XIII, 6: *because* is absent in the Verona and Gatian manuscripts; likewise in St. Cyprian, *To Fortunatus, on the Exhortation to Martyrdom*, ch. 11, p. 334.

[Col. 0135D] Matt. ch. XXII, 30: the Verona, Corbie, and Brescia manuscripts have *are*; likewise the Greek text and two manuscripts of the Queen of Sweden in the Divine Library of St. Jerome.

Matt. ch. XXIV, 15: the Verona manuscript has *standing*; likewise the Old Latin, which follows the Greek, as Mill testifies in the *Prolegomena*, p. 51.

John ch. I, 13: the Verona manuscript has, “but he was born of God.” Thus also St. Irenaeus in his books *Against Heresies*, Tertullian, St. John Chrysostom, Vigilius of Tapsus, and others.

John ch. I, 13: the Verona manuscript has *blood*, and so do all the manuscript copies of St. Hilary, bk. I, *On the Trinity*, no. 10.

John ch. I, 34: the Verona manuscript has, “because he is the chosen Son of God”; the Vercelli manuscript, “because this one is the chosen Son of God”; the Corbie manuscript, “because this one is chosen of God.” St. Ambrose [Col. 0136A], in his *Exposition of the Gospel according to Luke*, bk. V, vol. I, p. 1377, has, “because this one is chosen of God.”

Luke ch. XI, 4: the Verona and Corbie manuscripts have *our debts*; likewise St. Ambrose.

Matt. ch. III, 17: the Verona manuscript has *from heaven*; likewise St. Hilary, in his treatise on Psalm CXXXVIII, vol. I, p. 565.

Matt. ch. VI, 17: the Verona and Vercelli manuscripts have, “But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face”; likewise St. Ambrose, *On Elijah and Fasting*, ch. 10, p. 546. The St.-Germain manuscript has, “But when you fast, anoint your heads and wash your face.”

Matt. ch. VI, 18: the Verona and Vercelli manuscripts have, “that you may not appear to men as fasting, but to your Father . . . and your Father . . . will repay you.” St. Ambrose, *On Elijah and Fasting*, ch. 10, p. 546, has, “that you may not appear to men because you fast, but to your Father . . . and your Father . . . will repay you.” The St.-Germain manuscript has, “that you may not be seen by men as fasting, but by your Father . . . and your Father . . . will repay you.”

[Col. 0136B] Matt. ch. VI, 23: the Verona manuscript has, “and then I shall swear”; likewise St. Hilary, bk. IX, *On the Trinity*, no. 65.

Matt. ch. VI, 33: the Verona and St.-Germain manuscripts have, “they shall be supplied to you.” The Vercelli manuscript has, “and all these things are supplied to you.” St. Ambrose, *On Cain and Abel*, bk. I, ch. IV, p. 488, has, “they are at hand for you.”

Matt. ch. VII, 27: the Verona, Vercelli, and St.-Germain manuscripts have, “and its fall was great”; likewise St. Cyprian. The Brescia manuscript, however, has, “and a great fall occurred to it.”

Matt. ch. X, 22: the Verona and St.-Germain manuscripts have [Col. 0136C] *by all men*; likewise the ancient Corbie Bible and St. Augustine, in the *Mirror from the Gospel according to Matthew*, vol. III, pt. 1, p. 758.

Matt. ch. XI, 12: the Verona manuscript has, “the kingdom of heaven is constrained, and those who constrain seize it”; likewise St. Ambrose, *On Cain and Abel*, bk. I, ch. 4, p. 188; likewise in his exposition of Psalm XLIII, p. 902; and in Letter 63, first class, p. 1046. The Vercelli text is mutilated: “. . . is constrained, and those who constrain seize it.” The St.-Germain manuscript has, “seize it.”

Matt. ch. X, 38: the Verona manuscript has, “has received . . . and has followed me.” The Corbie manuscript: “has received . . . and has been following me.” St. Jerome, Letter CXLV to Exsuperantius, vol. I, p. 1073, has, “has taken up . . . and has followed me.”

[Col. 0136D] Matt. ch. XII, 1: the Verona, Corbie, and Brescia manuscripts have *on Sabbaths*; St. Ambrose, in the *Exposition of the Gospel according to Luke*, bk. V, vol. I, p. 1363, has *Sabbath-days*.

Matt. ch. XIII, 25: the Verona, Vercelli, and St.-Germain manuscripts have *among the wheat*; St. Irenaeus, *among the grain*; St. Ambrose, bk. III of the *Hexaemeron*, ch. 10, p. 49, *among the wheat*.

Matt. ch. XVII, 12: the Verona, Vercelli, and Corbie manuscripts have, “whatever they wished”; likewise the Old Latin, as Mill testifies in the *Prolegomena*, p. 55.

Matt. ch. XVIII, 3: the Verona and Vercelli manuscripts have, “like children”; the Corbie manuscript, “like this child.” St. Ambrose, in his exposition of Psalm XXXVI, p. 800, has, “like this child.”

Matt. ch. XIX, 12: the Verona, Vercelli, and Corbie manuscripts [Col. 0137A] have *eunuchs* in the first, second, and third places; likewise St. Ambrose, *On Virginity*, ch. VI, p. 220, and *On Widows*, ch. XIII. Tertullian, pp. 147, 158, 342, 525, 534, 543, has, “there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs,” etc.; likewise St. Ambrose, Letter 72, second class, p. 1075.

Matt. ch. XIX, 17: the Verona manuscript has, “if you wish to enter into eternal life,” etc.; likewise St. Ambrose, *On the Duties of Ministers*, ch. XI, p. 11. The Vercelli manuscript has, “to enter into life,” in agreement with St. Cyprian, p. 395. The St.-Germain manuscript has, “to come into life”; likewise Hilary the deacon, also called Ambrosiaster, on Romans, ch. 7, p. 66.

Matt. ch. XX, 30: the Verona manuscript has, “have mercy on us”; likewise St. Ambrose, bk. V, *On Faith*, ch. 8, p. 569.

[Col. 0137B] Matt. ch. XXI, 24: the Verona and Vercelli manuscripts have, “one word, which”; likewise St. Ambrose, *On the Blessing of the Patriarchs*, ch. VIII, p. 524.

Matt. ch. XXI, 32: the Verona and St.-Germain manuscripts have, “in the kingdom of God”; likewise St. Zeno in certain editions. The Vercelli manuscript: “. . . kingdom of God.” The Corbie manuscript has, “in the kingdom of heaven”; likewise St. Irenaeus.

Matt. ch. XXI, 34: the Verona, Vercelli, and Corbie manuscripts have *to the tenants*; likewise Lucifer of Cagliari, bk. II *For St. Athanasius*.

Matt. ch. XXI, 39: the Verona and Vercelli manuscripts have *the tenants*; likewise St. Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, bk. IV, vol. I, p. 277, and Lucifer of Cagliari, bk. II *For St. Athanasius*.

Matt. ch. XXI, 39: the Verona and Vercelli manuscripts have, “they killed [him] and cast [him] outside the vineyard”; likewise Lucifer of Cagliari [Col. 0137C] from Mark.

Matt. ch. XXI, 43: the Verona and Corbie manuscripts have *fruit*; likewise certain manuscript copies of St. Irenaeus.

Matt. ch. XXII, 12: the Verona and Corbie manuscripts have *you came*; likewise St. Irenaeus and Victor of Vita, *History of the Vandals*, p. 79, Ruinart edition.

Matt. ch. XXIII, 6: the Verona manuscript has *the first reclining-place*; St. Cyprian, bk. III of the *Testimonies against the Jews*, ch. 5, p. 374, has *the first place for reclining*.

Matt. ch. XXIII, 38: the Verona manuscript has *is left*; likewise St. Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, bk. IV, vol. I, p. 281.

Matt. ch. XXIV, 16: the Verona and Vercelli manuscripts have *into the mountains*; St. Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, bk. V, vol. I, p. 322, and St. Cyprian, *On the Exhortation to Martyrdom*, no. 11, have *to the mountains*.

[Col. 0137D] Matt. ch. XXIV, 46: the Verona and Corbie manuscripts have, “whom, when he comes,” etc.; likewise St. Hilary, bk. IX, *On the Trinity*, vol. II, p. 310.

Matt. ch. XXV, 33: the Verona manuscript has, “at his right [hand], but the goats at the left [hand]”; the Corbie manuscript, “at his right hand, but the goats at the left.” St. Cyprian has, “at the right hand, but the goats at the left.”

Matt. ch. XXV, 40: the Verona manuscript has, “to one of these least brethren of mine.” The Vercelli manuscript, “to one of these least brethren of mine.” St. Ambrose—bk. V, *On Faith*, ch. 14, p. 582; Letter I, first class, pp. 753 and 961; Letter 70, second class, p. 1065; and bk. I, *On Abraham*, ch. 5, p. 295—has, “to one of these least [ones].” The Corbie manuscript has, “to one of these least [ones],” [Col. 0138A] and likewise St. Hilary, in his treatise on Psalm CXXXII, vol. I, p. 515.

Matt. ch. XXVI, 29: the Verona manuscript has *the creature of the vine*; likewise St. Cyprian, Letter 63 to Caecilianus. The Vercelli manuscript is mutilated: “. . . creature . . .”

Matt. ch. XXVI, 41: the Verona manuscript has, “that you may not enter”; St. Cyprian, *On the Lord’s Prayer*, p. 270, “lest you enter.”

Matt. ch. XXVI, 52: the Verona manuscript has *take up*; likewise Lucifer of Cagliari, *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin against God*.

Matt. ch. XXVI, 64: the Verona manuscript has *with the clouds*, etc. The Vercelli manuscript is mutilated: “with . . . clouds”; likewise St. Ambrose, *On Joseph the Patriarch*, ch. 12, p. 506.

Matt. ch. XXVI, 73: the Verona and Vercelli manuscripts have, “your speech is similar.” I consider this reading genuine, but think that it was removed by copyists from the Vulgate, because [Col. 0138B] they preferred the explanatory rendering, *δῆλόν σε ποιεῖ* (“it makes you manifest”). Perhaps it migrated from the margin of Mark into the Gospel text itself. For this reason I believe that these very notable words were transferred from this passage of Matthew into Mark, since the Cambridge manuscript does not read them there, nor does the Coptic version, nor does Eusebius acknowledge them in bk. III of the *Demonstration of the Gospel*.

Matt. ch. XXVI, 75: the Verona and Corbie manuscripts have *most bitterly*; likewise St. Pacian, against the treatises of the Novatians, in Letter III.

Matt. ch. XXVII, 4: the Verona and Vercelli manuscripts have, “I have sinned, in that I have betrayed,” etc.; likewise St. Ambrose, bk. II, *On Repentance*, ch. 4, p. 422.

Matt. ch. XXVII, 39: the Verona and Vercelli manuscripts have *those passing by*. St. Ambrose, in his exposition of Psalm XLIII, p. 911, has *those who passed by*.

[Col. 0138C] Matt. ch. XXVII, 46: the Verona manuscript has *lama zaptani?*; likewise the older manuscript of the Queen in the Divine Library of St. Jerome. The Vercelli manuscript has *lema zahthani?*; the St.-Germain manuscript, *zabacthani?*

Matt. ch. XXVIII, 7: the Verona, Vercelli, and Corbie manuscripts have *I have told [you]*; likewise St. Augustine. The Brescia manuscript has *he told [you]*.

John ch. I, 4: the Verona manuscript has *in him*; likewise St. Hilary, bk. I, *On the Trinity*, vol. II, p. 7, and bk. II, vol. II, p. 37. The Vercelli, Gatian, and Mm. manuscripts have *in that one*; likewise St. Cyprian, bk. II of the *Testimonies against the Jews, to Quirinus*, ch. 3, p. 352.

John ch. I, 8: the Verona and Vercelli manuscripts have *the light*; likewise St. Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, bk. III, vol. I, p. 189.

John ch. I, 16: the Verona manuscript has, “because from [his] fullness,” etc.; likewise St. Ambrose, bk. IV, *On Faith*, ch. [Col. 0138D] 11, p. 548. Two manuscripts and certain editions of the same St. Ambrose, in his exposition of Psalm CXVIII, have *whence*, etc. The Vercelli manuscript has, “because from [his] fullness,” etc.

John ch. I, 18: the Verona, Gatian, and Mm. manuscripts have, “unless the only-begotten,” etc.; likewise St. Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, bk. IV, vol. I, p. 255; St. Ambrose, bk. III, *On Faith*, ch. 3, p. 501; *On the Holy Spirit*, ch. I, p. 605; Letter 22, first class, p. 875; and Sermon 12, p. 406. The Vercelli manuscript has, “unless the only [Son].”

John ch. I, 26: the Verona manuscript has, “I indeed baptize you”; the Vercelli manuscript, “I baptize you”; the Gatian manuscript, “I baptize you.” St. Cyprian, bk. II of the *Testimonies against the Jews*, ch. 19, p. 359, has, “I indeed baptize”; but another manuscript copy of the same St. Cyprian adds *you*.

[Col. 0139A] John ch. I, 32: the Verona manuscript has, “descending from heaven, and remaining,” etc.; likewise the Vercelli manuscript and St. Ambrose, bk. III, *On the Holy Spirit*, ch. I, p. 665. But in *On the Mysteries*, ch. 4, p. 331, he has, “descending from heaven . . . and remaining,” etc. St. Jerome likewise, in his commentary on Isaiah, bk. IV, ch. 11, p. 156, has *and remaining*.

John ch. III, 18: the Verona and Vercelli manuscripts have, in the third place, *has not believed*; likewise St. Augustine, on John’s Gospel, ch. III, Tractate 13, vol. III, pt. 2, p. 389. Thus it is also read in the ancient Bibles of Corbie, in accordance with the Greek, *πεπίστευκεν* (“has believed”).

John ch. III, 20: the Verona manuscript has, “lest they be reproved”; St. Irenaeus, “lest they be exposed.”

John ch. IV, 13: the Verona, Vercelli, Gatian, Mm., and Brescia manuscripts have *shall drink*; likewise St. Cyprian, p. 228.

[Col. 0139B] John ch. V, 4: the Verona, Vercelli, Gatian, and Mm. manuscripts have *in the pool*; the Corbie manuscript, *into the pool*; likewise St. Ambrose, *On the Mysteries*, ch. 4, p. 330.

In the same passage, the Verona and Vercelli manuscripts have *was held*; likewise St. Ambrose in the passage cited. The Gatian and Mm. manuscripts have *might be held*.

John ch. V, 43: the Verona, Vercelli, Corbie, Gatian, and Mm. manuscripts have *you received*; likewise St. Ambrose, bk. I, *On the Holy Spirit*, ch. 13, p. 628.

John ch. VI, 69: in the Verona manuscript *said* is added; in St. Cyprian, *saying*.

John ch. VI, 70: the Verona manuscript has, “because you are the Son of God”; the Corbie manuscript and St. Cyprian, “because you are the Son of the living God.”

John ch. VII, 15: the Verona and Vercelli manuscripts have, “he knows letters,” etc.; likewise St. Ambrose, bk. II, *On Faith*, ch. 9, p. 485.

[Col. 0139C] John ch. VII, 23: the Verona and Vercelli manuscripts have, “are you angry with me,” etc.; likewise St. Ambrose, in his exposition of Psalm CXVIII, p. 1092.

John ch. VII, 39: the Verona and Corbie manuscripts have *glorified*; likewise St. Ambrose, *On the Sacrament of the Incarnation of the Lord*, ch. VI, p. 714.

John ch. X, 38: the Verona and Brescia manuscripts have, “or by the works,” etc.; likewise St. Ambrose, *On the Mysteries*, ch. 2, p. 327, and in his exposition of Psalm CXVIII, p. 1118.

John ch. XII, 13: the Verona, Vercelli, and Corbie manuscripts have *palm flowers*. St. Ambrose, bk. IX of the *Exposition of the Gospel according to Luke*, vol. I, p. 1497, has *the piths of palms*; likewise the author of *Questions on the Old and New Testament*, question 82, Appendix 3 to the new edition of St. Augustine.

John ch. XII, 27: the Verona and Vercelli manuscripts have *is troubled*; [Col. 0139D] likewise St. Ambrose, bk. II, *On Faith*, ch. 5, p. 477.

John ch. XII, 40: the Verona manuscript has, “I shall heal them”; likewise St. Ambrose.

John ch. XII, 41: the Verona and Corbie manuscripts have *his majesty*; likewise St. Ambrose.

John ch. XVI, 13: the Verona manuscript has *what it hears*. St. Ambrose, bk. V, *On Faith*, ch. 11, p. 575, has *whatever it hears*; but in bk. II, *On the Holy Spirit*, ch. 11, p. 656, he has *what*.

John ch. XV, 5: the Verona and Vercelli manuscripts have *will bear*; the Corbie, Mm., and Brescia manuscripts, *bears*; likewise St. Jerome. Servatus Lupus, however, reads *will bear*.

Luke ch. I, 17: the Verona, Vercelli, and Corbie manuscripts have *unbelieving*; likewise two manuscript copies of the Queen of Sweden [Col. 0140A] cited in the Divine Library of St. Jerome.

Luke ch. I, 55: the Verona manuscript has *to Abraham*; likewise St. Irenaeus.

Luke ch. II, 28: the Verona manuscript has *in [his] hands*; the Brescia manuscript, *into his hands*; likewise St. Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, bk. I, vol. I, p. 40.

Luke ch. II, 32: the Verona manuscript has *for the revelation of eyes*. Certain manuscript copies of St. Irenaeus have *in the revelation of eyes*.

Luke ch. IV, 7: the Verona and Vercelli manuscripts have, “if, falling down, you worship before me”; the Brescia manuscript, “if, falling down, you worship me”; likewise St. Ambrose, in his exposition of Psalm XXXVI, vol. I, p. 797, and in *On Cain and Abel*, bk. I, ch. 5, no. 17, and elsewhere; as also certain manuscript books in the Divine Library of St. Jerome.

[Col. 0140B] Luke ch. VI, 35: the Verona manuscript has *love*; likewise St. Ambrose, *On Tobit*, ch. 16, p. 609.

Luke ch. VII, 47: the Verona manuscript has, “have been forgiven . . . because”; likewise St. Ambrose, *On Isaac and Anna*. But in bk. II, *On Repentance*, ch. 8, p. 431, he has, “have been dismissed,” etc.; whereas in Letter 41, first class, p. 953, “have been forgiven,” etc. The Brescia manuscript has, “are forgiven . . . because.”

Luke ch. XVI, 7: the Verona manuscript has, “and he said to him”; the Vercelli manuscript, “but he said also to this one”; St. Gaudentius, “and he said to him.”

Luke ch. XVIII, 14: the Verona and Brescia manuscripts have, “therefore I say”; the Gatian and Mm. manuscripts, “truly I say”; likewise certain manuscript copies of St. Cyprian.

Luke ch. XXIV, 49: the Verona and Corbie manuscripts have *the promised [thing]*; likewise St. Ambrose, bk. II, *On the Holy Spirit*, ch. 2, [Col. 0140C] p. 638.

Mark ch. XII, 31: the Verona manuscript has, “the second [commandment is] like that [one]”; the Vienna manuscript, “like this [one].” St. Cyprian, *On the Lord’s Prayer*, p. 271, has, “and the second [is] like this [one].”

Behold, most learned Muselli, this notable gleaning of the principal readings which I have extracted from the Verona Gospel-book and which agree with the Holy Fathers. Farewell, safeguard and ornament of the Church of Verona. May God, the Best and Greatest, long favor my prayers; and may he bring it about that you remain late into life for your native city, which honors and reveres you as a father—after the incomparable bishop John Bragadin—for your outstanding service in restoring ecclesiastical discipline and advancing sacred literature. I desire that you preserve for me your affection, whose memory indeed greatly refreshes me; and, if you wish to return like for like, preserve an affection that is no ordinary one. This will be the most excellent of all gifts, a gift which, because I am conscious of my own disposition toward you, I expect as though it were owed to me.

[Col. 0140D] If there is anything in which my work can be of use to your most distinguished and illustrious chapter, I shall undertake it of my own accord if I can recognize it myself; if otherwise, I shall do so when you have advised me, so that each of the reverend canons may understand how highly I value their goodwill toward me. Greet most warmly in my name the most learned and illustrious Count Ottolino Ottolini, whose wisdom and talent even Rome has admired. I hear that your nephew, the most noble Antonio Muselli, son of your brother, proves himself worthy of you in ancient morals and in ecclesiastical discipline. In proportion as he now esteems your praise—which is also especially dear to God—let him strive day by day more and more. In all things I desire to be like you. Farewell again.

[Col. 0141]

### Vercelli Manuscript

Matthan. + But Matthan begot Jacob. 16. But Jacob begot Joseph, to whom the Virgin Mary, being betrothed, bore Jesus, who is called Christ. 17. This . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . through

## Chapter II

1. Now when Jesus had been born in Bethlehem, the city

> [Note: Thus also the Greek text, *τῆς Ἰουδαίας* (“of Judea”).]

## Chapter III

4. Now John . . . wore . . . . . a garment of camel’s hair, and a leather belt around his waist; and his food was locusts and wild honey. 5. Jordan went out to him; and they were baptized . . . by him in the Jordan, con. . . . ing . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 7. And do not suppose that you can say among yourselves, ‘We have Abraham for our father.’ For I tell you that God is able from these stones to rai. . . . up chil. . . . . . 10. He has a winnowing shovel in his hand; and he has cleansed his threshing floor . . . and gathered the wheat [Col. 0155] into the granary, but he shall burn the chaff with unquenchable fire.”

13. Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan, to John, in order to be baptized 14. by him. But John tried to prevent him, saying: “I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?” 15. But Jesus answered and said to him: “Allow it now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.” Then he allowed him. And when he was baptized, a great light shone around from the water, so that all who had come were afraid. 16. And Jesus, having been baptized, immediately came up from the water; and behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending

## CHAPTER VI

1. Take heed not to do your righteousness before men in order to be seen by them; otherwise you shall have no reward from your Father who is in heaven. 2. Therefore, when you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before yourself, as hypocrites do in synagogues and streets, in order that they may be honored by men. Truly I say to you, they have their reward. 3. But when you give alms, do not let your left hand know what your right hand does, 4. so that your alms may be in secret; and your Father, [Col. 0171] who sees in secret, shall repay you openly. 5. But when you pray, do not be like . . . hypocrites, who . . . to stand praying in synagogues and at the corners of streets, in order to be seen by men. Truly I say to you, they have their reward. 6. But when you pray, enter your inner room; and, having shut the door, pray to your Father in secret. And your Father, who sees in secret, shall repay you openly. 7. But when praying, do not speak much, as the Gent . . . . For they think that . . . by their much speaking they shall be heard. 8. Therefore do not be like them. For your Father knows [Col. 0171] what you need before you ask 9. him. Therefore pray to him thus: Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name. 10. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in heaven and on earth. 11. Give us today our daily bread. 12. And forgive us our debts, as we also . . . . 13. . . . our debtors. And do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil. [Note: [Col. 0171] “Amen” is lacking, also in Cod. Cant.] 14. For if you forgive men their sins, your Father who is in 15. heaven will forgive you. But if you do not forgive . . . men, neither will your Father forgive [Col. 0173] your sins. 16. But when you fast, do not become gloomy like hypocrites. For they disfigure their faces in order to appear to men as fasting. Truly I say to you, [Note: [Col. 0173] Before “they have,” “because” is lacking. So too in Cod. Cant.] they have their reward. 17. But you, when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, 18. so that you may not appear to men as fasting, but to your Father who is in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, shall repay you openly. 19. Do not lay up treas . . . . for yourselves on earth, where rust and moth destroy, and where thieves break in and steal. 20. [Note: [Col. 0173] From here to verse 27 of chapter VIII all is lacking in the Greek Cod. Cant., according to Mill in the appendix.] But lay up [Col. 0173] treasures for yourselves in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves neither break in nor 21. steal. For where your treasure is, there [Note: [Col. 0173] So the Greek text, ἔσται, “will be.”] will be + your heart also. 22. The lamp of your body is your eye. If your eye is sound, your whole body is full of light. 23. But if your eye is evil, your whole body is dark. How great, then, is your darkness! 24. No one can serve two masters; for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will hold to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God [Col. 0175] and Mammon. 25. Therefore I say to you, do not be anxious in your heart about what you shall eat, nor about your body, what you shall wear. Is not the soul more than food, and the body than clothing? 26. Look at the birds of heaven: for they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not worth much more than they? 27. For which of you can add one cubit to his stature? 28. And why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they neither t . . . nor sp . . . . Yet 29. I say to you that not even Solomon in all his glory [Col. 0175] was clothed as one of these. 30. But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into an oven, how much more you, of little faith? 31. Therefore do not be anx . . . . saying: What shall we eat, or what shall we drink, or with what shall we be clothed? 32. For the Gent . . . . seek all th . . . things; and your Father knows that you need all these things. 33. Therefore seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be provided to you. 34. Do not be anxious about tomorrow. For tomorrow will be anx . . . . about it . . . . [Col. 0177] Suffic . . . . for the day is its own evil.

1. Do not judge, that you may not be judged. 2. For with the judgment by which you judge, you shall be judged; and with the measure by which you measure, it shall be measured to you. 3. But why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye and do not consider the beam that is in your own eye? 4. Or how do you say to your brother, “Let me take the speck out of your eye,” while behold, there is a beam in your own eye? 5. Hypocrite, first take the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see to take the speck out of your brother’s eye. 6. Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast your pearls [Col. 0177] before swine, lest perhaps they trample th . . . under their feet and, turning, t . . . . you to pieces. 7. Or if he asks for a f . . . will he hand him a serpent? 11. Therefore, if you, though evil, know how to give good gi . . . to your childr . . . , how much more shall your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him! 12. Therefore all things whatsoever you want men [Note: [Col. 0177] They add “good things”; so Cyprian, *On the Lord’s Prayer*. In the same place “thus” is added, according to the Greek text, οὕτω.] to do to you, good things, thus + do also [Col. 0179] to them. For this is the law and the prophets. 13. Enter through the narrow gate; [Note: [Col. 0179] The Latin Vulgate translates “because,” taking ὅτι in the Hellenistic sense for ὡς.] for + broad is the gate and spacious the way that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter through i . . . . . 14. nar . . . . is the way that leads to life, and few are those who find it! 15. Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravening wolves. 16. By their fruits you shall know them. Do men gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles? 17. Thus every good tree bears good fru . . . , but a bad tree bears bad fruits. 18. A [Col. 0179] good tree cannot bear bad fruit, nor can a bad tree bear good fruit. 19. Every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and cast into the fire. 20. Therefore by their fruits you shall know 21. them. Not everyone who says to me, “Lord, Lord,” shall enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will . . . . of my Fath . . . who is in heaven, he shall enter the kingdom of heaven. 22. Many shall say to me on that day, “Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name and cast out demons in your name?” 23. And then I shall say to them: “Because I never knew you; depart from me, workers of iniquity.” [Col. 0181] 24. Everyone who hears these words of mine and does them is like a wi . . . man, who bu . . . . his house upon 25. rock. Rain fell, floods came, winds blew, and struck that house; and it did not fall, for it was founded upon rock. 26. And everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them is like a fo . . . man, who built his house upon s . . . . 27. sand. For he was teaching them as one having authority, and not as their scribes and Pharisees.

And he said to them: ‘An enemy has done this.’ [Note: [Col. 0225] Thus also the Canterbury manuscript: *λέγουσιν αὐτῷ οἱ δοῦλοι*, “the servants say to him.”] The servants say [Note: [Col. 0225] The *m* in *fructum* has been erased by a corrector.] +: ‘Do you wish us to go and gather 29. them?’ He said to them: ‘No, lest perhaps while gathering the tares you uproot [Note: [Col. 0225] Thus also the Canterbury manuscript: *ἅμα καί*, “at the same time also.”] together with + the wheat. 30. Let both grow together until the harvest; and at harvest time I shall say to the reapers: Gather the tares first and bind them into bundles for burning, but gather the wheat into [Col. 0227] my barn.’ 31. He spoke another parable [Note: [Col. 0227] Thus also the Canterbury manuscript: *ἐλάλησεν*, “he spoke.”] + to them, saying: “The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed, which . . . a man sowed in his field: 32. it is indeed the smallest of all seeds; but when it has grown, it becomes greater than all garden plants, and becomes a tree so great that the bird- . . . of heaven come and dwell in its bran- . . . .” 33. . . . another para- . . . he said to them. “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven, which a woman, having taken it, hid in three measures of flour, until the whole was leavened.” [Col. 0227] 34. Al- . . . these thi- . . . Jesus spoke in parables . . . and without parables he did not speak to them, 35. so that . . . what was spo- . . . through the Pro- . . . might be fulfilled, saying: “I shall open my mouth in parables; I shall utter things hidden from the foundation of the world.” 36. Then, dismissing the crowds, he went into the house; and his disciples came to him, say- . . . : “Expl- . . . to us the para- . . . of the wheat and tares of the field.” 37. But Jesus answered and said: “He who sow- . . . the good se- . . . is the Son of Man. 38. The field is this world. The good se- . . . : these are the children of the kingdom. But the tares are the children of wickedness. [Col. 0229] 39. The enemy who sowed them is the devil. The harvest is the consummation of the age, and the reapers are angels. 40. Therefore, as the tares are gathered and burned with fire, so it shall be at the consummation of the age. 41. The Son of Man shall send his angels, and they shall gather . . . out of his kingdom all causes of stumbling and those who commit iniquit- 42. . . . ; and cast . . . them into the furnace of fire. There shall be weeping and gna- . . . of teeth. 43. Then the righteous shall shine like the sun in their Father’s kingdom. He who has ears, let him hear.

44. “The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure [Col. 0229] hidden in a field, which, when a man finds . . . , he hides . . . ; and, for . . . joy over it, goes and sells all that he has, . . . buys that field. 45. Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a mercha- . . . seek- . . . a fine pearl. 46. And when he found [Note: [Col. 0229] Before “precious,” “one” is lacking, also in the Canterbury manuscript.] a preciou- . . . pear- . . . , he went and sol- . . . whatever . . . had, and bought it. 47. Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea, which gathers fish of every kind. [Note: [Col. 0229] Thus also the Canterbury manuscript: *ὅτε δέ*, “but when.”] 48. But when . . . it was full, [Note: [Col. 0229] Thus also the Canterbury manuscript: *ἀνεβίβασαν αὐτήν*, “they drew it up.”] they drew it up + [Note: [Col. 0229] Thus also the Greek text: *ἐπὶ τὸν αἰγιαλόν*, “onto the shore.”] onto the shore + and, sitting down, selected [Note: [Col. 0229] Thus also the Canterbury manuscript: *τὰ κάλλιστα*, “the best.”] the best + [Col. 0231] fi- . . . into ves- . . . , but . . . put . . . . 49. So shall it be at the consummation of the ag- . . . : the an- . . . shall go out and separate . . . the wicked from among the righteous, 50. and cast them . . . into the furnace of fi- . . . ; there . . . be weeping and gnas- . . . of teeth.” And he said: 51. “Have you understood all these things?” They say to him: “Certainly.” [Note: [Col. 0231] They add “Lord,” as does the Greek text: *Κύριε*. *ὁ δέ*.] “Lor- . . .” + 52. he said to them: “Therefore every scr- . . . instructed . . . in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure things new and old.” 53. And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished these para- . . . , that he depart- . . . from there. 54. And com- . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . [Col. 0231] . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . “Whence has this man this wisdom and these mighty works? 55. . . . Is this not the son of Joseph the carpenter? Is not his mother called Mary, and his brother- . . . James, Joseph, Simon, 56. and Judas? And are not all his sisters . . . ? . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 57. . . . in his countr- . . . and in . . . . 58. Therefore he did not perform mighty works there . . . because of their unbelief.
