When his fellow servants saw what was happening, they were greatly distressed; and they came and reported to their master all that had occurred. Then his master summoned him and said to him: “Wicked servant, I forgave you all that debt because you begged me. Ought you not then also to have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I too had mercy on you?” And his master, angered, handed him over to the torturers until he should repay the entire debt. So also will my Father who is in heaven do to you, if each of you does not forgive his brother from your hearts.

And it came to pass, when Jesus had spoken these words, that he departed from Galilee and came into the borders of Judaea and beyond the Jordan; and great crowds followed him, and he healed them there.

[Note: Thus you should read in Hilary’s text of the *Commentary on Matthew*.]

And Pharisees came to him, testing him and saying: “Is it lawful for a man to dismiss his wife for any cause?” He answered them: “Have you not read that he who made them from the beginning made them male and female?”

[Note: The Vulgate: “he who made man from the beginning.” The Corbie manuscript omits both expressions, namely “man” and “from the beginning”; the Saint-Germain codex indeed reads “from the beginning,” but does not read “man.” And rightly so, since this wording is not found at all in Jerome’s *Commentary on Matthew*.]

“And he said: ‘For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and shall cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.’ Thus they are no longer two, but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let no human being separate.” They said to him: “Why then did Moses command that a certificate of divorce be given and that she be dismissed?” He said to them: “Because of the hardness of your hearts Moses permitted you to dismiss your wives; but from the beginning it was not so. But I say to you, whoever dismisses his wife, except on account of adultery, causes her to commit adultery.”

[Note: The Vulgate reads: “... except on account of fornication, and [whoever] marries another commits adultery.”]

The disciples said to him: “If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is not expedient to marry.” But Jesus said to them: “Not all accept this saying, but only those to whom it has been given. For there are eunuchs (*spadones*) who were born thus from their mother’s womb; and there are eunuchs who were made such by human beings; and there are eunuchs who have castrated themselves for the kingdom of heaven. Let the one able to accept this accept it.”

[Note: Tertullian and Cyprian, together with two of our manuscript codices, read “there are eunuchs” (*sunt spadones*); and thus they consistently retain the designation *spadones* elsewhere instead of “eunuchs.”]

Then little children were brought to him that he might lay hands upon them and pray. But his disciples were preventing them. Jesus, however, said: “Permit them, and do not prevent them from coming to me; for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these.” And after laying hands upon them, he departed from there.

And behold, one came to him and said: “Good Master, what good thing shall I do that I may have eternal life?” Jesus answered him: “Why do you ask me concerning the good? God alone is good.”

[Note: The Saint-Germain manuscript here has the wording found in Mark, chapter 10, verse 18: “No one is good except the one God.”]

“But if you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments.” He said to him: “Which?” Jesus said: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness; honour your father and your mother; and you shall love your neighbour as yourself.” The young man said to him: “I have kept all these things; what do I still lack?”

[Note: Lucas Brugensis observes that the words “from my youth,” which follow in our Vulgate, were not read in Greek by the Latin translator and consequently were not rendered in Latin. That this accords with the truth is shown by our two Latin manuscripts and other very ancient copies.]

Jesus said to him: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you possess and give to the poor, and you shall have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.” But when the young man had heard this word, he went away sorrowful; for he possessed many possessions. Jesus then said to his disciples: “Amen, I say to you: a rich person will enter the kingdom of heaven with difficulty. Again I say to you: it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven.” On hearing this, his disciples were greatly astonished, saying: “Who then can be saved?” But Jesus, looking at them, said: “With human beings this is impossible; but with God all things are possible.”

Then Peter answered and said: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you; what then shall there be for us?” Jesus said to them: “Amen, I say to you: you who have followed me, in the renewal, when the Son of Man shall sit on the throne of his glory, you too shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. And everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or children, or fields, for my name’s sake, shall receive a hundredfold and shall possess eternal life. But many who are first shall be last, and the last first.”

[Note: Certain words are omitted in the Corbie manuscript, namely “or father” and “or wife.” They are likewise absent from the Cambridge manuscript, as the Greek variant readings in vol. VI of the London Polyglot inform us.]

## XX.

The kingdom of heaven is like a householder who went out early in the morning to hire labourers for his vineyard. Having agreed with the labourers for a denarius a day, he sent them into his vineyard. And going out about the third hour, he saw others standing idle in the marketplace, and said to them: “Go also into my vineyard, and I shall give you whatever is just.” And they went. Again he went out about the sixth and the ninth hour, and did the same. But about the eleventh hour he went out and found others standing, and said to them: “Why do you stand here idle all day?” They said to him: “Because no one has hired us.” He said to them: “Go also and work in the vineyard.” When evening came, the lord of the vineyard said to his steward: “Call the labourers and pay them their wages, beginning with the last and ending with the first.” Therefore, when those who had come about the eleventh hour arrived, they each received a denarius. But when the first also came, they supposed that they would receive more; yet they too each received a denarius. And, receiving it, they murmured against the householder, saying: “These last have worked only one hour, and you have made them equal to us, who have borne the burden of the day and the heat.” But he answered one of them: “Friend, I do you no wrong. Did you not agree with me for a denarius? Take what is yours and go. But I wish to give this last one as much as to you. Or is it not lawful for me to do what I wish with what is mine? Or is your eye evil because I am good?” Thus the last shall be first and the first last. For many are called, but few chosen.

And as Jesus was going up to Jerusalem, he took the twelve disciples aside and said to them: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man shall be delivered to the chief priests and scribes; and they shall condemn him to death and hand him over to the Gentiles to be mocked, flogged, and crucified; and on the third day he shall rise again.”

[Note: Saint Hilary read here “secretly,” in accordance with the testimony of very many manuscript codices.]

Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee came to him with her sons, worshipping him and asking something of him. He said to her: “What do you wish?” She said: “Command that these two sons of mine may sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your kingdom.” But Jesus answered and said to them: “You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I am about to drink?” They said to him: “We are able.” Jesus said to them: “You shall indeed drink my cup; but to sit at my right hand and at my left is not mine to give you, but belongs to those for whom it has been prepared by my Father.” When the ten heard it, they were indignant concerning the two brothers. But Jesus called them to himself and said: “You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. It shall not be so among you. Rather, whoever wishes to be great among you shall be your servant; and whoever wishes to be first among you shall be your slave. Just as the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve and to give his life as a redemption for many.”

[Note: “But you seek to grow from the small and to become greater than the lesser. And when you go out,” etc.]

[Note: A manuscript codex of the monastery of Saint Andrew near Avignon retains the same addition, but in a more polished style, as follows: “But you seek to grow from the small and to become greater than the great. When you enter a banquet, do not recline in the highest places, lest someone more distinguished than you should arrive; and the one who invited you to the banquet, coming up, should say to you: ‘Move still farther down,’ and you be put to shame. But if you recline in a lower place, and one humbler than you should arrive, the one who invited you to the banquet will say to you: ‘Come still farther up.’ And this will be more advantageous for you.” There is no addition more notable in the whole volume of Matthew, owing to the most famous questions of learned men by which it has been debated. The presbyter Juvencus and Saint Hilary read it in their Gospel copies; but Leo the Great seems to have had no more added in his Gospel volume beyond what our Saint-Germain manuscript retains. Consult our *Annotations written on the Italian translation of Saint Matthew*, where we have discussed this addition at length.]

“But you seek to grow from the small and to become lesser than the great. When invited to a banquet, do not recline in the more prominent places, lest perhaps someone more distinguished than you arrive; and the one who invited you say to you: ‘Move still farther down.’ And it will be shame for you. But if you recline in a lower place, and one humbler than you arrives, the one who invited you to the banquet will say to you: ‘Come still farther up.’ And this will be more advantageous for you.”

And as they were going out from Jericho, great crowds followed him. And behold, two blind men sitting beside the road heard that Jesus was passing by; and they cried out, saying: “Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David.” But the crowds rebuked them so that they should be silent. Yet they cried out all the more, saying: “Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David.” And Jesus stopped and, calling them, said to them: “What do you wish me to do for you?” They said to him: “Lord, that our eyes may be opened.” But Jesus, having compassion on them, touched their eyes. And immediately they saw.

## XXI.

And when they drew near to Jerusalem and came to Bethphage, at the Mount of Olives, then Jesus sent two of his disciples, saying to them: “Go into the village opposite you, and immediately you will find a she-ass tied, and her colt with her. Untie them and bring them to me. And if anyone says anything to you, say that the Lord requires their service, and he will immediately send them.” This happened in order that what had been spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled: “Say to the daughter of Zion: Behold, your king comes to you, gentle, sitting upon a colt of a she-ass.” The disciples went and did as Jesus commanded them. And they brought the she-ass and the colt, laid their garments upon it, and he sat upon it.

[Note: The Syriac translator agrees with the Corbie manuscript codex; in him I read *usomou al ilo nahhthaihun*, that is, “and they placed their garments upon the colt.”]

And a very great crowd spread their garments on the road; while others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road. And the crowds that went before him cried out, saying: “Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; Hosanna in the highest.” And when he entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred, saying: “Who is this?” But many said: “This is Jesus, the prophet from Nazareth of Galilee.”

And Jesus entered the temple of God and drove out all those selling and buying in the temple; and he overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those selling doves. And he said to them: “It is written: ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer’; but you have made it a den of robbers.” And blind and lame persons came to him in the temple, and he healed them. But when the chief priests and scribes saw the wonderful deeds which Jesus performed, and the children crying out in the temple and saying, “Hosanna to the Son of David,” they were indignant and said to him: “Do you hear what these are saying?” But Jesus said to them: “Certainly; have you never read: ‘Out of the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise’?” And leaving them, he went outside the city to Bethany, and stayed there.

In the morning, while passing into the city, he was hungry. And seeing a fig tree beside the road, he came to it and found nothing on it except leaves only. And he said to it: “May fruit never grow from you for ever.” And immediately the fig tree withered. When the disciples saw it, they marvelled, saying: “How did it wither immediately?” Jesus answered them: “Amen, I say to you: if you have faith and do not doubt, not only shall you do what was done to the fig tree, but even if you say to this mountain, ‘Be lifted up and cast yourself into the sea,’ it shall happen. And whatever you ask in prayer, believing, you shall receive.”

And when he came into the temple, the chief priests and elders of the people came to him while he was teaching and said: “By what authority do you do these things? Or who gave you this authority?” Jesus said to them: “I also will ask you one question. Tell me, and I shall tell you by what authority I do these things. John’s baptism: whence was it—from heaven, or from human beings?” But they reasoned among themselves, saying: “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say to us, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’ But if we say, ‘From human beings,’ we fear the crowd, for they all held John to be a prophet.” And answering him, they said: “We do not know.” Jesus said to them: “Neither shall I tell you by what authority I do these things.

“What do you think? A certain man had two sons. Coming to the first, he said to him: ‘Son, go work today in the vineyard.’ He answered: ‘I will not.’ But afterwards, repenting, he went into the vineyard. Then he came to the other and said likewise. He answered: ‘I will go, sir,’ but did not go. Which of the two did the father’s will?” They said to him: “The last.”

[Note: Lucas Brugensis pronounces this reading to be spurious and not found in genuine copies. Nevertheless, he admits that Hilary read it, together with certain ancient copies mentioned by Jerome in his *Commentary on Matthew*. There are, however, books of every kind in which the reading is, “They say to him: The last,” not “They say to him: The first.” In this place Thomas Mareschallus should be consulted, *Observations on the Anglo-Saxon Version*, pp. 498–499. But the larger manuscript codex of Saint Andrew near Avignon must not be omitted: it reads, “They say: The last,” in accordance with the usage of the Corbie and Saint-Germain manuscripts and the other most ancient copies.]

Jesus said to them: “Amen, I say to you: prostitutes and tax collectors shall go before you into the kingdom of heaven. For John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him; but tax collectors and prostitutes believed him. Yet even when you had seen this, you did not afterwards repent so as to believe him.”

## XXII.

Hear another parable. There was a householder who planted a vineyard, surrounded it with a hedge, dug a pit in it, built a tower, leased it to tenants, and went abroad. When the season of fruit drew near, he sent his servants to the tenants to receive from the fruits of his vineyard. But the tenants seized the servants: some they beat, others they killed, and others they stoned. Again he sent other servants, more numerous than the first; and they treated them likewise. Finally he sent his only son, saying: “Surely they will respect my son.” But when the tenants saw the son, they said among themselves: “This is the heir. Come, let us kill him and take possession of his inheritance.” And seizing him, they threw him outside the vineyard and killed him. Therefore, when the lord of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those tenants?” They said to him: “He will miserably destroy those evil men, and lease the vineyard to other tenants, who will render him its fruits in their seasons.” Jesus said to them: “The stone which the builders rejected, this has become the head of the corner; this has been done by the Lord, and it is wonderful in our eyes. Therefore I say to you: the kingdom of God shall be taken away from you and given to a nation producing fruit.”

[Note: “This” (*iste*), with reference to Greek γωνίας (“corner”).]

[Note: The Corbie codex omits here an entire verse, numbered 44 in our Vulgate. The Cambridge copy likewise omits the same verse; for it is absent there in Greek and Latin. Thus those manuscript codices are found to agree in many respects: namely, our Latin and Greek Corbie manuscripts and the Latin and Greek Cambridge manuscript.]

And when the chief priests and Pharisees heard his parables, they understood that he was speaking about them. And seeking to seize him, they feared the crowds, because they regarded him as a prophet.

And Jesus answered and again spoke to them in parables, saying: “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who made a wedding feast for his son. And he sent his servants to call those invited to the wedding feast, but they would not come. Again he sent other servants, saying: ‘Tell those invited: Behold, I have prepared my dinner; my bulls and fattened fowl have been slaughtered, and everything is ready. Come to the wedding feast.’ But they disregarded it and went away, one to his farm, another to his business. The rest seized his servants, shamefully mistreated them, and killed them. When the king heard this, he was angry; and he sent his army, destroyed those murderers, and burned their city. Then he said to his servants: ‘The wedding feast is indeed prepared, but those invited were not worthy. Therefore go to the outlets of the roads, and invite whomever you find to the wedding feast.’ And those servants went out along the roads and gathered all whom they found, evil as well as good; and the wedding feast was filled with reclining guests. But when the king entered to see those reclining, he saw there a man not dressed in a wedding garment. And he said to him: ‘Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?’ But he was speechless. Then he ordered the servants: ‘Take him, with feet and hands bound, and cast him into the outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.’ For many are called, but few chosen.”

## XXIII.

Then the Pharisees went away and took counsel how they might ensnare him in speech. And they sent their disciples with the Herodians, saying: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful, that you teach the way of God in truth, and that you care for no one’s favour; for you do not regard the person of men. What do you think? Is it lawful to give tribute to Caesar, or not?” But Jesus, knowing their malice, said: “Why do you test me, hypocrites? Show me the tribute coin.” They brought him a denarius. Jesus said to them: “Whose image and inscription are these?” They said to him: “Caesar’s.” Then Jesus said to them: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” When they heard this, they marvelled; and leaving him, they departed.

On that day Sadducees came to him, denying the resurrection of the dead, and said to him: “Teacher, Moses said: ‘If anyone dies without children, his brother shall take that man’s wife and raise up offspring for his brother.’ Now there were seven brothers among us. The first took a wife and died without leaving offspring, and left his wife to his brother. Likewise the second and the third, down to the seventh. Last of all the woman also died. In the resurrection, therefore, whose wife among the seven shall she be? For all had her.” Jesus answered and said to them: “You err, not knowing the Scriptures nor the power of God. For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels of God in heaven. But concerning the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what was spoken to you by God, saying: ‘I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? He is not the God of the dead, but of the living.” And the crowds, hearing it, marvelled at his teaching.

But when the Pharisees heard that he had silenced the Sadducees, they gathered together; and one of them, a doctor of the law, questioned him, testing him: “Teacher, which commandment is great in the law?” Jesus said to him: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind. This is the greatest and first commandment. And the second is like it: You shall love your neighbour as yourself. On these two commandments hang the whole law and the prophets.”

But when the Pharisees had gathered together, Jesus questioned them, saying: “What do you think concerning the Christ? Whose son is he?” They said to him: “David’s.” Jesus said to them: “How then does David, in the Spirit, call him Lord, saying: ‘The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet’? If David therefore calls him Lord, how is he his son?” And no one was able to answer him a word; nor did anyone dare from that day onward to question him any further.

## XXIV.

Then Jesus spoke to the crowds and to his disciples, saying: “The scribes and Pharisees sit upon Moses’ seat. Therefore keep and do whatever they tell you; but do not do according to their works, for they speak and do not do. They bind heavy and unbearable burdens and place them upon people’s shoulders, but they themselves are unwilling to move them with their finger. They do all their works in order to be seen by people: they broaden their phylacteries and enlarge their fringes. They love the first places at banquets, the first seats in synagogues, greetings in the marketplace, and to be called Rabbi by people. But you are not to be called Rabbi; for one is your Teacher, and you are all brothers. And call no one your father upon earth, for one is your Father, who is in heaven. Nor be called masters, for one is your Master, Christ. The greatest among you shall be your servant. Whoever exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted.

“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who shut the kingdom of heaven before people. You yourselves do not enter, nor do you permit those entering to enter.”

[Note: An entire verse placed here in our Latin Vulgate is not recognized by our Latin manuscripts of the Old Latin version, nor by the Cambridge copy, nor by Jerome himself. See Lucas Brugensis, *Latin Variant Readings of the New Testament*, and Thomas Mareschallus, *Observations on the Anglo-Saxon Version*, p. 499.]

“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you traverse sea and land to make a single proselyte; and when he has become one, you make him twice as much a child of Gehenna as yourselves. Woe to you, blind guides, because you say: ‘Whoever swears by the temple, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gold of the temple is bound.’ Fools and blind persons! For which is greater, the gold or the temple that sanctifies the gold? And: ‘Whoever swears by the altar, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the offering that is upon it is bound.’ Blind persons! For which is greater, the offering or the altar that sanctifies the offering? Therefore whoever swears by the altar swears by it and by everything that is upon it. And whoever swears by the temple swears by it and by him who dwells in it; and whoever swears by heaven swears by the throne of God and by him who sits upon it.

“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you tithe mint, dill, and cumin, and have left aside the weightier matters of the law: judgment, mercy, and faith. These things it was necessary to do, and those not to omit. Blind guides, straining out a gnat but swallowing a camel. Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you cleanse the outside of cup and dish, but within you are full of plunder and uncleanness. Blind Pharisee, first cleanse what is inside cup and dish, so that what is outside may also become clean. Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful to people but inwardly are full of the bones of the dead and every impurity. So you also outwardly appear righteous to people, but inwardly you are full of hypocrisy and iniquity.

“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who build the tombs of the prophets and adorn the monuments of the righteous, and say: ‘If we had lived in the days of our fathers, we would not have been their partners in the blood of the prophets.’ Thus you bear witness against yourselves that you are sons of those who killed the prophets. And you, fill up the measure of your fathers. Serpents, brood of vipers, how shall you escape the judgment of Gehenna? Therefore behold, I send to you prophets, wise persons, and scribes; some of them you shall kill and crucify, and some of them you shall flog in your synagogues and persecute from city to city, so that upon you may come all righteous blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the temple and the altar. Amen, I say to you: all these things shall come upon this generation.”

XXV. Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you, how often I wished to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, and you were unwilling! Behold, your house shall be left desolate to you. For I tell you, you shall not see me henceforth until you say, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.”

And Jesus went out from the temple and was departing. His disciples came to show him the buildings of the temple. But he answered and said to them: “Do you see all these things? Amen, I tell you: not one stone here shall be left upon another that shall not be thrown down.”

And as he sat upon the Mount of Olives, the disciples came to him privately, saying: “Tell us, when will these things be? And what will be the sign of your coming and of the consummation of the age?” Jesus answered and said to them: “See that no one deceives you. For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am Christ,’ and they will deceive many. You will hear of wars and reports of wars. See that you are not troubled. For these things must happen, but the end is not yet. For nation shall rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom; and there shall be pestilences, famines, and earthquakes in various places. But all these things are the beginnings of sorrows.

“Then they will hand you over to tribulation and kill you, and you will be hated by all nations because of my name. Then many will be caused to stumble, and they will betray one another and hate one another. Many false prophets will arise and deceive many. And because iniquity has abounded, the love of many will grow cold. But whoever perseveres unto the end, that person shall be saved. And this Gospel of the kingdom shall be preached throughout the whole world, as a testimony to all nations; and then the consummation shall come.

“When therefore you see the abomination of desolation, spoken of through Daniel the prophet, standing in the holy place—let the reader understand—then those who are in Judaea must flee to the mountains. Let the one upon the roof not come down to take anything from his house; and let the one in the field not return to take his cloak. But woe to those who are pregnant and nursing in those days. Pray that your flight may not occur in winter or on the Sabbath. For then there shall be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the age until now. And unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved; but for the sake of my elect those days shall be shortened.

“Then, if anyone says to you, ‘Behold, here is Christ,’ or, ‘There,’ do not believe it. For false Christs and false prophets will arise, and will perform great signs and wonders, so as to lead even my elect, if possible, into error. Behold, I have foretold it to you. Therefore, if they say to you, ‘Behold, he is in the wilderness,’ do not believe it; or, ‘Behold, he is in the inner chamber,’ do not go out. For as lightning comes from the east and appears as far as the west, so shall be the coming of the Son of Man. Wherever the body may be, there the eagles shall be gathered.

“Immediately after the tribulation of those days, the sun shall be turned into darkness, the moon shall not give its light, the stars shall fall from heaven, and the powers of heaven shall be shaken. Then the sign of the Son of Man shall appear in heaven; and then all the tribes of the earth shall mourn, and they shall see the Son of Man coming upon the clouds of heaven with great power and his majesty. And he shall send his angels with a trumpet and a loud voice, and they shall gather his elect from the four winds, from their utmost bounds to their utmost bounds.

“Learn the parable from the fig tree: when its branch has already become tender and has put forth leaves, you know that it is near, at the doors. Amen, I tell you: this generation shall not pass away until all these things happen. Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away.

“But of that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, nor even the Son, but the Father alone.”

[Note: [Col. 0311] Hilary, Ambrose, Jerome, and other most eminent writers testify that this was the reading in the most ancient copies of Matthew.]

“For as were the days of Noah, so shall be the coming of the Son of Man. For as they were in the days of the flood, eating, drinking, taking wives, and did not know until the flood came and took them all away, so shall be the coming of the Son of Man. Then two will be in the field: one shall be taken and the other left.

[Note: [Col. 0312] On this addition, or variant reading, found in the Corbie manuscript, see Lucas Brugensis, *Notationes prolixiores*, and Th. Maresch, *Observationes in versionem Anglo-Saxonicam*, p. 500.]

“Two shall be lying in one bed: one shall be left, and the other taken. Watch therefore, because you do not know at what hour your Lord is coming. But know this: if the master of the house knew at what hour the thief would come, he would certainly keep watch and would not allow his house to be broken into. Therefore you too must be ready, because you do not know at what hour the Son of Man is coming.

“Who, then, is the faithful and prudent servant whom his master has appointed over his household, to give them their food at the proper time? Blessed is that servant whom his master, when he comes, finds doing so. Amen, I tell you: he will appoint him over all his possessions. But if that servant says in his heart, ‘My master delays his coming,’ and begins to strike his fellow servants, while eating and drinking with drunkards, that servant’s master will come on a day he does not know and at an hour he does not expect, and will cut him in two and assign his portion with the tax collectors. There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

“Then the kingdom of heaven shall be considered like ten virgins, who, having taken their lamps, went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride. Five of them were foolish and five prudent. The foolish, having taken their lamps, did not take oil with them in vessels; but the prudent took oil with them. While the bridegroom delayed, the foolish fell asleep. But at midnight a cry was made: ‘Behold, the bridegroom is coming; go out to meet him.’ Then all those virgins arose and trimmed their lamps. But the foolish said to the prudent: ‘Give us some of your oil, because our lamps are going out.’ The prudent answered and said: ‘Perhaps there will not be enough for both us and you; go instead to those who sell it and buy some for yourselves.’ But while they went to buy it, the bridegroom came; and those who were ready entered with him into the wedding feast, and the doors were shut. At last the remaining virgins also came, saying: ‘Lord, Lord, open to us.’ But he answered: ‘Amen, I tell you, I do not know you.’ Watch therefore, because you know neither the day nor the hour.

“For it is like a man going abroad, who called his servants and entrusted his property to them. To one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one, to each according to his ability; and he departed. Immediately the one who had received five talents went away, traded with them, and gained another five. Likewise, the one who had received two gained another two. But the one who had received one talent dug in the earth and hid his master’s money.

“After a long time, the master of those servants came to settle accounts with them. The one who had received five talents approached and offered another five talents, saying: ‘Master, you gave me five talents; behold, I have gained another five.’ His master said to him: ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. Since you have been faithful in a little thing, I shall appoint you over greater things. Enter into the joy of your master.’ And when the one who had received two talents came, he said: ‘Master, you gave me two talents; behold, I have gained another two talents.’ His master said to him: ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. Since you have been faithful in a small matter, I shall appoint you over greater things. Enter into the joy of your master.’

“But the one who had received one talent came and said: ‘Master, I knew you to be a hard man: you reap where you have not sown, and gather where you have not scattered. Therefore, being afraid, I went and hid your talent in the earth. Behold, you have what is yours.’ His master answered and said: ‘Wicked and lazy servant, you knew that I reap where I have not sown and gather where I have not scattered. You ought therefore to have entrusted my money to the bankers; then, when I came, I would have received it back with interest. Take the talent from him, then, and give it to the one who has ten talents. For to everyone who has, more shall be given, and he shall abound; but from the one who does not have, even what he has shall be taken away. And cast the wicked servant out into the outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.’

[Note: [Cols. 0319–0320] The Greek manuscripts have what is read here in the Corbie manuscript. Hilary likewise reads: “And what he has shall be taken away,” etc. But what follows in the same Corbie manuscript—“And cast the wicked servant out,” etc.—is represented by the Greek text of the Cambridge exemplar, where they read, βάλετε ἔξω, “cast out.”]

“But when the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all the angels with him, then he shall sit upon the throne of his majesty. All nations shall be gathered before him, and he shall separate them from one another, as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. He shall place the sheep at his right hand, but the goats at the left. Then the king shall say to those at his right: ‘Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the beginning of the world.

[Note: [Col. 0320] Cyprian, Lucifer of Cagliari, Gaudentius, bishop of Brescia, and Augustine read in the same way: “from the beginning of the world.”]

“For I was hungry and you gave me food; I was thirsty and you gave me drink; I was a stranger and you received me; naked, and you clothed me; sick, and you visited me; I was in prison, and you came to me.’ Then the righteous shall answer him, saying: ‘Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you, or thirsty and give you drink? When did we see you as a stranger and receive you, or naked and clothe you? When did we see you sick or in prison and come to you?’ But he shall answer them: ‘Amen, I tell you: insofar as you did it to one of these least ones, you did it to me.’

[Note: [Cols. 0321–0322] Some Greek copies support this reading of the Corbie manuscript, as may be seen among the Greek variant readings of the New Testament in vol. VI of the London Polyglot.]

“Then he shall also say to those at his left: ‘Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire which my Father prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry and you did not give me food; I was thirsty and you did not give me drink; I was a stranger and you did not receive me; naked, and you did not clothe me; sick and in prison, and you did not come to me.’ Then they too shall answer, saying: ‘Lord, when did we see you hungry and thirsty, or naked, or a stranger, or sick, or in prison, and did not minister to you?’ Then he shall answer them: ‘Amen, I tell you: insofar as you did not do it to one of these least ones, neither did you do it to me.’ And these shall go into eternal fire, but the righteous into eternal life.

[Additional apparatus: Col. 0305: *interficis*: “you murder”; *suas*: “her own.” Col. 0306: *ostenderent ei* / *ostenderet eis*: “that they might show him” / “that he might show them”; *enim*: “for.” Col. 0307: *Evangelium in*: “Gospel in”; *venit*: “comes.” Col. 0308: *descendat*: “let him not come down.” Col. 0309: *mundi usque modo, neque fiet*: “of the world until now, nor shall be”; *fuissent . . . fieret*: “had been shortened . . . would be saved”; *electos breviabuntur*: “for the elect [the days] shall be shortened”; *ecce illic*: “behold, there”; *Surgent*: “will arise”; *ducantur . . . etiam electi*: “even the elect may be led into error.” Col. 0310: “As in the Vulgate”; *ita erit et*: “so also shall be”; “As in the Vulgate, as far as ‘But concerning the day.’” Col. 0312: “As in the Vulgate, as far as ‘will come’”; *et unus, etc., ut Vulg.*: “and one, etc., as in the Vulgate.” Col. 0313: *perfodi*: “to break through”; *quia qua hora nescitis*: “because you do not know at what hour”; “Who thinks, etc., as in the Vulgate, as far as ‘gnashing of teeth’”; *est*: “is.” Col. 0314: “As in the Vulgate”; *erant*: “were”; “As in the Vulgate.” Col. 0315: *autem sumpserunt, etc., ut Vulg. usque, et dixerunt: Ne*: “but they took, etc., as in the Vulgate, as far as, ‘and they said: Lest’”; *Dum autem irent*: “But while they were going”; *clausa est janua*: “the door was shut.” Col. 0316: *reliquae*: “the remaining”; *vobis, nescio*: “you, I do not know”; *homo proficiscens, etc., ut in Vulg.*: “a man departing, etc., as in the Vulgate”; *statim abiit*: “immediately went away.” Col. 0317: *est alia, etc., ut in Vulg. usque, adquisivi*: “gained another, etc., as in the Vulgate, as far as ‘I have gained’”; *lucratus sum. Ait, etc., ut Vulg. usque timens*: “I have gained. He said, etc., as in the Vulgate, as far as ‘being afraid’”; *timens abii*: “being afraid, I went away.” Col. 0318: “And behold, etc., as in the Vulgate, as far as ‘to entrust the money’”; *mittere*: “to place”; *veniens ego, etc., ut Vulg.*: “I, when I came, etc., as in the Vulgate.” Col. 0319: *itaque*: “therefore”; *et abundabit*: “and he shall abound”; *videtur habere . . . inutilem servum injicite*: “seems to have . . . cast out the useless servant”; *illic*: “there.” Col. 0319: *quidem a dextris suis . . . a sinistris*: “indeed at his right hand . . . at the left.” Col. 0320: *rex, etc., ut Vulg.*: “the king, etc., as in the Vulgate”; *a constitutione*: “from the foundation”; *eram, et collexistis . . . operuistis*: “I was, and you received . . . clothed.” Col. 0321: *hospitem . . . aut nudum, etc., ut Vulg.*: “a guest/stranger . . . or naked, etc., as in the Vulgate”; *hospes*: “a guest/stranger”; *collexistis*: “you received.” Col. 0322: *visitastis*: “you visited”; *aut hospitem, aut nudum*: “or a guest/stranger, or naked”; *dicens*: “saying”; “As in the Vulgate”; *poenam aeternam*: “eternal punishment.”]

[Col. 0323] XXVI. And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished all these sayings, that he said to his disciples: “You know that after two days Passover will take place, and the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified.” Then the chief priests and elders of the people gathered in the courtyard of the high priest called Caiaphas, and they took counsel to seize Jesus by deceit and kill him. But they said: “Not on the feast day, lest there be an uproar among the people.”

But when Jesus was in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper, a woman came to him holding an alabaster vessel of precious ointment, and poured it upon his head as he reclined.

When the disciples saw this, they were indignant, saying: “Why this waste? For this could have been sold at a great price and given to the poor.” But Jesus, knowing it, said to them: “Why do you trouble the woman? She has done a good work toward me. For you always have the poor with you, but you will not always have me. For in pouring this ointment upon my body, she did it for my burial. Amen, I tell you: wherever this Gospel is preached in the whole world, what she has done shall also be spoken of in remembrance of her.”

Then one of the twelve, who was called Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests and said to them: “What will you give me, and I will hand him over to you?” And they agreed on thirty pieces of silver for him. From then on he sought an opportunity to hand him over.

On the first day of unleavened bread, the disciples came to Jesus, saying: “Where do you wish us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?” Jesus said: “Go into the city to a certain man and say to him: ‘The Teacher says, My time is near; with you I am keeping the Passover with my disciples.’” And the disciples did as Jesus directed them, and prepared the Passover.

When evening came, he reclined with the twelve disciples. And while they were eating, he said: “Amen, I tell you: one of you is about to hand me over.” Greatly distressed, they began each one to say: “Surely it is not I, Lord?” But he answered: “The one who dips his hand with me in the dish shall hand me over. The Son of Man indeed goes as it is written concerning him; but woe to that man through whom the Son of Man is handed over. It would have been good for him if that man had not been born.” Then Judas, who handed him over, answered and said: “Surely it is not I, Rabbi?” He said to him: “You have said it.”

And while they were dining, Jesus took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: “Take and eat: this is my body, which shall be handed over for you.”

[Note: [Cols. 0327–0328] The most ancient Greek and Latin exemplars do not add this. It is, one may suppose, an addition from the First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter XI, verse 24, where the matters pertaining to belief in Christ’s true body, delivered to the disciples as food, are clearly expressed. Compare also what is said at Luke XXII.19.]

And taking the cup, he gave thanks and gave it to his disciples, saying: “Drink from this, all of you. For this is my blood of the new covenant, which shall be poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins. But I tell you: henceforth I shall not drink of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in the kingdom of my Father.” And after a hymn had been sung, they went out to the Mount of Olives.

[Additional apparatus: Col. 0323: *venundari multo*: “to be sold for a high price.” Col. 0324: *habetis*: “you have.” Col. 0325: *At Jesus dixit*: “But Jesus said.” Col. 0327: *edite . . . meum. Et accipiens*: “eat . . . my body. And taking”; the following words, “which shall be handed over for you,” are absent from other most ancient Greek and Latin exemplars, as noted above. Col. 0328: *illis*: “to them.”]

XXVII. Then Jesus said to them: “All of you will be scandalized because of me this night. For it is written: ‘I shall strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered.’ But after I have risen, I shall go before you into Galilee.” Peter answered and said to him: “Even if all are scandalized because of you, I shall never be scandalized.” Jesus said to him: “Amen, I tell you: in this night, before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.” Peter said to him: “Even if I must die with you, I shall not deny you.” And all the disciples said likewise.

Then Jesus came with them to an estate called Gethsemane, and said to his disciples: “Sit here while I go there and pray.” And taking Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, he began to be sorrowful and distressed. Then he said to them: “My soul is sorrowful unto death. Remain here and watch with me.” Going a little farther, he fell upon his face, praying and saying: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me. Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.”

Then he came to his disciples and found them sleeping, and said to Peter: “Could you not then watch with me for one hour? Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” Again, a second time, he went away and prayed, saying: “My Father, if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, let your will be done.” And he came again and found them sleeping, for their eyes were heavy with sleep. Leaving them, he went away again and prayed a third time, saying the same words.

Then he came to his disciples and said to them: “Sleep now and rest. Behold, the hour has drawn near, and the Son of Man is handed over into the hands of sinners. Rise, let us go. Behold, the one who hands me over has drawn near.” While he was still speaking, behold, Judas, one of the twelve, came, and with him a great crowd with swords and clubs, sent by the chief priests and elders of the people. The one who handed him over had given them a sign, saying: “Whomever I kiss, he is the one; seize him.” And immediately, approaching Jesus, he said: “Hail, Rabbi,” and kissed him. Jesus said to him: “Friend, for what purpose have you come?” Then they approached, laid hands upon Jesus, and seized him.

And behold, one of those who were with Jesus stretched out his hand, drew his sword, and, striking the servant of the high priest, cut off his ear. Then Jesus said to him: “Put your sword back in its place. For all who take up the sword shall perish by the sword. Or do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he will immediately provide me with more than twelve legions of angels? How then shall the Scriptures of the Prophets be fulfilled, that it must happen thus?”

At that hour Jesus said to the crowds: “Have you come out with swords and clubs to seize me as though I were a robber? Every day I sat among you teaching in the temple, and you did not seize me. But all this has happened that the Scriptures of the Prophets might be fulfilled.” Then all the disciples left him and fled.

[Additional apparatus: Col. 0329: *mi Pater*: “my Father.” Col. 0330: *somno*: “with sleep.” Col. 0331: *omnis enim qui gladio percutit, gladio peribit*: “for everyone who strikes with the sword shall perish by the sword.” Col. 0332: *Scripturae, quia*: “the Scriptures, that.”]

XXVIII. But those who had seized Jesus led him to Caiaphas the chief priest, where the scribes and elders had assembled. Peter, however, followed him at a distance as far as the courtyard of the chief priest. Entering inside, he sat with the attendants to see the outcome. But the chief priests and the entire council sought false testimony against Jesus, in order to hand him over to death; and they found none, although many false witnesses came forward. At last [Note: [Col. 0333] however] two false witnesses came and said: “This man said, ‘I am able to destroy God’s Temple and build it again after three days.’” And the chief priest rose and said to him: “Do you make no answer to what these men testify against you?” But Jesus remained silent. And the chief priest said to him: “I adjure you by the living God: tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of God.” Jesus said to him: “You have said it. Nevertheless, I tell you: from now on you will see the Son of Man seated [Col. 0335] at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven.” Then the chief priest tore his garments, saying: “He has blasphemed. What further need have we of witnesses? Behold, now you have heard the blasphemy. What do you think?” And they answered and said: “He is guilty of death.”

Then they spat in his face and struck him with their fists; others slapped his face, saying: “Prophesy to us, Christ: who is it that struck you?” But Peter was sitting outside in the courtyard, and a maidservant came up to him, saying: “You too were with Jesus the Galilean.” But he denied it before them all, saying: “I do not know what you are saying.” And as he went out to the gateway, another woman saw him and said to those who were there: “This man too was with Jesus the Nazarene.” And again [Note: [Col. 0335] he swore] he denied it with an oath: “I do not know the man.” A little later those standing there came up and said to Peter: “Surely you too are one of them, for your speech makes you known.” Then he began to invoke curses and to swear that he did not know the man. And immediately the cock crowed. [Note: [Col. 0335] And he remembered Jesus’ word.] Peter remembered the word of Jesus, who had said: “Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.” And [Note: [Col. 0336] having gone outside,] he went [Col. 0337] outside and [Note: [Col. 0337] wept bitterly] wept most bitterly.

When morning came, all the chief priests [Note: [Col. 0337] and elders] and all the elders of the people took counsel against Jesus, to hand him over to death. They brought him bound and delivered him to Pontius Pilate the governor. Then Judas, who had betrayed him, seeing that he had been condemned [Note: [Col. 0337] had been], was seized with remorse and brought back the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders, saying: “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood.” But they said: “What is that to us? See to it yourself.” Throwing down the silver in the Temple, he departed; and he went away and hanged himself.

But the chief priests, having received the silver, said: “It is not lawful to put it into the [Note: [Col. 0338] into the *corban*:] treasury-offering, because it is the price of blood.” Having taken counsel, they bought with it the potter’s field as a burial-place for strangers. Therefore that field was called [Note: [Col. 0338] Acheldemach [ [Col. 0337] This name is reported to be written in Latin in the Cambridge manuscript as *Echeldemach*; in our manuscripts it is read as *Acheldamach* and *Acheldemach*. Corruptly, all read *Achel* or *Echel* for *Acel*, and *demach* and *damach* for *dama* or *dema*. For the Syriac word which signifies “blood” is written *demo*, not [Col. 0338] *demach*. In the Hebrew Gospel of Matthew, published at Paris in 1551, we read *bhacal dama*. In some Greek copies of Matthew, Ἀκέλδημα (*Akeldēma*); but in Acts of the Apostles, chapter 1, verse 19, it is written Ἀκελδαμά (*Akeldama*).] Acheldamach—that is, “Field of Blood”—to this day.

Then was fulfilled what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet, saying: “And they received the thirty pieces of silver, [Col. 0339] the price [Note: [Col. 0339] the price which they appraised for the sons] of him who was valued, whom they valued from the children of Israel; and they gave them for the potter’s field, as the Lord appointed me.”

But Jesus stood before the governor, and the governor questioned him, saying: “Are you the King of the Jews?” Jesus said to him: “You say so.” And when he was accused by the chief priests and elders, he answered nothing. Then Pilate said to him: “Do you not hear how many things they testify against you?” And he did not answer him a single word, so that the governor was greatly amazed.

Now on the festival day the governor was accustomed to release for the people one prisoner, whomever they wished. He had then a notorious prisoner called Barabbas. Therefore, when they had assembled, Pilate said: “Whom do you wish me to release to you—Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ?” For he knew that they had handed him over through envy. While he was sitting on the tribunal, his wife sent word to him, saying: “Have nothing to do with that righteous man; for today I have suffered much in a dream because of him.” But the chief priests and elders persuaded the crowds to ask for Barabbas and destroy Jesus. The governor answered and said to them: “Which of the two do you wish [Note: [Col. 0339] me to release?] to be released to you?” [Col. 0341] They said: “Barabbas.” Pilate said to them: “What then shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ?” They all said: “Let him be crucified.” The governor said to them: “For what evil has he done?” But they cried out the more, saying: “Let him be crucified.”

Seeing that he accomplished nothing, but that rather a tumult was arising, Pilate took water and washed his hands before the people, saying: “I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man. See to it yourselves.” And all the people answered and said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.” Then he released Barabbas to them; but Jesus, after having him scourged, he handed over to them to be crucified.

Then the governor’s soldiers took Jesus into the praetorium and gathered the whole cohort around him. They stripped him and put a scarlet cloak around him; and, plaiting a crown of thorns, they put it upon his head and a reed in his right hand. Kneeling before him, they mocked him, saying: “Hail, King of the Jews!” And spitting on him, they took the reed and struck his head with it. After they had mocked him, they took the cloak off him, dressed him in his own garments, and led him away to crucify him.

As they went out, they found a man of Cyrene named Simon; they compelled him to carry [Col. 0343] his cross. And they came to the place called Golgotha, which is called the place [Note: [Col. 0343] of Calvary. And] of a skull. They gave him wine mixed with gall to drink; and when he had tasted it, he would not drink. After crucifying him, they divided his garments by casting lots. [Note: [Col. 0343] The words which follow in the Sixtine Bibles, “that what was spoken might be fulfilled,” etc., are testified by learned men to be omitted in all ancient books of better authority; they have been transferred here in Matthew either from the Gospel according to John, or rather from Psalm XXI, verse 19. The variant readings of the Latin edition of the New Testament by Lucas of Bruges should be consulted at this [Col. 0344] point.] And sitting down, they kept watch over him. They placed over his head the written charge against him: “This is [Note: [Col. 0343] Jesus] the King of the Jews.”

Then [Note: [Col. 0343] they crucified . . . one . . . and one] two robbers were crucified with him, one at the right and one at the left. Those passing by blasphemed him, shaking their heads and saying: [Note: [Col. 0344] “He who [ [Col. 0344] Hilary agrees in this reading with the Corbie manuscript; other excellent and very ancient copies, according to the testimony of Lucas of Bruges, read with the Saint-Germain manuscript, “destroys, rebuilds.”] destroys the Temple and rebuilds it in three days:”] “You who were destroying God’s Temple and rebuilding it in three days, save yourself. If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross.” Likewise the chief priests, mocking him with the scribes and elders, said: “He saved others; he cannot save himself. If he is King of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him. He trusted in [Note: [Col. 0344] in God:] the Lord; let him deliver him now, if he wishes, for he said, ‘I am the Son of God.’” The robbers likewise, who [Note: [Col. 0345] were fixed] were crucified with him, reproached him.

From the sixth hour darkness came over the whole land until the ninth hour. About the ninth hour Jesus cried out in a loud voice, saying: [Note: [Col. 0345] Hebrew words unfamiliar to Latin writers are written variously in manuscript books, but everywhere corruptly, as the often-cited Bruges scholar noted before us. The Gothic translator writes *Helei*, with aspiration, for Ἐλί (*Eli*); and for the Greek [Col. 0346] Ἠλίαν (*Elian*) below and the Latin *Eliam*, there occur the Gothic *Helian* and Saxon *Heliam*. So Mareschal, *Observations on the Anglo-Saxon Version*, p. 500. Thus it is right that our manuscripts agree with these ancient barbarian versions.] “Heli, lema [Note: [Col. 0345] zabacthani?] sabachtani?” That is: “My God, my God, why [Note: [Col. 0346] have you forsaken me?] have you forsaken me?” But some standing there, on hearing it, said: “This man calls Elijah.” Immediately one of them ran, took a sponge, filled it with vinegar, put it on a reed, and gave him a drink. But the others said: “Leave him; let us see whether Elijah comes to save him.” Jesus, crying out again in a loud voice, gave up his spirit.

And behold, the veil of the Temple was torn in two from top to bottom, the earth shook, rocks were split, and tombs were opened; and many bodies of saints who had fallen asleep arose. Coming out of the tombs after his resurrection, they entered the holy city and appeared to many. But the centurion and those with him who were guarding Jesus, seeing the earthquake and the things that happened, [Col. 0347] were greatly afraid, saying: “Truly this man [Note: [Col. 0347] was] was the Son of God.”

There were also many women there at a distance, who had followed Jesus from Galilee, ministering to him; among them were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joseph, and the mother of the sons of Zebedee. When evening came, a certain rich man from [Note: [Col. 0347] Arimathia,] Arimathea, named Joseph, who was himself also a disciple of Jesus, came. He approached Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. Then Pilate ordered the body to be given over. Joseph took the body and wrapped [Note: [Col. 0348] it in a linen cloth] it in a clean linen cloth. He laid it in his own new tomb, which he had cut out in the rock; and he rolled a great stone to the entrance of the tomb and departed. Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were there, sitting opposite the tomb.

On the next day, which was after the Preparation, the chief priests and Pharisees assembled before Pilate, saying: “Lord, we remember that while he was still living that deceiver said, ‘After three days I shall rise.’ Therefore order the tomb to be guarded until the third day, lest perhaps his disciples come and steal him and say to the people, ‘He has risen from the dead’; and the last error will be worse than the first.” Pilate said to them: “[Col. 0349] You have [Note: [Col. 0349] guards [ [Col. 0349] An excellent reading in both manuscripts, as is shown by the learned Thomas Mareschal, *Observations [Col. 0350] on the Gothic Translation of Matthew*, p. 411.]] a guard; go, guard it as you know how.” They went and made the tomb secure, sealing the stone together with the guards.

But late on the Sabbath, as the first day of the week was dawning, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the tomb. And behold, there was a great earthquake; for an angel of the Lord descended from heaven, approached, rolled back the stone, and sat upon it. His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing white as snow. The guards were terrified from fear of him and became as dead men.

But the angel answered and said to the women: “Do not be afraid. For I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified. He is not here, for he has risen, as he said. Come, see the place where the Lord lay. Go quickly and tell his disciples that he has risen; and behold, he goes before you into Galilee. There you will see him. Behold, [Note: [Col. 0350] I have foretold] I have told you.” They quickly went out from the tomb with fear and great joy, running to announce it to his disciples. And behold, Jesus met them, saying: “Greetings.” They came up, took hold of his feet, and worshipped him. Then Jesus said to them:

[Col. 0351] “Do not be afraid. Go, announce to my brothers that they are to go into Galilee; there they will see me.” When they had gone, behold, some of the guards came into the city and reported to the chief priests all that had happened. Having assembled with the elders and taken counsel, they gave a large sum of money to the soldiers, saying: “Say, ‘His disciples came by night and stole him while we were asleep.’ And if this comes to the governor’s ears, we will persuade him and keep you safe.” They took the money and did as they had been instructed. And this report has been spread among the Jews to this day.

But the eleven disciples went into Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had appointed them to go. When they saw him, they worshipped him; but some doubted. Jesus came and spoke to them, saying: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Therefore go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit; teaching them to keep all things whatsoever I have commanded you. And behold, [Note: [Col. 0351] behold, I am with you.] I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age.”

## CODEX BRIXIANUS

[Col. 0142]

The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham. Abraham begot Isaac [Note: [Col. 0141] At the end, the *h* seems to have been erased; for *Isaach* was plainly written, as also in the following places. Since the erasure is likewise visible, we restore it.] (AA [Note: [Col. 0142] Wherever the sign (AA) occurs, the letters are gold up to that point.]). Isaac begot Jacob. Jacob begot Judah and his brothers. Judah begot Perez and Zerah by Tamar. Perez begot Hezron. Hezron begot Aram. Aram begot Amminadab. Amminadab begot Nahshon. Nahshon begot Salmon. Salmon begot Boaz by Rahab. Boaz begot Obed[h] by Ruth. Obed[h] [Note: [Col. 0142] Here too the aspirate was erased, though it is still plainly visible in the codex; hence we restore it, as we shall do elsewhere by using brackets.] begot Jesse. Jesse begot David the King. David the King begot Salo[Note: [Col. 0142] In this codex a letter is very rarely divided at the end of a line so as to be continued on the next. The scribe ordinarily prefers to leave parchment blank at the end of the line rather than divide a letter.]mon by her who had been Uriah’s. Solomon begot Rehoboam. Rehoboam [Col. 0144] begot Abijah. Abijah begot Asa. Asa begot Jehoshaphat. Jehoshaphat begot Joram. Joram begot Uzziah. Uzziah begot Jotham. Jotha[Note: [Col. 0143] The letter A is plainly seen to have been erased; we restore it at the end of the word *Joatha*.]m begot Ahaz. Ahaz begot Ezek[Note: [Col. 0143] The aspirate *h* has been erased, as in the following instance.]iah. Ezek[h]iah begot Manasseh. Manasseh begot Amon. Amon begot Josiah. Josiah begot Jeconiah and his brothers at the deportation to Babylon. After the deportation to Babylon, Jeconiah begot Shealtiel. Shealtiel begot Zerubbabel. Zerubbabel begot Abiud. Abiud begot Eliac[h]im. Eliac[h]im [Note: [Col. 0144] Brackets always indicate an erased aspirate *h*, traces of which are still visible in the codex.] begot Azor. Azor begot Zadok[h]. Zadok[h] begot Achim. Achim begot Eliud. Eliud begot Eleazar. Eleazar begot [Note: [Col. 0143] So also the Greek text, Ματθάν (*Matthan*).] Matthan. Matthan begot Jacob. Jacob begot Joseph, the husband of Mary, from whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ.

Therefore all the generations from Abraham to David are fourteen generations; from David to the deportation to Babylon, fourteen generations; and from the deportation to Babylon to Christ, fourteen generations.

[Col. 0146] The birth of Christ was thus. When his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together, she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit. Joseph, her husband, being a righteous man and unwilling to expose her publicly, wished to dismiss her secretly. As he considered these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying: “Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary your wife, for what will be born from her is of the Holy Spirit. She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he himself will save his people from their sins.” All this happened so that what had been spoken by the Lord through [Note: [Col. 0145] They add “Isaiah”; thus also the Cambridge codex, Ἠσαΐου (*Ēsaiou*).] Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled: “Behold, the Virgin shall be with child and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel,” which is translated, “God with us.”

Joseph, rising from sleep, did as the angel of the Lord commanded him and took his wife; and he did not [Note: [Col. 0145] So also Codex Cantabrigiensis, ἔγνω (*egnō*, “knew”).] know her until she bore her firstborn son, and he called his name Jesus.

When Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of [Note: [Col. 0145] So also the Greek text, τῆς Ἰουδαίας, “of Judea.”] Jud[Note: [Col. 0146] The letter *e* still appears whole in the codex, although it has been erased by someone.]ea [Col. 0148] in the days of King Herod, behold, Magi from the East came to Jerusalem, saying: “Where is he who has been born King of the Jews? For we saw his star in the east [Note: [Col. 0147] The letter *m* is visible, though erased.] and have come to worship him.” When King Herod heard this, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him. He gathered all the chief priests and scribes of the people and asked them where Christ was to be born. They said to him: “In Bethlehem of Jud[Note: [Col. 0148] Here also the letter *e* is clear, though somewhat rubbed away.]ea; for thus it is written through the prophet: ‘And you, Bethlehem of Jud[Note: [Col. 0148] Here likewise the letter *e* is clear, though somewhat rubbed away.]ea, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for from you shall come a ruler who will govern my people Is[Note: [Col. 0148] The letter *d* has plainly been erased, though its traces appear.]rael.’”

Then Herod secretly summoned the Magi and carefully ascertained from them the time when the star had appeared. He sent them to Bethlehem, saying: “Go and search carefully for the child; and when you have found him, report to me, so that I too may come and worship him.” After hearing the king, they departed; and behold, the star which they had seen in the East [Note: [Col. 0148] The letter *m* is erased, though its traces are apparent.] went before them until it came and stood over the place where the child was. Seeing the star, they rejoiced exceedingly with great joy; and entering [Col. 0150] [Note: [Col. 0149] So also the Greek text, εἰς τὴν οἰκίαν, “into the house.”] the house, they saw the child with Mary his mother. Falling down, they worshipped him; and opening their treasures, they offered him gifts: gold, frankincense [Note: [Col. 0149] An erased aspirate is visible.] and myrrh. Having been warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they returned to their own country by another way.

After they had departed, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream, saying: “Rise, take the child and his mother, flee into Egypt, and remain there until I tell you; for Herod is about to seek the child in order to destroy him.” He rose, took the child and his mother by night, and went into Egypt. He remained there until the death of Herod, so that what had been spoken by the Lord through the prophet might be fulfilled: “Out of Egypt I called my son.”

Then Herod, seeing that he had been deceived by the Magi, was greatly enraged.

Sending men, he killed all the boys in Bethlehem and throughout all its territory from two years old and under, according to the time which he had ascertained from the Magi.

Then was fulfilled what had been spoken through Jeremiah the prophet: “A voice was heard in Ramah, much weeping and lamentation. Rachel [Col. 0152] weeping for her children and unwilling to be comforted, because they are no more.”

After Herod’s death, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt, saying: “Rise, take the child and his mother, and go into the land of Israel; for those seeking the child’s life are dead.” He rose, took the child and his mother, and came into the land of Is[Note: [Col. 0151] An erased *d*, the traces of which remain.]rael. But when he heard that Archelaus ruled in Judea in place of Herod his father, he was afraid to go there. Warned in a dream, he withdrew to the regions of Galilee. Coming there, he dwelt [Note: [Col. 0151] So also the Greek text, εἰς πόλιν, “in a city.”] in a city called Nazareth, so that what had been spoken through the prophets might be fulfilled: “He shall be called a Nazarene.”

In those days John the Baptist came, preaching in the wilderness of Judea and saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.” For this is the one of whom Isaiah the prophet spoke: “A voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.”

[Col. 0154] John himself wore a garment of camel’s hair and a leather belt about his loins; his food was locusts and wild honey. Then Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0153] An erased *m*.] and all Judea and the whole region of the Jordan went out to him, and they were baptized by him in the Jordan, confessing their sins. But seeing many Pharisees and Sadducees coming for his baptism, he said to them: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath? Therefore bear fruit worthy of repentance, and do not presume to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you that God is able to raise up children for Abraham from these stones. Even now the axe lies at the roots of the trees. Therefore every tree which does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. I baptize you indeed with water unto repentance; but he who comes after me is mightier than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire. His winnowing-fan is in his hand; he will cleanse his threshing-floor and gather his whe[Note: [Col. 0154] The second letter *t* has been erased.]at [Col. 0156] into the granary, but he will burn the chaff with unquenchable fire.”

Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan, to John, in order to be baptized by him. But John tried to prevent him, saying: “I have need to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?” Jesus answered and said to him: “Permit it now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfil all righteousness.” Then he allowed him. After Jesus had been baptized, he immediately went up out of the water; and behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon him. And behold, a voice from heaven said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him.” Then Jesus was led into the wilderness by the Spirit in order to be tempted by the Devil.

After fasting forty days and forty nights, he was afterward hungry.

The tempter came to him and said: “If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become loaves of bread.” Jesus answered: “It is written: ‘A human being shall not live by bread alone, but by every word which proceeds from the mouth of God.’” Then the Devil took [Col. 0158] him to the holy city, set him on the pinnacle of the Temple, and said to him: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down. For it is written: ‘He has commanded his angels concerning you, that they may bear you up in their hands, lest you strike your foot against a stone.’” Jesus said to him again: “It is written: ‘You shall not tempt the Lord your God.’”

Again the Devil took him to a very high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. He said to him: “All these things I will give you if, falling down, you worship me.” Then Jesus said to him: “Go away, Satan; for it is written: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.’” Then the Devil left him; and behold, angels came and ministered to him.

When Jesus heard that John had been handed over, he withdrew into Galilee. Leaving the city of [Note: [Col. 0157] An erased *m*, whose traces are visible.] Nazareth, he came and dwelt in maritime Capernaum, in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali [Note: [Col. 0158] Here we have interrupted a line which is otherwise complete in the codex, because of the following letter, which projects into the margin as though beginning anew.], so that what had been spoken through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled: “Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, way of the sea beyond the Jordan, [Note: [Col. 0157] So also Codex Cantabrigiensis, Γαλιλαίας (*Galilaias*).] Galilee [Note: [Col. 0158] The final *e*, now erased, is still visible.] of the Gentiles: the people sitting in darkness [Col. 0160] saw a great light, and [Note: [Col. 0159] So also Codex Cantabrigiensis: καὶ οἱ καθήμενοι, “and those sitting.”] those sitting in the region and shadow of death—light has risen upon them.”

From that time Jesus began to preach and say: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.” As he passed [Note: [Col. 0159] “Jesus” is lacking also in Codex Cantabrigiensis.] beside the Sea of [Note: [Col. 0159] The final *m*, now erased, is still visible.] Galilee, he saw two brothers: Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother, casting nets [Note: [Col. 0159] Here likewise the final *m* has been erased.] into the sea, for they were fishermen. He said to them: “Come after me, and I will make you become fishers of human beings.” At once they left their nets and followed him.

Going on from there, he saw two other brothers, James son of Zebedee and John his brother, in a boat with Zebedee their father, mending their nets; and he called them. They immediately left the boat and their father and followed him. Jesus went around all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every disease and every infirmity among the people.

His report went through all Syria; and they brought him all who were ill, afflicted with various diseases and torments, poss[Note: [Col. 0160] The letter *a* has been erased, though its trace appears.]essed by demons, lunatics, and paralytics; and he healed them. Great crowds followed [Col. 0162] him from Galilee, the Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea, and from beyond the Jordan.

Seeing the crowds, he went up the mountain; and when he had sat down, his disciples came to him. Opening his mouth, he taught them, saying:

“Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. [Note: [Col. 0161] The fourth and fifth verses are transposed in the Greek and Latin Cambridge codex and in the Greek text, as in the Verona and Brixian codices.] Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted. Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled. Blessed are the merciful, for they shall receive mer[Note: [Col. 0161] . . . These three letters, *cor*, have been erased.]cy. Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God. Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.

“Blessed are you when people reproach you, persecute you, and falsely say every evil thing against you because of me. Rejoice and exult, because your reward is abundant in heaven. For so they persecuted the prophets [Col. 0164] who were before you.

“You are the salt of the earth. But if salt becomes tasteless, with what shall it be made salty? It is no longer good for anything except to be thrown out and trampled underfoot by people.

“You are the light of the world. A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden. Nor do people light a lamp and put it beneath a measuring-basket, but upon a lampstand, so that it may give light to all who are in the house.

“So let your light shine before people, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven. Do not think that I have come to abolish the law or the prophets. I have not come to abolish but to fulfil. Truly I tell you: until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota or one stroke shall pass from the law until all things are accomplished. Therefore whoever abolishes one of these least commandments and teaches people so shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven; but whoever does and teaches them shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven. For I tell you that unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven.

“You have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall not kill; and whoever kills shall be liable to judgment.’ But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother [Col. 0166] without cause shall be liable to judgment. Whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca’ [Note: [Col. 0166] Here an erased aspirate *k* is clearly visible.], shall be liable to the council. Whoever says, ‘Fool,’ shall be liable to the fire of Gehenna. Therefore, if you offer your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar [Note: [Col. 0166] The final *m*, still visible, has been cancelled.] and first go and be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer [Note: [Col. 0166] The final *s* has been erased.] your gift. Be quickly reconciled with your adversary while you are on the way with him, lest perhaps the adversary hand you over to the judge [Note: [Col. 0166] The second *i* has been erased.], the judge hand you over to the officer, and you be put in prison. Truly I tell you: you will not come out from there until you pay the very last quadrans.

“You have heard that it was said [Note: [Col. 0165] After ‘it was said,’ ‘to the ancients’ is lacking. So also in the Cambridge and Gothic codices.] ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.

“If your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you; for it is advantageous for you that one of your members perish, rather than your whole body be thrown into Gehenna. And if your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away from you; for it is advantageous for you that one of your members perish, [Col. 0168] rather than your whole body be thrown into Gehenna. It was also said: ‘Whoever dismisses his wife, let him give her a certificate of divorce.’ But I say to you: everyone who dismisses his wife, except on account of sexual immorality, makes her commit adultery; and whoever marries a dismissed woman commits adultery.
