There was there a large herd of pigs feeding; and they begged him that they might enter into them [Note: [Col. 0569] According to Codex Cantabrigiensis, ἵνα εἰς τοὺς χοίρους εἰσέλθωσιν.]. And he permitted them. 33. The demons therefore went out of the man and entered the pigs; and the herd rushed down the steep bank into the lake and was drowned. 34. But those who were feeding them, seeing what had happened [Note: [Col. 0569] According to the Greek text: ἰδόντες δὲ οἱ βόσκοντες τὸ γεγενημένον.], fled and reported it in the city and in the countryside.

35. They went out to see what had happened, came to Jesus, and found the man from whom the demons had gone out sitting at his feet, clothed and in his right mind; and they were greatly afraid. 36. Those who had seen it reported to them how the man who had been afflicted by demons [Note: [Col. 0571] According to the Greek text, ὁ δαιμονισθείς.] had been made whole. [Note: [Col. 0571] Before “who,” “and” is absent, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis.] 37. Then the whole multitude of the district of the Gerasenes begged him to depart from them, because they were held by great fear. He himself entered the boat and returned. 38. The man from whom the demons had gone out begged him that he might be with him; but he sent him away, saying [Note: [Col. 0571] Before “saying,” “Jesus” is absent, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis.], 39. “Return home and tell how great things the Lord has done for you.” And he went away through the whole city, proclaiming how great things Jesus had done for him.

40. When Jesus returned, the crowd welcomed him, for they were all waiting for him. 41. And behold, there came a man whose name was Jairus; he was a ruler of the synagogue. Falling at Jesus’ feet, he begged him to enter his house, 42. because … was his only …, about twelve years old, and she was dying. And as Jesus went, the crowd pressed upon him [Note: [Col. 0571] According to the Greek text, οἱ ὄχλοι συνέθλιβον αὐτόν.].

43. And a certain woman had had a flow of blood for twelve years; she had spent all her means on physicians and could not be healed by anyone. 44. She came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment, and immediately the flow of her blood stopped. 45. Jesus said, “Who touched me?” While all denied it, Peter and those with him said, “Master, such great crowds press around you, and you say, ‘Who touched me?’” 46. But Jesus said, “Someone touched me, for I myself perceived power going out from me.” 47. When the woman saw that she had not escaped his notice, she came trembling and fell at his feet; before all she would declare why she had touched him and how she had immediately been healed. 48. But he said to her, “Daughter, your faith has saved you; go in peace.”

49. While he was still speaking, there came from the ruler of the synagogue [Note: [Col. 0573] So also the Greek text, παρὰ τοῦ ἀρχισυναγώγου.], saying to him, “The daughter is dead … do not trouble …” 50. But Jesus, hearing this word, said to the girl’s father, “Do not fear; only believe, and she shall be saved.” 51. And when he came to the house, he allowed no one to enter with him except Peter, John, James, and the girl’s father and mother. 52. All were weeping and mourning for her. But he said, “Do not weep; she is not dead [Note: [Col. 0573] After “dead,” “the girl” is absent, also in the Greek text.], but sleeps.” 53. And they laughed at him, knowing that she was dead. 54. But he took her hand and called out, saying, “Girl, 55. arise.” And her spirit returned [Note: [Col. 0575] So also the Greek text, ἐπέστρεψε τὸ πνεῦμα αὐτῆς.], and she arose immediately; and he ordered that food be given her. 56. Her parents were astonished; but he commanded them to tell no one what had happened.

## CHAPTER IX

1. Having summoned the Twelve, his disciples [Note: [Col. 0575] So also the Greek text, μαθητὰς αὐτοῦ.], he gave them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases. 2. And he sent them to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal the sick. 3. He said to them, “Take nothing for the journey: neither staff nor bag nor sandals nor bread nor money, nor two tunics …” 4. “And whatever house you enter, remain there, and depart from there [Note: [Col. 0575] “Do not” is absent, also in the Greek text.]. 5. And whoever does not receive you, when you leave that city, shake even the dust from your feet as a testimony against them.” 6. … they … through villages and cities, proclaiming the good news and healing.

7. Now Herod the tetrarch heard of all that was being done, and was perplexed because some said, 8. “John has risen from the dead”; others, “Elijah has appeared”; and others, “One of the prophets of old has risen.” 9. But Herod said [Note: [Col. 0575] So also Codex Cantabrigiensis, δέ.], “John I beheaded. Who, then, is this of whom I hear such things?” And he sought to see him.

10. When the apostles returned, they told him all that they had done. Taking them with him, he withdrew privately to a deserted place belonging to Bethsaida. 11. But when the crowds learned of it, they followed him [Note: [Col. 0577] Following Veronensis and Brixianus, perhaps because οἱ ὄχλοι is masculine plural?]; and he welcomed them and spoke to them about the kingdom of God, and those who had need of … he healed … 12. But the day began to decline. The Twelve came to him [Note: [Col. 0577] Adds “to him,” also the Gothic version, αὐτῷ.] and said, “Dismiss the crowd [Note: [Col. 0577] So also the Greek text, τὸν ὄχλον.], so that they may go into the surrounding villages and countryside, find lodging, and obtain food; for we are here in a deserted place.” 13. But … “You give them something to eat.” They said to him, “We have no more than five loaves and two fish—unless we go and buy food for all this crowd.” 14. For there were about five thousand men [Note: [Col. 0577] So also the Greek text, γάρ.]. He said to his disciples, “Have them recline in groups of fifty.” 15. They did so, and all reclined. 16. Then Jesus took the five loaves and the two fish, looked up to heaven, blessed them [Note: [Col. 0577] So also Codex Cantabrigiensis, ἐπ’ αὐτούς.], broke them, and gave them to the disciples [Note: [Col. 0577] After “disciples,” “his” is absent, also in the Greek text.] to set before the crowds. 17. They ate and were all satisfied; and what was left over for them was taken up: twelve baskets of fragments.

18. And it came to pass, while he was praying alone, that his disciples were with him; and he asked … “Whom do the crowds say that I am?” 19. They answered and said, “John the Baptist; but others, Elijah; and others, that one of the prophets of old has risen.” 20. He said to them, “But you—whom do you say that I am?” Peter answered … “the … of God …” 21. He rebuked them and commanded them to tell this to no one, 22. saying, “The Son of Man must suffer many things, be rejected by the chief priests and scribes, be killed, and rise again after three days.”

23. He said to all, “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself and, taking up his cross, follow me. 24. For whoever wishes to save his life will lose it; but whoever loses his life for my sake, he [Note: [Col. 0579] Adds “he,” also the Greek text, οὗτος.] will save it. 25. For what does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but loses himself and suffers loss? [Note: [Col. 0579] Veronensis and Vercellensis omit *sui*; according to the Greek text, ὁ ζημιωθείς.] 26. For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him the Son of Man will be ashamed when he comes in his own glory and that of the Fa… and of the holy angels. 27. But I tell you truly: there are some standing here who shall not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.”

28. About eight days after these sayings, he took Peter, John, and James [Note: [Col. 0581] According to the order of the Greek text, καὶ Ἰωάννην καὶ Ἰάκωβον.] and went up on the mountain to pray. 29. And while he prayed, the appearance of his face became white and radiant. 30. And behold, two men were speaking with him: Moses and Elijah, 31. who appeared in glory and spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem. 32. But Peter and those who were with him were weighed down with sleep [Note: [Col. 0581] Veronensis omits *erant* after “with him,” in accordance with Greek syntax: καὶ οἱ σὺν αὐτῷ, ἦσαν βεβαρημένοι.]; and when they awoke, they saw his glory and the two men standing with him. 33. And as they were departing from him, Peter said, “Master, it is good for us to be here; let us make three tents: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah”—not knowing what he was saying. 34. While he was saying these things, a cloud came and overshadowed them; and they were afraid. And, as they entered the cloud, … 35. from … “This is my beloved Son; listen to him.” 36. And when the voice came, Jesus was found alone. They kept silent and told no one in those days anything [Note: [Col. 0581] According to Greek syntax, οὐδέν.] of what they had seen.

37. Now on the next day [Note: [Col. 0581] So also Codex Cantabrigiensis, Latin and Greek: διὰ τῆς ἡμέρας.], as they came down from the mountain, a great crowd met him. 38. And behold, a man from the crowd cried out, “Master, I beg you, look upon my son, for he is my only child. 39. And behold, a spirit seizes him; suddenly he cries out, throws him down, and convulses him with foaming; scarcely does it leave him, bruising him as it departs. 40. I begged your disciples to cast it out, but they could not.” 41. Jesus answered, “O faithless and perverse generation, how long shall I be with you [Note: [Col. 0583] A variant reading introduced into the text: “how long … shall I be”] and endure you? Bring your son here.” 42. While he was still coming, the demon threw him down and convulsed him [Note: [Col. 0583] So also the Greek text, ἔτι δέ.]. 43. But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit [Note: [Col. 0583] So also the Greek text, τῷ πνεύματι.], healed the boy, and gave him back to his father.

44. And all were astonished at the greatness of … While all were marvelling at everything he did, Jesus said to his disciples, 45. “Lay up these words in your ears: for the Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men.” But they did not understand this saying; it was … before them, so that they did not perceive it; and they were afraid to ask him about this saying.

46. A thought arose among them [Note: [Col. 0583] So also the Greek text, ἐν αὐτοῖς.] as to which of them would be greatest. 47. But Jesus, perceiving the thought of their hearts, took a child and set him beside himself, 48. and said [Note: [Col. 0583] After “said,” “to them” is absent, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis.], “Whoever receives this child in my name receives me; and whoever receives me receives not me, but him who sent me. For he who is least among all of you is the greatest.”

49. John answered, “Master, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we forbade him, because he does not follow you with us.” 50. Jesus said to them, “Do not forbid him; for whoever is not against you is for you. For there is no one who … in my name and will be able to speak evil of me.”

51. Now when the days of his being taken up were being fulfilled, he set his face steadfastly to go to Jerusalem. 52. He sent messengers before him; … going, they entered a city of the Samaritans to make preparations for him. 53. But they did not receive him, because his face was set toward Jerusalem. 54. When his disciples James and John saw this, they said, “Lord, do you wish that we command fire to come down from heaven upon them and consume them, as Elijah did?” 55. But turning, he rebuked them and said [Note: [Col. 0585] So also Codex Cantabrigiensis, καὶ εἶπεν.], “You do not know of what spirit you are. 56. For the Son of Man did not come to destroy human souls [Note: [Col. 0585] Adds “human,” also the Greek text, ἀνθρώπων.], but to save them.” And they went to another village.

57. As they were going along the road, someone said to him, “Lord [Note: [Col. 0585] Adds “Lord,” as does the Greek text, Κύριε.], I will follow you wherever you go.” 58. And [Note: [Col. 0585] Adds “and,” also the Greek text, καί.] Jesus said to him, “Foxes have dens, and birds of the sky nests in which to rest; but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.” 59. He said to another, “Follow me.” But he said, “Lord, first permit me to go and bury my father.” 60. But Jesus said to him [Note: [Col. 0587] So also the Greek text, δέ.], “Leave the dead to bury [Note: [Col. 0587] So also the Greek text, ἄφες τοὺς νεκροὺς θάψαι.] their own dead; but you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God.” 61. Another said, “I will follow … Lord … but first permit me to take leave of those at home” [Note: [Col. 0587] Greek text: ἀποτάξασθαι τοῖς εἰς τὸν οἶκόν μου. The article τοῖς, which serves both masculine and neuter gender, gave rise to this variant reading.]. 62. Jesus said to him, “No one who looks back and puts [Note: [Col. 0587] Read: ‘and puts.’] his hand to the plough is fit for the kingdom of God.” [Note: [Col. 0587] According to Codex Cantabrigiensis: οὐδεὶς εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω βλέπων, καὶ ἐπιβάλλων (and putting) τὴν χεῖρα αὐτοῦ ἐπ’ ἄροτρον.]

## CHAPTER X

[Note: [Col. 0588] Footnotes containing readings from the Codex Vindebonensis that depart from the Vulgate have been entered in a block following the Codex Brixianus.]

1. Jesus appointed [Note: [Col. 0587] Before “appointed,” “after these things” is absent, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis.] seventy others and sent them out two by two before his face into every place and city [Note: [Col. 0587] So also Codex Cantabrigiensis, εἰς πάντα τόπον καὶ πόλιν.] where he was about to come [Note: [Col. 0587] Before “about to come,” “he himself” is absent, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis.]. 2. And he said to them, “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the labourers are few. Therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send labourers into his harvest. 3. Behold, I send you as lambs among wolves [Note: [Col. 0587] So also the Greek text, ἐν μέσῳ λύκων.]. 4. Carry neither purse nor bag nor sandals; and greet no one on the road. 5. Into whatever house you first enter, say, ‘Peace to this house.’ And if a son of peace is there, your peace shall rest upon …; otherwise it shall return to you [Note: [Col. 0587] Greek text: ἐφ’ ὑμᾶς. The translator rendered it consistently with the preceding *super illum*, ἐπ’ αὐτόν.]. 7. Remain in that same house, eating and drinking what they have, for the labourer is worthy of his wages. Do not move from house to house. 8. And into whatever city you enter, if they receive you, eat what is set before you; 9. heal the sick who are in it, and say to them, ‘The kingdom of God has drawn near to you.’ 10. But into whatever city you enter and they do not receive you, go out into its streets and say, 11. ‘Even the dust from your city which clings to us upon our feet [Note: [Col. 0589] Adds “upon the feet,” also Codex Cantabrigiensis, εἰς τοὺς πόδας.] we wipe off against you. Yet know this: the kingdom of God has drawn near.’ 12. I tell you, it shall be more tolerable for Sodom in the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0589] So also Codex Cantabrigiensis, ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ (τοῦ θεοῦ).] than for that city.

13. “Woe to you, Chorazin; and Bethsaida [Note: [Col. 0589] So also Codex Cantabrigiensis, καὶ Βηθσαϊδά.]; for if the deeds done among you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented, sitting in sackcloth and ashes. 14. Yet it shall be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon in the judgment than for you. 15. And you, Capernaum … will you be exalted to heaven, or brought down into Hades? [Note: [Col. 0589] So also Codex Cantabrigiensis: μὴ ἕως οὐρανοῦ ὑψωθήσῃ, ἢ ἕως ᾅδου καταβήσῃ, “Will you be exalted as far as heaven, or descend as far as Hades?” The Greek text has καταβιβασθήσῃ, “you will be brought down, submerged.”] 16. Whoever hears you hears me; whoever rejects you rejects me; and … him [Note: [Col. 0589] Before “him,” “but whoever rejects me rejects” is absent, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis.] who sent me. [Note: [Col. 0589] Codex Cantabrigiensis also adds: ὁ δὲ ἐμοῦ ἀκούων, ἀκούει τοῦ ἀποστείλαντός με, “but whoever hears me hears him who sent me.”]

17. The seventy returned with joy, saying, “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name.” 18. He said to them, “I was watching Satan fall like lightning from heaven. 19. Behold, I have given you authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall harm you [Note: [Col. 0591] So also the Greek text, ὑμᾶς ἀδικήσει.]. 20. Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that evil spirits are subject to you; rather rejoice that your names are written in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0591] So also Codex Cantabrigiensis, ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ.].

21. In that same hour he rejoiced in [Note: [Col. 0591] Adds “in,” also Codex Cantabrigiensis, ἐν.] the Holy Spirit and said, “I give you thanks, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little children. Yes, Father, because thus was your good pleasure before you” [Note: [Col. 0591] So also the Greek text, ὅτι οὕτως ἐγένετο εὐδοκία ἔμπροσθέν σου.].

22. “All things have been delivered to me by my Father. And no one knows the Father except the Son; and … the Son … except the Father … and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal [him].” 23. Turning to the disciples [Note: [Col. 0591] After “disciples,” “his” is absent also in the Greek text.], he said, “Blessed, therefore, are the eyes that see what you see. 24. For I tell you that many prophets and righteous persons desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear [Note: [Col. 0591] Adds “you,” also Codex Cantabrigiensis, ὑμεῖς.], and did not hear it.”

25. As he said these things, behold, a certain expert in the Law stood up, testing him, and said, “Master, what must I do to possess eternal life?” 26. He said to him, “What is written in the Law? How do you read?” 27. He answered, “You shall love the Lord your God with [Note: [Col. 0593] So also Codex Cantabrigiensis, ἐν, here and almost wherever the Vulgate reads *ex*, “from/out of.”] all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength [Note: [Col. 0593] After “your strength,” “and with all your mind” is absent, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis.]; and your neighbour as yourself.” 28. He said to him [Note: [Col. 0593] So also the Greek text, δέ.], “You have answered correctly; do this, and you shall live.” 29. But he, wishing to justify himself, said to Jesus, “And who is my neighbour?”

30. Jesus, looking up, said, “A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers. They stripped him, inflicted wounds, and departed, leaving him … half alive. 31. A certain priest was going down by that same road; when he saw him, he passed by. 32. Likewise a Levite, when he came near the place and saw him, passed by. 33. But a certain Samaritan, travelling, came … to him; and seeing him, was moved with compassion. 34. And I bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine; then placing him on his own animal, brought him to an inn and took care of him. 35. On the next day he brought out two denarii, gave them to the innkeeper, and said, ‘Take care of him; and whatever you spend beyond this, I shall repay you when I return.’ 36. Which of these three, do you think, proved neighbour to the man who fell among the robbers?” 37. He said, “The one who showed mercy to him.” Jesus said to him, “Go, and do likewise.”

38. Now as they went, he entered a certain village; and a woman named Martha welcomed him into her house. 39. She had a sister named Mary, who also sat at Jesus’ feet [Note: [Col. 0595] So also the Greek text, τοῦ Ἰησοῦ.] and listened to his word. 40. But Martha was distracted with much service. She stood and said, “Do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her, therefore, to help me.” 41. Jesus answered her [Note: [Col. 0595] So also the Greek text, ὁ Ἰησοῦς.], “Martha, Martha, 42. Mary has chosen for herself the better part, which shall not be taken away from her.”

## CHAPTER XI
1. And it came to pass, when he himself was praying in a certain place—“he himself” is added, as also in the Greek text, αὐτόν (“him”)—and, when he had ceased, one of his disciples said to him: “Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples.” 2. And he said to them: “When you pray, say: ‘Father’—“our, who art in heaven” is added, as also in the Greek text, ἡμῶν ὁ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς—‘our, who art in heaven,’ may thy name be hallowed. May thy kingdom come. ‘May thy will be done in heaven and on earth’ is added, as also in the Greek text, γενηθήτω τὸ θέλημά σου, ὡς ἐν οὐρανῷ καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς. 3. Give us this day our daily bread. 4. And forgive us—so also Codex Cantabrigiensis: τὰ ὀφειλήματα ἡμῶν, ὡς καὶ ἡμεῖς ἀφίεμεν τοῖς ὀφειλέταις ἡμῶν—our debts, as we also forgive our debtors. And lead us not into temptation; “but deliver us from evil” is added, as also in the Greek text, ἀλλὰ ῥῦσαι ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ τοῦ πονηροῦ.

5. And he said to them: “Which of you has a friend and will go to him at midnight and say to him, ‘Friend, lend me 6. three loaves, because a friend of mine . . . from the road, and I have nothing to set 7. before him’; and he, from within, answering, will say”—so also Codex Cantabrigiensis, ἐρεῖ (“he will say”)—“‘Do not trouble me; the door is already shut, and my children are with me in bed; I cannot rise and give you anything.’ 8. I tell”—before “I tell” the words “even if he persists in knocking” are absent, also in the Greek text and in several Latin manuscripts and all Greek manuscripts—“you . . . rising . . . to him, because he is his friend; on account of his importunity he will rise and give him as many as he desires.” 9. And I say to you: Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened 10. to you. For everyone who asks receives; and he who seeks finds; and to him who knocks it shall be opened. 11. Or which of you, if his son asks him for bread, will offer him a stone? Or, if”—“if” is added, as also in the Greek, εἰ (“if”)—“he asks”—“asks” is added; Brixianus has *will have asked*; Codex Cantabrigiensis, αἰτήσῃ (“he asks”)—“for a fish, will he offer him a serpent instead of a fish? 12. Or if he asks for an egg, will he offer him a scorpion? 13. If then you, though you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father from heaven give”—so also Codex Cantabrigiensis, ἀγαθὸν δόμα—“a good gift to those who ask him?”

14. And he was casting out a demon, and it was dumb. And when he had cast the demon out of the dumb man—after “demon,” the words “the dumb man spoke” are absent, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis; likewise, “all . . . were astonished,” whereas Codex Cantabrigiensis has πάντες . . . ἐθαύμαζον, “all . . . marvelled”—all the crowds were astonished. 15. But some of the Pharisees said: “By Beelzebul, prince of demons, he casts out demons.” 16. And others, testing him, sought from him a sign from heaven. 17. But he, seeing their thoughts, said: “Every kingdom divided against itself is”—so also the Greek text, ἐρημοῦται—“laid waste; and house set upon house”—so also the Greek, πίπτει—“falls.” 18. So also Satan, if he is divided against himself, how shall his kingdom stand? Because you say that I cast out demons by Beelzebul, prince of demons. Gatianus reads *that I cast out*; Mm. *that I have cast out*; the Vulgate, *by Beelzebub I cast out*. 19. And if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they shall be your judges. 20. But if I cast out demons by the finger of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you. 21. When a strong man, fully armed, guards his own court, what he possesses is at peace. 22. But if one stronger than he comes upon him and overcomes him, he will take away all his weapons”—Gatianus and Mm.: *takes away*; Vulgate: *takes away*—“in which he trusted, and distribute the spoils. 23. He who is not with me is against me; and he who does not gather with me scatters.

24. “When”—“but” is added, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis, δέ—“an unclean spirit has gone out of a man, it passes through waterless places seeking rest; and, finding none, it says, ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’ Gatianus reads *out of a man . . . and seeking rest*; Mm., *. . . which has no rest, and does not*; the Vulgate, *from a man . . . seeking rest, and does not*. 25. And when it comes, it finds it swept and 25. adorned. Then it goes and”—after *takes*, *with itself* is absent, likewise in the Greek text—“takes seven other spirits more wicked than itself; and, having entered, it dwells there; and the latter condition of that person becomes much worse than the former.” 27. And it came to pass, as he said these things, that a certain woman raised her voice and said to him: “Blessed is the womb that bore thee, and the breasts which thou didst suck.” 28. But he said to them: “Blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep”—after *keep*, *it* is absent, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis—“.” 29. And as the crowds were gathering, he began to say: “This generation is an evil generation: it seeks a sign, and no sign shall be given it except the sign 30. of Jonah. For as Jonah was a sign to the Ninevites, so shall the Son of Man be to this generation. 31. The queen of the South shall rise in the judgment with the men of this generation and condemn them, because she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon; and behold, here is more than Solomon. 32. The men”—according to the Greek text, Νινευΐ—“of Nineveh shall rise in judgment with this generation and condemn it, because they repented at Jonah’s preaching; and behold, here is more than Jonah. 33. No one”—“but” is added, as also in the Greek text, δέ—“lights a lamp and puts it in a hidden place, nor under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, so that those who enter may see the light. 34. The lamp of your body is your eye. When your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light; but when it is evil, your body too will be dark. 35. If therefore the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness!” So also Codex Cantabrigiensis, εἰ οὖν τὸ φῶς τὸ ἐν σοὶ σκότος, τὸ σκότος πόσον, the latter phrase being drawn from Matthew. The following verse, 36, is absent, as also in Cantabrigiensis.

37. “Now, while he was speaking”—so also the Greek text, ἐν δὲ τῷ λαλεῖν; αὐτόν is read in Alexandrinus—“a certain Pharisee asked him to dine with him”—so also Codex Cantabrigiensis, μετ᾽ αὐτοῦ, “with him.” And he entered 38. and reclined at table. But the Pharisee began to reason within himself, saying: ‘Why was he not first washed before eating?’ 39. And the Lord said to him: ‘Now you Pharisees”—“hypocrites” is added, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis, ὑποκριταί, from Matthew—“cleanse the outside of cup or dish, but your inward part is full of robbery and wickedness. 40. Fools, did not he who made the outside make the inside also? 41. Nevertheless, give as alms what is within”—the Greek text reads τὰ ἐνόντα, “the things within”—“and behold, all things are clean for you; for these things ought to have been done, and those not omitted. 42. But woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who tithe mint and rue and every herb, and pass over judgment and the love of God. 43. Woe to you”—so also Codex Cantabrigiensis, Φαρισαῖοι—“Pharisees, because you love the first seats in synagogues and greetings in the marketplace; ‘and the chief places at feasts’ is added, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis, καὶ πρωτοκλισίας ἐν τοῖς δείπνοις, together with other Greek manuscripts cited by Mill. 44. Woe to you”—“scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites” is added, also in the Greek text, Γραμματεῖς καὶ Φαρισαῖοι ὑποκριταί—“because you are”—before *tombs*, *like* is absent, likewise in Codex Cantabrigiensis—“tombs which do not appear, and people walking over them do not know it.”

45. Then one of the lawyers answered and said to him: “Teacher, in saying these things you insult us also.” 46. But he said: “Woe also to you lawyers, because you load people with burdens which they cannot bear, and you yourselves do not touch the burdens with one of your fingers. 47. Woe to you, because you build the tombs of the prophets, while your fathers killed 48. them. Thus you bear witness”—Codex Cantabrigiensis: μὴ συνευδοκεῖν, “not to consent”—“not consenting to the deeds of your fathers; for they indeed killed them, but you build”—after *build*, *their tombs* is absent, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis—“them. 49. Therefore”—after *therefore*, the words “the wisdom of God also said” are absent, likewise in Codex Cantabrigiensis—“I send unto them prophets and apostles; and some of them they will kill and persecute, 50. so that the blood of all the prophets, shed from the foundation of the world, may be required from”—so also Codex Cantabrigiensis, ἕως τῆς γενεᾶς ταύτης—“this generation, 51. from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, who perished between the altar and the sanctuary. Yes, I tell you, it shall be required of this generation. 52. Woe to you lawyers, because you”—so also Codex Cantabrigiensis, ἐκρύφατε—“have hidden the key of knowledge; and”—“and” is added, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis, καί—“you yourselves have not entered, and you prevented those who were entering.” 53. As he was saying these things before”—so also Codex Cantabrigiensis, ἐνώπιον παντὸς τοῦ λαοῦ, “before all the people”—“all the people, the Pharisees and lawyers began to treat him harshly and to press 54. him, seeking to find some occasion against him in many matters”—so also Codex Cantabrigiensis, κακῶς ἔχειν, καὶ συμβάλλειν αὐτῷ, ζητοῦντες ἀφορμήν τινα λαβεῖν αὐτοῦ—“in order that they might accuse him.”

## CHAPTER XII

1. And when very many crowds had gathered round, so that they were trampling one another, he began to say to his disciples: “Beware”—“yourselves” is added, as also in the Greek text, ἑαυτοῖς—“of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy. 2. Nothing is covered that shall not be revealed, nor hidden that shall not be known. 3. Therefore what you have said in darkness shall be spoken in the light; and what you have spoken in the ear shall be proclaimed upon the housetops, and also in the streets. 4. But I say to you, my friends: take care not to be afraid of those who kill the body and after this have nothing more that they can do. 5. But I will show you whom you should fear: fear him who, after he has killed, has power to cast into Gehenna. Yes, I tell you, fear him. 6. Are not two sparrows sold for an *as*? Yet not one of them falls without the will of 7. God. But even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Do not fear: you are worth more than many sparrows”—after *are*, *you* is absent, also in the Greek text.

8. “I tell you: everyone who confesses me before people, the Son of Man also will confess him before the angels of God; 9. but whoever denies me before people, I too will deny him before my Father who is in heaven. 10. And everyone who speaks a word against the Son of Man, it shall be forgiven him; but whoever [the text is defective] against the Holy Spirit . . . 11. shall not be forgiven. But when”—so also Codex Cantabrigiensis, φέρωσιν (“they bring”)—“they bring you before synagogues and magistrates and authorities, do not be anxious”—after *how*, *or what* is absent, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis—“how you should answer or 12. what you should say; for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour”—so also the Greek text, ἅ (“what things”)—“what you ought to say.”

13. And someone from the crowd said: “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.” 14. But he said to him: “Man, who appointed me judge or arbiter over you?” 15. And he said to them: “Take care and guard yourselves against every kind of greed; for a person’s life does not consist in the abundance of what he possesses.” 16. Then he told them a parable, saying: “The estate of a certain rich man yielded abundant crops. 17. And he reasoned within himself, saying: ‘What shall I do, since I have nowhere to gather my crops?’ 18. And he said, . . . ‘I will tear down my barns and build larger ones, and there I will gather 19. all that has grown for me’”—after *for me*, *and my goods* is absent, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis—“‘and I will say to my soul: You have many goods’”—after *goods*, *laid up for many years: rest, eat, drink* is absent, likewise in Codex Cantabrigiensis—“‘feast.’ 20. But God said to him: ‘Fool, this night they demand your soul from you. . . . . . . whose shall they be?”’” Verse 21 is absent also in Codex Cantabrigiensis.

22. And he said to his disciples: “Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life”—after *life*, *your* is absent, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis—“what you shall eat; nor about your body, what you shall wear. 23. For”—*for* is added, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis, γάρ—“life is more than food, and the body more than clothing. 24. Consider the ravens: they neither sow nor reap; they have neither storehouse nor barn, yet God feeds them. How much more valuable are you than”—so also the Greek text, τῶν πετεινῶν—“birds? 25. And which of you, by worrying, can add one cubit”—after *one*, the words “if then you cannot do even the least thing, why are you anxious about the rest?” are absent, likewise in Codex Cantabrigiensis; similarly the continuation, καὶ περὶ τῶν λοιπῶν τί—“to his stature? 26. And why are you anxious about the rest? 27. Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they do not labour or spin”—“nor weave” is added, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis, οὔτε ὑφαίνει—“nor weave; but I tell you”—“that” is added, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis, ὅτι—“not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these. 28. Or consider the grass. . . [defective text] . . . is in the field . . . tomorrow it is thrown into the oven: God clothes it thus; how much more you, of little faith! 29. And do not seek what you shall eat or what you shall drink, and do not be anxious. 30. For the nations of this world seek these things. Your Father knows . . .”—“all” is added, also in the Ethiopic version and many other Greek manuscripts cited by Mill, in agreement with Vercellensis and Brixianus from Matthew—“that you need all these things. 31. But seek”—before *kingdom*, *first* is absent, likewise in the Greek text; and after *of God*, *and his righteousness* is absent, as in Vercellensis, Veronensis, and Brixianus—“the kingdom of God, and all these things shall be added to you. 32. Do not fear, little flock, for it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom. 33. Sell what you possess and give alms. Make for yourselves purses that do not grow old, an unfailing treasure in heaven, where no thief approaches, nor moth destroys, and where thieves do not break in and 34. steal. For where your treasure is, there also shall your heart be. 35. Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning; 36. and be like people waiting for their master, when he returns from the wedding, so that when he comes and knocks, they may open to him immediately. 37. Blessed are those servants whom the master, when he comes, finds watching. Amen, I tell you: he will gird himself, make them recline at table, and come forward and serve them. 38. And if he comes in the evening”—so also Codex Cantabrigiensis, τῇ ἑσπερινῇ—“watch and finds them so, blessed are they; for he will make them recline at table and serve them.”

> Note: “And if he comes in the evening watch and finds them so, blessed are those servants; he will make them recline at table and, passing among them, serve them. And if he comes in the second watch, and if in the third, and finds them so, blessed are they.” Gatianus: “and if he comes in the third watch, blessed.” Vulgate: “and if he comes in the second watch, and if he comes in the third watch, and finds them so, blessed are those servants.”

39. “But know this: if the master of the house knew at what hour the thief was coming, he would keep watch and would not”—Gatianus: *allow to be broken through*; Mm.: *will allow to be broken through*; Vulgate: *would allow to be broken through*—“allow his house to be broken into. 40. You too be ready, for at an hour when you do not expect him, the Son of Man will come.” 41. And Peter said: “Lord, are you saying this parable to us, or also to all?” 42. And Jesus said: “Who then is the faithful and prudent steward, whom the master appoints over his household, to give them their measure of wheat in due season? 43. Blessed is that servant whom his master”—*his* is added, also in the Greek text, αὐτοῦ; likewise *will find*, εὑρήσει—“when he comes, finds doing so. 44. Truly I tell you, he will appoint him”—before *over*, *that* is absent, also in the Syriac, Persian, and Ethiopic versions—“over all that he possesses. 45. But if that servant says in his heart, ‘My master delays his coming,’ and begins to beat the boys and maidservants and to eat and drink and get drunk, 46. the master of that servant will come . . . on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour”—Gatianus and Mm.: *which he does not know . . . with hypocrites*; Vulgate: *which he does not know . . . with unbelievers*—“that he does not know; and he will cut him in two and assign his portion with the unbelievers. 47. That servant who knew his master’s will and did not”—after *prepare*, *nor do according to his will* is absent, with the Syriac—“prepare . . . [defective text:] . . . shall be beaten much.” Mm. and Gatianus read *much*; the Vulgate, *with many stripes*. 48. But he who did not know and did what deserved a beating shall be beaten with few stripes. From everyone to whom much has been given, much shall be required; and from him to whom much has been entrusted, more shall be demanded.

49. “Do you not know that I came to cast fire upon the earth? And what do I desire”—Gatianus: *unless it be kindled?*; Vulgate: *unless that it be kindled?*—“if it is already kindled? 50. But I have a baptism”—so also the Greek text, Βάπτισμα; Gatianus: *But a baptism*; Vulgate: *But with a baptism*—“with which to be baptized; and how I am distressed until it is accomplished! 51. Do you think that I came to bring”—Gatianus: *peace upon the earth?*; Vulgate: *to give peace upon earth?*—“peace upon earth? No, I tell you, but division. 52. For there shall be five in one house divided, three against two and two against three; mother against daughter and daughter against mother; 53. father against son and son against his father; mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law and daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law.” 54. And he said also to the crowds: “When . . . [defective text] . . . from the east . . . the west, you immediately say, ‘A storm is coming,’ and so it happens. 55. And when you see the south wind blowing, you say”—Gatianus: *there will be heat, and so it happens*; Mm.: *there will be warmth, and so it happens*; Vulgate: *there will be heat, and it happens*—“‘There will be heat,’ and so it happens. 56. Hypocrites, you know how to discern”—“indeed” is added, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis, μέν—“the appearance of earth and sky; but this present time . . . [defective text] . . . 57. Why do you not judge for yourselves what is right? 58. For while you are going with your adversary to”—Greek text: ἐπ᾽ ἄρχοντα, “before a magistrate”—“the magistrate, make every effort on the way to be released from him, lest he”—so also Codex Cantabrigiensis, κατακρίνῃ—“condemn you before the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and the officer cast you into prison. 59. I tell you, you shall not depart from there until you have paid even”—Gatianus and Mm.: *the last quadrans*; a later hand: *the minutum*; Vulgate: *the last minutum*—“the last quadrans.”

## CHAPTER XIII

1. Now there came at that very time some people telling him about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mixed with their sacrifices. 2. And answering, he said to them: “Do you think . . . [defective text] . . . that these Galileans were sinners above all Galileans because they suffered such things? 3. No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you shall all likewise perish. 4. Or those eighteen upon whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed . . . [defective text] . . . do you think that they were debtors beyond”—Gatianus: *in Siloam . . . they all were debtors above all inhabitants in*; Mm.: *in Siloam . . . they had been debtors beyond all inhabitants in*; Vulgate: *in Siloam . . . they were debtors above all the people dwelling in*—“all the people who dwelt in Jerusalem? 5. No, I tell you; but unless you believe, all people shall perish.””

6. And he spoke this parable: “A certain man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard; and he came seeking fruit upon it and found none. 7. Then he said to the cultivator of the vineyard, ‘Behold, for three years I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree and find none. Cut it down, then; why does it even exhaust the ground?’ 8. But he answered and said to him, ‘Lord, leave it this year also, until I dig around it 9. and put”—thus St Ambrose, following Codex Cantabrigiensis, κόφινον κοπρίων—“a basket of dung; and if indeed it bears fruit; but if not, in the future you shall cut it down.’”

10. Now he was teaching”—so also the Greek text, ἐν μιᾷ τῶν συναγωγῶν, “in one of the synagogues”—“in one of the synagogues on the sabbath. 11. And behold, there was a woman who had had a spirit of infirmity for eighteen years, and she was bent over and could not at all straighten herself. 12. When he saw her, he called her to him and said: “Woman, you are released from your infirmity.” 13. And he laid . . . [defective text] . . . upon her, and immediately she was made straight and glorified 14. God. But the ruler of the synagogue, answering indignantly because Jesus healed on the sabbath, said to the crowd: “There are six days on which one ought to work; come therefore on those days and . . . [defective text] . . . and not on the sabbath day.” 15. The Lord answered”—so also the Greek text, ἀπεκρίθη—“him and said: “Hypocrite, does not each of you on the sabbath untie his ox or ass from the manger and lead it away to water it? 16. And ought not this daughter of Abraham, whom Satan has bound—behold, for eighteen years—to be loosed from this bond on the sabbath day?” 17. And as he said these things, all his adversaries were put to shame; and all the people rejoiced”—so also Codex Cantabrigiensis, ἐπὶ πᾶσιν οἷς ἐθεώρουν γινομένοις ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ, “at all the glorious things which they saw being done by him”—“at the glorious things which they had seen done by him. 18. Therefore he said: “To what is the kingdom 19. of God like, and to what shall I compare it? It is like a grain of mustard seed, which a man took and put in his garden; and it grew and became”—so also Codex Cantabrigiensis, ἐγένετο δένδρον—“a tree, so that the birds of heaven rested in its branches. 20. And again he said: ‘To what shall I compare the kingdom . . .?’ 21. It is like leaven, which a woman took and hid”—thus also St Ambrose—“in flour, until the whole was leavened.”

22. And he was going through cities and villages, teaching and making his journey toward Jerusalem. 23. And someone said to him: “Lord, are there few who are being saved?” But he said to them: 24. “Strive to enter through the narrow gate; for, I tell you, many will seek to enter and will not be able. 25. From the time the master of the house has risen”—so also the Greek text, ἀφ᾽ οὗ ἂν ἐγερθῇ—“and shut the door, and you begin to stand outside and knock”—after *knock*, *at the door* is absent, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis—“saying, ‘Lord, Lord’”—the Greek text likewise repeats Κύριε—“‘open to us,’ he will answer, ‘I do not know where you are from.’ 26. Then you will begin to say, ‘We ate and drank before you, and you taught in our streets.’ 27. And he will say to you, ‘I do not know where you are from; depart from me, all you workers of 28. iniquity.’ There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when you see Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and all the prophets entering into the kingdom of God, but yourselves cast 29. out. And they shall come from east and west and north and south, and recline at table in the kingdom of God. 30. And behold, there are last who shall be first, and there are first who shall be last.”

31. On that very day some Pharisees came to him, saying: “Leave and go from here, because Herod wishes to kill you.” 32. And Jesus said to them: “Go, tell that fox: ‘Behold, I cast out demons and perform healings today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am brought to completion.’ 33. Go on; for it is not fitting for a prophet to perish outside Jerusalem. 34. Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you! How often I wished to gather your children as a hen gathers her nest under her wings, and you were unwilling! 35. Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate. I tell”—after *you*, *that* is absent, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis—“you, you shall not see me until the day comes when you say: ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.’”

## CHAPTER XIV

1. And it came to pass, when he entered on the sabbath into the house of one of the chief Pharisees to eat bread, that they were watching 2. him. And behold, a man”—after *man*, *a certain* is absent, likewise in Codex Cantabrigiensis—“with dropsy was before him. 3. And Jesus answered the lawyers and Pharisees, . . . [defective text] . . . “Is it lawful to heal on the sabbath, or 4. not?””—“or not” is added, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis, ἢ οὔ—“But they were silent. And he took hold of him, healed him, and sent him away. 5. And”—before *said*, *answering* is absent, likewise in Codex Cantabrigiensis—“he said to them: ‘Which of you, if his ass or ox falls into a pit, will not immediately pull it out on the sabbath day?’ 6. And they could not answer him on these matters.

7. Now he spoke to those invited, observing how they chose the chief places at table, saying to them: 8. “When you are invited”—*by someone* is added, also in the Greek text, ὑπό τινος—“by someone, do not recline in the first place, lest someone more honourable than you has been 9. invited, and he who invited you and him comes and says to you, ‘Give this man your place’; and then you begin with shame to take the last place. 10. But when you are invited, go and recline in the lowest place, so that when he who invited you comes, he may say to you, ‘Friend, move higher.’ Then you will have honour before those reclining with you. 11. For everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and he who humbles himself shall be exalted.”

12. And he said also to the one who had invited him: “When you give a luncheon or a dinner, do not invite your friends, your brothers, your kinsmen, or neighbours”—“nor” is added, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis, μηδέ—“nor the wealthy, lest they also invite you in return and repayment be made to you. 13. But when you make a feast, invite the poor, the disabled, the lame, 14. the blind; and you will be blessed, because they have nothing with which to repay you. For you shall be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous.” 15. When one of those reclining with him heard these things, he said to him: “Blessed is he who shall eat bread in the kingdom of God.” 16. But he said”—after *said*, *to him* is absent, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis—“: “A certain man made a great dinner and invited 17. many. And he sent his servant at the hour of dinner to say to those invited, ‘Come’”—so also the Greek text, ἔρχεσθε—“for it is now ready. 18. And all alike began to excuse themselves. The first said”—after *said*, *to him* is absent, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis and the Gothic version—“‘I have bought an estate and must go out and see it; I ask you, have me excused.’ 19. And another said: ‘I have bought five yoke of oxen and am going to test them; and I cannot come’”—so also Codex Cantabrigiensis, διὸ οὐ δύναμαι ἐλθεῖν, “therefore I am unable to come.” 20. And another said: ‘I have married a wife; therefore I cannot come.’ 21. And the servant returned and reported these things to his master. Then the master of the house, angered, said to his servant: ‘Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in here the poor, the disabled, the blind, and the lame.’ 22. And the servant said: ‘Lord, what you commanded has been done, and still there is room.’ 23. And the master said to his servant”—after *servant*, *his* is added, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis, αὐτοῦ—“‘Go out into the roads and about the hedges, and compel them to enter, that my house may be filled. 24. For I tell you, none of those men who were invited shall taste my dinner.’”

25. Now crowds”—after *crowds*, *great* is absent, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis and Vercellensis—“were going with him; and he turned and said to them: 26. “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, yes, even his own life, he cannot be my disciple. 27. And whoever does not carry his cross and come after me cannot be my disciple. 28. For which of you, wishing to build a tower, does not first sit down and calculate the costs necessary, whether he has enough to finish it? 29. Otherwise, after he has laid a foundation and cannot finish, all who see it 30. will say”—Codex Cantabrigiensis: μέλλουσι λέγειν, “are about to say”; in the same manuscript *because* is absent before *this man*—“‘This man began to build and was not able to finish.’ 31. Or what king, going to wage war against another king, does not first sit down and consider whether he can meet, with ten thousand, the one coming against him with twenty thousand? 32. Otherwise, while he is still far away, he sends an embassy and asks for peace. 33. So therefore none of you who does not renounce all that he possesses can be my disciple. 34. Salt is good; but if salt”—“also” is added, likewise in Codex Cantabrigiensis, καὶ τὸ ἅλς, in agreement with Vercellensis—“has lost its savour, with what shall it be seasoned? 35. It is fit neither for soil nor for manure; they cast it out”—Greek text: βάλλουσιν αὐτό—“outside. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”

## CHAPTER XV
1. Now all the tax collectors and sinners were drawing near to hear him. 2. And the Pharisees and the scribes were murmuring, because he received sinners and ate with them. [Col. 0636] 3. And he spoke this parable to them:

4. “Which of you, having a hundred sheep, if one of them has gone astray, would not leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness and go after the one that has strayed, until he finds it? 5. And when he has found it, he … it upon his shoulders; 6. and, coming home, he calls together his friends and neighbours, saying to them: ‘Rejoice with me, because my sheep which was lost has been found.’ 7. I tell you that so there will be joy in heaven … over a sinner [Col. 0636] … who has repentance, more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance.

8. “Or what woman, having ten drachmas, if she loses one …, does not light a lamp, sweep the house, and search carefully until she finds it? 9. And when she has found it, she calls together her women friends and neighbours, saying: ‘Rejoice with me, because I have found the drachma.’ 10. So, I tell you, there will be joy before the angels of God over a sinner doing repentance.” [Col. 0638]

[Note: Col. 0635: Before *unam* (“one”), *drachmam* (“drachma”) is absent, also in the Codex of Canterbury.]

11. And he said: “A certain man had two sons. 12. And the younger said to him: ‘Father, give me the share of the estate that falls to me.’ And he divided his property between them. 13. And not many days later, having gathered everything together, the younger son went abroad into a distant country; and there he squandered his property by living extravagantly. 14. And after he had consumed everything, a famine arose throughout that country; and he too began to lack food. 15. And he went and attached himself to one of the citizens of that country. And that man sent him into his farm to feed swine. 16. And he desired to fill his stomach with the husks that the swine ate; and no one gave him anything. [Col. 0638]

17. “But, coming to himself, he said: ‘How many hired servants of my father have bread in abundance, while I am perishing here from hunger! 18. I will rise and go to my father, and say to him: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; 19. I am no longer worthy to be called your son; but make me like one of your hired servants.”’ 20. And rising, he came to his father. But while he was still far away, his father saw him; and, moved with compassion, he ran, fell upon his neck, and kissed him. 21. And his son said to him: ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’ [Col. 0640]

[Note: Col. 0637: So also the Greek text, *tōn misthiōn autou* (“of your hired servants”).]

[Note: Col. 0637: So also the Greek text, *apechontos* (“being far away”).]

22. “But his father said to his servants: ‘Quickly bring out for me that first robe, and clothe him; give him a ring for his hand and sandals for his feet. 23. Bring the fattened calf, kill it, and let us eat and feast; 24. for this son of mine had been dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found.’ And they began to feast.

25. “Now his elder son was in the field. And, as he came and approached the house, he heard music and dancing. 26. And he called one of the servants and asked what these things were. 27. And he said to him: ‘Because your brother has come, your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and sound.’ 28. But he became angry and would not go in. But his father went out and began to entreat him. 29. But he replied and said to his father: ‘Look, for so many years I have served you, and I have never transgressed your command; yet you have never given me … that I might feast with my friends. 30. But when this son of yours came, who devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him.’ [Col. 0642]

[Note: Col. 0639: It adds *quia* (“because”), as does the Greek text, *hoti*.]

[Note: Col. 0639: So also the Codex of Canterbury, *de* (“but/and”).]

31. “And he said to him: ‘Son, you have always been with me, and you are; and all that is mine is yours. 32. But we ought to feast and rejoice, because this brother of yours had been dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found.’”

## Chapter XVI

1. And he said to his disciples: “There was a certain rich man who had a steward; and this man was accused before him as though he had squandered his goods. 2. And he summoned him and said: ‘What is this that I hear concerning you? Render an account of your stewardship, for you will no longer be able to be steward.’ 3. But the steward said within himself: ‘What shall I do, since my master is taking the stewardship away from me? I am unable to dig; I am ashamed to beg. [Col. 0642] 4. I know what I shall do, so that, when I have been removed from the stewardship, they may receive me into their houses.’ 5. Therefore, having summoned each of his master’s debtors, he said to the first: ‘How much do you owe my master?’ 6. And he said: ‘A hundred baths of oil.’ And he said to him: ‘Take your documents, sit down, and quickly write fifty.’ 7. Then he said to another: ‘And how much do you owe?’ He said: ‘A hundred cors of wheat.’ He said to him: ‘Take your documents and write eighty.’ [Col. 0644]

[Note: Col. 0641: According to the Greek text, *egnōn* (“I have known / I know”).]

[Note: Col. 0641: So also the Latin and Greek Codex of Canterbury, *sou ta grammata* (“your documents”).]

[Note: Col. 0641: It adds *et* (“and”), as does the Greek text, *kai*.]

8. “And the master commended the unrighteous steward because he had acted prudently. And he said to his disciples: ‘The sons of this age are more prudent than the sons of light in this generation. 9. And I tell you: Make friends for yourselves from unrighteous mammon, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into their eternal dwellings. 10. Whoever is faithful in the least is faithful also in much; and whoever is unrighteous in little is unrighteous also in much. 11. Therefore, if you have not been faithful in unrighteous mammon, who will entrust to you that which is true? [Verse 12 absent in the supplied text.] 13. No servant can serve two masters. For either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will hold to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and mammon.’” 

[Note: Col. 0643: Before *fili*—read *filii*, “sons”—*quia* (“because”) is absent also in the Codex of Canterbury.]

[Note: Col. 0643: So also the Greek text, *Mamōna* (“mammon”).]

14. Now the Pharisees, who were avaricious, heard all these things and mocked him. 15. And he said to them: “You are those who justify yourselves before human beings; but God knows your hearts. For what is exalted among human beings is an abomination before God. 16. The Law and the Prophets were until John; from that time the kingdom of God is proclaimed as good news, and everyone forces his way into it. [Col. 0646] 17. But it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one stroke of the Law to fall. 18. Everyone who dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery; and whoever marries a woman dismissed by her husband commits adultery.

[Note: Col. 0643: It adds *in* (“among/in”), as does the Greek text, *en*.]

19. “There was a certain rich man who clothed himself in purple and feasted splendidly every day. 20. And there was a certain beggar, named Lazarus, lying at his gate, covered with sores, 21. desiring to be filled from what fell from the rich man’s table; but dogs also came and licked his sores. [Col. 0646]

[Note: Col. 0645: It adds *autem* (“but/and”), as does the Greek text, *de*.]

[Note: Col. 0645: After *divitis* (“the rich man’s”), ‘and no one gave him anything’ is absent, likewise in the Greek text.]

22. “And it came to pass that Lazarus the beggar died and was carried by angels into the bosom of … The rich man also died and was buried. 23. And, lifting up his eyes in Hades, while he was in torments, he saw Abraham far off and Lazarus resting in his bosom. 24. And he himself cried out and said: ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, because I am tortured in this flame.’ [Col. 0646]

[Note: Col. 0645: So also the Greek text: *kai etaphē, kai en tō Hadē eparas* (“and he was buried; and in Hades, lifting up …”).]

[Note: Col. 0645: It adds *requiescentem* (“resting”), as does the Codex of Canterbury, *anapauomenon*.]

[Note: Col. 0645: So also the Greek text, *kai* (“and”).]

25. “And Abraham said to him: ‘Son, remember that you received your good things during your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things; but now he is comforted here, whereas you are tortured. [Col. 0648] 26. And besides all these things, a great chasm has been fixed between you and us, so that those wishing to go from here to you cannot cross, nor can any cross from there to us.’ 27. And he said: ‘Then I beg you, Father, to send him to my father’s house. 28. For I have five brothers, so that he may testify to them, lest they too come into this place of torments.’ 29. And Abraham said to him: ‘They have Moses and the Prophets; let them hear them.’ 30. But he said: ‘No, Father Abraham; but if someone rises from the dead, he will persuade them.’ [Col. 0648] 31. And he said to him: ‘If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they believe if someone should go to them from the dead.’”

[Note: Col. 0645: It adds *tu* (“you”), as does the Greek text, *sy*.]

## Chapter XVII

1. And he said to his disciples: “It is impossible that stumbling-blocks should not come; nevertheless, woe to him through whom they come. 2. It would have been more advantageous for him not to have been born, or for a millstone to be placed around his neck and for him to be thrown into the sea, than for him to cause one of these little ones to stumble. 3. Take heed to yourselves. If your brother sins, rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive him. 4. And if he sins against you seven times in a day and seven times turns back to you, saying, ‘I repent,’ forgive him.” [Col. 0650]

[Note: Col. 0647: So also the Greek text, *de* (“but/and”).]

[Note: Col. 0647: Saint Clement also reads: *kalon ēn autō ei ouk egennēthē* (“it would have been good for him if he had not been born”).]

[Note: Col. 0647: Before *frater* (“brother”), *in te* (“against you”) is absent, also in the Gothic version.]

5. And the apostles said to him: “Lord, increase our faith.” 6. And he said to them: “If you had faith like a grain of mustard, you would say to this mulberry tree: ‘Be uprooted and transplanted into the sea’; and it would have obeyed you. 7. But which of you, having a servant ploughing or … tending …, when he returns from the field, will say to him: ‘Come at once and recline at table’? Rather, he will say to him: ‘Prepare what I may eat; gird yourself and serve me until I eat and drink; and afterwards you will eat and drink.’ 9. Does he thank the servant because he did what was commanded him? 10. I think not. So you also, when you have done what has been commanded, say: ‘We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we were obliged to do.’”

[Note: Col. 0649: So also the Codex of Canterbury: *ho de eipen autois* (“and he said to them”).]

[Note: Col. 0649: Greek text: *kai hypēkousen an* (“and it would obey”). Because the Greek text indicates past tense, the translator seems for that reason to have rendered it *obaudisset* (“would have obeyed”).]

[Note: Col. 0649: Vercelli also appears to have read “sheep,” together with the Syriac, Persian, Arabic versions, and Augustine.]

[Note: Col. 0649: So also the Greek text, *erei* (“he will say”).]

[Note: Col. 0649: So also the Codex of Canterbury, *all’ erei* (“but he will say”).]

[Note: Col. 0649: After *servo* (“the servant”), *illi* (“to him”) is absent, also in the Codex of Canterbury.]

[Note: Col. 0649: So also the Greek text, *ta diatachthenta autō* (“the things commanded him”).]

[Note: Col. 0649: After *feceritis* (“you have done”), *omnia* (“all”) is absent, also in the Codex of Canterbury.]

[Note: Col. 0649: The Greek text has *legete* (“say”), which also serves the present tense.]

11. And it came to pass, while he was going to Jerusalem, that he was passing through the midst of Samaria, Galilee, and Jericho. 12. And as he entered a certain village, behold, ten leprous men stood at a distance; 13. and they raised their voices, saying: “Jesus, Master, have mercy on us.” 14. When he saw them, he said: “Go, show yourselves to the priests.” And it came to pass, as they went, they were cleansed. [Col. 0652] 15. But one of them, when he saw that he was cleansed, returned, glorifying God with a loud voice; 16. and he fell upon his face at his feet, giving him thanks; and he was a Samaritan. 17. And Jesus answered … and said: “Were not these ten cleansed? Where are the nine? 18. Was none found to return and give thanks to God except this foreigner?” 19. And he said to him: “Rise, go; your faith has made you whole.”

[Note: Col. 0651: It adds *ei* (“to him”), as does the Greek text, *autō*.]

[Note: Col. 0651: So also the Codex of Canterbury, *houtoi* (“these”).]

20. Now, when questioned by the Pharisees, “When does the kingdom of God come?” … he said to them: “The kingdom of God does not come with observation; 21. nor will they say, ‘Behold, here!’ or ‘Behold, there!’ For behold, the kingdom of God is within you.” 22. And he said to his disciples: “Days will come when you will desire to see one day of the Son of Man, and you will not see it. 23. And they will say to you, ‘Behold, here!’ and ‘Behold, there!’ Do not go, nor follow them. 24. For just as lightning flashing from heaven shines upon the things under heaven, so also will the Son of Man be. 25. But first he must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation. 26. And as it happened in the days of Noah, so it will be in the days of the Son of Man. 27. They were eating and drinking, marrying wives and being given in marriage, until the day on which Noah entered into the ark; and the flood came and destroyed them all. [Col. 0654] 28. Likewise it happened in the days of Lot. They were eating and drinking, buying and selling, planting and building; 29. but on the day Lot went out from Sodom, fire rained from heaven and destroyed them all. 30. Thus will be the day on which the Son of Man is revealed. 31. In that hour, whoever is on the roof … his belongings being in the house, let him not come down to take them away; and whoever is in the field, likewise let him not turn back. 32. Remember Lot’s wife. 33. Whoever seeks to save his life will lose it, and whoever loses it for my sake will preserve it. [Col. 0654]

[Note: Col. 0651: It adds *et* (“also”), as does the Greek text, *kai*.]

[Note: Col. 0651: After *hominis* (“Man”), ‘in his day’ is absent also in the Codex of Canterbury.]

[Note: Col. 0653: It adds *propter me* (“for my sake”), also in the Gothic version.]

34. “I tell you: on that night two will be in one bed; one will be taken and the other left. 35. Two women will be grinding together; one will be taken and one left. Two will be in the field; one will be taken and one left.” 36. And they answered and said to him: “Where, Lord?” 37. And he said to them: “Wherever the body is, there also the eagles will be gathered.”

## Chapter XVIII

1. And he spoke a parable to them, that they ought always to pray and not lose heart, 2. saying: “There was a certain judge in a certain city who … did not fear God and did not respect any person. [Col. 0656] 3. And there was a widow in that city, who came to him, saying: ‘Vindicate me against my adversary.’ 4. And for a long time he was unwilling. After these things he said within himself: ‘Though I do not fear God or respect any person, 5. yet, because this widow troubles me, I will vindicate her, lest by her continual coming at last she wear me out.’” 6. And the Lord said: “Hear what the unjust judge says. 7. And will not God bring vindication for his elect, who cry to him day and night, while he is patient with them? 8. I tell you: he will bring their vindication swiftly. Yet when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith upon the earth?” [Col. 0656]

[Note: Col. 0655: So also the Greek text, *makrothymian* (“patience/long-suffering”).]

[Note: Col. 0655: Before *faciet* (“he will do”), *quia* (“because”) is absent, also in the Codex of Canterbury.]

9. And he spoke this parable to some who trusted in themselves as though they were righteous and despised others: 10. “Two men went up into the temple to pray, 11. one a tax collector and the other a Pharisee. The Pharisee, standing, prayed thus: ‘God, I thank you that I am not like other people—robbers, unjust persons, adulterers—or even like this tax collector. 12. I fast twice in the week; I give tithes of all that I possess.’ [Col. 0658]

[Note: Col. 0655: It adds *essent* (“were”), likewise the Greek text, *eisi*; Vercelli also has *sint* (“are/may be”).]

[Note: Col. 0655: It reads *sicut* (“as”), and so does the Greek text, *hōs*.]

13. “But the tax collector, standing at a distance, was unwilling even to raise his eyes to heaven; but only beat his breast, saying: ‘Lord God, be propitious to me, a sinner.’ 14. I tell you that this tax collector went down to his house justified rather than that Pharisee; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.

[Note: Col. 0657: So also the Codex of Canterbury, *mallon par’ ekeinon ton Pharisaiōn* (“rather than that Pharisee”).]

15. Now they were bringing infants to him so that he might touch them. When the disciples saw this, they rebuked them. 16. But Jesus, calling them together, said: “Allow the children to come to me, and do not forbid them; for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these. [Col. 0658] 17. Truly I tell you: whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child has not entered into it.”

18. And someone asked him, saying: “Good Teacher, what must I do to possess eternal life?” 19. But Jesus said to him: “… do you call me good? No one is good except one, God. 20. You know the commandments: ‘You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness; honour your father and your mother.’” 21. He said: “All these things I have kept from my youth.” [Col. 0660] 22. When Jesus heard this (sic), he said: “One thing still lacks for you: sell everything whatsoever you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.” 23. When he heard these things, he became sorrowful, because he was very rich. 24. And Jesus, seeing that he had become sorrowful, said: “How difficult it is for those who have riches to enter the kingdom of God! 25. It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.” 26. And those who heard said: “Then who can be saved?” [Col. 0660] 27. Jesus said to them: “The things impossible with human beings are all possible with God.” 28. But Peter said: “Behold, having left our nets, we have followed you.” 29. And he said to them: “Truly I tell you, there is no one who has left house, parents, brothers, wife, or children for the kingdom of God, 30. who will not receive sevenfold in this present time, and in the age to come possess eternal life.”

[Note: Col. 0657: It adds *tuam* (“your”), as does the Greek text, *sou*.]

[Note: Col. 0659: Codex of Canterbury: *ta idia aphentes* (“having left what was our own”).]

[Note: Col. 0659: So also the Codex of Canterbury, *heptaplasiona* (“sevenfold”).]

31. And he took his twelve disciples and said to them: “… we are going up to Jerusalem, and all the things written through the prophets concerning the Son of Man will be fulfilled. [Col. 0662] 32. For he will be delivered to the Gentiles, mocked, and spat upon; and, having been scourged, they will kill him; 33. and on the third day he will rise again.” 34. [Note: Col. 0659: So also the Greek text, *pros autous* (“to them”).]

35. And it came to pass, as he approached Jericho, that a certain blind beggar was sitting beside the road. 36. And when he heard the crowd passing by, he asked what this was. 37.
