And a leper came [Col. 0728] to him, begging him, [Note: [Col. 0727] So also the Greek text: καὶ λέγων, “and saying,” with *to him* omitted, which is also absent in Codices Cantabrigiensis and Brixianus. In the same place, before “saying,” “and kneeling” is absent in Verona, nor is it found in Codex Cantabrigiensis.] and saying +: “If you will, you can cleanse me.” 41. And stretching out [Note: [Col. 0727] After “hand,” “his” is absent also in the Greek text.] his hand +, he said to him: “I will; [Note: [Col. 0727] After “cleanse,” “and when he had said this” is absent in Codex Cantabrigiensis and in the Syriac, Persian, and Arabic versions.] be cleansed +.” 42. And the leprosy left him. 44. And he said to him: “See that you tell no one; but show yourself to [Note: [Col. 0727] So also the Greek text: ἱερεῖ, “the priest.”] the priest +, and offer for your cleansing what Moses commanded, as a testimony to them.” 45. But he went out and began to preach and spread the report, so that he could no longer [Col. 0728] enter a city openly; but people came to him from outside, in deserted places.

## CHAPTER II
1. And again he came to Capernaum after some days; and it was heard that he was in the house. 2. And many assembled, so that there was no longer room, not even at the door; and he spoke the word to them.  
[Note: Col. 0727. According to the Greek text, μηκέτι (χωρεῖν) μηδέ, “no longer—not even [to contain].” In the same place the Veronese manuscript has “to them”; and so Codex Cantabrigiensis, πρὸς αὐτούς.]

3. And they came to him, bringing a paralytic on a pallet.  
[Note: Col. 0727. Thus also the Greek text, ἔρχονται, “they come.”]

4. And since they could not approach because of the crowd, they uncovered the roof where he was; and they lowered the pallet on which the paralytic lay.  
[Note: Col. 0727. (g) Thus also the Greek text, προσεγγίσαι, “to approach.” In the same place, “to him” is absent in the Vercelli, Verona, Brixian, and Cantabrigiensis manuscripts.]  
[Note: Col. 0729. “Making an opening” is absent in Vercelli, Verona, and Codex Cantabrigiensis.]

5. But when Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, “Son, your sins are forgiven you.” 6. Now some of the scribes were sitting there and reasoning in their hearts, saying, 7. “This man blasphemes. Who can forgive sins except God alone?”  
[Note: Col. 0729. It adds “saying,” as does Codex Cantabrigiensis: λέγοντες.]

8. And Jesus, perceiving in his spirit what they were thinking within themselves, said to them, “Why do you think these things in your hearts?  
[Note: Col. 0729. Before “perceiving,” “immediately” is absent also in Codex Cantabrigiensis.]  
[Note: Col. 0729. After “spirit,” “his own” is absent also in Codex Cantabrigiensis.]

9. Which is easier: to say to the paralytic, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Rise and walk’? 10. But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority to forgive sins”—he said to the paralytic—11. “Rise, take up your pallet, and go to your house.” 12. And he rose, took up the pallet before them all, and went away, so that, marveling, they glorified God, because they had never seen such things.  
[Note: Col. 0729. After “God,” “saying” is absent also in Codex Cantabrigiensis.]

13. And he went out again beside the sea; and all the crowd came to him, and he taught them. 14. And as he passed by, he saw James, son of Alphaeus, sitting at the tax-office, and said to him, “Follow me.” And he rose and followed him.  
[Note: Col. 0729. Thus also Codex Cantabrigiensis, Latin and Greek: Ἰάκωβον, “James.”]

15. And it came to pass, while they reclined at table in the house, that many tax collectors and sinners reclined together with Jesus and his disciples; for there were many who also followed him.  
[Note: Col. 0729. Thus Codex Cantabrigiensis: κατακειμένων αὐτῶν, “while they were reclining.”]  
[Note: Col. 0731. Thus also the Greek text, ἠκολούθησαν, “followed.”]

16. And the scribes of the Pharisees saw that he ate with sinners and tax collectors, and they said to his disciples, “Why does he eat with tax collectors and sinners?”  
[Note: Col. 0731. Thus Codex Cantabrigiensis: καὶ εἶδαν, “and they saw”; elsewhere it often has εἶχαν, εἴδαμεν, ἤλθατε for εἶχον, εἴδομεν, ἤλθετε.]  
[Note: Col. 0731. After “eats,” “and drinks” is absent, also in the Greek and Latin Cantabrigiensis manuscript. In the same place, “your Master” is absent, as in the Greek text.]

17. And when Jesus heard it, he said, “Those who are strong have no need of physicians, but those who are ill do. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.”  
[Note: Col. 0731. Footnotes containing readings from Codex Vindobonensis that depart from the Vulgate have been entered in a block following Codex Brixianus.]  
[Note: Col. 0731. After “said,” “to them” is absent, likewise in Codex Cantabrigiensis.]  
[Note: Col. 0731. After “not,” “for” is absent, also in the Greek text.]

18. Now the disciples of John and the Pharisees were fasting; and they came and said to him, “Why do the disciples of the Pharisees and of John fast, but your disciples do not fast?” 19. And he said to them, “Can the sons of the wedding feast fast while the bridegroom is with them? 20. Days will come when the bridegroom shall be taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days.”  
[Note: Col. 0731. After “to them,” “Jesus” is absent also in Codex Cantabrigiensis.]  
[Note: Col. 0731. After “fast,” the words “as long as they have the bridegroom with them, they cannot fast” are absent, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis and Colbertinus: οὐ, in Mill’s edition.]

21. No one sews a patch of new cloth onto an old garment; otherwise the new patch pulls away from the old, and the tear becomes worse.  
[Note: Col. 0731. Thus also the Greek text, χεῖρον, “worse.”]

22. And no one puts new wine into old skins, but into new ones; otherwise it will burst the skins, and the wine and the skins will perish.  
[Note: Col. 0733. After “wine,” “will be poured out” is absent also in Codex Cantabrigiensis.]  
[Note: Col. 0733. After “will perish,” “but new wine must be put into new skins” is absent, likewise in Codex Cantabrigiensis.]

23. And it came to pass, as he was walking through the grainfields on the sabbaths, that his disciples began to pluck ears of grain.  
[Note: Col. 0733. “Again” is absent also in the Greek text.]  
[Note: Col. 0733. After “began,” “to go on” is absent also in Codex Cantabrigiensis.]

24. But the Pharisees said to him, “Look, why do your disciples do on the sabbaths what was not lawful for them?”  
[Note: Col. 0733. It adds “your disciples,” as does Codex Cantabrigiensis: οἱ μαθηταί σου.]  
[Note: Col. 0733. It adds “for them,” as does Codex Cantabrigiensis: αὐτοῖς.]

25. And he said to them, “Have you not read what David did when he was in need and was hungry, he and those who were with him? 26. How he entered the house of God and ate the loaves of presentation, and gave them to those who were with him—loaves which none but priests were permitted to eat?”  
[Note: Col. 0733. After “God,” “under Abiathar the chief priest” is absent, likewise in Codex Cantabrigiensis. Some think that Abimelech, not Abiathar, was high priest, and that for this reason the Gothic codex has simply “priest” instead of “chief priest.”]  
[Note: Col. 0733. It adds “only,” also in the Gothic version from Matthew.]

27. “But I tell you that the sabbath was made for humankind, not humankind for the sabbath; 28. therefore the Son of Man is Lord even of the sabbath.”  
[Note: Col. 0733. Before “not,” “and” is absent also in the Greek text.]

## Chapter III

1. And he entered the synagogue again; and there came to him a man with a withered hand. 2. And they watched him to see whether he would heal on the sabbath, so that they might accuse him. 3. And he said to the man who had the withered hand, “Rise into the midst.” 4. And he said to them, “Is it lawful on the sabbaths to do good, or to do evil? To save a life, or to destroy it?” But they kept silent.  
[Note: Col. 0735. Thus Codex Cantabrigiensis: εἶπε πρὸς αὐτούς, “he said to them.”]  
[Note: Col. 0735. It adds “anything,” also in the Latin and Greek Cantabrigiensis manuscript: τι.]

5. And looking round at them with anger, grieved … at the blindness of their heart, he said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” And he stretched it out; and his hand was restored like the other.  
[Note: Col. 0735. And so the Greek text: αὐτοῦ ὡς ἡ ἄλλη, “his, like the other.”]

6. But the Pharisees went out with the Herodians and took counsel against him, how they might destroy him.  
[Note: Col. 0735. Before “with,” “immediately” is absent, likewise in Codex Cantabrigiensis.]  
[Note: Col. 0735. The Greek text has ὅπως, “how/so that.”]

7. But Jesus withdrew with his disciples to the sea; and a great crowd from Judaea and Galilee, 8. and from Jerusalem, Idumaea, the region beyond the Jordan, Tyre, and Sidon, followed him, hearing how great were the things he did.  
[Note: Col. 0735. “Followed him” is absent also in Codex Cantabrigiensis.]  
[Note: Col. 0735. The Greek text reads ὅσα, “what things/how much.”]

9. And he told his disciples to keep a little boat ready for him because of the crowd, lest they crush him. 10. For he healed many, so that all who had afflictions rushed upon him in order to touch him. 11. And the unclean spirits, when they saw him, came forth before him and cried out, saying, 12. “You are the Son of God.” And he sternly charged them not to make him known, because they knew him.

13. And going up the mountain, he called to himself those whom he himself wished, and they came to him. 14. And he appointed twelve, that they might be with him and that he might send them out to preach the gospel, 15. and gave them authority to heal diseases and cast out demons.  
[Note: Col. 0737. Thus also the Greek text: δώδεκα, ἵνα, “twelve, that.”]  
[Note: Col. 0737. It adds “the Gospel,” also in Codex Cantabrigiensis: τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον.]

16. And he gave Simon the name Peter; 17. and James, son of Zebedee, and John, brother of James—whom he jointly named Boanerges, that is, “sons of thunder”; 18. and these were: Simon, Andrew, James, John, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, James of Alphaeus, Lebbaeus, Simon the Cananaean, 19. and Judas Scarioth, who also betrayed him.  
[Note: Col. 0737. Thus Codex Cantabrigiensis: Λεββαῖον, “Lebbaeus.”]

20. And he came again into a house, and the crowd assembled, so that they could not even eat bread.  
[Note: Col. 0737. Thus Codex Cantabrigiensis: ἔρχεται, “he comes.”]

21. And when the scribes and the others heard about him, they went out to seize him; for they said that he was astonishing them.  
[Note: Col. 0737. Thus Codex Cantabrigiensis: καὶ ὅτε ἤκουσαν περὶ αὐτοῦ οἱ γραμματεῖς καὶ οἱ λοιποί, “and when the scribes and the others heard about him.”]  
[Note: Col. 0737. Thus the Latin and Greek Cantabrigiensis manuscript: ἐξίσταται αὐτούς, “he astonishes them.” This reading has flowed in from Matthew, for it has καὶ ἐξίσταντο πάντες οἱ ὄχλοι, “and all the crowds were astonished.”]

22. And the scribes who had come down from Jerusalem said that he had Beelzebul, the prince of demons, and that through him he cast out demons. 23. And he called them to him and said in parables, “How can Satan cast out Satan? 24. If a kingdom is divided against itself, it cannot stand. 25. And if a house is divided against itself, that house cannot stand. 26. And if Satan casts out Satan and is divided against himself, his kingdom cannot stand.  
[Note: Col. 0739. After “said,” “to them” is absent also in Codex Cantabrigiensis. The same manuscript adds Jesus, ὁ Κύριος Ἰησοῦς, “the Lord Jesus,” as do Vercelli and Verona.]  
[Note: Col. 0739. Thus Codex Cantabrigiensis: ὁ Σατανᾶς Σατανᾶν ἐκβάλλει, μεμέρισται ἐφ᾽ ἑαυτόν, οὐ δύναται σταθῆναι ἡ βασιλεία αὐτοῦ: “Satan casts out Satan; he has been divided against himself; his kingdom cannot stand.”]

27. No one can enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man; then he will plunder his house. 28. Amen, I tell you: all sins and blasphemies shall be forgiven to the children of humankind; 29. but whoever blasphemes the Holy Spirit has no forgiveness, but is guilty of an eternal offence.” 30. For they were saying, “He has an unclean spirit.”  
[Note: Col. 0739. Before “Spirit,” “against/in” is absent also in Codex Cantabrigiensis.]  
[Note: Col. 0739. After “forgiveness,” “for ever” is absent in Codex Cantabrigiensis.]  
[Note: Col. 0739. Thus also the Greek text: ἐστίν, “is.”]

31. And his mother and his brothers came; and standing outside, they sent for him, calling him. 32. And a crowd sat around him and said to him, “Look, your mother, your brothers, and your sisters are outside, seeking to speak with you.”  
[Note: Col. 0739. Thus Codex Cantabrigiensis: ἔρχεται, “comes.”]  
[Note: Col. 0739. It adds “his,” likewise the Gothic version: αὐτοῦ.]  
[Note: Col. 0739. It adds “and your sisters,” also in Codex Cantabrigiensis: καὶ αἱ ἀδελφαί σου.]

33. But he answered and said, “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?” 34. And looking around at those sitting in a circle about him, he said, “Look: my mother and my brothers. 35. Whoever does the will of God is my brother, sister, and mother.”  
[Note: Col. 0741. Thus also the Greek text: ἀπεκρίθη, “he answered.”]  
[Note: Col. 0741. Before “sitting,” “his” is absent in Codex Cantabrigiensis, Greek.]  
[Note: Col. 0741. After “who,” “for” is absent, likewise in the Coptic version. Codex Brixianus supports this.]

## Chapter IV

1. And again he began to teach beside the sea; and a very great crowd gathered to him, so that, entering into a boat, he sat by the shore; and the whole crowd was on the shore.  
[Note: Col. 0741. It adds “into,” also in the Greek text: εἰς.]  
[Note: Col. 0741. Codex Cantabrigiensis has πέραν τῆς θαλάσσης, “across the sea.”]  
[Note: Col. 0741. Here likewise Codex Cantabrigiensis has πέραν τῆς θαλάσσης, omitting “on the ground.”]

2. And he taught them in parables, saying: 3. “Listen. Behold, the sower went out to sow. 4. And as he sowed, some fell beside the road; and birds came and ate it.  
[Note: Col. 0741. “Of heaven” is absent also in the Gothic version.]

5. Other seed fell upon stony ground; and because it did not have much earth, it sprang up, and quickly withered from the heat because it had no root.  
[Note: Col. 0741. Thus Codex Cantabrigiensis: καὶ ὅτι, “and because.”]

7. Other seed fell among thorns; and the thorns grew up and choked it, and it gave no fruit. 8. And other seed fell into good ground and gave fruit, springing up and increasing, and it bore one thirtyfold, one sixtyfold, and one a hundredfold.”  
[Note: Col. 0741. Thus Codex Cantabrigiensis: ἐπί, “upon.”]  
[Note: Col. 0743. Perhaps *adferet* should be read for *adfert*, “it bears,” with the Latin and Greek Cantabrigiensis manuscript: φέρει.]

9. And he said, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear; and he who understands, let him understand.”  
[Note: Col. 0743. It adds “and he who understands, let him understand,” also in the Latin and Greek Cantabrigiensis manuscript: καὶ ὁ συνιὼν συνιέτω.]

10. And when he was alone, his disciples asked him what this parable was. 11. And he said to them, “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God; but to those outside it is spoken in parables:  
[Note: Col. 0743. Thus the Latin and Greek Cantabrigiensis manuscript: ἐπηρώτων αὐτόν … τίς ἡ παραβολὴ αὕτη, “they asked him … What is this parable?” “His disciples” derives from Matthew or Luke.]  
[Note: Col. 0743. Thus Codex Cantabrigiensis: λέγει, “he says.”]  
[Note: Col. 0743. Thus Codex Cantabrigiensis: λέγεται, “it is spoken,” supported by Vercelli.]

12. ‘Seeing they may see and not perceive; and hearing they may hear and not understand, lest perhaps they turn and it be forgiven them.’ 13. And he said to them, “Do you not know this parable? How then will you understand all the parables? 14. The one who speaks the word sows it. 15. These are those sown beside the road: they receive the word carelessly, and when they have heard it, Satan immediately comes and takes away the word sown in their hearts.  
[Note: Col. 0743. According to Codex Cantabrigiensis: οἷς παρὰ τὴν ὁδὸν σπείρεται, “those for whom it is sown beside the road.”]

16. And these are those sown upon stony ground: when they hear the word, they immediately receive it with joy; 17. yet they have no root in themselves, but are temporary. Then, when tribulation or persecution arises because of the word, they immediately fall away.  
[Note: Col. 0743. After “are,” “likewise” is absent also in Codex Cantabrigiensis.]  
[Note: Col. 0745. Thus also the Greek text, ἤ, “or.”]

18. And others are those sown among thorns. They hear the word, 19. but the cares of life and the deceitfulness of the age, entering in together, choke the word, and they become fruitless.  
[Note: Col. 0745. Thus also Codex Cantabrigiensis: εἰς τὰς ἀκάνθας, “among the thorns.”]  
[Note: Col. 0745. Thus Codex Cantabrigiensis: βίου, “of life.”]  
[Note: Col. 0745. After “of the age,” “and desires concerning other things” is absent in Codex Cantabrigiensis and Colbertinus 2, in Mill’s edition.]  
[Note: Col. 0745. Thus Codex Cantabrigiensis: ἄκαρποι γίνονται, “they become fruitless.”]

20. And these are those sown upon good ground: they hear the word, receive it, and bear fruit, one thirtyfold, one sixtyfold, and another a hundredfold.”  
[Note: Col. 0745. It adds “and,” likewise the Greek text: καί.]

21. And he said to them, “Is a lamp brought in to be put under a measure or under a bed, rather than to be put on a lampstand? 22. For nothing is hidden except that it may be made manifest; nor has anything been made secret except that it may come into the open. 23. If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear.”  
[Note: Col. 0745. After “is,” “anything” is absent also in Codex Cantabrigiensis.]

24. And he said to them, “Take heed what you hear. With the measure with which you measure, it shall be measured back to you.” 25. “For to the one who has, it shall be given; and from the one who does not have, even what he has shall be taken away.”  
[Note: Col. 0745. Gatianus: “it shall be measured back to you.” Vulgate: “it shall be measured back to you, and it shall be added to you.”]  
[Note: Col. 0745. After “to you,” “and it shall be added to you” is absent also in Codex Cantabrigiensis and the Coptic version; likewise in other Latin manuscripts of the Old Version, according to Lucas Brugensis.]  
[Note: Col. 0745–0746. Gatianus: “does not have, it shall be taken away.” Vulgate: “does not have, even what he has shall be taken away.”]

26. And he said, “The kingdom of God is like a man who casts seed upon the earth; 27. and he sleeps and rises, night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows, though he does not know how. 28. For the earth bears fruit of itself: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear. 29. And when it has yielded its fruit, he immediately puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come.”  
[Note: Col. 0746. Gatianus and Mill: “if a man casts.” Vulgate: “if a man should cast.”]

30. And he said, “To what shall we compare the kingdom of God? Or in what parable shall we set it? 31. It is like a mustard seed, which, when sown upon the earth, though it is the least of all seeds, 32. grows and becomes greater than all vegetables, and puts forth great branches, so that the birds of heaven can dwell beneath its shade.”  
[Note: Col. 0747. Thus also the Greek text: ἐν ποίᾳ παραβολῇ, “in what parable.”]  
[Note: Col. 0747. Gatianus: “To what parable shall we compare it?” Vulgate: “To what parable shall we compare it?”]  
[Note: Col. 0747–0748. Gatianus: “which, when sown in the earth, grows.” Mill: “is least.” Vulgate: “which, when sown in the earth, is less than all the seeds which are in the earth; and when it has been sown, it grows.”]  
[Note: Col. 0747. Thus Codex Cantabrigiensis: ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν, “upon the earth.”]  
[Note: Col. 0747. Thus also the Greek text: μικρότερος πάντων τῶν σπερμάτων, “less than all the seeds.” In the same place, after “of all seeds,” “and when it has been sown” is absent also in Codex Cantabrigiensis.]  
[Note: Col. 0747. Thus also the Greek text: μεῖζον πάντων τῶν λαχάνων, “greater than all vegetables.”]

33. And with many such parables he spoke to them as they were able to hear; 34. but without parables he did not speak to them; yet privately he explained everything to his disciples.  
[Note: Col. 0748. Mill: “he spoke all things.” Vulgate: “he expounded all things.”]

35. And he said to them on that day, when evening had come, “Let us cross over.” 36. And they dismissed the crowd and took him with them, just as he was, in the boat; and many boats were with him.  
[Note: Col. 0747. Thus Codex Cantabrigiensis: πολλά, “many.”]

37. And a great windstorm arose, and waves were breaking into the boat, so that the boat was filling. 38. But he was in the stern, sleeping upon a cushion; and they awoke him and said to him, “Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?”  
[Note: Col. 0749. Thus Codex Cantabrigiensis: διεγείραντες, “having awakened.”]  
[Note: Col. 0749. According to the Greek text: οὐ μέλει σοι, “do you not care?”]

39. And rising, he rebuked the wind and said to the sea, “Be silent.” And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm.  
[Note: Col. 0749. Thus Codex Cantabrigiensis: τῇ θαλάσσῃ, καὶ εἶπε, “to the sea, and he said.”]

40. And he said to them, “Why are you afraid? Do you not yet have faith?” And they feared with great fear, and said to one another, “Behold, how even the sea and the winds obey him!”  
[Note: Col. 0749. Thus Codex Cantabrigiensis: ἄνεμοι, “winds.”]

## Chapter V

1. And they came across the strait into the region of the Gerasenes.  
[Note: Col. 0749. After “strait,” “of the sea” is absent also in Codex Cantabrigiensis.]

2. And when he came out of the boat, a man with an unclean spirit met him from among the tombs. 3. He had his dwelling in the tombs, and no one was any longer able to bind him, not even with chains; 4. for he had often been bound with fetters and chains, but had torn the chains apart and broken the fetters; nor could anyone tame him. 5. And night and day among the mountains and tombs he was crying out and cutting himself with stones.  
[Note: Col. 0749–0751. Thus Brixianus with Codex Cantabrigiensis: νυκτὸς δὲ καὶ ἡμέρας, “by night and by day”; the latter omits “always.” In the same place, “among the mountains and tombs,” according to the Greek text: ἐν τοῖς ὄρεσι καὶ ἐν τοῖς μνήμασιν.]

6. But seeing Jesus from a distance, he ran and worshipped him; 7. and crying out with a loud voice, he said, “What have I to do with you, Jesus, Son of God Most High? I implore you by God, do not torment me.” 8. For he said to him, “Come out of this man, unclean spirit.” 9. And he asked him, “What is your name?” And he answered, “Legion is my name, for we are many.”  
[Note: Col. 0751. Thus also the Greek text: ἀπεκρίθη, “he answered.”]

10. And he begged him greatly not to send him out of that region. 11. Now there was a herd of swine feeding there near the mountain.  
[Note: Col. 0751. After “swine,” “large” is absent also in Codex Cantabrigiensis. In the Verona manuscript, “feeding,” with the Latin Cantabrigiensis manuscript.]

12. And those spirits begged him, saying, “Send us into the swine, that we may enter them.” 13. And he permitted them. And the unclean spirits entered the swine, and the herd rushed down the steep slope into the sea—about two thousand—and they were drowned.

14. And those who tended them fled and reported it in the city and in the country. And people came out to see what had happened. 15. And they came to Jesus and saw the man who had been possessed by the demon sitting there, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid.  
[Note: Col. 0752. Gatianus: “what had happened.” Mill: “what had been done.” Vulgate: “what had happened.”]  
[Note: Col. 0752. Gatianus: “they came … were troubled.” Mill: “they came.” Vulgate: “they come … were troubled.”]  
[Note: Col. 0751. “And” is superfluous.]

16. And those who had seen it told them what had happened to the man who had had the demon, and about the swine. 17. And they began to beg him not to depart from their region. 18. And when he was getting into the boat, the man who had been demon-possessed begged him that he might be with him.  
[Note: Col. 0753. Thus also the Greek text: παρεκάλει, “he begged.”]

19. But Jesus did not permit him; rather, he said to him, “Go home to your own people, and tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and how he has had mercy on you.” 20. And he went away and began to proclaim in the Decapolis how much Jesus had done for him; and everyone marveled.  
[Note: Col. 0753. Thus also the Greek text: ὁ δὲ Ἰησοῦς, “but Jesus.”]

21. And when Jesus crossed over again, a great crowd gathered to him beside the sea. 22. And one of the rulers of the synagogue came, named Jairus; and seeing him, he fell at his feet 23. and begged him, saying, “My daughter is at the point of death. Come, lay your hands upon her, that she may be saved and live.”  
[Note: Col. 0753. Before “beside,” “and he was” is absent also in Codex Cantabrigiensis.]  
[Note: Col. 0753. Thus also the Greek text: εἷς, “one.”]  
[Note: Col. 0753. Thus Codex Cantabrigiensis: παρακαλῶν αὐτόν, “begging him.”]  
[Note: Col. 0753. Thus Codex Cantabrigiensis: ἅψαι αὐτῆς ἐκ τῶν χειρῶν σου, literally, “touch her with/from your hands.”]

24. And he went with him; and a great crowd followed him and pressed upon him. 25. And there was a woman who had had a flow of blood for twelve years, 26. who had suffered much under many physicians and had spent all that she had, yet had profited nothing, but rather grew worse.  
[Note: Col. 0753. Thus Codex Cantabrigiensis: ἥ, “who.”]

27. Having heard about Jesus, she came up behind him in the crowd and touched his garment, 28. saying, “If I touch even his garment, I shall be saved.” 29. And immediately the fountain of her blood dried up, and she knew in her body that she was healed.  
[Note: Col. 0753. Thus Codex Cantabrigiensis: λέγουσα, “saying.” In the Verona, Vercelli, and Colbertinus manuscripts in Mill’s edition, “because” before “if” is absent; Matthew does not have it.]

30. And Jesus, knowing that power had gone out from himself, turned about in the crowd and said, “Who touched my garments?”  
[Note: Col. 0755. Before “knowing,” “within himself” is absent also in Codex Cantabrigiensis.]  
[Note: Col. 0755. So also Codex Cantabrigiensis: καὶ … εἶπε, “and … he said.”]

31. His disciples said to him, “You see the crowd pressing upon you, and yet you say, ‘Who touched my garments?’”  
[Note: Col. 0755. Thus Codex Cantabrigiensis: λέγουσιν, “they say.”]

32. But he looked round to see who had done this. 33. And the woman, afraid and trembling, fell down before him and told him the whole truth. 34. But Jesus said to her, “Daughter, your faith has made you whole; go in peace, and be healed of your affliction.”  
[Note: Col. 0755. Thus Codex Cantabrigiensis: ὁ δὲ Ἰησοῦς, “but Jesus.”]

35. While he was still speaking, people came from the ruler of the synagogue, saying to him, “Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the Teacher any longer?”  
[Note: Col. 0755. “To him” is added, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis: αὐτῷ.]

36. But Jesus, having heard it, said to the ruler of the synagogue, “Do not fear; only believe.” 37. And he permitted no one to follow him except Peter, James, and John, the brother of James.  
[Note: Col. 0755. After “having heard,” “the word which was spoken” is absent also in Codex Cantabrigiensis and the Arabic and Ethiopic versions. Codex Vercellensis has “when he heard the word,” in conformity with Brixianus, which reads “having heard this word.”]

38. And they came to the house of the ruler of the synagogue, and he saw a tumult of people weeping and lamenting. 39. And entering in, he said, “Why are you disturbed, and why do you weep? The child is not dead, but sleeps.”  
[Note: Col. 0755. According to Codex Cantabrigiensis: θόρυβον κλαιόντων καὶ ἀλαλαζόντων, “a tumult of those weeping and lamenting.”]  
[Note: Col. 0755. It adds “why,” also in Codex Cantabrigiensis: τί.]

40. But they mocked him. And he, having put the crowd outside, took the child’s father and mother and those who were with him, and entered where the child was. 41. And taking her hand, he said to her, “Thabitha cumi,” which, translated, means, “Little girl, I say to you, rise.”  
[Note: Col. 0757. Thus Codex Cantabrigiensis: οἱ δέ, “but they.”]  
[Note: Col. 0757. Thus Codex Cantabrigiensis: ἐκβαλὼν τοὺς ὄχλους ἔξω, “having cast the crowds outside.”]  
[Note: Col. 0757. According to Codex Cantabrigiensis: εἰσεπορεύετο, “he entered.”]  
[Note: Col. 0757. After “child,” “lying” is absent also in Codex Cantabrigiensis.]  
[Note: Col. 0757. Codex Cantabrigiensis, Latin and Greek, reads Θαβιτά, *Thabitha*, with other Latin manuscripts and the Ethiopic version.]

42. And immediately the little girl rose and walked; for she was twelve years old. And they were overcome with great astonishment. 43. And he strictly charged them that no one should know this; and he told them to give her something to eat.  
[Note: Col. 0757. After “them,” “strictly” is absent also in Codex Cantabrigiensis.]

## Chapter VI
1. And departing from there, he went into his own country with his disciples; 2. and there he began to teach in the synagogue on the sabbath, so that they marvelled at his teaching, saying: “Whence has this man these things? And what is this wisdom which has been given him, and that such mighty works are accomplished by his hands?”  
[Note: Col. 0757. After “these things,” “all” is absent, also in the Greek text.]  
3. “Is this not the son of the carpenter and of Mary, the brother of James, and Joseph, and Jude, and Simon? Are not his sisters here with us?” And they took offence at him. 4. And Jesus said to them: “A prophet is not without honour, except in his own country, and among his own kin, and in his own house.” 5. And he performed no miracle there, except that he healed a few sick persons by laying his hands upon them, 6. because of their unbelief. And he went about the villages round about, teaching.

7. And having called the twelve disciples, he sent them out two by two, giving them authority over unclean spirits;  
[Note: Col. 0759. Thus also Codex Cantabrigiensis: ἀπέστειλεν, “he sent.”]  
[Note: Col. 0759. According to Codex Cantabrigiensis: δούς, “having given.”]  
8. commanding them to take nothing for the journey except a staff only: no bag, no bread, nor money in 9. their belts; but to be shod with sandals, and not to put on two tunics. 10. And he said to them: “Wherever you enter into a house, remain there until you depart 11. from there. And whoever do not receive you nor hear you, as you leave from there, shake off the dust of your feet as a testimony to them.”  
[Note: Col. 0759. Thus also Codex Cantabrigiensis: τῶν ποδῶν ὑμῶν, “of your feet,” with the Ethiopic version.]  
12. And going out, they preached that people should repent; 13. and some of them cast out many demons, and anointing many sick persons with oil, healed them.  
[Note: Col. 0759. Thus also Codex Cantabrigiensis: ἀλείψαντες, “having anointed.”]

14. Now King Herod heard of him—for his name had become known—and they said: “John the Baptist has risen from the dead; and therefore mighty works operate in him.” 15. Others said: “He is Elijah.” But others: “One of the prophets.”  
[Note: Col. 0761. Before “one,” “he is a prophet” is absent, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis.]  
16. When Herod heard this, he said: “John, whom I beheaded—he is the one; he has risen from the dead.”  
[Note: Col. 0761. The Veronese manuscript adds “he is the one”; the Vercelli manuscript, “this is he.” So also the Greek text: οὗτός ἐστιν, “this is he,” from Matthew.]

17. Herod himself had sent and seized John, and had bound him and put him in prison because of Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip, because he had taken her as his wife.  
[Note: Col. 0761. Thus also Codex Cantabrigiensis: ἔδησεν αὐτὸν καὶ ἔβαλεν εἰς τὴν φυλακήν, “he bound him and cast him into prison.”]  
18. For John said to Herod: “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.”  
[Note: Col. 0761. “Because” is added, as also in the Greek text: ὅτι.]  
19. But Herodias lay in wait for him and sought to kill him, but 20. could not. For Herod feared John, knowing him to be a righteous and holy man, and kept him safe. And on hearing him, he did many things, and heard him gladly.  
[Note: Col. 0761. The Greek text has συνετήρει, “kept him safe.”]  
[Note: Col. 0761. “Because” is superfluous.]

21. But when a favourable day had come, Herod gave a supper on his birthday to the chief men, the tribunes, and the principal men of Galilee.  
[Note: Col. 0761. The Greek text has καὶ γενομένης ἡμέρας εὐκαίρου, “and when a favourable day had come”; Codex Cantabrigiensis has δέ, “but,” in place of καί, “and.”]  
22. And when the daughter of Herodias entered and danced, and pleased Herod and those reclining with him, the king said to the girl: “Ask of me whatever you wish, and I will give it 23. to you.” And he swore to her: “Whatever you ask, I will give you, even if it be half my kingdom.”  
[Note: Col. 0761. After “daughter,” “his own” is absent, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis.]  
24. But the girl went out and said to her mother: “What do you wish me to ask for?” And she said: “The head of John the Baptist.” 25. And when she had entered before the king, she said: “Give me at once, on a dish, the head of John the Baptist.”  
[Note: Col. 0763. After “had entered,” “immediately with haste” is absent, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis.]  
26. And the king, grieved because of his oath and because of those reclining with him, was unwilling to refuse her.  
[Note: Col. 0763. Thus also the Greek text: περίλυπος γενόμενος, “having become grieved.”]  
27. And immediately, sending an executioner, he ordered his head to be brought. He went and beheaded him in prison,  
[Note: Col. 0763. “Immediately” is added, as also in the Greek text: εὐθέως.]  
[Note: Col. 0763. After “his head,” “on a dish” is absent, likewise in the Greek text.]  
[Note: Col. 0763. “And he went” is added, as also in the Greek text: ὁ δὲ ἀπελθών, “and he, having gone.” Brixianus: *Isque abiens*, “and he, departing.” Vercelli: “And when he had gone.”]  
28. and brought his head on a dish and gave it to the girl; and the girl gave it to her mother. 29. On hearing this, his disciples came and took his body and placed it in a tomb.

30. And the apostles gathered to Jesus and reported to him all that they had done and taught. 31. And Jesus said to them: “Come apart yourselves into a desert place and rest a little.” For there were many coming and going, and they did not even have time to eat.  
[Note: Col. 0763. “Jesus” is added, as also Codex Cantabrigiensis: ὁ Ἰησοῦς.]  
[Note: Col. 0763. “Yourselves” is added, as also in the Greek text: ὑμεῖς.]  
32. And they went away privately into a desert place. 33. But many saw them going and recognized them; and on foot, from all the towns, they ran together there and gathered there.  
[Note: Col. 0765. Codex Cantabrigiensis has καὶ συνῆλθον αὐτοῦ, “and they gathered there.” Mill thought that the words καὶ προῆλθον αὐτούς, “and they went before them,” which the Greek text has earlier, were deliberately deleted in Codex Cantabrigiensis, lest there be any conflict between this passage and Matthew, who says that this crowd followed Jesus.]

34. And going out, when Jesus saw a great crowd, he had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd; and he began to teach them many things.  
[Note: Col. 0765. According to Codex Cantabrigiensis: ἐξελθὼν δὲ καὶ ἰδών, “but having gone out and seen.”]  
35. And when the hour had now grown late, his disciples came to him, saying: “This is a desert place, and the hour is already past; 36. dismiss them, so that they may go into the neighbouring farms and villages and buy themselves bread to eat, for they have none here.”  
[Note: Col. 0765. “Because” is added, as also in the Greek text: ὅτι.]  
[Note: Col. 0765. After “place,” “here” is absent, also in the Greek text.]  
[Note: Col. 0765. According to the Greek text: ἄρτους τί γὰρ φάγωσιν οὐκ ἔχουσι, “bread—for they have nothing to eat.” An addition from chapter VIII, verse 2, of this Gospel.]  
37. But answering, he said to them: “You give them something to eat.” And they said to him: “Shall we go and buy two hundred denarii worth of bread and give it to them to eat?”  
[Note: Col. 0765. Thus also the Greek text: λέγουσιν, “they say.”]  
38. Jesus said to them: “How many loaves have you? Go and see.” And when they had found out, they said to him: “Five, and two fish.”  
[Note: Col. 0765. “Jesus” is added, as also Codex Cantabrigiensis: ὁ Ἰησοῦς.]  
39. And Jesus ordered them all to recline in groups upon the green grass. 40. And they reclined in divisions, by hundreds and by fifties.  
[Note: Col. 0765. “By” is added, likewise in the Greek text: ἀνά.]  
41. And Jesus, taking the five loaves and the two fish, looked up to heaven, blessed, broke the five loaves, and gave them to his disciples to set before them; and he divided the two fish likewise among them all.  
[Note: Col. 0767. “Five” is added; Codex Cantabrigiensis likewise has πέντε, “five.”]  
42. And all ate and were satisfied. 43. And they took up twelve full baskets of fragments, and also of the fish.  
[Note: Col. 0767. After “they took up,” “the remnants” is absent, likewise in the Greek text.]  
44. And those who had eaten were five thousand men.

45. And immediately, rising, he compelled his disciples to embark in the boat and go ahead of him across the lake to Bethsaida, while he dismissed the crowd.  
[Note: Col. 0767. “Rising” is added, as also Codex Cantabrigiensis: ἐγερθείς.]  
[Note: Col. 0767. “Into” is added, as also in the Greek text: εἰς.]  
[Note: Col. 0767. Thus also the Greek text: καὶ προάγειν, “and to go ahead.”]  
[Note: Col. 0767. Thus also Codex Cantabrigiensis: αὐτὸς δὲ ἀπολύει, “but he dismisses.”]  
46. And having departed from them, he went up the mountain to pray. 47. And when evening had already come, the boat was far away in the midst of the sea, while he was alone 48. on land. And seeing them rowing and labouring—for the wind was against them—about the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking upon the sea, and intended to pass them by.  
[Note: Col. 0767. Thus also Codex Cantabrigiensis, though with the order of words changed: βασανιζομένους καὶ ἐλαύνοντας, “being distressed and rowing.”]  
49. But when they saw him walking on the sea, they thought that it was a phantom and all cried out; 50. and they were troubled. But he immediately spoke to them, saying: “Take courage; it is I; do not 51. be afraid.” And he went up to them into the boat, and the wind ceased. And they were exceedingly astonished within themselves, and marvelled,  
[Note: Col. 0767. Thus also Codex Cantabrigiensis: καὶ ἀνέκραξαν πάντες καὶ ἐταράχθησαν, “and all cried out and were troubled.”]  
[Note: Col. 0767. According to Codex Cantabrigiensis: αὐτοῖς λέγων, “to them, saying.”]  
[Note: Col. 0769. “And marvelled” is added, as also in the Greek text: καὶ ἐθαύμαζον. Vercelli has “with amazement.”]  
52. for they had not understood concerning the loaves, but their heart was hardened.

53. And crossing over from there, they came into the land of Gennesaret.  
[Note: Col. 0769. “From there” is added; Codex Cantabrigiensis likewise has ἐκεῖθεν.]  
[Note: Col. 0769. Thus Codex Cantabrigiensis, Latin and Greek: Γεννησάρ, “Gennesaret.” In the Vercelli and Veronese manuscripts and Codex Cantabrigiensis, “and they moored” is absent.]  
54. And when they had come out of the boat, people immediately recognized him; 55. and running about through that whole surrounding district, they began to bring all who were ill on their beds; for wherever they heard that Jesus was, they carried them about.  
[Note: Col. 0769. Thus also Codex Cantabrigiensis: ἐπὶ τοῖς γραββάττοις πάντας τοὺς κακῶς ἔχοντας. περιέφερον γὰρ αὐτοὺς ὅπου ἂν ἤκουσαν τὸν Ἰησοῦν εἶναι, “all those who were ill upon pallets; for they carried them about wherever they heard Jesus to be.” Vercelli also agrees.]  
56. And wherever he entered, into villages or farms or towns, they laid all the sick in the marketplaces and begged him that they might touch even the fringe of his garment; and all who touched it were made well.

## CHAPTER VII

1. And Pharisees and certain scribes who had come from Jerusalem gathered to him. 2. And when they saw some of his disciples eating bread with unwashed hands—  
[Note: Col. 0769. After “bread,” “they found fault” is absent, also in Gothic, Coptic, Ethiopic, Alexandrian, and other manuscripts cited by Mill.]  
3. for the Pharisees, and all the Jews, do not eat unless they repeatedly wash their hands, holding to the tradition of the elders; 4. and when they come from the market, they do not eat unless they wash themselves. And there are many other things which they have received to observe: washings of cups, and jars, and bronze vessels, and couches.  
[Note: Col. 0769. “Bread” is added; Codex Cantabrigiensis likewise has ἄρτον.]  
[Note: Col. 0771. “When they come” is added, as also Codex Cantabrigiensis: ὅταν ἔλθωσιν. Brixianus, however, has “and returning.”]  
[Note: Col. 0771. Thus also the Greek text: ἃ παρέλαβον κρατεῖν, “which they received to observe.”]  
5. And the Pharisees and scribes asked him: “Why do your disciples not walk according to the tradition of the elders, but eat bread with unwashed hands?”  
[Note: Col. 0771. Thus also the Greek text: ἀνίπτοις, “unwashed.”]  
6. But he answered and said: “Isaiah prophesied well concerning you hypocrites, as it is written: ‘This people honours me with its lips, but their heart is far 7. from me. In vain do they worship me, teaching doctrines and commandments of men.’”  
[Note: Col. 0771. “Because” is added, likewise in the Greek text: ὅτι.]  
[Note: Col. 0771. According to Codex Cantabrigiensis: καὶ εἶπεν, “and he said.”]  
[Note: Col. 0771. Thus also Codex Cantabrigiensis: ἀγαπᾷ, “loves.”]  
[Note: Col. 0771. Before “commandments,” “and” is absent, likewise in the Greek text.]  
8. “You perform washings of bowls and pots, and many other similar such things, having forsaken the commandment of God and holding to human traditions.”  
[Note: Col. 0771. According to the order of Codex Cantabrigiensis: τοιαῦτα πολλὰ ποιεῖτε, ἀφέντες τὴν ἐντολήν, “you do many such things, having forsaken the commandment.”]  
9. And he said to them: “Well do you set aside the commandment of God, in order to establish your own tradition.  
[Note: Col. 0771. Thus also Codex Cantabrigiensis: στήσητε, “you may establish.”]  
10. For Moses said: ‘Honour your father and your mother’; and: ‘Whoever curses father or mother, let him surely die.’”  
[Note: Col. 0771. Thus also the Greek text: πατέρα, “father.”]  
11. “But you say: ‘If a man says to his father or mother, Corban’—that is, ‘a gift’—‘whatever benefit you might have received from me’; 12. you no longer allow him to do anything for his father or mother, 13. nullifying the word of God by your foolish tradition which you have handed down. And you do many such things.”  
[Note: Col. 0773. Thus also Codex Cantabrigiensis, Latin.]  
[Note: Col. 0773. After “father,” “his own” is absent, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis.]  
[Note: Col. 0773. “Foolish” is added, as also Codex Cantabrigiensis: τῇ μωρᾷ.]

14. And calling the crowds to him again, he said to them: “Hear me, all of you, and understand. 15. There is nothing outside a person which, entering into him, can defile him; but the things that come forth from a person are what defile a person. 16. If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear.”  
[Note: Col. 0773. According to the Greek text: προσκαλεσάμενος, “having called to himself.”]  
[Note: Col. 0773. According to the Greek text: ἔξωθεν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, “outside the person.”]  
17. And when he had entered into the house away from the crowd, his disciples asked him about the parable. 18. And he said to them: “Are you also without understanding? Do you not understand that everything entering a person from outside cannot defile him, 19. because it does not enter into his heart, but into his stomach, and goes out into the privy, purifying all foods?”  
[Note: Col. 0773. Thus also Codex Cantabrigiensis: οὐ γάρ, “for not.”]  
20. And he said: “What comes forth from a person, that defiles a person. 21. For from within, from the heart of persons, come evil thoughts: adulteries, 22. thefts, fornications, murders, covetousness, wickedness, deceit, licentiousness, an evil eye, blasphemies, pride, 23. foolishness. All these evil things come from within and defile a person.”  
[Note: Col. 0773. According to the order of Codex Cantabrigiensis.]  
[Note: Col. 0773. Thus Codex Cantabrigiensis: πλεονεξία, “covetousness,” [δόλος,] “deceit,” πονηρία, “wickedness,” ἀσέλγεια, “licentiousness,” βλασφημίαι, “blasphemies.”]

24. And rising, he went into the territory of Tyre; and entering a house, he wished no one to know, but he could not remain hidden.  
[Note: Col. 0775. After “Tyre,” “and Sidon” is absent, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis.]  
25. For as soon as a woman whose daughter had an unclean spirit heard about him, she came to him. 26. Now she was a Greek woman, a Syrophoenician by race. And she begged him to cast the demon out of her 27. daughter. But he said to her: “Let the children first be satisfied; for it is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to the little dogs.”  
[Note: Col. 0775. Thus the Greek text: δὲ . . . Ἑλληνίς, “but . . . a Greek woman.”]  
[Note: Col. 0775. Thus the Greek text: τοῖς κυναρίοις, “to the little dogs.”]  
28. But she answered and said to him: “Lord, yet even the little dogs under the table eat of the children’s crumbs.”  
[Note: Col. 0775. Before “Lord,” “indeed” is absent, likewise in Codex Cantabrigiensis.]  
[Note: Col. 0775. In the same place, with the same manuscript, it has ἀλλὰ καί, “but also.”]  
29. And he said to her: “Go; because of this saying, may it be granted you concerning your daughter as you desire.” 30. And when she had gone home, she found the girl lying upon the bed, and the demon gone out of her.

31. And again, leaving the territory of Tyre, he came through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, through the midst of the territory of the Decapolis. 32. And they brought to him one who was deaf and had an impediment in his speech, and begged him to lay his hand upon him. 33. And taking him aside from the crowd, he spat and put his fingers into his ears, and touched his tongue;  
[Note: Col. 0777. According to the order of Codex Cantabrigiensis: πτύσας ἔβαλε, “having spat, he put.”]  
34. and looking up to heaven, he groaned and said to him: “Ephphatha”—that is, “Be opened.” 35. And his ears were opened, the bond of his tongue was loosened, and he spoke plainly.  
[Note: Col. 0777. After “and,” “immediately” is absent, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis.]  
36. And he commanded them that they should tell no one. 37. But the more he commanded them, the more abundantly they proclaimed it; and they were exceedingly astonished, saying: “He has done all things well: he makes even the deaf hear and the mute speak.”  
[Note: Col. 0777. Thus also Codex Cantabrigiensis: οἱ δέ, “but they,” with “but the more he commanded them” omitted.]

## CHAPTER VIII

1. In those days, when again there was a great crowd and they had nothing to eat, he called his disciples and said to them:  
[Note: Col. 0777. Thus also the Greek text: δέ, “but.”]  
2. “I have compassion on this crowd, because it is already three days since they have been here, and they have nothing to eat; 3. and I do not wish to send them away fasting, lest they faint on the way, for some have come from afar.”  
[Note: Col. 0777. “This” is added, also Codex Cantabrigiensis: τούτου. Vercelli and Brixianus have “to this [crowd].”]  
[Note: Col. 0777. Thus also Codex Cantabrigiensis: ἤδη ἡμέραι τρεῖς εἰσιν ἀφ’ ὅτε ὧδε εἰσιν, “they have already been here three days.”]  
[Note: Col. 0777. So also Codex Cantabrigiensis: ἀπολῦσαι οὐ θέλω ἵνα μὴ ἐκλυθῶσιν ἐν ὁδῷ, ὅτι καί, “I do not wish to dismiss them lest they faint on the way, because also.” Vercelli is nearly in agreement with Veronensis.]  
4. And his disciples answered him: “From where can anyone satisfy these people with bread here in this wilderness?”  
[Note: Col. 0777. After “can,” “here” is absent, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis.]  
5. And he asked them: “How many loaves have you?” They said: 6. “Seven.” And he ordered the crowd to recline on the ground. Taking the seven loaves, giving thanks, he blessed and broke them and gave them to his disciples to set before the people; and they set them before the crowd. 7. They also had two small fish; and he blessed them and ordered them to be set before them. 8. And they ate and were satisfied; and they took up seven baskets of the fragments that remained.  
[Note: Col. 0779. Thus also the Greek text: κλασμάτων, “of fragments.”]  
9. Now those who had eaten were about four thousand persons; and he dismissed them. 10. And he himself, entering the boat with his disciples, came into the district of Magadan.  
[Note: Col. 0779. Thus also Codex Cantabrigiensis: αὐτός, “he himself,” with “immediately” omitted.]  
[Note: Col. 0779. So St Jerome, together with most other manuscripts, as Zacharias Chrysopolitanus testifies in the *Monotessaron*; Codex Cantabrigiensis Latin has *Magidan*.]

11. And the Pharisees came out and began to dispute with him, seeking from him a sign from heaven, testing him. 12. And groaning in spirit, he said: “Why does this generation seek a sign? Amen, I say to you: if a sign shall be given to this generation—” 13. And leaving them, he embarked and departed. And they had forgotten to take bread, and had no more than one loaf with them in the boat. 15. And he charged them, saying: “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod.”  
[Note: Col. 0779. After “beware,” “and take heed” is absent, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis.]  
16. And they reasoned with one another that they had no bread.  
[Note: Col. 0779. Before “that,” “saying” is absent, likewise in Codex Cantabrigiensis.]  
[Note: Col. 0781. According to Codex Cantabrigiensis: εἶχαν, in place of εἶχον, “they had.”]  
17. And Jesus, knowing it, said to them: “Why do you reason in your hearts because you have no bread? Do you not yet understand or perceive? Are your hearts still hardened? 18. Having eyes, do you not see? And having ears, do you not hear? Do you not remember the five loaves 19. which I broke for the five thousand persons, and how many baskets of fragments you took up?” And they said: “Seven.”  
[Note: Col. 0781. “In your hearts” is added, also Codex Cantabrigiensis: ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις ὑμῶν.]  
[Note: Col. 0781. Thus also Codex Cantabrigiensis: οἱ δὲ εἶπον, “and they said.”]  
21. And he said to them: “How is it that you do not understand?”  
[Note: Col. 0781. Thus also Codex Cantabrigiensis: λέγει, “he says.”]  
[Note: Col. 0781. Thus also the Greek text: οὐ, “not.”]

22. And they came to Bethsaida, and they brought to him a blind man and begged him to touch him. 23. And taking the blind man by the hand, he led him outside the village; and having spat upon his eyes, he laid his hands upon him and asked him whether he saw anything.  
[Note: Col. 0781. Thus also the Greek text: τὰς χεῖρας αὐτῷ, ἐπηρώτα, “his hands upon him, he asked.” Vercelli also supports this.]  
24. And looking up, he said: “I see people, as trees, walking.” 25. Then again he laid his hands upon his eyes; and after he had laid his hands upon him, he began to see and was restored, so that he saw everything clearly.  
[Note: Col. 0781. Thus also the Greek text: καί, “and.”]  
26. And he sent him home, saying: “Go to your house; and if you enter the village, tell no one.”

27. And Jesus and his disciples went into Caesarea Philippi; and on the way he asked his disciples, saying: “Who do people say that I am?”  
[Note: Col. 0783. Thus also Codex Cantabrigiensis: εἰς Καισάρειαν, “into Caesarea.”]  
[Note: Col. 0783. After “saying,” “to them” is absent, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis.]  
28. They answered him, saying: “John the Baptist; others, Elijah; but others, as one of the prophets.” 29. Then he said to them: “But who do you say that I am?” And Peter answered and said to him: “You are Christ Jesus, the Son of the living God.”  
[Note: Col. 0783. “The Son of the living God” is added, likewise in the Syriac and Persian versions, from Matthew.]  
30. And he sternly charged them that they should tell no one about him. 31. And he began to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things, be rejected by the elders and chief priests, be killed, and after three days rise again. 32. And he spoke the saying openly. Peter then took him aside and began to rebuke him, saying: “Lord, be merciful; for this shall not 33. happen.” But he turned, saw his disciples, and rebuked Peter, saying: “Get behind me, Satan; for you do not understand the things of God, but the things of human beings.”

34. And having called the crowd together with his disciples, he said: “If anyone wishes to follow after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.  
[Note: Col. 0783. After “said,” “to them” is absent, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis.]  
[Note: Col. 0783. Thus also the Greek text: ὀπίσω μου, “after me.”]  
35. For whoever wishes to save his life shall lose it; but whoever loses his life for the Gospel’s sake shall save it.  
[Note: Col. 0785. After “his life,” “for my sake” is absent, likewise in Codex Cantabrigiensis.]  
36. For what will it profit a person if he gains the whole world and suffers loss of his life? 37. Or what shall a person give in exchange for his life?  
[Note: Col. 0785. Thus also the Greek text: ἀντάλλαγμα, “exchange.”]  
38. For whoever is ashamed of me and my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, the Son of Man also shall be ashamed of him when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels.” 39. And he said to them: “Amen, I say to you, there are some standing here with me who shall not taste death until they see the kingdom of God coming in power.”  
[Note: Col. 0785. Thus also Codex Cantabrigiensis: δέ, “but.”]  
[Note: Col. 0785. Thus also Codex Cantabrigiensis: μετ’ ἐμοῦ, “with me.”]

## CHAPTER IX

1. And after six days Jesus took Peter, James, and John and led them up alone by themselves onto a very high mountain; and he was transfigured before 2. them. And his garments became shining, white as snow, such as no one can make on earth.  
[Note: Col. 0785. After “shining,” “exceedingly” is absent, also in Gothic.]  
[Note: Col. 0785. Codex Cantabrigiensis has τίς, “who”; “fuller” is absent.]  
3. And Elijah appeared to them with Moses, and they were speaking with Jesus. 4. And Peter answered and said to Jesus: “Rabbi, it is good for us to be here. Do you wish that I should make three tents: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah?”  
[Note: Col. 0787. Thus also Codex Cantabrigiensis: θέλεις ποιήσω, “do you wish that I should make?”]  
5. For he did not know what to say, since they were terrified with fear. 6. And a cloud came, overshadowing them; and a voice came from the cloud, saying: “This is my beloved Son; hear 7. him.” And looking round, they no longer saw anyone except Jesus alone with themselves.

8. And as they came down from the mountain, he commanded them to tell no one what they had seen, except when the Son of Man had risen from the dead. 9. And they kept this saying among themselves, questioning what this rising from the dead might mean.  
[Note: Col. 0787. “This” is added, also in the Greek text: τό.]  
10. And they asked him, saying: “Why do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?”  
[Note: Col. 0787. Thus also the Greek text: ὅτι, “that/because.”]  
[Note: Col. 0787. Before “scribes,” “Pharisees, and” is absent, likewise in the Greek text.]  
11. And answering, he said to them: “Elijah, when he comes first, will restore all things; and how is it written concerning the Son of Man, that he should suffer many things and be despised? 12. But I say to you that Elijah also has come, and they did to him whatever they wished, as it is written of him.”

13. And coming to the disciples, he saw a great crowd around them, and scribes disputing with them.  
[Note: Col. 0787. After “disciples,” “his own” is absent, likewise in the Greek text.]  
[Note: Col. 0787. The Greek text has πρὸς αὐτούς, “around them.”]  
14. And immediately all the crowd, seeing Jesus, were astonished; and falling down, they greeted him.  
[Note: Col. 0789. Thus also Codex Cantabrigiensis: ἰδόντες . . . ἐθάμβησαν, “seeing . . . they were astonished.”]  
15. And he asked them: “What are you disputing among yourselves?” 16. And one of the crowd answered him: “Teacher, I brought my son to you, having an unclean spirit. 17. Wherever it seizes him, it throws him down; he foams, grinds his teeth, and becomes rigid. And I told your disciples to cast it out, but they were unable to cast it out.”  
[Note: Col. 0789. Thus also Codex Cantabrigiensis: ἀπεκρίθη αὐτῷ, “answered him.”]  
[Note: Col. 0789. “His own” is added, as also in the Greek text: αὐτοῦ.]  
[Note: Col. 0789. “To cast it out” is added; Codex Cantabrigiensis likewise has ἐκβαλεῖν αὐτό, “to cast it out,” from Matthew.]  
18. And he answered them: “O unbelieving generation, how long shall I be with you? How long shall I endure you? Bring him to me.” 19. And they brought him. And when the unclean spirit saw him, it convulsed the boy; and falling to the ground, he rolled about foaming.  
[Note: Col. 0789. Before “spirit,” “immediately” is absent, likewise in Codex Cantabrigiensis.]  
20. And he asked him: “How long has this been happening to him?” 21. And he answered: “From childhood. And it often throws him into fire and into water, to destroy him. But if you can do anything, help us, Lord, having compassion on us.”  
[Note: Col. 0789. Thus also the Greek text: ἐφ’ ἡμᾶς, “upon us.”]  
22. But Jesus said to him: “If you can believe, all things are possible to one who believes.”  
[Note: Col. 0789. Before “to one who believes,” “are” is absent, also in the Greek text.]  
23. And immediately the father cried out with tears and said: “I believe, Lord; help my unbelief.”  
[Note: Col. 0791. Thus also Codex Cantabrigiensis: λέγει, “he says.”]  
24. And when Jesus saw that a crowd was running together, he rebuked the unclean spirit, saying to it: “Deaf and unclean spirit, I command you: come out of him, and take care never to enter into him again.”  
[Note: Col. 0791. Thus also the Greek text: ὅτι ἐπισυντρέχει, “that [a crowd] is running together.”]

27. And when he had entered into the house, his disciples asked him privately: “Why could we not cast it out?” 28. And Jesus said to them: “This kind cannot come out by anything except by prayers and fastings.” 29. Departing from there, they passed through Galilee, and they did not wish anyone 30. to know. For he taught his disciples and said to them: “The Son of Man will be delivered into the hands of human beings, and they will kill him; and when he has been killed, after three days he will rise again.”  
[Note: Col. 0791. Thus also Codex Cantabrigiensis: μετὰ τρεῖς ἡμέρας, “after three days.”]  
31. But they did not understand the saying, and they were afraid to ask him.

32. And they came to Capernaum. And when they were in the house, he asked them: “What were you discussing on the way?” 33. But they were silent, for they had debated among themselves on the way which of them was greater.  
[Note: Col. 0793. After “for,” “on the way” is absent, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis and Gothic.]

[Note: Col. 0793. Thus also Codex Cantabrigiensis: Τότε, “then.”]

[Note: Col. 0793. After “whoever,” “one” is absent, likewise in Codex Cantabrigiensis.]

[Note: Col. 0793. According to Codex Cantabrigiensis: καὶ εἶπε, “and said.”]

[Note: Col. 0793. After “forbid,” “him” is absent, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis.]  
[Note: Col. 0793. Thus also the Greek text: δυνήσεται, “will be able.”]  
39. For whoever is not against you is for you. 40. For whoever gives you a cup of cold water to drink in my name, because you are Christ’s, amen, I say to you, he shall not lose his reward.”  
[Note: Col. 0793. “Because” is added; Codex Cantabrigiensis likewise has ὅτι.]

41. “And whoever causes one of these little ones who believe to stumble, it is better for him if a millstone turned by an ass were hung about his neck and he were thrown into the sea.  
[Note: Col. 0793. Thus also the Greek text: περὶ τὸν τράχηλον, “about the neck.”]  
42. And if your hand causes you to stumble, cut it off and cast it from you. It is better for you to enter life maimed than, having two hands, to go into Gehenna, 43. where the fire is unquenchable, where their worm does not die and their fire is not quenched.  
[Note: Col. 0795. Thus also Codex Cantabrigiensis: ὅπου ἐστὶ τὸ πῦρ τὸ ἄσβεστον, “where the fire is unquenchable.”]  
44. And if your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off. It is better for you to enter eternal life lame than, having two feet, to be cast into Gehenna, 45. where their worm does not die and their fire is not quenched. 46. And if your eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out. It is better for you to enter the kingdom of God one-eyed than, having two eyes, to be cast into Gehenna, 47. where their worm does not die and their fire is not quenched.  
[Note: Col. 0795. After “Gehenna,” “fire” is absent, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis.]  
48. For every sacrifice shall be salted with salt.  
[Note: Col. 0795. Before “every,” “for everyone shall be salted with fire, and” is absent, also in Codex Cantabrigiensis, Greek and Latin, and in the Greek manuscripts Em. and Cov. I cited by Mill.]  
49. Salt is good; but if salt has become tasteless, with what will you season it? Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves.”
