[Col. 0823] At this point the Silver Codex is mutilated by an entire quire; for what we read in the Vulgate from chapter XII, verse [Col. 0824] 5, through XIII, verse 32, is missing here. Whether through the carelessness of the binder or through another act of sacrilege is uncertain.

[Col. 0825] At this point the Silver Codex is mutilated by an entire quire; for what we read in the Vulgate from chapter XII, [Col. 0826] verse 5, through XIII, verse 32, is missing here. Whether through the carelessness of the binder or through another act of sacrilege is uncertain. [Col. 0827] . . . no one knows, neither the angels in heaven nor the Son, except the Father. Therefore watch, be vigilant, and pray; for you do not know when the time will be. It is like a man going abroad: he leaves his house, gives authority to his servants, assigning each his work, and commands the doorkeeper to keep watch. Therefore keep watch, for you do not know when the master of the house will come: in the evening, or at midnight, or at cockcrow, or in the morning; lest, coming suddenly, he find you asleep. But what I say to you, I say to all: Keep watch.

Now the Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread were to occur after two days. And the chief priests and scribes sought how they might seize him by deceit and kill him. For they said, “Not during the festival, lest perhaps there be an uproar among the people.” And when Jesus was in Bethany, [Col. 0828] in the house of Simon the leper, while he reclined at table, a woman came having an alabaster flask of ointment, very costly pure nard. Breaking the alabaster flask, she poured it upon his head. But there were some who were indignant among themselves and said, “Why was this waste of ointment made? For this ointment could have been sold for more than three hundred denarii and given to the poor.” And they were harsh with her. But Jesus said to them, “Leave her alone. Why do you trouble her? She has done a good work for me. For you always have the poor with you, and whenever you wish, you can do them good; but you do not always have me. She has done what she could: she has anointed my body beforehand for burial. Amen, I say to you, wherever this Gospel shall be proclaimed [Col. 0829] in the whole world, what she has done shall also be spoken of in remembrance of her.”

And Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve, went to the chief priests in order to hand him over to them. When they heard it, they rejoiced and promised to give him money. And he sought how he might deliver him over conveniently. On the first day of Unleavened Bread, when they sacrificed the Passover, his disciples said to him, “Where do you wish us to go and prepare for you to eat the Passover?” And he sent two of his disciples and said to them, “Go into the city, and a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him. Wherever he enters, say to the master of the house, ‘The Teacher says, Where is my dining room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?’ And he will show you a large upper room, furnished and ready; prepare for us there.” And his disciples went away and came into the city and found [Col. 0830] it as he had told them; and they prepared the Passover. When evening came, he arrived with the Twelve.

As they reclined and ate, Jesus said, “Amen, I say to you, one of you who eats with me shall betray me.” And they began to grieve and say to him one by one, “Surely it is not I?” and another, “Surely it is not I?” He said to them, “One of the Twelve, who puts his hand with me into the dish. Yet the Son of Man goes as it is written concerning him; but woe to that man through whom the Son of Man is betrayed. It would have been good for that man if he had not been born.” As they ate, Jesus took bread; and having blessed it, he broke it, gave it to them, and said, “Take; for this is my body.” And taking the cup, giving thanks, he gave it to them, and they all drank from it. And [Col. 0831] he said to them, “This is my blood of the new covenant, which shall be poured out for many. Amen, I say to you, I shall no longer drink of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new in the kingdom of God.” And after singing a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.

Jesus said to them, “All of you shall stumble because of me, for it is written, ‘I shall strike the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered.’ But after I have risen, I shall go before you into Galilee.” Peter said to him, “Even if all stumble, yet I shall not.” Jesus said to him, “Amen, I say to you, this very night, before the cock crows twice, you shall deny me three times.” But he spoke all the more emphatically, “Even if I must die with you, I shall not deny you.” And they all said likewise.

And they came to a place whose name was Gethsemane. [Col. 0832] And he said to his disciples, “Sit here while I pray.” And he took Peter, James, and John with him and began to be fearful, distressed, and anguished. And he said to them, “My soul is sorrowful even unto death. Remain here and keep watch.” And going forward a little, he fell upon the ground and prayed that, if it were possible, that hour might pass from him. And he said, “Abba, Father, all things are possible for you. Remove this cup from me; yet not what I will, but what you will.” And he came and found them sleeping. He said to Peter, “Simon, are you sleeping? Could you not keep watch one hour? Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” Again he went away and prayed, saying the same words. And returning again, he found them sleeping, for their eyes were heavy, [Col. 0833] and they did not know what to answer him. He came a third time and said to them, “Sleep now and rest. The end is at hand; the hour has come. Behold, the Son of Man is delivered into the hands of sinners. Rise, let us go; behold, he who betrays me has drawn near.”

And immediately, while he was still speaking, Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve, came, and with him a crowd with swords and clubs, from the chief priests, scribes, and elders. His betrayer had given them a sign, saying, “Whomever I kiss, that is he. Seize him and lead him away securely.” And when he came, immediately approaching him, he said, “Rabbi,” and kissed him. But they laid hands upon him and seized him. One of those standing by drew a sword [Col. 0834] and struck the servant of the chief priest, cutting off his right ear. Jesus answered and said to them, “Have you come out with swords and clubs to seize me as though I were a robber?

“Daily I was with you, teaching in the temple, and you did not seize me. But let the Scriptures be fulfilled.”

And they all abandoned him and fled. A certain young man followed him, clothed only with a linen cloth over his naked body; and they seized him. But he left the linen cloth behind and fled from them naked. And they led Jesus to the chief priest, and they assembled . . . . . . . . .

The codex is mutilated by an entire page here, namely from verse 53 through verse 62.

But Jesus said to him, [Col. 0835] “I am; and you shall see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven.”

The high priest, tearing his garments, said, “Why do we still need witnesses? You have heard the blasphemy. What does it seem to you?” And they all condemned him as guilty of death. And some began to spit in his face, to strike him with their fists, and to say to him, “Prophesy to us.” And the attendants willingly struck him with slaps.

And while Peter was below in the courtyard, one of the maidservants of the high priest came to him; and, seeing [Col. 0836] Peter warming himself, she looked at him and said, “You too were with Jesus the Nazarene.” But he denied it, saying, “I neither know nor understand what you are saying . . .”

And he went outside before the courtyard, and the cock crowed. Again, when the maidservant saw him, she began to say to those standing by, “This man is one of them.” But he again denied it. And after a little . . .

The remaining two lines, which fill the facing page, are illegible; and, what is more regrettable, all the rest has perished.

# APPENDIX TO THE GOSPEL OF EUSEBIUS OF VERCELLI

[Col. 0837]

[Col. 0837]

## EDITOR’S NOTICE

Although in this appendix certain documents may be found which do not have a direct relation to the Gospel of Eusebius, whose works we have undertaken to publish here, we nevertheless judged that the reader should not be deprived of them, since they either furnish most valuable palaeographical information or serve to elucidate the manuscripts of the Old Latin version with which the text of our Eusebius has been compared.

[Col. 0837]

## LETTER OF BLANCHINI. Certain Variant Readings of the Evangelists Compared

To the most eminent and most reverend prince and lord, Lord Neri Corsini, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, most worthy protector of the kingdoms of Portugal, Joseph [Col. 0838] Blanchini of Verona, priest of the Roman Congregation of the Oratory, greetings.

Since [Note: [Col. 0837] Namely, on 21 April of this year, 1749.] the most holy lord [Col. 0839A] Benedict XIV, Supreme Pontiff, in that remarkable allocution which he delivered in secret consistory, amid the applause of the entire sacred senate of the most eminent cardinals of the Holy Roman Church, declared that he had, by his own motion, bestowed the highly honourable title of MOST FAITHFUL upon the Sacred Majesty of John V, King of Portugal and the Algarves, and upon his successors as kings, on account of the illustrious deeds by which that king himself and his royal forebears had most deservedly served the Catholic faith and the Apostolic See: allow me, most eminent prince, to approach you joyfully through this letter, as the most worthy protector of the kingdoms of Portugal.

I could not omit this duty owed by me to his devoted Name and Majesty, since the present fourfold Gospel-book of the ancient Italian Latin version, now almost [Col. 0839B] wholly printed at his expense and under his patronage, is about to be published very shortly. Indeed, most eminent protector, together with this honour of royal designation—on which I also warmly congratulate you—I shall be the first of all to publish a work in which the entire weight and splendour of this most honourable title is displayed. As you know, there is no book better able to urge most faithful conduct upon kings than the Gospel; and kingdoms which heed it never fall. No form of instruction is greater, none more useful to the commonwealth, none more divine. Those who receive its counsels with attentive ears are rightly called truly happy, prosperous, and fortunate, and they possess the best possible helper in governing peoples.

Great kings, most eminent prince, placed at the summit of affairs, are always occupied with public [Col. 0839C] concerns; accordingly, they could not even live unless they repeatedly devoted themselves to reading the most holy Gospel, and thus restored minds exhausted and distracted by the prolonged management of public affairs. For this restoration of the mind, so necessary to kings, what book among all books would John consider preferable to the Gospel? The Gospel relieves the cares and anxieties of royal rule; the Gospel imparts all weight and strength to the laws of dominion; finally, it seeks partnership with the throne—not, however, to diminish royal authority, but to protect and govern it with supports that will endure forever.

Therefore this Gospel-book had to be dedicated to John V, most faithful in piety, morals, and religion, because he has obtained the palm of the Most Faithful King and has added this also to his other praises: that by the common consent of all peoples he is called, and is, Most Faithful. It was fitting that the name of the great John should first be set together with this title on the front of the Gospels, because he has always gloried in employing it as a mirror in harmonizing his kingdom with the priesthood. Let this work of mine therefore gladly visit Lisbon and seek as its patron so great a king, who everywhere most faithfully supports the Catholic religion. The Roman faith, destined always to reign, has now embraced him with a closer bond; and, receiving him among the Most Faithful Kings, it claims by a certain special right [Col. 0840A] that he should more and more in future be willing to protect by his authority and patronage whatever pertains to it, since it now glories and rejoices not only in that old title of King, but also in this new one of MOST FAITHFUL.

I hear that you approve and even praise, most worthy protector of the kingdoms of Portugal, my plan to publish a portion of that golden allocution which the Supreme Pontiff delivered in consistory to the gathering of his most eminent purple-clad brethren on the twenty-first day of this month of April. As I copy it out, I am inflamed with certain sparks of Christian exultation, and I triumph and rejoice, because John V is exalted not so much by praise itself as by the supreme authority of the one praising him, and is endowed with that title of MOST FAITHFUL in which the Catholic Roman religion has always stood and shall stand. Behold, therefore, what he who is greatest and wisest on earth said of so great a king, for his commendation and everlasting glory:

[Col. 0840B]

> “Venerable brothers, we consider it altogether fitting, indeed necessary, to declare to you—as we now declare—that we have bestowed upon our dearest son in Christ, John, King of Portugal and the Algarves, and upon his successors, the most honourable title of MOST FAITHFUL, which indeed seemed deservedly to be assigned to him. For throughout the whole course of his life he has done most illustrious deeds, so that the glory of the Catholic religion and the dignity of this Holy See might be more greatly advanced, etc.
>
> “Moreover, how illustrious are this king’s merits toward the Christian commonwealth is more than sufficiently attested by [Col. 0840C] the apostolic letters of our predecessor Clement XI, which two published volumes contain.
>
> “For, in order to comply with the will and plans of that same pontiff, he supplied very many ships as assistance at the time when the tyrant of the Turks, threatening the island of Corcyra with a most powerful army, menaced ruin and disaster not only to the Venetian republic but also to all Italy and to this city, which is the head of the whole Christian religion.
>
> “We ourselves can and rightly do bear witness—and indeed we do bear witness—that this king has never allowed us to lack his assistance whenever the matter concerned either maintaining and enlarging religion or protecting the dignity of this Holy See. [Col. 0840D] Moreover, during our pontificate he founded several bishoprics in the remotest regions of his dominion, where only unbelievers lived, namely so that the Christian faith might there be propagated. We shall omit to speak here of the immense and truly royal expenditures which he makes in order that the necessities of ministers undertaking sacred missions may be supplied. Yet we must not pass over in silence the victories which he has recently gained in Asia and the new expeditions which he has undertaken; and we shall gladly compare wars of this sort with those successfully carried out by Gennadius, patrician and exarch of Africa, and shall affirm exactly what our predecessor Saint Gregory wrote to Gennadius himself [Col. 0841A] concerning them, in these words [Note: [Col. 0841] Book I, indiction 9, epistle 75, vol. II of his works, Paris edition of 1705, p. 360.]: ‘For where does the eloquent report of your merits not circulate? It declares that you frequently undertake wars not out of a desire to shed blood, but for the expansion of the commonwealth in which we behold God worshipped, so that the name of Christ may spread everywhere among subject peoples through the preaching of the Faith.’ We shall continue with the words of the same holy pontiff: ‘I have learned that Your Excellency has provided very many benefits for feeding the sheep of blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles.’ At last we shall conclude our discourse as Saint Gregory also concluded his letter: ‘Having rendered the address of paternal love, we ask our Lord and Saviour, who may mercifully protect Your Eminence [Col. 0841B] for the consolation of the holy commonwealth and strengthen it ever more by the might of his arm for spreading his name among neighbouring peoples.’”

Thus far the most wise Pope Benedict XIV, who, following the illustrious examples of his predecessors, bestowed upon John V—most deserving of the Catholic faith and the Apostolic See—the title and ornaments of MOST FAITHFUL. The most holy Pius V (what a great pontiff!) wished to confer upon the Sacred Majesty of Sebastian, King of Portugal and the Algarves, that excellent predecessor of John V, some honourable title as a lasting memorial of his deeds nobly accomplished, in return for the immense labours and works expended to promote the propagation of the Catholic faith; as Pope Benedict XIV ordered in letters, destined to endure forever, on the twenty-third day of December [Col. 0841C] 1748. But so great an honour was reserved for John V, whose memorials of piety and faith no age and no oblivion will ever erase. For the title of MOST FAITHFUL KING was first bestowed upon him; and when his descendants obtain it by hereditary right, they shall learn, through the title’s proclamation, the faith of John V, which is the root of all virtues, and, having learned it, they too shall proclaim it in emulous imitation.

Should I say that it has happened through your good fortune, most eminent cardinal, or through mine, that divine mercy has so long delayed the publication of this now mature fourfold Gospel-book? You indeed, if I probe your view, wish me to attribute this to my own good fortune: for, in this way, a more glorious entrance is opened for this work to King John V. It is presented to him [Col. 0841D] bearing on its front the title MOST FAITHFUL, in which the King himself will rightly take great pride. But it is also mine to show why in this matter I recognize an even greater weight of your good fortune. For if you hold such a view of me, it is fair that you grant me leave to hold it even more strongly of you, because you are the most worthy protector of the kingdoms of Portugal.

The most excellent Lord Emmanuel Pereyra de Sampajo, commander of the Militia of Our Lord Jesus Christ and plenipotentiary minister for the affairs of His Majesty at the Apostolic See, entrusted to your loyalty and wisdom this service of Christian exultation [Col. 0842A] which I am now performing. In rendering it, I congratulate him also from my heart. Although a great burden of most weighty affairs has been laid upon him, he bears it with the highest praise and everyone’s admiration; and it follows that he not only serves the will of the Most Faithful King—which is worthy of the highest praise—but also consults the interests of His Majesty, than which nothing can be more praiseworthy. May he therefore live many years, and live forever with Christ, whose Order and Militia he has entered. This is the aim of my prayers; this is the discipline and teaching of the fourfold Gospel-book which I bear in my heart.

But now, wisest cardinal, so far am I from deriving anything from your ancestors, who abound in every distinction, with which to adorn you, that there is even in you something which may redound to them. Yet if praise of you had to be sought from elsewhere, [Col. 0842B] whence could more adornments be supplied than from Clement XII, your uncle—a truly great pontiff, to the envy of many and the admiration of all—upon whom everyone testified that the College of Cardinals of the Holy Roman Church had bestowed the highest dignity on earth not as something desired, but as a debt owed? And how much might be written concerning your praises! But since I speak, as it were, with you, I do not wish to write more here, lest I seem to court your ears.

Therefore, wisest cardinal—to whom God has granted the utmost will to assist letters—since a new occasion now calls you to the outstanding glory of your inborn clemency, I beg you, undertake the patronage before the Most Faithful King of the continuation of this work. Restore to it what the perversity of the times—or, [Col. 0842C] to trace the cause more truthfully elsewhere, the force of my sins—has taken away. This is an act worthy of a cardinal, worthy of a prince; but most worthy of Neri both as cardinal and prince. While your great uncle was alive, gracious Rome saw your earlier life: from it nothing was ever low, obscure, or commonplace; all was ample, illustrious, and of unprecedented example. Since you cannot depart from yourself, you now bestow these things also upon all, and shall always bestow them.

Whatever profits may arise from this edition—especially in restoring the readings of the primitive holy Fathers, who either quote or expound in commentaries the four holy Gospels of Jesus Christ—I openly and plainly profess, with a mind as sincere as it is grateful, that all of them are owed to the wholly singular and incomparable munificence of John V, [Col. 0842D] and I shall always proclaim it. And would that, under the same patronage and at royal expense, I might also be permitted to publish two other outstanding volumes of Origen’s Hexapla, more precious than gold and silver, which wonderfully defend and aid the cause of the Catholic faith! This kind of subject, hitherto almost unattempted, desires a royal Maecenas, most eminent protector. But I shall speak with you of that another time.

For the present I send and submit for your wise examination certain omitted passages of the holy Fathers, so that from them you may determine whether I have rightly said that our Golden, Silver, Purple, [Col. 0843A] and Uncial manuscripts surpass others not only in antiquity but also in quality, and present the Old Latin version.

Matt. III.16. The Vercelli and Verona manuscripts have “coming upon him”; the Brescia manuscript, “coming over him.” The Vulgate translator of Matthew has “coming over himself”; nevertheless, in the Greek source one reads ἐπ᾽ αὐτόν, “upon him.”

Matt. V.12. The Verona and Saint-Germain manuscripts add “their fathers”; and so does St Cyprian in Epistle 26, p. 84.

Matt. VI.12. The Verona manuscript has “we forgive”; and so do some manuscript copies of St Cyprian.

Matt. VI.12. The Vercelli manuscript has “forgive”; and so does St Cyprian in *On the Lord’s Prayer*, p. 265.

Matt. VII.24. In the Vercelli manuscript the words “therefore . . . these” are absent; and so in St Cyprian, *Testimonies to Quirinus*, Book III, chapter 96, p. 387. In the Saint-Germain manuscript only “these” is absent.

Matt. IX.3. The Brescia manuscript has “they said among themselves”; the Greek has “they said within themselves.”

[Col. 0843B] Matt. XII.2. The Verona and Saint-Germain manuscripts have “it is not lawful for them”; and so do certain Greek copies and some Latin manuscript books cited in St Jerome’s *Divine Library*.

Matt. XII.7. The Vercelli, Verona, and Corbie manuscripts have “for if”; and so does St Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, Book IV, vol. I, p. 249.

Matt. XII.18. The Vercelli manuscript has “he announced”; the Verona, Corbie, and Brescia manuscripts have “he will announce”; and so does St Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, Book III, vol. I, p. 189.

Matt. XII.20. The Vercelli manuscript has “in victory”; the Brescia manuscript, “into victory.” St Cyprian, *Against the Jews*, and *On Mounts Sinai and Sion*, p. 497, have “in contention.”

Matt. XII.26. The Verona and Saint-Germain manuscripts have “for if Satan,” etc.; and so does St Ambrose, *On Repentance*, Book II, chapter 4, p. 421.

Matt. XII.29. The Verona manuscript has “has bound him,” etc.; and so do St Irenaeus and the Corbie manuscript.

Matt. XII.30. The Vercelli, Verona, and Saint-Germain manuscripts have “scatters.” St Ambrose, *On Repentance*, Book II, [Col. 0843C] chapter 4, p. 422, has “disperses.”

Matt. XII.40. In the Vercelli, Verona, Corbie, and Saint-Germain manuscripts, “and” is added before “Son”; and so in St Ambrose, *On Virgins*, chapter 19, p. 244, and *On Flight from the World*, chapter 4, p. 426.

Matt. XII.43. The Verona manuscript has “will find”; and so does St Hilary in his commentary on this passage of Matthew. The Corbie manuscript has “finding.”

Matt. XIII.4. In the Brescia manuscript “of heaven” is absent; and so in most Greek copies and in two Latin manuscript books of Queen Christina of Sweden kept at Rome.

Matt. XIII.11. The Corbie manuscript has *quoniam* (“because”) in place of *quia* (“because”); and so does St Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, Book IV, vol. I, p. 266.

Matt. XIII.13. The Vercelli, Verona, and Corbie manuscripts have “to them”; and so does St Irenaeus.

Matt. XIII.14. The Vercelli, Corbie, and Brescia manuscripts have “of Isaiah”; and so does St Irenaeus.

Matt. XIII.14. The Brescia manuscript has “might be fulfilled”; and so do several manuscript copies of St Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, Book IV.

[Col. 0843D] Matt. XIII.16. The Vercelli, Verona, and Corbie manuscripts have “which . . . hear”; and so does St Irenaeus.

Matt. XIII.17. In the Vercelli, Verona, Corbie, and Brescia manuscripts, *quippe* (“indeed”) is absent; and so in St Hilary, exposition on Psalm LXVII, vol. I, p. 234.

Matt. XIII.17. The Verona manuscript has “you heard”; the Saint-Germain manuscript, “you see . . . heard”; the Brescia manuscript, “you see . . . you hear”; etc.; and so do St Hilary in the passage cited and St Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, Book IV, p. 259.

Matt. XIII.38. The Verona manuscript has “wicked”; the Brescia manuscript, “evil”; and so does St Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, Book IV, vol. I, p. 288.

Matt. XIII.43. In the Vercelli and Verona manuscripts “for hearing” is absent; and so in nearly all manuscript copies of St Hilary’s *On the Trinity*, Book XI.

Matt. XIV.21. The Vercelli, Verona, and Corbie manuscripts have [Col. 0844A] “with boys and women excepted”; and so does St Ambrose, *On Virginity*, chapter 7, p. 223.

Matthew 15:27. The Vercelli and Verona [manuscripts]: “indeed, Lord”; Saint-Germain: “indeed.” The Greek: “Yes, Lord; for even the little dogs eat from the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table” (Ναὶ, Κύριε, καὶ γὰρ τὰ κυνάρια ἐσθίει ἀπὸ τῶν ψιχίων τῶν πιπτόντων ἀπὸ τῆς τραπέζης τῶν κυρίων αὐτῶν), which may be rendered, “indeed, Lord,” etc.

Matthew 16:17. Vercelli and Corbie: “who is in heaven”; and so Saint Jerome, *Commentary on Isaiah*, book XIV, chapter 52, vol. IV, p. 609.

Matthew 16:18. The word “and,” before “I,” is absent in Vercelli, as also in Saint Cyprian, Epistle 27, *To the Lapsed*, p. 56, and in *On the Unity of the Church*, p. 254.

Matthew 16:21. Corbie and Brescia: “him”; and so Saint Irenaeus.

Matthew 16:26. Verona: “shall gain”; Saint Cyprian, p. 621: “you shall gain.”

Matthew 16:28. Vercelli: “there are some of those standing here”; Verona: “because there are some of those standing here”; and so Saint Hilary, *Commentary on Matthew* chapter 17, and Saint Ambrose, *On Faith*, book III, chapter 12, p. 514. Yet in *On Faith in the Resurrection*, book II, p. 1159, he has: “of those standing here.” Corbie: “because there are some here among those standing”; Saint-Germain: “because there are some of those standing here”; Brescia: “because there are certain persons among those standing here.”

Matthew 17:16. Vercelli and Verona: “unbelievable”; and so Saint Hilary in his commentary on this passage of Matthew.

Matthew 18:5. Vercelli and Verona: “shall receive . . . a child . . . receives”; and so Lucifer of Cagliari, *For Saint Athanasius*, book II. Corbie: “shall receive . . . an infant . . . receives”; Saint-Germain: “shall receive,” etc.; Brescia: “shall receive . . . receives.”

Matthew 18:8. Corbie: “is for you”; and so Saint Augustine, *Mirror from the Gospel according to Matthew*, vol. III, part I, p. 760. Brescia: “is indeed for you.”

Matthew 18:15. Vercelli, Verona, and Corbie: “but if he shall sin”; and so certain manuscript copies of the works of Saint Ambrose.

Matthew 18:15. In Corbie, the word “and” is absent before the verb “rebuke”; and so in Saint Cyprian, *On the Twelve Abuses*, chapter 20, p. 596, and in Saint Ambrose, Epistle I, first class, vol. II, p. 948.

Matthew 19:35. Vercelli, Verona, and Corbie: “so also shall my Father who is in heaven do to you”; and so Saint Ambrose, Epistle I, first class, p. 958.

Matthew 24:41. In Vercelli there is added: “two on the roof: one shall be taken and one left.” In Verona: “two in bed: one shall be taken and one left”; and so in several Greek copies and some Latin books. In Corbie likewise: “two shall be lying in bed: one shall be left and the other taken.” But in the same codex the words “two women grinding at the mill: one shall be taken and one left” are omitted. In Brescia one reads: “two in one bed: one shall be taken and the other left.”

Matthew 26:28. “For” is absent in Vercelli and in Saint Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book V, vol. I, p. 332.

John 1:9. Verona: “for it was”; and so Saint Hilary, exposition of Psalm 131, vol. I, p. 501. Brescia: “but it was.”

John 1:18. In Gat., “Son” is absent; and so in Saint Ambrose, Epistle 10, first class, vol. II, p. 806.

John 4:23. Verona: “for indeed the Father”; and so Hilary, called Ambrosiaster, *Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans*, chapter 1, p. 29.

John 4:27. Vercelli: “th . . . wom . . . wondered”; Verona: “because he was speaking with a woman.” Saint Cyprian, p. 164: “because he was speaking with a woman.”

John 4:31. Vercelli: “meantime . . . the disciples . . . were asking, saying.” The Greek text is rendered word for word: “his disciples were asking him” (ἠρώτων αὐτὸν οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ).

John 4:34. Verona: “and that I may complete [it],” etc.; Brescia: “and complete [it]”; and so Saint Ambrose, *On Faith*, chapter 13, p. 581.

John 5:19. Vercelli: “does likewise”; Verona: “the Son also does the same likewise”; and so Saint Ambrose, *On Faith*, book II, chapter 8, p. 483; book IV, chapter 4, p. 528; and *On the Holy Spirit*, book II, chapter 12, p. 660. Gat.: “the Son likewise [does] the same.”

John 5:24. Verona: “shall pass from death to life”; Gat. and Mm.: “shall pass away from death to life”; Brescia, however, together with Vercelli and Saint Augustine, *Epistle* 55, book II, to Januarius concerning his inquiries, vol. II, p. 128: “shall pass from death to life.”

John 5:25. Verona and Brescia: “will come”; and so Saint Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book I, vol. VIII, p. 769.

John 5:29. Verona: “and they shall rise”; and so Saint Ambrose, p. 343.

John 6:43. Vercelli, Verona, and Brescia: “do not murmur among yourselves,” according to the Greek μετ᾽ ἀλλήλων, that is, “among yourselves,” or “against one another.”

John 6:58. Verona: “lives”; and so Saint Ambrose, p. 145.

John 7:28. Vercelli: “and I did not come of myself, but he is true,” etc.; Verona: “for neither did I come of myself, but he is true,” etc.; and so Saint Hilary.

John 7:34. Vercelli: “and where I go.” The Greek: “where I am” (ὅπου εἰμὶ ἐγὼ). The word εἰμὶ, marked with this accent, ought to be rendered “I am”; but when it is written εἶμι, it means “I go,” a spelling approved by some. Ancient codices lacked these marks, which grammarians later supplied in accordance with the different senses they understood to lie in the text. Thus the passage might be rendered: “and where I go, you cannot come,” in agreement with Vercelli.

John 7:52. “The Scriptures” is absent in Gat., Mm., and Brescia; and so in the Greek text and in some manuscript copies cited in Saint Jerome’s *Divine Library*.

John 8:6. Corbie, Gat., and Mm.: “with bowed head”; and so Saint Ambrose, Epistle 58.

Ibid. In Corbie and Mm., “downward” is absent; and so in the passage of Saint Ambrose just cited and in Saint Jerome’s *Dialogue against the Pelagians*, vol. II, p. 748.

John 8:44. Verona: “and desire,” etc.; Saint Cyprian reads, “and desires.”

John 8:58. Vercelli, Verona, and Corbie: “before Abraham, I am”; and so Saint Ambrose, *On Faith*, book III, chapter 9, p. 508.

John 9:7. In Vercelli and Verona, “wash” is absent; and so in Saint Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, book III, chapter 2, p. 364.

John 9:7. Vercelli and Verona: “woodland”; and so Saint Ambrose, Epistle 80, second class, p. 1096.

John 9:11. Verona: “and I began to see,” with Saint Ambrose, Epistle 80, second class, p. 1097. Corbie, Gat., and Mm.: “and I saw”; and so, more closely to the Greek archetype, certain manuscript copies cited in Saint Jerome’s *Divine Library*.

John 9:31. Vercelli: “but if anyone worships God and does [his] will”; Gat. and Mm.: “but he who is his worshipper.” Saint Cyprian has: “but he who has worshipped him and done his will”; and so Saint Augustine.

John 10:8. Gat.: “came before me.” The received Greek reads: “All who came before me” (Πάντες ὅσοι πρὸ ἐμοῦ ἦλθον). Yet the words “before me” are absent from a great many Greek codices, and from the Syriac, Persian, and Gothic versions, and from many Fathers cited by Mill in his *Various Readings*. Some learned men judge that they were removed at the very beginning of the Church because of the Manichaeans, who, as Theophylact attests, impiously inferred from them that all the prophets of the Old Testament had not been sent by God.

John 10:25. Vercelli: “I told you”; and so the Greek text, εἶπον ὑμῖν.

John 10:34. Vercelli: “because I,” etc.; and so Saint Cyprian, *Testimonies against the Jews*, book II, chapter 6, p. 314.

John 11:1. Gat. and Mm.: “of his sisters”; and so Saint Augustine, *Tractates on the Gospel of John*, chapter 11, tractate 49, vol. III, part 2.

John 12:6. Verona and Corbie: “he carried”; and so two manuscript codices cited in Saint Jerome’s *Divine Library*.

John 12:7. Verona: “leave her, that she may keep it until the day of my burial”; Gat.: “leave her,” etc.; Brescia: “leave her: she has kept it for the day of my burial.” The Greek text: “Leave her. She has kept it for the day of my burial” (Ἀφες αὐτήν· Εἰς τὴν ἡμέραν τοῦ ἐνταφιασμοῦ μου τετήρηκεν αὐτό). Yet many Greek codices, the Coptic and Ethiopic versions, and Nonnus agree with the Vulgate: “Leave her, that she may keep it for the day of my burial” (Ἄφες αὐτήν, ἵνα εἰς τὴν ἡμέραν τοῦ ἐνταφιασμοῦ μου τηρήσῃ αὐτό).

John 12:12. Vercelli: “the following day”; Brescia: “but on the following day.” The Greek τῇ ἐπαύριον: “on the following day.”

John 12:25. Vercelli and Verona: “shall bring”; and so Saint Ambrose, *Exposition of Psalm 43*, p. 894.

John 12:29. Vercelli: “thunders occurred”; Verona and Corbie: “a thunderclap occurred”; and so Saint Ambrose, *On Faith*, book II, chapter 15, p. 494. Brescia likewise has “a thunderclap.”

John 12:31. Vercelli: “is cast out”; Verona and Corbie: “shall be cast down”; and so Saint Gaudentius.

John 13:1. In Vercelli, Verona, and Brescia, “but” is added after “day”; and so in the Greek text.

John 13:2. Vercelli: “Scarioth”; Verona: “Scariotes”; Corbie: “Scarioth’s”; Gat. and Brescia: “Scariot’s”; and so two manuscript books in Saint Jerome’s *Divine Library*.

John 13:7. In Verona, “now” is absent; and so in the prologue to Saint Ambrose’s first book *On the Holy Spirit*, p. 603.

John 13:27. Before the word “entered,” “then” is added in Gat. and Brescia; and so in most manuscript books cited in Saint Jerome’s *Divine Library*.

John 14:1. Vercelli, Verona, Gat., and Mm.: “believe in God”; and so Saint Augustine, *Tractates on the Gospel of John*, chapter 14, tractate 67, vol. III, part II, p. 677; *Exposition of Psalm 68*, sermon I, vol. IV, part I, p. 697; *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, book I, vol. X, part I, p. 11; and *On the Gift of Perseverance*, vol. X, part I, p. 839.

John 14:3. Verona and Corbie: “I will bring you to myself,” etc.; and so Saint Ambrose, *On the Good of Death*, chapter 12, p. 411.

John 14:3. Vercelli and Verona: “to me,” omitting “him”; and so Saint Ambrose, *On Faith*, book V, chapter 12, p. 577.

John 14:7. Vercelli: “you know him”; Verona and Corbie: “you know him”; and so Victor of Vita, *History of the Vandal Persecution*, ed. Ruinart, p. 45. Saint Irenaeus, however, *Against Heresies*, book III, vol. I, p. 200, and book IV, p. 235, has “you have known him.”

John 14:18. Verona and Corbie: “I come to you”; and so the Greek text, ἔρχομαι, that is, “I come.”

John 14:27. Vercelli, Corbie, Gat., and Mm.: “I leave my peace to you”; Verona: “I give peace to you; I leave my peace to you.” Saint Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, book IV, chapter 3, p. 367: “I give my peace to you; I leave my peace to you”; and so Ambrosiaster, *First Epistle to the Thessalonians*, p. 284. But in the *Epistle to the Corinthians*, chapter 14, p. 159: “I give my peace to you; I leave peace to you.”

John 15:5. In Vercelli, Verona, and Mm., “are” is added; and so in Saint Ambrose, *Hexaemeron*, book III, chapter 12, p. 53, and *On Faith*, book IV, chapter 11.

John 15:5. Mm.: “but you”; Brescia: “and you”; and so Saint Jerome, *Dialogue against the Pelagians*, vol. II, p. 778.

John 15:13. “Anyone” is absent in Vercelli and Verona; and so in Saint Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Letter*, vol. X, part I.

John 15:15. Vercelli, Verona, Gat., Mm., and Brescia: “I call”; and so certain manuscript copies of Saint Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book IV, and Saint Cyprian, pp. 230 and 395.

John 15:26. In Vercelli at both occurrences, and in Verona only at the second, “my” is added after “Father”; and so in Saint Ambrose, *On Faith*, book II, chapter 9, p. 485, and *On the Holy Spirit*, book I, chapter 1, p. 605.

John 16:23. Vercelli: “on that day you will ask me nothing”; Verona: “on that day you ask me nothing”; Gat.: “you will ask me nothing”; and so the Greek text: Ἐμὲ οὐκ ἐρωτήσετε οὐδέν, that is, “you will ask me nothing,” or “you will request nothing.” For ἐρωτῶ is used in Luke and John both for “to request” and “to ask.”

John 16:24. Verona: “you have asked nothing.” Ambrosiaster, *Epistle to the Philippians*, chapter 2, p. 252: “you have asked nothing.”

John 16:27. Verona and Brescia: “loves . . . you love”; and so Saint Ambrose, *Exposition of Psalm 36*, p. 797. Corbie: “you love.”

John 16:32. Vercelli and Verona: “into his own region”; Corbie: “into his own [place]”; and so Saint Ambrose, *Exposition of Psalm 38*, p. 845, and Epistle 26, first class, p. 896.

John 17:5. Brescia: “glorify”; and so Saint Hilary, exposition of Psalm 2, vol. I, p. 46.

John 17:11. In Vercelli and Verona the words “whom you have given me, that they may be one, as we also are” are absent, as also in certain codices of Saint Zeno of Verona. They are likewise not read in Saint Hilary. In Corbie, however, they occur, but written in a later hand.

John 17:20. Vercelli and Brescia: “for these . . . for those”; and so Saint Cyprian, *On the Lord’s Prayer*, p. 271. Verona: “for these . . . for these.”

John 17:25. After the word “righteous,” Vercelli has “and,” as do the Greek text, the ancient Corbie Bible, and Saint Augustine both in *The Harmony of the Evangelists*, book III, vol. III, part II, p. 104, and *Against Adimantus, a Disciple of Mani*, vol. VIII, p. 122.

John 19:27. “And” is omitted in Vercelli; and so in Saint Ambrose, *Exposition of the Gospel according to Luke*, book II, vol. I, p. 1283.

John 20:27. Vercelli: “put your hands,” etc.; and so Saint Ambrose, *Exhortation to Virginity*, chapter 2, p. 280, and *Exposition of Psalm 118*, vol. I, p. 1250. Verona, however: “put [your] hand into,” etc., as Saint Ambrose likewise has in *Flight from the World*, chapter 4, p. 427.

John 20:31. Vercelli and Gat.: “because”; and so Saint Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book III, vol. I, p. 206.

John 21:17. Vercelli has “he said” on the third occurrence; Verona and Brescia, “he says”; and so the capitular Gospel-book of the church of Verona, written in the ninth century, for the Vigil of Saint Peter the Apostle.

John 21:17. Verona: “you know all things”; Corbie: “all things you know”; and so Saint Ambrose, *Apology of David*, chapter 9, p. 692. Gat. and Mm. codices: “you know all things,” in agreement with certain other manuscript books of Saint Jerome’s *Divine Library*.

Ibid. Verona and Corbie: “you know”; and so Saint Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, book II, chapter 7, p. 360, and *Apology of David*, chapter 9, p. 692.

Luke 1:31. In Verona and Brescia, “and” is added before “behold,” as in Saint Ambrose, *On Abraham*, book II, chapter 9, p. 339.

Luke 1:32. Vercelli: “to him”; and so Saint Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book III, vol. I, p. 185.

Luke 1:35. Corbie: “shall come upon you.” Most manuscript copies of Saint Augustine’s *On Correction and Grace* have “shall come over you.”

Luke 1:35. Verona has “you” after “overshadowed”; and so Tertullian, p. 515, and Saint Ambrose, *On the Incarnation of the Lord’s Sacrament*, chapter 6, p. 717. The Corbie codex reads “me” for “you.”

Luke 1:35. Gat.: “is born.” The Greek τὸ γεννώμενον is in the present tense, namely, “that which is being born.”

Luke 1:37. Vercelli, Verona, Corbie, and Brescia: “is not,” etc.; and so Saint Ambrose, Epistle, first class, p. 967.

Luke 1:37. Verona and Corbie: “with God”; and so Saint Ambrose, Epistle, first class, p. 967.

Luke 1:54. “His” is absent in Verona and Corbie; likewise in Saint Irenaeus and certain manuscript books of the Vatican Library’s Divine Scriptures. In Corbie it is added by a recent hand.

Luke 1:55. Vercelli: “for . . . ever . . .” Supply the lacuna from Saint Irenaeus, who has: “for ever.”

Luke 1:64. Vercelli: “his tongue was loosened”; Verona and Corbie: “his tongue was unbound”; and so Saint Ambrose.

Luke 1:73. Vercelli: “to give us,” omitting “himself”; Saint Irenaeus: “that he might give us,” likewise omitting “himself.”

Luke 1:74. Vercelli: “having been delivered, to serve him.” Saint Irenaeus has, according to the Greek text: “having been rescued, to serve himself.”

Luke 1:75. Vercelli: “in his pres . . . all days . . . ours.” Supply the lacuna from Saint Irenaeus, who has: “in his sight all our days.”

Luke 1:77. Vercelli: “to his people”; Corbie and Gat.: “to his populace”; Saint Irenaeus: “to his people.”

Luke 2:9. Vercelli: “the majesty of the Lord shone around them”; Corbie: “majesty shone around them.” The Greek text, δόξα Κυρίου, means “the glory of the Lord,” etc.; this term denotes the presence of the divine Majesty both in the Old and New Covenants.

Luke 2:18. In Vercelli, Verona, and Brescia, “and” is absent before “concerning these things.” This particle, *and*, is not read in the received Greek text, nor in most Greek codices and versions; nor does Saint Ambrose have it. Indeed, it seems wholly superfluous here.

Luke 2:22. “Him” is absent in Corbie and in Saint Irenaeus.

Luke 2:29. Verona and Gat.: “dismiss”; and so the Roman edition of Saint Ambrose, *On the Good of Death*.

Luke 2:35. Vercelli, Verona, Corbie, and Gat.: “of many hearts”; and so Saint Ambrose, *On Isaac and Anna*, chapter 6, p. 373, and *Exposition of Psalm 118*, p. 1119.

Luke 2:36. “Her” is absent in Vercelli; and so in Saint Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book I, vol. I, p. 40.

Luke 3:17. Vercelli: “for cleansing”; Saint Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book I, vol. I, p. 17: “to cleanse.”

Luke 3:23. Verona: “to be the son of Joseph”; Saint Augustine, *Questions on Deuteronomy*, book V, vol. III, part I, p. 572: “he was the son of Joseph.”

Luke 4:18. The words “to heal the broken-hearted” are omitted in Vercelli, Verona, and Corbie; and so in certain Greek codices, in Saint Ambrose, *On the Institution of Virgins*, chapter 10, p. 265, and in two manuscript books of the Queen of Sweden cited in Saint Jerome’s *Divine Library*. In one Vatican manuscript, however, they were added in a second recension.

Luke 6:26. “For” is absent in Vercelli, Verona, and Brescia; and so in two manuscript codices of the Queen of Sweden cited in Saint Jerome’s *Divine Library*.

Luke 6:30. “But” is absent in Verona; and so in Saint Jerome, *Dialogue against the Pelagians*, vol. II, p. 740.

Luke 6:30. Vercelli: “give”; and so Saint Jerome in the same *Dialogue against the Pelagians*, vol. II, p. 740.

Luke 6:32. At the first occurrence, “and” is absent in Brescia; and so in Saint Cyprian, *Testimonies to Quirinus*, book III, chapter 49, p. 382.

Luke 6:34. Vercelli: “And if you lend at interest.” The Greek word δανείζουσιν is sometimes rendered “they lend at interest,” sometimes “they lend”; for it has a double meaning. One who lends without interest δανείζει, and one who lends at interest δανείζει. But here it should invariably be rendered “to lend,” for the Evangelist is not speaking of usurers’ profit, but of the charitable loans which friends make to one another.

Luke 7:6. Verona, Corbie, and Brescia: “you would say”; and so certain manuscript books cited in Saint Jerome’s *Divine Library*.

Luke 7:36. Vercelli and Verona: “asked”; and so Saint Ambrose, Epistle 42, first class, p. 957, and one manuscript codex of the Queen of Sweden cited in Saint Jerome’s *Divine Library*. The Brescia codex: “will ask.”

Luke 7:37. Vercelli: “was bringing an alabaster flask of ointment.” Saint Cyprian, *Against the Novatian Heretic*, p. 436: “carrying a vessel of ointment.”

Luke 7:38. Vercelli: “was wiping”; Brescia: “was wiping”; Saint Cyprian: “wiped.”

Luke 8:15. Verona, Corbie, and Brescia: “through patience”; and so Saint Ambrose.

Luke 9:26. Vercelli: “in his gl . . . ory.” The Greek: ἐν τῇ δόξῃ, that is, “in glory.”

Luke 9:31. Vercelli: “appearing in glory”; Brescia: “were seen in glory,” with the Greek ἐν δόξῃ, “in glory.”

Luke 9:53. Vercelli: “because . . . he was going,” etc. Saint Jerome, Epistle 121, to Algasia, vol. I, p. 855: “because . . . he was proceeding,” etc.

Luke 11:3. For “daily,” Gat. has “each day”; and so, according to the Greek text, the ancient Corbie Bible codex, likewise one Vatican manuscript and another manuscript of the Queen of Sweden cited in Saint Jerome’s *Divine Library*.

Luke 11:4. Vercelli: “as . . . every debtor of ours.” Verona, Corbie, and Mm.: “as we also forgive our debtors”; and so Saint Ambrose. Vienna: “as,” etc.; Brescia: “as we also forgive all our debtors.”

Luke 11:17. Verona and Brescia: “is desolated”; and so certain Latin manuscript codices in Saint Jerome’s *Divine Library*.

Luke 11:23. Verona, Corbie, and Vienna: “against me”; and so Saint Cyprian, pp. 270 and 316. Gat., Mm., and Brescia: “against me.”

Luke 11:52. For “you have taken away,” Vercelli has “you have hidden”; Verona, “you hide”; and so Saint Ambrose, Sermon 16, p. 411.

Luke 12:10. In Vercelli, “to him” is added at the end after “shall be forgiven”; Verona, Corbie, and Vienna have “to him”; and so Saint Ambrose, *On the Holy Spirit*, book I, chapter 3, p. 611.

Luke 12:20. Vercelli: “they demand your soul,” etc. Saint Cyprian: “your soul is demanded.” Saint Augustine, *Conference with Maximinus, the Arian Bishop*, vol. VIII, p. 665: “your soul is demanded.” Vienna: “they demand your soul from you.” Saint Augustine, however, *Sermon 67 on the Words of the Gospel of Matthew*, vol. V, part II, p. 120: “they demand your soul.” Gat. and Mm.: “they will demand,” in accordance with the Greek text.

Luke 12:11. Vercelli: “do not be anxious how you may render an account,” etc.; Verona, Corbie, and Vienna: “how you may answer or speak”; and so Saint Ambrose, *On the Holy Spirit*, book I, chapter 4, p. 613.

Luke 12:47. Mm. and Gat.: “much”; and so Saint Ambrose, *Exposition of Psalm 38*, p. 858.

Luke 12:58. Brescia: “lest perhaps he hand you over to the judge.” Saint Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book I, vol. I, p. 104: “lest perhaps he give you to the judge.”

Luke 13:16. Vercelli: “ought she not to be loosed from this bond,” etc. Saint Irenaeus: “ought she not to have been loosed from this bond,” etc.

Luke 13:16. Verona does not read “this” after “bond”; and Ambrosiaster likewise has this in the *First Epistle to Timothy*, p. 292.

Luke 13:17. Before “opponents,” “all” is omitted in Verona and Vienna, and also in the Greek Canterbury codex.

Luke 14:21. Vercelli and Verona: “in flour.” Saint Ambrose, *Exposition of the Gospel according to Luke*, book VII, pp. 1455–1456, notes that “in flour” belongs to Luke, whereas “in three measures of flour” belongs to Matthew; and so it was then read in the received Greek codices. See Mill here. Corbie and Vienna: “into flour”; Gat.: “in sufficient flour for three [measures]”; Brescia: “in three measures of flour.”

Luke 14:23. Verona: “and compel [them], that they may enter.” Saint Ambrose: “and compel [them] to enter.”

Luke 15:21. Gat. adds: “make me one of your hired servants”; Mm.: “make me like one,” etc.; Brescia: “make me like one of your hired servants.” Many Greek and Latin codices cited by Mill in his *Various Readings* likewise add here: “make me like one of your hired servants.”

Luke 17:7. Verona: “returning.” Saint Cyprian, *Testimonies to Quirinus*, book III, chapter 51, p. 382: “coming.”

Luke 8:15. After “good,” “and excellent” is absent in Vercelli and Verona. Nor is it read in Saint Ambrose.

Luke 17:12. Vercelli: “into a certain village”; Greek: χώρην, “district” or “region.”

Luke 17:29. “But” is absent in Vercelli; and so in Saint Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book IV, p. 278.

Luke 19:13. Verona: “talents”; and so Lucifer of Cagliari, from Matthew.

Luke 19:37. For “disciples,” Gat. has “those descending”; Mm., “descending”; Brescia, “learners.” Certain manuscript books cited in Saint Jerome’s *Divine Library* have, as in the Greek Canterbury manuscript, “of those descending.”

Luke 20:35. Vercelli: “but those [who],” and so Saint Cyprian. The Vienna codex: “but those who,” etc.

Luke 20:35. Vercelli: “shall be worthy”; Corbie and Vienna: “are deemed worthy of that age and of the resurrection”; Saint Cyprian: “have been deemed worthy of that age and of the resurrection.”

Luke 21:20. Vercelli: “by armies”; and so the Greek reads in the plural, Ὑπὸ στρατοπέδων, that is, “by armies.”

Luke 21:23. Vercelli: “there shall be great distress upon the earth, and wrath upon this people.” The Greek reads: “For there shall be great distress upon the earth and wrath among the people” (Ἔσται γὰρ ἀνάγκη μεγάλη ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, καὶ ὀργὴ ἐν τῷ λαῷ).

Luke 22:6. Vercelli, Verona, Corbie, and Vienna: “without the crowd.” The Greek ἄτερ ὄχλου: “without a crowd,” “secretly,” “without the people,” or “without disturbance.”

Luke 22:26. Verona: “as the younger”; Gat., Mm., and Brescia: “as the junior”; and so the ancient Corbie Bible and Saint Augustine, *Mirror from the Gospel according to Luke*, vol. III, part I, p. 774, as well as *Harmony of the Evangelists*, book III, vol. III, part II, p. 104.

Luke 23:11. Brescia: “Herod with his soldiers.” The Greek likewise has σὺν τοῖς στρατεύμασιν αὐτοῦ, “with his soldiers,” namely, with his retinue; for Hellenistic writers use στρατιὰ and στράτευμα for any retinue.

Luke 23:28. Vercelli: “do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves”; Verona and Corbie: “do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves.” Saint Ambrose, *On Repentance*, book II, chapter 6, p. 427: “do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves.”

Luke 23:45. Vercelli: “the sun was darkened.” Nearly all Greek copies now have: “and the sun was darkened” (Καὶ ἐσκοτίσθη ὁ ἥλιος). Some others, however, read: “the sun failing.” Yet Origen observes, in his *Commentary on Matthew*, chapter 26, tractate 35, p. 128, col. 1, that the phrase “the sun failing” is absent from the best copies, and that copies preferring it have suffered a pious fraud by some unlearned Christian, who thought it should be substituted for clarity’s sake; or perhaps by some envious and deceitful person, who thereby found an occasion for constructing calumnies against the Church, as though accusing the Evangelists of foisting an eclipse upon an altogether unsuitable time. Whatever may have been the case with Origen’s copies, it is certain that scarcely any Greek copies now preserve that reading. Nevertheless, it is read in certain codices of the Roman Library. And in almost all [copies]: “and the sun was darkened.”

Luke 23:56. Vercelli and Brescia: “and indeed they rested on the Sabbath.” The Greek: ἡσύχασαν, “they rested.” The same word called *charasch* among the Hebrews means “to be silent,” “to rest,” and “to refrain”; the Greeks render it ἡσυχάζειν.

Luke 24:21. Vercelli: “since these things happened”; Greek: ἀφ᾽ οὗ, “since these things happened.”

Luke 24:38. Vercelli, Verona, Gat., Mm., and Brescia: “and why do thoughts,” etc. Saint Ambrose, *On the Patriarch Joseph*, chapter 12, p. 506: “why do thoughts,” etc.

Luke 24:39. Vercelli: “and my feet; because I am [he].” Verona: “see, behold my hands and my feet, because I myself am [he]”; and so Saint Ambrose in the passage just cited. Gat. and Mm. likewise: “my feet,” etc.; Brescia: “because I myself am [he].”

Luke 24:41. Corbie: “to eat”; and so Saint Augustine, Sermon 239, on the days of Easter, vol. V, part I, p. 997.

Mark 1:25. In Verona the words “unclean spirit” are added; in Gat. and Mm., “unclean spirit”; in Saint Ambrose, *On Faith*, book III, chapter 14, p. 517: “unclean spirit.”

Mark 7:19. In Vercelli, Verona, Gat., and Brescia, “goes” is absent; and so in Saint Augustine, *Mirror from the Gospel according to Mark*, vol. III, part I, p. 764.

Mark 8:31. Vercelli: “and to rise after the third day.” Certain Greek codices likewise read “to rise on the third day,” as Saint Matthew has in chapter 16, verse 21. Yet this old reading is that of a scribe who thought it truer to say that Christ rose on the third day than after three days from his death.

Mark 8:34. Verona: “if anyone wishes to follow after me”; Corbie: “if anyone wishes to follow after me”; Gat.: “if anyone wishes to come after me”; Vienna and Brescia: “if anyone wishes to follow after me”; and so the ancient Corbie Bible and one codex of Saint Augustine’s *Mirror from the Gospel according to Mark*.

Mark 8:34. Vercelli: “let him deny himself.” Saint Augustine, *Mirror from the Gospel according to Mark*, vol. III, part I, p. 764: “let him renounce himself”; Verona: “let him renounce himself”; Corbie: “let him deny himself to himself”; Vienna: “let him deny himself.”

Mark 9:11. Vercelli: “and Elijah, com . . . first, will restore all things.” The Greek: “Elijah indeed, coming first, restores all things” (Ἡλιὰς μὲν ἐλθὼν πρῶτον ἀποκαθιστᾷ πάντα).

Mark 10:7. Vercelli, Gat., and Brescia: “and he shall cleave to his wife,” in accordance with the Greek text, προσκολληθήσεται, etc.

Mark 10:29. Brescia: “shall leave”; and so Saint Cyprian, Epistle 56, to the Thibaritans, *On the Exhortation to Martyrdom*, p. 128, and *On the Lapsed*, p. 241.

Mark 10:30. Vercelli: “shall receive”; and so Saint Augustine, *Against Adimantus, a Disciple of Mani*, vol. VIII, p. 113.

Mark 10:30. After “only,” “now” is absent in Vercelli. Nor is it read in Saint Cyprian or in Saint Augustine, *Against Adimantus*, vol. VIII, p. 113.

Mark 12:30. Vercelli, Verona, and Vienna, instead of “and with all your mind,” have “with all your strength”; Corbie, “with all your strength.” Saint Hilary likewise reads “strength.”

Mark 12:44. Vercelli: “for all, from that which remained to them”; and so the Greek: Πάντες γὰρ ἐκ τοῦ περισσεύοντος αὐτοῖς, which may be rendered, “for all, from what was superfluous to them.”

Mark 14:36. Vercelli and Vienna: “all things [are] possible to you,” omitting “are.” Saint Hilary likewise, *On the Trinity*, book X, vol. II, p. 343: “all things [are] possible to you.”

Mark 14:36. Vercelli: “this cup.” Saint Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book X, vol. II, p. 343: “this chalice.”

Mark 15:29. Gat.: “destroys . . . builds”; and so one manuscript book of the Queen of Sweden cited in Saint Jerome’s *Divine Library*.

I have introduced into this epistle a vast forest of readings, for the purpose of the edition already explained: namely, that the excellence of our codices might become evident to you, most learned Cardinal, not so much from their remarkable antiquity as from these same passages, which I have borrowed from the Fathers of the earliest age. For these Fathers almost never fail to exhibit the chief readings of our codices. They are venerable monuments—although scribes have sometimes treated them badly—and they have not lost their original brightness and integrity. Therefore, under your protection, most eminent protector, I approach John V with them, and repeatedly commend to him myself and my own full brother Gaspar, his Commander in the Order of the Militia of Our Lord Jesus Christ. To the royal throne, most eminent Cardinal, not less the dignity than the condescension of most faithful John now calls [someone] “Brother,” that he may offer the work on my behalf. Farewell, most eminent Cardinal. Although it is difficult to requite your kindnesses, yet through unceasing zeal and a singular manner of respect I hope to satisfy [that obligation].

[Col. 0851]

## SECOND LETTER OF BLANCHINI. THE MORE NOTABLE READINGS OF THE BRESCIA GOSPEL-BOOK ARE ILLUSTRATED.

[Col. 0851D] To the most eminent and most reverend prince and lord, Lord Angelo Maria Quirini, Librarian of the Holy Roman Church and most deserving Bishop of Brescia: Joseph Blanchini, priest of the Roman Congregation of the Oratory, greetings.

It is the mark of supreme beneficence, most learned Cardinal, that whatever can be brought to light for the common benefit should not remain hidden in darkness or be shared with only a very few, but that each person should take every care to make it widely known for the advantage of the entire Christian commonwealth. Since nothing more divine or useful than the sacred Scriptures can ever be conceived, the greatest thanks are due to the distinguished Philip, Abbot Garbelli, Brescian patrician and provost of the church of Pontis vici, situated within the bounds of your most extensive diocese. Under your authority and patronage, he devoted all his industry to being the first of all to recover from the royal monastery of Saint Julia that notable silver Gospel codex—dearer to me than gold and jewels—in which the ancient Latin, or Itala, version is contained; to transcribe it; and to illustrate it in that distinguished preliminary letter of his. In that letter he set forth his opinion on the Old Translator in language of great elegance and with such an abundance of learning that, from the early Greek and Latin Fathers—among whom he himself spent almost his entire lifetime—nothing further can be drawn which he does not seem to have encompassed.

You received with the most attentive mind, and read with incredible pleasure, that opening part of the same letter which I included in the first volume of my *Vindications of the Canonical Scriptures*, and which won the great praise of you, whose judgment and wisdom are eminent. Recently, most eminent Prince, I received a letter from you in which you write that I should examine a certain passage of Saint John’s Gospel in the Gospel-book codex of Verona, of remarkable antiquity.

Such is the passage: “Who was born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of a man, but of God” (John 1:13). This reading, which first became known to you alone (for, so far as I know, it had not previously been published by others), afterwards appeared strange and foreign to the distinguished Scipione, Marquis Maffei, and to others; nor was it confirmed by the testimonies of the ancient holy Fathers. I had entered in my notes two parallel passages from St Irenaeus, and some others from Tertullian and Augustine [Col. 0853B], of still greater weight. But you, most learned Cardinal, so that no one might doubt that Irenaeus read the text in his copy as the Verona manuscript book has it, shared with me in letters full of substance and singular learning three further authorities from that most holy Bishop of Lyons which had escaped me. Therefore, as I cited the passage from the Verona Gospel-book, so, you say, it is read in Tertullian, John Chrysostom, Vigilius of Thapsus, and John Damascene; although some cannot examine this without concluding that the reading has been corrupted and must be corrected according to the present Greek, and especially the Latin, copies. In the works of the distinguished and most learned Sabatier—among whose other highest praises I certainly place first the fact that he brought to light all the Latin versions of the sacred books of the Old Testament that could be found in manuscripts and books of the Ancients—there are many Old Testament passages wholly peculiar to Irenaeus and Tertullian. Those, however, who have, so to speak, a fastidious palate will pass them by untasted in our fourfold Gospel-book. Father Ansaldus, the glory and ornament of the Dominican order, highly practiced in reading the holy Fathers and an outstanding judge in such matters, derived marvelous pleasure from you through the cited reading of the Verona codex. I hear that he is composing a remarkable work to show that St Irenaeus, Tertullian, and so forth, judged that it should be read thus, and that the Verona copy is not at fault because it differs greatly from the other surviving manuscript codices.

[Col. 0853D] I too explain that reading in a letter to the most illustrious and ever-to-be-honored Giovanni Francesco Muselli, Archpriest of the holy Church of Verona, who has deserved exceedingly well in letters, ecclesiastical discipline, and the conversion of the Hebrews to the Catholic faith. Whoever reads it will see that it cannot in any way be said that Irenaeus, Tertullian, and the other more ancient Fathers do not at all support the Verona Gospel-book—though, as I am told, this seems to be the opinion of the learned Barzani. In my judgment the distinguished Ansaldus will argue the case more successfully, for he will weigh everything most carefully. I for my part hold as certain that this reading is both extremely ancient and of good authority, although some persons, not understanding it, have dared to alter and corrupt the passage in Irenaeus and Tertullian; and where *natus est* (“was born”) was read, they imperiously ordered *nati sunt* (“were born”) to be read, in conformity with the Vulgate edition. The reading of the Fathers whom I have cited has strangely tormented the minds of those who wrote commentaries on the works of those same Fathers. Under your instruction and guidance, I maintain that the passage accords with certain copies of the earliest age. If anyone wishes to disagree, let him know that he will be excluded from the company of learned men. But now, most eminent Prince, I wish to send you certain passages from the Brixian codex which seem to me more noteworthy. Receive them as a pledge of my devotion. If you write anything in reply, it will be as welcome to me as though you loaded me with every kind of favor, O man of universal learning and chief glory and ornament of the Holy Roman Church.

Matthew 14:34. Brixian: “into the land of Gennesaret.” The Greek reads *Genesareth*. Some Greek codices have *Genesar* or *Genesera*.

John 8:59. Brixian: “He went out of the temple, passing through their midst, and went on.” The Greek has: “But Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple, passing through their midst. And thus he passed by” (*Ἰησοῦς δὲ ἐκρύβη, καὶ ἐξῆλθεν ἐκ τοῦ ἱεροῦ διελθὼν διὰ μέσου αὐτῶν. Καὶ παρῆγεν οὕτως*). These words, however, are not read in the Vulgate, St Chrysostom, St Cyril, St Augustine, or very many of the best codices.

Luke 8:54. Brixian: “But he, having put them all outside, and taking her hand,” etc. The Greek reads, “But he, having put all outside, and taking [her hand],” etc. (*Αὐτὸς δὲ ἐκβαλὼν ἔξω πάντας, καὶ κρατήσας*, etc.). These words are absent in St Ambrose and in certain Greek codices; and they are thought to have been removed because of the apparent contradiction that some perceived between verses 54 and 51, where it is said that Jesus admitted into the girl’s chamber only both her parents and three of his disciples.

Matthew 5:44. Brixian adds: “Bless those who curse you.” The Greek here adds: “Love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you” (*Ἀγαπᾶτε τοὺς ἐχθροὺς ὑμῶν, εὐλογεῖτε τοὺς καταρωμένους ὑμᾶς, καλῶς ποιεῖτε τοὺς μισοῦντας ὑμᾶς*). The words “bless those who curse you” appear to have been taken from Luke 6:28; they are absent from many codices. Most Greek codices do not have them, nor do Chrysostom, Augustine, Jerome, Salvian, Cyprian, Fulgentius, the Coptic version, Stephanus’s quarto Greek edition, or the Syriac version.

Matthew 5:47. Brixian: “only your friends.” Nearly all Greek codices likewise have “friends,” not “brothers.” So do all Stephanus’s codices, Bodleian manuscript 7 [Col. 0854D], and very many others. See Mill.

Matthew 6:1. Brixian: “Take heed that you do not perform your almsgiving before men”; and so do most, indeed nearly all, Greek codices. The Greek Fathers—Chrysostom, Theophylact, Euthymius, and most others—commonly follow this reading. Yet it does not conflict at all with the Vulgate, which is supported by certain Greek codices, the Syriac, Origen’s second homily on Exodus, and the ancient Latin Fathers.

Matthew 10:3. Brixian: “Lebbaeus, who is called Thaddaeus.” All Greek codices of Matthew read, “and Lebbaeus, who was surnamed Thaddaeus” (*Καὶ Λεββαῖος, ὁ ἐπικληθεὶς Θαδδαῖος*). From a comparison of the Evangelists, this Thaddaeus is the same person who was called Judas.

Matthew 10:8. In Brixian, “Raise the dead” is absent; and likewise in Stephanus manuscript 9, Colbert 3, Barberini 9, Bodleian 6, Selden 4, Ussher 2, and very many other Greek codices, on which consult Mill’s *Various Readings*. Yet the Vulgate, Syriac, Cambridge codex, and countless others contain it [Col. 0855A]. Some think it was added to Matthew’s text. Certainly, nowhere do we read that the Apostles restored the dead to life, at least before the resurrection of Jesus Christ. Chrysostom, Jerome, Euthymius, and Theophylact did not interpret these words; but it cannot at all be inferred from this that they were absent from the text, for commentators do not continuously explain every word of the divine writer.

Matthew 11:23. Brixian: “And you, Capernaum, which have been exalted to heaven, shall descend to hell.” The Greek has: “And you, Capernaum, which have been raised up to heaven, shall be brought down to hell.” But many ancient Greek codices agree with the Vulgate.

Matthew 15:8. Brixian: “This people draws near to me with its mouth, and honors me with its lips.” The Greek text: “This people draws near to me with its mouth, and honors me with its lips.”

Matthew 22:19. Brixian: “Show me a denarius.” Mark 12:15: “Bring me a denarius” (*φέρετέ μοι δηνάριον*). [Col. 0855B] Luke 20:24: “Show me a denarius” (*Ἐπιδείξατέ μοι δηνάριον*).

Matthew 27:8. Brixian: “That field was called the field of blood,” omitting *Haceldama*. *Hacel-dama* is a Syriac word and is not found in Greek codices. Perhaps it crept into Matthew from Acts. Yet ancient Latin books contain it, such as the celebrated Greek-Latin Cambridge codex and the old Vulgate of Matthew published by Martianay.

John 7:39. Brixian: “the Holy Spirit was not yet.” In present Greek codices one reads: “for the Holy Spirit was not yet” (*οὔπω γὰρ ἦν Πνεῦμα ἅγιον*). The reading of the Latin Vulgate is clearer: “for the Spirit had not yet been given.” This reading is ancient, as is evident from these words of St Augustine: “How is it understood that the Spirit had not yet been given, except because that definite giving or sending of the Holy Spirit was to occur after Christ’s glorification, of a kind that had never occurred before? For it was not that there had previously been none, if there had not been one of that kind.”

John 17:12. Brixian: “While I was with them in this [Col. 0855C] world.” Greek codices have: “I kept them in your name; those whom you gave me I guarded, and none of them,” etc. (*Ἐγὼ ἐτήρουν αὐτοὺς ἐν τῷ ὀνόματί σου, οὓς δέδωκάς μοι ἐφύλαξα, καὶ οὐδεὶς ἐξ αὐτῶν*, etc.). Thus read all Stephanus’s codices, many others cited here by Mill, the Coptic, Persian, Arabic, Syriac, Ethiopic, Cyril, and Theophylact (as is clear from their printed commentaries); and very many versions contain “while I was with them in the world.”

Luke 2:40. Brixian: “And he was strengthened in spirit.” The Greek likewise adds “in spirit” (*Πνεύματι*); this word is absent in certain Greek codices. The Persian and Ethiopic versions read “in the Holy Spirit.”

Luke 22:20. Brixian: “This cup, which is the New Testament in my blood, which shall be poured out for you.” The Greek reads: “This cup, the new covenant in my blood, which is poured out for you” (*Τοῦτο τὸ ποτήριον, ἡ καινὴ διαθήκη ἐν τῷ αἵματί μου, τὸ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν ἐκχυνόμενον*), which literally means: “This cup, which is the New Testament in my blood, is poured out for you.”

Luke 24:1. After “spices,” Brixian adds “and others with them” [Col. 0855D]. The Greek adds at the end of this verse that certain others joined them: “and some others with them” (*Καὶ τινες σὺν αὐταῖς*). The Armenian, however, has: “And the other women with them.” These words seem to have been taken from verse 10, where Mary Magdalene, Joanna, and Mary the mother of James, together with the others, are said to have come to the Apostles to report these things.

Mark 3:29. Brixian: “shall be guilty of eternal judgment.” The Greek also has: “is guilty of eternal judgment” (*Ἔνοχός ἐστιν αἰωνίου κρίσεως*). Some codices have *ἁμαρτίας*, “sin,” or *ἁμαρτήματος*, “offence.” Certain handwritten codices agree with the Vulgate.

Matthew 6:15. After “men,” Brixian adds “their sins”; and so does the Greek text.

Matthew 8:31. Brixian: “Command us to go.” The Greek text: “Permit us to depart.”

Matthew 12:35. Brixian: “from the good treasure of the heart,” in accordance with the Greek text. St Augustine, in the *Speculum on the Gospel according to Matthew* [Col. 0856A], III.1, p. 759: “from the good treasure of his heart.”

Matthew 24:18. Brixian: “to take his garments”; and the Greek likewise uses the generic term, “garments” or “garment.”

Matthew 26:3. Brixian: “the chief priests and the scribes.” The Greek and Syriac likewise add “and the scribes,” and this agrees with Luke 22:2 and Mark 14:7. Yet few handwritten codices of Matthew contain these words, according to Mill in the *Various Readings*.

John 8:25. Brixian, Gat., and Mm.: “the beginning, that,” etc.; Verona: “in the first place, because,” etc. The Greek text, and certain manuscripts of St Augustine’s *Confessions*, book II: “because,” etc.

John 7:26. Brixian: “Have the rulers truly recognized that this is truly the Christ?” And so the published Greek codices read: “Have the rulers perhaps truly recognized that this is truly the Christ?” (*Μὴ ποτε ἀληθῶς ἔγνωσαν οἱ ἄρχοντες, ὅτι οὗτός ἐστιν ἀληθῶς ὁ Χριστός*). But the second *ἀληθῶς* (“truly”) is absent in very many codices.

John 10:8. Brixian, Vercellian, and Veronese: “but not,” etc.; and certain Latin manuscript codices in the Divine Library of St Jerome have it more closely in accordance with the Greek [Col. 0856B].

John 11:2. Brixian and Vercellian: “who had anointed.” Greek: “who anointed the Lord with ointment” (*ἡ ἀλείψασα*); “who wiped [him]” (*ἐκμάξασα*).

John 11:50. Brixian and Gat.: “it is expedient for us”; and so most copies of the Greek text, certain manuscript books of the Divine Library of St Jerome, and St Augustine in his fiftieth tractate on John 11, III.2, p. 629.

John 14:9. Brixian and Vercellian: “he who has seen me has seen the Father,” in conformity with the Greek text, “he who has seen me has seen the Father” (*ὁ ἑωρακὼς ἐμέ, ἑώρακε τὸν Πατέρα*), and with St Augustine in *On Seeing God*, addressed to Paulinus, or Epistle 167, II, p. 478; likewise in *On the Spirit and the Letter*, X.1, p. 120. Verona: “he who saw me saw the Father”; and so the Claromontanus manuscript of St Irenaeus in book III *Against Heresies*, certain manuscript books of the Divine Library of St Jerome, and St Augustine in his sermon to catechumens, VI, p. 559. St Ambrose likewise, in his treatise *On the Trinity* [Col. 0856C], p. 324, has “saw.”

John 14:17. Brixian and Verona: “you know”; Vercellian: “you recognize.” Thus likewise the Greek text and certain manuscript books of the Divine Library of St Jerome. Corbie has “you know.”

John 14:17. Brixian, Vercellian, Verona, and Corbie: “remains . . . is”; and so Lucifer of Cagliari.

John 14:26. Brixian: “I said to you.” Greek: “which I said to you” (*ἃ εἶπον ὑμῖν*).

John 16:2. Brixian: “he will think that he has offered sacrifice to God.” Greek: “he may think that he is offering worship to God” (*δόξῃ λατρείαν προσφέρειν τῷ Θεῷ*).

John 16:13. Brixian: “will guide you into all truth”; Verona: “will lead you in all truth.” Greek text: “He will guide you into all truth” (*Ὁδηγήσει ὑμᾶς εἰς πᾶσαν ἀλήθειαν*). Some Greek codices: “He will guide [you] in all truth” (*Ὁδηγήσει ἐν τῇ ἀληθείᾳ πάσῃ*). Among Latin witnesses, some in Augustine read, “will lead you in all truth”; others, “will lead you into all truth”; and so Vercellian and St Ambrose in *On the Holy Spirit* [Col. 0856D], II.11, p. 656, and III.4, p. 685.

John 21:25. Brixian adds “Amen”; and so it is read at the end of this chapter in printed Greek codices, but not in the Vulgate or in the Coptic, Syriac, Persian, Arabic, and Armenian versions, nor in the very ancient Greek codices Alexandrinus, Cantabrigiensis, and Colbert 8.

Luke 1:66. Brixian, Vercellian, Veronese, Corbie, and Gat.: “what?” So likewise the Greek text, the ancient Corbie Bible, a Gospel-book of the Church of Verona, written about the ninth century on the feast of St John the Evangelist, certain manuscript books of the Divine Library of St Jerome, and St Augustine in book II *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, III.2, p. 36.

Luke 2:2. Brixian: “governor,” omitting the preposition “under”; so, in accordance with the Greek text, do two manuscript books of the Divine Library of St Jerome and St Augustine in book II [Col. 0857A] *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, III.2, p. 37.

Luke 6:26. Brixian, Vercellian, and Veronese have “all” before the word “men”; and so do the Greek text, the very ancient Corbie Bible codex, certain manuscripts of Queen Christina of Sweden in the Divine Library of St Jerome, and St Augustine in the *Speculum on the Gospel according to Luke*, III.1, p. 767.

Luke 6:35. Brixian, Vercellian, Veronese, and Corbie: “despairing of nothing.” Brugensis and Grotius render it: “lend, expecting no equivalent favor.” The Syriac, Arabic, Persian, Ludovicus de Dieu, and Tremellius: “lend, not frustrating hope.” Hammond and Beza: “lend, and do not let fear of want deter you from doing good.” These various readings arise from the ambiguous Greek verb *apelpizein*: to despair, to lose confidence, and to expect something from another. St Ambrose also appears to favor the Veronese and Vercellian codices.

Luke 14:5. Brixian: “Whose among you son, or ox, falls into a pit?” The Greek in very many of the best codices has: “Whose among you son, or ox, will fall into a pit?” (*Τίνος ὑμῶν υἱὸς, ἢ βοῦς εἰς φρέαρ ἐμπεσεῖται*) [Col. 0857B]; and so many manuscript codices in Mill, Theophylact, Titus of Bostra, and others. Cambridge Greek: “sheep, or ox” (*Πρόβατον, ἢ βοῦς*). Latin: “sheep, or ox.”

Luke 16:23. Brixian and Verona: “And in hell, lifting up his eyes.” The Greek likewise has: “And in Hades, lifting up his eyes” (*Καὶ ἐν τῷ ᾅδῃ ἐπάρας τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς αὐτοῦ*), etc.; and so the Preface of St Gaudentius. Vienna codex: “. . . lifting up his eyes.”

Luke 16:24. Brixian, Vercellian, and Verona: “and cool”; and so St Ambrose in *On Naboth of Jezreel*, ch. 12, p. 580.

Luke 23:15. Brixian: “Behold, nothing deserving death has been done by him”; and so the Greek text: “Behold, nothing deserving death has been done by him” (*Ἰδοὺ οὐδὲν ἄξιον θανάτου ἐστὶ πεπραγμένον αὐτῷ*). For some translate as though it read *ἀπ᾽ αὐτοῦ*, “by him,” as Erasmus, Illyricus, and Beza do: that is, “Behold, nothing deserving death has been done by him.” But the Vulgate’s explanation is better.

Mark 1:44. Brixian, Vercellian, and Corbie: “Show yourself to the priest” (Corbie: “to the priests”); Verona [Col. 0857C]: “Present yourself to the priest”; Gat.: “to the chief priests.” Greek: “Show yourself to the priest” (*Σεαυτὸν δεῖξον τῷ ἱερεῖ*). Some have *ἀρχιερεῖ*, “to the high priest,” such as Leicester manuscript, the Vélez codex, and Paris 6; see Mill here. The Syriac and Persian likewise have “show yourself to the priests,” in the plural. But certain Greek codices agree with the Vulgate and Gat. and have “to the chief priest.”

Matthew 1:20. Brixian, Verona, and St-Germain: “for what shall be born from her”; and so St Ambrose in *On the Institution of Virgins*, ch. 8, p. 263, and in *On the Holy Spirit*, II.5, p. 641, and II.9, p. 652.

Matthew 17:26. Brixian: “a denarius.” St Zeno of Verona, in book II *On Jacob’s Dream*, tract 13, p. 178: “two denarii.”

John 7:8. Brixian: “But I do not yet go up”; and Greek codices now have *οὔπω*, “not yet.” If that reading is ancient, every difficulty is removed. Grotius infers that it is not ancient because Porphyry would otherwise never have accused Christ of lying: the word *οὔπω*, “not yet,” would have solved the difficulty. But even if Greek codices had the simple *οὐκ*, “not,” the charge of lying is empty and impious.

John 21:22. Brixian here and in verse 23 has “if” in place of “thus”; likewise, in accordance with the Greek text, the manuscript of Queen Christina of Sweden, no. 14, said formerly also to have belonged to St Wenceslaus, a manuscript indeed of sound antiquity and authority.

John 5:2. Brixian: *Betesda*, and so the Greek codex: *Βηθεσδά*, “Bethesda”; Verona: *Betzeta*; Vulgate: *Bethsaida*. Learned men agree that this writing has been corrupted by copyists and others ignorant of Hebrew because of the similarity of these names, although it is read in Tertullian and in Theophylact of the Roman edition. For it is established that there was a district in the Holy City called by Josephus *Βηζεθά*, Bezetha, where the cattle market, or sheep market, stood. From this district, I think, the name was derived from the Hebrew *beth hazon*, that is, “house,” or “place,” of a sheep. In Greek, however, a sheep is called *πρόβατον*, whence the word *προβατική* was formed. Thus the Evangelist’s *probatica* is the sheep market, near which the pool was called Probatica; or that pool, whose water an angel occasionally stirred, was in the *probatica*, namely in the sheep market or beside it. In this district stood the Sheep Gate, which in the Hebrew text of 2 Esdras, chapter 3, verse 1, is called *shaʿar-hazon*, that is, “gate of the flock,” or “of the sheep”; and in the Greek version, “the sheep gate” (*πύλη προβατική*), which Eliashib the high priest is said to have built. Therefore some interpreters hold that the pool in question was called Probatica because it stood at the Probatica Gate—that is, the Gate of the Flock—or, if the Greek reading is approved, that the pool which was in the *probatica* stood beside the Gate of the Flock. But that the word *προβατική* denotes not so much a gate as a particular district is suggested by the Evangelist’s statement that the Probatica was called Bethsaida, in Greek [Col. 0858B] *Βηθεσδά*. For *Βηθεσδά* does not differ much in sound from *Βηζεθά*, the name, as we have said, by which Josephus calls the district where, by universal agreement, that pool was situated.
