Nevertheless, others think the name *Βηθεσδά* derived from another origin, namely from *Beth-cheseda* or *Betheseda*, meaning “house of mercy,” because of the benefits conferred on the sick in this pool. Others derive it from *Beth-esda*, that is, “house of effusion”—not from the shedding of victims’ blood, for sacrifices were slaughtered not there but at the altar, but from an aqueduct, whose founder was perhaps Hezekiah, who is said to have brought water into the City in 4 Kings 20:20.

Matthew 19:17. Brixian: “Why do you call me good?” And so certain more recent writers, namely Maldonatus, Jansen, Simon, and Martianay. But neither our Latin Vulgate version nor the Greek text of many ancient handwritten books agreeing with the Latin allows this explanation.

[Col. 0858C] Matthew 15:32. Brixian: “it is now three days that,” etc. St Ambrose: “it is a three-day period that.”

Matthew 16:6. Brixian: “. . . beware yourselves”; Vercellian, Verona, and St-Germain: “take heed to yourselves”; and so St Hilary and St Gaudentius, according to the St-Germain-des-Prés copy.

Matthew 16:12. Brixian: “he did not say,” etc. St Ambrose, *On Repentance*, I.15, p. 411: “He did not say that they should take heed of bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees.”

Matthew 17:21. Brixian, Vercellian, and Verona: “it is going to happen” (*futurum*; Brixian *futuru*) “that the Son of Man be handed over.” St-Germain has: “it is going to happen that . . . be handed over”; and so St Hilary in his commentary on Matthew 17.

Matthew 17:23. Brixian, Vercellian, Verona, and St-Germain: “they demanded”; and so St Hilary in his commentary on Matthew 17. Corbie: “they demand.”

Matthew 17:26. Brixian: “you will find in it”; Vercellian, Verona, and St-Germain: “you will find there”; and so St Ambrose in Epistle 7, first class, p. 781.

[Col. 0858D] John 8:39. Brixian, Vercellian, and Verona: “if you were Abraham’s children . . . you would do”; and so Ambrosiaster in his Epistle to Titus, ch. 1, p. 314; Rufinus, St Jerome, and St Augustine.

John 9:4. Brixian and Verona: “will come”; and so St Ambrose in his exposition of Psalm 118, p. 1054.

John 9:5. Brixian: “as long as I am in this world”; Vercellian and Verona: “when I am in this world”; and so St Ambrose in *On Faith*, III.7, p. 506. Corbie: “when I am in this world”; and so the same St Ambrose in Epistle 80, second class, p. 1096.

John 11:4. Brixian: “this sickness through him.” St Ambrose, *On Faith*, IV.10, p. 545: “this sickness,” etc., “but for the glory of God, that his Son may be glorified through it.”

John 13:5. Brixian: “poured”; Vercellian and Verona: “sent”; and so certain manuscript books of the Divine Library of St Jerome.

[Col. 0859A] John 13:32. Brixian and Verona: “and God has glorified him”; and so St Ambrose.

John 14:26. Brixian: “and will remind you of all things.” St Gaudentius: “and will admonish you of all things.”

John 18:28. Brixian: “to Caiaphas”; Vercellian, Corbie, Gat., and Mm.: “to Caiapham”; and so St Augustine in book III *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, III.2, p. 114, and in tractate 114 on John 18, III.2, p. 789. Verona: “from Caiaphan.”

Luke 2:22. Brixian: “they brought him.” St Irenaeus: “they placed him.”

Matthew 6:13. After the words “but deliver us from evil,” Brixian has: “For yours is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory for ever. Amen.” After the same words, the Greek adds: “For yours is the kingdom, the power, and the glory for ever. Amen.” This addition is also read in the *Apostolic Constitutions*, the *Incomplete Work on Matthew*, St Chrysostom, ancient Greek liturgies, and the Syriac and Gothic versions [Col. 0859B]. But it is highly probable that these words were added and crept from liturgical books into Matthew’s text; for Luke 11:4 does not contain them, nor does any ancient Latin Gospel codex apart from Brixian, nor the ancient Greek codices or the Coptic and Arabic versions.

John 17:13. In Brixian and Vercellian, “in this world” is added. St Jerome, in the *Dialogue against the Pelagians*, II, p. 749, has “in the world.”

Matthew 6:32. In Brixian, after “your Father,” “heavenly” is added; and so in the Greek version.

Matthew 6:31. Brixian: “to be anxious for tomorrow.” St Augustine, *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, II, III.2, p. 222: “to be anxious about tomorrow.”

Matthew 8:2. In Brixian, Vercellian, Verona, and St-Germain, after “a leper,” “a certain” is added; and so in St Hilary, tractate on Psalm 138, I, p. 566.

Matthew 13:38. In Brixian, Vercellian, Verona, and St-Germain, before “world,” “this” is added; and so in many editions of St Augustine’s *City of God*, book XX.

Matthew 14:22. Brixian: “he commanded the disciples.” Two manuscripts of Queen Christina of Sweden in the Divine Library of St Jerome have *iussit discipulis* (“he commanded the disciples,” with the dative), omitting “Jesus,” which is likewise omitted in Brixian and Corbie.

Matthew 18:7. Before “world,” “this” is added in Brixian, Vercellian, Verona, and Corbie; and so in St Cyprian, p. 153.

Matthew 26:39. Brixian: “My Father,” etc., “remove this cup from me.” St Hilary, in his commentary on Matthew: “My Father,” etc. St Ambrose, *On Faith*, II.5, p. 477: “My Father,” etc., “remove this cup from me.” Likewise, in *On the Sacrament of the Incarnation of the Lord*, ch. 7, p. 718, he has “My Father.”

John 14:17. Brixian, Vercellian, Verona, and Gat.: “this world”; and so St Ambrose in *On the Holy Spirit*, I.4, p. 611, and in his exposition of the Gospel according to Luke.

John 14:31. Brixian, Vercellian, Verona, and [Col. 0859D] Corbie: “this world”; and so St Ambrose in *On Faith*, V.7, p. 567.

John 17:16. Brixian and Verona have, in the first and second occurrence, “of this world”; and so St Ambrose in *Hexaemeron*, I, p. 14.

Luke 22:43–44. In Brixian these whole verses 43 and 44 are absent. Some, fearing that enemies of the Christian name might misuse this narrative to attribute indignities unworthy of Jesus Christ, expunged the whole text—that is, the present verses 43 and 44—from their copies. So likewise today these verses are absent from many ancient Greek codices: Alexandrinus; Bodleian 4 and 5; Leicester; Coptic; Paris 6; and from certain Syriac copies, according to Photius, Epistle 134. Formerly too they were absent from far more Latin texts: Jerome, book II *Against the Pelagians*; Hilary, book X *On the Trinity*; and Epiphanius, *Anchoratus*, chapters 31, 32, and 33. “We must certainly not be unaware,” says St Hilary, *On the Trinity* [Col. 0860A], X.41, “that in very many Greek and Latin codices nothing is found written either concerning the angel who appeared or concerning the sweat of blood.” He adds that no uncertainty about truth is thereby created, nor is error aided, because it is uncertain which reading among so many varieties of copies ought to be regarded as true: “Since we are uncertain whether this is absent or superfluous in various books—for this will remain uncertain to us because of the variety of books,” etc.

The aforementioned Epiphanius acknowledges in *Anchoratus*, chapter 31, that this passage from the Gospel had been erased from very many Greek codices through the pious fraud of certain Catholics, who feared that some harmful inference might perhaps be drawn from it, not understanding what injury to truth would result. He adds that St Irenaeus used this passage in book III, chapter 32, of his work *Against Heresies*, to prove the truth of the Incarnation.

The same St Epiphanius likewise uses the same passage in the cited place, chapter 37, p. 42, to establish that same doctrine. Grotius, on Luke 19:41, conjectures that this correction of copies was introduced only by the authority of bishops. Yet we certainly believe that this passage suffered what countless others did: it was expunged through the boldness of copyists or the excessive piety of certain semi-philosophers, who thought that the passage brought reproach upon Jesus Christ; or it was noted in the margin of a codex as requiring cautious reading, and thus furnished occasion for its suppression in certain copies.

Nevertheless this did not prevent most Greek and Latin manuscripts, and printed editions of our age, from remaining intact. Vercellian, Vienna, Verona, and Mm. contain these verses 43 and 44. We have seen an *Apology* drawn from St Epiphanius which adduces the passage from St Irenaeus in its support. St Hippolytus likewise reports the same view as Irenaeus in *Against Noetus*, ch. 18, Fabricius’s edition; likewise the Sermon on the Resurrection in Anastasius Sinaita’s *Hodegos*, p. 356; St Justin in the *Dialogue with Trypho*; St Chrysostom, *Homilies on Matthew*, homily 84; Ammonius in his *Harmony*; St Augustine [Col. 0860C] in *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*; and other Fathers after them. Writing to Theodore the Friend, Photius in Epistle 138 warns him never to allow himself, moved by the authority of certain Syrians who expunge this passage from Luke as alien, to reject it. Fear had persuaded those Syrians that it was unworthy of Jesus Christ to have been overwhelmed by pain so that a bloody sweat was forced out. By “Syrians” Armenians may readily be meant here, whom Nicon accuses, in *On the Most Wicked Religion of the Armenians*, of having expunged this passage and the history of the adulterous woman from the Gospel.

Matthew 6:22. In Brixian, after “eye,” “your” is absent; and so in St Augustine’s *Speculum on the Gospel according to Matthew*, III.1, p. 756.

Matthew 7:26. “This” is absent in Brixian and in St Cyprian.

Matthew 13:24. “Made” is absent in Brixian, Vercellian, and Verona, as in St Ambrose, *Hexaemeron*, III.10 [Col. 0860D], p. 49.

Matthew 16:23. In Brixian, Vercellian, Verona, and Corbie, “those things” is absent in the first and second occurrence; and so in St Hilary’s commentary on this passage of Matthew and in *On the Trinity*, VI.38, according to the authority of very many manuscript codices; likewise in St Ambrose, *On Faith*, II.7, p. 480.

Matthew 19:4. “Man” is absent in Brixian, Vercellian, Verona, Corbie, and St-Germain; and so in the Corbie Bible of the Vulgate version; in St Augustine, book X *On Genesis*, III.1, p. 256; in the *Speculum on the Gospel according to Matthew*, III.1, p. 761; in *City of God*, XIV.22; and in book XIX *Against Faustus*, VIII, p. 330.

Matthew 26:43. Brixian, Vercellian, and Verona: “let him now deliver him, if he wants him”; Corbie: “let him now deliver him, if he wants.” St Ambrose, *Exposition of Psalm 43*, p. 915: “now him.”

[Col. 0861A] John 18:11. “Your” is omitted in Brixian, Vercellian, and Verona; and so in certain Greek codices and some manuscripts in the Divine Library of St Jerome.

John 18:26. “To him” is absent in Brixian, Vercellian, and Verona; and so in the Greek text and certain manuscripts of the Divine Library of St Jerome.

Luke 2:46. After the word “questioning,” “them” is absent in Brixian and Vercellian; and so in St Augustine, sermon 22 on Psalm 118, IV.2, p. 1334.

Luke 8:32. “To you” is absent in Brixian, Vercellian, and Verona; and so in St Ambrose, *On Repentance*, II.6, p. 426, and in the royal manuscript of St Augustine’s *Speculum on the Gospel according to Luke*.

Luke 8:52. “Girl” is absent in Brixian, Vercellian, Verona, Gat., and Mm.; and so in certain manuscripts of the Divine Library of St Jerome.

Matthew 3:17. Brixian, Vercellian, and Verona: “in whom I have been well pleased”; and so St Hilary, *On the Trinity*, II, pp. 32 and 272; St Gaudentius [Col. 0861B] in his Reply to Paul the Deacon; and St Gregory the Great, *Moralia*, XXVIII.38, p. 895. St-Germain codex: “in whom I was well pleased.”

Matthew 6:19. Brixian: “upon earth”; and so St Cyprian in *On Works and Almsgiving*, p. 305.

Matthew 7:24. Brixian: “I shall liken him”; and so St Cyprian in book III of the *Testimonies to Quirinus*, ch. 96, p. 387.

Matthew 11:2. Brixian, Vercellian, Verona, and St-Germain: “in prison”; and so St Hilary in his commentary on Matthew, I, p. 721. Corbie: “into prison.”

Matthew 11:28. Brixian: “I shall make you rest.” St Jerome, Epistle 148 to Celantia, I, p. 1094: “I shall make you rest.”

Matthew 13:11. Brixian, Vercellian, and St-Germain: “mystery”; and so St Irenaeus.

Matthew 16:21. Brixian, Vercellian, and Verona: “it is necessary”; and so St Irenaeus.

Matthew 18:21. Brixian: “if he sins.” Lucifer of Cagliari likewise, in book II *For St Athanasius*, has “if he sins,” etc.

Matthew 19:21. Brixian and Corbie: “sell everything that you possess.” St Ambrose, *On the Duties of Ministers*, ch. 11, p. 11: “sell all your goods.” Philastrius, *Heresies*, 98: “sell, and everything that you have.”

Matthew 21:9. Brixian, Verona, and Corbie have “Hosanna” in both the first and second occurrences; and so St Irenaeus in book IV *Against Heresies*, I, p. 240.

Matthew 21:9. Brixian and St-Germain: “in the highest”; and so St Irenaeus.

Matthew 21:33. Brixian: “a tower”; Vercellian and Verona: “a tower . . . to tenants”; and so Lucifer of Cagliari in book II *For St Athanasius*. Corbie likewise: “. . . to tenants.”

Matthew 22:7. Brixian: “and, sending his army.” St Irenaeus has: “and, sending his armies,” etc.

Matthew 22:37. Brixian: “with all your soul”; and so St Zeno of Verona in book I, tract 2, *On Faith, Hope, and Charity*, p. 21.

Matthew 24:15. Brixian, Vercellian, and Verona [Col. 0861D]: “which was spoken”; and so St Irenaeus in book V *Against Heresies*, I, p. 322.

Matthew 26:9. Brixian: “to be sold for a high price”; Vercellian and Verona: “to be sold for a price”; and so St Ambrose in book VI of his exposition of the Gospel according to Luke. Corbie: “to be sold for a great price.”

Matthew 26:14. Brixian: “called Judas Scariothes”; Vercellian: “called . . . Judas Scarioth.” Supply the lacuna from the manuscripts of Queen Christina of Sweden reported in the Divine Library of St Jerome, which read: “called Judas Scarioth.” Verona: “Judas is called Scarioth”; Corbie: “Scariot.”

Matthew 26:36. The Brixian has, “until I go there to pray”; the Vercellian, “until I go there to pray”; and so also St Hilary in his Commentary on Matthew. The Veronese has, “until I go there to pray.”

Matthew 27:9. The Brixian has, “the sons of Israel.” So also St Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, book II, vol. III, part II, p. 114.

[Col. 0862A] Matthew 27:34. The Brixian has, “they gave him vinegar mixed with gall to drink.” The version of St Matthew also presents, in certain Greek copies, that Christ was offered vinegar mixed with gall. So too the Syriac, Origen, and Jerome. But most of the best manuscript codices, together with the Vulgate, read “wine,” as it also occurs in St Mark, and among many ancient witnesses, both Greek and Latin . . . . .

Matthew 27:55. The Brixian, Vercellian, and Veronese have, “seeing from afar”; the word *seeing* belongs to Mark.

Matthew 28:7. The Brixian, Vercellian, Veronese, and Corbie manuscripts have, “he goes before”; so also St Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, vol. III, part II, p. 133.

John 1:4. The Brixian, Vercellian, Veronese, Corbie, Gat., and Mm. have, “life is”; so also St Hilary and St Ambrose, *On Faith*, book III, chapter 6, p. 504.

John 3:4. The Brixian and Mm. have, “and be born”; so also certain manuscript books recorded in the *Divine Library* of St Jerome.

John 3:5. The Brixian has, “shall have been born”; so also St Cyprian, Epistle 72 to Pope Stephen, concerning the Council, [Col. 0862B] p. 180.

John 7:28. The Brixian has, “and you know me, and know whence I am.” St Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book VI, vol. II, p. 153, has: “Do you neither know me nor know whence I am?”

John 8:14. The Brixian, in the second place, has, “whence I come”; so also St Ambrose, p. 174.

John 9:25. The Brixian, Vercellian, and Corbie manuscripts have, “I was blind, and,” etc.; so also St Ambrose, Epistle class II, vol. II, p. 1097.

John 10:16. The Brixian, Veronese, and Corbie manuscripts have, “one flock”; so also St Cyprian, *On the Unity of the Catholic Church*, p. 255, and Epistle 76 to Magnus, concerning the baptism of Novatians, p. 209.

John 12:31. The Brixian and Vercellian have, “now is the judgment of this world”; so also St Gaudentius, Sermon 12, p. 146.

John 13:29. The Brixian has, “because,” etc. Certain manuscripts of the *Divine Library* of St Jerome, and almost all the codices of St Augustine, have, “because he says to him.”

[Col. 0862C] John 14:17. The Brixian has, “nor knows”; the Vercellian, “nor recognizes”; so also St Ambrose, *On the Holy Spirit*, book I, chapter 4, p. 611, and in his *Exposition of the Gospel according to Luke*. The Veronese has, “nor is acquainted with.”

Luke 1:2. The Brixian has, “And they became ministers of the word.” Budé, Hamm., Cappell., Vall., Vatab., Pisc., Gemar., and, among the ancients, Origen in Homily I on Luke, Ambrose, Euthymius here, Jerome in the Preface to Matthew, and the Greek text, have: “Having become ministers of the word” (*Hypēretai genomenoi tou logou*), “they became ministers of the word.”

Luke 2:49. The Brixian, Vercellian, Veronese, and Gat. have, “do you not know,” etc. Tertullian, p. 516, has, “do you not know.”

Luke 3:5. The Brixian has, “into a straight way”; so also the Clermont manuscript of St Irenaeus.

Luke 7:42. The Brixian has, “Which therefore of them,” etc. St Cyprian has, “Which of those,” etc.

Luke 24:24. The Brixian, Vercellian, Veronese, Corbie, and Gat. manuscripts have, “they did not see”; so also certain manuscripts in the *Divine Library* of St Jerome and St Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, book III, vol. III, part II, p. 140.

[Col. 0862D] Mark 5:43. The Brixian and Veronese have, “and he ordered food to be given to her.” St Irenaeus has, “and he ordered food to be given to her”; the Clermont codex of the same St Irenaeus has, “to be given,” etc.

Mark 11:25. The Brixian has, “for prayer”; so also St Cyprian, *Testimonies to Quirinus*, book III, chapter 22, p. 378.

Matthew 14:3. The Brixian and Veronese read, “of his brother Philip.” The Greek likewise adds “Philip” after the words “his brother,” from Mark 6:17.

John 3:5. “Holy” is absent in the Brixian and Veronese; so also today in all Greek and in most Latin copies; in Tertullian’s *On Baptism* and *On the Soul*; in St Cyprian, Epistle 73 to Jubaianus, on baptizing heretics, p. 187; and in St Ambrose, *On the Holy Spirit*, book III, chapter 10, p. 677.

Luke 1:3. The Brixian and Veronese have, “all.” The Greek codex likewise has *pasin*, that is, “all,” which the Syriac translator refers to persons, interpreting Luke [Col. 0863A] as though he said that he had followed eyewitnesses and ministers. Thus he does not understand the word *parēkolouthēkoti*, “having followed,” metaphorically, as attaining in the mind those things which were done and said, but properly, as following someone.

Luke 1:35. “From you” is absent in the Brixian and Veronese, as also in many Latin copies, in St Ambrose’s *Exposition of the Gospel according to Luke*, p. 1300, in several biblical books of Queen Christina of Sweden, and in most French manuscripts of St Augustine’s *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, book II. Yet the words are read by Irenaeus, Tertullian, Novatian, *On the Trinity*, chapter 19, and other ancient writers, and by the Syriac and Arabic versions reported by Mill in his edition of the Greek text.

Luke 6:26. The Brixian has, “to the prophets”; so also two manuscript books in the *Divine Library* of St Jerome.

Luke 9:48. The Brixian has, “whoever receives me receives him”; the Vercellian, “whoever receives me does not receive me, but him,” etc. The Veronese and Corbie manuscripts have, “does not receive me, but him,” etc. Hilary the Deacon, called Ambrosiaster, in his *Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans*, chapter II, p. 41, has, “he who receives me does not receive me, but him,” etc.

Matthew 22:35. In the Brixian and Corbie manuscripts these words are omitted: “that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet, saying: They divided my garments among themselves, and upon my clothing they cast lots.” Nor are they read in Origen, Euthymius, Theophylact, St Hilary, St Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, book II, vol. III, part II, p. 121, Titus of Bostra, the Syriac, Coptic, Arabic, and Ethiopic versions, the Complutensian edition, and very many handwritten Greek codices reported in Mill’s *Various Readings*. They are also absent from other codices preferring the Old Latin, Vulgate Latin, and Italic text. Some think that these words entered Matthew from John through the licence of copyists. I, however, follow the Vulgate reading.

John 10:22. The Brixian and Corbie manuscripts have, “Now the Dedication took place at Jerusalem.” That name, *ta enkaínia* (“the renewals” or “dedications”), is derived from *enkainízein*, “to make something anew,” by which word the Seventy Translators render the Hebrew verb “he initiated,” “he dedicated”; and among those translators *enkaínia*, *enkaínisis*, and *enkainismós* mean “renewals,” “renewal.” The Hebrew verb, like the noun, is used in the Old Testament of every dedication, whether first or renewed—for example, when a new house begins to be inhabited. Nevertheless, usage seems to have brought it about that *enkaínia*, *encaenia*, was understood as some renewal or restoration of the Temple. This is inferred from the Hebrew Calendar, in which only two celebrations of the Dedication of the Temple are mentioned, and no mention is made of Solomon’s dedication: the former in the month Kislev, on the twenty-fifth day, when the Maccabees restored the altar of burnt offerings; and therefore, as we read in 1 Maccabees 4:59, Judas, his brothers, and the whole assembly of Israel decreed that the days of the Dedication [Col. 0863D] (*enkainismoû*) of the altar should be observed in their season every year for eight days, from the twenty-fifth day of the month Kislev, with gladness and joy. The other *encaenia* found in the Jewish Calendar is the dedication, or restoration, of the Temple carried out under Zerubbabel in the month Adar, as may be seen in Ezra, chapter 6, verse 16.

John 11:56. The Brixian has, “What do you think? that he will not come to the feast?” Some read the Greek, *Ti dokei hymin? hoti ou mē elthē eis tēn heortēn*, with interrogation: “What do you think? Will he not come to the feast?”

Matthew 13:45. The Brixian and Veronese have, “trading”; so also St Cyprian, *Testimonies to Quirinus*, book III, p. 372, and in some manuscripts of *On Works and Almsgiving*; likewise St Ambrose, *On Abraham*, book II, chapter 9, p. 343.

Matthew 27:40. In the Brixian and Corbie manuscripts “Ah!” is omitted; so also in the Greek text and in St Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, book III, vol. III, part II, p. 127.

[Col. 0864A] Matthew 13:46. The Brixian has, “who, finding one precious pearl.” St Cyprian, *On Works and Almsgiving*, p. 305, has, “but when he found a precious pearl,” omitting the word “one,” which is likewise absent in the Vercellian, Veronese, and Saint-Germain manuscripts.

Matthew 20:15. The Brixian has, “Is it not lawful for me to do with what is mine what I will?” Certain ancient books have, “Or is it not lawful for me to do what I will with my property?” The Greek has, *Ē ouk exestin moi poiēsai ho thelō en tois emoís?*: “Or is it not lawful for me to do what I will with what is mine?” So too the Syriac and Old Vulgate. St Augustine, Sermon 87, has, “Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with what is mine?”

John 3:3. The Brixian and Gat. have, “shall have been born”; so also certain Latin manuscript codices recorded in the *Divine Library* of St Jerome, more closely conforming to the Greek text.

John 8:12. The Brixian and Vercellian have, “did not walk”; the Veronese, “will not walk.” St Ambrose, *On the Orthodox Faith against the Arians*, chapter 2, p. 350, has, “will not go.”

John 8:54. The Brixian, Gat., and Mm. have, “is ours”; [Col. 0864B] so too certain Greek copies and two Latin manuscript books reported in the *Divine Library* of St Jerome.

John 9:12. The Brixian and Veronese have, “but they said to him”; the Vercellian, “therefore they said to him”; so too certain manuscript codices in the *Divine Library* of St Jerome.

John 10:29. The Brixian, Vercellian, and Veronese have, “to snatch it,” etc. (The Veronese omits “it.”) St Ambrose, *On the Holy Spirit*, book III, chapter 16, p. 689, has, “to snatch them,” etc.

John 20:31. The Brixian and Veronese have, “Jesus Christ is the Son of God.” St Irenaeus likewise reads, “Jesus is the Son of God.”

John 11:50. The Brixian and Gat. have, “it is expedient for us”; so too the Greek, *hēmin*, “for us.”

John 12:7. The Brixian, Veronese, and Mm. have, “let [her] alone,” etc.; so also two manuscripts in the *Divine Library* of St Jerome and St Gaudentius, Sermon 13, p. 153 of the latest edition.

John 15:2. The Brixian, Veronese, and Corbie manuscripts have, “that it may bear much fruit.” St Hilary, *Commentary on Psalm 11*, vol. I, p. 87, has, “that it may bear more abundant fruit.” The Vercellian has, “that it may bring forth more abundant fruit.”

John 18:11. The Brixian has, “I shall not drink,” etc.; so also St Hilary, *Commentary on Psalm 138*, vol. I, p. 508, and *On the Trinity*, book X, no. 30. The Corbie manuscript has, “Shall I not drink?” etc.

John 20:31. The Brixian, Veronese, and Gat. have, “eternal life”; so also St Irenaeus.

Luke 1:51. The Brixian, Veronese, Corbie, and Gat. manuscripts have, “to remember”; so also the old translator, according to Mill’s *Prolegomena*, and certain manuscript books of the Bible reported in the *Divine Library* of St Jerome. St Irenaeus also, *Against Heresies*, book III, vol. I, p. 185, has “to recollect.”

Luke 2:38. The Brixian and Veronese have, “Jerusalem”; so too the very ancient Corbie biblical codex and many other Latin books. Likewise St Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book III, vol. I, p. 187, and St Augustine [Col. 0864D], *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, book II, vol. III, part II, p. 38. The Corbie manuscript has “Jerusalem”; Gat. has “in Jerusalem,” as does the Greek text.

Luke 7:37. The Brixian has, “he reclined”; the Vercellian, “to recline”; the Veronese, “he reclined”; Gat. and Mm., “he reclined at table”; so also St Ambrose and very many manuscript books in the *Divine Library* of St Jerome.

Luke 9:29. The Brixian has, “shall be ashamed of me . . . he shall put her to shame”; the Vercellian, “shall be ashamed . . . of me . . . . . . . . . . shall put . . . . . . .” St Ambrose, Epistle class II, vol. II, p. 1077, has, “shall be ashamed of me . . . I too shall be ashamed of him,” etc.

Luke 9:61. The Brixian has, “but first permit me to take leave of those who,” etc.; so also St Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, book II, vol. III, part II, p. 55. The Corbie Bible has, “of those who,” etc., in conformity with St Augustine, *Mirror: On the Gospel according to Luke*, vol. III, part I, p. 769.

[Col. 0865]

## SECOND LETTER OF BLANCHINI. DESCRIPTION OF A GREEK-LATIN MANUSCRIPT CODEX OF THE GOSPELS AND ACTS PRESERVED IN THE CAMBRIDGE LIBRARY

[Col. 0865A] Joseph Blanchini of Verona sends greetings and every good wish to the distinguished and most learned Philip, Abbot Garbelli, Brescian patrician.

You are not unaware, most learned Garbelli, how great a benefit students of Holy Scripture derived from that notable edition of the Old Latin and Italic Vulgate Version of the Gospel according to Matthew, drawn from the most ancient monuments through the study and labour of Dom Jean Martianay, Benedictine priest of the Congregation of Saint Maur, which he first gave to the learned world at Paris in 1695. This may plainly be known from the fact that the book was everywhere so favourably received that today it cannot be found for sale among our Italian booksellers; although no one ardently devoted to the study of Holy Scripture can possibly do without reading it. Therefore, in the Prolegomena to this Fourfold Gospel Book, since I had occasion to preface many remarks concerning the ancient Italic Latin version, lest I should appear to some to be undertaking a matter already handled by the most learned Martianay with much greater care and dignity than I could presume to promise of myself, I thought that this edition would be better served, and that I should act more prudently, if I invited you and the other lovers of the Italic version to read Martianay’s Prolegomena, [Note: [Col. 0865D] See the Prolegomena, col. 0000 and following.] in which he treated that subject with singular learning.

Now, therefore, in order to demonstrate that the Italic version—which adhered more closely to the Greek words while preserving clarity of meaning—is contained in our Fourfold Gospel Book, let us turn to the original Greek text, preserved in the older manuscript books. For, as St Jerome wrote to Damasus: “If faith is to be placed in Latin copies, let them answer: in which ones? For there are almost as many copies as codices. But if truth is to be sought from the many, why, returning to the Greek source, do we not correct those things which have either been badly rendered by faulty translators, more perversely amended by presumptuous ignoramuses, or added or changed by drowsy copyists?” And shortly afterward: “This present little preface promises only the four Gospels, etc., corrected by a comparison of Greek codices—but ancient ones.” St Augustine also sets out the same rule in book II of *On Christian Doctrine*.

It is not for me to decide whether some are right or wrong in holding that the translator of the Italic version should be corrected with the aid of Latin codices. But it is for me to show, by many arguments, that it is fair to grant me that I may judge no less safely concerning the Italic version from its adherence to the Greek words together with clarity of meaning. You have already worn out Mill’s edition of the New Testament by reading and perusing it. But since it is evident that most of the copies which he collated are very ancient, and since, to my knowledge, no one as yet—except Montfaucon and a few others—has stated their age and form, I thought it not inappropriate to declare to you what I think of them.

I shall first describe from Mill the Greek-Latin codex of the Gospels at Cambridge. And although some regard those parchments as almost Ogygian—that is, belonging to fabulous antiquity—I shall never be induced on their account to correct a single verse of my Fourfold Gospel Book; for if you follow them at any point, you will either be deceived or deceive. That codex is indeed very ancient, but, like the rest, corrupt. It retains the ancient Italic version, which nevertheless has readings rotten and toothless with age.

Greek codices must be consulted, but uncorrupt ones; without them no one should think that the Italic version can be found or, once found, published free from blemishes. I can neither sufficiently praise the undertaking of that greatest Doctor nor sufficiently wonder at the boldness of certain persons who disapprove Jerome’s labour, by which he opened for himself access to the purest Greek sources in order to correct the Latin text of the four Gospels, because he did not judge that his correction should be drawn from those muddy and turbulent pools of Latin translators.

Jerome had critics even in his own age. In order to obstruct his work, discredit it, and make the undertaking upon which he had entered suspect to the churches, they warned the ignorant populace to beware, because he departed from Latin copies. But in the defence which he wrote for himself to the most blessed Pope Damasus, wishing to remove that opinion from himself, he addresses him thus: “You compel me to make a new work out of an old one: that, after copies of the Scriptures have been scattered throughout the whole world, I should sit as a kind of arbiter and decide, since they differ among themselves, which are those that agree with the truth of the Greek. A pious labour, but a dangerous presumption, etc. For who . . . when he takes a volume into his hands and sees that what he reads differs from the taste which he has once imbibed, will not immediately burst out crying that I am a falsifier, proclaiming that I am sacrilegious, because I dare to add, alter, or correct anything in the old books?” Against this hostility, he says, a twofold reason consoles him: that you, who are the High Priest, command it to be done; and that even the testimony of detractors proves that what varies is not true.

And a little later: “A great error has become established in our codices: when one Evangelist said more about the same matter, they added it to another because they thought he had said too little; or, when one expressed the same sense differently, the man who had first read one of the four judged that the others also should be corrected according to its example. Hence it has happened that among us all things are mixed together: in Mark there are many things from Luke and Matthew; again, in Matthew, many things from John and Mark; and in the others are found things proper to the remaining Evangelists.”

This has happened more than once also to the Brixian codex, which I am publishing through your gift and which you, distinguished sir, splendidly illuminate in your notable letter printed at the head of the first part of this edition. But it has happened especially to the Greek-Latin Cambridge manuscript, whose description I append here, before presenting to you the principal readings of our Fourfold Gospel Book that agree more closely with the common Greek text and with ten other handwritten Roman codices.

### Description of the Greek-Latin manuscript codex of the Gospels and Acts preserved in the Cambridge Library

[Note: [Col. 0867D] Mill, *Prolegomena to the Greek New Testament*, p. 132.]

It is a parchment codex in a larger quarto format, as we commonly say. It contains the Gospels and the Acts of the Apostles. Beza acquired it at the beginning of the French civil war, in 1562, from the monastery of St Irenaeus at Lyons, after it had long lain there in the dust, torn and mutilated by sixty-six leaves; of these, a later hand supplied about ten from elsewhere. As soon as he had finished what he calls his larger annotations, he presented the manuscript to the University of Cambridge in 1581, sending at the same time a letter in which he disclosed his opinion of the codex.

So far as I know, Patrick Young was the first to collect its variant readings after it had been deposited in that university library. He in turn passed them on to the learned Putean brothers, the Puteans to Morin, and so forth; Morin, or someone else, to Étienne de Courcelles. Ussher also carefully collated this copy for the Elzevir edition of the New Testament of 1624, and communicated its variants, together with those of fifteen other manuscript codices, to Walton, for inclusion in the sixth volume, or appendix, of the Polyglot Bible.

As for the manuscript itself, it was written in rather large letters, or uncials, with no separation of words. The lines are not extended to one and the same length but are altogether unequal, some longer and others shorter, as if in the manner of *stichera*. The copyist took care that the Greek and Latin should correspond to one another, almost word for word, generally retaining even the same order of words. The Greek occupies the left-hand page and the Latin the right. The first two leaves have perished. On the third leaf, or fifth page, the Latin version begins at Matthew 1:12: “But after the deportation to Babylon,” etc.; on the sixth page the Greek text begins at chapter 1, verse 20: *paralabein Mariam*, etc.

In the Gospels, John immediately follows Matthew, and this by the compiler’s own design. For at the end of Matthew it has: “The Gospel according to Matthew has been completed; the Gospel according to John begins” (*Euangelion kata Matthaion etelesthē, archetai Euangelion kata Iōannēn*). Luke follows John, and Mark follows Luke, [Col. 0868A] with the same heading. The books were arranged thus so that the Gospels of apostles might take precedence over the Gospels of companions of apostles, just as Tertullian calls Mark and Luke companions of apostles.

[Note: [Col. 0867D] Book IV, *Against Marcion*, chapter 2.]

A note is also appended to Mark’s Gospel, indicating that the book of Acts is placed immediately after it. But this is by a later scribe. For the following leaf, which on one side presents the last twelve verses of the Third Epistle of St John and on the other the first part of Acts chapter 1, clearly indicates that the manuscript formerly contained, besides the Gospels and Acts, at least the Catholic Epistles; and that the Third Epistle of John—after Jude had been omitted, unless, perhaps, it was attached in this codex, as in certain others, to the Epistle of James the brother—was followed by the book of Acts. For the manuscript reads: “The Third Epistle of John ends. The Acts of the Apostles begin.”

Various annotations have been written in the margins of the codex itself, lest we pass over anything untouched:

1. Ammonian Sections, in a hand closely resembling that of the codex itself, but somewhat fuller and blacker. Here they stand alone, without the accompaniment of the Eusebian Canons which would show to which table each belongs. Evidently, since the scribe perhaps no longer had vermilion with which to mark the Canon in red characters, he seems to have postponed its transcription, following Eusebius’s intention, [Note: [Col. 0867D] Letter to Carpianus.] and afterward, through forgetfulness or some other impediment, was prevented from copying it according to plan.

2. Scattered here and there are the little words *archē*, *telos*, *kai lege*, *hōde stēke*—“beginning,” “end,” “and read,” “stand here”—denoting the beginning and end of liturgical readings; also titles of certain readings, written in a foul and barbarous hand.

[Note: [Col. 0867D] *Chy gene, anagnosma perē to sabbato, metaimorfos anagnosma, anagnosma peri tou kyriakē, anagnosma eis tin paraskygēn, anagnosma peri toou sabbatoou eis tēn enkēneoun enkainisin, anagnosma peri to kyriaky tōn profoutismatōn, ton apolysēon*, etc.—that is, with several forms corrupt, “Birth of Christ; reading concerning the Sabbath; reading for the Transfiguration; reading concerning Sunday; reading for Friday; reading concerning the Sabbath; reading for the Dedication; reading concerning the Sunday of the Illuminations; the dismissal,” etc.]

3. Certain chapter-headings of matters treated in the Gospels, written in a dreadful hand, sometimes in the margin but more often at the top of the page.

[Note: [Col. 0868D] At Matthew 9:35 and 10:1, where the healing of diseases and the election of the apostles are treated, appears this note: *tou therapeiei kai ton apostolon*, that is, *peri tou therapeuein, kai tōn apostolōn*, “concerning healing and the apostles.” Elsewhere: *ton grammateon kai phariseon*, that is, *peri tōn grammateōn kai pharisaiōn*, “concerning the scribes and Pharisees.” Elsewhere: *Apostolon kai ton hyiōn Zebedeon*, that is, *peri tōn apostolōn, kai tōn hyiōn Zebedaiou*, “concerning the apostles and the sons of Zebedee.”]

These notes, and the other annotations already mentioned, were not the work of one copyist or even of one century. Some are very ancient, others of a somewhat later age, others of a much more recent date; some are almost modern or wholly recent. They appear to be by various Latins who, for amusement, copied these monstrous forms of words as best they could. Certainly the Greek text of the codex, no less than the Latin, is by a Latin scribe.

Simon demonstrates this from the similarity of the characters in both texts; from purely Greek letters admitted into the opposite version; from the very purpose of Greek-Latin codices of this kind—which certainly could not have been useful to Greeks, for what had they to do with a Latin version or even the Latin language?—but which seem to have been made entirely for the benefit of Westerners. By placing the Greek text opposite the Latin, those having some competence in Greek could understand the sacred codex better and, where necessary, correct their Latin. Finally, this is evident from the manuscript’s scribal errors, some of which quite plainly betray a Latin copyist—for example, *Hērōdous*, *Iōannous*, *Iōannei*, *Samaritanōn*, *phlagellōsas*, *leprōsou*, and similar forms.

[Note: [Col. 0868D] Simon, *Critical History of the Text of the New Testament*, chapter 30.]

We now come to the parts of the codex itself. The Latin presents the Italic translation as it circulated at that time, almost everywhere interpolated, before Jerome’s revision. The Greek text, however, is remarkably corrupt and depraved, yet of such a kind that it certainly derived from the sources from which the Italic Version flowed.

I think that what happened to the copies used by the Italic translators, and to the transcripts derived from them, was this. The copies used by the translators themselves had suffered somewhat here and there from copyists—as is altogether clear from the Syriac and certain other versions made from codices similar to them—but in other respects they admirably represented apostolic diction. Yet once they came into Latin hands, corrupt codices were produced from them. For they were written not, as the other copies of the East, by Greek scribes familiar with their native language, who issued a text almost clean and carefully attended to, but by secretaries such as that age produced in the West: wretchedly ignorant and barbarous men, who knew virtually nothing about the books they were to copy except the letters themselves. Hence, in the course of time, a far greater—indeed, ultimately an altogether infinite—mass of errors and interpolated readings accumulated in those codices.

For as soon as some more learned Latins had written excerpts from various places, scholia, and notable pericopes in the margins of their copies, the copyists who were to transcribe them were given the task of transferring this entire marginal miscellany into the body of their transcript. Some such codices still exist today, wretchedly and beyond all measure mixed and stained. Most are very ancient and were once held in extraordinary authority among Westerners; and they had all the greater authority because other Latins made this version increasingly conform to these interpolated texts. Thus there was no doubt that the Greek texts to which this Latin corresponded so well exhibited that original text, whole and uncorrupted, after which the Italic version had been fashioned.

This agreement of Greek and Latin, as we have described it, certainly proceeded at first and, it seems, for a long time separately, in distinct volumes. Later, however, when the study of Greek began to flourish somewhat among Westerners, learned persons judged it useful to set the original text and translation before the eyes together: either on the same page, as we see done in some books, or on separate pages, as in others and particularly in this Cambridge codex.

As to the Greek text of the manuscript now under discussion, it can scarcely be said how excessively freely and downright wantonly the interpolator, whoever he was, behaved in arranging it. At first sight you would believe that his intention was not to present the text itself as the Evangelists issued it, but, while merely preserving the order and narrative of the sacred text, to make each Gospel more complete and fuller. This is shown by various fragments and entire periods from the other Gospels inserted into the text of each Gospel; by very numerous transpositions within each Gospel for the sake of narrative clarity; by pericopes transferred from one Gospel to another; and by innumerable other interpolations.

But certain words substituted for genuine ones, in no way more significant and contributing nothing to the clarity or richness of the narrative, point to an entirely different intention. So do changes of numbers, cases, genders, and tenses made everywhere without any reason; infinite transpositions for which no adequate reason can even be imagined; and, finally, many contractions and omissions here and there, including entire sentences that make a remarkable contribution to the integrity of the Gospel narrative. For a man who had determined to make from each Gospel a complete Gospel history and, as it were, a *Diatessaron*, would by no means have omitted such things. Indeed, the one certain conclusion is that the compiler of this text treated the books of the Gospels and Acts according to his own pleasure: he added, removed, and altered whatever he pleased; and, in a word, he took great pains to make the Evangelists’ text, in a large part, appear transformed into something else.

From the corrupt and interpolated passages of the codex, we shall note only a few here. In Matthew’s Gospel, that notable pericope concerning the chief places at dinner (chapter 20, verse 28) appears for the first time in these Greek interpolations: “But you seek to grow from smallness and to become less from greatness; but when you enter,” etc. (*Hymeis de zēteite ek mikrou auxēsai, kai ek meizonos elattoneisthai; eiserchomenoi de*, etc.; for thus it should be read). Everyone recognizes that its latter part is taken from Luke 14:8; while its former part—so far as I know, not yet observed by anyone—certainly arose from the Greek of the same Gospel’s chapter 22, verses 27–28: “For I came among you not as one reclining at table, but as one serving; and you have increased in my service, as one serving, [you] who have remained,” etc. (*Egō gar en mesō hymōn ēlthon ouch hōs ho anakeimenos, all’ hōs ho diakonōn kai hymeis ēuxēthēte en tē diakonia mou, hōs ho diakonōn, hoi diamemenēkotes*, etc.).

In chapter 21, verse 32, in the parable of the two sons commanded to go into the vineyard, of whom the first said that he would not go but did go, while the second said that he would go but did not: since in certain codices the *last*, or second, son was said to have done the Father’s will—as in corrupt Latin texts before Jerome—and since the interpolator’s copy could have had no other reading, by deleting the negative, he made it read, “when you saw [it], you repented,” contrary to all manuscript authority and to the Saviour’s meaning, so that the parable might fit the scribes and priests, who in his text were compared with the second son.

In Mark, chapter 2, verse 26, he removed the phrase “in the time of Abiathar the high priest” (*epi Abiathar tou archiereōs*) as not agreeing with historical truth; and likewise the words “for everyone shall be salted with fire” (*pas gar pyri halisthēsetai*), chapter 9, verse 49, perhaps because they seemed absurd. Other things he altered out of zeal for Gospel truth. In chapter 15, verse 25, because his copy had, “And it was the third hour, and they crucified him” (*ēn de hōra tritē, kai estaurōsan auton*), whereas the crucifixion had occurred only at the sixth hour, or a little before, he changed *estaurōsan*, “they crucified,” to *ephylasson*, “they were guarding,” lest the Evangelist should say anything false, as he supposed. Thus everything was preserved.

Of the same sort is “Why have you reproached me?” (*eis ti ōneidisas me*), chapter 15, verse 34. Someone could not endure—having forgotten that the same saying occurs in Matthew—that Christ, hanging upon the cross, should say that he had been forsaken by God. Accordingly, he wished *enkatelipes*, “you forsook,” to be softened in the margin into *ōneidisas*, “you reproached,” as especially fitting the Saviour, already assailed by the mockery and insults of the Jews; and this then entered into the text of this codex and doubtless some others.

In Luke’s Gospel, where this manuscript differs from others more notably than elsewhere, the interpolator has forced upon us a new genealogy of Christ, by which Luke is reconciled with Matthew. In it, the portion ascending from Joseph to Solomon—not to Nathan—is Matthew’s, with only Eliakim inserted in addition to Jeconiah and Josiah, and likewise Amaziah, Joash, and Ahaziah between Uzziah and Joram, whom that Evangelist had omitted in order to construct sets of fourteen generations. The remainder, from Solomon to Adam, differs in no respect from the codices of Luke. This is surely monstrous licence. Yet Jerome also testifies in his Preface to Damasus that some formerly acted thus with the Gospel text: “The man who had first read one of the four thought the others also ought to be corrected according to its example.”

At the end of Luke 6:4 appears in this codex, and in Stephanus β, the notable pericope concerning the man working on the Sabbath, which seems to have been taken from the Gospel according to the Hebrews. I do not know whether a tradition occurring in this codex, chapter 23, verse 54, concerning the size of the stone rolled to the door of Jesus’ tomb, likewise arose from some such narrative: it was such that twenty men could scarcely roll it.

In the Acts of the Apostles—for we pass over John’s Gospel, whose variants are less remarkable—the text teems with scholia imported from elsewhere and with more extended summaries (*periochai*), by which the interpolators wished the apostolic history to be conspicuously enlarged and elucidated. Some of these stand at the beginning of ecclesiastical readings, for in certain places their initial words, differing now and then from those supplied by the *Praxeis Apostolōn* (“Acts of the Apostles”), have entered this codex. Elsewhere also they have greatly enlarged this history by adding circumstances, with one or two exceptions not unsuitable—if anything can be called suitable that such reckless corrupters have thrust into the sacred text from their own invention.

Yet however remarkably interpolated the Greek text of this codex may be, because in many places it preserves the purity of the primitive sources from which it was derived, it supplies no small abundance of genuine readings differing from those now received. We do not speak of readings which the Cambridge manuscript has in common with other codices; here we shall touch only upon those which, so far as I know, occur in this Greek copy alone.

At Matthew 15:30, *chōlous, typhlous, kyllous*—“the lame, the blind, the maimed”—is without our *kōphous*, “the deaf,” which is evidently included in the following words, “and many others.”

For the meeting of the bridegroom and the bride, ch. XXV, v. 1; so too the Vulgate, Syriac, and Latin versions; nor do I doubt that this was the rendering of Matthew’s translator. But because below mention is made of the meeting with the bridegroom alone, and no meeting except that with the bridegroom is recalled, the Greeks deleted in later manuscripts the words “and the bride” (*καὶ τῆς νύμφης*), as having been wrongly added by the ancients. — “From this blood” (*Ἀπὸ τοῦ αἵματος τούτου*; “from the blood of this [man],” Cantabrigian Latin), ch. XXVII, v. 24, with *τοῦ δικαίου*, “of the righteous [man],” added. — “A sufficient sum of money” (*Ἀργύριον ἱκανόν*), ch. XXVIII, [Col. 0872B] v. 12, together with Stephanus’s second edition, the Cantabrigian manuscript, and the Vulgate, quite correctly. But since above, in the Greek of the preceding chapter, the plural *ἀργύρια* is used throughout and, what is more, a little below in v. 15 the soldiers are said to have received *ἀργύρια*, “pieces of silver,” it is not surprising that scholars long ago wrote *ἀργύρια ἱκανά*, “a sufficient quantity of silver,” in the margin at this point; scribes soon admitted it into the text. — “He eats with tax collectors and sinners” (*Μετὰ τῶν τελωνῶν καὶ ἁμαρτωλῶν ἐσθίει*), Mark ch. II, v. 16, correctly; and, I think, corresponding to the preceding “seeing him eating” (*ἰδόντες αὐτὸν ἐσθίοντα*). — “And the Pharisees questioned him” (*Καὶ οἱ φαρισαῖοι ἐπηρώτησαν αὐτόν*), ch. X, v. 2. *Προσελθόντες*, “having come up,” before *οἱ φαρισαῖοι*, which occurs now in all our copies, belongs to Matthew. — “And he comes to Jericho” (*Καὶ ἔρχεται εἰς Ἰερίχω*), ch. X, v. 46. Luke also has the singular, as Mark’s constant follower. The plural *ἔρχονται*, “they come,” appears to have been made from Matthew. — “Now the Passover was after two days” (*Ἦν δὲ τὸ πάσχα μετὰ δύο ἡμέρας*), ch. XIV, v. 1. Thus read the [Col. 0872C] Old Latin and Saxon versions. — “Sinners lend to sinners, that they may receive back” (*Οἱ ἁμαρτωλοὶ ἁμαρτωλοῖς δανείζουσιν, ἵνα ἀπολάβωσι*), ch. VI, v. 34. *Ἀπολάβωσι*, “may receive back,” simply, as in the former part of the clause. — “By Gentiles until they be filled” (*Ὑπὸ ἐθνῶν ἄχρις οὗ πληρωθῶσιν*), ch. XXI, v. 24—that is, the Gentiles, in conformity with St. Paul, in whom *πλήρωμα τῶν ἐθνῶν*, “the fullness of the Gentiles,” occurs more than once. — “This is the prophet” (*Οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ προφήτης*), John ch. VI, v. 14. — “Where they ate the bread” (*Ὅπου ἔφαγον τὸν ἄρτον*), ch. VI, v. 23; shortly after, “when the Lord had given thanks” (*εὐχαριστήσαντος τοῦ Κυρίου*).

But, leaving these matters, let us proceed to the Latin of the manuscript. Although the compiler of the work, in the greater part of it, fitted this Latin—which we said had been copied from some exemplar of the Old Latin version—accurately to the Greek text, retaining the same order even of words however much transposed, and indeed retaining the very faults [Col. 0872D] of his manuscript; for wherever the Greek fails (as happens in innumerable places through *homoeoteleuton* and scribal carelessness), the Latin fails as well, sometimes with the loss of all sense: nevertheless, from various places in which it departs here and there from the Greek, it is clear that this version was based on a text different from ours.

> **Note: [Col. 0871D]** Here are the variant readings. Readings placed first indicate those of the Cantabrigian manuscript; those placed second, the readings of the Greek manuscript from which the Latin version before us was copied:
>
> *Ἐλπίζουσιν, ἐλπιοῦσιν* — Matthew XII.21: “they hope,” “they will hope”;  
> *ἐλάλει, λαλῶ* — XIII.13: “he was speaking,” “I speak”;  
> *προσέχειν, προσέχετε* — XVI.12: “to beware,” “beware”;  
> *ἐμὸν τοῦτο δοῦναι, ἐμὸν δοῦναι* — XX.23: “it is mine to give this,” “it is mine to give.”
>
> *Δέρριν, τρίχας* — Mark I.6: “a skin,” “hairs”;  
> *ἐν σοί, ἐν ᾧ* — I.11: “in you,” “in whom”;  
> *εἰσεπορεύοντο, εἰσπορεύονται* — I.21: “they were entering,” “they enter”;  
> *ἐπερωτῶν, παρακαλῶν* — I.40: “asking,” “entreating”;  
> *στάχυας, στάχυη* — IV.28: “ears [of grain],” “an ear [of grain]”;  
> *βοσκομένη, βοσκομένων* — V.11: “feeding,” “of those feeding”;  
> *ἐθεώρει, θεωρεῖ* — V.38: “he was observing,” “he observes”;  
> *τοιαῦτα, ταῦτα* — VI.2: “such things,” “these things”;  
> *κατέγνωσαν, ἐμέμψαντο* — VII.2: “they condemned,” “they found fault”;  
> *ἀγαπᾷ, τιμᾷ* — VII.6: “he loves,” “he honors”;  
> *καθαρίζει, καθαρίζον* — VII.19: “he cleanses,” “cleansing”;  
> *φοίνισσα, συροφοίνισσα* — VII.26: “a Phoenician woman,” “a Syrophoenician woman”;  
> *ἐγγίζουσιν, ἤγγιζεν* — XI.1: “they approach,” “he was approaching”;  
> *προάγω, προάγει* — XVI.7: “I go before,” “he goes before”;  
> *πρώτοις, πρῶτον* — XVI.9: “to the first [ones],” “first”;  
> *ἐπικεφάλαιον, κῆνσον* — XII.14: “poll-tax,” “tribute”;  
> *ὠνείδισας, ἐγκατέλιπες* — XV.34: “you reproached,” “you forsook”;  
> *τρίτη, ἕκτη* — XV.33: “third,” “sixth.”
>
> *Βοσκομένη, βοσκομένων* — Luke VIII.32: “feeding,” “of those feeding”;  
> *εἰς ἑαυτούς, εἰς αὑτόν* — XXII.65: “against themselves,” “against him”;  
> *οὐκέτι θεωρεῖτε, οὐ θεωρεῖτε* — John XIII.16: “you no longer behold,” “you do not behold”;  
> *τρίτη, ἕκτη* — XIX.14: “third,” “sixth”;  
> *καὶ οὐκ ἐπίστευσεν, καὶ ἐπίστευσεν* — XX.8: “and he did not believe,” “and he believed.”
>
> *Εἰσῆλθεν, εἰσῆλθον* — Acts I.13: “he entered,” “they entered”;  
> *ὃ γνωστόν, καὶ γνωστόν* — I.19: “which [is] known,” “and [it is] known”;  
> *χρόνῳ ὡς, χρόνῳ, ἐν ᾧ* — I.21: “at the time when,” “at the time, in which”;  
> *πάσας σάρκας, πᾶσαν σάρκα* — II.17: “all flesh” [plural], “all flesh” [singular];  
> *ἐπερωτήσω σε, εἶπέ μοι* — V.8: “I will ask you,” “tell me”;  
> *οὐ παραγγελίᾳ, παραγγελίᾳ* — V.28: “not by command,” “by command”;  
> *δεξιᾷ, δόξῃ* — V.31: “at the right hand,” “in glory”;  
> *ἐκ τοῦ συνεδρίου, ἐν τῷ συνεδρίῳ* — V.34: “from the council,” “in the council”;  
> *οὗτοι ἐστάθησαν, οὓς ἔστησαν* — VI.6: “these stood,” “whom they appointed”;  
> *οἵ τινες προσευξάμενοι, καὶ προσευξάμενοι* — ibid.: “some having prayed,” “and having prayed”;  
> *τοῦτο, ταῦτα* — VII.1: “this,” “these things”;  
> *ἐφυγάδευσεν, ἔφυγεν* — VII.29: “he drove into exile,” “he fled”;  
> *σὺν χειρί, ἐν χειρί* — [Col. 0874D] VII.35: “with a hand,” “in a hand”;  
> *ἐπήγαγον, ἐπήγειραν* — XIV.2: “they brought upon,” “they raised up”;  
> *τούτῳ, οὕτῳ* — XV.15: “to this [one],” “thus”;  
> *ἀπαγγελοῦντας, ἀπαγγέλλοντας* — XV.27: “reporting,” “reporting”;  
> *εὐθέως, αὐτῇ τῇ ὥρᾳ* — XVI.18: “immediately,” “at that very hour”;  
> *προτεταγμένους, προστεταγμένους* — XVII.26: “previously appointed,” “appointed in addition”;  
> *ἐνθυμήσεως, ἐπιθυμήσεως* — XVII.29: “thought,” “desire”;  
> *κατασείσας, καταστείλας* — XIX.35: “having quieted by a gesture,” “having restrained”;  
> *ἐνομίσαμεν, ἐνόμιζον* — XXI.29: “we supposed,” “they supposed.”

Moreover, it is clear from these same divergences that the Latin version was interpolated in more than one place with Latin glosses and explanations [Col. 0873A], to which the Greek copy before us in no way corresponds. For example, what affinity of meaning is there between *κυλλούς*, “maimed persons,” and *sideratos*, “those struck by an evil astral influence”? Matthew ch. XV, v. 30. *Κυλλοί* are generally persons weak or mutilated in their limbs, crippled. Some reader who, for a reason unknown to me, took *κυλλούς* in this place to mean persons whose infirmity had arisen from *sideratio*, explained it as *sideratos*. Of the same kind are *ταλάντων*, “talents,” rendered *denariorum*, “denarii,” ch. XVIII, v. 24; *νόμισμα*, “coin,” rendered *denarium*, “a denarius,” ch. XXII, v. 19; and *παρασκευήν*, “Preparation,” rendered *coenam puram*, “the pure meal,” ch. XXVII, v. 62. For Parasceve was long ago called by this name. The old glosses are: *coena pura*, *παρασκευή*. The phrase occurs in Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, book V, ch. 4; and Augustine notes in his commentary on John that the Jews of his own time more commonly called Parasceve *coena pura*.

> **Note: [Col. 0874D]** Charles du Fresne, *Latin Glossary*, under the word *Coena*.

Why this meal was called “pure,” however, the most learned Du Fresne gives this explanation: not because it lacked meat, but because it was prepared for the sake of religion and the feast-day. For Jewish Preparations also had meat, and nevertheless are called pure meals because they were cooked for the sake of the feast-day; and they are still cooked today for the Sabbath, because it is not permitted to cook on the Sabbath. So he says. *Νόμισμα*, “a likeness,” Luke ch. XX, v. 24.

We have now seen what the Greek and likewise the Latin of this manuscript were like. One further question remains concerning the Greek: was it, in any respect, corrected against the Latin exemplar? For this was the explicit opinion concerning books of this kind held by certain learned men of our own and the preceding age. Since these texts agree remarkably with the Latin, against the other [Col. 0873C] Greek copies, even the best of them, they were readily persuaded either that these texts were not wholly of Greek origin but had been translated entirely from Latin, or at least that various parts had been revised and emended according to the Latin version. Thus Erasmus, Lucas of Bruges, Estius, Grotius, and others pronounce concerning them.

The matter seems now to stand thus. Various Greek copies, transcribed among the Latins from copies of the books from which the Old Latin version had been made, were severely damaged and interpolated through the ignorance of scribes and the meddlesomeness (*περιεργία*) of certain more learned Latins, who took care that scholia borrowed from Greek books should be inserted into the copies transcribed from their own. To these copies some persons subsequently adapted the Latin version. From this agreement it came about that an unlearned hand altered a few things here and there in the Greek text [Col. 0873D] to the form of the Latin copies and from the Latin version.

This is evident in the Cantabrigian Greek: *Ἡρῴδους*, *Ἰωάννους*, *Σαμαριτάνων*, and other forms of that kind, were made after the form of the Latin. In Matthew ch. V, v. 24, since the Latin had *offeres*, “you will offer,” the copyist changed *πρόσφερε*, “offer,” into *προσφερείς*, for that was to him the second person of the future. *Καταβαῖνον*, “descending,” was changed into *καταβαίνοντα*, because of the Latin *descendentem*, “descending,” ch. III, v. 16. In XI.22 and 24, because the Latin had *quam vobis*, “than you,” *ἢ ὑμῖν* was made to correspond to the Latin. Likewise, in v. 28 of the same chapter, *πάντες οἳ κοπιῶντες καὶ πεφορτισμένοι ἐστέ* was made because of the Latin *omnes qui laboratis, et onerati estis*, “all who labor and are burdened.”

In ch. XV, vv. 11 and 20, because of the obsolete Latin words—yet genuine in the translator of the Vulgate—*communicat, communicant*, that is, “defiles, they defile,” the copyist absurdly substituted *κοινωνεῖ, κοινωνοῦντα* for *κοινοῖ, κοινοῦντα*; likewise in Acts ch. XXI, v. 28, *ἐκοινώνησε τὸν ἅγιον τόπον τοῦτον*, “he made this holy place common,” because of the Latin *communicavit locum sanctum hunc*. Likewise Matthew ch. XVIII, v. 22, *ἐβδομηκοντάκις ἑπτάκις*, because of Latin *septies*, “seven times”; Acts ch. V, v. 9, *συνεφώνησεν* (for *συνεφωνήθη*) *ὑμῖν*, because of Latin *convenit vobis*, “it was agreed by you.” I pass over other examples.

[Col. 0874B]

## Letter of Theodore Beza

To the illustrious and in every respect most celebrated University of Cambridge, etc.

Having acquired some years ago from the monastery of St. Irenaeus at Lyons a Greek-Latin copy of the Four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles—a copy indeed mutilated, neither everywhere copied accurately from the beginning nor kept in the condition it ought to have been, as appears from certain pages inserted in a different hand and from some barbarous notes written by an unlearned Greek monk—I judged it proper to dedicate it especially to your most renowned University, etc., in whose sanctuary this monument of such venerable antiquity [Col. 0874C] is placed, unless I am mistaken.

And although no one will better assess than you yourselves how much authority is to be assigned to this copy, nevertheless I thought that I ought to warn you of the great discrepancy, especially in Luke’s Gospel, which I have found between this manuscript and all other copies, however ancient. It is so great that, to avoid giving offense to some, I think it should rather be preserved than published. Yet in this diversity, not of meanings but of words, I have found nothing whatever from which I could suspect that it had been corrupted by those ancient heretics. Indeed, I seem to have discovered many things worthy of observation; some things also so divergent from the received Scripture as nevertheless to agree with the writings of certain ancient Fathers, Greek and Latin; and, finally, not a few things by which the old Latin edition [Col. 0874D] is confirmed. Having compared all these with one another according to the measure of my ability, and collated them with the Syriac and Arabic editions, I have gathered them into my larger annotations upon the emended text, which will shortly appear.

But come: let the entire matter be subject, as is fitting, to your judgment. I ask only this of you: that you accept kindly and favorably this whatever-it-may-be memorial of my highest respect for your Excellencies [Col. 0875A], proceeding from one most devoted to you, etc.

Geneva, the eighth day before the Ides of December, in the year of the Lord 1581.

Theodore Beza, most devoted to the dignity of your whole illustrious University.

## Note Written by Theodore Beza’s Hand upon the Manuscript

[Col. 0876A]

This copy, of venerable antiquity, was formerly exported from Greece, as appears from certain barbarous Greek notes written in the margin; after it had long lain in dust, it was found, mutilated as it is seen here, in the monastery of St. Irenaeus at Lyons, when civil war broke out there, in the year of the Lord 1562.

[Col. 0875]

# Readings of the Fourfold Gospel Book Agreeing with the Greek Text in Places Diverging from the Vulgate Edition

## St. Matthew

[Col. 0875B]

### Chapter I

3. **Esron.** Greek: *Ἐσρώμ*, “Esrom.” So also the Veronese and Corbie manuscripts.

### Chapter II

1. **In Bethlehem of Juda.** In Greek: *τῆς Ἰουδαίας*, “of Judaea.” So in Vercelli, Saint-Germain, Verona, and Brescia. Why did the Greek books delete the other Bethlehem—which is in the tribe of Zebulun, Joshua XIX.15, and is located both in the Hebrew exemplar and in the Latin Vulgate—and write *Βαιθμών* for Bethlehem? But this other place too is called Bethlehem of Juda in Judges XIX.1.

4. **Where Christ was to be born.** Greek: *γεννᾶται*, “where Christ is born.” So Vercelli and Saint-Germain.

5. **In Bethlehem of Juda.** Greek: *τῆς Ἰουδαίας*, “of Judaea,” as in v. 1. So Vercelli and Brescia.

7. **He inquired diligently.** Greek: *ἠκρίβωσε*, “he investigated carefully.” So Vercelli, Saint-Germain, and Brescia.

8. **Inquire.** Greek: *ἐξετάσατε*, “search out.” Brescia: “seek diligently.”

[Col. 0875C] 11. **And, entering into the house.** Greek: *καὶ ἐλθόντες εἰς τὴν οἰκίαν*, “and, coming into the house.” Vercelli, Verona, and Brescia also read “into the house.”

14. **Who, rising up.** Greek: *ὁ δὲ ἐγερθείς*, “but he, having risen”; and so again in v. 21. Brescia: “but he, rising.” Vercelli and Verona: “but rising”; and so Saint-Germain.

### Chapter III

7. **From the wrath to come.** Here the Greek has *ἀπὸ τῆς μελλούσης ὀργῆς*, “from the future wrath.” So Corbie and Verona.

8. **Fruit worthy.** Greek: *καρποὺς ἀξίους*, “worthy fruits,” as in Luke. So Vercelli.

11. **He who is to come after me.** Greek: *ὁ ἐρχόμενος*, “he who comes.” Vercelli has: “but he who comes.”

14. **I ought from you.** Greek: *ἐγὼ χρείαν ἔχω*, “I have need.” So Brescia.

### Chapter IV

10. **Go, Satan.** In many Greek manuscripts one reads *ὕπαγε ὀπίσω μου, Σατανᾶ*, “Go behind me, Satan.” In Verona: “Go behind me, Satan.” But Vercelli and Corbie have: “Go behind, Satan.”

14. **The prophet.** Greek adds *λέγοντος*, “saying.” [Col. 0875D] So Brescia.

22. **And [their] father.** Greek adds *αὐτῶν*, “their.” So Saint-Germain and Verona.

24. **His report.** Greek: *ἀκοὴ αὐτοῦ*, “his report.” Saint-Germain has “fame.”

### Chapter V

1. **And Jesus, seeing the crowds.** The name Jesus is not in Greek, nor is it found in Brescia or Vercelli.

4. **They shall possess the earth.** Greek: *κληρονομήσουσι*, “they shall inherit.” Brescia has “they shall inherit”; Vercelli, “they shall possess by inheritance.”

22. **Whoever is angry.** Greek adds *εἰκῇ*, “without cause.” So Vercelli, Verona, Corbie, and Brescia. Incorrectly, although all Greek manuscripts, including the Cantabrigian, have this word, except the Vatican manuscript alone.

24. **And go first to be reconciled.** Greek: *καὶ ὕπαγε, πρῶτον διαλλάγηθι τῷ ἀδελφῷ σου*, “and go; first be reconciled to your brother.” Vercelli, Verona, and Brescia have: “and go, first be reconciled to your brother.”

41. **Another two.** The word “another” is not in Greek, nor in Brescia.

[Col. 0876B] 44. **Do good to those who hate you.** Greek manuscripts prefix these words: *εὐλογεῖτε τοὺς καταρωμένους ὑμᾶς*, “bless those who curse you.” Brescia likewise: “Bless those who curse you.”

**Likewise: for those persecuting and slandering you.** Greek: *ὑπὲρ τῶν ἐπηρεαζόντων ὑμᾶς, καὶ διωκόντων*, “for those who mistreat you and persecute [you].” Brescia has “for those slandering you and persecuting you.” Vercelli and Verona likewise: “for those slandering and persecuting you.”

46. **What reward will you have?** Greek: *ἔχετε*, “you have.” So Corbie.

48. **Heavenly.** Greek: *ὁ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς*, “who is in heaven.” So Verona and Saint-Germain.

### Chapter VI

1. **Your righteousness.** Greek: *τὴν ἐλεημοσύνην ὑμῶν*, “your almsgiving,” together with Brescia.

4. **Will repay you** (for “Blessed are the merciful, because they shall obtain mercy”). Greek manuscripts, both in this verse and in vv. 6 and 18, add *ἐν τῷ [Col. 0876C] φανερῷ*, “openly”; so Brescia. Vercelli and Saint-Germain likewise have “publicly”; Verona, “in public.”

10. **May it come.** Greek: *ἐλθέτω*, “let it come.” So Corbie.

13. **Amen.** Here Greek manuscripts add: *ὅτι σοῦ ἐστιν ἡ βασιλεία, καὶ ἡ δύναμις, καὶ ἡ δόξα εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας*, “for yours is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory for the ages.” Brescia has: “because yours is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory for the ages.”

### Chapter VII

19. **Will be cut down and cast into the fire.** Greek: *ἐκκόπτεται, καὶ εἰς πῦρ βάλλεται*, “is cut down and cast into the fire,” as in Matthew III.10. Vercelli reads “is cut down and will be cast into the fire,” taking *e* for *i*; Corbie similarly, “will be cut down and is cast into the fire.”

21. **He himself will enter the kingdom of heaven.** So Brescia. These words are not in Greek manuscripts.

29. **Their [scribes] and Pharisees.** These words are absent from Greek manuscripts. In Brescia too, “and Pharisees” is absent. The Pharisees, in my opinion, were omitted in certain manuscripts so that they should not be thought, besides the scribes, to have taught the people in an official capacity.

### Chapter VIII

7. **I will come and heal him.** Greek: *Ἐγὼ ἐλθὼν θεραπεύσω αὐτόν*, “I, having come, will heal him.” So Vercelli, Brescia, and Saint-Germain.

13. **In that hour.** Ten or more Greek manuscripts add here: *Καὶ ὑποστρέψας ὁ ἑκατόνταρχος εἰς τὴν οἶκον αὑτοῦ, ἐν αὐτῇ τῇ ὥρᾳ εὗρε τὸν παῖδα αὐτοῦ ὑγιαίνοντα*, “and the centurion, having returned to his house, found his servant well in that very hour”; and so Saint-Germain: “from that hour.”

### Chapter IX

2. **Are forgiven.** Greek: *ἀφέωνται*, “have been forgiven.” So Vercelli, Verona, and Saint-Germain: an Attic perfect, in place of the common *ἀφεῖνται*. The present is *ἀφίενται*.

12. **He says.** Greek: *εἶπεν αὐτοῖς*, “he said to them.” So Brescia.

13. **But sinners.** Greek adds *εἰς μετάνοιαν*, “to repentance.” So Saint-Germain, from Luke, where it occurs at V.32. It is not here in the Cantabrigian manuscript.

32. **Mute.** Greek: *κωφόν*, “deaf.” Vercelli, Verona, and Saint-Germain have “mute and deaf.”

### Chapter X

3. **And Thaddaeus.** Greek reads: *καὶ Λεββαῖος ὁ ἐπικληθεὶς Θαδδαῖος*, “and Lebbaeus, who was called Thaddaeus.” Brescia has: “and Lebbaeus, who is named Thaddaeus.”

[Col. 0877A] 5. **Into cities.** Greek: *εἰς πόλιν*, “into a city.” So Corbie.

8. **Raise the dead.** Certain Greek manuscript copies and Brescia do not have these words. Some also omit “cast out demons”; but those which contain both place “raise the dead” before “cleanse lepers.”

### Chapter XI

4. **What you heard and saw.** The things which Luke narrates summarily in ch. VII, v. 21. Greek: *ἀκούετε καὶ βλέπετε*, “you hear and see.” So Verona; Vercelli, however, has “you heard and see.”

10. **Before your face.** Malachi has “before my face,” and so Vercelli. But there is no difference, since Christ is himself God Most High and Lord, in accordance with that concerning the same John the Baptist, Luke I.76: “And you, child, shall be called prophet of the Most High; for you shall go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways.”

26. **It was pleasing.** Greek: *ἐγένετο εὐδοκία*, “it was good pleasure.” [Col. 0877B] So Saint-Germain and Verona.

### Chapter XII.1

1. **On the Sabbath.** Greek: *τοῖς σάββασι*, “on the Sabbaths.” So Vercelli, Corbie, Saint-Germain, Verona, and Brescia.

22. **Mute.** Greek: *κωφός*, “deaf.” Verona has “mute and deaf”; Corbie, “deaf and mute.”

31. **Will not be forgiven.** Greek adds *τοῖς ἀνθρώποις*, “to people.” So Brescia.

### Chapter XIII

4. **Birds of heaven.** In the standard Greek the word “heaven” is absent. So Corbie and Verona.

7. **The thorns grew.** Greek: *ἀνέβησαν*, “came up.” So Corbie and Brescia.

28. **Do you wish, shall we go?** Greek: *θέλεις οὖν ἀπελθόντες*, “do you wish, then, that we should go,” etc. Brescia has: “Do you wish, therefore, that we should go?”

30. **To burn them.** Greek adds *αὐτά*, “them.” So Brescia.

38. **Children of the wicked one.** Greek: *οἱ υἱοὶ τοῦ πονηροῦ*. Verona reads “children of the unrighteous”; Brescia, “children of the malignant one,” that is, of the devil. Therefore in the Latin edition *nequam*, “wicked,” is in the genitive case [Col. 0877C].

51. **Yes.** Greek: *ναί, Κύριε*, “yes, Lord.” Vercelli, Verona, Brescia, and Saint-Germain have “certainly, Lord.”

### Chapter XIV

30. **To sink.** Greek: *καταποντίζεσθαι*, “to go down, to be submerged.” Corbie has “to submerge.”

### Chapter XV

8. **Honors me.** The Greek text has: *ἐγγίζει μοι ὁ λαὸς οὗτος τῷ στόματι αὐτῶν, καὶ τοῖς χείλεσί με τιμᾷ*, “this people approaches me with their mouth and honors me with their lips.” Brescia: “this people approaches me with its mouth and honors me with its lips.”

10. **The crowds.** Greek: *τὸν ὄχλον*, “the crowd.” Brescia: “the crowd.”

30. **Mute persons.** Greek: *κωφούς*, “deaf persons.” So Corbie.

31. **Mute persons speaking.** Greek: *κωφοὺς λαλοῦντας, κυλλοὺς, ὑγιεῖς*, “deaf persons speaking, crippled persons well.” The Brescian copy has “mute persons speaking, crippled persons well.” Matthew seems to have omitted “crippled persons well” because he thought lesser miracles sufficiently understood from the greater ones.

### Chapter XVI

1. **They asked.** Greek: *ἐπηρώτησαν*, “they questioned.” So Corbie.

[Col. 0877D] 3. **The face.** Greek prefixes *Ὑποκριταί*, “hypocrites.” So Corbie and Brescia, which the Latin edition does not have.

5. **Across the sea.** Corbie: “across it was.” Greek: *εἰς τὸ πέραν*, “to the other side.” Greek books always use this expression. For four times in Matthew they wrote “across the sea,” *εἰς τὸ πέραν*, and likewise four times in Mark—V.1, 21; VI.45; and VIII.13.

13. **Whom do [people] say?** Greek: *τίνα με λέγουσιν*, “whom do they say that I am?” So Vercelli, Verona, Corbie, Brescia, and Saint-Germain.

22. **Far be it.** Greek: *ἵλεώς σοι*, “be gracious to yourself.” Brescia has “be propitious to yourself”; Vercelli, “propitious to you”; Verona, “far be it from you; be propitious.” The Syriac translator: “spare yourself.”

### Chapter XVII

11. **Will come.** Greek: *ἔρχεται πρῶτον*, “comes first.” Brescia has “will come first.” In Matthew XI.14 the Lord Christ says of John the Baptist: “He is Elijah who is to come”; that is, who was foretold as one who would come.

[Col. 0878A] 20. **By prayer and fasting.** Greek: *ἐν προσευχῇ καὶ νηστείᾳ*, “in prayer and fasting.” So Brescia, from Mark IX.28.

21. **While they were moving about.** Greek: *ἀναστρεφομένοις*. Corbie has “while they were returning.”

### Chapter XVIII

35. **From your hearts.** Here Greek manuscripts add *τὰ παραπτώματα αὐτῶν*, “their offenses,” with Brescia: “their sins.”

### Chapter XIX

4. **He who made man from the beginning.** Greek only: *ὁ ποιήσας ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς*, “he who made from the beginning.” So Vercelli and Saint-Germain.

7. **And to dismiss [her].** Greek adds *αὐτήν*, “her.” So Brescia.

12. **From the mother’s womb.** Greek: *ἐκ κοιλίας μητρός*, “from a mother’s belly.” Brescia has “from the mother’s womb.”

17. **Why do you ask me about the good?** Greek: *τί με λέγεις ἀγαθόν*, “why do you call me good?” So Brescia, as in Luke.

21. **What you have.** Greek: *σοῦ τὰ ὑπάρχοντα*, “your possessions.” Vercelli has “your goods.”

### Chapter XX

[Col. 0878B]

1. **Is like.** Greek adds *γάρ*, “for”: “for is like.” So Vercelli and Brescia.

7. **Go also into my vineyard.** Greek books add: *καὶ ὅ ἐὰν ᾖ δίκαιον, λήψεσθε*, “and whatever is just you shall receive.” Brescia: “and you shall receive what is just.” These words are absent only in the Cantabrigian manuscript.

15. **Is it not lawful for me to do what I wish?** Greek books add *ἐν τοῖς ἐμοῖς*, “with what is mine, in my own affairs.” Vercelli appears to have read likewise.

22. **Which I am about to drink.** Greek books add: *καὶ τὸ βάπτισμα, ὃ ἐγὼ βαπτίζομαι, βαπτισθῆναι*, “and to be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?” Similar words occur in the following verse, transferred here from Mark—except that, instead of “or,” they have *καί*, “and.” Brescia reads: “or to be baptized with the baptism with which I [am baptized].”

23. **You shall indeed drink my cup.** After “you shall drink,” the Greek text reads: *καὶ τὸ βάπτισμα, ὃ ἐγὼ βαπτίζομαι βαπτισθήσεσθε*, “and you shall be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized.” Brescia nearly agrees, reading: “and [with] the baptism with which I am baptized, you are baptized.”

### Chapter XXI

[Col. 0878C]

11. **But the peoples.** Greek: *οἱ δὲ ὄχλοι ἔλεγον*, “but the crowds were saying.” So Brescia and Corbie. In the Cantabrigian manuscript one reads *οἱ δὲ πολλοὶ εἶπον*, “but many said.”

17. **And he remained there.** Greek: *καὶ ηὐλίσθη ἐκεῖ*, “and he lodged there.” Brescia has “and he rested there.”

21. **Be taken up.** Greek: *ἄρθητι*, “be lifted up.” So Verona.

26. **For they all regarded John as a prophet.** Greek has *ἔχουσι*, “they regard.” So Verona and Saint-Germain.

31. **They say to him: The first.** In the Cantabrigian manuscript, *ἔσχατος*, “the last.” So Vercelli, Corbie, Saint-Germain, and Verona.

38. **And we shall have [it].** Greek: *καὶ κατάσχωμεν*, “and let us possess [it].” Corbie has “and let us possess.”

### Chapter XXII

5. **To his farm.** Greek: *εἰς τὸν ἴδιον ἀγρόν*, “to his own field.” Brescia has “to his field.”

7. **But the king.** Greek: *ὁ βασιλεὺς ἐκεῖνος*, “that king.” So Brescia; Verona, “that king.”

[Col. 0878D] 10. **Of those reclining.** Greek: *ἀνακειμένων*, “of those reclining.” Corbie reads “of those lying down at table.”

30. **They will be.** Greek: *εἰσίν*, “they are.” So Corbie, Verona, and Brescia.

### Chapter XXIII

5. **Fringes.** Greek adds *τῶν ἱματίων αὐτῶν*, “of their garments.” So Brescia.

14. **Praying long prayers.** Greek: *καὶ προφάσει μακρᾷ προσευχόμενοι*, “and praying under a pretext [with] a long prayer.” Verona reads “praying at length on an occasion”; Brescia, “under the pretext of prolonged prayer.” This entire v. 14 is absent in some Latin copies.

25. **And uncleanness.** Greek: *καὶ ἀκρασίας*, “and lack of self-control.” So Vercelli. In certain others, *καὶ ἀδικίας*, “and injustice”; so Brescia. But that “uncleanness” ought to be read is clear from the following verse, where it says: “First cleanse what is within.”

35. **Which was shed.** Greek: *ἐκχυνόμενον*, “which is being shed.” So Vercelli.

[Col. 0879A] 37. **And you would not.** Greek: *καὶ οὐκ ἠθελήσατε*, “and you would not.” So Verona.

### Chapter XXIV

6. **These things to happen.** Greek: *πάντα γενέσθαι*, “all things to happen.” So Brescia.

18. **His tunic.** Greek: *τὰ ἱμάτια αὐτοῦ*, “his garments.” So Brescia.

30. **With great power and majesty.** Greek: *μετὰ δυνάμεως καὶ δόξης πολλῆς*, “with power and great glory.” So Brescia.
