36. **Except the Father alone.** Greek: *εἰ μὴ ὁ πατήρ μου μόνος*, “except my Father alone.” So Brescia.

### Chapter XXV

2. **But five of them were foolish, and five prudent.** In Greek, contrariwise, the prudent are placed before the foolish, as in Brescia.

4. **With [their] lamps.** Greek adds *αὐτῶν*, “their.” So Verona and Brescia.

11. **But last of all.** Greek: *ὕστερον*, “afterwards,” as in Brescia.

31. **And all the angels.** Greek: *καὶ πάντες οἱ ἅγιοι ἄγγελοι*, “and all the holy angels.” So Brescia.

### Chapter XXVI

[Col. 0879B]

2. **Will be delivered up.** Greek: *παραδίδοται*, “is delivered up.” So Verona.

28. **Will be shed.** Greek: *ἐκχυνόμενον*, “which is being shed.” So Vercelli.

59. **That they might deliver [him] to death.** Greek: *θανατώσωσι*, “that they might put [him] to death.” Vercelli: “that they might kill [him].”

60. **Lastly.** Greek: *ὕστερον*, “afterwards.” So Vercelli.

61. **And after three days.** Greek: *καὶ διὰ τριῶν ἡμερῶν*, “and through three days.” Vercelli reads “and in three days,” and “and through three days.”

65. **The blasphemy.** Greek adds *αὐτοῦ*, “his.” So Verona and Brescia.

### Chapter XXVII

16. **But they had.** Greek: *εἶχον*, “they had.” So Vercelli, Verona, and Brescia, so that it refers to the Jews, not the governor.

22. **They all say.** Greek inserts *αὐτῷ*, “they all say to him.” So Brescia.

26. **He delivered [him] to them.** Greek books do not have “to them,” except the Cantabrigian manuscript. It is also absent in Verona.

### Chapter XXVIII

7. **Behold, I have told you.** Greek: *ἰδοὺ [Col. 0879C] εἶπον ὑμῖν*, “behold, I told you.” So Vercelli, Corbie, and Verona.

8. **To his disciples.** Greek books add: *ὡς δὲ ἐπορεύοντο ἀπαγγεῖλαι τοῖς μαθηταῖς αὐτοῦ*, “and as they were going to report it to his disciples.” Brescia: “but when they went away to announce [it] to his disciples.”

20. **Until the consummation of the age.** Greek adds *ἀμήν*, “Amen.” So Vercelli, Verona, and Brescia.

## St. John

### Chapter I

4. **In him was life.** The Cantabrigian Greek manuscript reads: *ἐν αὐτῷ ζωή ἐστιν*, “in him life is.” So Corbie and Brescia. Vercelli also, Gatianus, and the manuscripts read “in him life is”; Verona, “in him life is.”

15. **John bears witness concerning him and cries out.** Greek: *μαρτυρεῖ*—Vercelli and Verona, “bears witness”—*περὶ αὐτοῦ, καὶ κέκραγε*, “concerning him, and has cried out.”

27. **He is the one who is to come after me.** Greek: *αὐτός ἐστιν ὁ ὀπίσω μου ἐρχόμενος*, “he is the one coming after me.” So Vercelli, Verona, and Brescia.

43. **On the next day he wished to go out.** Greek: *τῇ ἐπαύριον*, [Col. 0879D] “on the following day,” as in vv. 29 and 35, where the Latin reads “on another day.” So Vercelli.

### Chapter II

4. **And Jesus says to her.** Greek: *λέγει αὐτῇ*, without the conjunction *καί*, “and,” which is likewise absent in Vercelli but present in the Alexandrian manuscript.

### Chapter III

3. **Unless someone is born again.** Greek: *ἐὰν μή τις γεννηθῇ ἄνωθεν*, “unless someone is born from above.” Brescia has “unless someone is born again”; Gatianus, “unless someone is born.”

25. **Now a question arose.** Greek: *ἐγένετο οὖν*, “therefore there arose.” Vercelli and Brescia have “therefore a question arose.”

### Chapter IV

1. **Therefore when Jesus knew.** Greek: *ὡς οὖν ἔγνω ὁ Κύριος*, “therefore when the Lord knew.” So Brescia.

2. **Although Jesus himself did not baptize.** Greek: *Ἰησοῦς αὐτός*, “Jesus himself.” So Vercelli, Verona, and Brescia. Gatianus and the manuscripts have “Jesus himself.”

3. **He left Judaea.** The Cantabrigian manuscript has [Col. 0880A] *Ἰουδαίαν γῆν*, “the land of Judaea”; so Verona, Gatianus, and the manuscripts; Vercelli likewise, “the Judaean land.”

28. **And she says to those men.** Greek: *καὶ λέγει τοῖς ἀνθρώποις*, without the pronoun “those.” So Vercelli, Verona, and Corbie. Another Greek manuscript has *πολίταις*, “to the citizens.”

31. **Meanwhile the disciples were asking him.** Greek: *ἐν δὲ τῷ μεταξὺ ἠρώτων αὐτὸν οἱ μαθηταί*. The word *ἐρωτᾶν* means not “to entreat” but “to question,” as Vercelli renders it. Yet in Greek books of the New and Old Testaments, especially in the Evangelists, this word occurs almost everywhere that Latin has *rogare*, “to ask.”

40. **They asked him.** Greek: *ἠρώτων αὐτόν*. So Vercelli and Verona.

42. **Not because of your speech.** Greek: *οὐκ ἔτι διὰ τὴν σὴν λαλιάν*. The Cantabrigian manuscript has *μαρτυρίαν*, “because of your testimony”; so Verona. The ancient translator considered it a word of testimony, more worthy than one of speech.

42. **Because this man is truly the Savior of the world.** Greek: *ὁ σωτὴρ τοῦ κόσμου ὁ Χριστός*, “the Savior of the world, the Christ.” So Brescia, and likewise the Syriac translator from the Greek.

[Col. 0880B] 46. **And there was a certain royal official.** Greek: *καὶ ἦν τις βασιλικός*. Vercelli reads *Basiliscus*, perhaps because the Latin translator carelessly read *βασιλίσκος*, “little king,” for what was written in Greek, *βασιλικός*, “royal official.”

47. **For he was beginning to die.** Greek: *ἤμελλε γὰρ ἀποθνήσκειν*, “for he was about to die.” Vercelli: “for he was going to die.”

49. **My son.** Greek: *τὸ παιδίον μου*, “my child.” Verona and Corbie have only “child.” The Alexandrian manuscript has *τὸν υἱόν μου*, “my son.”

51. **That his son was alive.** Greek: *ὅτι ὁ παῖς σου ζῇ*, “that your child lives.” Vercelli and Verona have “because your son lives.” The Cantabrigian manuscript has *ὁ υἱός*, “the son.”

### Chapter V

2. **Now at Jerusalem is the sheep-gate pool.** Greek: *ἔστι δὲ ἐν τοῖς Ἱεροσολύμοις ἐπὶ τῇ προβατικῇ κολυμβήθρᾳ*, “now there is at Jerusalem, by the Sheep [Gate], a pool.” Brescia: “now in Jerusalem there is at the Sheep [Gate] a pool.” Gatianus and the manuscripts likewise have “… at the Sheep [Gate].”

2. **Bethsaida.** Greek: *Βεθεσδά*, “Bethesda.” So Brescia and the Syriac translator from Greek. In the Coptic version the word *Βεθσαϊδά*, “Bethsaida,” is retained.

[Col. 0880C] 3. **Of the withered.** The Cantabrigian manuscript adds *παραλυτικῶν*, “of paralytics.” So Vercelli and Verona.

4. **For an angel of the Lord.** Greek: *ἄγγελος γάρ*, omitting the name “Lord” and using *γάρ*, “for,” in place of *δέ*, “but.” So Verona, Corbie, and Gatianus, who nevertheless reads “for” rather than “but.” In Beza’s Greek manuscript, which they call most ancient, this fourth verse is wholly omitted. The Alexandrian manuscript reads *Κυρίου*, “of the Lord.”

4. **Went down into the pool.** Greek: *κατέβαινεν ἐν τῇ κολυμβήθρᾳ*, “went down in the pool.” Vercelli: “went down into the bathing-place”; so the Veronese copy. In the Alexandrian manuscript, *ἐλούετο*, “was bathing.”

4. **And the water was moved.** Greek: *καὶ ἐτάρασσε τὸ ὕδωρ*, “and he stirred the water”—that is, the angel. So Vercelli, Corbie, Verona, Gatianus, and the manuscripts.

16. **Therefore the Jews persecuted Jesus.** Greek manuscripts add *καὶ ἐζήτουν αὐτὸν ἀποκτεῖναι*, “and they sought to kill him.” So Brescia.

27. **And gave him authority also to execute judgment.** Greek: [Col. 0880D] *καὶ κρίσιν ποιεῖν*, “and to execute judgment.” Brescia: “and authority of executing judgment.”

28. **They shall hear the voice of the Son of God.** Greek: *ἀκούσονται τῆς φωνῆς αὐτοῦ*, “they shall hear his voice.” So Vercelli, Gatianus, the manuscripts, Verona, and Brescia. Three or more Greek manuscripts in v. 25 read only *ἀκούσονται τῆς φωνῆς τοῦ Θεοῦ*, “they shall hear the voice of God,” not, as others have, *τοῦ Υἱοῦ τοῦ Θεοῦ*, “of the Son of God.”

30. **But the will of him who sent me.** Greek adds *πατρός*, “Father.” So Verona and Brescia.

46. **You would perhaps believe me also.** Greek: *ἐπιστεύετε ἂν ἐμοί*, “you would believe me.” Vercelli: “you would also believe me.”

### Chapter VI

1. **Across the Sea of Galilee, which is [the sea] of Tiberias.** Greek: *πέρας τῆς θαλάσσης τῆς Γαλιλαίας τῆς Τιβεριάδος*, “across the Sea of Galilee, [the sea] of Tiberias.” So Vercelli. In the Cantabrigian manuscript: *εἰς τὰ μέρη τῆς Τιβεριάδος*, “into the region of Tiberias,” as in Verona.

11. **Jesus therefore took the loaves.** Greek: *ἔλαβε δέ*, “but he took.” So Verona.

[Col. 0881A] 11. **He distributed [them] to those reclining.** Greek: *δέδωκε τοῖς μαθηταῖς, οἱ δὲ μαθηταὶ τοῖς ἀνακειμένοις*, “he gave to the disciples, and the disciples to those reclining.” Verona has: “and he gave to his disciples, and the disciples to those reclining.”

12. **That they should not perish.** Greek: *ἵνα μή τι ἀπόληται*, “that nothing may perish.” So Vercelli; Brescia and Verona likewise read “that nothing of them may perish.”

15. **He fled again.** Greek: *ἀνεχώρησε πάλιν*, “he withdrew again.” So Verona and Brescia.

22. Because there was no other small boat there except the one. The Greek reads: *ei mē hen ekeino eis ho anebēsan hoi mathētai autou*, “except that one into which his disciples embarked.” Verc. has: “except one, into which Jesus’ disciples had embarked.” In the Cambridge manuscript one likewise reads … *mathētai Iēsou*, “Jesus’ disciples.”

23. But other boats arrived. Greek: *alla de ēlthe ploiaria*, “but other boats came.” Thus Verc. and Brix.: “but other boats came.” The Greek Cambridge codex has *allōn ploiariōn elthontōn*, “other boats having come.”

24. They embarked in the small boats. Greek: *enebēsan kai autoi eis ta ploia*, “they too entered the boats.” In Cambridge one reads, *elabon heautois ploiaria*, “they took small boats for themselves.” In Veron.: “they took small boats for themselves.”

26. Not because you saw signs. Greek: *sēmeia*, “signs.” The Cambridge manuscript adds *kai terata*, “and wonders.” So too Verc., Gat., Veron., and Brix.

“And you have seen me, and do not believe.” The Alexandrian codex has *kai heōrakate, kai ou pisteuete*, “and you have seen, and do not believe.” Veron.: “and you saw, but do not believe.” Verc.: “and you see, and do not believe.”

37. I will not cast out. The Cambridge codex does not have “out” (*exō*), nor do Verc. or Veron.

45. Everyone who has heard from the Father. Greek: *pas oun ho akousas*, “therefore everyone who has heard.” But another reading has *akouōn*, “who hears,” as Verc., Veron., and Gat. have.

52. And the bread which I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world. Greek: *kai artos de hon egō dōsō, hē sarx mou estin, hēn egō dōsō hyper tēs tou kosmou zōēs*, “and indeed the bread which I shall give is my flesh, which I shall give for the life of the world.” Brix. reads thus: “For this bread, which I shall give, is my flesh, which I shall give for the life of this world.”

[Col. 0881C]

56. Truly is food … truly is drink. One of Stephanus’s manuscripts does not have *alēthōs*, “truly,” but has *alēthēs*, “true,” in both places; so too the manuscripts cited by Leontius and Apollinaris in the Catena.

57. And I in him. The Cambridge manuscript adds: *ean mē labēte to sōma tou huiou tou anthrōpou, hōs ton arton tēs zōēs, ouk echete zōēn en autō*, “unless you receive the body of the Son of Man as the bread of life, you do not have life in him.” Verc. and Corb. read: “If a man receives the body of the Son of Man as the bread of life, he will have life in him.” But Corb. has “in him” in place of “in it.”

60. In Capernaum. The Cambridge manuscript and another of Stephanus add *sabbatō*, “on the Sabbath.” Some Latin writers accordingly read, “teaching on the Sabbath in Capernaum,” as Verc. and Corb.

70. Because you are Christ, the Son of God. Greek: *tou Theou tou zōntos*, “of the living God.” Corb. has “of the living God.”

## CHAPTER VII

8. You go up to this feast. Greek: *eis tēn heortēn tautēn*, “to this feast.” But some copies omit *tautēn*, “this,” as do Verc. and Veron.

8. But I am not going up to this feast. [Col. 0881D] Greek: *egō oupō anabainō eis tēn heortēn tautēn*, “I am not yet going up to this feast.” Brix. has: “But I am not yet going up to this feast.” Thus almost innumerable Greek codices read, especially that most ancient Vatican manuscript, famed throughout the whole world.

9. Having said these things, he himself remained in Galilee. Greek: *tauta de eipōn autois* (Verc., “Saying these things to them”; Brix., “But he said these things to them”; Corb., “Having said these things to them”), *emeinen en tē Galilaia*, “but having said these things to them, he remained in Galilee.”

13. Yet no one spoke openly about him. Greek: *oudeis mentoi parrēsia*. Brix.: “Yet no one spoke boldly,” etc.

26. Have the rulers truly recognized that this is the Christ? Greek: *mēpote alēthōs egnōsan hoi archontes hoti houtos estin alēthōs ho Christos*, “Have the rulers perhaps truly recognized that this is truly the Christ?” [Col. 0882A] So too Brix. Corb.: “Have they perhaps truly recognized …” Likewise at verse 41 some Greek manuscripts have *houtos estin alēthōs ho Christos*, “this is truly the Christ,” where the Latin edition has only “this is the Christ.”

35. Of the Gentiles … the Gentiles. Greek: *Hellēnōn* and *Hellēnas*, “of Greeks” and “Greeks.” So too Verc., Corb., and Veron.

52. Are you also a Galilean? Greek: *mē kai sy ek tēs Galilaias ei*, “Are you not also from Galilee?” Brix. has: “Are you also from Galilee?”

52. Search the Scriptures and see. Greek: *ereunēson, kai ide*, “search and see.” So Gat., Mm., and Brix. Yet Cambridge reads *ereunēson tas Graphas*, “search the Scriptures.”

## CHAPTER VIII

6. He wrote with his finger on the ground. Greek: *eis tēn gēn*, “onto the ground.” So Corb., Gat., and the manuscripts. Some Greek manuscripts add *mē prospoioumenos*, “not pretending, not feigning”; that is, actually condemning them. Others, on the contrary, have *kai prospoioumenos*, “and assuming this for himself,” namely, by authority. For the word admits both meanings.

[Col. 0882B]

10. And the woman standing in the midst. Greek: *hestōsa*, “standing.” But the Cambridge manuscript has *ousa*, “being.” Corb. reads “was.” Other Greek witnesses omit the word altogether.

12. He who follows me does not walk in darkness. Greek: *ou mē peripatēsei en tē skotia*, “will certainly not walk in darkness.” So Veron.

19. Perhaps you would also know my Father. This particle “perhaps” is not one of doubt but of affirmation. Here “perhaps” has the same force as “certainly,” as is read in Verc.; Veron. and the Greek codices support this reading, since the word is absent from them.

25. The beginning, which I also speak to you. The obscurity of this passage, as it appeared to interpreters, arose from the Greek reading, which is certainly perplexing. It is as follows: *tēn archēn ho ti kai lalō hymin*, “the beginning, what I also speak to you.” Brix. has: “The beginning, which I also speak to you.” Veron.: “first of all, because I speak to you.” Gat. and Mm.: “The beginning, which I speak.”

27. And they did not understand that he was calling his Father God. Greek: *hoti ton patera autois elegen*, “that he was speaking to them of the Father.” Verc. [Col. 0882C] reads: “that he was speaking to them of the Father.” Brix.: “because he was speaking to them about the Father.” Veron.: “that he was speaking to them about … the Father.” Gat. and Mm.: “he was speaking to them of the Father.” Thus the Latin translator may have read *autois*, “to them,” in place of *autou*, “his.” The Syriac does so as well. The Cambridge manuscript has: *hoti ton patera autou legei ton Theon*, “that he calls his Father God.”

28. As the Father taught me. Greek: *ho patēr mou*, “my Father.” So Brix. But *mou*, “my,” is not present in Cambridge.

29. And he has not left me alone. Greek adds *ho patēr*, “the Father.” So Brix. But the word is not present in Cambridge.

38. And you, what you have seen. Greek: *kai hymeis oun ho heōrakate*, “and you therefore, what you have seen.” Verc.: “and you therefore what you have seen.” The Cambridge manuscript reads *ha ēkousate*, “what you have heard.” So too Brix.

39. If you are Abraham’s children, do the works of Abraham. Greek: *ei tekna tou Abraam ēte, ta erga tou Abraam epoieite an*, “if you were Abraham’s children, you would do the works of Abraham.” So Verc. and Brix.

45. But because I speak the truth, you do not believe me. [Col. 0882D] Greek: *egō de hoti tēn alētheian legō, ou pisteuete moi*. Gat. reads: “But because I speak the truth …” Verc., Veron., and Corb.: “Because I speak the truth, you do not believe me.”

49. And you dishonor me. Greek: *kai hymeis atimazete me*, “and you dishonor me.” So Corb. Verc. has “you do not honor.” Veron., “you dishonor.”

59. And he went out of the temple. Greek adds: *dielthōn dia mesou autōn, kai parēgen houtōs*, “passing through their midst, and thus he went on.” Brix. has: “passing through their midst, he went on.” These words are not in the Cambridge manuscript, but occur in the Syriac and Arabic.

## CHAPTER IX

1. And Jesus, passing by. In Greek, “Jesus” is absent, as it is in Verc., Veron., and Brix.

2. His disciples. Greek adds *legontes*, “saying.” So Verc., Veron., and Brix.

7. Siloë. Greek has *Siloam*, “Siloam.” So Verc. and Veron.

8. Those who had previously seen him, because he was a beggar. [Col. 0883A] Greek: *hoti typhlos ēn*, “because he was blind.” Verc.: “because he was blind and a beggar.” Veron.: “because he was a beggar and blind.”

11. The man who is called Jesus. Greek: *anthrōpos legomenos Iēsous*, “a man called Jesus.” So Verc., Veron., and Brix.

16. This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath. Greek: *hoti to sabbaton ou tērei*, “because he does not keep the Sabbath.” Brix. has: “because he does not observe the Sabbath.” Verc. and Veron.: “that,” etc.

17. What do you say of him, because he opened your eyes? Greek: *hoti ēnoixe*, “because he opened.” So Brix.; Verc. has “that he opened.”

22. That if anyone confessed him to be Christ. The verb “to be” is absent from Greek and is not read in Veron., Verc., or Brix.

27. I have already told you, and you heard. Greek: *kai ouk ēkousate*, “and you did not hear.” So Gat., Brix., and Verc.

30. The man answered. Greek: *apekrithē ho anthrōpos*, “the man answered.” So Verc., without the pronoun [Col. 0883B] *ekeinos*, “that one.”

38. And falling down, he worshipped him. In Greek the word “falling down” is absent, as it is in Verc.

## CHAPTER X

8. All, as many as came. Greek: *pantes hosoi pro emou ēlthon*, together with Gat.: “… came before me.”

10. And that they may have more abundantly. Greek: *kai perisson echōsin*. Mm.: “and that they may have more.”

11. For his sheep. In Greek the pronoun “his” is absent, as it is in Verc. and Brix. Likewise in verse 15, where “for my sheep” is read, “my” is absent in Greek and in Verc.

13. He does not care for the sheep. Greek: *ou melei autō peri tōn probatōn*, “there is no concern for the sheep in him.” So Brix.

25. I speak to you. Greek: *eipon hymin*, “I told you.” So Verc. Yet the Cambridge manuscript reads *lalō hymin*, “I speak to you.”

26. You are not of my sheep. Greek adds *kathōs eipon hymin*, “as I told you.” So Verc., Veron., [Col. 0883C] and Brix., as well as the Syriac and all Greek codices.

31. The Jews therefore took up stones. Greek: *ebastasan oun palin lithous hoi Ioudaioi*, “the Jews therefore again took up stones.” So Brix. Yet *palin*, “again,” is not in the Cambridge manuscript.

## CHAPTER XI

28. Secretly. Greek: *lathra*, “secretly, covertly.” So Brix. But Cambridge has *siōpē*, “in silence.”

29. She rises. Greek: *egeiretai*, “she rises.” Cambridge has *egerthē*, “she arose.” So Verc., Veron., and Brix.

37. Who opened the eyes of the blind man born. Greek: *tous ophthalmous tou typhlou*, “the eyes of the blind man,” without the word “born.” So Verc., Veron., and Brix.

41. Therefore they took away the stone. Greek adds *hou ēn* (“where he had been”) *tethnēkōs keimenos*, “lying dead” (Brix.: “where he had been”).

41. Having lifted up on high. Some manuscripts have, in place of “on high,” *eis ton ouranon*, “to heaven,” as Brix. Veron. has “toward heaven.”

45. Those who had come to Mary and Martha. The Greek does not have “and Martha”; it is likewise absent from Verc., [Col. 0883D] Veron., Brix., Gat., and Mm.

## CHAPTER XII

1. Where Lazarus had died, whom Jesus raised. Greek reads: *hopou ēn Lazaros ho tethnēkōs, hon ēgeiren ek nekrōn*, “where Lazarus was, who had died, whom he raised from the dead.” Brix. has: “where Lazarus was, who had died, whom Jesus raised from the dead.” Veron.: “where Lazarus was, who had died, whom he raised.”

4. Judas Iscariot. Greek: *Ioudas Simōnos Iskariōtēs*, “Judas, son of Simon Iscariot.” So Corb., but it reads *Iscariotis* in place of *Iscariotes*. Brix.: “Simon Schariotes.” Verc.: “Simon … Scarioth.” Veron.: “Simon Scariotes.”

6. Not because he cared about the needy. Greek: *ouch hoti peri tōn ptōchōn emelen autō*, “not because he cared for the poor.” Brix.: “not because he had concern for the poor.” Verc. and Corb.: “not that he had concern for the poor.”

Ibid. And having the money-box. Greek: *glōssokomon*. Brix.: “a money-box.”

7. Let her keep it for the day of my burial. [Col. 0884A] Greek: *aphes autēn, eis tēn hēmeran tou entaphiasmou mou tetērēken auto*, “let her be; she has kept it for the day of my burial.” So Brix., though it reads “on the day” instead of “for the day.” Veron. and the manuscripts also have “let [her be],” etc. Grotius and others prefer the Greek edition to the Latin. Yet the Latin is supported by the Cambridge and Vatican codices and others, which read: *hina eis tēn hēmeran tou entaphiasmou mou tērēsē auto*, “that she may keep it for the day of my burial.”

17. When he called Lazarus. Greek: *hoti*, “because.” Veron.: “because”; Verc.: “since,” etc.

19. Because we gain nothing. Greek: *ōpheleite*, “you profit.” So Verc.; Veron. has “you benefit.”

20. Certain Gentiles. Greek: *Hellēnes*, “Greeks.” So Verc., Corb., and Veron.

26. My Father will honor him. In Greek “my” is absent, as it is in Veron. and Brix.

28. Glorify your name. The Cambridge manuscript reads: *doxason (ton huion sou) en tē doxē hē eichon para soi pro touton kosmon genesthai*, “glorify your Son (so too in the manuscripts) in the glory which I had with you before this world came to be.”

[Col. 0884B]

31. Now is the judgment of the world. Greek adds *toutou*, “of this,” as do Verc. and Brix.

47. And has not kept. Greek: *kai mē pisteusē*, “and does not believe.” So Brix. Yet Alexandrian and Cambridge read *kai mē phylaxē*, “and has not kept.”

## CHAPTER XIII

24. And he said to him: Who is it? Greek: *pythesthai tis an eiē*, “to ask who it might be.” Verc. has: “Ask who it is.” Brix. and Corb.: “Ask who it is.”

27. Satan entered into him. Greek: *tote eisēlthen*, “then he entered.” Brix. and Gat. likewise read “then,” etc.

## CHAPTER XIV

1. You believe in God, and believe in me. Greek: *pisteuete eis ton Theon, kai eis eme pisteuete*, “Believe in God, and believe in me.” So Veron., Verc., Gat., and Mm.: “Believe in God,” etc. But Verc. has: “and you believe in me.” The Greek form *pisteuete* is ambiguous: it can be either indicative or imperative.

[Col. 0884C]

9. He who sees me sees the Father also. Greek: *ho heōrakōs eme, heōrake ton Patera*, “he who has seen me has seen the Father.” So Veron., Verc., and Brix., though they add “also” before “Father.” In Brix. “me” follows “who.”

10. You do not believe. Greek: *ou pisteueis*, “you do not believe.” So Verc., Veron., and Brix.

11. You do not believe. Greek: *pisteuete moi*, “believe me.” So Verc., Veron., and Brix.

## CHAPTER XV

2. He will take it away. Greek: *airei auton*, “he takes it away.” So Veron., Brix., and Verc. And shortly after, *kathairei*, “he cleanses,” with Verc. and Brix.

15. I will no longer call you. Greek: *ouketi hymas legō*, “I no longer call you.” So Verc., Veron., Brix., and Gat.; but the manuscripts have “… I call you.”

## CHAPTER XVI

2. To render service to God. Greek: *latreian prospherein tō Theō*, “to offer worship [or sacrifice] to God.” So Verc.

9. They did not believe in me. Greek: *ou pisteuousin*, “they do not believe,” etc. So Corb. and Veron.

[Col. 0884D]

13. He will teach you all truth. Greek: *hodēgēsei hymas eis pasan tēn alētheian*, “he will lead you into all truth.” So Verc. and Corb.; Veron. has “he will lead you into all truth.” Brix.: “he will guide you into all truth.”

20. But your sorrow will be turned into joy. Greek: *hē lypē hymōn eis charan genēsetai*. Brix. reads: “will become joy.”

22. No one will take [it] from you. Greek: *oudeis airei aph’ hymōn*, “no one takes [it] from you.” So Veron. Brix. likewise reads “takes away.”

## CHAPTER XVIII

5. Nazarene. Greek: *Nazōraion*. Veron. and Brix.: “Nazorean.”

## CHAPTER XIX

3. And they came to him. These words are absent from the Greek codices and from Brix.

34. He opened his side. Greek has *enyxe*, “he wounded [or pierced].” So Veron.; Verc. and Corb. have “struck.”

37. They will look upon him whom they pierced. In the Greek Septuagint of Zechariah 12:10 [Col. 0885A] one reads: *kai epiblepsontai pros me anth’ hōn katōrchēsanto*, “and they shall look upon me because—or for the reason that—they insulted [me].” But Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion have *eis hon exekentēsan*, “upon him whom they pierced.” Verc., Veron., and Corb.: “whom they pricked [pierced].”

## CHAPTER XX

1. And he saw. Greek: *blepei*, “he sees.” So Verc. and Brix.

20. And the side. Greek: *kai tēn pleuran autou*, “and his side.” So Gat. and Veron.

25. The mark of the nails. Greek: *ton typon tōn hēlōn*, “the imprint of the nails.” So Veron. Similarly, where the Latin reads, “and put my finger into the place of the nails,” Greek has *eis ton typon tōn hēlōn*, “into the imprint of the nails.” The author of our Latin Vulgate edition read *topon*, “place,” rather than *typon*, “imprint.”

## CHAPTER XXI

12. And none of those reclining dared. Greek: “… *etolma tōn mathētōn*.” Verc. and Brix.: “any of the disciples dared.” Veron.: “those reclining dared.”

22. Thus I will that he remain. Greek: *ean auton thelō menein*, “if I will that he remain.” So Brix.

# ST LUKE

[Col. 0885B]

## CHAPTER I

2. And they were ministers of the word. Greek: *tou logou*, “of the word.” Brix.: “of the Word.”

3. It seemed good to me also. In one Greek Canterbury manuscript, this passage adds *kai Pneumati hagiō*, “and to the Holy Spirit,” as also in Veron.

12. And fear fell upon him. Greek: *enepesen*. Veron. and Brix. read “fell.”

29. When she had heard. In Greek: *hē de idousa*, “but she, having seen.” Gat.: “but she herself, when she had seen.” Veron., Verc., Brix., and Corb. likewise read: “but she herself, when she saw.”

29. What sort of greeting this might be. At this point the Canterbury manuscript adds *hoti houtōs eulogēsen autēn*, “because he had thus blessed her.” Veron., Brix., and Corb. read: “because he had thus blessed him.” Verc. seems also to have had this reading, although some letters are now obliterated and can no longer be read.

35. That which shall be born. Greek: *to gennōmenon*, “that which is being born.” [Col. 0885C] So Gat. But it seems that the angel used the future tense, “that which shall be born.” For this passage concerns not Christ’s conception, but his very birth; otherwise the angel would have said “that which is in you,” not “that which is from you,” as in Matthew 1:20: “For that which has been born in her.”

50. And his mercy is from generation unto generations, to those who fear him; as in Psalm 102:17: “But the mercy of the Lord is from eternity and unto eternity upon those who fear him.” In Greek: *kai to eleos autou eis geneas geneōn*. Verc. and Veron. have: “and his mercy unto ages of ages.” Other manuscripts read *eis genean kai genean*, with Corb. and Brix.: “unto generation and generation.”

63. John is his name. Here the Cambridge manuscript adds *kai parachrēma elythē hē glōssa autou*, “and immediately his tongue was loosed.” Verc. likewise has: “and immediately his tongue was loosed.” Likewise Veron. and Corb.: “and at once his tongue was released.” Therefore, in the following verse, they omit the words “and immediately his tongue.”

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 0885D]

2. By the governor. Greek reads: *hēgemoneuontos tēs Syrias Kyrēniou*, “while Quirinius was governing Syria.” Those who wished “the whole world” in the first verse to mean the whole Roman empire judged that this registration of the whole world, as it is called in this second verse, could not have been said to have been made “by the governor of Syria.” They therefore deleted the preposition “by” from their copies, so that it would be understood only to have been made at the time when he was governor of Syria, but not by him.

4. Into Judaea. Cambridge manuscript: *eis gēn Iouda*, “into the land of Judah.” Verc.: “into the land of Judaea.”

9. Stood beside them. In Greek, *epestē autois*, “stood beside them.” So Brix.

The same verse. And the glory of God. Greek: *doxa Kyriou*, “glory of the Lord.” Verc. and Brix. likewise read “of the Lord.”

17. Concerning this child. Greek: *peri tou paidiou toutou*. But *toutou*, “this,” is absent from the Cambridge manuscript, Verc., and Brix.

[Col. 0886A]

18. And all who heard wondered, and at the things that had been told them by the shepherds. In Greek: *ethaumasan peri tōn lalēthentōn*, etc., “they wondered at the things that had been told,” etc.; the conjunction “and” is deleted. It is likewise absent from Verc., Veron., and Brix.

25. And the Holy Spirit was in him. Greek: *ep’ auton*, “upon him.” So Verc.

27. His parents. No Greek manuscripts have “his”; they have only *goneis*, “parents,” before *to paidion*, as does Verc.

33. And his father and mother. In Greek: *kai ēn Iōsēph kai hē mētēr autou*, “and Joseph and his mother were.” So Verc., Corb., Veron., and Brix. But the Cambridge manuscript reads *kai ēn patēr kai hē mētēr*, without *autou*, “his.”

34. And as a sign that will be contradicted. Greek: *antilegomenon*. Verc.: “which is contradicted.”

38. The redemption of Israel. Greek codices and the Gothic version have *lytrōsin en Ierousalēm*, “redemption in Jerusalem.” Veron. and Brix. read “the redemption of Jerusalem.” So Corb.: “Jerusalem.”

[Col. 0886B]

40. And he grew strong. Brix.: “he grew strong in spirit,” as St Luke himself also has in chapter 1:80 concerning John: “But the child grew and became strong in spirit.” In Holy Scripture, the verb “to grow strong” is sometimes understood of bodily strength, as in Acts 9:19: “And when he had taken food, HE WAS STRENGTHENED.” Therefore some Greek manuscripts read here *ekrataiouto pneumati*, “he grew strong in spirit.” Yet the Cambridge manuscript does not show this word.

42. According to the custom of the feast day. The Cambridge manuscript adds *tōn Azymōn*, “of Unleavened Bread.” So Verc.: “of Unleavened Bread.”

43. His parents. In Greek: *Iōsēph kai hē mētēr autou*, “Joseph and his mother,” as in verse 33. So Corb., Veron., and Brix. Cambridge has *hoi goneis autou*, “his parents.”

45. Seeking. Greek: *zētountes*. Verc. and Veron.: “searching.” Cambridge: *anazētountes*, “searching for.”

## CHAPTER III

7. That they might be baptized by him. In the Cambridge manuscript: *enōpion autou*, “before him.” So Veron.

[Col. 0886C]

8. And do not begin to say. In the common Greek text: *kai mē arxēsthe legein en heautois*. Brix.: “and do not begin to say within yourselves.” Cambridge: *kai mē doxēte legein en heautois*, “and do not suppose that you may say within yourselves.”

10. What then shall we do? The Cambridge manuscript adds *hina sōthōmen*, “that we may be saved,” which is repeated again in verse 14. Veron. and Gat. have “that we may live.”

14. But while the people were expecting. In Greek, including Cambridge: *prosdokōntos de tou laou*. Brix.: “but while the people were hoping.” Some suppose that the Vulgate translator read *dokountos*, “supposing,” for *prosdokōntos*, “expecting,” or that a Latin copyist wrote *existimante* (“supposing”) for *exspectante* (“expecting”).

16. But will come. In the common Greek text: *erchetai de*, “but he comes.” In Verc., Brix., and Gat.: “but he comes.” In Cambridge: *ho de erchomenos*, “but he who comes.” Thus wherever the Latin edition reads “he who is to come,” Greek has *ho erchomenos*, “the one who comes.”

19. His brother’s. The common Greek text adds *Philippou*, “Philip’s,” a word lacking from quite many other Greek manuscripts, as also from our Latin witnesses Veron., Verc., and Brix.

## CHAPTER IV

1. He was led by the Spirit. Greek: *ēgeto en tō pneumati*, “he was led in the Spirit.” So Corb. and Brix.

2. For forty days, and he was tempted by the devil. Greek: *hēmeras tessarakonta peirazomenos*, “being tempted for forty days.” Verc.: “for forty days while he was tempted.” Veron.: “for forty days he was tempted.” Gat.: “he is tempted.”

The same verse. He was hungry. Greek: *hysteron epeinasen*, “afterward he was hungry.” So Brix. Yet Cambridge lacks *hysteron*, “afterward.”

3. Tell this stone to become bread. Cambridge: *hina hoi lithoi houtoi artoi genōntai*, “that these stones may become loaves.” Verc. likewise seems to have read “that loaves may be made.” Perhaps from Matthew.

5. The world. In the common Greek text: *tēs oikoumenēs*, “the inhabited world.” Cambridge has *kosmou*, “of the world”; so Brix., from Matthew.

8. He says to him. Here the common Greek books add *hypage opisō mou, Satana*, “Go behind me, Satan,” with Veron.: “go behind me, Satan.”

[Col. 0887A]

15. And he was glorified. Greek: *doxazomenos*. Verc. reads “receiving honor.”

18. To heal the broken in heart.

19. To proclaim release to captives, and sight to the blind, to send forth the broken in release. Origen, Eusebius, Augustine, and Bede omit the former clause; Theophylact omits the latter while retaining the former. Jerome, in his commentary on Isaiah 61, when citing this passage of Luke, preserves both. Some Greek manuscripts cited by Lucas Brugensis, and the Cambridge codex, omit “to heal the broken in heart,” together with Verc., Veron., and Corb., although it occurs in Isaiah.

38. Into Simon’s house. The Cambridge manuscript adds *kai Andreou*, “and Andrew’s.” So Corb. and Veron., from Mark 1:29.

The same verse. With severe fevers. In Greek: *synechomenē* (in Cambridge, *katechomenē*) *pyretō*, “held by a severe fever,” as Verc. has. Corb. likewise reads the singular, “with a fever.”

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 0887B]

1. When the crowds pressed upon him. Greek: *en tō ton ochlon epikeisthai autō*. Verc.: “while the crowd pressed upon him.”

2. They had disembarked. Greek: *apobantes ap’ autōn*. Brix.: “disembarking from them.”

5. Master. Greek: *epistata*: “one set over others, governor, commander, one who presides and commands, one appointed to give commands.” Yet the Cambridge manuscript has *didaskale*, “teacher,” with Verc.: “master.”

6. But the net was breaking. Cambridge: *hōste ta diktya rhēssesthai*, “so that the nets were breaking.” Brix. likewise has: “so that the nets were breaking.”

7. So that they were nearly sinking. In the common Greek text “nearly” is absent, as it is in Verc., Corb., Veron., and Brix. In the Cambridge manuscript there is *para ti*, “nearly.”

10. You will be catching alive. Greek: *esē zōgrōn*. Veron. and Verc. have: “you will be making alive.” Corb. likewise reads “making alive.”

21. Except God alone? Greek: *ei mē monos ho Theos*. [Col. 0887C] Cambridge: *ei mē heis ho Theos*, “except one God.” So Verc.

## CHAPTER VI

10. And his hand was restored. Greek adds *hygiēs hōs hē allē*, “whole like the other.” Brix. likewise has “like the other,” and Veron. “like another,” from Matthew 12:13. In the Alexandrian manuscript and others only *hygiēs*, “whole,” is added.

17. And Tyre. The conjunction *kai*, “and,” is absent in Greek and in Verc., Corb., and Brix.

42. Not seeing the beam in your own eye. Cambridge: *kai idou hē dokos en tō sō ophthalmō hypokeitai*, “and behold, the beam lies beneath [or is present] in your own eye.” Verc., Veron., and Corb. have: “and behold, in your eye” (Corb., “his eye”) “a beam” (Veron., “of a beam”) “lies beneath.”

45. The mouth speaks. Greek: *lalei to stoma autou*, “his mouth speaks.” So Corb., Veron., and Brix. Verc. has “that one’s.” But Cambridge lacks *autou*, “his.”

## CHAPTER VII

4. To Jesus. In the Cambridge manuscript *pros ton Iēsoun*, “to Jesus,” is absent, as it is also in Verc.; but it is read in the common Greek text.

[Col. 0887D]

9. To the crowd following him. Greek: *tō akolouthounti autō ochlō*. So Verc.: “to the crowd following him.”

The same verse. Amen, I say to you. “Amen” is absent from the common Greek text and from Veron., but is present in Cambridge.

The same verse. In Israel. Greek: *oude en tō Israēl*, “not even in Israel.” Brix.: “not even in Israel.” Cambridge: *oudepote*, “never.”

11. Thereafter. Greek: *en tē hexēs*, “on the following [day].” In the Alexandrian manuscript: *ēn tō hexēs*. Brix. reads “on the following day.”

12. And many of his disciples went with him. Greek: *hoi mathētai autou hikanoi*, with Veron.: “many of his disciples.” Hence some suppose that others besides the Twelve were then accompanying Jesus.

12. Behold, one dead. Greek: *kai idou*, “and behold.” So Brix., Veron., and Verc.

The same verse. To his mother. Greek: *tē mētri autou*, “to his mother.” So Brix. The dative signifies “an only son to his surviving mother,” not “one whom his mother had borne as an only child.”

16. They magnified God. Greek: *edoxazon*, “they glorified,” as above elsewhere. So Verc.

17. Into all Judaea. Greek: *en holē tē Ioudaia*. So Verc.: “in all Judaea.” Veron. likewise has “in all Judaea.”

21. And with plagues. Greek: *kai mastigōn*, with Verc.: “and with scourges.”

37. A woman who was a sinner in the city. Greek: *gynē en tē polei, hētis ēn hamartōlos*, “a woman in the city, who was a sinner.” So Verc. and Veron.

42. Which of them therefore loves him more? Greek: *tis oun autōn*. So Brix.: “which of them therefore,” etc.

44. I entered your house. Greek: *eisēlthon sou eis tēn oikian*, in agreement with Verc., Veron., and Brix.: “I entered” (Brix., “I went into”) “your house.”

## CHAPTER VIII

2. From evil spirits. In one Greek manuscript: *apo nosōn*, “from diseases.” In Brix.: “from infirmities,” etc.; in Veron.: “infirmities,” etc.

[Col. 0888B]

3. Who ministered to him. The common Greek text has *autō*, “to him.” But Cambridge and another manuscript of Robert Stephanus have *autois*, “to them,” as Brix. and Gat. read, and as is likewise found in the Syriac version, so that it may refer jointly to the apostles and to Christ.

4. But when a great crowd assembled. Greek: *syniontos dē ochlou*. Verc.: “but while the crowd was assembling.” Cambridge: *synelthontos*, “having assembled.”

The same verse. He spoke by a parable. Greek: *dia parabolēs*, “by a parable.” Cambridge: *eipe parabolēn tautēn pros autous*, “he spoke this parable to them.” Veron.: “he spoke such a parable to them.” Verc.: “he spoke a parable,” etc.

27. A certain man. Greek adds *ek tēs poleōs*, “from the city.” Veron. and Brix.: “from the city.”

28. When he saw Jesus. Greek: *idōn de ton Iēsoun*, “but seeing Jesus.” So Verc.

28. I beseech you. Greek: *deomai sou*. Verc.: “I implore you.”

42. And it happened, as he went, that he was pressed by the crowds. [Col. 0888C] Greek: *en de tō hypagein auton, hoi ochloi synepnigon auton*. Verc.: “as he went, the crowd … so as to suffocate him.” Corb.: “… he was pressed, so as to suffocate him.”

47. And she fell at his feet. Greek: *kai prospesousa autō*, “and having fallen before him.” Brix.: “and she fell before him.”

49. To the ruler of the synagogue. Greek: *para tou archisynagōgou*, “from the ruler of the synagogue.” So Verc. and Veron.

## CHAPTER IX

1. To the twelve apostles. Greek: *tous dōdeka mathētas autou*, “his twelve disciples.” So Veron. But the Cambridge and Alexandrian manuscripts, and many others, have only *tous dōdeka*, “the twelve.”

4. And do not depart from there. Greek: *kai ekeithen exerchesthe*, in agreement with Verc., Veron., and Corb.: “and from there” (Verc., “go out”) “depart.” But Luke 10:7: “Do not move from house to house.”

10. Which is Bethsaida. Greek: *eis topon erēmon poleōs kaloumenēs Bēthsaida*, in agreement with Verc. and Brix., which read: “into a desert place called” (Brix., “is called”) “Bethsaida.” Gat. likewise has “Bethsaida.” Veron., however, “Betsaida.”

13. Into all this crowd. Greek: *eis panta ton laon touton*, “into all this people.” So Verc.

28. And James and John. In Greek the order of names is reversed: *kai Iōannēn, kai Iakōbon*, “and John, and James.” So Veron., Verc., Brix., and Gat. But the Cambridge manuscript follows the Vulgate edition.

31. His departure. Greek is *tēn exodon*, “the departure.” So Brix.

36. And while the voice came to be. Greek: *kai en tō genesthai tēn phōnēn*, “and when the voice had come to be.” Verc.: “and when the voice came to be.”

38. I beseech you. Greek: *deomai sou*, “I implore you,” as Verc.

39. And it tears him apart. Greek: *sparassei auton*, “it tears him apart.” Verc.: “it tears him apart.”

44. In your hearts. Greek: *eis ta ōta hymōn*, [Col. 0889A] “into your ears.” Verc., Veron., Brix., and Corb. read “in your ears.”

48. This one is greater. Greek: *houtos estai megas*, “this one will be great.” Verc.: “this one is great.”

54. And consume them. Greek codices add *hōs kai Ēlias epoiēsen*, with Verc., Veron., and Brix.: “as Elijah” (Brix., “and Elijah”) “did.”

56. To destroy souls. Greek: *psychas anthrōpōn*, “the souls of human beings.”

57. Wherever you go. Greek adds *Kyrie*, “Lord.” So Brix.

## CHAPTER X

1. Seventy-two. The common Greek text has only *hebdomēkonta*, that is, “seventy.” So Veron., Brix., and the Syriac version. The Cambridge manuscript has *obʹ*, that is, “seventy-two.” Another manuscript has “seventy disciples.” Perhaps so that these might be compared with the seventy elders of Israel mentioned in Numbers 11:16, 24, 25, and with the seventy palm trees that grew in Elim beside the twelve springs, some Greek manuscript books read not LXXII but LXII in this passage of Luke.

[Col. 0889B]

6. It will return to you. Greek: *eph’ hymas*, etc. Verc. and Veron.: “upon you,” etc. But Cambridge has *eph’ hymas anastrepsei hē eirēnē hymōn*, “your peace will return upon you.”

11. Even the dust which has clung to us. Alexandrian and Cambridge: *eis tous podas hēmōn*, “upon our feet.” Brix.: “on our feet.” Verc.: “onto [our] feet.” Veron., Mm., and Vind.: “on our feet.”

17. Seventy-two. Greek has only “seventy,” as in verse 1. So Veron., Brix., and Vind.

19. And nothing will harm you. Greek: *hymas ou mē adikēsei*. Verc., Veron., and Vind.: “… will harm you.”

20. In heaven. Cambridge: *en tō ouranō*, “in heaven,” singular. So Verc., Veron., Brix., and Vindeb.

38. Into a certain town. Greek: *eis kōmēn tina*. Verc.: “into a certain village.”

## CHAPTER XI

2. Let your kingdom come. Greek here adds: “Let your will be done, as in heaven, so on [Col. 0889C] earth.” So Vindeb., Brix., and the Syriac version. Veron. likewise reads: “let your will be done in heaven and on earth.” Verc. has only: “let your will be done.”

4. Into temptation. The Greek codices add, so that the prayer here may be complete, as it is in Matthew, “but deliver us from evil.” Corb. and Veron. likewise have, “But deliver us from evil.” Vind. and Brix., “but rescue us” (Vind., “snatch us”) “from evil.”

7. In bed. Greek: εἰς τὴν κοίτην, “into bed.” And so Vind., “into the bedchamber.” Cambridge, however, has ἐν τῇ κοίτῃ, “in bed.”

11. “But which father among you, if his son asks for bread,” etc. Greek: τίνα δὲ ὑμῶν τὸν πατέρα αἰτήσει ὁ υἱός, “Which father among you will the son ask?” Brix. has, “Which father among you, if a son should ask?” Veron., “From which one among you will a son ask?” Vind. and Corb., “From which father among you will a son ask?” Gat., “A son asked a father among you.” The manuscripts: “Among you a son asked his father.”

15. In Beelzebub. Greek: ἐν Βεελζεβοὺλ, “in Beelzebul.” So also Vindeb. and Brix.; but Veron. and Gat. have “Belzebul.” Corb., however, “Belsebul.”

20. The kingdom of God has come upon you. Greek: ἔφθασεν ἐφ᾿ ὑμᾶς [Col. 0889D], “has come beforehand to you.” Veron. and Brix. have, “has come beforehand upon you,” etc.

41. That which remains. The Greek reads τὰ ἐνόντα. Some translate this word as “the things available,” “the things in your possession”; others, “the things existing within”; others, “the things which are,” as the Veronese codex has.

44. Woe to you. The Greek adds: γραμματεῖς, καὶ Φαρισαῖοι ὑποκριταί, “scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites.” So also Veron., Brix., and Vind., though the latter omits “hypocrites.”

49. I will send to them. Greek: εἰς αὐτούς, “to them.” So Vind. and Veron.

## CHAPTER XII

1. But with many crowds surrounding [him]. Greek: ἐπισυναχθεισῶν, “having been assembled.” Brix. has “when [they had] gathered.”

Ibid. Take heed. In Greek: πρῶτον προσέχετε ἑαυτοῖς, “first take heed to yourselves, concerning the leaven.” Brix. has, “first take heed to yourselves concerning the leaven.” Veron., “... to yourselves ...”; Verc. and Vind., “first ...”

[Col. 0890A] 2. But nothing. In Cambridge, οὐδὲν γάρ, “for nothing.” So also Verc.

3. Will be spoken in the light. Greek: ἐν φωτὶ ἀκουσθήσεται, “will be heard in the light.” So Brix.

3. In inner rooms. Greek: ἐν τοῖς ταμείοις, “in store-rooms.” So Vind.; as at verse 24, ταμεῖον means “store-room.”

12. What you ought to say. Greek: ἃ δεῖ εἰπεῖν, “the things which it is necessary to say.” Verc., Veron., Brix., and Vind. have, “the things which ought to be said.” Mm., “the things.”

18. And I will make larger ones. Greek: οἰκοδομήσω, “I will build.” So Verc. and Brix. But Cambridge reads ποιήσω, “I will make.”

20. Whose will they be? Greek: τίνι ἔσται, “to whom will they be?” So Vind. But Cambridge manuscript has τίνος ἔσται. The genitive denotes possession and ownership; the dative, use.

31. Seek first. That word “first” is not in the Greek; nor is it read in Veron., Verc., Brix., Corb., Gat., or Mm.

31. And his righteousness. These words too are absent from the Greek [Col. 0890B], and from Verc., Veron., Brix., and Vind.

35. In your hands. These words occur in no Greek codex, whether printed or manuscript, nor in Verc., Veron., Brix., or Gat.

39. At what hour the thief would come. Greek: ἔρχεται, “comes.” So Veron., Brix., and Vind.

42. Whom he appointed. Greek: ὅν καταστήσῃ, “whom he will appoint.” So Vind. and Brix.

49. And what do I desire, unless it be kindled? Greek: καὶ τί θέλω, εἰ ἤδη ἀνήφθη, “and what do I desire, if it has already been kindled?” Veron., Corb., and Vind., “and what do I desire, if it be kindled?” In Corb. and Vind., however, “etc.” is absent.

## CHAPTER XIII

4. At Siloam. Greek: ἐν τῷ Σιλωάμ. Brix. and Vind., “Siloam”; Gat., “Syloam.”

7. It occupies the ground. Greek: τὴν γῆν καταργεῖ, “it renders the ground unproductive.” Veron. and Corb. have, “it empties the ground.”

8. And this year. In the received Greek text: καὶ τοῦτο τὸ ἔτος, “and this year.” In Verc., “and this year.” In Cambridge, ἔτι τοῦτον τὸν ἐνιαυτόν, “yet this year.”

[Col. 0890C] 10. On the sabbaths. Cambridge has τῷ σαββάτῳ, “on the sabbath.” So Vind., “on the sabbath.”

Ibid. In their synagogue. Greek: ἐν μιᾷ τῶν συναγωγῶν, “in one of the synagogues.” So Veron.; but Brix. has, “in a certain synagogue.” The Cambridge manuscript, following the received edition, reads ἐν τῇ συναγωγῇ αὐτῶν, “in their synagogue.”

12. He called her to him. Greek: προσεφώνησε, simply, “he addressed [her].” Brix., Gat., Mm., and Vind. have, “he called [her] to himself.” But Cambridge omits the entire phrase, “he called her to himself.”

15. Hypocrite. Greek: ὑποκριτά, singular, “hypocrite.” So Brix.

16. A daughter of Abraham. Greek: θυγατέρα Ἀβραὰμ οὖσαν, “being a daughter of Abraham.” Verc., “since she is a daughter of Abraham.”

25. But when the master of the house has entered. Greek: ἀφ᾿ οὗ ἂν ἐγέρθη, “from the time when he rises.” Veron., “after he has risen.” Yet the Cambridge manuscript, following the received edition, has εἰσέλθῃ, “has entered.”

## CHAPTER XIV

2. A certain man with dropsy was before [Col. 0890D] him. In the received Greek: ἦν ὑδρωπικὸς ἔμπροσθεν αὐτοῦ, “there was a man with dropsy before him.” In the Cambridge manuscript the word “certain” is absent; so also in Veron. and Corb.

4. But he, having taken hold [of him]. Greek: καὶ ἐπιλαβόμενος, “and having taken hold.” Verc., “he therefore, taking hold [of him].”

8. When you have been invited. Greek adds ὑπὸ τίνος, “by someone.” So Veron. and Brix., “by someone.”

28. To complete it. Greek: τὰ πρὸς ἀπαρτισμόν, “the things needed for completion.” Verc. has, “the things necessary to finish it.” Brix., “the things necessary to complete it.”

33. All that he possesses. Greek: πᾶσι τοῖς ἑαυτοῦ ὑπάρχουσι, “all his own resources.” So Verc.

35. But it will be cast out. Greek, without the adversative particle “but”: βάλλουσιν αὐτόν, “they cast it out.” Veron. likewise has simply, “they will cast it out.”

## CHAPTER XV

1. Tax collectors. Greek: πάντες οἱ τελῶναι, “all the tax collectors.” So Verc., Brix., and Vind.

[Col. 0891A] 14. And after he had spent everything. Greek: δαπανήσαντος δὲ αὐτοῦ πάντα, “but after he had spent everything.” Verc. has, “and when he had spent everything.” Veron., Brix., and Vind., “... he spent ...”

17. Here I perish from hunger. The Greek lacks the adverb “here,” which indicates a place far removed from his father’s house. Thus it is written there also: πόσοι μίσθιοι πατρός μου, “how many hired servants of my father!” So Verc., Veron., Brix., Corb., Gat., and Mm. Vind. likewise has, “... hired servants of [my] father ...,” instead of the received Latin edition’s “in my father’s house.”

23. And let us eat. Greek: καὶ φαγόντες, “and, having eaten.” Brix., “and eating.”

25. And dancing. Greek: καὶ χορῶν, “and dances.” So Veron.

## CHAPTER XVI

1. He was accused. Greek: διεβλήθη. Vind. has, “he had been denounced.”

2. To act as steward. Greek: οἰκονομεῖν. Verc., “to administer.”

6. Take your bond. Greek: γράμμα, “a document” or “letter.” [Col. 0891B] So Veron. and Corb. It is called a *cautio* (“bond”) because by means of such a document the creditor is secured against the debtor’s denying the debt.

9. Mammon. The sequence and coherence (*ἀκολουθία*) of this discourse indicate that this Syriac word signifies riches. In the received Greek it is written μαμονᾶ; and so in Verc., Veron., and Brix. In the Cambridge manuscript, however, μαμμονᾶ.

14. Who were covetous. Greek: φιλάργυροι, “lovers of money.” Verc., “lovers of money.” Every love of money conjoined with avarice is condemned by God.

21. And no one gave to him. These words are absent from all Greek books, as also from Verc., Veron., and Brix.

22. And he was buried in hell. Greek: καὶ ἐτάφη, “and he was buried.” Veron. and Brix. have, “and he was buried.” A striking antithesis shines out in the received Latin text: the final lot of the beggar is excellently set against the equally final lot of the rich man. For the one is said to have been carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom; the other, not merely to have been buried, as the Greek [Col. 0891C] and two of our codices read, but to have been “buried in hell.”

24. Into water. Greek: ὕδατος, “water.” So Brix.

25. You received good things. Greek: ἀπέλαβες σὺ τὰ ἀγαθά, “you received your good things.” So Veron.

28. Into this place of torments. Greek: βασάνου, “of torment.” Verc., “of suffering.”

## CHAPTER XVII

14. As they went. Greek: ἐν τῷ ὑπάγειν αὐτούς, “while they were going.” Veron., Corb., and Vind. read, “while they go.”

16. Giving thanks. Greek adds αὐτῷ, “to him.” So Veron.

22. And he said to his disciples. The pronoun “his” is absent in all Greek books, and in Brix.

## CHAPTER XVIII

4. For a long time. Greek: ἐπὶ χρόνον, “for a time.” Verc., “for a time.”

5. She may blacken my eyes. Greek: ὑποπιάζῃ με, “may bruise my eyes with a black-and-blue mark.” Some Greek manuscripts have ὑποπιέζῃ με, “may press me hard.” Veron. and Corb. have, “may constrain me.”

[Col. 0891D] 7. And will he have patience with them? Greek: μακροθυμῶν ἐπ᾿ αὐτοῖς, “being patient with them.” Veron., Verc., and Vind., “having patience.” In the Alexandrian manuscript, μακροθυμεῖ. Thus in the Greek of Ecclesiasticus, chapter XXXV, verse 18 (the passage corresponding to the Latin edition, chapter XXXV, verse 22), one reads: οὐδὲ μὴ μακροθυμήσει ἐν αὐτοῖς, “nor will he be patient with them.”

8. Do you think? Greek: ἆρα, “indeed?” Veron. and Vind., “does he then?”

14. Justified ... rather than him. “Than him” clearly refers to that Pharisee, and has the same sense as “in preference to him.” The Greek reads ἢ ἐκεῖνος, “than that one.” So Veron., Brix., Gat., Corb., and Vind. Cambridge, however, has μᾶλλον παρ᾿ ἐκεῖνον τὸν Φαρισαῖον, “rather above that Pharisee”; in others, merely παρ᾿ ἐκεῖνον, “than that one.” Verc. has “before that one,” imitating Greek syntax.

20. And [your] mother. Greek adds σου, “your.” So Verc. and Veron.

## CHAPTER XIX

7. Had lodged. Greek: εἰσῆλθε καταλῦσαι [Col. 0892A], “entered to lodge.” Verc. has, “had entered to stay.” Brix., “entered to stay.”

15. Servants. Greek: τοὺς δούλους τούτους, “those servants.” Brix. reads, “those servants.”

Ibid. That he might know how much each had gained by trading. Greek: ἵνα γνῷ τίς τί διεπραγματεύσατο, “that he might know who had gained what by trading.” Verc. has, “that he might know what each had gained by trading.”

23. So that, when I came. Greek: καὶ ἐγὼ ἐλθών, “and I, having come.” So Veron. and Brix.

26. And he shall abound. This is absent from the Greek, as also from Verc., Brix., Corb., and Vind.

28. He went before. Greek: ἐπορεύετο, “he went.” So Verc.

37. The entire crowd of disciples. Greek: πᾶς ὄχλος, “the whole multitude.” So Verc.

39. From the crowds. Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ ὄχλου, “from the multitude,” as in verse 37. Verc. and Brix., “from the crowd.”

43. They will hem you in. Greek: συνέξουσι, “will confine you.” So Verc.

47. Of the people. Greek: λαοῦ. Verc., Brix., and Gat., “of the people.”

## CHAPTER XX

[Col. 0892B]

1. They came upon [him]. Greek: ἐπέστησαν. Verc. has, “they stood by.”

3. Answer me. Greek: καὶ εἴπατέ μοι, “and tell me.” So Brix.

20. Him in [his] speech. Greek: αὐτοῦ λόγου, “his speech.” Corb. and Vind., “his speeches”; Verc., “... his ...”

27. Who deny. Greek: οἱ ἀντιλέγοντες, “those who deny that there is a resurrection.” So Verc.

37. At the bush. Greek: ἐπὶ τῆς βάτου, “at the bush.” So Corb. and Brix.

## CHAPTER XXI

4. From what was superfluous to them. Greek: ἐκ τοῦ περισσεύοντος αὐτοῖς. Verc. has, “from that which was left over for them.” Brix., “from that which abounded to them.”

7. When these things begin to happen. Greek: ὅταν μέλλῃ ταῦτα γίνεσθαι, “when these things are about to happen.” Corb. and Vind., “when they will happen.”

14. Not to prepare beforehand how you are to answer. Greek: μὴ προμελετᾷν ἀπολογηθῆναι, “not to rehearse beforehand a defense.” Verc., “do not first meditate on how you are to render an account.”

16. By parents. Greek: καὶ ὑπὸ γονέων, “and by parents.” [Col. 0892C] So Verc.

23. Great distress. Greek: ἀνάγκη μεγάλη, “great necessity.” Verc., “great necessity.”

25. Distress of nations. Greek: συνοχὴ ἐθνῶν, “constriction of nations.” Verc., “compression of nations”; Brix., “collision of nations.”

26. Fainting away. Greek: ἀποψυχόντων. Verc. reads, “growing cold.”

Ibid. The powers of heaven will be shaken. Greek: αἱ γὰρ δυνάμεις τῶν οὐρανῶν σαλευθήσονται, “for the powers of the heavens will be shaken.” Cambridge: αἱ γὰρ δυνάμεις αἱ ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ, “for the powers which are in heaven.” Verc. and Corb., “for the powers” (Corb., “indeed, the powers”) “which are in heaven.”

27. With great power and majesty. Greek: μετὰ δυνάμεως καὶ δόξης πολλῆς, “with great power and glory.” Verc., “with great power and glory.”

30. Put forth [leaves]. Greek: προβάλωσιν, “they put forth.” Veron., “they may put forth.” The Greek then adds, which is absent from our Latin texts: βλέποντες ἐφ᾿ ἑαυτοῖς γινώσκετε, “seeing these things, you recognize for yourselves.”

## CHAPTER XXII

2. But they feared. Greek: ἐφοβοῦντο [Col. 0892D] γάρ, “for they feared.” So Verc. and Brix. Cambridge has, with the received edition, ἐφοβοῦντο δέ, “but they feared.”

3. Who was called. The Greek reads τὸν ἐπικαλούμενον, as in Verc., “who is called.” In Cambridge, τὸν καλούμενον.

3. Of the twelve. Greek: ἐκ τοῦ ἀριθμοῦ τῶν δώδεκα, “from the number of the twelve.” Verc., “from the number of the twelve.”

Ibid., 6. To betray him without crowds. Greek: ἄτερ ὄχλου, “without a crowd.” So Verc., Corb., Vindeb., and Veron.

7. To be sacrificed. Greek: θύεσθαι, “to be offered in sacrifice.” So Corb., Vindeb., and Brix.

26. Let him become as the younger. Greek: ὡς ὁ νεώτερος, “as the younger.” So Gat., Mm., and Brix. Veron. has, “the more youthful.”

51. Permit [them] as far as this. Verc., Corb., and Vind. have “as far as this,” instead of “as far as here,” corresponding to Greek μέχρι δεῦρο.

[Col. 0893A] 52. And the officers of the temple. The Greek codices at this point read στρατηγούς, “commanders.” Verc., “chief priests.”

## CHAPTER XXIII

10. Vehemently. Greek: εὐτόνως. Verc. has, “forcefully.”

11. With his army. Greek: σὺν τοῖς στρατεύμασιν αὐτοῦ, “with his forces.” So Veron. and Corb. Brix., however, has, “with his soldiers.”

16. Having punished [him]. Greek: παιδεύσας, “having disciplined [him].” Verc. reads, “having chastised [him].”

19. Thrown [into prison]. Greek: βεβλημένος. Verc., “cast.”

22. Therefore I will punish him and release him. Greek: παιδεύσας οὖν αὐτὸν ἀπολύσω, “therefore, having disciplined him, I will release him.” Verc., “therefore I will release him after chastising him.” Brix. has, “therefore, punishing him, I will release him.” See what we said on verse 16.

23. They pressed [their demand]. Greek: ἐπέκειντο, “they were pressing upon [him].” So Verc.

29. Days will come. Greek: ἔρχονται, “are coming.” So Mm. Cambridge has ἐλεύσονται, “will come.”

33. And the robbers. Greek: καὶ τοὺς κακούργους, “and the criminals.” So in verse 39: Greek has κακούργοις, “criminals.” [Col. 0893B] So Codex Verc. has it.

42. When you come into your kingdom. Greek: ὅταν ἔλθῃς ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ σου, “when you come in your kingdom.” So Verc.; Veron. has, “when you will come in your kingdom.”

48. And all the crowd. Greek: καὶ πάντες ὄχλοι, “and all the crowds.” Verc., “and all ... crowds.”

51. And their deeds. Greek: καὶ τῇ πράξει αὐτῶν, “and their action.” Verc. has, “and their work.”

51. A city of Judea. Greek: πόλεως τῶν Ἰουδαίων, “a city of the Jews.” So Verc. and Brix.

56. They were silent. Greek: ἡσύχασαν, “they were quiet.” So Verc. and Brix.

## CHAPTER XXIV

1. Of the sabbath. Greek: σαββάτων, “of the sabbaths.” So Verc., as in Mark XVI.2.

Ibid. The spices which they had prepared. The Greek codices add here, καί τινες σὺν αὐταῖς, “and certain others with them.” The Brixian codex also has, “and other women together with them.” The Syriac translator rendered, “and other women were with them.”

4. While they were bewildered in mind. Greek: ἐν τῷ διαπορεῖσθαι [Col. 0893C] αὐτὰς, “while they were perplexed.” Brix., “while they hesitated.”

11. These words. Greek: τὰ ῥήματα αὐτῶν, “their words.” So Brix.

20. To the condemnation of death. Greek: εἰς κρῖμα, “for judgment.” Verc., “in judgment.”

24. But they did not find him. Greek: αὐτὸν δὲ οὐκ εἶδον, “but they did not see him.” So Corb., Veron., and Brix., with which Verc. and Gat. agree, except that they read “but” instead of “indeed.” Cambridge has αὐτὸν δὲ οὐκ εἴδομεν, “but we did not see him.”

26. And thus to enter. In Greek books the adverb “thus” is absent; so also in Verc.

29. And he went in with them. Greek: καὶ εἰσῆλθε τοῦ μεῖναι σὺν αὐτοῖς, “and he went in to remain with them.” Gat., “and he went in to remain with them.” Verc., “and he went in, so that he might remain with them.” Brix., “and he went in with them, so that he might remain.” Veron., “and he went in with them, and remained.” The Cambridge manuscript reads similarly: καὶ εἰσῆλθε τοῦ μεῖναι μετ᾿ αὐτῶν, “and he went in to remain with them.” Some Greek manuscripts omit this entire clause.

30. And he handed [it] to them. Greek: καὶ ἐπεδίδου αὐτοῖς. [Col. 0893D] Brix. has, “and he gave [it] to them.”

31. He vanished. Greek: ἄφαντος ἐγένετο, “he became invisible.” Veron. and Brix., “he was made unseen.”

32. While he spoke on the road. The Greek adds ἡμῖν, “to us.” So Brix.

35. The things which had happened on the road. Greek: τὰ ἐν τῇ ὁδῷ, “the things on the road.” So Verc.

36. Jesus stood [among them]. Greek: καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἔστη, “and Jesus himself stood.” Gat. and Brix., “Jesus himself stood” (in Brix., “but” is absent). Verc. and Veron., “he himself stood.”

38. Arise in your hearts. Greek: ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις ὑμῶν, “in your hearts.” So Brix.

41. While they still disbelieved for joy and wondered. Greek: ἔτι δὲ ἀπιστούντων αὐτῶν ἀπὸ τῆς χαρᾶς, καὶ θαυμαζόντων, “but while they still disbelieved for joy and wondered.” So Brix.

43. And after he had eaten before them, taking the remains, he gave [the remains] to them. The Greek has only: Καὶ λαβὼν, ἐνώπιον αὐτῶν [Col. 0894A] ἔφαγεν, “and, having taken [it], he ate before them.” So Brix. and Verc. But Brix. reads *ipsis* (“themselves”) for *eis* (“them”); and Verc. places “before them” after “he ate.”

47. Beginning from Jerusalem. In the received Greek, ἀρξάμενον, “beginning.” In Verc., “beginning.” In Cambridge, ἀρξαμένων, “having begun.”

49. Remain in the city. Greek adds Ἱερουσαλήμ, “in the city of Jerusalem.” Brix. has, “in this city, Jerusalem.”

# MARK

## CHAPTER I

5. All. So Brix. alone. That word is absent from the Greek books.

10. And remaining. This is absent from the Greek, and from Verc. and Brix.

11. In you I am well pleased. Greek: ἐν ᾧ, “in whom.” So Veron. Cambridge has ἐν σοί, “in you.”

13. And forty nights. These words are absent from Greek books, as also from Verc., Corb., Veron., and Brix.

15. And believe the Gospel. Greek: ἐν Εὐαγγελίῳ, “in the Gospel.” So Verc.

18. Having left their nets. Greek adds αὑτῶν, “their own.” So Brix.

38. Into the neighboring villages and towns. Greek: εἰς τὰς ἐχομένας κωμοπόλεις, “into the neighboring market-towns.” Verc. reads, “into the neighboring villages.” Veron., “the adjoining villages.”

39. And in all Galilee. Greek: εἰς ὅλην τὴν Γαλιλαίαν, “into all Galilee.” So Verc., without “and.”

44. To the chief priest. Greek: τῷ ἱερεῖ, “to the priest.” So Verc., Veron., and Brix.

## CHAPTER II

2. And they gathered. Greek: καὶ εὐθέως συνήχθησαν, “and immediately they were gathered.” Verc. reads, “and immediately” (Brix., “and at once”) “they gathered.”

3. And they came. Greek: καὶ ἔρχονται, “and they come.” So Verc. and Veron.

5. Are forgiven. Greek: ἀφέωνται, “have been forgiven.” So Veron.; Brix., “have been forgiven.”

7. He blasphemes. Greek: τί οὗτος οὕτω λαλεῖ, “why does this man speak thus?” So Verc. and Brix.

[Col. 0894C] 16. Your teacher. These two words are absent from Greek, as also from Verc., Veron., and Corb.

17. The healthy. Greek: οἱ ἰσχύοντες, “the strong.” So Veron. Ibid. But sinners. Greek adds εἰς μετάνοιαν, “to repentance.” It is also found in Verc. and Vind., perhaps added from Luke.

26. Under Abiathar the chief priest. These words are absent from the Cambridge manuscript and also from Verc., Veron., and Vind.

## CHAPTER III

3. Rise into the midst. Greek in some manuscripts: ἐγέρθητι καὶ στῆθι ἐν μέσῳ, “rise and stand in the midst.” Brix., “rise, stand in the midst.”

5. And his hand was restored. Greek adds αὐτοῦ ὑγιὴς ὡς ἡ ἄλλη, “whole as the other,” perhaps from Matthew. Gat. has, “... his [hand], restored to health like the other.” Verc. and Veron., “his, like the other” (in Veron., “and” is absent).

10. Scourges. Greek: μάστιγας, “scourges.” Verc., “blows.”

21. He has gone out of his mind. Greek: ἐξέστη. Verc., Veron., Corb., and Vind. read, “he is beside himself.”

22. Beelzebub. Greek has Βεελζεβούλ. So Brix. [Col. 0894D] Vind., however, “Behelzebul”; Veron., “Belzebul.”

## CHAPTER IV

10. And those who were with him were the twelve. Greek: οἱ περὶ αὐτὸν σὺν τοῖς δώδεκα, “those around him with the twelve.” Brix. reads, “those who were with him together with the twelve.”

18. And others are. Greek: καὶ οὗτοί εἰσιν, “and these are.” Brix., “and these are.”

19. Cares. Greek: μέριμναι. So Corb., Veron., and Brix. Vind., however, has “anxiety.”

19. Of the age. Greek: τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου, “of this age.” So Brix.

24. And it will be added to you. Greek adds τοῖς ἀκούουσι, “to those hearing.” Brix. reads “to those believing” in place of “to those hearing.”

40. Who, do you think? Greek: τίς ἄρα, “who then?” Corb. and Vind., “who indeed?”

## CHAPTER V

2. He met. Greek adds αὐτῷ, “him.” So Brix. and Veron.

[Col. 0895A] 10. Lest [he send] them. Greek: ἵνα μὴ αὐτούς, “lest [he send] them.” Brix., Corb., and Vind. have, “lest ... them.”

12. Spirits. Greek: πάντες οἱ δαίμονες, “all the demons.” Verc., “all the demons.” Brix. has simply, “demons.”

13. It was hurled down. Greek: κατὰ τοῦ κρημνοῦ, “down the steep bank.” Veron., “headlong.”

13. About two thousand. Greek: ἦσαν γὰρ ὡς δισχίλιοι, “for they were about two thousand.” Verc. seems to have read, “but they were about two thousand.” Brix. and Vind. have, “but they were as it were two thousand.”

34. Go in peace. Greek: εἰς εἰρήνην, “into peace.” So Vindeb.

## CHAPTER VI

2. And miracles. Greek: ὅτι καὶ δυνάμεις, “that also miracles.” Brix. reads, “that miracles.”

26. To grieve [her]. Greek: ἀθετῆσαι, “to reject [her request].” Verc., “to refuse.”

27. But. Greek: καί, “and.” So Veron.

Ibid. And beheaded [him]. Greek: ὁ δὲ ἀπελθὼν ἀπεκεφάλισεν, “and he, having gone, beheaded [him].” Brix., “and he, going away, beheaded [him].” Verc. and Vind., “and when he had gone, he beheaded [him].” Veron., “and he went and beheaded [him].”

35. And the hour has already passed. Greek: καὶ ἤδη ὥρα [Col. 0895B] πολλή, “and the hour is already late.” Verc., “and the hour [is] now late,” etc.

51. And exceedingly more. Greek: καὶ λίαν ἐκ περισσοῦ, “and exceedingly beyond measure.” Veron. has, “and more abundantly.”

Ibid. They were astonished. Greek adds καὶ ἐθαύμαζον, “and they marveled.” So Veron. and Brix. Verc. reads, “with amazement.”

56. In the streets. Greek: ἐν ταῖς ἀγοραῖς, “in the marketplaces.” Verc., “in the forum.”

## CHAPTER VII

3. Often. Greek: πυγμῇ, literally “with the fist.” Corb. and Vind., “with the fist”; Veron., “repeatedly”; Verc., “for a moment.”

7. And commandments. In Greek “and” is absent, as also in Corb. and Veron.

14. The crowd. Greek: πάντα τὸν ὄχλον, “the whole crowd.” So Brix.

26. A Gentile woman. The Greek here is Ἑλληνίς, “a Greek woman.” So Verc., Corb., and Vind.

32. Mute. Greek: μογιλάλον, “having an impediment in speech.” Gat. has, “mugillatum” [an obscure transliteration].

37. He made [them] hear. Greek: ποιεῖ, “he makes,” etc. So Verc. and Brix.

## CHAPTER VIII

1. Having summoned the disciples. Greek adds ὁ Ἰησοῦς, “Jesus.” So Brix.

20. How many baskets full of fragments? Greek: πόσων σπυρίδων πληρώματα κλασμάτων, “how many baskets full of fragments?” Brix. reads, “how many baskets full of fragments?”

25. And he began to see. Greek: καὶ ἐποίησεν αὐτὸν ἀναβλέψαι, “and he made him look up.” So Brix. and Verc. (which, however, has “him” in another form).

26. And if you enter the village, tell no one. Greek: μηδὲ εἰς τὴν κώμην εἰσέλθῃς, μηδὲ εἴπῃς τινὶ ἐν τῇ κώμῃ, “do not even enter the village, nor tell anyone in the village.” Verc., “and do not enter the town, nor tell anyone,” omitting ἐν τῇ κώμῃ, “in the village.”

10. What then do they say? Greek: ὅτι λέγουσιν, “what do they say?” Veron. and Vind., “what they say.”

37. And we forbade him. Greek adds οὐκ ἀκολουθεῖ ἡμῖν, “because he does not follow us”; so Brix. Veron. and Verc. have, “who does not follow us” (Verc., “follow us”).

## CHAPTER X

17. That I may inherit eternal life. Greek: κληρονομήσω, “may inherit.” [Col. 0896A] Verc. and Brix., “may possess.”

21. And follow me. Greek adds ἄρας τὸν σταυρόν, “taking up the cross.” Verc., “and having taken up the cross.”

29. Or mother. Greek adds ἢ γυναῖκα, “or wife.” So Brix.

40. It is not mine to give to you. “To you” is absent from Greek, Verc., Corb., Vindeb., and Veron.

## CHAPTER XI

1. Bethany. Greek reads εἰς Βηθφαγὴ καὶ Βηθανίαν, “to Bethphage and Bethany.” Brix. has, “to Bethphage and Bethany.” An addition from Luke XIX.29.

23. It shall be done for him. Greek: ἔσται αὐτῷ ὃ ἐὰν εἴπῃ, “whatsoever he says shall be for him.” Verc. has, “whatever he may say will happen to him.” Veron., Corb., and Vind., “whatever he says.”

## CHAPTER XII

6. Most dear. Greek: ἀγαπητόν, “beloved.” So Verc.

15. Craftiness. Greek: ὑπόκρισιν, “hypocrisy.” Verc., “pretense.”

26. I am. Greek and Veron. omit “am.”

27. Of the living. Greek: ζώντων, “of those living.” So Gat.

31. But the second is like it. Greek: καὶ δευτέρα ὁμοία αὕτῃ, “and a second [commandment] is like this.” [Col. 0896B] Veron., “a second [is] like it.”

38. Beware of the scribes. Greek: βλέπετε ἀπὸ τῶν γραμματέων, “beware of the scribes.” So Corb., Vindeb., and Veron.

38. Who wish to walk in robes and [receive] salutations. Greek: καὶ ἀσπασμούς, “and salutations.” So Veron.

40. Under the pretext of a lengthy prayer. Greek: καὶ προφάσει μακρᾷ προσευχόμενοι, “and praying under a long pretext.” Verc. and Corb., “praying on the occasion of a lengthy [prayer].” Vind., “praying a long prayer.”

## CHAPTER XIII

14. Where it ought not. Greek: ὅπου οὐ δεῖ, “where it is not proper.” So Verc. and Corb.

## CHAPTER XIV

3. Spikenard. Greek: νάρδου πιστικῆς, “genuine nard.” So Gat., Brix., and Vindeb. Perhaps from John XII.3, where “nard of pisticus” is read.

14. My guest room. The pronoun μοῦ, “my,” is absent from Greek, and from Corb. and Vind.

15. Furnished. Greek adds ἔτοιμον, “prepared.” So Corb., Brix., and Vindeb.

[Col. 0896C] 19. Is it I? Greek adds καὶ ἄλλος, μήτι ἐγώ, “and another [said], ‘Is it I?’” So Corb., Verc., Vindeb., and Brix.

22. Take. The received Greek adds φάγετε, “eat”; Corb., “eat.” Yet φάγετε is absent from the Alexandrian and Cambridge manuscripts.

34. And watch. Greek adds μετ᾿ ἐμοῦ, “with me.” So Gat.

50. Then his disciples. These three words are absent from Greek books, and from Verc. and Brix.

56. And agreeing. Greek: ἶσα, “equal.” So Verc.

## CHAPTER XV

7. Had committed murder. Greek: οἵ τινες ἐν τῇ στάσει φόνον πεποιήκεισαν, “who had committed murder in the insurrection.” Verc. seems to have read, “who had committed murder in the insurrection.”

8. And when the crowd had gone up. Greek: καὶ ἀναβοήσας ὁ ὄχλος, “and the crowd, having cried out.” Verc., “the whole crowd being stirred up,” a reading which appears to approach ἀναβοήσας more closely (though ἀναβοᾷν means “to cry out”) than ἀναβήσας, which is translated “when it had gone up.”

[Col. 0895]

33. Manuscripts 2: οἱ μὲν δὲ ἐν τῷ πλοίῳ προσεκύνησαν αὐτῷ, “but those in the boat worshipped him,” with Cor.

4. Manuscript 1: ποιήσω ὧδε σκηνὰς τρεῖς, “I will make three tents here.” Veron., “I will make three tents here.” Cor., “I will make three tents.”

5. Manuscript 1: τοιοῦτον ἐπὶ τῷ ὀνόματί μου, “such a one in my name,” with Veron. and Brix.

29. In manuscripts 9 one reads εἰς τοὺς πόδας αὐτοῦ, “at his feet.” In Brix., “at his feet.”

20. Manuscript 1 does not read ἐκ νεότητός μου, “from my youth,” with Corb.

22. Manuscripts 10: ἢ τὸ βάπτισμα, “or the baptism.” Brix., “or the baptism.” But these words have slipped into Matthew’s text from Mark chapter X.

5. Manuscripts 9 add τῶν ἱματίων αὐτῶν, “of their garments.” Brix., “of their garments.”

14. Manuscripts 2: καὶ κηρυχθήσεται τὸ εὐαγγέλιον, “and the gospel will be proclaimed,” with Verc.

32. Manuscripts 8: ἐκφύῃ, “puts forth.” Verc. and Veron., “they sprout”; Cor., “it brings forth.”

29. Manuscripts 8: καὶ ὃ ἔχει, ἀρθήσεται, “and what he has will be taken away,” with Verc., Veron., and Corb.

39. Manuscripts 6: καὶ προσελθὼν μικρόν, “and having gone forward a little.” Verc. has, “and having proceeded a little.”

59. Manuscripts 9 read καὶ οἱ πρεσβύτεροι, “and the elders.” Brix., “and the elders.”

35. The words ἵνα πληρωθῇ τὸ ῥηθὲν, etc., through the end of the verse, are not found in the ten manuscripts, nor in Corb. and Brix.

## ST. JOHN

### CHAPTER I

16. Manuscript 1: ὅτι ἐκ τοῦ πληρώματος, “because from the fullness.” Verc., “because”; Veron., “because from the fullness.”

### CHAPTER II

12. Manuscript 1: μετὰ ταῦτα κατέβη, “after these things he went down.” Veron., “after these things he departed”; Brix., “after these things he went away.”

### CHAPTER IV

1. Manuscripts 9: ἔγνω ὁ Κύριος ὅτι, “the Lord knew that,” with Brix.

41. Manuscripts 10 read ἐπίστευσαν διὰ τὸν λόγον αὐτοῦ, “they believed because of his word.” Verc. and Veron., “they believed through” (Veron., “because of”) “his word.”

42. Manuscripts 9 add ὁ Χριστός, “the Christ,” with the support of Brix.

### CHAPTER V

30. Manuscripts 9 add πατρός, “of [the] Father”; Veron. agrees with them.

### CHAPTER VI

10. Manuscripts 2: ἀνέπεσον οὖν οἱ ἄνθρωποι, “therefore the men reclined.” Verc., “therefore the men reclined.”

Manuscript 1: ἃ ἐποίησε σημεῖα, “which signs he performed,” with Verc.

[Col. 0898A] 15. Manuscripts 4: βασιλέα, ἀνεχώρησεν, “king, he withdrew.” Veron. and Brix. read, “king, he withdrew.”

Ibid. Manuscripts 9 read ἐκεῖνο, εἰς ὃ ἐνέβησαν οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ, “that one into which his disciples had embarked.” Veron., “that ...”; Verc., “... into which the disciples of Jesus had embarked.”

55. Manuscript 1: ἀληθής ἐστι βρῶσις, καὶ τὸ αἷμά μου ἀληθής ἐστι πόσις, “is true food, and my blood is true drink.” Mm. reads, “true food ... is true drink.”

### CHAPTER VII

26. Manuscripts 6: ὅτι οὗτός ἐστιν ἀληθῶς ὁ Χριστός, “that this is truly the Christ,” with Brix.

### CHAPTER VIII

Two manuscript codices omit eleven complete verses of chapter VIII—namely, from the words Ἰησοῦς δὲ ἐπορεύθη, “but Jesus went,” to the words ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν μηκέτι ἁμάρτανε, “from now on, sin no more”—which are likewise absent from Verc. and Brix. In Veron., although they are absent, it nevertheless appears that they were obliterated by age.

6. Manuscripts 2: κατέγραφεν εἰς τὴν γῆν, “he wrote down upon the ground.” Corb., Gat., and Mm., “... on the ground.”

14. Manuscripts 4: ἢ ποῦ ὑπάγω, “or where I am going.” Brix., Gat., and Mm. have, “or where.”

42. Manuscripts 3 do not read οὖν, “therefore,” which is likewise absent [Col. 0898B] in Verc. and Veron.

59. Manuscripts 9 add διελθὼν διὰ μέσου αὐτῶν, καὶ παρῆγεν οὕτως, “passing through their midst, he went on thus.” Brix., “passing through their midst. And he went.”

### CHAPTER IX

16. Manuscript 1: καὶ σχίσματα ἦν ἐν αὐτοῖς, “and there was division among them.” Verc. has, “and there were disagreements among them.”

28. Manuscripts 10 do not have οὖν, “therefore,” which is likewise absent in Veron.

### CHAPTER X

8. Manuscripts 4: ἦλθον πρὸ ἐμοῦ, κλέπται, “came before me, thieves,” with Gat.

### CHAPTER XI

41. Manuscripts 9 read οὗ ἦν τεθνηκὼς κείμενος, “where the dead man had been laid.” Brix. has only, “where he had been.”

### CHAPTER XII

31. In manuscripts 10 one reads νῦν κρίσις ἐστὶ τοῦ κόσμου τούτου, “now is the judgment of this world.” In Verc. and Brix., “now is the judgment of this world.”

### CHAPTER XIII

24. Manuscript 1: Σίμων Πέτρος, καὶ λέγει αὐτῷ· εἰπὲ τίς ἐστιν περὶ οὗ λέγει, “Simon Peter, and he says to him: ‘Tell [us] who it is about whom he speaks.’” Brix., “Simon Peter, and he says to him: ‘Ask who it is about whom he speaks.’” Veron., “... Tell ...”

### CHAPTER XIV

17. Manuscripts 2: ὅτι ἐν ὑμῖν μένει, καὶ ἐν [Col. 0898C] ὑμῖν ἐστι, “because he remains among you and is in you.” Verc. has, “because he remains with you and is in you.” Brix., “because he remains with you and is in you.” Veron. and Cor., “because he remains with you and is with you.”

14. MS 1: “which I command you.” Vercelli reads: “which I command you.”

## CHAPTER XVIII

11. Eight MSS: “the sword into the sheath,” together with Vercelli, Verona, and Brescia.

40. MS 1: “Then they all cried out.” Verona: “Therefore they all cried out.” Vercelli: “But they all cried out.”

## CHAPTER XIX

28. Four MSS: “Jesus, having seen,” with Vercelli.

31. Four MSS: “of that Sabbath,” with Vercelli, Verona, and Corbie.

## CHAPTER XXI

1. MS 1: “to his disciples upon the,” with Vercelli, Verona, and Brescia.

# ST LUKE

## CHAPTER I

35. Ten MSS read: “and the holy thing being born,” with Brescia. But Corbie has: “what shall be born, Holy.” Verona: “Therefore what shall be born, Holy.”

50. Three MSS: “unto generation, and generation.” Corbie and Brescia [Col. 0898D] read: “unto offspring and offspring.” MS 1: “unto generations and generations.”

## CHAPTER II

40. Nine MSS add “in spirit.” Brescia likewise: “in spirit.”

## CHAPTER III

2. In ten MSS is read: “under the high priest.” In Verona: “under the chief of the priests.”

4. In nine MSS the word “saying” is added; likewise in Brescia, “saying.”

22. Nine MSS add “saying.” Brescia and Vindobonensis: “saying.”

## CHAPTER IV

4. Nine MSS have “saying.” Brescia likewise: “saying”; but Vercelli has “and he said.” Verona: “he said.”

7. MS 1: “if, falling down, you worship.” Verona, Vercelli, and Brescia likewise read: “if, having fallen down, you worship.”

8. Nine MSS add: “Go behind me, Satan.” Verona: “Go behind me, Satan.”

## CHAPTER VI

10. MS 1: “all of them, in anger, said to him.” Vercelli has: “all those to be in anger; he said [Col. 0899A] to the man.” Verona and Corbie: “to all those in anger, he said to the man.” Brescia: “all those, he said to the man.”

10. Nine MSS add: “sound as the other.” Verona: “as another”; Brescia: “as the other,” without “sound” (*hygiēs*, “healthy”).

## CHAPTER VII

11. In nine MSS there is “many.” In Verona: “many.”

31. The words “And the Lord said” are absent from ten MSS, as from Vercelli, Verona, Corbie, Gatianus, and Munich.

42. Two MSS: “Which then of them will love him more?” Brescia: “Which therefore of them loves him more?”

## CHAPTER VIII

3. Eight MSS: “they ministered to them,” with Brescia.

9. In nine MSS “saying” is added; likewise in Brescia, “saying.”

## CHAPTER IX

17. MS 1: “and they took up what had remained over to them.” Brescia reads: “and they took up what was left over to them.”

23. Nine MSS: “and let him take up his cross, and follow.” Verona has: “and, having taken up his cross, let him follow.”

54. Nine MSS read: “as Elijah also did”; Brescia likewise. But Vercelli and Verona have “as Elijah did,” [Col. 0899B] without “also,” etc.

57. In nine MSS there is “Lord”; likewise in Verona and Brescia.

## CHAPTER X

11. MS 1 adds: “from your city onto the feet,” with Vercelli; but Vercelli, Brescia, Munich, and Vindobonensis read: “on the feet.”

22. Eight MSS add: “and, turning to the disciples, he said,” agreeing with Vercelli and Verona: “and, turning to the disciples, he said.”

23. Nine MSS read: “privately.” Brescia: “apart.”

## CHAPTER XI

4. Nine MSS add: “but deliver us from evil,” and Verona likewise. Vindobonensis and Brescia, however: “but deliver” (Brescia, “rescue”; Vindobonensis, “snatch”) “us from evil.”

25. MS 1: “he finds it vacant, swept.” Brescia reads: “vacant, cleaned with brooms.”

53. Two MSS: “to be grievously afflicted,” and Vindobonensis likewise: “to be severely afflicted.” Verona: “to be ill.” Vercelli: “to be unwell.”

## CHAPTER XII
