23. In the Verona manuscript there are seventy-two generations. St Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book III, chapter 22, no. 3, p. 219, writes: “For this reason Luke shows that the genealogy, which is from the generation of our Lord down to Adam, has seventy-two generations; joining the end to the beginning and signifying that he is the one who has recapitulated in himself all the nations from Adam onward.” Moreover, Irenaeus seems to make the number of nations and languages equal to the generations, and in this he has several Greek Fathers in agreement with him. In the Syriac and Persian versions there are seventy-seven generations; in Arabic, seventy-eight; and in Ethiopic, eighty.

# Testimonies of the Old Testament Cited by Christ, the Apostles, and the Evangelists in the Four Holy Gospels

They are presented in this index according to the Hebrew truth, the Latin Vulgate edition, the Greek edition of the Seventy, and the ancient Old Latin, so that, when these are compared with the Greek text and the Old Latin version of the New Testament itself, they may determine whether Christ, the Apostles, and the Evangelists, in citing the Old Testament, adhered more closely to the translation of the Seventy than to the Hebrew truth.

Number 1 indicates the Hebrew text; 2, the Vulgate edition of the New Testament; 3, the Greek version of the Seventy; 4, the Greek New Testament; 5, the ancient Old Latin version of the Old Testament; 6, the Vulgate edition of the Old Testament; 7, the ancient Old Latin version of the New Testament.

[Col. 0918D] 2. Matthew 19:4; Mark 10:6. He made them male and female (Mark adds, “God”).

[Col. 0919A] 3. Genesis 1:27. “Male and female he made them.” He made them male and female.

4. Matthew 19:4, and Mark 10:6. “Male and female he made them” (Mark: “God”). He made them male and female (Mark: “God”).

5. Genesis 1:27. He made them male and female.

6. Genesis 1:27. He created them male and female.

7. Matthew 19:4. Vercelli, Verona, Corbie, and Brescia: “Because he who made [them] from the beginning” (in Corbie, *from the beginning* is absent), “made them male and female” (in Verona and Corbie, *them* is absent).

Mark 10:6. Vercelli, Verona, Corbie, and Brescia: “God made them male and female” (Verona, Corbie, and Brescia omit *them*).

[Col. 0947]

**LETTERS OF SAINT EUSEBIUS, BISHOP OF VERCELLI AND MARTYR.**

From Galland, *Bibliotheca* (C, S).

**FIRST LETTER. TO THE EMPEROR CONSTANCIUS.** Having received the letter summoning him to the synod, the sainted president informs the Emperor that he is hastening to Milan.

[Col. 0947C]

Eusebius to Constantius, Augustus the Emperor, greetings.

Most gracious Emperor, seeing that your devoted mind desires this: that ecclesiastical peace may endure throughout the world, I received your letter with great joy. I also received letters from my brothers and fellow bishops, who deigned to inform me of this, so that, through those very persons who obey your [Note: Supply “command in this matter.” So Baronius. Yet the sense of this passage still seems obscure. Galland.] command in this matter, I might receive a full report; I judged it necessary to hasten to Milan. Whatever, Lord Emperor, when I come into your presence, shall seem just [Col. 0947D] and pleasing to the Lord, I promise that I shall do. May God preserve you, most glorious Emperor.

(See Constantius’s letter convoking the council in volume XIII of our *Patrology*, col. 564.)

**LETTER II. TO THE PRESBYTERS AND PEOPLE OF ITALY.** The holy pastor, rejoicing with his flock over its faith, exhorts it to continue on the path of salvation.

To the most beloved and greatly longed-for brothers, [Col. 0948C] the presbyters, and also to the holy peoples standing firm in the faith at Vercelli, Novara, Ivrea, and likewise Dertona: Eusebius, bishop, eternal salvation in the Lord.

I. Although our Lord sustained us with many blessings while we were separated from you in body, and afforded us your presence in the coming and visitation of very many brothers, nevertheless we were sorrowful and sad, and not without tears, because for a long interval of time we did not receive writings from your holiness. [Note: Another reading: “not receiving writings, we feared lest any . . .” The same editor.] For we feared lest some diabolical subtlety had ensnared you, or human power had subjected you to unbelievers. While we were afflicted by these thoughts, therefore, and turned every consolation of the brothers who came to us from different [Col. 0948D] provinces more into sorrow at your absence than into joy, the Lord deigned to grant this: that I might learn what had troubled me not only from the letters expressing your sincerity, but also from the presence of our dear ones, the deacon Syrus and the exorcist Victorinus. Thus, most beloved brothers, I learned that you were safe, as I had desired. And, as though I had suddenly been snatched across every distance of the earth—as happened to Habakkuk, who was carried by an angel [Col. 0949A] to Daniel—I judged that I had reached you when I received the letters of each one and ran through your holy friends and your love in your written messages.

II. Tears mingled with my joy, and my mind, eager to read, was held back by the occupation of weeping. Both were necessary, so that each affection might strive to anticipate the offices of love in fulfilling this desire. Thus, during these days, judging that I was serving with you in this occupation, I forgot my past hardships. For joys surrounded me on every side—here displaying steadfast faith, there love, there fruit—so that, placed amid so many and such great blessings, I suddenly judged, as I said above, that I was not in exile but with you.

[Col. 0949B] Therefore I rejoice, most beloved brothers, in your faith; I rejoice in the salvation which follows faith; I rejoice in your fruits, because you are not merely established there but also go far beyond. For just as a farmer grafts onto a good tree that which, for the sake of its fruits, does not suffer the axe or become subject to fire, so we too wish and desire to render to your holiness not only service according to the flesh, but to spend our very souls for your salvation. As I said, you have extended firm branches with fruit, and have laboured to reach me across so great a distance of lands. I, the farmer, rejoice and gladly gather the fruits [Note: Another reading: “of our labour.” The same editor.] of your labour, because you were willing to do so much; and not only I, or our most holy presbyters and deacons who are with me, or the other brothers, but all of us who long for you.

[Col. 0949C] For, as the most blessed Apostle says (Philem. 7, 20), you have filled my heart, since you fulfilled the divine commands which [Note: Another reading: “To fulfil . . . befits men.” The same editor.] Christians ought to fulfil toward a bishop or churchmen whom you know to be labouring in exile for the faith’s sake. You fulfilled what brothers ought to do for brothers, and what children ought to render to a father. Yet while we, according to the divine commands, wished to produce heavenly fruits for you from earthly things, lasting fruits from perishable things, everlasting fruits from frail things, we began, constrained by necessity, to sow daily in patience. The poor rejoiced in your fruits; not only the people of that city but everyone glorified God; and those able to see the love you bore me, seeing it from these very fruits, glorified God and named us with every honour, together with your blessing.

[Col. 0949D] III. Seeing this, the devil—the enemy of the innocent, foe of righteousness, adversary of faith—because God was blessed in this work, stirred up against us his Ariomaniacs, who for a long time had been eager, not only because of this work but also because of their unbelief, to which they could not persuade us, to resort to violence. This was his customary practice: to terrify by force and power those whom he could not persuade.

[Col. 0950A] Accordingly, he gathered a multitude of his followers, who drag us to the workshop of their unbelief and mock us; and they say that the whole power has been granted to them by the Emperor. While they said much and boasted of their power, I wished to show them in this matter that their power amounted to nothing: silently, I handed over my body to the executioners, which the Lord said could be given up in persecutions. How free my mind was while I suffered at their hands, was shut up, kept for four days, and heard the reproaches and persuasions of various persons, I showed by saying not a single word.

They wished to add this to their wickedness: that the brothers—that is, the presbyters and deacons—should cease to visit me; and they said that they would prevent the others also [Col. 0950B] from approaching me. Therefore, lest I should eat food from the hands of unbelievers—or rather, what is worse, of transgressors who are unbelievers, as the Apostle says—I addressed to them a petition in this manner:

**COPY OF THE PETITION ADDRESSED TO PATROPHILUS AND HIS ASSOCIATES**

Eusebius, servant of God, together with his fellow servants who labour with me for the faith’s sake, to Patrophilus, custodian, with his associates. [Note: For why Eusebius calls Patrophilus, the Arian prelate, “custodian” rather than “bishop,” see Baronius, year 356, no. 97. The same editor.]

IV. Since, in the fury and violence of a multitude, you not only dragged me upon the ground, but at times carried me, lying on my back with my body stripped naked, from this lodging which you had given me through your agents and officials, and from which I never departed except by your violence: God knows it, and the city knows it; nor can you deny it here or hereafter. [Col. 0950C] Therefore I reserve the matter for God, so that it may receive its end as he himself shall ordain. Meanwhile, know that I have resolved this (so that justice may now and hereafter, and here, be able to stand): in the lodging in which you hold me shut up, where, after the first carrying-away, you thrust me back more cruelly and dared to carry me away again in the same manner and cast me into a single cell, I will eat no bread nor drink water unless each one of you first declares, not merely by word but also by hand, that you will not prevent my brethren, who gladly suffer these things with me for the sake of the faith, from bringing necessary food from the lodging where they reside, nor prevent those who may deign to visit me. Indeed, I ought to depart from the body, lest I be compelled repeatedly to tell those who wish to know of so great a crime which you have committed against divine and public law. [Col. 0950D] But lest any unbeliever should call you cruel toward us, or suppose that we, ignorant of the divine commands, were unwilling to avoid confusion rather than obey the Lord, I have presumed to undertake this course. I say again: unless you make this declaration both verbally and in writing, you will be murderers by preventing it.

> [Note: “You who, in the fury of many, not only dragged me along the ground, but sometimes carried me lying on my back with my body stripped naked, from this lodging which you had given me through your agents and officials, and never allowed me to leave except through your violence. And God knows,” etc. This appears less correct.]

V. Almighty God knows this; his only-begotten Son, born ineffably from him, also knows it—he who, [Col. 0951A] for the sake of our salvation, God of eternal power, put on a perfect man, chose to suffer, conquered death and rose on the third day, sits at the right hand of the Father, and will come to judge the living and the dead. The Holy Spirit also knows it. The Catholic Church is witness, which thus confesses: that I shall not be guilty in my own person, but you, who wished to prevent my fellow servants from ministering necessary provisions. And if you prepare this, [the text is syntactically uncertain: “you ought to despise …”]—not as though I feared death, but lest, after my departure, you should say that I wished to leave by a voluntary death and find for yourselves some mist of accusation against us. I shall summon the Churches which I can reach by letters while confined; I shall also summon the servants of God, so that, when they gather there, the whole world may recognize what the sound faith, approved by all [Col. 0951B] Catholic bishops, suffers from the Ariomaniacs, whom it had previously condemned. Likewise, I, Eusebius the bishop, subscribed.

> [Note: Another reading: “And some mist of excuse for yourselves.”]

> [Note: Another reading: “Confined.” Immediately after: “that I may summon them.”]

I adjure you who read this letter, by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, not to suppress it, but to pass it on for others to read.

VI. Thus, scarcely on the fourth day, somewhat softened by this letter, they compelled us, hungry as we were, to return to the lodging in which we had stayed. Meanwhile they saw how the people received us as we returned with joy. They surrounded our lodging with lamps. With the Lord’s assent we began again to minister to those in need. Their inhumanity could not endure this, and they turned our love into their own hatred. They could scarcely tolerate it for twenty-five days. [Col. 0951C] They burst out again and, with a lawless crowd of many people, came to our lodging armed with clubs. They broke through the wall by means of another’s enclosures and violently reached us. Again they seized me and shut me up under stricter guard, with only my most beloved presbyter Tegrinus. They also seized and imprisoned all our brethren—that is, the presbyters and deacons. After three days, by their own authority, they sent them into exile in various places. Other brethren who had come to visit us they put into the public prison and kept shut up for many days. Rushing again upon the lodging, they destroyed everything that had been acquired either for expenses or for the poor. But because this public crime of theirs was being noted by all the citizens, they adopted this expedient: they returned some less important things and boasted that they had restored our possessions to us. [Col. 0951D] Yet they kept the provisions for themselves. And after so great a crime, they sought, if possible, to deny it in such a way that they would permit none of my people to come to me with food necessary for the body. Only on the sixth day, when various persons cried out against them, did they permit one person to come. So far as they were concerned, they displayed murderous intent; and lest they desist from malice, they dismissed him on the fourth day. Afterwards, scarcely on the sixth day, [Col. 0952A] when we were failing, they allowed someone at last to come with provisions. These, then, are the works of the Ariomaniacs.

> [Note: Another reading: “Appeased.” A little later: “They saw upon the ground.” Erroneously.]

> [Note: Another reading: “They perceived.”]

> [Note: Another reading: “Wishing.” Very corrupt.]

> [Note: Read: “they plunder.”]

VII. See, most holy brethren, whether this is not persecution, while we who preserve the Catholic faith suffer these things. Consider more deeply whether it is not even far worse than that which was carried out by those who served idols. They sent people to prison, but did not prevent their own people from coming to them. How greatly, then, has Satan wounded the Churches through the cruelty of the Ariomaniacs! Those who ought to set free send people into public custody. Those who are taught to suffer for righteousness’ sake inflict violence. Those who are taught by divine law not to reclaim their own plundered possessions plunder the possessions of others. I pass over the extent of the cruelty which has invaded them while they delight in temporal wealth. Prisoners confined with robbers are not denied by interrogators [Col. 0952B] or judges the opportunity to see their own people; but even our own are forbidden to visit us. Devout brethren are prevented not only from coming to the lodging in which we are held, but are terrified by threats lest they approach the prison. Thus they have subjugated everyone, as I have most plainly learned. I shall begin with the bishops: while certain men fear losing their rank, they have themselves lost the faith; and while they do not wish to lose earthly possessions and immunities, they have judged heavenly treasures and true security to be nothing. The rest, led in the same way, seeing bishops afraid to lose these things, began to love what they cannot possess forever.

> [Note: “Lest they approach the prison, they are threatened.” Another reading: “lest they approach, the prisons threaten.”]

> [Note: The passage is mutilated.]

VIII. Thus the Ariomaniacs intimidate the rich by threatening them with proscription; thus they intimidate the poor, because they have the power to imprison them. And what madness! [Col. 0952C] In the place where we are held, they send not only men who serve us to prison, but also consecrated maidens, shutting them up in public custody without any fear of God. But just as the wicked elders who sought to violate Susanna’s chastity did not rejoice, so neither will these always rejoice, who seek by manifold persecution and extreme oppression to subject the Church to their unbelief. For holy Daniel said to them: “Thus the daughters of Israel, being afraid, lay with you” (Dan. 13:57). But let human fear depart from your hearts, most holy ones, since you have the consolation of the Lord, who says: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:18). This is a time of testing; it is a time for those who have been tested to become manifest. Therefore they have received [Col. 0952D] human aid, because they do not possess divine aid. Had they possessed it, they would never, by earthly power, subjugate to themselves the souls of innocent people.

> [Note: Another reading: “made manifest.”]

IX. We ought to have written much concerning their evils, by which not I alone but very many are oppressed. Yet, lest we should be able to do this and make their cruelty known by letters, they keep us under the strictest guard. Therefore both our own people and friends are forbidden [Col. 0953A] to approach us. But the Lord granted me to send this letter to you through our most beloved Syrian deacon, whom I had the ability to send, because, by the providence of our Lord, he had gone at that time to visit the holy places and was not found with the other brethren.

X. Moreover, we scarcely wrote this letter in whatever way we could, continually asking God to restrain the guards from hour to hour and grant that the deacon might bring you not rather news of our suffering, but at least some sort of letter of greeting. Therefore I earnestly ask you to guard the faith with every vigilance, preserve concord, devote yourselves to prayer, and remember us without ceasing, so that the Lord may deign to deliver his Church, which suffers throughout [Col. 0953B] the whole world, and so that we who are oppressed may, once liberated, be able to rejoice with you. May the Lord grant this at your request, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed with him from the ages and unto all ages of ages. Amen.

> [Note: This word is absent in Baronius, though other printed editions have it.]

XI. Again I ask and beseech you, through God’s mercy, that each person name his or her greeting in this letter, because necessity has prevented me from writing, as I used to do, individually [Col. 0954A] to each of you. Thus in this letter I address you all—brethren, holy sisters, sons and daughters, every sex and every age—and ask that, content with this greeting and with our service, you may deign also to greet in our name those who are away and who deign to love us. Our brethren who are with me—presbyters and deacons, and indeed all our people—greet you. Together with me they earnestly ask that, remembering us, you may deign to greet all your people in our name. Moreover, I have sent the letter which I composed to Patrophilus, my keeper, so that from it you may know that we can neither be frightened by the threats of the Ariomaniacs nor led into their fellowship by the serpent-like subtlety of their blandishments. May the Godhead protect you and cause you to flourish and live both here and hereafter with all your own people, [Col. 0954B] brethren most beloved and most deeply longed for.

## LETTER III. TO GREGORY, BISHOP OF SPAIN

Eusebius congratulates Gregory because, while Hosius and very many others fell at Rimini into communion with Valens and Ursacius, he had resisted.

(This letter may be found in volume X of our *Patrology*, among the historical works of St Hilary, Fragment XI, col. 713. See also the letters of Pope Liberius to Eusebius, *Patrology*, vol. VIII, cols. 1350, 1355, 1356.)

[Col. 0953]

# CONFESSION CONCERNING THE TRINITY OF SAINT EUSEBIUS, BISHOP OF VERCELLI AND MARTYR

FROM THE *SACRED ANECDOTA* OF EUGENIO DE LEVIS. (C, G, S)\*

## NOTICE

[Col. 0953]

After recounting at the beginning of the preface both the occasion and the usefulness of his intended publication of the *Anecdota*, the most learned de Levis proceeds as follows:

“I shall begin by resolving to publish the confession of faith against the Arians of Saint Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, the first of that name—called the Hammer of the Arians. I found this formula of faith, and caused it to be copied, on three parchment leaves belonging to the very distinguished monastery of Saints Michael and Januarius Martyr at Lucedio. This monastery was founded in the seventh century, as may be seen in its proper place, and was under the special protection of the bishops of Vercelli. It is probable that the holy bishops of the Church of Vercelli assumed the administration of this monastery perhaps in the eighth century and retained it until the death of Saint Bonomius, in 1026, on the third day before the Kalends of September [30 August].

“It is true that no modern writer known to me has ascribed to this holy bishop Eusebius of Vercelli another confession against the Arians besides that commonly called the *Quicumque* Creed, concerning which John Stephen Ferrerius, bishop of Vercelli, Father Corbellini, Marcus Aurelius Cusanus, and others have written. Yet, if we carefully weigh what the holy doctor wrote together with Saint Athanasius to the Antiochenes, we cannot assent to this opinion; and therefore very many have judged that the *Quicumque* Creed was composed in later centuries, an opinion with which we readily agree.

“The aforementioned Bishop Ferrerius reports, on the authority of one codex in the Vatican Library, that Saint Eusebius wrote a work *On the Unity of the Trinity*. Hyacinth Galizia follows him in the *Lives of the Saints*, vol. I, p. 177, writing that a copy of this work is preserved in the library of the Fathers of the Oratory of Saint Philip Neri at Turin, as a gift of Abbot Lawrence Scotus. I saw that copy in 1762 and caused another to be transcribed from it. From this transcription I learned that he had written another book, *On the Best Method of Interpreting Sacred Scripture*, on the words, ‘Out of Egypt I called my son,’ as is read at the end of Book V after the Profession of the Arians. Yet, when I compared these five books, or the work *On the Unity of the Trinity*, with the works of Saint Athanasius, I found these books, or work, to be attributed to the presbyter Faustinus, although arranged in a different order from that found in the printed editions.

“I also investigated with the greatest diligence whether there was anything in this work that could indicate its author with certainty, especially in the letter addressed to the Empress Flaccilla, to whom he dedicated his work. Yet I found nothing except several variant readings. After the *Profession of the Arians*, which here appears in the fifth book, several unpublished passages occur, among them—as I have already said—a mention of his own book *On the Best Method of Interpreting Sacred Scripture*.

“Whether this work was written by Saint Eusebius has been doubted by many very learned men. Among them should not be omitted the distinguished Father John Baptist Audifredi, of the Order of Preachers, prefect of the Casanatensian Library. Since, in 1771, I had asked him to examine this Vatican codex with his tireless care, he answered me in a letter dated 29 November 1776 that, in codex no. 1319, p. 253, there occurs the work: ‘… of Saint Eusebius, bishop: the book *On the Unity of the Trinity* begins.’ The work begins with these words: ‘You, one Father, and Son, and Holy Spirit, who have declared unity and deity to us,’ etc., and ends after four books. The last book ends with the words: ‘Their operation in creation is one’; and immediately follows: ‘The fourth book ends. The book on the Catholic profession begins’; and immediately another book, *On the Impious Profession of the Arians*, which ends with these words: ‘If the ears of the rest are deaf,’ etc. In that letter he did not hesitate to affirm that the work was not by the presbyter Faustinus but rather by Saint Eusebius.

“Indeed, in another letter, dated 13 June 1778, he affirmed that the letter or tract *On the Canons of the Gospels*, which is read in several editions of Holy Scripture, is by the same author, even though in many editions of Holy Scripture this is read only in Greek. Finally, he observed that in the edition of the *Orthodoxographers* this letter occurs written in Greek and Latin, from an old Latin version, and translated into Latin in volume VI of Fabricius’s *Greek Library*. All these matters must be considered with more mature judgment, so that the truth may emerge.

“For although, after considering these observations, I found the Turin copy of the Congregation of Saint Philip Neri conformable in substance, it nevertheless said nothing about whether that Vatican Library codex was written on parchment, nor did it state the character of the script or the age of the codex. Therefore I judged that the authority of this work ought not to be used here to demonstrate the unity of Saint Eusebius’s doctrine against the Arians in the confession which we are publishing, nor that it was appropriate to publish all the unpublished material found in this work attributed to Faustinus.

“As to how highly the confession of faith of our holy doctor Eusebius ought to be valued, I refer the reader to the short preface placed before the text and to the brief commentaries made upon the confession itself. In them are found sure and more evident arguments concerning the true author of this creed, his genuine profession of faith, and Catholic doctrine. Having weighed all these points, I do not believe that the reader will depart from my counsel and opinion. For in them it has been demonstrated how concordant Saint Eusebius’s teaching is with that of Saint Athanasius of Alexandria and the other holy Fathers, and what particular propositions Saint Eusebius put forward that conform to Sacred Scripture, the ancient Fathers, and the councils. Once these matters are published, the reader will have new arguments for refuting the Arian heresy and new circumstances for illuminating the history of that period.”

## PRELIMINARY INQUIRY CONCERNING THE EXPOSITION OF EUSEBIUS OF VERCELLI’S FAITH, OR CONCERNING THE AUTHOR OF THIS CREED

[Col. 0955]

[Col. 0955] The *Quicumque* Creed has already been vigorously disputed by many most distinguished scholars. Some claim it for Saint Athanasius; others for Anastasius of Sinai; many argue that it was composed by a Latin author; some maintain that it was produced by a Gallic writer. Of the latter, many contend that Vigilius of Thapsus was the author, while others name Vincent of Lérins. They support their opinions by showing that the creed condemns the heresies of Eutyches and Nestorius, which arose after the death of Saint Athanasius. But what follows from this if someone were to say that the holy Fathers anticipated and guarded against these heresies, as historians have already observed in many earlier holy Fathers? Those arguments would then have no force.

What many theologians have judged to be of some difficulty, I would say, is that the Latins did not by means of the authority of this creed demonstrate against the Greek schismatics that origin of the Holy Spirit from the Son—that is, his procession—as theologians teach. But anyone might readily counter this argument by pointing to Saint Basil the Great and Didymus of Alexandria, who acknowledged and handed down this procession; theologians have cited their authorities against the Greeks. No one denies that these Fathers lived in the age of Saint Athanasius and Saint Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli. Therefore it was not necessary to bring against the latter all the Fathers and their writings, especially perhaps those matters which were on everyone’s lips, in order to prove that what was transmitted by tradition had been strengthened by the authority of the Fathers.

For, although among those who argue for the authors mentioned above there are few who have written in favor of Saint Eusebius of Vercelli or stated this opinion as the common one, we nevertheless know that this creed was customarily recited in the Church of Vercelli from very ancient times. The tradition of that Church teaches us that this creed was written in Latin at Alexandria, in the presence of Saints Athanasius, Asterius, and the aforesaid Saint Eusebius; and that, after the acts celebrated there had been rendered into Latin, it was presented by Eusebius himself to Pope Liberius.

All writers on the Church of Vercelli report that, in the Eusebian rite and in the canonical hours, the recitation of this creed was prescribed in ancient times and a feast of the Most Holy Trinity was celebrated. From this rite Alcuin Flaccus, in the time of Charlemagne, in order to provide novice priests with an easy method of celebrating the sacred liturgy, prescribed on Sundays the Mass of the Most Holy Trinity, repeatedly customarily celebrated in the Church of Vercelli—without mentioning another Alcuin, bishop of Vercelli, who was administering that Church at that very time—until those novice priests could easily learn the use of many other books. This opinion receives very great support from the synodical letter sent by Athanasius to the Antiochenes, which has the following near its end:

> “We determined these matters in this fashion both because it is impious to demand anything beyond the Nicene Council or receive contentious opinions, and also for the sake of peace alone, lest those who think rightly be regarded as rejected. We who remained at Alexandria briefly made known their CONFESSION, whatever it was, in common with our fellow ministers Asterius and Eusebius. For the rest of our people had gone, each to his own province. You in turn will see that these matters are published in common where you customarily hold your assemblies, and call everyone together. For it is fitting that the letter first be read in that place,” etc.

Therefore, from this authority and from the confession of Saint Eusebius and Asterius reported to the Antiochenes by Athanasius, it is demonstrated that he presented his creed together with the letter.

What those confessions or creeds were is unknown to us: whether the *Quicumque* Creed or this confession which we are publishing. Writers dispute among themselves concerning the former, as was observed above. But this latter confession, which is the subject of our inquiry, is one which, without the author’s name, was written on three large leaves in the ninth century, as the form of the script seems to indicate. These three parchment leaves, among other materials belonging to the monastery of Saints Michael and Januarius Martyr at Lucedio in the diocese of Vercelli, were copied at our direction. The *Quicumque* Creed and this confession differ little from each other in style, yet in many respects they are unlike; and I would consider this one older than that.

If, however, we consider the doctrine of hypostasis, this confession explains it in the same Greek words used by Saint Athanasius in his already-mentioned synodical letter. Accordingly, the terms ὁμοούσιον (*homoousion*, “of the same substance”) and οὐσία (*ousia*, “substance”) are read in this creed to explain that the substance of the Son and Father is one and the same. Speaking of the hypostases in his confession made at the Synod of Alexandria and reported at the end of the same letter already mentioned to the Antiochenes, Saint Eusebius says:

> “As regards the hypostases, I confess that I too think the same; nor do I merely add my vote to this, but I also assent to the incarnation of our Savior: namely, that, although he was the Son of God, he became man and assumed all that belonged to our former humanity, except sin. And, according to the argument of the letter, I confirm this by my support.”

What clearer evidence could we desire, both from Saint Athanasius and from Saint Eusebius himself, who approves all that Saint Athanasius wrote? Moreover, from Saint Jerome we learn that Saint Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, translated Origen’s commentaries on David’s Psalms from Greek into Latin, correcting their errors so that anyone might read them with an unblemished and unhindered step. In this confession, moreover, while treating of the resurrection of this flesh of ours, he corrects Origen’s error concerning the resurrection of bodies. Therefore I would think that this creed ought to be attributed to no one more fittingly than to Saint Eusebius. Perhaps this is that from which, in later times, the creed commonly called the *Quicumque* was composed.

Finally, if we consider the acts of this same Saint Eusebius published by Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. IV, p. 759, they themselves inform us that he gave his confession to Pope Liberius at Rome before setting out for Vercelli:

> “But Saint Eusebius, athlete of Christ, having given the confession of his faith and deposited it at Rome in the sacred archive, took leave of Pope Liberius and set out on his journey with the other brethren.”

All this appears consistent with what Rufinus wrote in *History*, book I, chapters 28, 29, 30, etc. For he recounts that Eusebius went to Alexandria with other confessors sound in the faith, treated the lapsed there more leniently, and was entrusted with the oversight of the West, as Asterius was with that of the East. Indeed, the decree of that council adds a fuller discussion concerning the Holy Spirit: that the Holy Spirit also was to be believed to be of the same substance and deity as the Father and Son (ch. 29, p. 211), and that absolutely nothing in the Trinity was to be called created, inferior, or later. It also dealt, at the prompting of Scripture, with the distinction between substances and subsistences. “The Greeks call them *ousiai* [οὐσίαι] and *hypostases* [ὑποστάσεις]. For some said that substance and subsistence appeared to be one; and because we do not speak of three substances in God, neither ought we to speak of three subsistences…” It also determined concerning the Lord’s incarnation that the body which the Lord assumed was neither without sensation nor without a soul. All these matters, carefully and moderately arranged, being settled, each person departed on his journey in peace.

All these matters are treated in this confession. Moreover, Rufinus, in the same book, chapter 30, describes Eusebius as traveling through the East and Italy, exercising at once the office of physician and priest, recalling individual Churches—after their renunciation of unbelief—to the health of right faith. Especially so because he found Hilary of Poitiers, who, as we have recalled, had formerly been thrust into exile with the other bishops but had now returned and was in Italy, undertaking the same work of restoring the Churches and renewing the faith of the Fathers. Behold how the doctrine against the Arians was disseminated and proclaimed among Italians and Gauls.

Nor would I think myself mistaken in saying that this confession or creed was known to the author of the *Summary of Faith*. The Ballerini brothers hold that the *Summary of Faith against the Arians* should be attributed to Pope Saint Leo I on the authority of two codices, although Sirmond, Gallandi, and some others formerly assigned it to an uncertain author. For several statements occur there copied word for word from this confession. Alcuin Flaccus, moreover, in his book *On Faith in the Trinity* addressed to Charlemagne, and in the *Questions to Fredegesius*, has quoted certain passages from it here and there without naming the author. A few have been indicated in their proper places, lest I be more prolix than the subject requires.

# CONFESSION CONCERNING THE HOLY TRINITY

[Col. 0959]

[Col. 0959A] 1. We confess and believe that the holy and undivided Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is naturally one Lord, of one substance, one nature, and likewise one majesty and power. We profess that the Father is neither made, created, nor begotten. For he derives his origin from no one; from him the Son receives birth and the Holy Spirit procession. Thus he himself is the fountain and origin of the whole Godhead; likewise the Father of his own essence, who ineffably begot the Son from his ineffable substance, yet begot not something other than what he himself is: God from God, light from light.

II. Therefore all fatherhood in heaven and on earth is from him. We likewise confess that the Son, born from the substance of the Father before the ages and without beginning, was not made. [Col. 0959B] For neither was the Father ever without the Son, nor did the Son ever exist without the Father. Yet the Father is not from the Son in the way that the Son is from the Father, because the Father did not receive generation from the Son, but the Son from the Father. Therefore the Son is God from the Father. The Father indeed is God, but not from the Son: Father of the Son, but not God from the Son. The Son, however, is Son of the Father and God from the Father, yet in every respect equal [Col. 0960A] to God the Father, because he did not at some time begin to be, nor did he cease to be… The Son is believed to be of one substance with the Father, so that he is also called *homoousion* [ὁμοούσιον] with the Father—that is, of the same substance as the Father. For *homo* [ὁμο] in Greek means “one,” while *ousia* [οὐσία] means “substance”; joined together, the two signify one substance. For the Son must be believed to have been begotten not from nothing nor from another substance, but from the Father’s womb—that is, from the substance or nature of the Father himself.

> [Note: The term *homoousion* [ὁμοούσιον] means that the Son is not merely like the Father, but is altogether of the same nature and essence as he. Accordingly, the Arian heresy is here overthrown—a heresy which Saint Athanasius abhorred in all his works and during his exile, in order to demonstrate, with the Fathers of the Nicene Synod, the true consubstantiality of the Son of God. The same holy doctor Athanasius wrote the history of that most sacred synod concerning this faith of the Fathers; see p. 415 of his works.]

> [Note: “Many in number, who were present at Rimini or Nicaea under the authority of your name, were compelled to accept the permission concerning *ousia* [οὐσία], a term once devised by you against the heresy of the Ariomaniacs and always received by us reverently and faithfully.” Thus the Fathers of the Council of Paris, held in 362, as is read among the fragments of Saint Hilary of Poitiers, vol. II, p. 533. Meanwhile, the emperor compelled the delegates of the Council of Rimini on our side to unite with the communion of the heretics, and gave them a creed drafted in deceitful words, which, beneath concealed perfidy, spoke as though it upheld Catholic doctrine. For, under the pretext of false reasoning, he represented the word *ousia* as ambiguous, rashly employed by the Fathers, and not derived from the authority of Scripture, lest the Son be believed to be of one substance with the Father. That creed professed the Son to be like the Father; but within it lay prepared deceit, so that he might be like yet not equal. Thus Sulpicius Severus, *Sacred History*, book II, ch. 43, in Gallandi, *Library of the Fathers*, vol. VIII, p. 389. Behold, therefore, the meaning of Saint Eusebius is all the clearer against this decree of that synod. Lest it support fraud, our holy doctor uses the Greek terms *ousia* and *homoousion*—that is, “the same substance”—while writing in Latin, in order to explain himself more clearly, in accordance with the customs of his time. Saint Hilary, his disciple, did the same in book I, no. 12, of *On Faith in the Trinity*.]

III. Therefore the Father is eternal and the Son eternal. Since the Father always existed, he always had a Son of whom he was Father; and for this reason we confess that the Son was born from the Father without beginning. Nor do we call this same Son of God, because he was begotten from the Father, a small portion of a divided nature. Rather, we affirm that the perfect Father begot the perfect [Col. 0960B] Son without diminution and without division, because it belongs to the Godhead alone not to have an unequal Son. This Son of God is Son by nature, not by adoption. God the Father must be believed to have begotten him neither by will nor by necessity, because no necessity can obtain in God, nor does will precede wisdom.

> [Note: Concerning this division of nature, no one before Tatian, in his *Oration to the Greeks*, explained that it was impossible in this manner: “He was born by communication, not by severance.” Saint Justin continues in his *Dialogue with Trypho*: “The Son is properly called begotten because he has a Father who begot him.” Alcuin Flaccus follows, *On Faith in the Holy Trinity*, book I, no. 5, ch. 15, p. 717, ed. André du Chesne: “But there is no DIVISION or SEVERANCE between the Father and the Son, because each is in the other.” Saint Justin Martyr, *Dialogue with Trypho the Jew*, no. 70: “We see something similar occurring among ourselves. When we utter a word, we beget a word, but not by SEVERANCE, so that the word which is within us is diminished when we utter it. We also see one fire kindled from another without diminishing the fire from which it is kindled. The fire kindled from it exists and appears, yet does not diminish that from which it was kindled. The WORD OF WISDOM himself shall be my witness: he is God, begotten from the Father of all, and is also the Word, Wisdom, Power, and Glory of the Savior.”]

> [Note: Here Saint Eusebius overthrows the heresy of Sabellius, as also in the works of Saint Hilary, Fragment XI, or *The Catholic Faith Set Forth at the City of Larissa by the Gallican Bishops to the Eastern Bishops*, no. 2: “We have embraced the term HOMOOUSION as expressing the true and lawful birth of the only-begotten God from God [Col. 0960C] the Father, repudiating the union according to Sabellius’s blasphemies and not understanding the Son to be ANY PART of the Father. Rather, from the whole and perfect unbegotten God, the whole and perfect only-begotten God was born; we therefore confess him to be of one *ousia*, or substance, with God the Father, so that he may not be regarded rather as a creature, an ADOPTION, or a mere designation.”]

> [Note: Here he refutes the Arian heresy, concerning which Hilary wrote against it in *On the Trinity*, book VI, no. 26: “Although the mere simple confession of the names of nature shows that the one of whom it is said, ‘This is my Son,’ and the one to whom it is said, ‘My Father,’ are what they are called, nevertheless, lest the Son’s name be merely one of adoption or the Father’s merely one of honor, let us see what properties belonging to the Son have been added to the name ‘Son.’” The same doctor, *Against Emperor Constantius*, no. 9: “He cries, ‘This is my beloved Son,’ etc., and you decree that he is not Son and that there is no Father, but only external designations of adoption.”]

> [Note: God would not be the highest good if he needed anything. Nor would he be eternal God, immeasurable, or the beginning and origin of all goods, if he needed anything or if will preceded wisdom. Therefore he is rightly called the highest good, the fountain and origin of all things, who made the world and everything in it. Being Lord of heaven and earth, he does not dwell in temples made with hands, nor is he served by human hands, as though needing anything, since he himself gives to all life, breath, and all things (Acts 17:24–25).]

[Col. 0961A] **IV.** We also believe that the Holy Spirit, whom we believe to be the third person in the Trinity, is one God, equal with God the Father and the Son, of one substance and one nature; yet not begotten or created, but proceeding from both, and being the Spirit of both. This Holy Spirit is believed neither to be unbegotten nor begotten. For if we were to call him unbegotten, we should speak of two Fathers; or if begotten, we should absurdly proclaim two Sons. Yet he is called the Spirit neither of the Father alone nor of the Son alone, but jointly of the Father and the Son. For he does not proceed from the Father into the Son, or from the Son to sanctify the creature; rather, he is shown to proceed simultaneously from both, because he is acknowledged to be the love or holiness of both.

[Note: [Col. 0961B] Alcuin Flaccus writes thus in *On the Trinity*, Book I, chapter 15: “The Holy Spirit is nowhere called either unbegotten or begotten, lest, if he were called unbegotten like the Father, two Fathers should be understood in the holy Trinity; or if he were called begotten like the Son, two Sons should likewise be thought to exist in the same holy Trinity. But, with the faith preserved, he is to be said only to proceed from the Father and the Son. Yet he does not proceed from the Father into the Son, nor from the Son to sanctify the creature, as some who misunderstood badly thought should be believed; but he proceeds from both, because the Father begot such a Son that, just as the Holy Spirit proceeds from himself, so also he proceeds from the Son.”]

This Holy Spirit, then, is believed to be sent by both, as the Son is sent by the Father; yet he is not regarded as inferior to the Father and the Son, just as we testify that the Son, because of the flesh he assumed, is inferior to the Father and the Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0961C] If someone perhaps says, “He is inferior because he is said to be sent,” what will he say when he reads in the prophet Isaiah Christ speaking in his own person: “The Lord has sent me, and his Spirit”; and elsewhere: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me . . .”? How, then, is he to be believed inferior who is also God, who, like Christ himself, is equal to the Father? Thus the author of the *Brief Statement of Faith against the Arians*, Sirmond, p. 231, B–C.]

[Note: [Col. 0961C] From all historians it is most evident that the Socinians, Macedonians, and Arians held that the Holy Spirit is nothing other than gifts of charisms. The Fathers of the Councils of Nicaea and Alexandria showed this false doctrine of theirs to be contrary to Holy Scripture and the testimonies of the holy Fathers—by Matthew 28:19; by the history of Ananias in Acts 5; and by Paul’s words in Hebrews 3 and 1 Corinthians 3, to omit the authorities of the Old Testament cited in many places by holy Fathers and councils to prove the existence of the Holy Spirit, his divinity, and his equal dignity and majesty with the Father and the Son. This is the doctrine which Rufinus records as having been defined by the Council of Alexandria (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book I, chapter 29, p. 211): “Indeed, a fuller discussion concerning the Holy Spirit was also added in that decree of the council, so that the Holy Spirit too should be believed to be of the same substance and divinity as the Father and the Son,” Saint Asterius, representative of the East, and Saint Eusebius, of the Western Church, taking the lead. All these matters are fully discussed in the *Brief Statement of Faith against the Arians* (*Bibliotheca Patrum* of Gallandi, vol. VIII, p. 592 ff.); and thus the matters noted in the preface are more clearly proved here. Indeed, so far as we know, no one has left this doctrine to us formulated in such closely similar words.]

[Col. 0961B] **V.** This is the holy Trinity which, according to the transmitted account of the faith, may be called and believed not a triple eternity but eternity. Nor should one properly say that Trinity exists in one God; rather, the one God is Trinity. In the relative names of the persons, the Father is referred to the Son, the Son to the Father, and the Holy Spirit to both. Though three persons are thus spoken of relatively, yet one nature—that is, one substance—is believed. We do not proclaim three substances as we do three persons, but one substance and three persons.

[Note: [Col. 0962C] Alcuin Flaccus, Book I of *On Faith in the Trinity*, chapter 4, p. 710, says: “Certain things are said of God substantially: God is great, almighty; whatever is said with reference to himself is the same as the substance of divinity. Other things are said relatively: the Father in relation to the Son, the Son in relation to the Father, and the Holy Spirit relatively to the Father and the Son. But with reference to himself, whether Father, Son, or Holy Spirit, he is called God. Thus the Father, in that he is God, is by that very fact substance; because the Son is of the same substance, undoubtedly the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God. But God, in that he is Father, is said relatively, since ‘Father’ is not a name of substance but refers to the Son. We do not say that the Son is Father as we say that the Son is God, nor do we say that the Father is Son as we say that he is God; for God is said substantially, while Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are said relatively. The Holy Spirit is likewise said relatively to the Father and the Son, though not in the same manner as the Father and the Son are related to one another.”]

[Col. 0962A]

[Note: [Col. 0962D] “Therefore let three persons be believed, but not three substances; three properties, but not three powers.” *Brief Statement of Faith against the Arians*, Sirmond, vol. I, p. 225.]

**VI.** For what the Father is is not said with reference to himself, but with reference to the Son. Likewise the Holy Spirit is referred not to himself but relatively to the Father and the Son, in that he is proclaimed the Spirit of the Father and the Son. Again, when we say “God,” this is not said in relation to something else, as Father is said in relation to Son, Son in relation to Father, or Holy Spirit in relation to Father and Son; but “God” is said specially in relation to himself. For even if we were questioned concerning each individual person, we must confess God. Therefore: God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit; God is said in the singular, yet not three Gods, but one God.

[Note: [Col. 0962D] “For if you ask the Catholic Church what the Father is, it says, ‘God’; it also says that the Son is God, and that the Holy Spirit is God; and yet it does not say three Gods.” Ibid.; also in Gallandi, *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. VIII, p. 592, question 19.]

**VII.** Likewise, the Father is called almighty, the Son almighty, and the Holy Spirit almighty, each in the singular; yet not three almighties, but one almighty. Likewise one light and one principle are proclaimed. Thus each person is confessed and believed individually to be fully God, and all three persons to be one God; their majesty, divinity, and power are one, undivided, and equal. They are neither diminished in the individual persons nor increased in the three.

[Note: [Col. 0962D] Q. “Is the Father one light and the Son another?” A. “By no means another; rather, the Father and the Son are one light, just as they are one substance. Therefore ‘light from light’ is rightly said, as ‘God from God’; just as the Father and the Son are one God, so they are one light.” Thus Alcuin Flaccus, *To Fredegisus on the Trinity*, question 19, p. 764. “For just as many fires are kindled from one torch, yet the light of the first torch is not diminished by the many torches kindled from it, so the Word proceeding from the Father’s power did not leave the begetter of the Word devoid of it.” Thus Tatian the Assyrian, *Address against the Greeks*, no. 5, in Gallandi, *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. I, p. 641. Justin Martyr also uses this illustration of a torch to explain the eternal generation in which God communicated his entire substance to the Son, *Dialogue*, no. 128. We should distinguish eternal generation and procession from temporal coming forth. Thus: “That power which prophetic discourse, as has similarly been demonstrated in many cases, calls both God and angel, is not numbered merely by name, as the light of the sun is; rather, it is also in number something other. This I briefly discussed above, when I said that that power was united from the Father by his power and will, not by division, as though the Father’s substance were divided; just as all other things that are divided and cut apart are not the same as they were before being divided.” In Gallandi, *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. I, p. 580.]

[Note: [Col. 0963D] “To be another in number” is the same as saying that he is other than the Father, as is clear from what follows; for he is distinguished from the Father not by substance but only by subsistence, or person.]

[Note: [Col. 0963C] “Among human beings, a father begets a son inferior to himself because he too was begotten inferior by a father. Therefore, as the son grows, the father grows old; and when the father dies, the son is shown to succeed him and sometimes becomes better and more powerful than his father. But with God this is not so; for where divinity does not admit growth or aging, it is fitting that love should have the Son equal.” *Brief Statement of Faith against the Arians*, Gallandi, as above, p. 688.]

**VIII.** For nothing is lacking when each person is individually called God, nor is anything additional present when all three persons are declared to be one God. Therefore this holy Trinity, which is the one true God, neither departs from number nor is comprehended by number. Number is discerned in the relation of the persons; but what is unnumbered in the substance of divinity is not comprehended. Thus only this indicates number: that they are from one another; and only in this are they without number: that they are in relation to themselves. For one natural name belongs to this holy Trinity in such a way that it cannot be plural in the three persons. Accordingly, as Scripture says: “The Lord, our Lord, and great is his power, and of his wisdom there is no number” (Ps. 146:5). Yet, because we say that these three persons are one God, we cannot say that the Son is the same person as the Father, or that the Father or Son is the same person as the Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0963D] “Supply: is present.”]

[Note: [Col. 0964C] “Whatever, then, is said of God in relation to himself is said of each individual person—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—and also of the Trinity itself together, not in the plural but in the singular.” Alcuin, *On Faith*, chapter 8, p. 712: “That is, understand three persons and one God. They do not say it once, lest you believe in singularity; nor twice, lest you exclude the Holy Spirit; nor ‘Holy Lords of Sabaoth,’ lest you confess three Gods after the manner of the Gentiles. Rather they say, ‘Holy, Holy, Holy, the Lord God of Sabaoth’” (Isa. 6:5).]

[Note: [Col. 0964C] “Where one God is believed, there lesser and greater are excluded. Unity knows no number, and equality admits no rank.” *Brief Statement of Faith against the Arians*, Sirmond, p. 215.]

[Col. 0963B] **IX.** For the Father is not himself the Son, nor the Son himself the Father, nor the Holy Spirit himself either the Father or the Son. Yet the Father is what the Son is, the Son what the Father is, and the Holy Spirit what the Father and the Son are—that is, one God by nature. For when we say that the Father is not the same person as the Son, this refers to the distinction of persons.

**X.** But when we say that the Father is what the Son is, the Son what the Father is, and the Holy Spirit what the Father and the Son are, this is shown to concern the nature by which he is God, or the substance. As regards substance they are one; for we distinguish persons, not divide the Godhead. Therefore we acknowledge the Trinity in the distinction of persons, and profess unity because of the nature or substance. These three, then, are one by nature, not by person. Yet these three persons must not be regarded as separable, since none is believed ever to have existed before another, after another, or without another, nor ever to have performed anything separately. For they are found inseparable both in what they are and in what they do. Thus we believe that between the begetting Father, the begotten Son, and the proceeding Holy Spirit there was no interval of time in which the begetter at any time preceded the begotten, or the begotten was lacking to the begetter, or the proceeding Spirit appeared later than the Father or the Son. Therefore this Trinity is proclaimed and believed by us to be inseparable and unconfused.

[Note: [Col. 0964C] Alcuin Flaccus, Book I, chapter 4, p. 617: “He wrote the whole chapter in which he proves that the Holy Trinity is not separable either in nature or in persons.”]

[Note: [Col. 0964C] “But perhaps you still say, according to a carnal understanding, that between the begetting Father and the begotten Son there could not but have been some interval. Hours make an interval; hours denote time. If you place time before the Son, you do not confess that all things were made through him.” *Brief Statement of Faith against the Arians*, Sirmond, p. 224. And shortly afterward: “Thus, according to you, the Father was without the Son, just as he was without power, without wisdom, without life, without truth. But because he must be believed never to have been without these, it accords with your salvation that, according to the Catholic faith, you confess the Son coeternal and equal with the Father.”]

[Col. 0964B] These three persons, therefore, are spoken of, as the Fathers define, in order that they may be known, not in order that they may be separated. For if we attend to what Holy Scripture says about Wisdom, “She is the brightness of eternal light” (Wis. 7:26; Heb. 1:3), then, just as we see brightness inseparably adhering to light, so we confess that the Son cannot be separated from the Father. Therefore, while we do not confuse those three persons of one and inseparable nature, neither do we in any way proclaim them separable. For the Trinity itself has deigned clearly to show us this: even in those names by which it willed that the individual persons should be recognized, it does not permit one to be understood without another. The Father is not known without the Son, nor is the Son found without the Father. The very relation expressed by the word forbids the persons to be separated; even when it does not name them together, it implies them together. No one can hear any one of these names without being compelled to understand the other also.

[Note: [Col. 0964D] Here Saint Hilary of Poitiers appears to have taken this from Book VII of *On the Trinity*, no. 29, though in another manner and using the comparison of fire, as in Book VI, no. 12, concerning light or a lamp.]

[Col. 0965A] **XI.** Although, then, these three are one and one is three, each person nevertheless retains its own abiding property. For the Father has eternity without birth; the Son has birth with eternity; and the Holy Spirit has procession without birth, with eternity. Of these three persons, we believe that the person of the Son alone, for the deliverance of the human race, assumed a true human being without sin from the holy and immaculate Virgin Mary. From her he was begotten in a new order and by a new birth, because untouched virginity knew no intercourse with a man and, made fruitful through the Holy Spirit, supplied the material of flesh. This Virgin’s birth is neither reached by reasoning nor shown by example. If it is reached by reason, it is not marvelous; if shown by example, it is not unique. Yet the Holy Spirit must not be believed to be Father of the Son because Mary, overshadowed by that same Holy Spirit, conceived, lest we seem to assert Fathers of the Son—which it is impious to say.

[Note: [Col. 0965D] Saint Hilary, *On the Trinity*, Book X, no. 15: “For the Virgin bore what she bore only from her own Holy Spirit.”]

In this wondrous conception, as Wisdom built a house for itself, “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). Yet the Word itself was not converted or changed into flesh so as to cease being God because it had willed to become human. Rather, the Word became flesh in such a way that not only the Word of God and human flesh are there, but also a rational human soul; and this whole is called both God because of God and human because of the human being. In this Son of God we believe there are two natures: one of divinity, the other of humanity.

[Note: [Col. 0965D] “And the Word became flesh”—or what else could he be than God made flesh of our flesh? Saint Hilary, *On the Trinity*, Book XI, no. 16; and in the book *On the Synods*, or *On the Faith of the East*, anathema 11, p. 384.]

[Col. 0965C] **XII.** These the one person of Christ united in himself in such a way that divinity can never be separated from humanity, nor humanity from divinity. Thus perfect God and perfect human being are one Christ in unity of person. Yet because we have said that there are two natures in the Son of God, we shall not posit two persons in him, lest, God forbid, a quaternity appear to be added to the Trinity.

[Note: [Col. 0965D] Saint Hilary treats this argument clearly throughout his exposition of Psalm 138, and in Book X, no. 17, of *On the Trinity*. These things correspond to what was defined at the Council of Alexandria, for which reason Saint Eusebius, subscribing the synodal letter to the Antiochenes sent by Saint Athanasius, writes: “But I also consent concerning the incarnation of our Savior . . .”]

**XIII.** For God the Word did not assume the person of a human being, but human nature; and into the eternal person of divinity he assumed the temporal substance of flesh. Again, although we believe that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are of one substance, we do not say that the Virgin Mary gave birth to the unity of this Trinity, but only to the Son, who alone assumed our nature into the unity of his person. We must also believe that the entire Trinity effected the incarnation of this Son of God, because the works of the Trinity are inseparable. Yet the Son alone assumed the form in the singularity of his person, not in the unity of the divine nature. That form was joined to what is proper to the Son, not to what is common to the Trinity, for the unity of person; so that the Son of God and the Son of Man are one Christ. That is, Christ in these two natures consists of three substances: the Word, which must be referred to the essence of God alone; and body and soul, which belong to the true human being. Thus he has in himself the twofold substance of his own divinity and our humanity. Further, in that he came forth from God the Father without defect, he is only begotten; for he is understood neither as made nor as predestined.

[Col. 0966B] **XIV.** Yet in that he was born of the Virgin Mary, he must be believed to be predestined. Both generations in him are marvelous: he was begotten of the Father before the ages without a mother, and at the end of the ages was begotten of a mother without a father. Yet, inasmuch as he is God, he created Mary; inasmuch as he is human, he was created from Mary—himself both Father and Son of Mary, his mother.

**XV.** Again, in that he is God, he is equal to the Father; in that he is human, he is inferior to the Father. Likewise, he must be believed both greater and lesser. In the form of God, the Son himself is greater than himself because of the humanity he assumed, since divinity is greater. In the form of human being, the Son himself is greater than himself in relation to the humanity which is understood to be less than divinity. Thus, according to divinity, which is equal to the Father, both he and the Father are greater than the human being whom the person of the Son alone assumed. Again, insofar as this question may be asked, the Son is believed to be both equal and lesser. We answer: according to the form of a servant (Phil. 2:7), he is lesser than both the Father and the Holy Spirit, because the Holy Spirit is not called Father and did not assume flesh. But the person of the Son alone assumed flesh, through which he is believed to be lesser than those two persons.

[Note: [Col. 0965D] “In this flesh he is greater than the Father: equal in the Word, greater in flesh; equal to him through whom he made us, greater than him who was made for us. For although many testimonies set forth above clearly teach that the Son is God, I have nevertheless judged that a few more should be added. It is written in Genesis: ‘God created heaven . . .’; and certainly the Evangelist confirms that all things were created through the Son . . . Since the Son is shown to be God by testimonies both present and previously adduced from the holy Scriptures, I wonder why some do not fear to blaspheme him by calling him LESSER, since God is nowhere at all read to be lesser.” *Brief Statement of Faith against the Arians*.]

Again, this Son is believed to be personally distinct, though inseparable, from God the Father and the Holy Spirit, from the human being assumed from Mary. Yet in the human being there exists one person, while with the Father and the Holy Spirit there exists the substance of the divine nature. Nevertheless, the Son must be believed to have been sent not only by God the Father but also by the Holy Spirit, as he himself says through the prophet: “And now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit” (Isa. 48:16). He is also understood to have been sent by himself, because the will and operation of the whole Trinity are recognized to be inseparable.

[Note: [Col. 0966D] Supply: “nor did [the Holy Spirit] assume flesh.”]

[Note: [Col. 0966D] That is, a person distinct from the human being, or humanity, assumed from Mary. For whenever he employs the term “human being,” he consistently uses it for humanity, as may be seen in many places. I therefore ask that this alone be noted here by all, lest I become longer than the matter requires.]

[Note: [Col. 0966D] “His descent from heaven is the cause of an origin conceived from the Spirit. For Mary did not give origin to the body, though she contributed everything natural to her sex for the growth and birth of the body. That he is the Son of Man belongs to the birth of flesh assumed in the Virgin; but that he is in heaven belongs to the power of a nature that always remains, which, having itself initiated and created flesh, did not confine itself, by the power of its infinity, within the limits of a bounded body.” Saint Hilary, *On the Trinity*, Book X, no. 16, p. 331.]

[Note: [Col. 0967B] “But perhaps someone says: ‘He is inferior because he is said to be sent.’ What will he say when he reads Isaiah the prophet speaking in Christ’s person: ‘The Lord has sent me, and his Spirit’ . . .? He who is known to be everywhere must be believed to be sent.” *Brief Statement of Faith against the Arians*, following Saint Hilary. “We remember that the Paraclete was sent by the Son, and faith itself declared this at the beginning. But because, by the power of an undifferentiated nature, he frequently said that his own works were the works of the Father, saying, John 10:37, and because he often promised to send the Paraclete, he sometimes said that he would be sent by the Father, since he was accustomed dutifully to refer to the Father all that he did. From this heretics frequently seize an occasion, saying that the Son himself is the Paraclete who will be sent and for whose sending he will ask the Father, so that there may be a difference between the one sent and the one asking.” Thus Saint Hilary, *On the Synods of the East*, or *On the Faith of the Easterners*, no. 20, p. 494; and he continues, no. 21: “If anyone says that the Holy Spirit is a part of the Father or of the Son, let him be anathema.”]

He who before the ages was called only-begotten spiritually was made firstborn. He is only-begotten because of the substance of divinity; firstborn because of the nature of assumed flesh. In the form of the human being assumed, according to Gospel truth, he is believed to have been conceived without sin, born without sin, and to have died without sin; he alone was made a sinner for us, that is, a sacrifice for our sins. Yet, with his divinity preserved, he endured the passion itself for our offences; condemned to death and the cross, he underwent a real death of the flesh. On the third day, too, raised by his own power, he rose from the tomb.

[Note: [Col. 0967C] The words read here—“he is believed to have been conceived without sin, born without sin, and to have died without sin”—should, I believe, be referred to the words of Saint Eusebius subscribing the already-mentioned synodal letter sent by Saint Athanasius to the Antiochenes. At its end Eusebius wrote: “And [he assumed] all things which belonged to our former humanity, except sin,” etc.]

[Col. 0967B] **XVI.** By the example of this our head, therefore, we confess that a true resurrection of the flesh of all the dead will take place. We believe that you will rise again not in an aerial body or in any other flesh, as some speak wildly, but in this flesh in which we live, stand, and move. When the example of this holy resurrection had been completed, the same Lord and Savior returned, by ascending, to the Father’s seat, which he had never left in respect of divinity. There he sits at the right hand of the Father, awaited at the end of the ages as Judge of all the living and the dead.

[Note: [Col. 0967D] From this it is plainly inferred that Eusebius is contending against the error of Origen, who taught that not flesh but bodies would rise, and that these would not be the same bodies but other, subtle, aerial, heavenly bodies, which souls would assume in place of the coarser material and fleshly body that they now govern and animate. He taught or confirmed this doctrine, or heresy, in his *Commentary on Psalms*, vol. I, recent Venetian edition, pp. 398–399, and on Matthew, pp. 344, 446, vol. XIII, or vol. III. This heresy was subsequently followed by Bardesanes the Syrian and many others. Against them the Fathers of Aquileia added the pronoun “this” to the article “resurrection of the flesh” in the Apostles’ Creed, as Rufinus teaches in Book I of his *Invective against Saint Jerome*, no. 4: “The holy Church of Aquileia, God’s Spirit foreseeing future calumnies against us, when it hands down ‘the resurrection of the flesh,’ adds one syllable of a pronoun; and instead of saying ‘the resurrection of the flesh,’ we say ‘THE RESURRECTION OF THIS FLESH.’” In this creed, therefore, it is laid down against those who taught resurrection in alien flesh or matter rather than that of this our body. Thus, as we have already said in the preface with Saint Jerome, Saint Eusebius produced a Latin translation of Origen’s commentaries on the Psalms from Greek, with the errors corrected. Anyone may readily recognize here against whom the author of this confession defined this doctrine, especially since in the remaining creeds nothing was established so plainly against Origen’s error in the very words found here. Concerning this heresy of Origen, Saint Epiphanius wrote specifically in the *Ancoratus*, p. 356: “But I think enough has been said about these matters, since we have offered a few examples from many. As for those who appear to be Christians but truly believe Origen, and who confess the resurrection of the dead—both our flesh and the holy body of the Lord assumed from Mary—yet say that this flesh will not rise, but that another will be given from God in its place, how shall we not say that they hold an opinion more impious than others, and more foolish than the Greek [one]?” The latter is a heresy which he refuted elsewhere, as here.]

[Col. 0968A] **XVII.** From there he will come with all the saints to execute judgment, rendering to each one the reward properly due according to what each has done while dwelling in the body, whether good or evil (2 Cor. 5:10).

We believe that the holy Catholic Church, purchased at the price of his blood, will reign with him forever. Established within her bosom, we believe in one baptism and confess it for the remission of all sins. Under this faith, we truly believe in the resurrection of the dead and await the joys of the age to come.

This alone must be our prayer and petition: that, when judgment has been accomplished and brought to its end, and the Son has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father, he may make us participants in his kingdom, so that we who cleave to him through this faith may reign with him without end.

[Col. 0968B] This is the faith of our confession set forth: through it the doctrine of heretics is destroyed; through it the hearts of believers are purified; through it, too, one approaches God gloriously. Having, during a three-day fast, poured forth this sacred savor by the continuous presentation and discussion of the accounts, we passed on to the matters laid down for exposition on the following day.

[Note: [Col. 0968D] Although in this period the author seems to indicate that he spoke on this mystery of the most holy Trinity for two other days, nevertheless the manuscript contains nothing further and has its final page blank. These materials must perhaps be sought elsewhere.]

[Col. 0969]

# Supplement to the Edition of Eusebius’s Works, in Which Certain Matters Concerning the Author’s Life and Writings Are Set Forth

## I. On the Life and Writings of Eusebius of Vercelli, from Gallandi

[Col. 0969A]

Eusebius, a Sardinian by birth, having left his native land and kindred and preferred pilgrimage to domestic leisure, as Saint Ambrose says, was first reader of the Roman Church and afterward was ordained bishop of Vercelli.

[Note: [Col. 0969D] Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 96.]

[Note: [Col. 0969D] Ambrose, Letter 63, §68, *Works*, vol. II, p. 1038, edition of the Benedictines, Paris.]

And indeed it was rightly believed that he had been chosen for the episcopal office by divine judgment. For the electors, who had never known him before, set aside their fellow citizens and, as soon as they saw him, approved him; and the interval between seeing and approving was no greater than that required for him to be seen. Thus he deservedly proved so great a man: every church chose the man whom it recognized as divinely called.

[Note: [Col. 0969D] Ambrose, ibid., §2, p. 1023.]

He was the first in the western regions to unite monastic life with clerical life. This was, no doubt, after his return from Egypt, where in exile he had diligently investigated the rule of the holy monks, according to Baronius.

[Note: [Col. 0969D] Ambrose, ibid., §66, p. 1038.]

[Note: [Col. 0969D] Baronius, under the year 328, §22.]

In the year 354, when Arian impiety was especially harassing the Church, Pope Liberius sent a letter to Eusebius, asking him to undertake, together with the legates of the Apostolic See, the defense of the faith before Constantius.

[Note: [Col. 0969D] Liberius, Letter to Eusebius of Vercelli, vol. VIII of our *Patrology*, col. 1349 ff.]

Obeying the Roman pontiff, the blessed bishop received the legates honorably and courteously at Vercelli; he offered himself as their companion both on the journey and in the embassy, and went with them to the emperor in Gaul. When the supreme pontiff learned of this, he immediately wrote back to him, declaring how great his joy had been when he learned that Eusebius had joined himself to his legates.

[Note: [Col. 0969D] The same, ibid.]

Eusebius therefore pressed his case vigorously before Constantius and obtained everything sought by that embassy: namely, that a council should be held. It was accordingly convened at Milan in the following year. In that council Eusebius’s courage and steadfastness of spirit shone forth; for, fearing neither threats nor chains nor even a drawn sword, he undertook exile for the duty of his ministry in the year 357, being banished to Scythopolis. There he was at first received with great kindness by Count Joseph; afterward he was cruelly harassed by Patrophilus, a former associate of Arius and a man altogether savage. Eusebius himself declares in a written pamphlet addressed to that same Arian Patrophilus, which he enclosed with letters sent to his own people in Italy, what and how great were the sufferings then endured by this most steadfast confessor of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0970D] Athanasius, *History of the Arians*, §34, p. 363.]

[Note: [Col. 0970D] Epiphanius, *Heresies*, 30, §5.]

[Note: [Col. 0970D] Eusebius of Vercelli, letter; see above.]

Afterward he was transported from Scythopolis to Cappadocia and thence to Egypt. Finally, when Julian issued an edict in 362 restoring exiled bishops, Eusebius went to Alexandria at Athanasius’s request, and there attended the synod convened by Athanasius. But to recount individually the matters transacted at that Alexandrian synod would be more lengthy than the scope of our undertaking permits.

[Col. 0970A] Nevertheless, we think this must not be omitted: Eusebius subscribed in Latin to the acts of that Alexandrian synod. Athanasius himself reports this in the following words:

[Note: [Col. 0970D] Athanasius, *Tome to the Antiochenes*, *Works*, vol. I, part II, p. 776.]

> I, Eusebius, agree, in accordance with your exact confession on both sides, by which you have concurred in the same judgment concerning the hypostases, with that same judgment. I also agree concerning the incarnation of our Savior: namely, that the Son of God became human and assumed everything that belonged to our former humanity except sin; and I have confirmed this by my vote in accordance with the tenor of the letter. And since the document of the Council of Sardica is said to have been excluded, lest anything beyond the Nicene faith seem to be set forth, I consent also to this, lest the Nicene faith appear to be excluded through it; and I judge that it should not be produced. I wish you well in the Lord.

Thus far Eusebius’s subscription. Athanasius prefaces it with these words: “Τούτοις καὶ Εὐσέβιος ὑπέγραψε Ῥωμαϊστὶ, ὧν ἡ ἑρμηνεία· Ἐγὼ Εὐσέβιος κ. τ. λ.”—“Eusebius also subscribed to these things in Latin, of which this is the translation: ‘I, Eusebius,’ etc.”

[Col. 0970B] Tillemont therefore seems to have argued less than correctly that Eusebius perhaps did not know Greek well because he subscribed in Latin to the Alexandrian synod. Was that bishop of Vercelli really unskilled in Greek who, according to Jerome’s testimony, produced Eusebius of Caesarea’s commentaries on the Psalms, which he had **translated from Greek into Latin**?

[Note: [Col. 0970D] Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, vol. VII, p. 530.]
