[Note: [Col. 0970D] Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 96; and Letter 61 to Vigilantius, §2.]

[Col. 0970C] It would be better, then, to suppose that Eusebius perhaps did not know how to speak or write Greek fluently, rather than that he was wholly ignorant of the Greek language; or, what I would prefer, that although learned in Greek, he wished to subscribe in Latin to the acts of the Greek synod, so that the agreement of both Churches in defining doctrines might stand forth more fully and clearly.

Now, after the celebration of the Synod of Alexandria, the holy bishop of Vercelli, as Socrates relates after Rufinus, journeyed through the eastern provinces like an eminent physician and restored to complete health those who were weak in faith, instructing and educating them in ecclesiastical doctrine. Departing thence, he came into Illyricum; and finally, having reached Italy, he continued to perform the same offices of piety and religion. At the return of this [Col. 0971A] excellent bishop, to use Jerome’s words, “Italy exchanged its garments of mourning.” When at last he had returned to his church at Vercelli, he gladly visited it, finding it most admirably ordered and firmly established in the true faith. After giving forth so many and such illustrious examples of virtue, under the emperors Valentinian and Valens, on the Kalends of August in the Dionysian year of Christ 370, this excellent bishop departed this life, according to the judgment of more exact chronologists.  
[Note: [Col. 0970D] Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, ch. 9.]  
[Note: [Col. 0970D] Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History*, book I, chs. 30–31.]  
[Note: [Col. 0971C] Jerome, *Dialogue against the Luciferians*, §19, p. 191.]  
[Note: [Col. 0971C] Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, vol. VII, pp. 559 and 777, note 11.]

Only three letters of Saint Eusebius have come down to us. The great Baronius wove the first two, recovered from the archive of the church of Vercelli, into his *Ecclesiastical Annals*, whence we have copied them. We have appended the third, excerpted from the historical work of Saint Hilary, bishop of Poitiers.  
[Note: [Col. 0971C] Baronius, under the year 355, §7; and under the year 356, §92 and following.]  
[Note: [Col. 0971C] Hilary, Fragment XI, §5.]

There also survives a codex of the Gospels copied in the hand of this same Saint Eusebius [Col. 0971B]. Preserved to this day in the greater church at Vercelli, it was splendidly published at Milan in 1748 by Giovanni Andrea Irico, V.C.; and in the following year our Blanchini incorporated it at Rome in his learned work entitled *The Fourfold Gospel Book*.

## II. On his writings and their editions, from Schöenemann

There survive three letters of Eusebius: the first, to the Emperor Constantius; the second, to the presbyters and peoples of Italy; the third, to Gregory, bishop of Spain. There is besides a *Little Book of the Deed*, addressed to Patrophilus, the Arian bishop [Col. 0971C], which he had attached to the letter to the people of Vercelli.  
[Note: [Col. 0971C] Gallandius therefore does not number it separately; nor in the older Libraries of the Fathers, in all of which only the one letter to the presbyters and peoples of Italy is expressly listed, although this *Little Book of the Deed* is everywhere appended to it [Col. 0972C]. Oudinus considers it a separate letter.]

The translation of his Commentary on the Psalms has been lost [Col. 0972A]. A codex of the Gospels copied in Eusebius’s own hand is preserved at Vercelli and was published, after Giovanni Andrea Irico’s edition (Milan, 1748, quarto), in Blanchini’s *Fourfold Gospel Book*.

The first two letters, with the *Little Book of the Deed*, were published—first, as Gallandius says—after being recovered by Baronius from the archive of the Church of Vercelli, in the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, under the year 355, §7, and under the year 356, §92 and following. Yet I should ask him from what source that single letter to the people of Vercelli, with the *Little Book of the Deed*, was published, since it already appears, if I understand Ittigius correctly, in volume I of the Paris *Library of the Fathers* of 1575; for Ittigius mentions a letter of Eusebius of Vercelli, and it can be no other.  
[Note: [Col. 0972C] Not “the three later letters,” that is, these two together with the first, to Constantius, as Oudinus says in the cited place. He likewise states that they were reprinted in the second edition of Bigne’s *Library*, in 1589; this is false, if Ittigius compiled his catalogue correctly.]

Thereafter the same material was published in the Supplements to the fourth edition of the Paris *Great Library* (Paris, Aegidius Morellus, 1639), vol. I, pp. 627–628 [Col. 0972B]; likewise in the fifth Paris edition of that *Library* (at the expense of the same Aegidius Morellus, 1654), which Ittigius describes. Unless perhaps this is entirely the same edition, merely with its title revised—which is highly probable.  
[Note: [Col. 0972C] Compare Ittigius.]

This is especially so if one considers what Ittigius also noticed: no account whatever was taken there of the new Combefisian Supplement published in 1648. Finally, they are found in the Lyons *Great Library of the Fathers* (the Anisson brothers, 1677), vol. V, pp. 1127–1128. The letter mentioned in third place began to be published among Hilary’s Fragments, Fragment XI, §5. From there Gallandi most recently printed it, together with the preceding items copied from Baronius, in vol. V, no. 7 (Venice, 1769), with brief notes and a few variant readings, preceded by an account of Eusebius in the *Prolegomena*, ch. 7 [Col. 0972C].

# A.D. 353–355. JULIUS FIRMICUS MATERNUS

[Col. 0971]

# NOTICE

We had assigned Firmicus Maternus a place between Constantine and the Arian Candidus, as chronological order required, and would have given him there, had not the almost insuperable difficulty of obtaining Münter’s excellent edition stood in the way. But when the time for sending this work to the press pressed upon us, when we had vainly solicited every bookseller and library, and when many persons elsewhere urged us to hasten the course of the *Patrology*, we yielded to the eagerness of subscribers and to the necessity of circumstances. We intended to publish Firmicus, as soon as we acquired him, in the place from which he would depart least from his proper chronological position. We employ, and shall employ, the same procedure whenever we cannot devote ourselves to chronological precision without creating delays equally unwelcome to ourselves and to our subscribers.

# PROLEGOMENA

## I

[Col. 0971D]

The tenth year is now passing since Johannes Michael Hertz, provost of the cathedral church at Roskilde and shortly afterward bishop of Ribe, a most deeply missed colleague, at my urging published, for the due attainment of the highest honours in theology [Col. 0972D], an inaugural dissertation full of sound learning on Julius Firmicus Maternus.  
[Note: [Col. 0971D] *Inaugural Dissertation on Julius Firmicus Maternus and Especially on His Little Book On the Error of Profane Religions*. Copenhagen, 1817.]

That treatise was, as it were, a forerunner of an edition of this writer, for preparing which he would undoubtedly have girded himself, had it pleased God to grant him a longer life [Col. 0973A]. But since he was taken from among the living when old age had scarcely begun, I judged it to be my duty to carry out what I had urged upon him and to devote some spare hours to bringing fresh light upon this writer, long neglected.

The times also seemed opportune to me. For this year the Danish Church celebrated the memory of the conversion of our forefathers from the darkness of paganism to Christian light, begun by the preaching of Ansgar in the year 826. Therefore, since that holy bishop—as likewise his colleagues and successors, and in general all who proclaimed Christ’s doctrine to Gentiles—had necessarily to follow one and the same course, if they acted wisely: namely, to destroy the ancestral superstitions of those peoples before instilling heavenly doctrine into their minds [Col. 0973B]; I thought I should perform a welcome service if, in the absence of writings from the age in which Ansgar flourished that attacked the religions of the Germans and northern peoples, I recalled the arguments with which Christians assailed the polytheism prevailing in the Roman Empire. Thus I hoped that readers would receive with favour this new edition also of Firmicus, who deals exclusively with this subject.

## II

Editors of any ancient author ordinarily begin by writing about the author whom they have undertaken to elucidate; and the nature of the matter requires this. But all students of ecclesiastical antiquities know that I can scarcely, indeed hardly at all, follow in their footsteps [Col. 0973C]. For my Firmicus suffered the unhappy fate that not a single writer mentions anyone of this name before Honorius of Autun, a writer of the thirteenth century, who in book II, chapter 5, of *The Philosophy of the World* cites Firmicus’s *Astronomicon*. This, however, helps our inquiry little, since that book is wholly different from our *On the Error of Profane Religions*, and, in my judgment, adequate arguments cannot establish that both books proceeded from the same author.

The name Firmicus itself is obscure. It is absent from writers and does not occur in literary monuments. In Gruter we read only of persons named *Maternus*, at pp. 220.9; 1009.2; 1468.8; and 1482.11; and of a *Materna*, at p. 1225.3. Those who maintain that Firmicus—whether one man wrote both books or two authors must be posited—was Sicilian will find nothing in Sicilian inscriptions collected by Gabriele Lancellotto, Prince of Torre Mutia, from which to draw arguments for their opinion. For the *Firmii* mentioned there, pp. 145.30 and 182.55, must by no means be confused with the *Firmici* [Col. 0973D].

We must therefore consult the surviving books which profess Firmicus as author, if perhaps anything can be gathered from them. And, as I have already said, we have two inscribed with the name of Julius Firmicus Maternus: one astrological, by a man devoted to polytheism [Col. 0974A]; the other polemical, against the worship of deities, written by a Christian. In the title of both, the author is called *V.C.* If these letters are understood to mean *vir consularis*, “a man of consular rank,” you will find no Julius Firmicus Maternus who rose to the height of the consulship in Constantine’s age, insofar as the Fasti inform us. Yet perhaps he governed a province and for that reason, as was customary in that age, was called consular; or he was adorned with this purely honorific title, of which Gothofredus collected examples from the history of those times.

That both books were composed in Constantine’s age is clearly evident from passages occurring in them. For *Mathematica*, book I, ch. 2, asserts that the eclipse of the sun which occurred under the consuls Optatus and Paulinus, in 334 [Col. 0974B], had been predicted by astrologers, and lists it among recent phenomena.  
[Note: [Col. 0973D] In the year 1087 from the foundation of the City. Almeloveen, *Consular Fasti*, p. 161.]

It was therefore written, or at least begun, shortly thereafter. The same period also suits the other book, *On the Error of Profane Religions*. Dedicated to the emperors Constantius and Constans, sons of Constantine the Great, it was composed after Constans’s British expedition, which it mentions; perhaps also at the beginning of the Persian war conducted by Constantius, and before the repeated defeats in which this emperor was shortly afterward routed by Shapur; certainly before the killing of Constans, murdered through Magnentius’s plot in 350. It therefore belongs between the years 343 and 350.

Hence it is evident that both books were published in approximately the same years; but the first somewhat earlier, under Constantine the Great, for whose safety the author offers pious prayers near the end of book I. Nor does the other passage in the preface to book I appear to obstruct this conclusion: it indicates that the author dedicated the books of *Mathematica*, which he had dedicated to Mavortius Lollianus when the latter was appointed to the fasces of the province of Campania, to the same Lollianus as proconsul and consul designate [Col. 0974C]. The Fasti indeed list a certain Lollianus as consul in 355; and Ammianus Marcellinus praises Mavortius, praetorian prefect, for his lofty constancy.  
[Note: [Col. 0973D] Book XVI, 8.]

But it is not established that these two were one and the same person—namely, the same Mavortius Lollianus to whom Firmicus addressed his book. On the other hand, it must be admitted that Mavortius Lollianus may have been designated consul many years before actually entering upon the consulship, as occurred not infrequently under Constantine’s immediate successors [Col. 0974D]. Perhaps the reason for the postponement of those highest honours promised to Mavortius Lollianus may be sought in Magnentius’s rebellion and the civil turmoil arising from it, which was not suppressed until the destruction in 353 of that tyrant, at whose discretion the city of Rome itself lay.

We shall therefore maintain that the books of *Mathematica* were published shortly after that solar eclipse, which occurred in 336, and before the death of Constantine the Great; but that *On the Error of Profane Religions* was written between 343 and 350, or rather 348, when the Romans were defeated by Shapur at Singara.

## III

[Col. 0975A]

The first book presents its author as a man devoted to the superstitions of the pagans; the second, as a Christian. Yet I can scarcely bring myself to believe that Firmicus the astrologer, already advanced in age—as he himself declares in his astronomical work—changed his mind, renounced the worship of deities to which he had adhered throughout his earlier life, and embraced Christian rites. If he had done so, he would surely have mentioned his conversion to Christ in *On the Error of Profane Religions*, and would have left at least some traces, however unconscious, of his former superstition.

Although he knows pagan religions well, he knows them from reading and from the accounts of other people rather than from personal experience. He is skilled in Holy Scripture [Col. 0975B], and uses it in teaching and argument as was customary in an age to whose manner he could have become accustomed only by long practice. Thus it can scarcely be believed that he had become a Christian so recently; rather, one must conclude that he had been a Christian from birth, or at least from youth.

To this is added the difference in Latin style in the two little works, universally acknowledged to be very great. In the astronomical book there appears very slight knowledge of either language, Greek or Latin. It is full of barbarous words and phrases, such as, to cite a few: *horoscopare*, “to cast a horoscope”; *ferarum mansuetarii*, “tamer of wild beasts”; *cardinaliter*, “cardinally”; *quiescentia* for *quies*, “rest”; *intimare alicui* for *significare*, “to signify to someone”; *concordiale* for *sociale*, “social”; *partiliter* for *per partes*, “by parts”; *caballarius* for *eques*, “horseman”; and *computus* for *computatio*, “calculation” [Col. 0975C].  
[Note: [Col. 0975D] Fabricius, *Latin Library*, ed. Ernesti III, p. 115.]

These suggest Lombard times rather than Constantine’s age, or at least remind us of the Gallic Latin found in the translation of Irenaeus.

But as regards *On the Error of Profane Religions*, it is written in a purer style, such as authors of Constantine’s age use: not indeed the Latin of the golden age, but still tolerable and sufficiently eloquent. Yet this book too displays only moderate knowledge of Greek. From this, however, one cannot in the least infer that the two books proceeded from one and the same author. We therefore embrace the opinion that Firmicus the astrologer is wholly distinct from Firmicus the theologian. This view has long been defended, among many others listed by Hertz, by Caelius Rhodiginus [Col. 0975D], Baronius, Glandorpius, and Lipsius. But, leaving aside the astrologer, let us consider the theologian alone.  
[Note: [Col. 0975D] *On Julius Firmicus Maternus*, pp. 11–12.]

## IV

It is greatly to be regretted that all things are so uncertain and obscure that we must frankly confess our complete ignorance of the author of *On the Error of Profane Religions*. Some maintain, for no reason known to me, that he was Sicilian by birth.  
[Note: [Col. 0975D] Mongitore calls him a Sicilian of uncertain birthplace—namely, in Sicily. Renda, *Old Sicilian Library* (Rome, 1700), p. 167.]

I should consider him African, if the almost constant use of African biblical manuscripts observed in him sufficed to establish this opinion; though these could very easily have been brought from Africa to Italy, Spain, and Gaul. Nor have I found in his book clear signs of African Latin, well known from Apuleius, Tertullian, and Cyprian [Col. 0976A].

Baronius believes that he was bishop of Milan and attended the Roman Synod convened in 357 by Julius I, bishop of Rome. But that synod is a fabrication of Pseudo-Isidore.  
[Note: [Col. 0976D] Walch, *History of Church Councils*, p. 165.]

All are ignorant of a Julius who was bishop of Milan in the time of Julius, bishop of Rome. Maternus of Milan, however, presided over the Christian worship of that city under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, in 307 or 311, and died for religion.  
[Note: [Col. 0976D] Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, IV, p. 307. Bisoizius, *History of the Bishops of Milan*, p. 15.]

Thus falls the claim of Binius and Cajetanus [Col. 0976B], who list him among the saints of the Catholic Church.  
[Note: [Col. 0976D] *Idea of the Holy Sicilians*, pp. 15 and 125.]

Thus only this may be maintained: Julius Firmicus Maternus, as is clear from his book *On the Error of Profane Religions*, was a pious and learned man and an opponent of pagan religions. He attacks them fiercely, sometimes with excessive zeal, when he urges emperors violently to destroy their remnants. But this must be attributed to the times in which he lived and to the examples before his eyes, rather than counted as his fault.

## V

In an examination of any ancient author, investigation of the sources from which he drew claims a principal place, especially when the subject is historical [Col. 0976C]. That it ought not be neglected in an ecclesiastical writer is self-evident. Therefore, when I was assembling notes for my Firmicus, I carefully considered earlier authors whom he had consulted. Yet I took care not to suppose that every item he shares with other apologists for Christianity was always drawn from their books. The nature of the subject itself undoubtedly required that all who sought to overthrow polytheism should recount and refute nearly the same myths; and these might have become known to them through learned conversation and instruction of catechumens.

But I chiefly attended to those passages in which Firmicus recounts the same myths found in other apologetic writers in almost the same order and nearly in the very words of earlier writers [Col. 0976D]. Such agreement, as will be apparent from the notes, is observed quite often with Clement of Alexandria’s *Exhortation to the Greeks*, Minucius Felix’s *Octavius*, and above all Arnobius’s books *Against the Nations*. He also seems often to have consulted Lactantius, and certainly studied with constant care Cyprian’s three books of *Testimonies*. For very many sayings from the Old and New Testaments which he adduces agree with Cyprian’s text—not merely in common and worn passages, but also where they offer readings different from those supplied by manuscripts and citations in the works of other Fathers [Col. 0977A].

Nor did he wholly neglect pagan writers. From not a few passages it is evident that Firmicus studied Cicero’s books *On the Nature of the Gods* carefully. He drew some things from Porphyry’s *On the Cave of the Nymphs*, perhaps also from another of his treatises, *On Abstinence from Eating Flesh*. In chapter 14 he further cites that philosopher’s book *On Philosophy Derived from Oracles* (*Περὶ τῆς ἐκ λογίων φιλοσοφίας*), which long ago perished through the injury of time.

Yet Firmicus also contains myths found in no other pagan or Christian writer; for this reason, modern writers on mythology quite frequently appeal to his testimony [Col. 0977B]. From where, then, did he draw these matters unknown to others? I shall state my opinion: from Euhemerus’s *Sacred Inscription* (*Ἱερὰ Ἀναγραφή*). For since he understood and explained pagan myths only historically, scorning every physical or mystical interpretation, that exposition by Euhemerus of all Greek mythology must have greatly pleased him. It is plainly evident that Firmicus followed Euhemerus in what he says concerning Jupiter.

How a Greek writer, Euhemerus, became known to him is obvious to all. Ennius had rendered Euhemerus into Latin; many fragments of this translation are cited or transcribed by Lactantius in *Divine Institutions*, book I, chs. 11, 13, 14, 17, and 22. It is likewise cited by Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, I.42; Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Greeks*, ch. 2, p. 20 of Potter’s edition; Minucius Felix [Col. 0977C], *Octavius*, ch. 21; and Arnobius, *Against the Nations*, IV.29. It is therefore no wonder that this author, a destroyer of pagan religions, was known to Firmicus, pleased him, and was consulted by him.

Rather, one is moved to wonder that apologists for Christianity, so diligent in handling the same subject as Euhemerus, nevertheless cited his name, book, and passages from it less frequently than they ought. Only a few fragments excerpted from ancient authors—especially from the Ennian translation—have thus far been collected. Yet I do not doubt that, from Firmicus and from other writers alike, many such remnants (*λείψανα*) could be recovered, if greater diligence and sound critical judgment in distinguishing and assessing them were applied; these could enrich Hessel’s collection in his edition of Ennius.  
[Note: [Col. 0977D] Amsterdam, 1707, quarto.]  
[Note: [Col. 0977D] The passages in which he is cited were diligently collected by the late Johannes Conrad Orelli in his notes on Arnobius IV.20, vol. II, p. 245 [Col. 0978D]; John Lydus and the scholiasts may perhaps supply others.]

This would certainly have been accomplished by the remarkably learned Johannes Lundblad, Doctor of Sacred Theology and ordinary public professor of eloquence and poetry at the University of Lund. In two dissertations on Euhemerus (Lund, Gothland, 1804), he had begun to publish and elucidate his fragments; but he was taken from the living before he could complete the work he had begun. Following in the footsteps of that excellent man and my dearest friend, I have resolved—if God grants leisure—to collect and publish whatever remains of Euhemerus I can discover.

## VI

[Col. 0978A]

Firmicus, wholly unknown until the middle of the sixteenth century, was first published in print by Matthias Flacius Illyricus at Strasbourg in 1562, from a manuscript discovered at Minden in Westphalia. This is the only manuscript that preserved our author for posterity. The same fortune befell Phaedrus, Velleius Paterculus, the first five books of Tacitus’s *Annals*, Hesychius, the First Epistle of Clement of Rome to the Corinthians, Minucius Felix, and Arnobius.

Where the manuscript of our Firmicus lies hidden today—for “lies hidden” I say, since it is mentioned nowhere—I do not know. Ritter mentions Flacius’s edition in his *Biography of Illyricus* (Frankfurt, 1725), p. 353, but does not give the place or year of printing; from this I infer that Ritter had not seen it [Col. 0978B]. It is exceedingly rare. It is lacking from our libraries, both the Royal and the University; nor was it in the Bunavian library, now joined with the Royal Library at Dresden. But I found it in the select library of the Reverend Hansen, pastor of Slangerup in the diocese of Zealand, who generously gave me this precious possession (*κειμήλιον*).

Flacius speaks thus in his preface to Andreas Meiendorfius concerning the manuscript from which he drew his edition:

> “For awakening this pious gratitude and zeal in our minds, while certain pious writings and even some impious writings have been useful, so too is this work of Julius Firmicus against the errors of profane religions, which I discovered at Minden, an ancient and not undistinguished city of Westphalia, and now for the first time publish for the public benefit. It is indeed a little book most worthy to survive, both because of the elegance of its style and because of the knowledge it contains of pagan antiquity and also of Christianity. From it, if only you consider somewhat more attentively what is said concerning Christ, sacrifices, heavenly bread, images, and other matters, you may learn not a little about the purity of doctrine and the simplicity and purity of the Church’s rites.” [Col. 0978C]

So he writes. Moreover, there is scarcely any hope that another manuscript of this author of ours will emerge. Copies are absent from the richest libraries: namely, they are absent from Vienna, Munich, Paris, St Mark’s in Venice, and St Gall; nor are they held in British and Belgian libraries, although Dutch editors were certainly attentive to investigating this matter. Nor are they in the Vatican, which is, as it were, the library of libraries [Col. 0978D], and which for two centuries has had as its custodians the most learned men—Holstenius, Leo Allatius, Zaccagnius, Marinius, and others—who would by no means have neglected such a discovery (*εὕρημα*).

Unless, perhaps, chance reveals it in some palimpsest manuscript, or brings it to light from a corner of a monastic library not yet adequately explored, we shall continue to have the use of that one copy alone which emerged almost three centuries ago.

Flacius did not state its age. But the whole character of the text shows that it was copied by a scribe not unskilled [Col. 0979A]. For it has not very many errors, and these are easily corrected. The gaps should not be charged to the scribe; they undoubtedly existed in the manuscript which he copied. The preface is mutilated at the beginning, but Flacius’s words, “Some things are lacking,” seem to indicate that not very much was missing in the Minden manuscript. At the place, moreover, where Wower’s edition and those following it (in this edition, col. 983) display a gap, Flacius found none in his manuscript, or at least did not note one. Nevertheless, the context teaches that something is missing, since Firmicus did not fulfil his promises.

In chapter 5, after the words “but let him follow the laws of the Persians,” there is one gap in Flacius and the same one in Wower; and shortly thereafter a second gap occurs, which Flacius did not note [Col. 0979B]. It therefore seems to have been marked conjecturally by Wower. The remaining gaps seem to arise only from individual words having been erased and do not seriously impede the sense.

Wower and Gronovius corrected certain errors; I too have added a few emendations in the notes, supplying a correction to the text itself in only two places, in chapter 16, where *Abaris the Scythian* must plainly be read instead of *Avarus the Scythian*.

My chief concern in this new edition of Firmicus was to elucidate, as briefly as possible, what he recounts about pagan rites. To that end I transcribed the notes of Wower and other learned men on Firmicus, adding much that Hertz observed in his dissertation on Firmicus. Nor did I neglect the editors of Fathers older than Firmicus, in whom things similar to his statements are read: namely Ouzelius, Heraldus, Rigault, Davis, and Lindner on Minucius Felix; Walch on Lactantius; Elmenhorst and above all Orelli on Arnobius; not to mention others whom I consulted here and there [Col. 0979C].

I have also added much from my own resources, especially to the later chapters from 18 onward, which Wower almost entirely neglected and the editors following him failed to address. They treated the elucidation of this author, far from contemptible, lightly and perfunctorily.

Finally, since quite a number of biblical passages are cited from pre-Jerome Latin translations, I judged it necessary to examine their actual readings. This was not difficult. I quickly found that Sabatier had diligently collated them in his *Ancient Latin Versions of the Holy Bible*. Therefore I especially sought to determine which among the many manuscripts of the old version—or, rather, old versions—Firmicus had before him. Almost every page taught me that, among all Latin Fathers, he agrees most closely with Cyprian, especially with that bishop’s books of *Testimonies against the Jews* and *On the Unity of the Church*. Thus the sacred texts he uses were borrowed either from these works or from manuscripts very similar to those read by Cyprian [Col. 0979D].

This, then, is the sum of the labour I have expended upon Firmicus. I admit that one kind of inquiry remains, which judges of such matters may perhaps desire: a comparison of our author’s exegesis and theological opinions with the interpretation of the same passages and exposition of doctrines mentioned by Firmicus in the other apologists and Fathers [Col. 0980A]. I have not wholly neglected it. Yet since Firmicus, viewed exegetically and dogmatically, is of only slight use to theologians, whereas pagan mythology and mystery religions derive from him a light not to be despised, I judged the latter matters more important and applied myself more carefully to elucidating them.

I wish that the most learned Orelli had also bestowed upon Firmicus the wealth of his learning, as he had promised in his preface to Arnobius, p. XVI. Then my labours would certainly not have been needed. But after being occupied for several years by other learned labours, he recently departed this life, greatly to be lamented.

## VII

Before proceeding to expound the argument of the book which I shall discuss, I shall make a few remarks about its title. Since only one copy exists, or ever existed—the one brought to light by Flacius—the only title that may be regarded as genuine is that which Flacius assigned it, and which he undoubtedly read in the Minden manuscript itself: *On the Error of Profane Religions*. Therefore, if modern writers who have mentioned this book stated the title somewhat differently—for example, Balthasar Bonifacius in his *Ludicrous History* (Brussels, 1656, p. 456), who calls the work *On the Error of Profane Nations and Religions* [Col. 0980C], and Baronius, in whom the book is called *On the Mysteries and Errors of Profane Religions*—they undoubtedly cited its title from memory, without consulting the book.  
[Note: [Col. 0979D] Hertz, *On Julius Firmicus Maternus*, p. 36.]

The author’s name is clearly given in the Minden manuscript. Thus no credence should be given to Giraldi, who calls him Villius, or to Glandorpius, who calls him Quintus Villius.  
[Note: [Col. 0979D] In Hertz, p. 11.]

Both moreover confuse him with the astrologer. The former reports, on the authority of others, that the name was read in a very ancient manuscript and on an ancient stone.  
[Note: [Col. 0980D] Ibid.]

The latter cites no authority.  
[Note: [Col. 0980D] *Onomasticon*, p. 905.]

The title further says, “To the Emperors Constantius and Constans”; and rightly so, for the book is addressed to these emperors, as is abundantly clear from numerous passages. Baronius is therefore wrong in believing the book to have been written to Constantine and Constans [Col. 0980D]. For all the historical events it mentions occurred after the death of Constantine, which took place in 340. I have already explained the letters *V.C.* added to Firmicus’s name.

## VIII

I now proceed to expound the argument of the book, generally following Hertz. I shall first make only this preliminary observation: in the mutilated preface, in my opinion, not much is missing. The leaves do not appear to have been cut from the Minden manuscript, since the title is present and Flacius has at the beginning only, “Some things are lacking.” If the title had been absent from the beginning and merely added at the book’s end in these words—“Here ends Julius Firmicus Maternus, V.C., *On the Error of Profane Religions*”—as such subscriptions occur in many ancient books, Flacius would certainly have indicated it.

What is missing, therefore, is a brief address to the emperors and an exposition of the subject. Firmicus seems to have moved on to certain Christian doctrines concerning the creation of the world and the fall of the first-created human beings, deceived by the devil’s snares [Col. 0981A]. Through these he prepared his way to admonish pagans—for, although the book is dedicated to emperors, he frequently addresses pagans—to guard themselves against a similar fraud.

From this there is an easy transition to the origin of oracles and divinations, according to Hertz’s opinion, based upon editions which have a gap immediately after the beginning. But the Minden manuscript, as the first Flacian edition teaches, has no such gap. Nor do I see why it is necessary to take the preface’s words, “By manifest arguments and the testimony of examples we shall prove that divination was invented and perfected by the devil,” to mean that the writer had initially determined to treat only this topic, when he returns to it repeatedly in what follows.

Hertz has demonstrated—or at least made highly probable by numerous arguments—that Firmicus touched upon certain Christian doctrines at the beginning of the little book [Col. 0981B]. “If what survives is only a fragment,” he says, “if an exposition of certain Christian doctrines preceded it, it does not seem to me at all inconsistent with truth that Firmicus composed an apology for the Christian religion suited to his age, and, changing what seemed to require change according to the circumstances of the times, preserved in constructing it the same order which he saw earlier apologists had maintained.”

I readily grant this to Hertz, provided the doctrines were indicated only very briefly rather than expounded. But when he adds: “That is, in the first part of the treatise he defended the doctrines and rites of divine religion, and also the entire conduct of Christians, against pagan calumnies; while in the latter he exposed the errors of profane religions,” I would observe that Firmicus acted rather as an adversary of pagan superstition than as an apologist for Christian doctrine and worship [Col. 0981C].

In that age apologies were no longer needed in the sense in which Athenagoras, Justin, Tertullian, Minucius Felix, and others had composed them while the worship of deities flourished. For in Constantine’s age all pagan affairs were already tottering: the emperors had devoted themselves to Christ; an immense multitude had deserted the altars of the gods; laws had already been enacted against pagan worship, which, once dominant, was now almost oppressed [Col. 0981D–0982A].

These facts must certainly be considered and weighed when Firmicus is compared with earlier apologists. From them is to be explained the difference in his entire discourse, which more than once urges and incites emperors to destroy pagan worship by force. Such a thought could never have occurred to earlier apologists, although they too almost everywhere declare their hostility toward the religion which they attack.

## IX

The editions of Firmicus known to me are the following:

Julii Firmici Materni, *A Man of Consular Rank, Book on the Error of Profane Religions, addressed to the Emperors Constantius and Constans*, never before brought to light. Printed at Strasbourg by Paul Machaeropoeus, at the expense of Johann Oporinus, 1562, octavo. The preface is signed by Matthias Flacius Illyricus. First edition.

—Paris, 1575. —With the Latin Mythographers, edited by Hieronymus Commelin. Heidelberg, 1599, octavo. —Paris, 1610. —*Julius Firmicus, On the Error of Profane Religions*, edited by Johannes a Wower (Hamburg, 1603), octavo. —In the works of Cyprian, edited by Philippe le Prieur. —Paris, 1666, folio. —With Wower’s notes, Oxford, 1678, octavo. —In Galland, *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. V, pp. 65 ff. [Col. 0982C] —In *Bibliotheca Patrum Maxima*, vol. IV, pp. 164–179.

In N. Rigault’s edition of Minucius Felix and Cyprian’s *On the Vanity of Idols*, with notes by J. a Wower and a new index. Leiden, 1645, octavo.

—The same edition reprinted, with the editorial work of Jacob Oiselius, Leiden, 1652, quarto. —In Jacob Oiselius’s Minucius Felix. Leiden, 1672, octavo. —Appended to le Maire’s edition of Minucius Felix, Leiden, 1632, quarto. —In Jacob Gronovius’s Minucius Felix and Cyprian’s *On the Vanity of Idols*. Leiden, 1709. The same edition, at least with a new title, appeared at Rotterdam in 1743, octavo. —With Arnobius in Oberthür’s edition of the Latin Fathers. Würzburg, 1783, vol. V. From this edition [Col. 0982D] we divided Firmicus’s text into separate chapters.

Translated into Dutch and illustrated with notes by G. Kempfer, 1718.

[Col. 0981]

# JULIUS FIRMICUS MATERNUS, A MAN OF CONSULAR RANK, ON THE ERROR OF PROFANE RELIGIONS. (C)*

## PREFACE

[Col. 0981D]

. . . that which the Craftsman did in the making of man, as we said before, must be specifically unfolded again through the yearly admonitions and communications of the lost. [Note: We discussed the lacuna in the preface (preceding column, no. VIII, beginning), where we also presented Hertz’s opinion concerning the omissions. They do not seem to be so extensive as Flacius’s words indicate. [Col. 0982D]] We shall prove, by evident reasoning and by the testimony of examples, in witness to the truth, that divination was invented and perfected by the Devil, [Note: The Fathers agree in this assertion. For example, Tertullian: “the demon of the Pythian oracle,” *On Prayer*, ch. 13. In the same sense Athenagoras, *Embassy for the Christians*, ch. 23, Minucius Felix in the *Octavius*, ch. 26, Arnobius, *Against the Nations*, I, ch. 56, and Firmicus himself, ch. 27, unanimously attributed all errors and false religions to demons; Athenagoras calls them “deceivers of men” (ἀπατηλοὺς τῶν ἀνθρώπων). It is unnecessary to demonstrate at length from historical examples that not all pagans put faith in divinations. Under the leadership of Xenocrates, the Eleatic philosophers are known to have rejected all divination; see Cicero, *On Divination*, I.3; Plutarch, *Opinions of the Philosophers*, I.1, who makes the same assertion concerning Epicurus; Brandis, *Commentary on the Eleatics*, I, p. 71.] so that, by a thought corrupted in spirit, by the hope of fleeting prosperity, and by perverted judgment, he might overthrow wretched human beings entangled in perpetual disasters. [Note: After the word *entangled* (*implicitos*), Wower and other editors mark a lacuna; yet there is no indication of one in the first edition. If there was one, Firmicus kept his promise and assembled much material from history and antiquities concerning the origin of divination in the Devil’s cunning and in the hatred with which he pursued the human race.] . . .

## CHAPTER I. He establishes the elements as principles of things; but, because they are diverse and contrary in power, none of them is the supreme divinity (although here he speaks only of fire, having refuted the worship of the others in the following chapters). Rather, all have God as their maker and governor.

No one doubts that the four Elements are the principles of created things—that is, fire, water, air, [Col. 0983B] and earth. But these Elements are diverse, indeed opposed in power. Therefore those nations are in error which, while assigning primacy to the elements, [Note: Athanasius briefly touches upon the worship of the Elements in *Against the Greeks*, ch. 9. That these too were worshipped by the Persians is taught by Creuzer, *Symbolism and Mythology of Ancient Peoples*, I, p. 651; Klenker, *Persica*, in the appendix to the *Zend-Avesta*, chs. 20 and 114.] still designate fire as though it were the supreme God, [Note: He means the Persians. On fire-worship among the Persians, see Herodotus I.131; Maximus of Tyre, Oration 38; Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, V.39; Evagrius, *Ecclesiastical History*, ch. 14. Since these writers were almost contemporaries of Firmicus, it is sufficient to cite them here. Add Eustathius on Dionysius, *Description of the World*, who says of the Persians: “They honor fire” (τιμῶσι τὸ πῦρ). More in Brisson, *On the Royal Principate of the Persians* (Strasbourg, 1710), p. 349, and Creuzer, *Symbolism and Mythology*, I, pp. 692, 713. On the highly celebrated Persian worship of the Sun and Mithras, see Creuzer IV, p. 410; on water as sacred among the Persians, Brisson, p. 356. “They still designate . . .”: thus Tertullian, *Against the Valentinians*, ch. 32: “If perhaps we are assigned to the Persians,” i.e. if we are taught to follow the Persian religion; *Apology*, ch. 16: “I am assigned as an angel, not an angel or a female angel”; *On Prescription*, ch. 21, and frequently. See Semler’s index of Tertullianic Latin, vol. VI.] as though all the rest received their substance from its heat. They do not know that all the Elements are joined together by their very contrariety, and that they themselves have God [Col. 0984A] as their maker: he established each in its own place and order, and created everything which we grasp either by mind or by thought, or certainly behold with our eyes, as composed through the fellowship of his divine Word (John 1:2–3), through the balanced regulation of bodies in this whole universe.

## CHAPTER II. He refutes the worship of water among the Egyptians.

The inhabitants of Egypt, receiving the benefits of waters, worship water, [Note: Athanasius, *Against the Greeks*, ch. 24: “Above all, the Egyptians have especially honored water and proclaim it to be gods” (Πάντων μάλιστα Αἰγύπτιοι τὸ ὕδωρ προτετιμήκασι, καὶ θεοὺς ἀναγορεύουσι). The same in *On the Incarnation of the Word of God*, ch. 45. Likewise Plutarch, *On Isis and Osiris*, ch. 5, asserts that nothing was held by the Egyptians in greater honor than the Nile. Wower.—They worshipped it as a god and represented it in statues and coins (Eckhel, *Doctrine of Ancient Coins*, IV, p. 36). The sanctity of Nile-water is well known: it was transported even to Rome for sacred use. Lactantius, *Divine Institutions*, II.6, doubtless has this Egyptian superstition chiefly in view. Constantine the Great had already forbidden the worship of the Nile (Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, III.25). The Indians regarded water as the principle of all things (Creuzer I, p. 595), and among the Greeks so did Thales; Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, I.25; Lactantius II.10; Arnobius II.9, with Elmenhorst and Orelli there.] pray to waters, and venerate waters through the superstitious persistence of vows. But in their sacred rites—what they call mysteries—[Note: A gloss. Wower.—Nevertheless these secret rites are contrasted with the public rites mentioned by Firmicus in the opening words of this chapter. On these mysteries of later times, especially those to which Firmicus refers, see San-Crucius, *Mysteries of Paganism*, vol. II, p. 151 ff., and Creuzer I, p. 259 ff.] they add tragic deaths and mournful contests attended by the fear of disaster. [Note: Plutarch treated this entire tale in a separate work; the interpretation of Firmicus’s words should be sought from him. Wower.] They say that incest with a sister and adultery were committed, and that this crime was punished by the severe vengeance of a husband. Isis is the sister; [Note: Minucius Felix, *Octavius*, ch. 21, attests that the history of Isis was narrated by Euhemerus: “Euhemerus recounts the births, native countries, and tombs of the gods and points them out through the provinces: the Dictaean Jupiter, the Delphic Apollo, Pharian Isis, and Eleusinian Ceres. Prodicus speaks of men assumed into divinity who, wandering about, benefited humankind through the discovery of new crops.” See Ouzelius on this passage.] Osiris, the brother; Typhon, the husband. When Typhon discovered that his wife Isis had been corrupted by the incestuous desires of her brother, he killed Osiris, tore him limb from limb, and scattered the quivering parts of the miserable body along all the banks of the river Nile. [Note: Plutarch, *On Isis and Osiris*, ch. 18; Diodorus Siculus I.21. On Osiris’s death and dismemberment see the material collected by Creuzer, *Symbolism and Mythology*, I, p. 259 ff. and 302 ff.] Isis, having rejected Typhon, enlisted as companions, in order to bury both brother and husband, her sister Nephthys [Note: She was Typhon’s sister and wife; he [Anubis] was the son of Osiris and Nephthys. Plutarch, *On Isis and Osiris*, ch. 14; Jablonski, *Egyptian Pantheon*, III, pp. 46, 112–113, 118–119. According to Jablonski’s conjecture, the name has an Egyptian origin, either from a word meaning “that which is exposed to the wind” or from another meaning “that which sets a boundary,” pp. 120–121.] and Anubis the hunter. [Note: Perhaps more correctly, “the barker.” Thus “barking Anubis” in Virgil, *Aeneid*, VIII.698, and “the barking Anubis” in Propertius, *Elegies*, III.10.41—unless he is called a hunter because, by the skill of a tracking dog, as Firmicus says, he found the limbs of the dismembered body.] For this reason a dog’s head [Note: The dog-headed one is called an inventor in Minucius Felix, *Octavius*, ch. 21. Apuleius likewise describes him: “Anubis, raising high the neck of a dog, bearing a caduceus in his left hand.” Athanasius, *Against the Greeks*, ch. 9.] was placed upon him, because by the skill of a tracking dog he found the parts of the torn body. Thus Isis gave the recovered Osiris to burial.

These men had indeed been kings in Egypt [Note: Synesius, *On Providence*, pp. 91 ff. through 121, ed. Petavius. Wower.] as well as tyrants; but Osiris was just, apart from what he committed with his sister. Typhon was mad, ungovernable, and proud. Therefore the one is worshipped, the other avoided. [Note: Yet Typhon was worshipped in idols and temples. See my programme, *On the Typhonians of the Egyptians*, Copenhagen, 1822. Remains of these Typhonians still survive.] This is the substance of the Isiac rite. In the inner sanctuaries they keep the buried idol of Osiris; they mourn it with annual lamentations, [Note: Athanasius, *Against the Greeks*, ch. 10. Wower.] shave their heads, [Note: Plutarch, *On Isis and Osiris*, ch. 4; Artemidorus, *Interpretation of Dreams*, I.23; Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, II.1; Prudentius, *Against Symmachus*, I.609: “of Isis, forever lamenting her lost Osiris.” “And rites of mimicry and ridicule among their bald-headed celebrants.” Synesius, *Encomium of Baldness*, p. 79, ed. Petavius. That people customarily shaved in mourning is well known from Plutarch, *On Superstition*, and other sources. Wower.] so that they may bewail the pitiable fate of their king with the disgrace of a disfigured head; they beat their breasts, [Note: Herodotus II.61 recounts this concerning the festival of Isis at Busiris, adding that Carians living in Egypt wounded their faces with knives. Lactantius, *Divine Institutions*, I.21: “The Egyptian rites of Isis are performed because she either lost or found her little son. First, her priests, their bodies shaven, beat their breasts and lament, as she herself did when she lost him. Then the boy is brought forth as though found, and that mourning is turned into joy.” Theophilus, *To Autolycus*, I.14. Wower.—Athenagoras, *Embassy*, ch. 12; Minucius Felix, *Octavius*, ch. 21. Similar material occurs in the poem addressed to a senator who had deserted Christianity, among the works attributed to Cyprian. Lampridius, *Commodus*, ch. 9: “[Commodus] compelled the devotees of Isis continually to strike their breasts in the rain until they perished.”] tear their arms, reopen the scars of old wounds, so that through yearly mournings the destruction of that baleful and pitiable death may be renewed in their souls. And when they have done these things on appointed days, they then pretend that they find the remains of the dismembered body; and, having found them, rejoice as though their grief had been lulled to sleep. [Note: Minucius Felix, ch. 22, says the same concerning the lost son of Isis: “When the little one is then found, Isis rejoices and the priests exult.”]

O wretched and perishable mortality: you send funeral offerings to your kings every year, while neglecting the supreme God who has ordered all things by the governance of his divine craftsmanship; and you lose both your hope and your life. You are not corrected by the splendor of the light shown to you; you do not seek the marks of liberty restored; you do not acknowledge the hope of salvation returned to you; nor do you request, in repentance for former crimes, pardon. You vainly suppose that this water which you worship [Note: The water of the Nile (*On Isis and Osiris*, ch. 5), and also the water of sacred springs and rivers worshipped by pagans.] will at some time benefit you. There is another water through which renewed human beings are reborn. This water which you worship every year is dried up by some other force that drains the channels of its veins, or else is polluted by the ill-omened blood of your king [Note: Osiris.]. [Col. 0986A] That water which you despise [Note: Namely, baptismal water.] is adorned by the fiery majesty of the venerable Spirit, [Note: He alludes to the history of Christ’s baptism: Luke 3:21; John 1:32–33.] so that healing health may flow from it to believing people through the old scars of conscience.

But in these funerals and mournings—which truly are funerals—concerning things that happened and whose remnants still exist today (for even now Osiris’s tomb is in Egypt, [Note: He means Busiris, where Diodorus Siculus I.85 relates that the body of Osiris, enclosed in a wooden cow, was buried by Isis. The same author records other sepulchral cities of Osiris according to another tradition; besides Busiris, the more celebrated were Philae, Abydos, and Memphis. Nor does he omit the depths of the Nile between Elephantine and Syene. See Creuzer I, p. 259 ff., and *Herodotean Commentaries*, I.2, §§10, 11, 13: “And not only is the tomb of Osiris displayed, but also the embalming places” (Καὶ οὐ μόνον ὁ τάφος τοῦ Ὀσίριδος δείκνυται, ἀλλὰ καὶ ταριχεῖα), Athanasius, ch. 25. Many Egyptian amulets survive on which is represented the column in which Isis concealed Osiris’s body (Plutarch, *On Isis and Osiris*, ch. 15); their form is as follows:] and the remains of the burned body are seen), [Note: I do not know from where Firmicus drew this. It seems to be a new tale, and scarcely from Euhemerus. But in Egypt corpses were never cremated.] their defenders wish to attach a physical explanation. Calling Osiris the seeds of crops, [Note: Athenagoras, ch. 19; Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, II.1 and III.12; differently Plutarch, *On Isis and Osiris*, ch. 33. See Suidas under Δόγμα. Wower.] Isis the earth, [Note: Compare Ouzelius on Minucius Felix, p. 162–163, and Creuzer, *Symbolism and Mythology*, IV, p. 220.] and Typhon heat, [Note: Plutarch, *On Isis and Osiris*, ch. 33: Typhon is the scorching and pestilential wind called *Semum* among Eastern peoples. Jablonski, *Egyptian Pantheon*, III, pp. 84–85, 91–92. See Norberg’s dissertation, “On the Wind Semum,” in *Academic Opuscula*, London and Gothenburg, 1819, III, p. 302.] they say that, because ripe crops are gathered by heat for human use and are separated from companionship with the earth, then sown again as winter approaches, this is the death of Osiris when crops are yielded; [Note: Read: “are yielded” (*redduntur*). Wower.] but his discovery is when crops, conceived by the generative nourishment of earth, [Note: Wower changed the reading *genitalis* of the first edition to *gentiali*.] begin once more to be produced through a new generation.

Suppose this to be the true explanation of those rites; suppose that vows are paid to divinities on account of crops: why do you add incest, adultery, the destruction wrought by pitiable punishment? What evil example do you display from your rites to people wandering astray and simply desiring to sin? The physical explanation you allege should be concealed by some other method. But why should what is known to everyone have needed concealment? Why do you mourn the crops of the earth and lament the growing seeds? All these things have been bestowed for the support of the human race by the generosity of the supreme God. Thanks should be given [Col. 0986C] to the supreme God for this; the gift of the supreme God is not something to be mourned. Mourn rather because you are in error, and lament because you renew your error by perpetual mourning. Do not seek another’s funeral in yearly rites; rather, prepare comforts for your own funerals every year. O wretched person! You rejoice that you have found something or other, while through these rites you lose your soul every year. There you find nothing except an image which you yourself set up, nothing except something that you must either seek again or mourn again. Seek rather the hope of salvation; seek the origin of light; seek that which may either commend you to the supreme God or restore you to him. And when you have found the true way of salvation, rejoice; then, with the freedom of speech raised upright, proclaim: “We have found; we rejoice together” (Εὑρήκαμεν, συγχαίρομεν), [Note: The customary words of those crying out in the Isiac rites after the discovery of Osiris’s body. The scholiast on Juvenal’s *Satires*, VIII.29, “The people cry out as they cry to Osiris when he has been found,” adds: “The people of Egypt, when Osiris was found, said: ‘We have found him; we rejoice together’” (Εὑρήκαμεν, συγχαίρομεν). For they believed that Isis cried this when she found Osiris’s limbs; see Cramer’s edition of this scholiast (Hamburg, 1823), p. 312. Athenagoras, *Embassy*, ch. 19, has the same words. Wower.—Compare also Minucius Felix, *Octavius*, ch. 21, and Augustine, *City of God*, VI.10.] when, after your repentance, you have been liberated from these calamities by the pardon of the supreme God.

## CHAPTER III. He refutes the worship of earth among the Phrygians.

[Col. 0987B] The Phrygians who live at Pessinus [Note: Strabo XII.7; Ammianus Marcellinus XXII.22 [or 9]. On the πέτρα διοπετής, “heaven-fallen stone,” of Pessinus, which was transported to Rome during the Second Punic War (Livy XXIX.11 and 14), see Appian, *Hannibalic War*, ch. 56; Herodian I.2; Arnobius, *Against the Nations*, VI.11 and VII.46 [Orelli]; Augustine, *City of God*, III.12; Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 25; Lactantius II.7; Cicero, *On the Responses of the Soothsayers*. Compare Falconet’s dissertation on the stone of the Mother of the Gods, *Memoirs of the Academy of Inscriptions and Belles-Lettres*, vol. XXIII, p. 213; and, if it is worth so much, my antiquarian dissertations published in German, p. 257 ff.] around the banks of the river Gallus [Note: Stephanus, *On Cities*, under “Gallus.” Wower.] assign to earth primacy over the other elements and wish it to be the mother of all things. [Note: Arnobius II.52: “We see that others among the wiser people say that the earth is the mother of human beings”; VII.33. Lactantius II.10. Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, chs. 3–4. Servius on *Georgics* II.268. Orpheus, *Hymn* 25: “Earth, divine mother of the blessed gods and mortal human beings” (Γαῖα θεὰ μήτηρ μακάρων θνητῶν τ’ ἀνθρώπων). On Cybele see the notes of Rigault, Ouzelius, and Elmenhorst on Minucius Felix, ch. 21; Heraldus and Davies on the same author; Cambridge edition, pp. 42 and 105. Compare also Orelli’s notes on Arnobius, vol. I, p. 79.]

Then, so that they too might establish for themselves an annual sequence of sacred rites, they consecrated with annual mourning the love of their wealthy queen, who tyrannically wished to avenge the arrogance of her beloved young man. [Note: By removing his genitals, because he had not kept faith (*Altis*). Refer to this what follows concerning the angry woman. Lactantius, *Epitome*, ch. 8. The tale is told differently; some, indeed most, relate that Attis himself did what is here attributed to the angry Cybele. See the following note.] And, either to satisfy the angry woman or to seek solace for her repentance, they claimed that the man whom they had shortly before buried had come back to life; and when the woman’s mind burned with the impatience of excessive love, they built temples for the dead young man. Then what the angry woman had done in response to the injury of beauty spurned, the priests chose to undergo themselves. [Note: If the preposition were absent here, the Latin would be better: Gronovius.—The Mother of the Gods loved Attis; driven mad by Acdestis, he cut off his own genitals with a potsherd. The Galli, her priests, imitate this in honor of the Great Mother. Arnobius V.7, 39, and Orelli on the passage; Augustine, *City of God*, II.4; Lucian, *On the Syrian Goddess*, ch. 15; Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, II.4; and many others. Wower.—“What? Would one who makes an offering from his own blood and prays through his wounds not be better irreligious than religious in this fashion?” These are the words of Minucius Felix, ch. 24, Cambridge edition, p. 123; compare the notes on the passage.]

Thus, in their annual rites, a funeral procession is arranged together with honor for this earth; and while people are persuaded that they worship the earth, they venerate the destruction of a miserable death. Here too, most sacred Emperors, so that this error may be concealed, they maintain that these rites have been devised with a physical explanation. [Note: On Phrygian worship, its physical explanation, and its syncretism with similar cults, compare especially Creuzer II, p. 36 ff. Firmicus, however, refers everything to the fertility of the earth and crops renewed at an appointed time.] They say that crops love the earth, and that what grows from the crops is itself loved; the punishment [Col. 0988A] he endured, they say, is what the reaper does to ripe crops with a sickle. His death, they say, is when collected seeds are stored away; and his life again is when scattered seeds are restored in their yearly cycles.

I should like them now to answer my inquiry: why have they joined this simple matter of seeds and crops with crime, death, arrogance, punishment, and love? Was there nothing else that could be said? Was there nothing by which wretched mortality might give thanks to the supreme God for crops? In order to give thanks for crops reborn, you howl; in order to rejoice, you mourn. Nor, even when you have seen the true explanation, are you ever sorry to have done this; rather, you act in such a manner that, occupied by annual lamentations, you always flee life and seek death. Let them tell me what benefit this gives the crops: that they sow their tears with yearly howlings in sorrow, groan amid the disasters of a death that has been slain, and say that this is composed according to a physical explanation. You mourn and lament, and conceal your mourning under another explanation.

The farmer knows when to break open the earth with the plough, when to entrust grain to the furrows. He knows when to harvest crops ripened by the sun’s heat, and when to thresh the parched grain. This is the physical explanation; these are the true sacrifices, performed by people of sound mind through yearly labor. Divinity seeks this simplicity: that people serve in gathering fruits according to the ordered laws of seasons. Why have inventions of a wretched death been sought for this order? Why is concealed with tears what ought not to have been concealed? From this they must admit that these rites [Col. 0988C] were devised not in honor of crops, but in honor of another’s death.

For when those who assign first place to this element say that the earth is the mother of all the gods, [Note: Orpheus, cited above; Plato, *Statesman*; Lucretius II.598; Varro, *On the Latin Language*; Elmenhorst on Arnobius, p. 94.] it is truly the mother of their gods, and we do not deny or reject this: for from it they make their assembled gods always either of stone or of wood. [Note: Said ironically.] Seas flow around the entire earth, and it is in turn enclosed and constrained by the circle of the encircling Ocean. It is covered also by the rounded height of heaven, swept by winds, sprinkled by rains, and confesses its fear by tremblings of continual motion. Consider what awaits you who worship these things, when your gods reveal their weakness to you by their daily declarations.

## CHAPTER IV. Likewise, the worship of air among the Assyrians and certain African peoples.

The Assyrians and part of the African peoples hold that air has leadership among the elements, and worship it under an imagined figure. [Note: Thus the Phoenicians, according to the very ancient testimony of Sanchuniathon in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, I.10: “[Usoos] consecrated two pillars to fire and wind, worshipped them, and at the same time poured libations to them from the animals he hunted” (τὸν Οὔσωον . . . ἀνιερῶσαι δύο στήλας πυρί τε καὶ πνεύματι, καὶ προσκυνῆσαι, ἅμα δὲ σπένδειν αὐταῖς ἐξ ὧν ἤγρευε θηρίων; ed. Orelli, p. 18). That the Assyrians—or Syrians, for the two names are often interchanged by ancient writers—worshipped air under the name of Juno or Venus we learn from Plutarch, *Crassus*, ch. 17, concerning the goddess of Hierapolis: “Some call this goddess Aphrodite, others Hera, others believe her to be the originating cause and nature that furnished all things with seed from moisture and revealed to humankind the beginning of all good things” (Γίνεται δὲ πρῶτον αὐτῷ σημεῖον ἀπὸ τῆς θεοῦ ταύτης, ἣν οἱ μὲν Ἀφροδίτην, οἱ δὲ Ἥραν, οἱ δὲ τὴν ἀρχὴν καὶ σπέρματα πᾶσιν ἐξ ὑγροῦ παρασχοῦσαν αἰτίαν καὶ φύσιν νομίζουσι, καὶ τὴν πάντων εἰς ἀνθρώπους ἀρχὴν ἀγαθῶν καταδείξασαν). On the worship of this Venus Urania, called among the Babylonians Ὀμόρκα or Ὀμορώκα, and Θαλάτθ (“Mother”) according to Berosus (ed. Richter, Leipzig, 1825, p. 50), as well as Μυλίττα or Μόλις, see Herodotus I.199 and Pausanias I.14. She was also worshipped with great reverence among the Carthaginians and Cypriots; compare my dissertations *On the Religion of the Carthaginians*, p. 62 ff., and *On the Temple of the Heavenly Goddess at Paphos*.]

They consecrated this same air under the name of Juno, or of virgin Venus—if virginity ever pleased Venus. To ensure that incest should not be absent even from her, they maintain that Juno became Jupiter’s wife from being his sister. [Note: This sacred marriage of the highest gods among all peoples—compare Creuzer I, p. 281—belongs not only to Jupiter and Juno but also to Liber and Libera (ibid., III, p. 370). On the incestuous marriages of gods, to which our author alludes, compare Minucius Felix, ch. 31: “Thus you worship incestuous gods, joined with mother, daughter, and sister.” The same is found in Athenagoras, chs. 16 and 27; Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation*, ch. 2, p. 14; Tatian, chs. 13 and 16; Arnobius IV.35 and V.9. For more, see Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, III.265: “Queen Juno, both sister and wife of Jupiter”; Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 14: “Jupiter shamefully mounting his sister”; Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, I.16.]

They feminized this element, [Note: Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, II.26: “The air lying between sea and heaven is consecrated under the name of Juno, who is Jupiter’s sister and wife, because it resembles the ether and is most closely joined with it.” They feminized it and attributed it to Juno because nothing is softer than it. Firmicus plainly had Cicero’s passage in view. So also in Heraclides Ponticus, *Homeric Allegories*, ch. 10, p. 53, ed. Schow: “Hera, after it [the Ether], is air, a softer element, and therefore female” (Ἡ δὲ Ἥρα μετ’ αὐτὸν [Αἰθέρα] ἔστιν ἀήρ, μαλακώτερον στοιχεῖον, διὰ τοῦτο καὶ θῆλυ); also ch. 25, p. 87. See Creuzer on Cicero’s passage; Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, I.13, on Juno as representing an aerial substance. Seneca, *Natural Questions*, III.14, states that the Egyptians assigned a double sex to every element.] moved by some sort of reverence, I know not what. Is it because air lies between sea and heaven that they pursue it with the effeminate voices of priests? Tell me: is this what they seek—the woman in a man, whom the chorus of their priests cannot otherwise serve unless they feminize their face, polish their skin, and disgrace male sex with women’s adornment? [Note: Clement of Alexandria, *Instructor*, III.3, p. 261, elegantly titles the chapter: “Against men who beautify themselves” (Πρὸς τοὺς καλλωπιζομένους τῶν ἀνδρῶν). Arnobius II.41: “For this reason [the ruler of the world] sent souls, that, forgetting their divine weight and dignity, they might acquire gems, little stones, and pearls at the cost of chastity; hang them from their necks; pierce their ears for plates of metal; seek cosmetics to make up their bodies; diminish their foreheads with bands; darken their eyes with soot; and not blush in male bodies to curl their hair with tongs, smooth their bodily skin, walk with bare knees, and by every other adornment both expose and soften the strength of manhood into the dress and luxuries of women.” See the notes in Orelli’s edition. Philochorus gives the reason in Macrobius III.8, where he teaches that Moon and Venus are the same divinity, and adds: “Men sacrifice in women’s dress, and women in men’s, because the same deity is considered both male and female.” Compare Creuzer, *Symbolism*, II, p. 163. Similar material occurs in the poem to the Senator who had returned from Christianity to idols, among the Cyprianic writings:

> V.3. A shameful disgrace brands the worshippers of the Great Mother.  
> For her priests in women’s tunics confess, by their inward apparel,  
> the inward vice.  
> They think lawful what is unlawful; therefore throughout the world  
> they walk softly, speak with softened words,  
> hold their ruined loins with an outstretched thumb,  
> and change their own sex by a crime openly practiced.  
> And when they celebrate their rites, they say that on these days  
> they are chaste—as though they were chaste only then;  
> if, as they claim, they are chaste then, what are they the rest of the time?  
> But because they are compelled at least once to be modest,  
> they rage in spirit, tear their bodies, and shed blood.
>
> V.21. Now you also say that age has not made you bald,  
> but your religion has; and that your feet, their shoe removed,  
> are bound with soft Gallic papyrus.

Compare our book *On the Religion of the Carthaginians*, pp. 82 and 84. The following verses of Commodian, an African poet, I think, agree with these:

> *Instructions*, XVII:  
> You have seen the Dindymarians: with what uproar  
> they enter upon their excesses while seeking to feign madness;  
> or when with a foul double axe they strike their own backs,  
> preserving by their teaching what they heal with blood.

Compare the notes of Rigault and Davies.]

One may see in the very temples, amid public groaning, pitiable spectacles: men suffering womanly acts [Note: “Where are debaucheries more readily procured by priests than among altars and shrines? Where are arts of seduction practiced and adulteries contemplated?” Minucius Felix, ch. 25. Especially in the temples of Isis: Ovid, *Amores*, II.2.25, and *Art of Love*, III.392; Juvenal, *Satires*, VI.488, and the scholiast, ed. Cramer, p. 445. Yet similar things were not absent from other temples. See Ouzelius’s and Davies’s notes on Minucius’s passage. Athanasius, *Against the Greeks*, ch. 26, likewise says that men underwent womanly acts in the worship of the Great Goddess.] and revealing, with glorious display, the stain of their impure and shameful bodies. They publicize their crimes and confess the defect of their contaminated bodies with the greatest mark of delight—perhaps “detestation.” [Note: Perhaps: *detestation* rather than *delight*. Wower.] They dress their long-nurtured hair as women do, and, clothed in delicate garments, scarcely support their heads upon wearied necks. Then, having thus made themselves alien to men, filled with the sound of pipes, they invoke their goddess, so that, filled with a wicked spirit, they may foretell future events as though they knew them to frivolous people.

What monster or portent is this? They deny that they are men, yet they are; they wish to be believed women, but the bodily condition they possess, whatever it may be, declares something else. It should also be considered what kind of divinity it is that delights in the lodging of an impure body, attaches itself to shameful limbs, and is appeased by the pollution of bodily defilement. Blush, wretched people, at your prostrate degradation; [Note: The first edition has *summitatem*, “height”; the others, *sublimitatem*, “sublimity.” Wower restored *supinitatem*, “prostration” or “degradation.”] God made you otherwise. When your company comes before the tribunal of God the Judge, you will bring with you nothing that God who made you will recognize. Cast off this error of so great a calamity, and at last abandon the pursuits of a profane mind. Do not condemn, by the criminal law of the Devil, the body that God made. While time still permits, help yourselves in your calamities. God’s mercy is rich; [Note: He has Matthew 18:27 in view.] he gladly forgives. Leaving ninety-nine sheep, he seeks the one that was lost (Matthew 18:12; Luke 15:4). And the father restores a garment to the prodigal son when he returns, and prepares a feast (Luke 15:22). Let no multitude of crimes cause you to despair. The supreme God, through his Son Jesus Christ our Lord, frees those who are willing and gladly forgives those who repent; he does not demand much [Note: Wower suggests: “he exacts no penalty” (*nec mulctam exigit*). The correction does not seem necessary.] in order to forgive. By faith and repentance alone you can redeem whatever you have lost through the criminal persuasions of the Devil.

## CHAPTER V. Likewise, fire among the Persians. He exposes their mysteries and tales, denounces their lascivious and mournful rites, often mingling exhortations drawn from Christian sacred writings; and at the end of the chapter, after a second lacuna, where he speaks of the human soul, he also presents a philosophical argument concerning the indissolubility of the soul.

[Col. 0992A]

The Persians and all the Magi who inhabit the borders of the Persian land carry fire before them [Note: [Col. 0991A] Xenophon testifies that fire was carried before Cyrus as he proceeded, *Cyropaedia*, book VIII, ch. 3, §12. This custom of carrying fire before a person later passed from the Persians to the Romans; for it is evident from Herodian, book I, ch. 8, §16, II, 8, and other passages in that writer, that fire was carried before the Augusti, if not earlier, at least from the time of Marcus Aurelius and Commodus onward, as a symbol of imperial and Augustan honor. On the Phoenicians as worshippers of fire, consult the passage from Sanchuniathon cited at ch. 4 in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, I, ch. 10. [Col. 0991C]] and think that it ought to be set above all the elements. [Note: [Col. 0991C] Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation*, ch. 5, p. 56: “The Magi among the Persians have honored fire, as have many of those who inhabit Asia.” Maximus of Tyre, Oration 38; Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, VII, ch. 8; Rufinus, *History*, II, ch. 26; and many others. The Persians worship all the elements as the illustrious offspring of God—“those who deify the elements”—but assigned the foremost place to fire and light. For all exalted and sacred conceptions ultimately look to and are referred to these. Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, V, ch. 38, Schulz ed., III, p. 1082. On the Babylonians’ worship of fire and water, compare Berosus in Clement, *Exhortation*, ch. 5, p. 57, Potter ed.]

Accordingly, they divide Jupiter [Note: [Col. 0991C] In Xenophon: “Zeus, greatest and king.” His supreme divinity, penetrating the universe with fire, gives it life and motion.] into two powers, [Note: [Col. 0991C] These are the divine powers, according to the doctrines of the philosophy of nearly all ancient peoples: the male, generative power, and the female, bringing-forth power.] transferring his nature to both sexes, [Note: [Col. 0991C] They undoubtedly refer to Mithras the god and Mithra [Col. 0991D] the goddess of the Persians; see Creuzer, *Symbols and Mythology*, I, 728 ff. Both were male and female fire. The Greeks likewise represented Jupiter, insofar as he was associated with air, as “of double nature” (*diphyēs*), according to Athenagoras, ch. 18. Plato calls Pan “of double nature” in the *Cratylus*, not, I would suppose, as some maintain, because of the lower and animal part of his body, but because he was regarded as the divinity of nature endowed with that twofold power which we have indicated.] and assign the substance of fire to images both male and female. [Note: [Col. 0991D] Add [a word] before *viri* (“male”), or, preferably, before *ignis* (“fire”). For they have two statues, one male and the other female, which are for them images or symbols of the twofold substance of fire. Strabo, who speaks of the statues, XI, ch. 8, p. 478, Tzschucke ed., prefers “torch”: those of Anaitis and Omanus and Anadatus, Persian genii, set upon the same altar at Zela by the Sacae and Massagetae. Clement of Alexandria, on Berosus’s authority (*book III*, p. 70, Richter ed.), reports that this worship of images among the Persians was introduced by Artaxerxes, son of Darius Ochus. [Col. 0992A]]

They portray the woman, indeed, with a threefold face, [Note: [Col. 0992A] Insofar as, in Greek thought, Mylitta, Artemis, and Persephone had coalesced in her (Creuzer I, 735). For there is no reason to think of a triple-headed idol fashioned in the likeness of Hecate. And although Mithras was often represented in works of art, I do not recall ever reading that Mithra was represented in the same works, unless the following words bear upon this.] binding her with monstrous serpents. [Note: [Col. 0992A] I do not know whether the following may be referred to this matter, or whether they have some resemblance to Firmicus’s account: Diodorus Siculus, book II, ch. 9, p. 123, Wesseling ed., tells of a statue of Ops seated upon the summit of the pyramid which Belus had built at Babylon. Two serpents [Col. 0992C] attended her; nor should we wonder that they were attendants or companions of the divine nature. Moreover, Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, I, chs. 19 and 20, explains why the image of a dragon was customarily attached to statues of the Sun.]

They do this so that they may not in any respect depart from their author, the Devil, [Note: [Col. 0992C] He refers to the story of the Fall of the first-created human beings, Genesis III.] but so that their goddess, defiled by serpents, may be adorned with the stained badges of the Devil.

But they worship the man as a driver-off of oxen [Note: [Col. 0992C] Mithras. For he was called *Bouklopos*, “ox-driver.” Porphyry, *On the Cave of the Nymphs*, ch. 18: “and the ox-driving god, secretly hearing generation.” Hence “driver-off of oxen,” which Statius expressly rendered, *Thebaid*, I, v. 720:

> Angry, she follows Mithras, who twists the horns.

His initiation is therefore called *bouklopiē*; and because it returned in its cycle every year, the poet spoke of the “cycles of Ox-driving,” that is, the regular festival returning in its yearly circuit. Joseph Scaliger in Wower—

> Moreover, you still depict him as a thief . . .

Commodian, *Instructions*, XIII, likewise called him a thief—

> He was forever turning away another’s cattle in caves,

confusing him with Cacus driving off Hercules’ cattle. Compare Zoëga, *Abhandlungen*, Welcker ed., p. 131. On this Mithras *Bouklopos*, see Creuzer, *Symbols*, I, p. 785 ff. According to Kleuker, the bull is a symbol of the female. I do not know whether that is correct; for it never has the form of a cow, but always of a bull. Yet Luctatius, on Statius’s *Thebaid*, I, vv. 719–720, understands by the bull the Moon subdued by Mithras. It will rather be the symbol of the primeval bull killed by the poisonous creatures of Ahriman, whose seed the good genii were believed to preserve in the Moon. Perhaps for this reason Mithras, the active principle of nature, is represented in monuments as killing the bull with a dagger, so that all plants might spring from its corpse and all animals from its seed. Zoëga proposes this explanation among others, though he does not seem to approve it. These, moreover, are Mithraic mysteries; on them compare Sainte-Croix, *Historical and Critical Researches on* [Col. 0993A] *the Mysteries of Paganism*, II, p. 121, and Zoëga, *Dissertation on Works of Art Relating to Mithraic Worship*, in the proceedings of the Royal Danish Society of Sciences for 1806; in German in Zoëga’s *Abhandlungen*, Welcker ed., notes 1–5. Compare Kleuker, in his Persian studies (*Appendix to the Zend-Avesta*, II, 2, p. 128), who praises Firmicus’s extensive knowledge of Persian religion.] and transfer his rites to the power of fire. As their prophet has handed it down to us, saying:

> “Bind together . . . of theft . . . the noble father.” [Greek text: *Miktabō mystaky ho klopiēs syndete patros agauou*.]

[Note: [Col. 0993A] Correct it: “Initiates of the lowing ox . . . sing together the cycles of Ox-driving of the noble father.” [Greek: *Mūkētao boos mystai . . . Kukla Booklopiēs synaeidete patros agauou.*] Wower. Firmicus deliberately truncated the ending of the preceding verse, as authors often do. But the gaps in the following verse come from scribes, or from the man who first edited Firmicus, because he could not make out the difficult-to-read letters. Joseph Scaliger in Wower, p. 122.—Compare Wower’s *Letters*, Century II, no. 38. Yet in Scaliger’s letter cited here no mention of fire appears; and who would believe that the first part of the former verse would be quoted together with the following verse, as though Scaliger intended there to be so great a gap? Gronovius.—The words “of the noble father” receive some illumination from words cited by Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation*, ch. 2: “the bull is father of the dragon, and the dragon father of the bull”; Arnobius, V, 21, has the same words; see also Orelli’s note.]

They call this one Mithras. [Note: [Col. 0993B] On Mithras, the genius of the Sun among the Persians, see Creuzer, *Symbols and Mythology*, I, p. 720 ff. He is frequently mentioned by authors, but mostly in accordance with pagan notions. Those eager to form a more correct conception should consult the sacred Persian book, the *Zend-Avesta*. Ancient stones also, not infrequently [Col. 0993C] but of a later age and, so far as I know, only Latin, commemorate “Mithras, the unconquered god.” They refer to Mithraic rites either discovered or propagated by those Cilician pirates subdued by Pompey the Great, and spread through nearly all the West after the time of Antoninus Pius.]
