But they hand down his rites in hidden caves, so that, always plunged in the filthy darkness of obscurity, they may not see the grace of brilliant and clear light. O blind consecration of a divinity! O criminal inventions of a law to be shunned! You believe him to be a god [Col. 0994A] whose crimes you acknowledge. [Note: [Col. 0993C] The classic passage is in Porphyry, *On the Cave of the Nymphs*, ch. 6. Eubulus relates that Zoroaster first among the Persians consecrated a naturally formed cave in the mountains of Persia in honor of Mithras, the maker and father of all things, in order to signify by the cave the world created by Mithras. Luctatius says this on the passage in Statius, *Thebaid*, I, v. 719:

> Or beneath the rocks of the Persian cave  
> Angry, she follows Mithras, who twists the horns.

Hence it is clear how different Mithras’s religion was from Zoroastrian doctrine. For pure Magianism consistently taught that the world was created by Oromasdes. Mithraic rites are mentioned by Justin Martyr, *Dialogue with* [Col. 0993D] *Trypho*, Jebb ed., p. 213; the appendix to Tertullian, *On the Prescription against Heretics*, ch. 40; and *On the Soldier’s Crown*, ch. 15: “Blush, his fellow-soldiers, now to be judged not by himself but by some soldier of Mithras: when he is initiated in the cave, in truly the camp of darkness, a crown is offered to him upon a sword, as if in imitation of martyrdom; then, when it has been placed on his head, he is instructed to push it away from his head with the hand held out to meet it, and perhaps transfer it to his shoulder, saying that Mithras is his crown.” Wower. The reliefs seen throughout Italy, Gaul, and Germany depict Mithras slaughtering a bull, often in a cave (Zoëga, cited work, pp. 145, 161; Seel, *The Mithraic Mysteries*). In collections of engraved gems there commonly occur carved gems displaying ravens, lions, and scorpions, alluding to the same rites. Luctatius, on Statius’s cited passage concerning Mithraic caves, mentions reliefs of this kind. If [Col. 0994A] you want more, see what Lindenbrog, in his notes on Luctatius, and Kleuker, in the Persian studies just cited, have gathered from the cited writers, as well as from Jerome and Agathias.]

Therefore you who say that sacrifice is rightly offered in these temples not according to the Persian rite of the Magi, [Note: [Col. 0994A] Firmicus mentions no other crime committed by Mithras than his driving away the oxen. But he does not understand the symbols of this worship.] why do you praise these Persian rites? I know that you think this worthy of the Roman name, and of Persian rites. [Note: [Col. 0994A] Thus he holds Mithraic rites to differ from Persian religion; and yet in the foregoing passage he confuses the two. [Col. 0994B]] But let him follow Persian laws. [Note: [Col. 0994B] I do not grasp the sense. For why would Romans, who practiced an entirely different religion, think it worthy of the Roman name to maintain that Zoroastrian rites differed from Mithraic ones? I for one do not see how the words “and of Persian rites” cohere with what precedes. Nor will interpretation become easier if you change *dignum* (“worthy”) to *dignius* (“more worthy”).] . . . . . . . [Note: [Col. 0994B] A corrupt passage, which I do not attempt to emend. Even if you correct the solecism *legibus sequi*, I still do not see how these words are to be connected with those preceding. A gap follows this passage, by which the sense is interrupted.]

. . . . . . . so that she is consecrated armed with shield, cuirass, breastplate, sword, and spear. [Note: [Col. 0994B] These words, placed like an island between two gaps, seem to cohere neither with what precedes nor with what follows. Yet if you maintain that some connection exists with what precedes, the discussion will concern Mithraic initiations, with the slight alteration of *armata* (“armed,” feminine) to *armatus* (“armed,” masculine). For it is established that Mithraic initiates were called soldiers of Mithras; see Tertullian, *On the Soldier’s Crown*, ch. 15, and Zoëga, cited work, p. 138. If, however, this is unsatisfactory, one should perhaps think of a secret rite of Zoroastrian religion, for whose mention the words preceding this fragment may have paved the way: “But let him follow Persian laws.” For Plutarch, in his *Artaxerxes*, ch. 3, relates that this Persian king, called Mnemon by the Greeks—the same man whom Berosus, book III, Richter ed., p. 70, reports to have set up images of Anaitis for worship in various cities of his empire—received the higher teachings of initiation at Pasargadae in the temple of a certain goddess whom he calls “warlike” and in some way compares with Minerva. Xerxes too seems for the same reason to have performed rites for Trojan Pallas (Herodotus VII, 43). For, unless I am mistaken, he compared her with Anaitis. I suspect that Anaitis, the same divinity as Astarte or Mylitta, was worshipped by the Comanian rite, though I do not understand how her religion could have been joined with the purer Zoroastrian religion in Artaxerxes’ own age, in Persia itself and not far from Persepolis, as it were the Capitol and citadel of the whole people. In other [Col. 0994D] places Persian Artemis is mentioned, for example by Plutarch in his *Lucullus*; Pausanias III, ch. 16 (see also VII, ch. 6); and Strabo XVI, ch. 1, §18, who calls the sanctuary of this goddess Azora—the correct reading seems to be Zara, whence Artemis Zaretis. Therefore, if Plutarch’s account is true, this divinity will be identical with Mithra: Mithra among the Persians, a symbol of generative nature, was armed in that temple, as Venus Urania was worshipped on the island of Cythera. See also Creuzer’s discussion of this subject, I, p. 730: “Perhaps the Parthian tetradrachms belong here, on which Pallas is seen standing before a seated king and offering him a crown, or placing a crown upon his head. But sometimes in place of Pallas there stands a woman in a stola or turreted crown, with various attributes, or Victory. The matter is therefore uncertain. These are coins of Arsaces XV, Phraates IV, and their successors.” Mionnet, *Catalogue*, V, p. 656 ff.; Eckhel, *Doctrine of Ancient Coins*, III, pp. 530, 534. Perhaps likewise relevant is a coin of Hierocaesarea in Lydia, published by Seguinus, *Selected Ancient Coins*, pp. 9–10 (Eckhel III, p. 193), on which Artemis—I think the Comanian goddess—is dressed as a woman but equipped with a quiver, with the inscription “Persian.” Its reverse has a burning altar decorated with sphinxes, indicating mystical fire worship. On this Diana of the Diocaesareans, compare Tacitus, *Annals*, III, 62, and Spanheim on Callimachus, *Hymn to Diana*, v. 37, where you will find much material collected concerning this divinity.]

. . . There is also a third part, to which they assign dominion in the rough and secluded places of forests and of wild beasts. [Col. 0995A] The last part of that threefold division concerns the paths of desires, which display the evil cravings and enticements of perverse lust. Therefore they assign one part to the head, so that it may in some fashion signify a human being’s anger. They place another in the heart, so that it may seem to contain, as forests do, the variety of diverse thoughts which we conceive by manifold intention. The third part is placed in the liver, whence lust and pleasure arise. For there the accumulated fertility of generative seed, by natural stimuli, stirs up the desire of lust.

Consider carefully, therefore, what that division accomplishes, so that you may see how easily the reason of truth may assail a fabrication. If the soul is divided, and its substance is separated into kinds of differing efficacy, then, its order dissolved, it begins to be what it had been. [Col. 0995B] For mind is one thing, anger another, lust another. Thus that separation dissolves the soul, and it suffers the greatest loss from that partition; nor does this thing preserve its whole form, which is separately divided into three contrary parts and, to speak the truth, becomes mortal through the division itself. [Note: [Col. 0995C] Athenagoras, ch. 7: “Now Socrates, being generated and perishable, is compounded and divisible into parts; but God is ungenerated, impassible, and indivisible.” In place of “Socrates” he might also have said “a human being” or “an animal.” But he preferred to use the name of an individual thing. Lindner on Athenagoras.]

For what can be divided is a body. But whatever is a body must necessarily be mortal. [Note: [Col. 0995C] There can be no doubt that Firmicus is here attacking philosophers, especially the Pythagoreans, who are known to have posited three parts or faculties of the human soul: *nous*, “intellect”; [Col. 0995D] *phrenes*, “mind”; and *thymos*, “spirit,” and to have assigned the first two their place in the brain and the third in the heart. Hertz, *On Julius Firmicus Maternus*, p. 39.] Therefore, if the soul is divided, it is a body. If it is a body, it must necessarily be a mortal thing. Excellent and splendid consequences of that error! By this inference a great benefit is bestowed upon us. Through the inventions of these absurdities they wish souls to be mortal.

## CHAPTER VI. From the worship of the elements he passes to other superstitions and exposes their secrets; first, indeed, he recounts the story of the two Liberi, the Cretan and the Theban.

Thus, most sacred emperors, have the elements been consecrated by depraved human beings. But there still remain [Col. 0996A] other superstitions [Note: [Col. 0995D] He now passes from refuting the worship of the elements to attacking other parts of mythology, which he drew partly from popular tradition and from the fables of poets whose songs time has preserved; partly, as I suspect, from Euhemerus’s *Sacred Inscription*. He begins with Liber and Libera.] whose secrets must be exposed: those of Liber and Libera, [Note: [Col. 0995D] Lactantius I, ch. 10; Minucius Felix, ch. 21; Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, II, 24; Arnobius does not have it; Creuzer III, 376, 381.] all of which must be especially made known to your sacred understanding, so that even in these profane religions you may know that the deaths of human beings have been consecrated.

Liber, then, was the son of Jupiter, [Note: [Col. 0995D] He tells the story of two Libers (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, II, 24), [Col. 0996C] the Cretan and the Theban; and, if you consider the Cretan Liber, the story is very close to a fable. Whether in it he followed Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation*, ch. 2—as Wower, in his notes on Firmicus, thinks, but Ursinus denies in *Biblical Questions*, II, ch. 19—I would readily doubt, since at least in his account of Liber’s burial he departs from Clement, while otherwise being supported by the authority of no writer. Hertz, *On Julius Firmicus Maternus*, p. 40. This fable is mentioned by Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, II, 5; Arnobius I, chs. 36, 41, V, 19, and repeatedly, especially in book V; although the Theban can not everywhere be easily distinguished from the Cretan. Hyginus, *Fables*, 167. Macrobius, *Commentary on Scipio’s Dream*, I, ch. 12.] that is, of the Cretan king. [Note: [Col. 0996C] Thus Commodian, *Instructions*, VI:

> But Jupiter reigned in Crete, and there he died.

Arnobius likewise states, I, chs. 36–41, the opinion of Euhemerus that the gods had been human beings. See the inaugural dissertation of Peter Krog Meier, most deeply missed colleague, *On the Method and Argument of Arnobius’s Apologetic Work* (Copenhagen, 1815), pp. 158–159. Arnobius, moreover, brings forward nearly the same examples as Firmicus. Athanasius, *Against the Greeks*, ch. 9, also reports that Jupiter was counted among the gods by the Cretans.]

Since he had been born of an adulterous mother, he was reared in his father’s house with greater care than was fitting. Jupiter’s wife, whose name was Juno, [Note: [Col. 0996D] This whole fable is told by Firmicus alone: is it from Euhemerus?] stirred by the frenzy of a stepmother’s heart, prepared every kind of plot for the infant’s murder. When his father set out on a journey, because he knew his wife’s concealed indignation, he entrusted the protection of his son to suitable guardians, as it seemed to him, lest some deception be practiced by the angry woman.

Then Juno, having obtained an opportunity for her plot, was still more strongly inflamed because the departing father had entrusted both the royal throne [Col. 0996B] and the scepter to the boy. First she corrupted the guards with royal rewards and gifts; then she placed her followers, called Titans, [Note: [Col. 0996D] In Antoninus Liberalis they are regarded as attendants of Saturn, ch. 36, whence it is written: “Zeus, having driven out the Titans, deprived Cronus of sovereignty.” Gronovius.] in the inner parts of the palace. By trinkets and a skillfully made mirror she so enticed the child’s mind that, abandoning the royal residence, he was led by childish desire to the place of ambush.

There he was seized and slaughtered. So that no trace of the murder could be found, the band of attendants divided the limbs, torn into pieces, among themselves. Then, to add one crime to another, because they greatly feared the cruelty of the tyrant, they boiled and consumed the boy’s limbs in various ways, feeding upon a human corpse in a banquet unheard of until that day. His sister, whose name was Minerva, kept the heart for herself, both because she too had shared in the crime [Col. 0996C] and so that there might be clear evidence of an accusation, and so that she might have something by which to mitigate the onrush of her enraged father.

When Jupiter returned, his daughter set forth the course of the crime. Then the father, moved by the deadly calamity of the disaster and the bitter violence of his grief, [Col. 0997A] killed the Titans after torturing them with various kinds of punishment. [Note: [Col. 0997C] On these, see Commodian, *Instructions*, XX, where he says:

> For you foolishly worship evil beings who have perished by a blow.]

No torture or penalty was omitted in avenging his son; raging through every kind of punishment, he avenged his son’s death in whatever way he could—by a father’s feeling, indeed, but with tyrannical power.

Then, since the father could no longer endure the torments of his grieving heart, and since grief arising from bereavement was eased by no consolation, he made an image of him from gypsum, in modeled work; and he placed in the part of the figure in which the outlines of the breast had been formed the heart which his sister, having denounced the crime, had revealed. After this he built a temple in place of a tomb and appointed the boy’s tutor as priest. His name was Silenus. [Note: [Col. 0997C] On this tutor of Bacchus, see Lactantius I, ch. 21, and Creuzer III, 514.]

The Cretans, to alleviate the savagery of the frenzied tyrant, [Note: [Col. 0997C] For passages of ancient writers on Jupiter’s worship in Crete, see Meursius, *Crete* (Amsterdam, 1675), p. 198.] established festive days of mourning [Col. 0997B] and devised an annual rite with triennial consecration, performing in sequence all that the boy either did or suffered as he died. They tear a living bull to pieces with their teeth, [Note: [Col. 0997C] Hesychius: “Dionysus, the bull-eater.” Suidas says the same [Col. 0997D] concerning Bacchus. Wower.—The words which Photius has in his *Lexicon*—“Bull-eater: Sophocles in the *Tyrians* calls Dionysus this, either because a bull was given to those who won the dithyramb, or because he was a raw-eater; from him Aristophanes transferred the name to Cratinus”—do not belong here.] reviving cruel feasts in annual commemorations; and, through the secluded places of forests, wailing with discordant cries, they feign the madness of a frenzied mind, so that that crime may be believed to have been committed not through treachery but through madness. A chest is carried before them, in which the sister had secretly hidden the heart; by the sound of pipes and the ringing of cymbals they imitate the trinkets by which the boy had been deceived.

Thus, in honor of a tyrant, a god was made by a serving populace—a god who could not have a burial.

There was also another Liber, a tyrant at Thebes, [Note: [Col. 0997D] From what source he drew his account of the Theban Dionysus is not clear to me, since Homer, *Iliad* VI, 130; Hyginus, *Fables*, 132; Apollodorus, *Library*, III, ch. 5; and others relate that Bacchus was indeed first put to flight, but not torn apart, nor was Lycurgus left unavenged. Compare Heyne on Apollodorus, II, p. 571 ff.] conspicuous for the power of magical art. Having captivated women’s minds by certain drugs and spells, he commanded frenzied women, at his own pleasure, to perform cruel acts, so that he possessed noble women deprived of their senses both as servants of lusts and of crimes. What crimes he committed, and how great a crime he ordered mother against son or sisters against brother to perpetrate, is related daily on the stage by writers of tragic verse, [Note: [Col. 0997D] Such were the plays of Aeschylus: *Bacchae*, *Bassarae*, *Nurses of Dionysus*, *Hedonoi*, *Lycurgus*, *Xantriae*, *Pentheus*, *Semele*; the *Dionysiacus* of Sophocles, if that is the genuine title; and Euripides’ surviving *Bacchae*—perhaps the same play which is listed among lost works under the title *Pentheus*—and the *Cyclops*, judging from its chorus.] so that the criminal cruelty of the wicked [Col. 0998A] tyrant may continually be renewed in the minds of hearers by deadly recitals.

Lycurgus, [Note: [Col. 0997D] The story of Lycurgus is told in various ways. Apollodorus, III, 5, makes him king of the Edonians of Thrace and says that he drove Bacchus from his region, but not from his native country. On [Col. 0998C] him compare Zoëga’s dissertation, *Lycurgus Overcome by the Maenads*, and Welcker’s additions. A relief is explained there. Firmicus seems to have derived all this from Euhemerus. There once existed a play of Aeschylus entitled *Lycurgus*.] protected by a sober conspiracy of men, stripped him of his kingdom and drove him from his native land. For that effeminate man could not long sustain the united will of men. That he was effeminate and served the lusts of male lovers is sung in the gymnasia of the Greeks. [Note: [Col. 0998C] This seems to refer to musical contests established in gymnasia and elsewhere during celebrations of the gods’ feast days; perhaps also to songs which were very probably sung almost every day in the same places, where learned youth and all who favored the Muses used to gather even on non-festival days.]

Nor was Lycurgus content merely with his flight and exile; fearing that the fugitive, received by others, might sow in another land the shameful seeds of his crimes, he armed himself with a sword and pursued the disgrace of his native country with a threatening decree.

Then Liber cast aside the fillets which he bound with circles of vine-leaf crowns and fled with a half-male retinue—for only companions in his debaucheries, disgraceful acts, and lusts followed him. In utmost terror and despair he wandered through every coast [Col. 0998B] of the neighboring sea. There, among drunken girls [Note: [Col. 0998D] What others tell of Bacchus traveling through the world in a triumphal procession, our author holds to have happened during his flight. On the Bacchae, see Creuzer III, 186.] and wine-soaked old men, while the procession of his crimes still preceded him—one man foul in black clothing, another terrible with a snake displayed, [Note: [Col. 0998D] Arnobius V, ch. 19: “Let us pass over the monstrous Bacchanalia . . . in which, with feigned madness . . . you wrap yourselves with serpents and . . . scatter with bloodied mouths the entrails of bleating goats.” Scholiast on Lycophron, v. 143, concerning the Bacchae: “They carried lions and other wild animals in their own hands, and had serpents coiled around their hair.” Wower.—Creuzer III, 187, mentions dragons or serpents in Bacchic religions.] another bloody at the mouth as he tore apart the living limbs of an animal—Lycurgus seized him and hurled him from a nearby cliff, which made an immense precipice with inaccessible rocks, into the sea, so that his mangled body, long tossed about by the waves of the sea, might by stern punishment call the minds of wandering peoples back to the order of sanity and sobriety.

Homer, to reveal Liber’s flight and terror and to show his death, says that this was Liber’s end:

> . . . and Dionysus, frightened,  
> Plunged beneath the wave of the salt sea; Thetis received him in her bosom,  
> Terrified, for a mighty trembling possessed him at the man’s outcry. [Note: [Col. 0998D] Homer, *Iliad* VI, v. 135.]

[Col. 0998C] You imitate Lycurgus, and follow his sober institution; nor does our consul Postumius depart from your salutary laws. [Note: [Col. 0998D] Livy gives this history at length, XXXIX, chs. 8–19. The senatorial decree concerning the Bacchanalia is famous. Compare Matthew the Egyptian, *On the Senatorial Decree concerning the Bacchanalia*, and Bynkershoek, *On Foreign Religion*, among his works. Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 6: “The consuls, by the authority of the senate, drove Liber Pater with his mysteries out not only from the City but from all Italy.” On the Bacchanalia see also Caspar Barth on Statius, *Thebaid* II, vv. 74 and 77. [Col. 0999D]]

For, as we find in the books of the Annals, the crimes of the Bacchanalia were exposed when a certain young man, Ebutius, laid information. At that time sound morals still remained in the city of Rome, and no one, with morals dissolved, sought out foreign superstitions. Then neither did the senate fail the consul, nor the laws of the commonwealth, nor the consul the laws. But after investigation of all who transmitted the criminal inventions of this rite, capital punishment was decreed by resolution of the senate, after judicial examination, against all slaves—indeed, against Romans. Nor did the avenging swords of the consul rest until this evil had been cut out by the roots. O punishment worthy of the Roman name! O constancy of ancient virtue worthy of praise! The consul was unwilling to spare even his fellow citizens when foreign vices were being corrected in order to cleanse the fatherland.

## CHAPTER VII. He expounds the story of Libera, or Proserpina, and maintains that Liber is worshipped as the sun and Libera as the moon.

There follows this contagion of a rite, and the order of a funeral is imitated: the death of a daughter, consecrated by Ceres, a woman of Henna. [Note: [Col. 0999D] Arnobius I, 36, says that she was born in the region of Trinacria. I suspect that Firmicus also drew this account from Euhemerus.]

For all that the father had done in Crete on account of his son, Ceres likewise established at Henna, when her daughter was lost, in the impatience of maternal grief. I shall briefly set out how this happened.

Many sought the only daughter of Ceres, whom the Greeks call Persephone and our people, with altered pronunciation, Proserpina, for marriage. Her mother carefully weighed the merits of each man. And while the mother’s decision still seemed uncertain to all, a wealthy rustic, whose name was Pluton because of his wealth, driven by a reckless heat of desire, unable to endure the delay of postponement and complaining of the flames of ill-ordered love, near the lake of Percus [Note: [Col. 0999D] That is, the lake. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* V, 385:

> Not far from the walls of lofty Henna is a lake,
Pergus by name, a body of water. Ovid, Aristotle, Solinus, and Diodorus describe the place as covered with flowers of every kind, especially violets. Firmicus seems to have borrowed this image from it. See further Cluverius, *Sicily*, 319, 20; 323, 24.] he carries off the maiden whom he has found [Col. 0999C]. The lake Pergus, however, situated in the territory of the city of Henna, is quite delightful and pleasant; its charm arises from the variety of its flowers. For throughout the whole year it is crowned with flowers succeeding one another in turn. There you will find whatever hyacinth swells into stalk; there the tresses of the narcissus, or whatever paints the golden rose above; there white ivy gently creeps over the ground, and sweetly blushing marjoram is found together with purple violets; nor do white lilies desert this garland. In every way it was a place suited by its charm both to invite and to hold maidenly minds.

In this place, when the maiden had been discovered by Pluto near evening, she is carried off by force, [Note: [Col. 0999D] Apollodorus, *Library*, I, ch. 5, and Heyne on this passage; Diodorus Siculus V, ch. 3; Ovid, *Fasti* IV, vv. 420–620; Hyginus, fable 146; Arnobius V, ch. 24. See also Le Clerc in *Bibliothèque Universelle* VI, p. 55.] placed upon a vehicle, [Col. 1000A] and driven away with her clothing torn and her hair dishevelled. Her nails, kept in reserve against the rustic lover, were of no use; neither cries nor wailing helped, nor the commotion of the other girls. Then one girl, running swiftly, made quicker by fear itself when no one came from the city to help, reports the maiden’s abduction to her mother.

The mother, enraged against the ravisher, leads an armed band. Pluto was not unaware of the woman’s approach; but when he turned his eyes back toward the city and saw countless companies coming with the mother, he adopted a deadly plan in desperation. He drove the four-horse chariot that drew the vehicle into the middle of the lake. It was sunk in deep chasms; there, submerged together with his beloved maiden, he offered the pitiable mother the deadly sight of her daughter’s death.

The people of Henna, that they might find some consolation [Col. 1000B] for the mother’s grief, invented that the king of the underworld had carried off the maiden. And, that belief might follow the invention, they asserted that he had re-emerged with the maiden at another place near Syracuse. [Note: [Col. 1000D] Diodorus Siculus, book V, ch. 4, p. 333, and Ovid, *Metamorphoses* V, in the passage cited, report that Pluto descended to Orcus with the abducted Proserpina, and that the spring Cyane arose at the place where he descended. See Cluverius, *Sicily*, p. 177.] They build a temple, indeed, both for the ravisher and for the maiden, with carefully contributed expenses, [Note: [Col. 1000D] Syracuse was founded by Archias many years after the cult of Ceres and Proserpina had become established among the Greeks, in Olympiad XI, year 2 or 4, in 735 before Christ’s birth: Thucydides, book VI, ch. 3; Cluverius, *Sicily*, p. 139.] and decree annual vows in the temple.

But the mother’s grief is overcome by no means, nor are the torments of feminine impatience cured. Believing that her daughter had truly been seen near Syracuse, she comes, with Triptolemus her rustic guide, by journeys through the night to the shore of the Syracusan city, clad in mourning dress and filthy squalor; nor was there lacking someone to deceive the credulous mother concerning her misfortunes. Then a certain Pandarus, I know not who, says that he had seen the ravisher board a ship with the maiden not far from Pachynus. [Col. 1000C] The woman is persuaded, since she longed to hear by any means that her daughter was alive; she rewards the city with countless gifts. The Syracusans, stirred by the woman’s generosity, consecrate the abduction of the maiden and, seeking to soothe the mother’s grief, adorn the pageant of the miserable funeral with the honour of temples.

But even this does not suffice for the mother. Boarding a ship, she seeks her daughter along foreign shores. Thus tossed by waves and storms, she arrives at a place in the region of the Attic city. [Note: [Col. 1000D] Arnobius V, 25.] There, having been received as a guest, she distributes grain hitherto unknown to the inhabitants. The place received its name from the woman’s homeland and arrival. For it was called Eleusis, [Note: [Col. 1000D] The author of the *Etymologicum Magnum*, under “Eleusis,” gives the same account: “Because of the coming of Demeter; for there, when she came, she found the crop . . . or from Eleusinus, son of Hermes.”] because Ceres had come there after leaving Henna. And so she herself—though the transmitted *dispensatio* leaves the construction corrupt [Note: [Col. 1000D] Since the word *dispensatio* has no verb with which it can be joined, perhaps the reading of this passage would be more correct if either it were assumed that after the word *disciplinam* something such as this had fallen out: “was the cause of divine worship for her, and after death . . .”; or if the word *dispensatio* were deleted and, further, *ipsa tum* were read for *tum ipsa*.]—both because she had brought grain and because she had handed down instruction for gathering crops, after her death, on account of the benefit arising from an abundance of grain, was buried in that place [Note: [Col. 1001C] Nothing is read in the writers concerning a tomb of Ceres at Eleusis. Our author seems to have drawn this from Euhemerus.] and at the same time consecrated and called by a divine name together with her daughter.

For the frivolity of the Greeks loves to call by divine names those who have bestowed something upon them or assisted them by counsel or courage. Thus the favour received is repaid by them: they call gods, and believe to be gods, those who have at some time benefited them. Thus Nysa does not doubt concerning Liber, [Note: [Col. 1001C] Creuzer III, 122, 124: “If the name must be sought from India, you have the city Nischadabura.” Creuzer IV, 237: “The authors teach that Liber was called Nysius.” Arnobius V, 28: “Whether he received the name from a city or from a man is uncertain.” Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* III, ch. 25, has a fifth Liber, born of Nysus and Dione. Compare Creuzer’s note. Likewise Commodian, *Instructions* XII: “He is taken up and given to Nysus to be nourished as a foster-child.” The classic passages on Nysa and Bacchus Nysius are in Diodorus Siculus I, ch. 15 (where see Wesseling), and III, 67–70; Orelli on Arnobius V, 28.] nor Sparta concerning its new stars, [Note: [Col. 1001C] The Dioscuri.] and sorrowful Oeta burns and consecrates Hercules; [Note: [Col. 1001C] Justin Martyr, *First Apology* I, ch. 29. Theophilus, *To Autolycus* I, ch. 14: “Heracles burned himself.” Tatian, *Address to the Greeks*, ch. 36. Minucius Felix, ch. 21: “Hercules, that he may cast off the human being, is burned up in the Oetaean fires.”] [Note: [Col. 1001D] Vibius Sequester, *On Mountains*; Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, ch. 1; Minucius Felix, ch. 21; and the notes of Elmenhorst and Ouzelius on this passage; Lactantius I, 9; Augustine, *City of God* XVIII, 4; Hyginus, fable 30; Arnobius IV, 25.] and the tomb of Jupiter, long dead, is still worshipped by the foolish Cretans. [Note: [Col. 1001D] Suidas, under “Picos.” [Uncertain OCR: “Wow.—I do not find it in Kuster’s edition.”]] [Note: [Col. 1001D] Theophilus, *To Autolycus* I, ch. 15; II, 3; Athenagoras, ch. 26; Tatian, ch. 44; Origen, *Against Celsus* III, ch. 43, p. 475; Rigaltius’ Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 25; Arnobius IV, ch. 25; Lactantius I, 11. You will find passages from the ancient authors collected in Meursius, *Crete*, II, ch. 4. Compare Creuzer IV, 427. Ennius preserved Euhemerus’ testimony concerning this tomb of Jupiter: “When his life had been brought to its end by age, he departed from life in Crete and went to the gods; and his sons, the Curetes, tended and honoured him; and his tomb is in Crete [Col. 1002C] in the town of Knossos.” See Ennius in Hessel, p. 323.]

Yet, most sacred Emperors, this is added to increase this profane error: they defend these men—that is, Liber and Proserpina—as if by a greater authority. For Greek inventions wish to refer Liber to the Sun, [Note: [Col. 1002C] Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I, ch. 18, where he shows that Father Liber is the very same god as the Sun.] while, calling Proserpina Libera, they fabricate that she is the Moon. [Note: [Col. 1002C] Creuzer IV, 188, 220.] How absurd and miserable this is, we may gather from reason itself, from the truth. Who saw the Sun as a child? Who deceived him? Who killed him? Who tore him apart? Who divided him? Who feasted upon his limbs? Who carried off the Moon? Who hid [Note: [Col. 1002C] I would prefer *abscondidit*, “hid,” though Nonius also has *abscondit*.] her? Who made her Pluto’s wife?

But again they seek to protect this error by physical reasoning, [Note: [Col. 1002C] Arnobius III, chs. 29–34 sets out the disagreement and conflict of opinions concerning the nature of each deity, the force and meaning of its name, and the number of those addressed by a common designation. See Meyer, *On Arnobius*, pp. 233–238.] thinking that they can worship by this reasoning the undivided and divided mind—that is, *ton ameriston kai ton memerismenon noun*, “the indivisible and the divided intellect.” [Note: [Col. 1002C] From Neo-Platonic philosophy. Proclus Diadochus, *Elements of Theology*, ch. 109, ed. Creuzer, p. 160, has *nous merikos*, “particular intellect,” which shares in the Whole and exists through both the universal soul itself and the particular intellect itself. In the same work, ch. 171, p. 254, he has *nous ameriston*, “indivisible intellect,” an undivided essence, because it lacks magnitude and is incorporeal and immovable.]

Tell me, O mortals: why do you add funerals to natural things? Why do you pollute God’s ordering by the atrocity of cruel deaths? Why [Col. 1001C] was such harsh and cruel torment necessary? What [Col. 1002A] is the point of this persuasion, that the sequence of deadly calamity should be joined with divine things, and mortal disaster with mourning should be joined to the nature of the heavenly bodies which the highest God made under fixed laws? What benefit is there in what you do? You mingle earthly things with heavenly, perishable things with things above, darkness with brightness, consecrating human pains and griefs as divine honours.

## CHAPTER VIII. It consists for the most part of a prosopopoeia in which the Sun is imagined, in a speech addressed to men, to refute and reject the divine worship which they themselves paid him.

If the Sun, with the whole human race assembled, were to speak in a public address, perhaps he would strike your despair with the following speech:

“Who has driven you, perishable human beings, [Col. 1002B] rebelling every day against the highest God in various ways, to so great a crime that, in the profane error of wicked desire, you say that I die and live according to your judgment? And would that the inventions of your insane thought proceeded according to the customary fashion, or at least in one form! Would that the wickedness of your criminal thought ran riot without insult to me! But now, while hurling yourselves over precipices, you do not spare me either; your speech has no reverence at all, but you hasten to your own ruin and death through dishonouring me.

“Some, in Egypt, submerge me in the waters and rushing eddies of the Nile through an obstinate madness of mind. [Note: [Col. 1002D] Correct *vorticibus*, “eddies.” [Uncertain OCR: “Wow.”]] [Note: [Col. 1002D] Namely, those who maintain that the Sun is the same deity as Osiris; see Macrobius I, ch. 21, and who assert that Adonis, Attis, Osiris, and Horus are nothing other than the Sun.] Others mourn me after cutting off their genitals. [Note: [Col. 1002D] Namely, those who maintain that the Sun is the same deity as Osiris; see Macrobius I, ch. 21, and who assert that Adonis, Attis, Osiris, and Horus are nothing other than the Sun.] Others, after I have been cut down by a cruel death, either boil me in a cauldron or fasten the mangled limbs of my body upon seven spits. [Col. 1002C] [Note: [Col. 1002D] Clement, *Protrepticus*, ch. 2, p. 15: “And the Titans, after tearing him apart, placed a certain cauldron on a tripod, threw into it the limbs of Dionysus, first boiled them, then threaded them on spits and held them over the fire of Hephaestus.” See also Justin Martyr, *First Apology* I, ch. 29; Arnobius V, ch. 19: “We refrain from proclaiming the Bacchanalia, in which the secret and unspeakable matter is revealed to the initiated: Liber, occupied in childish games, is torn away by the Titans; by the same men he is cut limb from limb and thrown into little pots to be cooked.” [Uncertain OCR: “Wow.”] And Arnobius I, 41: “Do not you also sacrifice Father Liber, torn limb from limb by the Titans, by consecrating shrines?” [Col. 1003C] The same tale is told by Hyginus, fable 167, and Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* II, 15. In this passage the Sun plays the part of Liber, with whom pagans of the later period often identified him. — “Upon seven spits.” Perhaps it should be corrected: “either they boil me in a cauldron, or they fasten upon spits the mangled limbs of my torn body.” For in Homer, *Iliad* I, v. 463: “. . . beside it they held in their hands five-pronged spits.” [Uncertain OCR: “Wow.”] Yet the number seven is mystical.]

“Anyone who has flattered me a little with smooth [Col. 1003A] speech invents me as the driver of a four-horse chariot. [Note: [Col. 1003C] So on a coin of Elagabalus in Beger, *Thesaurus Brandenburgicus* II, 712, where a conical stone—the symbol of the god—is in a quadriga; likewise a human figure in a quadriga in the same author, p. 768, and on a coin of Maximinus, ibid. p. 792.] At last cast away the ruin of so great a madness, and, convinced by a saving persuasion, seek the true path of salvation. He is an enemy of God who has either imagined or invented these things. Nor does a simple or customary punishment attend his crime, who pollutes sacred things with profane notions, who invents so much concerning God’s splendid work [Note: [Col. 1003C] Namely, the Sun.].

“Mourn your dead—and you yourselves will die a like death. Send funerary offerings to your kings if you wish, and soothe their bereavements by some other kind of remedy. Mourn Liber, mourn Proserpina, mourn Attis, mourn Osiris, [Note: [Col. 1003C] In the Mysteries, and also in public cults.] but without insulting our dignity. I do not want you to lead me through their tombs and ashes; I do not want my name to furnish fuel for your error. I was made by God for the daylight; [Col. 1003B] that alone is enough for me. Why do you deprive me of the dignity of an honourable office? God made me one thing and commanded me to be another, yet you divide me according to your pleasure [Note: [Col. 1003C] As the Persians did Mithra-Mitram, and the Greeks and Romans Apollo and the Sun.] and tear me apart according to the desire of your own choice. Whatever I am, I simply obey God; and I do not want you to understand anything else concerning me than what you see. This is pleasing to God; this God willingly embraces; this leads human beings onto the path of salvation: that, casting away errors, you should simply and faithfully heed the grace of God.”

Let it suffice, most sacred Emperors, that I have spoken these things in a prosopopoeic manner. But now, formed by the instruction of sacred readings, I address ruined people in religious speech. If those whom you worship are gods, why do you mourn them? [Note: [Col. 1003C] Minucius Felix, ch. 21: “Is it not ridiculous either to mourn what you worship, [Col. 1003D] or to worship what you mourn?”] Why do you lament them with yearly griefs? If they are worthy of tears and mourning, [Note: [Col. 1003D] Clement of Alexandria, *Protrepticus*, ch. 2, p. 21, has precisely these words: “If you consider them gods, do not mourn them or beat yourselves; but if you mourn them, no longer regard them as gods.” They are, moreover, words of Xenophanes of Colophon addressed to the Egyptians. Plutarch, *On Isis*, ch. 70: “Xenophanes of Colophon held that the Egyptians, if they considered them gods, ought not to mourn; but if they mourned them, ought not to consider them gods. Otherwise it is absurd at once to mourn them and to pray that they may make the fruits appear again and bring them to maturity for themselves, so that they may again [Col. 1004C] be consumed and mourned.” [Uncertain OCR: “Wow.”] This passage shows that Firmicus had read Clement. Minucius too reproduced it in ch. 21. See also Athenagoras, *Embassy*, chs. 12 and 25.] why do you heap divine honour upon them?

Therefore do one of two things: either do not mourn them, if they are gods; or, if you think them worthy of grief and tears, do not call them gods, lest the majesty of the divine name be polluted by your griefs and tears. But because a ruined mind, entangled in the snares of criminal desire, cannot be recalled by any reasoning, I shall pursue the remaining matters, [Col. 1004A] so that, once everything which profane wickedness has consecrated has been publicly exposed and uncovered, the mercy of God, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, may raise up the fallen, call back to himself those who flee, strengthen the wavering, correct those who err, and—what is of greatest importance—give life to the dying.

## CHAPTER IX. He briefly treats the mourning for the death of Adonis, struck by Mars transformed into a boar, and briefly recalls the Gospel narrative concerning the expelled demon.

In many cities of the East—although this evil has also passed over to us—Adonis [Note: [Col. 1004C] Writers do not mention when the Mysteries of Adonis reached Rome; nevertheless, it is probable that this occurred in the age of Hadrian or at least of Elagabalus.] [Note: [Col. 1004C] Arnobius VII, 33; Lactantius I, 17. On this entire fable see Fikenscher, *Explanation of the Myth of Adonis* (Gotha, 1800), and Creuzer II, p. 95 ff.] is mourned as Venus’s husband, and his killer is displayed standing by, together with the wound. For Mars, transformed in appearance and shape into a wild boar, in order to claim for himself [Col. 1004B] the foremost place in Venus’s love, strikes down the young man as he rashly rushes against him. [Note: [Col. 1004C] In the first edition *serentem*, “sowing,” occurs in this place. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* X, vv. 710 ff.: “By chance the dogs, following the sure tracks of a boar from his hiding-place, roused him; and the young son of Cinyras, as he was preparing to leave the woods, had pierced him with a slanting thrust. Immediately the boar shook the hunting spear from his curved snout.” [Uncertain OCR: “Wow.”]]

If Adonis was a god, why did he not know the ambushes of his rival? If he was a human being, why did he contend with one above him? But I hear that another had marital intercourse with Venus. [Note: [Col. 1004C] And in ch. X: “I hear of Cinyras of Cyprus.” These words seem to indicate a man who acquired a more intimate knowledge of Greek sacred rites from the reports of others, since he himself had been educated in the Christian religion from childhood. Nor do the words in ch. 8 conflict: “But now, formed by the instruction of sacred readings, I address ruined people in religious speech.” For *now* should not be pressed too strongly, as though he had only at an advanced age finally begun to read Holy Scripture. It should rather be referred to what follows: “I address ruined people . . .”] Vulcan, unless I am mistaken, is said by these worshippers of the gods to be Venus’s husband. O laughable belief of foolish men! An adulterer placed between two husbands is caught by one and defeats the other. But see: that the adulterous god might defeat the husband, he preferred that body which he chose to be a boar. If he had the power to change his body, he ought rather to have assumed the appearance and shape of a lion. But those who know the natures of animals say that the lion, amid that wildness of spirit, preserves the virtue of chastity. Therefore the form of the lion is rightly rejected by an adulterer [Col. 1004C] and that of a lustful animal chosen.

Let us now consider the mysteries of the Gospel tradition. When the demon is expelled, the Lord gives it a herd of swine (Matthew VIII, 31–32; Mark V, 13; Luke VIII, 32–33). Nor without reason: so that, tossed with lustful animals over steep precipices and through waves, the unclean spirit might be destroyed by a death worthy of it through the various deaths of the swine. [Col. 1005A]

## CHAPTER X. He denounces the abominations in the worship of Venus of Paphos.

I hear that Cinyras of Cyprus [Note: [Col. 1005B] This whole narrative has the flavour of Euhemerus.] gave a temple to his mistress, a prostitute; [Note: [Col. 1005B] Namely, the secret doctrine in the Mysteries of Venus, transmitted to the initiates in the temple at Paphos and its sacred grove, whose name, *hieros kēpos*, “sacred garden,” still survives today: *Voyage d’Ali-Bey* II, p. 129.] her name was Venus. He also initiated many people into the cult of Cyprian Venus and assigned them to empty consecrations. He further ordained that whoever wished to be initiated, after Venus’s secret had been communicated to him, [Note: [Col. 1005B] Clement of Alexandria, *Protrepticus*, ch. 2, p. 12; Lactantius I, 17; and Theodoret, *Cure of Greek Affections*, discourse 3, ed. Schultz, vol. IV, p. 767. All from Euhemerus: “She—Venus—instituted the art of prostitution and was the originator among the women of Cyprus of their publicly earning money by their bodies.” Ennius in Hessel, p. 325. Justin, from his Trogus, reports the same in XVIII, ch. 5. Commodian, *Instructions* XVI: “. . . together with the heavenly woman of Pharos, the virgins and Venus, for whom your wives make themselves wanton.” Arnobius IV, 25 likewise has this prostitute enrolled among the gods by Cinyras.] should give the goddess an as in his hand as payment. [Note: [Col. 1005B] “In his hand”: so Wower corrected it. Scaliger: “one as,” whereas the first edition read: “after Venus’s secret had been communicated to him, he should give an as, the hand of payment, to the goddess.” [Col. 1005C]]

What this secret was, we must all understand silently, because on account of its obscenity we cannot explain it more openly. [Note: [Col. 1005C] From Clement’s *Protrepticus*, ch. 2, p. 13, and Arnobius V, ch. 12, we learn what this secret was. The latter writes that a “grain of salt and a phallus” were handed over; the former: “Nor do we pass over those hidden initiations of Cyprian Venus, whose founder is said to have been King Cinyras of Cyprus, in which those who receive them pay fixed contributions as to a prostitute and bring back phalluses bestowed as a token of the favourable deity.” Compare Orelli on this passage; Lucian, *On the Syrian Goddess*, ch. 16; Meursius, *Cyprus*, p. 109; and our dissertation, *The Temple of the Heavenly Goddess at Paphos*, p. 17. Constantine the Great had destroyed the temple of Venus at Aphaca on Mount Lebanon, notorious for the crimes committed there. This may perhaps explain Firmicus’s recent recollection of the temple at Paphos and its mention here. Athanasius also touches on these abominations in temples of Phoenician Venus in *Against the Greeks*, ch. 26.] Cinyras, a good lover, obeys the laws of prostitutes: he ordered that an offering be given by their priests to Venus when consecrated, as to a whore.

## CHAPTER XI. Likewise, the abominations of Jupiter Sabazius.

[Col. 1005B]

Those who worship Jupiter Sabazius [Note: [Col. 1005C] Inscriptions speak of this god, who is Dionysus (Creuzer III, 344) [Col. 1005D] or Lunus (Creuzer, p. 350), and belongs to Phrygian religions (ibid. 358); in conformity with Justin Martyr, *First Apology* I, p. 45, and Firmicus, they make him Jupiter through the syncretism of later paganism, which confuses nearly all deities.

“Quintus Nunnius Alexander gave this gift to Jupiter Sabazius” (Gruter, p. XXII).

“Sixtus Metius Zetus to Jupiter Sabazius Alexander, willingly and deservedly fulfilled his vow” (Gruter, ibid.).

“To Jupiter Sabazius, Quintus Nunnius Alexander willingly and deservedly fulfilled his vow” (ibid.). They write *Sabazius* and *Sebazius* interchangeably. Hesychius, Suidas, and Harpocration have *Zabazios*. Macrobius I, ch. 18 has *Sebadius*. The Greeks seek the derivation of the name in *sabazein*, that is, *bakcheuein*, “to revel as a Bacchant.” Zonaras, in his lexicon: “Sabadius: an epithet of Dionysus; and *saboi*: a Bacchic cry.” Photius, in his lexicon, says from Demosthenes’ *On the Crown* that *saboi* are initiates of Sabazius, that is Dionysus, just as *Bacchi* are initiates of Bacchus. I would rather believe that the name has a foreign origin. The great Bochart derives it from the Hebrew or Phoenician [word not recoverable in the supplied text], “to become intoxicated.” The scholiast on Aristophanes (*Wasps*, v. 9), however, maintains that it is a Thracian word. If this is so, perhaps it may be compared with German *Saufen*, Swedish *Suppa*, and Danish *Sobe*. Perhaps it will be derived with greater right from Persian languages: for *Zabzeba* in Pahlavi is a name for the Sun, from a Chaldean [word not recoverable in the supplied text], “he shone”; if one adds [a word not recoverable in the supplied text], likewise found in that language, one obtains the notion of most intense splendour (Eusèbe Salverte, *Essay on the Names of Men, Peoples, and Places*, Paris, 1824, vol. II, p. 93). Yet I gladly acknowledge that all etymologies of this sort are uncertain. On Sabazius further see Arnobius V, 21, and [Col. 1006C] Orelli’s note; Santa-Cruz, *On the Mysteries* II, p. 93; Welcker, appendix to Zoëga’s treatises, p. 401.] draw a snake through their bosom when they are initiated. [Note: [Col. 1006C] Arnobius V, 21: “The sacred rites themselves, and the rite of initiation itself, called Sebadian, will be able to bear witness to the truth: in them a golden snake is lowered into the bosom of the consecrated and is drawn out again from the lower and deepest parts.” Similarly Justin Martyr, *First Apology* I, p. 45. Clement of Alexandria, *Protrepticus*, ch. 2, p. 14: “The token of the mysteries of Sabazius for those being initiated is the god passing through the bosom; and this is a serpent, drawn through the bosom of those being initiated, an exposure of Zeus’s lack of self-control.” See more in Orelli’s notes on Arnobius’s passage.]

The vices of the first error still spread abroad, [Col. 1006A] and whatever destroyed the human being is worshipped, and the cunning, malicious cruelty of the deadly serpent [Note: [Col. 1006C] Namely, the serpent of Paradise.] is adored.

## CHAPTER XII. Likewise, the abominations and foul rites of the Corybants.

In the sacred rites of the Corybants, parricide is worshipped. [Note: [Col. 1006C] Minucius Felix, ch. 21; Lactantius I, ch. 13—though in these passages there is no mention of parricide. Arnobius V, 19: “Let the Corybantic sacred rites also be consigned to oblivion, in which that holy mystery is transmitted: a brother slaughtered by brothers.” So likewise Clement, *Protrepticus*, ch. 2: “If you wish to view the orgies of the Corybants too, after these had killed the third [Col. 1006D] brother,” etc. See further Santa-Cruz, *Mysteries of Paganism*, I, p. 79, and Creuzer II, 41, 767 ff.] For one brother was killed by two, and, lest any evidence disclose the murder of a brother’s death, he was consecrated by his parricidal brothers beneath the roots of Mount Olympus. [Note: [Col. 1006D] Clement, *Protrepticus*, ch. 2, p. 15.] The foolish belief of the Macedonians worships this same person. [Note: [Col. 1006D] Lactantius I, ch. 15 says that the Macedonians worshipped Cabirus with the highest veneration.] This is Cabirus, to whom the Thessalonians once offered supplication with blood-stained hands, to the blood-stained god. [Note: [Col. 1006D] He is seen on coins of the Thessalonians. See Eckhel, *Doctrine of Ancient Coins* II, p. 77: games in his honour were celebrated among them, the *Kabeiria*. He also occurs elsewhere on coins, for example those of Tripolis in Phoenicia, III, p. 373, and of the emperor Claudius Gothicus, inscribed “To the god Cabirus,” VII, p. 472. Firmicus alone testifies that he was propitiated with human sacrifices.] It must therefore be considered what kind of deity that is which parricidal madness devised in order that it might worship parricide. [Note: [Col. 1006D] I would prefer *celaret*, “conceal,” rather than *coleret*, “worship.” [Uncertain OCR: “Wow.”] The first edition has the latter; [Col. 1007B] nevertheless *coleret* seems better to accord with the sequence of the argument.]

## CHAPTER XIII. He teaches that every kind of abomination is commended to human beings by narratives of the gods’ crimes, and that names more base and worse than human are portrayed.

[Col. 1006B]

Therefore, whoever reveres these sacred rites with devout mind, [Col. 1007A] whoever finds pleasing the dreadful contagion of that superstition, either seeks consolation for his evils or silently approves their crimes in thought—wishing, seeking, and most earnestly desiring this: that he too may be permitted what was permitted to his gods, and that likeness of conduct may lead him too into fellowship with such a life.

Does someone delight in adultery? [Note: [Col. 1007B] Reproaches of this kind occur frequently in the Acts of the Martyrs. Thus, for example, the martyr Symphorianus said before the judge: “Who does not know that Apollo was a shepherd of King Admetus at the river Amphrysus, and that, recalling the allurements of his pleasures, he loves laurel crowns wreathed in garlands?” Ruinart, *Authentic and Selected Acts of the First Martyrs*, p. 72. Bishop Achatius, ibid., p. 140, on Apollo: “Being shamefully inclined toward boys, captivated by the beauty of a certain Hyacinthus, as you well know, he grew inflamed; and miserable and ignorant of the future, he killed with a discus the person whom he longed to see.” The following passages mention Asclepius struck by lightning, Venus the adulteress, and Jupiter buried in Crete. The martyr Theotechus exposes the crimes of Jupiter, Mars, and Vulcan in the *Acts of St Theodotus* (ibid., p. 363). Nor will other testimonies of this sort be lacking if you examine the Acts of the Martyrs. See [Col. 1007C] p. 47 on Venus; p. 468 on Jupiter’s fornication with his sister Juno; p. 446 on Hercules and Asclepius. Compare Justin Martyr, *First Apology* I, ch. 9; Arnobius IV, ch. 26, where the filthy loves of the gods are enumerated; and Orelli and Meyer, *On Arnobius*, p. 244. Clement of Alexandria has nearly the same material in the *Protrepticus*, ch. 2, p. 27. The unworthy acts of the gods clearly prove that those supposed gods are not gods: Athanasius, *Against the Greeks*, ch. 12. For the individual cases see the mythographers. We shall note only a few.] Let him look to Jupiter and seek there incentives for his own desire; he approves, imitates, and praises the fact that his god deceives in the form of a swan, [Note: [Col. 1007C] Leda.] carries off in the form of a bull, [Note: [Col. 1007C] Europa.] sports as a satyr, [Note: [Col. 1007C] Antiope: Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VI, 110; Hyginus, fable 8; Apollodorus III, ch. 5, 5; Nonnus, *Dionysiaca* VII, 123, XVI, 232; and the scholiast on Apollonius Rhodius IV, 1090, in the later Brunck edition; Arnobius IV, 26. “Sports” has a sexual sense. Ovid, *Art of Love* I, 91, 613; *Metamorphoses* VI, 131; and Burmann on Ovid, *Art of Love*, p. 546.] and, so that he may become accustomed to being lavish in abominations, corrupts a royal maiden shut away by gold flowing freely. [Note: [Col. 1007C] Danaë: Horace, *Odes* III, 16.]

Does someone delight in the embraces of boys? Let him seek Ganymede in Jupiter’s bosom; [Note: [Col. 1007C] Minucius Felix, ch. 22: “and Jupiter’s violation of Ganymede [Col. 1007D] consecrated in heaven.”] let him see Hercules seeking Hylas in impatient love; [Note: [Col. 1007D] Arnobius also has this, borrowed from Clement: Orelli, cited passage.] let him learn of Apollo captured by longing for Hyacinthus. [Col. 1007B] [Note: [Col. 1007D] Arnobius says the same: “Another is occupied with Hyacinthus.” Ovid, *Metamorphoses* X, 160 ff. Orelli.—Commodian, *Instructions* XI: “That final day was the day of Hyacinthus, his companion.”] Let one look upon Chrysippus, [Note: [Col. 1007D] Pausanias VI, ch. 20, and Hyginus, fable 85, treat Chrysippus, son of Pelops, carried off by Laius because of his beauty, rescued by Pelops, and then killed by Atreus and Thyestes; but we do not read that he was loved by any god.] another upon Pelops, [Note: [Col. 1007D] Arnobius likewise enumerates him as loved by Neptune. Pindar, *Olympian* I, 38: “Pelops, whom Poseidon, the earth-shaking lord, loved.” Orelli.—“Poseidon loves the youth”: Philostratus, *Images* I, on Pelops.] so that through his gods he may say that he is permitted [Note: [Col. 1008B] “They do not show the gods to be better than human beings”: Athenagoras, ch. 9. Xenophanes had already sung:

> Homer and Hesiod attributed to the gods  
> all those things among human beings that are shameful and blameworthy—  
> stealing, adultery, and deceiving one another.

Lindner on Athenagoras.—Tertullian agrees with Athenagoras, *Apology*, ch. II: “Your justice is a disgrace in heaven” (*heaven*, thus Havercamp); “you make gods out of every criminal person.” Athanasius, *Against the Greeks*, ch. 25, likewise teaches that the shameful examples of false gods led people to do similar things.] whatever is now punished with the utmost severity by Roman laws. [Note: [Col. 1008B] For example, the Julian law on adultery and illicit sexual relations; compare Johann Wilhelm Hoffmann, *On the Julian Law for the Punishment of Adulteries*, Frankfurt, 1732. Those convicted were banished to an island. The Peducaean law on incest; the Papian-Poppaean law. The successors of Augustus frequently enacted laws against adultery and other crimes of this kind: for example, Tiberius’s law on chastity (Suetonius, *Tiberius*, ch. 35), Caracalla’s law against adulterers, *Digest* XLVIII, title 5, law 13, §5. But Firmicus seems most directly to have in view the laws of Constantine the Great concerning marriage: *Theodosian Code* III, title 16; IX, title 7; *Justinian Code* IV, title 39; V, title 27. He repressed with severe laws the obscenities especially associated with divine worship in Syria: Eusebius, *Life of Constantine* III, chs. 56, 58; Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History* I, 18; Sozomen, *Ecclesiastical History* II, 4.]

[Col. 1008A] It is difficult to enumerate all their adulteries. Who rebukes Amymone? [Note: [Col. 1008C] Clement of Alexandria, in the cited passage, p. 27, and Arnobius IV, 26, mention her.] Who Alopê? [Note: [Col. 1008C] The same authors.] Who Menalippe? [Note: [Col. 1008C] The same authors.] Who Chione and Hippothoe? [Note: [Col. 1008C] Clement mentions Chione—Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XI, 301 ff. Clement and Arnobius mention Hippothoe. The mythographers write that all these women were violated by Neptune. See Orelli’s notes on Arnobius’s passage. Ovid, however, has Chione violated by Apollo.] Surely your god is said to have done these things. He whom they wish to correct the sins of wandering people by stern oracles loves Sterope, [Note: [Col. 1008C] Clement and Arnobius, in the cited passages, say that Sterope was violated by Apollo, [Col. 1008D] as were likewise Aethusa, Prothoe, and Arsinoe, whom Clement and Arnobius include in the cited passages. Compare Orelli’s notes. I have read nothing concerning Zeuxippe.] carries off Aethusa, violates Zeuxippe, seeks Prothoe, and courts Arsinoe with adulterous desire. But from this flock of corrupted women, one maiden both avoided and overcame the god who loved her: Daphne. [Note: [Col. 1008D] Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I, v. 490 ff.; Hyginus, fable 203; Commodian, *Instructions* XI:

…he who wantonly began to love Daphne in this manner. For a god who divines and foretells the future was unable either to find her or to violate her. Does someone suffer womanish passions and seek consolation for an effeminate body? Let him look at Liber, who, even after death, displays to his lover the rewards of promised lust by imitating a shameful intercourse. [Note: Clement of Alexandria, *Protrepticus*, ch. 2, p. 29, and Arnobius V.28 tell this filthy tale; compare Firmicus. “Can you,” in Arnobius’s words, “make known to your beardless youths and those wearing the bordered toga the agreements which Liber made with his lovers?” It is also mentioned by Gregory of Nazianzus in the *Stelīteutikos* [?].]

If anyone, under a monstrous blaze of desire, arms himself for the destruction of his father, let him take Jupiter as his example. [Note: In fleeing from his father. The story is well known and was also told by Euhemerus; Ennius, Hessel, p. 320.] Let one who longs for his brother’s blood follow the precedent of the Corybantes; and let those who desire incest take their examples from Jupiter. He lay with his mother, [Note: Cybele on the summit of Mount Agdis, as Arnobius V.9 has it.] married his sister, [Note: Juno.] and, that he might complete the whole crime of incest, he even made an assault, with a seducer’s intent, upon his daughter. [Note: Proserpina; Tatian, ch. 16; Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* VI, p. 251, Elmenhorst; Nonnus, *Dionysiaca* VI.157.]

Does someone pursue inferiors with the shrieking rage of jealousy and wish to torture an opponent with cruel savagery? From the fate of Marsyas let him learn the methods of cruel tortures from Apollo. [Note: Apollodorus, *Library* I.4; Hyginus, *Fables* 165; Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VI.384 ff., and *Fasti* VI.703.] Does someone covet another’s property and attempt to accomplish this through the owner’s death? Let him see how Hercules, having killed Geryon, drove off the Iberian cattle. [Note: Apollodorus II.5.] If anyone delights in the indiscriminate slaughter of human beings, let him carefully consider the perverse desires of Mars. From the crowd of their sinning gods he has collected the seeds of nearly every crime. [Note: Thus Wower corrected the reading of the first edition, which has “from his pious [gods].”] And so that a ruined mind might commit its crime with impunity, it defends itself with greater authority by the precedents of earlier crimes.

If a seducer seeks the rewards of fornication, if he desires to learn the way of solicitation, let him see Jupiter’s gold in the lap of the corrupted woman. [Note: Understand Danaë.] If a public parricide desires, in wicked greed, to betray the guardianship of a kingdom entrusted to him, let him look back to those who betrayed Saturn to his son. [Note: Prometheus and his companions; see Aeschylus’s *Prometheus*. Or, if he has in view the final betrayal, by which Saturn was mutilated by his son, see Lycophron, v. 869, and Tzetzes on the same passage.] How the right of hospitality may be violated, how the obligations of friendship may be disturbed, or how the sacred bond of a shared table may be profaned—[Note: Something seems to have fallen out here, for the examples found in the other cases are missing, although the story of Tantalus may be referred here. Firmicus, however, uses it as an example of vengeance taken for an injury.]—if anyone, inclined to wrongdoing, seeks to be so, let him learn the sequence of crimes from the history of Tantalus. [Note: For the authorities who relate Tantalus’s deeds, see Hederich, *Mythological Lexicon*.]

O gloomy consolation of criminal desire! O lamentable delusion of humankind! O bloody contemplation of disastrous imitation! You have made the sky into a stage, [Note: The correct emendation reads *scenam*, “stage,” in place of *coenam*, “banquet,” found in the first edition. It closely reproduces Clement, *Protrepticus* ch. 4, p. 52: “Alas for your godlessness! You have made heaven a stage, and the divine has become a drama for you.” The surviving tragedies, in which gods play roles, sufficiently confirm this complaint of Firmicus.] and have led erring minds over sheer precipices into cruel disaster, since to men wishing to sin the path of crimes is pointed out by the examples of gods.

But amid this law of crimes, amid this confession of wickedness, let us thank those who, although we did not know it, handed down even the destructions and deaths of these gods, [Note: For example, Euhemerus and others.] so that we might learn everything through so many opposing testimonies. For even among the ancients—although the venerable condescension of our Lord Jesus Christ had not yet illuminated the earth—there was a religious steadfastness in rejecting superstitions. Chaste and sober Diomedes wounds Venus; he conquers and strikes Mars. [Note: *Iliad* V.883 ff., 846 ff.; Clement, *Protrepticus* ch. 2, p. 31, Potter; Tertullian, *Apology* ch. 14; Minucius Felix ch. 22; Longinus, *On the Sublime* ch. 9; Arnobius IV.25; Gregory of Nazianzus, *Oration* IV against Julian.]

By the decree of Otus and Ephialtes, [Note: *Iliad* V.384; Diodorus Siculus V.51.] Mars, mighty in war, was condemned to a temporary exile [Note: For thirteen months: *Iliad* V.386; Hyginus, *Astronomy* II.40.] and endured the iron shackles of chains. Jupiter weeps for his son Sarpedon, dead at Troy. [Note: Homer relates Sarpedon’s death in *Iliad* II.459.] Neptune did not receive from a proud king the payment due for the walls he built. [Note: Laomedon, king of Troy; Homer, *Iliad* Φ.443, and Eustathius on the passage.] Apollo tends the flocks of another king. [Note: Admetus; Hyginus, *Fables* 50; Tatian, *Address to the Greeks* ch. 35. Commodian, *Instructions* XI also relates that Apollo tended Admetus’s cattle.] Another reports to the Sun, who sees all things, the death of his slaughtered cattle. [Note: Lampetia, *Odyssey* M.374.] Sparta buries the Castors, [Note: Pausanias III.13, though he believes that they were buried in Messenia; Arnobius IV.25.] Hercules burns on Mount Oeta, [Note: See above on ch. 7.] and Aesculapius is elsewhere struck by lightning. [Note: Justin Martyr, *Apology* I.29; Tertullian, *Apology* ch. 14; Minucius Felix ch. 21: “Aesculapius, so that he may rise as a god, is struck by lightning”; Apollodorus III.10; Hyginus, *Fables* 49; Arnobius IV.24 and Orelli’s notes; Pindar, *Pythian* Ode III, antistrophe 3, in Clement, *Protrepticus* ch. 2, p. 25; Theodoret, *Cure of Greek Maladies*, discourse 3, *Works*, ed. Schultz, IV, p. 767.] Vulcan, cast down by his father, breaks his foot. [Note: *Iliad* A.590–90; Clement, ibid.; Tertullian, *Apology* ch. 14; Arnobius IV.24 and Orelli on the passage.] Liber dies while fleeing Lycurgus. [Note: I do not know whence Firmicus has this; perhaps from Euhemerus.] Venus is exposed when caught in adultery, [Note: Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IV.170; Minucius Felix ch. 22.] and, after marrying a god, she pursues the bed of the human Anchises. [Note: Arnobius V.27.]

Saturn, fearing for his kingdom, devours his children. [Note: Apollodorus I.1; Tatian, *Address to the Greeks* ch. 42.] Fleeing from Crete, [Note: Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII.319:

> First Saturn came from heavenly Olympus,  
> fleeing Jupiter’s weapons, an exile from a kingdom taken away.

Ovid, *Fasti* I.235:

> I remember that Saturn was received in this land;  
> Jupiter had driven him from the realms of heaven.] he is hidden in Italy by the Spartans. [Note: Arnobius IV.24: “Was it not an old man driven out by us who hid in the territories of the Italians?” Minucius Felix ch. 22; Lactantius I.13–14; Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* III.3; Tertullian, *Apology* ch. 10; and Orelli’s notes on Arnobius. Euhemerus in Ennius, p. 320: “Jupiter, having learned of Saturn’s plots, again claimed the kingdom for himself and drove Saturn away. Tossed through all lands, and pursued by armed men whom Jupiter had sent to seize or kill him, he scarcely found a place in Italy in which to hide.” But this passage says not a word of Spartans. I do not know whence Firmicus drew it. Clearly an error of an ancient copyist lies concealed here, who confused the name of the Spartans with the name of some not dissimilar Italian people.]

Because of love for a catamite, Juno is despised, [Note: That is, Ganymede. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* X.155; Justin Martyr, *Apology* I.33; Tatian ch. 16; Minucius Felix ch. 22; Arnobius IV.44: “And what [shall we say] for those Ganymedes who were carried off and installed as instructors in lust?” Cyprian, *Letter* 1.2, has *catamitum*. Arnobius IV.26: “The catamite is carried off to become a pleasure-object and keeper of cups.” Lactantius I.11: “He is said to have carried off the catamite in the form of an eagle.” Theodoret, *Cure of Greek Maladies*, discourse 3, *Works* IV, p. 767. Festus: “They said *catamitus* for Ganymede.” Papias: “Catamitus … Ganymede. Ganymede was effeminate; hence effeminate persons are called catamites.” More in Orelli. Add Plautus, *Menaechmi* I.2.35:

> Tell me: have you never seen a painted picture on a wall,  
> where an eagle carried off a catamite, or where Venus [carried off] Adonis?

Cf. Taubmann, *Observationes*, p. 587.] and the Moon descends to Endymion. [Note: Arnobius IV.27. A very familiar story; Apollodorus I.7 and Heyne on the passage.] And Jupiter, bringing aid to the Trojans against the will of his wife and daughter, is deceived and sleeps. [Note: *Iliad* Ξ.352; Minucius Felix ch. 22.]

O shameful confession, O pitiable and lamentable cults, O wretched condition of harsh slavery! The sacrilegious power of tyrants has dragged holy men, who worship God with devoted mind, into the worship of these gods; and, that one crime might be added to another, death was decreed for those unwilling to do so. [Note: Hertzius understands this passage as referring to Sapor’s persecution of Christians: Sozomen, *Ecclesiastical History* II.1–13; Cassiodorus, *Tripartite History* III.2. But it is closely connected with what Firmicus had just said concerning Greek and Roman mythology, of which the Persians plainly knew nothing. Thus it refers to the persecutions by which Roman emperors harassed Christians before the reign of Constantine the Great.]

Transfer the temples instead to the theatre, so that the secret rites of these religions may be handed down upon the stage, [Note: Tertullian, *Apology* ch. 6, calls theatres “the breeding-grounds of corrupted morals”; elsewhere, “the consistory of shamelessness,” *On Spectacles* ch. 16, and “the sanctuary of Venus,” ibid. ch. 10. Cyprian, *Letter* 2 to Donatus: “Then what a ruin of morals! What incentives to disgrace! What nourishment for vices! To be polluted by an actor’s gestures.” Augustine, *City of God* II.13, praises ancient Rome: “For a long time Roman virtue had not known those theatrical arts, which, although sought for the delight of human pleasure, crept in through the corruption of human morals. The gods had demanded that they be performed for them.” Havercamp on *Apology*, loc. cit.] and, so that depravity may omit nothing, make actors priests. No place more fitting for such religions can be found. There let a contemptible crowd sing the loves of the gods. There let dancers display their disasters and deaths … There, in the temples of the gods, [Note: The passage is mutilated. Wower proposed this supplement: “There let dancers display their disasters and deaths; there, in the temples of the gods,” etc. I approve; at least a few words seem to be missing.] a ruined and womanish mind is better instructed in crime by impious and criminal masters.

## Chapter XIV

He maintains that Serapis, his name and rites, were fabricated from the history of the patriarch Joseph; that demons gather in images through continual sacrifices and are nourished by the blood of victims. From Porphyry he proves that Serapis obeyed human commands and was compelled to speak against his will; and he asserts the same of all the remaining gods of the Gentiles, as subject to the authority of Christians.

Learn also, most sacred emperors, from what origin the venerable divinity of Alexandria [Note: Serapis. Many Fathers teach that the Gentiles drew much from the most ancient Jewish sources—for example, Theophilus, *To Autolycus* III.19; Justin’s *Exhortation* chs. 8–10—but corrupted it in many ways. See Justin’s *Exhortation* ch. 14 ff.; Tatian, *Address* ch. 40; Tertullian, *To the Nations* II.2; Meyer, *On Arnobius*, p. 196. Among more recent writers, Peter Daniel Huet undertook to demonstrate the same in his otherwise learned *Evangelical Demonstration*.] derived its beginning; and let the discourse, having exposed [the matter] from the common frailty of us all, recall our mortality to the beginning of truth. When a grievous famine came upon the crops as they withered, Joseph, the young man descended from the stock of the devout patriarch Jacob, interpreted the king’s dream and explained all that it signified (*Genesis* XLI).

Joseph—he was Jacob’s son [Note: A gloss which slipped from the margin into the text; the first edition read “and.”]—was sent to prison because of his chastity; after interpreting the dream, he was rescued and made a partner in the kingdom. For, by collecting and preserving the crops of seven years, the providence of the divine hand alleviated the want of another seven-year period. After his death, the Egyptians built temples for him according to the ancestral custom of their nation; [Note: A fiction arising solely from the confusion of Joseph with Serapis. Rufinus II.23 says that Apis was Joseph. On Apis, see Orelli’s notes on Arnobius I.36, p. 317.] and, so that posterity might learn the just favor of his administration, the measure-basket (*modius*) by which he had distributed grain to the hungry and purchasers was placed upon his head. [Note: Wower’s emendation, *quo modio*, “by what measure-basket,” in place of *quomodo*, “how.” It refers to the *modius* placed upon Serapis’s head.]

He also received his name from the first founder of the race, so that he might be worshipped more sacredly. For because he was Sarah’s great-grandson, and Abraham, by God’s favor, had received a son from her when she was ninety years old (*Genesis* XXI.2), he was called Serapis in Greek—that is, **Σαρᾶς ἀπό**, “from Sarah.” [Note: Paulinus of Nola, *Natalicia* XI, on St. Felix, v. 100, already identifies Serapis with Joseph:

> …so that Serapis might represent holy Joseph,  
> concealing the venerable name beneath a deadly name,  
> though the very form of the image taught the truth,  
> since a measure-basket rests upon its head.

This doubtless refers to the grain shortage relieved for the Egyptians by Joseph. Likewise Suidas, as Firmicus, under **Σάραπις**: “Others said that he was Joseph.” But the name Serapis is clearly of Egyptian, not Greek, origin. Georg Zoëga attempted its difficult etymology in his excellent work *On the Origin and Use of Obelisks*, p. 306, and identified an Egyptian word meaning “father of darkness,” corresponding to Greek **ᾅδης** or **ἀΐδης**, “Hades.” That the origin of the name had long been uncertain is evident from Plutarch, *On Isis* ch. 29, since he lists several opinions. On this deity, whose force and power were believed to extend widely, see Creuzer I, pp. 312 ff.]

But this happened against Joseph’s will—indeed, after he was dead. For a devout soul devoted to the highest God could not have been brought to such a crime as itself to furnish superstitious people with the allurements of error from its own name, especially since it knew that the most sacred laws of God forbade anyone to venerate or worship anything of that sort. Here in Egypt he is worshipped; here he is adored; a body of *neocori* guards his image; [Note: On the *neocori*, temple-attendants and guardians: this title of honor was held not only by individual persons, but was eagerly sought and repeatedly assumed—three or four times—by many peoples and cities, especially in Asia Minor. See Eckhel, *Doctrine of Ancient Coins* IV, p. 288. The present reference is to the *neocori* of Serapis. One of them—there were many, since Firmicus speaks of a “body” of *neocori*—is mentioned in the Farnese inscription in Gruter, p. 314.1, M. Aurelius Asclepiades, called:

> **Ὁ ΠΡΕΣΒΥΤΑΤΟΣ ΤΩΝ ΝΕΩΚΟΡΩΝ ΤΟΥ ΜΕΓΑΛΟΥ ΣΑΡΑΠΙΔΟΣ**  
> “The senior of the *neocori* of great Serapis.”]

and, in memory of antiquity, the erring people still preserve with contentious zeal the order of rites established in honor of a most upright and prudent man. [Note: Joseph, in Firmicus’s understanding, who identifies him with Serapis.]

Yet in this image, as in the others, unclean spirits of demons gather through continual sacrifices. [Note: Ancient Christians consistently held that demons lurked beneath consecrated statues and images. Compare Krog-Meyer, *On Arnobius*, p. 254. Minucius Felix, ch. 27, makes the same assertion in these very words; but one must read “beneath consecrated statues and images,” not “consecrated,” as the editions have it, since the statues, not the unclean spirits, were consecrated. See Lindner on this passage of Minucius. Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols* ch. 4, likewise states: “These spirits lurk beneath consecrated statues and images”—perhaps drawn from Minucius. Lactantius II.15–16. Tertullian, *Apology* ch. 21, end: “If this is the divinity which, once known, reforms one toward good, it follows that every contrary divinity found false must be renounced—above all that one which, lurking beneath the names and images of the dead, produces belief in divinity by certain signs, miracles, and oracles.” Compare *On Spectacles* ch. 12: “Demons dwell in idols of the dead, if we consider even their titles.”]

For souls accomplish nothing; nor does the blood poured out by the continual slaughter of cattle do anything except nourish from that blood the substance of demons, generated by the procreation of the devil. [Note: The belief that divine beings were nourished by the savor from the blood and flesh of sacrifices was common among ancient peoples: Porphyry, *On Abstinence* II.42, p. 182, Goës; Lucian, *On Sacrifices* ch. 9; Aristophanes, *Birds* vv. 183 ff. and 1513 ff. It accordingly passed also to Christians, who held the same concerning demons. Athenagoras, ch. 22: “The demons are those previously mentioned, who attend upon the blood from the victims and lick it around”; and ch. 23: “The demons concerned with matter are greedy for the odors of fat and the blood of victims.” Justin Martyr, *Apology* II.6: “[The evil angels] brought some things about … through the teaching of sacrifices, incense, and libations, of which they became needy after becoming enslaved to passions and desires.” Minucius Felix ch. 27: “They feign diseases, terrify minds, distort limbs, in order to compel worship of themselves; then, fattened by the odor of altars or the victims of cattle, they seem to have healed those whom they had afflicted.” Clement of Alexandria, *Protrepticus* ch. 2, p. 35, may likewise be cited: “The demons themselves, it seems, confess their own gluttony: ‘Libation and the savor of fat—for this is the portion we received as our honor.’” Tertullian, *Apology* ch. 22: “…that he may procure for himself, as his proper food, the savor and blood offered to statues and images.” See further Havercamp’s notes. I add only Arnobius VII.3: “unless perhaps the god devours the souls of victims, or pursues the savor and smoke from burning altars, and feeds on the odor of fat which burning entrails, still wet with blood and soaked from earlier sacrifices, emit.” Compare also V.19 and VII.28.]

Porphyry, defender of the Stoics and enemy of God and truth, disclosed to us with manifest proofs that this is so in many writings of criminal impiety.
