For in the books which he calls **περὶ τῆς ἐκ λογίων φιλοσοφίας**, “On Philosophy Derived from Oracles,” [Note: Read **περὶ τῆς ἐκ λογίων φιλοσοφίας**, not *περὶ τῆς εὐλογίων φιλοσοφίας*. Creuzer I, p. 215. The book has long been lost. It is cited by Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* III.4 and often elsewhere; Augustine, *City of God* X.23; Theodoret; and others. Holstenius, *On the Life and Writings of Porphyry* ch. 9, p. 55; and Fabricius, *Greek Library* IV, pt. II.] while proclaiming Serapis’s majesty, he confessed his weakness. For at the very beginning of the work [Note: “That is, placed in the very opening” appears to have entered from a gloss.] he said: “Serapis, having been summoned and placed within a human body, gave such replies.” [Note: Firmicus undoubtedly refers to Porphyry’s words. Strabo XVII.1.17 testifies to miraculous cures, especially cures effected by incubation, performed in the temple of Serapis at Canopus; Tzschucke VI, p. 533; Cicero, *On Divination* II.59. Serapis the Saviour is likewise mentioned in inscriptions: Gruter, p. XXIII, nos. 7–10. Perhaps this sanctuary was still frequented in Firmicus’s age. From roughly the age of Alexander Severus it became especially celebrated through restored rites, to which Platonic philosophers gave careful attention. Creuzer, *Dionysus* I, p. 122.]

Now let ruined men tell me: who is superior, he who summons, commands, and confines, or he who is summoned and obeys? When he has come, he is confined within the body of the person receiving him by the power of the one commanding. We thank you, Porphyry, because in your books you disclosed to us the substance of your gods. Through you we have learned to what extent your gods serve living human beings. Your Serapis is summoned by a human being and comes; and when he has come, he is immediately confined at command, and perhaps against his will the necessity of speaking is imposed upon him.

Thus, when your gods begin to harm human beings, the scourges of religious utterance punish them among us. [Note: That is, exorcisms. The demon clinging to a person is torn, burned, beaten, and immediately confesses the crimes he has committed: Origen, *Homilies on Joshua* 24. “If the hostile force of a demon besieges someone’s body, and many invocations of exorcists are used, and yet the deaf demon remains in the possessed body through all this, more easily enduring the penalties of exorcists and the tortures inflicted upon him through invocation of God’s name”: Tertullian, *Apology* ch. 23. Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols* ch. 4: “You may see them [the demons], by our voice and the operation of hidden majesty, beaten with whips, scorched with fire, stretched out by the growing force of punishment, howling, groaning, and begging.” The same, *To Demetrianus*, p. 191 Fell: “When they are adjured and tormented by us with spiritual scourges and verbal tortures, they are driven from possessed bodies.” The same, *Letter* 78: “Through exorcists, by human voice and divine power, the devil is whipped, burned, and tortured.” *Letter* 191: “Exorcists [use] spiritual scourges,” and often elsewhere. Minucius Felix ch. 27: “Adjured through the true and only God, they unwillingly and miserably shudder in bodies, or leap out immediately, or vanish gradually, according as the faith of the sufferer helps or the grace of the healer breathes upon him.” Lactantius II.15: “Adjured by his name, they depart from bodies; beaten as though by whips with his words, they not only confess that they are demons but even give their names … Hence, often with loud howls, they cry out that they are being beaten and burned and are on the point of departing.” V.21: “Thus forced out, they howl under the power of the divine divinity.” Arnobius I.46: “There was one among us … whose name, when heard, puts harmful spirits to flight.” Prudentius, *Apotheosis* 438:

> Apollo is tortured, struck by the name of Christ;  
> nor can he bear the thunderbolts of the Word—  
> so many blows of the tongue agitate the wretch!

It should be noted from ecclesiastical history that Catholics rebuked the erring spirit and even forbade it to speak of its own accord, whereas Montanists urged it to speak at greater length: Routh, *Reliquiae Sacrae* I, p. 416. A passage in Firmicus’s *Astronomy* II.9 teaches that Gentiles likewise held this belief about the power of adjurations: “It will make exorcists, who free people afflicted by demonic assault with suitable remedies.” For more on exorcists see Bingham, *Origines Ecclesiasticae* II, p. 19 ff.]

Thus your gods, established in human bodies, are tortured by the fire of spiritual flames through the word of God; and those who are worshipped among you as gods are, among us, subject to human authority through the healing grace of Christ and religious faith: though resisting, they endure tortures, and, conquered by avenging punishments, are subdued.

## Chapter XV

He discusses the Penates, deriving their name from *penus* (“provisions”), and Vesta from merely domestic fire: thus, things useful and agreeable to human beings which they made into gods.

I shall also undertake to explain who the Penates are, so that nothing may be omitted by me. Those who think that life is nothing but license to eat and drink fashioned these gods for themselves out of the baseness of their own desire, consecrating under this name, for the preservation of mankind, the nourishment of the body obtained from daily meals. Because bodily weakness is restored through food, they decreed that food alone was God, ignorant of the truth of the divine oracle.

For when our Lord Jesus Christ, concerned for our salvation, was struggling with the devil in the divine conflict of his majesty, and wished to free from the devil’s jaws the human being whom he bore, he shattered him with this reply. For when the devil said to him: “If you are the Son of God, make these stones become loaves” (*Matthew* IV.3; *Luke* IV.3), [Note: *Make* is found only in Firmicus. In all other manuscripts and Fathers preserving the pre-Jerome version of Matthew and Luke, the reading is “say.”] the Lord answered him: “A human being does not live by bread alone, [Note: “Not by bread alone.” The others have *solo*, “by bread only.” Maximus of Turin agrees with Firmicus. See Sabatier, *Bibliotheca Sacrorum Latinorum Veterum*, III, p. 277.] but by every word of God” (*Luke* IV.4).

Ignorant, therefore, of the substance of humankind, they consecrated daily meals under this name. For everything that human beings eat is called *penus*; hence also the pantry (*cella penaria*), and hence the Penate gods—things composed in miserable imagination by abject and degraded persons. [Note: Festus: *Penora*. Varro, *On the Latin Language* IV.]

Now learn what Vesta is, [Note: On Vesta see Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II.27; Ovid, *Fasti* III.45 and VI.250 ff.; Arnobius III.32, IV.35; Isidore, *Etymologies* IX.11.] lest you suppose her something ancient or discovered amid supreme awe. She is domestic fire, serving daily uses upon hearths. Therefore let her have cooks, [Note: A mockery.] not wretched virgin priestesses, who, scorning the sparks of that fire, are either compelled to sin with prostituted bodies [Note: I do not understand how Vestal virgins can be said to have been compelled to sin, since Roman pontifical law punished their unchastity with the utmost severity. Nor does Firmicus’s phrase “scorning [the sparks]” seem to accord with the following words, “or, while remaining in virginity, they lose,” etc. The entire passage is defective and can scarcely be restored intact.] or, while maintaining virginity, lose the honorable dignity of a glorious name. [Note: That is, because they consecrated their celibate life not to God but to the unclean demon Vesta.]

## Chapter XVI

He explains the origin of the Palladium, and maintains that its divinity preserved neither Troy nor Rome from fire, nor will preserve its worshippers in the future.

Hear also what divinity the Palladium is. It is an image made from the bones of Pelops. [Note: He has in mind Pelops’s shoulder, which Ceres, insufficiently cautious while mourning the loss of Proserpina, ate at the banquet prepared by Tantalus for the gods. Servius on Virgil, *Georgics* III.7: “When he was restored to life by the gods, Ceres replaced his missing shoulder with an ivory one.” Hyginus, *Fables* 83. Servius, loc. cit. Lycophron v. 152: “When this [shoulder] was thereafter being carried from Pisa to Troy—because they had received an oracle that Ilium was **Ἴλιον δυσάλωτον**, ‘Ilium hard to capture,’ without that bone and Philoctetes’ bow—it was lost in a shipwreck near Euboea. But the Eretrian fisherman Damarmenus hauled it up and was charged to preserve it, as were his descendants.” Pausanias, *Elis* I.13. From that tradition—that Pelops’s shoulder had been brought to the Greeks besieging Troy—arose the further tale that the Trojans made the Palladium from it. Besides Firmicus, Clement of Alexandria, *Protrepticus* ch. 4, p. 41, ed. Potter, relates this:

> “Many would perhaps be astonished if they learned that the Palladium called ‘fallen from Zeus,’ which Diomedes and Odysseus are said to have removed from Ilium and deposited with Demophon, was made from Pelops’s bones, just as the Olympian [statue] was made from other bones of an Indian beast.”

Philostratus, *Images* ch. 30, also mentions this ivory shoulder. Arnobius IV.25 agrees with Clement: “Who declared that the Palladium was put together from the remains of Pelops? Was it not you?” Meursius considers that Cassandra’s words in Lycophron, v. 53, refer to this:

I behold you, wretched woman, being burned a second time

By the hands both of the Aeacidae and of Tantalus,

Keeping house as a serving-woman with the remnants of the fire

Of the devoured child, your body blackened with soot.

[Col. 1016D] From Clement’s comparison of the Palladium with Olympian Jupiter, it is probable that he had Pelops’ ivory shoulder in mind. Perhaps he had received the report that the Palladium preserved among the Roman Vestals was made from bone; he therefore gave credence to the old tale. Of the Palladium—whose earliest authors are said to have been Lesches and Arctinus (Hesychius, s.v. Διομήδειος)—the latest information, so far as I know, is supplied by Herodian, book I, chapter 14: when Vesta’s temple was destroyed by fire in the time of Commodus, the Vestal virgins carried the Palladium, together with the other pledges of Roman imperial security which they kept, to the chief pontiff, who was also the emperor, in the Palatine residence. From what source Firmicus drew his account of the Palladium we do not know. He has more than Clement: he says that it was sold and put up for auction. One may conjecture that he took this from Euhemerus.

[Note: In the editions “Avarus the Scythian” is read twice. Without hesitation I have corrected it to “Abaris the Scythian,” whom Aristotle calls Baris. Compare Scaliger in Gronovius’ edition of Minucius Felix and Firmicus, p. 434.]

Abaris the Scythian is said to have done this. Consider, then, what kind of thing it is that a barbarian Scythian consecrated. Is there among the Scythians anything fashioned by human reason? Could that savage people, ever given to cruel and inhuman violence, discover anything right in establishing religions? Abaris sold this image to the Trojans, promising vain things to foolish people. A god was sold, in order to benefit its purchaser; and the purchaser worshipped in supplication whatever he had shortly before seen put up for auction. The material of the image itself, moreover, consists of the bones of Pelops. If human power compels unhappy people to venerate bones, gather at least the remains of a purer and more chaste man.

[Note: Neptune, that is, is said to have loved Pelops. Pindar, Olympian Ode I, 38; Tatian, Oration to the Greeks, ch. 42; Arnobius IV.26. See above, col. 1008, note k.]

Let the idol you make possess merit derived from the virtues of a human being. Pelops was the darling of a lover, and long bore the shameful consequences of prostituted modesty. Yet crime did not fail him even in adulthood. For he killed, through the treachery of a betrayer, the man whose daughter he sought in marriage.

[Note: This story is narrated by Firmicus alone.]

He also assailed the betrayer himself with perjuries and, so as not to render the reward he had promised, hurled that same man down sheer precipices. Behold the man whose bones were selected so that a god might be made, one who would preserve cities and kingdoms. But he never preserved or benefited them; and from the disasters of the cities in which he was kept, he saw what awaited himself. Troy was burned by the Greeks, Rome by the Gauls; and in both conflagrations the Palladium was preserved.

[Note: In the first instance by Aeneas; in the second by the Vestal virgins during the Gallic war, in the 365th year from the founding of the City. Livy V.40 does not mention a third occasion under Commodus. Perhaps, however, Firmicus did not have Aeneas in mind, but Caecilius Metellus, who, when the temple of Vesta was burning (A.U.C. 512), rescued from the flames the sacred pledges abandoned by the Vestals. Ovid, Fasti VI, vv. 437 ff.]

But it was preserved not by its own powers, but by human protection: for men rescued it from each place, and it was transferred so that it might not be consumed by a human fire. So great a divinity required human protection and sought human help lest it burn. The Palladium was delayed from the fire, not delivered from it.

[Note: Accordingly, when Firmicus wrote, it still remained unharmed under the guardianship of the Vestal virgins, during the reigns of the emperors Constantine and Constans. For the reports which John Malalas and the author of the Alexandrian Chronicle relate from Byzantine tradition—that Constantine the Great transferred this image to Byzantium and buried it in the forum named after him—are fables. John George Roeser, *On the Palladium*, in Johann Christoph Martini, *Treasury of Dissertations*, etc., vol. II, part I (Nuremberg, 1765), p. 290. But at what time the Palladium perished has not been handed down in the authors’ records. The Vestal virgins, however, after the laws against idolatry enacted by Gratian and Valentinian II, were held in contempt and gradually disappeared. Nadal, *History of the Vestals*; *Memoirs of Literature Drawn from the Register of the Academy of Inscriptions and Belles-Lettres*, vol. V, octavo edition; Johann Friedrich Eisenhart, *On the Vestals and the Vestal Law of the Roman People*, Helmstedt, 1752; also in his *Opuscula*, p. 99 ff.]

The sentence stands; the punishment remains; fire is imminent, fire presses hard—a fire it will be unable to escape. Already the heavenly flame is in travail; already the coming of divine judgment is being shown; already the destruction of the coming catastrophe is announced. In this conflagration the Palladium will not be able to find hiding places. That fire searches hidden things and seeks what is concealed; and whatever has ruined wandering people by vain persuasions it embraces in the swift devastation of its flames. “For,” he says, “the day of the Lord comes, burning like an oven.”

[Note: Firmicus alone has this reading. Sabbatier, II, p. 1011.]

You have heard what is coming. There is nothing gathered from you that can be stored in the Lord’s granaries. You shall burn like stubble, whose empty worthlessness is reserved for ashes and embers, which the consuming fire feeds upon by the force of its innate breath. This is your outcome and end; this is the punishment God has established for those who have deceived human beings: that whoever, against God’s will, has either deceived or ruined a wretched person should burn in everlasting flames.

I wish, indeed, to inquire carefully of which Minerva they wish this to be the sign.

[Note: Namely, the Palladium.]

For it is agreed that there were several Minervas, and no one disagrees on this point. Let us therefore state the lineage, character, art, and purpose of each, so that from all these it may be discovered in whose Minerva’s name the Palladium is consecrated.

## CHAPTER XVII. He treats of five Minervas. He urges that the Palladium, dedicated to the fifth, daughter of Pallas, should be burned and its temples destroyed; at the same time he attacks as shameful and bloody the rites of sacred worship by which people are taught to sin, and demands their abolition.

[Col. 1018B]

Antiquity hands down to us readers that there were five Minervas.

[Note: Compare Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* III.25, who enumerates them all with little difference. Compare Creuzer’s notes. Clement also has the first as daughter of Vulcan, the second as daughter of the Nile, and the third—Cicero’s second—as daughter of Saturn, *Protrepticus* ch. 2, p. 24; he calls her “the inventress of war” (τὴν τοῦ πολέμου εὑρέτιν), the fourth daughter of Jupiter, and the fifth daughter of Pallas. Our author follows Clement, who treated of the five Minervas in ch. 2, p. 8. See further Arnobius IV.17 and Epiphanius, *Ancoratus*, p. 513.]

One is Vulcan’s daughter, who founded Athens; a rustic crowd followed her from country places into the order of civic life. There was another in Egypt,

[Note: In Cicero and Arnobius likewise she is the second, the Saïtic goddess, designated by the Egyptians with a name that in Greek means “Merciful” (Ἐλεήμων). Thus in Cyprus too the heavenly Venus was called “Merciful”: “Ἐλεήμων: Aphrodite in Cyprus” (Hesychius). Compare Arnobius IV.16 on Neith; Jablonski, *Egyptian Pantheon* I, p. 53 ff.; and Zoëga, *Treatises*, p. 101.]

daughter of King Nile,

[Note: “Daughter of King Nile.” Elmenhorst on Arnobius III.21, p. 117.]

a teacher of the weaving art. A third was born of Saturn as father. But they record that she was mannish: for she never kept herself within the modesty proper to the female sex, but always pursued arms, the din of battles, and the bloody pursuits of war. The fourth was daughter of Jupiter, king of Crete, and brought to her father the slain Liber. The fifth was born of Pallas as father and Tritonis as mother.

[Note: Clement of Alexandria gives the same account. But he, like Ampelius, ch. 9, calls her a daughter of the Titans. Compare Creuzer on Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book I, p. 326.]

Called after her father’s name, she was named Pallas by men. Driven by parricidal madness and the impulse of insane recklessness, she slaughtered her father Pallas by a cruel death.

[Note: L. Ampelius, ch. 9; Tzetzes on Lycophron, v. 255; Heraclides of Pontus, *Allegories of Homer*, p. 73. On the third Minerva: “The third Athena, by one plot acting impiously against father and mother” (τρίτη δ᾽ Ἀθηνᾶ, διὰ μιᾶς ἐπιβουλῆς εἰς πατέρα καὶ μητέρα δυσσεβοῦσα).]

Nor, content with her father’s mere death, she adorned herself with the spoils of his body, so that she might enjoy her evils longer and triumph more cruelly over her father’s death, making public the crime of parricide by this cruel display. To this woman the Palladium is consecrated—an outrage!—in name. This is the Pallas who is worshipped; this is she who is guarded under pontifical law,

[Note: That is, the Palladium was guarded by the Vestals, priestesses of Vesta. Gutherius, *On the Ancient Pontifical Law of the City of Rome*, p. 21. In an ancient inscription they are called:

PONTIFICES VESTAE V. V. C. C.

“Priestesses of Vesta, most chaste Vestal Virgins.” Ibid.]

and whose image is worshipped with supplication. Apply fire; increase the flames, so that she may be said to burn in your daily sacrifices. For what else does a parricide deserve than to be consumed daily in avenging flames, with the flames endlessly renewed, before God’s judgment? These should be called funeral pyres, most sacred emperors, not temples.

[Note: They despise temples as funeral pyres. Minucius Felix, ch. 8. Tertullian, *On the Spectacles*, ch. 13: “We despise temples no less than monuments.” That is, since corpses of the dead were laid and buried in very many pagan temples—as Clement of Alexandria, Arnobius, Eusebius, and others demonstrate at length—Christians often designated and regarded them accordingly.]

They should rather be called the pyres of the wretched. For pitiable human servitude makes buildings in honour of ruined human beings as though they were tombs. Here the ashes of burned bodies are kept; here the ashes of the dead are deposited by an irreligious law, so that the event of bitter deaths may be renewed by the daily blood of victims; so that the outcome of sorrowful lamentation may be reborn in annually renewed griefs; so that a fresher wailing may stir up tears that had fallen silent; and so that the wretched mind of man may learn, from the ritual of sacred things, both to worship and to commit parricides, incest, or killings.

These things, most sacred emperors, must be cut away utterly and destroyed, and corrected by the most severe enactments of your edicts, so that the fatal error of this presumption may no longer defile the Roman world, and the wickedness of a pestilent custom may not gain strength. Whatever strives to destroy the man of God

[Note: He appears to have borrowed this designation from 1 Timothy 6:11 and 2 Timothy 3:17. Hertz.]

must no longer rule on earth. They are unwilling, indeed, and resist; in headlong desire they long for their own destruction. Yet assist the wretched; set free those who are perishing. For this purpose God Most High has entrusted empire to you: that through you the wound of this affliction may be healed. We know the danger of their crime; the punishments of their error are known. But it is better that you save them against their will than that you grant destruction to those who desire it.

Those who are ill delight in harmful things; and when adverse illness has taken possession of a human body, perverse things are demanded by sufferers contrary to their health. A mind captured by the defect of sickness always desires the increase of its diseases, despises and scorns the remedies of healers,

[Note: Wowerius corrected this to *aspernat ac contemnit*, “he despises and scorns.” I do not know why.]

rejects the remedy of medicine, and hastens with headlong spirit toward its own destruction. Then, if the evil of the disease grows stronger, stronger remedies are sought, and medicine vigorously sets itself against the patient for his safety. Harsh foods and bitter drinks are administered to the unwilling; and if the evil has become entrenched, fire and steel too are applied. Thus a person, once health has been recovered and safety restored, acknowledges with a sound mind that everything he endured unwillingly through the infirmity of a sick body was done for his benefit.

## CHAPTER XVIII. He explains the etymologies, or origins, of the names attributed to the gods. He then explains the symbols and signs of the worship of the gods, adducing many biblical passages wherever an opportunity seemed to him to arise from the character of the age and from the manner of interpreting sacred Scripture. He is especially occupied with explaining five symbols.

[Col. 1020B]

Receive also, most sacred princes, the manner in which their names were formed. They wished this light, which by God’s command, after darkness has been driven away, restores day to human beings and regulates the course of its journey through the space of twelve hours,

[Note: He divides the day, during which the sun shines in heaven, into twelve hours, according to Roman practice.]

to be called “sun” (*sol*), not because it is alone, as some wish—for there are also the heavens, the moon, and many other stars which we see, some of which shine in one continuous and connected series, joined together, while others, scattered over the whole sky, measure their wandering courses by their own deviations.

[Note: These words readily recall the elevated passage in Cicero’s *Dream of Scipio*, in *On the Republic* VI.17–18.]

But it is called *Sol* because, when it has risen and the other stars have been obscured, it alone shines above the other stars.

[Note: Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II.27: “It was called *Sol* because it alone, among all the stars, is so great.” Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy* V, metrical poem 2:

> Him, because he alone beholds all things,  
> You may rightly call the true Sun.

Likewise Apollo, understood mystically according to the observation of the many, is the one god: Ἀπόλλων, μυστικῶς κατὰ τήρησιν τῶν πολλῶν νοούμενος, ὁ εἷς ἐστι θεός—Clement, *Stromata* I.24, p. 419, Potter edition. See Creuzer’s note on the cited passage; Varro, *On the Latin Language* IV.10; Isidore, *Etymologies* III.70.]

This same moon (*luna*) also received the name Lucina from its nocturnal light.

[Note: Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II.27: “The moon is named from shining; for she is the same as Lucina.” Compare Creuzer, note 96.]

Some also wished her to be called Diana, because, shining by night, she makes for human beings almost another day. They wished Neptune’s name to derive from swimming (*natando*), fashioning the substance of the name from what they believed he gladly did.

[Note: Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II.26: “Neptune is from swimming, with the first letters somewhat altered.” See Creuzer’s note 83. Arnobius III.31 gives another derivation: that water marries the earth. Varro, *On the Latin Language* IV, does likewise. Perhaps it seems derivable from νέφος, νεφόω, “cloud, to cloud over” (Orelli on Arnobius III.31), unless it is of foreign origin. Hermann derives another etymology from *Nepto unus*; and one might indeed think of Nephthys, since the Etruscans, Rome’s teachers in religious matters, had so many connections with the Egyptians and therefore could easily have received this deity’s name from them. Yet among Etruscan monuments that have survived there is no trace of Neptune. Nor is it established with certainty that the god Consus, worshipped by the earliest Romans and Sabines, was the same deity as Neptune. He seems rather to have been a god of counsels, from *conso*, that is, *consulo*, “I deliberate.” Daniel Wyttenbach’s ingenious conjecture derives the etymology from the ancient νέπος, “fish,” or νίπτειν, “to wash upon”: *Select Scholarly Notes on Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods*, Creuzer edition, p. 754. Böttiger’s view also deserves closer examination: that Neptune was in antiquity called Ποτιδᾶν, “Gift of Springs” (*Ideen zur Kunstmythologie*, p. 269).]

They call the whole power and nature of the earth Father Dis, because this is the nature of earth: that all things fall back into it, and things which arise from it proceed forth again. This showed the earth’s abundance and riches. They wish to call the substance of crops Proserpina, because crops, when they begin to be sown, benefit human beings. They call the earth itself Ceres.

[Note: Arnobius V.35 and 37 calls Ceres “earth.” Theodoret, *Cure of Greek Maladies*, discourse 3, *Works*, vol. IV, p. 771, Schulze edition.]

This name is taken from the bearing of crops.

[Note: Read “from bearing crops” (*a gerendis fructibus*), Creuzer’s correction, in accordance with Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II.26, p. 312: “For Ceres is mother from bearing crops, *Ceres* as though *Geres*”; see Creuzer’s note 86. Schelling attempted another etymology from the Hebrew language in his dissertation *On the Samothracian Deities*, p. 63, deriving the name Ceres from an Arabic root which among other meanings also has that of ploughing.]

Mars (*Mavors*) received his name from the events of wars, as though he “turns great things.”

[Note: From averting evil? Hermann and Creuzer, *Letters on Homer and Hesiod*, p. 202. Payne Knight, *Prolegomena to Homer*, p. 163, Ruhkopf edition, derives it from μάω, with Aeolic digamma μάϝω: “I rush violently; I desire intensely.”]

Minerva likewise has a martial name, as though she either diminishes or threatens.

[Note: The name appears to be Etruscan. On Etruscan bowls *Menrva* and *Menerva* are frequently read; the Romans seem to have received it from the Sabines or Etruscans. Compare Creuzer on Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II.26, note 88. Varro, *On the Latin Language* IV.10, and Festus say that Minerva came from the Sabines. Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II.26 and III.24, derives Minerva from one who either diminishes (*minueret*) or threatens (*minaretur*). Festus: “Minerva is called so because she advises well.” Firmicus took both etymologies from Cicero; see Creuzer’s note 88 on Cicero II.26. G. J. Vossius derives it from the old verb *meneo* for *moneo*, “to advise,” from μένος; Lauzius agrees, *Essay on the Etruscan Language*, pp. 199 ff., 203, 209. Arnobius III.31 derives it from memory, as though *Meminerva*. Compare Orelli’s note. Finally Daniel Wyttenbach seeks the origin in *minari*, “to threaten,” because the goddess’s other name, Pallas, is derived from πάλλειν, “to brandish a spear” (Creuzer’s Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 75).]

Human beauty (*venustas*) is called Venus.

[Note: Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II.27: “Our people named Venus, and from her comes *venustas*, rather than Venus from *venustas*.” In Daniel Wyttenbach’s scholia in Creuzer, p. 788, an etymology from ἑνός, “of one,” is attempted, because in the deity Venus the power of joining is discerned, from which, with Aeolic F prefixed, comes Venus. Yet, with the leave of such great men, I would observe that the deity is of Eastern origin and that Astarte could easily have been called by a plural of majesty, like Κόρη, which was a name of Proserpina. Hence 2 Kings XVII.30 and the name of the Numidian city Sicca Veneria.]

They fashioned Apollo’s name from human misfortunes, in Greek speech, as though he either loses or destroys everything entrusted to him. They also call the sun Apollo because, when it sets each day, it loses the brilliance of its light. Now the Greeks call “to destroy” ἀπόλλειν.

[Note: Firmicus was poorly versed in Greek: he writes ἀπόλλειν in place of ἀπολλύειν. Arnobius did not attempt the name, nor did the other Christian writers whom I have examined. The *Etymologicum Magnum* derives the etymology from ἀπολύων τῶν κακῶν, “releasing from evils,” which Plato also gives among others in the *Cratylus*, Heindorf, p. 74.]

You see how turbulent error devised your lying and fictitious gods, so that both forms and names were handed down to you through old women’s superstitions. But truth uncovered all these things, and sound reason discovered them, so that, once everything which sacrilegious error had hidden had been investigated and exposed, the path of truth might shine forth. For when all these things had been badly fashioned, they were at first a terror to mortals.

[Note: “Fear first made gods in the world …” Fragment of Petronius, Burmann edition, p. 676.]

Then, once their novelty had worn away, a certain contempt was born from wonder, as among people recovering from a long illness. Thus, little by little, the mind dared carefully to investigate what had astonished it, and promptly sent its keen intelligence into the secrets of fabricated and vain superstitions. Then, through continual consideration, it gathered the explanation of hidden things and reached their causes, so that the human race first learned the pitiable inventions of profane religions, then despised them, and finally rejected them.

## CHAPTER XIX. 1. In the Eleusinian rites: “I have eaten from the drum,” etc.; here he says much about heavenly bread, perhaps eucharistic.

It now pleases me to explain by what signs or symbols the pitiable throng of human beings recognizes itself within these superstitions. For they have their own signs and their own responses, which the Devil’s teaching handed down to them in these assemblies of sacrilege. In a certain temple,

[Note: Of Eleusinian Ceres.]

so that a mortal person may be admitted into the inner parts,

[Note: The language is scarcely about a person near death; for there is nothing to prove or indicate that such persons were admitted before death into the inner parts of the temple and its sanctuary, or even into the underground chambers, where, unless I am mistaken, the principal and most secret part of the mysteries was celebrated. Rather, the person “about to die” is mortal.]

he says: “I have eaten from the drum; I have drunk from the cymbal; and I have thoroughly learned the secrets of the religion.” In Greek this is said:

> ἐκ τυμπάνου βέβρωκα, ἐκ κυμβάλου πέπωκα, γέγονα μυστικός.  
> “I have eaten from the drum; I have drunk from the cymbal; I have become an initiate.”

[Note: On these Eleusinian mystic words, which were the token of initiates—the “password of the Eleusinian Mysteries,” as Clement of Alexandria calls it—see Clement, *Protrepticus* ch. 2, p. 14. Compare Meursius, *Eleusinia*, and the passages cited there, p. 30; and L. B. Sylvestre de Sacy’s note on Santa-Cruz, *Mysteries of Paganism* I, p. 304. Firmicus slightly alters these symbolic words: he has γέγονα μυστικός, which he translates badly into Latin as “and I have thoroughly learned the secrets of the religion.” Clement has neither of these phrases, but: ἐκερνοφόρησα, ὑπὸ τὸν παστὸν ὑπέδυον: “I carried the kernos; I secretly entered beneath the bridal chamber.” See Potter’s notes on this passage.]

Wretched man, you wrongly confess the crime you have committed. You have swallowed the deadly venom of poison, and under the impulse of impious frenzy you taste a lethal draught. Death always follows that food, and eternal punishment. What you proclaim that you drank constricts the life-giving vein unto death, and the seat of the soul, polluted by the continuance of evils, throws you into disorder. There is another food that grants salvation and life; another food that commends and restores a human being to God Most High; another food that relieves the fainting, recalls the wandering, raises the fallen, and grants to the dying the tokens of eternal immortality. Seek Christ’s bread and Christ’s cup.

[Note: The context seems to teach that, when Firmicus adduces the Eleusinian symbolic formula, “I have eaten from the drum; I have drunk from the cymbal,” every thought of the Eucharist was not absent from his mind. For the words which he subsequently quotes from Psalm XXXIII—in the Hebrew Bible Psalm XXXIV—were interpreted mystically by certain ancient teachers concerning the Lord’s Supper, as Theodoret testifies in his paraphrase of this psalm, v. 9: “It should be known, however, that the stated sense is fitting for the Jews of old; but the meaning hidden in the depth of the letter hints at the grace of the divine mysteries. For through most holy baptism true illumination—he refers to the preceding sixth verse—comes to those who approach, and the tasting of life-giving food clearly displays the goodness of the Savior. For what shows his love for humankind as clearly as the cross, the passion, the death undergone for us, and his becoming at once food and fountain for his own sheep?” Theodoret, *Works*, Schulze edition (Halle, 1769), vol. I, p. 815. I do not doubt that this interpretation of these words was already current in Firmicus’ age. Moreover, his very words seem to imply the sacred Supper: “And again he himself, that he might impart the substance of his majesty to believers, said: Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood …” Hertz. Justin Martyr, *First Apology* ch. 86 and *Dialogue with Trypho*, p. 237, Tebb edition, asserts that demons imitated the Eucharist in Mithraic rites. The same is found in the appendix to Tertullian’s *On Prescription against Heretics*, ch. 40. See also Grabe, *Spicilegium Patrum* II, p. 240.]

So that, once earthly frailty has been despised, the human substance may be nourished with immortal food. But what is this bread or this cup, concerning which great Wisdom proclaims loudly in the books of Solomon, saying: “Come, eat of my breads and drink the wine which I have mixed” (Proverbs IX.5).

[Note: Much as Augustine, *City of God* XVII.20.]

And Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, offered the returning Abraham the grace of blessing with bread and wine.

[Note: From Hebrews VII.1 it is clear that Melchizedek was a type of Christ to ancient Christians; thus the offering of bread and wine was a type of the Eucharist.]

Isaac also, when he had blessed Jacob and Esau humbly sought the same thing from his father, replied to him: “He has made him your lord, and I have made all his brothers servants; I have strengthened him with wheat and wine” (Genesis XXVII.37).

[Note: The words of this verse in the Sabbatier edition are taken from Firmicus.]

Then Esau bewailed his misfortunes in miserable lamentation because he had lost the grace of wheat and wine—that is, of future blessedness. But that this divine bread is bestowed by God upon consecrated persons, the Holy Spirit declares through Isaiah: “Thus says the Lord: Behold, those who serve me shall eat, but you shall hunger. Behold, those who serve me shall rejoice, but you shall be put to shame; the Lord shall slay you” (Isaiah LXV.13–14; V.13).

[Note: As in Cyprian, *Testimonies against the Jews* I, and Fulgentius, *To Monimus* I.25, v. 14. Cyprian omits the final words, “the Lord shall slay you.”]

Not only is this bread denied by God Most High to the sacrilegious and impious, but punishment is also promised and the destructions of bitter death decreed, so that the outcome of divine judgment may be administered to hungry throats. The venerable responses of Psalm XXXIII also follow this same point; for the Holy Spirit says through David: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet.” Sweet is heavenly nourishment, sweet the food of God; it does not contain the sorrowful torment of miserable hunger, and it expels from the marrow of men the poisonous force of the former venom.

[Note: Cyprian, *Testimonies* I; Augustine on Psalm XCIX: “Taste and see how sweet the Lord is.”]

The following words of the oracle declare this to be so. For he says: “Fear the Lord, his saints, because there is no want for those who fear him. The rich have lacked and hungered; but those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing” (Psalm XXXIII.10–11).

[Note: Much as Cyprian, *Testimonies* I and III.11: “they shall not lack any good thing,” as in the author of the *Imperfect Work on Matthew* and the Mozarabic Breviary.]

You who walk so clad in the praetexta in the temple, who shine in purple, whose head is crowned either with gold or with laurel: shameful want follows your error, and the burdensome weight of poverty hangs over your neck. The poor man whom you despise is lavish and rich;

[Note: Perhaps read *lautus*, “splendidly provided for.” Wowerius.]

Abraham prepares a place for him in his bosom (Luke XVI.22 ff.). Then, across the intervening spaces of flame, to soothe the wounds of your conscience, you will ask him for a small drop of dripping water; nor will Lazarus, even if willing, be able either to give or obtain relief for your pain. For the merits of each are weighed in equal justice: to him life will be granted because of this world’s evils; to you, because of this world’s goods, the everlasting punishment of torments is decreed.

But so that it might be said more plainly what that bread is through which the destructions of miserable death are overcome, the Lord himself marked it with holy and venerable speech, lest people’s hopes should be deceived by corrupt interpretations through divergent expositions.

[Note: He refers to perverse interpretations of the prophets. Compare Justin, *First Apology* chs. 54, 56, 59; *Dialogue with Trypho* ch. 69. See Heinrich Georg Clausen, *The Ante-Theodosian Apologists of the Christian Church as Judges of Plato and His Philosophy* (Copenhagen, 1817), p. 81. Minucius Felix, ch. 27: “Demons both are deceived and deceive,” so that, being ignorant of sincere truth, they do not acknowledge even the truth they know, to their own destruction.]

For he says in John’s Gospel: “I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst” (John VI.35).

[Note: Cyprian, *Testimonies* I has, however, “he who comes.”]

Likewise, in what follows he signifies the same in similar fashion: “If anyone thirsts, let him come and drink—he who believes in me.”

[Note: This does not occur in the following verses; the words are almost the same as verse 35, which he had just quoted.]

And again he himself, that he might impart the substance of his majesty to believers, said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (ibid., 54).

[Note: Cyprian, *On the Lord’s Prayer* and *Testimonies* I and III.]

Therefore, wretched mortals, have nothing to do with drums—the food of hatred. Seek the grace of saving food and drink the immortal cup. Christ calls you back to the light by his feast, and brings to life limbs decayed by grievous poison and torpid members. Renew the ruined human being with heavenly food, so that whatever in you is dead may be reborn through divine gifts. You have learned what you ought to do; choose what you will: from there death is born, from here immortal life is bestowed.

## CHAPTER XX. 2. Perhaps in the Mithraic rites: “Hail, bridegroom; hail, new light”; on this occasion he says much about Christ as bridegroom and light of the world.

You also say: “Hail, bridegroom; hail, new light.” Why, disastrous persuasion, do you hurl a wretched man over precipices? Why do you promise him the tokens of a false hope? With you there is no light, nor is there any bridegroom worthy to hear this. There is one divine power, one bridegroom of humankind, whose favor Christ has received [Note: Another hymn or creed customarily sung in rites reminds pagan readers of this; whether it was drawn from certain mysteries, I do not know. Perhaps from Mithraic rites, since the sun is there saluted. Yet the mention of a bridegroom and new light leads Firmicus to explain and apply it to Christ, whom Christians venerated as the bridegroom of his Church and the light of the world (John 8:12).].

You cannot transfer to yourself the glory of another’s blessedness, nor can you be adorned with the splendor of heavenly divinity. You have been cast into darkness and filth; there foulness, squalor, gloom, darkness, and the horror of perpetual night hold sway. If you wish even a faint brilliance of light to shine upon you, lift up your face and raise your sunken eyes; abandon these things and turn to him who said: “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). By his divine commandments we are bound to make our work shine each day in this earthly life. But it cannot shine unless the adornments of an unstained conscience protect us, unless a whole and incorrupt life commends us. Then the grace of the true light will arise for us; then the author of light will reveal himself to us; then we can both receive and see the true light.

But, to restrain the wickedness of this sacrilegious utterance, I shall establish by the oracles of sacred readings who is truly the bridegroom: namely, that Christ is the bridegroom and the Church the bride, from whom spiritual children are begotten day after day for that venerable Father. In this proof let the venerable mysteries of the prophets be disclosed. Let the authority of the holy oracles assist us. Joel, prompted by the divine Spirit, speaks thus:

> “Blow the trumpet in Zion; sanctify a fast and proclaim a healing; gather the people, sanctify the Church, receive the elders, assemble the nursing little ones; let the bridegroom come forth from his chamber, and the bride from her bridal room” [Note: As in Cyprian, *Testimonies*, book II.] (Joel 2:15–16).

Jeremiah indicates the same thing in similar terms, when he threatens Jerusalem with a grim oracle:

> “And I shall take away from the cities of Judah and the towns of Jerusalem the voice of those rejoicing, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride” [Note: Cyprian, *Testimonies* II, has “from the crossroads of Jerusalem”; our author omits it, as well as “and the voice of those making merry.”] (Jeremiah 16:16).

The Holy Spirit also proclaims the bridegroom’s coming forth through the Psalms. In Psalm 18 this oracle is found:

> “And he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber, exulted as a giant to run his course. His departure is from the height of heaven, and his circuit reaches to its height; and there is none who hides from his heat” [Note: Cyprian, *Testimonies* II, differs only in one word: *profectio* (“departure”), where Cyprian has *egressio* (“going forth”).] (Psalm 18:6–7).

Let more hidden mysteries be revealed. In the Apocalypse [Note: The gloss “that is, in the Revelation,” found in the first edition, was deleted by Wowerius.] we shall find who the Bridegroom is; for it is written:

> “Come, I shall show you the new bride, the wife of the Lamb. And he led me in the Spirit onto a great mountain, and showed me the holy city Jerusalem descending from heaven” [Note: As in Cyprian, *Testimonies*, book II.] (Revelation 21:9–10).

We must investigate what Gospel teaching also hands down to us on this matter. For in the Gospel of John we find it recorded thus:

> “You are my witnesses that I said to those who were sent to me from Jerusalem that I am not the Christ, but that I was sent before him. For he who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice” [Note: As in Cyprian, *Testimonies* II.] (John 3:28–29).

The mystery of this matter has been shown. The chorus of wise virgins awaits this bridegroom; holy virginity, with sleepless care, bears lamps before him; and to servants awaiting the bridegroom the reward of blessed prizes is promised (Matthew 25:1 ff.). For we find in Luke’s Gospel:

> “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning; and be yourselves like men awaiting their lord when he comes from a wedding, so that when he comes and knocks they may open to him. Blessed are those servants whom the Lord, when he comes, finds watching” [Note: Cyprian, *To Fortunatus*, *Testimonies* II.] (Luke 12:35–36).

Behold: by the oracles of venerable responses the bridegroom has been shown. Why do you, placed amid bitter misfortunes, give yourself a blessed name? If, once freed, you wish to follow the bridegroom’s light, cast away errors; and, vigilant in sleepless care, chastise the former deeds of your life by devout religious commitment. Then, when the bridegroom finds you watchful in his name and recognizes the merits of your faith, he will give the greatest reward, give the whole gift. You will enter with him into heaven’s bridal chamber; you will see the kingdoms of the world; and, that you may become their participant, the grace of immortality will be bestowed upon you by the most merciful and most just Lord.

## CHAPTER XXI

**3. In another, certainly Mithraic, formula: “God from the Rock” (*Theos ek Petras*), where he gathers much from the sacred Scriptures concerning Christ the stone.**

[Col. 1026D]

The formula of another profane sacrament is: “God from the Rock” [Note: Of Mithras, in whose mysteries this sacramental formula was used. Jerome, *Against Jovinian* I, writes that, according to pagan myths, Mithras was generated in a rock through the heat of lust. Justin, *Dialogue with Trypho* 70: “Those who transmit the mysteries of Mithras say that he was begotten from a rock.” Wowerius. Commodian, *Instructions* XIII:

> “Invincible, born from a rock, if he is held to be a god.”

Augustine, *On Amos* 3.9; “rock-born Mithras” (*petrogenēs Mithras*) in John Lydus, *On the Months*, p. 47. “They say that the Romans above all worship Vesta, just as the Persians worship rock-born Mithras, because of the point of fire and the moist substance, while those beneath the Bear do so because of the point of water.” These passages were collected by Philippus a Turre in *Monuments of Ancient Antium*. See further Creuzer I, 177; Zoega, *Abhandlungen*, p. 132. The same name perhaps also refers to the caves (*spelaea*) in which Mithraic mysteries were celebrated. “The formula of another profane sacrament,” says Firmicus. For the first was that exclamation in chapter 20: “Hail, bridegroom; hail, new light.” As he endeavored to claim that phrase for Christ by sentences from sacred Scripture, so he also adapted to this formula the words of the sacred text, using Old Testament passages. These are the following: Deuteronomy 27:3, “and you shall write upon the stone all the words of this law”; and Joshua 24:26–27, concerning the great stone which Joshua took and set up beneath the terebinth—whereupon his words refer: “the stone which God promised that he would send in establishing the foundations of the promised Jerusalem.”].

Why do you transfer this holy and venerable mystery to profane acts by a counterfeit profession? There is another stone, which God promised to send when establishing the foundations of the promised Jerusalem. Christ is shown to us by the meaning of the venerable stone [Note: It is customary among the Fathers of the ancient Church to compare Christ with a stone. Thus Justin Martyr, *Dialogue with Trypho*, frequently, taking occasion from Matthew 21:42; Mark 12:10; Luke 20:17; Acts 4:11; and Psalm 118:22. Tertullian, *Against the Jews* 9. In Damasus’s poem on the names of the Lord he is greeted as “Rock”; in a similar poem of Ennodius of Pavia, “Stone” and “Mountain”; and in Orientius of Illiberis he is called “Mountain” and “corner-stone.” All this, if it is worth the trouble, may be seen in our *Symbols and Artistic Representations of the Ancient Christians*, fascicle I, p. 17 ff.].

Why do you, by stealthy fraud, transfer the dignity of a venerable name to polluted superstitions? Ruin follows your stone, and the deadly collapse of falling roofs. Our stone, established by God’s hand, builds, strengthens, raises, fortifies, and adorns the grace of the restored body with the splendor of everlasting immortality. For Isaiah, prompted by the Holy Spirit, says of it:

> “Thus says the Lord: Behold, I lay in the foundations of Zion a precious, chosen, most excellent corner-stone, honored; and he who believes in him shall not be put to shame” [Note: These words agree entirely with Cyprian, *Testimonies*, book II.] (Isaiah 28:16).

The Psalms likewise contain a similar response. In Psalm 117 the Holy Spirit says:

> “The stone which the builders rejected, this has become the head of the corner. Was not this made, and is it marvelous in our eyes?” [Note: Verse 22 is exactly as in Cyprian’s *Testimonies* II and the author of *On Jewish Unbelief*, addressed to Vigilius. Verse 23 differs little from Cyprian.] (Psalm 117:22–23).

Through many prophets the Holy Spirit shows the sequence of this name. For Zechariah the prophet says:

> “Behold, I bring my servant; his name is Rising, because the stone which I set before Jesus—upon that one stone are seven eyes” [Note: It differs little from Cyprian.] (Zechariah 3:8–9).

But, that it may be more clearly established, let us reveal the more ancient secrets of the venerable readings. In Deuteronomy it is set down thus:

> “And you shall write this entire law upon the stone” [Note: Cyprian in the cited passage adds the words “very clearly.”] (Deuteronomy 27:8).

Joshua son of Nun likewise specifically records this by divine command:

> “And he took a great stone and set it before the Lord. And Joshua said to the people: ‘Behold, this stone shall be for me a witness, because it heard all the words spoken by the Lord when he spoke to you. And it shall be for us a witness in the last days, when you depart from your Lord’” [Note: Cyprian, *Testimonies* II, reports almost the same words.] (Joshua 24:26–27).

Daniel further explained clearly in venerable oracles that through this stone—that is, through our Lord Jesus Christ—these gods and the multitude of temples will fall. For, when interpreting the king’s dream, he said:

> “And behold, an image, an exceedingly great image, and the sight of that image was dreadful; it stood lofty before you. Its head was of fine gold; its breast and arms were silver; its belly and thighs bronze; but its feet were partly iron and partly clay, until a stone was cut from a mountain without hands cutting it, and struck the image upon its feet of iron and clay and crushed them into small pieces. Then iron and clay and bronze and silver and gold became together as fine fragments, like chaff and dust in a dry summer; the wind blew them away, so that nothing remained of them. And the stone which struck the image became a great mountain and filled the whole earth” [Note: With a few exceptions, as in Cyprian.] (Daniel 2:31–35).

What place on earth has not Christ’s name possessed? Where the sun rises, where it sets, where the north is raised, where the south slopes—everywhere the majesty of the venerable name has filled all things [Note: There are many testimonies in ancient ecclesiastical writers concerning Christianity’s spread throughout almost the whole world in its earliest centuries; stripping away all rhetoric, they show that it had passed beyond the boundaries of the Roman Empire. But, since these matters do not belong to this passage, we pass them over. See Elmenhorst on Arnobius I.55, p. 53; Mosheim, *On the Affairs of Christians before Constantine the Great*, pp. 203, 448 ff.].

And although in certain regions the limbs of idolatry still twitch [Note: He speaks especially of the Roman Empire. Nor does the history of the following age at all bear out that idolatry had been so weakened in Firmicus’s time. For although Constantine the Great had already destroyed many temples and idols, the worship of the gods was not overthrown until under Theodosius and his sons. Yet remnants remained even into the sixth century under Justinian, and longer.], nevertheless the situation is such that in every Christian land this pestilential evil may be cut out by the roots. What does the oracle of the prophets answer concerning the stone of idolaters [Note: He returns to the Mithraic religion, which, joined with the worship of the Sun, had in the West absorbed almost all the remaining paganism.], of which they say, “God from the Rock”? Who has withstood this stone, or whom does it spare?

This holy stone—that is, Christ—either supports the foundations of faith; or, placed at the corner [Psalm 118:22; Matthew 21:42; Mark 12:10; Luke 10:17; Acts 4:11; 1 Peter 2:7], joins by an equal moderation the members of two walls, that is, gathers together into one the peoples of the Old and New Testaments; or certainly unites the diversity of body and soul in a human being by inviolable immortality; or proclaims the law; or bears witness against sinners; or—rather—strikes the image of the devil [Note: Idols and the whole apparatus of idolatry.], so that, when he has been overcome, cast down, and turned into ashes and embers, it may raise the summit of its loftiness and possess a pure dominion of rule.

And now it is for you, Constantius and Constans, most sacred emperors, and for the strength of your venerable faith, to be invoked: that faith which is raised above humankind, separated from earthly frailty, joined to the fellowship of heavenly things, and which in all its acts follows, so far as it can, the will of the most high God. Only a little remains [Note: This should be read thus, not *talium* as in the first edition. He urges the princes utterly to destroy the worship of idols; likewise in chapter 30.], for the devil to lie utterly cast down by your laws and for the deadly contagion of extinguished idolatry to perish. The poison of this venom has ebbed away, and day by day the substance of profane desire expires.

Raise the banner of faith. Divinity has reserved this task for you; by its favor you stand eminent as destroyers of all your enemies, through whose deeds the Roman Empire was weakened [Note: Wowerius thus corrected the reading *firmabatur* (“was strengthened”) of the first edition.]. Raise the standard of the venerable law; enact and proclaim what is advantageous. Let it be fortunate and auspicious for the commonwealth that you have overthrown the army amid such heaps of slain enemies. God has also made you participants in his glory and will; propitious Christ has reserved for your hands the destruction of idolatry and the ruin of profane shrines for your people. He conquered evil spirits with spiritual weapons; you have conquered earthly evils. Raise the trophies of victory [Note: That is, the signs of the cross. See chapter 29; *Epistle of Barnabas* 9; Justin Martyr, *First Apology*, p. 82; *Dialogue with Trypho*, pp. 325, 336.], and let the mighty inscription of triumphs be displayed. Rejoicing in the destruction of profane things, exult more strongly; exult confidently. Your prosperity is joined with God’s power: with Christ fighting for humanity’s salvation, you have conquered.

## CHAPTER XXII

**4. In the Bacchic formula: *Elilikeros demorphoi*—more correctly, “O twisting-horned, two-formed one” (*Helixikerōs dimorphe*); this he understands of the devil as dragon, whose horns he relates to Christ’s cross.**

[Col. 1030A]

Let all the symbols of profane religion be presented in order, so that we may prove that the most wicked enemy of the human race transferred them from the holy and venerable oracles of the prophets to the polluted crimes of his madness. For we find this also said: “twisting-horned, two-formed” [Note: Correct to *Helixokerōs, dimorphe*, or rather *hēlie dikerōs dimorphe*: “O Sun, two-horned, two-formed.” A formula of the orgies of Bacchus or of the Sun. For both bear the same name, as Macrobius shows at length, *Saturnalia* I.18. Bacchus, moreover, was anciently worshipped as bull-formed, bull-horned, and two-formed. Scholiast on Nicander, *Alexipharmaca*, verse 31. Orpheus, Hymn 29:

> “I call upon Dionysus, loud-thundering celebrant of the Bacchic cry,  
> Wild, ineffable, hidden, two-horned, two-formed,  
> Ivy-flourishing, bull-faced . . .”

Plutarch also reports in *On Isis and Osiris* 35 and *Greek Questions* 36 that Bacchus was called by the Greeks “ox-born”; and Nonnus describes Bacchus in the same way, *Dionysiaca* XXI.217:

> “. . . since in their double form  
> are hybrid bulls and men; for they possess both  
> the appearance of an ox and a man’s face.”

For all these points see Creuzer’s *Dionysus* I, p. 267, and Böttiger’s *Ideas toward an Art-Mythology* I, p. 323, note 14.].

This god of yours is not two-formed but many-formed. For the form of the deceiver changes into many kinds. He is the basilisk and scorpion [Note: That scorpions were regarded as harmful creatures in Persian religion is clear from Mithraic reliefs, where a scorpion clings to the genitals of the sacred bull. They also occur in monuments of Babylonian religion. In the New Testament, Luke 10:19, “serpents and scorpions” are presented as adversaries of the Christian religion. See Kuinoel on this passage. In Revelation 9:3, 5, 10, destructive locusts are compared to scorpions and described as closely resembling them. Creuzer, I, 722.], trodden beneath the secure footsteps of believers [Note: He doubtless refers to the protoevangelium of Genesis 3:15.] (Luke 10:19); he is the malignant serpent whose head deceived mortality seeks; he is the twisting dragon [Note: Leviathan (Job 40:20). For the pre-Jerome text reads: “Will you draw out the dragon with a hook? Will you put a bridle around his nostrils?” Jerome’s text has “Leviathan.”], drawn by a hook and shut up captive. This god of yours is adorned with the locks of the Lernaean serpent [Note: I confess that I do not know where Bacchus or Mithras was adorned with serpent locks. Apollodorus, II.5, tells the story of the Lernaean Hydra.], seeing that, when its lord has been struck, a multitude of dying serpents succeeds.

Why do you multiply like new-born hydras? Why do you array yourself in a fertile offspring of crimes? We have learned the path to your death; we know by what remedies the poisons of your art are overcome. We drink Christ’s immortal blood; Christ’s blood has been joined to our blood. This is the saving remedy against your crimes, which excludes deadly poison from God’s people. Who has seen this god whom they bewail with horns? What are these horns that he boasts of possessing? There are other horns, which the prophet, prompted by the Holy Spirit, mentions [Note: As appears from what follows, he refers to Habakkuk 3:4.], and which you, devil, think you can transfer to your polluted face. From where do you seek ornaments and glory?

The horns signify nothing other than the venerable sign of the cross [Note: Augustine, *City of God* XVIII.32: “Horns are in his hands” (Habakkuk 3:4): what else is this but the trophy of the cross? The horn, especially of the unicorn, was understood as the cross. In the *Dialogue with Trypho*, ed. Jebb, p. 275, Justin Martyr declares that it can be compared to nothing except the sign of the cross; and on p. 310 he maintains that the unicorn’s horn alone among all horns is the sign of the cross. Tertullian, *Against Marcion* III says that Christ is indicated by that horn, since the beam of the cross is a unicorn. Others interpreted this horn as the seat “upon which those who are crucified sit,” as Justin Martyr says (*Dialogue with Trypho*, p. 276). Irenaeus, *Against Heresies* II.42—chapter 24 in Massuet’s edition—speaks of the five horns of the cross, and one in the middle, on which the person fastened to the cross rests. Tertullian, *Against the Jews* 10. The unicorn’s stake is the central upright. See Henricus Kipping, *On the Cross and Those Crucified* (Bremen, 1671), Exercise 19, p. 131.].

By one extended and upright horn of this sign the world is sustained and the earth held together. And by the framework of the two [Note: I understand: “and by the two that extend along the side,” namely the crossbeams of the cross, from which Christ hung. By their framework the east is touched and the west supported—they looked toward east and west—so that the whole world, strengthened by the threefold stability of the upright beam and two crossbeams of the fixed work, the cross planted in the earth, may hold the foundations of the root of immortality. The cross is called the root of immortality. But *teneant* (“may hold”) is preferable to *teneantur* (“may be held”), as the sense seems to demand.], which extend at the sides, the east is touched and the west supported, so that the whole world, strengthened by the threefold stability of the fixed structure, may hold fast the foundations of the root of immortality. This venerable mystery has been handed down to us by the prophet’s oracle. For in Habakkuk we find it written thus:

> “His power covered the heavens, and the earth is full of his praise. His splendor shall be like light; horns shall be in his hands. And there the power of his glory was established, and he shall establish his love. The Word shall go forth, and shall proceed according to his steps” [Note: For the most part it agrees with Cyprian, *Testimonies* II.] (Habakkuk 3:3–5).

Behold the venerable horns of the Cross; behold the immortal summit of holy power; behold the divine framework of the glorious work. You, Christ, sustain the world and earth with outstretched hands; you uphold the heavenly dominion. Our salvation clings to your immortal shoulders. You, Lord, bear the sign of eternal life; by the prophets you proclaim this to us through venerable inspiration. For Isaiah says:

> “Behold, a son has been born to us; sovereignty is upon his shoulders, and his name has been called Messenger of Great Counsel” [Note: The passage is cited from memory and more briefly; in its final words, “Messenger of Great Counsel,” it agrees with Cyprian, book I. These two alone have the word *cogitatio* (“counsel” or “thought”).] (Isaiah 9:6).

These are the horns of the Cross, by which all things are both raised up and held together. Upon these horns human life securely rests. That Amalek might be defeated, Moses imitated these horns with outstretched hands (Exodus 17:12); in order more readily to obtain what he earnestly sought, he made himself a cross from the rod. Hasten swiftly to these horns [Note: I do not know from where Firmicus drew this. The Talmudists tell many fables concerning Moses’ miraculous rod. It is said that God created it on the eve of the Sabbath and entrusted it to Adam, from whom it passed to Enoch, Noah, and Joseph. After Joseph’s death it was brought into Pharaoh’s palace; Jethro secretly took it away and planted it in his garden. Finally it yielded to Moses when he could read the name of God inscribed upon it. This is related in the book *Midrash Vayoscha*. Since Firmicus speaks only of the rod, one cannot suppose that he means the wood on which the bronze serpent was suspended in the desert (Numbers 21:8–9), to which, from ancient times onward as a type of Christ (John 3:14), the form of a cross was attached. See *The Origin, Nature, and Transmission of a Sacred Science, Writing, and Language among the Patriarchs of the Human Race; or, Explanation of Obscure Fables and Traditions concerning Adam, Seth, etc.* (Breslau, 1786), p. 136.]; flee to these horns in humble veneration. May justice, equity, chastity, mercy, patience, and faith fasten you to these horns, so that, bearing the venerable emblems and rejoicing in the majesty of the consecrated font, you may share in both Christ’s burial and his life.

## CHAPTER XXIII

**5. In Isiac rites, concerning Osiris restored to life: “Take courage, initiates,” where, on the occasion of the ointment with which the initiates’ throats were anointed, he speaks of the devil’s poisonous ointment.**

[Col. 1032A]

Let us set forth another formula [Note: We find this dramatic representation, in which a dead person was mourned and lamented in darkness with songs of rhythmically arranged grief until, after lights were kindled, mourning turned to joy, in varying forms in almost all Mysteries. For they mourned and joyfully greeted Osiris and Adonis, dead and restored to life; Cabirus, dead—whether restored to life I do not know; and Proserpina, lost and found again. There is no doubt that similar rites were celebrated in Mithraic mysteries. “The death of your god is known,” Firmicus says below. Therefore I think that this well-known exclamation in Firmicus’s age—to which, as far as I know, he alone refers—should be connected with it: “Take courage, initiates, [because] the god has been saved,” by which, from the salvation of their god rescued from great dangers, they also wish one another an end to their toils and troubles.], so that by the effort of reflection their crimes may be exposed. Its whole order must be described, so that everyone may recognize that the law of divine dispensation has been corrupted through the perverse imitation of the devil.

On a certain night an image is laid supine in a bier and mourned with lamentations arranged in measured rhythms. Then, when they have satisfied themselves with their feigned mourning, a light is brought in. At that point the priest anoints the throats of all who had wept; and, after they have been anointed, the priest whispers in a slow murmur:

> “Take courage, initiates, [for] the god has been saved;  
> for from our labors there shall be salvation for us.”

Why do you urge wretches to rejoice? Why do you compel deceived people to be glad? What hope, what salvation, do you promise them by deadly persuasion? Why do you disturb them with a false promise? The death of your god is known; his life does not appear. No divine oracle has ever spoken of his resurrection [Note: As it did concerning Christ’s resurrection.]; after death he did not show himself to people so that they might believe in him; he promised no proofs of this act, nor did he set forth preceding examples that he would do it [Note: Jairus’s daughter, the young man of Nain, Lazarus.].

You bury an idol, you mourn an idol, you bring an idol forth from burial; and, miserable man, after doing these things, you rejoice. You free your god; you arrange the prostrate limbs of stone; you repair an insensible rock. Let your god give you thanks, reward you with like gifts, and wish you to share in his own condition: may you die as he dies, may you live as he lives. As for the anointing of throats with ointment, who would not, scorning vanity, despise this crime? Therefore the devil has his own christs [Note: The initiates of Mithraic rites were also anointed on the forehead. “Mithras marks his initiates on the forehead,” says Tertullian, *Prescription against Heretics* 40. Zoega, *Abhandlungen*, p. 178. “His own christs” alludes to the Greek etymology from *chriein*, “to anoint.”], and because he himself is Antichrist, he draws wretched people into a criminal association to disgrace his own name.

Reserve this ointment for the dying [Note: Homer, *Iliad* II.680: Apollo anointed the dead body of Sarpedon with ambrosia. Pliny, *Natural History* XIII.1: “The use of perfumes began to be extended also to the dead.” Minucius Felix 12: “You reserve ointments for funerals.”], so that those whom you have caught in your snares, having made them forgetful with poisonous ointment, you may always plunge into gloomy and deadly ruin.

## CHAPTER XXIV

**He speaks of the ointment which the Father gave to the Son, and which the Son bestows upon believers.**

There is another ointment, which God the Father gave to his only Son and which the Son bestows upon believers through the divine majesty of his name. Christ’s ointment is made with an immortal composition and blended with the spiritual fragrances of spices. This ointment strips the decaying limbs of humankind from mortal snares, so that, when the first human being has been buried, another human being may immediately be born more happily from that same human being.

And, that this may be explained more clearly, the mysteries of sacred readings must be disclosed. David, to convey the grace of this ointment, says:

> “Fair in form beyond the sons of men, grace has been poured out upon your lips; therefore God has blessed you forever. Gird your sword upon your thigh, most mighty one; in your splendor and beauty aim onward, proceed prosperously and reign, because of truth and gentleness and justice; and your right hand shall lead you wondrously. Your arrows are sharp, O most mighty one; peoples shall fall beneath you in the heart of the king’s enemies. Your throne, O God, is for age upon age; a straight scepter is the scepter of your kingdom. You loved justice and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions. Myrrh and stacte and cassia flow from your garments, from ivory buildings, from which they made you glad” [Note: In these words of the sacred text he differs variously from Cyprian and others. See Sabatier on the readings of the ancient Church. Concerning Christ’s external appearance while he lived on earth, I recently discussed this in *Symbols and Artistic Representations of the Ancient Christians*, II, p. 1 ff.] (Psalm 44:3–10).

We have perceived the mysteries of the immortal ointment, and the order of divine dispensation has been shown to us. Everlasting kingship and heaven’s diadem were bestowed upon our Lord together with the majesty of the ointment. But another oracle shows us who he is who received the power to rule the world and is adorned with the majesty of the venerable name. The same David says:

> “Why have the nations raged, and the peoples devised vain things? The kings of the earth stood up, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ” [Note: At the beginning he differs from the others, agreeing with Augustine on Psalm 1 in having “Why?”] (Psalm 2:1–2).

Why do you so exalt yourself, sacrilegious persuasion? Why do you ensnare wretched people with unbridled rashness? Christ’s ointment grants heaven’s rule; your ointment kindles the flames of Gehenna.

## CHAPTER XXV

**Having made this excursus on the wretched error of these profane people, he gives a grave warning; he teaches that the kingdom given to Christ is signified by this anointing, adducing many passages of Scripture, and at the same time touches upon Christ’s descent into the underworld.**
But I should like to examine closely and with careful inquiry what this priest puts together with impure mouth and the defiled contamination of his words. With his god having been delivered, he urges his companions to take courage and place confidence in good hope. O into what wretched, what mournful snares has fleeting cunning entangled itself! Who delivers your god? For whom has he performed this service—that he should be in distress? Learn, learn what you do not know; learn what you do not see. Christ, the Son of God, endured all these things in order to free the human race from the snares of death; in order to remove the yoke of harsh captivity; to restore humankind to the Father; to reconcile humankind with God in a favourable reconciliation after the offence had been appeased; to show by his own example the fruit of the promised resurrection. The Son of God did what he had promised before: he shut the gates of the infernal abode, and, having trampled down death, overthrew the necessity imposed by the harsh law. For three days a company of the righteous was newly gathered by him,

[Note: I would prefer *recensita*, “reviewed/recounted”: it is better; if you punctuate thus, everything will hang together. He is plainly speaking of Christ’s descent into hell, 1 Peter 3:19: “a company of the righteous.” Tertullian, *On the Soul*, ch. 7: “But what is that which is conveyed to the regions below after its separation from the body—the soul? What is detained? What is reserved for the day of judgment? To what did Christ also descend when dying? I suppose, to the souls of the patriarchs, if the soul is not beneath the earth.” And ch. 55: “Nor did he ascend into the higher regions of heaven before he descended into the lower regions of the earth, in order there to make the patriarchs and prophets partakers of himself.” Justin Martyr, *Dialogue with Trypho*, p. 220, Jebb, cites a lost passage of Jeremiah: “But the Lord God remembered those of Israel who had fallen asleep in the land of the grave, and he descended to them to proclaim to them his salvation.” Irenaeus has the same passage, *Against Heresies* III.20.22; IV.33; V.31; Massuet. Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* VI.6, p. 762; *Gospel of Nicodemus*, ch. 24 ff.; and many others, whom you will find listed by Dittelmaier in his *History of the Doctrine of Christ’s Descent into Hell*, and by Pott, Excursus 3 on 1 Peter 3:19, “On the Descent of Jesus Christ into Hell.” Firmicus joins those who denied that Christ brought all persons out of hell after unbelievers had been restored to a better mind (Augustine, *On Heresies*, ch. 79; Philastrius, *Heresies* 121), and maintained that Christ liberated from there only believers who had departed this life in hope of the Messiah to come. So likewise among Latin writers Cassiodorus on Psalm 48, and Gregory the Great, *Letters* V.15. Lactantius and Arnobius make no mention of this doctrine. It acquired particular importance from the Apollinarian disputes concerning the human soul of Jesus Christ. The second part of the *Gospel of Nicodemus*, which narrates Christ’s descent into hell at greatest length, also seems to be assignable to those times. There is, so far as I know, only one surviving ecclesiastical monument from the Middle Ages on which Christ’s descent into hell is represented: namely, the lead bull of Albert, Patriarch of Jerusalem (1204–1214). On its reverse Christ leads a soul, released from its bonds, back from hell, while another accompanies and applauds; two crowned figures stand by, I suppose the king and queen of Jerusalem. The inscription is H ANACTACIC [“The Resurrection”]. On the obverse one reads: “Albert, Patriarch of Jerusalem.” I published this bull in my second dissertation on the coins of the Franks in the East, printed in the *Proceedings of the Royal Danish Society of Sciences* for 1821.]

so that the wickedness of death might not rule against them any longer, and so that the merit of the righteous might not collapse under long despair.

[Note: That they had awaited Christ’s coming in vain.]

He broke the everlasting bars, and at Christ’s command the iron doors fell down.

[Note: In the speech delivered by Thaddaeus at Edessa, in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* I.13: “…and how Christ was crucified, descended into Hades, and tore apart the barrier that had not been torn from eternity,” etc. *Gospel of Nicodemus*, ch. 21: “When all the saints heard these things from Isaiah, they said to the prince of hell: ‘Now open your gates and remove the iron bars, for you shall be bound and have no power.’” Eusebius, *Demonstration of the Gospel* IV.12: “Tearing apart the gates of the dark recesses that have stood from eternity.” Athanasius, *On the Passion and Cross of the Lord*: “Then, when the wretch had been cast out of Hades, sitting beside the gates he watches all those in chains being led out by the Saviour’s courage.” Proclus, homily on the Lord’s Passion: “Today he shattered brazen gates and broke iron bars—the one swallowed as a mere dead man, yet burning as God the Word.”]

Behold, the earth shook, and, its foundational stability being disturbed, recognized the divine power of Christ present. The revolving course of the world hastens the day toward its end before the appointed time; and, before the full course of the daylight hours had elapsed, the sun hastened in its course toward night (Luke 23:44). Behold, the upper extremities of the veil are torn, and the darkness of night hides the world beneath deeper shadows (Matthew 27:51). All the elements were disturbed while Christ fought—at the very time when he first armed a human body against the tyranny of death. This struggle was fought for three days, until death, its powers of malice overcome, should be broken.

Why, devout man, man of Christ, do you despair and fail in your habitual impatience? Can you not endure a delay of three days? Do you confess your anxiety and despair in new prayers? The Holy Spirit signifies in solemn utterance that you will do this on that day, when he says through David: “We have been reckoned as sheep for slaughter. Arise, why do you sleep, O Lord? Arise, and do not destroy us utterly. Why do you turn away your face? Do you forget our poverty and affliction? For our soul has been humbled into the dust; our belly clings to the earth. Arise, O Lord, help us, and deliver us for your name’s sake” (Psalm 43:22–26).

[Note: It differs little from the Sabatier text.]

Behold, after three days a day brighter than usual rises, and the sun receives again the grace of its former light. Christ, almighty God, is adored amid the sun’s more splendid rays. The saving divinity rejoices, and a company of the righteous and saints accompanies his triumphant chariot. Then, in exalted joy, exalted mortality cries: “Where, O death, is your sting?” (1 Corinthians 15:56). Then the saving divinity, going before, commands the heavenly gates to be opened for him: “Open, open, and tear away the immortal bars. Christ God, having trampled death, calls back to heaven the human being whom he had assumed.”
