[Note: Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*, ch. 16: “[The Son of God], being about to assume even the very substances of human beings, flesh and soul.” But *assumere*, “to assume,” is also used by Firmicus in ch. 26. So too Novatian, *On the Trinity*, ch. 19: “The true Son of God assumes that holy thing born from Mary”; and Hilary, *On the Trinity* X.15: “If he had assumed only a body from the Virgin, he would also have assumed a soul from her”; XI.13: “He assumed the form of a servant.” Tertullian also uses *induere*, “to put on,” *Against Praxeas*, ch. 27: “When the Word became flesh … was he clothed in flesh? Indeed, clothed”; and *On the Flesh of Christ*, ch. 11: “…he is clothed in flesh through the cooperation of the Holy Spirit.”]

This is foretold by the holy prophet in sacred utterance, and the commanding voice is heard from the prophet’s mouth. For the Holy Spirit says, in order to show us the power of Christ’s command: “Lift up your gates, O rulers, and be lifted up, everlasting gates, and the King of glory shall enter” (Psalm 24:7).

[Note: Others read, “of your ruler.” Tertullian, *Against the Gnostics*, Cassiodorus, and Cyprian, *Testimonies* II, have “your.”]

This command is given to angels who did not know; for they could not know when the Word of God descended to earth. Thus they themselves answer with anxious inquiry: “Who is this King of glory?” (ibid., v. 8).

[Note: Cyprian, *Testimonies* II, has “king of brightness.”]

To their inquiry Christ replied clearly in the majesty of his divinity: “The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle.”

[Note: As in the Sabatier text. The *Gospel of Nicodemus* also contains the same words of the Psalm in its account of Christ’s descent into hell, ch. 21.]

The Son of God is immediately recognized by the guardians of heaven, and they acknowledge whatever had previously escaped them. They see the spoils of the vanquished enemy, and, remembering the order of the first dispensation, they too cry out in a repeated voice together with those ascending: “Lift up the gates, you who preside over them” (ibid., v. 9),

[Note: Firmicus alone has “you who preside over them.”]

“and be lifted up, everlasting gates, and the King of glory shall enter.” When the Son returned, the Father restored to him the promised sceptres of the kingdom and granted him the throne of the kingdom with equal authority: that he might command, reign, hold power, and rule in the perpetual majesty of his divinity.

[Note: One of the alternatives appears superfluous; perhaps better: “that he might command, that he might hold the kingdom.” VOW.]

Hear what the Holy Spirit commanded Daniel to say concerning him: “I was looking in a vision by night, and behold, one like a Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven came even to the Ancient of Days and stood in his presence; and those who stood by presented him. And royal power was given to him, and all the kings of the earth and the kingdom and all glory served him. And his power is eternal and shall not be taken away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed” (Daniel 7:13–14).

[Note: Justin Martyr, in the *Dialogue*, p. 87, departing alike from the Hebrew and the Greek text of the Septuagint, drew Tertullian, *Against the Jews* ch. 14, Cyprian, and Firmicus after him. Verse 13 is as in Cyprian, *Testimonies* II, although he has “and those who stood by him.” Verse 14 differs little, for it has “by race,” and “all glory shall serve him.”]

The same things are shown to us by holy revelation. For we find this written in the Apocalypse: “And I turned to see the voice which spoke with me, and I saw seven golden lampstands; and in the midst of the lampstands one like a Son of Man, clothed in a robe reaching to the feet, and girded above the breasts with a golden belt. His head and hair were white, like white wool, like snow; his eyes were like a flame of fire; his feet like bronze refined as in a fiery furnace; and his voice like the sound of many waters. In his right hand he held seven stars; from his mouth came a sharp two-edged sword; and his face shone like the sun in its strength. And when I saw him, I fell at his feet as dead. And he laid his right hand upon me, saying: ‘Do not fear. I am the first and the last, and the living one; I was dead, and behold, I am alive for ages of ages, and I hold the keys of death and of hell’” (Revelation 1:12–18).

[Note: “Clothed in a robe reaching to the feet” (*endymenon podērē*, ἐνδεδυμένον ποδήρη). *Poderis*, according to Isidore XIX.21, is a tunic fitted to the body and descending to the feet; it occurs in Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, ch. 11, from the pre-Jerome translation of Ezekiel 9:2.]

[Note: Apart from small details, Firmicus agrees with the Sabatier text and with Cyprian, *Testimonies* II.]

After the resurrection also, when he gave his disciples certain commands, he concluded the order of his immortal commandments with this injunction: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit; teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you” (Matthew 28:18–19).

That God the Father, making him a sharer in the kingdom, granted him the seat of the royal throne, is taught by this oracle: “The Lord said to my Lord: ‘Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet. The Lord shall send forth from Zion the rod of your strength: rule in the midst of your enemies. With you is dominion in the day of your power, in the brightness of the saints; from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you. The Lord has sworn and will not repent’” (Psalm 109:1–4).

[Note: It generally agrees with Cyprian, *Testimonies* II, except at verse 3, where this author has the Sabatier reading: “in the splendours of the saints.”]

These, most sacred emperors, are the enemies of God who disturb the order of truth by an opposing law; who, prompted by perverse desire, conceive sacrilegious vows; who in the frenzy of a profane mind always worship either wood or stone. Here we must set forth the order of the holy dispensation, so that whatever the holy word of God has handed down to us in prophetic teaching may be explained specifically for refuting the stains of profane error, lest … as we have said, those who handed down sacrilege to the erring may have fabricated it.

[Note: A few words have fallen out.]

[Note: Read *commentitii sunt*, “they invented/fabricated.” *Commentior* in the sense “I lie” occurs in Apuleius, *Apology*, p. 314: “You were not ashamed to invent a piece of wood which I had sought throughout the whole town.”]

Thus let the order of truth be more carefully investigated by us. Therefore, setting the remaining matters aside briefly, let our discourse turn to explaining these things which are true.

## CHAPTER XXVI

He briefly sets forth the Church’s doctrine concerning Christ in comparison with Adam: that Christ, born of the Virgin Mary, recovered everything Adam had lost. He returns to his course.

Grant me, lords emperors, the patient attention of your sacred ears,

[Note: Lactantius I.1, “to grant patient attention”; and Arnobius, “to lend one’s ears,” I.6, IV.33, VII.33; “to lend assent,” I.54, VII.25. — “Sacred.” Emperors are also called “most sacred” by writers of that age.]

that we may fully explain to your clemency what we promise. Why God—that is, the Son of God—submitted to becoming human will be shown to your piety in a brief and true account. When God made the first human being, Adam, in his own image (Genesis 2:27), he gave him a definite law of commandments. Deceived through the woman, that is, Eve, by the devil’s persuasions, he lost the dignity of the glory promised him. There was a tree in Paradise:

[Note: The tree of knowledge; Genesis 3:3.]

he lost the grace of the rewards promised by God. The human being was made from the clay of virgin earth; for, as Scripture says, rain had not yet fallen upon the earth. This man, despising God’s commands, afflicted the human race with the snares of mortality. All this had to be remade and corrected; and the restoration of the origin had to restore its beginnings.

Adam, made from the clay of virgin earth, lost through his own transgression the life promised him. Christ, born through the Virgin Mary and the Holy Spirit, received both immortality and kingdom. The wood of the tree furnished those who had been deceived with deadly food;

[Note: Death.]

the wood of the cross restored life in an immortal structure. Adam despised; Christ obeyed God. Thus, by the divine dispensation, Christ recovered everything Adam lost. For after many ages, in the final periods of time—that is, almost in the last week of the ages—the Word of God joined himself to a human body,

[Note: Arnobius I.60: “He therefore assumed human form and concealed his power beneath the likeness of our race, so that he could be seen and beheld, speak and teach, and accomplish all the deeds for whose performance he had come into the world, while preserving the command and dispositions of the highest King.” Lactantius IV.10 and 12; Augustine, *City of God* X.29; and others in Elmenhorst’s observations on Arnobius, p. 56. Compare also ch. 25.]

in order to free humanity, conquer death, and join the frailty of the human body to divine immortality. For what would such a multitude of saints have gained? What hope of salvation would they have had? What reward for their merits, if they too were held bound under one and the same condition of lot by the inescapable snares of mortality? Abel, Enoch, Noah, Shem, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob could promise themselves nothing from God’s mercy and majesty. After such great merit of faith, they too would go away, consigned with all the rest; one destruction of death would receive all God’s saints alike, and piety would have no reward with God if one and the same condition of death engulfed them all.

But God had promised Abraham a kingdom brighter than the stars of heaven. Therefore the Virgin Mary, descending from Abraham’s race, conceives God, so that the offspring of the persons mentioned above might be joined by the bond of immortal fellowship; and so that the human race, united through the human being who is at once God by an equal association of fellowship, might attain the dominion of immortality through the merit of obedience. Since, therefore, most sacred emperors, we have satisfied your attentive ears, let us proceed with what remains, so that even thus our discourse, cleansing the filth of polluted ears, may be able to purify them.

## CHAPTER XXVII

He explains the final symbol of the Mithraic initiations, “The bull [is] the father of the serpent, and the serpent [is] the father of the bull.” He mentions the serpent, deceiver of the first-formed humans and object of its deadly cult, and says that the dragon was struck down on the day Christ appeared.

There follows another symbol,

[Note: From the Sabazian mysteries.]

which is handed down to the credulous ears of wretched people as something great: “The bull [is] the father of the serpent, and the serpent [is] the father of the bull.”

[Note: Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation* ch. 2, p. 15: “A certain idolatrous poet says: ‘The bull is the father of the serpent, and the serpent the father of the bull.’” Arnobius V.21: “If anyone should ask for the author of the matter, then we shall cite the Tarentine and the well-known iambic trimeter which antiquity sings: ‘The bull begot the serpent, and the serpent the bull.’” There he reports the origin of the tale: Jupiter, hiding under the form of a serpent, violated Persephone. Heraldus conjectures that the Tarentine poet—not an obscure figure, as Meursius thought—was the comic poet Rhinthon. See Orelli’s notes on Arnobius V.21; cf. Creuzer III.361; Santa Croce II, p. 96.]

At times, devil, you have revealed to us the signs of your stained name; at times you have confessed your infamous name in your own voice. I know who you were and what you dared; I know what the malicious persuasion of your crimes has done. This was what you earnestly promised Eve when you were destroying her, when you said to her: “You shall be like gods” (Genesis 3:5). Then you were preparing temples and shrines for yourself and your own followers, and consecrating the filth of your venomous mouth by abominable rites. You creep through temples and feed miserably on the blood of slaughtered victims. Nor did your poisons lack blood; nor did you lack the portions of half-burned bodies of those cremated.

[Note: Thus Wower restored the corrupt reading of the first edition: “Nor did you make yourself bloody with unjust blood.” As in what follows, the reference is to human victims.]

You have frequently stained yourself with the blood of human victims. And you glut yourself on the blood of the temple of Latiaris; or your frenzy has been nourished by the altar of Carthage and by the poisons of your parched throat.

[Note: It must certainly be corrected to “and of Latiaris.” Porphyry, *On Abstinence*: “But even now, does anyone not know that in the great city a human being is slaughtered at the festival of Jupiter Latiaris?” On Jupiter Latiaris see Justin Martyr, *Apology* II.12; Theophilus, *To Autolycus* III.6; Tatian ch. 46; Minucius Felix chs. 21, 30; Tertullian, *Apology* ch. 2, *On the Shows* ch. 6, *Against the Gnostics* ch. 7; Lactantius I.2; Athanasius, *Against the Greeks* ch. 25; Rycquius, *On the Capitol* ch. 25; and Valesius’s notes on Eusebius’s Oration in Praise of Constantine, p. 264. One might well wish that some learned person would narrate the history of human sacrifice from its beginnings to the victory of the Christian religion: it would indeed be a long work, full of tedium; but whoever completed it well would render an outstanding service to the history of the religions of the ancient world.]

[Note: Ennius’s very famous verse: “The Carthaginians are accustomed to sacrifice their little children.” Justin Martyr, *Apology* II, p. 128; Athenagoras, *Embassy* ch. 23. See what we have discussed at length concerning this superstition in the book *On the Religion of the Carthaginians*, p. 17 ff.]

While doing these things, you boast to wretched people that you benefit them—so as to destroy them by your cruelty, deceive them by persuasion, and cast them down by promises. Thus you provide for your own, parricide! Flee, wretched people, flee, and abandon this contagion with whatever speed you can. What is worshipped is a dragon. It cannot remain hidden: it has itself confessed the proper character of its name. Punishment follows the defendant who has confessed. Hear what the holy prophet proclaims under divine inspiration. Faith has handed down to us this oracle of Isaiah; for he says: “On that day God will bring his holy, great, and strong sword upon the dragon, the great and twisting serpent, and he will kill the dragon” (Isaiah 27:1).

[Note: Firmicus differs from the Sabatier reading, drawn from Jerome’s commentary on Isaiah 27, and does not agree with the other manuscripts.]

The will of God is the substance of the completion of the work.

[Note: Perhaps, “the completion of the work is imminent.” Wower.]

The sentence against the dragon has rightly been pronounced: whatever God has said has been done. This is the dying dragon’s consolation: a great crowd of the lost accompanies its ruin. If the day of its death is sought, it was struck down when it saw the God-man, when Christ’s divine power appeared to us. After that day, whoever follows the institution of this serpent must die with the serpent. He himself fashioned and composed these gods whom you worship.

[Note: From the continuous assertion of the Fathers that all idolatry is an invention of the devil and demons.]

If your stubborn minds remain in this error, you too will burn together with your gods, so that whatever your authors have deserved by divine judgment may be transferred, through this partnership of association, also to your destruction. Believe me: the devil has omitted nothing that might either weaken or destroy the wretched human being. Therefore he transformed himself into every form through manifold variety; therefore he fashioned himself with cunning of every kind, so that he might kill people entangled by diverse and manifold deceits.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

He calls the dragon the author of fictitious deities and says that it always arranged for its rites to be renewed through wood. From this he notes the misuse of wood in idolatrous rites through a few examples drawn from the Phrygian rites and those of Osiris and Proserpina. Then, as he is about to expound the doctrine of the cross, he adduces passages of the New Testament which the ancient Church and that age interpreted concerning the cross. Thus, after setting forth and refuting the principal symbols and signs then current in the worship of idols, he gathers his arguments so that the emperors to whom he wrote might proceed all the more confidently to abolish idols and their rites utterly.

The ruined executioner—

[Note: The devil.]

—arranged, monstrous to say, that his rites should always be renewed through wood,

[Note: Since, that is, he had deceived the first-formed humans through wood, the fruit of the forbidden tree.]

because he knew this would happen:

[Note: Perhaps, “as one who knew,” or “because he knew this would happen.” Justin Martyr, *Apology* I, p. 82.]

that human life, fastened to the wood of the cross, would be bound in the structure of perpetual immortality. Therefore he would deceive those who were to perish by an imitation of wood. In the Phrygian rites, which they call those of the Mother of the Gods, every year a pine tree is cut down and an image of a young man is bound to the middle of the tree.

[Note: Arnobius V.39: “That pine which is solemnly brought into the sanctuary of the Mother of the gods—is it not an image of that tree beneath which Attis, after cutting off his genitals, took away his own manhood, and which, they relate, the Goddess consecrated as a consolation for her grief?” V.16: “What does that pine signify which on the appointed days you always bring into the sanctuary of the Mother of the gods? Is it not a likeness of the tree beneath which the frantic youth laid violent hands upon himself?” And shortly afterwards: “What do the branches of the tree, adorned with violet garlands and bound about, indicate? Do they not show that the mother adorned the pine with the first flowers, as an indication and testimony of pitiable grief?” This occurred on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, as recorded in the Roman Calendar of Constantine the Great for that day (Orelli on V.16). See also Zoega, *Abhandlungen*, p. 179. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* X.104, relates that Attis was transformed into a pine. Servius, however, says that priests of Rhea found him mutilated at the roots of this tree and carried him into the goddess’s temple, where he died (*on Aeneid* IX.114). The story is in fact a repetition of that of Osiris and Typhon. Cf. Santa Croce I.85. Pliny, *Natural History* XVI.10.15, mentions a statue of Attis suspended from a tree. See Creuzer II, pp. 38 ff., 53, 108. The pine is an image of flight and destruction; Creuzer I.117.]

In the Isiac rites, a trunk is cut from a pine tree.

[Note: This note is missing in Migne’s printed edition.]

The middle portion of this trunk is carefully hollowed out;

[Note: He undoubtedly speaks of the later Isiac rites. I do not know whether any other writer mentions this ritual. See nevertheless Plutarch, *On Isis and Osiris*, ch. 42.]

there an image of Osiris made from its fragments is buried.

[Note: Wower correctly emended the reading of the first edition, *illis de seminibus*, to *illīs de segminibus*. See Plutarch, *On Isis and Osiris*, ch. 21.]

In the rites of Proserpina, a felled tree is fashioned into the likeness and form of a maiden;

[Note: I do not know whether any other author mentions this ritual. I observe indeed that Santa Croce, I, p. 157, cites Tatian ch. 16, but Tatian is speaking of Rhea, as are the passages of Arnobius just cited concerning the Mother of the Gods. Sylvestre de Sacy also warns readers of this. Santa Croce should certainly have cited Firmicus, apparently the sole source for this account. Creuzer gives a few details, IV.453.]

and, after it has been brought into the city, it is mourned for forty nights; on the fortieth night it is burned. The same flame also consumes those other pieces of wood of which I have spoken; for after a year flame devours the pyre of those very woods.

[Note: Thus, once the year was completed and the festival days returned, these three images were burned together by the priests.]

You have erred, wretch, and erred grievously. That fire can do you no good. In vain do you take comfort from its flame, always renewing this fire for your inventions. The fire that exacts penalties for your crimes rages in the perpetual continuance of torments. Learn the order of the divine and liberating wood, so that you may know that no help can come to you by any means. A wooden ark saved the human race from the flood (Genesis 7–8). Then Abraham laid wood upon the shoulders of his only son (Genesis 22:6). A wooden rod protected the people of God as they departed from Egypt (Exodus 14:21, 26). Wood gave the bitter waters of Marah a sweet taste (Exodus 15:25). By a wooden rod saving water is brought forth from the spiritual rock (Exodus 17:6; 1 Corinthians 10:4). And, so that Amalek might be defeated, Moses stood with arms extended around the rod (Exodus 17:11–12).

[Note: The sacred text says nothing about the rod, nor do the Latin interpreters.]

The patriarch dreams that an angel is leaning on a wooden ladder, and sees some ascending and others descending by the same ladder (Genesis 28:12).

[Note: Moses says not a word, nor do the Latin interpreters, about a wooden ladder seen in the dream.]

And the law of God is entrusted to a wooden ark (Exodus 40:20), so that by all these things, as though by certain steps, the salvation of humankind might arrive at the wood of the cross. Therefore the wood of the cross sustains the structure of heaven, strengthens the foundations of the earth, and leads to life the people fastened to it. The devil’s wood always burns and dies, and carries believing people down to the depths of Tartarus with its ashes.

Let its nature too be considered rationally. As the devil consecrates his tree, at the dead of night he has a ram sacrificed at the roots of the felled tree.

[Note: He is undoubtedly speaking of the pine, but does not say in which mysteries. This ritual seems not to be known from elsewhere.]

Who persuaded you to do this, criminal one? From where did you learn it in your deadly desire? Do you always array yourself against the highest Lord with wicked desire? Therefore the severe judgment of divinity casts you down from heaven into abject humiliation; therefore God’s sentence decrees eternal punishment for you: because every day a new crime is always added to your crimes; because you attempt to deceive the human being of God by fraudulent persuasion. See what the mocking enemy has devised.

When Abraham was about to sacrifice his son at God’s command, a ram was substituted and bound at the roots of a nearby tree (Genesis 22:13). When the highest God was about to free his people from Egyptian tyranny, he commanded that a ram be slain at night and ordered its blood to be smeared upon the doorposts.

[Note: The paschal lamb; Exodus 12:4 ff.]

He commands it to be consumed in a night-time meal by a fixed number of persons and gives the sacrifice itself the name Pascha, “Passover.” But divine majesty’s providence devised this as an image of future things, in order to show us the true Passover by means of the sign. Therefore, when the Prophet, commanded by the divine Spirit, foretold the passion of our Lord, he said: “Like a sheep he was led to sacrifice; like a lamb before its shearer, so he did not open his mouth. In humiliation his judgment was taken away. Who has told of his generation? For his life shall be removed from the earth” (Isaiah 53:7–8).

[Note: It differs little from the Sabatier text. Verse 8 nearly agrees with Cyprian, *Testimonies* II, down to words absent in Cyprian.]

Another prophet also gave a similar oracle in answer concerning these same matters: “Lord, make it known to me, and I shall know; then I saw their designs. I was led like a lamb without malice to sacrifice. They devised a design against me, saying: ‘Come, let us put wood into his bread, and let us erase his life from the earth’” (Jeremiah 18:18–19).

[Note: It agrees entirely with Book II of Cyprian’s *Testimonies*.]

That our Lord is called the Lamb is shown us by holy revelation. For in the Apocalypse we find this written: “And I saw in the midst of the throne and the four living creatures, and in the midst of the elders, a Lamb standing as though slain, having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent throughout the world. And he came and received the book from the right hand of him who sat on the throne. And when he had received the book, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb, each holding golden lyres full of the spices of petitions, which were the prayers of the saints; and they sang a new song, saying: ‘You are worthy to receive the book and to open its seals, because you were slain and redeemed us to God by your blood from every tribe and language and people and nation, and made us a kingdom and priests to our God, and we shall reign upon the earth.’”

[Note: With a few exceptions he has the same text as Cyprian, agreeing with him also in having at verse 8 “golden lyres full of spices of petitions,” omitting the intervening words and “golden bowls.”]

John also calls the Son of God by the name of Lamb, so that he too may answer the prophetic promise. For he says in the Gospel: “On the next day John sees Jesus coming toward him and says: ‘Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world’” (John 1:35–36).

[Note: Quoted from memory.]

For the salvation of humankind the venerable blood of this Lamb is poured out, so that the Son of God may redeem his saints by the outpouring of precious blood; so that those freed by Christ’s blood may first be consecrated by the immortal majesty of that blood. Blood poured out among idols has helped no one. And lest the blood of cattle deceive or destroy wretched people: that blood defiles; it does not redeem, and through various misfortunes it presses people down into death. Wretched are those stained by the shedding of sacrilegious blood. The *taurobolium* or *criobolium* drenches you in the criminal pollution of blood.

[Note: *Taurobolium* or *criobolium*. The *taurobolium*, *criobolium*, and *aemobolium* were purifications by the blood of victims in which the initiate was drenched. Introduced into the Roman West in the age of Antoninus Pius and his successors, they properly belonged to the mysteries of the Mother of the Gods and were compared with Christian baptism, so that one purified by them was called “reborn,” and the term *percipere*, used among Christians of baptism, was applied to these purifications. Yet this bath of regeneration was repeated not once but often. The entire rite is described by Prudentius in his Hymn on the Roman Martyr. Of the inscriptions mentioning it, collected in Fleetwood’s *Sylloge of Inscriptions*, pp. 12–18, I select the one which Wower had already used to illustrate Firmicus: “To the Great Gods, the Mother of the Gods and Attis: Sextilius Agesilaus Aedesius, a man of senatorial rank, distinguished advocate of the African tribunal, reborn through taurobolium and criobolium for eternity [i.e. for a long time], dedicated this altar, when our lords Valens, for the fifth time, and Valentinian were consuls.” The *aemobolium* occurs in only one inscription: “Petronius Marcellus, priest, member of the council of the imperial household, decurion, performed at his own expense a criobolium and aemobolium for Primo and Justo” (in Luca Camara, *On Ancient Chieti*, Rome, 1651; and in Zorn, *Bibliotheca Antiquaria Exegetica*, p. 1080). For the *taurobolium* generally, see Nathan Friedrich Kautsch’s learned dissertation *On the Taurobolium*, Leipzig, 1738; Creuzer II.59, IV.347; and Zoega, *Abhandlungen*, p. 141.]

## CHAPTER XXIX

He gathers from the sacred writings testimonies to the vanity of idols, and exhorts the emperors regarding the prosperous and flourishing condition of the commonwealth under their rule and the punishment of pagan impiety, now most imminently approaching.

[Col. 1043B] Let those defilements, then, which you gather, be washed away. Seek untainted springs, seek pure waters, so that there, after many stains, the blood of Christ may make you white with the Holy Spirit (Rev. VII.14). But to bring wretched people back to sound judgment by full persuasion, greater authority is needed, so that, once minds have been cured and healed, no trace of the former pestilence may remain. What idols are, therefore, and what substance they possess, has been shown by the oracles of the prophets and by the divine voice. All this must be stated particularly, so that it may be recognized that this has been set forth not by our rashness but handed down to us by divine teaching and sealed by a heavenly voice. What their substance is, the venerable voice of Wisdom shows; for [Col. 1043C] it says in the books of Solomon:

“All the idols of the nations they regarded as gods, though they have neither sight of eyes to see, nor nostrils to perceive breath, nor ears to hear, nor fingers of hands to touch. Their feet also are slow for walking. For a human being made them, and one who borrowed breath fashioned them. No human being can form a god for himself; for, being mortal, he fashions a dead thing with lawless hands. Yet he is better than those whom he worships, since he himself lived, whereas they never did” [Note: [Col. 1044D] It agrees for the most part with Cyprian.] (Wis. XV.15–16).

What more do we seek? Wisdom confronts us with a divine voice, teaches what it had seen in the hidden counsels of God, and shows what was salutary, lest frail and perishable mortality hasten toward its own destruction and death. The Holy Spirit gives the same warning beforehand in the Psalms. For in Psalm CXXXIV we find it written thus:

“The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands. They have a mouth and do not speak; they have eyes and do not see; they have ears and do not hear. For there is no breath in their mouth. Those who make them are like them” [Note: [Col. 1044D] As in Cyprian; but he omits the addition in the Roman Psalter and follows the Hebrew text.] (Ps. CXXXIV.15–17).

If the craftsman who either carved or cast an image for display of his skill is struck by the divine punishment of a curse, one must consider what he ought to hope for who calls a god what another has sold. Jeremiah also, when by God’s command he gave precepts to the people, addressed the people in these words:

“But say in your hearts: ‘You, Lord, must be worshipped.’ My angel is with you, and I shall require an account from your souls. Their tongue has been polished by a craftsman; they are themselves overlaid with gold and silver, yet they are false and cannot speak. As a lover, at the prompting of desire, gives gold to a virgin, so crowns have been made for the heads of their gods. At times their priests take gold and silver away from their gods and spend it upon themselves. They even give some of it to prostitute-harlots, and clothe them as though they were human beings—gods of silver, gold, and wood” (Baruch VI.5–10).

He adds in what follows, to shake off every trembling doubt:

“Over their body and head owls, swallows, and birds likewise fly. From this you shall know that they are not gods. Therefore do not fear them. The gold which they have about them is for appearance; unless someone wipes away the rust, it will not shine. For when they are melted down, they feel nothing. They were bought at a price, and there is no spirit in them. Being without feet, they are carried on shoulders” (ibid. 21–24).

He further adds, that the confirmed mind may be strengthened more firmly: “Knowing, therefore, from these things that they are not gods, do not fear them” (ibid. 28). And to expose the wretched disgrace of their priests, he adds:

“In their houses their priests sit, with torn tunics and shaven heads and beards; their heads are bare. They roar and cry out against their gods, like the dead in Gehenna” (ibid. 30–31).

The same prophet also indicates in a prophetic voice that kings and nations will pronounce these judgments concerning them:

“Later it shall be known that they are false, by all nations and kings; for it is evident that they are not gods, and that no work of God belongs to them. They will not raise up a king for a country, nor give rain to human beings. They will not discern judgment, nor free a country from injury, because they can do nothing. And if fire falls upon the house of gods of wood, gold, and silver, their priests will save themselves, but the gods themselves will be burned in the midst like beams. They will not withstand king or war. How, then, are they to be thought or accepted to be gods? Gods of wood, gold, and silver will not free themselves from thieves and robbers; those who are strong will take from them the gold and silver with which they are covered” [Note: [Col. 1045C] These words are not found in Cyprian. Sabatier noted quite a number of variant readings.] (ibid. 50–57).

Remove, remove without hesitation [Note: [Col. 1045C] Without fear of obstacles or rebellions.], most sacred Emperors, the ornaments of the temples. Let the fire of the mint or the flame that melts metals consume these gods. Transfer all the votive offerings to the use of yourselves and of the Lord. After the destruction of the temples [Note: [Col. 1045C] The law of Constantius and Constans is given in the Theodosian Code, book XVI, title 10, law 4. Libanius, *Oration in Defense of the Temples*, p. 23, speaks of palatine temples given as a gift to private persons; Reiske II, p. 185. On temple revenues dispersed, see the same author, *Oration on the Death of Julian*. Yet the history of later times, down to Theodosius and his sons, teaches that not all temples were destroyed. Symmachus, *Letters* 10, no. 54, testifies that Constantius himself acted moderately at Rome, visited temples, and confirmed the privileges of the Vestal Virgins.], you have advanced more greatly in God’s power; you have conquered enemies, [Col. 1045B] extended the Empire [Note: [Col. 1045D] These passages are full of flattery. For Roman affairs went rather unsuccessfully in the Persian war.], and, that greater glory might accrue to your prowess, disregarding and reversing the order of the seasons, in winter [Note: [Col. 1045D] Toward the end of January 343, Constans, after pacifying Gaul, set sail with a fleet from Boulogne to invade Britain: Libanius, *Oration* 3; Ammianus Marcellinus, book XX, 1. A large bronze coin bears witness to this expedition. On its obverse: BONONIA OCEANEN. A woman stands in a trireme; she holds a shield in her left hand and hurls a spear with her right toward a swimming figure. At the trireme’s prow is Victory; at its stern, two military standards. Banduri reproduces the coin, *Numismata imperatorum Romanorum* II, p. 348. It admirably explains Firmicus’s words: “you trod beneath your oars the raging waves of Ocean.” See the coin in the catalogue of this edition.]—a thing which has neither ever been done nor will be done—you trod beneath your oars the swollen and raging waves of Ocean. The wave of a sea now almost unknown to us trembled, and the Briton was terrified by the unexpected sight of the emperor [Note: [Col. 1046C] Not indeed the inhabitant of the Roman province, long since pacified, but a Caledonian threatening an incursion into Scotland. The outcome of the war is unknown; but coins proclaim victory, though they may also have been struck in remembrance of the war waged with the Franks. It remains uncertain, however, whether these peoples were reduced to obedience more by arms or by money. Yet the large coin on which the emperor, mounted on horseback, attacks with his spear an unarmed enemy who has sunk to his knees (see Banduri, cited place), and which bears the inscription *DEBELLATOR GENTT. BARBARR.* (“Subduer of Barbarian Nations”), together with others proclaiming the Victory of Augustus and the Glory of the Romans, seems to have been minted on the same occasion as the first coin bearing the name of Boulogne and to refer to the Caledonian expedition. On these, moreover, see Le Beau, *Histoire du Bas-Empire*, II, p. 62, and Tillemont, *Histoire des Empereurs*, IV, p. 336. Others also will pertain to the Frankish war. Eckhel, *Doctrina Nummorum Veterum*, VIII, pp. 3, 112.].

What more do you desire? The elements, conquered by your valour, yielded. That God commands idols not to be made is declared by the writings of the most sacred Law. For in Exodus we find it written thus: “You shall not make for yourselves gods of silver, nor gods of gold” (Exod. XX.23). And again, in the same book, I find the voice of God commanding: “You shall not make for yourself an idol, nor the likeness of anything” [Note: [Col. 1046D] It agrees with Cyprian, *Exhortation to Martyrdom*.] (ibid. IV). The Holy Spirit enjoins shame upon the wretched because he wishes to recall those who err, not to destroy them. And through Isaiah he says:

“You shall be utterly ashamed, you who trust in carved images, who say to molten images, ‘You are our gods’” [Note: [Col. 1046D] It differs little from Sabatier’s text.] (Isa. XLII.17).

He also gives a law for the consecrated people to observe with devoted constancy, and commands thus: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Deut. VI.13; Matt. IV.10; Luke IV.8). Similar commands of God are known in Deuteronomy; for he says: “You shall have no other gods besides me” (Deut. V.7). He adds also, in order to impress upon their minds the weight of his majesty:

“See, see that I am he, and there is no God besides me. I kill and I make alive; I strike, and I myself heal; and there is none who can deliver from my hands” [Note: [Col. 1046D] Almost as in Cyprian, book I.] (Rev. XVI.6–7).

In the Apocalypse this same teaching is also shown by sacred revelation; for it is written thus:

“And I saw another angel flying in mid-heaven, having the eternal Gospel to proclaim over the earth to every nation and tribe and tongue and people, saying with a loud voice: ‘Fear the Lord rather, and give him glory, because the hour of his judgment has come; and worship him who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all things that are in them.’”

Our Lord Jesus Christ also, preserving the institutions of his Father’s Law, proclaims the same thing by a venerable ordinance; for he says:

“Hear, Israel: the Lord is your God, and you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength. This is the first commandment; and the second is like it: you shall love your neighbour as yourself. On these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets” [Note: [Col. 1046D] Like Cyprian, book I, he seems especially to have had Mark before his eyes.] (Deut. VI.5; Matt. XXII.37–40; Mark XII.29–31; Luke X.27).

This divine and venerable command is followed by the holy conclusion of the immortal Lord; for, to show the way of salvation more plainly, he adds and says: “And this is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom you sent” (John XVII.3). You know the order of the sacred commands; you have learned by a venerable and immortal voice what you ought to follow and what you ought to flee. Hear [Col. 1046C] again the destruction awaiting those who despise them, and by what disasters the necessity of the venerable Law has bound them. For the conclusion of the venerable commands is summed up in these words: “Whoever sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out, except to the Lord alone” [Note: [Col. 1046D] As the author of *On Gamblers* among the Cyprianic works.] (Exod. XXII.20).

If the dreadful penalty struck the sacrilegious person alone, if the severity of the Law threatened the sinner alone, then one obstinately committed to sacrilege might indeed fortify himself by the rashness of furious resolve [Col. 1047A]; but now it threatens even his stock and offspring, intending that no part of the most wicked seed may remain and that no trace of the profane race may endure. “Whoever sacrifices,” it says, “to gods shall be rooted out” (Deut. XXXII.17). Consider what you do, miserable and mournful delusion. Your crime destroys very many, and the fruitful punishment is distributed through the entire substance of your race. Why it rages so against sacrificers is shown by the clear declaration of the authority of the ordained Law in Deuteronomy; for we find it written thus: “They sacrificed to demons, and not to God” (ibid.). Do not transfer yourself to defiled and polluted spirits; do not hope for help from lower powers. Do not supplicate those over whom, by God’s grace, you ought now to rule. Behold: the being you worship is a demon. When it hears the name of God and of his Christ, it trembles; and, in order to answer us when we question it, it scarcely gathers its faltering words [Note: [Col. 1047D] Compare above, at chapter 14, p. 57, note a.]. Clinging to a human being, it is torn, burned, beaten, and immediately confesses the crimes it has committed. Do not worship it; do not supplicate it; do not fall prostrate and bend your knees to it: you are forbidden by the command of the venerable Law. Hence comes the penalty of severity; hence the dreadful sentence of punitive judgment. Why, when God’s indulgence has granted you freedom, do you choose instead the yoke of slavery [Note: [Col. 1047D] A lacuna follows this word.]? . . . . . . . . . . . .

The supreme God does not cease to assail this crime with a saving voice; rather, in his mercy, he hastens to correct erring human beings with repeated threats. Hear what the divine voice says through the prophet Isaiah:

“They worshipped the gods which their fingers made; man bowed down, and the man was humbled, and I will not release [Col. 1047C] them” [Note: [Col. 1047D] Cyprian supports Firmicus: *Letter* 64, *Exhortation to Martyrdom*, and *On the Lapsed*.] (Isa. II.8–9).

And now, O profane people, the angry divinity addresses you, and still confronts your errors with a sacred voice; for through the same prophet he says in what follows: “You have poured libations to them and offered sacrifices to them. Shall I not be angry over these things, says the Lord?” [Note: [Col. 1047D] As Cyprian, *Exhortation to Martyrdom*.] (Isa. LVII.6). God still delays his saving indignation and suspends severity, in case you may perhaps repent of sinning and somehow abandon the destruction of your sacrilegious will. Behold, in the very force of indignation he again persuades in a moderated voice and restrains the goads of his wrath; for through the prophet Jeremiah he says:

“Do not go after foreign gods, to serve them; do not worship them, and do not provoke me by the works of your hands, to your destruction” [Note: [Col. 1048D] As the same author.] (Jer. XXV.6).

Why here, you who are inclined to sacrilege, do you close your ears? Why here do you hasten, in the burning of stubborn madness, toward destruction and death? God made you free; it lies in your hand either to live or to perish. Why do you hurl yourself over precipices? Set upon a slippery path and already at the point of falling, at least check your tottering steps. Behold, sentence is pronounced; behold, punishment is decreed. Divine forbearance long spared your crimes; long it regarded your wicked deed with dissimulation. You have arrived [Col. 1048A] at that critical point where hope and prayers fail. And that you may be more plainly instructed, learn the destruction wrought by judgment. The whole tenor of the answer concerning this matter is found in the Apocalypse; for it is written thus:

“If anyone worships the beast and its image, and receives its mark upon his forehead and hand, he too shall drink of the wine of God’s wrath, mixed in the cup of his anger. And he shall be punished with fire and sulphur before the eyes of the Lamb, and the smoke of their torments shall rise for ages of ages. And those who worship the beast and its image shall have no rest day or night” [Note: [Col. 1048D] It agrees for the most part with Cyprian, *Testimonies*, book III, and *Exhortation to Martyrdom*.] (Rev. XIV.9–10).

## CHAPTER XXX. Finally, he urges upon the emperors the divine command concerning the extirpation of idolaters (Deut. XIII); if they obey it, both a prosperous outcome and a happy future [Col. 1048B] reign are promised to them.

But upon you also, most sacred Emperors, the necessity of avenging and punishing this evil is imposed; and by the law of the supreme God this is commanded you: that your severity should pursue the crime of idolatry in every way. Hear and commit to your holy minds what God commands concerning this crime. This law is prescribed in Deuteronomy; for it says:

“If your brother, or your son, or your wife who is in your bosom, or your friend who is equal to your own soul, secretly entices you, saying, ‘Let us go and serve other gods of the nations,’ you shall not consent to him, nor listen to him; your eye shall not spare him, nor shall you conceal him. You shall certainly denounce him. Your hand shall be first upon him to put him to death, and afterward the hand of all the people. They shall stone him, and he shall die, because he sought to turn you away from your Lord” [Note: [Col. 1048D] Cyprian, *Exhortation to Martyrdom*, generally supports him.] (Deut. XIII.6–10).

He commands that not even a son be spared; he brings the avenging sword even through a beloved wife. He also pursues a friend with lofty severity, and all the people are armed to tear sacrilegious bodies apart. Entire cities too, if they are caught in this crime, are decreed destruction. And so that your foresight may learn this more clearly, I shall set forth the ruling of the established Law. In the same book the Lord fixes punishment for entire cities in these words:

“If you hear, in one of the cities which the Lord your God gives you to inhabit, people saying, ‘Let us go and serve other gods, whom you do not know,’ you shall surely kill all who are in the city by the slaughter of the sword, and burn the city [Col. 1048D] with fire; it shall remain without inhabitant. It shall never be rebuilt” [Note: [Col. 1048D] It agrees for the most part with Cyprian, book I.] (ibid. 12, 13, 15).

“And the Lord will turn from the indignation of his wrath, and will give you mercy, have mercy on you, and multiply you, if you obey the voice of the Lord your God and keep his commandments” (ibid. 17–18). The supreme God promises you, most sacred Emperors, the rewards of his mercy and decrees the increases of the greatest enlargement. Therefore do what he commands; fulfill what he prescribes. Your auspices [Col. 1049A] have been heaped with greater gifts; from the beginning of your faith you have felt the increase of divine favour. The venerable hand of God has never abandoned you, nor, when you laboured, has it ever denied you aid. The battle-lines of opponents have been laid low, and rebellious arms have always fallen before your sight. The proud have been sent beneath the people’s yoke, and Persian hopes have collapsed [Note: [Col. 1049A] In 344 Constantius appears to have conducted affairs with the Persians not unsuccessfully; hence, as Theophanes testifies (*Chronographia*, p. 30, *Scriptores Rerum Byzantinarum*, vol. X), he celebrated a triumph over the Persians. This may indeed have provided Firmicus with occasion to write of Persian hopes having collapsed. In this bloody war, however, Constantius was defeated by Shapur nine times, especially at Singara in 348; and only an invasion of the Massagetae recalled the victor from the siege of Nisibis. Zonaras, book XIII, ch. 5: “Emperor Constantius, having engaged the Persians many times, had the worse part and lost many of his own men.” Eutropius X.6: “Constantius suffered many grave losses at the hands of the Persians, with towns frequently captured, cities besieged, and armies slaughtered; and he had no successful battle against Shapur, except that at Singara he lost an unquestionable victory through the ferocity of his soldiers, who, as daylight was already failing, mutinously and foolishly demanded battle contrary to the strategy of war.”].

Nor will cruelty, armed with its evils, be able to stand long against you. You have experienced God’s power in contrary outcomes for each side. To you the crown of heavenly victory has been bestowed, and by your good fortune our hardships are relieved. These [Col. 1050A] are the rewards which the supreme God has rendered you for your faith, most sacred Emperors [Note: [Col. 1050A] Firmicus could have said this only of Constans, who embraced the Nicene faith and protected it in the East. Constantius, on the contrary, openly favoured the Arians.]. Having meanwhile rewarded you with these distinctions, he invites you into the mysteries of the venerable Law. Let your clemency always look to heaven with a pure mind, a devoted conscience, and an uncorrupted spirit; always await help from God; implore the venerable divinity of Christ; and offer spiritual sacrifices to the saving God for the welfare of the whole world and of yourselves. Thus all things will prosper for you: victories, wealth, peace, abundance, health, and triumphs; so that, protected by the divine majesty, you may govern the world in a happy dominion.

# SAINT PHILASTRIUS, BISHOP OF BRESCIA

[Col. 1049]

[Col. 1049]

## FIRST DEDICATORY EPISTLE

[Note: [Col. 1049D] In this and the following letter the reader will readily observe that the discussion concerns Philastrius not exclusively, though particularly. That this may not surprise the reader, it is necessary to know that the collection from which we have excerpted the works of our saint is composed under this title: *Works of the Ancient Bishops of Brescia—St Philastrius and Gaudentius—together with the shorter works of Blessed Rampertus and Venerable Adelmannus*. We considered it a duty not to deprive the reader of these letters, since they shed some light both upon Philastrius and upon the edition of his works.]

[Col. 1049C] To our most holy lord Clement XII, pope: ANGELUS MARIA QUIRINI, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Mark, librarian of the Apostolic See, and bishop of Brescia.

The reason which impelled me, Most Blessed Father, when I had been appointed by Your Holiness to the charge of the Vatican Library, to set my mind upon bringing forth from that most richly stocked literary storehouse a new edition of Saint Ephraem the Syrian, now itself brings it about that, to increase both the name and the glory of the Church of Brescia, over which I likewise preside, I present the four ancient bishops of that Church, who were also writers, now for the first time brought together in one volume. This reason, of course, is the love of sacred literature, which, by the highest gift of the immortal God, was implanted in me from my tender years, afterward grew up with me, and throughout every stage of life and in every place remained so faithful a companion that it has been found not only to travel, spend the night, and live in the country with me—things which, according to a saying of Cicero, letters are accustomed to do with us—but even, if I may speak thus, to serve as bishop with me. In this last office, surely, no more praiseworthy discharge seems possible than to direct one’s efforts and labours toward bringing greater light and reverence to the ancient monuments of the Churches.

Indeed, Most Blessed Father, although the Church of Brescia is remarkably adorned by several monuments of this kind, most illustrious is the fact that four bishops sat in its see, equally distinguished by holiness and published writings. Two of them—Saints Philastrius and Gaudentius—lived in the age of the holy Augustine, bishop of Hippo; while Blessed Rampertus flourished about nine hundred years ago, and Venerable Adelmannus about seven hundred years ago. Moreover, Philastrius was so nearly contemporary with Augustine that, when the latter was asked by letter from the deacon Quodvultdeus to write a treatise on heresies, he replied that Philastrius, known to him at Milan in the company of Ambrose, had already performed that very task amply. Gaudentius, meanwhile, received the Church of Brescia, offered to him while he was still in vigorous age, through the exertions of that most holy bishop of Milan himself, while Gaudentius was making a pilgrimage in the East to the Holy Places. Rampertus’s elevation to that see is commended by the translation of Saint Philastrius into the greater church, the construction of the monastery where the bodies of Saints Faustinus and Jovita rest, and many other matters. Finally, Adelmannus is made illustrious by his zeal for the Catholic faith, with which he fought against Berengar of Tours concerning the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, and for that reason is attacked even by the Innovators of our own time.

How much these four ornaments of the Church of Brescia now owe to Paolo Galeardi, canon of my cathedral and a man of renowned name in the republic of letters, is shown by the eloquent prefaces placed by him in their respective locations. In them he records that he has first revised Fabricius’s notes on Philastrius and then enlarged them with a new *Spicilegium*; that he has supplied fuller notes on Gaudentius; and that by his industry he has contributed many other things worthy of the work. As I present all these things to Your Holiness on bended knees, I do not doubt that you will accept favourably my labour in procuring this edition. For since the Roman Pontiff, out of apostolic benevolence, is accustomed to call all bishops his brothers and professes a common solicitude with them, there will be no part of their office which he does not embrace with the same benevolence; consequently, he will embrace this effort of mine, such as it is, in support of learning. For the surviving monuments of talent and scholarship left by the most holy bishops of old openly show that they devoted themselves to cultivating learning—even philological learning. Who could imagine that tasteless judgment by which, as the very worthy old man once told me at Paris, certain inhabitants of that region complained that the most Christian King had treated them badly in appointing as their bishop the most celebrated and learned Pierre-Daniel Huet, then bishop of Avranches in Normandy, because his scholarly pursuits were not yet finished? We know that even the Roman Pontiffs, amid the weightiest affairs of the whole Christian commonwealth, which they governed in the most difficult times, found sufficient leisure to compose works of no small bulk. This most certainly demonstrates that, as that ancient writer said, for accomplishing great matters in a short span, human beings lack diligence more than strength or time.

May God, greatest and best, grant that Your Holiness may enjoy for many more years a happy lifetime, and that the excellent deeds upon which you expend diligence, strength, and time may establish among posterity an immortal remembrance of your name; so that the sacred annals of the Corsini family may glory both in a bishop of Fiesole enrolled among the saints and in the wisest governor of the universal Church.

[Col. 1051]

## DEDICATORY EPISTLE II

[Col. 1051C] To ANGELUS MARIA QUIRINI, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and bishop of Brescia, from PAULUS GALEARDUS, canon of Brescia.

As soon as the plan was undertaken to publish this collection of the ancient Fathers of the Church of Brescia, most eminent Quirini, I judged that I must chiefly devote myself to ensuring that the undertaking, begun at your command and through your beneficence, should meet the public expectation of mankind and the greatness of your name. For what could be more splendid, what more worthy of being done, than for the bishop of Brescia to take thought for the bishops of Brescia, and to place in an ever better light their writings, by which the Christian cause is wonderfully fortified, defended, and instructed? And so, since I particularly desired what I most wished for—to obtain some manuscript copy in which Philastrius’s book *On Heresies*, which occupies the first place in this collection, had been transcribed—I needed to invoke your authority, so that the variant readings of the Corbie manuscript, which I had learned from reliable indications was held in France, might be sent to us in Italy. You promptly and generously granted what I so earnestly desired. Meanwhile, lest anything further that might assist in elucidating Philastrius be lacking, you sent letters to Hamburg, asking the distinguished Johann Albert Fabricius himself to provide for inclusion in this edition anything more that he had worked out after arranging the Hamburg edition of Philastrius in 1721.

The outcome answered our wishes no less fully than it did your diligence and kindness. First, the distinguished Hermann Reimarus, Fabricius’s son-in-law—for Fabricius had died—sent to Brescia his father-in-law’s later studies on Philastrius; we appended these at the end of Philastrius in this edition as the excellent fruit of that outstanding man [Note: [Col. 1051D] We have inserted these posthumous notes of Fabricius among the earlier notes at the foot of the pages. (EDITORS.)]. Then Bernard de Montfaucon, distinguished and renowned throughout the entire world of letters, complying with your request and employing the services of Monsieur Jean Raverdy, arranged for the variant readings of Philastrius, carefully excerpted from the Corbie manuscript, to be brought from Paris to us. Although they reached Italy later, and therefore were placed in an appendix after Fabricius’s posthumous notes [Note: [Col. 1051D] We have likewise given these variant readings at the foot of the pages, but distinguished by a separate sequence. [Col. 1052D] (EDITORS.)], they nonetheless brought to this edition not merely a singular ornament but indeed the very greatest usefulness. For nearly six entire chapters, which Philastrius had lacked until this day, occur in them; Philastrius may now be considered complete and finished, whereas previously he was defective and mutilated in a great part of himself. The corrections by which Philastrius’s text from the same manuscript is improved, supplemented, or restored are almost so numerous and substantial that our *Spicilegium* is practically composed from them; we placed it after those variant readings at the very end of the Philastrian work [Note: [Col. 1052D] As with the preceding materials, for the reader’s convenience we have moved the notes of the *Spicilegium* and placed them beside Fabricius’s earlier and posthumous notes. (EDITORS.)].

These, most eminent and most reverend prince, are your services to Philastrius. To respond to them in some measure, according to my ability, I have newly revised from the beginning Gaudentius, who follows Philastrius, after the Paduan edition of 1720, and carefully compared him with a manuscript codex of the best quality which chance had offered me; I have corrected and enlarged in many places the notes of the prior edition. Finally, I added to the same Gaudentius Rampertus and Adelmannus, who complete this distinguished quartet of bishops of Brescia and who, together with Gaudentius, had appeared in print at Padua in the same year, after revising them somewhat, so that these excellent lights of the Church of Brescia, contained in one volume, might come into the hands of readers.

These, most illustrious cardinal, are concerns worthy in the highest degree of a librarian of the Apostolic See. In that office the things you accomplish by your zeal, even while absent, are so great and such that you have eclipsed the luminaries of earlier men who held the same post. The enlarged spaces of the Vatican Library, enlarged by the supreme pontiff Clement XII, bear witness to this, as do the books which you have generously added to it. I say nothing at all of the most splendid edition of Saint Ephraem, which you have advanced with such zeal, although far from Rome, and brought almost to its finishing point, so that from this one work you may truly be called *hekáergos* (ἐκάεργος, “far-working” or “far-shooting”). As for the Church of Brescia, over which you have now presided for a twelfth year, I could not easily say by what great advances you have enlarged it. I shall mention only this: the great structure of the principal church has, through your care and at the great expense of your own treasury, been advanced so far that everyone hopes that, after its larger and nobler portion has long been completed and enriched with great ornaments, the remainder too will be finished within no long interval of time.

In this matter I truly cannot restrain myself from comparing you with that great Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, whom this collection mentions frequently and praises not slightly because, among the other monuments of his industry, he completed the church of our mistress, Saint Mary Mother of God, whose foundations he had laid, chiefly with the assistance of Cnut, king of the Danes. The two churches share the same name; they share grandeur and majesty. But you have no Cnut to lend a hand; therefore all hope and all support rest upon your generosity and greatness of spirit. Yet this is not the place for your praises. It is not my purpose to pursue them; nor, if I wished to do so, could I easily find an end to this speech. I shall therefore turn to prayers and earnestly beseech God, greatest and best, that he may allow us to possess longer this good which we enjoy through divine bounty, and preserve you safe for us for many years.

[Col. 1054B] Long may you live in safety for the Church of Brescia; long may you live for the good of letters. May the people of Brescia, as one of our poets finely sang, have in their late posterity this virtue of yours—your religion, humanity, moderation, and the other adornments of mind in which you abound:

> Let later generations have their own ruler; let later generations boast of you as their prince.

But if perhaps some event should occur—as human affairs are changeable—or rather, as I foretell, if the supreme dignity of the Church should someday take you from us, the memory among us of your benefactions will not therefore perish, since, entrusted to enduring monuments, it will live forever. Indeed, even after a long succession of years, when almost all things ordinarily sink into oblivion and times change with times, among the citizens of the city of Brescia, exempt from this common law,

> Your honour, your name, and your praises shall always remain.

Given at Brescia, on the Kalends of December, 1738.

[Col. 1053]

## PREFACE OF PAULUS GALEARDUS TO THE BOOK OF SAINT PHILASTRIUS, *ON HERESIES*
1. The name of Philastrius has been so well known among ecclesiastical writers from antiquity itself that it needs no man’s words to make it clearer or more illustrious. For he was the predecessor in the episcopal see of Brescia of Gaudentius, bishop of Brescia, who celebrates him with exceptional praises in more than one passage. [Note: Preface to Benivolus, p. 218; Sermon 16, p. 334; Sermon 21, p. 370.] Moreover, when his book *On Heresies* was first published, it enjoyed such distinguished renown that Augustine not only mentions him before other writers on this subject, indeed before Epiphanius himself, but also infers from Philastrius’s very work—who enumerated so many more heresies than Epiphanius—how difficult it is to compose a treatise *On Heresies*; and hence he seeks an excuse for himself from undertaking such a work, writing to Quodvultdeus. [Note: Vol. VI of the Works, col. 6, Froben edition.]

Although Augustine declares Epiphanius more learned than Philastrius, he nevertheless does not therefore assert that the former included fewer and the latter more heresies because Philastrius numbered among heresies many things which are not truly heresies. For this many have long accused him, together with Bellarmine [Note: *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 133.], and more recently Bochart [Note: *Phaleg*, bk. I, ch. 11.] and Cave [Note: *History of Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 176.]; rather, because one thing seemed a heresy to one of them, another to the other. Augustine himself warns that it is truly difficult to define this precisely.

And indeed, although I have no wish to deny that Philastrius, in this book *On Heresies*, perhaps in more than one place gave more to zeal for religion and love of Catholic truth than to judgment and care, nevertheless it is well known that the designation αἵρεσις (*hairesis*) has a broad range, and sometimes signifies not so much an error in faith as an institution or a sect. Augustine uses it in this sense when speaking of the various schools of philosophers. [Note: Vol. VI of the Works, col. 10.] Indeed, it occurs frequently in the same sense in Acts of the Apostles: 24:5, πρωτοστάτην τῆς τῶν Ναζαραίων αἱρέσεως, “the originator and leader of the sect (heresy) of the Nazarenes”; 24:14, κατὰ τὴν ὁδὸν ἣν λέγουσιν αἵρεσιν, “according to the sect which they call a heresy”; and 26:5, ὅτι κατὰ τὴν ἀκριβεστάτην αἵρεσιν τῆς ἡμετέρας θρησκείας ἔζησα Φαρισαῖος, “that according to the strictest sect (heresy) of our religion I lived as a Pharisee.”

Melchior Cano therefore rightly observes, in *On Theological Topics*, book 12, chapter 8, that among ancient Greeks and Latin authors the name *heresy* is generic, and designates any school whatsoever—for example, the Platonic, Stoic, or Peripatetic. [Col. 1055B] Later Christian writers, however, narrowed the word *heresy* to mean a sect and division by which someone separates himself from the common faith of the Church. In Augustine, *Against Cresconius*, book II, chapter 4, heresy is “the sect of those who follow a different way”; and in the book *On the Singularity of Clerics*, the author of that work—whoever he may finally have been, certainly ancient and at least contemporary with Origen or Cyprian—calls heresy the corruption of the *Agapetae*, which had then especially invaded the morals of the Church. [Note: Among Cyprian’s Works, Amsterdam edition, p. 148, col. I.]

2. The manner in which Philastrius’s name ought to be written and pronounced does not seem sufficiently certain; for I find that the ancients use both *Philaster* and *Philastrius* indiscriminately. Augustine, in his letter to Quodvultdeus, after calling him Philastrius more than once, [Note: Place cited, col. 6.] again writes in the *Catalogue*, chapter 41: “Philaster, bishop of Brescia.” Then in chapter 45: “Philaster places both of these under separate and individual numbers”; in chapter 53: “But Philaster also attributes this abstinence to them”; and thus he always calls Philastrius *Philaster* wherever he names him in that Catalogue.

Likewise, *Philaster* is read at the beginning of the Acts of the Council of Aquileia [Note: In Labbe, vol. II, col. 978.], and shortly afterwards: “while the bishops of Aquileia were seated in the church … Philaster, bishop of Brescia,” after Justus, the legate of the Gauls. [Note: Ibid., col. 979.] Later below: “Philaster, bishop of Brescia, said.” [Note: Ibid., col. 990.] Philaster is also called such by Gregory the Great, book VI, letter 15: “Philaster in the book which he wrote *On Heresies*”; and by the author of the *Praedestinatus*, chapter 52: “Philaster writes that Macedonius calls the Holy Spirit the deity of the Father and the Son.”

Conversely, Gaudentius consistently calls him Philastrius in Sermon 21, on the life and death of Philastrius, [Col. 1055D] bishop and his own predecessor [Note: P. 370.], as also in the Preface to Benivolus: “you have been imbued with the admirable teachings of our father Philastrius, an apostolic man in every respect”; [Note: P. 218.] and in Sermon 16, on his own ordination: “after that most learned voice of my father Philastrius, of venerable memory.” [Note: P. 334.] Philastrius is also the form used by Rampertus in the Sermon on the Translation of Blessed Philastrius, [Note: P. 387.] to pass over more recent writers: the author of the Appendix to Ildefonsus, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 3; John Trithemius, chapter 84; and very many others, who preferred to call him Philastrius rather than Philastrus.

*Filastrius* also occurs—with the sixth letter of the name written as *f* rather than φ—in two inscriptions preserved with the aid of manuscripts of the people of Brescia, which we publish in the Notes to Rampertus’s Sermon: [Note: P. 388.] “THE ASSUMPTION OF THE MOST BLESSED FATHER FILASTRIUS”; and “FILASTRIUS, OF MOST BLESSED MEMORY, RESTS HERE IN PEACE.” The same form of the name is read in the rhythm, or acrostic poem, on Philastrius at the end of Gaudentius’s Sermons, [Note: P. 377.] where it is expressed thus: “FILASTRIUS, BISHOP OF BRIXIA” [*BRICSIENSIS*, thus]; and likewise in manuscript no. 244 of the Saibante Library at Verona, which we cite in our Notes to Gaudentius. [Note: P. 374.] For it contains: “At the city of Brescia, the deposition of Filastrius, bishop of that same city.”

I do not think we need trouble ourselves greatly over the origin of the name. The distinguished Johann Albert Fabricius noted a few matters in the preface to the Hamburg edition of 1721, but they are not of such weight that we ought to seek from them a certain etymology (ἔτυμον) of the name. Some, as he says, would derive *Filastrius* in Latin from *filiastro*, a word used in later centuries for “stepson,” with only a slight alteration; but Fabricius himself does not find this origin sufficiently convincing. Rather, he judges truer the derivation by which Greek *Philastrius* means “lover of the stars.”

Certainly this man is also called *Filiaster* by Peter de Natalibus, bishop of Equilio, *Catalogue of the Saints*, book VI, chapter 115. Perotti, moreover, says this concerning the definition of the word in his *Cornucopiae*, p. CIX:

> Catullus is a proper name, from which comes *Catulaster*, just as from Antonius comes *Antoniaster*. Names of this kind ending in *-aster*, *-astra*, and *-astrum* are not diminutives, as some suppose, but rather imitative.

And shortly after:

> *Filiaster*, which some use for “stepson,” does not mean “a little son,” but one who imitates a son; and *Parasitaster* does not mean “a little parasite”—for the comic poet would not call a little parasite *Parasitaster*—but one who imitates a parasite.

3. We do not know Philastrius’s lineage any more than his native country. Gaudentius, comparing him with Abraham and, by examples of faith and works, calling him Abraham’s son, writes as follows: [Note: Sermon on the Life and Death of Blessed Philastrius, p. 371.]

> Believing God with fullest faith, he too departed from his own land, from his kindred, and from his father’s house, and followed the word of God, stripped of all the encumbrances of the world.

And shortly afterwards:

> Traversing almost the entire circuit of the Roman world, he preached the word of the Lord, proving himself a worthy imitator of the apostle Paul.

Great indeed is this praise of Philastrius, by which Gaudentius seems in some fashion to rank him with Abraham and Paul. Yet although he says, “he departed from his own land, from his kindred, and from his father’s house,” when he seems to come closer to the matter itself, he adds nothing further by which he might show us Philastrius’s native country or lineage. Rampertus says nothing about this, [Note: Sermon on the Translation of Philastrius, found at p. 387.] nor does anyone else. Rather, in that rhythm or poem on Philastrius which we mentioned a little above, and which is certainly older than the ninth century, it is expressly said that even then Philastrius’s origin was wholly unknown. These are the words of that rhythm: [Note: P. 377.]

> Of what towers [or city] this man was born,  
> None among us remembers or knows;  
> But this we know: that he followed  
> Blessed Abraham.

What grounds, then, led Ughelli to call him a Spaniard [Note: Vol. IV, *Italia Sacra*, col. 525, Venetian edition.], or Cave to call him perhaps Italian by race, [Note: P. 176.] I do not at all perceive. For I cannot believe that something was known to Ughelli or Cave which Gaudentius passed over and which was in no way established in the eighth or ninth century.

Baronius, moreover, recounts Philastrius’s deeds under A.D. 369, no. 27. There, employing Gaudentius’s testimony, he places among Philastrius’s chief praises the fact that at Milan he resisted Auxentius, defender of the Arian heresy, with unconquered constancy; and that for this reason he was beaten with whips and stoutly contended for the defense of the Catholic faith. Gaudentius’s testimony is as follows:

> For, filled with the Holy Spirit—he speaks of Philastrius—he fought with such vigor of faith not only against pagans and Jews, but also against every heresy, and especially against the raging Arian perfidy of that time, that he was even subjected to beatings and bore in his body the marks of our Lord Jesus Christ. For he was formerly a worthy guardian of the Lord’s flock in the city of Milan, resisting the Arian Auxentius before blessed Ambrose was chosen. [Note: Sermon on the Life and Death of Blessed Philastrius, p. 372.]

Gaudentius recounted these things about Philastrius to the people of Brescia, as he himself says, fourteen years after Philastrius’s death—thus in A.D. 401, if Philastrius’s κοιμησις (*koimēsis*, “falling asleep” or death) and Gaudentius’s succession are, according to the common reckoning of writers, placed in the year 387, as most, indeed nearly all, do. Samuel Basnage, called Flotte-Manville, however, places Philastrius’s death in 386, [Note: Vol. III, *Annals*, p. 106, no. 10. See below in this Preface, no. 9.] and there records in his *Annals* Gaudentius’s splendid eulogy of Philastrius as well.

Gaudentius’s testimony certainly proves that Philastrius’s conflicts must be assigned to the period before Ambrose’s elevation to the Milanese see. Hence Baronius recounts them under A.D. 369, [Note: No. 27.] when—after Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, had been compelled to depart Milan through Auxentius’s intrigues, an event which Pagi rightly observes occurred in 365 [Note: *Critique* on A.D. 369, no. 2.]—Baronius conjectures that Philastrius remained in Milan after Hilary’s departure in order, by whatever means he could, to keep the Catholic people faithful to their duty. [Note: Baronius, A.D. 369, no. 27.] Therefore, since Ambrose’s election falls in the year 374, [Note: Baronius, A.D. 374, nos. 9 and 10.] if Baronius’s conjecture is approved, it plainly follows that the protection and defense of the Church of Milan must be assigned to Philastrius within the decade from 365 to 374. For Gaudentius’s words make this interval quite clear: “He was formerly a worthy guardian of the Lord’s flock in the city of Milan, resisting the Arian Auxentius, BEFORE BLESSED AMBROSE WAS CHOSEN.”

In the same rhythm on Philastrius, the things he suffered at Milan for the safeguarding of the Catholic faith are denoted in these verses: [Note: P. 378.]

> Beloved minister of the eternal King,  
> He always declared the teachings of the perfidious sect—  
> And still more those of the Arians—  
> To be false everywhere,  
> Opposing them as it were with inward conviction.  
>
> With diligent scourges they struck his limbs,  
> So that, beaten, they often poured forth  
> Running blood of rosy colour.

And shortly afterwards:

> But against you, wretched, ignorant Auxentius,  
> He stood firm in the strength of faith.

4. That Philastrius was already invested with episcopal dignity when he exposed himself to so many and such great perils for the Church of Milan may be inferred even from this: it would have been of very little use for a private individual, in a matter of such consequence, to offer himself as the foremost soldier and leader of the Catholic cause. This is especially so because resistance had to be made to Auxentius, the Arian bishop, who, after Dionysius had been driven from the Milanese see, [Note: Baronius, A.D. 355, nos. 17, 19, 30.] relied on the authority of Emperor Valentinian—for he had deceived him by his frauds and tricks—and dared and obtained everything; Hilary himself having been ordered to leave Milan as the supposed author of disturbances and discord. [Note: Baronius, A.D. 369, no. 19.]

Furthermore, the other defenders of the Catholic cause who had most to do with Auxentius were distinguished by episcopal office: namely, Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli; Hilary of Poitiers; and Evagrius of Antioch. Although Baronius confesses that he does not know who this Evagrius was, [Note: Ibid., no. 28.] Pagi clearly shows that he was bishop of Antioch. [Note: *Critique* on A.D. 389, nos. 9 and 10.]

Likewise, Gaudentius’s words by which Philastrius is called in the city of Milan “A WORTHY GUARDIAN OF THE LORD’S FLOCK” openly show that he was a bishop, since the care of the people is entrusted only to bishops and they alone can be called worthy guardians of the Lord’s flock. Nor should it move us that it may seem unworthy of a bishop to be subjected to scourges and beatings; for we read that Eusebius also, bishop of Vercelli, was punished in the same manner by the Arians under Emperor Constantius in the affair of Athanasius. The Acts of the Passion, or Life, of St Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli—produced by Ughelli from a very ancient manuscript of the monastery of Nonantola in his account of the bishops of Vercelli [Note: Vol. IV, *Italia Sacra*, col. 749, Venetian edition.]—teach us this. They contain: [Note: Ibid., col. 756.]

> Then the Arians rushed upon him, snatched blessed Eusebius from the company of the bishops, and, beating him violently with lashes, left him half dead.

And shortly afterwards:

> Again, after he had been beaten with lashes, they asked whether he would now confess in agreement.

Athanasius shows this to have been a customary crime of the Arians in his letter *To the Solitaries*:

> The Eusebians—that is, the Arians—therefore send letters to Philagrius and direct that he go as quickly as possible with Gregory into Egypt; and immediately thereafter bishops were beaten and bound in harsh chains.

Then shortly after, in the same place: “Alas, how many bishops there were cut to pieces with rods!” And below, speaking of the same Arians:

> Liberius [the pope] sent Eutropius the presbyter and Hilary the deacon to Caesar. One of them, namely the presbyter, they sent into exile; but the other, stripped of his clothes, they cut his back to pieces with lashes, and after flogging him made him an exile.

Sulpicius narrates that Martin of Tours was publicly beaten with rods when the Arian heresy had spread throughout the whole world, and especially through Illyricum.
