[Note: *Life of Blessed Martin*, ch. 6.] Felix the abbot, together with Fulgentius, afterwards bishop of Ruspe, are said by the author of the *Life of Blessed Fulgentius*, chapters 10 and 11, to have been beaten with lashes at the order of a certain Arian presbyter. [Note: *Library of the Fathers*, vol. IX, col. 2.]

5. The time when Philastrius began to hold the episcopate of Brescia is not clear. The matters just stated may persuade us that before the year 365, when Hilary was ordered to leave Milan, he held episcopal rank. Hence Baronius himself, when discussing the contests conducted at Milan by bishops against Auxentius, joins Philastrius with Eusebius of Vercelli and Evagrius of Antioch: [Note: “Although Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, Evagrius, and Philastrius of Brescia often caused him—that is, Auxentius—trouble and strongly harassed him.” Baronius, A.D. 369, no. 6.] Indeed, shortly afterwards, recounting Auxentius’s outrages by which he harassed the bishops of the Catholic Church, he expressly calls Philastrius a bishop: [Note: “Auxentius insults the holy bishops of the Catholic Church, and among others harasses Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, and likewise Philastrius, bishop of Brescia.” Ibid., no. 27.]

That which may seem to oppose this opinion must nevertheless be considered. In the Council of Aquileia, held in 381, the bishops are listed in order: Limenius of Vercelli is fourth, while Anemius of Sirmium is fifth. Since it is certain that these became bishops long after 365, one might conclude that Philastrius cannot have been older in the episcopate than Limenius and Anemius, because he is listed eighth at the same council.

For the discipline was that bishops at councils, both in sitting and in subscribing, should observe the order in which they had been raised to the episcopate. Gregory openly states this in book IX, letter 108 of the Benedictine edition, letter 113 in other editions, where, after preserving the metropolitan’s place and honour, he adds:

> We decree that the other bishops shall observe their own places according to the date of their ordination, whether in sitting in council, in subscribing, or in any other matter.

The First Council of Braga, canon 24, says:

> While preserving the primacy of the metropolitan bishop, the other bishops, according to the date of their ordination, shall yield one another their places in sitting. [Note: Baronius recognizes this same practice of ecclesiastical discipline under A.D. 451, no. 16; Pagi under A.D. 402, no. 25; Peter de Marca, *Dissertation on Primacies*, no. 80; Noris, Dissertation 5 *On Synods*, ch. 10.]

That Limenius and Anemius were made bishops long after 365 is shown by the fact that Limenius was appointed bishop of the Church of Vercelli after Eusebius’s death, and Baronius places Eusebius’s death in 371. [Note: Baronius, A.D. 371, no. 116.] Anemius, moreover, must be placed either in the very year 380, immediately preceding the Council of Aquileia in 381, as Baronius thinks, [Note: Baronius, A.D. 380, no. 18; Tillemont agrees, vol. X, *Life of Ambrose*, p. 122.] or at least after 374, the year assigned to Ambrose’s election to the Milanese see, on the authority of Paulinus in the *Life of Ambrose*. For Ambrose was present at Anemius’s ordination at Sirmium, and there restrained the Arians, who, relying on Justina’s influence, stirred up disturbances and tried to drive Ambrose himself from the church.

But although these things are so, the considerations that lead us to believe Philastrius was made bishop much earlier than Limenius and Anemius are of greater weight. Gaudentius’s authority is evident, and the words quoted above can apply only to a bishop. Nor, as we have already said, could the cause of the Catholic Church amid so many storms have been suitably undertaken by a private person, considering the magnitude of the matter, nor defended with sufficient dignity by anyone other than a bishop.

One must also seriously consider whether so many bishops subscribing to the Council of Aquileia after Limenius and Anemius—there are nearly twenty-eight—can be thought to have been created and installed in their sees in so short a time, so that one must suppose they subscribed in due order after Limenius and Anemius, as men older in the episcopate; especially if Anemius was made bishop of Sirmium in 380, only one year before the Council of Aquileia, as Baronius held. It is certainly sufficiently clear that Philastrius was older in the episcopate than Anemius, since Anemius was ordained bishop of Sirmium in Ambrose’s presence, whereas Philastrius, before blessed Ambrose was chosen, is called by Gaudentius “A WORTHY GUARDIAN OF THE LORD’S FLOCK” in the city of Milan while resisting the Arian Auxentius. [Note: Sermon on the Life and Death of Blessed Philastrius, p. 372.]

It remains, then, that in the subscriptions to that council the exact order prescribed by ecclesiastical rule was not observed. One proof may be that Philastrius is counted eighth in the list of bishops prefixed to the council, but appears eleventh at the beginning of the Acts; and the Gallic delegates Constantius of Orange, Proculus of Marseilles, and Justus of Lyons are placed among the bishops in one order in the list and another at the beginning of the Acts. Learned men have long observed [Note: In the Benedictine edition of Gregory, vol. II, p. 1014. See Peter de Marca, *Dissertation on Primacies*, no. 80.] that nothing is more disordered than the sessions and subscriptions not only of bishops but even of metropolitans in synods; consequently, no certainty can be drawn from them when their published Acts are consulted. Augustine, in Letter 217, teaches us that this was sometimes also the case in circular letters, with bishops subscribing them in a disturbed order. Complaining to Bishop Victorinus of this very matter, he says:

> Then it was written to the Numidians themselves in such a disordered and neglected order that I found my own name in third place, although I know after how many bishops I was made bishop; a practice quite injurious to others and invidious toward me.

6. That what has thus far been said about the Council of Aquileia and the names of the bishops listed there may become still clearer, it seemed good to set before the reader’s eyes the beginning of the council itself, from which everyone may more easily discern for himself how great was the disorder in the names of the bishops assigned to this council.

## Council of Aquileia

[Note: Vol. III of the Councils, Royal edition, 1644, p. 386; vol. II of Labbe, p. 1164, Venetian edition.]

Held in the time of Pope Damasus I.

### Bishops who attended this Council

Valerian, bishop of Aquileia.  
Ambrose, bishop of Milan.  
Eusebius, bishop of Bologna.  
Limenius, bishop of Vercelli.  
Armenius [read: Anemius], bishop of Sirmium in Illyricum.  
Sabinus, bishop of Piacenza.  
Abundantius, bishop of Trent.  
PHILASTER, bishop of Brescia.  
Constantius, bishop of Orange (*Arausio*).  
Theodorus, bishop of Octodorus [read: Octodurus].  
Domninus, bishop of Grenoble.  
Amantius, bishop of Nice.  
Maximus, bishop of Emona.  
Basilianus [otherwise Bassianus], bishop of Lodi.  
Proculus, bishop of Marseilles.  
Heliodorus, bishop of Altinum.  
Felix, bishop of Jadera.  
Eventius, bishop of Citinium [otherwise Tinium; read: Ticinium].  
Exuperantius, bishop of Dertona.  
Diogenes, bishop of Genoa.  
Constantius, bishop of Siscia, legate of the Gauls.  
Justus, legate of the Gauls.  
Felix, legate of the Africans.  
Numidius, legate of the Africans.  
Evagrius, presbyter and legate.  
Artemius, Almachius, Januarius, Jovinus, Macedonius, Cassianus, Marcellus, Eustathius, Maximus, Chromatius, presbyters.

If you remove the last of these, Chromatius, who is called not a bishop but a presbyter, and also Evagrius, who is called twenty-fifth in number a presbyter and legate, thirty-three bishops remain, although at the very outset of the council they are incorrectly said to have numbered thirty-two:

> At this council, Palladius and Secundianus, Arian bishops, together with a certain presbyter Attalus, are condemned by thirty-two Italian, Gallic, and Pannonian bishops, in the presence of Gallic and African delegates.

This numerical notation, corruptly prefixed to the beginning of the council, deceived Baronius [Note: A.D. 381, no. 82.] and Basnage as well, [Note: Vol. III, *Annals*, p. 82, no. 16.] who count only thirty-two bishops. And indeed only thirty-two appear at the beginning of the Acts, which we shall set down immediately; but Eventius of Citinium, or Ticinium, [Note: Fabricius certainly added him when he presented the Acts of the Council of Aquileia in the testimonies concerning Philastrius.] must be added there, since he is inscribed eighteenth in the list of bishops.

All of this number were bishops, although the names of their sees are not added for Justus, Felix, Numidius, and the others following Evagrius. For at the beginning of the Acts, where the names are listed anew, Evagrius and Chromatius the presbyters are omitted, and at the end of the list it is said: “Januarius … Maximus, Macedonius, Cassianus, Marcellus, and Eustathius, bishops.” Tillemont also rightly observes [Note: Vol. X, *Life of St Ambrose*, p. 129.] that the names of the last nine, to whom neither the title bishop nor the name of a see is assigned, are not only intermingled with bishops’ names at the beginning of the Acts, but are also included among bishops by that general closing formula; and that one of them, Januarius, is designated by the title bishop when he delivers his judgment. [Note: Vol. II of Labbe, p. 1176.]

The Acts of the council proceed as follows:

> In the consulship of Syagrius and Eucherius, most illustrious men, on the Nones of September, while Valerian of the city of Aquileia, Ambrose, Eusebius, Limenius, Anemius, Sabinus, Abundantius, Artemius, Constantius, Justus, PHILASTER, Constantius, Theodorus, Almachius, Domninus, Amantius, Maximus, Felix, Basilianus, Numidius, Januarius, Proculus, Heliodorus, Jovinus, Felix, Exuperantius, Diogenes, Maximus, Macedonius, Cassianus, Marcellus, and Eustathius, bishops, were seated with the bishops in the church at Aquileia: Bishop Ambrose said.

Thus far are the names of bishops listed at the beginning of the Acts. If they are compared with the list prefixed to the Acts, it will immediately appear how disorderedly these names have been set down, so great and such is the discrepancy and disagreement between the two lists. For whereas Constantius of Orange is placed after Philastrius in the list, Constantius is again placed before Philastrius at the beginning of the Acts, together with Justus, who was the Gallic delegate. Artemius also precedes them, though he lacks the name of a see and is listed in the catalogue after Constantius and Justus, with several bishops intervening, as twenty-sixth in order, whereas at the beginning of the Acts he is read as eighth.

Again, that same Justus, legate of the Gauls, who precedes Philastrius as tenth in number at the beginning of the Acts, appears in the list after Philastrius, with thirteen bishops intervening: fourteenth in the list, but twenty-second in rank. Who could ever establish or infer anything certain from such variety and inconsistency?

Furthermore, something must be noted that, so far as I know, no one has observed up to this time: Constantius, bishop of Siscia, twenty-first in the list, is altogether wrongly called a legate of the Gauls, when this office was rather held by the other Constantius, of Orange, the ninth. For Siscia is, in Ptolemy, a city of Pannonia in the region of Savia; in Pliny it is Siscia, [Note: Pliny, bk. III, ch. 25.] and in Strabo Syscia; formerly it was an episcopal see under the archbishop of Kalocsa. Therefore a Pannonian bishop had nothing whatsoever to do with the Gauls, such that he should have attended the Council of Aquileia as their delegate.

There were likewise three delegates of the Gauls at this council, though only two appear in the list: Constantius of Orange, Proculus of Marseilles, and Justus of Lyons, from the Viennensis, Narbonensis, and Lugdunensis provinces of Gaul. Baronius [Note: A.D. 381, nos. 82, 84.] and Binius [Note: Notes on the Council of Aquileia, vol. II of Labbe, col. 1182, Venetian edition.] rightly state this, as do Sirmond [Note: Ibid., col. 1178: Constantius is called legate of the Gauls in the Acts of the council, as is Justus at col. 1167; Proculus, however, in the letter to the bishops of Gaul at col. 1178.] and the Sammarthani.

But the names of cities also contain some error. Theodorus, the tenth bishop in the list, called bishop of Octodorus, should rather be called bishop of Octodurus, from the town Octodurus in Narbonensian Gaul, commonly Martigny. And Eventius of Citinium, eighteenth in the list—for whom *Tiniensis* is entered in the margin—must certainly be written *Ticinensis*, or *Ticiniensis*, as Hardouin reads from manuscripts. [Note: Vol. I of the Councils, col. 837.] For although Tinia, commonly Tine and called Kerka by the Dalmatians, a city of Bosnia, was subject to Anemius, primate of Illyricum, who attended the Council of Aquileia, nevertheless one must understand here not a bishop of Tinium or Ceneta, as Ughelli thought, [Note: Vol. V, *Italia Sacra*, in the bishops of Ceneta, col. 172, Venetian edition.] but Eventius or Juventius of Ticinum, as the most diligent Tillemont determined after others. [Note: Vol. X, note 14 to the *Life of St Ambrose*, p. 738.]

Chifflet [Note: Notes on Vigilius, p. 65.] and Hardouin [Note: Notes on the Council of Aquileia, p. 1164, Venetian edition.] also warned that an error entered into the date on which the synodal proceeding was held. Reading manuscripts, they give “the third day before the Nones of September,” which was Friday, in place of the “Nones of September” found in the Acts. For the latter day was Sunday, not especially suited to so lengthy a disputation of bishops; moreover, it is entirely incompatible with Sunday that Palladius, the Arian bishop, said in the council: [Note: P. 1173.] “I shall not answer unless the authorities come after the Lord’s day.” And so much thus far concerning the Council of Aquileia.

7. Splendid are the things which Gaudentius records concerning Philastrius’s preaching: [Note: Sermon on the Life and Death of Blessed Philastrius, p. 372.]

> When, through the laying on of the hands of the presbytery, he had been chosen as a steward of the divine word, [Note: See our notes on this passage of Gaudentius, ibid.] he did not at all permit the grace of God to be neglected; but traversing almost the entire circuit of the Roman world, he preached the word of the Lord, proving himself a worthy imitator of the apostle Paul.

He who says “almost the entire circuit of the Roman world” surely means almost the entire world which was then subject to Roman rule. Thus Ovid, *Fasti*, book I:

> When Jupiter, from his citadel, looks upon the whole world,  
> He has nothing but the Roman world to protect.

Perhaps with this passage of Ovid in view, Namatianus, in his *Itinerary*, says—in flattery, as the distinguished Barth notes [Note: Notes on the *Itinerary* of Rutilius Namatianus, p. 180.]—that the entire οἰκουμένη (*oikoumenē*, inhabited world) was subject to Roman rule, addressing Rome in these verses:

> For you extend gifts equal to the rays of the sun  
> Wherever the surrounding Ocean flows.  
> Phoebus himself, who contains all things, revolves for you,
[Col. 1064B] He likewise keeps among your own [possessions] horses bred from your own [stock]. Certainly, that edict issued by Caesar Augustus, that the whole world should be enrolled [Note: [Col. 1064D] Luke II.], meant nothing other than the Roman dominion under the name of the whole world; Pseudo-Hegesippus also called it the Roman world in Book II of *On the Destruction of Jerusalem*, chapter 9: “The world of lands, which is enclosed and defined by the Roman Empire, is called by most people the Roman world.”

That Philastrius remained at Rome for some time is attested by Gaudentius himself [Note: [Col. 1064D] P. 372.]: “Having also stayed at Rome for no short time, he won many to the faith by both public and private disputation.” From these words of Gaudentius Ughellus perhaps inferred that Augustine became acquainted with Philastrius at Rome, and that from Philastrius’ public as well as private discussions on sacred matters he adopted new sentiments of Christian piety; this Ughellus expressly affirms in his account of Philastrius [Note: [Col. 1064D] Vol. IV of *Italia Sacra*, col. 525.], even citing Augustine himself and Gaudentius as witnesses, although neither of them says a single word about a matter so important. Surely neither Augustine himself nor Gaudentius, Philastrius’ successor, ought to have passed it over in silence in that often-cited Sermon on the Life and Death of Blessed Philastrius.

Augustine’s testimony concerning Philastrius has long been known to all. His words are these [Note: [Col. 1064D] Augustine, Epistle to Quodvultdeus.]: “A certain Philastrius, bishop of Brescia, whom I myself also saw at Milan together with Saint Ambrose.” From this passage of Augustine it is plainly established that Philastrius was known to Augustine at Milan only by sight, and that no intimacy existed between Augustine and Philastrius. Thus these are, as we also said in our annotations on Gaudentius [Note: [Col. 1064D] P. 372.], more the prophecies of idle minds [Col. 1064D] than conjectures.

Similar is what some persons report of Philastrius on the occasion of this Roman stay: namely, that he was graciously received by Pope Damasus and taught publicly at Rome [Col. 1065A]. This is found both in the Lessons of a certain manuscript Breviary of the Monastery of the Nuns of St Catherine at Brescia, reported in volume IV of the *Acta Sanctorum* for June, p. 383, and in Malvetius’ *Chronicle* [Note: [Col. 1065D] Vol. XIV of *Rerum Italicarum*, p. 809.], distinction 4, chapter 3. Ferrarius likewise reported it in his *Catalogue of the Saints of Italy* for 18 July, in these words: “At Rome, liberally treated by Pope Damasus, he taught publicly.” But since Gaudentius has absolutely nothing on this point, I do not know how safely it can be affirmed, especially since it is not very probable that Philastrius was at Rome under Damasus; rather, about the time of Damasus, who began to hold the see in 367 [Note: [Col. 1065D] Pagi places it in 366.], he was involved at Milan amid the conflicts of the Arians, as we have seen [Note: [Col. 1065D] See above, no. 3.].

Whether, however, he could have been present at the Council of Nicaea—as Malvetius reports in his *Chronicle*, distinction 4, chapter 2, and Capreolus after him in Book III of the *History of Brescia*—is not without reason doubted by Ferrarius in the annotations to the same catalogue under 18 July [Col. 1065B]. For since the Council of Nicaea was held in 325, if Philastrius had sat in it, he must then have been very young [Note: [Col. 1065D] The same is said of Sabinus, bishop of Piacenza, in the *Acta Sanctorum* for January, vol. II, p. 163. See Tillemont, vol. X, note 5 on the Life of St Ambrose, p. 744.], whereas fifty-six full years later, namely in 381, he is found also to have attended the Council of Aquileia.

8. After Philastrius had passed through the villages and hamlets of various regions, Gaudentius says [Note: [Col. 1065D] Sermon on the Life and Death of Blessed Philastrius, p. 372.], “the faithful disciple of Christ never ceased to preach the word of God.” At last he settled at Brescia, “that the Apostolic man might have some fruit also in this city, as among the other nations.” Let us therefore hear from Gaudentius himself what, having now become bishop, he bestowed upon this city. “After those circuits,” says Gaudentius [Note: [Col. 1065D] Ibid.], “so salutary to many souls, Brescia—once untutored [Col. 1065C] but eager for instruction—received him: ignorant indeed of spiritual knowledge, yet praiseworthy in its zeal for learning. Like a good husbandman, he immediately cut down from their deepest roots the dreadful forest of diverse error; bending eagerly over the plough of teaching, he overturned with all his strength the virgin soil, and by unceasing furrows turned the neglected ground into fruitful new fields, abundantly implanting in its bosom the seeds of life-giving commandments.”

Certainly nothing is said here except that the discipline and morals of Brescia were reformed and improved by Philastrius; although elsewhere Gaudentius himself says that the Church of Brescia was founded in the Faith by Philastrius [Note: [Col. 1065D] Sermon on His Own Ordination, p. 334.]: “After that most learned voice of Philastrius, my father of venerable memory, which, flowing forth abundantly through the grace of the Holy Spirit, founded this Church in the Faith of the adorable Trinity.”

Some weight is added to this statement of Gaudentius—which seems to indicate that the Church of Brescia was then first established by Philastrius—by the fact that other Churches in this district, even into the fourth century, [Col. 1066A] lacked their own bishop: namely Vercelli, Novara, Ivrea, and Tortona [Note: [Col. 1065D] Ughellus, vol. IV. See Tillemont, vol. VII, note 2 on the Life of St Eusebius, p. 772.]. Indeed, that at that time several Churches were governed simultaneously by one and the same bishop is taught by the Letter addressed by Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, to the peoples of Vercelli, Novara, Hipporegia—read Eporedia—and also Tortona [Note: [Col. 1066D] In Baronius, A.D. 356, no. 92.].

But since, among the other subscriptions of the Fathers of the Council of Sardica, held in 347, there occurs [Note: [Col. 1066D] Labbe, vol. II, p. 688.] the signature of a bishop of Brescia in this form, “Ursacius, from Italy, of Brescia” (whom our writers call Ursicinus); and since moreover Rampertus, bishop of Brescia, who lived in the ninth century, expressly calls Philastrius the SEVENTH bishop of Brescia [Note: [Col. 1066D] Sermon on the Translation of Philastrius, p. 391. See the Preface to Rampertus, p. 383.], it is altogether necessary that the Church of Brescia had several bishops before Philastrius [Col. 1066B].

What is certain is that, in Philastrius’ time, considerable remnants of idols and paganism still existed at Brescia. Therefore he frequently attacks them in a sharper style [Note: [Col. 1066D] Ch. 61, where he treats of the Manichaeans.], those “who worship demons, adore the elements, invoke the names of gods and goddesses like pagans . . . and do not cease to enslave many souls by falsehood and brutish shamefulness”; and elsewhere [Note: [Col. 1066D] Ch. 109.]: “The utterly depraved will of men preferred to devise idols for the purpose of committing its own crime and shamefulness, so that their worshippers might possess unrestrained licence to do evil.”

Moreover, not only in Philastrius’ time but also in the time of Gaudentius, who succeeded him, worshippers of idols were still rather numerous in the city of Brescia itself and in its surrounding territory. Gaudentius himself censures them in more than one passage, especially in Sermon 13, where he says [Note: [Col. 1066D] P. 319.]: [Col. 1066C] “Do you suppose that the lukewarm and negligent Christian loves God, when he permits idols to be worshipped on his estates, when he allows the shrine of a demon and the altar of the devil to stand as an insult to God?” Thus the Brescian writers must by no means be heard when they maintain that the whole city of Brescia had already been converted to Christ’s faith under Bishop Apollonius, from the second century of Christ onward, as Ughellus reports [Note: [Col. 1066D] Vol. IV, col. 524.]. For two or more centuries after Apollonius, remnants of paganism and temples of idols still survived, as we long ago observed in our annotations on Gaudentius [Note: [Col. 1066D] P. 319.].

9. Philastrius had in the Church of Brescia two distinguished pupils in piety and doctrine: Benivolus and Gaudentius. We have spoken more fully of Benivolus [Col. 1066D] in the Preface prefixed to Gaudentius’ Sermons [Note: [Col. 1066D] No. 9, p. 190.]. Baronius treats at greater length, under A.D. 386 [Col. 1067A] [Note: [Col. 1067D] Nos. 5 ff.], of his noble act in resisting the commands of the Empress Justina, refusing to dictate a law contrary to the Catholic faith. In that year, when Justina favoured the Arians, so many and such great disturbances were stirred up against the Catholics at Milan that Ambrose’s constancy was almost overwhelmed by the violence and factions of the heretics.

Benivolus, then, trained in Philastrius’ discipline, presided over the archives of memorials; and when he was instructed to dictate imperial decrees against the faith of the Fathers, being offered also a higher rank of office if he did so, he voluntarily renounced the honours of the court, adding these words [Note: [Col. 1067D] Rufinus, Book XI, ch. 16.]: “Why do you promise me a higher rank as the reward of impiety? Take away even this rank which I possess; only let my conscience of faith remain uninjured.” Saying this, he cast his belt at the feet of those issuing the impious commands.

Gaudentius attributes Benivolus’ outstanding deed to Philastrius’ instruction and teaching. For Benivolus was still at that time [Col. 1067B] a catechumen, and consequently had been formed by Philastrius in the precepts of the Catholic faith. Gaudentius therefore later addresses him as a Christian flourishing in piety [Note: [Col. 1067D] Preface to Benivolus, p. 218.]: “Nor is it surprising that today you conduct yourself thus in the fear of the Lord, since, before you had received the grace of baptism, you fought so for the truth of the heavenly faith that you gave proof of a constancy so great, having been imbued with the admirable teachings of our father Philastrius, a man wholly apostolic.”

Gaudentius himself everywhere calls Philastrius father: for example, in the Sermon on His Own Ordination [Note: [Col. 1067D] P. 334.], “After that most learned voice of Philastrius, my father of venerable memory”; and in the Preface to Benivolus [Note: [Col. 1067D] P. 218.], “having been imbued with the admirable teachings of our father Philastrius, a man wholly apostolic.” So too in the Sermon on the Life and Death of Blessed Philastrius, where he calls himself the least part [Col. 1067C] of the care that Philastrius expended in instructing the Church of Brescia [Note: [Col. 1067D] P. 373.]: “But I am the least part of him.”

Indeed, Gaudentius everywhere reflects Philastrius’ teaching. What he treats more distinctly in Sermon 19 concerning Christ’s divinity occurs here and there in Philastrius in almost the same words. Gaudentius says [Note: [Col. 1067D] P. 357.]: “In Christ there is a double substance, one his own and the other ours; that is, one of God and the other of man.” Philastrius says [Note: [Col. 1067D] Ch. 127.]: “Although his generation is twofold, one unlimited, of divinity; the other temporal, of incarnation through the Virgin.” Gaudentius says [Note: [Col. 1067D] P. 360.]: “His Passion was undergone not in the divinity, which is impassible, but in his humanity; and it came to the aid of the whole stricken world.” Philastrius says [Note: [Col. 1067D] Ch. 92.]: “He therefore suffered in passible flesh, not in divinity, which is naturally impassible.” Gaudentius says [Col. 1067D] [Note: [Col. 1067D] P. 364.]: “He remained equal to the Father, as he had always been.” Philastrius says [Note: [Col. 1067D] Ch. 127.]: “We do not fail to know that he remains with the Father for ever, and has always remained [with him].”

Likewise, in Tractate 3 Gaudentius says that Christ’s preaching was completed in only [Col. 1068A] one year [Note: [Col. 1068D] P. 249.]: “From the Baptism which he underwent for our sake in the Jordan until the day of his Passion, the period of one year is fulfilled.” Although several ancient Fathers held this view, as we noted on that passage of Gaudentius, Gaudentius nevertheless seems to have derived it from Philastrius. For Philastrius says in chapter 106 [Note: [Col. 1068D] P. 78 (of this edition, col. 1220).]: “The Lord commanded that only those things which he did and taught in one year should be written down.”

Likewise notable is Philastrius’ teaching [Note: [Col. 1068D] Chs. 136, 150, 453, and elsewhere. See Fabricius’ notes there.] concerning the threefold state of human nature: namely, that of Commandment, Law, and Grace. He calls *Commandment* the time before the Law of Moses, in which the first parents and the patriarchs lived according to the unwritten law of nature. Gaudentius expressly repeats the same thing in more than one passage, as in Tractate 10: “The law of commandment is” [Note: [Col. 1068D] P. 298.], [Col. 1068B] “‘From every fruit of the tree which is in Paradise you shall eat for food; but from this one you shall not eat’; and whatever else the Lord is known to have commanded by word alone before Moses.” Especially in Tractate 8 [Note: [Col. 1068D] P. 273.]: “The first day, therefore, was under COMMANDMENT, from Adam to Moses; the second day was under the LAW of Moses; the third day is under the GRACE of the Saviour.”

Gaudentius also frequently employs words distinctive of Philastrius, such as *positio* (“position”), *incorporatio* (“incorporation”), *suballigaturae* (“bindings beneath”), and *umbratiliter* (“in shadow-like fashion”). This will be evident to anyone comparing the vocabulary of both writers, especially their exotic terms. Thus you may clearly recognize Philastrius as Gaudentius’ master not only in thought but also in expression.

10. In what particular year Philastrius became known to Augustine at Milan is uncertain. Augustine writes [Col. 1068C] [Note: [Col. 1068D] Epistle to Quodvultdeus.] that he saw him at Milan, where he was staying with Saint Ambrose. Now Augustine himself was sent from Rome to Milan by Symmachus, prefect of the city, before the consulship of Bauto, which fell in 385 [Note: [Col. 1068D] Book III against the Letters of Petilian, ch. 25; Book V of the *Confessions*, ch. 13.]. But he could not have moved there except in the thirtieth year of his life—that is, 384—since at the age of twenty-nine he heard the Manichaean Faustus at Carthage [Note: [Col. 1068D] Book V of the *Confessions*, ch. 3]. Having received baptism, he then returned to Africa and departed Milan in the thirty-third year of his life [Note: [Col. 1068D] Book IX of the *Confessions*, ch. 11], namely in 387. It follows that Philastrius became known to Augustine in one or another of the years from 384 to 387.

Since there is a certain correspondence and concurrence between the dates of Augustine, Ambrose, and Philastrius, from which some light may in some degree be shed on Philastrius’ affairs [Col. 1068D], it will not be inappropriate to set before the reader, in the following diagram, several corresponding dates.

[Note: [Col. 1069A] The following three texts, headed “ST AUGUSTINE,” “ST AMBROSE,” and “ST PHILASTRIUS,” are printed in parallel in Migne.]

### ST AUGUSTINE

[Col. 1069]

Born on the Ides of November, A.D. 354. In 383, at the age of twenty-nine, he hears the Manichaean Faustus at Carthage.

Sent from Rome to Milan before Bauto’s consulship in A.D. 384, at the age of thirty. On the Kalends of January, when Bauto, the consul, opened the year, he delivers at Milan a panegyrical oration in A.D. 385, at the age of thirty-one [Note: [Col. 1069] Book III against the Letters of Petilian, ch. 25.].

When persecution is stirred up against Ambrose, he is present at Milan in A.D. 386, at the age of thirty-two; in that same year he sees there the relics of the holy martyrs Protasius and Gervasius discovered [Note: [Col. 1069] Book IX of the *Confessions*, ch. 7; Sermon 39 *On Various Subjects*. See Puricelli, *Nazarian Dissertation*, ch. 43; Noris, 50, *Somnia*, 18.].

At Milan he is baptized at Easter in A.D. 387, at the age of thirty-three; then, departing from Milan, when he reached Ostia on the Tiber, he was bereaved of his mother [Note: [Col. 1069] Book IX of the *Confessions*, ch. 11. See Noris, 50, *Somnia*, 49.].

### ST AMBROSE

[Col. 1069]

In A.D. 381 he attends the Council of Aquileia together with Philastrius [Note: [Col. 1069] *Acts of the Council of Aquileia* in Labbe, vol. II, p. 1164, Venice edition.].

In A.D. 386 the Empress Justina raises disturbances against Ambrose at Milan [Note: [Col. 1069] Baronius, A.D. 386; Noris, 50, *Somnia*, 18.].

In A.D. 397 Ambrose dies [Note: [Col. 1069] Baronius, A.D. 397, no. 36; and Notes on the Martyrology, 4 April. See Tillemont, notes on the Life of St Ambrose, note 56, vol. X, p. 761.].

### ST PHILASTRIUS

[Col. 1070]

In A.D. 381 he attends the Council of Aquileia together with Ambrose [Note: [Col. 1070] *Acts of the Council of Aquileia*, Labbe, vol. II, p. 1164.].

In A.D. 386, or in the preceding or following year, he becomes known to Augustine in Ambrose’s presence.

In A.D. 387, according to the common opinion of writers—and certainly before Ambrose’s death—he has Gaudentius as his successor [Note: [Col. 1070] See what we add below, no. 9.].

[Col. 1069A] Certainly, if there were room for conjecture, I should not judge it implausible that Philastrius, while staying at Milan, became known to Augustine in the year when, after disturbances had broken out against Ambrose, Benivolus preferred the integrity of the Faith to courtly honours—in 386, as we said a little above [Note: [Col. 1069C] No. 9.]. Perhaps this was chiefly at Philastrius’ prompting and urging, since Gaudentius attributes Benivolus’ noble deed to him [Note: [Col. 1069C] Preface to Benivolus, p. 218.]. Or perhaps Philastrius stood by Ambrose in that same year when Ambrose transferred the relics of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius amid an unprecedentedly crowded public celebration [Note: [Col. 1069C] Ambrose, Epistle 85, on the discovery of the bodies of Sts Gervasius and Protasius.]. But since these matters are uncertain and ambiguous, we leave the whole question open.

Rampertus, bishop of Brescia, who lived in the ninth century, associates Philastrius with Ambrose as his companion in that Arian sedition [Note: [Col. 1069C] Sermon on the Translation of Philastrius, p. 399.]: “What manner of man did Ambrose, bishop of Milan, of most holy memory, understand him to be in the time of the wicked tempest of the Arians—a man whom he had as his colleague?” He then continues: “And how great did the neighbouring bishops consider his merit to be, if the fourth bishop of Bergamo took care to mention in the epitaph of the third bishop—that is, his predecessor, unless I am mistaken—that Ambrose, the bishop himself, had been ordained deacon by Philastrius?”

Certainly, if this epitaph of the third bishop of Bergamo survived, perhaps further information might be extracted from it highly suitable for illuminating the dates of Philastrius’ life. But since the inscription mentioned by Rampertus appears nowhere [Note: [Col. 1069C] Ughellus, vol. IV, col. 412; Coelestinus, Book XIII, *History of Bergamo*, ch. 4.], [Col. 1070A] we can derive no light from it.

11. Most modern writers place Philastrius’ death in A.D. 387: Labbe [Note: [Col. 1069C] *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. II, p. 212.], Vossius [Note: [Col. 1069C] Book III, *On Latin History*, ch. 2.], Moreri, and Cave [Note: [Col. 1069C] P. 176.]. Others, namely Ughellus [Note: [Col. 1070C] Vol. IV, col. 528, under Gaudentius; although a little earlier, under Philastrius, col. 525, he had said that Philastrius presided over the Church of Brescia for eight years.] and Papebroch [Note: [Col. 1070C] *Acta Sanctorum* for March, vol. II, p. 14.], assign it to A.D. 385. Baronius [Note: [Col. 1070C] A.D. 386, no. 7.] and Basnage Flotte-Manuville [Note: [Col. 1070C] *Annals*, vol. III, p. 106, no. 10.] assign it to 386. All, however, lack support from antiquity.

Certainly, if the date of Gaudentius’ pilgrimage to the East were known—for he was summoned back from there to succeed Philastrius in the episcopate—something certain could readily also be stated about Philastrius’ death. For some interval must be allowed between Philastrius’ death and the return of Gaudentius, travelling so far away. But one may wish; one may by no means divine.

Faynus, one of our own writers, with quite astonishing confidence and making light of all antiquity [Col. 1070B], plainly fixes the dates of Philastrius in both *The Heaven of Brescia* [Note: [Col. 1070C] Ch. 29.] and his notes on the Martyrology of Brescia [Note: [Col. 1070C] 18 July, p. 100.] in these words: “He succeeded Faustinus in the see of Brescia in A.D. 354, and died in A.D. 385.” By this calculation thirty or more years of episcopacy are assigned to Philastrius, although Ughellus gives him no more than eight [Note: [Col. 1070C] Vol. IV, col. 525.]. Indeed Labbe, in *On Ecclesiastical Writers* [Note: [Col. 1070C] Vol. II, p. 212.], says: “He died on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August in A.D. 387, after presiding for about eight years.”

The very learned William Cuper also rightly observed that Faynus differs very greatly from Ughellus, in section 2, no. 14, of his Commentary on [Col. 1071A] St Philastrius [Note: [Col. 1071D] *Acta Sanctorum* for July, vol. IV, p. 386.]. But since we too, together with Labbe, Vossius, and others, have assigned Gaudentius’ beginnings to A.D. 357 [Note: [Col. 1071D] Preface to Gaudentius, no. 4.], it would certainly be desirable that both the years during which Philastrius occupied the see and the year of his death might be established by some more certain ancient testimony. Since such testimony is unavailable, nothing should rashly be affirmed or denied.

Labbe places the beginning of Philastrius’ episcopate in A.D. 380 [Note: [Col. 1071D] Vol. II, p. 211.], while Faynus assigns it to A.D. 354. The year 354 is assigned by Giovanni Francesco Florentini, in his *Chronological Index of the Bishops of Brescia* [Note: [Col. 1071D] Brescia, Bartholomew Fontana, 1614.], to Faustinus, Philastrius’ predecessor; Faynus in *The Heaven of Brescia* [Note: [Col. 1071D] P. 20.] assigns Faustinus more than thirty years in office. Thus, on Florentini’s reckoning, Philastrius’ episcopate began in 384; but on Faynus’ reckoning [Col. 1071B] it ended in 385, and would therefore be limited to a single year. Nor would this permit Philastrius to have been a bishop attending the Council of Aquileia in 381. Everything is wholly reversed and badly put together.

A passage of Philastrius occurs in chapter 106, where he says that more than four hundred years have now passed and been completed since the Lord came; perhaps someone may think that Philastrius’ lifetime must therefore be extended beyond the close of the fourth century. But since it is certain that Philastrius died while Ambrose was still alive, and Ambrose died in 397—something clearly established from Gaudentius, for Gaudentius, having become bishop, addresses Ambrose as present in the Sermon on His Own Ordination [Note: [Col. 1071D] P. 334.]—either that passage must be corrupt and supplemented, as Fabricius proposed [Note: [Col. 1071D] See the fourth note in order on ch. 106, EDITOR.], “more or less than four hundred years have now passed”; or Philastrius spoke not very precisely but by *auxēsis* (rhetorical amplification), using a complete number [Col. 1071C] for an incomplete one.

Thus in the *Testimonies concerning Philastrius*, Johann Albert Fabricius rightly corrects Thomas Malvenda, calling it a manifest blunder of Baronius to affirm from the aforesaid sermon of Gaudentius that Philastrius died while Ambrose was still alive, since Fabricius himself had elsewhere also noted that Philastrius wrote the book *On Heresies* before Parmenian’s death, that is, before A.D. 391 [Note: [Col. 1071D] Notes on chapters 83 and 106.]. Therefore Philastrius cannot have said, while writing it, that more than four hundred years had passed and been completed since the Lord came.

12. Gaudentius does not permit us to doubt the day of Philastrius’ death; for he says [Note: [Col. 1071D] P. 374.]: “On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August he put off the human being.” On precisely that day the Roman Martyrology, Maurolycus, Galesinius, and other later martyrologists commemorate Philastrius [Col. 1071D]. The *Nomenclature of Authors* prefixed to Du Cange’s Glossary wrongly assigns Philastrius’ death to the first of August, although otherwise it sets the year of his death, together with the others, at 387.

In the Martyrology of Alexander Peregrinus, under 18 July, these words are read concerning Philastrius: “In the city of Brescia, the heavenly birthday of St Philastrius, bishop and confessor of that same city. How great his holiness and merit were, and by what miracles he shone forth, the most blessed Gaudentius, likewise bishop of the same city, set forth in a truthful style.” More on the day of Philastrius’ death may be found in the Notes on Gaudentius’ Sermon on Philastrius, p. 374.

Philastrius occupied the see of Brescia after Faustinus, and Gaudentius succeeded him, as all catalogues of the bishops of Brescia report. Rampertus calls him the SEVENTH bishop of Brescia [Note: [Col. 1072D] Sermon on the Translation of Philastrius, p. 391.]. Since the entire account necessary for correctly establishing the bishops of Brescia, both those before Philastrius and his successors, depends on this numerical designation, we have carefully weighed in the Preface to Rampertus [Col. 1072B] [Note: [Col. 1072D] P. 389.] both further evidence from antiquity and arguments of reason in support of retaining it firmly—although Rampertus’ authority alone suffices. I ask you to consult it, as well as the preliminary Admonition to the ancient Rhythm concerning Philastrius, p. 375.

Whether Philastrius ought to be classed under the title of martyr, as the recent continuator of Gavantius thinks [Note: [Col. 1072D] Vol. II, p. 559, Roman edition of 1738.], in the manner of Numidicus, Eutychius, Sosthenes [Note: [Col. 1072D] Roman Martyrology, 9 August, 24 August, 28 November.], and others whom it is known endured tortures in former times but later died a natural death—since he is by no means called by that title in the martyrologies, nor does the Church of Brescia honour him under that cult—I leave undecided.

He was buried together with his wooden *lituus*, or pastoral staff, which is still preserved in the treasury of the Church of Brescia, as Ferrarius also relates in the *Catalogue of the Saints of Italy*, following Capreolus, Book III of the *History of Brescia* [Note: [Col. 1072D] 18 July.]. The very learned William Cuper recently repeated this information from Florentini’s *Chronological Index of the Bishops of Brescia* [Col. 1072C] in section 2, no. 16, of his Commentary on St Philastrius, Bishop of Brescia [Note: [Col. 1072D] *Acta Sanctorum* for July, vol. IV, p. 387.]. In that place the Sermon of Rampertus on the Translation of Philastrius, carefully corrected and elucidated from the Padua edition of 1720, was republished.

The place of burial, at St Andrew’s, is mentioned in two manuscripts of the Church of Brescia, excerpts from which we produced for Rampertus’ sermon [Note: [Col. 1072D] Notes on Rampertus, p. 388.]. Malvetius, moreover, mentions the cathedral Church of St Andrew in his *Chronicle*, distinction 3, chapter 11, and distinction 4, chapter 3. Brescian writers testify that Rampertus first translated Philastrius’ sacred body from this place. Florentini’s words are these [Note: [Col. 1072D] *Chronological Index*, under Philastrius.]:

“On 9 April in the year 838, his body was translated, together with his wooden crozier, from the crypt of St Andrew, where it had lain hidden for almost five hundred years, into the winter cathedral church, the church subsequently built above which is commonly called the ROTUNDA.”

The same Cuper recounts other translations of Philastrius in section 2, no. 16, of the mentioned Commentary on St Philastrius [Note: [Col. 1072D] *Acta Sanctorum* for July, vol. IV, p. 387.]. Since mention has occurred of the wooden staff or crozier found together with Philastrius’ body [Col. 1073A], I think it not irrelevant to note here that this staff is wooden and curved at its head or upper end; its outline has the same shape as that drawn by Montfaucon from a Cassinese manuscript in his *Italian Diary*, p. 323.

Baronius, under A.D. 504, mentions the pastoral staff of St Augustine, translated together with his body from Africa to Sardinia [Note: [Col. 1073D] No. 38.]. This shows that such *koimēlia* (“relics, treasured objects”) used to be buried with bishops’ bodies. Ughellus reports the same concerning the archbishops of Milan [Note: [Col. 1073D] Vol. IV, col. 78.], where, following Puricelli, he relates that the body of Archbishop Anselm, who lived until 822, was found at the right side with his wooden staff and a jewelled, gilded silver ring.

That the day of Philastrius’ death was once solemn among the citizens of Brescia is shown by the testimonies of Gaudentius and Rampertus. The former says [Note: [Col. 1073D] Sermon on the Life and Death of Blessed Philastrius, p. 374.] that he had now renewed the observance of this solemnity for fourteen years; the latter says that Philastrius’ episcopal successors at Brescia [Note: [Col. 1073D] Sermon on the Translation of Philastrius, p. 387.], venerating the day of his passing, honoured it reverently and ordered the people of Brescia to refrain from every earthly labour. But this kind of observance has long since become obsolete; indeed, even the title of patron, once long customarily given both to Philastrius and Apollonius [Note: [Col. 1073D] Notes on Gaudentius, p. 374.], has ceased to be applied to them:

> So great is the power of remote antiquity to change things with the passage of time.

13. Besides the book *On Heresies* written by Philastrius, certain other works are attributed to him which in no way acknowledge Philastrius as their author. These include the ancient [Col. 1073C] Latin translation of the Epistle of St Barnabas, attributed to Philastrius by Papebroch in the *Acta Sanctorum* for June, vol. II, p. 457; and, following Papebroch, also by Fabricius in the Preface to Philastrius prefixed to the Hamburg edition and again placed before this Brescia edition.

Papebroch professes that he particularly values that translation because it bears Philastrius’ name as author. “And it is,” in Papebroch’s words, “to be valued all the more highly because in an ancient Corbie manuscript it is found as though rendered into Latin by St Philostorgius”—read *Philastrius*—“bishop of Brescia.” Papebroch perhaps drew this from Puccinelli’s *Life of St Barnabas*, Book II, p. 69. But the error of those eminent men, Papebroch himself and Fabricius as well, was quite extraordinary [Col. 1073D] [Note: [Col. 1073D] Ittig likewise made the same error, *Ecclesiastical History*, century I, p. 23.]. For in that manuscript of Corbie, which both mention, there was contained, besides Philastrius’ book *On Heresies*, a Latin translation of the Epistle of St Barnabas and also several other pieces. Without sufficiently examining the matter, each thought that the old translation was presented in that codex under Philastrius’ name.

Yet neither Menard nor Cotelerius, the very learned editors of that epistle, ever conceived of attributing that translation to Philastrius. Rather, in volume II of the *Library of the Fathers*, p. 16, where that Latin translation was published again, these few words are prefixed, which make the entire issue clear:

> “When the Reverend Father Hugo Menard at some time came upon a manuscript volume of Philastrius, bishop of Brescia, from the monastery of Corbie, he found there, immediately after Tertullian’s Epistle *On Jewish Foods*, an epistle bearing the name of Barnabas, together with the Epistle of the Apostle James.”

Thus, in that codex several little works by different authors had been collected together. Since the first of them, namely the book *On Heresies*, bore Philastrius’ name, the ancient Latin translation—which perhaps lacked an author’s name—was easily attributed to Philastrius as well. But we shall discuss this below, when we treat expressly of the Corbie manuscript [Col. 1074B] [Note: [Col. 1074D] No. 20.].

Certainly Menard, who handled the Corbie codex and extracted that Latin translation from it—for, as Papebroch himself relates [Note: [Col. 1074D] *Acta Sanctorum* for June, vol. II, p. 457.], he had the Greek exemplar from the papers of Turrianus—would by no means have passed this over in silence if he had seen the translation marked in the Corbie manuscript with Philastrius’ name.

The Acts of Saints Faustinus and Jovita are likewise attributed to Philastrius. From these Jacobus Riccius declares that he published their Life; he printed it in 1511, according to Ascanio Martinengo in the preface to his Italian Life of the same saints, published at Brescia in 1602. But Martinengo himself rightly doubts whether such Acts are truly by Philastrius. Henschenius also intimates this [Note: [Col. 1074D] *Acta Sanctorum* for February, vol. II, p. 806.], because they differ entirely in style and manner of writing from the book *On Heresies* [Col. 1074C].

We gladly deny that these Acts are Philastrius’ work, as we also deny that he wrote the Passion of Afra, which Ughellus attributes to him in the Preface to the Bishops of Brescia [Note: [Col. 1074D] Vol. IV, col. 523.]. Ughellus had received this from Galesinius, who states in his notes on 24 May that Afra’s history was composed by Faustinus and Philastrius, bishops of Brescia.

If anyone were to attribute to Philastrius the Creed commonly called Athanasian, an exposition of which was at one time attributed also to our Gaudentius, that conjecture might perhaps not be judged wholly implausible. For in Philastrius there occur often not only the ideas but the very words of that Creed. Thus the Creed says: “Therefore the right faith is that we believe and confess that our Lord Jesus Christ is God, begotten from the substance of the Father before the ages.” Philastrius says [Note: [Col. 1074D] Ch. 127.]: [Col. 1074D] “Therefore it is shown to be right, and the firm foundation of faith, that we recognize him as begotten properly from the Father, yet not in time but before all ages.”

The distinguished Fabricius had also noticed this at Philastrius’ words [Note: [Col. 1074D] Ch. 51.], “As the Father is immeasurable, so is the Son, so is the Holy Spirit,” adding: “In almost the same words in the Creed which we call Athanasian: ‘The Father immeasurable, the Son immeasurable, the Holy Spirit immeasurable.’”

Elsewhere Philastrius says [Col. 1075A] [Note: [Col. 1075D] Ch. 93.]: “There is a true person of the Father, and there is a true person of the Son, and there is a true person of the Spirit. Therefore, of these three persons there is one truth, majesty, equality of substance, and divinity.” But the Creed says: “The person of the Father is one, of the Son another, and of the Holy Spirit another; but the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one divinity, equal glory, coeternal majesty.” Therefore it does not seem implausible either that Philastrius was the author of that Creed, or that the Creed’s author, whoever he was, sometimes borrowed from Philastrius not only doctrines but the very words themselves.

## § I. On the usefulness and employment of the book *On Heresies* written by Philastrius.

14. Fabricius rightly observed—and we too noted above—that Philastrius’s book *On Heresies* was written before Parmenian’s death, that is, before the year 391 [Note: [Col. 1075D] No. 11, at the end.]. But that it was composed after 380 (a point Fabricius did not note) is indicated by Philastrius’s inclusion among heretics of the Abstainers [*Abstinentes*] [Note: [Col. 1075D] Ch. 84.], namely the Priscillianists, whom Philastrius plainly censures under this name [Note: [Col. 1075D] Fabricius, note on ch. 84, “They are in Gaul.” EDIT.], and whose heresy began to emerge around the year 380 [Note: [Col. 1075D] Fabricius, same place; Tillemont, vol. VIII, p. 798.]. Even if nothing else commended the usefulness and value of this book, this at least would demonstrate them: Augustine himself excerpted much from Philastrius in his little book *On Heresies*, without at all concealing his name, so that anyone might know through whom he had profited. Yet, because this fact has not been sufficiently considered by some as it ought to have been, Augustine has seemed unfairly to give too little credit to our Philastrius [Col. 1075C].

Moreover, the material Augustine took from him appears in Augustine’s own little work *On Heresies* from chapter 58 onward. For there, after reviewing the heresies mentioned by Epiphanius, he says: “I now add those which Philaster included and Epiphanius did not.” Thus, if Philastrius’s book *On Heresies* did not survive, we should be wholly ignorant of the heresies of Seleucus and Hermias concerning a corporeal God, the matter of the world, the creation of souls, and other similar matters—heresies which Augustine copied from Philastrius in almost the same words. Likewise, we should be ignorant of the Proclianists, Patricians, Ascites, Aquarians, and many others, whom Augustine, having received them from Philastrius, included in his list.

Philastrius confirms the immortality of the soul in several places; he reports that it was also recognized and maintained by Carpocrates [Note: [Col. 1075D] Ch. 35.] and Valentinus [Col. 1075D] [Note: [Col. 1075D] Ch. 38.]. Indeed, he rebukes and counts among heretics the Samaritans, who do not recognize that a human being has an immortal soul [Note: [Col. 1075D] Ch. 7.]. He speaks so plainly and openly concerning the mystery of the Trinity [Col. 1076A] that several statements found in the Creed commonly attributed to Athanasius seem to have been drawn from Philastrius, as we have just observed [Note: [Col. 1075D] No. 13, at the end.]. Especially noteworthy is what he says in chapter 93, where among errors he lists a certain heresy that makes God threefold; and chapter 109, where he shows from Scriptural testimonies that knowledge of the Trinity had been announced to human beings from the very origin of the world.

On the grace of God, a doctrine not sufficiently explained before Augustine, he speaks lucidly in more than one passage, namely in chapter 98: “Inspiration, therefore, is not the soul, but a grace of dignity from the divine Spirit”; and a little above: “The inspiration of the divine Spirit is a certain grace and advancement in dignity.” So too in the preceding chapter: “There is no doubt that the soul was made first, but the flesh was afterward [Col. 1076B] formed; and thus afterward, when God’s inspiration was infused, spiritual grace was conferred, so that the human being, now capable of the divine law, might be shown not powerless by the Lord.”

15. But since we are here discussing the usefulness and value of Philastrius’s work, we must not pass over the critique and praise of this book recorded by Louis Ellies Dupin in his *Ecclesiastical Library* [Note: [Col. 1075D] Vol. II, section 4.]. Dupin’s criticism first concerns the charge almost universally brought against our Philastrius: namely, that he invented for himself many heresies that never existed [Note: [Col. 1075D] “He invents a quantity of heresies which never were.”], such as the Nazaraeans, Heliognosts, Musorites, Muscaccaronites, Troglodytes, Fortunatians, and, not to mention others, the Cybelites—imitators, that is, of the worshippers of Cybele.

Philastrius says not a single word [Col. 1076C] about the Cybelites, who are mentioned by both Epiphanius and Augustine under the name Valesians [Note: [Col. 1076D] Epiphanius, *Heresies* 38; Augustine, *On Heresies* ch. 37.]. The rest, however—many of whom should be called not heretics but rather idolaters—are mentioned by Scripture, in whose tracks Philastrius follows. The Nazaraeans are likewise acknowledged by Epiphanius and Augustine [Note: [Col. 1076D] Epiphanius, *Heresies* 29; Augustine, ch. 9.]. The Troglodytes are mentioned by Theodoret, who writes that the Eunomians and Aetians were called by the same designation because they met *en oikeiais lanthanousais*—“in concealed private dwellings” [Note: [Col. 1076D] Note on Philastrius, p. 11.], as Fabricius observed long ago.

How wrongly Dupin further asserts that no one besides Philastrius spoke of the Judaites, Passalorinchites, Rhetorians, Barefooted Ones, we pointed out in our *Spicilegium* [Note: [Col. 1076D] See among the notes on ch. 76, the note “There are other Passalorinchites.” EDIT.]; and the same is fully evident from Fabricius’s notes on these heresies [Note: [Col. 1076D] Chs. 34, 76, 81, 91.]. Dupin then continues to blame Philastrius because he sometimes places among heresies opinions either true or at least certainly open to dispute on either side [Col. 1076D] [Note: [Col. 1076D] “Sometimes he includes among heresies opinions which are true, or at least problematic.”], for example the Millenarians [Note: [Col. 1076D] Ch. 59.], those who deny that the elements will one day be consumed by fire [Note: [Col. 1076D] Ch. 80.], those who attribute Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews to Luke or Barnabas [Note: [Col. 1076D] Ch. 89.], [Col. 1077A] and others of this kind.

Yet some allowance should be made for Philastrius’s temperament. He was carried along by a particular zeal for love of Catholic truth; and whenever he thought he detected a trace of error, he directed his pen against it with greater vehemence. Not to mention that the Millenarians, or Chiliasts, are more than once counted among heretics by the Fathers; that to believe the world incorruptible is altogether an error, as the Scriptural testimonies adduced by Philastrius prove; and that modern critics have laboured greatly to establish that the Epistle to the Hebrews is a true and genuine offspring of Paul [Note: [Col. 1077D] See Fabricius’s notes on ch. 89.].

Dupin adds that Philastrius committed many serious errors in this little treatise [Note: [Col. 1077D] “He makes several gross errors in this small treatise.”]. Although I know well that charges of this kind ought to be made more sparingly against such men—as indeed Fabricius made this same charge against Philastrius more sparingly and modestly [Col. 1077B] whenever he found him in error—I nevertheless would not obstinately deny that Philastrius made quite a few statements in which greater care and diligence might be desired, unless his zeal for religion and piety might in some measure excuse his lack of exactness and care.

Meanwhile Dupin, while harshly attacking Philastrius as his critic, himself falls shamefully into error when he reproaches Philastrius for deriving the Samaritans from King Samarius, son of Canaan [Note: [Col. 1077D] “He says that the Samaritans derive from a king called Samarius, son of Canaan; what a blunder!”]. Philastrius did not say that King Samarius was the son of Canaan. Rather, he said: “The Samaritans are called after King Samarius”; then: “Others say that they were named after the son of Canaan, who was called Samarius” [Note: [Col. 1077D] Philastrius, ch. 7: “The Samaritans are so called after the Samaritan king. Others, however, say [they were named] after the son of Canaan, who was called Samarius by this name, from whom the Samaritans received their designation”; hence Dupin may be answered: *quelle bévue!*—“what a blunder!”]. We noted the same point in the *Spicilegium*.

Dupin is likewise mistaken in being angry with Philastrius [Col. 1077C] because he condemns those who used the book of Ecclesiasticus as canonical [Note: [Col. 1077D] “He condemns those who admit Ecclesiasticus as a canonical book.”]. Philastrius does not condemn those who used this book as canonical, but those who used it as a book of Solomon, as Fabricius correctly explains in his notes on Philastrius [Note: [Col. 1077D] See the note on ch. 56, “One book of Wisdom.” EDIT.].

16. Yet, although Dupin seems not to have thought very favourably of Philastrius, he nevertheless noticed that some passages in him deserve particular attention [Note: [Col. 1077D] “There are nevertheless some noteworthy passages.”]. We too have selected a few examples above to indicate the usefulness of the book [Note: [Col. 1077D] No. 14.]. Such are the immortality of the soul, asserted by Philastrius in several places, as we have said; the mystery of the Trinity, lucidly and clearly explained; the eternal generation of the Word, plainly and distinctly set forth [Col. 1077D] [Note: [Col. 1077D] Ch. 127.]; Christ’s descent into hell, and how it profited nothing to the impious enemies of God [Col. 1078A] [Note: [Col. 1078D] Ch. 125. See also Fabricius, *Codex Apocryphus Novi Testamenti*, p. 1005.]; and many other matters, which sufficiently show from elsewhere the importance and usefulness of Philastrius’s work.

No one has better indicated than Philastrius that Pythagorean and Platonic doctrines opened sources of error for many heretics. In his account Valentinus is called more a Pythagorean than a Christian [Note: [Col. 1078D] Ch. 38.]; while the Passalorinchites are said to follow Pythagorean vanity rather than the heavenly life and wisdom of the Prophets [Note: [Col. 1078D] Ch. 76.]. When speaking of the errors of Seleucus and Hermias, Philastrius expressly notes that their visible Paradise was drawn from Plato [Note: [Col. 1078D] Ch. 55. Augustine, however, in *On Heresies*, ch. 59, speaking of the Seleucians, says contrary to Philastrius: “They also deny a visible Paradise”; whereas Philastrius says: “They affirm a visible Paradise.”]. Finally, here and there many things occur in him by which more hidden recesses of ecclesiastical antiquity are opened to students. Thus the distinguished Fabricius quite rightly and candidly declares that he does not at all regret [Col. 1078B] spending some hours reviewing and elucidating Philastrius’s little book, and that he learned various things from it [Note: [Col. 1078D] Preface to Philastrius.].

Philastrius aptly ridicules the vanity and empty philosophical opinion concerning Pythagorean or Platonic metempsychosis, the transmigration of souls [Note: [Col. 1078D] Ch. 124.], as also their *didagma* (δίδαγμα), “teaching,” concerning infinite worlds [Note: [Col. 1078D] Ch. 113.]. Dupin too noted this latter point. From these passages of Philastrius, one may easily defeat with Philastrian weapons such errors as still adhere to some minds. In chapter 88 he expressly sets out the authority (*authentia*, αὐτενθία) of the canon of Scripture. Fabricius aptly observed concerning this passage [Note: [Col. 1078D] See the note on ch. 38, “It was established by the apostles.” EDIT.] that Philastrius omits Revelation and the Epistle to the Hebrews in his list, although elsewhere Philastrius himself testifies that he embraces both writings.

In the same [Col. 1078C] chapter 88 Philastrius rightly says that the Valentinians, possessing separate apocryphal writings of the Prophets and Apostles—that is, Acts—despised the canonical Scriptures. This should certainly be understood of Valentinus’s disciples, not of Valentinus himself. Massuet proved from Tertullian that Valentinus himself added nothing to, and subtracted nothing from, the canon, but merely adapted the Scriptures to his own meaning through depraved interpretations [Note: [Col. 1078D] Dissertation 1 on Irenaeus, no. 9.].

Dupin further praises Philastrius’s excellent statement [Note: [Col. 1078D] Ch. 128.], in which he teaches that we ought first to run by our own will, and then not, with presumption and boasting, to suppose that we deserve to be saved by our own strength and worthy righteousness rather than by Christ’s mercy. Dupin likewise praises Philastrius’s further remark, reproving anyone who says, “I can be a martyr; I can be an apostle,” and does not say, “If Christ wills,” since increase in that office and grace is conferred by him [Col. 1078D].

He also commends Philastrius’s book especially for brevity, although Augustine, by contrast, calls it extremely lengthy [Col. 1079A] [Note: [Col. 1079C] *On Heresies*, ch. 41.]: “Philaster, bishop of Brescia, in the very lengthy book which he composed on heresies.” Fabricius notes that Augustine’s statement must be understood [Note: [Col. 1079D] Testimonies concerning Philastrius.] not of the physical size of the volume, but of the extensive number of heresies it mentions, far exceeding Epiphanius.

17. Although Philastrius generally showed himself more diligent in enumerating heresies, so that he sometimes mentioned the same heresy more than once, as Dupin says [Note: [Col. 1079D] “He makes so numerous a catalogue of heresies that he multiplied them further by mentioning the same heresy several times.”], he nevertheless omitted some heresies listed by Epiphanius, which Augustine therefore includes in his own catalogue: the Archontics, Severians, Elcesaites, Samsaeans, Bardesanites, Valesians, Angelics, [Col. 1079B] Apostolics, Origenists, Hieracites, Anthropomorphites, Apollinarists, Antidicomarianites, Psallians, Martyrians, and Satanians, whom Augustine places last among those derived from Epiphanius [Note: [Col. 1079D] Augustine, *On Heresies*, chs. 20–57.]. These, then, are the heresies listed by Epiphanius and omitted by Philastrius which Augustine incorporated into his catalogue.

Conversely, among the heresies Augustine says that he received from Philastrius, he mentions the Priscillianists [Note: [Col. 1079D] Ibid., ch. 70.], although the name of the Priscillianists is not found in Philastrius’s book, as Fabricius noted in the *Testimonies concerning Philastrius*, where he cites Augustine’s testimony about Philastrius. Philastrius, however, censures them under the name of Abstainers in chapter 84, as Fabricius there observes [Note: [Col. 1079D] See the note on ch. 84, “They are in Gaul.” EDIT.]. Augustine likewise lists the Passalorinchites [Col. 1079C] in chapter 63 among the heresies “which Philaster included and Epiphanius did not.” Yet Epiphanius does include the Passalorinchites, as Fabricius notes on Philastrius chapter 76 [Note: [Col. 1079D] See the note on ch. 76, “There are other Passalorinchites.” EDIT.], as he does also the Colluthians, whom Augustine has in chapter 65 as mentioned by Philastrius but not by Epiphanius [Note: [Col. 1079D] See Fabricius, note on ch. 79, “Not the maker of evils.” EDIT.].

Augustine also omitted several heresies which neither Epiphanius nor Philastrius listed. Among them were the Masbotheans, so called from Masbotheus, one of the first seven heretics enumerated by Eusebius [Note: [Col. 1079D] Book IV of the *Ecclesiastical History*, ch. 22.]; likewise the Gorthaeans, from a certain Gorthaeus [Note: [Col. 1079D] Eusebius, ibid.], although Epiphanius also lists the Gorthenians [Note: [Col. 1079D] *Heresies* 12.], whom Augustine nevertheless omits. The Asclepiodoti [Col. 1080A] were named after Asclepiodotus, a disciple of Theodotus the leather-worker [Note: [Col. 1079D] On Theodotus, Philastrius ch. 50; Augustine ch. 33, where the reading is not *Theodotus* but *Theodotio*.], and he taught that Christ was merely a human being [Note: [Col. 1079D] Eusebius, book V, ch. 28.].

The Saccophori were a certain kind of Manichaeans, so called as though carrying a sack; they are mentioned in the Theodosian Code [Note: [Col. 1079D] Book XVI, title 5, law 9.]. Tillemont [Note: [Col. 1079D] Vol. VIII, p. 798.] criticizes Baronius for wrongly thinking, under the year 383 [Note: [Col. 1079D] Nos. 34, 36.], that they were identical with the Messalians, whom Augustine in chapter 57 calls not Messalians but Psallians. The Helvidians, named after Helvidius, a disciple of Auxentius, against whom Jerome wrote a book, are omitted by Epiphanius, Philastrius, and Augustine—although perhaps they are the same as those whom Epiphanius calls Antidicomarites [Note: [Col. 1080C] *Heresies* 78.] and Augustine Antidicomarianites [Note: [Col. 1080D] Ch. 56.].

Eusebius mentions Macrianus [Note: [Col. 1080D] Book VII, ch. 10. Consult Valesius’s notes on this passage of Eusebius.], who, having been a Catholic—that is, rational—man, became chief of the synagogues of Egyptian magicians [Col. 1080B] and the Emperor Valerian’s guide and teacher in every impiety. He neither understood the providence governing all things nor reflected upon the judgment of him who is before all things, in all things, and above all things: God.

The *Chronicon Alexandrinum* repeatedly calls the Arians Exocionites [Note: [Col. 1080D] P. 704, Rader’s edition, and elsewhere.]. They are also called Exucontians by Athanasius and other writers, because they maintained that the Son of God—whom they denied to be consubstantial and coeternal with the Father—was created *ex ouk ontōn* (ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων), that is, “from things not being,” or from nothing. Ittig has made several excellent observations about them [Note: [Col. 1080D] *Observationes Miscellaneae* VIII, p. 239, Leipzig, 1700.].

The heresy of Bonosus, a certain bishop—whether of Sardica, as Marius Mercator makes him, or rather of Naissus, as Holstenius judges [Note: [Col. 1080D] Ittig, *Observationes Miscellaneae* IX, p. 244.], is not sufficiently established—consisted in this: the Bonosians not only denied Christ’s divinity, but also believed that several children [Col. 1080C] had been born to Mary. This is sufficiently clear from the case of Bonosus heard at the Synod of Capua in A.D. 389 [Note: [Col. 1080D] Ibid., p. 246. See Tillemont, vol. X, pp. 236, 754.].

And this is enough concerning the heresies omitted by Epiphanius, Philastrius, and Augustine. Since it is not the purpose of this place to give a longer treatment of them, these remarks will suffice [Note: [Col. 1080D] Those wishing more may consult Euthymius’s *Panoply*, vol. XIX of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, p. 6, in the translation of Peter Francis Zini of Luni, archpriest; and the *Dogmatic Panoply* of Nicetas Choniates Acominatus, whose complete *synopsis* (σύνοψις) from a cotton-paper manuscript in the library of the distinguished Stephen Baluze was published by the most learned Montfaucon in *Greek Palaeography*, book IV, ch. 9, p. 327. See also, if desired, Thomas Ittig’s *Dissertation on the Heresiarchs of the Apostolic Age*, Leipzig, 1690; Hartmann’s *Treatise on Events under the Apostles*; and Arnold’s *History of Heresies*, cited by Ittig himself, *Observationes Miscellaneae* IX, p. 244.]. Our purpose calls us elsewhere: namely, to bring forward and assess various judgments concerning Philastrius made by non-Catholics.

## § II. The judgments of heterodox writers concerning Philastrius are reported and assessed

18. First come the Magdeburg Centuriators [Col. 1081A]. Though greatly hostile to the Catholic cause through their zeal for novelty, they nevertheless praise Philastrius in more than one place with exceptional commendation as a man most fervent in zeal for Catholic truth. Thus in Century 4, chapter 5 [Note: [Col. 1081D] P. 182.], where they treat the Arian heresy, they write: “Other eminent men of this age also opposed this heresy, such as Ambrose, Epiphanius, PHILASTER, Marius Victorinus, and others like them.”

They then quote in full Philastrius’s passage against Arius [Note: [Col. 1081D] P. 192.]: “Man and angel were made from nothing; but since the Son is true, he must be recognized as begotten from that divine substance of the Father,” together with the remaining material in Philastrius, chapter 66. Later, when speaking of the Semi-Arians [Note: [Col. 1081D] Ch. 5, p. 202.], they add the words of Philastrius alone against their own hypothesis concerning the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 1081D] Philastrius, ch. 67.]: “Christ the Lord joined the Spirit to the Father and to himself in the faith of baptism unto eternal salvation.” This alone sufficiently shows how highly Philastrius and his authority stood with them [Col. 1081B].

Elsewhere also they praise Philastrius and note particular passages of his wherever the subject allows them to use his dictum and authority: in Century I, chapter 5 [Note: [Col. 1081D] P. 370.], they state from Philastrius that Simon was overcome before Nero by Peter’s teaching and miracles—although Philastrius [Note: [Col. 1081D] Philastrius, ch. 29.] mentions neither teaching nor miracles, but only that Simon was defeated by the prayer of the blessed Apostle. In Century 2, chapter 5 [Note: [Col. 1081D] P. 65.], they derive light from Philastrius regarding the heresies of Marcus and Valentinus; in Century 3, chapter 5 [Note: [Col. 1081D] P. 82.], they note from him that the Manichaean heresy was especially powerful in Spain and the five provinces. Finally, they show in every way [Col. 1081C] that they had studied Philastrius with the greatest care.

When, in Century 5, chapter 4, they discuss the doctrine of the Church [Note: [Col. 1081D] P. 48.], they place Philastrius among all the most illustrious men of that age and count him together with John Chrysostom, Augustine, Cyril, and other great men. Then in chapter 10, where they discuss bishops and teachers, they offer this judgment concerning Philastrius [Note: [Col. 1081D] P. 744.]:

> Although Augustine ranks this author below Epiphanius, it is nevertheless clear from this very work—in which, while refuting every kind of heresy with remarkable brevity and skill, he incidentally combines many things worthy of knowledge—that he was a learned man, possessed judgment concerning matters, and had extensive knowledge of antiquity, of ancient histories including pagan ones, and above all of the sacred Scriptures.

A little later they say: “He was skilled in the Greek language, for he cites Greek authors: Solon, Plato in the *Timaeus*, Hesiod, Hermes Trismegistus, Democritus.” Finally they add:

> In his catalogue of heresies he contends with great zeal against every sort of vanity, superstition, and error among pagans, Jews, and Christians. For, enumerating one hundred and fifty-six heresies—both those which existed before Christ’s coming and those which existed afterward, among both the people of God and the nations—he refutes most of them, especially those which arose among the Christian people after Christ’s glorification: briefly indeed, but still with sufficient lucidity and clarity [Col. 1082A].

19. These praises by the Magdeburg writers sufficiently dispel the perverse judgment of Philastrius offered by Jean Daillé in book II, chapter 1, of *On the Use of the Fathers* [Note: [Col. 1081D] P. 206.] in these words:

> Philastrius, bishop of Brescia, counted among heresies, as though alien from the public faith of all Christians, those things of which he himself did not approve, with a judgment so deceptive [Col. 1082B] and sometimes so foolish that it is utterly devoid of every appearance of truth that what he slays, the Church too condemned.

Daillé was serving a cause; consequently, he could hardly praise Philastrius highly when he had undertaken to criticize Justin, Irenaeus, Chrysostom, and nearly all the other Fathers. Moreover, Daillé seems in that book to be paving a broad and well-fortified road toward scepticism, since, once the authority of the Fathers has been removed, he leaves us almost nothing certain.

Now, if Philastrius stumbled anywhere, he is not for that reason immediately to be entirely cast aside and rejected. For he contains much that is excellent, by which both Catholic doctrine and ecclesiastical discipline are defended and illuminated. But Daillé criticizes Philastrius more sharply elsewhere, namely in book II, chapter 3 of the same work [Note: [Col. 1081D] P. 245.], where [Col. 1082C] he says:

> Philastrius relates as a certain fact—and, lest you suppose him to speak without an authority, confirms it by the testimony of Hesiod, the Greek poet—that the pagans were so called from a pagan king, the son of Deucalion and Pyrrha. These are so many dreams, unheard of both by Hesiod and by all learned men.

Selden likewise criticizes Philastrius in nearly the same language in *On the Syrian Gods*, Syntagma I, p. 95; Fabricius quoted the passage in his *Testimonies concerning Philastrius* [Note: [Col. 1082D]]. Fabricius had also noted that the passage of Hesiod cited by Philastrius no longer survives [Note: [Col. 1082D] Note on Philastrius, ch. 111, “As Hesiod says.”], although he did not at all perceive that these alleged dreams were unheard of by Hesiod and all learned men.

What if Philastrius shortly thereafter states more clearly who that pagan king was: namely, the son of Deucalion and Pyrrha, named Hellen, after whom the Greeks were later called *Hellēnes* (Ἕλληνες)? On this point Philastrius has the agreement of learned writers, as Fabricius himself correctly observes [Note: [Col. 1082D] See the note on ch. 111, “From the pagan king.” EDIT.]. Indeed, Philastrius expressly says this very thing [Note: [Col. 1082D] In the aforementioned ch. 111.]: namely, that the Greeks were named after the Greek king, that is, Hellen. Above, Philastrius had called him “a pagan king,” from whom the Pagans were named [Col. 1082D]—for Fabricius himself observed that Philastrius understands “Pagans” as Greeks [Note: [Col. 1082D] In the note on ch. 113, “To the Greeks,” Fabricius teaches that Philastrius takes Greeks for pagans there, just as above in ch. 111 he called Greeks “Pagans.”].

William Cave judged Philastrius more moderately and cautiously. His words are these [Note: [Col. 1082D] *Historia Ecclesiastica Scriptorum*, p. 176.]:

> He wrote a book *On Heresies*, in which he everywhere breathes love for Catholic truth; but he often displays less accurate judgment in counting among heresies those doctrines which by no means deserved to be marked by that name [Col. 1083A].

This is the same accusation Dupin brings against Philastrius, as we saw above [Note: [Col. 1083D] No. 15.]; therefore there is no need to repeat here what we said there. It is, however, plainly evident from what has been said thus far how undeservedly, not to say insolently, Joseph Scaliger pronounces concerning Philastrius in the sayings called *Scaligerana* [Note: [Col. 1083D] P. 310, Cologne edition]: “Philastrius is worthless,” when Philastrius’s book was so useful to many learned men, indeed to Augustine himself.

Besides, Scaliger had long been hostile to Philastrius of his own accord, or rather through a certain defect of character, as will be clear to anyone who consults the *Elenchus Trihaeresii* of that author [Col. 1083B]. In it he makes many charges against Philastrius, some justly and some unjustly; among other things, that Philastrius makes no mention of *tōn hyper nekrōn baptizomenōn* (τῶν ὑπὲρ νεκρῶν βαπτιζομένων), “those baptizing for the dead” [Note: [Col. 1083D] *Elenchus Trihaeresii*, ch. 1.]. Yet Philastrius expressly says, when treating the heresy of the Cataphrygians [Note: [Col. 1083D] Ch. 49.]: “These baptize the dead.” Fabricius noted this [Note: [Col. 1083D] *Testimonies concerning Philastrius*], and the Magdeburg Centuriators observed it before Fabricius [Note: [Col. 1083D] Century 2, ch. 5, p. 78.].

But enough concerning Philastrius. We must now treat of the Corbie manuscript of Philastrius, whose variant readings have been added to this edition of ours as a precious supplement.

## § III. On the Corbie manuscript and the corrections derived from it

20. Scholars had long desired a manuscript copy of Philastrius.
