Fabricius himself testifies that, at his request, the distinguished Gisbert Cuper had searched for one in Italy in vain when Fabricius was preparing the edition of Philastrius published at Hamburg in 1721. Thus, disappointed of every hope, Fabricius declared in the preface to that Hamburg edition that he had to rely solely on printed editions [Col. 1083C].

For my own part, shortly after publishing Gaudentius, I had already conceived the plan of a new edition of Philastrius. Although the distinguished Fabricius anticipated me, and I was considering changing my plan and directing my efforts elsewhere, I still could not wholly despair of finding a manuscript of Philastrius, or entirely cease further searching for one. Yet a manuscript copy of Philastrius was sought in vain in Italian and transalpine libraries alike; it appeared nowhere [Col. 1083D].

Then, while I was reading for another purpose, I encountered the prefatory notice to the Latin translation of the Epistle of Barnabas in volume II of the Lyons edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, p. 16. There, excerpted from a letter of d’Achery [Note: [Col. 1084D] This letter of d’Achery also appears in vol. XVI of Jean de la Haye’s *Bibliotheca Maxima*, before the Epistle of Barnabas, p. 901.], are these words:

> When the Reverend Father Hugo Menard once came upon a manuscript volume of PHILASTRIUS, BISHOP OF BRESCIA, from the monastery of Corbie, he found immediately after TERTULLIAN’S Epistle *On Jewish Foods* an EPISTLE bearing the name of BARNABAS, together with the EPISTLE OF JAMES THE APOSTLE [Col. 1084A].

When I read this, I immediately became certain that a manuscript Philastrius would be found at Corbie. For, since that volume contained besides the Latin translation of the Epistle of Barnabas—which Menard published at Paris in 1645 from the Corbie manuscript—several other little works of different kinds, I readily understood that Philastrius’s book *On Heresies* was also concealed among them.

Moreover, I saw that both Papebroch, in volume II of the *Acts of the Saints for June*, p. 457, and Fabricius, in the preface to Philastrius, as we said above [Note: [Col. 1084D] No. 13.], cited the Corbie manuscript as though the Latin translation of Barnabas’s Epistle contained in it, lacking its author’s name, were attributed to Philastrius. Although each wandered far from the truth and substituted one thing for another—since neither Menard, who had the manuscript in his hands, nor Vossius or Cotelerius, editors of Barnabas’s Epistle, had ever thought of assigning that translation to Philastrius—still, this assertion of Papebroch and Fabricius, whatever its worth, indicated that the manuscript contained something identifying Philastrius as its author [Col. 1084B].

Accordingly I immediately directed my wishes and requests to Corbie, so that I might obtain more certain information about, and access to, that manuscript. But Philastrius was sought at Corbie in vain: he had long since migrated to the Parisian monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. The monks of that house had long before borrowed the book from the Corbie monks. Scipio Maffei, the distinguished scholar, did indeed inform me in a letter written to me at Paris on 5 February 1733 [Col. 1084C] [Note: [Col. 1084D] It survives among the *Gallic Antiquities*, p. 76, where 1730 is printed in error for 1733.] that the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés possessed a manuscript copy of Philastrius, no. 625. This gave us what seemed a certain hope of finding another manuscript of Philastrius’s work in the library of Saint-Germain.

But it was the very Corbie manuscript itself—as we shall shortly see—that I so eagerly sought. Meanwhile, when I inquired, no further answer was given by which I might learn anything more certain concerning this Paris manuscript. Therefore, since I made no progress and had no suspicion that the Corbie manuscript had been transferred to the Parisian monastery, I submitted petitions to the Most Eminent Cardinal Quirini, bishop of Brescia, requesting that, in accordance with his great kindness toward all, especially toward letters and learned men, he would deign to send letters to Paris [Col. 1084D] and seek from there more definite knowledge and information concerning this Corbie manuscript.

That eminent man, worthy of immortality, most fully performed what was requested. In two subsequent letters sent to him, we learned, to our great delight, that the Corbie manuscript was in the library of Saint-Germain and that Philastrius’s book *On Heresies* was contained in it. The first of these letters, written to the Most Eminent Cardinal on 29 August 1736, says:

> I have already had the honour of informing Your Eminence that I had seen Dom Bernard de Montfaucon concerning the manuscript of Saint Philastrius. I also informed you, Monseigneur, that there was one in the library of the Abbey of Saint-Germain which was very ancient and came from Corbie [Col. 1085A].

The other, written a little later in the same month of September, confirms almost the same thing, but much more fully:

> The manuscript of Saint Philastrius which is in the library of the Abbey of Saint-Germain is the very same one from Corbie which Father Menard used. Since the Fathers of Corbie had lent it to these monks, who needed it, it remained here, and will remain here as long as they wish.

Upon receiving letters of this kind, I was filled with no small joy, seeing that the event had so splendidly confirmed my conjecture concerning the Corbie manuscript. At the same time I began to wonder how eminent men speaking of this Corbie manuscript had been so greatly deceived—especially why Fabricius, trusting Papebroch, neglected, while preparing his edition of Philastrius, to investigate more certainly the Corbie manuscript or seek some aid from it.

Meanwhile I did not cease to press on with my purpose and repeatedly request the variant readings of the same manuscript, again employing the authority of the Most Eminent Cardinal Quirini. In letters to Montfaucon, he strongly supported my undertaking, until the variant readings themselves were carefully excerpted and sent to Italy. Since they arrived late and the edition of Philastrius was already [Col. 1085C] under way and almost begun, they were therefore placed after Fabricius’s posthumous notes in an appendix [Note: [Col. 1085D] They appear on p. 152, together with the letter sent by Dom Jean Raverdy, Benedictine monk, to the Most Eminent Cardinal Quirini.—We, however, have placed these variant readings at the foot of the pages, as you have been advised, reader, at col. 1095, note b. EDIT.].

21. If anyone further wishes to know what benefit or illumination the variant readings of the Corbie manuscript have brought to Philastrius, let him consult our *Spicilegium*, in which he will find several passages of Philastrius that, through the assistance of this manuscript, have been restored, supplemented, or improved. Among these, for example, is chapter 47 [Note: [Col. 1085D] We have restored this chapter to the text, though marking its supplementary origin by a special note. EDIT.], on the four elements, which he had taken from the *De Mundo*, where a sense wholly incomplete and mutilated has been restored and supplied from the Corbie manuscript [Note: [Col. 1085D] See this edition, col. 1163. EDIT.]; likewise chapter 51 [Note: [Col. 1085D] See this edition, col. 1167. EDIT.], where the text of Philastrius mistakenly introduces pseudo-prophets from the heresy of the Cataphrygians, an error removed with the help of the same manuscript. Likewise, that passage in chapter 66 [Note: [Col. 1085D] See this edition, col. 1180. EDIT.] was utterly corrupted in the editions: “The everlasting likeness therefore of the Son also according to works,” although Fabricius gave no warning of this fault; but the Corbie reading corrects it with little difficulty: “The everlasting likeness therefore of the Son is according to works,” [Col. 1086A] with the words that follow restored and punctuated in a better manner. So too in chapter 110 [Note: [Col. 1085D] See this edition, col. 1232. EDIT.], where the editions read *conjunctum* (“joined”) quite wrongly, the Corbie codex appropriately substitutes *conjugium* (“marriage”); without this correction, the passage in the Hamburg edition cannot in any way be understood.

There are many such instances, which plainly show how undeservedly the distinguished Fabricius said in the preface to the Hamburg edition: “There are still few passages in which I should wish for light from manuscript codices,” when so many errors remained in that edition and have been healed by the aid of the Corbie manuscript. Remarkable, moreover, is that passage in chapter 144 [Note: [Col. 1086D] See this edition, col. 1279. EDIT.], “of those earlier Saints, who [are] of the Seventy-Two in other ways”; where, through the loss of one line, not Oedipus himself could have discovered what Philastrius meant without the correction of the Corbie manuscript. So also [Col. 1086B] chapter 148 [Note: [Col. 1086D] See this edition, col. 1283. EDIT.], where, instead of the word *praeputii* (“foreskin”), the editions absurdly thrust in *praecepta* (“precepts”). For in that place Philastrius, discussing the figure of the Gentiles and of the Jews, had unquestionably written a suitable account of the foreskin and circumcision, as the reading of the Corbie codex rightly has.

Indeed, not a few passages still remain to which the Corbie codex brought no assistance, such as that in chapter 88 [Note: [Col. 1086D] See this edition, col. 1199. EDIT.], “for the Manichaeans [have] Apocrypha”; Fabricius too, following Germonio, had noted that this passage of Philastrius was corrupt [Note: [Col. 1086D] *Cod. Apocr. N. T.*, part 3, p. 598.—Compare this edition, col. 1200, note “Nam Manichaei.” EDIT.]. So too chapter 6 [Note: [Col. 1086D] See this edition, col. 1120. EDIT.], “they assert that certain times are opposed to Christ our Lord,” where Fabricius thought that *quaedam testimonia* (“certain testimonies”) should be written instead of *quaedam tempora* (“certain times”), though he judged that this should not be done without the authority of manuscript codices. That passage in chapter 122 [Note: [Col. 1086D] See this edition, col. 1247. EDIT.] has also not yet been sufficiently clarified: “which indeed was afterwards, after years, in Thessaly, sometimes in a small place.” Though Fabricius, in my view undeservedly, disturbed the received reading, wishing *inter Oetam et Pindum* (“between Oeta and Pindus”) to be read instead of *interdum* (“sometimes”), if the manuscript codices supported it.

Obscure too—unless perhaps it is faulty and corrupt—is the passage in chapter 152 [Note: [Col. 1086D] See this edition, col. 1293. EDIT.]: “so that even a nature wholly alien may be found not deprived of Christ’s gift, that is, not even a catechumen”; where neither the Corbie codex nor Fabricius is of any help. The same is true of another passage in chapter 150 [Note: [Col. 1086D] See this edition, col. 1290. EDIT.], “likewise in Christ’s presence,” and of chapter 153 [Note: [Col. 1086D] See this edition, col. 1293. EDIT.], “and after the Faith of Christ, election, begetting [persons] of the Catholic faith, of a few”; in these places the water altogether sticks fast. Unless perhaps some other manuscript codex should come to the rescue, from which they may be recovered, no one, however fortunate and skilled in conjecture, will easily extricate himself from such perplexities [Col. 1086D].

## § IV. On the Six Chapters of Philastrius Recently Found in the Corbie Manuscript

22. Although the Corbie codex has furnished Philastrius with so many, and such excellent, corrections, [Col. 1087A] still greater benefit has nevertheless been derived from it, because it has given us Philastrius, hitherto incomplete and mutilated, complete and entire. For although Philastrius, as Augustine testifies, divided his work into one hundred and fifty-six chapters, only one hundred and fifty appeared in the editions. Augustine’s passage is clear in the letter to Quodvultdeus prefixed to his catalogue *On Heresies* [Note: [Col. 1087D] Vol. VI of the Works, col. 6.]:

> A certain Philastrius, bishop of Brescia, whom I myself also saw at Milan together with St. Ambrose, wrote a book on this subject. He did not omit those heresies which existed among the Jewish people before the Lord’s coming, and he mentioned twenty-eight of them; and, after the Lord’s coming, one hundred and twenty-eight.

The two numbers therefore make up one hundred and fifty-six heresies, or one hundred and fifty-six chapters, [Col. 1087B] from which Philastrius composed his book *On Heresies*. This is also confirmed by the fact that the catalogue of those charged with heresy before Christ’s advent, placed by Philastrius at the beginning of the work and ending with the Herodians, contains twenty-eight chapters or heresies, as Augustine likewise states. But the remaining heresies, both those after Christ’s advent and those arising under the Apostles, number in the published editions only one hundred and twenty-two, although Augustine says that they are one hundred and twenty-eight. That same number is indeed given by Augustine also in chapter 41 of the book or catalogue which he wrote *On Heresies*.

Later writers who mention Philastrius’ work agree with Augustine: the author of the Appendix to Ildefonsus’ *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 3, [Col. 1087C] says:

> Philastrius, bishop of Brescia, published a book *On Heresies*, setting forth each one, whether those which existed among the Jewish people before the Incarnation of Christ, of which he enumerates twenty-eight; or those which arose against the Catholic faith after the coming of the Lord and Saviour, of which he describes one hundred and twenty-eight.

Likewise John Trithemius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 84, speaking of Philastrius, says: “It is reported, Augustine being witness, that his notable work was written on one hundred and fifty-six heresies.”

The distinguished Fabricius, in the *Testimonies concerning Philastrius*, having cited Augustine’s passage, from which the number of heresies listed by Philastrius is inferred, observed that six chapters were missing, and conjectured that they were absent from the end of Philastrius’ work: “It is credible that the final chapters of the book [Col. 1087D] of Philastrius, in which there is no trace of a conclusion, have perished.” But this conjecture turned out not very happily for that most distinguished man. For in the Corbie manuscript, by which the deficiency of these six chapters is splendidly supplied, the same chapters are placed in various locations and under different numbers.

Thus, after chapter 106 of the Hamburg edition, and also of ours—marked in the manuscript as no. LXXVII, and presenting the heresy that doubts concerning the years and time of Christ—there follows in the same manuscript, with the same number LXXVII repeated, another heresy on the end of the world and the consummation of the age, absent from the editions. Then after chapter 112 (113 in our edition), concerning the seven planets and marked in the manuscript no. [Col. 1088A] LXXXIV, there is added in the same place, under no. LXXXVI, a heresy concerning a double God and the judgment of the devil. After chapter 114 (116 in ours), concerning the blindness of Adam and Eve, no. LXXXVII in the manuscript, there occurs in the same manuscript, no. LXXXVIII, another heresy concerning the skins or tunics which the Lord made for the first parents after their transgression. And after chapter 136 (139 in ours), which treats of the four living creatures in the Prophets and is marked no. CVIII, no. CIX of the same Corbie manuscript contains a heresy concerning the day of Epiphany—all absent from the editions.

Thus, in the editions, after chapter 146 (150 in ours), no. CXIX in the manuscript, concerning Solomon’s wives, follows chapter 147 (152 in ours), concerning the breath Adam received. But in the manuscript there is inserted, no. CXX, a heresy concerning stone knives and the circumcision of the Jews. Likewise, after chapter 148 (153 in ours), where the editions place [Col. 1088B] the heresy concerning the measuring-line in the prophet Zechariah, which is no. CXXII in the manuscript, the same manuscript codex adds under no. CXXIII another heresy concerning the birds that ministered to Elijah. By these supplements, the deficiency of six chapters in Philastrius’ work is completely restored; and consequently, by the benefit of the Corbie codex, we possess Philastrius, hitherto maimed and incomplete, whole and complete.

23. Since in our *Spicilegium*, appended to the variant readings of the Corbie manuscript, we have touched very little, or not at all, on the matters set forth in these six Philastrian chapters, it will, I think, not be inappropriate to make some observations here, which may both cast greater light upon the chapters themselves and disclose and clarify Philastrius’ meaning concerning opinions that perhaps prevailed more widely at that time.

[Col. 1088C] Thus, in the Corbie manuscript, no. LXXVII, there is placed a heresy concerning the end of the world and the consummation of the age, by which some maintained that the determination of the times had been fixed by God Christ the Saviour. But Philastrius, rejecting that view—which supposed that a fixed number of years, neither more nor fewer, would precede the consummation—says that the prophets everywhere announced that the consummation of the age would occur about the five-hundredth year, and that the Lord would thus come again from heaven.

This opinion of Philastrius rested upon a principle common to almost all the Fathers in the first centuries of the Church: namely, that the world would be consummated six thousand years after its creation. On this point see the Epistle bearing the name of Barnabas, chapter 15; Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book V, chapter 28; Lactantius, book VII of the *Divine Institutes*, [Col. 1088D] chapters 14 and 25; our Gaudentius; and others. Since, however, according to the computation commonly accepted at the time, more than five thousand years were thought to have elapsed from the creation of the world to Christ, it followed that the consummation of the age and Christ’s return from heaven were believed not to be far distant.

Indeed, Hippolytus the martyr, according to the testimony of Photius, codex 202, and Syncellus, p. 315, thought that Christ was born at the beginning of the year 5501 from the creation of the world, but that the judgment would occur five hundred years after Christ’s birth—an opinion that nearly agrees with Philastrius’. There were those who placed the number of five hundred years, at whose end the consummation of the world and Christ’s return from heaven were to take place, after the completion of the sixth millennium, and thus added these five hundred years to the six-thousandth year from the creation of the world. Cotelerius teaches this in his note on the Epistle of Barnabas, p. 44. Whether Philastrius held the former or the latter of these opinions is not sufficiently clear.

See further Augustine, *City of God*, book XVIII, chapter 53; Cotelerius on the Epistle of Barnabas, p. 44, where he also discusses another passage in Philastrius, who says in chapter 106 that those are mistaken who think that from Christ’s first advent to the second—that is, to the consummation of the age—three hundred and sixty-five years, neither more nor fewer, must be counted; likewise Clement of Alexandria, Potter edition, p. 407, in the collected notes on book I of the *Stromata*, chapter 21; and Feuardentius on Irenaeus, [Col. 1089B] book V, chapter 28, Massuet edition, p. 199. I pass over both ancient and modern interpreters, who have ranged widely over this subject in commenting on Matthew, chapter XXIV, verse 36, and 1 Thessalonians, chapter V, verse 1.

24. At number LXXXVI in the Corbie manuscript is added a heresy concerning a double God, which Philastrius there attributes to the Manichaeans, Gnostics, Nicolaitans, and other depraved persons who agree in this error, saying that one God is good and another evil. Elsewhere Philastrius likewise accuses the Manichaeans of this error, namely in chapter 61, to which we added some remarks in the *Spicilegium*. The origin of this error, however, is assigned by Philastrius himself in chapters 44 and 45 to Cerdo and Marcion, Cerdo’s disciple. Epiphanius rebukes them for this error, volume I, pp. 300, 303, observing that Marcion established not merely two principles but three—a point noted also by Grabe on Irenaeus, book III, chapter 43, Massuet edition, p. 144. Before Epiphanius, Irenaeus refuted the same error, himself in book I, chapter 27, book III, chapters 9 and 43—indeed, almost throughout book III, as Feuardentius observes on Irenaeus, book I, chapter 29, Massuet edition, p. 77—and throughout book IV, as Massuet notes in Dissertation 3 on Irenaeus, no. 55, p. CXXX.

What Philastrius adds—“Therefore God did not cast our father out of paradise through envy, but rather, consulting for his good, did not spare him while he sinned in a small matter” [Note: [Col. 1089D] Irenaeus speaks similarly of Adam, book III, chapter 23, no. 6, p. 222, Massuet edition.], “lest by sparing him he should find him, as he advanced to a greater age, proceeding even to greater other crime[s]” (read: “to still greater crimes”), “and afterwards condemn him more severely when, by criminal judgment, he had been made guilty”—resembles what he says in [Col. 1089D] chapter 129 concerning Cain’s sin: that he was rebuked by the Lord so that, if thereafter the fruit of good works followed him, he would without doubt receive remission of so great a crime.

Moreover, the words “as he advanced to a greater age” seem to indicate that Philastrius held the opinion that the first parents were not created at a mature age. Irenaeus sets out this view in book III, chapter 22, no. 4. Although Massuet predicts in his note on that passage of Irenaeus that it will not have many defenders [Note: [Col. 1089D] P. 219.], Clement of Alexandria expressly teaches it in the *Protrepticus*, chapter 11, where he says of Adam: *παρήγετο ἐπιθυμίαις ὁ παῖς*, “the child was led astray by desires”; likewise Theophilus of Antioch, book II to Autolycius, p. 314, in the *Orthodox*, saying that Adam could not yet eat of the tree of knowledge because *ἔτι νήπιος ἦν*, “he was still an infant,” or child.

As for what follows concerning the sentence and judgment of the devil, by which Philastrius seems to suggest that after his fall the devil still had room for repentance: perhaps this accords with the familiar opinion of not a few ancient writers that the devil had not yet received the sentence of his condemnation and had not yet been assigned to eternal torments, but would suffer this at the last judgment. For Philastrius says: “Since the devil is seen to be more obstinate toward repentance, he awaits from Christ the Lord a greater servitude”—perhaps *severitatem*, “severity,” should be read—“at the future judgment.” See Massuet on Irenaeus, [Col. 1090B] book V, chapter 26, p. 324; also Dissertation 3, on Irenaeus’ doctrine, article 9, nos. 108–109; Feuardentius, annotations on Irenaeus, Massuet edition, pp. 11 and 198; and Petavius, volume III of *Dogmatic Theology*, book I, *On Angels*, chapter 8, and book III, chapter 4.

25. What Philastrius relates at no. LXXXVIII of the Corbie codex concerning the skins or tunics of the first parents is directed at refuting the heresy of those who thought that the human being was already “material” (*choicus*), as Irenaeus says [Note: [Col. 1090D] Book I, chapter 5, no. 5, p. 27.], that is, composed of matter, though he received his form not from this dry earth but from an invisible substance; and that he then put on the fleshly and perceptible surface or form of the body when Genesis says that the Lord made skins or tunics for the first parents (Gen. III:21). The Valentinians in particular were charged with this view, as is clear from Tertullian, *Against the Valentinians*, chapter 24:

> Meanwhile, the Valentinians say that afterwards a fleshly surface was woven over the material man, and that this is the skin-tunic subject to sense.

And in chapter 7 of *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*:

> For those skin-tunics which Adam and Eve, stripped of paradise, put on will not, as some wish, themselves be the restoration of flesh from mud; for somewhat earlier Adam had already recognized in the woman’s flesh the propagation of his own substance: “This now is bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh” (Gen. II:23). And the very portion of the male, transferred into the woman, was supplied with flesh—a flesh, I suppose, that must be supplied with mud, if Adam is still mud.

What Tertullian called “skin-tunics,” Irenaeus called the *dermatine tunic*, when recounting this error of the Valentinians [Note: [Col. 1090D] Book I, chapter 5, no. 5.]:

> Afterwards, they say, a *dermatine tunic* was placed around him; and by this they mean sensible flesh.

Sixtus of Siena, book V of the *Sacred Library*, annotation 53, reports that Methodius ascribed this error to Origen, as though he had thought it utterly ridiculous that God should prepare skins from flayed dead animals and sew skin-tunics, as if he were a tanner or a maker of fur garments. But Sixtus clears Origen of this error in the same annotation 53, adding:

> I suspect that this passage was corrupted by Origen’s enemies; for he sets forth his own mind in a Catholic manner on this matter in Homily 6 on Leviticus, where he writes: “God made [Col. 1091A] skin-tunics and clothed Adam and his wife. Those tunics, therefore, were made from skins taken from animals; for it was fitting that the sinner should be clothed in such things.”

Therefore the objection that it would be unbecoming for God to prepare skin-tunics for human beings should be attributed not so much to Origen as to his followers [Note: [Col. 1091D] See Sixtus of Siena, book V, *Sacred Library*, annotations 54–55.]. To answer it, some said that the skin-tunics in that passage of Genesis signify the bark of trees; for just as animal hides are called skins, so tree-bark is also called skin. But our Philastrius takes another route to dissolve the objection. He says that the skin-tunics do not at all signify the bodies of the first parents, but that in this way God is declared, through divine power, to have given them wisdom so that they might make garments for their bodies.

What Philastrius says here, namely that on the seventh day the Lord took earth from clay and fashioned their bodies, is altogether the same as what he had affirmed in chapter 97, where he treats of the image of God in the human body. For there too he has: “On the seventh day Scripture says concerning Adam: ‘And the Lord took earth from clay and formed the human being whom he made.’” Yet Scripture plainly says that God created nothing on the seventh day, but completed all his works on the sixth and rested from all his works on the seventh, as Fabricius rightly noted on that passage [Note: [Col. 1091D] Note: “The soul on the sixth day.”]. For this reason he calls Philastrius’ opinion incredible and contrary to the common view, since it conflicts with the sacred writer’s narrative, which expressly affirms the contrary.

26. Then there is added in the Corbie manuscript, at no. CIX, another heresy concerning the day of Epiphany. According to Philastrius, some held that only the Nativity of the Lord [Col. 1091C] ought to be celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of January [25 December], but not the day of Epiphany. Augustine, *Sermon 32 on Time*, the fourth on Epiphany, states that the Donatists in Africa were formerly followers of this opinion:

> With good reason the Donatist heretics never wished to celebrate this day with us, because they neither love unity nor communicate with the Eastern Church, where that star appeared.

Perhaps Philastrius also distinguished the two days so precisely—the Lord’s Nativity and the coming of the Magi—when he said that the Saviour fulfilled all things carnally in himself and from himself, so that he was born on VIII Kalends of January and appeared on the sixth [day, namely, of the same month]; and shortly afterward: “These four greater feast-days were established: first, that on which he was born; then that on which he appeared, that is, twelve days later.” Perhaps he did so in order to find fault with the Greeks, who commemorated the adoration of the Magi on VIII Kalends of January, on the same day as the Lord’s Nativity, as the Menologia of both Sirlet and Basil report, in Florentinius’ annotations on the more ancient Western Martyrology [Note: [Col. 1091D] Exercise 4, p. 235.].

Florentinius himself, to be sure, argues from several considerations [Note: [Col. 1091D] P. 237.] that both mysteries—the Lord’s Nativity and the coming of the Magi—could have occurred on the same day, 25 December, although in different years. Perhaps this is also supported by the fact that among Eastern Christians both feast-days, the Lord’s Nativity and the coming and adoration of the Magi, were called Epiphany, as Macrius observes in the *Hierolexicon*; and Suidas calls the very Incarnation of Jesus Christ an Epiphany: *Ἐπιφάνεια, ἡ τοῦ Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ ἔνσαρκος οἰκονομία*—“Epiphany is the incarnate dispensation of our Saviour Jesus Christ.”

Philastrius is correct here in using the name Epiphany for the adoration of the Magi, although elsewhere, namely in chapter 149, he calls the Lord’s Ascension an Epiphany, as Fabricius noted on that passage [Note: [Col. 1091D] Note: “The third at Epiphany.”], a view with which we too agreed in the *Spicilegium* [Note: [Col. 1092D] See the note appended to chapter 149. EDIT.]. Here, moreover, he assigns four greater annual feast-days: the Lord’s Nativity, Epiphany, thirdly the day on which he suffered and rose again, [Col. 1092B] and fourthly that on which he ascended into heaven around Pentecost. Elsewhere, in chapter 141, he enumerates eight festivals which the Catholic Church knows and observes; but they are almost the same as those he mentions here, with only the Lenten fast and Wednesday added there. On these see, if desired, Fabricius’ notes on that passage [Note: [Col. 1092D] Note: “On the eight festivals.”], as well as what we added in the *Spicilegium* [Note: [Col. 1092D] See the note appended to chapter 141. EDIT.].

Finally Philastrius adds that some think the day of Epiphany to be the day of baptism, and others the day of the transfiguration on the mountain. Both interpretations certainly fit well enough, if we consider the force of the word, which signifies an appearing or manifestation. On each day the Lord appeared and was manifested, both by the Father’s voice and by John’s testimony.

27. Concerning the stone knives used for circumcision, [Col. 1092C] of which Philastrius speaks at no. CXX of the Corbie codex, we have said something in the *Spicilegium*. Here it is enough to observe that Philastrius in this passage rejects the use of stone knives, saying that the Jews could more easily be endangered by them than cured. Yet elsewhere [Note: [Col. 1092D] Chapter 118.], citing the passage in Exodus (Exod. IV:25), he writes that Zipporah, Moses’ wife, took a stone and circumcised the boy; and in Joshua V, the passage with which Philastrius is here concerned, it is expressly said: “Make for yourself stone knives.”

Whether Joshua used a stone or a sword for circumcision is indeed a much-debated question among interpreters. Masius especially, and Drusius on Joshua V:2, should be consulted; both incline toward a stone rather than a sword. Masius even adds in support of this opinion the judgment of Moses Maimonides, the most learned of the Jews, who thinks that Joshua used hard flints, not sharp little swords. Also fitting and highly apt is that familiar anagoge by which the rock is called Christ (1 Cor. X), so that circumcision of the heart through Christ might be signified, as Ambrose says in the preface to the Epistle to the Galatians. Yet Philastrius here intends, when he says that the Jews were circumcised with stone knives, that Jews are daily circumcised—that is, that saving knowledge of Christ is instilled into them—by Gentiles, whose very hard and stony minds had formerly been devoted to impiety, but who afterward became believers in [Col. 1093A] the Lord, having abandoned their stony mindset. In this trope Philastrius has Gaudentius in agreement with him, who in Tractate 2 calls the Gentiles converted to Christ stones once exceedingly hard.

I confess, together with many others, that I wholly do not know how the Jews who used a stone knife for circumcision could more easily be endangered than healed, as Philastrius here maintains. Rather, the fact that iron causes a more grievous wound than stone seems indicated by the great usefulness and suitability of flint knives for more difficult incisions, as Stephanus Morinus explains at length in *Exercises on Languages*, part II, chapter 9, p. 290. Pliny also says, XII.25, that balsam shrinks from injury by iron and is therefore cut with glass, stone, or bone knives; this is confirmed and elucidated by Salmasius, *Plinian Exercises*, chapter 35, p. 417.

28. Finally Philastrius adds at no. CXXIII of the Corbie manuscript another heresy, as he calls it, concerning the birds that ministered to Elijah. By it, he says, some suppose that ravens brought him meat for food in the evening and bread in the morning. This displeases Philastrius. For he says that the holy and most blessed prophet, who had despised every such food by voluntary abstinence, did not at any time eat meat; and that on account of such great dignity he deserved to obtain from God the honor of being carried aloft into paradise, where he was placed with all the saints.

He then adds: “For if someone says that ravens brought him bread, this is sometimes reasonable; but concerning meat it is found incongruous.” Certainly the ravens brought bread only to Paul, as Jerome relates in his *Life*; and Malvenda, translating the passage where ravens feed Elijah [Note: [Col. 1093D] 3 Kings XVII:6: “And the ravens caused bread to come to him.” *Bibliotheca Maxima* of John de la Haye, vol. IV, p. 693.], mentions bread alone. But both the Hebrew text and the Septuagint version, 3 Kings XVII, have bread and meat; all the other versions likewise mention bread and meat. Indeed, Basil, an eminent advocate of abstinence, acknowledges that bread and meat were brought to Elijah, in Homily 3 *On Avaricious Rich Men*; and Augustine agrees with Basil in *Sermon 146 on Time*.

There was, moreover, a Jewish tradition that the food supplied to Elijah by ravens was taken, through the ministry of angels, from Ahab’s own table. The sacred text expressly relates that the ravens did this twice a day: “The ravens also brought him bread and meat in the morning, and likewise bread and meat in the evening” (3 Kings XVII:6). Yet Philastrius remembers meat as brought to Elijah only in the evening: “There are certain heretics who suppose concerning blessed Elijah that ravens brought him meat for food in the evening and bread in the morning.” [Note: [Col. 1093D] Augustine too agrees with Philastrius, both in the cited *Sermon 146 on Time* and in Homily 18, where he says: “Did not a raven offer him [Col. 1094D] bread in the morning and meat in the evening?”]

It should also be observed that the end of this chapter was cut away by copyists, perhaps weary because Philastrius differed so openly from the history of the sacred text. Learned men long ago observed that something similar happened, for a not very dissimilar reason, to the last five chapters of Irenaeus [Note: [Col. 1094D] Feuardentius, *Annotations*, p. 205; Grabe, *Prolegomena*, p. 16, Massuet edition.]: namely, [Col. 1094A] because copyists in a later age did not wish to copy further the doctrine of the millennial kingdom, which had become hateful to them, and therefore broke off the thread. Yet, as Feuardentius rightly says, this evil should have been remedied by some warning, not by erasure; that is, by the pen, not the knife.

## § V. On the Plan and Order of This Edition

29. It remains for us now to say a few words about the plan and arrangement of this edition. Our chief purpose was to present Philastrius’ book, which holds the first place in this collection, as corrected and complete as possible. Several editions of Philastrius had already appeared, but none of them was sufficiently corrected or accurate; every one abounded in many errors. It therefore seemed altogether necessary to have the assistance of some manuscript codex, by whose aid the text of Philastrius might be restored and healed.

Now, from France we had been given almost certain hope that we would obtain the variant readings of the Corbie manuscript. But because they were delayed for a long time and the typographical undertaking could not endure a longer delay, it became necessary to turn our attention to the published copies and employ them to advance the work. The Basel edition prepared by John Sicard in the year of Christ’s birth 1528, in which Philastrius then first saw the light, seemed better and more corrected than the Helmstedt editions printed later, in 1611 and 1621, and consequently also better than those subsequent to the Basel edition offered in the Parisian, Cologne, and Lyons *Libraries of the Fathers*. But since it was evident that the latest of all, published at Hamburg in 1721 by the distinguished John Albert Fabricius, had been corrected by him in many places and restored to the genuine reading, we resolved to reproduce it as better and more excellent than all the others.

Furthermore, Fabricius himself affirmed that, in preparing and embellishing the Hamburg edition, he had chiefly used the Basel edition [Note: [Col. 1094D] Preface to Philastrius.]. Therefore, where manuscript codices were lacking, it seemed that little or nothing further was to be desired when the two editions agreed, especially since Fabricius’ edition had been illuminated and enlarged by the learned man’s numerous and substantial annotations. Meanwhile, the most eminent Cardinal Quirinus had arranged for Fabricius’ later *Curae* on Philastrius to be sent to us from Hamburg, lest any small fragment (*ἀποσπασμάτιον*) of that great man be lacking from our edition. Finally, the variant readings of the Corbie codex arrived at Brescia; their very numerous corrections, and corrections of no small importance for supplementing and restoring the text of Philastrius, we placed in our *Spicilegium*.

30. The order of this edition has been arranged by us thus: first is presented **PHILASTRIUS’ BOOK ON HERESIES, WITH THE CORRECTIONS AND NOTES OF JOHN ALBERT [Col. 1095A] FABRICIUS**, everywhere reproducing the text of the Hamburg edition. If any fault occurs in it that can be removed by the aid of the Corbie manuscript, the reader will find it dealt with in the *Spicilegium*.

There follow **THE POSTHUMOUS NOTES OF THE SAME JOHN ALBERT FABRICIUS ON PHILASTRIUS**. From them the reader will easily perceive how extensive and manifold was the reading of this great man. In transcribing them, the pages of both editions, the Hamburg edition and ours, are marked, so that the passages may be found more easily. They are found on page 147 of this Brescia edition, together with the letter sent by Hermann Samuel Reimarus to the most eminent Cardinal Quirinus.

Afterwards, on page 152, are added **VARIANT READINGS IN PHILASTRIUS, FROM THE CORBIE MANUSCRIPT**, together with the letter of Dom John Raverdy, Benedictine monk, to that same most eminent Cardinal Quirinus. In presenting them, we wish the reader to be warned that the reading of the Corbie manuscript has been reproduced exactly, retaining even its very errors and faults, lest anything be lacking in fidelity.

To these is appended our *Spicilegium* to the notes of the distinguished Johann Albert Fabricius, in which the principal and more ample place is occupied by emendations drawn from the Corbie manuscript. For, as has already been said, the various readings of this codex reached us rather late, namely at the time when everything was ready for publication—indeed, when this edition itself had already been begun. Therefore no other provision could then be made, either for the public benefit in restoring Philastrius’s text or for the private considerations of the printer [Col. 1095C]. Moreover, I should certainly be unfair—I whom Fabricius himself called an impartial judge of his diligence in editing Philastrius [Note: [Col. 1095D] Preface to Philastrius.]—if I wished anything to be detracted from the reputation or labours of this eminent man, who has deserved exceedingly well not only of Philastrius but of all letters.

[Note: [Col. 1095D] In this latest and, as we hope, most perfect of all editions, the studies of the most learned Galeardus will be brought back to unity and method, from both of which he was compelled by typographical necessity to depart, in the following manner:

1. The variant readings of the Saint-Germain codex will be placed in due order beneath the individual columns, with corresponding small letters referring the reader to them.

2. All the chapters which the Fabrician edition gained from the aforementioned codex will be inserted in their proper places in the text, [Col. 1096D] so as to continue both the sequence of subjects and that of the numbering.

3. Fabricius’s posthumous notes, fitted to and intermingled with his earlier annotations, will accompany the text in continuous elucidation.

4. Whatever notes Galeardus collected in the *Spicilegium* at the end of his edition will be arranged beneath the text in the same order as Fabricius’s notes.

5. The author’s name will be attached to every note, lest any confusion arise. EDITORS.]

The things which he himself did for Philastrius are splendid and almost innumerable; consequently, if he left anything still untouched or insufficiently polished, no one should on that account justly charge this against him as a fault. But since it is the rule that, in editing and emending ancient writings, there is always room for the diligence of a later scholar, we ask and in turn grant this indulgence: that everyone engaged in the same arena may frankly and simply express his judgment concerning matters which earlier scholars have observed or said otherwise [Col. 1095D]. Such freedom of judgment is not usually construed maliciously except by persons insufficiently candid and insufficiently devoted to truth.

In this edition, moreover, special care has been taken to correct faulty punctuation, as will be evident everywhere to those comparing both copies—the Hamburg edition and our own [Col. 1096A]. In all other respects we have almost always reproduced the Hamburg edition, changing very few things, where the Basel edition appeared superior to the Hamburg one. The index of scriptural passages cited by Philastrius was compiled by the Reverend Antonio Guelfi of Brescia, almoner to the Most Eminent Cardinal Quirini. I gladly wish here to testify that his assistance in collating the variant readings, and consequently in refining this entire edition, was never lacking to me.

## § VI. Various editions of the works of St Philastrius

Philastrius first saw the light in 1528, published by Johann Sichard together with Lanfranc’s little treatise against Berengar [Col. 1096B]. Galeardus found this edition superior and more correct than the subsequent Helmstedt editions and those found in the Paris, Cologne, and Lyons *Libraries of the Fathers*. Finally, in the present century, in 1721, Johann Albert Fabricius, in the Hamburg edition, assisted him admirably—not indeed with manuscripts, but with his critical acumen—and illuminated him with most learned annotation. Then, in 1738, Galeardus’s very fully equipped edition appeared, presenting Fabricius’s text but enriched with Fabricius’s posthumous notes, the variants and emendations of the Corbie manuscript; in it Philastrius was for the first time enlarged and completed with six chapters which had hitherto been lacking. Andreas Gallandius likewise retained Fabricius’s text, immediately placing beneath it the variants of the Corbie codex and inserting in their proper places the six chapters supplied from that manuscript [Col. 1096C]. To him is due the latest edition of this author.

## SIXTEENTH CENTURY

**1528. Basel, octavo.** *Catalogue of Heresies* by Philastrius, bishop of Brescia. Added is the most learned little work of Lanfranc, bishop of Canterbury, on the sacrament of the Eucharist against Berengar. Now newly published.

Sichard, whom we have said brought these little works to light, is the same man who in precisely the same year caused the *Antidote against All Heresies* to be published. He wrote a dedicatory letter to Balthasar, elected coadjutor of Constance—postulate of Hildesheim, bishop of Malta, ambassador and vice-chancellor of His Imperial Majesty—at Basel on 26 November 1528 [Col. 1096D]. In it he declares that by publishing these writings of the ancients he was avenging the sorrow which he derived from the calamity of an age shaken by similar heresies. Meanwhile he left us uncertain about the documents from which he brought forth Philastrius; although perhaps there is room for conjecture [Col. 1097A], since he testifies that in the preceding year he had gone to Trier to inspect ancient libraries, where an occasion may have arisen for him to pay homage to Balthasar in this preface. The text was simply transcribed, with an index of noteworthy matters prefixed.

**1539. Basel, … octavo.** *Catalogue of Heresies* by St Philastrius, bishop of Brescia, with a supplement by an anonymous recent writer; 114 sayings of the Fathers concerning the duty of true rulers of God’s Church; and an excerpt from the letter of Nicephorus Chartophylax to Theodosius the Monk on the power of binding and loosing.

**1575. Paris, at Michel Sonnius, folio.** *Catalogue of Heretics* by St Philastrius, in volume V of Bignius’s *Library of the Fathers*.

**1589. Paris, folio.** *Book on Heresies* by Philastrius, bishop of Brescia, in volume IV of the second edition of Bignius’s *Library of the Fathers*.

## SEVENTEENTH CENTURY

[Col. 1097B]

**1611. Helmstedt, by Jacob Lucius, quarto.** *Catalogue of Almost All Heresies* by St Philastrius, with the supplement of an anonymous author; edited by Johann von Fuchte.

**1618. Cologne, folio.** *Book on Heresies* by Philastrius, in volume IV of the *Library of the Fathers*.

**1621. Helmstedt, by Jacob Lucius, quarto.** Reprint of Fuchte’s edition.

**1644. Paris, printed by three booksellers, folio.** *Book on Heresies* by Philastrius, in volume IV of the *Library of the Fathers*, of this edition and of that bearing the date 1654 in its title.

**1676. Helmstedt, … quarto.** Second reprint of Fuchte’s edition.

**1677. Lyons, at the Anissons, folio.** *Book on Heresies* by St Philastrius [Col. 1097C], in volume V of the *Great Library of the Fathers*, pp. 701–726.

## EIGHTEENTH CENTURY

**1721. Hamburg, at the expense of Theodor Christoph Felgner, octavo.** *Book on Heresies* by St Philastrius, bishop of Brescia, with the emendations and notes of Johann Albert Fabricius, and enriched with very extensive indices.

Although Fabricius had no manuscripts at hand and had to rely solely upon the old editions, this Philastrius nevertheless appears considerably more correct [Col. 1098A] and is everywhere learnedly and aptly explained. He acknowledges that a few passages still remain in which he wished for light from manuscripts:

> “The illustrious Gisbert Cuper once gave me hope, he says, of obtaining a handwritten copy from Italy; but after an interval he informed me again that all that hope had vanished. Thus I had to rely solely upon the editions, especially the Basel ones. What I have nevertheless accomplished in editing this writer, I shall gladly allow impartial and learned judges to assess—above all Paul Gagliardus, canon of Brescia, whom I learned, somewhat later, from the *Venetian Journal of the Learned Men of Italy* to be preparing an edition of Philastrius and Gaudentius. I did not wish to omit the chapter headings, although added by someone other than Philastrius himself and sometimes less suitable. But I omitted the appendix or supplement of a recent writer, since it is not very accurate and has no authority, intending to add in its place the little book on heresies which Claudius Menardus published under Jerome’s name. Yet, being occupied with the fairs, I intend to publish that little work of Pseudo-Jerome in a separate volume, to add to it other brief ancient writers on heretics, and to prefix a dissertation opposing the error and prejudice of those who allow themselves to be so offended by the heresies of Christians, and by their number and variety, that they think too unworthily and irreverently of the truth of religion itself.”

After the preface is placed the *Life of St Philastrius* by St Gaudentius—namely, his sermon delivered on the anniversary of Philastrius’s solemn commemoration, fourteen years after Philastrius’s death—and certain testimonies of earlier editors concerning him [Col. 1098C]. The notes beneath the text abound in wide reading, elucidating the author’s opinions, and are sometimes critical.

**1738. Brescia, from the press of Giovanni Maria Rizzardi.** *Book on Heresies* by St Philastrius, bishop of Brescia, with the complete notes of Johann Albert Fabricius. There were added Variant Readings from the Corbie manuscript codex and the *Spicilegium* of Paolo Galeardus, canon of Brescia: in Angelo Maria Quirini’s collection of the ancient Fathers of the Brescian Church, pp. 1–183.

[Col. 1097]

## PREFACE OF JOHANN ALBERT FABRICIUS TO THE BOOK OF ST PHILASTRIUS ON HERESIES, PREFIXED TO THE HAMBURG EDITION OF 1721

[Col. 1097D]

I do not at all regret having spent certain hours in editing and elucidating the little work of St Philastrius, the most ancient writer after Tertullian whom we have among Latin authors on heresies.

I acknowledge that I have learned various things from him; nor can I refrain from embracing and commending the doctrine and zeal of this devout Doctor and lover of Christ. Yet St Augustine long ago rightly observed, as many have since, that Philastrius here and there proscribes among heresies quite a number of things which are not heresies, but either misinterpretations (*parermēneiai*, παρερμηνεῖαι) [Col. 1098D], or hallucinations of whatever kind, or errors—if indeed they are errors. For there are certain chapters, though few, in which the opinion that he himself charges with heresy appears even more true.

Likewise, a few passages still remain in which I should wish for light from manuscript codices. The illustrious Gisbert Cuper once gave me hope of obtaining a handwritten copy from Italy, but after an interval he again informed me that all such hope had vanished. Therefore I had to rely solely upon the editions, especially those of Basel [Col. 1099A]. But what I have accomplished in editing this writer I shall gladly allow fair and learned judges to assess, above all Paolo Galeardus, canon of Brescia, whom I learned somewhat later, from the *Venetian Journal of the Learned Men of Italy*, to be preparing an edition of Philastrius and Gaudentius. I did not wish to omit the chapter headings, although they were added by someone other than Philastrius himself and are sometimes less appropriate. But I omitted the appendix or supplement of a recent writer because it is not very accurate and has no authority, intending to add in its place the little book on heresies which Claudius Menardus published under Jerome’s name. Yet, being occupied with the fairs, I intend to publish that little work of Pseudo-Jerome in a separate volume, to add to it other brief ancient writers on heretics, and to prefix [Col. 1099B] a dissertation opposing the error and prejudice of those who allow themselves to be so offended by the heresies of Christians, and by their number and variety, that they think too unworthily and irreverently of the truth of religion itself.

Besides this book on heresies, an ancient Latin translation of the Epistle of St Barnabas is ascribed to our Philastrius. It bears Philastrius’s name in the Corbie manuscript codex; in the *Acts of the Saints*, 11 June, vol. II, pp. 460 and 457, “Philostorgius” is wrongly printed in its place [Col. 1100A]. There are also those who ascribe to Philastrius the *Acts of Saints Faustinus and Jovita* in Surius and Bollandus, 15 February, as well as the *Acts of St Afra, virgin and martyr of Brescia*, in the *Acts of the Saints*, 24 May. But an attentive and experienced reader will not doubt that both works are by a wholly different and much later writer.

Those who maintain that the name is Latin in origin think it no different from *filiaster*, used for “stepson,” though Cange and Friedrich Lindenbrog, in his work on the *Code of Ancient Laws*, p. 1400, note it in a later age. Fulbert of Chartres, Letter 33: “If anyone has held his stepson or stepdaughter before the bishop for confirmation, let him be separated from his wife and not take another.” But to Greek ears *Philastrius* sounds more attractively and more correctly as “lover of stars”; this was also the name of Philastrius [Col. 1100B], a Studite monk, by whom Constantine Harmenopulus was trained about A.D. 1340, according to Nicetas Comnenus Papadopoli in the *Mystagogical Preludes*, p. 143.

From the monuments and testimonies of the ancients which I have appended, it cannot be clearly and certainly inferred at what time the bishop of Brescia departed this life. Yet conversely I see that nothing can be objected to the opinion of learned men who say that he did not live beyond the year 388 after Christ’s birth. Farewell.

[Col. 1099]

## LETTER OF JOHANN RAVERDY, TRANSMITTING TO THE MOST EMINENT CARDINAL QUIRINI THE VARIANT READINGS OF THE SAINT-GERMAIN MANUSCRIPT CODEX

[Note: [Col. 1099D] This manuscript is the same codex of the monastery of Corbie which Fabricius mentions in the preface to the Hamburg edition of Philastrius, where he calls it the Corbie manuscript [Col. 1100D]; it is discussed more fully above in the preface to this edition. It is a parchment manuscript, elegantly written in the ninth century, numbered 717, formerly 625.]

[Col. 1099C]

As soon as I learned that Your Eminence needed the variant readings of our manuscript of Philastrius, I eagerly undertook this small task. What moved me to do so, Monseigneur, was the high esteem which I have always retained for the solid piety and profound learning of Your Eminence. These astonished me and won my admiration twenty-eight years ago, when I was studying at Saint-Denis in France, where I often had the honour of seeing Your Eminence, as also at Saint-Germain and Saint-Remy of Rheims.

I am fully persuaded, Monseigneur, that Your Eminence has no recollection of me, because, being then only a schoolboy, I did not merit your attention; whereas I never tired of hearing you speak on subjects of every kind, so much was there to learn from it. It is through these first [Col. 1099D] impressions, Monseigneur, and through these feelings of esteem and admiration, that I have always taken a wholly particular interest in everything concerning Your Eminence. I have never lost sight of you, and I was filled with joy when I saw you clothed in the Roman purple and enter the Sacred College, of which you are now an ornament, as well as the honour and glory of the Order of St Benedict. I do not despair of seeing you one day splendidly fill [Col. 1100C] the foremost see of the Church.

These are the wishes I make, Monseigneur, for Your Eminence; they are likewise those of our congregation and our superiors, who are full of veneration for you and will never neglect anything by which they may deserve the honour of your protection. I hope, Monseigneur, that Your Eminence will be satisfied with the variants which I have the honour to send you: I have prepared them with every possible exactness. You will find six chapters missing from the printed text. One could wish that the manuscript were more correct; for though it is very beautifully written and belongs to the ninth or tenth century, it contains many scribal mistakes. But it is enough to know that Your Eminence takes the trouble to revise this ancient author, in order to be assured that he will reappear in all his purity.

I shall count myself fortunate, Monseigneur, if my small task can be useful to you, all the more because I undertook it only to give you tokens of my attachment, veneration, and most profound respect, with which I have the honour to be,

Monseigneur,  
Your Eminence’s most humble, etc.

From Saint-Germain-des-Prés, 14 February 1737.

[Col. 1101]

## LETTER OF HERMANN SAMUEL REIMARUS, TRANSMITTING THE POSTHUMOUS NOTES OF J. A. FABRICIUS ON PHILASTRIUS

[Note: [Col. 1101B] Hermann Reimarus himself mentions that he sent these notes to the Most Eminent Cardinal Quirini in his *Commentary on the Life and Writings of Johann Albert Fabricius*, published at Hamburg in 1737, p. 167. In another letter to the same Eminence, dated 29 January 1737, he also writes that his veneration for the virtues of that Most Eminent person had been greatly increased after his friend Conrad Widovius, senator of Hamburg, who had spent much time with him in the Longueville residence at Paris, had extolled them extraordinarily to him.]

[Col. 1101A]

The letter written by Your Eminence to Fabricius, my father-in-law, was delivered to me after his death, though rather late. In it I see that you desire Fabricius’s later work on Philastrius, and whatever he had lately discovered concerning the Syriac text of St Ephraim. Indeed, I regard the opportunity offered me to write to a man of such rank, such proven virtue, and such extensive learning as an honour of the highest kind, as is fitting. Yet I confess that I should embrace it much more gladly if I were able to provide material of greater importance in answer to the questions raised.

For there are very few things at all which the man of pious memory noted on Philastrius, and I do not know whether even these will contribute much to the embellishment of the splendid edition being prepared among you. Yet I did not think I should fail, for the sake of testifying to my veneration and devotion toward Your Eminence, to answer something—whatever its quality—rather than nothing [Col. 1101B]. In copying, however, I knowingly omitted what had been taken from the distinguished Galeardus’s [Col. 1102A] edition, since it is better known in Italy. Nor do I think you are unaware of what Marquis Scipio Maffei records in his *Antiquities of Gaul*, p. 76, concerning the manuscripts sought for Philastrius and one found in the library of the Benedictines of Saint-Germain, codex 625. I may also pass over what is noted concerning Philastrius in the *Index Expurgatorius* of Brassichellanus.

Moreover, lest the final page of the attached sheets should be blank, I added a few things especially about the Syriac text of St Ephraim, although perhaps they are already known in themselves or from Fabricius’s earlier letters. The aforementioned Kohl, formerly professor at the Academy of St Petersburg, gave me the opportunity to inspect with my own eyes the Slavonic codex which I mention there. But lest I detain Your Eminence longer than is fitting with trifles, I make an end of writing, hoping that my boldness will be excused. Farewell.

[Col. 1102B]

Written at Hamburg, 15 October 1736.

[Col. 1101]

## SELECT TESTIMONIES OF THE ANCIENTS CONCERNING ST PHILASTRIUS

St Gaudentius, successor of St Philastrius in the see of Brescia, Sermon on the Life and Death of St Philastrius.

[Note: [Col. 1101D] Gaudentius delivered that sermon in the fourteenth year of his episcopate. Philastrius is commemorated on 18 July and Gaudentius in the Roman Martyrology on 25 October. Blondel, *On the Eucharist*, p. 36, reports that Gaudentius died in A.D. 404. But Tillemont, vol. X, p. 588, proves that he was still alive in 406, indeed in 410, if he is the same person to whom Rufinus dedicates his translation of Clement’s *Recognitions*.]

[Col. 1101C]

Beloved, today mindful of Christ’s promises, we render due honour to our father Philastrius as one truly living. For he is a son of the Patriarchs, their companion in faith, and an emulator of their manner of life. Most like them in sincerity, and proclaiming that they live to God as Christ declares, he refutes, by a powerful written refutation (or: condemnation), the unbelief of the Sadducees (Matthew 22), when he says that he who is called the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob is not God of the dead but of the living. “For all,” he says, “live to him” (Matthew 22:32). And indeed divine Scripture declares that they were dead in Christ according to the condition of the flesh, although it had foretold that they would be buried in a good old age, as their surviving tombs demonstrate [Col. 1102C]. (For the complete sermon, if you wish, consult the works of Gaudentius.)

The same St Gaudentius, Homily 16, on his Ordination.

[Note: [Col. 1101D] Gaudentius, Philastrius’s successor, delivered this homily while St Ambrose was still alive. He mentions him in these words: “But blessed Father Ambrose and the other venerable bishops, bound by the vow whereby you rashly bound yourselves, sent me such letters through your embassy that I could no longer resist without injury to my soul; for even the Eastern bishops would deny me saving communion unless I promised to return to you.” And again, after some intervening words: “I entreat our common father Ambrose that, after the scant dew of my discourse, he himself may water your hearts with the mysteries of the divine Scriptures.” Thomas Malvenda is mistaken in calling, in his work *On Antichrist*, p. 108, Baronius’s conclusion an evident error: namely, that Philastrius died while Ambrose was still alive, as inferred from these words of Gaudentius. St Ambrose died in A.D. 397, on 4 April. Labbe, however, places Philastrius’s death in A.D. 387, vol. II, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 213.]

To what, then, is this discourse directed? Clearly, that your belovedness may plainly understand how great was the force which compelled my lowliness to obey lofty commands and to open my mouth in the presence of so many priests, and especially after that most learned voice of my father Philastrius, of venerable memory, which [Col. 1103A], abundantly flowing through the grace of the Holy Spirit, founded this Church in faith in the adorable Trinity, established it in true hope and perfect charity, raised it toward virtues, and left it in peace.

The same author, Preface to Benevolus, Servant of Christ, p. 942.

Nor is it surprising that you now live thus in the fear of the Lord, since, even before receiving the grace of baptism, you fought so for the truth of the heavenly faith that, instructed by the admirable teachings of our father Philastrius, a man apostolic in every respect, you demonstrated a testimony of such constancy.

St Augustine, Preface to Quodvultdeus, prefixed to his book *On Heresies*.

A certain Philastrius, bishop of Brescia, whom I myself saw at Milan with St Ambrose, wrote a book on this subject [Col. 1103B], not passing over those heresies which existed among the Jewish people before the Lord’s advent; and he recorded twenty-eight of them, and 128 after the Lord’s advent.

[Note: [Col. 1103D] This number is consistently found not only in Augustine’s manuscripts here and in chapter 41, but is also confirmed by the author of the appendix to Ildefonsus’s *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 3, and by Trithemius, chapter 84, following Augustine’s account. Yet in the published book of Philastrius you will find no more than 122 heresies after the Lord’s advent; and it is credible that the final chapters of Philastrius’s book, in which there is no trace of a conclusion, have been lost.]

On this matter Epiphanius, bishop of Cyprus, illustriously renowned for his doctrine of the Catholic faith, also wrote in Greek. But he, collecting the heresies of both periods, embraced eighty of them.

[Note: [Col. 1103D] Epiphanius also wrote before Philastrius, who profited from his writings.]

Since, therefore, both wished to do what you ask of me, you see how much they nevertheless differ from one another in the number of sects. This certainly would not have occurred unless one thought one thing to be heresy and the other another. Nor should it be imagined that Epiphanius was unaware of any which Philastrius knew; for we find Epiphanius far more learned than Philastrius, so that we should rather say that Philastrius was unaware of very many, if Philastrius had in fact included more and Epiphanius fewer. But without doubt, in the question in which it is debated what heresy is, the two did not hold the same view; and in truth it is altogether difficult to define this.

The same author, *On Heresies*, chapter 41.

Philaster, bishop of Brescia, in the very lengthy book [Note: [Col. 1103D] Augustine calls it a “very lengthy book” not because of the size of its volume, but because of the lengthy number of heresies which it records, far greater than that in Epiphanius [Col. 1104D].] which he composed on heresies, judged that 128 heresies should be counted, placing the Sabellians immediately after the Noetians, etc.

He names Philastrius again in chapters 45, 53, 57, 67, 71, and 80, and implies that he drew from Philastrius everything which he gives from chapters 58 through 80. “He himself also mentions others,” he says in chapter 80, “but they do not seem to me to deserve to be called heresies. But those which I have set down without names, he likewise did not record by name.” Conversely, in chapter 70 [Col. 1103D], he gives the name Priscillianists, which is not found in Philastrius’s book.

Author of the *Praedestinatus*, chapter 52.

Philaster writes that Macedonius called the Holy Spirit the divinity [Col. 1104A] of the Father and the Son; by this statement he seems to deny the Holy Spirit his own proper character. These words are found nowhere in Philastrius, but were taken from Augustine, chapter 52, as Cotelerius rightly noted, vol. I of the *Monuments*, p. 773.

The same author, chapter 57.

But because Philaster himself, in his books in which he recounts diverse histories, also records the heresies which have arisen in every other period, we now set forth only the heresies by excerpting from his books. He then expressly cites chapter 72: “We find, Philaster writing, that the seventy-second heresy is that of the Rhetorians, begun by Rhetorius.” But this and other material from chapters 58 through 80 he transcribed not from Philastrius himself, whom he apparently never consulted, but from Augustine [Col. 1104B].

St Damasus, synodal letter of A.D. 371, in Holstenius’s Roman Collection, published in 1662, octavo, p. 166.

But from the report of our brothers among the Gauls and Venetians [Note: [Col. 1104D] By the “Venetian brothers” Damasus, and Theodoret, *History* II.22, Sozomen VI.23, and Nicephorus XI.31—where the same letter is read in Greek—mean Philastrius and Evagrius; and by the “Gauls,” Hilary, as Valesius noted in his remarks on Sozomen, p. 142.] we have learned that some men, not from zeal for heresy—for so great an evil cannot befall God’s bishops—but through ignorance or a certain simplicity, heated by harsh interpretations, do not sufficiently discern which opinion of our Fathers ought chiefly to be maintained, when conflicting views are put into their mouths. Finally, they write that Auxentius of Milan was condemned principally for this reason.

Acts of the Council of Aquileia [Note: [Col. 1104D] In the collections of councils, vol. II of Labbe, p. 979; vol. I of Hardouin, p. 825; among the works of St Ambrose, vol. II of the new Benedictine edition, p. 802; and among the writings of Vigilius of Tapsus published by François Chifflet.] against the heretics Palladius and Secundianus, Arians, A.D. 381.

[Col. 1104C]

Under the consulship of the most illustrious men Syagrius and Eucherius, on the Nones of September, at Aquileia, while the following were seated in the church with the bishops: Valerian of the city of Aquileia; Ambrose of Milan; Eusebius of Bologna; Limenius of Vercelli; Anemius of Sirmium in Illyricum; Sabinus of Piacenza; Abundantius of Trent; Artemius; Constantius, bishop of Siscia and legate of the Gauls; Justus, legate of the Gauls; Philastrius, bishop of Brescia; Constantius, bishop of Orange; Theodore of Octodurum; Almachius; Domninus of Grenoble; Amantius of Nice; Maximus of Emona; Felix; Basilianus of Lodi; Numidius; Januarius; Proculus of Marseilles; Heliodorus of Altinum; Jovinus; Felix of Jadera; Eventius of Ticinum; Exsuperantius of Dertona; Diogenes of Genoa; Maximus; Macedonius [Col. 1104D]; Cassianus; Marcellus; and Eustathius—Bishop Ambrose said, etc.

Philaster, bishop of Brescia, said: “Together with all the rest, I condemned the blasphemies and wickedness of Palladius, who follows [Col. 1105A] and defends Arian doctrine.”

St Gregory the Great, Book VI, Letter 15, to George, priest, and Theodore, deacon, of Constantinople.

But lest I detain your belovedness in my discussion, consider what Philaster said about this heresy in the book which he wrote on heresies. His words are these [Note: [Col. 1105D] Chapter 122.]: “There are heretics who say that the Lord descended into hell and there proclaimed himself to all even after death, so that those confessing there might be saved; whereas this contradicts the prophet David, who says: ‘For who shall confess to you in hell?’ And the Apostle: ‘As many as sinned without law shall perish without law.’” Blessed Augustine also agrees with his words [Note: [Col. 1105D] Chapter 79 of *On Heresies*.] in [Col. 1105B] the book which he wrote on heresies.

St Rampertus, Treatise on the Translation of St Philastrius.

Although it is certain that, through heavenly providence, manifest examples of divine miracles shone forth at the translation of our venerable pope, our people need these things to be committed to writing. For the crowd of sick common people, gathering from every direction, receiving healing and returning home, proclaims these events everywhere and abundantly with a thousand voices. The surrounding villages likewise report to us a heavenly miracle: their sick, afflicted with varied and hidden ailments, came amid so great a multitude to the venerable body; through God’s merciful working, through the merits of that saint, and with their faith assisting, they returned restored from their illnesses. Those who had known their infirmities on the previous day testify to this miracle, and so many are witnesses of God’s miracles who had previously known the sick—unless the wavering faith of the sick themselves obstructs it.

But since the death due to all awaits both their witnesses and ourselves, for the sake of future persons, whose loving devotion to the observances owed our father we hope will be zealous and eager to hear of them, we consider it best truthfully and concisely to write at least a few of the many miracles which Christ mercifully performed when crowds flocked to the bier of the blessed Philastrius, his confessor, lover, and preacher. Thus, not only report transmitted by word of mouth and by successive generations, but also the written record published by us, to whom God granted the sight of these things, may bear witness [Col. 1105C]. (For the complete sermon, see the edition of Rampertus.)

Roman Martyrology, 18 July.

At Brescia, the heavenly birthday of St Philastrius, bishop of that city, who fought vigorously against heretics, especially Arians, by word and writing, and suffered much at their hands; finally, illustrious in miracles, he rested in peace as a confessor.

Caesar Baronius, Notes on the Martyrology.

[Col. 1106A]

There survives a sermon of St Gaudentius, his successor as bishop, in which his life is described. There is also a sermon by Rampertus, bishop of the same Church, on the Translation. Lipomannus, vol. II, and Surius, vol. IV, contain all these things. Philastrius lived under Theodosius the Elder and attended, with St Ambrose and the other holy bishops, the Council of Aquileia against the Arians, as is clear from the acts of that council. St Augustine mentions him in his book *On Heresies*, addressed to Quodvultdeus, and testifies that he knew him. He died while St Ambrose was still alive, as is clear from the sermon delivered by St Gaudentius, his successor, at his ordination. Hence it is evident that either the manuscript is corrupt or the statement has been added by someone else which occurs in Philastrius, *On Heresies*, chapter 111: namely, that 430 years had elapsed from Christ the Lord to the time when he was writing [Col. 1106B]. For it is clear that St Ambrose, who outlived him, had departed human life long before that time, in the consulship of Caesarius and Atticus, A.D. 397. Compare the same Baronius under A.D. 386.

Author of the Appendix to Ildefonsus, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 3.

Philastrius, bishop of Brescia, published a book on heresies long before the most blessed Augustine, setting forth each one: both those which existed among the Jewish people before Christ’s incarnation, of which he enumerates twenty-eight; and those which arose after the advent of the Lord and Saviour against the Catholic faith [Col. 1106C], which he likewise describes as numbering 128.

[Note: [Col. 1105D] There are only 122 in the published editions, as I noted above on Augustine’s passage.]

Thus the same man of great renown, Augustine, also mentions him.

Johannes Trithemius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 84.

Philastrius, bishop of Brescia, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature, known to and intimate with blessed Ambrose of Milan, whom St Augustine mentions in a certain letter to Quodvultdeus, wrote several distinguished little works for the common benefit, none of which I recall having come into our hands. Augustine, in the passage cited above, testifies that the following notable work is his:

*One Book on 156 [Note: [Col. 1105D] In the published editions there are no more than 150. Trithemius himself, chapter 95, also says that Epiphanius wrote on [Col. 1106D] ninety heresies, though the published editions contain no more than eighty. He likewise lists among Jerome’s writings, chapter 100, a book on eighty-four heresies beginning “The Simonians, from Simon.” But that book belongs to Augustine, not Jerome.] Heresies: The Simonians, from Simon.*

I have not seen the rest. He flourished under the most Christian Emperor Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 380 [Col. 1106D].

Elias Capreolus, Book III of the *History of Brescia*.

To him (that is, to Faustinus) PHILASTRIUS was immediately appointed as successor. When the Arian heresy had arisen, Constantine—who had already sided with it—summoned a council of three hundred and eighteen bishops to examine it; among them Philastrius argued with the greatest keenness. Afterwards committing the disputation itself to writing, he won no small glory for the whole people of Brescia. Concerning him the holy Augustine writes these words in his letter to the deacon Quodvultdeus: “Philastrius, bishop of Brescia, whom I myself saw at Milan together with blessed Ambrose, wrote a book on this subject, not passing over those heresies which existed among the Jewish people before the coming of the Lord; and he enumerated twenty-eight of them.”

Christophorus Sandius, *On the Origin of the Soul*, p. 141.

PHILASTRIUS of Brescia, in Heresy 97, says that the soul was created before the body, and proves this from the Psalms. Moreover, in an Origenistic manner, he interprets the inner and outer human being, and calls the flesh the instrument of the rational soul. It is therefore unsurprising that he made no mention of the heresy of the Origenists, although he counts even other very slight errors among heresies.

John Mill, Preface to the New Testament, §831.

[Col. 1107B]

We do not dwell long on PHILASTRIUS’s citations, since, apart from that passage, Matthew 22:29, “You do not know the Scriptures, and are ignorant of their power,” and the other, Luke 12:49, “How I wish that it were kindled”—which are likewise cited by Maximus of Turin, Remigius, Rufinus, and Jerome—the rest appear to be cited in wording different from our manuscripts, or from memory.

John Selden, *On the Syrian Gods*, Syntagma I, p. 95.

In very many matters, PHILASTRIUS, as I warn once for all, speaks rather rashly about those ancient Syrian “heresies,” as he calls them. Nor is he at all able to sustain his credit in those things which he often thrusts forward much too boldly concerning their rites and deities, as though inventing dreams for himself.

Joseph Scaliger, *Refutation of Serarius’s Trihaeresium*, ch. 1.

[Col. 1107C]

Serarius dispatches the Catalogues of the heretics by PHILASTRIUS, bishop of Brescia, with far too light a hand. For it was the business of one who had undertaken a discussion of heretics to examine them more carefully. We shall say more about them below. Meanwhile, anyone moderately educated in Greek will not deny that *Heliognostoi* is incorrectly named. For sound grammatical analogy—which they call *analogia*—requires Ἡλιογνῶσται (*Hēliognōstai*), not Ἡλιόγνωστοι (*Hēliognostoi*). Yet if the former is correct *according to analogy* (*kat’ analogian*), it is not correct *according to sense* (*kat’ ennoian*). They ought to have been called Ἡλιολάτραι (*Hēliolatrai*, “sun-worshippers”) or Ἡλιοσεβεῖς (*Hēliosebeis*, “sun-reverers”). These are those who worshipped toward the rising sun, as is recorded in Ezekiel 8, contrary to the divine institution of the Mosaic law. From them came those called Σαμψαῖοι (*Sampsaioi*), “sun-devotees,” ἡλιάζοντες (*hēliazontes*), ἡλιασταί (*hēliastai*), and ἡλιακοί (*hēliakoi*). Epiphanius, Heresy 33: “For the Sampsaeans are interpreted as ‘solar people’” (Σαμψαῖοι γὰρ ἑρμηνεύονται ἡλιακοί), although he was silent concerning worship of the rising sun.

But they were Essenes, or derived from the Essenes, as will be shown elsewhere. [Note: Scaliger, ch. 20 of the *Refutation of the Trihaeresium*.] Why the usage prevailed that they should be called *Kaiani* rather than *Kainiani*, let learned men inquire. For here analogy has been violated. *Musoritae* is a barbarous compound, and no grammar can extricate me from it. Whether the Troglodytes—who in chapter 22 are also called Subterraneans, and are repeated by Philastrius without any reason—are rightly derived from Ezekiel 8:11–12 will be made evident by comparing Philastrius’s words with those of the prophet. He says: “The elders, dwelling in hidden caves, worship idols with censers.” The prophet’s words are:

“And seventy men of the elders of the house of Israel, and Jaazaniah son of Shaphan standing in the midst of them, stood before the images; and each had a censer in his hand, and the vapour of a cloud of incense arose. And he said to me: Surely you see, son of man, what the elders of the house of Israel do in darkness, each one in the secret place of his chamber.”
