In Greek: ἐν σκότει, ἐν τῷ κοιτῶνι τῷ κρυπτῷ αὐτῶν—“in darkness, in their hidden chamber.” Neither Τρωγλοδύται (*Troglodytai*, “cave-dwellers”), nor Ὑπόγειοι (*Hypogeioi*, “underground people”), nor Ἀποχθόνιοι (*Apochthonioi*, “subterranean people”) can be so called where there are no caves at all, but rather inner rooms of a house and hidden bedrooms.

“Fly-worshippers,” that is, Μυιολάτραι (*Myiolatrai*), “from the fly of Ekron,” he says, “to whom King Ahaziah sent.” In 2 Kings 1:2 we read: “Go, inquire of Baalzebub, the god of Ekron.” Here there is no “fly of Ekron,” but Baalzebub of Ekron; hence they ought to have been called Baalzebubites. But Baalzebub, that is, “God of the Fly,” is so called by Scripture as an insult, as we have shown elsewhere; not because the Ekronites wished to dishonour their deity by that name—for who insults what is revered? (τίς γὰρ τὸ σεβιζόμενον ὑβρίζει?)—but because there were many Baals, and among those nations, madly devoted to idols as they were, Baal was never said without a genitive construction. There was Baal-Shamayim, “Baal of Heaven,” the Οὐράνιος (*Ouranios*, “Heavenly One”); Baal-Reem, the Βροντεύς (*Bronteus*, “Thunderer”), whom Scripture, with a ridiculous name, calls Baal-Peor, which means Πορδεύς (*Pordeus*, “Farter”), not Βροντεύς.

Thus that idol of the Ekronites, which in my judgment was called Baal-Zebahim, “God of victims, immolations, sacrifices,” Scripture jocularly called “God of the Fly,” because in the Temple at Jerusalem flies did not lick up the flesh of sacrificial victims, whereas pagan shrines were infested with flies because of the smell of the sacrifices. Therefore in Arcadia rites were performed for a certain hero, Myiagros (“Fly-Chaser”), before the victims were slaughtered, lest flies alight upon them. Pausanias says: “At this festival they sacrifice beforehand to Myiagros, praying over the sacrificial victims to the hero and invoking Myiagros” (Ἐν ταύτῃ τῇ πανηγύρει Μυιάγρῳ προθύουσιν, ἐπευχόμενοι τε κατὰ τῶν ἱερείων τῷ ἥρωι, καὶ ἐπικαλούμενοι τὸν Μυίαγρον).

Therefore, from the fact that King Ahaziah sent to inquire of the oracle of Baalzebub, the Ekronites’ idol, it neither follows nor is true that any heresy of Fly-worshippers arose from this. Only one Baal was called without a genitive construction *par excellence*, namely Baal-Shamayim, of whom Scripture speaks so often. The other gods are called *Baalim* absolutely in the sacred books, although among those peoples each was conceived together with his own genitive qualification. Therefore Baalites ought not to have been distinguished from Fly-worshippers, if there had been any heresy of Fly-worshippers. But Philastrius wrongly separated them, just as he separated Troglodytes [Col. 1108D] from Subterraneans.

The Astarites and Remphanites, I think, are Ἀστρῖται (*Astritai*, “star-people”): “the star of your god Remphan” (τὸ ἄστρον τοῦ θεοῦ ὑμῶν Ῥεμφάν; Amos 5:26; Acts 7:43). Therefore the Molochites mentioned next by the same Philastrius belong to these, from the same passage in Amos: “You took up the tent of Moloch” (Ἀνελάβετε τὴν σκηνὴν Μολόχ). Nor ought the Tophetites to have been separated from them any more than Troglodytes from Subterraneans; for in the place Topheth children were purified by fire for the idol Moloch.

“The Puteorites,” he says, “who dug for themselves wells that cannot hold saving water.” I understand this to be a hybrid word, *puteoryctae*, [Note: Philastrius actually wrote *Puteoritas*, as he did *Musoritas* and *Hermioritas*.] compounded of Latin and Greek. But the Greek has λάκκους ὤρυξαν, “they dug pits”; they ought therefore to have been called Λακκορύκται (*Lakkoryktai*), not *Puteoryctae*. Yet if one must conjecture a heresy from that clause, why should I not say that another heresy existed from verse 27, which called wood its father and stone its mother? For who would deny that the inference is the same?

Nor is anything certain about the Bahalites or Balaamites. “A heresy,” he says, “which maintains that it took its name from the idol Bahal, or from Balaam the false prophet, who came from Mesopotamia against most blessed Moses.” How can those who maintain this derive it from the idol Bahal if it was derived from Balaam the false prophet? Certainly there were no Pythonissaeans, nor can any consistent rationale be produced. But he gave himself too much licence in divining heresies which neither existed nor could have existed. If they were to be investigated in this manner, far more probable ones could be adduced, such as Soccothbenothites, Nergelites, Asimaeans, Nebahasites, Tartacites, Adrammelechites, and Anamelechites. For those idols had their worshippers. But on this principle, as many idols as there were, so many kinds of heresies or sects would have had to be established.

Likewise, in the second part of the same writer’s work, how many heresies are said to have existed after Christ which never existed at all? And yet not only there [Note: Philastrius, Heresy 129, mentions those who baptize the dead.], but also in Epiphanius, the most ancient of all was omitted: ἡ τῶν ὑπὲρ νεκρῶν βαπτιζομένων, “the sect of those baptized on behalf of the dead.”

Erasmus, *Defence against Luther’s Epistle*, vol. IX of the Basel edition of the *Works*, p. 1265.

If there is danger that someone may recoil from the Christian religion upon learning that the Church was harassed by various errors of heretics, then Saint Epiphanius and PHILASTER among the Greeks, and Augustine among the Latins, undertook a pernicious task in setting before the world a catalogue of all heresies. Erasmus is mistaken in counting Philastrius among Greek writers, just as elsewhere he irrelevantly doubts whether Irenaeus wrote in Greek or Latin.

Ferdinand Ughelli, vol. IV of *Sacred Italy*, p. 729, where he recounts the bishops of Brescia.

Saint PHILASTRIUS, a Spaniard [Note: To others, an Italian.], governed this Church in A.D. 381, a most noble man both in learning and in holiness of life. For while Auxentius was still distinguished at Milan by the title of bishop, Philastrius fiercely assailed and conquered the Arians in disputations of his own, so that he may now be counted among the brightest lights of that age. He attended the Council of Aquileia with Saint Ambrose [Col. 1109D] and sat eighth among the fathers of that council, as Baronius relates from its acts. Augustine mentions him in his book *On Heresies* addressed to Quodvultdeus, and affirms that he introduced himself into Philastrius’s friendship at Rome; and that through his public and private discussions of sacred matters he acquired new perceptions of Christian piety, as Gaudentius, Philastrius’s successor, writes when recounting his life. He presided for eight years and died on the Kalends of August [1 August], while Saint Ambrose was still alive, as the same Gaudentius relates in his Sermon on his own Ordination. He was buried near Saint Andrew, where Bishop Rampertus is said to have found him wrapped in linen in A.D. 838, on the fifth day before the Ides of April [9 April], with this brief inscription:

PHILASTRIUS, OF MOST BLESSED MEMORY, HERE RESTS IN PEACE.

Thereafter Bishop Rampertus transferred his sacred body to the Major Church; and the people of Brescia honour and venerate him as one of their patron saints.

Philippus Ferrarius, *Catalogue of the Saints of Italy*, 18 July.

PHILASTRIUS, a Spaniard by birth, highly learned in sacred and secular letters, gained no small increase of learning through travel. Sailing to Athens, he quickly made great progress there; and at Rome, generously received by Damasus, he taught publicly. Then, having been initiated into the sacred ministry, he departed and everywhere contended against the Arians. At Milan, disputing against Bishop Auxentius and other Arians, he refuted them and wrote books against heresies. He suffered much from heretics: frequently beaten and wounded by them, he would even have perished crucified, had he not been rescued by Catholics.

When he had gone to Brescia to venerate the relics of Saints Faustinus, Jovita, and Afra, he was most kindly received by Saint Faustinus the bishop and chosen as his assistant and successor. He devoted himself wholly to reading, signing documents, preaching, establishing churches, and refuting heresies. Concerning him the holy Augustine says in his letter to the deacon Quodvultdeus: “Philastrius, bishop of Brescia, whom I myself saw at Milan together with blessed Ambrose, wrote a book on this subject, not passing over those heresies which existed among the Jewish people before the coming of the Lord; and he enumerated twenty-eight of them.”

NOTE. Some write that Philastrius attended the Council of Nicaea under Pope Saint Sylvester and Constantine the Great. If this is true, he must have been a young man and attended as a hearer, not as a disputant. He died, however, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August [18 July], before Saint Ambrose, by whom Saint Gaudentius, his successor, was ordained.

Tillemont may also be consulted, vol. VIII of the *Memoirs*, p. 541, etc.

[Col. 1109]

CRITIQUE OF CERTAIN PASSAGES OF PHILASTRIUS

[Note: So that the reader may lack nothing concerning Philastrius, we append the testimony of F. J. M. of Brescia concerning Philastrius, together with his critique, which warns that certain passages of Philastrius should be read cautiously. This critique of the Brescian refers to the second Paris edition of the *Library of the Fathers*, produced in 1589 by Margarin de la Bigne, Parisian theologian. It appears in the *Index of Expurgated Books*, pp. 115 ff., first at Rome and then at Bergamo, printed by Comino Ventura in 1608, octavo.]

[Col. 1109D]

The notes on the Roman Martyrology for 18 July will show you more about Saint Philastrius from approved authors; on that day the feast of Saint Philastrius is entered among the sacred observances in the public registers of the Roman Church. Yet although Saint Philastrius was eminent in holiness and learning, his work *On Heresies* should nevertheless be read cautiously and judiciously in certain passages, because it contains some matters insufficiently consistent with the principles of sound theology. Saint Augustine, in the preface to his own book *On Heresies* addressed to Quodvultdeus, observes that Saint Epiphanius wrote more learnedly on heresies than Saint Philastrius.

**Heresy 49**

Before the beginning of the chapter, note: “Read this chapter cautiously, for Saint Philastrius thinks that the soul of the first human being … [some words are lacking]”; whereas almost all the holy Fathers and interpreters of Genesis understand, learnedly, piously, orthodoxly, historically, and properly, the “breath of life” in the aforesaid passage as a soul partaking of reason. See Castro, book II *Against Heresies*, under “Soul,” Heresy 2, and Sixtus, book V of the *Bibliotheca*, annotation 27.

**Heresy 56**

At the beginning of the chapter write: “Read this chapter cautiously, for Saint Philastrius counts it as a heresy to hold that before the construction of the Tower of Babel there was only one language in the world; whereas Sacred Scripture and almost all the holy Fathers most clearly teach that there was only one language among humankind before the building of Babel.” Add the more recent interpreters of Genesis 11, Castro, book IX *Against Heresies*, under “Language,” and Sixtus, book V of the *Bibliotheca*, annotation 87.

**Heresy 63**

There in the text, where it says, “from the Lord until now, 430 years,” place in the margin: “Latinius, a learned man, thought that an error had crept into the number here and that by a slight change it should be restored as 380. For there is an obvious reason why Saint Philastrius could not have reached the year 430: he died while Saint Ambrose survived him, as is certain from the sermon on his Ordination delivered by Saint Gaudentius, Philastrius’s successor; and it is known that Saint Ambrose died in the consulship of Caesarius and Atticus, in the year of salvation 397. See the notes on the Roman Martyrology for 18 July.”

**Heresy 69**

There in the text, where it says, “since they were sanctified even in the womb, such as the Patriarchs, Prophets, Judges, Jeremiah, and John the Baptist, etc.,” write in the margin: “Read cautiously: if we speak of true sanctification from original sin, theologians teach that only Jeremiah, John the Baptist, and the Mother of God were sanctified in the womb.”

**Heresy 79**

At the beginning of the chapter write: “This chapter must be read cautiously; for it is neither heresy nor error to believe that not all the Psalms were published by David, since many Fathers and more recent writers hold this, and the question is still debated among learned persons. Consult Sixtus, book I of the *Bibliotheca*, and the interpreters of the Psalms in their prefaces.”

**Heresy 82**

At the beginning of the chapter write: “This chapter must be read cautiously, for it is not heresy to think that the stars are fixed in the heaven, since philosophers, Peripatetics, astronomers, and scholastic theologians affirm this with the greatest agreement, although some of the ancient Fathers dissent. See Saint Thomas, Part I, question 70, article 1, reply to objection 3, and Sixtus, book V of the *Bibliotheca*, annotation 14.”

**Heresy 89**

Remove the marginal note: “The numerous multitude of Solomon’s wives and concubines in 3 Kings 11 is to be understood mystically,” and replace it with: “Saint Philastrius does not mean the passage in 3 Kings 11:3, which is undoubtedly to be understood historically, but the passage in Song of Songs 6:7, which most Fathers interpret mystically.”

[Col. 1111]

THE BOOK OF SAINT PHILASTRIUS, BISHOP OF BRESCIA, ON HERESIES.

[Col. 1111]

[Note: In the Saint-Germain manuscript, the Preface and the Catalogue which immediately follows, of those charged with heresy before Christ’s coming, are lacking; and it begins with these words: “Here begins the book of Filaster on Heresies. After the passion of Christ, etc.”]

PREFACE.

[Col. 1111D]

It is necessary to speak of the various pestilence [Note: “Of heresies.” Latin writers not infrequently use a plural genitive of this Greek type, as is shown by the titles *Metamorphoseon* and *Halieuticon* of Ovid, Fulgentius’s *Mythologicon*, Petronius’s *Satiricon*, and C. Hyginus’s *Poeticon Astronomicon*. Also below, chapter 29, *haereseos*. FABRICIUS.] of heresies and of the various errors which have emerged from the beginning of the world, have flowed down among the Jews, and, since our Lord Jesus the Saviour came in the flesh, have sprung up; and gradually to set forth their number; and to recognize that the enemy of humankind was not undeservedly compared by the prophet Jeremiah [Note: “To a partridge by the prophet Jeremiah.” Jeremiah 17:11. Saint Ambrose, *Hexaemeron* VI.3: “We know the crafty partridge, which steals another partridge’s eggs and broods them with its own body; yet it cannot possess the fruit of its fraud, because when it has hatched its chicks, it loses them: when they hear the voice of the one that laid the eggs, they abandon it and, by a certain natural instinct and affection, go to that one…. The devil imitates this partridge: he strives to seize the offspring of the eternal Creator, and if he can gather together any foolish persons lacking strength of their own understanding, he broods them with bodily allurements; but as soon as Christ’s voice is instilled into the little ones, they depart and go to that mother who embraces her young, like a bird, with maternal love.” The same is handed down by Cassiodorus, *Variae Epistles* II.14, and very many others. Cotelerius, in his notes to vol. II of *Monuments of the Greek Church*, p. 547; Huet, on Origen, pp. 16 ff.; Bochart, vol. II of the *Hierozoicon*, p. 84; and Allatius, on Eustathius of Antioch, pp. 132 ff., cite their passages. See also Ambrose, Epistle 32 to Irenaeus, vol. II, pp. 918 ff.; Athanasius, vol. I, p. 363, latest edition; Johann Camerarius, *Symbola* III.68; Combefis, on Hippolytus, *On Antichrist*, ch. 55; Ducaeus, notes on Saint Basil, vol. I, p. 44. FABRICIUS.] to a partridge. Since it suffers barrenness, it frequently secretly broods over the offspring of others and for some time cherishes and claims them as though they were already its own children. But when, as they grow, the time of age enabling discernment has arrived [Note: “The time of age enabling discernment”: the time when they can, by age, distinguish true parents from false ones. Early childhood, even in a human being, does not know how to distinguish right from left, good from evil. Compare Grotius on Deuteronomy 1:39 and Jonah 4:11. Thus the earliest age of the world did not immediately recognize and follow its Lord and Saviour, but allowed itself to be shamefully led away by the devil into various kinds of idolatry and superstition. FABRICIUS.], then, abandoning [Note: “Having abandoned false parents.” Earlier editions less correctly read “having lost.” Thus below, after a few intervening words: “having abandoned the falsehood of the most deceitful parent.” FABRICIUS.] false parents, recalling the rights of their parents by their own understanding and openly beholding them with their eyes, they delay no longer in following them. This comparison has been given to us for this reason: that, having abandoned the devil, the cause of impiety, who imagined that he held the world under his own dominion, and having seen and recognized Christ as parent, having abandoned the falsehood of the most deceitful parent, every person who recognizes him delays no longer [Note: “Every person delays no longer”: that is, no one who has recognized him delays. Thus in Florus II.18: “There was not one Numantine man who was led away in chains.” Similar expressions occur in the sacred writers: Luke 1:37, οὐκ ἀδυνατήσει παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ πᾶν ῥῆμα, “no word will be impossible with God”; Romans 3:20, ἐξ ἔργων νόμου οὐ δικαιωθήσεται πᾶσα σάρξ, “by works of the law no flesh shall be justified.” FABRICIUS.] in following the footsteps of the true parent, Christ.

For we know that Jeremiah’s prophecy is being fulfilled daily in an enigmatic manner [Note: “Being fulfilled daily in an enigmatic manner”: through the multitude of neophytes daily joining the Church, we understand to be fulfilled what the prophet signified would occur through the partridge allegory. Accordingly he immediately adds: “because now all nations daily abandon idolatry,” etc. Although I seem to have somewhat improved this passage through more suitable punctuation—for previously the words “recognizing daily through the enigma” were joined, followed by a full stop—the construction is still very broken and difficult, but many passages in this book will teach the reader that such is not foreign to Philastrius’s usage. FABRICIUS.], saying: “The partridge cried out; it gathered what it did not bear; making riches for itself not with wisdom, in the midst of its days they will abandon it, and in its end it will be foolish” (Jeremiah 17:11). [Note: “They will abandon it.” Thus the Septuagint, which Philastrius follows here; but the Vulgate and Pagninus read, “it will abandon them.” Compare Jerome on this passage of Jeremiah, who cites the prophet’s testimony in both forms. On the reported characteristic of the partridge, Bochart, vol. II of the *Hierozoicon*, pp. 84–85, must certainly be consulted; he throws no little light on this preface of Philastrius. GALEARD.]

For now, as all nations daily abandon the deadly idolatry of the enemy [Note: “All nations”: some persons even from every, including the most remote, nations.], hear of Christ, the true Lord, from the Law and the Prophets, believe and remember that he is always with the Father, and fly speedily to him in every manner as suppliants [Note: The Helmstedt edition incorrectly reads “simple.”], so that the prophecy may be fulfilled [Note: At this place Philaster inserted Christ’s name for explanatory purposes.]: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord Christ” (Psalm 22:27).

CATALOGUE OF THOSE CHARGED WITH HERESY BEFORE THE COMING OF CHRIST.

[Note: Certain heresies reported by Philaster up to chapter 32 did not exist before Christ’s coming, nor did they arise among the Jews, as Philaster says in the Preface; although they took the occasion for their error from the Old Testament (ἀπὸ νόμου ἐξ Ἰουδαίων φύσασαι, “arising from the Law among the Jews”: Epiphanius, *Ancoratus*, ch. 12, vol. II, p. 18). Such are immediately the Ophites, Caiani, and Sethians. Tertullian therefore speaks more correctly, calling them in chapter 45 “heretics of Judaism,” in contrast to others who chose to be heretics from the Gospel, or, in Jerome’s words, “who mangled the Gospels.” FABRICIUS.]

[Col. 1113]

[Note: Fabricius had published these first three chapters of Philastrius in vol. V, p. 136, of the *Codex Pseudepigraphus*, with nearly the same notes as are appended here. GALEARD.]

## I. OPHITES

[Col. 1113D]

[Note: “The Ophites are first”—not in chronological order, but because they stumbled, as it were, immediately at the first beginning and threshold of the first book of the Old Testament. They are mentioned by Augustine, *On Heresies*, by the author of *Praedestinatus*, ch. 17, and others. FABRICIUS.]

The Ophites are first—those called Serpentines [Note: That is, those whose name may thus be rendered in Latin. Instead of Ophites, or Offites, as the pseudo-Jerome catalogue incorrectly writes, Origen, Clement of Alexandria (*Stromata* VII, p. 765), and Theodoret also have the name Ophians; and Sophronius corruptly has “Sophians,” unless they were also so named because, according to Irenaeus, they said that Sophia had assumed the image of a serpent. In Theodoret and Procopius of Gaza, they appear under the Hebrew designation Ναασηνοί (*Naasenoi*—so it should be read, not Ἐσθηνοί), from the Hebrew word for serpent corresponding to Greek ὄφις. See Cotelerius, vol. I of *Monuments of the Greek Church*, p. 769; and Thomas Ittigius, “the blessed one,” dissertation *On Heresiarchs Nearest to the Apostolic Age*, p. 120.

I am persuaded that these Ophites arose from the Gnostics, Valentinians, or Marcionites, because the Ophite teaching found in Epiphanius 37.3 ff.; Tertullian, appendix to *On Prescription*, ch. 47; Origen, *Against Celsus* VI, pp. 295 ff.; and Nicetas, *Treasury* IV.9 is closely related to Valentinian fictions and to the Gnostics who worshipped Prunicus, with whom Saint Irenaeus also joins the Ophites. Moreover, Theodoret, *Fables of Heretics* I.24, and Nicetas, *Treasury* IV.14, state that the Marcionites preferred the serpent to the Creator and worshipped it with distinctive cult.

Yet it is remarkable that Origen relates, p. 294, that no one was admitted by the Ophites, whose founder was Euphrates, into their assembly “unless he pronounced curses against Jesus” (ἐὰν μὴ ἀρὰς θῆται κατὰ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ). He likewise writes in *Against Celsus* III, p. 119, that Ophians and Caiani were wholly alien to the teaching of Jesus, and in book VII, p. 358, that Jesus was altogether denied by them. In book VI, p. 291, he calls the Ophites’ doctrine absurd, not persuasive even to the simplest people, and their heresy utterly obscure (ἀσημοτάτην); Procopius calls it most impious (δυσσεβεστάτην). FABRICIUS.]

They worship the serpent, saying that it first brought us the knowledge of good and evil. Hence they assert that the Lord was envious of it [Note: They taught that Jaldabaoth, the God of the Jews, was envious of humankind because it had recognized the higher God and Father; therefore a certain power, produced in the form of a serpent, deceived Eve. See Epiphanius 37.3–5. FABRICIUS.] because it first conveyed to the woman knowledge of a good thing and an evil thing [Note: This is the same as what he said shortly before: “knowledge of good and evil,” from Genesis 2:9, τὸ εἰδέναι γνωστὸν καλοῦ καὶ πονηροῦ. FABRICIUS.]. Through her this knowledge thus spread to the whole human race. For this reason, they say, he was cast down from the first heaven into the second [Note: For they posited eight heavens, as Epiphanius teaches in 37, section 4, although in section 5 he afterwards writes simply that he was cast down from heaven (ἀπὸ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ). FABRICIUS.], whence they say that he will come from heaven; and they consider him to be, as it were, some power of God, and proclaim that he ought to be worshipped. [Note: Some earlier editions incorrectly read *ut velut*, “as though.” Besides Epiphanius 37.5, the scholiast on book XXI of the *Basilica*, p. 581, using the words of Damascene, also mentions the cult with which the Ophites honoured the serpent and the chest in which they customarily kept it. Such chests were also used in pagan rites; see Laurentius Begerus’s learned inquiry *On Serpent-bearing Coins*. FABRICIUS.]

## II. CAIANI

[Note: The author of the appendix to Tertullian, ch. 47, calls them Cainaei; Augustine, *On Heresies*, and the author of *Praedestinatus*, ch. 18, Cainiani. But Irenaeus, I.35, and Epiphanius and Damascene, Heresy 38, likewise have Καϊανοί (*Kaianoi*); Josephus calls Cain Καΐς (*Kais*). Theodoret, book I of *Fables of Heretics*, ch. 15, has Καϊνοί (*Kainoi*) and Καϊνισταί (*Kainistai*), while Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* VII, p. 549, has Καϊανισταί (*Kaianistai*). Tertullian, *On Prescription* ch. 33, and Jerome, Epistle 83, call it the Caian heresy; Jerome in his work against Vigilantius notes that Tertullian attacked the Caiani in his *Scorpiace*. Jerome, however, says not “Caian heresy” but *Caina* in both places: namely, both in Epistle 82 [otherwise 83] to Oceanus, “Behold, the Caina heresy rises against me,” and in *Against Vigilantius*, “which was formerly called the Caina heresy”; whereas Tertullian in the cited passage has *Caiana*.

Lambert Daneau, on Augustine’s *On Heresies*, ch. 18, thinks that copyists, when transcribing Epiphanius, mistakenly made Caiani out of Cainiani, and that Augustine too was deceived by this error when he names the Caiani. But Bayle, *Critical Dictionary*, under “Cainites,” observes that the Fathers used the name Caiani long before Epiphanius and Augustine used the term. GALEARD. Sophronius also has Καϊνοί in the catalogue of heresies in Act XI of the Sixth General Council; Nicetas, *Treasury* IV.11–12, has both Καϊνοί and Καϊανοί; and before them Origen, *Against Celsus* III, p. 119, writes that they were wholly alien to Jesus’s teaching, as were the Ophites. Distinct from this Gnostic heresy are the Caianite Aphthartodocetae, named after a certain Caian of Alexandria, concerning whom Damascene writes in Heresy 84. FABRICIUS.]

The Caiani praise Cain [Note: “Praise Cain”: δοξάζουσι—honour and worship him. In Honorius of Autun’s little book *On Heresies*, Caiani are said to be those who hate Cain; on the authority of Augustine one should read *onorant*, that is, “honour.” FABRICIUS.], the fratricide, the firstborn of our father and blessed Adam, the first-created man. They say that Cain came from another power, that is, the devil [Note: “From another power, that is, the devil.” I think the words “that is, the devil” were added either by Philastrius or another person contrary to the Caiani’s meaning. For although Theodoret, *Fables of Heretics* I.11, reports that the Archontics taught that Cain and Abel were children of the devil (τοῦ Διαβόλου παῖδες), just as the *Pirke of Rabbi Eliezer* calls Cain the offspring of Samael, and other rabbis cited by Gaulmin, *On the Death of Moses*, p. 216, relate that he was born from the seed of the first serpent and was the author of magic through serpents, this seems remote from the Caiani’s opinion. They held that Cain, rather than Abel, was descended from a stronger and more excellent power, as Epiphanius and others testify. Compare what Philastrius says in the following chapter from the Sethians’ view: “When the angels were in dissension, the feminine power prevailed in heaven.” FABRICIUS.]; whereas blessed Abel was born from another. And the greater power which was in Cain prevailed so that he killed his brother.

## III. SETHIANS

[Note: The author of the appendix to Tertullian’s *On Prescription*, ch. 47, calls them Sethoitae. Others call this class of Gnostics Sethites, such as the pseudo-Jerome catalogue, ch. 9; yet in ch. 17 it too calls them Sethians, as do Epiphanius and Damascene in Heresy 39, Augustine and the author of *Praedestinatus*, ch. 19, Nicetas, *Treasury* IV.12, Rabanus Maurus, *On the Institution of Clerics* II.58, and Honorius of Autun, Heresy 31. But in Gennadius, *On Dogmas*, ch. 52, where Sethianus and Theodosius are said to have introduced three barbarous principles, *Scythianus* seems to be required instead of *Sethianus*. FABRICIUS.]

The heresy of the Sethians worships Seth, Adam’s later-born son, and calls itself by this name because he was born after the murder of blessed Abel. From him they are called Sethians, worshipping him and saying that, when two human beings had been created in the beginning and the angels were in dissension, the feminine power prevailed in heaven [Note: “Prevailed,” *tenuit*, that is, κεκράτηκε: it gained the first place. Epiphanius 39.2: “For there was a conflict among the angels, contending concerning the generations of these two human beings—the one who begot Cain and the one who begot Abel—and the power above, which they call mother and female, prevailed. For they think there are mothers above, female and male.” (Ἦν γὰρ ἡ στάσις τοῖς Ἀγγέλοις, ἀγωνιζομένοις περὶ τῶν γενεῶν τῶν ἀνθρώπων τούτων τῶν δύο, τοῦ γεγεννηκότος τὸν Καΐν καὶ τοῦ γεγεννηκότος τὸν Ἄβελ, κεκρατηκέναι δὲ τὴν ἄνω δύναμιν, ἣν μητέρα φάσκουσι καὶ θήλειαν. Δοκεῖ γὰρ αὐτοῖς εἶναι καὶ μητέρας ἄνω, καὶ θηλείας καὶ ἄρσενας.) See, if you wish, what follows there and what Philaster translated into Latin and abridged. For, as I shall note in the appropriate places, he often follows Epiphanius’s tracks; and according to Theodore the Studite, Epistle to Naucratius, vol. V of Sirmond’s *Works*, p. 324, no one wrote better on heresies. FABRICIUS.]. For among them males and females, gods and goddesses, are believed to exist.

Perceiving this, they say, the mother, because righteous Abel had been killed, planned to bear righteous Seth, and placed in him a spirit of great power, so that hostile powers might be destroyed [Note: Earlier editions less correctly read “may be destroyed.” Epiphanius more fully expresses this as follows: “so that through this constitution and this seed the powers of the angels who made the world, and the two human beings from the beginning, might be overthrown” (Ὅπως διὰ τῆς ταύτης συστάσεως καὶ τούτου τοῦ σπέρματος καθαιρεθῶσιν αἱ δυνάμεις τῶν Ἀγγέλων τῶν τὸν κόσμον πεποιηκότων, καὶ τοὺς δύο ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς ἀνθρώπους). FABRICIUS.].

Concerning Seth himself, they say that the Lord Christ derives his lineage from him [Note: They would not err in this if the Sethians thought it thus, since Saint Luke too does not hesitate to trace Christ’s lineage to Seth. But Philaster did not sufficiently grasp Epiphanius’s meaning, who states the Sethians’ view in these words, 39.4: “From Seth, by seed and succession of lineage, Christ came—Jesus himself not by generation, but appearing wondrously in the world, just as Seth himself then was; and Christ now visited the human race, sent from the Mother above.” (Ἀπὸ δὲ τοῦ Σὴθ κατὰ σπέρμα καὶ κατὰ διαδοχὴν γένους ὁ Χριστὸς ἦλθεν, αὐτὸς Ἰησοῦς οὐχὶ κατὰ γένη, ἀλλὰ θαυμαστῶς ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ πεφηνὼς, ὥς ἐστιν αὐτὸς ὁ Σὴθ ὁ τότε, καὶ Χριστὸς νῦν ἐπιφοιτήσας τῷ γένει τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἀπὸ τῆς μητρὸς ἄνωθεν ἀπεσταλμένος.) The meaning is that Christ did not derive descent from Seth in the ordinary and natural way, but that Seth himself miraculously returned to the world, so that he who was then Seth might now be Christ. Jacob Rhenferd argues, irrelevantly, that this charge is falsely imputed to the Sethians, pp. 173 ff. of his *Philosophical Works*, where he discusses fictitious Jewish heresies. FABRICIUS.]. Some of them, however, assert and maintain not merely that he derives his lineage from Seth, but that Seth himself is Christ.

## IV. DOSITHEUS

[Col. 1118A]

[Note: [Col. 1117C] A certain Dositheus later appeared, a Jew by origin. He is the one mentioned in Jewish books and said, together with Sabia (from whom the sect of the Sebuaeans derives in Nicetas, *Treasury*, book I, chapter 35), to have taught the Samaritans during the Assyrian captivity in the time of Sennacherib. See Drusius, *On the Sects of the Hebrews*, III.4; his notes on Serarius’s *Minerval*, chapter 10; and Lightfoot’s chorographical dissertation on John, p. 934 of the Leipzig edition. Eulogius, in Photius, codex 230, p. 466, calls him Δόσθης (*Dosthēs*), and his followers Δοσθηνοί (*Dosthenoi*); others call him Δοσίθεος (*Dositheus*) and them Δοσιθεανοί, Δοσί, and Δοσίθεοι. Epiphanius, *Heresy* 13, and Nicetas in the cited passage write that he was Jewish by nation and subsequently joined the Samaritans. Hence some call him a Samaritan, write that he was the author of their errors among the Samaritans, and even that he corrupted the Samaritan Pentateuch. Ancient writers also commonly confuse this ancient Dositheus with the deeds of a later Dositheus, likewise a Samaritan, whom they make a contemporary of Simon Magus and report to have claimed that he was the Messiah. Compare, if desired, Cotelerius on the *Apostolic Constitutions* VI.8, and D. Th. Ittigius at the beginning of his learned book *On the Heresiarchs of the Apostolic Age*. Thus the author of the *Recognitions* transmitted under Clement’s name, I.54, speaks of Dositheus as the leader of the Sadducean doctrine; and shortly afterward, II.8, mentions Dositheus as master of thirty disciples, among whom was Simon Magus. Origen seems to have drawn from him what he has in *Against Celsus* VI, p. 282; he also mentions this Dositheus in many other places, as in I, p. 44, and Homily 27 on Matthew and 14 on John, pp. 219 ff. of Huet’s edition; so too Hegesippus in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* IV.22, Hippolytus in Photius, codex 121, and Theodoret, *Compendium of Heretical Fables* I.2, who says that the Dositheans sprouted from Simon’s heresy as from a most bitter root. But it is clear that our Philaster speaks not of some contemporary of Simon Magus, but of that far more ancient man [Col. 1118A], because immediately afterward, in chapter 5, he calls Saddoc, the founder of the Sadducees, his disciple, just as does the author of the appendix to Tertullian and Jerome in *Against the Luciferians*, who describe the Sadducees as arising from the root of Dositheus’s error; and Epiphanius, *Heresy* 14, calls them an ἀπόσπασμα ἀπὸ Δοσιθέου, “an offshoot from Dositheus.” Nicetas likewise does so in *Treasury* I [Col. 1118B], chapter 38. FABRIC.]

A certain Dositheus later appeared, a Jew by origin, who dared to say

[Note: [Col. 1118B] “That one must live in the Law of the Lord only according to the flesh.” That is, as explained in the following chapter, that the external rites of the Law must be observed—something which Damascene, Nicetas, and others write was done more scrupulously by the Dositheans. Philaster calls this “living carnally” in chapter 8. Yet since he shortly afterward affirms that they denied the resurrection, those words may also be understood to mean that Dositheus taught that one lives only in this body, as is said below, chapter 7, of the Samaritans. Or, that the promises of the Law do not extend beyond the present life. FABRIC.]

that one must live in the Law of the Lord only according to the flesh;

[Note: [Col. 1118B] “And that he did not hope for a future resurrection from it.” Namely, because he denied that it could be proved from the Law. Of Dositheus, Eulogius says in Photius, codex 230, p. 467: Ἀπεκήρυττε καὶ τὴν ἀνάστασιν, “He rejected the resurrection”; there Eulogius confirms it from the books of Moses. The author of the *Recognitions* likewise gives no obscure indication that the Sadducees received this error from Dositheus. On the other hand, Epiphanius, Nicetas, and others explicitly write that they did admit the resurrection. The author of the appendix to Tertullian and Jerome in *Against the Luciferians* also report [Col. 1118C] that the Sadducees added to the heresy of Dositheus the error of denying the resurrection. St John Damascene, as though seeking to reconcile opinions so diverse and conflicting, writes that at least some Dositheans believed in a future resurrection. FABRIC.]

and that he did not hope for a future resurrection from it;

[Note: [Col. 1118C] “Neither the Spirit of God nor an angel.” See Eulogius in Photius, p. 468. Yet Epiphanius, *Heresy* 14, denies that angels were rejected by the Samaritans, testifying that this was peculiar to the Sadducees’ heresy. Observe further that the words in Acts 23:8, οὔτε Ἄγγελον, οὔτε Πνεῦμα, “neither angel nor spirit,” are interpreted by Philaster as referring to the Holy Spirit. So also Epiphanius says of the Sadducees: Πνεῦμα δὲ ἅγιον οὐκ ἴσασι, “They do not acknowledge the Holy Spirit,” and likewise Theophylact. But understand *spirit* (*pneuma*) as the human soul, which the Sadducees denied to be an immortal spirit or to remain after its departure from the body, according to Josephus, XII.12. FABRIC.]

believing that neither the Spirit of God nor an angel exists,

[Note: [Col. 1118C] “Nor a future judgment.” For Dositheus taught, according to the same Eulogius, that souls are mortal [Col. 1118D] and the world incorruptible. FABRIC.]

nor a future judgment

[Note: [Col. 1118D] “From the Law and the Prophets.” Indeed, the author of the appendix to Tertullian’s *On Prescription* and Jerome in *Against the Luciferians* write that he was the first to reject the Prophets, on the ground that they had not spoken in the Holy Spirit; and thereby they indicate that he was also the author among the Samaritans of their own error, since below, chapter 7, they are said to accept the books of the Law alone. FABRIC.]

to be expected from the Law and the Prophets.

## V. THE SADDUCEES

After him, the Sadducees—

[Note: [Col. 1118D] “From Saddoc, a Jewish man.” Epiphanius and Damascene call him Σαδούκ (*Sadouk*); the Arabs, Zendik; among the Jews, he was a disciple of Antigonus of Socho. See Maimonides on *Pirke Aboth*, vol. IV of the splendid Surenhus edition of the *Mishnah*, p. 411, where there is also discussion of Boethus, another disciple of Antigonus and founder of the Boethusians. On these, as also on the Sadducees, there is an abundance of material in the learned writers Fuller, Pococke, Drusius, Serarius, Scaliger, and others.]

from Saddoc, a Jewish man [Col. 1119A] who bore that name, who

[Note: [Col. 1119B] “Was his disciple”: Dositheus’s. For this is what other ancient writers have likewise left in writing, as I noted in the preceding chapter. And one who heard Antigonus could also follow the traces of another teacher.]

was his disciple, and who confirmed this heresy, so that they were called Sadducees after him, likewise proclaim that one must live only according to the flesh, be circumcised, and have the body baptized. But from the divine Law they expect

[Note: [Col. 1119B] “Nothing else”: no other life and no promises of a better, eternal, blessed life. For Josephus reports of the Sadducees, *Antiquities* XVIII.2, τὰς ψυχὰς συναφανίζουσι τοῖς σώμασι, “they cause souls to perish together with the bodies”; and that they denied the resurrection is clear from Acts 23:8. See, if desired, Menasseh ben Israel, *On the Resurrection* I.6.]

nothing else,

[Note: [Col. 1119B] “Epicurean madness.” The most distinguished Gerhard Johann Vossius, *On the Origin of Idolatry* I.10, observes that the Sadducees were at least better than the Epicureans in this respect: although, like Epicurus, they held souls to be mortal, they nevertheless did not deny that God watches over human affairs—though only in this life. Yet one who persuades himself that human souls are subject to the same fate as their bodies easily slips into denying providence.]

following Epicurean madness rather than the ordinances of the divine Law. Of them it is written also

[Note: [Col. 1119C] “In the Gospel”: Matthew 21:23; Mark 12:18; Luke 20:27 ff. See also Matthew 16:6 ff., where the best Saviour commands his followers to beware of the ζύμη, “leaven,” of the Pharisees and Sadducees.]

in the Gospel, with the Lord teaching and preaching against this destructive heresy.

## VI. THE PHARISEES

The Pharisees have another doctrine, which

[Note: [Col. 1119C] “Confesses a future resurrection.” In this they were distinguished from the Sadducees, Acts 23:8. St Epiphanius, XVI.2: ὡμολόγουν δὲ οὗτοι ἀνάστασιν νεκρῶν, “these confessed a resurrection of the dead.” Yet it is uncertain whether they believed that the impious too would rise again. See Flavius Josephus, *Antiquities* XVIII, chapter 2, and *Jewish War* II, chapter 12.]

confesses a future resurrection [Col. 1120A],

[Note: [Col. 1119C] “It accepts the Law and the Prophets.” Learned men have already proved that the Sadducees did this as well; and Menasseh ben Israel, *On the Resurrection*, p. 43, affirms that it is certain from the Talmud. But besides τὰ γεγραμμένα, “the written things,” the Pharisees also employed many πατροπαράδοτα, “traditions handed down from the fathers,” and maintained certain additions to the Law, as Tertullian says, which the Sadducees were unwilling to embrace.]

accepts the Law and the Prophets,

[Note: [Col. 1119C] “It awaits Christ as a righteous man.” The Pharisees persuaded themselves that the Messiah to come would not be God but a mere human being; similarly, below in chapter IX, this is said of the Essenes. Yet in Philaster’s age scarcely even the name of the Pharisees remained; Eusebius, earlier than Philaster, attests this of his own time in his commentary on the Psalms, pp. 268 and 396.]

but awaits Christ as a righteous man.

[Note: [Col. 1119D] “These Judaize”: that is, they are Jews. Take care not to understand this of Christians who Judaize.]

They Judaize and do not accept the Gospels; and

[Note: [Col. 1119D] “Certain times.” It would be easy to write *testimonies* [instead of *times*], but to do this without the authority of manuscript codices would be to cut the knot rather than untie it. Another way of explaining this passage has therefore occurred to me: namely, that the Pharisees held that certain times—that is, the festivals of the year, the Jubilee, new moons, and Sabbaths commanded in the Law—are contrary to the teaching of Jesus, whose Apostle forbids the observance, παρατηρεῖσθαι, “of days and seasons and years” (Galatians 4:10; Colossians 2:16).]

they assert that certain times are contrary to Christ our Lord.

## VII. THE SAMARITANS

The Samaritans

[Note: [Col. 1119D] “From Samarius, a king.” Epiphanius, vol. I, p. 24: ἀπὸ ἀρχαίου τινὸς Σωμόρων υἱοῦ Σωμήρ, οὕτω τοῦ ἀνδρὸς καλουμένου, “from an ancient man named Somēr, son of Somoron.” See 3 Kings 16:24. FABRIC.—“From Samarius, a king.” Thus the Basel and Hamburg editions; but the Lyon edition reads, “from Samarus, a king,” which may perhaps be better. The Vulgate at 3 Kings 16:24 has Somer, as does Epiphanius, Σωμήρ; the Septuagint and Pagninus, Semer, Σεμήρ; the Arabic, Samer. See Josephus VIII.7, where Gelenius translates: “he called it Samaria from Samarus,” confirming the reading of the Lyon edition. GALEARD.]

are so named from King Samarius.

[Note: [Col. 1120B] “From a son of Canaan.” In Genesis 10:18 he is called Σαμαραῖος (*Samaraeos*). FABRIC.—“Others, however, [derive them] from a son of Canaan.” Dupin wrongly criticizes Philaster on this point in his *Ecclesiastical History*, century IV. Philaster does not say that King Samarius was a son of Canaan, as Dupin, reading much too hastily, supposed. GALEARD.]

Others, however, say that they are from a son of Canaan named Samarius, from whom the Samaritans were called. They accept the Law of Moses—that is,

[Note: [Col. 1120B] “Only four books.” Since other ancient writers—Origen, Epiphanius, Leontius, and many others—report that the Samaritans admitted only the Pentateuch, as the surviving remnant of them is known still to do, while rejecting prophetic writings composed after Moses, it may seem surprising that Philaster reports that they accepted only four books of Moses. [Col. 1120C] Nor is this a copyist’s error, since below, chapter 115, there recurs a distinct heresy concerning the rejection of Deuteronomy. But I fear that Philaster was misled by the double meaning of the terms δευτερώσεως (*deuterōseōs*) and δευτερονομίου (*Deuteronomion*). For it is known, even from Maximus on Epistle 9 of Dionysius the Areopagite, that just as δευτερώσεις can signify the Hebrews’ unwritten ancestral traditions, so *Deuteronomy* can sometimes signify them as well; these traditions the Samaritans certainly rejected. As far as I know, Philaster alone wrote—and, I think, incorrectly—that the Samaritans rejected Moses’ fifth book. Further, I have retained the ancient genitive *Moysi* for *Moysis*, following the earlier editions and because Tertullian and other ancients spoke thus, just as *Achilli* and *Ulyssi* occur conventionally for *Achillis* and *Ulyssis*, and similarly elsewhere; see, if desired, Vossius, *On the Art of Grammar* IV.9, and Claude Dausqueius, *Orthography*, p. 95. The accusative *Mosea* for *Mosen* occurs in Juvencus IV.15 and others. FABRIC.—“Only four books.” Fabricius rightly noted that Philaster’s assertion that the Samaritans accepted only four books of Moses is singular. (In the index to the Hamburg edition, “Sadducees” is printed for “Samaritans” under “four books.” EDIT.) This is not stated by the other ancients who speak of the Samaritans’ reception of the Pentateuch, and is wholly ἄγνωστον, “unknown.” Could it be that, granted Philaster’s statement is certain, the Samaritans rejected Deuteronomy—Fabricius understands him to mean that book—because it contains certain things that scholars now agree were by no means written by Moses’ own hand? See Simon, *Critical History of the Old Testament* I.6; Huet, *Evangelical Demonstration*, p. 179, Paris edition; neither notices Philaster’s passage. But that Deuteronomy was not anciently rejected by the Samaritans is clearly shown by the notable passage in that book, 27:4, corrupted by the Samaritans: in place of Mount Ebal, they substituted Gerizim, against the testimony of all Hebrew manuscripts and all ancient versions. On this see Walton, *Prolegomena* XI to the London Bible, no. 16 [Col. 1121B]; likewise Étienne Morin, *Exercises on the Languages*, part II, chapter 7, p. 201. See below, note on heresy 116. GALEARD.]

only four books—expecting no future judgment, [Col. 1121A] denying the resurrection,

[Note: [Col. 1121B] “Christ the Lord, the Son of God.” From this passage do not infer that Philaster asserts that the Samaritans denied the Messiah to have been promised in the Law—I am surprised that Rabbi Joseph Albo adds “and in the Prophets,” which they wholly rejected. About A.D. 1400 Albo had such brazen effrontery as to write in his *Ikkarim* that neither the Law nor the Prophets contains an oracle from which the Messiah’s coming can necessarily be inferred. Philaster merely denies that the Samaritans believed that the Messiah foretold would be the Son of God. Leontius, *On Sects*, p. 423: Περὶ δὲ τὴν ἐνανθρώπησιν τοῦ Χριστοῦ οὕτως ἔχουσιν· Οὐ πιστεύουσιν ὅτι ἦλθεν, ἀλλ᾽ ὅτι μέλλει ἐλθεῖν, οὐδὲ ὅτι Θεὸς ὁ ἐρχόμενος, ἀλλὰ προφήτης: “Concerning Christ’s incarnation they hold thus: they do not believe that he has come, but that he is going to come; nor that the coming one is God, but a prophet.” FABRIC.]

not believing that Christ the Lord, the Son of God, had been announced beforehand in the Law and the Prophets;

[Note: [Col. 1121B] “That a human being possesses an immortal soul according to the Law.” The same Leontius says: οὔτε δὲ ἄγγελον δοξάζουσιν εἶναι οὔτε ψυχὴν ἀθάνατον, οὔτε ἀνάστασιν, “Nor do they hold that an angel exists, nor an immortal soul, nor a resurrection.” Learned men, however, prove that these errors are falsely charged upon the Samaritans [Col. 1121C]. See Christoph Cellarius, *Samaritan History*, chapter 3; compare nevertheless Adriaan Reland, *Dissertations*, part II, dissertation 7. There is mention of Samaritans even in Justinian’s age in Procopius. Niccolò Alemanni notes laws enacted by Justinian against them in his notes on the *Secret History*, pp. 130 ff. FABRIC.]

nor that a human being possesses an immortal soul according to the Law. They think that one must live only in this body, and that the future resurrection consists in the begetting of children, which occurs daily in this age;

[Note: [Col. 1121C] “This”: wrongly; another reading, *haud*, “not.”]

they reckon this to be it, and proclaim it to be vanity—likened indeed to irrational beasts, as it is written in the Prophet: “Man, though in honour, did not understand; he was compared with irrational beasts and became like them” (Psalm 49:12).

## VIII. THE NAZARENES

[Col. 1122A]

[Note: [Col. 1121C] “Of the Nazarenes.” This term is used simply for Christians in Acts of the Apostles 15:5, where St Paul is called πρωτοστάτης τῆς τῶν Ναζαραίων αἱρέσεως, “leader of the sect of the Nazarenes,” the designation being taken from Jesus the Nazarene. It then appears to have been used more particularly for those Jews who had given their allegiance to Christ. Subsequently it denoted those who, having become Christians from among Jewish ζηλωταὶ τοῦ νόμου, “zealots for the Law” (Acts 21:20), still clung rather firmly to Jewish rites and believed in Christ as God while observing the Law, as Sulpicius Severus says in book II—such as there were not a few even in the Apostles’ own times. Thus Philaster too, following his Epiphanius as usual, takes the name in this sense.]

The heresy of the Nazarenes is one which accepts the Law and the Prophets,

[Note: [Col. 1121D] “Carnally”: that is, only by observing the external rites of the Law, as our author said above in heresy 4, “to live in the Law of the Lord only according to the flesh.” Thus, shortly afterward, “carnal observance” is nothing other than that external observance understood according to the letter.]

yet declares that one must live carnally, and supposes that all justification consists in carnal observance.

[Note: [Col. 1121D] “Growing the hair of their heads.” St Epiphanius does not charge this upon his Nazarenes, and I fear Philaster incorrectly applied to them what in his own time presented itself to his mind concerning persons devoted under Numbers 6.]

They also grow the hair of their heads, believing that all the power of righteousness consists in this,

[Note: [Col. 1121D] “From Samson”: Judges 16:17. Compare what Tzetzes says concerning the fateful locks of Pherelai and Nisus, *Chiliads* 2, History 37.]

as though deriving this presumption of judgment from that Samson, because they were called Nazarenes; and afterward pagans, appropriating mighty men from his image,

[Note: [Col. 1121D] “Hercules.” They relate that the lion slain by Samson when he went to Timnah was the Nemean lion killed by Hercules; Delilah was Omphale; the two columns of the Gaza house were the columns at Gades, which marked the limit of Hercules’ journeys, just as the former marked the end of Samson’s life. This is set out by the illustrious Huet, *Evangelical Demonstration*, p. 336. Add, if desired, Louis Cappel, *Posthumous Works*, p. 426 ff. The name itself also agrees, for Samson means “sun of strength” and is explained by Flavius Josephus as ἰσχυρός, “strong.” Indeed Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I.20, says that Hermes is the sun “as is evident even from his name.” For what else is Ἡρακλῆς (*Hēraklēs*) than Ἥρας, that is, “of the air,” κλέος, “glory”? And what other glory of the air is there than the sun’s illumination? And so forth. I omit what the most eminent and learned Gisbert Cuper in his *Harpocrates*, and Jacob Rhenferd in his explanation of a Phoenician coin in Jean Le Clerc, vol. XI of the *Bibliothèque choisie*, pp. 109 ff., observed about Hercules as the sun. FABRIC.—“As though deriving this presumption of judgment from that Samson, [because] they were called Nazarenes.” The Basel edition reads thus also; but the Paris and Lyon editions read, “because he was called a Nazarene,” with which the Corbie manuscript agrees, and this reading is certainly easier and better. On this passage of Philaster, Barthius, *Adversaria* V.46: “These words of Philaster are unquestionably corrupt. The phrase ‘because he was called a Nazarene,’ from the Gospel, I think belongs to those Nazarenes whom Humbert testifies to have been semi-Christians. Therefore I think that in Philaster it should be read so that Samson’s typical role follows the blessed name of Christ or Jesus.” But I do not understand what this critic of greater nations means. For Philaster immediately adds that the pagans called their mighty men Hercules, appropriating them not from Christ or Jesus but from Samson himself and his image; Fabricius also noted this from Huet. GALEARD.]

called them Hercules.

## IX. THE ESSENES

But the Essenes are those who

[Note: [Col. 1122C] “Practise the life of monks.” Josephus, *Antiquities* XVIII.2, testifies that they neither had wives nor slaves and that they held their possessions in common. He discusses the Essenes’ life more fully in *Jewish War* II, chapter 12; likewise Philo does so in his *Apology for the Jews* and in *That Every Good Man Is Free*. Josephus’s words occur also in Porphyry, *On Abstinence* IV, and Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* IX.3; Philo’s, in Eusebius VIII.11–12. FABRIC.—“The Essenes are those who practise the life of monks.” The great father of the *Annals* acknowledges them to be Christians under A.D. 64, nos. 4 and 5, following both ancient and more recent writers who have written about them—excepting the Innovators, because, he says, they pursue monastic institutions with the utmost hatred. The familiar question is whether monks derive their origin from the Essenes. There are debates conducted with the greatest vigour between Serarius and Scaliger on this matter, and each adduces Philaster’s passage in support of his own opinion: Serarius, *Trihaeres* III.10; Scaliger, *Elenchus Trihaeres* 31, where he rebukes Serarius as though he had not quoted Philaster’s testimony in full. Yet this is quite unjust, for Serarius had cited above, at the end of chapter 4, the final words which he omits there, where he treats of the Essenes’ doctrines or institutions. Salmasius notes in his commentary on Solinus, p. 431, that they drew something from Christian teaching but were not wholly Christians: for besides other things conformable to Christian practice, they had mutual love, a commitment to chastity, contempt for riches, prayers before dawn, and other such practices. But since Philaster [Col. 1123B] adds that the Essenes did not expect Christ the Lord as the Son of God, but believed he would be only a prophet or righteous man, it is clear even from this that they cannot be counted among Christians. This conclusion from Philaster’s passage also appears to have pleased Samuel Basnage, *Annals*, vol. I, p. 172. GALEARD.]

practise the life of monks, taking no luxurious food, making no display in dress, and owning nothing; but applying themselves to reading and good works,

[Note: [Col. 1123B] “Dwelling also in separate places.” Josephus affirms that they gathered in considerable numbers not outside cities or in a single city, but in various cities, where they lived together in a common fellowship. Philo, on the contrary, states that they lived κωμηδόν, “village by village,” and avoided cities, τὰς πόλεις ἐκτρεπομένους, “shunning cities.” That both speak of the same people is evident because Philo, like Josephus, counts them at more than four thousand. To reconcile the two, I would say that Philo’s τὰς πόλεις, “cities,” and Josephus’s μίαν πόλιν, “one city,” should be understood of Jerusalem; then, what Josephus wrote—that the Essenes lived through several cities—Philo expressed by κωμηδόν. Philo, *On the Contemplative Life*, p. 899, Paris edition: Τειχῶν ἔξω ποιοῦνται τὰς διατριβὰς ἐν κήποις ἢ μοναγρίοις ἐρημίαν μεταδιώκοντες, “They make their dwellings outside the walls, in gardens or solitary places, pursuing the wilderness.” Josephus, at the end of book XVII, p. 866, mentions Simon, ἀνὴρ γένος Ἐσσαῖος, “a man of Essene stock”; likewise Judas, Ἐσσηνὸς τὸ γένος, “Essene by birth,” XIII.2 §2, p. 665. FABRIC.]

dwelling also in separate places. Yet they await Christ the Lord,

[Note: [Col. 1123C] “Not expecting [him as] the Son of God.” Like Jews, the Essenes expected the Messiah to come; but they did not expect that he would be the Son of God, only that some prophet promised in the Law and the Prophets would come. Philaster makes the same observation above, chapter 6, concerning the Pharisees, and chapter 7 concerning the Samaritans. FABRIC.]

not as the Son of God, nor acknowledging that he was announced in the Law and the Prophets as Lord, but expecting him as only a prophet or righteous man.

## X. THE HELIOGNOSTICS

[Note: [Col. 1123C] “Heliognostics and Devictiacs.” Gabriel Prateolus reads *Heliognostici*, which is not altogether displeasing, and *Devictiatici*, a reading no less obscure than the common one. The most learned Jean-Baptiste Cotelerius, in his notes on Damascene’s *On Heresies*, p. 762, suspected *Heliactiaci*, from ἥλιος, “sun,” and [Col. 1123D] ἀκτίς, “ray.” Thus the name Heliognostics would refer to what Philaster adds as their belief, that the sun knows all things belonging to God; while Heliactiacs would refer to the illumination of people by the sun’s rays. Dr Christoph August Heumann, *Poecilia*, vol. III, book IV, p. 533, wishes to read: “Egyptians.” Justin, *Dialogue with Trypho*, pp. 274b, 349d, infers from Deuteronomy 4:19 that the stars were left by God to be worshipped by the nations. See Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* VI, p. 669; Origen, vol. II of Huet’s edition, p. 48; also Athanasius, *Against the Gentiles* I, p. 49d; Isidore of Pelusium III, epistle 391. FABRIC.]

The Heliognostics, who are also called Devictiacs, worship the sun and say that the sun

[Note: [Col. 1123D] “Knows all things.” Recent Jews also attribute knowledge to the sun, as to other stars. So Maimonides, *Guide for the Perplexed* II.5, and *Madda, Hilchoth Yesode ha-Torah* 3 §9.]

knows all things which belong to God; that no one other than the sun illuminates human beings, and that the sun supplies them with all nourishment. They fail to recognize that, being placed in servitude, it daily pursues the course

[Note: [Col. 1124B] “Pursues.” Another reading is *peragat*, “performs.” But because I found the common reading in the printed codices, and Philaster more frequently uses the indicative in constructions of this kind, I preferred it. FABRIC.]

appointed by God the Father through Christ the Lord [Col. 1123B] in the Holy Spirit,

[Note: [Col. 1124B] “Of whom it is written.” In Job 9:7 only the latter clause is found: ὁ λέγων τῷ ἡλίῳ, καὶ οὐκ ἀνατέλλει, “who says to the sun, ‘Do not rise,’ and it does not rise.” Philaster added the former clause from Genesis 1:3, 14 ff., and 2 Corinthians 4:6. ID.]

of whom it is written: “He who tells the sun to rise, and it rises; and not to rise, and it does not rise.”

[Note: [Col. 1124B] “Hermes.” I do not know whether Philaster had in view these words found near the end of Hermes’ *Asclepius*: “When they had left the sanctuary and began to pray to God, they faced south. For, when the sun is setting, whoever wishes to pray to God ought to look in that direction; as also, when the sun is rising, toward what is called the east.” ID.]

That vain pagan Hermes [Col. 1124A] Trismegistus taught that, after the almighty Lord, human beings ought to worship no one but the sun itself. When he had gone

[Note: [Col. 1124B] “To the province of the Celts.” Caesar, *Gallic War* VI.17, observes that the Celts especially worshipped the god Mercury, that he had very many images, and that they considered him the inventor of every art. Hence Paul Pezron, in *Antiquities of the Celtic Nation and Language*, p. 118, rightly had no doubt that Hermes also had ruled among the Celts. The present passage of Philaster would perhaps have delighted that distinguished man by expressly confirming this, had he encountered it. Yet Philaster, when he wrote this, did not believe—or did not consider—that this Celtic Hermes was distinct from the Egyptian one to whom the *Asclepius* and other writings are attributed. ID.]

to the province of the Celts, he is known to have taught them and persuaded them to submit to this error. The captive Jews worshipped this sun, as the prophet Ezekiel, rebuking and condemning those same Jews, declares and charges with greater severity the crime of majesty—

[Note: [Col. 1124C] “The crime of majesty”: namely, the violation of the divine majesty by worship rendered to the sun, which God created. I think Philaster refers to Ezekiel 8:16, and that at the end of this section the words have fallen out: “And behold, they are as though mocking.” FABRIC.]

as it is written (Ezekiel 8:16).

## XI. WORSHIPPERS OF FROGS

There are others

[Note: [Col. 1124C] “Who worship frogs.” Prateolus calls them *Ranatitae*, citing Philaster as his authority, though I do not know whether this came from a more ancient manuscript of our writer or from his own invention. “I suspect,” says Cotelerius, “that these are the people called Batrachitae in law 5 of the Code *On Heretics*, and by Balsamon Βατραχῖται”—so I read, instead of [Col. 1124D] Βαθραχῖται—“for βάτραχος means ‘frog.’” Philaster may have written *Ranoritae*. ID.]

who worship frogs, which, under Pharaoh, the land of the Egyptians then brought forth by God’s wrath,

[Note: [Col. 1124D] “The land brought forth.” Exodus 8:3: ἐξερεύξεται, “the river shall teem forth” or “bubble up frogs.” ID.]

so that their stench might weary the Egyptians;

[Note: [Col. 1124D] “Might weary.” Thus Bochart rightly reads, *Hierozoicon* II, V.4, p. 673, in place of *defatigent*, “they weary,” found in the editions. Cotelerius preferred *defatigaret*, with the land understood as subject. It is not surprising that frog-worship existed among the Egyptians, worshippers of so many prodigies; great numbers of frogs could cause them serious inconvenience, especially after the Nile’s inundation. ID.]

and they still persevere in this wickedness, believing that God’s anger can be appeased by this observance.

## XII. THE MUSORITAE

[Col. 1124B]

[Note: [Col. 1124D] “Musuritae.” The name is derived from *mures*, “mice,” with only the sort of ending found below in chapter 20, *Puteoritae*, and chapter 56, *Hermioritae*. ID.]

The Musoritae are certain people by name who worship shrews. When, under the priest

[Note: [Col. 1124D] “Musoritae.” The name is derived from *mures*, “mice,” with only the sort of ending found below in chapter 20, *Puteoritae*, and chapter 56, *Hermioritae*. ID.]

Eli, the Ark of the Covenant was captured [Col. 1125A]

[Note: [Col. 1125B] “Under the priest Eli.” I have written this from 1 Samuel 4, since the earlier editions absurdly had *Belo*, “Belus.” FABRIC.]

by the Allophylians,

[Note: [Col. 1125B] “By the Allophylians.” It is well known that in Holy Scripture the Philistines are called by this name. For the whole narrative concerning the punishment of the Philistines, compare the great Bochart, *Hierozoicon* III.34. Yet I am surprised that on p. 1033 he takes these Musoritae of Philaster to be Christian heretics, when they are said to accept the Law and the Prophets but not the Gospel. Although perhaps there were nowhere any such Christian or Jewish heretics, and Philaster rather thoughtlessly derived heretics from the Philistines’ action, as Selden says, *On the Syrian Gods*, Syntagma I.6. ID.]

and, in God’s anger, the land had produced shrews so that their crops might perish, they were instructed by their own people to make golden mice and to send them, together with the Ark and

[Note: [Col. 1125B] “Five golden seats.” The Greek version of 1 Samuel 6:4 adds no number for the mice. Yet verse 18 shows that not merely five golden mice were given, just as there were five ἕδραι, “seats,” but as many as there were cities in the five Philistine satrapies. To reconcile the reading of the Hebrew text in verse 4 with verse 18, [Col. 1125C] one must say that their priests directed them to give only five golden mice, corresponding to the number of satrapies; but then, to secure a more certain deliverance from the plague, they chose to give one for each individual city. That those mouse-images were talismanic and στοιχειωματικά, “elemental,” as John Gregory was persuaded in chapter 8 of his *Observations*, does not seem likely, since the Philistines did not keep them but gave them to the Israelites. It is more credible that they dedicated as an offering mere images of the animals by which they had been punished, and images of the afflicted body part—whether they suffered from haemorrhoids, mariscae and cancerous ulcers, or, as Flavius Josephus thought, dysentery and diarrhoea. Jacob Philipp Thomasin observes in *On the Votive Offerings of the Ancients*, chapter 35, that such a custom prevailed among other peoples and among Christians too. FABRIC.]

five golden seats; and immediately the plague ceased from them. Therefore, though they accept the Law and the Prophets, they do not recognize that this

[Note: [Col. 1125C] “Plague.” Philaster denotes by this general term the evil with which God punished the Philistines. After learned interpreters and Bochart’s diligence, I would not add a word regarding it. But it is worthwhile to note the passage of Herodotus reported by Longinus, p. 162 of the splendid Toll edition: τῶν Σκυθέων τοῖς συλήσασι τὸ ἱερόν, ἐνέβαλεν ἡ ἐν Ἀσκάλων πόλει Θεὸς τὴν Θήλειαν νοῦσον: “Upon the Scythians who plundered the sanctuary, the goddess in the city of Ascalon inflicted the female disease.” For what that Θήλεια νοῦσος, “female disease,” was, see, if desired, the discussion of the distinguished Jacob Tollius in his notes, and of Hieronymus Mercurialis, *Various Readings* III.7, in chapter 31 of his *Fortuita*. ID.]

is vain and abominable, despised by everyone and ridiculed in every way.

## XIII. THE MUSCACCARONITAE

[Note: [Col. 1125D] “Muscaccaronitae.” I have written this instead of the printed reading *Musca-Accaronitae*. Prateolus incorrectly has *Moscaranitae*.]

There are others who worship

[Note: [Col. 1125D] “The fly of Accaron.” An idol of Ekron, or the Philistine city Accaron, not far from Gath, which the people of Accaron worshipped under the image of a fly: Μυῖα, Θεὸς Ἀκκαρών, “Fly, god of Accaron.” George of Pisidia, *Cosmurgia*, verse 978: Καὶ μέχρι μυίας ἐκθεοῦντες τὴν φύσιν, “Deifying nature even as far as a fly.” Pseudo-Jerome, *On the Perfect Man*, vol. V, p. 52: “That any compensation whatsoever might rather follow than that I should come to the Fly of Accaron’s worship.” Compare Bochart, *Hierozoicon* II, IV.9; and John Selden, *On the Syrian Gods*, Syntagma II.6, where among other things you may read: “From Baalzebub Philaster constructs the heresy of the Muscae-Accaronitae, who, in his words, worship the Fly in the city called Accaron.” See also Salmasius on Solinus, p. 12, on the god Myiagros; G. Outhovius, *On the Judgments of Jehovah*, pp. 102 ff.; and Drusius, *On the Hebrew Terms of the New Testament*, under *Beelzebub*. Moreover, in Syncellus, p. 190, read ἐν εἰδολείῳ, “in a shrine,” rather than ἐν εἰδολίᾳ μυίας Ἀκκαρών. FABRIC.]

the Fly of Accaron in the city so named, as it is written in the Book of Kings (4 Kings 1:2, 16): King Ahaziah of the Jews, being ill, had sent to the Fly

[Note: [Col. 1126B] “To the city of Accaron.” Earlier editions omit the preposition: “Accaron city.” On this city see Adriaan Reland, *Palestine*, pp. 745–746. ID.]

in the city of Accaron to learn whether he might recover from his bodily sickness. For this reason the blessed prophet Elijah, angered with divine zeal because the king of the Jews had chosen to hope for healing not from God but rather from the Fly and the city of Accaron, angrily pronounced through the divine Spirit that he would not escape, but would die at once in his bed.

## XIV. THE TROGLODYTES
[Note: [Col. 1126B] Troglodytes. The Greek name derives from τρώγη or τρώγλη, meaning “a hiding-place,” and δύω, “I enter.” See Hadrian Turnebus, *Adversaria* XXIV.42, and Johann Rhodius on Scribonius Largus, p. 154. Theodoret, *On Heretical Fables* IV.4, accordingly writes that Eunomians and Aetians were also called by this name [Col. 1126C] because they met “in concealed private houses” (ἐν οἰκείαις λανθανούσαις). On the Troglodyte Nomads, an ancient wandering people of Africa, mentioned by Herodotus IV.185; Strabo XVII, p. 775; Diodorus Siculus III, p. 165; Mela I.8; Pliny V.5; Porphyry, *On Abstinence from Animal Food* I, p. 9, and IV, p. 427; and other ancient authors, there is an exceptional dissertation by the distinguished Johann Esberg, published at Uppsala in 1699, octavo. Job Ludolf, in his commentary on the *Ethiopian History*, p. 199, and Peter Kolbe, in his very worthwhile description of the Cape of Good Hope, published in German at Nuremberg in 1719, folio, do not doubt that the Hottentots, well known from recent travellers’ accounts, are remnants of these Troglodytes. See pp. 352, 355, 370, 405, 425, 448, 453, 455. In the same people Kolbe believed he observed traces of Jewish rites, pp. 352, 413, 414, 416, 425, 429, 431, 433, 449, 457 ff. Pliny, XXXVII.8, writes that in the Troglodytes’ language *topazion* means “to seek.” ID.] The Troglodytes are so called among the Jews: they lived in hidden caves and did not cease worshipping idols. As the prophet [Note: [Col. 1126D] The prophet Ezekiel. In the vision, VII.11–12, from which our author repeats these matters below in chapter 22. Compare, if you wish, Porphyry’s little work *On the Cave of the Nymphs* concerning caves of this sort. FABRIC.] Ezekiel says, the Lord showed him how, in hidden caverns, the elders of the people, holding censers, sacrificed to idols and worshipped them with blinded minds.

## XV. HERESY CONCERNING THE FORTUNE OF HEAVEN

[Note: [Col. 1126D] The heading of this chapter in earlier editions was “Fortune of Heaven.” But it ought to be “Heresy concerning the Fortune of Heaven,” as below in chapter 18, “Heresy concerning the idol Moloch and Remphan,” and similarly throughout this book. FABRIC.]

There is another heresy among the Jews: they call her [Note: [Col. 1126D] The Queen and Fortune of Heaven. That the moon was worshipped under this name has already been observed by very learned men: Hugo Grotius on Jeremiah VII.18; Peter Faber, *Semestria* III.2, p. 27; Johann Selden, *On Syrian Gods*, Syntagma I, chapter 1, and Syntagma II, chapter 2; and Gerhard Vossius, *On the Origin of Idolatry* II.21 and 24. Kircher is mistaken when he understands the Pleiades, *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*, I, pp. 361 ff. FABRIC.] the Queen, [Col. 1127A] and Fortune of Heaven; in Africa she is also called [Note: [Col. 1127B] She is called the Heavenly One in Africa. Herodian V.6: “The Libyans call her Urania, while the Phoenicians call her Astroarchē [elsewhere this is Astarte], intending her to be the moon” (Λίβυες μὲν οὖν αὐτὴν Οὐρανίαν καλοῦσι, Φοίνικες δὲ Ἀστροάρχην—ἄλλοις αὕτη Ἀστάρτη—ὀνομάζουσι, σελήνην εἶναι θέλοντες). I omit passages from Tertullian and other ancients, already noted by Peter Faber, *Semestria* III.1 ff., the illustrious Gisbert Cuper in Harpocrates, p. 11, Conrad Rittershausen on Salvian, *On Providence* VIII, Samuel Boussac, *Theological Nights*, Dissertation 26, “On the Empress of Rain and Fair Weather,” pp. 311 ff., Paris, 1698, octavo; Thierry Ruinart on Victor of Vita, [Col. 1127C] p. 144; and Raffaele Fabretti, *Inscriptions*, p. 667. FABRIC.] the Heavenly One. They did not hesitate to offer sacrifices to her. Thus the Jews in the time of the prophet Jeremiah openly said, when he warned them to withdraw from idols, serve the Lord, and worship him alone, that, angered, they cried out (Jer. XLIV.27): from the time when they ceased sacrificing to that Fortune or Queen of Heaven, all evils and dangers had befallen them. Therefore blessed Jeremiah, leaving their people and city, composed Lamentations because of their impiety and foretold that destruction would come upon them and their city [Note: [Col. 1127C] Would come not long afterward. Philaster therefore agrees with those who regard Jeremiah’s Lamentations as a writing announcing future calamity, rather than lamenting a calamity already present and inflicted. Yet one should rather agree with whoever prefixed these words to the ancient Greek version of Lamentations: “And it came to pass, after Israel had been taken captive and Jerusalem laid waste, that Jeremiah sat weeping and uttered this lament over Jerusalem” (Καὶ ἐγένετο μετὰ τὸ αἰχμαλωτισθῆναι τὸν Ἰσραήλ, καὶ Ἱερουσαλὴμ ἐρημωθῆναι, ἐκάθισεν Ἰερεμίας κλαίων, καὶ ἐθρήνησε τὸν Θρῆνον τοῦτον ἐπὶ Ἱερουσαλήμ). Origen, Eusebius, Athanasius, Olympiodorus, and others held the same opinion.] not long thereafter.

## XVI. BAALITES

[Note: [Col. 1127C] “Baalites among them”: that is, among the Jews, as in the preceding chapter and chapter 25; or, as this chapter itself says, among those who professed the Law under the name of Judaism. Earlier editions printed *Bahalitae* and *Bahal*. Below, chapter 24, *Belitae*. FABRIC.]

There are also Baalites among them, who retained in memory [Note: [Col. 1127D] Baal, the name of the king of the Tyrians. Jezebel’s father, Ethbaal, Ahab’s father-in-law, was king of the Sidonians (III Kings XVI.31). But the worship of Baal was far older—apparently spread throughout the East from Belus, king of the Assyrians—and is already mentioned in Judges II.13, where also at verse 11, as frequently afterward elsewhere, *Baalim* occurs in the plural of multitude. Selden treats these matters copiously and learnedly in *On Syrian Gods*, Syntagma II, chapter 1; to omit Kircher, *Oedipus Aegyptiacus* I, pp. 262 ff.; John Owen, *Theologoumena*, p. 342; Anthony van Dalen, *On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry among the Jews*, chapter 2; etc. Yet perhaps Philaster wrote “king of the Syrians,” as below in chapter 27—that is, of the Assyrians—rather than “king of the Tyrians.” FABRIC.] Baal as the name of the king of the Tyrians. Worshipping his image, they sacrificed to it, as the Book of Kings relates, when Ahab, king of the Israelites, and Jezebel his wife did not cease sacrificing to that idol. Moved by divine zeal, the blessed prophet Elijah, sent by the Lord, said to those who professed the Law under the name of Judaism but ruinously served pagan impiety, [Note: [Col. 1127D] Another reading: “pernicious.” FABRIC.] and to all the people (III Kings XVIII.21): “How long do you limp [Note: [Col. 1128B] “On both your knees”: ἰγνύαις. The word is ambiguous, as is the Hebrew word; it also denotes a meaning or disposition of mind. See, if you wish, Cotelerius on *Apostolic Constitutions* VIII.1. FABRIC.] upon both your knees? Either God—God; or Baal—Baal.” Nevertheless, because the king and queen favoured the priests of the groves, they perished by various punishments and torments. The people too, not abandoning idols, perished in repeated captivities.

## XVII. ASTARITES

There are others who [Note: [Col. 1128C] Astar, a man. Philaster is mistaken in inventing for himself here and below in chapter 27 an Astar as a man—that is, a male—since in sacred Scripture Astar never occurs in the singular; rather, Astoreth, in III Kings XI.5, 33, is the goddess Astarte, and the plural Astaroth, Ἀστάρται, and Ascheroth denote the groves in which those idols were worshipped. Compare Selden, *On Syrian Gods*, Syntagma II, chapter 1; Spencer, *On Hebrew Laws* II.16; and Allatius on Eustathius, *Hexaemeron*, pp. 314 ff. FABRIC.] worshipped Astar, a man, and [Note: [Col. 1128C] Chamos. An idol of the Moabites, otherwise called Baal-peor. See the commentators on Numbers XXI.29; Judges XI.24; III Kings XI.33; IV Kings XXIII.13; Jeremiah XLVIII.7, 13; and Selden, *On Syrian Gods*, Syntagma I, chapter 5. Suidas: “Chamos was a god of the Tyrians and Ammonites, just as Astarte was the goddess of the Sidonians, whom Solomon served” (Χαμὼς Θεὸς ἦν Τυρίων καὶ Ἀμανιτῶν, ὥσπερ ἡ Ἀστάρτη Θεὸς Σιδονίων, ᾗ ἐλάτρευσε Σολομών). FABRIC.] Chamos, the abomination of the Canaanites and Sidonians—that is, [Note: [Col. 1128C] “Idols of men and women”: that is, images of males and females. Thus below, chapter 24, “of many as it were men and many women”; and chapter 27, “Astar and Astaroth, men and women.” It is well known that among Hebrews, Greeks, Gauls, and other peoples *homo* (“man”) is used for a male, as also among the Latins. See Johann Henel, *Wrocław Leisure*, chapter 42; Scipio Gentili, *Parerga* I.3; and Taubmann on Plautus, pp. 251 and 292. In III Esdras IV.17: “And these women make the garments of men, and these women bring glory to men; and men cannot exist without women” (Καὶ αὗται ποιοῦσι [Col. 1128D] τὰς στολὰς τῶν ἀνθρώπων, καὶ αὗται ποιοῦσι δόξαν ἀνθρώποις, καὶ οὐ δύνανται ἄνθρωποι χωρὶς γυναικῶν εἶναι). Likewise Tobit VI.7, 14; Matthew XIX.10; and I Corinthians VII.1. FABRIC.] idols of men and women—and offered them various sacrifices. On their account captivity repeatedly came upon those kings and their people at that time, with the Lord permitting it, as is related in the Books of Kings. Apart from the blessed king David, [Col. 1128B] holy Hezekiah, Josiah, and [Note: [Col. 1128D] And Joshua son of Nun. It may seem surprising that Joshua is mentioned here after the kings; thus at first sight one might suspect that some king lies concealed under this name. Yet one must not demand from Philaster such exact and punctilious precision as perhaps one might desire elsewhere in this little book. FABRIC.] Joshua son of Nun, all the others allowed the people to sacrifice to idols; and, often together with their own destruction, they themselves [Note: [Col. 1128D] “Worshipped.” I have restored this for *versabantur* (“were occupied”), which earlier editions intruded. Moreover, understand “their destruction” as the destruction of the kings themselves and of the people. FABRIC.] worshipped them, not destroying them, but rather hastening to become supporters of their impiety—as did the other kings, as the Books of Kings attest.

## XVIII. HERESY CONCERNING THE IDOL MOLOCH AND [Note: [Col. 1129B] Remphan. Thus the name is written in the manuscripts of Irenaeus, in the Vulgate Latin version, and commonly. The Greek version of the Seventy, as also some Greek manuscripts of Acts, has Ῥαιφάν, as though the translators had read [uncertain reading omitted in the source] in Amos. In lists of Egyptian planetary names in Kircher’s *Coptic Forerunner to Oedipus Aegyptiacus*, I, p. 385, II, pp. 415, 431, there is Ῥηφάν, which he notes corresponds to Saturn. Ῥηφάν also occurs in the Coptic version published by David Wilkins. This name may also be seen written or corrupted in various other ways: Ῥομφᾶ, Ῥαιμφάν, Ῥαμφάν, Ῥαφάν, Ῥεφάν, Ῥεφάμ, Ῥεφφάν, Ῥεφᾶ, as the industry of Louis de Dieu and John Mill has noted on the passage in Acts. For Grotius, Ῥεμφάν is the same as Ῥιμμών in IV Kings V.18, because the Hebrew may be pronounced either way. There was also Remphis, king of Egypt, mentioned by Diodorus Siculus I, p. 56. FABRIC.] REMPHAN
