There is another heresy among the Jews, concerning which [Note: [Col. 1129B] The Lord speaking prophetically. In Amos V.26. To elucidate this difficult passage, in addition to the commentators, Selden, [Col. 1129C] and Vossius on idolatry, one should consult the most distinguished Samuel Petit, book and chapter 1 of *Various Readings*; John Spencer, book III of *On Hebrew Laws*, pp. 32 ff.; John Braun, book IV of *Sacred Selections*, chapters 8–10; Campegius Vitringa, book II of *Observations*, pp. 245 ff.; and Heinrich Mü hlius, who subjected the learned man’s opinion to examination in the second dissertation of *Scriptural Demonstration*. FABRIC.] the Lord, speaking prophetically, accused them, and concerning which the blessed martyr Stephen rebuked them, saying: “Did you offer me victims and sacrifices in the wilderness for forty years, house of Israel, says the Lord Almighty? And now you have taken up [Note: [Col. 1129C] The tabernacle of your Moloch: a little shrine (ναΐσκον) and booth (παστόν) in which the Ammonite image of Moloch was worshipped. *Moloch* is Hebrew; some maintain that Saturn, others the sun, was worshipped under this name, although Baal and Moloch appear to be general names common to several gods, as Spencer, following Samuel Petit, not implausibly observed. FABRIC.] the tabernacle of your Moloch and the star of your god Remphan, [Note: [Col. 1129C] “Forms of fashioned carved idols.” The words “fashioned carved idols,” like others which I have caused to be printed in a different typeface, Philaster added himself. Moreover [Col. 1129D] I have written *fictorum* (“fashioned”) for *fixorum* (“fixed”), which earlier editions had. FABRIC.] forms of fashioned carved idols” (Acts VII.42 ff., from Amos V.27). Therefore the Lord says: “I shall cause you to be carried away in captivity into Babylon, and into the [Note: [Col. 1129D] “I shall spare.” II Maccabees I.19. In the prophet Amos there is only: “And I shall deport you beyond Damascus” (καὶ μετοικιῶ ὑμᾶς ἐπέκεινα Δαμασκοῦ)—Damascus, which Justin Martyr assigns to Arabian territory, p. 238. In its place Saint Stephen said: “And I shall deport you beyond Babylon” (καὶ μετοικιῶ ὑμᾶς ἐπέκεινα Βαβυλῶνος), which is farther away, and the outcome confirmed it. In Philaster’s words I have here followed the edition found in the *Libraries of the Fathers*: for the Basel edition had all the same, except that it lacked the words “in the wilderness,” “your,” and “your,” and wrote *Babylone* for *Babylonis*; whereas John a Fuchte edited it thus: “In Babylon and the interior dry places of the Persians, and in the remotest part of all lands.” For *interiora* one may also read *ulteriora* (“more distant”), unless one prefers to rest with me in the received reading [Col. 1130B]. FABRIC.] elevated and dry interior regions of the Persians, and to the farthest extremities of all the earth.”

## XIX. HERESY CONCERNING THE ALTAR OF TOPHET

There are also [Note: [Col. 1130B] Those who set up an altar thus called, Tophet, after the name of someone. Tophet does not appear to be the name of an idol, but of a place. Although in the Greek Fathers’ Catena on Jeremiah, p. 624, “altar of Tophet” is explained as “altar of Pluto” (Βωμὸς τοῦ Πλούτωνος), and the very learned Andreas Mulier thinks in his *Sacred Glossary* that Tophet is the Egyptian Tautus. Others consider it to correspond to Vesta, whom the Scythians called ταβιτί, according to Herodotus IV.152. Certainly the Targum on Isaiah XXX.33 renders Tophet as Gehenna, and Kimchi on IV Kings XXIII.10, with other Hebrews, notes that Tophet is called from [Hebrew word absent in the supplied text], a word meaning “drum,” because they customarily made a din with drums when they sacrificed people to Moloch, so that the cries of those being burned should not be heard. Procopius on the same passage writes that Tophet among the Hebrews means “fall” or “ruin” (πτῶσιν), as though it were [missing term]. But what Jeremiah VII.31 calls “the high places of Tophet” are, in the same prophet, “altars to Baal” (βωμοὶ τῇ Βαάλ), XXVII.35: in the one case the word is drawn from the place, [Col. 1130C] in the other from the idol’s general name. FABRIC.] those who set up an altar thus called Tophet, after the name of someone, [Col. 1130A] in the valley of the son of Hinnon. [Note: [Col. 1130C] In the valley of the son of Hinnon: Nehemiah XI.30, or Joshua XVIII.16 and elsewhere. This designation certainly suggests that Hinnon was the proper name of a man who gave his name to this valley, though it suits the place well that some derive it from [Hebrew root absent in the supplied text], “to groan.” From it comes the name Gehenna, whose fires in the sacred books of the New Covenant are used for the everlasting punishments of hell. There is also a kind of disease called “the fire of Gehenna” because of its intense heat, in the account of the passing of Saint Eleutherius, bishop of Tournai. FABRIC.] There the Jews sacrificed their sons and daughters to demons. [Note: [Col. 1130C] They sacrificed to demons. Philaster is right here in writing that sons and daughters were not merely passed and purified through fire, as Maimonides, *Guide for the Perplexed* III.38, believed, but were also sacrificed—that is, burned in fire. See Selden, *On Syrian Gods* I.6; Grotius on Deuteronomy XVIII.10; Gregory Michaelis on Gaffarel’s *Unheard-of Curiosities*, pp. 95 ff.; Spencer II.10, *On Hebrew Laws*; Episcopius, *Institutes of Theology*, [Col. 1130D] p. 134; Jacob Goezius, *Human Victims* I.11. FABRIC.] Of these the Lord says [Note: [Col. 1130D] Through the prophet Ezekiel. Only the first words are found in Ezekiel VIII; what follows is taken from Jeremiah VII.31; Philaster himself added the last words from his own invention. FABRIC.] through the prophet Ezekiel: “Behold, son of man, see what this people Israel does: it sacrifices its sons and daughters in the valley of Tophet to demons, to whom I did not command this iniquity to be done among the people Israel.”

## XX. WELL-WORSHIPPERS

[Note: [Col. 1130D] Puteorites. A word formed from *puteus*, “well,” just as above, chapter 12, *Musoritae* from mice. Yet it is surprising if Philaster took literally what the prophet had said allegorically and fashioned a distinct heresy from it. FABRIC.]

The Well-worshippers are those who worship wells, digging them deep and drawing from them, as though hoping for some water of salvation in them. Yet the Lord says [Note: [Col. 1130D] Through the prophet. Jeremiah II.13, where Apollinaris in the Catena on this passage understands the broken cisterns as demons and idols. FABRIC.] through the prophet in admonition: “They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves broken cisterns that cannot contain saving water.” What he had formerly said through the prophet, he fulfilled in his own divine [Note: [Col. 1130D] Presence. I have written this for *praescientia* (“foreknowledge”), which the Helmstedt edition had. The words immediately quoted are Christ’s, John IV.13. FABRIC.] presence, saying: “Everyone who drinks from this earthly water will thirst again; [Col. 1131A] but if he drinks from the water that I shall give him, he shall never thirst, but it shall become in him a spring leaping up to eternal life.” [Note: [Col. 1131B] “For it was.” Earlier editions less well: “it will be.” FABRIC.] For it was the saving grace of Christian baptism granted by the Lord and Saviour to humankind.

## XXI. HERESY CONCERNING THE BRONZE SERPENT

There is also a heresy among the Jews which sacrificed to the serpent and practised the same impiety as far as Hezekiah, king of the Jews. For the Jewish people sacrificed to the bronze serpent, as is related [Note: [Col. 1131B] In the Books of Kings. In IV Kings XVIII.4 you read that the Israelites burned incense (θυμιᾶσαι) to the bronze serpent until the time of King Hezekiah. Philaster has added the rest from tradition. FABRIC.] in the Books of Kings, which Moses had been commanded to make (Num. XXI.9) when Israel departed from Egypt. When the Jews, murmuring wickedly, were bitten by serpents and perished, the Lord ordered Moses to make a bronze serpent and hang it on a wooden pole in the midst of the people; and those who looked upon it were saved from plagues and various wounds. Thus the Jewish people sacrificed to that bronze serpent until King Hezekiah; they also made [Note: [Col. 1131B] Formations as well. By “formations,” as Philaster calls them, and “incisions” and “impressions,” he means [Col. 1131C] magical characters and figures engraved on that column, to which superstitious people attributed an apotropaic power—just as to the bronze serpent found in Paris, mentioned by Gregory of Tours VIII.33. Nor were there lacking those who regarded the serpent itself, erected by Moses, as such a talisman; this opinion is refuted by Natalis Alexander in *Selected Chapters of the Ancient Ecclesiastical History of the Old Testament*, age IV, dissertation 6, and by Gaffarel in *Unheard-of Curiosities*, chapter 6, §7. FABRIC.] formations on a great stone, like an obelisk, placed in the temple as a column. On it the Jews carved human-made incisions and impressions, including certain letters; and [Note: [Col. 1131C] Taking up various formulas. The sense is that there were persons who copied certain of these characters onto thin plates and wore the copies like amulets—what he shortly calls *phylacteries*, and, by a Latin word of the same meaning, *tutamina* (“protective charms”), and *alligaturae* (“bindings”), or περιάμματα. Johann Christian Frommann treats them copiously in his book *On Fascination*, and Jacob Wolf in his *Examiner of Amulets*. FABRIC.] taking up various formulas and placing them on plates, they wore them around their necks. They also taught incantations [Col. 1132A] and had things like phylacteries—or rather practised sorceries; they worshipped these things and derived from them the bindings and protective charms which they wore, and wear, on their breasts. The Lord everywhere [Note: [Col. 1131C] In the Law: Leviticus XXVI.1 and Deuteronomy XVI.22, which are [Col. 1131D] the thirteenth and fourteenth negative commandments. FABRIC.] forbade these things in the Law, because this was the impiety of pagan blindness. Therefore the most blessed King Hezekiah ordered these impressions or carvings to be erased, scraped wholly away with iron, and cut out; he also ordered the bronze serpent to be taken down and [Note: [Col. 1131D] Broken. IV Kings XVIII.4: that is, crushed to pieces, as Moses’ calf was in Deuteronomy XI.21. Let those, therefore, consider this who still display that serpent intact upon a column in the church of Saint Ambrose at Milan—the serpent described in a separate book by Pietro Paolo Bosca, prefect of the Ambrosian Library. Compare Georg Hieronymus Welsch, *On the Medinensis Vein*, pp. 67 ff., and Wagenseil, *τὸν μακαρίτην*, in the preface to the German book on the Jewish practice of writing German with Hebrew letters, where he provides an image of that serpent. FABRIC.] broken. [Note: [Col. 1131D] “For which merit.” The ancients commonly use *meritum* for a virtue and good action pleasing to God, which he considers worthy of rewards. Thomas Morton collected passages in his *Antidote*. It is called *meritum* because it “earns,” that is, obtains, grace; for this is what *mereri* means, as in that saying of Pope Zosimus: “O happy fault, which merited having such a Saviour!” [Col. 1132B] Andreas Schott, *Humanistic Observations* II.16, and Desiderius Heraldus on Arnobius I, p. 50, noted that *meritum* can also signify guilt. FABRIC.—Add Elmenhorst on Arnobius, p. 48; Buchner on Prudentius, *Hymn on the Nativity of Christ*, line 110:

> He renders fitting things in return for merits;

[Col. 1132C] from which you may rightly infer that this term is *meson*, or “middle,” and denotes an action done either well or badly. For more, see the Fabro-Buchnerian *Thesaurus*, p. 1451, with which Martinus agrees in his *Philological Lexicon*. GALEARD.] For this merit he was delivered by the Lord from the great siege of the [Note: [Col. 1132C] Persians and Assyrians. Sennacherib, who unsuccessfully besieged Jerusalem, IV Kings XVIII ff., is called king of the Assyrians and Arabs by Herodotus II.141. FABRIC.] Persians and Assyrians, who had then come to take the Jewish people and city captive. Thus, on that night when King Hezekiah feared the barbarians, [Note: [Col. 1132C] An angel of the Lord from heaven. From the fact that he accomplished the deed without tumult, Saint Anthony, in Athanasius’s *Life* of him, infers that he was a good angel. Saint Nilus, in his second narrative, describes this slaughter by the angel elegantly and vividly. FABRIC.] an angel of the Lord descended from heaven and, in the silence of night, struck down one hundred and eighty-five thousand foreigners besieging the city, [Col. 1132B] displaying to the king in the morning, and to all the Jewish people, all these men lifeless and dead.

## XXII. HERESY FITTED FOR EVERY SHAMEFUL ACT IN SUBTERRANEAN PLACES

[Note: [Col. 1132C] Another heresy. It was already mentioned above in chapter 14, from Ezekiel VIII.10–12. FABRIC.]

There is another heresy: as Ezekiel the prophet, by God’s command, saw seventy elder men of the Jews standing underground in a cave, holding censers, sacrificing to and worshipping the same [Note: [Col. 1132C] With various carved forms. The great Hugo Grotius indeed contends that these images of the subterranean Pantheon were merely painted [Col. 1132D] images. (Jerome favours Grotius on Ezekiel VIII.10: “Not only the idol of jealousy, but all the Temple walls were painted with various images of idols, so that there was no beast which the wall’s painting did not represent”; and certainly not only the Vulgate but also the Chaldean Paraphrase mentions painting. Grotius adds on this same passage in Ezekiel that, according to Philaster, the Troglodytes customarily painted such forms on walls; the most eminent man is mistaken, for in chapter 14, where Philaster speaks of the Troglodytes, he says not a word about painting. GALEARD.) Yet the word which the Seventy rendered διαγεγραμμένον may also quite reasonably be understood of a carved image. Moreover, I gladly persuade myself that all this was shown by God only in a vision to Ezekiel, who was then living in Babylon, and was not an event set before his present eyes while he was bodily present in the Temple at Jerusalem. FABRIC.] various [Col. 1133A] carved forms.

## XXIII. HERESY OF THE WOMEN WITH THE IMAGE OF THAMUS

There is another heresy of the Jews which the prophet is compelled, by God’s command, to see beneath a cave (Ezek. VIII.14): women [Note: [Col. 1133B] Sitting and weeping. For mourners sit, as learned men note on Virgil XI.350: “the whole city sat down in mourning.” See also John Doughty, *Sacred Analects*, on this prophetic passage. FABRIC.] sitting and lamenting a certain [Note: [Col. 1133B] Thamus. Earlier editions wrongly have *Thamur*, for in Hebrew it is Θαμμούζ. Thamous is an Egyptian king in Plato’s *Phaedrus* and Philostratus VI.5; elsewhere Ἀμοῦς. I discussed him in *Greek Library* I.2. In Manetho, quoted by Josephus, *Against Apion* I, pp. 1040 ff., he is Θούμμωσις and Τέθμωσις; in Syncellus, p. 63, Ἄμωσις, likewise Τέθμωσις, son of Aseth, whose son Amosis was also called Ἄμωσις and by another name Μισφραγμύθωσις, [Col. 1133C] as is read in Syncellus there and at p. 122. In manuscripts of Josephus, Ἀλισφραγμούθωσις occurs less correctly. Manetho writes that his son was Τέθμωσις, the king who expelled the Israelites from Egypt. In Herodotus II.42, Ἀμμοῦς is the Egyptian Jupiter; Plutarch teaches the same in *On Isis and Osiris*, p. 354. We note that Manetho explains the same name as “hidden” (κεκρυμμένον), and that this is the Greeks’ Jupiter Ammon. Diodorus Siculus I, p. 15, and Theodoret testify that Osiris too was called Ἅμμων by some. According to Theodoret: “Thamous is Adonis in the Greek language” (Ὁ Θαμοῦς ὁ Ἄδωνίς ἐστι κατὰ τὴν Ἑλλάδα φωνήν). (Add Procopius of Gaza, pp. 258 ff., on Isaiah. For the worship of Thamus among the Egyptians, see the writers cited by John Jarki on Elias Schedius, p. 103. GALEARD.) Hence learned men have made more than enough observations on this passage about the lament for Osiris and Adonis. The distinguished commentator on Philostratus, p. 234, writes, on the testimony of Syncellus cited above, that Thamus, king of Egypt, perished when torn apart by a hippopotamus. But Syncellus, p. 54, reports this about Menes, not Thamus, though Marsham, *Chronicle*, p. 31, confuses Menes with Thamus [Col. 1133D]. FABRIC.] Thamus, [Note: [Col. 1133D] Who was the king’s son. He himself was also, as Philaster immediately adds, king of the Egyptians. FABRIC.] the son of a king of the Gentiles. The women of Judaea worshipped his image with weeping; practising Gentile impiety, they did not cease offering sacrifices to him. For Thamus [Note: [Col. 1133D] That Pharaoh. Africanus, quoted in Syncellus, pp. 62 ff., holds the same view: he calls that king Ἄμωσις, as Manetho does in Josephus, p. 1041: “Tethmosis, the king who expelled them from Egypt” (Τέθμωσιν, ὁ ἐκβαλὼν αὐτοὺς ἐξ Αἰγύπτου Βασιλεὺς Τέθμωσις). If he was the one whom the Jewish women mourned, then the cause of their mourning was that this king perished with his army, swallowed up by the Red Sea. Others think that the Egyptian king was Chenchres, or Acherres; others, Petisonius. But in this matter I willingly trust Manetho. FABRIC.] was called that Pharaoh, king of the Egyptians, who ruled the Egyptians at the time of blessed Moses.

## XXIV. BELITES

[Col. 1133B] There is another heresy among the Jews: worshipping idols of many [Note: [Col. 1134B] “As it were men”: that is, males, as above in chapter 17. FABRIC.] men, as it were, and many women, in the hidden caves of the Baalites they did not cease offering sacrifices to them. Scripture says [Note: [Col. 1134B] “As it were many males and females.” In sacred Scripture not only the singular but also the plural occurs, as in Judges II.11; I Samuel VII.4; II Chronicles XXVIII.2; and frequently elsewhere. FABRIC.] that there was a number, as it were, of many males and females. This showed that from [Note: [Col. 1134B] King Belus. Founder of Babylon, on whom, as on others of this name, Marsham’s *Chronicle Canon* should be consulted. They hold that he is the one whom the sacred writer Moses calls Nimrod, Genesis X.10. FABRIC.] King Belus, who held the East under powerful rule for a long time, and from his wife and sons or daughters, all their [Col. 1134A] progeny had proceeded as born from those parents, so that from them they were called [Note: [Col. 1134B] Baalites. As Baalites or Belites above in chapter 16 were not inappropriately called worshippers of Baal or Bel, so throughout this chapter the more suitable sense would result if, instead of *Baalitarum*, *Baalitae*, and *Belitae*, one read *Baalim* everywhere. Philaster’s meaning is that all Belus’s descendants are included under that common name. FABRIC.] Baalites. For just as there is a family of the [Note: [Col. 1134C] Gracchi. I thought this should be written *Graccorum* rather than *Graecorum*, which earlier editions had. Note that among the Romans the family of the Gracchi existed, just as that of the Anicii; on the Anicii, besides Glandorp and others who wrote on Roman families, see Vinetus on Ausonius, Epistle 16, and Reinesius, *Letters to Hofmann*, pp. 633 ff. Terentius Scaurus, from Varro, noted in his work on orthography that the name of the Gracchi was anciently written *Graccorum*, without the sign of aspiration. Compare Johann Rhodius’s notes on Scribonius Largus, pp. 218 ff. FABRIC.] Gracchi, or of the Anicii and others, so their whole progeny emerged from their parents, and from one name the impious race came to be called Belites. Thus, when the dead were placed in tombs and their descendants likewise buried in that place, they deserved to be called by their people and posterity by this name: Belites, after their ancient lineage. Belus acquired this name or surname either from his own proper name [Note: [Col. 1134C] Or from prowess in war. This derivation is no less far-fetched than the statement in the *Paschal Chronicle*, p. 36, that Belus was called, as it were, βέλος, “a missile,” “because he was most keen” (διὰ τὸ ὀξύτατον εἶναι). Hyginus, fable 274: “The Africans and Egyptians first fought with clubs; afterward Belus, son of Neptune, waged war with the sword, [Col. 1134D] whence *bellum* [war] is so called.” Barth, on Statius II, p. 889, wrongly treats the final words as a gloss; for Cassiodorus too, I.30, after observing that *pugna* [fight] was called so because combat was first carried on with fists, says: “Afterwards Belus first brought forth an iron sword, from whom it pleased them that war should be called *bellum*.” This passage has already been noted by Vossius in his *Etymological Dictionary* and by Muncker on Hyginus. FABRIC.] or from prowess in war, because at that time he surpassed many. Because the Jewish people followed the Gentiles’ impiety in this matter, divine Scripture accuses them: sacrificing to these persons—that is, to kings, their sons, and all their kin—they were handed over to various captivities [Col. 1134B] in consequence.

## XXV. HERESY INVOLVING THE IDOL BAAL

There is another heresy among the Jews which maintains that the idol Baal took its name from Balaam the false prophet, [Note: [Col. 1134D] From Balaam the false prophet. I have written this, since earlier editions wrongly had: “Or Balaam the false prophet.” FABRIC.] who came from Mesopotamia against the most blessed Moses, because Balak, king of the Moabites at that time, [Col. 1135A] had asked him to go [Note: [Col. 1135C] “To go to him”: that is, to King Balak, Numbers XXII.5. He would therefore have said more clearly, “to go to himself.” But such neglect of the reflexive pronoun, and conversely use of it in place of the demonstrative, is frequent among writers especially of this and the following ages. Thus the illustrious Huet entitled his autobiography *On Matters Pertaining to Him*. FABRIC.] to him and curse the Jewish people. Because he was formerly called [Note: [Col. 1135C] “Called a prophet in the Scriptures formerly.” Saint Jerome, in the *Hebrew Questions* on Genesis XXII, after saying that the Hebrews identify Balaam with Elihu in the Book of Job and trace his lineage to Nahor, Abraham’s brother, writes: “At first he was a holy man and prophet of God” (Num. XXIV.3 ff.); “afterward, through disobedience and desire for gifts, while he wished to curse Israel, he is called by the title of diviner” (Josh. XIII.22). Eucherius wrongly has, where he transcribes Jerome’s words, “he is deprived of the title of diviner.” FABRIC.] a prophet in the Scriptures but afterward, having despised the Lord’s command, fell into destruction as a false prophet (Num. XXI.8; Josh. XIII.22), plotting against God’s people, the Jews, like pagans, made an idol of him [Note: [Col. 1135C] Under this name: worshipping Balaam under the name of Baal. So far as I recall, no other ancient writer has left this tradition. FABRIC.] under this name and did not cease [Note: [Col. 1135D] “Did not cease worshipping it”: that is, worshipped it. This manner of expression is very familiar to Philaster. Thus chapter 14: “they did not cease worshipping idols”; chapter 16: “Ahab and Jezebel his wife did not cease sacrificing to that idol”; chapter 23: “practising Gentile impiety, they did not cease offering sacrifices to him.” FABRIC.] worshipping it.

## XXVI. SUPERSTITIOUS HERESY CONCERNING THE WOMAN WITH A PYTHON-SPIRIT
Another heresy concerns the woman with a familiar spirit (Pythoness): they covered the woman in garments and hoped to obtain certain answers from her. [Note: Philaster misunderstood the passage read at 1 Samuel 28: Saul covered himself and, having changed his garments, pretended to be someone else. FABRIC.] [Note: The fuller reading was *posse se consequi*, “that they could obtain for themselves”; perhaps the copyist neglected to repeat the same syllable that precedes. FABRIC.] Hence they say that this Pythoness summoned up from the underworld the soul of the blessed Samuel; and, chiefly on that ground, very many people to this day suppose that the words which the most blessed Prophet had spoken to King Saul while he was still alive were likewise proved true in their fulfilment, as though he had again uttered responses from God. [Note: That is, they were recognized as true as though he had again uttered God’s responses; the things Samuel had said to Saul while still alive were being proved to be God’s responses. Earlier editions, in my view corruptly, read: “as though he is recognized to have uttered true responses to him again.” FABRIC.] Since very many prefer to acquiesce in this falsehood, they descend into everlasting destruction, although the Prophet says: “The souls of the righteous are in the hand of the Lord, and death does not touch them.” [Note: These are words from the Book of Wisdom, chapter 3:1. Many ancient writers also call the author of this book a prophet, as Lucifer of Cagliari does when citing this very passage, p. 194: “The Holy Spirit says through the mouth of Solomon”; shortly afterwards, “Sacred Scripture says”; and again, p. 195: “The Holy Spirit,” he says, “speaks through the mouth of the Prophet.” Yet the most learned authorities, along with St Jerome, Augustine, Eusebius, and Basil the Great—not to mention the Jews—deny that it was written either by Solomon or by a prophet. For the words “in the hand of the Lord, and death does not touch them,” the Greek in Lucifer is: ἐν χειρὶ Θεοῦ, καὶ οὐ μὴ ἅψηται αὐτῶν Βάσανος, “in the hand of God, and torment shall not touch them”; in Lucifer, *tormentum malitiae*, “the torment of wickedness.” FABRIC.]

How, then, could an impious soul summon from the underworld a holy and righteous soul, especially that of a Prophet? [Note: A sound argument by which Philaster proves that the figure brought before Saul by the witch of Endor was not the real Samuel. Tertullian uses the same argument in *On the Soul*, ch. 57; Gregory of Nyssa in his Letter to Theodosius; and others, whose passages Leo Allatius collected in *Syntagma de Engastrimytho*, ch. 10 ff. FABRIC.] But because they do not understand that souls departing from the faith of Christ the Lord make themselves already devoted to impiety and submit themselves to it with every zeal: for every person is possessed of free choice, so that he may choose what he wishes to do, God permitting it. [Note: This was the common teaching of Greek and Latin writers before Augustine, though they confessed with the Apostle that God gives both the willing and the accomplishing. St Jerome, *Hebrew Questions on Genesis* 4:6: “But because you possess free choice, I warn you that you should rule over sin, not sin over you.” Philaster refers to Sirach 15:14 ff. FABRIC.] But because he departed from the Lord—Saul, namely, for he is the subject here—an unclean spirit came to rule him. This is so with those who are wavering and limping in the divine law, as blessed Elijah said: “Either God, God; or Baal, Baal” (3 Kings 18:21). For whoever clings to Christ is one body with him (1 Cor. 6:17), and whoever clings to an unclean spirit is of one accord with it.

And King Ahab of the Jews, when he believed Zedekiah and the other false prophets and despised Micaiah, the true prophet of the Lord, was granted by Christ the Lord, for a time still, a place of mercy: so that, if he wished to believe the true Prophet, he might avoid the storm of danger; but if he refused, and preferred to believe the false prophets, he would without doubt perish. [Note: That is, he was still granted time for repentance and for embracing sound counsel. FABRIC.] Thus the Lord questions the unclean spirit, saying: “Who will deceive Ahab, king of the Israelites, so that he may go to battle and be killed?” And behold, the unclean spirit came, saying: “I will go and do it.” And the Lord said to the unclean spirit: “How will you do this?” And the unclean spirit said to the Lord: “I will make myself like an angel of light and utter similar words; I will lead him into battle, and there I will abandon him, and thus he will die.” And the Lord said to him: “Go; thus you shall do” (2 Chronicles 18:19). Therefore the Apostle also says: “It is no great thing if Satan too transforms himself into an angel of light, when his agents transform themselves” (2 Cor. 11:14). Thus they deceive many by vision, word, or persuasion of no other thing—that is, of something good, as he immediately adds—indeed by a seemingly plausible vision. [Note: Perhaps *verisimilis*, “plausible,” should be read; or *verisimili* should be referred to the preceding words, “by word or persuasion.” FABRIC.] Thus, when people wish in due time to believe and to cling to them through words as though similar, and visions as though good and not evil, they incur the unavoidable sentence of eternal death and, after the departure of the body, are plunged into diverse punishments and torments. The same danger befell the king of the Jews at that time, because he preferred to believe false rather than true prophets of God.

## XXVII. ON THE IMAGES OF ASTAR AND ASTAROTH: A HERESY

There is a heresy among the Jews: after the death of Moses and the succession of Joshua son of Nun, they worshipped Astar and Astaroth and were handed over into the captivity of the Gentiles. For Astar and Astaroth were men and women, and they worshipped their images—figures of men and women. [Note: That is, images of males and females. FABRIC.] [Note: See, if you please, what was said above on chapter 17. Earlier editions read *Asthar* and *Astharoth*. FABRIC.] These were names of Syrian—that is, Assyrian—and Egyptian kings. When their sons and daughters were worshipped by their peoples, those peoples afterwards also built temples for them; burying their descendants there after the rulers’ deaths, they likewise offered sacrifices to them under the name of gods and goddesses. [Note: Earlier editions less well read *nomina*, “names.” They offered in the name of gods and goddesses—that is, as to gods and goddesses—sacrifices. FABRIC.]

For there is an Astarteion or Astartion in Syria—a temple of Astarte—and there are many various such sanctuaries elsewhere. [Note: Ἀσταρτεῖον or Ἀστάρτιον, a temple of Astarte: 1 Samuel 31:10; Josephus, *Antiquities* VI.15 and *Against Apion* I. Earlier editions gave this passage in a most corrupt form: “For there is an Asturtium in some Syria, diverse and many.” Philaster means that there were also many different temples of Astarte elsewhere, as ancient evidence confirms. See Petrus Faber, *Semestria* III.2; Astarte standing on a ship in coins: Beger, III, p. 52. FABRIC.] All this impiety was then ablaze among the people of the Canaanites, a people which Moses was commanded by the Lord to root out together with all its people. [Note: He was commanded not merely to destroy the altars, idols, and groves of the Canaanites: Exodus 23:24; 34:13. FABRIC.]

## XXVIII. HERODIANS

Others are Herodians, so called from Herod, king of the Jews. [Note: Very learned men, following Epiphanius, heresy 20, and Nicetas, *Treasury* I.34, contend that Herod the Great gave the Herodians their name. But the Herodians of Matthew 22:16; Mark 3:6 and 12:13 were officials or soldiers of Herod Antipas, who killed John the Baptist and was the son of Herod the Great. There the name no more signifies a heresy or sect than “Caesarians,” “Pompeians,” and the like; compare Tertullian’s Attinians, Nigrinians, and Cassians. Thus the Herodians were Jews who favoured Herod and, with him, the Roman party. St Jerome on Matthew 22: “The Pharisees therefore send their disciples with the Herodians, that is, Herod’s soldiers; or those whom the Pharisees, mocking them because they paid tribute to the Romans, called Herodians, as not devoted to divine worship.” Some Latin writers absurdly suppose that the Herodians believed Herod to be Christ, which we nowhere at all read. The Herod struck by an angel in Acts 12:23 was Herod Agrippa, son of Aristobulus and Berenice; Josephus also recounts his death, *Antiquities* XIX.8. FABRIC.—Add to Jerome John of Damascus, for whom the Herodians were those who paid tribute to the Romans in order to please Herod; the Pharisees called them Herodians in mockery. Macer, *Hierolexicon*, s.v. “Herodians,” corrects Philaster at this point. Compare, if desired, Scaliger, *Elenchus Trihaeresii*, chs. 1–2. GALEARD.]

They confess the resurrection, receive the Law and the Prophets, and await Herod, the king of the Jews who was struck by the angel, hoping in him as Christ himself. [Note: Philaster therefore did not agree with those who thought that the Herodians held the same views about spirits and the resurrection as the Sadducees: John Hardouin, *On the Coins of the Herods*, p. 97 ff.; an anonymous English writer in the *Fortuita*, Rotterdam, 1727, octavo, p. 40; and before him Hugo Grotius on Matthew 16:6 and Mark 8:15. Nor did he confuse the Herodians with the Dositheans, whose position Grotius likewise refutes on Mark 3:6. FABRIC.]

[Note: Philaster accordingly persuaded himself that Herod Agrippa—whom flatterers called God, according to St Luke, Acts 12:22, and Josephus, *Antiquities* XIX.8, p. 679—was regarded by the Herodians as the Messiah yet to come: “they await him,” he says, “hoping in him as Christ.” Yet, according to Epiphanius and Nicetas, as already noted, Herod the Great was considered Christ by the Herodians. The eminent Hugo Grotius was mistaken through lapse of memory when, on Matthew 16:6, he says that Epiphanius applied to Herod the murderer of the Baptist what belonged to the Great. The author of the appendix to Tertullian’s *On Prescription*, St Jerome *Against the Luciferians*, John of Damascus *On Heresies*, and the pseudo-Jerome catalogue, when they mention Herod simply, seem to mean the Great. The scholiast on Persius also understands Herod the Great in Satire 5.80, “when Herod’s days came”; and it is unsurprising that the day on which Augustus granted the kingdom to Herod the Great was celebrated annually even among his successors and descendants. Incidentally, Theophylact, Letter 13, uses “Herodians” for those who imitate Herod’s cruelty. FABRIC.]

[Note: Thomas Malvenda, *On Antichrist* I.11, reads *expetunt*, “seek after,” rather than *exspectant*, “await.” But there is no need to alter the received reading. FABRIC.]

## CATALOGUE OF THOSE ACCUSED OF HERESY AFTER CHRIST’S PASSION

## XXIX. SIMON MAGUS

[Note: In the manuscript, the names of the ἑτεροδόξοι, “heterodox persons,” are lacking; in their place the articles or chapters are distinguished by numbers—I, II, etc.]

After the passion of Christ our Lord and his ascension into heaven, there was a certain Simon Magus, a Samaritan by birth, from a village called Gitta in Samaria. [Note: On the one Simon Magus, see Johann Laurentius Mosheim, *Dissertation on the One Simon Magus*, Helmstedt, 1734; and Augustin Calmet, *Dissertation on Simon Magus*, vol. VII, p. 815 ff. FABRIC.] [Note: The correct reading is *Githeus*, from Gitta in Samaria, rather than *Citheus*: ἀπὸ Γιτθῶν or Γετθῶν. Compare Cotelerius’s notes on the *Apostolic Constitutions* VI.7, p. 334, and *Clementine Recognitions* I.12, p. 489. The learned Stephanus le Moyne is mistaken in concluding that Simon was a Κιτταῖος, or citizen of the well-known Cypriot town of Citium. FABRIC.] Engaged in magical arts, he deceived many, saying that he was a certain power of God above all powers (Acts 8:11). [Note: Acts 8:10: Ἡ δύναμις τοῦ Θεοῦ ἡ μεγάλη, “the great power of God.” Justin Martyr, *First Apology*, p. 69: “A certain Simon, a Samaritan from a village called Gitta, under the emperor Claudius performed magical works in your royal city Rome by the art of demons who worked through him and was considered a god.” And in the *Dialogue with Trypho*, p. 349: “I said that the Samaritans who obey Simon, the magician from their own people, are deceived; they say that he is God above every rule, authority, and power.” *Clementine Recognitions* II.7: “This Simon was born to a father Antonius and a mother Rachel; a Samaritan by people, from the village of Gethon; a magician by art, yet most excellently educated in Greek liberal learning, exceedingly desirous of glory and self-display beyond every kind of human being. Thus he wished himself believed to be the lofty Power above the Creator God, and to be thought Christ, and to be called ‘the Standing One.’” Irenaeus I.20: “the highest Power, that is, he who is Father above all, whatever people may call him.” Tertullian, ch. 46: “He dared to call himself the supreme Power, that is, the supreme God.” In Jerome: “I am the Word of God; I am the Beautiful One; I am the Paraclete; I am the Almighty; I am all things of God.” FABRIC.]

The Samaritans venerate him as though he were the Father and perniciously exalt him as founder of their own heresy, striving to prefer him with many praises. [Note: Epiphanius 21.1 concerning Simon: “He called himself the Father to the Samaritans, but to the Jews he called himself the Son.” FABRIC.] [Note: This heresy is of course distinct from the Samaritan heresy discussed above in chapter 7. FABRIC.] [Note: Another reading: *efferre*, “exalt,” instead of *praeferre*, “prefer.” FABRIC.]

Though baptized by the blessed Apostles, he departed from their faith [Note: By Saint Philip, Acts 8:13. FABRIC.] and sowed a wicked and destructive heresy, declaring that he had been transformed only ostensibly—that is, as though in a shadow—and thus had suffered, though, he said, he did not truly suffer. [Note: “As though a shadow”: compare *umbratiliter*, “shadowily,” below in ch. 31, and “as though in a shadow, ostensibly,” in ch. 32. Tertullian: he “did not suffer in God’s phantom-form, but as though he suffered.” Epiphanius 21.1: παθόντα δὲ μὴ πεπονθέναι, ἀλλὰ δοκήσει μόνον, “having suffered, yet not having suffered, but only in appearance.” Augustine, *On Heresies*, ch. 1: “in the reign of Tiberius [he said that he] appeared ostensibly in the person of the Son . . . but that Christ neither came nor suffered anything at the hands of the Jews.” FABRIC.]

He also dared to say that the world was made by angels, and that the angels had been made by certain perceptions endowed from heaven, and that they had deceived humankind. [Note: Simon, in Epiphanius 21.2: “Through her [Ennoia, Thought] I created the angels, and the angels created the world and human beings.” Irenaeus I.20 and Theodoret, *Heretical Fables* I.1 say the same. For writers on Simon’s life and heresy, see those cited by Johann Vogt, fascicle 3 of the *Bibliotheca Haeresiologica*, p. 567 ff. The Sabbath of Simon after eleven days: *Clementines* II.35, p. 630. FABRIC.] [Note: Philaster intended to render Simon’s ἔννοια, “Thought,” discussed by Epiphanius in the cited place: “that I might escape notice by my angelic powers and descend upon the Ennoia, who is also called Prunicus and the Holy Spirit, through whom I created the angels.” Instead of *praeditis*, “endowed,” I would prefer *proditis*, “produced.” FABRIC.]

He further asserts that a certain other Intellect descends into the world for the salvation of human beings: namely, that Helen who, he says, is reported by the most frivolous poets in connection with the Trojan War. [Note: Rather, it is the same Intellect. For in Epiphanius, whom Philaster plainly seems to follow, Intellect, “the power descending from above,” Simon’s ἔννοια, and Helen are one and the same. In Theodoret’s account of Simon’s doctrine, however, they are distinguished: first, νοῦς or ἐπίνοια, “Mind” or “Conception”; second, φωνὴ καὶ ἔννοια, “Voice and Thought”; third, λογισμός καὶ ἐνθύμησις, “Reasoning and Reflection.” FABRIC.] [Note: “That Helen”: others call her Selene, Σελήνη, as Augustine does at the beginning of *On Heresies*: “He also wished himself believed to be Jupiter, and a certain prostitute, Selene—whom Philaster adds was from Tyre—he represented as Minerva and made his accomplice in crimes.” Fabricius omitted to note here the name Selene given to this woman, whom Philaster calls Helen, remembered by poets in the Trojan War. Others call her Selene, as Sichardus long ago observed in the preface to his Basel 1528 edition of Philaster. Similarly Philaster’s *Carpocras* is elsewhere *Carpocrates*, and his C. Bassus is elsewhere Colorbasus. Fabricius observed both: in ch. 35 he reads Carpocras, Καρποκρᾶς, following Philaster’s first edition; but in ch. 43 he rightly replaced C. Bassus with Colorbasus, departing from Sichard’s edition and following Latinius. The Codex Corbeiensis, recently discovered in France, confirms Latinius’s correction: where Sichard’s Basel edition has “After him, C. Bassus,” it reads “After him, Colorbasus.” On Colorbasus and the doctrine of the Colorbasians, consult Irenaeus I.12 ff., with Feuardentius’s notes in Massuet’s edition, p. 56. GALEARD.]

And the Powers which had made the world, he says, stirred up rebellion, led by desire for that Helen. For she, by giving desire to those Powers and appearing in a woman’s form, could not ascend into heaven, because the Powers in heaven would not allow her to ascend. But she awaited another Power, namely the coming of Simon the Magician himself, who would come and save her. [Note: Epiphanius 21.2, p. 57: “Those same angels came into conflict with one another over her; she herself suffered nothing, but caused them to work mutual slaughter upon themselves, since she had implanted in them desire for herself. Holding her fast so that she could not return above, each of them had intercourse with her in each female bodily form, as she passed from one to another,” etc. FABRIC.] [Note: Simon in Epiphanius 21.3: “This is she who is now with me; for her sake I have descended, and she awaited my coming.” FABRIC.]

He also allegorically maintains that the wooden horse, which the most frivolous poets say was present in the Trojan War, was a device signifying the ignorance of all impious nations. [Note: The famous wooden—or “Dardanian”—horse of Epeius, celebrated in Homer and Virgil, may be considered in Laurentius Beger’s commentary on the Fabretti Iliac Table, ch. 58. Simon Magus said that it was an image of the ignorance of the nations, which refused to recognize the salvation offered them in Simon: “The wooden horse devised by Homer, which the Greeks think was deliberately made, that sorcerer again said was the ignorance of the nations.” Epiphanius 21.3. FABRIC.] Yet it is established that this Helen who was with the Magician was a prostitute from Tyre; she followed this same Simon Magus and committed with him various magical practices and various crimes. [Note: This passage should be punctuated thus: “For she was Tyrian, originating from among the Tyrians,” Epiphanius 21.2; “taken from Tyre,” ibid. 21.3. Irenaeus I.20 calls her a prostitute from the city of Tyre. Nicetas and others likewise call her a Tyrian prostitute. FABRIC.]

When he fled from the blessed apostle Peter, departing from the city of Jerusalem and coming to Rome, and there contended with the blessed Apostle before the emperor Nero, he was defeated on every side by the blessed Apostle’s argument and prayer; struck by an angel, he thus came to his death, so that the manifest falsehood of his magical arts might become known to all people. [Note: Extensive accounts of Simon Magus’s arrival at Rome, his dispute with the apostle Peter, his magical flight, and disgraceful death appear in the *Recognitions* attributed to Clement, Pseudo-Abdias, and Pseudo-Marcellus. Many writers more deserving of credence also touch on the matter; their testimonies are noted by B. Ittigius in his dissertation *On the Heresiarchs of the Apostolic Age* and by Tillemont, vol. I of the *Memoirs for Ecclesiastical History*, to omit innumerable others. If Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers* 1, is believed, this occurred in the second year of the emperor Claudius. FABRIC.] [Note: In Greek usage, Βασιλέα, “king,” means “emperor.” FABRIC.] [Note: Arnobius, II, p. 50, says that Simon Magus’s fiery chariot and four-horse team were blown apart by Peter’s speech and vanished when Christ was named. Theodoret: “Having prayed, he dashed him down from a great height.” The prayer of Peter in Pseudo-Abdias I.18 is given as follows: “Lord Jesus, show your power, and do not permit the people who are to believe in you to be deceived by these vain arts. Let him fall thus, Lord, so that, while alive, he may know that he could do nothing against your power.” FABRIC.] [Note: Or, as Isidore of Seville says in his *Chronicle*, he was struck down by the demons who carried him in the air: Peter adjured them by God, Paul prayed, and Simon, released, burst apart. FABRIC.] [Note: That is, he died. Although the sentence here can aptly mean that this befell Simon deservedly, it is certain that *mereri*, like Greek ἀξιοῦσθαι, very often denotes not merit but occurrence. FABRIC.]

## XXX. MENANDER

After him came one named Menander, who became Simon’s disciple and followed his impiety in every respect. [Note: Epiphanius 22.1: “A certain Menander, originating from the Samaritans, became for some time a disciple of this Simon.” Irenaeus I.20 and Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* III.26 call Menander Simon’s successor. FABRIC.] [Note: Epiphanius, p. 61: “Weaving together in every respect doctrines like those of his teacher, he did not refrain from sorceries and other magical practices. Nor did he differ at all in doctrine, except only that he called himself greater even than the teacher who had preceded him.” Hence John of Damascus, ch. 22, writes that the Menandrians differ from the Simonians in certain respects: διαφερόμενοι δὲ πρὸς τοὺς Σιμωνιανοὺς κατά τι. Tertullian, ch. 46: “Saying the same things as Simon himself, whatever Simon had said, Menander declared himself to be; he denied that anyone could obtain salvation unless baptized in his name.” Yet if we follow Theodoret and Irenaeus, he did not call himself the First Power, τὴν πρώτην δύναμιν, as Simon did, but wished to be regarded as the Saviour of humankind sent by that Power. FABRIC.]

## XXXI. SATURNINUS

[Note: He is called *Saturninus*, like Phaedrus and Evandrus; others use Phaeder, Evander, and Menander. Propertius says of the comic poet: *docte Menandre*, “learned Menander.” Isaac Vossius gathers many such forms in his note on Ovid, *Tristia* II.369; see also writers cited by me in *Bibliotheca Latina* II.3. From Menander come the names Menandrians and Menandrianists, as Cotelerius notes on the *Apostolic Constitutions* VI.8. FABRIC.]

A little later Saturninus likewise drew thence the seeds of deadly doctrine. He maintained that the world had been made by angels; that the angels were separated from that Power; that the world had been apportioned in order among the angels; and that they devised the making of humanity. [Note: Epiphanius 23.1: “They are separated from the Power above.” Philaster shortly calls it the “supernal Power.” Tertullian, ch. 46: “[Saturninus held] that the unbegotten Power—that is, God—dwells in the highest and infinite regions; but that angels far distant from him, that is, inferior angels, made the lower world.” FABRIC.] [Note: Irenaeus writes that, according to Saturninus, seven angels made the world; Epiphanius adds that the world was allotted among those seven angels: “He says that seven certain beings made the world and the things in it; and that the world was allotted in portions to each angel.” FABRIC.]

They therefore made a human being, and the human being, he says, was their work. For they say that a light was sent down from the supernal Power; it illuminated this world, stirred the angels to desire, and immediately ascended to heaven. [Note: Epiphanius: “For, he says, when that Light from above had looked down, it produced some stimulus in these angels; they undertook, desiring the likeness above, to make the creature, humanity.” The reading should be *φωτός*, “light,” rather than *φωνῆς*, “voice”: in old manuscripts word-endings are commonly represented by abbreviations, so that the false reading *φωνῆς* readily led also to *τῆς* for *τοῦ* and *παρακυψάσης* for *παρακύψαντος*. FABRIC.] But they, having become desirous of that light, wished to behold its Power. Since they were unable to do so, they said to one another: “Let us make a human being according to our image and likeness.” [Note: Unless the word “our” was added, as in some manuscripts of Irenaeus and in Theodoret by another hand, Philaster erred in adding it. For he attributes to the angels the words of God in Genesis 1:26, holding that they made humanity not in their own image but in the image of that Light and the supreme Power. Thus he wrote only: Ποιήσωμεν ἄνθρωπον κατ` εἰκόνα καὶ καθ` ὁμοίωσιν, “Let us make a human according to image and likeness,” omitting ἡμετέραν, “our,” as Epiphanius expressly testifies. FABRIC.]

After the human being had been made, because he was powerless, he could not be saved. [Note: Epiphanius: “Because he could not attain completion through the angels’ weakness, he lay and crawled on the ground.” Irenaeus: “When the creature had been made and could not rise because of the angels’ weakness, the Power above took pity on it, since it had been made in her likeness, and sent forth a spark of life, which raised up the human, formed its joints, and made it live.” Epiphanius: ἐζωογόνησε, “made alive.” Theodoret: “When the creature could not rise but crawled like a worm, the divine Power, he says, taking pity, sent down a spark of life and brought the incomplete human to perfection.” FABRIC.] The supernal Power, therefore, seeing what they had done, sent a spark which restored the human being, raised him up, and made him live. [Note: Fabricius’s Hamburg edition reads *fecit enim vivere*, through a printer’s error; Sichard rightly has *fecit eum vivere*, “made him live.” What Philaster here calls a spark may perhaps be the same as Horace’s *divinae particulam aurae*, “a little portion of divine breath,” *Satires* II.2. Prudentius likewise calls it a spark, *Hamartigenia*, v. 852. See below, ch. 126, and Fabricius there; also Gataker on Marcus Antoninus II.2, p. 48, London edition, with Dacier’s notes, p. VIII. The Seleucians and Hermianites, moreover, held that human souls are from fire and spirit, as Philaster reports below, ch. 55. GALEARD.]

They hold that the spark is to be saved, but that the rest is to be abandoned and left to those Powers that made it. [Note: Understand the spark as the soul, which Saturninus taught would return to God; the rest of the human being would perish and be dissolved. Tertullian: “That light and power, having taken pity, [sent] a spark, which is to be saved; the rest of the human being perishes.” He denied altogether that there would be a resurrection of the flesh. FABRIC.] They affirm that Christ appeared only in a shadow, that he did not take true human flesh and soul, and that he thus completed the entire economy—the incarnate and saving work—of the Saviour’s mystery. [Note: “Only in a shadow”: κατὰ δόκησιν, “in appearance,” and *putative*, “ostensibly.” Tertullian: “Christ was not in the substance of a body, and suffered only in a phantom, as though he suffered.” Irenaeus, Epiphanius, Theodoret, and others say the same of Saturninus. FABRIC.] [Note: The ancient writers commonly use *oeconomia*, “economy,” to embrace the Incarnation and everything Christ either did or suffered for our sake. See the distinctive dissertations of Elias Veiel and Johann Philipp Pfeifer on this word; Ducaeus’s notes on Chrysostom, vol. VIII, Savile edition, p. 372; Casaubon on Gregory of Nyssa’s letter, p. 105; Vulcanius on Cyril, p. 116; Grabe on Irenaeus, p. 419; Gataker on Antoninus, p. 330; and Suicer’s *Thesaurus*. FABRIC.]

## XXXII. BASILIDES

Basilides, who is also called a heresiarch by many, violated the laws of Christian truth by setting forth and speaking of the Law, the Prophets, and the Apostles, while thinking otherwise. [Note: Eusebius, *Chronicle*, in the seventeenth year of Hadrian: “Basilides, the heresiarch, dwells at Alexandria; from him come the Gnostics.” FABRIC.] When he had come to Egypt, he taught and defined as follows: from the unbegotten and only God there was born Intellect; from Intellect, Word; from Word, Understanding; from Understanding, Power and Wisdom. [Note: Philaster follows, as usual, Epiphanius 24.1, where Basilides’ sequence is given: first, τὸ ἀγέννητον, ὅ μόνος πάντων πατήρ, “the Unbegotten, who alone is Father of all”; second, Νοῦς, “Mind”; third, Λόγος, “Word”; fourth, Φρόνησις, “Understanding”; fifth, Δύναμις καὶ Σοφία, “Power and Wisdom”; sixth, Ἀρχαὶ, ἐξουσίαι, ἄγγελοι, “Principalities, Authorities, Angels.” From the angels, the first and highest heaven was created, along with the angels inhabiting it. From these another heaven and angels were made, then from those another, down to the last heaven nearest us, the three hundred and sixty-fifth. Compare Irenaeus I.23 and Theodoret, *Heretical Fables* I.4. FABRIC.]

[Note: *Intellecto* stands for *intellectu*, as though it were a genitive of *intellectus*, like *senati*, *ornati*, and *tumulti* for *senatus*, *ornatus*, and *tumultus*, with similar examples collected by Claudius Dausqueius, *Orthographia*, pp. 96 and 103. FABRIC.]

[Note: Epiphanius requires the reading: “from Understanding, Power and Wisdom,” ἐκ δὲ τῆς φρονήσεως Δύναμις καὶ Σοφία. The Basilidian amulets, apart from Macarius and Chiffletius, are treated by T. Ittigius, *On Heresiarchs*, p. 101 ff.; Athanasius Kircher, *Arithmologia*, p. 169 ff.; and Raffaele Fabretti, *Inscriptions*, p. 531 ff. FABRIC.—The Corbie manuscript reads: *de sensu autem et virtutem*, “from Understanding, however, and Power”; but the transposition of the conjunction is obvious. It should therefore read *de sensu autem virtutem et*—“from Understanding, Power and”—as Fabricius too observed from Epiphanius. To illustrate this Basilidian heresy, permit me to produce an unpublished letter of the very eminent Nicolas-Claude Peiresc, supplied to me by a manuscript collection of that most distinguished author’s letters, from the library of the most eminent Cardinal Quirini, born for the good of letters.]

*Letter of Sieur de Peiresc on the Abraxases.*
> “It was my error to write to Your Lordship that the first author of the word ΑΒΡΑΞΑΣ had lived in Julian’s time, since he died under Hadrian and was called Basilides (see Baronius, under the year 1700, no. 7 and following, and his Additions to no. 13, printed at the end of vol. XII, p. 570). It is true that his heresy sprang up again in those times and endured even to Valentinian and later; it was enlarged by those of the Nicolaitans, Gnostics, Carpocratians, Marcosians, Heracleonites, Ophites, Archontics, Severians, Sampsaeans, Bardesanists, Cathars, and many others, which were nearly all born at one and the same time. Although there was some diversity among them, they nevertheless all maintained that the world had been made by angels, or by certain imagined angelic powers, baptized with certain barbarous names, almost all drawn in an occult sense from the poetic fictions of Hesiod and the other Greeks, often observing the manner of Hebrew or Syriac speech. Almost all agreed upon seven heavens, in the highest of which they said there was Sabuoth, Saldabaoth, or the maker of this world, son of Achamoth, called by others Barbelo, Prunnicus, or Methra. Basilides alone, together with some others, believed in as many as 365 heavens and an equal number of powers governing them—that is, angels barbarously named—all ruled by the chief ΑΒΡΑΞΑΣ, which in Greek letters amounts numerically to 365. From this they infer the number of the heavens, powers, days of the year, and members of the human body, assigning it a power for each member. Others introduce thirty chief aeons, all with their barbarous names. In short, I should be too prolix if I wished to recount in detail the articles of [Col. 1145C] their heresies. It will be better for Your Lordship to consult Epiphanius himself, against the eighty heresies, in which I am sure Your Lordship will find many things to your taste; and, once you have understood their mysteries, you will easily be able to supply an explanation for most of your false hieroglyphics.
>
> “Nevertheless, on reviewing the impressions sent me by Your Lordship, it seemed to me that the three figures seen on Your Lordship’s white carnelian and chalcedony almond-shaped gem may perhaps be interpreted thus: the taller woman, namely the veiled one, is the Achamoth of the Valentinians; the other, who appears to be an Eros, is her son Saldabaoth, in the act of breathing the animal essence into man, his creature, at his mother’s prompting. The letters on the chalcedony almond-shaped gem, between the kneeling figure and that of Achamoth, are the same as those on the reverse of the white carnelian; but little sense can be extracted from them, except that ποιῶ means ‘I make,’ ΧΑΡΙΣ ‘grace,’ and ΚΥΠΡΙΣ ‘beauty.’ ΒΟΥΒΑΣΤΙ may perhaps be the name [Col. 1145D] of a handsome Egyptian city, or of a neighboring prefecture, called the Bubastite nome or Bubastites, where these heretics especially lived.
>
> “On the reverse of the chalcedony almond-shaped gem, I should suppose that the three barbarous names in the middle are those of three of these principalities. The repeated letters around the circumference, I should suppose, denote the seven heavens according to the doctrine of the Marcosian heretics: Α the first; ΕΕ the second; ΗΗΗ the third; ΙΙΙΙ the fourth; ΟΟΟΟΟ the fifth; ΡΡΡΡΡΡ the sixth; ΩΩΩΩΩΩΩ the seventh. Your Lordship may see their mysteries in the aforementioned Epiphanius. Likewise, I judge that the names of the seven angels on the reverse of the green jasper signify the seven heavens according to the Valentinian heresy: Michael, Gabriel, Uriel, Raphael, Ananiel—whom, to complete the number seven, I think they invented—Prosorael, and Chabediel. In the middle of the shield of the [Col. 1146A] monstrous figure on the other side of the said jasper appear the letters ΙΑΩ. This is a word uttered by the Boundary when it sought to frustrate Achamoth’s designs; it was afterwards given as the name of the principality nearest to us, Achamoth’s son, called the patron of the World. He swallows all souls that leave human bodies, except those of these heretics; then, together with the excrement, he ejects them through his serpent-shaped tail and sends them to be [Col. 1146B] shut up in the bodies of beasts. The same name ΙΑΩ is found under a similar figure on Your Lordship’s carnelian, which bears a lion and seven stars on its reverse and holds one hand upon the head of a little human figure—perhaps one of these heretics. The same letters also appear on one of your carnelians beneath a figure unlike the other but equally fantastical: it has the head of Serapis, a naked body, angelic wings, a bird’s tail, and besides this another serpent tail, with letters among certain rods: MNHCTHP, which I remember having interpreted for Your Lordship before.
>
> “On the large agate there may perhaps be that very powerful Boundary of the Valentinians, imagined to stand in the first quaternity of aeons or angels, above the male and female. That ADONAI and SADDAI in relief may perhaps pertain to the Archontics. PERIESC. ‘From Padua, 8 March 1602.’”

The Basilideans and Valentinians illustrated by Peiresc [Col. 1146C] may be read of in his Life written by Gassendi, book I, p. 36; likewise, on p. 60, Pignorius there testifies to the account of Irenaeus, Epiphanius, and perhaps also our Philastrius concerning the ancient sectarians. Fabricius should be given credit for everything that we publish from the precious repositories of Natalis Benedictus; for all that we have brought forward to elucidate the history of Epiphanius, Irenaeus, and the other Fathers in their attacks on ancient sectarians derives from them. GALEARD.

“From understanding and power, Wisdom”; from power, moreover, and Wisdom, principalities and powers and diverse angels were made.

[Note: [Col. 1144B] **“And power, Wisdom.”**]

For the angels themselves, he says, made heaven.

[Note: [Col. 1146C] **Heaven.** Understand that highest and first of the 365 heavens, whose number, corresponding to the days of the year, is indicated by the name ΑΒΡΑΞΑΣ, common on Basilidean amulets. FABRIC.]

After them other angels made a heaven; and thus, produced from others, other angels made a third heaven. Those in their order, and others again, he says, made [Col. 1146A] 365 heavens; and he assigns to those powers angelic names.

[Note: [Col. 1146C] **Angelic names.** Epiphanius, XXIV.2, says that Basilides formed the angels’ names “by mimic name-making” (κατὰ μιμολογίαν ὀνοματοποιουμένους). Irenaeus: “They also invent certain names, allegedly of angels, and declare that these are in the first heaven, those in the second; and thereafter they endeavor to expound the names, origins, angels, and powers of 365 fabricated heavens.” Theodoret: “having fabricated names of angels” (καὶ ἀγγέλων δὲ ὀνόματα διαπλάσαντες). Damascene: “For he says that the heavens exist and assigns angelic names to them” (λέγει γὰρ τοὺς οὐρανοὺς εἶναι, καὶ τούτοις ὀνόματα ἀγγελικὰ ἐπιτίθησι). FABRIC.]

And he himself, occupied with magical arts, likewise deceived many ignorant persons.

[Note: [Col. 1146D] **Occupied with magical arts.** The same Irenaeus says of Basilides’ school, book I, ch. 23: “They also employ magic, incantations” (ἐπῳδαῖς, “spells,” in Theodoret), “invocations, and every kind of other illicit art.” Epiphanius: “Nor did this deceiver cease to devote himself to magical contrivances and illicit practices” (Οὐ μὴν δὲ ἀλλὰ καὶ μαγγανικαῖς μηχανίαις προσανέχων οὐκ ἐπαύσατο καὶ περιεργίαις). FABRIC.]

He asserts that man was made by angels.

[Note: [Col. 1146D] **Man by angels.** Epiphanius: “that man was fashioned” (πεπλάσθαι τὸν ἄνθρωπον), and “that this creation came into being” (τὴν κτίσιν ταύτην γεγενῆσθαι). Basilides held that human beings and all these lower things were made by the 365th heaven and its angels. See Augustine, *On Heresies*, ch. 4, and Theodoret. FABRIC.]

He even dares to call the true omnipotent Lord an angel, and says that he received the Jewish people as his inheritance and brought them out [Col. 1147A] of the land of Egypt.

[Note: [Col. 1146D] **And he dares to call him an angel.** Epiphanius: “Blaspheming the omnipotent Lord himself, the truly existing God, the only God and no other . . . he wishes to represent him as one of the angels of whom he speaks” (Βλασφημῶν αὐτὸν τὸν παντοκράτορα Κύριον τὸν ὄντως ὄντα Θεὸν μόνον καὶ οὐχ ἕτερον . . . ἕνα βούλεται παριστᾷν τῶν ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ λεγομένων ἀγγέλων). Basilides considered the God of the Jews to be [Col. 1147B] the chief of the angels of the 365th heaven. Irenaeus, book I, ch. 23: “The angels of the heaven that contains the lower one—which is also seen by us—made all things that are in the world and assigned to themselves portions of the earth and of the nations upon it. Their chief, moreover, is he who is thought to be the God of the Jews. Since he wished to subject the other nations to his own people, that is, the Jews, all the other rulers opposed and resisted him.” FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1147B] **Out of the land of Egypt.** Epiphanius, XXIV.2: “The Jews came into his allotted portion; and he, more self-willed than the angels, brought the children of Israel out of Egypt by the self-will of his own arm, because he was more rash and self-willed than the others” (Ἐληλυθέναι δὲ τοὺς Ἰουδαίους ἐς κλῇρον αὐτοῦ καὶ τὸν αὐτὸν ὑπὲρ ἀγγέλων αὐθαδέστερον, ἐξαγαγεῖν δὲ τοὺς υἱοὺς Ἰσραὴλ ἐξ Αἰγύπτου αὐθαδείᾳ Βραχίονος ἰδίου, διὰ τὸ εἶναι αὐτὸν ἰταμώτερον τῶν ἄλλων καὶ αὐθαδέστερον). FABRIC.]

Thus, becoming more audacious, he was exalted, he says, against the other angels; desiring to hold the others in subjection, he acquired hostile nations, which were stirred up by powers hostile to him. Therefore various nations, he says, rose against the Jews.

[Note: [Col. 1147B] **Having become more audacious.** The same Epiphanius, p. 70: “Therefore, because of his self-will, their God resolved to subject all the other nations to the race of Israel; and for this reason he prepared wars” (Ὅθεν διὰ τὴν αὐθάδειαν αὐτοῦ βεβουλεῦσθαι τὸν αὐτὸν αὐτῶν Θεὸν καθυποτάξαι τῷ γένει τοῦ Ἰσραὴλ πάντα τὰ ἄλλα ἔθνη . καὶ διὰ τοῦτο παρεσκευακέναι πολέμους). FABRIC.]

But he says that Christ suffered only seemingly, as a shadow.

[Note: [Col. 1147B] **“As a shadow.”**]

[Note: [Col. 1147C] **Seemingly, by means of a shadow.** Ὡς δοκήσει πεφηνότα, “having appeared only in seeming,” shadowily; compare above, chs. 29 and 31. Basilides in Epiphanius, XXIV.3: “It was not Jesus who suffered, but Simon of Cyrene” (οὐχὶ Ἰησοῦν πεπονθέναι, ἀλλὰ Σίμωνα τὸν Κυρηναῖον), etc. Irenaeus: “Accordingly, he did not suffer, but a certain Simon of Cyrene, compelled to bear his cross in his stead, was crucified through ignorance and error after being transformed by him, so that he might be thought to be Jesus; while Jesus himself took Simon’s form and stood by laughing at them.” A trace of this Basilidean fiction about Simon survives in the Muhammadan impostor-gospel published under the name of St Barnabas the Apostle. FABRIC.]

He also affirms that Simon of Cyrene came to the Passion in his place; “for he,” he says, “bore his cross.”

[Note: [Col. 1147B] **“He bore the cross . . .,” said of Christ the Lord.**]

[Note: [Col. 1147C] **He bore his cross.** Matthew 27:32; Mark 15:21; Luke 23:26. From Luke’s words one might suppose that Simon gave Christ, carrying his own cross (John 19:17), not a substituted or vicarious assistance, but rather a shared assistance. Even if Simon alone bore the cross in Christ’s stead for a time, it does not follow—unless all the Jews were so stupid and visually deceived—that anyone should imagine that all the Evangelists and Apostles were likewise ignorant or acting in bad faith in reporting that Christ was crucified by the Jews, and that Paul should glory that all his knowledge consisted in knowing Christ, and him crucified (1 Corinthians 2:2). FABRIC.]

He also wrongly permits men to live, and gives them license to adhere to worldly vices; he even forbids people to suffer martyrdom for Christ’s name, saying thus: “You do not know what you desire. For Christ,” he says, “did not suffer [Col. 1148A] or undergo crucifixion. How then can you confess that he was crucified, when he was not crucified, and when you do not know who suffered?”

[Note: [Col. 1147D] **Wrongly permits them to live.** As Epiphanius teaches, after the example of Simon Magus: “He permits those who follow his teaching to perform every practice of malicious contrivance and licentiousness; he teaches those persuaded by him a certain promiscuity of men with women, on a wicked principle” (Πᾶσαν ἐπιτήδευσιν κακομηχανίας καὶ ἀσελγείας ἐπιτρέπει τοὺς αὐτῷ μαθητευομένους ἐπιτελεῖν, ἄνδρας μετὰ γυναικῶν πολυμιξίαν τινὰ κακῆς ὑποθέσεως τοὺς αὐτῷ πεισθέντας διδάσκει). Irenaeus: “[They teach] contempt for things sacrificed to idols, considering them nothing, and use of them without any apprehension; and they regard the use of all other practices and of every form of lust as indifferent.” FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1147D] **He forbids suffering martyrdom.** Epiphanius, XXIV.4: “He teaches that one must not bear witness [i.e. suffer martyrdom]” (διδάσκει μὴ δεῖν μαρτυρεῖν). Irenaeus: “Know all men, they say, but let no one know you. Accordingly, such persons are ready for denial; indeed, they cannot even suffer for the Name [of Christ], since they are like everyone else, including non-Christians.” FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1148B] **“You do not know what you desire.”** ποθεῖς ὃ ἀγνοεῖς. FABRIC.—“You do not know what you desire.” Ittigius, *Ecclesiastical History*, second century, p. 301, cites these words of Philastrius—or rather Basilides—where “23” is incorrectly printed for ch. 32, and “Philostrius” for Philastrius. GALEARD.]

### XXXIII. NICOLAUS OF ANTIOCH

Let us see by what madness Nicolaus of Antioch, a proselyte, was deceived. He lived under the Apostles and was chosen by them as the seventh deacon, as is written in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 6:5). Later, withdrawing from them and from sound doctrine, he was ruined by various errors and deceptions. He was at first with the Apostles and the most blessed martyr Stephen. He too says that there are very many Powers, from which the Gnostics—who imagine that they know something—especially arose. They venerate Barbelo and a certain woman, Noria. [Col. 1149A] Others among them worship a certain Jaldabaoth; others, a man called Cavlacav. They also advance the following doctrines: “At first there were only darkness, depth, and water; and in their midst a division of the earth occurred, and the Spirit separated these elements. Then darkness, rushing upon the Spirit, produced four aeons, and these four produced four other aeons. Right and left are light and darkness.” They also say that a certain being had intercourse with that woman and Power, from whom gods, men, angels, and seven spirits of demons were born. They add that certain prophets were born from her, bearing the splendid name Barcaban. Others assert that they see a Gospel of Perfection, empty visions full of deceit, and various dreams, raving madly.

[Note: [Col. 1148B] **A proselyte.** Προσήλυτον, “proselyte” (Acts 6:5). Nicetas, indeed, in book IV of the *Treasury*, calls him an Antiochene of Daphne. There were more than ten other cities called Antioch besides the celebrated Syrian city named Antioch at Daphne, which, according to Epiphanius XXIII.1, was Saturninus’s seat. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1148B] **Withdrawing from them.** Many ancient writers also absolve Nicolaus himself of heresy and crimes, blaming Nicolaus’s disciples. See Gobarus in Photius, codex 232, and Cassian, *Conferences* XVIII.16, together with modern writers; [Col. 1148C] D. Ittigius, “the blessed man” (τὸν μακαρίτην), *Dissertation I on the Heresiarchs of the Apostolic Age*, ch. 9; and Cotelerius on book VI, ch. 8, pp. 336 ff., of the *Apostolic Constitutions*. Augustine appears doubtful in ch. 5 of *On Heresies*. Ambrosius Gardebosc, vol. I, part IV, dissertation 3 of his *Ecclesiastical History*, disputes against Natalis Alexander that Nicolaus was the author of the Nicolaitans. *Mémoires de Trévoux* (1713), pp. 1494 ff. D. Johann Wilhelm Janus likewise maintains in a separate dissertation that the Nicolaitans should be expunged from the catalogue of heretics; published at Wittenberg in 1723, quarto, and reprinted in vol. II of the *New Philologico-Theological Treasury*, p. 1016. Against this, however, see Johann Lorenz Mosheim, *Dissertations on Ecclesiastical History*, pp. 389, 457; also Grotius on Acts 20:30, and Buddeus, *The Apostolic Church*. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1148C] **“He.”** That is, Nicolaus, not Stephen. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1148C] **Powers.** That is, aeons or angels, concerning whom more follows shortly. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1148C] **Whence also the Gnostics.** Others also report that the Gnostics took their beginnings from Nicolaus, as does Nicetas. Indeed Irenaeus, III.11, calls the Nicolaitans an offshoot of falsely so-called knowledge. Epiphanius, XXVI.1, says of the Gnostics: “These are those joined to this Nicolaus” (οὗτοι δὲ οἱ τούτῳ τῷ Νικολάῳ συνεζευγμένοι). Compare Augustine, ch. 6. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1148D] **Barbelo.** From *A*, “son,” and *Domina*, “Lady”: as though one said “the Lady’s son,” as Jean Croius noted. Compare what learned men have written on Irenaeus, book I, ch. 33. Hence the Gnostics were called Barbelites or Barbeliotes; see Cotelerius on Damascene, p. 764. Nicetas incorrectly has Borborites, although he had already mentioned the Borborians above. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1148D] **Noria.** I have written this for *Nora*: for they reported that this name, derived from fire or light—as the Greek name Pyrrha, wife of Deucalion—belonged to the wife of the patriarch Noah. Irenaeus, book I, ch. 34; Epiphanius, XLVI.1. In Damascene, *On Heresies*, ch. 26, for Βαρβέλλω καὶ Βερῶ one seems to need to read [Col. 1149B] Βαρβελὼ καὶ Νωρίαν, “Barbelo and Noria,” or rather Βάρβελον καὶ Βαρβελώ, “Barbelo and Barbelō”; for Irenaeus, book I, ch. 33, mentions these two distinctly, though Epiphanius, XX.2, reads Βαρβερὼ ἤτοι Βαρβηλώ, “Barberō, that is, Barbelō.” FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1149B] **Jaldabaoth.** As though “God of strength.” The distinguished Samuel Basnage, *Annals*, under A.D. 83, no. 6. Compare Irenaeus, book I, ch. 34, and Nicetas IV.9, where one sees that the God of the Jews was called by this name among the Ophites. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1149B] **Cavlacav.** I have written this for the corrupt *Calacaum*. Theodoret has Καυλακούαν. The name is taken from Isaiah 28:10, as, besides Epiphanius XXV.4, Jerome on Isaiah and Nicetas noted (*Bibliotheca Patrum*, Lyons, vol. XXV, p. 109), where Daniel’s twelfth vision is wrongly cited for Isaiah. Petavius on Epiphanius, p. 44; Wetstein on Origen, p. 102; and Samuel Basnage, vol. I of the *Annals*, p. 790, discuss the name. The person whom Philastrius says is worshipped by the heretics in this passage Epiphanius, XXV.3, calls “a certain ruler” (ἄρχοντά τινα), that is, an aeon or angel. Theodoret, however, suggests that they revered Christ himself under this name, book I, ch. 4, *Fables of the Heretics*; thus Cavlacav would have been, for them, as it were the awaited one. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1149B] **“At first,” he says, “there was darkness alone.”**]

[Note: [Col. 1149C] **Depth and water.** This should be read instead of “depth from water.” Epiphanius XXV.5: “They say that there was darkness and depth and water” (λέγοντες ὅτι σκότος ἦν καὶ βυθὸς καὶ ὕδωρ). FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1149B] **“And from these a division.”**]

[Note: [Col. 1149C] **Division of the earth.** That is, the separation of earth from water: Genesis 1:9. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1149C] **Darkness rushing in.** Thus it should be read instead of the printed “darkness beholding,” *tenebras intuentes*. Epiphanius: “But the darkness was angry with and hostile to the Spirit; the darkness rushed up and entwined itself with the Spirit” (τὸ δὲ σκότος ἦν χαλεπαῖνον τε καὶ ἐγκοτοῦν τῷ πνεύματι, ὅπερ σκότος ἀναδραμὸν περιεπλάκη τῷ πνεύματι). FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1149D] **Four others.** Epiphanius has fourteen others. But Philastrius’s reading is correct, and the manuscripts of Epiphanius ought rather to be corrected from it. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1149D] **“The left, they say, is light.”** It seems one should read: “The right and the left, they say, are light and darkness.” Epiphanius: “And right and left came to be—light and darkness” (καὶ γέγονε δεξιά τε καὶ ἀριστερὰ φῶς καὶ σκότος). FABRIC.—**“The left, they say, is light.”** Fabricius adds: “It seems one should read: ‘The right and the left, they say, are light and darkness.’” This is a wholly certain emendation, supported, besides the Epiphanius cited by Fabricius, also by the Corbie manuscript, which reads: “right and left, he says, are light and darkness.” Then, with the conjunction omitted, “a certain being.” Likewise, in the same place Fabricius rightly restored *Barcaban* for *Barabbas*, where the Corbie manuscript also correctly reads “from her, bearing the splendid name Barcaban,” whereas the editions most wrongly have *Barrabam*. And in ch. 36, where the printed editions had “and the Lord himself [to be] Jews,” he restored from Cotelerius “the Lord of the Jews.” Thus also in ch. 51, where the editions absurdly read μετάννισμον, or μεταννικοὶν, as the especially corrupt Lyons edition has it—the error long ago observed and corrected in Potter’s notes on Clement of Alexandria, p. 516—Fabricius also noticed it and supplied μεταγγισμόν; the Corbie manuscript has *metangesmon*. From this come Augustine’s and others’ *Metangismonites*. Therefore that great man’s diligence and ingenuity in restoring Philastrius’s text deserve the praise they have received. [Col. 1150C] GALEARD.]

[Note: [Col. 1150C] **And men.** Epiphanius XXV.5 makes no mention here of human beings. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1150B] **“From her, bearing the splendid name Barcaban.”**]

[Note: [Col. 1150C] **Barcaban.** Βαρκαββάν. I restored this from Epiphanius XXVI.2, Eusebius, *History* IV.7, Jerome, ch. 21 of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, Theodoret, and others, in place of *Barraba*, which earlier editions had wrongly introduced. Philastrius, however, added on his own authority that the Gnostics claimed these prophets were born from that Power. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1150C] **Gospel of Perfection.** Εὐαγγέλιον τελειώσεως. Epiphanius XXVI.2. FABRIC.]

### XXXIV. HERESY DERIVED FROM JUDAS THE TRAITOR

[Col. 1150A]

Others established a heresy derived from Judas the traitor, saying that Judas did a good work in betraying the Savior. For he, they say, became for us the author of all good knowledge, through whom the heavenly mysteries were revealed to us. Since the Powers in heaven were unwilling for Christ to suffer, knowing that, if he suffered, he would give life to humanity, Judas, they say, knowing that Christ’s suffering would bring salvation to humanity, therefore betrayed the Savior. This evil of their impious assertion sometimes appears plausible to certain vain and foolish people, although it is in every respect contrary and abominable, since the blessed prophet David beforehand (Psalm 69:25; 109:8), the Lord [Col. 1150B] and Savior (Matthew 26:24; John 17:12), and [Col. 1151A] the blessed Apostles, confirming the Lord’s judgment against him, have condemned him (Acts 1:18, 25).

[Note: [Col. 1150C] **Derived from Judas the traitor.** Pseudo-Jerome calls them Judaites in ch. 8 of his list of heresies. Below, in ch. 36, our Philastrius attributes a similar opinion to Cerinthus. Others attribute it to the Cainites, treated in ch. 2. On more recent persons reheating the same madness, see, if you wish, the blessed and learned Ittigius, *On the Heresiarchs of the Apostolic Age*, dissertation 2, p. 115; and Johann Heinrich Otho, *Anabaptist History*, p. 267. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1150D] **Author of good knowledge.** That is, of the divine plan for our salvation through Christ’s death. Thanks for this must be attributed to Christ alone, not Judas; nor should betrayal be regarded as the cause of our salvation, since divine Wisdom, which chose to turn Judas’s malice toward a good end, could also have provided for our salvation in other ways. St Chrysostom expresses this view excellently in Homily 82 on Matthew, p. 854, and Homily 84, p. 875. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1150D] **The Powers in heaven unwilling, he says, that Christ should suffer.** Some ancients once thought that the fall or sin of angels was envy of humankind—not merely because humans were made in God’s image, but also because God was to send the Savior to sinners—as the blessed and learned Spener taught in his German *Vindications against Daniel Hartnack*, pp. 19 ff. The same opinion pleased Sherlog in more recent times in his *Mirror of Hebrew Antiquities*: he says that Lucifer took it furiously when, among other great secrets, he learned of the future mystery of the Incarnation. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1150B] **“Unwilling,” he says, “that Christ should suffer.”**]

[Note: [Col. 1150B] **“Although the blessed prophet David beforehand.”**]
