[Note: [Col. 1151B] **The blessed Apostles.** In the Helmstedt edition, the word *Apostles* had wrongly dropped out. FABRIC.]

### XXXV. CARPOCRAS

After him arose Carpocras by name. He too says that there is one Principle, from which Principle—that is, from God—there came forth angels and Powers; but those Powers that are below made this visible creation in which we dwell. He thinks that Christ was born not of the Virgin Mary and the divine Spirit (Luke 1:35), but as a human being from Joseph’s seed, and born carnally, like all human beings. After suffering, he says, Christ was found among the Jews to be better in upright life and conduct; he declares that his soul was received into heaven, but thinks that his flesh was left on earth, and holds that salvation belongs only to the soul and not to the flesh.

[Note: [Col. 1151B] **Carpocras.** Epiphanius XXVII also has Καρποκρᾶς; others, such as Irenaeus, Eusebius, Timothy the Presbyter, and Theodoret, have *Carpocrates*. His followers are Καρποκράσιοι, “Carpocrasians,” in Epiphanius; in others, such as Augustine, ch. 7, and Epiphanius XXX.1, *Carpocratians*; in Nicetas, *Carpocrateni*. Johann Friedrich Hebenstreit, *Dissertation on the Heresy of the Carpocratians*, Wittenberg, 1712. Hugo Grotius suspects that the Second Epistle of Peter and the Epistle of Jude were directed against the Carpocratians; see his notes on vv. 4, 7, 8. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1151B] **One Principle.** “One supreme Principle and Father of all, unknown and incapable of being named” (Μίαν ἄνω ἀρχὴν καὶ πατέρα τῶν ὅλων, ἄγνωστον καὶ κατονομάστον). Epiphanius XXVII.2.]

[Note: [Col. 1151B] **“But the Powers of gods.”**]

[Note: [Col. 1151B] **The Powers that are below.** I did not hesitate to write this instead of the corrupt reading in the editions, “but the Powers of gods.” The angels are called powers existing below, “having descended far beneath the unknown Father” (πολύ τι ὑπὸ τοῦ πατρὸς τοῦ ἀγνώστου ὑποβεβηκότες) and “having departed from the power above” (ἀποστάντες ἀπὸ τῆς ἄνω δυνάμεως), as Epiphanius has it. Tertullian calls them “Powers far distant from the higher Principle”; Irenaeus’s translator, “angels much inferior to the unbegotten Father.” [Col. 1151C] FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1151C] **This visible creation.** “The world and the things in the world” (Τὸν κόσμον καὶ τὰ ἐν κόσμῳ). Epiphanius. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1151B] **“Where,” he says, “we dwell.”**]

[Note: [Col. 1151C] **A man born from Joseph’s seed.** Epiphanius: “Jesus our Lord was born from Joseph, just as all human beings are born from the seed of a man and woman” (Ἰησοῦν τὸν κύριον ἡμῶν ἀπὸ Ἰωσὴφ γεγενῆσθαι καθάπερ καὶ πάντες ἄνθρωποι ἐκ σπέρματος ἀνδρὸς καὶ γυναικὸς ἐγενήθησαν). FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1151C] **After suffering.** That is, after overcoming and passing beyond the world-making angels (κοσμοποιούς), once he had endured the sufferings imposed as punishments. Epiphanius, p. 103, from Irenaeus, book I, ch. 24: “Jesus’ soul, having been raised among Jewish customs, despised them; and therefore it received powers through which it was able to perform the acts imposed upon human beings as punishments, and to transcend the world-makers” (Τὴν δὲ ψυχὴν τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἐν τοῖς Ἰουδαίων ἔθεσιν ἀνατραφεῖσαν καταφρονῆσαι αὐτῶν, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο δυνάμεις εἰληφέναι δι᾽ ὧν τὰ ἐπὶ κολάσεσι πάθη προσόντα τοῖς ἀνθρώποις δυνηθεῖς πρᾶξαι, ὑπερβῆναι τοὺς κοσμοποιούς). FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1151C] **Better.** Tertullian, ch. 48, says, following Carpocras’s view, that Christ was merely born a man, yet better than the rest in devotion to justice and integrity of life; [Col. 1151D] that he suffered among the Jews, and that his soul alone was received into heaven because it was stronger and more robust than the others. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1152D] **His flesh left on earth.** Cast into the tomb and left there. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1152D] **Salvation of the soul.** He uses *salvation* for immortality. Thus he says that Carpocras denies salvation to the flesh because he denied the resurrection. From this, Tertullian says, he inferred that, since the salvation of souls alone had been attempted, there were no resurrections of bodies. Tertullian frequently speaks thus in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*. Below, in ch. 38, Philastrius says of Valentinus: “He thinks that the soul alone is saved, but the human body is not saved.” FABRIC.]

### XXXVI. CERINTHUS

Cerinthus succeeded to this error and likeness of vanity. He taught similarly concerning the Savior’s generation and the creation of angels, differing from Carpocras in nothing except that he agrees only in part with the Law—namely, that it was given by God—and considers the Lord of the Jews to be the one who gave the Law to the children of Israel. But he teaches circumcision and Sabbath observance, and declares that Christ has not yet risen from the dead but will rise. He does not accept the Apostle Paul; he honors Judas the traitor; he accepts only the Gospel according to Matthew and rejects the three Gospels; he rejects the Acts of the Apostles and blasphemes the blessed martyrs. Under the Apostles he stirred up a contentious dispute, saying that people ought to be circumcised. Because of this, the Apostles decided against him and his heresy in their Acts, determining that those coming from the Gentiles who believed in Christ our Lord and Savior ought no longer to submit to Judaism—that is, circumcision and other such carnal observances of vain superstition.

[Note: [Col. 1152D] **Cerinthus succeeded.** Tertullian—or whoever enriched his book *On Prescription* with an appendix—also makes Cerinthus later than Carpocras. But although Irenaeus, Epiphanius, and Jerome in *Against the Luciferians* mention Carpocras first, they do not testify that he was earlier in time; nor is it credible, since Cerinthus had already spread his errors during the time of John the Apostle, as Irenaeus himself and many others report, not to mention that he had already stirred up the dispute of sedition against the Apostles Peter, James, and Paul, as will be discussed below. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1152B] **On the Savior’s generation.** Cerinthus taught with Carpocras that Jesus was the son of Joseph and Mary, but differed from him in holding that Christ descended upon Jesus after the baptism, thus separating Christ from Jesus. See Irenaeus, book I, ch. 25; Epiphanius XXVIII.1. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1152B] **On the creation of angels.** That is, the world created by angels, as Epiphanius XXVIII.1, Augustine ch. 8, Damascene, [Col. 1152C] and others report, besides Irenaeus himself. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1152C] **Only in part.** The editions corruptly read *ex patre*, “from the Father,” and shortly thereafter “and the Lord himself [to be] Jews,” instead of “the Lord of the Jews,” as Cotelerius also noted, vol. I of the *Monuments*, p. 765. Philastrius says that Cerinthus agrees with the Law in part, which Epiphanius, p. 110, describes as “adhering in part to Judaism” (προσέχειν τῷ Ἰουδαϊσμῷ ἀπὸ μέρους). FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1152C] **The Law as given by God.** Not by the highest God, but by the God of the Jews, one among the angels by whom the world was created. Epiphanius: “He says that the Law and the prophets were given by angels, and that the giver of the Law was one of the angels who made the world” (Φάσκει δὲ οὗτος νόμον καὶ τοὺς προφήτας ὑπὸ ἀγγέλων δεδόσθαι, καὶ τὸν δεδωκότα νόμον ἕνα εἶναι τῶν ἀγγέλων τῶν τὸν κόσμον πεποιηκότων). Tertullian on Cerinthus: “He declares that the Law itself was given by angels, and pronounces the God of the Jews not Lord—that is, not the highest God—but an angel.” FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1152C] **To be circumcised.** See Epiphanius XXVIII.5 and our author below in this very chapter. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1152C] **To observe the Sabbath.** I have written this for *sabbatizari*. This was common to Cerinthus and other Judaizers in the Apostles’ time, who maintained that Sabbaths must be observed in the Jewish manner. Rejecting this, Paul warns the Colossians, 2:16: “Let no one judge you in a matter of festival, new moon, or Sabbaths” (Μήτις ὑμᾶς κρινέτω ἐν μέρει ἑορτῆς ἢ νουμηνίας ἢ σαββάτων). FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1152D] **Christ has not yet risen.** St Augustine and the author of the *Predestined* are mistaken when, in ch. 8 of *On Heresies*, they write that Cerinthus held Jesus not to have risen but to be destined to rise. For Cerinthus separated Jesus from Christ, as I have just noted; he did not deny that Jesus rose but denied it of Christ. Irenaeus is quite clear, book I, ch. 25: after baptism Christ descended upon him in the form of a dove . . . but in the end Christ flew back again from Jesus; Jesus suffered and rose again, whereas Christ remained impassible, being spiritual. Therefore neither Epiphanius [Col. 1153A] XXVIII.6, followed by Timothy the Presbyter in Cotelerius, vol. III, *Monuments*, p. 388—“Christ suffered and was crucified, but has not yet risen; he will rise when the universal resurrection of the dead occurs” (Χριστὸν πεπονθέναι καὶ ἐσταυρῶσθαι, μήπω δὲ ἐγηγέρθαι . μέλλειν δὲ ἀνίστασθαι ὅταν ἡ καθόλου γένηται νεκρῶν ἀνάστασις)—nor the appendix to Tertullian on Cerinthus is accurate when it says: “Christ was born from Joseph’s seed.” It ought rather to have said Jesus. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1153B] **He does not accept Paul.** Epiphanius XXVIII.5: “They reject Paul because they do not obey circumcision; indeed, they cast him out because he said, ‘All you who are justified by the Law have fallen away from grace’ [Galatians 5:4], and, ‘If you are circumcised, Christ will benefit you nothing’ [Galatians 5:2]” (Τὸν δὲ Παῦλον ἀθετοῦσι, διὰ τὸ μὴ πείθεσθαι τῇ περιτομῇ· ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐκβάλλουσιν αὐτὸν διὰ τὸ εἰρηκέναι Ὅσοι ἐν νόμῳ δικαιοῦσθε, τῆς χάριτος ἐξεπέσατε . καὶ ὅτι ἐὰν περιτέμνησθε, Χριστὸς ὑμᾶς οὐδὲν ὠφελήσει). FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1153B] **He honors Judas the traitor.** Others attribute this not to Cerinthus but to the Cainites, as I said above on ch. 34. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1153B] **He accepts Matthew alone.** Nor even the Gospel in its entirety, but only insofar as it did not oppose Cerinthus’s heresy. See Epiphanius XXVIII.5 and XXX.14. [Col. 1153C] FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1153C] **He rejects the Acts of the Apostles.** Epiphanius notes that the Ebionites also rejected these, XXX.16. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1153C] **He blasphemes the blessed martyrs.** Basilides agreed with Cerinthus in this, for he too forbade martyrdom; see above, ch. 32. But it is not known whence Philastrius drew this statement concerning Cerinthus, since it is not found in Irenaeus or Epiphanius. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1153A] **“Under the blessed Apostles, [he stirred up] a dispute.”**]

[Note: [Col. 1153C] **A contentious dispute.** Epiphanius recounts three disturbances (ταραχή, “sedition”) concerning circumcision and the observance of Jewish rites stirred up by Cerinthus before he spread his heresy in Asia: one at Antioch, when James and the other Apostles wrote to the troubled Antiochenes (Acts 15:24); another in Jerusalem, when Peter had returned from Cornelius to Jerusalem (Acts 11:2–3); and a third, likewise at Jerusalem, against Paul (Acts 21:28). Timothy the Presbyter charges the same three disturbances to Cerinthus. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1153C] **The Apostles decided in their Acts.** With Peter and James taking the lead, they judged “not to trouble those from among the Gentiles who are turning to God” (μὴ παρενοχλεῖν τοῖς ἀπὸ τῶν ἐθνῶν ἐπιστρέφουσιν ἐπὶ τὸν Θεόν), Acts 15:19. Jerome, Epistle 89 to Augustine: “We lapse into the heresy of Cerinthus and Ebion, who, though believing in Christ, were anathematized by the Fathers for this reason alone: that they mixed the ceremonies of the Law with Christ’s Gospel, and so professed the new things in such a way as not to relinquish the old.” Agobard aptly observed that all that Cerinthus maintained was Jewish, in *On Jewish Superstitions*, vol. XIV of the *Library of the Fathers*, p. 257. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1154A] **“The blessed Apostles decided in their Acts.”**]

### XXXVII. EBION
[Note: [Col. 1153D] Ebion, disciple of Cerinthus. Tertullian—or whoever was the author of the appendix to *On Prescription*, ch. 48—calls Ebion Cerinthus’s successor; Jerome, *Against the Luciferians*, p. 304, supports this. I know that there are learned men who think that no Ebion ever existed; but among the ancients there is no one who denies it, while many affirm that he did exist: besides Jerome in several places, our Philastrius, and Tertullian himself, ch. 33 of *On Prescription*, there are Pacian, [Col. 1154A] Epistle 1; Hilary in his books *On the Trinity*; Rufinus on the Creed; Theodoret, *Compendium of Heretical Fables*, book II, ch. 1; [Col. 1154B] Cassian, *On the Incarnation*, book I, ch. 2; book III, ch. 5; book V, ch. 10. Compare Mosheim, *Sacred Observations*, ch. 5, p. 233 ff.; dissertation on *Ecclesiastical History*, p. 552 ff.; Buddeus, *Apostolic Church*. William Whiston, *Authentic Records*, p. 949 ff., disputes concerning Ebionite inventions and assigns to the Ebionites Papias, pp. 680, 951; Hegesippus, pp. 950, 952; the Clementine Homilies, p. 953 ff.; and Josephus also, p. 954 ff. Jacob Rhenferd wrote an Apology for the Ebionites, in his dissertation *On the Fictitious Heresies of Judaizers*. Finally, Epiphanius expressly testifies, XXX.2, that Ebion lived in the village of Cocabe in the district of Basanitis; and in ch. 17, p. 141, having noted that the name Ebion means “poor” in Hebrew, he adds: “But he was in fact called Ebion by nature—Ebion, I think, the poor and wretched man—having inherited the name from his father and mother.” The interpolated Epistle of Ignatius to the Philadelphians, ch. 6: “Such a man is poor in understanding, as the name Ebion indicates.” Hence there is frequent wordplay in ancient writings upon [Col. 1154C] the name of poverty when they speak of the Ebionites. Yet one may by no means infer from this that there was no Ebion; rather, it is credible that Origen took the occasion for that wordplay from Ebion’s very name, when, in *Against Celsus* II, p. 56, he says that the Ebionites are “named after the poverty, according to the interpretation, of the Law,” because they still clung to the “poor elements” of Jewish rites. Thus the Ebionites are called “poor in understanding” by Origen himself, *On First Principles* IV and *Homilies on Genesis* 3, and by Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* III.27 and *On Ecclesiastical Theology* I.14. And Origen, in his commentary on Matthew XX, p. 428, calls an Ebionite one “poor with respect to faith in Jesus,” or one who thinks poorly and humbly of Christ, to use Eusebius’s words, *Ecclesiastical History* III.27. John Lightfoot noted that a certain Ebion is mentioned in the Talmud, vol. II of his works, p. 148. FABRIC.]

Ebion, a disciple of Cerinthus, [Note: [Col. 1154C] Similarly mistaken with him in many matters. Not in all matters. Nor do I agree with the learned men who read in Irenaeus, book I, ch. 26, concerning the Ebionites: “But concerning matters relating to the Lord, he thinks in the same way as Cerinthus and Carpocrates.” For Epiphanius, XXX.14, testifies that the reading should be “not in the same way.” For, after saying that Cerinthus and Carpocrates tried to prove from Christ’s genealogy in Matthew’s Gospel that Christ was begotten from the seed of Joseph and Mary, he immediately added concerning the Ebionites: “But these men maintain certain different views.” He then teaches that they cut off the genealogy, regarded Jesus as a mere human being, and held that Christ, having descended upon him in the form of a dove, denied that he himself was human when, stretching out his hand toward his disciples, he said: “Behold my mother and my brothers” (Matt. XII.49). FABRIC.] erred like him in many things. He held that our Savior was carnally born [Note: [Col. 1154D] Born of Joseph. “From a man’s seed, that is, Joseph’s.” Ebion in Epiphanius XXX.3. Eusebius says of the Ebionites, *Ecclesiastical History* III.27: “They regarded him as lowly and ordinary, justified only by progress in character as a mere man, and born through the union of a man and Mary.” Theodoret and others say similar things. FABRIC.] of Joseph, and taught that there was nothing divine in him; [Col. 1155A] rather, [Note: [Col. 1155B] Like all the prophets. Yet they professed that Christ surpassed the other prophets in this respect: the other prophets had wisdom merely from their own natural ability and understanding, whereas Christ was a true prophet. This, I think, is how Epiphanius XXX.18 should be understood: “They say that the prophets are prophets of understanding and not of truth . . . but they call Christ a prophet of truth.” Hence Methodius, in the *Banquet of the Virgins*, p. 113, says concerning the Ebionites: “They stubbornly maintain that the prophets spoke from their own impulse.” FABRIC.] he asserted that, like all the prophets, Christ too had God’s grace; but he did not believe that he was the Lord of majesty and the Son of God the Father, eternal with the Father—although the divine Scriptures everywhere testify and proclaim the Lord to be eternal, [Note: [Col. 1155B] Truly with the Father. Thus God is Christ’s true Father, and Christ is God’s own only-begotten Son: Rom. VIII.32; Ps. II.7; Matt. III.17, XVII.5; John I.14, 18; III.16, 18; Heb. I.8. FABRIC.] truly and equally eternal with the Father.

### XXXVIII. VALENTINUS

[Note: [Col. 1155C] After him. This was during the time of the Roman bishops Hyginus, Pius, and Anicetus. Hyginus held office from A.D. 138; Pius from A.D. 150; Anicetus from A.D. 153 to 162. See what learned men have written on Irenaeus III.4. FABRIC.]

After him a certain Valentinus arose, [Note: [Col. 1155C] A Pythagorean. Irenaeus himself says of the Valentinians, II.19: “Their wish to reduce this whole universe to numbers they received from the Pythagoreans; for these first posited numbers as the origin of all things, and the origin of numbers themselves as even and odd, from which they derived both sensible and insensible things.” On this doctrine of the Pythagoreans, see, if you please, Iamblichus, *Theologoumena of Arithmetic*, and John Meursius’s *Pythagorean Decad*; and, specifically concerning the rival doctrines of the Valentinians, Renatus Massuet’s preliminary dissertations to Irenaeus, p. 28. FABRIC.] more a Pythagorean than [Note: [Col. 1155B] A Christian. For—FABRIC.] a Christian, belching forth a certain empty and destructive teaching—a kind of arithmetical, that is, [Note: [Col. 1155B] A deceptive doctrine of multiplicity. FABRIC.] [Note: [Col. 1155C] A new deceptive doctrine of multiplicity. Numerous Aeons, pairings of Aeons, and manifold successions, concerning which more below. The word *numerositas* (“multiplicity”) is commonly found in Augustine, Macrobius, Orosius, Sidonius, and other medieval writers, perhaps also among more ancient authors. FABRIC.] a new deceptive doctrine of multiplicity—and captured the souls of many ignorant people. At first, indeed, [Note: [Col. 1155D] He was in the Church. In Egypt and at Rome, as long as he lived there, he remained in communion with the Church, or, as Tertullian says in *On Prescription*, ch. 19, believed in Catholic doctrine and had not yet disclosed his errors. But after he was conveyed to the island of Cyprus, he finally poured forth his heresy, as Epiphanius relates, XXXI.7: “For before this he was thought to have some share in piety and right faith in the places mentioned; but in Cyprus he advanced at last to the uttermost impiety.” FABRIC.] he was in the Church. [Note: [Col. 1155D] But afterward, becoming more ambitious. Tertullian, *Against the Valentinians*, ch. 4: “Valentinus had hoped for the episcopate, because he was capable both in talent and in eloquence. But offended that another had obtained the position through the prerogative of martyrdom, he broke away from the Church of the authentic rule—as minds aroused by ambition are wont to be inflamed by the presumption of revenge—and turned to assail the truth.” I am persuaded that the episcopate which Valentinus lost was on the island of Cyprus. FABRIC.] But afterward, becoming more ambitious, he was deceived by no small error; and while residing in the province of Cyprus, he began to define the matter thus:

“There was nothing else in the world at first,” he says, “except [Note: [Col. 1155B] The depth of the sea and the silence of the sea—FABRIC.] [Note: [Col. 1156B] The Depth. For the Kabbalists, *Bythus* is *En Soph*: God, alone filling infinite space from eternity. FABRIC.] the Depth and [Note: [Col. 1156B] Silence. *Sigē*: in the author of the *Praedestinatus*, *eine tiefe Stille*, “a deep silence.” God hidden within himself and manifested by no created thing. It is not necessary to suppose that St. Ignatius had this Valentinian *Sigē* in view when he wrote that the Son of God was “the eternal Word, not proceeding from silence”; those words mean only that the Logos was eternal and that no more ancient silence had existed in God before him. Photius also attributes these Valentinian doctrines concerning Bythus and Sigē to the Manichaeans, *Against the Manichaeans* III, p. 34, vol. II of Wolf’s *Anecdota*. FABRIC.] Silence—which [Note: [Col. 1156B] The chaos of the poets. On close consideration, the poets’ chaos is one thing and the Valentinians’ *Sigē* another. For the poets’ chaos is the eternal, rough, unformed mass of matter; the Valentinians’ *Sigē* preceded in time all matter and every created thing. FABRIC.] poets call chaos. Teaching that from this Depth [Note: [Col. 1156B] and Silence proceeded—FABRIC.] and Silence proceeded [Note: [Col. 1156C] Mind and Truth. *Nous* and *Alētheia*: the intelligible world, or angels created by God before the world, after whose fall or sin the Valentinians thought the creation of the visible world subsequently followed. Hence, they say in Irenaeus II.35, that the Demiurge is the product of a fall. FABRIC.] Mind and Truth; from Mind and Truth, [Note: [Col. 1156C] Word and Life. *Logos* and *Zōē*: the rational world of human beings before Christian times. FABRIC.] Word and Life; [Note: [Col. 1156B] and from Word and Life proceeded—FABRIC.] and from Word and Life, [Note: [Col. 1156C] Man and Church. *Anthrōpos* and *Ekklēsia*: human beings gathered into the Christian Church. FABRIC.] Man and Church; and from Man and Church there proceeded [Note: [Col. 1156C] Twelve Aeons. From the names of these Aeons in Irenaeus, book I, ch. 1, Tertullian, Epiphanius, and others readily available, it may be established that Valentinus meant nothing other than to designate, under the names of presiding angels, the various prerogatives of the Christian condition. Similarly, the names of the ten Aeons signify the various virtues of the rational world; lastly, the names of the eight highest Aeons signify the excellences of the intelligible world, whose first-born octonary he called the root and substance of all things. FABRIC.] twelve [Note: [Col. 1156D] Aeons, that is, Ages. I doubt that Valentinus intended by Aeons to denote as many successive periods of time; it is truer that, by metonymy, he meant lesser gods and angels living in the age. God himself is, for Valentinus, “the perfect Aeon before all” in Irenaeus at the beginning of book I: “The Aeon may rightly be called God” (Plotinus, p. 329). Hilary too seems to have used *saecula* for angels, *On the Trinity* II: “Archangels do not know; angels have not heard; the ages do not comprehend.” FABRIC.] Aeons, that is, Ages. From [Col. 1157A] Word and Life there proceeded ten Aeons; from Mind and Truth, eight Aeons. This [Note: [Col. 1157B] The *Triacontad* of Ages. Cotelerius advised that this should be written *Triacontad* rather than *thirty*, vol. I of *Monuments of the Greek Church*, p. 768. So also in Tertullian. FABRIC.] Triacontad of Ages, that is, [Note: [Col. 1157B] Thirty Aeons. FABRIC.] thirty Aeons, is therefore made up of the Ogdoad, [Note: [Col. 1157B] and the Decad consists—FABRIC.] the Decad, and the Duodecad. He [Note: [Col. 1157B] Raves. Earlier editions incorrectly read “he deliberates.” See the same Cotelerius, vol. III, p. 629. FABRIC.] raves about these thirty Aeons.

He says that Christ was sent by the Father—whom he calls [Note: [Col. 1157B] By the name of Depth. *Bythus*, mentioned above. FABRIC.] “Depth”—[Note: [Col. 1157B] For the salvation of the whole world. Hence he is called Savior, “the most perfect beauty and star of the Pleroma, the perfect fruit,” as Irenaeus has it, p. 14. FABRIC.] for the salvation of the whole world; that he brought flesh down from heaven and [Note: [Col. 1158B] received nothing—FABRIC.] received nothing from the holy Virgin, but, as water [Note: [Col. 1157B] As water through a channel. Epiphanius XXXI.7: “They say that he brought his body down from above and passed through Mary the Virgin as water through a pipe, taking nothing from the Virgin’s womb.” Irenaeus, book I, [Col. 1157C] ch. 7: “This one passed through Mary as water goes through a pipe.” Thus the ancient Latin translator of Irenaeus. Some have conjectured that Philastrius likewise should read “through a pipe,” because, after a scribe wrote *per tuvum*, another who did not understand corrected it to *per rivum* (“through a channel”). But nothing should be altered: a *rivus* is a constructed watercourse. Vitruvius VIII.7: “Water conduits are made in three kinds: channels by constructed watercourses, lead pipes, or earthenware tubes.” Perhaps in Augustine, *On Heresies*, ch. 11, one should read not “through a crevice” but “through a channel” or “through a pipe.” Certainly the author of the *Praedestinatus*, who commonly follows Augustine’s lead, says in ch. 11 on the Valentinians: “The Son assumed nothing from the Virgin Mary, but passed through her as water through a channel or pipe, without any assumption of flesh.” The author of the appendix to Tertullian’s *On Prescription*, ch. 49: “Bringing down some sort of spiritual body from heaven, he passed through the Virgin Mary as water through a pipe, receiving or borrowing nothing from her.” FABRIC.] through a channel, so he passed through her. [Note: [Col. 1157D] Only the soul is saved. The Valentinians denied the resurrection of this body, as is clear from the same appendix to Tertullian’s *On Prescription*, ch. 49. Epiphanius says, XXXI.7: “They deny the resurrection of the dead.” Our author also used “salvation of the soul” above, ch. 35, to mean immortality. FABRIC.] He therefore holds that the soul alone is saved, and that the human body is not saved.

### XXXIX. PTOLEMY

[Col. 1157B] There are other [Note: [Col. 1157D] His successors. Refer this not to Ptolemy alone but also to Secundus and the others subsequently mentioned—especially in the next chapters, Heracleon, Marcus, and Colorbasus. FABRIC.] successors of his: Ptolemy, who [Col. 1158A] introduced an equally empty doctrine, saying [Note: [Col. 1157D] There are four Aeons and another four. Understand these as in addition to and prior to the thirty Aeons posited by Valentinus. Thus the author of the appendix to Tertullian, ch. 49, says of Ptolemy and Secundus: “They agree with Valentinus in every respect; they differ only in this: Valentinus invented only thirty Aeons, but these added several more—first four, then another [Col. 1158B] four.” Irenaeus, book I, ch. 5 (Massuet’s ed., 11): “Others again among them named the first and original Ogdoad by these names: first Proarchē, then Anennoēton, third Arrhēton, and fourth Aoraton. From the first, Proarchē, they say Archē was emitted in first and fifth place; from Anennoēton, Acatalēpton in second and sixth; from Arrhēton, Anonomaston in third and seventh; and from Aoraton, Agennēton in fourth and eighth.” This is the Pleroma of the first Ogdoad. They wish these Powers to have existed before Bythus and Sigē, so that they may appear as perfections of the perfect ones. These words of Irenaeus set forth Ptolemy’s view. Then in ch. 6 (Massuet, 12), Irenaeus observes that [Col. 1158C] certain disciples of Ptolemy added still further inventions to their master’s doctrines: “Those who are more learned among Ptolemy’s followers say that their Bythus has two consorts, which they call dispositions: Ennoia and Thelēsis,” etc. Tertullian, *Against the Valentinians*, ch. 33: “There arose from his school disciples who corrected their master Ptolemy and assigned a double consort to their Bythus: Thought and Will.” Epiphanius, XXXIII.1, less accurately attributes this to Ptolemy himself, as Massuet aptly observed, p. 49 of his preliminary dissertations on Irenaeus. St. Athanasius agrees with Epiphanius, *Against the Arians* III, p. 608 of Montfaucon’s edition: “For Ptolemy, Valentinus’s follower, said that the Unbegotten has two consorts, Thought and Will; and he first thought, then willed, and what he had thought he was unable to bring forth until the power of Will came upon him.” FABRIC.] that there were four Aeons and another four, wishing to devise some new false invention beyond what his teacher Valentinus had fabricated.

### XL. SECUNDUS

After him, a certain man named Secundus, likewise teaching that Aeons were [Note: [Col. 1158B] made, asserts them to be infinite. FABRIC.] made, nevertheless asserted [Note: [Col. 1158C] Nevertheless, he asserts them to be infinite. I do not find this in other writers who mention the heretic Secundus—Epiphanius and Damascus, *Heresy* 32; [Col. 1158D] Augustine and the author of the *Praedestinatus*, ch. 12; Theodoret, *Compendium of Heretical Fables* I.8; Tertullian, *Against the Valentinians*, ch. 38; the author of the appendix to Tertullian, ch. 49; and, older than all these, Irenaeus, book I, ch. 5. Yet it is clear from the *Apostolic Constitutions* VI.8 that some heretics introduced infinite Aeons. FABRIC.] that they were infinite. He also supposes that Christ appeared to humankind as though in a phantom, that is, [Note: [Col. 1158D] As a shadow. Above, pp. 29, 31, 32. Hence Damascus writes that the Secundians denied Christ’s flesh. FABRIC.] like a shadow, and did not possess true human flesh.

### XLI. HERACLEON

After him Heracleon, [Note: [Col. 1158D] His disciple. I think this testimony should not be given much weight; nor do I think it establishes that Heracleon was truly Secundus’s disciple, or that Marcus—discussed in the following chapter—was Heracleon’s successor. For in Epiphanius, Colorbasus follows Marcus and Heracleon follows Colorbasus. Conversely, Tertullian, *Against the Valentinians*, ch. 4, places Secundus after Heracleon and the magician Marcus after Secundus. FABRIC.] his disciple, arose [Col. 1158B] and said: “The Principle is one, whom he calls Lord; then [Col. 1159A] [Note: [Col. 1159B] Another was born from this. Rather, two from that Monad. The author of the appendix to Tertullian, ch. 49: “He first introduces that which he declares to have existed, and then two from that Monad, and afterward the remaining Aeons. Then he introduces [Col. 1159C] the whole of Valentinus.” Compare what Epiphanius and Damascus say of Heracleon in *Heresy* 36, Augustine, and the author of the *Praedestinatus*, ch. 16. Like Valentinus, he also denied that grace and truth were in the Law. See Photius, *Amphilochia*, ch. 246, and Epistle 134. FABRIC.] another was born from this.” From these two he asserts the generation of many Principles, raving likewise with his teachers.

### XLII. MARCUS

A certain Marcus, after him, [Note: [Col. 1159C] His successor. See what I noted on the preceding chapter. St. Jerome, in Epistle 29 and on Isaiah LXIV, confuses this Marcus with the much later Priscillianist Marcus, as Cotelerius noted on the *Apostolic Constitutions* VI.8. FABRIC.] his successor, by making numerical and metrical calculations, including [Note: [Col. 1159C] The calculation of letters. Epiphanius discusses these absurdities of Marcus at length in *Heresy* 34, drawing on Irenaeus, book I, ch. 10 ff., and learned commentators on Irenaeus. FABRIC.] computations of letters, imagined himself the inventor of something plausible and new. Thinking that he might win praise from some persons, he likewise fell into no slight madness of error. For he says:

“There are twenty-four letters, which contain the perfection of all things. Therefore Christ said, ‘I am Alpha and Omega’” (Rev. I.8).

He also said that in the last time Christ [Note: [Col. 1159C] Descended. I have written this in place of the future “will descend,” which was corrupt in earlier editions. FABRIC.] descended upon Jesus in the form and likeness of a dove; and [Note: [Col. 1159C] Christ as a dove. Marcus proved this from the fact that the Greek letters of *peristera*, meaning “dove,” yield the number 801, the same number produced by the letters alpha and omega. See Grabe’s Irenaeus, [Col. 1159D] pp. 68 and 71. FABRIC.] he taught that Christ himself was the dove which descended, he says, upon the twelve Aeons—that is, the twelve apostles—and he held that one of them fell, namely Judas. He says that Christ [Note: [Col. 1159D] In appearance only. Above, ch. 32. FABRIC.] appeared only in appearance, and [Note: [Col. 1159B] He is thought to have suffered. FABRIC.] believes that he suffered as though in a shadow, but not that he truly suffered in the body.

### XLIII. COLORBASUS

[Note: [Col. 1159D] After him, Colorbasus. This is the correct reading in Philastrius instead of “C. Bassus,” as Latinus Latinius correctly noted long ago. In Nicetas IV.7, “Colobarsus” is incorrect. Moreover, Henry Dodwell argues, in his dissertation on Irenaeus, p. 326 ff., that Colorbasus was not after Marcus but before him. Nor is “after” always an indication of time; as Greek *meta*, it often means “besides.” FABRIC.]

After him [Note: [Col. 1159B] After him, Colorbasus, who likewise—FABRIC.] Colorbasus likewise held that in letters and in the number of the elements and the seven stars [Col. 1160A] were established [Note: [Col. 1159D] The life of all human beings. The author of the *Praedestinatus*, ch. 15, says of Colorbasus: “He affirmed that the whole life of human beings was placed in the seven stars, and tried to establish that these are the seven Churches and the seven golden lampstands.” FABRIC.] the life and generation of all human beings; he did not perceive that true human salvation was to be hoped for in Christ’s majesty and power, nor [Note: [Col. 1159B] nor in his . . . true—FABRIC.] in his bodily presence.

### XLIV. CERDON

[Note: [Col. 1159D] Cerdon. In the *Life of Stephen the Younger*, he is Κερδονᾶς, vol. IV of Cotelerius’s *Monuments*, p. 441. In Sophronius’s Epistle, [Col. 1160B] Κέρδων ἀκέρδων, “Cerdon, without gain.” Similarly, III, p. 627; below, ch. 53, Noetus is called ἀνόητος, “senseless.” FABRIC.]

After these, a certain Cerdon arose, teaching worse things than his masters. Having come to Rome from Syria, he dared to say [Note: [Col. 1160B] Two Principles. Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, ch. 52: “And the other plagues of this origin or order, which introduce for themselves [Col. 1160C] two unknown Principles, as Cerdon and Marcion do; or contrary Principles, as Mani does,” etc. But there is no doubt that Cerdon too posited two Principles mutually opposed and contrary: one good and the other cruel. The good one was higher; the cruel one was the creator of this world, according to the appendix to Tertullian’s *On Prescription*, ch. 51. FABRIC.] that there are two Principles: one God good, and another evil; and that the good God does good things while the evil one does evil things. He maintains that Jesus the Savior [Note: [Col. 1160C] Was not born of the Virgin. This must be understood not concerning Mary’s virginity but concerning the reality of the birth, which Cerdon held to have occurred only shadowily and *kata dokēsin*, “in appearance.” Epiphanius XLI.1: “Christ was not born from Mary, nor did he appear in flesh”; neither born of a virgin, but not born at all, according to the appendix to Tertullian. See Christian Kortholt’s notes on Justin, p. 53b ff. FABRIC.] was not born of the Virgin, did not appear in the flesh, [Note: [Col. 1160C] Nor descended from heaven. This was the opinion of Valentinus and Apelles. FABRIC.] nor descended from heaven, but was seen by human beings only in appearance. “He did not truly appear,” he says, “but was a shadow”; hence some thought [Col. 1160B] that he suffered, though he did not truly suffer.

### XLV. MARCION

Marcion, his disciple, a native [Note: [Col. 1160C] Of Pontus. See Isaac Vossius, p. 34, on Catullus, and my excellent teacher Thomas Ittig’s dissertation *On Heresiarchs*, [Col. 1160D] p. 135. FABRIC.] of Pontus, from the city of Sinope, [Note: [Col. 1160D] He came to Rome before the middle of the second century. Compare Blondel, *On Bishops*, p. 19 ff. FABRIC.—He came to Rome before the middle of the second century. The subject is Marcion, concerning whom Lambert Daneau also says in his commentary on Augustine, *On Heresies*, ch. 22: “He came to Rome, as Tertullian writes in book I against him, under Antoninus Pius, around the 115th year after Christ’s passion, under Hyginus, as Platina says; according to Tertullian, under Eleutherus. But after Cerdon, the heresy began to become known under the emperor Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher and Anicetus, bishop of Rome, around the 133rd year after Christ’s passion—although Clement, *Stromata* VII, holds that the heretic Valentinus was still living at Rome at that very time, and that Marcion saw him as an old man while Marcion was young.” Bayle, *Critical Dictionary*, under “Marcionites,” noticed several errors of Daneau in this passage. GALEARD.] came to Rome. While living there he sowed a wicked heresy; questioning the holy presbyters of the Catholic Church, he offered them his own [Note: [Col. 1160B] Deadly errors—*erroris* in place of *errores*, since *e* is very often written for *i*. FABRIC.] deadly error, saying:

[Note: [Col. 1160B] What is it, he says, that—FABRIC.] “What is this which is written in the Gospel, when the Lord says: [Col. 1161A] [Note: [Col. 1161B] It is written. In St. Archelaus’s disputation with Mani, p. 33: “Just as, if someone sews a patch of unshrunk cloth onto an old garment, the tear becomes greater, so too the body, if joined to a most excellent work, would perish.” FABRIC.] ‘No one puts a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment, nor new wine into old wineskins; otherwise [Note: [Col. 1161B] the wineskins are burst and the wine is spilled. FABRIC.] the wineskins will burst and the wine will be spilled’” (Matt. IX.16)? [Note: [Col. 1161B] And again. Mani used the same saying to introduce two Principles. Even before Mani, Marcion condemned the Law and the Prophets, as Augustine testifies, *Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets* I.1. FABRIC.] “And again: ‘There is no good tree which produces bad fruit, nor a bad tree which produces good fruit’” (Matt. VII.8).

Having received an interpretation of this from the holy presbyters, he did not submit to the truth; rather, he confirmed still more firmly the lie of his master Cerdon. Likewise he proclaimed [Note: [Col. 1161B] One God good and one evil. [Col. 1161C] Relevant to this error of Marcion and the Manichaeans is the outstanding passage in Gaudentius, Sermon 7 on Exodus, p. 74, Patavian edition: “If Marcion and Mani had deserved to understand this, they would never have said that one God of the New Testament is good, while another, evil one spoke through the old Law. In the aforementioned Law of Unleavened Bread they even dared to impute cruelty to him, saying that a human soul is destroyed because of the leaven of bread—than which nothing could be more cruel.” Philastrius contains nothing concerning this alleged cruelty of God among the errors of Marcion and Mani; nor does he say that they called the God of the New Testament good and that of the Old evil. Yet Gaudentius teaches us both points, which Fabricius might fittingly have included here in his notes on Philastrius. GALEARD.] one God good and another evil. He believed that Christ [Note: [Col. 1161C] Appeared only in appearance. Marcion appealed, among other passages, to Phil. II.7, where Christ is said to have come “in the likeness of human beings.” On this passage see, if you please, Theophylact; also Chrysostom, [Col. 1161D] Homily 83 on Matthew, pp. 863, 865. FABRIC.] appeared only in appearance—that is, as though in a shadow—and suffered shadowily, but not in true flesh. [Note: [Col. 1161D] The Gospel according to Luke. But it was mutilated in various ways and, apparently, lacked Luke’s name at its head; Marcion’s antitheses were prefixed to it. See Tertullian, *Against Marcion* IV.4; Irenaeus I.29, III.11; Origen, *Against Celsus* II, p. 77, and *Philocalia*, ch. 5; Epiphanius XLII.10 ff.; and Nicetas IV, *Treasury of Orthodox Faith*, ch. 10. In this as in other matters Marcion followed the steps of his teacher Cerdon, of whom the appendix to Tertullian’s *On Prescription*, ch. 51, says: “He receives only the Gospel of Luke, and not even the whole of it.” FABRIC.] He accepts only the Gospel according to Luke, not the Gospels, [Note: [Col. 1161D] Nor the Epistles of Paul, except—Rather, Marcion accepted Paul’s other epistles, rejecting only those to Timothy and Titus, as is evident from Tertullian, *Against Marcion* V.20, Jerome, and Epiphanius. FABRIC.] nor the epistles of the apostle Paul, except those to Timothy and Titus. Passages which say [Col. 1161B] of Christ [Note: [Col. 1161B] but passes over those concerning the true God. FABRIC.] as of a true God he passes over; but passages of Scripture which speak as though of a human being he accepts. [Col. 1162A] Nor does he confess [Note: [Col. 1162B] That Christ is judge of all. This is why Marcion rejected the Epistles to Timothy, in the latter of which it is expressly written, IV.1, that Jesus is “about to judge the living and the dead.” FABRIC.] that Christ is judge of all. Defeated and expelled [Note: [Col. 1162B] By the blessed John the Evangelist. “How can it be,” asks Latinus Latinius, “that Marcion, Cerdon’s disciple, was known in the time of the apostle John, when neither Cerdon was known before Hyginus—who is believed to have been bishop of Rome from A.D. 138 to 150—nor Marcion before Anicetus—from A.D. 150 to 154—as Irenaeus, Tertullian, and Cyprian teach?” FABRIC.] by the blessed John the Evangelist and by the presbyters of the city of Ephesus, he sowed this heresy at Rome.

### XLVI. LUCANUS

[Note: [Col. 1162C] Lucanus. He is called Lucian by Epiphanius and Damascus, *Heresy* 45, and by Nicetas IV of the *Treasury of Orthodox Faith*, ch. 15. He is distinct from Lucian, the Arian martyr, from whom the Lucianists derive their name. Moreover, Ittigius rightly noted, in his dissertation *On Heresiarchs*, p. 136, that the name “Lycus of Pontus” in Rhodo, cited by Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V.13, denotes not Lucanus, as Baronius held under A.D. 146, but Lucanus’s teacher Marcion. Besides Tertullian, *On the Resurrection*, ch. 2, and *On Prescription*, ch. 51, Lucanus is mentioned by Origen, *Against Celsus* II, p. 77: “I know of no others who have altered the Gospel except the followers of Marcion and Valentinus, and, I think, those of Lucanus.” FABRIC.]

A certain Lucanus arose after him. Maintaining and decreeing views similar to Marcion’s, he falsely taught in all things, like Marcion his master.

### XLVII. APELLES
Apelles was [Note: [Col. 1162C] His disciple. Understand: not Lucanus’s, but Marcion’s—whom Tertullian, *On Prescription*, ch. 30, calls Apelles’s instructor and fashioner. Origen, *Against Celsus*, p. 267: “Apelles, an acquaintance of Marcion”; *Homilies on Genesis*, homily 2: “Apelles, indeed a disciple of Marcion, but the inventor of a heresy differing more from that which he received from his teacher. While he wishes to maintain that the writings of Moses contain nothing of divine wisdom and nothing of the Holy Spirit, he piles up sayings of this sort,” etc. Epiphanius, vol. I, p. 380, calls Apelles Lucanus’s fellow-pupil (*syscholastēs*). FABRIC.] his disciple, preaching in some respects doctrines similar to Marcion’s. When certain persons asked him [Note: [Col. 1162B] “how”] how he understood the faith, he replied: [Note: [Col. 1162D] “I have no need to learn.” Cotelerius, *Monuments*, vol. I, p. 772, rightly emended this from “to say,” which stood in the editions. FABRIC.] “I have no need to learn from Marcion in order to assert two coeternal Principles. For I proclaim one Principle, whom I know as God; this God made the angels and also made another Power, [Note: [Col. 1162D] “Whom I know to be the second God.” Thus again Cotelerius rightly restores the text, in place of what the editions read: “whom I know to be God; the second, who is also the Power of God, which made him.” Epiphanius and John of Damascus, *Heresies* 44; Augustine; the author of the *Praedestinatus*, ch. 22; and John Zonaras in Cotelerius, *Monuments*, vol. III, p. 470, likewise report this concerning Apelles: “He confesses one supreme God, and says that the One in turn made another,” etc.] whom I know to be the second God, who is also the Power [Col. 1163A] of God, [Note: [Col. 1163A] “which made the world”] which made the world.” But this God who made the world is not, he says, good like the one who made him; rather, he is subject to that God by whom this one also was made, and he obeys that one’s will, command, and [Note: [Col. 1163B] “and obeys his precepts in all things.” This was added by Philastrius contrary to Apelles’s own view. For Apelles held that the inferior God, whom the supreme God had produced, had fallen away from that goodness through wickedness. Epiphanius, Augustine, and others state this expressly. The author of the *Praedestinatus*, ch. 22: “Apelles confesses one Principle, that is, the good; and another made by it—that is, another was made by the one Principle. When this was found wicked, it was cast out by the good. And this Principle, cast out by the good Principle because it acted wickedly against the will of the good Principle, made the world in its wickedness.” FABRIC.] precepts in all things. The Arians are now [Note: [Col. 1163B] “The Arians are now his associates.” The Arians agreed with Apelles only in introducing a second God inferior to the first; in every other respect they were far removed from his heresy. FABRIC.] his associates and supporters in thus preaching and believing.

He says that Christ appeared [Note: [Col. 1163B] “in the flesh.” He did not acquire it by birth from a mother, but fitted it to himself from the four elements. See Tertullian, *On the Flesh of Christ*, ch. [Col. 1163C] 6, and *Against Marcion*, III, ch. 11. Tertullian also attacked these inventions of Apelles more extensively in his lost work *Against the Apelleians*. FABRIC.] in the flesh, but not [Note: [Col. 1163C] “as Valentinus.” Above, ch. 38. FABRIC.] as Valentinus, as having taken flesh from heaven. [Note: [Col. 1163A] “taken flesh”] He also says [Note: [Col. 1163C] “that after the Passion he did not rise in the flesh.” Apelles maintained that Christ left his flesh in the tomb, so that it might again be scattered into the elements from which it had been taken. Gregory Nazianzen likewise touches upon this opinion of Apelles in Epistle 1, to Cledonius. See John Pearson, *On the Apostles’ Creed*, p. 480 of the Latin edition.] that after the Passion he did not rise in the flesh, but that Christ had received it from the four [Note: [Col. 1163C] “from the four elements which he had taken from the world.” This is the reading of the Hamburg edition, with which the other editions agree, but it makes no sense whatever. Yet the eminent Fabricius gave no warning at all of so evident a corruption. The Corbie manuscript opportunely supplies the passage: “Christ received from the four elements—that is, from the dry” (perhaps “the moist” should be added, which is absent from the manuscript), “the hot, and the cold—and in the resurrection again gave back to the elements [Col. 1163D] those things which he had received from the world.” In the same way our author speaks in ch. 120: “Different mixtures were established—hot, cold, dry, and moist—for the four corners of the world,” which the editions badly transmit. So, a little earlier in this same ch. 47, apart from the Hamburg edition, the Basel and Lyons editions wrongly read, “the Power of God, which made him”; but the Corbie manuscript rightly reads, “the Power of God, which made the world.” Then the Basel and Lyons editions read, “but he is subject to that God,” while the Hamburg edition has the less satisfactory “or rather, he is subject to that God.” Philastrius’s account in this ch. 47 of Apelles’s error—that Christ gave back to the four elements what he had received from the world—does not greatly differ from Virgil’s statement concerning Pallas, *Aeneid* XI.51:

[Col. 1164B] “We bring the youth lifeless, now owing nothing to any heavenly powers.”

On this passage Servius comments: “The living belong to the gods above; the dead belong to those below, as in Book XII:

‘Be gracious to me, O shades,
since the will of the gods above has turned away.’

We owe all things to the gods above while we live, because, as the natural philosophers say, when we begin to be born we receive spirit from the Sun, body from the Moon, blood from Mars, intelligence from Mercury, desire from Jupiter, appetites from Venus, and moisture from Saturn; and when dead, men seem to render these things back, each to its respective giver.” GALEARD.] elements—namely, from the dry, hot, and cold [Note: [Col. 1163A] “elements—that is, from the dry, hot, and cold—Christ received [it], and in the resurrection again gave back to the elements [Col. 1164A] what he had received from the world.”] elements which he had received from the world—and that he dismissed these into the earth, [Note: [Col. 1164A] “but he himself [ascended] into heaven”] while he himself ascended into heaven without flesh.

[Note: [Col. 1164B] “Under the Apostles.” This must be understood broadly, as including times after those of the Apostles. The words which the editions here prefixed to the following chapters as though they were a new heading—“Catalogue of heresies which arose under the Apostles” [Col. 1164C]—I have rightly deleted as extraneous and wholly inappropriate in this place. FABRIC.] These, then, were the heresies in order under the Apostles.

### XLVIII. [Note: [Col. 1164C] Tatian. In Sicardus’s Basel edition, *Tacianus*, with which the Corbie manuscript agrees. Isidore, *Etymologies* VIII.5, does not distinguish Tatianists from Encratites, saying: “The Tatianists are so called from a certain Tatian, and are also called Encratites, because they abhor meat.” Epiphanius, however, distinguishes Tatianists and Encratites by calling the Encratites schismatics of Tatian, as Augustine reports in *On Heresies*, ch. 25. On the Encratites, see Philastrius, ch. 72. GALEARD.] TATIAN

[Note: [Col. 1164C] “After the persecution of Decius.” This is an error either of Philastrius or, as I prefer to think, of a copyist: Tatian’s heresy preceded the persecution of Decius, which afflicted Christians in A.D. 250, by nearly a hundred years. Thus Allatius, *On Eustathius of Antioch*, p. 7, reads “Hadrian” instead of “Decius.” “Aelius” would be nearer the truth. FABRIC.] After the persecution of Decius there was [Note: [Col. 1164A] “Tatian, moreover, a disciple of St Justin”] a certain Tatian, a disciple of Saint Justin Martyr. He withdrew from the truth [Note: [Col. 1164C] “after his [master’s] passion.” Theodoret, *Compendium of Heretical Fables*, I.20: “After the completion [death] of the teacher”; Epiphanius [Col. 1164D] XLVI.1: “When holy Justin died,” etc.; Irenaeus, I.31: “After his martyrdom.” Saint Justin suffered martyrdom in A.D. 150, in the twelfth year of Antoninus Pius. FABRIC.] after his martyrdom, and despised in every respect the teaching [Note: [Col. 1164A] “of so great and blessed a [martyr]”] of so great and blessed a martyr and teacher, saying that certain [Note: [Col. 1164D] “Aeons.” Augustine, *Heresies* 25, calls them “fabulous emanations of ages.” Irenaeus, I.31, observes that Tatian agreed with Valentinus in this respect; hence the author of the appendix to Tertullian’s *On Prescription*, ch. 51, says that he entirely savoured of Valentinus. FABRIC.] Aeons had been emitted from heaven. He further added this: [Note: [Col. 1164D] “Adam is not saved.” On this opinion of Tatian see B. Ittigius, *On Heresiarchs*, p. 206 ff.; Samuel Andreae, dissertation *On Adam’s Salvation*; and Vossius, *Theological Theses*, dissertation 2, thesis II, p. 50. Saint Irenaeus refuted Tatian superbly in III.34, 35, and 39. FABRIC.] that Adam, [Col. 1165A] our forefather, the first-created man, is not saved. In proclaiming Aeons he raved [Note: [Col. 1165B] “as Marcion.” Rather, as Valentinus. Philastrius says nothing above, in ch. 45, concerning Aeons in Marcion. FABRIC.] as Marcion did. He also [Note: [Col. 1165B] “Human generation.” Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* I, p. 223, testifies that the Encratites abhorred procreation (*paidopoiia*) together with marriage. Compare Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* IV.29, drawing on Irenaeus.] detests human procreation, rejects the lawful right of marriage, and does not acknowledge that this institution was established by God.

### XLIX. CATAPHRYGIANS

After these, others arose: [Note: [Col. 1165B] “Cataphrygians.” The Montanists, from Phrygia as their native land of origin, were called “those of Phrygia” (*hoi kata Phrygas*), also “Phrygians,” and by Epiphanius “Phrygasts.” Nazianzen, *Oration* 14, p. 221: “the madness of the Phrygians still even now.” FABRIC.] Cataphrygians, dwelling in the province of Phrygia. They [Note: [Col. 1165C] “accept the Prophets and the Law.” Epiphanius XLVIII.1: “They accept all Scripture, Old and New Testament.” FABRIC.] accept the Prophets and the Law; [Note: [Col. 1165C] “confess the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.” Epiphanius likewise: “Concerning Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, they think in the same manner as the holy catholic Church.” This is sufficiently apparent also from the writings of Tertullian after he had become a Montanist. Therefore, the error of Sabellius which certain ancient writers charge against the Montanists must be attributed neither to Montanus himself nor to the whole sect, but to a few persons from Montanus’s school who departed from their teacher on this point. FABRIC.] they confess the Father, the Son, and the Spirit; and they expect [Note: [Col. 1165C] “the resurrection of the flesh.” Epiphanius: “And they likewise affirm a resurrection of the dead.” Tertullian, already Montanus’s disciple, also defended this doctrine excellently in his special work *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*. In the final chapter and in ch. 11 he praises the new prophecy of the overflowing Paraclete, concerning whom Prisca spoke strikingly through a prophetess: “They are flesh and hate the flesh.” FABRIC.] the resurrection of the flesh, which the catholic Church also proclaims.

They proclaim certain persons of their own as prophets—namely, [Note: [Col. 1165D] “Montanus, Priscilla, and Maximilla.” Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*, ch. 1: “For at that time Praxeas compelled the bishop of Rome [Victor, about A.D. 198], who had already acknowledged the prophecies of Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla and who, as a result of that acknowledgement, was bringing peace to the churches of Asia and Phrygia, to revoke letters of peace already issued and to desist from his plan to receive the charismatic gifts, by making false assertions concerning those prophets and their churches and by defending the authority of his predecessors.” Tertullian, *On the Soul*, ch. 9: “There is among us today a sister endowed with gifts of revelations,” etc. Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, vol. II, p. 419 ff., discusses these alleged prophecies with his usual care and learning. See Didymus in the *Catena* on Acts X.10, in Wolf’s *Anecdota*, vol. IV, p. 49 ff. FABRIC.] Montanus, Priscilla, and Maximilla—whom neither the prophets nor Christ proclaimed. They further add that the fullness [Note: [Col. 1165D] “the fullness of the Holy Spirit.” The Montanists denied that Christ’s promise to bestow the Holy Spirit had been completely fulfilled in the outpouring upon the Apostles in Acts II. Rather, they held that its more perfect manifestation [Col. 1166B] was fulfilled in Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla, and that no prophets thereafter were to be expected. Maximilla in Epiphanius XLVIII.2: “After me there will no longer be a prophetess, but the consummation.” FABRIC.] of the Holy Spirit was not granted through [Note: [Col. 1165B] “the blessed Apostles, Christ giving [it]”] the Apostles by Christ’s gift, but judge it to have been imparted through their own false prophets. They separate themselves from the catholic Church [Note: [Col. 1165B] “because of their own prophets . . . Pepuza”] through those false prophets and false teachers.

These people [Note: [Col. 1166B] “baptize the dead.” See Vossius, *Disputations on Baptism*, XII, thesis 2, p. 159 ff., who rightly distinguishes from this Montanist abuse another practice of the Cerinthians and Marcionites, who baptized the living on behalf of the dead, [Col. 1166C] concerning which see Grotius on 1 Corinthians XV.29 and William Wall, *History of Infant Baptism*, English edition, p. 239 ff. FABRIC.] baptize the dead; [Note: [Col. 1166C] “celebrate mysteries publicly.” Epiphanius XLVIII.14, speaking of the Cataphrygian Pepuza: “Those who go there perform certain mysteries in the place and sanctify it, as they suppose.” FABRIC.] they publicly celebrate mysteries; and they call their village [Note: [Col. 1166C] “Pepuza.” Earlier editions incorrectly read *Pepura*. Epiphanius XLVIII.14: “Such people also honour a certain deserted place in Phrygia, once called the city of Pepuza, but now razed to the ground; and they say that the Jerusalem above comes down there.” On the Pepuzians see XLIX.1. FABRIC.] Pepuza, so called in Phrygia, Jerusalem. There Maximilla, Priscilla, and Montanus himself are known to have spent their vain and unfruitful lives. There too the [Note: [Col. 1166C] “mystery of the Cynics.” Another reading is “of the stage-players,” but I think *Cyntillianorum* should be read, written in place of *Quintillianorum*. Epiphanius XLVIII.14: “In the allied sect of this heresy, called that of the Quintillians—that is, the Priscillians and Pepuzians—they say that a terrible and unlawful deed takes place. For at a certain feast they prick a very small child all over his body with bronze needles and obtain his blood for the supposed practice of sacrifice.” FABRIC.] mystery of the Cynics is celebrated, together with an execrable impiety involving an infant. For they say that at Easter they mix the infant’s blood into their sacrifice, [Note: [Col. 1165B] “and thus send forth their destructive satellites.”] and in this way send out everywhere their destructive and false emissaries.

### L. THEODOTUS

After these there was [Note: [Col. 1166D] “Theodotus the Byzantine.” This is the tanner, distinct from Theodotus the Montanist, mentioned by Asterius Urbanus in Eusebius V.16, and from Theodotus the banker, the founder of the Melchizedekians, discussed below at ch. 52. On Theodotus the Tanner see B. Ittigius, *On Heresiarchs*, p. 259 ff.; to this add Pearson, part II of the *Vindication of Ignatius*, p. 23, and his posthumous works, p. 147 ff.; also my notes on Saint Hippolytus’s *Against Noetus*, vol. II, p. 7. FABRIC.] a certain Theodotus, Byzantine by origin, [Col. 1166B] a denier of Christ [Note: [Col. 1166B] “of our God”] our God [Note: [Col. 1166D] “in the persecution.” Behold the shameful reason for stripping Christ of divinity: in order, evidently, that his denial during persecution, as the denial of a mere man, might seem more excusable. Pappus’s *Synodicon*, ch. 3, on Theodotus of Byzantium: “Having denied Christ, and being severely reproached by the faithful, he could not bear the disgrace. The impious man dared to say, ‘I did not deny God, but a mere man.’” FABRIC.] and Savior during persecution. He began to teach as follows: [Note: [Col. 1166B] “He was a common man . . . he denied”] “Christ was a common [Col. 1167A] man, like all human beings.” He said this so that he might no longer endure from people the reproach of his denial. For he thought that if someone said to him, “Why did you deny Christ, God and Lord?” he could answer, “I denied a man, not God.”

They use [Note: [Col. 1167B] “passages of Scripture.” A specimen may be found in the *Excerpts of Theodotus* at the end of Clement of Alexandria. FABRIC.] passages of Scripture which teach concerning Christ as though he were a human being; [Note: [Col. 1167B] “but those which speak of him as God . . . they do not accept.”] but they do not accept those which speak of him as God. Reading but in no way understanding, they show themselves to be associates of pagan impiety and Jewish blindness rather than sharers in Christian salvation.

### LI. THE HERESY CONCERNING THE SUBSTANCE OF FATHER AND SON

There are others who speak of [Note: [Col. 1167B] “saying *metangismon*, that is”] [Note: [Col. 1167C] “*Metangismos*.” I have written this in place of the worthless word *metanismon*. Augustine and the author of the *Praedestinatus*, ch. 58, mention heretics called Metangismonites, from the word *angeion*, meaning a vessel, because they taught that the Son was in the Father as a smaller vessel within a larger vessel. Compare Nicetas, *Treasury*, I.3–4; II.59; and II.82. FABRIC.] *metangismos*: that is, that the Son enters into the Father and exists in him as a vessel within a vessel. They do not understand what they assert. For the Savior did not say that the Son enters [Col. 1167B] into the Father; rather, he taught equality in divinity and power, not [Note: [Col. 1167C] “entry or containment”—by which the Son would be contained within the Father as the greater. FABRIC.] entry or containment, [Note: [Col. 1167C] “as they suppose . . . thinking this.” The Corbie manuscript rightly reads: “as those madmen rave . . . thinking this.” I do not know how the remaining words intruded here from the heresy of the Cataphrygians, where precisely the same words occur above in ch. 49. Certainly the reference here to false prophets—appropriate there because of Montanus and Priscilla—is out of place; all the rest is likewise superfluous and absurd, a point Fabricius wholly failed to observe. GALEARD.] as they suppose, to have been imparted.

And they separate themselves from the catholic Church because of their own false prophets; [Note: [Col. 1167B] “as those madmen rave, agreeing with them”] as madmen, holding this opinion and failing to understand that as the [Note: [Col. 1167C] “Father is immense, so also are the Son and the Holy Spirit.” In almost the same words, the creed called Athanasian states: “The Father is immense, the Son immense, the Holy Spirit immense.” FABRIC.] Father is immense, so also are the Son and the Holy Spirit—equal in all things—so that the Trinity is immutable, immense, [Col. 1168A] omnipotent, and eternal everywhere. [Note: [Col. 1168B] “everywhere to us”] This is most plainly proclaimed to us in the holy Scriptures: there are three Persons, living forever, equal in all majesty and power; yet the Son and the Holy Spirit are properly from the Father.

### LII. CONCERNING MELCHIZEDEK

After these, [Note: [Col. 1167D] “Others.” In this chapter Philastrius seems to refer to Theodotus the Banker, founder of the Melchizedekians, as Latinius rightly observed. He taught that Melchizedek was a Power of God superior to Christ, because Christ is said to be a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek; Christ acts for human beings, having become their intercessor and advocate, while Melchizedek acts for the heavenly angels and powers. See the appendix to Tertullian’s *On Prescription*, final chapter; Epiphanius and John of Damascus, *Heresies* 55; Augustine and the author of the *Praedestinatus*, ch. 34; Theodoret, *Compendium of Heretical Fables* II.6; and our author below, ch. 143. FABRIC.] others departed from these and said similar things. They also assert that Melchizedek the [Note: [Col. 1168B] “priest [is], they say, a great Power . . . departing [from the faith].”] priest is a great Power of God, and they maintain certain different names for human beings, departing from the catholic faith. [Note: [Col. 1167D] “Certain different names for human beings.” From Epiphanius LV.2, where the Melchizedekians are said to have claimed names for Melchizedek’s parents: his father Heraclas, his mother Astaroth or Asteria. FABRIC.]

### LIII. NOETIANS

Others are called Noetians after a certain [Note: [Col. 1168B] “of a certain senseless man named Noetus.” This passage should be read and punctuated thus; the editions wrongly had: “Other senseless Noetians, of a certain man named Noetian.” It is plainly an allusion to the name *Noetus* (*noētos*), since “senseless” is *anoētos*. Thus Cerdon was called *akerdōn*, Eunomius Anomius, Sibyl *abylla*, Macarius *amakarios*, Eudoxius Adoxius, Eusebius Asebius, Eutyches Atyches, Eutactus Atactus, and similarly. The heresy of Noetus, which first emerged from him around A.D. 245, was effectively refuted by Saint Hippolytus, whose work is available in Greek and Latin in the latter volume of the works of that holy martyr, recently published by me. FABRIC.] senseless man named Noetus. He said that the almighty Father himself is Christ, and that he himself was born, himself suffered, and himself died in the body. He also said [Col. 1168B] that he was Moses and that his brother was [Note: [Col. 1168C] “the prophet Elijah.” Rather, Aaron. Saint Hippolytus, p. 6, *On Noetus*: “This man said that he was Moses and that his brother was Aaron.” Epiphanius and John of Damascus, *Heresies* 57, repeat the same from Hippolytus. FABRIC.] the prophet Elijah.

### LIV. SABELLIUS

After him Sabellius, [Note: [Col. 1168C] “from Libya.” Basil, Epistle 63, calls him a Libyan heretic; so do Nicephorus VI.25 and Nicetas of Byzantium, *For the Council of Chalcedon*, p. 675. Sabellius’s heresy broke out around A.D. 257. We lack D. Ittigius’s [Col. 1168D] *Tou Makaritou* dissertation, which he promised in the *Heptad of Dissertations*, p. 432. Meanwhile one may consult the Reverend Christian Worm’s *History of Sabellianism*, published in octavo in 1696. See also Epiphanius and John of Damascus, *Heresies* 62; Augustine and the author of the *Praedestinatus*, ch. 41; Victor of Vita III.6; Euthymius’s *Panoply*, title X, vol. XIX of the Lyons edition of the *Library of the Fathers*, p. 61; the Benedictines’ notes on Saint Ambrose, vol. II, p. 445; and Petavius, *Theological Dogmas concerning the Holy Trinity*, p. 33 ff. FABRIC.] a disciple of his from Libya, likewise followed the likeness and error of his teacher. Thus they were later called Sabellians, and also [Note: [Col. 1168D] “Patripassians,” because they taught that the Father suffered under the form (*schēma*) of the Son. Compare Petavius, *On the Incarnation*, I.5; Pearson, *On the Apostles’ Creed*, pp. 281, 566; Elmenhorst on Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, p. 103; and Beveridge on the *Synodicon*, p. 92. FABRIC.] Patripassians; Praxeans, after [Note: [Col. 1168D] “Praxeas.” Tertullian’s distinguished book *Against Praxeas* survives. FABRIC.] Praxeas; and Hermogenians, after [Note: [Col. 1168D] “Hermogenes.” Augustine and the author of the *Praedestinatus*, ch. 41, infer from Philastrius that Hermogenes belonged to Sabellius’s company. But Tertullian, who refuted Hermogenes’s error concerning the eternity of matter in a special work, says not a word (*ne gry*) about any Patripassianism of Hermogenes. FABRIC.] Hermogenes. They were [Note: [Col. 1168B] “in Africa, and thus”] in [Col. 1169A] Africa, and because they held these views were cast out from the catholic Church.

### LV. THE HERESY OF SELEUCUS AND HERMIAS CONCERNING A CORPOREAL GOD

What is this folly [Note: [Col. 1169B] “of the Galatians.” Below, ch. 56, Hermiorites and Proclianites are said to dwell in parts of Galatia. In Nazianzen, *Oration* 14, p. 221, “the folly of the Galatians” refers to similar heretics, while also repeating words from Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians III.1. Jerome observes that the Apostle reproaches them with the characteristic quality of their own region; and the poet Callimachus likewise reproaches the Galatians with stupidity in his *Hymn to Delos*, v. 184, calling them “a senseless race.” FABRIC.] of the Galatians—of the heretics [Note: [Col. 1169B] “Seleucus and Hermias.” Compare Augustine and the author of the *Praedestinatus*, ch. 59, on the Seleucians and Hermians. The Hermias of Philastrius and Augustine is the same as the Hermogenes to whom Tertullian addressed a special book in opposition. FABRIC.] Seleucus and Hermias? When they maintain that God [Note: [Col. 1169B] “to be incorporeal . . . not made.”] is corporeal, they also assert that *hylē*, that is, the matter of the world, is coeternal with God. They do not understand matter—the matter of the elements, which is without soul and therefore irrational—to have been made by God the Father through the Son from nothing, so that what had not previously existed might exist. [Note: [Col. 1169B] “They do not understand it thus.” They do not understand, as the catholic [Col. 1169C] Church understands, that matter was created from nothing by God the Father through the Son, and was commanded into existence (*ex ouk ontōn*), though it had not existed before; nor that souls were made by the same God through the Son. Rather, they make that matter, lacking a rational soul and mother of the elements, a goddess coeternal with God. They maintain that rational souls are not created by God but proceed from matter through angelic creators. Philastrius states this, in his usual manner, somewhat obscurely. FABRIC.]

They say that the spirit of a human being—that is, the soul—was not made by God through the Son, but [Note: [Col. 1169C] “is from the earth.” That is, as I have already shown, it proceeds from matter. Therefore Hermogenes in Theodoret, *Compendium of Heretical Fables* I.19, taught that the devil and demons would likewise be poured back into matter: “The devil and the demons will be poured back into matter.” FABRIC.] is from the earth. They assert that evil [Note: [Col. 1169C] “at one time [comes] from God, at another from matter.” This is a remarkable stupidity of these heretics, unlike nearly all the others who posit two coeternal Principles: they sought the cause of evil even in the good God, not in [Col. 1169D] matter alone. FABRIC.] sometimes comes from God and sometimes is from matter. They deny that the Savior sits in the flesh at the Father’s right hand, but say that he [Col. 1170A] [Note: [Col. 1169D] “laid aside the flesh.” That is, he stripped himself of flesh and deposited it in the sun as his future dwelling-place. The Seleucians and Hermians taught that Christ’s body did not ascend beyond the sun, but was stripped off by Christ there and deposited in it. Augustine and the author of the *Praedestinatus*, ch. 59, correctly draw this from Philastrius: “They deny that the Savior sits in the flesh at the right hand of the Father; instead, they say that he laid it aside and placed it in the sun.” Pearson rightly observed, *On the Apostles’ Creed*, p. 482, that this double invention pleased the Manichaeans as well. Gregory Nazianzen, Epistle 1 to Cledonius, concerning them: “For where is the body now, if not with the one who assumed it? Surely it has not, according to the babblings of the Manichaeans, been deposited in the sun, in order to be honoured through dishonour.” Augustine, *Against Faustus* XX.2, teaches that, according to the Manichaeans, the Father had established his seat in inaccessible Light, the Son in the light of sun and moon, and the Holy Spirit throughout the whole expanse of the air. In Tractate 34 on John, he says that they held Christ himself to be the sun: “The Manichaeans thought that this sun, visible to bodily eyes and exposed openly for viewing not only by human beings but even by cattle, was Christ the Lord.” The *Catena of the Fathers* on Psalm XVIII: “For attention must not be paid to the foolish talk of heretics who say: ‘After the resurrection the Savior deposited in the solar sphere the body which he wore, to be kept until the second coming.’” Theodoret, *Compendium of Heretical Fables* I.19, on Hermogenes: “He said that the Lord’s body was deposited in the sun.” In the *Excerpts of Theodotus*, p. [Col. 1170C] 808: “He placed his tabernacle in the sun.” “Some say that the Lord placed his body in the sun, as Hermogenes [did].” Is. Vossius, ch. 5 of *On the Sibylline Oracles*, also thinks the following Sibylline verse pertains to this:

“Then from the sun God will send a king,
who will bring the whole earth to rest from the evil of war.” FABRIC.] laid aside the flesh and placed it in the sun. For the Prophet said—though they do not know what he said—[Note: [Col. 1170C] “The Prophet said.” Psalm XVIII (XIX), 6 (4), whose meaning Justin, *Questions to the Orthodox*, 63, takes to be: “He made the heavens the sun’s tabernacle.”] “He placed his tabernacle in the sun.”

They maintain that Paradise is visible [Note: [Col. 1170B] “they, like Plato, affirm a visible Paradise.”] in accordance with [Note: [Col. 1170C] “from Plato.” *Phaedo*, p. 401. FABRIC.] Plato. Serving such vanities, and thinking that human souls come [Note: [Col. 1170C] “from fire and spirit.” The author of the *Praedestinatus*, ch. 59: “They do not attribute the soul to God the Creator, but maintain that angels are creators of souls from fire and spirit.” FABRIC.] from fire and spirit, they do not use this baptism because of the saying of John the Baptist: [Note: [Col. 1170C] “He himself will baptize you . . .” John the Baptist’s saying. From this passage of Philastrius it cannot, I think, be proved that the Seleucians and Hermians used a baptism of fire as well; John Gottfried Olearius rightly observed this in his dissertation *On the Baptism of the Holy Spirit and Fire*, defended at Leipzig under R. D. John Schmid in 1706, §14. FABRIC.] “He himself will baptize you in Spirit and fire” (Mark I.8).

[Note: [Col. 1170D] “These say that angels are the creators of our souls.” The heresy of Seleucus and Hermias—that angels are the creators of our souls—which Fabricius treats very thinly above in note c, is examined more fully by Desiderius Heraldus, *Observations on Arnobius*, II, p. 89. Compare Fevardentius’s notes on Irenaeus II.2. GALEARD.] These say that angels, not Christ the Savior, are the creators of our souls. They assert that this world is hell; and they proclaim that the resurrection is this procreation of children which occurs daily in the human race. They do not proclaim or await that future and glorious resurrection unto immortality.

### LVI. PROCLIANS
Other disciples of these persons are called Proclianites, and Hermiorites. They add further errors, teaching that what is written in Ezekiel concerning the four living creatures means that the lion represents the king of the Parthians, the calf the Egyptians, the eagle the Romans, and the man the devout—that is, Christians.

[Note: Col. 1170B: They are called Prodianites and Hermeonites.]

[Note: Col. 1170D: Proclianites. The earlier editions wrongly read “Prodianites.” See Augustine and the author of the *Praedestinatus*, ch. 60, who states that they were named after a certain Proclus. They are therefore different from the Montanists κατὰ Proclum (“according to Proclus”), concerning whom see the appendix to Tertullian’s *On Prescription*, ch. 52. Proclus is also mentioned by Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VI.20. FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1171A: Hermiorites. That is, disciples of Hermias, mentioned in the preceding chapter; they are elsewhere called Hermians or Hermogenianians. I have written “Hermiorites” rather than “Hermiotites,” because I observed that Philastrius delights in this termination, as above in Musorites and Puteorites. FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1171B: In Ezekiel. See Ezekiel 1:5 ff. Philastrius’s opinion concerning these four living creatures will be known below, in heresies 135, 148, and 149. FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1171B: King of the Parthians. I believe this should be written instead of “of the shepherds,” which the earlier editions presented and which rightly seemed obscure to the most learned Jacob Thomasius, who discussed this passage of Philastrius at length in his *Prefaces*, pp. 385 ff. The name “Parthians” is used here either for Persians, as Salmasius noted that Tertullian and others did, in his notes on *On the Pallium*, p. 119—likewise “Persians” for Parthians: Valesius on Ammianus XXXI.2, p. 620; Ez. Spanheim, p. 149b, on Julian, *Oration* 1—or, as I prefer, since they are placed before the Egyptians, for Assyrians. Thus Ammianus Marcellinus also used “Parthians” for Assyrians, XXVIII.4: “With enormous deformity of flattery, feeling their way before a newcomer, they exalt him so highly that the Parthians [exalt] Semiramis, Egypt Cleopatras, the Carians Artemisia, or the Palmyrenes Zenobia.” (“The Palmyrenes Zenobia.”) Herm. Witsius, *Miscellanea Sacra*, vol. I, dissertation 8, noted that Assyrians are thus put for Persians, who, after defeating the Babylonians, subjected Assyria to themselves. There was also in Egypt a royal dynasty, the seventeenth in number, called that of the Shepherds. But the distinct subsequent mention of the Egyptians does not permit Philastrius to be explained of that dynasty. FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1171C: The calf of the Egyptians. As they assigned the lion to the Assyrians because of their power, so they assigned the calf to the Egyptians because Apis was worshipped by them in the form of a calf, as was Mnevis also. See Herodotus III.28, Strabo XVII, p. 555, Ammianus XXII.13, Pliny, *Natural History* VIII.46, and others. FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1171C: The eagle of the Romans. Because of the eagle standard which the Romans had long employed, especially since the time of Gaius Marius, according to Pliny, *Natural History* X.4. Nicholas of Lyra, and Rabbi Eliezer among the Jews, also understood the eagle in Ezekiel’s vision as the Roman Empire. See the cited *Prefaces* of Jacob Thomasius, pp. 389, 399. FABRIC.]

They use the book of Wisdom of that Sirach who wrote after Solomon—that is, many ages later—as the one book of Wisdom.

[Note: Col. 1171D: The devout. That is, Christians. This interpretation of Ezekiel’s living creatures, which Philastrius here attributes to heretics, is scarcely to be found elsewhere. FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1171D: One book of Wisdom. It is well established that the volume of Ecclesiasticus is commonly called by the ancients sometimes “the Wisdom of Sirach” or “of Jesus,” sometimes “all-virtuous Wisdom,” sometimes praised under Solomon’s name, and sometimes simply “Wisdom,” with no author’s name attached. One may therefore reasonably be surprised that Philastrius lists among the Proclianites’ heresies their use of Sirach’s Wisdom as though it were Solomon’s. Although it is entirely true that it was written long after Solomon’s time, Philastrius ought not to have overlooked that many other sound and catholic writers did likewise. A great number of them are cited by Serarius on the first epistle of St Boniface and by Cotelerius on the epistle of Clement of Rome, pp. 178 ff. See also St Ambrose on Psalm 36, vol.
