I of the Benedictine edition, p. 807. FABRIC.]

Denying that Christ came in the flesh, and disbelieving in the Resurrection and Judgment, they dwell in regions of Galatia and, hiding like foxes, plunder many, as Solomon testified when he said: “Catch for us the little foxes, destroying the vineyard of the Lord the Saviour.”

[Note: Col. 1172B: Denying that he came in the flesh. Augustine, in his chapter 60 on heresies, excerpted this single error of the Proclianites from Philastrius in the same words. But the author of the *Praedestinatus* says: “These people say that the Son of God appeared on earth as the angel Raphael or Gabriel did—not by assuming flesh, but as an appearance; that is, only κατὰ δόκησιν [“in appearance”], not in a true human body.” Since he adds that they entertain no other error, I infer that this writer—something I suspect from other arguments too—did not consult Philastrius, who mentions more errors, but had only Augustine’s book at hand, which he continually follows κατὰ πόδα, “step by step.” FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1172B: In regions of Galatia. See, if you please, what was said in the preceding chapter. FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1172B–C: Hiding like foxes. The author of the *Praedestinatus*: “They mingle with the people of God so that they are not recognized. Finally, because they entertain no other error, they communicate with us; and this is the worse, because whenever they find simple-minded persons, they make them think and believe as they do.” FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1172C: Solomon. The true Solomon, of course, not that of the Proclianites: Song of Songs 2:15. This passage is very frequently applied by the ancients to heretics who rend the Church. Moreover, that foxes especially lie in wait for grapes is well known from Nicander, Theocritus, and others, whose passages Bochart cites, *Hierozoicon* III.13. FABRIC.]

## LVII. FLORIANS, OR CARPOCRATIANS

The Florians, also called Carpocratians, who are also called Soldiers because they came from military people, deny Judgment and the Resurrection. They do not believe that Christ was born of the Virgin. They suppose that the entire Resurrection consists in the begetting of children through abominable intercourse. Thus, in their church after sunset, with the lamps extinguished, they have not hesitated to mingle with women, thinking to fulfil the commandment of the Law: “Increase and multiply” (Gen. 1:28). They hasten to submit rather to abominable Judaism and paganism than to rest in Christian truth, maintaining instead the life and madness of beasts—whom Scripture also likened to the life of beasts (2 Pet. 2:12).

[Note: Col. 1172C: Florians. They should rather be called Florinians, from Florinus; nevertheless Augustine and the author of the *Praedestinatus*, ch. 66, also call them Florians, although the latter calls him Florian. He is Florinus, the Valentinian presbyter at Rome in the time of Emperor Commodus, about AD 182, against whom St Irenaeus wrote a book *On the Ogdoad* and a book *On Monarchy, or That God Is Not the Author of Evils*. See Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V.20; Theodoret, *Compendium of Heretical Fables* I.23. There was also a certain Flora to whom the heretic Ptolemy wrote, in Epiphanius XXXIII.3. FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1171A: Others are Florians, or …]

[Note: Col. 1172C–D: Carpocratians. It is surprising that Philastrius inserts the Carpocratians here, since he had already spoken of Carpocrates above in ch. 35. Neither Augustine nor the author of the *Praedestinatus* adds a word about the Carpocratianism of the Florians; and Dodwell, in his sixth dissertation on Irenaeus, p. 432, rightly doubts whether Philastrius transmitted this on adequate authority. FABRIC.—“Florians, or Carpocratians.” This passage from Philastrius is cited in the *Collections* on Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* III, p. 514, Potter edition. Concerning Florinus and his associate Blastus, see Eusebius V.15, Valesius edition; Massuet rightly corrects the translation of this passage, dissertation 2 on St Irenaeus, art. 3, §59. Philastrius criticizes Florinus again below, ch. 79. GALEARD.]

[Note: Col. 1172D–1173B: Soldiers. In Epiphanius XXVI.3, and thence in Damascene, heresy 26, the name στρατιωτικῶν, “Soldiers,” occurs among Gnostic appellations. Certainly, what Philastrius subsequently reports of these heretics and their doctrines accords more with Epiphanius’s Gnostics than with Florinus. FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1173B: Resurrection. Florinus taught that our flesh is the cause of evil, as Gennadius notes in ch. 126 of *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*. FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1173B–C: Born of the Virgin. Those denied that he was truly born who, with Valentinus, taught that Christ had flesh of a special quality from heavenly matter and received nothing from the holy Virgin. Above, ch. 38. FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1173B: “consists in … after sunset, with lamps …”]

[Note: Col. 1173C: With lamps extinguished. The foulness of certain heretics gave pagans an occasion for slandering all Christians as though they delighted in such lusts and indiscriminate sexual intercourse. See B. D. Christian Kortholt, *The Pagan Slanderer*, p. 99 and pp. 546 ff.; and John Bona, *Liturgical Matters* I.4. Grotius observed that the licentiousness of the Carpocratians is censured in Jude, verse 7. FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1173C: “Increase and multiply.” Greek: Αὐξάνεσθε καὶ πληθύνεσθε, “Increase and multiply.” FABRIC.]

## LVIII. HERESY CONCERNING THE FEAST OF EASTER

There are also those who dispute about the most salutary day of Easter, asserting that Easter must be celebrated on the fourteenth day of the moon, not as the catholic Church celebrates it, and that it must always be celebrated in March. When they do this, they do not always observe the Lord’s Day as Easter; they do not reckon the hours and days, but celebrate on the second, third, fourth, fifth, or sixth day. Through this error they do not recognize the one true and saving day of the Easter of our Lord, established for the whole world and confirmed by the Lord through the numerical course of the moon, the months, and intercalations. Since they do not calculate these things, they do not know what they celebrate.

[Note: Col. 1173B: Others who concern themselves with the day …]

[Note: Col. 1173C: The fourteenth moon. On the fourteenth day of the month, whatever weekday it might fall upon. Hence they were called Quartodecimans, or Tessarescaedecatites; see below, ch. 87. Concerning Blastus, see the author of the appendix to Tertullian’s *On Prescription*, ch. 53: “He wishes secretly to introduce Judaism; for he says that Easter is not to be observed otherwise than according to the Law of Moses, on the fourteenth of the month. But who does not know that evangelical grace is nullified if he reduces Christ to the Law?” FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1173D: Not as the catholic Church. The Church celebrates Easter on the Lord’s Day after the full moon; Augustine says in Letter 119 (new edition, 55), ch. 9, that this is characteristic of Christian religion. FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1173D: Always in March. That is, in the month corresponding to the Hebrew Nisan. Petavius, *On the Doctrine of Times* II.58, should be consulted on this passage of Philastrius. FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1173D: Hours and days. From Christ’s burial to his resurrection. FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1173D–1174B: On the second, third, fourth, fifth, or sixth day. Namely, according as the fourteenth lunar day falls upon the second, third, fourth, fifth, or sixth weekday. See Bochart, *Hierozoicon* II.10, vol. I, p. 562. FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1174B: The day of Easter of our Lord. Sunday: κυριακὴ ἡμέρα, “the Lord’s Day,” Rev. 1:10; μία σαββάτων, “the first day of the week,” Acts 20:7 and 1 Cor. 16:2. Thus the Lord’s Day replaces the Sabbath as a weekly Church holiday; see learned writers on the Epistle of Barnabas, ch. 15. FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1174C: By the numerical course of the moon, months, and intercalations. By the numerical course of the moon, so that it is celebrated after the full moon; by the months, now March and now April; by intercalations, that is, insertion of days, and especially of a Sabbath, until the day of the sun appointed for the celebration of Easter arrives. FABRIC.]

## LIX. CHILIONETITES

There is another heresy of the Chilionetites—that is, “of a thousand years”—which teaches thus: when Christ comes from heaven, those thousand years will again be ours for living carnally, begetting children, and eating, as happens daily now in this age. They are ignorant that heavenly food will be present—that is, the reward of immortality, not this perishable and passing thing. For when certain Jews supposed this, the Lord said in the Gospel: “You do not know the Scriptures, and you are ignorant of their power; for on the day of judgment they will neither marry nor be given in marriage, but will be like angels” (Matt. 22:29). And again the Apostle says: “The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness, peace, and everlasting joy in the Spirit of the Lord” (Rom. 14:17).

[Note: Col. 1173B, 1174C: Chilionetites. Augustine says of the Cerinthians in ch. 8 of *On Heresies*: “They also invent a fable that for a thousand years after the resurrection there will be an earthly kingdom of Christ, according to the carnal pleasures of the belly and lust; hence they are also called Chiliasts.” “Chilionetites” is a more explicit designation than Chiliasts, Milliasts, or Millenarians, for in the latter names only the trace of the number appears, whereas Chilionetites are called from a chiliad ἐτῶν, “of years.” Thus Epiphanius used χιλιονταετηρίδα, “a thousand-year period,” LXXVII.26, p. 1031. In Victor of Vita I.10, “Millenarians” are commanders over a thousand soldiers among the Vandals under Genseric. FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1174C–D: “When Christ comes … for living.” Petersenius wrongly cites this passage of Philastrius concerning the Chilionetites, as Ittigius notes, *Ecclesiastical History*, first century, p. 296. GALEARD.]

[Note: Col. 1174D: Heavenly food. Of those reclining with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of God, Matt. 8:11. FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1174B: “when the Lord … and their power”]

[Note: Col. 1174D: And their power. In Matthew and Mark 12:24 it is also: μηδὲ τὴν δύναμιν τοῦ Θεοῦ, “nor the power of God.” In the Clementine *Homilies* 2.51, 3.50, and 18.20: Διὰ τοῦτο πλανᾶσθε, μὴ εἰδότες τὰ ἀλεθῆ τῶν γραφῶν, οὗ εἵνεκεν ἀγνοεῖτε καὶ τὴν δύναμιν τοῦ Θεοῦ: “For this reason you are deceived: you do not know the truths of the Scriptures, and for that reason you are ignorant also of the power of God.” FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1174B: “nor are given in marriage, but …”]

[Note: Col. 1174D: Like angels. In Matthew: ἀλλ᾽ ὡς ἄγγελοι τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐν οὐρανῷ εἰσι, “but are as the angels of God in heaven.” Mark likewise: Ἀλλ᾽ εἰσὶν ὡς ἄγγελοι οἱ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς, “but are as angels in heaven.” FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1174D: Everlasting in the Spirit of the Lord. As is his habit, Philastrius cites the words of Scripture from memory. Paul has χαρὰ ἐν Πνεύματι ἁγίῳ, “joy in the Holy Spirit.” FABRIC.]

## LX. HERESY REJECTING THE GOSPEL OF JOHN AND HIS APOCALYPSE

After these are heretics who do not accept the Gospel according to John or his Apocalypse. Since they do not understand the power of Scripture and do not wish to learn, they remain in their heresy and perish. They even dare to say that the Apocalypse likewise belongs to that heretic Cerinthus and is not by blessed John the Evangelist and Apostle, but by Cerinthus the heretic, who at that time was exposed as a heretic by the blessed apostles and cast out of the Church.

[Note: Col. 1174D–1175B: The Gospel and the Apocalypse. Epiphanius and Damascene refute the Alogi under this name; see heresy 51. The Ebionites, Cerinthians, Cerdonians, Theodotus of Byzantium, and Marcion rejected the Gospel of John. Theodore Scutariotes, in a scholium on Nicetas, *Treasury of the Orthodox Faith* IV.22, appears to attribute this also to the Quartodecimans, though it is certainly not true of all of them. FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1175B–C: Of that heretic Cerinthus. No one at all attributed the Gospel of John to Cerinthus as its author. Philastrius’s words must therefore be restricted to the Apocalypse alone, which the Alogi, according to Epiphanius LI.3, attributed to Cerinthus, as did some others mentioned by Dionysius of Alexandria in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VII.25. Dionysius and Epiphanius show how far this opinion is from plausibility. FABRIC.—“So that they even dare to say … the Apocalypse likewise.” This is the reading of the Hamburg edition, with which the Basel and Lyon editions agree. From it Fabricius inferred that these heretics might have attributed not only the Apocalypse but also the Gospel of John to Cerinthus; he therefore warned that Philastrius’s words should be restricted to the Apocalypse alone. But the Corbie manuscript reads much more suitably: “so that they even dare to say that the Apocalypse likewise belongs to that heretic Cerinthus.” With the conjunction removed, no suspicion remains concerning the Gospel. GALEARD.]

[Note: Col. 1175A: “say, and the Apocalypse likewise”]

[Note: Col. 1175C: Likewise. Cotelerius, *Monuments* I, p. 775, in the same place. FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1175C: By the blessed apostles. Above, ch. 36. FABRIC.]

## LXI. MANICHAEANS

After these came the Manichaeans from Persia, named after a man Mani, or Turbo as he was called. Taking destructive supports from those earlier sects, they assert that there are two gods, one good and one evil, and proclaim a conflict between God and the Lord. They hold that the human soul is properly from God, but suppose that the body was made by the devil. Denying the Resurrection and not hoping for Judgment, they worship demons and adore the elements; like pagans, they invoke the names of gods and goddesses. They say that there are certain male-females, sharing in both natures, and devote themselves to abominable shamefulness. Having been defeated in disputation by the holy bishop Archelaus, rejected, branded, and exposed, they became known to all at that time. Yet, like thieves, under the guise of Christian confession, they do not cease to enslave many souls by falsehood and bestial shamefulness (2 Tim. 3:6). They are said to hide in Spain and its five provinces, and daily ensnare many by this deception.

[Note: Col. 1175C–D: Turbo. Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* VI.13, and Photius, *Against the Manichaeans* I, state that the Persian word *Manes* means a quarrelsome speaker, ὁμιλητής, and one eager for disputation, πρὸς διάλεξιν δραστήριον; although Thomas Hyde, *History of the Religion of the Ancient Persians*, p. 284, denies that any trace of this meaning survives today in Persian. From Augustine, *On Heresies*, ch. 46, one might suspect that *Urbicus* should be read instead of Turbo—the name elsewhere being Cubricus or Curbitius. But the received reading is sound, for there certainly was a disciple of Mani named Turbo, Τύρβων, mentioned by Epiphanius, vol. I, pp. 623, 642. FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1175A: “from those destructive persons”]

[Note: Col. 1175D: From those earlier ones. Such as the school of Valentinus and of Marcion, above chs. 38 and 45. FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1175D: Those who assert two gods, one good … See above, ch. 47, note l. GALEARD.]

[Note: Col. 1175D–1176A: Between God and the Lord. Between the good God and the Lord who gave the Law through Moses and spoke in the Hebrew prophets. Mani blasphemed that this one was not the true God but one of the princes of darkness, as is clear from Augustine, Epiphanius LXVI.31, and others. FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1175D–1176B: Denying the Resurrection. Rufinus observes in his *Explanation of the Creed* that Mani followed Valentinus’s footsteps in this also. FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1176B: Not hoping for Judgment. Understand this in respect of bodies; for there is no doubt that they assigned a spiritual resurrection to souls, and Augustine admits this, *Against Faustus* IV.2. FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1176A: “worshipping demons … teaching … and bestial …”]

[Note: Col. 1176B: Adoring the elements. Understand the sun and moon, which are called στοιχεῖα, “elements,” by Cyril, *Against Julian* VI, pp. 205, 211, and by other writers whose passages I cited on Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 45. Alexander of Lycopolis, *On the Manichaeans*, p. 5: Τιμῶσι μάλιστα ἥλιον καὶ σελήνην οὐχ ὡς Θεούς, ἀλλ᾽ ὡς ὁδὸν δι᾽ ἧς ἐστιν πρὸς Θεὸν ἀφικέσθαι, “They especially honour the sun and moon, not as gods, but as a way through which one may come to God.” Athanasius and Chrysostom, in the *Synopsis of Scripture* where they discuss the Book of Wisdom, call them στοιχειολάτραι, “element-worshippers.” Peter Pithoeus argues from Philastrius, p. 175 of his *Works*, that they did not abstain from pagan rites. FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1176B: Male-females. Like the Valentinian aeons, ἀρρενοθήλεις, “male-female,” concerning whom see Irenaeus and Tertullian. Concerning Mani’s hermaphrodite demon, see Epiphanius LXVI.52, p. 664. FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1176C: Archelaus. The acts of the disputation in which Archelaus, bishop of Carrhae in Mesopotamia, brought Mani’s errors to light and refuted them were formerly read. They were written in Syriac and later translated into Greek by Hegemonius. Cyril of Jerusalem, in his sixth catechesis, and Epiphanius, heresy 66, quoted much from them. Valesius published part in Latin from an old translation in his notes on Socrates, p. 197; Laurentius Alexander Zaccagnius published more complete portions in *Collections of Ancient Monuments*, Rome, 1698, quarto. From Zaccagnius’s edition I also gave them in the *Spicilegium of the Fathers of the Third Century*, at the end of the second volume of the works of St Hippolytus, Hamburg, 1718, folio. Compare, if you please, what I noted on this disputation of Archelaus with Mani in *Bibliotheca Graeca* V.1, p. 262, and on Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 72. FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1176C–D: Under the guise of Christian confession. As though they were confessors and martyrs, who could no longer openly and safely express their doctrines, but only secretly and within private walls while hiding. FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1176D: Bestial shamefulness. Or *pecudalis*, as the manuscripts of Martianus Capella read. Cato and other ancients said *pecuinus*; Venantius, Sedulius, and others, *pecualis*. FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1176D: In Spain and the five provinces. Spain was then divided into five provinces, as is clear from Sextus Rufus’s *Breviary*, ch. 5: Tarraconensis, Carthaginensis, Lusitania, Gallaecia, and Baetica. The sixth province of the Spains was not in Spain but on African soil, Tingitanian Mauretania. FABRIC.]

## LXII. PATRICIANS

The Patricians are named after a certain Patricius, who lived at Rome. They assert that human flesh was not made by God but believe that it was made by the devil. They decree that it must be despised and discarded by every means, so that some of them have not hesitated even voluntarily to inflict death upon themselves.

[Note: Col. 1177A: Others are Patricians, from a certain Patricius who was in the city of Rome. These …]

[Note: Col. 1177B: From Patricius. The author of the Commentary included among the works of St Ambrose, on 1 Timothy 4:1, mentions him with the Marcionites and Manichaeans. Augustine, *Against the Adversary of the Law and Prophets* II, final chapter, after naming Basilides, Carpocrates, Cerdon, Marcion, and Apelles as forerunners of the Manichaeans, adds: “There were also, or are, certain Patricians—from a certain Patricius; in some manuscripts, Patricini—who likewise oppose the ancient divine books.” Otherwise mention of these Patricians is rather rare in ancient writings, for what Augustine reports about them in *On Heresies*, ch. 61, was copied from Philastrius, as Isidore and later writers repeat it from Augustine. FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1177B: Not by God but by the devil. Like the Manichaeans mentioned in the preceding chapter: “they suppose that the body was made by the devil.” FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1177B–C: Inflict death on themselves. The author of the *Praedestinatus*, ch. 61, says of the Patricians: “They say that the substance of human flesh was created not by God but by the devil, and they detest it so much that they call the person who can steadfastly kill himself perfect. Some among them even ask strangers whom they encounter to kill them. This madness began long ago in parts of Upper Numidia and Mauretania. The wretched Donatists later followed them,” etc. FABRIC.]

## LXIII. SYMMACHIANS

The Symmachians, disciples of that man—that is, Patricius—hold the same opinions in all respects. Not hoping for Judgment, they proclaim that one must serve worldly vices and carnal desires.

[Note: Col. 1177C–1178B: Symmachians, disciples of that man. “That man,” namely Patricius. Augustine, the author of the *Praedestinatus*, and other writers on heresies say nothing of these Symmachians. I agree with Petavius, who thinks Philastrius’s Symmachians were named after someone other than Symmachus the Ebionite, Greek translator of the books of the Old Testament, in his notes on Epiphanius, p. 400. But Valesius rightly observed, in his note on Eusebius VI.17, p. 119, that other Symmachians, mentioned by the author of the Commentary included among St Ambrose’s works in the prologue to the Epistle to the Galatians, derived their name from Symmachus the Ebionite: “Such also are the Symmachians, who trace their origin from the Pharisees, who, while preserving the whole Law, call themselves Christians, and, in the manner of Photinus, define Christ not as God and man, but as man only.” Faustus the Manichaean, in Augustine, book XIX of the work written against him, ch. 4: “If someone of the Nazarenes, whom others call Symmachians, objected to me that Jesus said that he had not come to abolish the Law,” etc. Augustine himself, XIX.17, after speaking of believers from the circumcision who persisted in such perversity that they compelled Gentiles to Judaize, says: “These are the people whom Faustus mentioned by the name Symmachians or Nazarenes, who endure even to our times, indeed in a small remnant but nevertheless still endure even in that small number.” The same Augustine, *Against Cresconius the Donatist* I.31: “Even now there are certain heretics who call themselves Nazarenes but are called Symmachians by some; they have Jewish circumcision and Christian baptism.” FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1178A: Other Symmachian disciples.]

[Note: Col. 1178B: Not hoping for Judgment. The same was said above, ch. 61, of the Manichaeans. FABRIC.]

## LXIV. PAUL OF SAMOSATA

After these, there was in Syria a certain Paul of Samosata, who denied that the Word of God—that is, Christ God the Son—was substantial, personal, and eternal with the Father. Instead, he taught that it was uttered, that is, a kind of air, not, however, to be believed as the eternal living person of the Son with the eternal Father. He preached that Christ was a righteous man, not true God, inclining rather to Judaism; he also taught circumcision. Therefore he taught a certain Queen Zenobia in the East at that time to Judaize.

[Note: Col. 1178B: After these. That is, besides these. So μετά is used in Acts 5:37. An ancient writer in the catena on Acts 2:22, in Wolfius, *Anecdota* IV, p. 6, makes Paul of Samosata a follower of Artemon. Philastrius’s chronological language is not to be taken so precisely as though every heretic whom he places after another necessarily arose later than those whom he named before. Paul of Samosata was deposed from the bishopric of Antioch for heresy in AD 270. But Mani’s heresy, of which Philastrius spoke in ch. 61, was refuted by Archelaus in AD 278. Thus Paul also precedes in Augustine, ch. 44, and in Epiphanius. FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1178A: “substantial and personal … to be believed”]

[Note: Col. 1178B–C: Substantial … uttered. Epiphanius, LXV.1, reports Paul of Samosata’s doctrine: Μὴ εἶναι δὲ τὸν Υἱὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐνυπόστατον, ἀλλὰ ἐν αὐτῷ τῷ Θεῷ … ἐλθόντα δὲ τὸν Λόγον καὶ ἐνοικήσαντα ἐν Ἰησοῦ, ἀνθρώπῳ ὄντι: “The Son of God is not hypostatic, but is in God himself … and the Word came and dwelt in Jesus, who was a human being.” Marius Mercator, *Letter on the Difference between Paul and Nestorius*: “Nestorius dealt with the Word of God, not indeed as Paul thinks, who defines it to be not a substantial but an uttered, effectual Word of God’s power.” The same, dissertation *On the Twelve Anathemas of Nestorius*, no. 19: “Paul understood the Word of God as a προφορικὸν καὶ πρακτικὸν Λόγον καὶ ἐνεργητικόν—that is, an uttered Word, effective in power—not as substantial, which the Greeks call οὐσιῶδες.” For other material concerning Paul and this heresy, see Garnerius on Mercator, vol. II, pp. 307 ff., and Tillemont, *Memoirs*, vol. IV. FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1178C–D: He taught circumcision. Although Paul of Samosata seemed by his denial of Christ’s divinity to support the Jews, and Epiphanius, LXV.7, accordingly assigns him to “the servants of the Jewish heresy,” τῆς τῶν Ἰουδαίων αἱρέσεως ὑπερέταις, other ancient writers do not attribute to him the teaching that circumcision was necessary for Christians. Augustine nevertheless infers in *On Heresies*, ch. 44, that the Paulianists did not retain the baptismal formula because canon 19 of Nicaea commands that they be rebaptized. The learned annotations of William Beveridge on that canon may profitably be consulted. FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1178D–1179B: Zenobia. After the murder of her husband Odaenathus, Septimia Zenobia held Syria and Phoenicia from AD 267, while Paul of Samosata held the bishopric of Antioch. Since she observed Jewish rites, he is accused of denying that Christ was God in order to gain her favour. Theodoret, *Compendium of Heretical Fables* II.8: “Paul of Samosata was bishop of the Antiochenes, while Zenobia held power at that time—for after defeating the Romans, the Persians handed over to her the rule of Syria and Phoenicia. He drifted into the heresy of Artemon, believing that by this he would serve her, since she held Jewish opinions.” St Athanasius, *Letter to Those Living the Solitary Life*, vol. I, p. 857: “Zenobia was a Jewess, and she supported Paul of Samosata.” St Chrysostom, Homily 7 on John, p. 57, concerning Paul of Samosata: “They say that, to gratify a certain woman, he sold his own salvation.” Abulfaragius, *History of Dynasties*, p. 81: “Eusebius the Chronologist reports that this Paul was aided by a certain Jewess whom Gallus Caesar had placed over Syria, and that, approving his knowledge and opinion, she installed him in the patriarchate of Antioch.” FABRIC.]

## LXV. PHOTINUS

Photinus, following his doctrine, preached similarly in every respect. Persisting in this falsehood, he was expelled from the Church of the city of Sirmium, having been overcome by holy bishops.

[Note: Col. 1179A–B: Following his doctrine. Photinus, an Ancyrean by birth, following in the footsteps of his teacher Marcellus of Ancyra, whom Eusebius refuted, began to defend the heresy of Paul of Samosata around AD 341. See Socrates I.36 and II.18; the writers cited by me in vol. VIII of *Bibliotheca Graeca*, p. 314; and Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs* VI, pp. 760, 765 ff.; Matthieu Larroque, *Considerations Serving as an Answer to What Mr David Wrote against the Dissertation on Photinus*, Rouen, 1671, quarto. FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1179A: After that one, Fotmus.]

[Note: Col. 1179B–D: He was expelled from the Church of the city of Sirmium. Sirmium, capital of Illyricum, whose bishopric Photinus held until AD 351, when he was deposed by eastern bishops and Basil of Ancyra, successor of Marcellus, through the second Synod of Sirmium. For the decrees of the Council of Antioch in AD 345 and the first Council of Sirmium in AD 349, which did not take effect, see Pappus’s *Synodicon*, chs. 43 and 50. Compare Socrates II.29 ff. and Hardouin, *Councils* I, pp. 702 ff. Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 107, writes that Photinus was expelled by Valentinian, who began to reign in AD 364; evidently he was expelled again, after Julian the emperor had recalled him from exile in AD 362. Julian also mentions Photinus in his first book *Against the Christians*, quoted by Cyril of Alexandria, VIII, p. 262, Leipzig edition. FABRIC.]

[Note: Col. 1179D: Overcome by holy bishops. I think *separated* should be read instead of *overcome*. No disputation with Photinus is mentioned here, nor any contest by bishops by which he could be said to have been overcome; it merely says that he was expelled from the Church of the city of Sirmium. GALEARD.]

## LXVI. ARIANS
Arians. [Note: [Col. 1179B] “The Arians are . . . saying ‘under the emperor of blessed memory’”] [Note: [Col. 1179D] From Arius. He was first a deacon at Alexandria, but was expelled by Meletius. After the latter’s death, however, he was received by Achillas, bishop of Alexandria, as a presbyter and made head of the Alexandrian school, as is recorded in chapter 32 of Pappus’s *Synodicon*. Thereafter, following Achillas’s death not long after A.D. 312, Arius coveted the episcopate; indignant that Alexander had been preferred to him, he began about A.D. 316 to spread his heresy. It was condemned at the Council of Nicaea, [Col. 1180B] convened by the emperor Constantine in A.D. 325. Consult, if you please, the writers on Arius and the Arians cited by me in Book V, chapter 23, of the *Bibliotheca Graeca*, vol. VIII, pp. 308 ff. FABRICIUS.] They derive from Arius, a presbyter of the city of Alexandria, who lived under Alexander, bishop of blessed memory, and under the holy emperor Constantine. He said that the Son of God was [Note: [Col. 1180B] Like God: *homoiousios*, not *homoousios*. FABRICIUS.] like God—like only in name—and, by not believing him to be of the divine substance of God the Father himself, [Note: [Col. 1179B] “and not of his own . . . divine . . . substance”] fell into a dangerous heresy. For a creature too is called like God, since Scripture says: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. [Col. 1180A] 1:26). Yet neither man nor angel has been begotten from God properly and naturally—that is, from that ineffable and eternal divine substance of the Father—as [Note: [Col. 1180B] Only-begotten Son. *Monogenēs*, John 1:14, 18; 3:16, 18; and 1 John 4:9: begotten not merely *monos ek monou* (“alone from the alone”), but also *monotropōs* (“in a unique manner”), as Gregory Nazianzen rightly says, *Oration* 36, p. 590. The words in Theodoret, *Haeretical Fables*, V.2, are: “But if he is created, he is not only-begotten, for he has creation as a sister [Col. 1180C] and all the parts of creation.” FABRICIUS.] the only Son was begotten, [Note: [Col. 1180C] Properly from the Father. The Jews professed that they had heard this from Christ himself: “He called God his own Father” (*patera idion elege ton Theon*), John 5:18. Alexander of Alexandria, in Theodoret, *History*, I.4, p. 14: “Paul declared his genuine, proper, natural, and exceptional sonship” (*gnēsian autou kai idiotropon kai kataxaireton huiotēta*), saying thus of God (Rom. 8:32): “He who did not spare his own Son,” but delivered him up for us—not, plainly, for natural sons, “those who are not sons by nature” (*tōn mē physei huiōn*). For, to distinguish him from those who are not sons properly, “by contrast with those who are not proper” (*pros antidiastolēn tōn ouk idiōn*), Paul called him his own Son. FABRICIUS.] properly and eternally from the Father. But man and angel were made from nothing.

[Note: [Col. 1180C] “The Son . . . against.” Begotten from the Father’s essence, so that from him he possesses from eternity identity of nature, and is “the imprint of his substance” (*charaktēr tēs hypostaseōs autou*), Heb. 1:3. Psalm 110:3: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (*ek gastros pro heōsphorou egennēsa se*). The ancients, with great unanimity, opposed this passage to Arius as referring to the eternal and proper [Col. 1180D] generation of the Son. See Petavius, *Dogmatic Theology on the Most Holy Trinity*, V.7. FABRICIUS.]

But since the Son is true, [Note: [Col. 1179B] “it is necessary that he be . . . of the Son is according to”] it is necessary to recognize that he was begotten from that divine substance of the Father. For a true God cannot otherwise be the only Son, unless he has been properly begotten from that divine substance of the Father.

[Note: [Col. 1180D] “The eternal likeness of the Son is according to works.” The passage is wholly corrupt in the printed editions; the Corbie manuscript has assisted it. It reads thus: “The eternal likeness of the Son is according to works”; then, where the printed text continued, more badly, “and he is begotten from the divine substance of God himself’s quality,” the manuscript rightly omits the conjunction: “begotten from the divine substance of his quality.” Therefore we owe the restored complete passage to the Corbie manuscript. Thus too in chapter 68 the editions read: “They assert that the Son, who is a creature, made the Spirit; and they assert that the Son is not like the Father.” But the Corbie reading is somewhat better: “They assert that the Son, who is a creature, made the Holy Spirit. They assert that the Son is not like the Father.” GALEARDUS.]

Therefore the eternal likeness [Note: [Col. 1180A] “of the Son is according to”] of the Son is also according to works, because “as the Father does, the Son likewise does” [Note: [Col. 1180B] “all things, from his own quality”] all things (John 5:19); and he is begotten from the divine substance [Note: [Col. 1180D] “of the quality of God himself.” Endowed with a nature of the same kind as God himself. Thus below, chapter 66: “believing there to be one substance of quality, one divinity.” FABRICIUS.] of God himself’s quality, because he was born from him properly and eternally, not made from nothing like man and angel, [Note: [Col. 1180B] “or some creature, which is subject to all decline”] or any creature whatsoever.

## LXVII. SEMI-ARIANS

[Col. 1181A]

[Note: [Col. 1181A] Semi-Arians. It is clear that Philastrius includes under this name those afterward called Macedonians or Pneumatomachians, condemned at the Council of Constantinople in A.D. 381. Macedonius himself was deposed from the episcopate of Constantinople for heresy in A.D. 361. FABRICIUS.]

There are also Semi-Arians. They [Note: [Col. 1181B] “Think rightly concerning the Father and the Son.” Ratramnus says the same of Macedonius in Book II, chapter 2, *Against the Greeks*. Yet Epiphanius, *Heresy* 73.23 and 27, sufficiently shows that this cannot be affirmed of all Semi-Arians. FABRICIUS.] think rightly concerning the Father and the Son, believing there to be one substance of quality and one divinity. But they proclaim that the Spirit is neither from the divine substance nor true God, but a [Note: [Col. 1181B] Made and created. *Ktisma* and *poiēma*. John Zonaras, in his canon concerning the Mother of God: “Let us leave Macedonius to babble utterly, when he says that the uncreated Spirit of God is a creature and a work” (*Makedonion pantōs lērein aphentes ton legonta ktisma te kai poiēma einai to aktiston Pneuma Theou*). FABRICIUS.] made and created Spirit, so as to associate and compare him with creation. Yet the Lord Christ joined him to the Father and himself [Note: [Col. 1181B] In the faith of baptism. The baptismal formula is “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” Matthew 28. Baptism is one of eternal salvation, bestowed in hope of obtaining eternal salvation. FABRICIUS.] in the faith of baptism for eternal salvation, and commanded that he be worshipped by all believers together with the Father and the Son. [Note: [Col. 1181B] To be worshipped by all believers. From that baptismal formula itself the ancient Christians inferred invocation (*epiklēsis*) and religious worship of the Holy Spirit; for them, “to be baptized into the name” (*baptizesthai eis to onoma*) is “to be baptized having invoked the name” (*baptizesthai epikalesamenon to onoma*) of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. This is demonstrated from passages in Origen, Firmilian, and others by our blessed Gotfridus Olearius, in his dissertation *On the Worship and Glorification of the Holy Spirit with the Father and the Son against William Whiston*, published at Leipzig in 1711, pp. 12 ff. See also Basil, *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 19. FABRICIUS.]

And he established that throughout all ages the Spirit should be proclaimed [Note: [Col. 1181C] True God. I do not doubt that Philastrius wrote this instead of “him true.” FABRICIUS.—“True God.” Fabricius adds: “I do not doubt that Philastrius wrote this instead of ‘him true’”; but he does not indicate where “him true” is read instead of “true God.” Certainly Sichardus, in the Basel edition of 1528, correctly has “true God,” although Fabricius does not cite that edition here; whereas “him true” is read in the Lyons edition of the *Library of the Fathers*, V, p. 708. The Corbie manuscript agrees with Sichardus’s edition in reading “true God.” GALEARDUS.] as true God. They do not understand that, when the Evangelist says, “All things were made through him, [Note: [Col. 1181D] “And without him nothing was made.” Philastrius agrees with those who begin a new clause in John with the words, “What was made in him was life.” This punctuation is also known to have been used by Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, Theophilus of Antioch, Origen, Tertullian, Lactantius, Eusebius, Augustine, and many others, even more recent writers such as Honorius and Peter Bruno. Therefore it is not right, with Epiphanius in the *Ancoratus*, I, p. 80, to condemn that punctuation as heretical and injurious to the Holy Spirit, even though certain heretics such as Valentinus and Heracleon also followed it. FABRICIUS.] and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3), he is not speaking of the Holy Spirit, as though the Spirit had been made by the Son. For the Prophet declares that the Trinity made all visible and [Col. 1182A] invisible things, saying: [Note: [Col. 1181D] The ancients [Col. 1182B] commonly understand this passage of the Holy Trinity. See Faverdentius on Arnobius and Serapion’s conflict, p. 523, and Gregory’s disputation, p. 9. FABRICIUS.] “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their host” (Ps. 33:6).

Therefore, in all creation, which was made through the Spirit, he omitted nothing that was not made through him. Otherwise, [Note: [Col. 1182B] In the faith. In the baptismal formula, in which the Holy Spirit is joined with the Father and the Son. Thus above our author had said: “when the Lord Christ joined the Spirit to the Father and himself in the faith of baptism for eternal salvation.” FABRICIUS.] a servant would not be joined with the Lord in the faith, if the divine and holy Spirit were a creature. For this reason all Scripture and the Lord [Note: [Col. 1182B] “All sins to be forgiven to men.” That is, “to be pardoned.” Ovid, *Tristia*, II.1:

> But if I had not sinned, what could you have granted?

Suetonius, *Nero*, 29: to those who had confessed obscenity before him, he granted pardon also for their other offenses. Ennodius, IV.8: “Confidence granted became the mother of boldness”; and Epistle 12: “Appeased by a simple gift, I pardoned errors”; and in the *Life of St. Epiphanius, Bishop of Pavia*: “For at the holy man’s entreaty he forgave the injury inflicted upon the mother by men of his jurisdiction.” GALEARDUS.] declared by a heavenly judgment that all sins are forgiven to men, except blasphemy against the divine and worshipped Spirit. [Note: [Col. 1182B] “Declared by a heavenly judgment.” Thus I have written with Cotelerius, in his notes on John Damascene, *On Heresies*, vol. I of the *Monuments*, p. 782. Earlier editions wrongly read “declared by a heavenly essence”; and the Helmstedt edition has “foretold.” There is also one that reads: “declared blasphemy concerning the heavenly essence of the divine and worshipped Spirit.” But I greatly prefer Cotelerius’s emendation. FABRICIUS.] (Matt. 12:31).

## LXVIII. EUNOMIANS

After these come the Eunomians, from Eunomius, [Note: [Col. 1182C] A disciple of Arius. Eunomius did not hear Arius himself, who had already died in A.D. 336, but Aetius from A.D. 356 onward. Eunomius lived until A.D. 396, certainly until A.D. 392. Jerome, chapter 120 of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, says: “He is said to be still living in Cappadocia and to write much against the Church.” Philastrius calls him Arius’s disciple because he imitated his heresy. Augustine, chapter 54 of *On Heresies*, calls him Aetius’s disciple, as other writers also attest. FABRICIUS.] Arius’s disciple and enemies of the true faith in every respect. They say that there are [Note: [Col. 1182C] Three substances of differing quality. Elsewhere: “of different quality.” But thus in chapters 67 and 92 our author said “one substance of quality.” St. Augustine, on Eunomius, chapter 54: “He asserted that the Son was unlike the Father in every respect, and the Holy Spirit unlike the Son.” The Arians above, chapter 66, and the Semi-Arians in Augustine, chapter 51, denied only that the Son was *homoousios* with the Father, though they acknowledged that he was *homoiousios* and like him. But Eunomius, with his Aetius, denied even this; his followers, the Eunomians, were accordingly called Anomoeans. I remember that I have supplied Eunomius’s exposition of faith and *Apology* in Greek and Latin in Book V, chapter 22, of the *Bibliotheca Graeca*, where see the discussion if you please. Add the remarks of the Reverend Vogt, fascicle 3 of the *Bibliotheca Haeresiologica*, pp. 485 ff., where there is a dissertation of Jacob Basnage; and p. 605, where there is a catalogue of writers. FABRICIUS.] three distinct substances of different quality, [Note: [Col. 1182D] As of gold, silver, and bronze. Compare Epiphanius, 76.2, p. 914. FABRICIUS.] as gold, silver, and [Col. 1183A] bronze. They assert that the Father made the Son, and then that the Son, [Note: [Col. 1183B] “who is a creature”] who is a creature, made [Note: [Col. 1183B] “they assert [that the Son] made the Holy Spirit.”] the Spirit. They also assert that the Son is not like the Father, because he is a creature; nor is the Spirit like the Son, because [Note: [Col. 1183B] “made by the Son, [they submit] to impiety”] he was made by the Son. They agree more openly with pagan impiety and Jewish wickedness [Note: [Col. 1183B] “openly [rather] than to Christian”] than they wish to obey Christian teaching and the Catholic faith, [Note: [Col. 1184B] “wishing to contend against the Catholic [faith]”] [Note: [Col. 1183B] “Wishing to submit.” Thus above, chapter 57, concerning the Florians: “to submit rather to accursed Judaism and paganism.” FABRICIUS.]

## LXIX. THE HERESY THAT CHRIST DID NOT HAVE A TRUE SOUL

There are others who err [Note: [Col. 1183B] Concerning the incarnation. *Tēn enanthrōpēsin tou Logou*, “the incarnation of the Word.” St. Hilary calls it “the embodiment of the Word of God,” p. 637, and “embodiment” in many places. FABRICIUS.—[Col. 1183C] “There are others who err concerning the incarnation.” I cited this passage in my notes on Gaudentius, who had used the word *incorporatio* for *enanthrōpēsis*, p. 39 of the Padua edition. Yet there are several other passages in which Philastrius uses the same word, noted in the index to the Hamburg edition of Philastrius under “Incorporatio.” Some further passages omitted even from Fabricius’s index may be added: chapter 126, “David himself, patriarch and so great a witness indeed of the INCARNATION of Christ the Lord”; chapter 124, “Although his generation is twofold, one OF DIVINITY, the other OF INCARNATION”; likewise chapter 135, “Appearing afterward IN THE INCARNATION”; and shortly before: “he announced in a vision his coming INCARNATION.” GALEARDUS.] concerning the incarnation, saying that the Savior did not assume [Note: [Col. 1183C] A true rational human soul. The Arians taught that the Word (*Logos*) assumed only a body without a soul, and himself occupied the place of soul—not Arius himself, if Marius Mercator is to be trusted. Yet St. Athanasius attributes this to Arius in *On the Coming of Christ*: “Arius acknowledges only flesh, in order to conceal [Col. 1183D] the divinity” (*Areios de sarka monēn pros apokryphēn tēs Theotētos homologei*). Theodoret, *Haeretical Fables*, V.11, says of Arius and Eunomius: “Concerning the dispensation of the Savior: Arius and Eunomius said that he assumed a body, but that the divinity performed the function of the soul” (*Areius de kai Eunomios sōma men auton ephasan eilēphenai, tēn Theotēta de tēs psychēs energekēnai chreian*). Rufinus of Palestine, *On the Faith*, vol. I of Sirmond’s works, p. 309: “If Jesus Christ had not possessed a soul, as the impious Arians suppose, or if again he had possessed a soul indeed but not a rational one, as the mad Apollinaris defined, he could surely never have advanced in wisdom.” Epiphanius, 69.19, and, following him, Augustine, the author of the *Praedestinatus*, heresy 49, and Damascene, 69, attribute this view to the Arians. Caesarius refutes the error in Questions 25 ff. FABRICIUS.] a true rational soul of a human being, but only a human body. By removing the soul from the body, they deny the true [Note: [Col. 1183D] “They deny the salvation of human beings.” For unless Christ assumed a human soul, he could not be the Savior of souls, according to the theological maxim: “What he did not assume, he did not redeem.” Theophilus of Alexandria, First Paschal Letter: “And thus the very course of the argument proves that nothing imperfect was assumed by the Lord, but that humanity was assumed by him wholly and perfectly saved.” FABRICIUS.] salvation [Note: [Col. 1184B] “of humanity’s salvation . . . and for whose sake”] of human beings.

How, then, can a soul be said to be present which was not assumed by the Savior, when [Col. 1183B] the Savior says: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26:36)? Otherwise, it could not be called soul unless it were in him for whose sake he came. Therefore both these were present in the Savior: that is, body and soul, which he deigned to assume for our salvation. We must know that he also possessed [Note: [Col. 1184C] A true human soul, possessing understanding. Against the heresy of Apollinaris, who taught that Christ assumed an ensouled body, but that the Word (*Logos*) himself occupied the place of mind and understanding. Facundus, IX.3: “The Apollinarists indeed believe that the Lord assumed the nature of flesh and soul without mind; the Arians, that of flesh only.” See John Pearson on the Creed, pp. 285 and 422 of the Latin edition, and Suicer, vol. II of the *Thesaurus*, pp. 264 ff. FABRICIUS.] a true human soul possessing understanding, and a human body [Note: [Col. 1184C] Likewise bodily sensation. The Arians taught that the sensation of suffering was assumed not by Christ’s soul, which they denied, but by the Word; and, as Phoebadius says, that God had become passible. St. Athanasius, *On the Incarnation*: “Therefore the Arians vainly imagine that the Savior assumed flesh alone, wickedly referring the apprehension of suffering to the impassible divinity” (*Matēn oun Areianoi phantazontai sarka monēn hypotithmenoi aneilephenai ton Sōtēra, tēn de tou pathous noēsin epi tēn apathē Theotēta anapherontes asebōs*). See the same Pearson, p. 334; the Benedictine prolegomena to Hilary, pp. 35 and 47; and Elmenhorst on Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Doctrines*, p. 112. FABRICIUS.] with bodily sensation likewise, so that he could suffer in his body and die.

Nevertheless, this flesh is known to have been made [Note: [Col. 1184D] By the Holy Spirit. Prudentius, *Apotheosis*, v. 435:

> From the time when the Spirit touched the mortal womb,  
> That Spirit, the God of God, clothed himself in the mother’s body  
> And created man from virginity.

Damascene, *On the Orthodox Faith*, III.2, says: “not seminally but creatively” (*ou spermatikōs alla dēmiourgikōs*). FABRICIUS.] by the Holy Spirit, and the soul created, as it is written in the Gospel: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High [Note: [Col. 1184B] “will overshadow you . . . Whose soul”] will overshadow you.” And that he had a true soul appears when he says: [Note: [Col. 1184D] “I lay down my soul for you.” He refers to John 10:11: “I am the good shepherd; the good shepherd lays down his soul for the sheep” (*Egō eimi ho poimēn ho kalos; ho poimēn ho kalos tēn psychēn autou tithēsi hyper tōn probatōn*). FABRICIUS.] “I lay down my soul for you.” And, concerning his passible flesh, [Note: [Col. 1184D] To Thomas. In the Gospel passage whose words are cited, there is no mention of Thomas. FABRICIUS.] he said to Thomas: “A spirit does not have bones and flesh, as you see that I have” (Luke 24:39). And the apostle Peter bore witness concerning the Savior, saying: [Note: [Col. 1184D] “For you will not abandon my soul to Hades, nor will you allow your Holy One to see corruption” (*Hoti ouk enkataleipseis tēn psychēn mou eis Hadou, oude dōseis ton hosion sou idein diaphthoran*). FABRICIUS.] “His soul was not left in hell, nor did his flesh see corruption” (Acts 2:27, from Ps. 16:10). Since he was incarnate and became man for our salvation, he is believed, acknowledged, worshipped, and proclaimed in the Catholic Church as true God.

## LXX. TROPITAE

[Note: [Col. 1184B] “There are other Tropitae who”] The Tropitae are those who say that the Word was [Note: [Col. 1184D] The Word changed into flesh. Hence the name *Tropitae*, from *tropē*, “change.” Tertullian refutes this heresy—which was later revived among the Eutychians—in *On the Flesh of Christ*, chapter 10 ff. FABRICIUS.] changed into flesh. They do not understand what the apostle John says: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). They do not attend to the fact that the Word [Col. 1185A] is unchangeable, [Note: [Col. 1185B] and incorruptible] and incapable of conversion—that is, God the Son of God. But he himself, having fashioned the flesh which he assumed for our salvation, assumed and put it on because of [Note: [Col. 1185C] “our incapacity.” Because we could not see him unless he were clothed in flesh. It may also be punctuated thus: “because of our incapacity to see him.” FABRICIUS.] our incapacity.

Accordingly, in order that he might be seen, these things were joined together into one for our salvation. They disclosed not a change of the Word into flesh, but rather the assumption of something visible, so that the invisible one might be seen, believed, and known through visible flesh, and worshipped fittingly [Note: [Col. 1185C] Fittingly: apprehended by sense itself and by sight. FABRICIUS.] by humankind.

## LXXI. HERESY CONCERNING CHRIST’S PASSION

[Note: [Col. 1185B] “There are also heretics who”] There are also heretics who err concerning the Passion, saying that in the Passion Christ our God laid aside [Note: [Col. 1185B] “our Lord . . . into heaven, and he is no longer”] his flesh and [Note: [Col. 1185C] “Thus ascended into heaven.” Compare what is said above concerning Apelles in chapter 47. Tertullian, *On the Flesh of Christ*, chapter 24: “That those too may blush who affirm that the flesh sits in heaven devoid of sensation, like a sheath stripped from Christ; or who say that there are only flesh and soul, or soul alone, but flesh no longer.” Gregory Nazianzen, Epistle 1 to Cledonius: “If anyone says that he has now laid aside the flesh, and that the divinity is naked of body, and that he neither exists nor will come with what he assumed, may he not see the glory of the coming” (*Ei tis apotithesthai nyn tēn sarka legei, kai gymnēn einai tēn Theotēta sōmatos, alla mē meta tou proslēmmatos kai einai kai hēxein, mē idoi tēn doxan tēs parousias*). FABRICIUS.] thus ascended into heaven, so that the divinity is no longer in flesh. For, they say, after the Passion he did not rise in flesh, nor ascend into heaven with flesh. Yet the salvation [Note: [Col. 1185B] “of every human being . . . by the Passion of his flesh and resurrection”] of all human beings rests upon the Passion of his flesh, his Resurrection, and his Ascension into heaven, [Note: [Col. 1185B] “rests . . . the blessed angels”] without hesitation, for us and all believers. For the angels said to the apostles, for our faith and joy, in the Acts of the Apostles: “As you saw him ascending into heaven, [Note: [Col. 1185C] “Thus expect him again.” Philastrius roughly conveys the sense, as is his custom, but does not reproduce the sacred writer’s words. For Acts 1:11 reads: “Thus he will come, in the manner in which you saw him going into heaven” (*Houtōs eleusetai, hon tropon etheasasthe auton poreuomenon eis ton ouranon*). FABRICIUS.] so expect him to come again from heaven.”

## LXXII. AERIANS

[Col. 1186A]

[Note: [Col. 1186B] “There are other Aerians, so called from Aerius . . . who”] [Note: [Col. 1185D] Aerians. Epiphanius and Damascene, Heresy 75, call them *Aerianoi*; Augustine and the author of the *Praedestinatus*, chapter 53, call them *Aeriani*. In Damascene, Heresy 98, I think *Aereianōn* should be read in place of *Areianōn*, although Epiphanius and others report that Aerius also adhered to Arius. Aerius was still alive when Epiphanius wrote, in A.D. 375. FABRICIUS.]

The Aerians are so called after a certain Aerius. They practice abstinence and dwell in great numbers [Note: [Col. 1185D] In Pamphylia. Epiphanius testifies that Aerius himself had been a monk in Pontus, or Lesser Armenia. FABRICIUS.] in the province of Pamphylia. They are also called [Note: [Col. 1185D] Encratites. Augustine, on Philastrius’s authority alone, records that the Aerians shared the views of these people, for Epiphanius says not a word—*not even a grunt* (*oude gry*)—about this. Epiphanius himself, however, says much about the Encratites in Heresy 46, writing that in his own time a great number of them existed in Pamphylia and other provinces of Asia, vol. I, p. 399. FABRICIUS.] Encratites, that is, “the abstinent.” They possess nothing, [Note: [Col. 1185D] “They possess nothing.” Epiphanius says of Aerius: “He preaches renunciation” (*apotaxian kēryssei*). Damascene, on the contrary, says: “He rejects renunciation” (*apotaxian apokēryssei*). FABRICIUS.] abominate foods [Note: [Col. 1186C] “They abominate foods.” Damascene, on the contrary: “He freely employs every kind of meat-eating and luxury” (*Sarkophagiais pantodapais kechrētai kai tryphais adeōs*). Besides Epiphanius and others, John Zonaras in his canon concerning the Mother of God, published in vol. III of Cotelerius’s *Monuments*, p. 470, relates that they rejected the Church’s fasts and offerings for the dead. FABRICIUS.] which God gave with blessing to the human race, and even condemn marriages sanctioned by the Law, asserting that they were not instituted by God.

## LXXIII. BORBORIANS

[Note: [Col. 1186C] Borborians. Epiphanius, 26.3, p. 85, relates that certain Gnostics were called thus “from muddy obscenity” (*apo tēs aischrourgias borborōdous*), or the foul depravity of their life. Theodoret, *Haeretical Fables*, I.13: “Barbeliotes, that is Borborians” (*Barbēliōtai ēgoun Borborianoi*), whose “mystic rites” he testifies surpass every thought in foulness: “For the things done by them as divine surpass every evil calculation and every filthy conception” (*Panta gar logismon ponēron hyperbainei kai pasan ennoian mysaran ta par’ ekeinōn hōs theia prattomena*). See also Nicetas, *Thesaurus*, IV.2. FABRICIUS.—Borborians. Augustine calls them Borborites, as though “filthy,” because of the excessive indecency which they are said to practice in their mysteries, as Fabricius also noted from Epiphanius [Col. 1186D] and Theodoret. But Philastrius presents literally what they present allegorically, adding: “Thus they go into mud and, daubed with it, disfigure their faces and limbs, thereby showing God’s creation as blameworthy to all.” In the Corbie manuscript, *eademque* (“and thereby”) stands in place of *eadem re* (“by the same thing”), and is better; this reading should therefore also be restored in Gangius under “Borboriani,” where he cites this passage of Philastrius. GALEARDUS.]

There is another heresy, that of the Borborians. Entangled in the vices of the world and enslaved to evil [Note: [Col. 1186B] “lusts, they do not”] lusts, they do not expect a future judgment, but instead praise the world’s carnal desire. Thus they go into mud and, daubed with mud, disfigure their faces and limbs, [Note: [Col. 1186B] “and thereby show to all . . . permission”] thereby displaying God’s creation to all as though blameworthy. Yet that abyss of faults and ruinous condemnation of vices proceeds from human will, not through permission of the divine Law.

## LXXIV. ARTOTYRITES

[Note: [Col. 1186B] “There are other Artotyrites by name in Galatia.”] [Note: [Col. 1186D] Artotyrites. Compare Epiphanius and Damascene, Heresy 49. Augustine and the author of the *Praedestinatus*, chapter 28, state on the authority of the presbyter Timothy, in Cotelerius, vol. III of the *Monuments*, p. 379, that they descended from Marcion’s heresy: “The Artotyrites, then, derive from the heresy of this Marcion” (*Hoi oun Artotyritai ek tēs haireseōs toutou tou Markiōnos katagontai*). But Epiphanius joins them with the Montanists and Priscillianists. Their compound name comes from *artos*, “bread,” and *tyros*, “cheese.” FABRICIUS.]

The Artotyrites are so called from the thing itself. They are in Galatia and offer bread and cheese, not [Col. 1187A] [Note: [Col. 1187B] “That which the Catholic Church [does].” These heretics did not use flour kneaded with water in the sacred Supper, but flour kneaded with milk. The same Timothy says: “For kneading leaven with milk, they offer it to their own initiates” (*Galakti gar phyrōntes zymēn tois oikeiois mystais oregousin*). FABRICIUS.] that which the Catholic and Apostolic Church offers in its celebration.

## LXXV. ASCODROGITAE

[Note: [Col. 1187B] “In one sequence without a number. There are again other Ascodrogitae.”] There are [Note: [Col. 1187B] Ascodrogitae. Augustine, who follows Philastrius, more correctly calls them Ascites in Heresy 62; for *askos* in Greek is called *uter* in Latin, a wineskin, which they are said to carry about while it is inflated and covered, [Col. 1187C] in Bacchic frenzy. The author of the *Praedestinatus*: “Though they have nothing evil in doctrine, they nevertheless place a huge wineskin beside the altar, inflate it while empty, cover it with linens, and worship it, because they place in it the consecrated blood of the Lord. They cite the Gospel saying (Matt. 9:17): ‘They put new wine into new wineskins, and both are preserved.’” Epiphanius’s Tascodrogitae are entirely different from these, but identical with the Passalorinchites, whom our author discusses below in chapter 76. The Ascites used a wineskin to preserve the wine used in the sacred Supper. FABRICIUS.] Ascodrogitae in Galatia, who place an inflated and covered wineskin in their church. They go round it mad with [Note: [Col. 1187B] “rather”] drink and revelry, [Note: [Col. 1187C] Like the pagans in honor of Father Liber. Julian, Epistle 41: “Just as those who, at Dionysus’s beating of the thiasus, are carried unrestrainedly toward the dance” (*Kathaper hoi tō Dionysō ton thiasōn krousanti pros tēn choreian anetoi pherontai*). FABRICIUS.] like the pagans devoted to Father Liber, raging in deranged minds according to Gentile custom. They do not understand what the Savior says: that new wineskins should be taken and new wine put into them, not into old ones (Matt. 9:17).

And when they hasten to serve [Note: [Col. 1187B] “Or: to be mad?”] their own blindnesses, they prove utterly alien to Christian salvation. For the Apostle rejects that Jewish justification and carnal vanity, but affirms Christ’s true and complete knowledge, saying: “The old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new through Christ” [Col. 1187B] (2 Cor. 5:17). The Lord was speaking of the Law and shadow, and of the fullness of his own grace; and of the two human beings, as the Apostle says: “The first man is earthly, from the earth; the second man is heavenly, from heaven” (1 Cor. 15: [Col. 1188A] 47). For he announced in teaching and confirmed by events what was through shadow, and what was to be greater and better in the Lord’s presence.

## LXXVI. HERESY OF THE PASSALORINCHITES

[Note: [Col. 1187C] “There are other Passalorinchites.” Epiphanius, 48.14, p. 416, testifies that they were called Tascodrogitae, and that in their language *taskos* means “peg,” while *droungos* means “nose” or “snout”: “Among them *taskos* is called a peg, and *droungos* a nostril or snout” (*Taskos par’ autois passalos kaleitai, droungos de myktēr eitoun rhynchos kaleitai*). Since, therefore, while praying they affected the practice of putting the index finger of the hand upon the nose, “for the sake of sternness and self-righteousness they were called by some Tascodrogitae, that is, Passalorinchites” (*Katēpheias charin kai ethelodikaiosynēs, eklēthēsan hypo tinōn Taskodrougitai, toutesti Passalorynchitai*). This name has been remarkably abbreviated or corrupted among writers, as Cotelerius observed, vol. I of the *Monuments*, p. 774. Add that Theodore Studites calls them *tascodourgoi* in his Letter to Naucratius, vol. V of Sirmond’s works, p. 324. Nicetas Comnenus Papadopoli calls them *Perticonasati* in his *Mystagogical Preliminaries*, p. 152. FABRICIUS.—“There are other Passalorinchites.” Here Fabricius produces Epiphanius’s words, in which they are expressly called *Passalorynchitai*. Dupin is therefore wrong in asserting, *Ecclesiastical History*, section IV, that no ancient writer except Philastrius said a word about these heretics. Augustine also mentions them, *On Heresies*, 63, as he does the Barefooted, Heresy 68, [Col. 1188B] and the Rhetorians, Heresy 72; although Dupin asserts that these too were unknown to all writers except Philastrius. GALEARDUS.]

There are other Passalorinchites, who, placing a finger upon their noses and mouths, [Note: [Col. 1188B] “and lips . . . as though they pursued a practice”] and [Note: [Col. 1188B] Upon their lips, as though observing silence. Thus Harpocrates, the god of silence, is depicted restraining his lip with a finger in an ancient relief, illustrated by John Smetius, *Antiquities of Nijmegen*, pp. 127 ff.; John Lomeier, *Days of Joy*, dissertation 3, and especially in his *Harpocrates*, an illustrious and very learned work by Gisbertus Cuperus, published at Utrecht in 1687, quarto. FABRICIUS.] upon their lips, as though they practiced perpetual silence. They devote themselves to no other thing [Note: [Col. 1188C] “Other” for “otherwise.” See Vossius, *Aristarchus*, IV.6. FABRICIUS.] except silence, as though it were a pursuit.

They do this as though desiring to imitate [Note: [Col. 1188B] “They desire to imitate the blessed prophets . . . Blessed David: Set”] the prophets, because David the prophet says: “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth, and [Note: [Col. 1188C] “A door of enclosure.” *Thyran periochēs*.] a door of enclosure about my lips” (Ps. 141:3). And because the blessed prophets devoted themselves to fasts (Ps. 35:13; 69:10) and often [Note: [Col. 1188C] “Applied themselves to silence.” The Corbie manuscript likewise reads this; but the Lyons edition more rightly has “commended.” Arnobius, *Against the Nations*, V, said “to apply the mind to nourishment”; I do not remember ever reading “to apply silence to fasts.” GALEARDUS.] applied themselves to silence, these people take this up and think they observe something worth observing. [Note: [Col. 1188B] “They think they observe something.”] They hasten instead to follow Pythagorean [Note: [Col. 1188C] Pythagorean vanity. The reports about the five-year silence of the Pythagorean school are well known; see learned men on Gellius, I.9, and Laertius, VIII.10; Holstenius on Porphyry, p. 80; Rittershusius; and Andreas Schottus, Book II, *On the Good of Silence*. I add a passage from Procopius of Gaza, Epistle III: “Pythagoras of Samos, they say, did not honor silence without limit, but a fixed time brought a change toward speech, and they changed. Yet even during the time in which they kept silent, they surely were not required to know nothing from one another; rather, the tongue had silence, but the hand served the tongue, and by written characters they spoke again” (*Pythagoras Samios, touton phasin hōs ou mechri pantos etima sigēn, all’ hōristo chronos autēs metabolēn agōn epi logois kai meteballonto. All’ oude par’ hon esiōpōn chronon edei dēpouthen mēden par’ allēlōn eidenai, alla tēn men glōttan eiche sigē, hē de cheir diēkoneito tē glōttē, kai dia grammatōn palin ephthengonto*). FABRICIUS.] vanity rather than the heavenly life and wisdom of the prophets.

## LXXVII. AQUARII

[Note: [Col. 1188B] “There are others called Aquarii, who”] [Note: [Col. 1188D] Aquarii. Augustine and the author of the *Praedestinatus*, chapter 64. These are the Hydroparastatae, “offering water instead of wine” (*hydōr ant’ oinou prospherontes*), of whom Theodoret speaks in *Haeretical Fables*, I.21. The Ebionites are known, on the testimony of Epiphanius, 30.16, and Irenaeus, V.1, to have used water alone in the sacred Supper; so also did the Encratites, followers of Tatian, concerning whom see Epiphanius, 47.3, and the presbyter Timothy published by Cotelerius in vol. III of the *Monuments*, p. 379, who also calls them *Akkaophoroi*. So did certain others from Marcion’s school, the Manichaeans, and perhaps others assailed by Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, I, p. 137: “There are some who give thanks even over bare water” (*eisi gar hoi kai hydōr psilon eucharistousin*). Cyprian attacks them at length in Epistle 63 to Caecilius, pp. 148 ff. See also Chrysostom, Homily 83 on Matthew, p. 864; Beveridge on Trullan Canon 32; and Ittigius, *On Heresiarchs*, pp. 211 ff. The Aquei, or Hydrotheitae, of whom Augustine and the author of the *Praedestinatus* speak in chapter 75, and our author below in chapter 96, are distinct from these Aquarii. FABRICIUS.]

The Aquarii are so called because in the heavenly sacraments they [Col. 1189A] [Note: [Col. 1189B] “offer water”] offer water alone, not that [Note: [Col. 1189C] “which the Church [does].” The Catholic and Apostolic Church offers wine in the sacred Supper, whether unmixed or diluted with water. Cyprian especially strongly approved dilution, by which the people are signified through water as united to Christ’s blood. Compare, if you please, Edmund Martène, *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, pp. 322 ff.; John Bona, *Liturgy*, II.9; Gerhard Vossius, *Theological Theses*, p. 304; and Elmenhorst on Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Doctrines*, p. 174. The Greeks pour some hot water into the wine, so that it may represent more closely the blood of a living human being. See Peter Arcudius, *On the Agreement of the Two Churches in the Doctrine of the Sacraments*, III.39, p. 321. FABRICIUS.] which the Catholic and Apostolic Church customarily performs.

## LXXVIII. HERESY CONCERNING THE PROPHETS
Some assert that prophets arise every day and proclaim that prophecies are being made, not knowing that the Law and the Prophets extended only to John the Baptist (Matt. 11:13), and that the end of the Law and the Prophets was fulfilled and completed in Christ’s coming.

> **[Note: Col. 1189C] “The Law and the Prophets.”** In the same sense St John Chrysostom cites Daniel 9:24: “For when he for whom it is reserved has come, prophecy and vision shall be sealed.”  
> Greek: *Ὅτι ἐλθόντος ᾧ ἀπόκειται, σφραγισθήσεται καὶ προφητεία καὶ ὅρασις.*  
> FABRICIUS.

## LXXIX. THE COLLUTHIANS

> **[Note: Col. 1189B] “But there are other Colluthians.”**

The Colluthians, so called in Egypt after a certain Colluthus, say that the Lord is not the maker of evils.

> **[Note: Col. 1189D] “Colluthus.”** This is Colluthus, a presbyter of Alexandria, who, Epiphanius relates, disturbed the Church and disseminated false doctrines at the same time as Arius: *Panarion* LXIX.2, p. 728. Epiphanius also mentions his followers, who did not hesitate to call themselves Colluthians: “Some named themselves Colluthians” (*οἱ μὲν Κολλουθιανοὺς ἑαυτοὺς ὠνόμασαν*). Alexander of Alexandria censures Colluthus’s ambition in Theodoret, *History* I.4, p. 9; Athanasius testifies, in his *Apology to the Emperor Constantius*, vol. I, p. 732, that he died in the rank of presbyter.  
> FABRICIUS.

> **[Note: Col. 1189D] “Not the maker of evils.”** Augustine repeats this from Philastrius in chapter 65, and Isidore repeats it from Augustine in *Origins* VIII.5. The author of the *Praedestinatus*, chapter 65, is therefore mistaken in supposing that the Colluthians’ error consisted in teaching that God created both evils and goods.  
> FABRICIUS.

> **[Note: Col. 1190B] “But another.”** Florinus, concerning whom see above at chapter 57.  
> FABRICIUS.

But another opposed them, saying that the Lord is the maker of evils; he too is equally a heretic. Though both were carried away by empty controversy, they did not know the force of reason. For Scripture has proclaimed that God makes good things, and nevertheless also evils, when the prophet says: “I am the Lord, who make peace and create evils” (Isa. 45:7).

> **[Note: Col. 1190C] “Who make …”** LXX: *ὁ ποιῶν εἰρήνην καὶ κτίζων κακά*—“who make peace and create evils.”  
> FABRICIUS.

And another prophet says: “Is there evil in a city which the Lord has not made?” (Amos 3:6).

> **[Note: Col. 1190C] “Is there …”** LXX: *εἰ ἔσται κακία ἐν πόλει ἣν Κύριος οὐκ ἐποίησε*—“Will there be evil in a city which the Lord has not made?”  
> FABRICIUS.

But Scripture says that these evils were not made by God as evils by nature, but arise from human causes—namely, from people who sin against the Lord under the Law. They are trials, persecutions, and various distresses, which, by God’s permission, rise against sinners, as it is written: “Who gave Israel over to plunder? Was it not the Lord, against whom they sinned and would not walk in his ways?” (Isa. 42:24).

> **[Note: Col. 1190C] “These evils are not by nature.”** The sense is that they were not created by God in such a way as to be evil in nature, or to possess an evil nature. Below: “God did not make evil nature.”  
> FABRICIUS.

Scripture elsewhere says that God did not make an evil nature: “Behold, all things which God made were very good,” in the book of Genesis—that is, the creation of the world (Gen. 1:31).

> **[Note: Col. 1190C] “The creation of the world.”** Chalcidius, p. 372, speaks of the generation of the world. It has been observed by Humphrey Hody, in his learned work *On the Greek Sacred Scriptures*, p. 115, that Alexandrians used *genesis* (*γένεσις*) for creation (*κτίσις*).  
> FABRICIUS.

And elsewhere the prophet says: “For God did not make evil, nor does he delight in the destruction of the living” (Wisdom 1:13).

> **[Note: Col. 1190C–D] “For God …”** LXX: *ὅτι ὁ Θεὸς θάνατον οὐκ ἐποίησεν, οὐδὲ τέρπεται ἐν ἀπωλείᾳ ζώντων*—“For God did not make death, nor does he delight in the destruction of the living.” Philastrius wrote *evil*, using the genus for the species of evil, namely death, a term which he found in the Book of Wisdom. Ancient Christian writers frequently cite that book under the name of “the Prophet,” as I recall having noted above at chapter 26.  
> FABRICIUS.

Therefore evils are not natural through the agency of God the creator, but through human will, which is bound by the law of God, convicted by judgment, and restrained by correction. For the sake of conversion, these things are inflicted upon people daily by the Lord.

> **[Note: Col. 1190D] “By correction.”** Good writers used *coertio* or *coerctio* for *coercitio* (“restraint,” “correction”), and both forms occur indiscriminately in manuscripts.  
> FABRICIUS.
>
> **“But human … binds by correction.”** The passage is more obscure in the printed editions than could be restored by conjecture, unless the true reading had occurred in the Corbie manuscript: “which is bound by the Law of God and will be convicted by judgment, and is restrained by correction.” The Hamburg edition wrongly has *constringit* (“restrains”); the Basel and Lyons editions correctly have *constringitur* (“is restrained”). Shortly afterward, the Corbie manuscript as well as the Basel and Lyons editions have *dicuntur et ignorantur* (“are said and are not understood”) for *dicunt et ignorant* (“they say and do not know”), which appears in the Hamburg edition.  
> GALEARD.

When, therefore, they say these things, they do not understand them as they have been said. For the things which they suppose to be evils for people in correction are full of instruction and benefit; these are what perverse human will deserves to suffer. For the Apostle says: “Is God unjust, who inflicts his wrath upon human beings?” (Rom. 3:3).

> **[Note: Col. 1191B–C] “Is God unjust …?”** Greek: *Μὴ ἄδικος ὁ Θεὸς ὁ ἐπιφέρων ὀργήν;*  
> FABRICIUS.

Yet all these things are permitted to happen to humankind not without benefit and future advantage. For the righteous person is proved more faithful and more righteous by enduring tribulation; while the sinner either ceases from sin after amendment, or, if persisting, is taken from the world lest, while remaining in the body, he appear to commit further offences. Thus, either when amended he will not delay to perform good work while he still remains in the body, or his mind is restrained so that he may cease from sin, as the Apostle says: “He who has died has been justified from sin” (Rom. 6:7).

> **[Note: Col. 1191C] “He who has died …”** Greek: *ὁ ἀποθανὼν δεδικαίωται ἀπὸ τῆς ἁμαρτίας*—that is, “he sins no longer.”  
> FABRICIUS.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1191C] “Yet not without benefit.”** St John Chrysostom sets out certain outstanding benefits clearly and elegantly in Homily I *To the Antiochenes*. Add Gaudentius, Preface to Benivolus; Paulinus, Epistle 18 to Delphinus, bishop of Bordeaux; Isidore of Pelusium, Epistle 282 to the monk Boethus; and Nilus, Epistle 319 to the presbyter Ephestion.  
> FABRICIUS; GALEARD.

## LXXX. THE HERESY CONCERNING THE WORLD

There is another heresy which says that the world will not be changed but will always remain in the same state, even after the coming of our Lord Christ from heaven. Yet he himself says: “All things shall pass away and be changed” (Matt. 24:35; Mark 13:31; Luke 21:33).

> **[Note: Col. 1191C–D] “Will not be changed.”** Although below he judges more mildly concerning the opinion of those who believe that the world will perish and return into nothing, he already ranks among heresies the view of those who taught, with Ocellus of Lucania, Timaeus, and other pagan philosophers, that the world would remain eternal in its present state; and also with Philo the Jew, who defends the same view in *On the Incorruptibility of the World*, as does the anonymous Christian writer cited by Photius, *Codex* 36—“that the heavens are indissoluble” (*ὅτι ἀκατάλυτοί εἰσιν οἱ οὐρανοί*)—namely Cosmas Indicopleustes, book VII, pp. 275 ff. Danaeus, on Augustine’s *On Heresies*, chapter 67, calls them “Eternalists.” The author of the *Praedestinatus*, chapter 67, calls them “Satannians,” after some unknown Satannius.  
> FABRICIUS.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1191D] “After the coming of our Lord Christ from heaven.”** Understand this as referring to the Judgment and, as Augustine expresses Philastrius’s opinion, to the time after the resurrection of the dead.  
> FABRICIUS.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1191D] “All things shall pass away.”** Greek text: *ὁ οὐρανὸς καὶ ἡ γῆ παρελεύσονται*—“heaven and earth shall pass away.” All things are contained in heaven and earth.  
> FABRICIUS.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1191D] “Be changed.”** *Ἀλλαγήσονται*, Heb. 1:12, from Psalm 102:26.  
> FABRICIUS.

They do not understand that the Lord spoke of this for the sake of the changing of the elements, so that, once these have been changed, a new creation may be re-formed (Rev. 21:1). David also teaches this: “They shall perish, but you remain the same forever” (Ps. 102:26).

> **[Note: Col. 1191D] “They shall perish.”** LXX: *Αὐτοὶ ἀπολοῦνται, σὺ δὲ διαμένεις*—“They shall perish, but you remain.”  
> FABRICIUS.

And the Lord says: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Matt. 24:35; Mark 13:31; Luke 21:33). And: “I make a new heaven and a new earth,” says the Lord (Isa. 65:17).

The elements, therefore, are announced as to be restored rather than destroyed. And although it is not impossible for God—who made all things from nothing—to erase all things again, as blessed Job says, “If he destroys all things, who will say to him, ‘What have you done?’” (Job 9:12), nevertheless, if you think in this way, you will recognize the omnipotence of the Lord Christ. But if anyone judges that they are to be restored, he will understand consistently as well. For although Scripture shows that the seeds are perishable—that is, that the world itself can return to nothing—yet what God has made does not perish.

> **[Note: Col. 1192B–C] “To be restored rather than destroyed.”** He used *pereunda* (“things to be destroyed”) for *peritura* (“things that will perish”), contrary to the usage of better writers. So below: “For although Scripture shows the seeds to be destroyed”; and again: “In the resurrection of human beings, seeds not to be destroyed.” Similarly, shortly afterward he says *permanenda* for *permansura*: “The elements, then, will pass into greater glory, and are to remain in it with human beings.” As to the matter itself, most early doctors of the Church held that heaven and earth would not be annihilated at the consummation of the age, but changed and renewed through the *restoration* (*ἀποκατάστασις*, Acts 3:10) and *renewal* (*παλιγγενεσία*, Matt. 19:28).
>
> Barnabas, Epistle, chapter 15: “When his Son comes, he will abolish his time, judge the ungodly, and change the sun, the moon, and the stars; then he will rightly rest on the seventh day.”  
> Greek: *Ὅταν ἐλθὼν ὁ υἱὸς αὐτοῦ καταργήσει τὸν καιρὸν αὐτοῦ καὶ κρινεῖ τοὺς ἀσεβεῖς καὶ ἀλλάξει τὸν ἥλιον καὶ τὴν σελήνην καὶ τοὺς ἀστέρας, τότε καλῶς ἀναπαύσεται ἐν ἡμέρᾳ τῇ ἑβδόμῃ.*
>
> It would be lengthy to produce other testimonies of the ancients, which may be seen in Vossius, *Theological Theses*, pp. 248 ff.; Paul Sherlog, *Dioptra of Antiquity*, p. 285; Thomas Burnet, *Sacred Theory of the Earth* IV.1 ff.; Gataker, on Antoninus XI.1; Elmenhorst, on Gennadius, *Ecclesiastical Doctrines*, p. 164; D. Bebelius, *Ecclesiastical Antiquities of the Fourth Century*, vol. II, p. 610; Suicer, vol. II of the *Thesaurus*, p. 151; and Jacob Thomasius, *On the Stoic Conflagration of the World*, p. 17. For the agreement of the Jews, see Menasseh ben Israel, *On the Resurrection*, book III, chapter 4. Vincent Placcius, *of blessed memory* (*ὁ μακαρίτης*), collected the opinions of Dr Luther and our theologians in his vernacular work *On the Immortality of the Soul*, pp. 65, 93 ff.  
> FABRICIUS.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1192C–D] “It is not impossible for God.”** Against the opinion of the pagans, to which Philo agrees in *On the Incorruptibility of the World*, p. 728.
