For, if one listens to them, it is their established position that “it is impossible for anything to come into being from what is nowhere existent, and impossible and unceasing for what exists to perish” (*ἐκ τοῦ οὐδαμῆ ὄντος ἀμήχανόν ἐστι γενέσθαι τι, τό τε ὂν ἐξαπολέσθαι ἀνήνυστον καὶ ἄπαυστον*): nothing from nothing, and nothing can return into nothing.  
> FABRICIUS.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1192D] “If he …”** LXX: *ἐὰν ἀπαλλάξῃ, τίς ἀποστρέψει; ἢ τίς ἐρεῖ αὐτῷ, Τί ἐποίησας;*—“If he removes, who shall turn him back? Or who will say to him, ‘What have you done?’”  
> FABRICIUS.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1192D] “Scripture shows.”** In the passage cited above, Psalm 102:26.  
> FABRICIUS.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1192D] “What he made does not perish.”** For God hates none of the things he has made: “You abhor nothing that you have made” (*οὐδὲν βδελύσσῃ ὧν ἐποίησας*), Wisdom 11:24.  
> FABRICIUS.

For Solomon says that he made all things from nothing so that things which did not exist might exist (Wisdom 1:14).

> **[Note: Col. 1192D–1193C] “He made all things from nothing so that they might exist.”** LXX: *Ἔκτισε γὰρ εἰς τὸ εἶναι τὰ πάντα*—“For he created all things for existence.” Philastrius renders *ἔκτισε* (“he created”) by “he made from nothing.” He also has in view the passage in Hermas, book II, Mandate I, which he cites again below in chapter 123: “First of all, believe that God is one, who created, ordered, and made all things from non-being into being” (*Πρῶτον πάντων πίστευσον ὅτι εἷς ἐστιν ὁ Θεὸς ὁ τὰ πάντα κτίσας καὶ καταρτίσας καὶ ποιήσας ἐκ μὴ ὄντος εἰς τὸ εἶναι*).  
> FABRICIUS.

In the resurrection of human beings, too, he shows seeds that are not to perish but are coming into greater glory, as the Apostle says: “A natural body is sown; a spiritual body rises” (1 Cor. 15:44); “it is sown in corruption; it rises in incorruption” (ibid., 42).

> **[Note: Col. 1193C] “A natural body is sown … a spiritual body.”** Greek: *Σπείρεται σῶμα ψυχικόν, ἐγείρεται σῶμα πνευματικόν.*  
> FABRICIUS.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1193C] “It is sown … in corruption.”** Greek: *Σπείρεται ἐν φθορᾷ, ἐγείρεται ἐν ἀφθαρσίᾳ.*  
> FABRICIUS.

And the Apostle himself again says: “For the expectation of creation awaits the revelation of the children of God. For creation was subjected to vanity, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope of the dignity of future glory. Therefore creation itself also shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Rom. 8:19 ff.).

> **[Note: Col. 1193C] “In hope of the dignity of future glory.”** After *ἐπ’ ἐλπίδι* (“in hope”), Philastrius supplied from himself the words “of the dignity of future glory.”  
> FABRICIUS.

Thus he shows that the elements—that is, human beings together with this visible creation—are to advance from glory to glory, when the Lord says: “Then the light of the sun shall shine sevenfold” (Isa. 30:26).

> **[Note: Col. 1193C] “Then the sun shall shine sevenfold.”** LXX: *Τὸ φῶς τοῦ ἡλίου ἔσται ἑπταπλάσιον ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ*—“The light of the sun shall be sevenfold on that day.”  
> FABRICIUS.

The elements, then—the sun, moon, and stars—will pass into greater glory and are to remain in it with human beings, although the Lord who made all things can also bring them to nothing. Yet Christ’s majesty and power are eminent in this: that he permits the same elements to pass into greater glory. For the Apostle also announces and prophesies that these elements will be dissolved and come to nothing.

> **[Note: Col. 1193C–D] “Dissolved.”** 2 Peter 3:10: *Στοιχεῖα καυσούμενα λυθήσονται, καὶ γῆ καὶ τὰ ἐν αὐτῇ ἔργα κατακαύσεται*—“The elements, burning, shall be dissolved, and the earth and the works in it shall be burned up”; and v. 12: *Οὐρανοὶ πυρούμενοι λυθήσονται, καὶ στοιχεῖα καυσούμενα τακήσεται*—“The heavens, being set on fire, shall be dissolved, and the elements, burning, shall melt.”  
> FABRICIUS.

## LXXXI. THE BAREFOOTED

The heresy of the Barefooted holds that people ought to walk without shoes, because, they say, under Moses it was commanded: “Take off your shoes” (Exod. 3:5).

> **[Note: Col. 1193D] “The Barefooted.”** The author of the *Praedestinatus* and Augustine, chapter 68, following in Philastrius’s footsteps, call them *Gymnopodes*, because they always walked barefoot. Prateolus calls them *Nudipedes*.  
> FABRICIUS.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1193D] “Take off your shoes.”** LXX: *λῦσαι τὸ ὑπόδημα ἐκ τῶν ποδῶν σου*—“Untie the sandal from your feet.”  
> FABRICIUS.

They also appeal to Isaiah’s having gone barefoot for three years. But such practices belong rather to human and empty superstition, not to the tradition of the saints or to the command, authority, and power of our Lord Jesus Christ.

> **[Note: Col. 1193D] “Three years.”** As a sign of the impending captivity of the Egyptians and Ethiopians at the hands of the Assyrians.  
> FABRICIUS.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1193D] “Human and empty superstition.”** This is not said of Isaiah, who did this by God’s command, but of those who placed some supposed element of religious worship in that superstitious imitation.  
> FABRICIUS.

## LXXXII. THE NOVATIANS

The Novatians arose after the last persecution, from a certain Novatus. Before this, they believed as the catholic Church did, accepting the Old and New Testaments. But during persecution, because many believers had fallen and had been received into repentance by the catholic Church, they became angry—or rather, were led by presumption and pride—and attempted to sow an empty doctrine. They separated themselves from the catholic Church, disagreed with the goodness and mercy of Christ, and said that no place for repentance remains to a believer after baptism.

> **[Note: Col. 1194C] “After the last persecution.”** The last, or tenth, persecution began under Diocletian and Maximian Herculius around AD 285. But the Novatians had already troubled the Church after the eighth, Decian persecution, around AD 251. See Tillemont, vol. III, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*.  
> FABRICIUS.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1194C] “From a certain Novatus.”** The ancients mention two leaders of this heresy, Novatus and Novatian: the latter a presbyter of the Roman Church, the former of the African Church. See William Beveridge’s notes on Nicene Canon 8.  
> FABRICIUS.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1194C] “They formerly believed as the catholic Church.”** Novatian admits, in Atticus of Constantinople cited by Socrates VII.25, p. 367, that they had “introduced no innovation concerning the faith” (*οὐδὲν περὶ τὴν πίστιν καινοτομῆσαι*).  
> FABRICIUS.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1194C–D] “No place for repentance … after baptism.”** Eulogius attacks this Novatian error in Photius, *Codex* 182 and 208. Among modern writers, in addition to Tillemont and Beveridge, consult Gabriel Albaspinaeus, *Observations*, pp. 195 ff., and John Forbes, *Historico-Theological Instructions*, pp. 666, 710 ff.  
> FABRICIUS.

They do not know that the Lord cries through the prophet: “As I live, says the Lord, I do not will the death of the sinner, but rather that he should return and live” (Ezek. 33:11).

If, therefore, they say that Scripture spoke this of those who are to be baptized, but not of believers, let them hear the Saviour, after baptism by water, speaking thus of another baptism, namely that of penitential suffering: “I have a baptism with which to be baptized, and how I am constrained until it be accomplished” (Luke 12:50).

> **[Note: Col. 1194D] “I have a baptism with which to be baptized.”** Note the phrase *ἔχω βαπτισθῆναι* (“I have to be baptized”) for *μέλλω βαπτισθῆναι* (“I am about to be baptized”), of which John Bois has gathered many examples in his notes on Chrysostom, Savile edition, vol. VIII, pp. 41 ff.  
> FABRICIUS.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1194D] “Until it be accomplished.”** This should be read instead of the worthless words *si sciretis* (“if you knew”), which stood in earlier editions. The Greek is: *πῶς συνέχομαι ἕως οὗ τελεσθῇ*—“how I am constrained until it is accomplished.”  
> FABRICIUS.

Thus he plainly shows us that after the baptism which he had previously given through water, another baptism also—of penitential suffering—must be granted to fallen human beings by his own goodness and mercy and bestowed by the same Lord.

> **[Note: Col. 1194D] “Another baptism of penitential suffering.”** On this baptism of repentance, see John Morin’s extensive work *On the Sacrament of Penance* III.4; IX.2 and 13; X.6.  
> FABRICIUS.

The Apostles understood this from his most salutary suffering and proclaimed that, after that first grace, he had also bestowed this upon humankind. For, as provident and almighty, he grants sinners through repentance that one who has fallen may rise, fight again in that warfare, persevere in it, and hope to obtain from the Lord the victory he desires.

> **[Note: Col. 1195B] “One who has fallen, rising and fighting again.”** In the sacred warfare against the devil, into which he had been enlisted through baptism.  
> FABRICIUS.

For in Christ, his mercy, justice, and goodness abound daily toward sinners and penitents. Paul testified concerning those who had not repented because of sin, when he said in his Epistle: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (2 Cor. 11:29).

> **[Note: Col. 1195B] “Who is weak …?”** Greek: *Τίς ἀσθενεῖ καὶ οὐκ ἀσθενῶ;*  
> FABRICIUS.

And again: “Lest, when I come to you, the Lord should humble me again because of certain persons who have not repented” (2 Cor. 12:21).

> **[Note: Col. 1195B–C] “Lest I come …”** These are Paul’s full words: *Μὴ πάλιν ἐλθόντα με ταπεινώσῃ ὁ Θεός μου πρὸς ὑμᾶς καὶ πενθήσω πολλοὺς τῶν προημαρτηκότων, καὶ μὴ μετανοησάντων ἐπὶ τῇ ἀκαθαρσίᾳ*—“Lest, when I come again, my God humble me before you and I mourn many of those who had sinned previously and did not repent of their uncleanness.” Philastrius, as is his custom, abridged them.  
> FABRICIUS.

The Apostle Peter had said to Simon Magus: “Repent, if perhaps what you have done may be forgiven you.” And Paul, after a time, commands that the person whom he had rejected be received again.

> **[Note: Col. 1195C] “Whom he had rejected.”** The man whom he had delivered to Satan in 1 Corinthians 5:4, he receives again after proof of repentance in 2 Corinthians 2:7.  
> FABRICIUS.

Such persons, therefore, may suffer loss of rank, but not loss of salvation, as the Lord says: “There are many dwelling places in my Father’s house” (John 14:2).

> **[Note: Col. 1195C–1196A] “There are many dwelling places …”** *Ἐν τῇ οἰκίᾳ τοῦ Πατρός μου μοναὶ πολλαί εἰσιν*—“In my Father’s house are many dwelling places.” Ancient doctors of the Church understood this text not only as referring to the multitude of heavenly dwellings but also to the diversity of ranks.  
> FABRICIUS.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1195C] “Loss of rank.”** In the practice of the ancient Church, clergy were reduced to lay communion in order to remove scandal; and all who were admitted to public penance for apostasy or a graver crime lost their sacred orders, as Gabriel Albaspinaeus and John Morin observed at length in the works cited above. But here Philastrius, as below in chapter 89, understands “rank” as a higher degree of heavenly glory.  
> FABRICIUS.

## LXXXIII. THE MONTANISTS

The Montanists are those who rebaptize any persons whom they have deceived, and, in their madness, promise their own baptism in addition to the baptism of the catholic Church. They are also called Donatians, after a certain Donatus established in Africa, who sowed this heresy; and they are now called Parmenianists, after a certain Parmenio, who recently succeeded to their errors and falsehood.

> **[Note: Col. 1195C–D] “Montanists.”** The Donatists were called *Montenses* because, as Jerome testifies in his *Chronicle* under AD 356, they first began to have a church at Rome on a hill. Isidore, *Origins* VIII.5: “The heretics called Montani are so called because they hid in the mountains during persecution.” They are also called Montenses in Optatus, book II, chapter 4, and elsewhere. In Augustine, *On the Unity of the Church*, chapter 3, they are Rupitani; and in Epistle 53 (old edition 165), *Cuzupitani* also seems to be the reading for *Rupitani*. On the other Montanists, followers of Montanus, see above, chapter 49.  
> FABRICIUS.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1195D] “They rebaptize.”** See D. Thomas Ittig, *History of the Donatist Schism*, appended to his dissertation *On Heresiarchs*, §122 ff., and the writings of learned men on Optatus and in vol. IX of the new edition of Augustine’s works.  
> FABRICIUS.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1195D–1196C] “After a certain Donatus in Africa.”** The ancients mention two Donati as leaders of this heresy: one of Casae Nigrae, called “of the Huts,” and the other Donatus the Great, bishop of Carthage. Both were promoters of schism, but the former was earlier. Hence Augustine, *Heresies* 69: “The Donatians or Donatists … we understand Donatus, who came from Numidia and divided the Christian people against Caecilian, to have been the leader of this heresy. Having joined to himself bishops of the same party, he ordained Majorinus bishop at Carthage. Majorinus was succeeded, in the same division, by another bishop Donatus, who so strengthened this heresy by his eloquence that many think they are called Donatists more particularly after him.”  
> FABRICIUS.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1196C] “After a certain Parmenio.”** This is Parmenianus, who succeeded Donatus in the episcopate of Carthage in AD 368, and against whom the surviving writings of Optatus and Augustine were composed. The author of the *Praedestinatus*, chapter 69: “These heretics are called Montenses in parts of Italy, Parmenianists in inland Africa, and Donatists in the region of Carthage.” Parmenianus died in AD 391; from this passage one may rightly infer that Philastrius wrote while he was still alive.  
> FABRICIUS.

## LXXXIV. THE ABSTINENT

There are, in Gaul, Spain, and Aquitaine, certain persons who call themselves Abstinent. They likewise follow and do not hesitate to preach the most pernicious faction of the Gnostics and Manichaeans, separating human marriages by their persuasions and advocating abstinence from foods.

> **[Note: Col. 1196C] “They are in Gaul and Spain.”** I have written “in Gaul and Spain” instead of “in the Gauls and Spaniards.” It is clear that Philastrius is attacking the Priscillianists, who began to emerge about AD 380. See Tillemont, vol. VIII, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, p. 798; and the work against them, ascribed to Ambrose, on the Apostles’ Creed.  
> FABRICIUS.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1196C–D] “Of the Gnostics and Manichaeans.”** Augustine, *Heresies* 70: “The Priscillianists, whom Priscillian established in Spain, follow chiefly an amalgam of Gnostic and Manichaean doctrines.” Compare H. Dodwell, Dissertation 5 on Irenaeus, chapter 10, pp. 405 ff.  
> FABRICIUS.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1196D] “Separating human marriages.”** Leo the Great, Epistle 15 to Turibius (old edition 93), chapter 7, concerning the Priscillianists: “They condemn marriages and recoil from the procreation of offspring; in this, as in almost everything, they agree with the profanity of the Manichaeans.” First Council of Braga, AD 561, canon 11: “If anyone condemns human marriage and recoils from the procreation of offspring, as Manichaeus and Priscillian said, let him be anathema.”  
> FABRICIUS.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1196D–1197C] “Abstinence from foods.”** The same First Council of Braga, canon 14: “If anyone considers unclean meats, which God gave for human use, to be unclean and abstains from them not because of bodily affliction but because he supposes them unclean, so that he will not even taste vegetables cooked with meat, as Manichaeus and Priscillian said, let him be anathema.”  
> FABRICIUS.

This grace was granted by Christ to human choice, not as a commandment of the Law, but for the sake of heavenly advancement and rank (Matt. 19:12). For the Lord says to Peter: “Not all can receive this saying” (ibid., 11).

> **[Note: Col. 1197C] “Heavenly advancement.”** Greek: *διὰ τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν οὐρανῶν*—“for the sake of the kingdom of heaven.” He uses “rank” for a higher degree of heavenly glory, as in chapters 82 and 89.  
> FABRICIUS.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1197C] “Not all …”** Greek: *οὐ πάντες χωροῦσι τὸν λόγον τοῦτον*—“Not all can receive this saying.”  
> FABRICIUS.

And the same Lord again says: “Whoever dismisses his wife without a ground of sexual immorality makes her commit adultery” (ibid., 9).

> **[Note: Col. 1197C] “Without a ground of sexual immorality.”** Greek: *Εἰ μὴ ἐπὶ πορνείᾳ*, or, as other manuscripts have it, *παρεκτὸς λόγου πορνείας*.  
> FABRICIUS.

It is one thing, therefore, for this to take place by mutual consent (1 Cor. 7:5), with the purpose of attaining from the Lord the praise of greater merit; it is another thing to urge it contrary to the Law and contrary to the will of both parties.

> **[Note: Col. 1197C] “By mutual consent.”** Greek: *Ἐκ συμφώνου πρὸς καιρόν*—“by agreement for a time.”  
> FABRICIUS.

And again: “Let not the one who does not eat despise the one who eats, and let not the one who eats judge the one who does not eat” (Rom. 14:3).

> **[Note: Col. 1197C] “Let not the one who does not eat …”** The Greek text has the order reversed: *ὁ ἐσθίων τὸν μὴ ἐσθίοντα μὴ ἐξουθενείτω, καὶ ὁ μὴ ἐσθίων τὸν ἐσθίοντα μὴ κρινέτω*—“Let the one who eats not despise the one who does not eat, and let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats.”  
> FABRICIUS.

What is voluntary, then, is a desire for fuller praise—indeed, for heavenly reward. But what is outside the Law was not handed down by God Christ, but was invented through empty human presumption and error. For it is written: “I give you all things to eat as grass.”

> **[Note: Col. 1197C] “I give you all things to eat …”** LXX: *Ἰδοὺ δέδωκα ὑμῖν πάντα χόρτον*—“Behold, I have given you every herb”; not *ὡς χόρτον* (“as grass”).  
> FABRICIUS.

They do this in order that, gradually despising foods, they may say that they are not good, and consequently may hold and assert that foods were not granted by God to human beings for food, but were made by the devil. In this way they endeavour to proclaim that creation was made not by God but by the devil; and through this lie they have enslaved many souls.

> **[Note: Col. 1197C] “Made by the devil.”** This is expressly attributed to the Priscillianists by Augustine, *Heresies* 70, and by the First Council of Braga, canon 13.  
> FABRICIUS.

## LXXXV. THE WANDERERS

In Africa there are persons called Wanderers (*Circuitores*). They travel around the countryside and force those whom they encounter on the road to kill them, saying that they desire to suffer martyrdom; and under this pretext many of them at times commit robbery.

> **[Note: Col. 1197C–D] “Wanderers.”** These are those whom others, including Augustine and the author of the *Praedestinatus*, chapter 69, call Circumcellions. In Isidore VIII.5, *Campitae* should be read instead of *Crotopites*.  
> FABRICIUS.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1197D] “They force them to kill them.”** They threatened those persons with death unless they did so. Compare D. Thomas Ittig, *History of the Donatists*, §82. Similar is the drive toward self-destruction among the Patricians, discussed above in chapter 62.  
> FABRICIUS.

Some of them die as *biothanati*, throwing themselves over precipices and suffering a different ruinous death. Since they hasten so to perish without cause, they incur the loss of an honourable death and rather entangle themselves in the coming judgment of God than free themselves from it.

> **[Note: Col. 1197D–1198C] “Biothanati.”** The word is derived not from *βίος* (“life”) but from *βία* (“violence”), like *βιαιοθάνατος*: they rush toward death by a kind of violence, or take their own lives by violence done to themselves. See Du Cange in both glossaries; Elmenhorst on Arnobius, pp. 37 ff.; and Peter Wesseling, *Probabilia*, p. 35.  
> FABRICIUS.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1198C] “They incur the loss of an honourable death.”** Through their own fault they deprive themselves of the honour of the honourable death which awaited them by nature.  
> FABRICIUS.

## LXXXVI. HERESY CONCERNING FOOD AND THE HOLY SPIRIT

There are also those who do not eat with other people, led by empty presumption and thinking that they are doing something better. “For the prophets did this too,” they say (1 Kings [3 Kingdoms] 13:9), not understanding that a different dispensation was established for human beings by Christ the Lord.

> **[Note: Col. 1198C] “They do not take food with other people.”** Augustine, *Heresies* 71: “Philastrius says that there are other heretics who do not eat with people; but he does not state whether they do this with others not of their sect, or even among themselves.” The author of the *Praedestinatus*, chapter 71, calls them Adelophagi, saying that a Christian should not take food in such a manner as to be seen by another while eating.  
> FABRICIUS.

They think rightly concerning the Father and the Son, but do not understand rightly concerning the Spirit; they believe that the Holy Spirit is created and made, rather than God, as the Scriptures declare and the catholic Church proclaims.

> **[Note: Col. 1198C] “They do not understand rightly concerning the Spirit.”** Augustine repeats this from Philastrius. It is therefore surprising that the author of the *Praedestinatus* says that his Adelophagi confess the Trinity to be of one substance. Meanwhile, it is uncertain whom Philastrius is denouncing, since he had already spoken above, in chapter 67, of other Pneumatomachians.  
> FABRICIUS.

## LXXXVII. ANOTHER HERESY CONCERNING PASCHA

There is another heresy which maintains that Pascha ought to be celebrated with the Jews. These people live in Galatia, Syria, Phrygia, and Jerusalem; and, following the Jews, they perish in an error like theirs. In this way the Jews also confirm their own falsehood, when they see certain uneducated Christians following the vanity of their law rather than the rule of catholic truth. Yet the Jews celebrate with them, so that these persons are shown and recognized by all as partners in the Jews’ guilt and crime.

> **[Note: Col. 1198C–D] “Pascha ought to be celebrated with the Jews.”** On the fourteenth day of the moon; hence they were called Quartodecimans and Tessarescaedecatites. See Epiphanius and John of Damascus, *Heresies* 50; Augustine and the author of the *Praedestinatus*, chapter 29; and what was said above in chapter 58.  
> FABRICIUS.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1198D] “The Jews confirm their own falsehood.”** So that they may thereafter cling all the more stubbornly to the errors of Judaism.  
> FABRICIUS.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1198D] “They celebrate together with these persons.”** The Hamburg edition is wrong; the Corbie manuscript more correctly reads *cum istis concelebrant* (“they celebrate with these”). The Basel edition agrees with Hamburg; the Lyons edition reads *cum istis celebrabant* (“they were celebrating with these”). Then the Corbie manuscript reads *manifestarentur, atque ab omnibus dignoscerentur* (“that they might be exposed and recognized by all”), whereas the Hamburg and Basel editions have *manifestantur, atque ab omnibus dignoscuntur* (“they are exposed and recognized by all”).  
> GALEARD.

## LXXXVIII. THE APOCRYPHA
There is another heresy, called Apocryphal, that is, secret; which accepts only Prophets and Apostles, not the Canonical Scriptures, that is, the Law and the Prophets—namely, the Old and New Testament.

[Note: [Col. 1199B] Another heresy exists which is called Apocryphal, that is, secret and belonging only to the Prophets and Apostles.]

[Note: [Col. 1199B] Only the Prophets and Apostles. Heretics circulated and read various apocryphal writings. To recommend these to everyone, they did not consult the canon of sacred books received by the Church, but thought it sufficient if they were inscribed with the name of some Prophet or Apostle [Col. 1199C]. Yet the Church of Christ could never receive them or count them among the Canonical Scriptures. I formerly catalogued most of these apocrypha in two separate books: one, published A.D. 1713, *Codex Pseudepigraphus Veteris Testamenti*; the other, *Codex Novi Testamenti Apocryphus*, printed in 1709, with a supplement in 1719, octavo. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1199C] Not … the Law and the Prophets. The Valentinians, Manichaeans, and other heretics rejected the Law, attributing it to an evil god. It is established that these same people also rejected a large portion of the prophetic books, all those which are canonical. FABRIC.]

And when they wish to read only those apocryphal writings, they deliberately hold views contrary to the Canonical Scriptures, and gradually formulate doctrines, rendering judgments against them: against the Law and the Prophets, and advancing counsels contrary to the ordinances of the most blessed Apostles. Among these are especially the Manichaeans, Gnostics, Nicolaitans, Valentinians, and very many others, who, possessing apocrypha of Prophets and Apostles—that is, separate Acts—despise reading the Canonical Scriptures.

[Note: [Col. 1199C] And contrary to the ordinances of the most blessed Apostles. He will shortly say that a ruling about sacred books was laid down by the Apostles and their successors; see, if you please, my notes thereon. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1199C] And very many others, such as the Ebionites, Encratites, Apotactites, and Priscillianists. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1199C] Separate Acts: documents wholly different from those [Col. 1199D] used by the Catholic Church. FABRIC.]

For this reason it was decreed by the Apostles and their successors that nothing else ought to be read in the Catholic Church except the Law, the Prophets, the Gospels, the Acts of the Apostles, the thirteen Epistles of Paul, and seven others: two of Peter, three of John, one of Jude, and one of James; these seven are joined to the Acts of the Apostles. But the hidden writings, that is, the apocrypha, although they ought to be read by the perfect for the sake of moral instruction, ought not to be read by everyone, because persons without understanding have added and removed many things, as the heretics wished.

[Note: [Col. 1199D] Decreed by the Apostles and their successors. In canon 85, or the last of those which we call Apostolic, there is a ruling concerning the sacred books to be retained in the Church. There too, as in Philastrius, the Apocalypse and the Epistle to the Hebrews are omitted, though our author elsewhere testifies that he accepts both writings, as in chapters 60 and 89. Philastrius may also have had in mind Laodicean canon 60 (A.D. 367): “What books ought to be read”; except that there the fourteen Epistles of Paul are mentioned. On the order of the sacred books and on the joining of Acts of the Apostles to the Catholic Epistles, see my notes in the *Codex Apocryphus Novi Testamenti*, p. 750, and Humphrey Hody, *De Bibliis Originalibus*, IV.4, p. 644 ff.]

[Note: [Col. 1199D] They ought to be read by the perfect, not by everyone. Philastrius therefore did not doubt that the Canonical Scriptures ought to be read by everyone. The “perfect” are οἱ μεμνημένοι: those no longer merely sprinkled with Christian teaching, but thoroughly imbued with it. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1200B] Not by everyone, because they do not understand.]

[Note: [Col. 1200B] Because persons without understanding added and removed many things. In earlier editions *qui* wrongly stood for *quia*. Moreover, he used *tulerunt* in the sense of “they removed.” FABRIC.—“Although they ought to be read … persons without understanding.” The reading of the Corbie manuscript is decidedly better: “although they ought to be read by the perfect for the sake of moral instruction, they ought not to be read by everyone, because [*quia*, to be restored for *qui*] persons without understanding …” Fabricius had also advised this correction. Likewise, shortly afterward, the Corbie manuscript has “of Peter likewise the Apostle, and equally of Paul the Apostle,” as do the Basel and Lyons editions; but “and equally of Paul the Apostle” has dropped out in the Hamburg edition. GALEARD.]

[Note: [Col. 1200C] For the Manichaeans [have] apocrypha. I am certain that the word “Manichaeans” is out of place here. Whether “Matthew” should be written in its place, or “the apocrypha of Matthias and of the blessed Andrew,” or whether the word “Manichaeans” was inserted wholly at random and should therefore be deleted without replacing it with anything else, I would prefer to have determined by the judgment of manuscript codices rather than by my own. Concerning all those Acts and writings falsely attributed, by Manichaeans and other heretics, to Matthew, Matthias, Andrew, John, Peter, and other Apostles, I do not wish to repeat what I set forth in the *Codex Apocryphus Novi Testamenti*. FABRIC.]

For the Manichaeans have apocrypha of the blessed Apostle Andrew—that is, Acts concerning what he did when he came from Pontus into Greece, written down at that time by disciples following the Apostle. Hence the Manichaeans and others of that sort possess Acts of the blessed Andrew, of John the Evangelist, and likewise of the blessed Apostle Peter, in which, because they performed great signs and wonders, so that cattle, dogs, and beasts spoke, the ruined heretics have also judged the souls of human beings to be like those of dogs and cattle.

[Note: [Col. 1200B] Following the blessed Apostle.]

### LXXXIX. THE HERESY OF CERTAIN PERSONS CONCERNING PAUL’S EPISTLE TO THE HEBREWS

There are others also who do not maintain that Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews is his own, but say that it belongs either to the Apostle Barnabas, or to Clement, bishop of the city of Rome. Others say that it is Luke the Evangelist’s; they also wish to read an Epistle to the Laodiceans as a writing of the blessed Apostle. Because they added into it certain things while holding unsound views, it is not read in the Church; and even if it is read by some, it is nevertheless not read publicly to the people in church. Only his thirteen Epistles are read, and at times the Epistle to the Hebrews.

[Note: [Col. 1200B] There are others who … [say it] is, but.]

[Note: [Col. 1200C] There are others also. Especially in the West; nevertheless, they should not for that reason be classed as heretics. Peter of Blois: “The Epistle to the Hebrews is considered by many Latins uncertainly to be Paul’s because of the difference in style; some suspect that Barnabas wrote it, others that Clement did.” Friedrich Spanheim discusses this question fully and learnedly in his book on the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, which he vindicates for the Apostle Paul; so too Tillemont, vol. I, *Mémoires ecclésiastiques*, pp. 311, 607 ff. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1200D] Barnabas. Thus Tertullian, *On Modesty*, ch. 20; Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 5, and Primasius, preface to the Epistle to the Romans, refer to that passage. See, if you please, my notes in Book IV of the *Bibliotheca Graeca*, ch. 5, p. 161. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1200D] Or Clement. Because of similarity of language, not a few people in former times thought that at least the Greek translation of the Epistle to the Hebrews, made from Hebrew, was by Clement, as is clear from Eusebius, *History* III.38, Gobarus in Photius, *Codex* 222, and Theophylact. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1201B] Luke. Lanfranc of Canterbury, in his preface to Paul’s Epistles, also mentions the opinion which unhesitatingly attributes the Epistle to the Hebrews to Luke. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1201B] The Epistle to the Laodiceans: falsely attributed to Paul on grounds drawn from Colossians IV.16. It was already mentioned by Jerome, Theodoret, and others, as I showed in the *Codex Apocryphus Novi Testamenti*, p. 853 ff. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1201B] Some wish to read [it as] a writing of the blessed Apostle because they added.]

And because he wrote in it in a rhetorically persuasive style, they therefore do not think it belongs to the same Apostle. And because it says in it that Christ was “made,” it is therefore not read. Likewise, [they object] concerning repentance (Heb. VI.4; X.26), on account of the Novatians. Yet when it says that Christ was made (Heb. III.2), it says that he was made in respect of his body, not his divinity, since it teaches in the same place that the Son is of the divine and paternal substance, who is, it says, “the radiance of glory and the image of his substance” (Heb. I.3). Nor does it exclude repentance in its teaching, but shows a different degree of standing between one who has remained whole and one who has sinned. Thus loss concerns standing in the person who sinned, not loss of salvation. For if anyone has fought courageously through martyrdom, he shall receive his former standing; or if he has lived worthily in this age, he obtains what he desires to attain.

[Note: [Col. 1201B] And in it, rhetorically.]

[Note: [Col. 1201C] In persuasive speech. Origen, in Eusebius, *History* VI.25, p. 227, observed that the Epistle to the Hebrews is “more Greek in the composition of its expression, not having the Apostle’s unpolished manner of speech” (συνθέσει τῆς λέξεως ἑλληνικωτέραν, οὐκ ἔχουσαν τὸ ἐν λόγῳ ἰδιωτικὸν τοῦ Ἀποστόλου). FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1201B] And because [it says] Christ was made … between this one.]

[Note: [Col. 1201C] Christ made. Greek: πιστὸν ὄντα τῷ ποιήσαντι αὐτόν, “faithful to him who made him”—that is, made him high priest (ἀρχιερέα), as Photius correctly explains, III.10, p. 46, against the Manichaeans. It must be understood in the same sense as Acts II.36: “God made him both Lord and Christ” (Ὅτι Κύριον καὶ Χριστὸν αὐτὸν ὁ Θεὸς ἐποίησε). FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1201C] The radiance of glory. Greek: “the radiance of [his] glory and the exact imprint of his substance” (Ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης καὶ χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ). FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1201C] Loss of standing. So above, ch. 81, concerning the Novatians: “Such persons can therefore suffer loss of standing, not loss of salvation.” FABRIC.]

Moreover, in the Epistle itself it excludes rebaptizers; it does not deny the baptism of repentance. It should be considered that repentance is at times found fruitful in many penitents, who were afterward commended by the Lord in faith, life, and good work in this age, as they persevered in good things and fruitful works. For the Lord said through the prophet: “I shall not remember his evils, but rather his good deeds, if he shall henceforth remain in good works” (Ezek. XXIII.16).

[Note: [Col. 1201C] It excludes rebaptizers. For ἅπαξ φωτισθέντας, Heb. VI.4, means “those once baptized.” Thus Jonas of Orléans, Book I against Claudius of Turin (in the *Orthodoxographi*, p. 1221): “It is impossible for sins committed after baptism to be cleansed by repetition of baptism. For as Christ died once in the flesh on the cross, so we die once in baptism—not in the flesh, but to sin. Therefore, as he cannot be crucified again, so neither can we be baptized. Sins committed after baptism, however, are washed away by the tears of repentance and by generous almsgiving.” FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1202B] Former soundness.]

[Note: [Col. 1202B] It will be found fruitful in many.]

[Note: [Col. 1201D] “I shall not remember …” LXX: “All his sins which he has committed shall by no means be remembered, because he has done judgment and righteousness; in them he shall live” (Πᾶσαι αἱ ἁμαρτίαι αὐτοῦ, ἃς ἥμαρτεν, οὐ μὴ ἀναμνησθῶσιν, ὅτι κρῖμα καὶ δικαιοσύνην ἐποίησεν, ἐν αὐτοῖς ζήσεται). The same sense occurs in XVIII.28. FABRIC.]

### XC. MELITIANS

The Melitians derive from a certain Melitius in Egypt, who had belonged to the Arian party and was cast out of the Catholic Church. Later he was received back, as though he were following the truth, together with his disciples. But afterward, wishing to act without discrimination, they communicated both with heretics and with the Catholic Church. When the Catholic Church learned of their indiscriminate conduct, it excluded them from its communion.

[Note: [Col. 1202B] There are others from Melitius.]

[Note: [Col. 1201D] Melitius. Meletius, or Melitius, an Egyptian and bishop of Lycopolis in the Thebaid, was deposed by Peter of Alexandria because he had sacrificed to idols during persecution. Around A.D. 301 he created a schism. See Athanasius, *Apology* 2, p. 777; Pappus, *Synodicon*, ch. 32; Socrates, *History* I, pp. 14 and 28 ff.; Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History* I.8 and *Compendium of Heretical Fables* IV.7; Augustine and the author of the *Praedestinatus*, heresy 48 [Col. 1202C]. Other Meletians derive from Meletius of Antioch; concerning them see Tillemont, vol. VII, *Mémoires*, p. 9. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1202C] He had belonged to the Arian party. Sozomen, I.15, testifies that Arius at first supported the schism of Melitius the Egyptian, but that, after abandoning Melitius, Arius was ordained deacon by Peter of Alexandria and later again disapproved Peter’s actions against the Melitians. Theodore the Studite, however, denies that the Melitians themselves held heterodox doctrine, Epistle 40, vol. V of Sirmond’s edition, p. 326; and Epiphanius testifies that Melitius taught nothing contrary to the faith of the Catholic Church, *Panarion* LXVIII.1 and 3. Indeed, he relates that Melitius discovered Arius’s heresy and reported it to Alexander of Alexandria, LXVIII.4. Yet he also reports that the Melitians later communicated with the Arians, LXVIII.6: “but now, having allied themselves with the Arians” (νῦν δὲ Ἀρειανοῖς συναφθέντες). John of Damascus, *Heresies* 68. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1202C] Received as though following the truth. At the Council of Nicaea, Meletius retained the title of bishop, and [Col. 1202D] the Melitians were permitted to carry out the functions of their office in the Church, with only their right to vote in elections removed. See Valesius on Socrates, I.9. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1202D] And with heretics—namely, Arians. See Epiphanius, vol. I, p. 721; Tillemont, vol. VI, *Mémoires*. FABRIC.]

### XCI. RHETORIUS

[Note: [Col. 1202D] Rhetorius. In the author of the *Praedestinatus*, ch. 72, citing Philastrius through Augustine, they are called Rhetorians. Athanasius, *Against Apollinaris* I, p. 926: “For you will grant to all heretics the most impious notion of the one once called Rhetorius, whose impiety it is even frightening to utter” (Δώσετε γὰρ πᾶσιν αἱρετικοῖς κατὰ τὴν τοῦ ποτε λεγομένου Ῥητορίου ἔννοιαν ἀσεβεστάτην, οὗ καὶ τὴν ἀσέβειαν ἐξειπεῖν φοβερόν). In Augustine’s judgment, the doctrine Philaster ascribes to the Rhetorians is so absurd that it seems incredible even to him. Cotelerius compares it with the doctrine of Apelles in his notes on the *Apostolic Constitutions* VI.10. FABRIC.]

There are others in Egypt and Alexandria deriving from a certain Rhetorius, who praised all heresies, saying that all thought rightly and none of them erred, but that all of them walked rightly; and he thought it wrong not to believe this. If, then, he praised everyone, whom did he condemn? Therefore he does not hold what is true.

[Note: [Col. 1202D] From a certain Rhetorius. I suspect that the rhetor Themistius lies concealed under this Rhetorius. In his twelfth oration to Valens, p. 159, and his fifth to Jovinian, p. 69, Themistius teaches that the Deity is so far from being offended by that diversity of opinions concerning divine matters [Col. 1203C] that it even delights in it. Symmachus expresses the same view in Prudentius II, 772 [Col. 1203D]:

> Yet he persists in affirming that, when the one God is sought,  
> the road of travel is manifold and varied.  
> Hence some hasten in one direction, others in another,  
> each through his own winding paths; but the meeting-points  
> are constrained by the same end, and converge together into one.  
> FABRIC.]

And therefore the heretic Photinus is to be praised, who denies that Christ the Lord existed with the Father before the ages; and so is every heresy which blasphemes either the Father, or the Son, or the Spirit. Why, then, does he praise blaspheming heretics, when Christ the Lord has already condemned them from this present age, saying that blasphemy against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven to persons who blaspheme and persevere, neither here nor in the age to come (Matt. XII.31)? It is therefore evident that this man too is a heretic—or rather, that he knows nothing—since he judged that they ought to be praised rather than reproved and rejected.

[Note: [Col. 1203D] Photinus. On whose heresy, see above, ch. 65. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1203C] In the age to come.]

### XCII. HERESY CONCERNING THE DIVINITY OF CHRIST

There is another heresy which says that the Divinity suffered when the flesh, joined to the Divinity, suffered on the cross. It errs in this: not only can the Divinity naturally neither suffer, nor be held, nor be seen, but neither can the soul of a human being, made by God, as the Lord says: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Matt. X.28). Thus in every respect those persons err who say that Christ’s Divinity is passible by nature, and impiously suppose that it suffered pain, or wept, or groaned. For Christ’s suffering is natural to the flesh, not [a suffering] of the Divinity.

[Note: [Col. 1203D] The Divinity suffered pain. This error is noted especially in those who taught that Christ assumed flesh without a soul, and that the Logos (Λόγος) was in him in place of a soul, as I said above on ch. 69. The author of the *Praedestinatus*, ch. 73, calls them Theophonites; Danaeus, on Augustine, ch. 73, calls them Theopassians; Nicephorus, XV.28, and others, call them Theopaschites. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1203C] Erring in that.]

[Note: [Col. 1203D] “Do not fear …” Yet Philastrius wrongly infers from this passage that the soul is not subject to pain; he himself rightly observed in ch. 69, from Matt. XXVI.38, that Christ’s soul suffered pain. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1203C] Is passible by nature.]

[Note: [Col. 1203C] Or wept.]

[Note: [Col. 1203C] Or groaned.]

[Note: [Col. 1203D] Naturally in the flesh. I added the word “flesh,” since the sense requires it. FABRIC.—“Naturally in the flesh, not with the Divinity suffering.” Fabricius adds: “I added the word FLESH, since the sense requires it.” Correctly; for Philastrius himself shortly afterward says: “He suffered in passible flesh, not in Divinity naturally impassible”; and on the following page, “when human flesh naturally suffered.” GALEARD.—(Fabricius thought the word “flesh” should be added because the sense required it. But, it seems, in vain. For immediately afterward the holy Father repeats the same thought, demonstrating that “flesh” is superfluous there. Thus he shortly says: “He suffered in passible flesh, NOT in Divinity naturally impassible.” Those latter words agree perfectly with the earlier words, “naturally, with the Divinity not suffering.” GALLAND.)]

For this reason he who was in passible flesh was not recognized by the Jews: he who was proclaimed by the Law and Prophets as the true God and openly foretold as coming in the flesh. The Prophet says: “God shall come openly” (Ps. L.3). Again, the same prophet David says: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup” (Ps. XVI.5). For what is the cup except his suffering? While he bestowed upon the human race the gift of so great goodness and mercy, he was unknown to the most wicked people of the Jews.

[Note: [Col. 1204D] “God shall come openly.” LXX: “Our God shall come and shall not keep silence” (Ἥξει ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν καὶ οὐ παρασιωπήσεται). FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1204D] “The Lord [is] the portion of my inheritance.” LXX: “The Lord [is] the portion of my inheritance and of my cup” (Κύριος μερὶς τῆς κληρονομίας μου καὶ τοῦ ποτηρίου μου). FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1204D] What is the cup except his suffering? From Matt. XX.22. Compare the works of St Maximus, vol. I, p. 73 ff. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1204C] Most wicked.]

He therefore suffered in passible flesh, not in Divinity naturally impassible; he is acknowledged and believed, with the Divinity nevertheless not absent but joined equally with the body, on account of the mystery of consummation decreed and defined beforehand. Knowing this, the Apostle did not separate the Divinity from the flesh on the cross, saying: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (I Cor. II.8). Paul therefore joined both together to manifest to us Christ’s most complete goodness and mercy.

[Note: [Col. 1204C] In passible flesh, not [one] who is both acknowledged and believed, not joined with the body.]

[Note: [Col. 1204D] The mystery of consummation. Below in this chapter: “The mystery, for the sake of our salvation, was consummated by the Lord, so that there might be a complete conquest of the enemy.” From John XIX.30: τετέλεσται, “It is finished.” FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1204D] Lord of glory: Κύριον τῆς δόξης. Compare Alcimus Avitus, Epistle 3. FABRIC.]

But the Apostle Peter openly taught both what is passible by nature and what is impassible, saying: “He was put to death indeed in the body, but made alive in the Spirit.” Therefore neither was the flesh absent from the Divinity, nor the Divinity from the flesh, when human flesh naturally suffered; and in this very event, by the permission of Christ’s Divinity, the mystery for our salvation was consummated by the Lord, so that there might be a complete conquest of the enemy: so that he who was seen to suffer as a human being, though he was God in flesh, might then conquer the enemy, not for himself but for us; and so that, although we had previously been conquered, he might in his suffering open to those believing in him the power to conquer, and grant heavenly glory to those following him.

[Note: [Col. 1204D] “Put to death indeed …” Greek: “having been put to death in the flesh, but made alive in the spirit” (θανατωθεὶς μὲν σαρκί, ζωοποιηθεὶς δὲ τῷ πνεύματι). FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1204C] And in this very event.]

[Note: [Col. 1204D] And we, already conquered. Easily to be conquered, unless we were protected by his aid and assistance. FABRIC.]

Therefore no such natural passion or pain was produced in his Divinity, as some suppose; otherwise he was merely human, not God and human, as it is written (John I.14 and elsewhere). Rather, the mystery of our eternal salvation was consummated, which had been foretold beforehand alike by the Law and the Prophets.

[Note: [Col. 1205C] Therefore no natural.]

### XCIII. HERESY MAKING GOD THREE-FORMED

There is a heresy which says that God is, as it were, three-formed and composite, so that one part is of the Father, one part of the Son, and one part of the Holy Spirit; and it maintains that this is what should be believed. In saying this, it neither knows nor understands the teaching of divine Scripture. For in declaring a certain threefold substance, it blasphemes greatly, being ignorant that one is he who sent and another he who was sent.

[Note: [Col. 1205C] Another heresy.]

[Note: [Col. 1205C] A three-formed God. In Danaeus on Augustine, heresy 74, they are the Triforms or Triformians. In the author of the *Praedestinatus*, ch. 74, they are Triscilidae—or perhaps Triselidae or Triscelidae—distinct from the Tritheists, but closer to the Sabellians, concerning whom Philastrius spoke above in ch. 54. Add Chiffletius on Vigilius, p. 145. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1205C] It maintains this, and in saying this neither knows nor understands.]

[Note: [Col. 1205C] In declaring … it blasphemes greatly … in ignorance.]

There is therefore a true Person of the Father, who sent the Son; a true Person of the Son, who came from the Father; and a true Person of the Spirit, who was sent by the Son and Father. Accordingly, these three Persons possess one truth, majesty, equality of substance, and eternal divinity. For as the Father’s Person is immense and ineffable, so is that of the Son and so is that of the Holy Spirit, so that in the distinction of names and the three Persons there is no diversity of nature.

[Note: [Col. 1205C] The true Person of the Father. The Athanasian Creed: “The Person of the Father is one, of the Son another, and of the Holy Spirit another. But the divinity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one, their glory equal, and their majesty coeternal.” FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1205C] And equality of substance.]

[Note: [Col. 1205D] For as [the Father] is. In the same Creed: “Such as the Father is, such is the Son, and such the Holy Spirit.” FABRIC.]

This Trinity is therefore immeasurable, invisible, and ineffable; it is known by faith alone, yet cannot be worthily expressed by the exposition of human speech and mortal understanding.

[Note: [Col. 1205D] Immeasurable. Others say “immense”; Salvianus said “unmeasurable.” FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1205C] And invisible and.]

For when he says that the Father sends the Son and the Son sends the Holy Spirit, he says it on account of the Persons; he does not show them to be separated by distance of place. This is because of the heretics Sabellius and Photinus, who refused to understand God rightly. The Lord says: “To whom have you made me like, and to whom shall I be like?” (Isa. XL.18). “For as heaven is distant from earth, so are your understandings, thoughts, and counsels distant from my understandings and thoughts,” says the Lord (Isa. LV.9).

[Note: [Col. 1205D] For when he says. The Savior uses human speech in John V.30, 37; VIII.16, 18; XV.26; XVI.7. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1205D] Sabellius and Photinus: the former confounds the Persons; the latter divides the nature of God. Photinus was discussed in ch. 65. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1205D] “To whom …?” Greek: “To whom did you liken the Lord, and with what likeness did you liken him?” (Τίνι ὡμοιώσατε Κύριον, καὶ τίνι ὁμοιώματι ὡμοιώσατε αὐτόν). FABRIC.]

When, therefore, he says that the Father sent and that the Son was sent, he says it on account of the Persons, lest anyone suppose that the Father himself is the Son or that the Son himself is the Father—a delirium held by Sabellius. And lest the Son, sent from heaven, should be thought not to be everywhere in the Father, he indeed said that he was sent by the Father, but he also showed that he is everywhere with the Father, saying: “The Father who sent me is with me” (John VIII.16).

[Note: [Col. 1205C] And was sent.]

[Note: [Col. 1205D] “The Son was sent forth.” Thus the Hamburg, Basel [Col. 1206C] and Lyons editions—certainly incorrectly. The Corbie manuscript rightly has “and the Son was sent”; then, shortly after, the Corbie manuscript reads “chiefly established in the flesh,” with the conjunction removed; perhaps it ought to be restored after “might be made manifest to the human race.” GALEARD.]

[Note: [Col. 1205C] In holding this view.]

[Note: [Col. 1205C] Everywhere with the Father.]

[Note: [Col. 1206C] Yet he showed himself to be.]

[Note: [Col. 1206C] “The Father who sent [me] …” Greek: “I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me” (Ὅτι μόνος οὐκ εἰμί, ἀλλ᾽ ἐγὼ καὶ πέμψας με πατήρ). FABRIC.]

Therefore he did not speak of a separation in place, since the Son himself, with the Father and Holy Spirit, fills and contains all things. Rather, he spoke so that we might believe in the Father’s true Person, in the Son’s Person such as is the Father’s, and in the true Person of the Holy Spirit such as is the Son’s; and so that we might recognize one substance of quality, majesty, and power in these three Persons. He deigned to teach these things, especially while established in the flesh, in which both his humility shone forth to the world and his ineffable goodness was displayed; and [he showed] the condescension to human frailty in such abundant mercy and generosity that it might be made manifest to the human race. He deigned thus to act and speak for our salvation, that we might be able in some measure to know, grasp, and understand concerning God.

[Note: [Col. 1206C] Such as is the Father’s.]

[Note: [Col. 1206C] Let us believe the true Person … the Person of the three Persons. For let us recognize the substance of quality; these things thus.]

[Note: [Col. 1206C] One substance of quality. Against Eunomius, who taught three different substances of quality, ch. 68. [Col. 1206D] Below, ch. 109: “[David] proclaimed a Trinity of Persons, yet one equal power of majesty, substance, and divinity.” FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1206C] In the flesh.]

[Note: [Col. 1206C] He deigned [to do] these things.]

### XCIV. ON THE DIVERSITY OF THE HEAVENS

There is a heresy which disputes concerning the diversity of the heavens. For Scripture declares that on the first day heaven and earth, these two elements, were made; on the second day, that the firmament of water was made, and nevertheless testifies that the firmament itself was called heaven. David speaks thus concerning the heavens: “Praise the Lord, heavens of heavens, and waters that are above the heavens” (Ps. CXLVIII.4). Therefore, if anyone wishes to understand six heavens according to David, and this firmament as a seventh, he does not err. For Solomon says that there are three heavens: “Heaven, and the heaven of heaven” (III Kings VIII.27). Likewise the Apostle Paul confesses that he was caught up as far as the third heaven (II Cor. XII.3). Thus whether anyone understands seven, as David does, or three, or two, he does not err, since the Lord also says: “Our Father who is in the heavens” (Matt. VI.9). For even the pagans sometimes profess one heaven, and sometimes heavens. David therefore taught what is complete; Solomon and the blessed Paul likewise what is partial. But the book of Genesis has announced two heavens to us.

[Note: [Col. 1206D] On the diversity of the heavens. The arguments Philastrius makes in this chapter are not very sound, and Augustine rightly passed over this whole matter, as he did several others, in his own work on heresies. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1206C] Another heresy disputes concerning the diversity of the heavens.]

[Note: [Col. 1206D] Scripture: Gen. I.1 and 8. From these passages he concludes below that the book of Genesis announces two heavens to us. Cosmas Indicopleustes likewise maintains that there are no more than two heavens, III, p. 177; VII, p. 276; IX, p. 312. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1206D] “Praise the Lord …” LXX: “Praise him, heavens of heavens, and the water above the heavens” (Αἰνεῖτε αὐτὸν οἱ οὐρανοὶ τῶν οὐρανῶν, καὶ τὸ ὕδωρ τὸ ὑπεράνω τῶν οὐρανῶν).]

[Note: [Col. 1206C] “Praise the Lord, [you] heavens of heavens.”]

[Note: [Col. 1207B] Six heavens. Since the word in the dual number occurs three times in David, Philastrius infers six heavens from his words; and, counting the firmament as one alongside them, he affirms below that David understands seven heavens. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1207B] This firmament as the seventh. From Gen. I.8. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1207B] LXX: “Heaven and the heaven of heaven will not suffice for you” (Ὁ οὐρανὸς καὶ ὁ οὐρανὸς τοῦ οὐρανοῦ οὐκ ἀρκέσουσί σοι). FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1207C] Greek: “caught up as far as the third heaven” (ἁρπαγεὶς ἕως τρίτου οὐρανοῦ). FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1207B] He confesses that he was caught up.]

[Note: [Col. 1207C] Greek: “Our Father who is in the heavens” (Πάτερ ἡμῶν ὁ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς). FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1207B] The most foolish pagans profess one heaven and one pole.]

[Note: [Col. 1207C] And heavens. Simplicius, in his commentary on Epictetus, p. 233, mentions eight heavens according to the opinion, namely, of those who count the planetary orbits as heavens. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1207B] The blessed David taught what is complete.]

[Note: [Col. 1207B] It announced two heavens to us.]

### XCV. HERESY WHICH DOES NOT KNOW AND REJECTS THE LAND OF BLESSEDNESS

There is another heresy which disputes concerning the earth, saying that this is the only earth and that there is no other. It is ignorant that there is another earth, which is as it were the womb of all things and contains the universe; which is found in Scripture as ὕλη (*hylē*), that is, matter; which is invisible and unformed; and which was made by God on the first day. But this earth in which we dwell is shown to be founded upon water, as David said: “You founded the earth upon the waters” (Ps. CXXXVI.6).

[Note: [Col. 1207C] The land of blessedness. As the chapter titles are not by Philastrius himself, so the present one is also foreign to Philastrius’s purpose; for he is not speaking of a land of blessedness, but of that invisible and unformed earth of Gen. I.2. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1207C] Another heresy. Augustine was quite right to pass over this one too. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1207C] This one alone. Philastrius thinks two earths must be distinguished from one another: one, given as a kind of common matter to all things, concerning which Moses speaks in the opening words of Genesis, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth”; and another, the dry land which afterward emerged above the waters, Gen. I.10. Below, ch. 96: “There is one earth which contains all things, and another which is founded upon water.” FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1208B] The womb of all things … which as it were.]

[Note: [Col. 1207D] As it were the womb of all things. Other ancient writers thought likewise with Philastrius, including Augustine in *On Genesis against the Manichaeans* and elsewhere; Caesarius, Question 51, vol. I of the Ducaean supplement, p. 582. See Petavius, *Theological Dogmas*, *On the Work of the Six Days*, I.2. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1207D] In the Scriptures. In Wisdom XI.17: “Your all-powerful hand, which created the world from unformed matter” (Ἡ παντοδύναμός σου χεὶρ κτίσασα τὸν κόσμον ἐξ ἀμόρφου ὕλης). FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1207D] Invisible and unformed. Gen. I.2. See Chalcidius, p. 372. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1207D] LXX: “To him who established the earth upon the waters” (Τῷ στερεώσαντι τὴν γῆν ἐπὶ τῶν ὑδάτων). Likewise II Pet. III.5: “earth composed out of water and through water” (γῆ ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ δι᾽ ὕδατος συνεστῶσα). Not “out of water” as its material, but because it rises out of the waters; this is what Grillus called “rising out of water” (ἐξ ὕδατος ἀνασχεῖν), *Against Julian* VI, p. 192. “For water bears the earth” (καὶ γὰρ γῆν τὸ ὕδωρ φέρει), as the Indian Jarchas says in Philostratus, III.11. The Egyptians and Thales held the same view. See Simplicius, *On the Heavens* II, p. 127; Thomas Burnet, *Archaeologia*, II.3; and Andreas Dounaeus, notes on Chrysostom, vol. VIII, p. 283. FABRIC.]

For the womb of all things is that former, immeasurable earth made on the first day, which contains the water and this earth inhabited by us. It abundantly supplies grain and the fruits of trees to the human race, birds, reptiles, cattle, and all other creatures, being commanded by Christ the Lord and Savior, as it is written in the book of Genesis, to serve creation (Gen. I.11 and 30 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 1208B] Grain and fruits. *Fruges* of the earth are grain; *fructus* of trees are fruits. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1208B] Abundantly, commanded by Christ the Savior.]

[Note: [Col. 1208C] Commanded by Christ. Christ is the Word of the Father, through whom he created all things: John I.3; Col. I.16. FABRIC.]

### XCVI. HERESY DENYING THAT WATER WAS MADE BY GOD
[Note: [Col. 1208C] Another heresy. In Danaeus, On Augustine, ch. 75, they are the Aquaei; in the author of the *Praedestinatus*, ch. 75, the Hydrotheitae. FABRICIUS.] Another heresy raises a question concerning water: [Note: [Col. 1208C] That it was not made by God. That is, because Moses mentions not that the waters were made, but only that they were gathered together. FABRICIUS.] it maintains that water was not made by God, but exists eternally of itself [Col. 1208B]—[Note: [Col. 1208B] They assert, in ignorance, that the Lord always . . .]—being ignorant that, [Note: [Col. 1208C] If the greater element . . . by the earth. I do not see on what grounds Philastrius says that water is contained by the earth, since Genesis 1:9 rather proves the contrary: “Let the waters be gathered into one place, and let the dry land appear.” For if the dry land was concealed by the waters, it is plain that the earth was smaller than the waters. I am surprised that Fabricius did not note this at all, nor even Scaliger in his *Elenchus Trihaeresii*, where he observes far slighter errors of Philastrius. But if Philastrius means that earth which he called the womb of all things in the preceding chapter—as I indeed think he does, and in this he savours of Platonism—then it cannot truly and properly be called an element, but was rather *hylē* (ὕλη), that is, the universal matter containing all things, as he himself said there. Elsewhere Philastrius calls even the sun, moon, and stars “elements,” as Fabricius explains in chs. 61, 108, and 120; indeed, he calls human beings so as well, ch. 80 at the end: “thus showing that the elements—that is, human beings—are to proceed from glory to glory.” The Apostle, in Galatians 4:3, calls the legal observances, or those bodily rites of worship under which they served as under visible elements, “the elements of the world” (στοιχεῖα τοῦ κόσμου), as Isidore Clarius of Brescia, bishop of Foligno, says on this passage. GALEARD.] if the greater element was made, that is, earth, how much more the lesser, that is, water, which is contained by the earth! Thus the prophet Jonah says: [Note: [Col. 1208D] LXX: “I am a servant of the Lord, who made the sea and the dry land” (Δοῦλος Κυρίου εἰμὶ ἐγὼ ὃς ἐποίησε τὴν θάλασσαν καὶ τὴν ξηράν). FABRICIUS.] “I am a servant of God, who made the sea [Note: [Col. 1208B] and the earth] and the dry land” (Jonah 1:9). [Note: [Col. 1208D] And David. Psalms 104:3 and 6. Compare Severian of Gabala, Homily 1, *On the Creation of the World*, p. 215, vol. I of the latest Combefisian supplement. FABRICIUS.] David also says that water was made [Col. 1209A] by the Lord; and likewise [Note: [Col. 1209C] The three children likewise. In their hymn, among other created things, they summon even the waters to celebrate the Creator’s praises, v. 11: “Bless all waters” (εὐλογεῖτε, ὕδατα πάντα). FABRICIUS.] the three children. [Note: [Col. 1209C] Another earth. This twofold earth was discussed in the preceding chapter. FABRICIUS.] Therefore, one earth contains all things, and another is founded upon water: namely, this earth inhabited by us, of which the Prophet says: “You founded the earth upon the waters” (Ps. 131:6). He certainly does not mean that first earth.

[Note: [Col. 1209B] We know that this earth is to be renewed . . . “I make.”] This earth, therefore, [Note: [Col. 1209C] To be renewed and purified. At the consummation of the age. See above, ch. 80. FABRICIUS.] must be renewed and purified. [Note: [Col. 1209C] Which is also moved. See the remarks on ch. 102. FABRICIUS.] We also know that it is often shaken by earthquake. Of it the Lord says: [Note: [Col. 1209C] LXX: “For the heaven shall be new and the earth new” (Ἔσται γὰρ ὁ οὐρανὸς καινὸς καὶ ἡ γῆ καινή). FABRICIUS.] “I will make a new heaven and a new earth” (Isa. 65:17). Again the Lord says in the Gospel that heaven and earth shall pass away (Luke 21:33). Thus this earth is understood to derive its substance, as it were, from the roots of that prior earth which was commanded to stand above the waters, and which [Note: [Col. 1209C] Abundantly. Some editions wrongly have *copioso* (“abundantly,” instrumental/ablative) instead of *copiose* (“abundantly,” adverb). FABRICIUS. — “Abundantly.” Fabricius notes that in certain editions *copioso* is read in place of *copiose*, but does not state which editions. The Basel edition of Sichard certainly has *copiose* correctly, although *copioso* is not altogether impossible. GALEARD.] abundantly supplies food to humankind.

## XCVII. HERESY CONCERNING THE IMAGE OF GOD IN THE HUMAN BODY

[Col. 1209B]

[Note: [Col. 1209B] Another heresy which . . .] [Note: [Col. 1209C] There is also a heresy. The author of the *Praedestinatus*, ch. 76, calls them Homuncionites—a poorly suited name, and one known to have been applied by others to those who regarded Christ as a mere human being; thus, at the very beginning of the dispute between Arnobius and Serapion, the same persons are called Homuncionates. Danaeus notes in the index prefixed to Augustine’s book *On Heresies* that Philastrius’s heretics here are called Melitonians. But in the index published by the Benedictines in vol. VI of Augustine’s works before the book *On Heresies*, there is no mention of Melitonians; one reads only: “Those who say that the image of God is not the soul.” FABRICIUS. — In this opinion, that the human soul was created before the body, Philastrius had several Fathers agreeing with him. Among them Augustine, *On Genesis according to the Letter*, VII.24, says: “Let us then see whether perhaps this can be true, which certainly seems to me more tolerable to human opinion: that God, in those first works which he created all at once, also created the human soul, which in its own time he would breathe into the limbs of a body formed from mud. For we rightly understand neither what was said, ‘after his image,’ except of the soul, nor what was said, ‘male and female,’ except of the body. Therefore let it be believed, if no authority of Scripture or reasoning of truth contradicts it, that human beings were so made on the sixth day that the causal principle of the human body was indeed in the elements of the world, while the soul itself was already created, as the day was originally created; and, having been created, it lay hidden in God’s works until, in its proper time, he placed it in the body formed from mud by breathing—that is, by inspiring—it into it.” Hilary on Psalm 129, Gregory of Nyssa, *Philosophical [Treatises]* II.6, and others give similar teachings. Against them stands the authority of Pope Leo I, in Sixtus of Siena, *Sacred Library*, annotation 208 at the end, where he criticizes Gregory of Nyssa’s view as a Platonic fiction. Yet Cotelerius observed, in his notes on the *Clementine Recognitions*, p. 493, that it should be placed outside the errors of the Platonists. GALEARD.] There is also a heresy which says that before the human body, not the soul, was made; that the body, not the human soul, is the image of God; and that [Note: [Col. 1210C] According to predestination. As though Moses had merely set forth God’s plan, and the words “God made” signify not what he did, but what he predestined himself to do. FABRICIUS.] it was according to predestination that Scripture spoke thus. [Note: [Col. 1209B] They suppose that the Lord said . . .] This is their view, although Scripture says: “God made the human being; in his image he made him; male and female he made them” (Gen. 1:27).

[Note: [Col. 1210B] Being ignorant [of] what the prophet . . . the rational [soul].] They are ignorant of what the Prophet said. [Col. 1210A] For when he says, “Let us make,” he promises that he will make; but when he says, “God made,” he shows that the work has already been done, and declares that what was made was not flesh, but the rational soul. For there is no doubt that flesh cannot speak without a soul; therefore flesh is the instrument [Note: [Col. 1210B] of the soul, which is a rational thing] of the rational soul. When Scripture says “male and female,” [Note: [Col. 1210D] Not the sex of bodies here. Philastrius will have few supporters on this point. FABRICIUS.] it indicates not the sex of bodies, but the distinction between the ruling and the subject soul. [Note: [Col. 1210D] And that bodies were not previously made and lying there. Petavius does not hesitate to affirm that what Philastrius maintains here is plainly false; see *Theological Dogmas*, book II, *On the Work of the Six Days*, ch. 4, §16. FABRICIUS.] Nor is it uncertain that bodies were not previously made and lying there, as some imprudent persons suppose, since Adam’s flesh and that of the woman were made afterward. For on the seventh day Scripture says concerning Adam: “And the Lord took earth from the clay and formed the man whom he had made.” You see, then, how it first shows that the human being—that is, the rational and [Col. 1210B] immortal soul—was made by the Lord, and is called the image of God; but it shows that the earth taken from clay, joined to the soul—that is, the outer human being, the fragile body—was formed on the following day. [Note: [Col. 1210B] and thus, when sleep had been sent] Scripture testifies and proclaims that, after sleep was sent upon Adam, the Lord afterward took from his rib and made the woman. And it is not uncertain that the soul was first made [Note: [Col. 1210D] Soul on the sixth day; body on the seventh. Again and again in this chapter Philastrius presses his incredible opinion, contrary to the common view and no less contrary to the explicit words of the sacred writer, who writes in Genesis 2:2 that God created nothing on the seventh day, but completed all his works on the sixth, and rested from all his works on the seventh. Yet because Genesis 2:7 follows, “And God formed the human being from dust of the earth” (καὶ ἔπλασεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸν ἄνθρωπον χοῦν ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς), Philastrius persuaded himself that this occurred on the seventh day, though it is merely a repetition and explanation of what had been done on the sixth day, when Moses had said in Genesis 1:27, “And God made the human being” (καὶ ἐποίησε ὁ Θεὸς τὸν ἄνθρωπον). Likewise, it cannot be proved that Genesis 1:27 speaks only of the soul, as Philastrius contends; it must surely be understood of the whole human being, as is shown by what follows there: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth.” Alphonsus de Castro, book II, p. 56, classified Philastrius’s opinion that the soul was created before the body—which Jerome also criticized in John of Jerusalem, *Letter to Pammachius*—among heresies. FABRICIUS.]—that is, on the sixth day—and that Adam’s body was formed from earth on the seventh day. [Col. 1211A] Likewise, that the woman was made from the man’s [Note: [Col. 1211B] body—from his side . . . and that] body, that is, from his side, is not uncertain; and that the soul was made first, but the flesh was formed afterward, and then afterward, by God’s breathed inspiration, [Note: [Col. 1211C] Spiritual grace bestowed at the end. By a gracious inspiration added to and infused into the soul, of which below, ch. 98. FABRICIUS.] spiritual grace was bestowed at the end, [Note: [Col. 1211C] “So that.” The Helmstedt edition wrongly has “that it may be.” FABRICIUS.] so that [Note: [Col. 1211C] The human being now capable of the divine Law. Below, ch. 98: “that the human being might be capable of the heavenly Law.” FABRICIUS.] the human being might be shown by the Lord to be now capable, not incapable, of the divine Law. The reasoning of truth is evident: blessed David also said that the soul was made first and the body then formed: [Note: [Col. 1211C] LXX: “Your hands made me and formed me” (αἱ χεῖρές σου ἐποίησάν με καὶ ἔπλασάν με). Caesarius, Question 76: “The term ‘making’ seems to me to be understood of the soul, and ‘forming’ of the manifold fashioning of the body” (τὴν ποίησιν ἐπὶ τῆς ψυχῆς μοι δοκεῖ νοεῖσθαι, τὴν δὲ πλάσιν ἐπὶ τῆς σωματικῆς πολυπλασίας). FABRICIUS.] “Your hands,” he says, [Note: [Col. 1211B] he says, made] “Lord, made and formed me” (Ps. 119:73). He also declared that the Spirit was afterward [Note: [Col. 1211C] The Spirit infused. The grace of the Holy Spirit infused into the soul, of which below in the next chapter. The ancients also interpret the “spirit” of 1 Thessalonians 5:23 in this way. FABRICIUS.] infused, saying: [Note: [Col. 1211C] LXX: “Do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Τὸ Πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιόν σου μὴ ἀντανέλῃς ἀπ’ ἐμοῦ). FABRICIUS.] “Do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Ps. 51:11).

## XCVIII. HERESY CONCERNING THE BREATHING OF THE HUMAN SOUL

[Note: [Col. 1211D] Another heresy. Augustine judged that this and the following heresies down to ch. 113 should be passed over. Sixtus of Siena, book V of the *Sacred Library*, annotation 27, does not doubt that the present case is one of those of which Augustine says that Philastrius numbered many assertions among heresies which are not heresies. “With due respect to Philastrius,” says Alphonsus de Castro, book II *Against Heresies*, p. 55, “I do not see why he branded this assertion as heresy. First, I find it to be the teaching of many truly Catholic doctors, who maintain that the breath which God breathed into the human face was the human soul, which he either created then by breathing it in, or, having created it, infused into the body.” Yet many ancients interpret the breath of life which God breathed into the first human as the Holy Spirit infused into him together with the soul: Jerome, Cyril, Basil, and Severian. See Bull, *Defence of the Nicene Faith*, sect. 2, ch. 9, §21, p. 211; Petavius, *Theological Dogmas, On the Trinity*, p. 824 ff.; and *On the Work of the Six Days*, p. 314. FABRICIUS.] Another heresy says that the breathing was the soul [Col. 1211B] (Gen. 2:7), rather than [Note: [Col. 1212B] The breathing given into the soul. The Helmstedt edition wrongly has “by breathing into the soul.” FABRICIUS. — “The breathing into the soul.” Perhaps here too Fabricius did not inspect Sichard’s Basel edition sufficiently carefully: for it retains the very reading, *inspiratione in animam*, which Fabricius criticizes as peculiar to the Helmstedt edition. The Corbie manuscript, recently discovered in France, as also the Lyons edition, has *inspirationem in animam*, which is undoubtedly the true reading, and is also printed in the Hamburg edition. GALEARD.] that a breathing was given into the soul. [Note: [Col. 1211B] Being ignorant that . . . how it can be judged] They are ignorant that, if the inspiration [Col. 1212A] is the soul, [Note: [Col. 1212C] How can it judge? Elsewhere, “indicate.” The sense is that the soul cannot be regarded as God’s special grace, properly infused, because it is common to all. FABRICIUS. — “How can it be judged?” Fabricius adds: “Elsewhere, ‘indicate.’” Sichard’s edition has *quomodo judicari* (“how it can be judged”), but this reading too escaped Fabricius’s attention. The Corbie manuscript has *quomodo dijudicari*; likewise on the following page, p. 190, where editions wrongly have *itaque quae non*, while Corbie has *itaque non*, and therefore *quae* must be deleted altogether. Similarly, another scribal error occurring at the end of ch. 103—*non aliter nisi Deus Christus*—must be emended according to the Corbie manuscript, which has *non alter nisi Deus Christus*: “no other than God Christ.” GALEARD.] how can it judge what has properly been infused by God, since it does not [Note: [Col. 1212B] attend to . . . and advancement] attend to the fact that the inspiration of the divine Spirit is a certain grace and [Note: [Col. 1212C] Advancement in dignity. By which a human being greatly excels other human beings. Thus below: “the inspiration, then, which is not the soul, but a grace of dignity.” And again: “the unjust, being negligent and contemptuous, lose so great a merit of dignity.” Compare Augustine, *City of God*, XIII.24. FABRICIUS.] an advancement in dignity, by which a human being may be [Note: [Col. 1212D] Capable of the heavenly Law. Capable of observing it willingly and eagerly through the grace of the Holy Spirit. Thus above, ch. 97: “The flesh was formed afterward, after the soul; and afterward, when God’s inspiration had been infused, spiritual grace was finally bestowed, so that the human being might now be shown by the Lord capable, not incapable, of the divine Law.” FABRICIUS.] capable of the heavenly Law.

The Lord shows in the Gospel that inspiration was given to our father Adam when he already possessed a soul, and that no soul was breathed into him. [Note: [Col. 1212D] In Greek: “He breathed on them and said to them, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’” (Ἐνεφύσησε καὶ λέγει αὐτοῖς· λάβετε Πνεῦμα ἅγιον). FABRICIUS.] For just as he himself had formerly breathed into Adam, so afterward, when the Apostles already had souls, he breathed into them after the Resurrection a greater grace of the divine Spirit, saying: “Receive the Holy Spirit.” He did not say, “Receive a soul,” but, “Receive the Holy Spirit.” Therefore, he who breathed into Adam, a created human being possessing a soul, afterward breathed into the blessed Apostles, who possessed souls; [Note: [Col. 1212B] so that it may be known that all things were made through him] so that it may be known that all things are through him, [Note: [Col. 1212D] Nothing was made without him. See above, ch. 67. FABRICIUS.] and that nothing was made without him (John 1:3).

Therefore it is wholly unreasonable [Col. 1212B] for anyone to suppose that inspiration is the soul, since the soul is known to have been made; [Col. 1213A] it is placed under the condition of the Law and found liable to judgment. Of it he says: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both body and soul in Gehenna” (Matt. 10:28). The inspiration, [Note: [Col. 1213B] therefore, is not] therefore, is not the soul but [Note: [Col. 1213C] A grace of dignity. Above he had called it “an advancement in dignity.” FABRICIUS.] a grace of dignity, coming from the divine Spirit through God Christ to all. Those who possess and keep it receive an increase of graces, [Note: [Col. 1213C] Like the Apostles. The Helmstedt edition corruptly reads “and like the Apostles.” FABRICIUS. — Fabricius again criticizes the Helmstedt edition, which wrongly reads “and like the Apostles”; but Sichard’s edition correctly has “like the Apostles,” the conjunction omitted. The Lyons edition has “and like the Apostles,” wrongly. GALEARD.] like the Apostles, the Prophets, and all the righteous. But the unjust, being negligent and contemptuous, lose so great a merit of dignity, like that Saul of whom it was said: [Note: [Col. 1213C] LXX: “And the Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord choked him” (Καὶ Πνεῦμα Κυρίου ἀπέστη ἀπὸ Σαούλ, καὶ ἔπνιγεν αὐτὸν πνεῦμα πονηρὸν παρὰ Κυρίου). FABRICIUS.] “The Spirit of the Lord departed from him, and an unclean spirit afflicted him” (1 Sam. 16:14). Scripture also testifies that [Note: [Col. 1213C] LXX: “Wisdom shall not enter into a soul skilled in evil” (Εἰς κακότεχνον ψυχὴν οὐκ εἰσελεύσεται σοφία). FABRICIUS.] the spirit of wisdom shall not enter a malicious soul (Wis. 1:4).

## XCIX. HERESY CONCERNING THE HUMAN SOUL AND INTELLECT

[Note: [Col. 1213C] Concerning the soul. *Peri tou thyrathen nou* (Περὶ τοῦ θύραθεν νοῦ), “concerning the intellect from without,” to use Origen’s words, *Against Celsus* III, p. 159. FABRICIUS.]

[Col. 1213B]

Another heresy says that the human soul was not made by God under the name “soul,” but [Note: [Col. 1213C] “Formerly,” they say, “it was called Intellect.” The opinion of the Platonists was that understanding spirits, or Intelligences, first lived in heaven and then, having fallen into sin, were cast down into bodies as punishment. On this opinion see extensively Augustine Steuchus of Gubbio, *On Perennial Philosophy*, IX; Livius Galantes, *Comparison of Christian and Platonic Theology*, XIII; and Giovanni Battista Crispus, *On Reading Philosophers with Caution*, divisions 1 and 2. FABRICIUS.] that it was formerly called Intellect and was in heaven; but later, because it desired earthly things, it departed from heaven, and for that reason they suppose it is now called Soul.
