They are ignorant that in the beginning the soul was made by God and created after the angels; that it was called “Soul” by the Lord; and that it received this proper name from God, so that it should be called Soul, not Intellect. Scripture says: [Note: [Col. 1213D] LXX: “His soul shall lodge among good things” (Ἡ ψυχὴ αὐτοῦ ἐν ἀγαθοῖς αὐλισθήσεται). FABRICIUS.] “His soul shall dwell among good things” (Ps. 25:13). Again: [Note: [Col. 1213D] LXX: “For you will not abandon my soul to Hades” (Ὅτι οὐκ ἐγκαταλείψεις τὴν ψυχήν μου εἰς ᾅδην). FABRICIUS.] “You will not abandon my soul [Col. 1214A] in Hades” (Ps. 16:10). Again: [Note: [Col. 1213D] LXX: “Return, my soul, to your rest” (Ἐπίστρεψον, ψυχή μου, εἰς τὴν ἀνάπαυσίν σου). FABRICIUS.] “Return, my soul, to your rest” (Ps. 116:7). Again: [Note: [Col. 1213D] LXX: “My soul has been greatly troubled” (Ἡ ψυχή μου ἐταράχθη σφόδρα). FABRICIUS.] “My soul is greatly troubled” (Ps. 6:3). Again: [Note: [Col. 1213D] LXX: “So my soul longs for you, O God” (Οὕτως ἐπιποθεῖ ἡ ψυχή μου πρὸς σέ, ὦ Θεός). FABRICIUS.] “So my soul longs for you, O God” (Ps. 42:2). Again: [Note: [Col. 1213D] Blessed [be the Lord]. Compare Jeremiah 38:16: “As the Lord lives, who made this soul for us” (Ζῇ Κύριος ὅς ἐποίησεν ἡμῖν τὴν ψυχὴν ταύτην). FABRICIUS.] “Blessed is the Lord, who made my soul.” Thus they maintain that vain teaching of the philosophers [Note: [Col. 1213B] They adhere to empty opinions, which sacred Scripture does not proclaim] which divine Scripture does not proclaim.

## C. HERESY OF THE GNOSTICS AND MANICHAEANS CONCERNING SERPENTS AND BIRDS

There is a heresy which considers cattle, serpents, and birds [Note: [Col. 1214C] Cattle, serpents, and birds. Fish are omitted, as in ch. 95, although their no less remarkable cleverness is also observed; likewise that of bees, ants, and spiders. See Plutarch, *Whether Land or Water Animals Are More Intelligent*, p. 732 ff., and Vossius, *On Idolatry*, IV.14. FABRICIUS.] rational, like human beings. So do [Note: [Col. 1214C] The depraved Manichaeans and Gnostics. Glycas notes, *Annals*, p. 145, that the Manichaeans taught that brute animals were by no means devoid of reason, and confirmed this by the fact that God punished the serpent. Alexander of Lycopolis, p. 19, also testifies that the Manichaeans made it a religious scruple to eat animals. On other heretics see Cotelerius on the *Apostolic Constitutions*, VI.10, p. 339. FABRICIUS.] the depraved Manichaeans and Gnostics, and whatever [Note: [Col. 1214B] and indeed most vainly suppose concerning poets and Stoic philosophers] poets [Note: [Col. 1214C] Poets. Parmenides and Empedocles in Stobaeus, *Physical Eclogues*, p. 93. See the notes on Sextus Empiricus, p. 512. FABRICIUS.] and Stoic philosophers [Note: [Col. 1214C] And Stoic philosophers. Not all of them, certainly; for I have shown in my notes on the same Sextus, p. 18, that Cleanthes and Chrysippus held the opposite opinion. FABRICIUS.] imagine. They do not understand that the rational human being possesses the mind’s understanding concerning God—[Col. 1214B] that is, [Note: [Col. 1214D] Being able to know and believe in God. Whatever degree of sensation or reason one attributes to brute animals, one must nevertheless admit that they do not attain to matters concerning religion and virtue, contemplation of heavenly things and things remote from sense, or concern for glory enduring after death and blessed immortality. FABRICIUS.] the ability to know and believe in God. Humans share bodily sensation with cattle and other similar creatures, which may indeed have bodily sensation; but they can in no way have the mind’s understanding concerning God, nor an immortal and rational soul like the human being, who is called the image of God. Scripture says: [Note: [Col. 1214D] LXX: “Do not become like horse and mule, which have no understanding” (Μὴ γίνεσθε ὡς ἵππος καὶ ἡμίονος, οἷς οὐκ ἔστι σύνεσις). FABRICIUS.] “Do not be like horse and mule, in which there is no understanding” (Ps. 32:9). And: [Note: [Col. 1214D] LXX: “A human being, though in honour, did not understand; he was compared to irrational cattle and became like them” (Ἄνθρωπος ἐν τιμῇ ὢν, οὐ συνῆκε, παρασυνεβλήθη τοῖς κτήνεσι τοῖς ἀνοήτοις, καὶ ὡμοιώθη αὐτοῖς). FABRICIUS.] “A human being, though in honour, did not understand; he was compared to senseless cattle and became like them” (Ps. 49:23).

Thus bodily sensation is shared with us by cattle, birds, and serpents; but understanding belongs to human beings alone: it is the power of the immortal [Col. 1215A] mortal [Note: [Col. 1215C] power of the soul] soul, [Note: [Col. 1215C] Infused into it by the Holy Spirit. See above, chs. 98 and 99. FABRICIUS.] infused into it by the Holy Spirit. It is called the image of God, and it rules, governs, and possesses all these things abundantly, as it is written: [Note: [Col. 1215C] LXX: “Behold, I have given you every herb” (Ἰδοὺ δέδωκα ὑμῖν πάντα χόρτον). FABRICIUS.] “I have given you all things under your authority” (Gen. 1:29).

## CI. HERESY CONCERNING FALSE PROPHETS, ATTRIBUTING ALL EVILS TO GOD

Another heresy says that wicked kings and false prophets do not arise and act by their own will, but are sent forth at God’s command. [Note: [Col. 1215C] sent out, being ignorant] It is ignorant that Scripture declares that false prophets and wicked kings do not become such through God, but come forth against God’s will, through their own will and the enemy’s prompting. Thus [Note: [Col. 1215C] Jannes and Mambres. 2 Timothy 3:8. See, if you wish, what I have noted concerning them in the *Pseudepigraphic Code of the Old Testament*, p. 813 ff. But do not agree with the learned man who, in *Sacred Observations*, II, pp. 32 and 156, considers Jannes and Mambres fictitious names for unknown persons, like “Peloni Almoni” in Ruth 4:1, 1 Samuel 21:3, and 2 Samuel 6:8. (“Like Peloni Almoni.” These words ought to have been printed in Hebrew letters, since they are Hebrew text and one seeks them in vain in the Vulgate at the passages indicated by Fabricius. These expressions signify nothing in Hebrew, but are used in place of a proper name which is omitted as known, or which we do not wish to name, as Vatablus notes on Ruth 4:1. Thus 1 Samuel 16:2: “I have appointed my servants to such-and-such a place,” where Münster says: “I have assigned my servants some such place.” Now *peloni* means “covered,” and *almoni* “hidden”; Hebrew idiom applies these names to things whose particular names are not expressed. GALEARD.) Pliny certainly mentions Jannes among the magicians, XXXI.1. FABRICIUS.] Jannes and Mambres came against [Note: [Col. 1215C] the blessed Moses and] Moses and Aaron, [Note: [Col. 1215D] Priests of God. In what sense Moses was a priest, see Grotius on 2 Samuel 8:18 and *On Authority in Sacred Matters*, ch. 9. FABRICIUS.] priests of God under Pharaoh, by their own [Col. 1215B] will. Scripture says: [Note: [Col. 1215D] LXX: “They ruled for themselves and not through me; they governed and did not make it known to me” (Ἑαυτοῖς ἐβασίλευσαν καὶ οὐ δι’ ἐμοῦ, ἦρξαν καὶ οὐκ ἐγνώρισάν μοι). FABRICIUS.] “They reigned, but not through me; [Note: [Col. 1216C] Nor through my Spirit. Philastrius added these words from Genesis 6:3. FABRICIUS.] nor through my Spirit,” says the Lord (Hos. 8:4). And concerning [Note: [Col. 1216C] LXX: “Thus says the Lord Almighty: I did not send the prophets, yet they ran; nor did I speak to them, yet they prophesied” (Οὕτος λέγει Κύριος παντοκράτωρ· οὐκ ἀπέστελλον τοὺς προφήτας, καὶ αὐτοὶ ἔτρεχον, οὐδὲ ἐλάλησα πρὸς αὐτούς, καὶ αὐτοὶ ἐπροφήτευον). FABRICIUS.] false prophets: “Thus says the Lord: I did not send them, yet they went to prophesy in my name” (Jer. 23:16, 21). Therefore, too, the Lord often pronounces against them [Note: [Col. 1215C] death, and in this] a sentence of death deserved in this world, [Note: [Col. 1216C] A sentence of death, as in 1 Kings 13. FABRICIUS.] declaring it.

False prophets, therefore, are not sent by God, nor are wicked kings who depart from the Lord. But although wicked persons are sometimes raised against wicked persons [Note: [Col. 1216C] The Lord permitting. FABRICIUS.] with the Lord’s permission, [Note: [Col. 1215C] The Lord, so that by evil persons . . .] this occurs so that evil persons may be destroyed by evil persons. But the good, who endure persecution and [Col. 1216A] possess righteousness before the Lord, await the great bestowal of their future reward. The wicked, however, are sometimes destroyed by the wicked, and not only by the good, so that their iniquity may be punished in part even in this age.

## CII. HERESY CONCERNING EARTHQUAKES

[Note: [Col. 1216C] Another heresy which does not [hold] earthquakes to occur by God’s . . .] A certain heresy believes that earthquakes occur not by God’s command and indignation, [Note: [Col. 1216C] but from nature] but from the very nature of the elements. It does not understand what Scripture says: [Note: [Col. 1216C] LXX: “He looks upon the earth and makes it tremble” (Ὁ ἐπιβλέπων ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν καὶ ποιῶν αὐτὴν τρέμειν). FABRICIUS.] “You look upon the earth,” it says, “and shake it with an earthquake.” Again: [Note: [Col. 1216C] LXX: “I shake heaven and earth” (Ἐγὼ σείω τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν). Perhaps Philastrius should read: “And again, further: I will shake heaven and earth.” FABRICIUS.] “Yet once more I will shake heaven and earth.” Failing to heed God’s power, they dare to attribute the power of movement to the nature of the elements, like certain vain [Note: [Col. 1216C] prattlers, who] philosophers who, by attributing this to the nature of things, did not acknowledge God’s power. But in such matters God’s indignation and power act, and he [Note: [Col. 1216C] Shakes. I preferred this to *commonet* (“warns”).] shakes his creation for the sake of conversion and benefit—especially for the many who sin and return to the Lord, Savior and Creator.

## CIII. HERESY OF HERMES TRISMEGISTUS CONCERNING BEASTS AND STARS

Another heresy professes various names of stars [Note: [Col. 1216D] According to pagan folly. I have restored this in place of the reading found in editions, “according to the folly of beasts of the pagans.” Yet Philastrius should be excused for having, carried away by excessive zeal, condemned the innocent names of stars as pagan folly and ridiculously counted them among heresies. FABRICIUS.] according to pagan folly, like [Note: [Col. 1216D] Hermes. Below, ch. 112, he calls him most deceitful; in ch. 10, a vain pagan. FABRICIUS.] that Hermes Trismegistus, who ought rather to be judged vain than great; and certain poets like him, who apply such names as Comets, [Note: [Col. 1216D] Pogonias. A kind of comet, whose long rays extend in the likeness of a beard; see Hardouin on Pliny, vol. I, p. 178. FABRICIUS.] Pogonias, Hyades, [Note: [Col. 1216D] Kids. Virgil, *Georgics* I.204: “Moreover, Arcturus’s star, the days of the Kids, and the shining Serpent must be observed by us.”] the Kids, [Col. 1217A] [Note: [Col. 1217B] and other] and other such [Note: [Col. 1217B] They assert names. Earlier editions wrongly have *nomine* (“by name”). FABRICIUS.] names in their madness. Scripture, however, has given us only a few names of stars. Job the prophet says—before the pagans had transferred the names of stars from the sacred Scriptures—[Note: [Col. 1217C] LXX: “He who makes the Pleiad and Hesperus and Arcturus and the chambers of the South” (Ὁ ποιῶν πλειάδα καὶ Ἕσπερον καὶ Ἀρκτοῦρον καὶ ταμεῖα Νότου). FABRICIUS.] Job himself says: “He who made the Pleiades and Arcturus,” he says, “and Hesperus, and the South, and Orion, [Note: [Col. 1217C] And Lucifer. Philastrius added this from Job 38:32, where learned persons interpret Μαζουρώθ as Lucifer. On those stellar names, besides Drusius, see Ludovicus Cappellus, pp. 460 ff. of his posthumous works. FABRICIUS.] and Lucifer” (Job 9:9).

[Note: [Col. 1217C] From the sacred Scriptures, etc. On the contrary, the Septuagint translators transferred these names into the Greek translation of the sacred books from common pagan usage and convention. Eucherius: “Why is it that in the book of Job we read Pleiades, Orions, and Arcturus, according to the convention of secular authors? Not because they are called by these names among the Hebrews, but because the translator—the author of the Greek version—wished to call them by names found in pagan usage, so that the meaning of these stars might be clearer to us.” FABRICIUS.] We receive these few names as reported from the sacred Scriptures. Scripture did not state the names of all the stars, but reserved them to God’s power, declaring through the prophet: [Note: [Col. 1217C] LXX: “He numbers the multitude of stars, calling them all by names” (Ὁ ἀριθμῶν πλήθη ἄστρων, καὶ πᾶσιν αὐτοῖς ὀνόματα καλῶν). FABRICIUS.] “He numbers the multitude of the stars and calls them all by names” (Ps. 147:4). Reading these few names in the sacred Scriptures, [Note: [Col. 1217B] the poets and false] poets afterward, and false philosophers, dared to appropriate them and attach many others by their lies, proclaiming to the world seeds of impiety, so that people might suppose that the names of all, or at least most, stars could also be comprehended from them. Yet no one other than God Christ, through whom the Father made all things, has assigned and known the names of all the stars, and called each one by its name, as it is written (ibid.).

## CIV. HERESY CONCERNING THE VARIOUS LANGUAGES

[Note: [Col. 1217C] Alphonsus de Castro classified this opinion of Philastrius among heresies. Add Marianus Valguarnera, *Antiquities of Palermo*, p. 71, vol. XIII of the *Treasury of the Antiquities of Sicily*. FABRICIUS.]

There is another heresy which raises doubts about language and languages, although Scripture speaks both of one language and of languages.

[Note: One language and languages. One language, Gen. 11:1: “And the whole earth was of one lip,” χεῖλος ἓν καὶ φωνὴ μία πᾶσι, “one lip and one voice for all”; and languages, because in Gen. 10:5, where the various nations are mentioned, each is said to be κατὰ γλῶσσαν, “according to its language”; and in 10:20 and 31, κατὰ γλώσσας αὐτῶν, “according to their languages”; and in 11:7, συγχέωμεν αὐτῶν ἐκεῖ τὰς γλώσσας, “let us confound their languages there.” For certain manuscripts read thus, as was noted on Origen, *Against Celsus*, V, p. 250. Certainly, v. 11: Ὅτι ἐκεῖ συνέχεε Κύριος τὰ χείλη πάσης τῆς γῆς, “For there the Lord confounded the lips of all the earth.” Philastrius evidently therefore judged from Genesis 10 that, many ages before the building of Babel, there had already been a great diversity of languages among human beings. But when Genesis 11 then says that all were of one lip, he thought this meant that, although there were different kinds of languages, all nevertheless understood one another; and thus there was one language for all, not indeed through the use of the same words, but through the same understanding among all speakers and hearers. Learned men, indeed, says the most distinguished Perizonius, ch. 14 of *Origines Babylonicae*, p. 296, reject both this very absurd interpretation and that diversity of languages before the Babylonian confusion; but then they should also reject the separation into various colonies before the Babylonian dispersion, since the reasoning in both matters is altogether the same, and each opinion is derived from the same tenth chapter, or from the order of chapters 10 and 11 of Genesis. What then? These things are the clearest indication that that order of Mosaic narration, or of those chapters, does not prevent us from confidently maintaining that all the events of that division or separation mentioned in chapter 10 finally occurred after the dispersion and confusion of speech in chapter 11, from which the diversity of languages at last began. FABRIC.]

If, therefore, there was one language before, because there were few people, or many afterward, because many human beings had by then been born and multiplied in the world, it is not altogether useless to think thus. For from Adam to Heber, after the fifteenth generation, there were two thousand seven hundred years, under whom the confusion of languages was sent because of the sin they committed in building the tower and the city; and they suffered this because they rebelled against God. For, possessing angelic grace—that is, knowledge of many languages—they did not acknowledge the Lord, giver of so great a wisdom; and, striving to advance against him, they had lost the grace which they had received from God without any labor.

[Note: 2,700 years. From Adam to Heber are 2,700 years, half the age of the world from its creation until Christ the Savior’s birth in the year 5,400. Below, chs. 112 and 105. Others, who thought Christ was born in the year 6,000 from the world’s creation, placed Peleg son of Heber, or Heber himself, in A.M. 3,000. Thus the presbyter Hesychius, in the fragment *On the Birth of Christ*; Josephus, ch. 1 of the *Hypomnesticon*; Procopius of Gaza on Gen. 11:18; and Eustathius, p. 54, on the *Hexaemeron*. FABRIC.]

[Note: Angelic grace. Philastrius believed that, without study and naturally, through the power of the divine image, human beings were divinely granted before the Babelic confusion the ability to understand whatever languages were spoken, like angels. Below: “It belongs to angelic power to know the languages of all human beings.” FABRIC.]

[Note: “They had lost.” Someone prefers “they lost.” But above the wording is: “which they had done in building,” etc. FABRIC.]

And what had before been bestowed naturally by the Lord upon all, without study, as upon the image of God, afterward, when forgetfulness had been sent by the Lord, they could scarcely learn through study and instruction: not all languages, nor many, but scarcely a few, so that a person might manage to learn three or four and with difficulty speak even those. Yet all knowledge of languages, which human beings had lost by offending two thousand seven hundred years earlier, the Lord again bestowed after his ascension, through the Holy Spirit and without any labor, upon believers in the time of the Apostles, as is written in the Acts of the Apostles.

[Note: “Without any labor . . . afterward, however, through.” FABRIC.]

[Note: Human beings had lost it through offending 2,700 years earlier. If they had lost it 2,700 years earlier, they could not have used that knowledge before the Babelic confusion. The meaning, therefore, is that through the sin committed by the first-created humans 2,700 years earlier, it came about that afterward they did not preserve it continually, but after an intervening time lost it in the confusion at Babel. See below, ch. 105. FABRIC.]

[Note: Under the Apostles. Acts 2:4, 7, 12. On these passages it will be useful to consult Johann Caspar Santorocci’s dissertation *On the Miracle of Languages*, published at Marburg in 1718. Gregory Nazianzen rightly observed, *Oration* 44, on Pentecost, p. 738, that the miracle was in the speakers rather than in the hearers; for Luke, the sacred writer of Acts, explicitly and repeatedly mentions people λαλοῦντες ἑτέραις γλώσσαις, “speaking in other languages.” FABRIC.]

For it belongs to angelic power to know the languages of all human beings; but through faith in Christ, knowledge of all languages is supplied without labor to believers. Thus we read that, under the instruction of the divine Spirit, the Apostles—and likewise the Gentiles then believing in Christ the Lord and Savior—proclaimed, without labor, the knowledge of all languages bestowed upon them. Thus, under Peter and Paul and the others, when they taught the Gentiles that the Spirit of God had come from God, they were able to speak in many languages, so that the human hearers among the Gentiles marvelled that they too had, through faith in Christ, knowledge of so many languages granted without instruction.

## CV. HERESY CONCERNING THE NAME OF A LANGUAGE

Another heresy says that the name of a language first proceeded from the Jews; others say from the pagans. Yet both parties, holding this opinion, have been deceived by no small error.

[Note: The name of a language—from the Jews, according to some; from the pagans, according to others. That is, the most ancient language was held to be that of the Jews, or the Greek language of the pagans. FABRIC.]

For the human being was made a participant in reason. Therefore, one who spoke with reason—how was he devoid of reason?

[Note: How was he devoid of reason? I think *orationis*, “speech,” should be read. FABRIC.]

It is therefore prior and greater to be a participant in reason and to be called rational than to possess the special and local name of some language, and to possess something from the name of a human being. For two thousand seven hundred years passed from Adam to Heber.

[Note: Down to Heber, father of Peleg, under whom that celebrated dispersion of languages occurred, Gen. 10:25. The number of 2,700 years has already been discussed in the preceding chapter. FABRIC.]

Therefore, the name “language” was one name for all human beings, and there was one language. But once they devised things against the Lord, that heavenly knowledge was taken away from them—that is, the insight and wisdom of all languages.

[Note: The one name “language” for all names. Whatever idiom human beings spoke, it was called human language. In this sense Augustine, *City of God*, XVI.11: “Then it was necessary for it—that is, the Hebrew language—to be distinguished from the other languages by a proper name, just as the other languages too were called by proper names. But when it was one, it was called nothing other than human language or human speech, which alone the whole human race spoke.” GALEARD. It came by no other individual name, because all understood one another and, as Philastrius immediately adds, possessed knowledge of all languages. FABRIC.]

[Note: This heavenly knowledge. In ch. 104 he called it angelic grace: the ability to understand whatever languages were spoken. FABRIC.]

But holy Heber, who did not depart from God in accordance with his own name, God willed to cause his race to flourish more abundantly, and to be called in the world first by this name also: so that from Heber, who had not consented to the construction of the rebels’ tower, they should be called Hebrews after his name.

[Note: In accordance with his own name. Heber has his name from departing or passing over. *Book of Hebrew Names*, vol. II of Jerome’s works, ed. Jean Martianay, p. 203: Ἕβερ, διάβασις ἢ διαπερῶν, “Heber: passage, or one passing through.” Jerome: *Eber*, “a passer-over.” FABRIC.]

[Note: Hebrews from Heber. Compare Bochart’s *Phaleg*, book II, ch. 14, and book IV, final chapter. FABRIC.]

Heber, then, is known to have been most righteous before not only the pagans but also the Jews—that is, seven hundred years before Moses, founder of the Jewish commonwealth. Believing in the Lord and separated from the conspiracy of wicked people, he deserved to obtain from the Lord this first designation from his own name.

[Note: Seven hundred years earlier: seven hundred years before Moses. FABRIC.]

Hence the vain poets, transferring that building to their falsehoods, taught that the rebellious Aloadae had wished to ascend into heaven by piling mountains upon one another, and had therefore been condemned.

[Note: They transferred that building to their falsehoods. This is far more credible than Celsus’s assertion in Origen, IV, p. 174, that Moses drew from the fable of the Aloadae what he handed down concerning the tower of Babel and the confusion of languages. FABRIC.]

[Note: The Aloadae: Otus and Ephialtes, sons of Aloeus, concerning whom Homer, *Iliad* XI.314:

> They strove to set Ossa upon Olympus,  
> and upon Ossa the leaf-rustling Pelion, so that heaven might be climbed.

Compare Philo the Jew, *On the Confusion of Languages*, p. 251; and among more recent writers, the distinguished Huet, book II of *Alnetan Questions*, ch. 12, §6, p. 189 ff. FABRIC.]

Their ravings did not escape Christian learning and discernment.

## CVI. HERESY DOUBTING ABOUT THE YEARS AND TIME OF CHRIST

Another heresy doubts concerning the proclaimed year, of which the prophet Isaiah says: “To proclaim the acceptable year of God, and the day of recompense” (Isa. 61:2).

[Note: Concerning the proclaimed year: concerning the time meant by the acceptable year proclaimed in Isaiah’s words cited at Luke 4:19. FABRIC.]

[Note: LXX: Εὐαγγελίσασθαι ἐνιαυτὸν Κυρίου δεκτὸν καὶ ἡμέραν ἀνταποδόσεως, “to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of recompense.” It is evident, however, that the prophet means neither “day” nor “year” precisely and strictly, but the time in which it pleased God to reveal and impart to human beings the grace of his favor in Christ. FABRIC.]

Some therefore think that from the Lord’s coming until the consummation of the age, the number of years will be neither more nor less than three hundred and sixty-five, until the divine presence of Christ the Lord again comes from heaven. This proves contrary to fact, if those who hold it reason thus; for we know that already more than four hundred years have passed and been completed since the Lord came. How, then, can their view of the year be reasonable, as very many have wished to think?

[Note: Three hundred and sixty-five: because a year consists of that many days. Augustine, *City of God*, XVIII.53, mentions an oracle, or response of demons, by which that number of 365 years was fixed. They fabricated certain Greek verses, supposedly uttered by a divine oracle to an inquirer. In them they declare Christ innocent of this supposed sacrilege; but they add that Peter performed magical acts so that Christ’s name might be worshipped for 365 years, and that when this stated number had been completed it would immediately come to an end. Later they describe the imaginary magic: an old child was killed, cut to pieces, and buried in a profane rite. FABRIC.]

[Note: “Those who had thought . . . already more.” FABRIC.]

[Note: Already more than four hundred years. I think it should be read, “already about four hundred years.” For the full four hundred years had not yet elapsed when Philastrius wrote this. I remember having noted above, at ch. 83, that Philastrius wrote before Parmenian’s death, that is, before 391. And in ch. 112: “From the Lord until now, three hundred and eighty years and more”; ch. 27: “and more than a hundred in the psalm”; Cicero, *For Sextus Roscius*, ch. 14: “more than forty years old.” FABRIC.]

[Note: How can this be reasonable? Above, heresy 98: “therefore it has no reason”; below, 146: “therefore it is reasonable.” FABRIC.]

[Note: “It will be tradition.” FABRIC.]

[Note: “As very many wished to think.” This should be read thus in place of the defective wording in earlier editions: “As very many wished to think this.” FABRIC.]

For the things which he did and taught in one year, the Lord commanded alone to be recorded. For of the things he did and said in the first thirty years, blessed John says that the world could not contain them if all the things he had done were written individually.

[Note: What he did in one year. This was not merely the view of the Valentinians, attacked by Irenaeus, book II, ch. 36 ff.; it was also held by many Catholic doctors: Philastrius, Clement of Alexandria, Tertullian, Origen, Lactantius, Orosius, and Evagrius in the disputation of Simon the Jew with Theophilus the Christian, vol. V of Edmond Martène’s *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, p. 13, as well as others who, relying on Isaiah’s words, thought that Christ preached for one year after baptism and that all the matters described by the Evangelists were done within that one year. See Scaliger, book VI of *On the Correction of Times*, p. 551 ff.; Grotius on Luke 6:19; Blondel, preface to *On Bishops and Presbyters*, p. 27 ff.; Montagu, *Origins of the Church*, vol. I, pp. 330 ff., 341, 343; and John Potter’s notes on Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* I, p. 407 (old ed., 340). FABRIC.]

[Note: According to blessed John. John 21:25: Ἔστι δὲ καὶ ἄλλα πολλὰ ἃ ἐποίησεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς, “There are also many other things that Jesus did.” I am persuaded that these words should be understood not of the thirty years before baptism, as Philastrius wishes, but especially also of the time of Jesus’ ministry after baptism. FABRIC.]

[Note: The world could not contain. On this hyperbole I spoke in *The Apocryphal Codex of the New Testament*, p. 321. Nor do I think John’s meaning is what the very learned Jacob Eisner attributes to him in his excellent *Sacred Observations*: that the ungodly world would not receive them even if they were individually written down. For John’s addition αὐτόν, “itself,” plainly opposes that interpretation: οὐδὲ αὐτὸν οἶμαι τὸν κόσμον χωρῆσαι τὰ γραφόμενα βιβλία, “I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books being written”—referring to magnitude, not impiety. FABRIC.]

Isaiah the prophet, therefore, spoke of that year of the Lord Savior in which he taught until his passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven, as the most blessed writers handed down; not of three hundred and sixty-five years, as some imagine, but of that year after baptism, in which, preaching, he disclosed to believers the mysteries of salvation from the Law and the Prophets, testifying to and bringing to fulfillment the things once spoken.

[Note: “As the most blessed handed down”: the Evangelists and Apostles. It is Philastrius’s customary practice to give sacred writers the title “most blessed.” FABRIC.]

## CVII

[Note: This heresy, absent from all printed editions, has been added from the excellent Saint-Germain manuscript, although it is not supplied with names of heretics.]

There is another heresy whose adherents assert that the consummation of the age was fixed according to a definition of times by God, Christ the Savior. Hence they infer that the number leading to the consummation is certain, and suppose that it will be neither more nor less, since the prophets everywhere announced that the consummation of the age would occur about the five-hundredth year, and that thus the Lord would come again from heaven.

For Daniel reckons seventy weeks, hearing from Christ the Lord: “Hear,” he says, “man greatly beloved: seventy weeks have been decreed for your people until Christ the leader, that all the things spoken concerning the city Jerusalem and the people might come to pass” (Dan. 11:23, 25). But just as this was said to Daniel before Christ came in the flesh and was almost fulfilled, so also the same number, from the law received by Moses to the entry into the promised land, does not fall very far short of five hundred years.

When the Lord spoke of signs and various things—famines, persecutions, floods, earthquakes, pestilences—which would come near the end (Matt. 24:7; Luke 21:25–26), he also spoke in a riddle to the blessed Peter about the multitude of years. When Peter said, “Lord, how often shall I forgive a brother who sins?” the Lord said, “Not seven times, but seventy times seven” (Matt. 18:21–22). He showed both that the infinite daily number of the human race’s sins ought to be forgiven by one human being to another, and that every debt must be forgiven by all believers to a Jew returning, or to a pagan and other carnal persons returning from impiety to the faith of Christ and to his Church.

For the Jewish historians also taught, saying that more than four hundred and eighty years had passed from nothing, and that thus the Lord came in the flesh.

[Note: “From nothing.” Perhaps “from Daniel,” as a little earlier and immediately below. FABRIC.]

You also have in Genesis the mystery very plainly proclaimed: vengeance sevenfold upon Cain, but seventy-sevenfold upon Lamech (Gen. 4:24). There can be no doubt that Scripture thereby foretold, in two persons, the impiety of one people and the iniquity of the other. For “the Law is spiritual,” according to the Apostle (Rom. 4:14); and “these,” he says, “are the two covenants” (Gal. 4:14). Nor do we discard the historical fact that the people spent seventy years in Persia, nor do we despise spiritual knowledge.

Therefore the seventy weeks spoken of by Daniel are four hundred and ninety years, then almost completed, and so Christ came in the flesh; and from Christ’s manifestation to the consummation of the age, you will find almost the number of years remaining to be completed. For the interpreters taught concerning the seventy weeks Daniel saw. Those first wise interpreters understood seven times seventy, four hundred and ninety years: the jubilee which the Jews—not those of the present time, but the ancient and learned Jews—awaited with the greatest joy as the year of Christ’s remission and pardon, celebrating beforehand in a figure his bodily presence, as Leviticus contains.

But the lesser jubilee has fifty years; it cannot have fewer, nor can it have more. For the greater jubilee has five hundred years and the lesser jubilee fifty. Thus the greater has five hundred years less a tenth, so that from this one jubilee might signify Christ’s presence and the consummation of the age.

Although the seventy years of the people’s captivity in Persia are understood historically, and after their return to Jerusalem nearly five hundred years are found completed until the incarnation of Christ the Lord, this must also be understood spiritually: that after seventy times seven—that is, after approximately four hundred and ninety years—the Jews must be under Antichrist, when he is found to be a deceiver by the Jews themselves who had first considered him to be Christ. But not long afterward, when his treachery and deceit have become known, all who remain, undertaking repentance, will hasten to the faith of Christ the Lord; and, repenting, will obtain pardon for their sins from Christ the Lord, as the rest do, so that what was said may be fulfilled: “Amen, I say to you, you will see me no more until you say, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord’” (Matt. 23:39).

And so that this may be fulfilled: “Until the fullness of the Gentiles enters, and thus all Israel will be saved, as it is written” (Rom. 11:25); and, “Though the people of Israel be as the sand of the sea, the remnant will be saved” (Rom. 9:27). And blessed Isaiah openly taught concerning Christ (Isa. 61:1) that he would grant pardon to all who return; the Lord himself said thus: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; therefore he anointed me, sent me to proclaim good news to the poor, to preach release to captives, sight to the blind, to announce the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of recompense” (Luke 4:18). When the Lord had received the book of Scripture in the temple and had seen this passage, he said to the Apostles and to all that it had then been fulfilled in his own presence—what the most blessed Daniel also observed, when the Lord said to him: “Hear, man greatly beloved, and understand from the going forth of God’s word,” that is, from Christ’s incarnation, until his divine judgment and return from heaven, and the consummation of the age, when it will be present with the angels (Dan. 9:23).

## CVIII. HERESY CONCERNING THE GIANTS IN THE TIME OF NOAH

There is another heresy which maintains concerning giants that angels mingled with women before the flood, and conjectures that giants were born from this union. Yet Nimrod was born afterward not from a spirit—that is, not from an angel—but from the human being Cush, who was a son of Ham; and he is the first called a giant in Scripture, because he began to be a hunter and a strong man, so that he was called a giant on earth: “Therefore,” it says, “they will say, ‘As Nimrod the giant, so strong is he’” (Gen. 10:9), whenever someone might afterward be seen to resemble him in strength.

[Note: Concerning giants. From the Greek version of Gen. 6:2, many ancient doctors of the Church persuaded themselves of this, as I remember noting concerning the fragment of Pseudo-Enoch in *The Pseudepigraphic Codex of the Old Testament*, p. 172 ff. One may also consult Suicer, *Thesaurus*, p. 37 ff.; Christian Schotanus’s notes on Sulpicius Severus; and Cotelerius on the Apostolic Fathers, vol. I, p. 493. FABRIC.]

[Note: From the human being Cush. Gen. 10:8: Χοὺς δὲ ἐγέννησε τὸν Νεβρώδ, οὗτος ἤρξατο εἶναι γίγας ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς· οὗτος ἦν γίγας κυνηγὸς Κυρίου τοῦ Θεοῦ· διὰ τοῦτο ἐροῦσιν· Ὡς Νεβρώδ γίγας κυνηγὸς ἐναντίον Κυρίου: “Cush begot Nimrod; he began to be a giant upon the earth. He was a giant hunter before the Lord God. Therefore they will say: ‘Like Nimrod, a giant hunter before the Lord.’” FABRIC.—Διὰ τοῦτο ἐροῦσιν, Ὡς Νεμβρὼδ γίγας κυνηγὸς ἐναντίον Κυρίου, “Therefore they will say: ‘Like Nimrod, a giant hunter before the Lord’” (Gen. 10:9). Philastrius translates this: “Therefore they will say, ‘Like Nimrod the giant, so strong is he.’” The Vulgate: “like Nimrod, a mighty hunter before the Lord.” On this proverb see Bochart, *Sacred Geography*, IV.12, col. 228; to which may be added Vatablus in Pearson’s *Critics* on this passage of Genesis, and Delrio, *Proverbs of the Old Testament*, vol. I, p. 17. GALEARD.]

Human beings, then, were strong; from youth they were rapacious, ravagers, javelin-throwers, runners, devoted to plunder, and thus, as though alien not only from human character but even from human appearance, they were called giants, being huge and committing such great crimes contrary to the nature of other human beings.

[Note: Human appearance: presenting, as it were, another kind of appearance and form. FABRIC.]

[Note: “They were considered enormous, contrary . . . not from another.” FABRIC.]

For a giant, by etymology, is called an earth-born monster, compounded from two names, whether in form, life, appearance, strength, or bulk of limbs.

[Note: An earth-born monster. Orpheus, in the eighth *Sacred Discourse*, cited by the author of the *Great Etymological Dictionary*:

> Whom among the blessed they call giants by surname,  
> because they were born from earth and heavenly blood.

FABRIC.]

[Note: From two names: γῆ, “earth,” and γυῖα, “limbs,” properly feet. FABRIC.]

For, that you may know that giants were not of another nature but were produced from human stock, you have the six-fingered persons, ἐξαδακτύλους, in the books of Kings, whom those books declare to have been of the race of giants because of their great form, their enormous bulk of limb, and immense strength, two thousand three hundred years after the flood; as also that Goliath whom the most blessed King and Prophet David alone struck down in battle. “A wagon,” he says, “carried the equipment of weapons” belonging to him and others of this sort.

[Note: In the books of Kings. 2 Sam. 21:20: Καὶ ἦν ἀνὴρ Μαδών (Procopius: ἐκ Γάδης), καὶ οἱ δάκτυλοι τῶν χειρῶν αὐτοῦ καὶ οἱ δάκτυλοι τῶν ποδῶν αὐτοῦ ἓξ καὶ ἓξ, εἰκοσιτέσσαρες ἀριθμῷ: “And there was a man of Madon [Procopius: from Gath], and the fingers of his hands and the toes of his feet were six and six, twenty-four in number.” FABRIC.]

[Note: Two thousand three hundred years after the flood. So Livy, III.5: “the Romans, five thousand three hundred”; and XXXIII.27: “denarii, thirty-four thousand five hundred and fifty.” See more in Gronovius on Livy XXXIX.7. On the methods of calculating years which Philastrius uses from the flood until David’s time, see below on ch. 112. FABRIC.]

[Note: That Goliath. On him see commentators on 1 Sam. 17, and the Reverend Paul Christian Hillischer, pastor of the Dresden Church, in *The Life of Goliath*, published at Bautzen in 1716, quarto, adorned with learned and agreeable observations, together with a commentary on the apocryphal Psalm 151 and a letter concerning Og the giant. FABRIC.]

[Note: “A wagon carried the equipment of weapons.” *Carrus* or *carra* properly denotes a kind of Gallic wagon on which baggage was placed; hence Caesar’s Greek translator calls it σκευοφόρος, “baggage-bearing.” See Johann Scheffer, *On Vehicular Matters*, II.28, p. 329. But I do not know whence Philastrius obtained his interpretation of *carra*, where others understand an armor-bearer, 1 Sam. 17:7: Ὁ αἴρων τὰ ὅπλα αὐτοῦ προεπορεύετο αὐτοῦ, “The one carrying his weapons went before him.” Augustine Calmet notes that the weight of Goliath’s armor exceeded 272 pounds. FABRIC.—*Carra* and *carrae*, a word in the feminine gender not especially common, occurs twice in King Theodoric’s order exempting the carts of Saint-Denis from toll throughout Gaul, in Mabillon, *On Diplomatics*, p. 471: “Let none of our judges or toll-collectors presume to demand or exact anything from that cart”; and shortly after: “From every cart of the monastery of lord Saint-Denis.” Capitular II of Charlemagne, 813, ch. 10, ed. Baluze, p. 519: “Let the king’s provisions be conveyed in a cart.” More is found in Du Cange under *carrae*; but *carrus* and *carrum*, masculine and neuter, are more usual among writers of the better age, Caesar and Hirtius. Du Cange also shows in his *Glossary* that *carrum* was commonly used by writers of the lower age. GALEARD.]

Since people of this kind had therefore been devoted from childhood to plunder in a bestial manner, Scripture described them as though alien from human nature and character. For there is no doubt that those angels who were cast down from heaven are not merely like human nature, except that they were able to enter human beings—that is, to persuade them—and to suggest things shameful and contrary to the Law, as they still do now.

[Note: “Merely human.” FABRIC.]

[Note: Entering into human beings: by suggesting and inciting them to evil, which the ancients commonly called ἐμβάλλειν, ὑποβάλλειν, ἐγγλύφειν, ὑποτίθεσθαι, διεγείρειν: “to cast in,” “to insinuate,” “to implant,” “to suggest,” “to stir up.” See Damascene’s *Sacred Parallels*, vol. II, p. 648. FABRIC.]

Thus the enemy of the human race persuaded the Jews to perpetrate such crimes against God and against the holy prophets, as it is written: “Satan entered into Judas.” Likewise, before that time, unclean spirits entering the souls of men and women—that is, persuading them—had spread throughout the world crimes of evil persuasion.

[Note: “Against the Lord.” FABRIC.]

[Note: Greek text: Εἰσῆλθεν εἰς ἐκεῖνον ὁ Σατανᾶς, “Satan entered into him.” FABRIC.]

[Note: Men and women. He uses *homines*, “human beings,” for men, as above in ch. 17: “Idols of men and women”; see, if you please, my notes there. FABRIC.]

But if anyone thinks it just to say that angels sinned thus after being transformed into flesh and remaining in that flesh, or believes that they were made fleshly in this way, he forcibly imposes this interpretation upon the narrative; just as the falsehoods of pagans and poets assert that gods and goddesses, transformed, committed shameful marriages.

[Note: “That they remained in that flesh.” FABRIC.]

[Note: “He determines the history.” Above, ch. 101: “the Lord determines a fitting judgment by pronouncing it.” FABRIC.]

[Note: The falsehoods of pagans and poets. Again and again Christian writers reproached them with these things in their distinguished apologies against the Gentiles: Justin Martyr, Clement of Alexandria, Arnobius, Tertullian, Lactantius, Minucius Felix, Commodian, Julius Firmicus, and others. FABRIC.]

If this happened at any time, it will not be doubtful that it may happen now; but what did not happen at any time is plainly not happening now either.

[Note: “If this happened at any time.” See commentators on Eccles. 1:9; Gataker, p. 257, on Marcus Aurelius VII.1; and Gassendi, *The Philosophy of Epicurus*, p. 166. Melissus of Samos, in Palaephatus: ἔστιν, ἃ ἐγένετο, νῦν, καὶ ἔσται, “Things that happened exist now and will be.” Marcus Aurelius XII.26: πᾶν τὸ γινόμενον οὕτως ἀεὶ ἐγίνετο, καὶ γενήσεται, καὶ νῦν πανταχοῦ γίνεται, “Everything that happens has always happened thus, will happen, and is now happening everywhere.” FABRIC.]

But “giant” is also taken in a good sense because of strength: “For he shall rejoice like a giant to run his course.” This is shown to be proved and fulfilled in Christ’s divine manifestation.

[Note: LXX: Ἀγαλλιάσεται ὡς γίγας δραμεῖν ὁδὸν αὐτοῦ, “He shall rejoice like a giant to run his way.” The pious ancients gladly interpret this of Christ: Rufinus, Gregory the Great, Bernard, and others. FABRIC.]

## CIX. HERESY ATTRIBUTING PAGANISM AND ALL CRIMES TO GOD
[Col. 1226B] Another heresy says that [Note: [Col. 1226D] Paganism instituted by God. *Paganitas*, like *paganismus* and *pagania*, denotes the religion and rites of the Gentiles. It is well known that they were called pagans from the rural districts (*pagi*), in which they worshipped gods after the worship of idols had been banished from the temples of cities and towns. Pelagians and certain others have persuaded themselves that this paganism, no less than Christianity or Judaism, has hitherto been approved by God, so that one who lives in it free from crime may attain eternal salvation. FABRICIUS.] paganism was instituted by God, rather than devised through human wickedness and the enemy’s suggestion, as a cause of vices and the production of crimes. How, then, can that which was instituted by God be condemned by that same God? For there is no doubt that, from the beginning of the world, knowledge of God [Note: [Col. 1226D] Of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Philastrius undertakes to demonstrate that the doctrine of the most holy Trinity was delivered by God to human beings immediately at the very beginning of things, using arguments of no very firm force. FABRICIUS.] the almighty Father, [Col. 1227A] and of his Son and the Holy Spirit, was proclaimed. For in [Note: [Col. 1227C] In the book of the world’s creation. Above, chapter 79. FABRICIUS.] the book of the creation of the world—that is, in Genesis—you find written: “And God said,” and “God made” (Gen. 1:3, 7). Again: “God said, ‘Let there be lights’” (ibid., 14). And on the sixth day God said: [Note: [Col. 1227C] “Let us make.” Basil, Homily 10 on the *Hexaemeron*, p. 44, Greek Basel edition: “Why did he not say, ‘I shall make’ [read thus instead of ‘Make’], but, ‘Let us make a human being’? So that, while recognizing the Father, you may not be ignorant of the Son; so that you may know that the Father made through the Son, and the Son created by the Father’s will; and that you may glorify the Father in the Son and the Son in the Holy Spirit. Thus the work became common to both, so that you might be a common worshipper of both, not dividing worship but uniting the Godhead.” FABRICIUS.] “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26). And God made him—not, plainly, upon an angel’s persuasion [Note: [Col. 1227C] Not with an angel, surely, as persuader. Saturninus, according to Epiphanius, vol. I, p. 62, taught that when God said, “Let us make man,” he was addressing the angels. The Jews [Col. 1227D] think the same. See Maimonides, *Moreh Nevukhim*, part II, chapter 6, and Manasseh ben Israel, *Conciliator* on Genesis, question 6. FABRICIUS.] in the creation of man, but, manifestly, with his Son, Christ our Lord, and the Holy Spirit.

For in Genesis, that is, in the first book, you have the holy and adorable Trinity proclaimed beforehand to human beings. For it says thus: “The Lord [Note: [Col. 1227D] “The Lord from the Lord.” Below, chapter 110, from Genesis 19:24: Κύριος παρὰ Κυρίου, “the Lord from the Lord.” The ancients explain this passage as meaning that the Son inflicts punishment upon the Sodomites from the Father. Although the Hebrew idiom permits “the Lord from the Lord” to signify the same as “from himself,” as Theodor Hackspan noted in *Sylloge*, p. 150 ff.; Gataker, chapter 17 of *Adversaria*; Grotius on 2 Tim. 1:18. FABRICIUS.] rained from the Lord sulphur and fire” (Gen. 19:24). And again, concerning the Spirit on the first day: [Note: [Col. 1227D] LXX: Καὶ Πνεῦμα Θεοῦ ἐπεφέρετο ἐπάνω τοῦ ὕδατος, “And the Spirit of God moved over the water.” FABRICIUS.] “And the Spirit of God was borne over the water” (Gen. 1:2). And Pharaoh, [Col. 1227B] king of Egypt, says: [Note: [Col. 1227D] LXX: Μὴ εὑρήσομεν ἄνθρωπον τοιοῦτον ὃς ἔχει πνεῦμα Θεοῦ ἐν αὐτῷ, “Shall we find such a man as this, who has the Spirit of God in him?” FABRICIUS.] “Who,” he says, “will interpret these things [Note: [Col. 1227C] “Will interpret for us.”] for us, unless he has the Spirit of God?” (Gen. 41:38). And David: [Note: [Col. 1227D] LXX: Τῷ Λόγῳ τοῦ Κυρίου οἱ οὐρανοὶ ἐστερεώθησαν, καὶ τῷ Πνεύματι τοῦ στόματος αὐτοῦ πᾶσα ἡ δύναμις αὐτῶν, “By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their host.” See above, chapter 67. FABRICIUS.] “By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their host” (Ps. 32:6).

But afterward the depraved human will, departing from so great a knowledge of piety, hastened eagerly to serve the falsehoods and vanities of idols and chose rather to give itself to a most shameful life. It was held liable to the judgment [Note: [Col. 1227D] Liable to a condemning judgment. Thus the editions; but the Corbie manuscript, somewhat better, has “liable to the judgment of condemnation.” Thus chapter 98: “Placed under the condition of the Law, it is found liable to judgment” [Col. 1228C]; chapter 79: “liable to God’s Law”; and chapter 134: “when the soul is found sinning and liable to judgment.” See Jacob Spiegel’s commentary on Prudentius Weitz, p. 208. GALEARD.] of condemnation, so that the prophets had previously said: [Note: [Col. 1228C] LXX: Ὁ θυσιάζων Θεοῖς, πλὴν Κυρίῳ, θανάτῳ ἐξολοθρευθήσεται, “He who sacrifices to gods, except to the Lord, shall be utterly destroyed by death.” FABRICIUS.] “Whoever sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out” (Exod. 22:20). And again: “The gods who did not make heaven shall be rooted out” (Ps. 95:5). Therefore the Lord did not display [Note: [Col. 1228C] Not his new presence. He did not now come for the first time, but had long already been present with his Church. FABRICIUS.] his presence as something new, saying: [Note: [Col. 1228C] “He who spoke in the prophets: behold, I am present.” I think this refers to John 8:56, 58, although you will look for the actual words there in vain. FABRICIUS.] “He who spoke [Note: [Col. 1227C] “I who spoke … so that those who worship them.”] in the prophets, behold, I am present” (Isa. 52:6).

Nor did the Lord anywhere command that angels be worshipped, nor [Note: [Col. 1228C] The elements of the world: the sun, moon, and stars, as above, chapter 61. Theophylact on Colossians 2:8: Στοιχεῖα κόσμου ἥλιον καὶ σελήνην λέγει, “By ‘elements of the world’ he means sun and moon.” FABRICIUS.] the elements of the world, nor any creature, nor idols. These the utterly depraved human will chose to invent for the sake of committing its own wickedness and shamefulness, so that their worshippers might have unrestrained licence to do evil. For even [Note: [Col. 1228D] The very name *idol* is a semblance of deceit and a falsification of form. “Form” is εἶδος in Greek, and falsification or deceit is δόλος; hence Philastrius composes the name of *idol* as though from εἶδος δόλος. FABRICIUS.] the very name *idol* is called, in Greek interpretation, a semblance of deceit and a falsification of form.

The Trinity of Christianity, therefore, was proclaimed from the beginning of the world, and the truth of piety was everywhere taught without interruption. David too teaches: “The Lord said to my Lord” (Ps. 109:1); and, “Your good Spirit [Note: [Col. 1228C] “Your good Spirit will lead me into …”] will lead me in the right way” (Ps. 142:10); and again: “The Spirit of the Lord [Col. 1228B] filled the world” (Wis. 1:7); and, “Where shall I flee from your Spirit, and where shall I go from your presence?” (Ps. 138:7). For Solomon teaches (Wis. 14:15) [Note: [Col. 1228C] Blessed Solomon teaches.] that [Note: [Col. 1228D] That idolatry. For illumination of this passage compare Philo, *On the Decalogue* and *On the Contemplative Life*; Athanasius, *Against the Gentiles*, vol. I, p. 10 ff.; Lactantius, book I, chapter 15 ff. Among later writers, Vossius, book I, *On Idolatry*, chapter 11; John Faes on Gyraldus, p. 698 ff. FABRICIUS.] idolatry was instituted by man. When a certain father mourned for a long time over his lost son, he made an image of him and took pleasure in looking upon it; and from this, handed down to posterity, a different material of impiety sprang up within the human race.

## CX. HERESY CONCERNING CHRISTIANS WHO BELIEVE IN THE WORD OF GOD IN THE LAST TIME

[Note: [Col. 1228D] The Word of God. Understand the Word to be Christ, whose worshippers this heresy babbled had only begun the other day. FABRICIUS.]

Another heresy says that [Note: [Col. 1228D] Christians as most recent. This objection of novelty against Christians was formerly frequent on the lips of Gentiles and Jews. See Elmenhorst’s notes on Arnobius, book I, p. 19; D. Kortholt, *The Pagan Detractor of Makarios*, chapters 1 and 5; and on Justin [Col. 1229B] Martyr, pp. 31 and 55. Christians replied that their doctrine was no less ancient than that Word which was in the beginning: Διὰ τὸν λόγον ὃς ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν, ἀρχαΐζομεν, “Because of the Word who was in the beginning, we are ancient,” says Clement of Alexandria in the *Protrepticus*, p. 5. Compare Agobard, *Against Abbot Fredegisus*, vol. XIV of the Lyons edition of the *Library of the Fathers*, p. 277 ff. FABRICIUS.] Christians were created very recently, [Col. 1229A] [Note: [Col. 1229B] “More recent and …”] and later than Jews and pagans. It is ignorant that Christians were created before Jews and pagans by nature, and also in [Note: [Col. 1229B] By faith, life, sacrifice, and manner of life. Philaster subsequently treats these four items distinctly, point by point; from them he concludes that Christians are prior to Jews and pagans both by nature and by time—that is, that their doctrine is both more excellent and older than Jewish and Gentile doctrine. FABRICIUS.] faith, life, time, sacrifice, and manner of life.

In faith, indeed, because from Adam to Moses, during [Note: [Col. 1229C] Three thousand seven hundred years. Here, as below in heresies 112 and 156, Philastrius follows the numbers of the LXX interpreters, as almost all ancient Christians customarily did. According to the Hebrew codices he ought to have stated a far shorter interval; for in them, from Adam, or the creation of the world, to the birth of Moses, who lived 120 years, not more than 2,373 years are counted, so that the departure from Egypt and the giving of the Law on Mount Sinai fall in the year 2453. FABRICIUS.] three thousand seven hundred years, all the righteous, worshipping [Note: [Col. 1229B] “Both God and Lord.”] [Note: [Col. 1229C] “God and God.” That is, God the Father and God the Son. The ancients customarily cite in support of this meaning Genesis 1:27: “And God made man; according to [Col. 1229D] the image of God he made him.” FABRICIUS.] God and God, Lord and Lord, and also the Holy Spirit, proclaimed the true Trinity. Thus from those blessed, ancient predecessors you may readily recognize the whole Trinity, and that this too was afterward revealed to us by the Lord. [Note: [Col. 1229D] “You may recognize.” Thus I have written from the Basel and Lyons editions instead of the erroneous *possit* in the Helmstedt edition. I have also removed the stop after *antiquis* and retained *hoc*, which Lyons wrongly omits. In the same place *aliis* is wrongly printed for *illis*, and Basel has *manifestata*, others *manifestam*. The sense is that one may readily understand that, through and after those ancient persons themselves, the doctrine of the most holy Trinity was revealed to us by God. FABRICIUS.]

For when Scripture says: [Note: [Col. 1229D] “Rained …” Compare above, chapter 108. FABRICIUS.] “The Lord rained from the Lord sulphur and fire upon Sodom and Gomorrah” (Gen. 19:24), what does it seem to proclaim to you? Does it not declare that God the Father, through his Son—that is, [Col. 1229B] Christ God—performed all signs and wonders? David, knowing this, proclaimed the Lord Father and the Lord Christ, that is, his Word, and the Holy Spirit: a Trinity of persons, but one majesty, substance, and equal power of divinity. Yet he demonstrated that the Son is from God the Father, who is [Note: [Col. 1229D] Prior. Correctly so in Helmstedt and Basel; Lyons wrongly has *priorem*. The Father is prior to the Son in origin, not in time or nature. FABRICIUS.] prior, and properly demonstrated the Holy Spirit, teaching: [Note: [Col. 1229D] “By the Word of the Lord.” Compare above, chapter 108. FABRICIUS.] “By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their host” (Ps. 32:6). And again elsewhere: “The Lord said to my Lord” (Ps. 109:1). And all the prophets proclaimed the Word and Spirit, [Note: [Col. 1229D] “They proclaimed.” A comma should be placed here, not after *ubique*, as earlier editions do. FABRICIUS.] everywhere speaking thus: “And the word of the Lord came to me” (Isa. 38:4); and, “The Spirit of the Lord was upon me” (Isa. 61:1; Ezek. 11:5).

Therefore Christianity is not a matter of faith [Note: [Col. 1230B] “Temporal Christianity.”] of recent origin; [Note: [Col. 1229D] “Christianity is not temporal in the matter of faith.” An old gloss: *temporalis*, ὀλιγοχρόνιος, “short-lived.” Philastrius means that the faith of Christianity, or of Christians, [Col. 1230B] did not arise only recently and is not of brief duration; Christians are not χρονῖται, “men of recent time,” the abusive term by which Aetius attacked Catholics. Athanasius rightly asks him, *Dialogue 2 on the Trinity*, p. 193, vol. II: “Whom do you call ‘men of recent time’? Those who, from the holy Apostles until today, praise Father, Son, and Holy Spirit? Or those who have appeared yesterday or today, stemming from you, and possess a heresy?” In the same sense our author frequently uses *temporalis* for something that has arisen recently or lasts only a short while; so also do Tertullian and others. FABRICIUS.—“Christianity is not temporal in the matter of faith.” So the editions read; but the Corbie manuscript has *temporalis Christianitas*, “temporal Christianity,” which is preferable. Here and elsewhere Philastrius uses *temporalis* for something that has arisen recently, as Fabricius correctly noted on heresies 110, 112, and 129, where he brands pagan falsehoods with the same mark of temporality; and on heresy 111, where *temporalitatis* means “recent and by no means ancient,” again explained by Fabricius. *Temporalitas* is absent from Du Cange’s glossary; *temporalis* occurs there, but not in the sense Philastrius uses. GALEARD.] rather, before the Jews and pagans it had been revealed to those who studied and sought within the Law; but [Note: [Col. 1230B] “But not to those desiring the Father Almighty …”] [Note: [Col. 1230C] “But not to those desiring.” I judged that this must be written instead of *nunc*, “now,” which yielded no sense. *Capientibus*, “to those receiving,” also came to mind in place of *cupientibus*, “to those desiring”; but I preferred the latter because it better corresponds to “to those studying and seeking.” Isaiah 65:1: “They found me who did not seek me.” Moreover, the phrase “knowledge of the Father and Almighty” means the doctrine of God, almighty Creator of heaven and earth, and of his worship and Law; no simultaneous mention is made of the Son the Saviour or of the Holy Spirit. FABRICIUS.—“But not to those desiring.” Fabricius adds: “I judged that this must be written in place of *nunc*, which made no sense.” The emendation is by no means necessary if one reads *nuntiatur*, “is proclaimed,” for *nuntiabatur*, “was proclaimed”; anyone inspecting the entire passage will readily be convinced that this is the true reading, especially since *nunc*, “now,” corresponds to what he had said earlier, “before Jews and pagans.” Fabricius’s Corbie manuscript supports his reading; but Sichard’s edition has *nunc autem cupientibus*, “but now to those desiring.” GALEARD.] the word and knowledge of the Father Almighty was proclaimed to those who desired it by those holy [Col. 1230B] and perfect teachers.

In life also, those earlier saints employed no life other than that in which we live. For until Abraham, though they did not have [Note: [Col. 1230D] They did not have circumcision. Eusebius argues excellently on this point in book I of the *Evangelical Demonstration*; consult it if you please. FABRICIUS.] circumcision and did not delight in [Note: [Col. 1230D] They did not delight in sacrifices. Yet it is certain that sacrifices were offered to God from the earliest human beings. But the Levitical [Col. 1231B] ceremonial ordinances of sacrifice had certainly not yet then been instituted, which is sufficient against the Jews. FABRICIUS.] sacrifices, [Col. 1231A] they pleased God and were proclaimed righteous by him in all things. For David said: “A contrite heart is a sacrifice to God” (Ps. 50:19), and, “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. 49:14).

And because, compelled by the necessity of their lack of teachability, temporary sacrifices—not perpetual, [Note: [Col. 1231B] Nor true: such as could truly expiate divine wrath and reconcile salvation to human beings. Christ offered himself for us as the one true and saving sacrifice of this kind. FABRICIUS.] nor true, nor saving—were prescribed to the Jews, the prophet says to the Jews: “Behold, I make new things” (Isa. 43:19), and: [Note: [Col. 1231C] “Before they come.” Below, heresy 144. FABRICIUS.] “Before they come, they were announced to you” (Isa. 48:5–6). Thus Isaiah the prophet testified before the Jews: “For who required these things from your hands?” (Isa. 1:12). And again: “Circumcise your hearts, and not your bodies” (Jer. 4:4).

But what kind of sacrifice was that which Melchizedek first offered [Note: [Col. 1231C] Under Abraham. Already in Abraham’s time, Genesis 14:18, Melchizedek, with Abraham present, offered a victory-sacrifice, ἐπινίκιον. FABRICIUS.] in Abraham’s time, before four hundred years had passed before the Jews were named, or [Note: [Col. 1231C] “Before Judah was born.” I emended thus, since I found the earlier editions reading “before Judas was born,” which cannot be accepted. For who would say that 340 years elapsed from Abraham until Judah’s birth—those years which the Apostle counts, Galatians 3:17, from Abraham’s first arrival in Canaan to the Israelites’ departure from Egypt? FABRICIUS.—“Before Judas was born.” Here too the most learned Fabricius’s emendation seems quite unnecessary, since the earlier editions rightly have “before Judas was born,” supported by the Corbie manuscript. Philastrius’s meaning is not that 340 years elapsed from Abraham to Judah, but that Melchizedek offered sacrifice before the Jews were named or Judah was born, and before four hundred years had elapsed before they received the book of Genesis. Here he uses a complete number for an incomplete one, and a certain μετάθεσις, or transposition of words, which Fabricius recognized also in the phrase “foreseeing the mystery of Christianity,” rightly observed to refer to Melchizedek. Perhaps “four hundred years” slipped into a place not its own; one should accordingly read: “before the Jews were named, and before four hundred years had passed before they received the book of Genesis.” GALEARD.] Judah was born, and before they [Col. 1231B] [Note: [Col. 1231B] “Received in the book … you perceive.”] received the book of Genesis, [Note: [Col. 1231D] “Foreseeing the mystery of Christianity?” I believe these words must be joined with the preceding ones and accordingly expressed as a question. Earlier editions separate them and place a stop after “Genesis,” producing an insipid sense. FABRICIUS.] foreseeing the mystery of Christianity? Thus you may recognize that everything which belongs to Christianity—whether faith, life, or [Note: [Col. 1231D] Sacrament: the sacrifice of Christ, of which he has just spoken. FABRICIUS.] sacrament—[Col. 1232A] was not temporary but established and proclaimed, indeed rather celebrated, from the beginning of the world.

But in Christ and through Christ, [Note: [Col. 1231D] Through whom all things were made: John, the first verse and chapter of the Gospel. FABRICIUS.] through whom all things were made, we ought to see and [Note: [Col. 1231B] “And recognize what was …”] recognize from him what was the greater mystery concerning him in the Law, proclaimed beforehand [Col. 1232B] and fulfilled; and to receive it from him more fully as completed and brought to perfection.

[Note: [Col. 1231D] “For that chastity also …” He shows that the celibate life led by many Christians was not new, but that some prophets under the Law had already followed such a practice. On Daniel see Huet, *Evangelical Demonstration*, p. 466; and on the three youths, notes of that same most learned man on Origen, p. 66. Cosmas Indicopleustes VIII, p. 307: “For divine Scripture records neither marriage nor child nor anything of the sort concerning any of them; but tradition and custom, in accordance with the prophecy, portray them in images as beardless and smooth-faced.” St Jerome, to Eustochium, *On the Guarding of Virginity*: “Elijah was a virgin; Elisha a virgin; many sons of the prophets were virgins.” Jeremiah 16:2 says: “And you shall not take a wife.” FABRICIUS.]

For there is no doubt that a similar chastity existed among very many prophets—Elijah, Elisha, Daniel, Jeremiah, Ezra, the three youths, and many other most blessed persons—so that, in Christ’s presence, it might be recognized as [Note: [Col. 1232C] What was above the Law. For the Law nowhere commands celibacy. Earlier editions wrongly join the words “what was above the Law was proclaimed beforehand,” which gives no sense. FABRICIUS.] something above the Law, proclaimed beforehand by them. And marriage, which belonged to the Law, was confirmed in Christ’s presence by his divine pronouncement [Note: [Col. 1232C] “Marriage.” The editions wrongly have *conjunctum*, but the Corbie manuscript rightly has *conjugium*, “marriage.” For since Philastrius had previously said that celibacy, proclaimed beforehand by Elijah, Elisha, and the other prophets, was above the Law, he fittingly adds that marriage, which belonged to the Law, was confirmed in Christ’s presence—that is, in the Gospel—by Christ’s own divine pronouncement, namely Matthew 19:6: Ὃ οὖν ὁ Θεὸς συνέζευξεν, ἄνθρωπος μὴ χωριζέτω, “What therefore God has joined together, let no human being separate.” Thus on the following page, p. 224 in the Hamburg edition, “regarding Jews and pagans” is corruptly printed through the fault of the printers; the Basel and Lyons editions correctly have “rejecting Jews and pagans.” This reading is also supplied by the Corbie manuscript; likewise, in chapter 156, “who can tame the testimonies” is altogether wrongly printed in the Hamburg and Lyons editions, but Basel and the Corbie manuscript correctly have “who can tame all things.” GALEARD.] was confirmed by his divine pronouncement, so that this grace might be recognized as granted to human will and zeal. [Note: [Col. 1232D] Granted to will and zeal: even under the Law and before the Law, not reserved only for the grace of Christianity. FABRICIUS.]

Therefore the Lord himself joined those earlier [Note: [Col. 1228D] Saints before the Law—for example Abraham, who attained righteousness through the same faith by which we attain it. FABRICIUS.] saints before [Col. 1232B] the Law to us, and us to those earlier saints, according to the righteousness of faith. But he looked upon [Note: [Col. 1232B] “But the Jews, and between commandment …”] Jews and pagans, who were placed in the intermediate period [Note: [Col. 1232D] Between commandment and grace: that is, between the pre-legal state and the grace of the Gospel. You find *mandatum*, “commandment,” in this sense below in heresy 148. Most explicitly in heresies 150 and 153 he distinguishes these three: commandment, the Law in the intermediate period, and Christ’s grace. St Maximus, vol. I, pp. 86, 269, and elsewhere calls them τὸν φυσικὸν νόμον, “the natural law”; τὸν γραπτόν, or τοῦ γράμματος, “the written law” or “law of the letter”; and τὸν πνευματικόν, or the law of χάριτος, “grace,” as it is also called by Proclus of Constantinople, Homily 2, where he counts seven laws. Photius, book IV against the Manichaeans, pp. 113, 129, 131, 150–56, 165, 167, 171, 178, similarly contrasts Law and Grace; there Christ is “legislator of grace,” τῆς χάριτος νομοθέτης. Chrysostom, vol. VI, new edition, p. 324, and vol. IV, p. 593 ff., distinguishes an angelic commonwealth before Moses, the Law of Moses, and Christ’s commonwealth. The same author, vol. II, p. 276, says that Job was πρὸ τῆς χάριτος καὶ πρὸ τοῦ νόμου, “before grace and before the Law.” On τῆς χάριτος in the same sense, see p. 228d, 229a. FABRICIUS.] between commandment [Col. 1233A] and grace, and who, by a hostile and destructive will, are found ruined in carnal vices, enemies and adversaries of heavenly doctrine, reserved for the eternal judgment of punishments.

## CXI. THE MOST HARMFUL HERESY CONCERNING THE HUMAN BODY AND SOUL

There is a heresy which says that [Note: [Col. 1233C] Pagans are born naturally: by the natural propagation of souls, not by a new creation every day. Philastrius thus agrees with the rather implausible opinion, approved by Hilary, Jerome, and many other doctors of the Church (see Elmenhorst on Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, p. 131). He maintains that souls are created daily by God through Christ, an opinion which initially pleased Augustine too; but Augustine afterward remained doubtful when Pelagius objected that, if the soul is not propagated by descent, it does not deserve the punishment for original sin. Augustine says in Letter 28 [new edition, 166] to Jerome that he could find no answer to this objection by prayer, reading, thought, or reasoning. Compare Henry Noris, *Augustinian Vindications*, pp. 101, 110; and Jacob Thomasius, *The Blessed One*, dissertation *On the Origin of the Soul*, section 3, §§34 ff. FABRICIUS.] pagans are born naturally, [Note: [Col. 1233D] Not Christians. Tertullian too affirms that the soul is propagated by descent, in *On the Soul*, chapters 9, 19, 22, 27, 36. His famous saying in chapter 18 of the *Apology* is: “Christians are made, not born”; it was long ago explained by D. Matthias Zimmermann in a learned historical-theological dissertation, Leipzig, 1662, quarto.] but not Christians; that is, it holds that the human body and soul are not created daily by God through Christ by the [Note: [Col. 1233D] Nature of things: that is, generation. Thus below, chapter 112: “Therefore the nature of things must be ascribed to God, not to human vanity.” FABRICIUS.] nature of things, but proceed in this way by pagan vanity. For from Adam to Abraham, and afterward to Judah, who after Abraham was [Note: [Col. 1233D] Fourth in descent. Judah, from whom the Jews have their name, was Jacob’s son, Isaac’s grandson, and Abraham’s great-grandson. FABRICIUS.] fourth in descent, [Note: [Col. 1233B] “In descent, pagans …”] [Note: [Col. 1233D] Not pagans. Philastrius denies that Greek idolaters then existed, and that the name of Greeks or pagans had been heard. FABRICIUS.] there were neither pagans nor people called Jews; rather, they were called nations from the names and diversity of provinces. [Col. 1233B]

But pagans, after the Jews, were so called either from a *pagus*, that is, a place, or from a single [Note: [Col. 1234B] From one province: Greece. FABRICIUS.] province, or [Note: [Col. 1234B] From King Paganus: Hellen, or Greek, of whom below in this chapter. FABRICIUS.] from King Paganus. That this is true is manifest, as Hesiod the Greek poet says. [Note: [Col. 1234C] “As Hesiod says.” Below: “that pagans were called from King Paganus, as Hesiod the Greek poet says.” And again: “and, as Hesiod says, Greeks were called from the Greek king (Hellen).” The verses in which Hesiod wrote this no longer survive, so far as I know. Yet Strabo, VIII, p. 370, after observing that Homer called only the inhabitants of Thessaly Ἕλληνες, “Hellenes,” adds that Hesiod and Archilochus called Ἕλληνες also those who were πανέλληνες, “Panhellenes.”]

If then the name is from a *pagus*, it indicates a place, [Note: [Col. 1234C] As is also said now. It remains customary now to designate someone from this or that *pagus*, whether *pagus* denotes a village or an administrative district; compare Caesar, in whom the entire Helvetian nation is divided into four *pagi*.] as is still said of that particular district. But if it is from idols—because those worshipping images were called pagans, that is, Gentiles—this is because idols were invented not by God but by the most depraved human will, as our Scripture also says (Wis. 14:15 ff.). Very many pagans likewise declared that human beings invented these things [Note: [Col. 1234B] For the seduction and condemnation of souls.] for the seduction and condemnation of souls, because the people, looking upon them, delighted in banquets; and in the vanity of these they brought destruction upon their own souls (Exod. 32:6).

But a surer and stronger proof is that pagans were called from King Paganus, as Hesiod the Greek poet says: [Note: [Col. 1234C] “Who afterward.” Thus the Hamburg edition through scribal error; but the Corbie manuscript, as also the Basel and Lyons editions, correctly has *qui postea*, “who afterward.” Then, shortly afterward, the editions have “this is the falsehood of the name,” whereas Corbie more correctly has “this falsehood of the name.” In the same way, in chapter 112, where Hamburg corruptly reads “under holy Eber, who had not agreed to the building of the tower,” one should restore “under holy Eber, who had not agreed,” as in the Corbie manuscript and the Basel and Lyons editions. It may seem surprising that the great Bochart did not think of this passage, in which Philastrius expressly affirms that Eber did not agree to the building of the tower—the same thing that Bochart himself teaches in *Phaleg*, I.10. Compare Augustine, *City of God* XVI.11, and Louis Vives there; also, if desired, Stephen Morin, *Exercises on Languages*, part I, chapter 8, p. 44 ff., though Huet takes the contrary position, *Evangelical Demonstration*, proposition 4, p. 68. Philastrius said the same above in chapter 105. GALEARD.] afterward, from the pagan king, son of Deucalion and Pyrrha, they bore his name as though it were [Note: [Col. 1234D] From King Paganus: Hellen, son of Deucalion and Pyrrha, according to the agreement of Thucydides, Apollodorus, Strabo, and Eusebius. From this Hellen came Ἕλληνες, “Hellenes.” Compare Erasmus Vinding, *Hellen*, in volume eleven of Gronovius’s *Treasury of Greek Antiquities*, p. 321; and Salmasius, *On Hellenistic Language*, p. 348 ff. FABRICIUS.] pleasing and attractive; indeed, rather, worshipping his memory until the present day, they maintain this falsehood [Note: [Col. 1234B] “Possible … this falsehood.”] of the name through continued reverence.

Helles, therefore—that is, a Greek man—is so called from the language and name of the king, who was Deucalion’s son, and was named thus; just as Italians received their name from Italus, Romans from Romulus, and Latins from Latinus, [Col. 1235A] not from the impiety of idols. For idols, that is, [Note: [Col. 1235C] Forms. εἴδη, from which comes the name εἴδωλον, “idol.” “Forms of sculptured human beings”: sculptured human images. FABRICIUS.—“Forms of sculptured human beings.” I would suppose one should read “forms of sculptures,” followed by a comma: “afterward the most evil human will invented them.” The sense and syntax are then clearer, though Fabricius thinks otherwise. Thus earlier in this same chapter 111 Philastrius uses *sculptilia*, “sculptures,” absolutely for idols, and immediately afterward says that idols were invented by the most depraved human will. GALEARD.] forms of sculptured human beings, were afterward invented by the most evil human will.

But the Greek language was indicated by the distinctive character of a single province; King Paganus confirmed it with his own name, just as Romulus named the Romans. And, as Hesiod says, [Note: [Col. 1235C] Greeks called from a Greek king: that is, from Hellen, as he said above: “Helles, that is, a Greek man, is so called from the language and name of the king.” Otherwise they were also called Γραικοί, “Graikoi,” from Graecus, son of Thessalus; this was a name older than that of Ἕλληνες, “Hellenes.” See what learned men say on Stephanus of Byzantium under Γραικοί. FABRICIUS.] Greeks were called after the Greek king, who was Greek by name, son of Deucalion.

## CXII. HERESY CONCERNING THE UNCERTAINTY OF THE YEARS OF THE WORLD
Another heresy asserts that the number of years from the world’s beginning is uncertain and that people do not know the courses of time; although from Adam to the Flood there are ten generations and 2,242 years.

> [Note: From Adam to the Flood. If one adds together the individual figures recorded by Philastrius, there result 5,341 years from the creation of things to Christ’s birth. It is sufficiently clear, moreover, from other passages in his work that he follows the computation of the Seventy Interpreters, not the Hebrew codices; for in chapters 110 and 156 he reckons 3,700 years down to Moses, and in chapter 104, 2,700 years from Adam to Eber. I noted the computations of other ancients approaching most nearly to Philastrius’s in *Bibliographia antiquaria*, ch. 7, p. 191. FABRIC.]

And from the Flood to the confusion of tongues under holy Eber—who had not consented to the building of the tower—there are five generations, nearly 600 years; at that time the names of provinces too were divided, as it were, into seventy-two languages.

> [Note: [Col. 1235B] “as it were, of 75 languages, and thence…”]

> [Note: Seventy-two languages. See Cotelerius on Clement, XVIII.4; Potter on Clement of Alexandria, p. 404; Bochart, *Phaleg*, book I, ch. 15. FABRIC.]

From there to Abraham the patriarch are five generations, 540 years. From Abraham to Moses are seven generations, 430 years, as the blessed Apostle says.

> [Note: The blessed Apostle. Galatians 3:17; compare, if you please, Ussher’s *Sacred Chronology*, ch. 8 ff., and Scaliger on Eusebius, p. 17. FABRIC.]

And from Moses to Samuel the judge are 629 years.

> [Note: [Col. 1235B] Samuel: 629.]

From Samuel and David to the captivity of the Jews in Persia are nearly 500 years. From the captivity to the appearance of our Lord are nearly 500 years. And from the Lord until now are more than 380 years.

> [Note: From the Lord until now: more than 380 years. Earlier editions read: “more than 430.” But Philastrius indicates that he wrote before A.D. 391 in ch. 83, and he attended the Council of Aquileia in A.D. 387, under the consulship of Syagrius and Eucherius. (This is a scribal *sphalma* [error], which should by no means be charged to Fabricius; for how could that eminent scholar have failed to know that the Council of Aquileia must be assigned to A.D. 381, as its Acts in Baronius for that year demonstrate, while the consular epoch elsewhere also supplies the correct date, A.D. 381?
