Fabricius certainly could not have forgotten that he himself had included, among the testimonies concerning Philastrius at the beginning of the book, the Acts of the Council of Aquileia against the heretics Palladius and Secundianus—Arians—in A.D. 381, from Labbe and Chifflet. Latinus Latinius makes the same mistake when he too says of Philastrius: “He attended the Council of Aquileia, held when Syagrius and Eucherius were consuls,” that is, in the year of the Lord 387. Incorrectly. GALEARD.) Hence Latinus Latinius judged that the manifestly corrupt number should be restored thus; other learned men agree with him. Compare also ch. 106, where Philastrius wrote that “somewhat more or less than four hundred years” had elapsed since the Lord came. FABRIC.—From the Lord until now, more than 380 years. The Corbie manuscript suitably has *plus minus* (“more or less”), although it too contains the error of earlier editions, which read “more than 430”; Fabricius noted and, following Latinius, corrected this. The Lyons edition is even more corrupt: “more than 1,430.” Above too, in ch. 106, where editions read “now more than four hundred years,” Fabricius rightly supplied “now more or less than four hundred years.” Yet Philastrius also uses *plus* without *minus* in ch. 130 and in “the hundredth plus,” that is, Psalm 144, as Fabricius notes there. GALEARD.]

Therefore, if this faith existed in those earlier holy fathers of ours which exists in us, and was handed down and preached beforehand from them—that is, the faith of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—how is this divine knowledge temporary, as some suppose, and not Christian knowledge, announced beforehand to all human beings from the beginning of the world, as is shown by its manifestation and proclamation in the commandment and the Law?

> [Note: If this was the faith. He showed this above, ch. 110. FABRIC.]

> [Note: How is it temporary? *Temporale* means “of recent and short duration,” as also in chs. 110, 121, and 122. FABRIC.]

But if, in the middle of time under Moses, something was said less fully through a shadow, this was certainly not envy on the part of the Lord who gave it; rather, the weakness of the people unable to receive the heavenly mystery—the incapacity and frailty of human beings who could not bear it—will be blamed.

> [Note: [Col. 1236B] “under a shadow.”]

Finally, Christ the Lord himself, what he had earlier announced through the holy prophets, subsequently commanded and confirmed, saying: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:9), so that he might declare not only that this was the ancient faith from the world’s beginning, but also approve the life in which we live today: in the circumcision of the heart, not in the boasting of the flesh (Gal. 6:13).

> [Note: [Col. 1236B] “the ancient faith.”]

Thus those are greatly mistaken who dare to ascribe the human race either to pagan impiety or to Jewish vanity.

> [Note: The human race, or pagan impiety. That is, those who think that the religion of Greeks or Jews is as ancient as the human race, so that people are naturally born pagans or Jews—a claim our author denied in the preceding chapter, 111. FABRIC.]

For one may not call a person a Jew unless the eighth day has received him, nor likewise a pagan unless he has believed that human beings made the false gods.

> [Note: The eighth day. Before circumcision he will not be a Jew. FABRIC.]

> [Note: Unless he has believed false gods to have made humankind. That is, unless he persuades himself that false gods, or idols, are humanity’s makers and demiurges. FABRIC.]

Therefore the nature of things must be ascribed to God, not to the vanity of any of these; but the teaching which fructifies after nature, if it is true, must be joined to faith in God and united to the most health-giving service. It does not depart from that faith, but rather recognizes its own Lord through faith and remembers the Creator by nature.

> [Note: The nature of things. Human generation, as above in ch. 111: “the nature of things [does not hold] that the body and soul of a human being are created daily by God through Christ.” FABRIC.]

> [Note: Which fructifies after nature. So that not merely human nature but also the teaching professed by parents may be propagated: a pagan may be born from a pagan, a Jew from a Jew, a Christian from a Christian. FABRIC.]

Accordingly, it is not a natural weakness of the human soul but rather a perverse will that must be blamed, as the Lord says: “And now, if you are willing and obey me, you shall eat the good things of the earth; but if you are unwilling and do not obey me, the sword shall devour you. For the mouth of the Lord has spoken these things” (Isa. 1:19–20).

> [Note: LXX: “And if you are willing and obey me, you shall eat the good things of the earth. But if you are unwilling and do not obey me, a sword shall devour you. For the mouth of the Lord has spoken these things.” FABRIC.]

And again: “Come to me, all you who are burdened, and I will relieve you” (Matt. 11:28).

> [Note: [Col. 1237C] “has spoken this. And the Lord: Come…”]

> [Note: Greek text: “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest.” Philastrius omitted *kopiōntes* (“those who labor”) for brevity. FABRIC.]

## CXIII. HERESY CONCERNING THE SEVEN PLANETS

> [Note: [Col. 1237C] “Another heresy…”]

> [Note: It must also be regarded as a heresy. One would scarcely find anyone who believed that those names were assigned to the days by God; but using those names is as indifferent and as remote from heresy as using the names of the stars discussed in ch. 103. Justin Martyr certainly did not hesitate to call it “the day of the Sun” in *Apology* 2, p. 99. Yet Irenaeus, V.23, preferred to call Venus’s day *tēn pro tēs Kronikēs*, “the day before Saturn’s,” that is, the day before the Sabbath. FABRIC.]

It must also be regarded as a heresy to say that the names of the days—Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn—were so assigned by God from the beginning of the world, rather than named by the empty presumption of human beings. For from the first beginning down to the Greek kings and that utterly deceitful Hermes, who dared falsely to assign these most vain and frivolous names, if you investigate, you will find that much time elapsed, and that the pagans—that is, the Greeks—thus assigned these names.

> [Note: To the Greek kings. As above, in ch. 111, he used “pagans” for Greeks; so here he uses “Greeks” for pagans or gentiles. Thus below in this chapter: “and so the pagans, that is Greeks, assigned these names.” Yet the naming of days after the seven planets is owed not to Greeks but to Egyptians, as the highly authoritative witnesses Herodotus, book II, ch. 82, and Dio Cassius, book XXXVI, p. 37, attest; Philastrius himself confirms this when, just as in ch. 103, he reproaches Hermes the Egyptian by name. FABRIC.]

Indeed, they even said that human generation depends upon the seven stars, as that same madman himself determined.

> [Note: Since even according to the seven stars. Earlier editions incorrectly read: “since these names also [were assigned] according to the seven stars.” Human generation is made dependent upon the seven planets also in writings circulating under the name of Hermes Trismegistus, as in *Poimandres*, ch. 9, and *Minerva Mundi*, p. 29; not to mention matters from the *Panaretus* of Trismegistus in Paulus Alexandrinus, K.3, and in the astrological *Balance of Hermes*, the two books on revolutions of nativities, the aphorisms, and the iatromathematical writings. FABRIC.]

For the numbering of days—first, second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh—was named by God (Gen. 1); it was not proclaimed or handed down in the beginning in this shameful vanity of naming.

## CXIV

> [Note: Here too the deficiency of the printed copies is supplied from the cited manuscript codex of Saint-Germain.]

There is a heresy which, when it reads in Genesis the word spoken by the Lord concerning Adam, “Behold, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil. And now, lest he stretch out his hand, touch, and taste of the tree of life, and live forever” (Gen. 3:22), says that the Lord expelled him from paradise because of envy. First, they hold that one God made the soul and another the flesh, as Manichaeans, Gnostics, Nicolaitans, and other lost people suppose, saying that one God is good while the other, they say, is evil. They think that this evil God said that they should be expelled from paradise, failing to attend to the fact that the one and same God, the Father, through the Son made Adam our father and gave him a commandment: if he kept it, he would remain immortal; if he transgressed the commandment, he would be expelled from paradise, as it is written. And because he suffered this through the enemy’s persuasion, when they do not attend to Christ’s mercy, they descend into the abyss of everlasting death.

Therefore God did not enviously drive our father from paradise so that he might not remain there or taste from the tree of life; rather, he was looking to his welfare. He did not spare one who had sinned in a small matter, lest, by sparing him, he should find him guilty later in life of other and greater offences, and then condemn him more severely when made liable by a criminal judgment.

> [Note: Crime. Perhaps: “crimes.” FABRIC.]

For between the human being and the devil stood Christ, at once hearer and judge, most just and good in all things. Likewise, he did not spare the human being who had sinned in a small matter, while nonetheless giving him a sentence suited to the sin he had committed; and he likewise left the devil room for repentance. But because the devil did not understand that he should repent of so great an evil suggestion, a greater judgment was being kept for him afterward. The human being, when expelled from paradise, was found more inclined to repentance; but the devil, shown harder toward repentance, awaits a greater severity of future judgment from Christ the Lord, as it is said: “He was unwilling to understand so as to do good” (Ps. 35:4). And again: “But he did not hate wickedness” (ibid., 5).

> [Note: Servitude. Perhaps: “severity.” FABRIC.]

Therefore Adam, having sinned in a small matter by being persuaded by the devil to eat, immediately repented and deserved to obtain forgiveness for his offence, and to return to paradise, into Christ’s presence, also through the procreation of children. But the devil, not repenting, and his followers are reserved for a greater judgment, as the Lord said: “Depart from me into the eternal fire which my Father prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41).

## CXV. HERESY CONCERNING INFINITE WORLDS

> [Note: This heresy is lacking in the Saint-Germain codex.]

Another heresy says that worlds are infinite and innumerable, according to the empty opinion of certain philosophers, whereas Scripture has said and taught that there is one world.

> [Note: According to certain philosophers. Accordingly, in Augustine’s index, ch. 77, one should read “philosophers” instead of “Ophites,” or, as some have it, “Orphics”; though it was also an Orphic doctrine that the moon and other stars are inhabited, on which I spoke in *Bibliotheca Graeca*, book I, ch. 20, §8 ff. In the author of the *Praedestinatus*, ch. 77, this heresy is called that of the Ametritae. Jerome, *Against Rufinus* I, writes that Origen introduced innumerable worlds. See Christian Gottlieb Jöcher, inaugural program *On the Heresy of the Ophites, or Orphics*, Leipzig, 1730, quarto. FABRIC.]

> [Note: Scripture says there is one world. It makes mention of one heaven and one earth in Genesis 1:1; nevertheless, no conclusion can thereby be drawn that the stars are inhabited by no dwellers. FABRIC.]

They also draw this from the apocrypha of the prophets—that is, from secrets, as the pagans themselves called them—and from Democritus, who asserted that there are many worlds. While proclaiming this as part of his own wisdom, he stirred many souls and unsettled minds into diverse errors.

> [Note: From the apocrypha of the prophets. He means the prophets and theologians of the gentiles, just as Epimenides is called “a prophet of the Cretans” by Paul in Titus 1:12. Proclus, *Commentary on the Timaeus* IV, p. 279, expressly attests that they, as also the Pythagoreans and others, taught a plurality of worlds: “It is evident that it has been rightly said that each of the spheres is a world, and that the theologians too teach these things.” FABRIC.]

> [Note: That Democritus. Democritus in Hippocrates’ *Letter to Damagetus*: “Because worlds are many beyond number, do not in any way niggardly limit nature, which is rich.” Ammianus, XV.1, and Augustine, *Against the Academics* III.10, also mention Democritus’s infinity of worlds, besides other testimonies noted by Andreas Schott, *Nodi Ciceroniani*, book II, ch. 7, and Menage on Diogenes Laertius IX.44. Simon Magus in the Ebionite writer of the Clementines, III.39: “Accordingly Adam, who had come into being according to his likeness, is created blind and handed over without knowledge of good or evil.” Add III.42. FABRIC.]

## CXVI. HERESY CONCERNING THE BLINDNESS OF ADAM AND EVE

> [Note: There are certain heretics. Augustine attributes this opinion to the unlearned multitude, not to heretics; see *City of God* XIV.17 and Leonhard Coqueius’s notes there. FABRIC.]

There are certain heretics who suppose that our father Adam and our mother Eve were blind before they tasted from the tree, and that afterwards their eyes were opened and they then perceived that they were naked. Yet Scripture had previously said (Gen. 3:7) that Eve saw with her eyes the tree and its fruit, that it was good in appearance and pleasant to behold; and, stretching out her hand, she tasted it.

> [Note: [Col. 1239C] “and afterwards opened their eyes.”]

> [Note: [Col. 1239C] “Eve, it says, saw with her eyes.”]

> [Note: She also saw with her eyes. The Hamburg, Basel, and Lyons editions read this way, certainly wrongly: for who saw? But the Corbie codex correctly reads, “Eve saw with her eyes,” as is expressly handed down in Genesis 3:6. At the end of this same chapter, after “the man who had been invited to the wedding,” the words of Matthew 22:12 have fallen out: “Friend, how did you enter here?” They are, however, found in the Corbie manuscript and the Lyons edition. GALEARD.]

It is therefore madness on the part of heretics, and rather the blindness of Jews, to think this, because they do not understand the manner of nakedness. Scripture teaches us that this was a loss of immortality through transgression of the commandment, not bodily nakedness.

> [Note: [Col. 1240C] “that is, thus.”]

This the Apostle teaches us when he says: “And if clothed in Christ, we shall not be found naked” (2 Cor. 5:3). And again: “Put on Christ Jesus” (Rom. 13:14). And the Lord reproves in the Gospel the person who had no wedding garment, though he had been invited to the wedding (Matt. 22:11).

## CXVII

> [Note: This heresy, lacking in the printed editions, has been added from the cited Saint-Germain codex.]

There is a heresy which, when it hears in Genesis that after the transgression the Lord clothed our first parents in tunics of skins, supposes that he made their bodies at that time and thus clothed them. Yet Scripture says that on the seventh day the Lord took earth from clay and formed their bodies, and afterwards made the woman’s flesh from Adam’s rib.

> [Note: To clothe. It seems one should read *vestierit*, “clothed.” FABRIC.]

Therefore here it was not their bodies that he called tunics of skins; rather, he declared that by divine power they had been given wisdom to make bodily garments for themselves, as it is written: “Who gave women wisdom to weave tunics?” But if anyone wishes to take it that the Lord made tunics for them, the Almighty made from nothing that which is written: “He calls into existence things which are not as though they were” (Rom. 4:17). Therefore, whether he made tunics by their own wisdom, as the Prophet says, this is reasonable; or whether God granted them this by his own power, it is not unacceptable. For in the Temple women and virgins worked purple, fine linen, flax, and other articles for the honor of the Temple, as well as coverings and diverse, varied ornaments of the Temple.

> [Note: “that covering.” Perhaps: “covering.” FABRIC.]

## CXVIII. HERESY TRANSFERRING THE GUILT OF CHILDREN ONTO PARENTS

There is a heresy which, when it hears in Exodus that an angel met Moses at the lodging place where he had stopped and wished to kill him, not his son who had not yet been circumcised, finds in this no small cause for offence.

> [Note: In Exodus. Exodus 4:24; in addition to the commentators on this passage, compare Johann Frischmuth’s *Diatribe* and the author of *Vesperae Gorinchemenses*, p. 5 ff. FABRIC.]

But if anyone wishes to understand it this way—that the angel threatened them because, after the appointed days had passed, namely eight, on which the male child ought to have been circumcised, they had not done it and thus despised God’s commandment—the fault in those of such a small age belongs not to the children but to their parents, as it is written.

> [Note: [Col. 1241B] “eight, on the eighth of which he ought…”]

> [Note: [Col. 1241B] “in equal age.”]

> [Note: Their parents, as it is written. That is, the person who had not circumcised his son on the eighth day was to be cut off, Genesis 17:14. FABRIC.]

Therefore, when she understood that the fault was that of the parents, not of the infant, the mother of the boy immediately, it says, took a stone and circumcised the child; and at the sight of the blood the angel at once withdrew from him (Exod. 4:25–26), completely removing the penalty of death which he had threatened to inflict upon him.

> [Note: Having taken a stone, she circumcised the child. Thus the LXX, *psēphon*, “stone,” which Philastrius follows in this word, although he expresses the rest differently. Pagnini’s Hebrew version has “rock”; the Vulgate, “a very sharp stone.” Augustine, *Against Pelagius on Original Sin* II.30, mentions a stone knife used for circumcision—not because it was necessary to use a stone knife, but because such a knife first came to the hurried mother’s hand, since these things occurred near Petra in Arabia, where stone is more plentiful and more commonly used than iron, as Lapide correctly notes on Exodus 4:25. For more on stone knives used in sacred and secular contexts, see Stephanus Morinus, *Exercitationes on Languages*, part II, ch. 9, p. 288 ff.; see also Münster and Drusius in the *Critici Sacri* on Joshua 5:2. GALEARD.]

> [Note: His mother. Zipporah, Moses’ wife. FABRIC.]

> [Note: LXX: “and he departed from him.” FABRIC.]

For Moses is not known to have been circumcised at that time, as some suppose; rather, his son was circumcised. For what was commanded under the Patriarchs and the Law was fulfilled slowly, not promptly, by the people or by the parents of some persons, as it is written (Josh. 5:5, 7).

> [Note: As some suppose. This is also the opinion of the learned Hermann von der Hardt; see, if you please, his book *On the Circumcision of the Jews*, ch. 4. FABRIC.]

## CXIX. HERESY CONCERNING THE BOOK OF DEUTERONOMY

There are certain heretics who are disturbed about Deuteronomy, in which Moses, when he was about to depart from the body, composed this book by repeating the four books, establishing in it, as it were, the foundations of the earlier Law, and more fully testifying to Christ’s bodily presence. Those who think otherwise are led into no small error.

> [Note: Heretics concerning Deuteronomy. It is obscure what Philastrius intends by this heresy, unless perhaps that those erred who thought that Deuteronomy does not repeat matters written in the preceding four books, but relates what befell Moses after them. FABRIC.—Heretics concerning Deuteronomy. Fabricius considers it obscure what Philastrius means by this heresy, although he clearly enough indicates that these anonymous heretics rejected Deuteronomy because Moses gives fuller testimony in it to Christ’s bodily presence. For he immediately says that the same things written in Exodus are contained in the book of Deuteronomy itself; he then says that this alone seems to have been said more fully by Moses because he added, “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among our brothers”; and finally he concludes that what belonged to Law and Grace concerning Christ the Lord should be made manifest and committed in the book itself—namely, Deuteronomy—as a testimony to all. This perhaps refers to the Samaritans, whom he said above in ch. 7 accept only four books of Moses; they too did not expect Christ the Lord as the Son of God, as Philastrius testifies there: “not believing that Christ the Lord, the Son of God, was announced beforehand in the Law and the Prophets.” GALEARD.]

> [Note: When he was leaving the body. Not long before his death. FABRIC.]

> [Note: Christ’s bodily presence. By the words from Deuteronomy 18 cited immediately below. FABRIC.]

For the things written in the Law—that is, in Exodus—are contained also in this book itself; but this alone seems to have been said more fully by him, because he added: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among our brothers, like me; you shall hear him” (Deut. 18:15, 18). But whoever does not hear him shall be uprooted utterly (ibid., 19).

> [Note: [Col. 1242B] “For in … Exodus, things written before…”]

> [Note: In the book itself. Deuteronomy. FABRIC.]

For some think this was said by him concerning Deuteronomy, because in it too (Deut. 5:5) he received on the mountain stone tablets written anew, whereas in Exodus he is known to have received them twice (Exod. 24:12) and to have ascended the mountain.

> [Note: [Col. 1242B] “they think Deuteronomy…”]

Therefore it is reasonable that what belonged to Law and Grace concerning Christ the Lord should be made manifest: that what is celebrated in the Law through a shadow should, in Christ’s bodily presence, be announced to believers through grace poured out from heaven, and be written in that book itself and delivered to all as a testimony.

> [Note: It is therefore reasonable. Thus ch. 98: “it is therefore of no rational account.” FABRIC.]

> [Note: Of Law and Grace. Above, ch. 109. FABRIC.]

> [Note: That what is celebrated in the Law through a shadow. This difficult and obstructed passage seems, through scribal fault, to require restoration as follows. First, for *celebratur* (“is celebrated”), which occurs in the Hamburg edition, one should read *celebrabatur* (“was celebrated”), as the Corbie codex and also the Basel and Lyons editions have. Then, for *in Christo et ipsumque*, which the three editions present, one should read from the manuscript, *in Christo et ipsoque*, yielding: “In Christ’s bodily presence, grace poured out from heaven should be announced to believers, and it should be written in the book itself and delivered to all as a testimony.” GALEARD.]

## CXX. CONCERNING THOSE WHO DESPISE LAWFUL MARRIAGE

> [Note: Certain are heretics. Valentinians and others, whom Clement of Alexandria, *Stromateis* III, p. 469, and Chrysostom, on Psalm 51.5, censure: “Therefore he does not accuse marriage, as some foolishly suppose … but brings forward the lawlessness ventured by the ancestors from the beginning, and declares that it became the source of these streams.” Compare John Potter on Clement of Alexandria, p. 557. FABRIC.]

There are certain heretics who, hearing David say in the fiftieth Psalm, “I was conceived in iniquity, and my mother bore me in sin,” suppose that the prophet said that the lawful right of marriage is iniquity and sin. Yet it was said beforehand in Genesis: “Be born, multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. 1:28). And: “Marriages are honorable” (Heb. 13:4).

> [Note: Greek text: “Marriage is honorable in all things.” FABRIC.]

For if anyone thought thus, then so many and such great righteous persons were conceived in iniquity, even though they were sanctified in the womb: the Patriarchs (Gen. 25:23), the Prophets (Jer. 1:5), the Judges (Judg. 13:5, 7; 16:17), Jeremiah (as above), and the most blessed John the Baptist (Luke 1:15), as it is written.

> [Note: [Col. 1243C] “were conceived, though in…”]

But they do not know that David the prophet spoke in another sense: not of natural generation, but of the transgression of our father Adam and Eve, who, after transgressing the commandment and being expelled from paradise, begot children. Thus he teaches that she, as it were the mother of all, conceived them after the iniquity of the transgression of the commandment and gave birth to them in that manner.

For how could David have said of himself that he was conceived in iniquity and born in sin, when he was born by lawful right and, chosen by God (1 Sam. 16:12; 1 Chron. 29:4), was sought for such great royal glory, as is written concerning him? Therefore he was not here teaching that he was born in iniquity or sin; rather, he wished to show that our parents Adam and Eve, after they had first committed sin—that is, transgression of the commandment—then begot children, and that from them all of us likewise have been born.

> [Note: [Col. 1243C] “conceived in iniquity or in…”]

> [Note: Our parents Adam and Eve. This testimony from Philastrius should be added to other testimonies of the ancients concerning original sin in Vossius, *Historia Pelagiana*, p. 145. FABRIC.]

Therefore, after the transgression, it says: “In pain you shall bear children” (Gen. 3:16).

> [Note: LXX: “In pains you shall bear children.” FABRIC.]

For we have from those first parents a common iniquity of the flesh arising from their transgression, a general inheritance descending from the first inheritance upon all, as the Apostle said: “Just as through one human being death entered into all human beings” (Rom. 5:12).

> [Note: Greek text: “Just as through one human being sin entered into the world, and death through sin, and thus death passed into all human beings.” Philastrius, in his customary manner, cited these words in abbreviated form. FABRIC.]

For this law of marriage, promulgated by God, is praised daily and customarily blessed. For David showed what was at first sorrow and announced what Christ’s heavenly grace was to bring as great joy to believers, saying: “Unless anyone is reborn of water and Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:5). Therefore, in that psalm, foreknowing the coming joy, he bore witness, saying: “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop and I shall be cleansed; you shall wash me and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Ps. 50:8), so that we too who believe may rejoice together with him in saving baptism.

> [Note: Marriage is customarily blessed. Among Jews and Christians there has always prevailed the custom of solemnly inaugurating marriage by *hierologia*, or priestly blessing. On this see John Selden, *Uxor Hebraica*, book II, chs. 28–29; Jacob Gretser, *On Blessings*, book II, ch. 43; and the author of the French dissertation, *Dissertation historique sur l’usage de la bénédiction nuptiale* (*Journal des Savants*, 1703, pp. 23–72). I pass over other writers on this subject whom I cited in *Bibliographia antiquaria*, ch. 20, §3. Edmund Martène collected ancient formulas for blessing married couples at the end of part two of book I of *De Antiquis Ecclesiae Ritibus*. FABRIC.]

> [Note: He showed. David, namely, in the words cited above from Psalm 50:6. FABRIC.]

> [Note: [Col. 1244C] “heavenly grace.”]

> [Note: Greek text: “He is not able to enter.” FABRIC.]

> [Note: You shall sprinkle me with hyssop. On the cleansing use of hyssop, see Cotelerius on the Epistle of Barnabas, ch. 8, p. 26, and D. Theodorus Dassovius’s dissertation *On the Purification of the Hebrews*, published at Wittenberg in 1692. FABRIC.]

## CXXI. HERESY CONCERNING THE DIVISION OF THE WORLD
There are certain heretics who hold erroneous views concerning the division of the earth and the apportionment of its habitation. They argue that the Greeks, Egyptians, or Persians began to map the whole world, and that blessed Noah did not, after the Flood, divide, assign, delimit, and orderly distribute it among his three sons.

[Note: [Col. 1244D] Not blessed Noah. If we listen to George Syncellus, p. 45, Noah, instructed by a divine oracle, divided the inhabited world among his sons, κατὰ τὸν θεῖον χρησμὸν, “according to the divine oracle,” in the 934th year of his life, the 2576th year of the world. But Jacob Perizonius, p. 288 of *Origines Babylonicae*, considers all this invented from a misunderstanding of the words of Genesis 11:4, πρὸ τοῦ διασπαρῆναι, “before they were scattered.” And the great Bochart, *Phaleg*, book I, final chapter, says: “I do not sufficiently understand how Noah could have divided the world among his sons when by far the greater part of it was not yet known.” You will say that Noah was a prophet and, by God’s revelation, assigned to his sons the individual parts of the world known to himself. But when Scripture is silent, it is not for us to conjecture these things. Yet Philastrius clung to this opinion so obstinately that he counts as heretics those who doubt it. FABRIC.]

From this, later historians, following as it were certain paths,

[Note: [Col. 1244D] Paths—that is, from a single path of falsehood once opened. FABRIC.]

have fabricated different falsehoods. Noah therefore divided and handed over the whole world to his three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth.

[Note: [Col. 1244D] Shem indeed received the eastern regions of India. Sulpicius Severus, book I, chapter 6: “But the world was so divided among Noah’s sons that Shem was contained within the East, Japheth in the West, and Ham in the middle regions.” Compare, besides Syncellus, Epiphanius, Heresy LXVI, 83; Eutychius, *Annals*, vol. II, p. 52 ff.; the *Paschal Chronicle*, p. 26; Cedrenus, p. 13; Freculph, *Chronicle*, book I, chapter 27. To these more recent writers should be added, besides Bochart in the *Phaleg* and learned interpreters on Genesis 10, Allatius on Eustathius’ *Hexaemeron*, p. 237 ff.; Edward Bernard on Flavius Josephus, *Antiquities*, book I, chapter 6; and Francesco Bianchini, *Historia veterum monumentis illustrata*, chapter 18, p. 203 ff. Following Lactantius, book I, chapter 11, Bianchini thinks that the Greeks hence invented the division among Saturn’s sons: Jupiter, to whom the East fell; Pluto, to whom part of the West fell; and Neptune, to whom the sea-coasts with the islands fell. The author of the Clementine *Recognitions*, book I, chapter 30, disagrees with Philastrius. There he says that the eldest of Noah’s children, Shem, received the region in the middle of the earth, in which Judaea is situated; that the youngest, Japheth, received the eastern quarter; and that Ham received the West. FABRIC.]

To Shem, indeed, he assigned the eastern regions of India and Persia, extending to a portion of the South; he confirmed by fixed decree that his firstborn should possess the boundaries from the West and North as far as Mount Lebanon. To Ham also, his second son, he apportioned all the Syrians,

[Note: [Col. 1245B] And the dioceses. FABRIC.]

the dioceses of Egypt, Africa, the vast expanse of the Ethiopians stretching almost to the borders of Ocean, and the Spains; and by the divine Spirit he foretold that this territory should be possessed and inhabited.

[Note: [Col. 1245B] Foretold. FABRIC.]

In the middle region, however, he allowed him boundaries extending as far as Cappadocia, that is, Mount Taurus. But to the third, Japheth, he assigned by divine command, for those entering Cappadocia and departing from Cilicia, the cold regions—those of Armenia,

[Note: [Col. 1245B] Those of Armenia, the Bosporus, Pontus, and Thrace. FABRIC.]

the Bosporus, Pontus,

[Note: [Col. 1245C] Bosporus, Pontus. An error has crept into the Hamburg edition, in which *Bosphorici* occurs in place of *Bosphori*, as also in the Lyons edition; but in the Corbie manuscript and the Basel edition, *Bosphori* is correctly read. Thus on the following page the Hamburg and Lyons editions read, not very well, “Shem, when [with] the younger”; and the Basel edition agrees. But the Corbie codex better reads, “Shem, to whom with the younger.” GALEARD.]

Thrace, the Pannonias, Illyricum, Italy, and all the western regions.

And from the first, indeed,

[Note: [Col. 1245D] Twenty-five generations. Genesis 10:22 ff. names twenty-seven descendants of Shem: (1) Elam, (2) Asshur, (3) Arpachshad, (4) Lud, (5) Aram, (6) Cainan, (7) Uz, (8) Hul, (9) Gether, (10) Meshech, (11) Salah, (12) Eber, (13) Peleg, (14) Joktan, (15) Almodad, (16) Sheleph, (17) Hazarmaveth, (18) Jerah, (19) Hadoram, (20) Uzal, (21) Diklah, (22) Obal, (23) Abimael, (24) Sheba, (25) Ophir, (26) Havilah, (27) Jobab. FABRIC.]

he counts twenty-five generations descended. From the second—

[Note: [Col. 1245D] From the second, thirty-five. Genesis 10:6 ff. counts thirty descendants of Ham: (1) Cush, (2) Mizraim, (3) Put, (4) Canaan, (5) Sheba, son of Cush, (6) Havilah, (7) Sabtah, (8) Raamah, (9) Sabteca, (10) Sheba, son of Raamah, (11) Dedan, (12) Nimrod, (13) Ludim, [Col. 1246B] (14) Naphtuhim, (15) Anamim, (16) Lehabim, (17) Pathrusim, (18) Casluhim, (19) Philistim, (20) Caphtorim, (21) Sidon, (22) Hethite, (23) Jebusite, (24) Amorite, (25) Girgashite, (26) Hivite, (27) Arkite, (27) Sinite, (28) Arvadite, [Col. 1246C] (29) Zemarite, (30) Hamathite. FABRIC.]

thirty-five, that is, from Ham. But of Japheth, whose line was then reckoned smaller—that is,

[Note: [Col. 1246C] Only fifteen. Genesis 10:2 gives Japheth fifteen descendants: (1) Gomer, (2) Magog, (3) Madai, (4) Javan, (5) Elishah, son of Japheth, (6) Tubal, (7) Meshech, (8) Tiras, (9) Ashkenaz, (10) Riphath, (11) Togarmah, (12) Elishah, son of Javan, (13) Tarshish, (14) Kittim, (15) Rodanim. FABRIC.]

only fifteen—an increase was promised to him by blessed Noah, to come in the future:

[Note: [Col. 1246B] And greater. FABRIC.]

“May the Lord enlarge Japheth; may he dwell in the tents of

[Note: [Col. 1246C] Enlarge. This alludes to the name Japheth, which derives its meaning from the verb “to enlarge.” FABRIC.]

Shem” (Gen. 9:27).

[Note: [Col. 1246B] Shem, to whom with the younger. FABRIC.]

With the younger son a smaller number of generations was found to have been granted at that time; but as he increased, a larger number was afterward destined to be extended to him than to his two brothers, so that he might hold the middle and outer regions—that is, the dominions of the Canaanites, Egyptians, Africans, and Persians. From him afterward arose the Romans, conquerors of the world and rulers of all nations. Hence we recognize that Romans, Latins, and Italians trace their descent from Japheth, and that they hold the world under their dominion

[Note: [Col. 1246C] Daily—namely, at the time when Philastrius was writing this. FABRIC.]

daily, and have often held it before.

[Note: [Col. 1246B] But if anything is considered ancient by the falsehood of the Greeks . . . to be before. FABRIC.]

But whatever is deemed ancient by Greek falsehood is shown, by the testimony of their own authors, to be in every respect recent—

[Note: [Col. 1246C] Temporal: of recent and not very remote antiquity. Thus above, chapters 110 and 112, and immediately in this same chapter: “when they wish to veil and conceal their own recentness”; and in the next chapter, “what is most vainly recent among the pagans.” FABRIC.]

Solon himself testifying to the Athenians that

[Note: [Col. 1246D] Solon. In Plato, *Timaeus*, p. 474: “O Solon, Solon, you Greeks are always children; no Greek is an old man. . . . You are all young in soul; for you possess in it no ancient belief derived from old report, nor any learning made grey by time.” Justin Martyr, *Exhortation to the Greeks*, p. 13; Cyril, *Against Julian*, I, p. 15; Chalcidius, p. 12; and very many others cite the same passage. FABRIC.]

he heard this from an Egyptian priest:

[Note: [Col. 1246D] He heard it from an Egyptian priest. Proclus, *Commentary on the Timaeus*, p. 31—drawing, I suspect, on Manetho—reports the names of Egyptian priests with whom Solon associated in various provinces of Egypt, and conjectures that the man who spoke these words to him was a Saitic priest named Pateneit: “Solon encountered at Saïs a priest named Pateneit, at Heliopolis Ochlapi, and at Sebennytus Ethimon, as Egyptian histories report. And perhaps this is the Saitic priest who spoke the following words to him.” FABRIC.]

“Solon, Solon, you Greeks are always young and children. No Greek will ever be old or ancient; nor do you possess any ancient teaching or knowledge. Rather, you possess what you have seized and appropriated from others, and you present it altered by various falsehoods, and thus instruct humankind.” Plato, indeed, says this in the *Timaeus*.

For after the confusion of languages, different names then began to arise. Taking these up, Greek historians composed two or three different records, as though they were monuments; and when they wish to veil and hide their own recentness,

[Note: [Col. 1247B] Recentness: the short span during which they have existed. FABRIC.]

they have been judged and proved by their own witnesses to be most deceitful. For when fifty of them—the Greeks, Egyptians, Chaldaeans, and Syrians—agree concerning our antiquity, but two or three disagree, it is more just to rest with the many historians who agree in one judgment than with two or three who disagree, because the many have spoken more truly than the two.

## CXXII. HERESY CONCERNING THE FLOOD

[Note: [Col. 1247B] Another heresy . . . to have been more ancient. FABRIC.]

There is also a heresy which says that the flood under Deucalion and Pyrrha was earlier than that which occurred under Noah.

[Note: [Col. 1247B] Under Deucalion and Pyrrha. This matter has been endlessly rehearsed in the writings of poets and other authors. I do not wish to add a word after what learned men have written on Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, I: Francesco Bianchini of Verona, in his most learned Italian work, published at Rome in 1699, quarto, *De Historia Veterum monumentis probata*, chapter 17, p. 187 ff.; Octavius Falconerius, *On the Apamean Coin Exhibiting a Type of Deucalion’s Flood*, Rome, 1667, and in volume X of Gronovius’ *Thesaurus antiquitatum Graecarum*; likewise George Schubart, *Parergetic Explanation of Ovid’s Metamorphosis concerning Deucalion’s Flood*, found in the same volume X and separately published at Jena in 1684, quarto. FABRIC.]

The pagans, wickedly transferring the event and changing its names, claim that the ark after the Flood was, as it were, in Greece,

[Note: [Col. 1247C] The ark, as it were, in Greece—resting on Mount Parnassus. See Plutarch, *On the Intelligence of Animals*, p. 968; Lucian, *On the Syrian Goddess*, vol. II, p. 661. FABRIC.]

and what is most vainly recent among pagans

[Note: [Col. 1247C] What is recent: what happened not so many centuries previously, around 1514 years before Christ’s birth, more than eight hundred years after the Flood described by Moses. See Scaliger on Eusebius, number 490. FABRIC.]

is proclaimed by them, with much falsehood, as though it were ancient. And what occurred in a small place in Thessaly is represented by thieving pagans as having occurred everywhere—that is,

[Note: [Col. 1247B] In the whole world. FABRIC.]

in the world. What happened later in Thessaly,

[Note: [Col. 1247D] What occurred later in Thessaly. Earlier editions read less well, “what occurs.” FABRIC.]

in a place at times limited in extent,

[Note: [Col. 1247D] In a place at times small. He uses *interdum* in the sense of “meanwhile,” as Seneca, *Epistles*, 95: “those who undertake the guardianship of humankind, meanwhile attentive to individuals.” If the manuscripts supported it, I would read “between Oeta and Pindus” instead of *interdum*. FABRIC.]

that Flood, however, occurred throughout the whole world,

[Note: [Col. 1247D] In the whole age: throughout the whole world. Thus below, in the following chapter, “the four corners of the age,” that is, of the world. FABRIC.]

as the writing of the Gentiles also testifies.

[Note: [Col. 1247D] As their Scripture too. When pagan poets describe Deucalion’s flood, they say that it prevailed throughout the whole world: “All was sea; even shores were lacking to the sea.” FABRIC.]

## CXXIII. HERESY CONCERNING THE SIGNS OF THE ZODIAC AND HUMAN BIRTH

Another heresy says that human beings are born according to the twelve

[Note: [Col. 1247D] That people are born according to the twelve signs of the Zodiac: long-lived or short-lived, fortunate or unfortunate, according as the horoscope of the natal chart fell upon this or that degree of the Zodiac. Especially in Philastrius’ time, the Priscillianists believed human beings to be bound by the powers of the stars, as is clear from Leo the Great, Epistle 15 (93), to Turibius. FABRIC.—According to the twelve Zodiacs. [Col. 1248C] In Sichard’s Basel edition one reads *secundum XII Zodia*, “according to twelve Zodiacs,” a reading also found in the Corbie manuscript, as likewise below: “Therefore they are ignorant that these twelve Zodiacs.” Here Fabricius retained the Basel reading, although earlier he altered the phrase by substituting “according to the twelve signs of the Zodiac,” as the Lyons edition also, less correctly, has it. Philastrius used the Greek word ζῴδιον, “celestial sign,” just as above, chapter 109, he derives the name *idol* from a Greek formation, as though it were εἴδους δόλος, “a falsification of form”; and as in chapters 85 and 103 he uses *biothanatos* and *pogonias*. Indeed, in chapter 129 he has *ana septuaginta duo*, “seventy-two each,” which Fabricius says in the same place might perhaps seem incredible in a Latin writer. GALEARD.]

signs of the Zodiac, as those most foolish astrologers,

[Note: [Col. 1248C] Those most foolish mathematicians: genethlialogical astrologers. See, if you please, what I noted on Sextus Empiricus, p. 214. FABRIC.]

the defenders of all error and wickedness, say. Hearing these things, very many unlearned people at times set aside God’s Law

[Note: [Col. 1248C] God’s Law set aside—the Law which prohibits divinations of this kind: Leviticus 20:6, 27; Deuteronomy 18:10; Isaiah 8:19. FABRIC.]

and do not hesitate to enslave themselves to the vanities of astrologers. Thus the apostolic saying is fulfilled: “They worshipped and served the creature rather than the Creator” (Rom. 1:25). And again: “See that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit according to the

[Note: [Col. 1248D] Elements of the world: the stars. See above, chapters 61 and 109. FABRIC.]

elements of the world, and not according to Christ; for in him all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. 2:8).

Therefore they do not understand that these twelve zodiacs of which they speak are diverse climatic zones and diverse regions of the inhabited world, arranged by God for habitation, and that distinct temperaments of places and times were ordained: hot, cold, dry, and moist,

[Note: [Col. 1248B] Four. FABRIC.]

as the four corners

[Note: [Col. 1248D] The four corners of the age: the four cardinal points of the world, from which comes the powerful fourfold company of the winds. FABRIC.—“Moist as the four corners of the age.” The *ut* (“as”) was gratuitously added here by unlearned copyists, although both the editions and the Corbie manuscript retain it. The same, in my judgment, is true of the particle *in* occurring a little later, where the reading is *respirantes in invicem*; better is *respirantes invicem*, “breathing upon one another.” Thus in the preceding chapter 122, where Fabricius emended, “what occurred later in Thessaly in a place at times limited in extent,” I do not know whether the received reading, to which the Corbie manuscript also agrees, should rather be retained: “what occurs later in Thessaly in a place at times limited in extent.” For perhaps Philastrius used Thessaly for all Greece, in order to unite the Thessalian flood under Deucalion and Pyrrha with the Boeotian flood of Ogyges; and for that reason he said “what occurs later, at times, in a small place,” as though such a flood in Thessaly—that is, in Greece—were customary after a brief intervening period of years. For Augustine, *City of God*, XVIII.8, as noted there by Ludovicus Vives, reckons about one hundred and seventy years between the flood, or cleansing, under Ogyges and that under Deucalion. In the same chapter 122, where the Hamburg edition reads “having happened everywhere, that is, in the world,” the Basel edition reads somewhat better “in the whole world,” and the Corbie manuscript reads likewise. What Philastrius says shortly afterward, “in the whole age,” must mean “in the whole world”; just as in the following chapter “the four corners of the age” means “the four corners of the world,” as Fabricius also observed. GALEARD.]

of the world, from which, as though full fountains overflowing with their proper quality, they pour forth by their breath, mutually breathing upon one another by their great inherent power; and when their mixture is again diffused everywhere, a pleasant and healthful temperature is thereby supplied to all inhabitants. Thus it is known that by divine power a sweet and prosperous life has been granted and bestowed upon mortals by the Lord.

## CXXIV. HERESY CONCERNING THE SOULS OF EVILDOERS

[Note: [Col. 1249B] Another heresy . . . of usurers. FABRIC.]

Nor is there lacking a heresy which says that the souls of usurers,

[Note: [Col. 1249C] Usurers: those who oppress the poor with unjust interest. Firmicus, *Mathesis*, III.8, associates usurers and the deceitful. Cato, *On Agriculture*, preface: “Our forefathers held and established in their laws that a thief should be condemned in double damages, but a usurer in fourfold.” FABRIC.]

evildoers, murderers, and other such persons pass into demons,

[Note: [Col. 1249C] Pass into demons. In the index to Augustine, chapter 78, this heresy is called that of the Tertullians. In Isidore, Honorius, Rabanus, and Gratian, the same teaching is attributed to the Tertullianists. Yet in the surviving writings of Tertullian himself it is certainly nowhere defended. See Jacobus Pamel, *Tertullianic Paradox* 11. The author of the *Praedestinatus*, chapter 78, not very aptly calls those who support this heresy Peripneumones. John Baptist Crispus shows, *On Philosophers to Be Read with Caution*, p. 464 ff., that it is wrongly charged against Origen. FABRIC.]

and cattle, beasts, and serpents. They do not understand that, when the human soul has departed from the world, whether good or evil—that is,

[Col. 1249B]

pious or impious—it is led by an angel

[Note: [Col. 1249D] By an angel. See commentators on Luke 16:22 and St Macarius, Homily 22. You will also learn that this was the opinion of the Jews from the Samaritan version of Genesis 5:24 and the Targum on Song of Songs 4:12. Compare Jacob Vindet, *On the State of the Departed*, pp. 46 and 70. FABRIC.]

to its appointed place, so that in the future it may receive what is decreed according to what it has done in this world. But if anyone thinks this happens so, he seems to have more fellowship with paganism and the vanity of philosophers

[Note: [Col. 1249D] Paganism and the vanity of philosophers—especially those from the school of Pythagoras or Plato who maintained the doctrine of metempsychosis, that is, the migration of souls into other bodies, not merely human bodies but also those of other animals. Zacharias, bishop of Mytilene, notes in his book *Against the Eternity of the World*, p. 184, that this doctrine was derived from the Egyptians. FABRIC.—(An elegant Italian translation of this book from the Greek was published at Padua in 1735 by the distinguished Giovanni Antonio Vulpius; we rightly congratulate the most eminent Domenico Lazzarini of blessed memory, recently appointed in his place to teach humane letters in the University of Padua. GALEARD.)]

than with Christianity,

[Note: [Col. 1249B] “Seems to seek.” FABRIC.]

since the Apostle says: “We must all be made manifest

[Note: [Col. 1250C] Greek: “For we must all be made manifest before the judgment-seat of Christ, that each may receive the things done through the body, according to what he has done.” Philastrius, for brevity’s sake, omitted here and in chapter 125 the words that follow, “whether good or evil.” Rufinus, *On the Creed*, p. 26: “that each may receive what belongs to his own work, according as he has done, whether good or evil.” FABRIC.]

before the tribunal of Christ, that each may receive the things he has done in this body” (2 Cor. 5:10).

[Note: [Col. 1249B] “And again, ‘You will not abandon my soul in hell.’ ‘Who will confess to you?’ The soul therefore . . .” FABRIC.]

And again: “For who shall confess to you in hell?” (Ps. 6:6). Therefore the nature of the soul is not changed

[Note: [Col. 1250C] Into another nature—that of demons or beasts. For he had said above that some hold that the souls of the wicked pass into demons or beasts. FABRIC.]

into another nature. But when by its will

[Note: [Col. 1250C] By its will: voluntarily, through the misuse of free choice. FABRIC.]

it despises and neglects God’s command, and refuses

[Note: [Col. 1250C] “Refuses,” that is, declines, denies, rejects. Thus Augustine, *Sermons on Various Subjects*, 121.22: “If, then, those who ignored Noah while he was building the ark deserved to perish, what do those deserve who ignore salvation while Christ builds the Church?” FABRIC.]

to adhere to lawful and saving pursuits, it devotes itself to future judgment and punishments. It is recognized as comparable to cattle for no reason other than its morals,

[Note: [Col. 1250B] “Not to other [beings] except cattle, on account of morals.” FABRIC.]

not by nature but by manners, as it is written.

[Note: [Col. 1250D] As it is written: Psalm 32:9; 2 Peter 2:22; and other passages in which wicked people are compared with animals. FABRIC.]

Thus such pagan persons, Jews, and very many others become like beasts in this world, not in the nature of beasts but in their morals.

[Note: [Col. 1250B] And very many others. FABRIC.]

For when the Savior said to the Jews, “You are of your father the devil” (John 8:44),

[Note: [Col. 1250D] Greek: “You are from your father, the devil.” Not because the Devil created them, but because they imitate him, Augustine says on that passage. FABRIC.]

he showed them to be alike, rebuking and judging them, not by nature but by the habits of wickedness and beastly dispositions.

[Note: [Col. 1250B] He showed them similar in dispositions. FABRIC.]

And John said to the Jews: “Offspring of vipers” (Matt. 3:7).

[Note: [Col. 1250D] Greek: γεννήματα ἐχιδνῶν, “offspring of vipers.” Christ himself likewise addresses the Jews thus in Matthew 12:34 and 23:33. FABRIC.]

## CXXV. HERESY CONCERNING CHRIST’S DESCENT TO HELL

[Note: [Col. 1250D] Other heretics. Gregory the Great cites this present passage of Philastrius, book VI, Epistle 15. Danaeus, on Augustine, chapter 79, calls this heresy that of the Liberati; the author of the *Praedestinatus*, chapter 79, that of the Adecerditae. Yet not only Origen and his teacher Clement of Alexandria, but many other doctors of the Church also—namely Augustine, *On Genesis according to the Letter*, XII.33; Epiphanius, Heresy 46; and the Ambrosiaster on Ephesians 4, cited by Cornelius a Lapide on 1 Peter 3:19, “Second Question,” who also cites Philastrius and says that this fable and heresy were refuted by him among others—approved what Philastrius ascribes in this chapter to heretics. See Latinus Latinius on this passage of Philastrius. GALEARD. Allatius, *Dissertation 2 on the Ecclesiastical Books of the Greeks*, p. 244 ff., and Cotelerius on Hermas, *Shepherd*, book III, chapter 16, p. 117, show that this opinion pleased not only Origen and his teacher Clement of Alexandria, but many other teachers of the Church. FABRIC.]

Other heretics say that the Lord descended into hell and there also proclaimed to everyone after death, so that those who confessed there might be saved. But this conflicts with the prophet David, who says: “For who shall confess to you in hell?” (Ps. 6:6), and with the Apostle: “As many as sinned without the Law shall perish without the Law” (Rom. 2:12).

And he also says:

[Note: [Col. 1251C] Greek text: “It shall be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment than for you”; and, verse 24: “But I say to you, it shall be more tolerable for the land of Sodom on the day of judgment than for you.” FABRIC.—“And he also says.” He seems tacitly to raise the objection from Matthew 11:22, “It shall be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment than for you,” to which he immediately replies that this was said συγκριτικῶς, comparatively. The Corbie manuscript reads, “But when he says.” GALEARD.]

“It shall be more tolerable for some than for that city which did not believe the doctrine of the Apostles

[Note: [Col. 1251B] The teaching of the Gospel. FABRIC.]

and the Gospel” (Matt. 12:22). He says, by comparison of many punishments, that they endure lesser torments than those others; nevertheless he does not affirm that they are thereby saved.

For they are mistaken more grievously and depart from truth who think that false poets and vain philosophers, rebellious against God, can be saved.

[Note: [Col. 1251C] Poets and philosophers. Among the pagans especially, Philastrius seems to think it even more incredible that some Pythagoras or Homer should be released from infernal punishments, because, as teachers and champions of pagan errors, they deserve even heavier punishments. FABRIC.]

For those vain poets and philosophers, and no others, have planted in human minds the seeds of pagan impiety and the names of gods and goddesses. Yet the Prophet cries out concerning the future judgment, asking that forgiveness might be granted to him here in repentance: “Forgive me, that I may be refreshed, before I go away and exist no more” (Ps. 38:14).

[Note: [Col. 1251D] Septuagint: Ἄνες μοι ἵνα ἀναψύξω πρὸ τοῦ με ἀπελθεῖν καὶ οὐκέτι μὴ ὑπάρξω, “Release me, that I may be refreshed, before I depart and am no more.” On this passage Origen in the *Catena*: “Unless you forgive me sin and I am refreshed before I depart there, I shall have no opportunity for repentance.” FABRIC.]

If, then, righteous persons who sin scarcely received repentance while still in this life, repenting, as Solomon says, “and if the righteous is scarcely saved, where shall the ungodly and sinner appear?” (Prov. 11:31),

[Note: [Col. 1251D] Septuagint: Εἰ ὁ μὲν δίκαιος μόλις σῴζεται, ὁ ἀσεβὴς καὶ ἁμαρτωλὸς ποῦ φανεῖται, “If the righteous is scarcely saved, where shall the ungodly and sinner appear?” The Apostle Peter cites it in his First Epistle, 4:18. FABRIC.]

then, had they believed that God exists,

[Note: [Col. 1251D] “If they had believed that God exists.” Because idolaters wandered from the knowledge of the true God, they are therefore called atheists and strangers to deity in Ephesians 2:12. In the Stoics’ judgment also, the bad and impious person is an atheist: ὁ δὲ φαῦλος ἄθεος, “the base man is an atheist,” as in Diogenes Laertius VII.119. FABRIC.]

they would not have spread the shameful names of gods and goddesses, and would have obtained pardon in Christ’s descent into hell.

[Note: [Col. 1251D] Would have obtained pardon. Gregory the Great, book VI, Epistle 15, to George, priest, and Theodore, deacon of Constantinople: “I have learned that your affection has said that our almighty Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, descending into hell, saved and freed from deserved punishments all those who confessed him to be God there. On this matter I desire your fraternity to think quite differently. For in descending into hell he delivered by his grace only those who both believed that he would come and kept his commandments in their lives.” FABRIC.]

Since, therefore, the impious are everywhere enemies of God, how shall they be saved by confessing there after death? For the Apostle teaches (Heb. 9:27) that every human being must die, and afterward be judged,

[Note: [Col. 1251B] “And thereafter be judged” (omitting what follows up to the words “when he simply thus confesses diverse things to people” in Heresy 127). Thus in the manuscript [the material stands] in one and the same sequence. FABRIC.]

as it is written (Rom. 14:10), before Christ’s tribunal, and receive according to what he has done in this world (2 Cor. 5:10).

The Savior further declares of them that they have not believed even the Father (John 8:19, 55); thus he declared that they too would be judged (John 12:48). But whoever believed in the Father before Christ came in the flesh has passed from the judgment of the ungodly (John 3:18).

Among sinners and the ungodly, however, there is diversity of penalties and punishments:

[Note: [Col. 1252C] Diversity of penalties and blows. Just as our author taught above, chapter 82, from John 14:2, that different degrees of glory are given in heavenly rewards, Tertullian, *Scorpiace*, chapter 6, says: “How are there many dwelling places with the Father, if not according to diversity of merits—just as one star differs from another in glory (1 Cor. 15:41), if not according to diversity of rays?” Philastrius called this lesser degree “loss of rank” or “detriment” in chapters 82 and 89. Thus, too, on the common doctrine of the ancient Church, he teaches that in hell there are varied and different measures of penalties and punishments, in accordance with Luke 12:47 and Matthew 11:24. See Isidore of Pelusium, *Letters*, IV.42 and V.220–222; Allatius, *On Purgatory*, p. 232 ff.; and Suicer, *Thesaurus*, p. 91. FABRIC.]

there is not complete acquittal for either group, but the justice of judgment and a recompense proportionate to sin—even for those who had been swallowed by water under Noah, as Scripture teaches (1 Pet. 3:20).

## CXXVI. HERESY CONCERNING THE HUMAN SOUL

There is another heresy which, uncertain about the constitution of the soul,

[Note: [Col. 1252D] Concerning the constitution of the soul. I preferred this reading to that in other copies, “concerning the sense of the soul.” For he calls *census* the nature by which a thing is constituted; Tertullian likewise uses this term for the soul. FABRIC.]

supposes that it consists of elements, as do many most foolish philosophers:

[Note: [Col. 1252D] As many philosophers [do]. See Plutarch, *Opinions of the Philosophers*, IV.2 ff.; Galen, *History of Philosophy*, chapter 16; Stobaeus, *Physical Eclogues*, p. 93 ff.; John Philoponus, *Prolegomena*; Aristotle, *On the Soul*, I; Nemesius, chapter 2; Macrobius, *Commentary on the Dream*, I.14; Justin Martyr, *Exhortation to the Greeks*, p. 8; Theodoret, *Therapeutics*, V, p. 72; and the remarks of learned men on Hermias, *Mockery of the Gentile Philosophers*, chapter 2, and Tertullian, *On the Soul*, chapter 5. FABRIC.]

some think it is of fire,

[Note: [Col. 1252D] Now of fire. According to Democritus, Hippocrates, and Hipparchus, the soul is fire and a πυρῶδες σύγκριμα, “a fiery compound.” According to Heraclides of Pontus it is light; according to Heraclitus, a spark of starry essence. FABRIC.]

some of water,

[Note: [Col. 1253C] Of water. This was the opinion of Thales and Hippo, and also of the Egyptians, who thought the soul to be ὕδωρ γονοποιοῦν, “generative water.” See Thomas Gale on Iamblichus, *On the Egyptian Mysteries*, p. 303. FABRIC.]

some of spirit,

[Note: [Col. 1253C] Of spirit. Understand *spiritus* here as καπνός and ἀναθυμίασις, “smoke” and “exhalation,” as the Stoics held the soul to be πνεῦμα νοερὸν καὶ θερμόν, “an intelligent and warm breath.” See commentators on Wisdom 2:3. FABRIC.]

some of matter,

[Note: [Col. 1253C] Of matter. στοιχεῖον ἀπὸ στοιχείων, “element from elements,” from some fifth substance, according to Critolaus and the Peripatetics. FABRIC.]

some of a fountain,

[Note: [Col. 1253C] Now of a fountain. The fountain, or crater, of pre-existent souls in the heavens, from which Plato’s school brings them down. FABRIC.]

some of atoms,

[Note: [Col. 1253D] Now of atoms, as in the Epicurean school. FABRIC.]

and some of what is, as it were, air.

[Note: [Col. 1253D] Now, as it were, air. The soul is ἄνεμος, “wind,” or an αεροειδὲς σῶμα, “air-like body,” according to Anaxagoras and Anaximenes. FABRIC.]

Yet the human soul was made by the Lord, namely from nothing, as it is written: “He made all things from nothing, that they might exist which had not existed” (Wis. 1:14).

[Note: [Col. 1253D] “Who made . . .” See above, chapter 80, where the same passage is cited. FABRIC.]

The soul, therefore, made by God, is called the image of God, after the creation of the angels:

[Note: [Col. 1253D] After the creation of angels—not only later in time, but also inferior in dignity: humanity is lower than the angels. “The creation of angels,” as shortly “the nature of angels,” is used for the angels themselves, who are a creation, that is, a thing created by God. FABRIC.]

for the human being is less than the nature of angels, as it is written: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Ps. 8:5).

[Note: [Col. 1253D] “You made him lower . . .” See commentators on Hebrews 2:9 and the dissertation on that passage by the late Thomas Ittig, found among his miscellaneous works. FABRIC.]

But if he keeps the commands of the Law,

[Note: [Col. 1253D] If he keeps the commandments of the Law. The Savior promises eternal life to those who keep the Law’s commands, Luke 10:28; but for those unable perfectly to fulfil it, yet believing, faith is reckoned as righteousness, Romans 4:5. FABRIC.]

then he will be like the angels.

[Note: [Col. 1254C] Like angels: ἰσάγγελος, “equal to angels,” Luke 20:36. FABRIC.]

If, therefore, angels are servants of God placed under Law,

[Note: [Col. 1254C] Angels, servants of God: λειτουργικὰ πνεύματα, “ministering spirits,” Hebrews 1:14. FABRIC.]

how much more is the human soul under the Law that has been proclaimed? If it keeps what has been commanded it, then it ought to say what the Lord said to the apostles: “Even when you have done all things, say that

[Col. 1253B]

we are unprofitable servants” (Luke 17:10).

[Note: [Col. 1254C] Unprofitable servants. Below, chapter 128, “most wicked servants.” FABRIC.]

## CXXVII. HERESY CONCERNING CHRIST’S NATIVITY
[Note: [Col. 1254C] Another heresy. In the author of the *Praedestinatus* and in Augustine, ch. 80, no name for this heresy occurs; Danaeus therefore did not very aptly call it, in Augustine, that of the Nativity-men, or Initiates. FABRICIUS.] Another heresy says of the Savior that [Note: [Col. 1254C] He was first with the Father. Having no proper *hypostasis*, hidden as it were in the Father’s essence, [Col. 1254D] before He willed that He should proceed from Him *hypostatically*, in order to create the world through Him. This was the opinion of certain ancients, such as Tertullian in ch. 3 against Hermogenes. See George Bull’s *Defence of the Nicene Faith*, section 3, chapters 5 and 10, pp. 337, 398; Petavius, *Dogmatic Theology concerning the Holy Trinity*, book I. FABRICIUS.] he was first with the Father and was thus born; and when it confesses this [Note: [Col. 1254D] Simply. Openly, and without sufficient consideration. FABRICIUS.] simply, it furnishes people with various stumbling-blocks. For to exist before and afterwards to be born are contrary in every way. And although his generation is twofold—one, of divinity, unbounded and eternal; the other, of incorporation through the Virgin, [Note: [Col. 1253C] temporal—and there is no doubt. Yet according to] temporal—yet there is no doubt that, according to divinity, we must understand [Note: [Col. 1254D] That he was never at any time lacking in being with the Father. Thus the Father never did not have the Son, but was always both God and Father, to use Arnobius’s words in his conflict with Serapion, p. 523. FABRICIUS.] that he was never at any time lacking in being with the Father; [Note: [Col. 1254D] Nor was he who was always with the Father from himself. For everything that is in the Father is from itself and subsists unbegotten (*agennēton*); therefore, if the Son before generation had existed without hypostasis in the Father, he too would then have had to be from himself and unbegotten. FABRICIUS.] nor was he who [Col. 1254A] was always with the Father from himself, nor was he known as not begotten from the Father, as certain persons strayingly suppose.

If both points are expressed with a sound interpretation, [Note: [Col. 1253C] of right faith . . . that begotten] what is right and a foundation of faith is shown: namely, that we acknowledge him as truly begotten from the Father, this only Son, yet not in time; but that before all ages and every creature he was truly begotten from the Father, as is fitting, and that we believe it. Nor should we fail to know that he remains with the Father forever and has always remained with him. There is therefore no separation or contradiction between always being and having been, and being begotten. [Note: [Col. 1253C] For “always being” is said on account of eternity] For “always being” is said on account of eternity, lest the Son be thought temporal; but “begotten” is said because the Church, in its proclamation, recognizes [Note: [Col. 1254C] Not from himself] that he was born not from himself but from the Father. [Col. 1254B] Therefore one must not be separated from the other: the eternity of the Son must be joined together with generation, and generation coupled with eternity. Confession concerning the Father must be believed and held in such a manner that for us there is one Father, the begetter, [Note: [Col. 1254C] And one Son] and one Son, the Father’s only Son, rightly recognized as begotten from the Father.

Therefore, always being and being begotten accord with [Note: [Col. 1254C] Pious faith] pious faith: so that his eternal generation may not be temporal, and so that the true proper relation and eternity of the only-begotten Son from the Father and with the Father may not be unknown. But if anyone first confesses that he was unbegotten, and then afterwards begotten [Col. 1255A] from the Father, he does not know what he confesses. For while [Note: [Col. 1255C] He thinks he is escaping one heresy. That of the Arians, who deny the *homoousion* and the eternity of the Son. FABRICIUS.] he thinks that he is escaping one heresy, [Note: [Col. 1255C] He falls into another] he falls into another, worse one, by confessing an unbegotten Son—indeed, rather by denying both Father and Son, preaching two unbegottens, and denying the truth of the one unbegotten Father and the one Son, properly the only-begotten from the Father.

## CXXVIII. HERESY CONCERNING GOD’S HARDENING

There are certain heretics who suppose that the Lord said thus through Moses concerning Pharaoh: “For this purpose [Note: [Col. 1255C] I raised you up. Exodus IX, 16; Romans IX, 17: *exēgeira se*. See, if you please, Wolfgang Franz’s excellent work on the interpretation of Scripture for a right understanding of these passages. FABRICIUS.] I raised you up, that I might show my power in you” (Exod. IX, 16). And: [Note: [Col. 1255D] “Hardening, I will harden.” Exodus IV, 21, and VII, 3: *egō sklērynō*. Through a lapse of memory Philastrius wrote “hardening, I will harden” instead of “I will harden.” FABRICIUS.] “I will harden Pharaoh’s heart, so that he will not let you go” (Exod. IV, 21). And the Apostle says: [Note: [Col. 1255D] Greek text: *Ara oun ou tou thelontos, oude tou trechontos, alla tou eleōntos Theou*—“So then it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who has mercy.” At this place Meric Casaubon notes a paronomasia of three Hebrew words, in his *Disquisition on Languages*, p. 84, and in his notes on Optatus, book II, ch. 20. FABRICIUS.] “Therefore it is neither of the one who wills nor of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy.”

But the Apostle says these things not as a definition, but as an argument and instruction concerning what is true, lest anyone suppose that God [Col. 1255B] spoke in this way. For one must attend to what the Lord says: “That I might show in you indeed [Note: [Col. 1255D] All my power. Exodus IX, 16, and Romans IX, 17: *hopōs endeixōmai en soi tēn ischyn mou*. Philastrius added “all” for purposes of explanation. FABRICIUS.] all my power,” that is, magnanimity, goodness, and forbearance, which is surely [Note: [Col. 1255C] Poured out upon all] poured out upon all in this age.

For when he says this to Pharaoh, he says it to every human being embodied in the flesh: amid prosperity, resources, and temporal power, he gives warning. Those who attend to riches become more sluggish and negligent concerning the fear and grace of God Christ, and forget their own [Note: [Col. 1255C] Thus to the end] salvation even to the end, becoming unmindful of the fear of God. When Pharaoh himself was afflicted, he unwillingly acknowledged the Lord, as is written (Exod. VIII, 8, 25; IX, 27; X, 24). But when he was again released by God, he returned like a dog to [Col. 1255C] his vomit (Prov. XXVI, 11; II Pet. II, 22).

Accordingly, the souls of pagans, Jews, heretics, the rich, and likewise sinners are sometimes found contemptuous of God amid prosperity. Therefore [Note: [Col. 1255D] Instruction. Through afflictions and calamities. FABRICIUS.] instruction is beneficial and saving for the human race [Col. 1256A] in all things, as the Prophet says: “It is good for me, Lord, that you humbled me, that I might learn your ordinances” (Ps. CXVIII, 71). And again, concerning rebuke: [Note: [Col. 1255D] LXX: *Hotan apekteinen autous, ezētoun auton, kai epestrephon kai ōrthrizon pros Theon*—“When he killed them, they sought him, and returned and rose early toward God.” From this someone might conjecture that Philastrius wrote “toward God” instead of “toward him.” FABRICIUS.] “When the Lord killed the Jews,” he says, “then they sought him and kept watch toward him” (Ps. LXXVII, 34).

The blessed Apostle does not, then, say that [Note: [Col. 1255D] We should not run or will. When he said in Romans IX, 16 that it is not of the one who runs nor of the one who wills: “It belongs,” says Optatus, II, 20, “to the Christian person to will what is good and to run in what he has willed well; but it has not been granted to the human being to bring it to completion, so that after the courses which one must complete, something may remain for God, whereby he may aid the one who fails.” FABRICIUS.] we should not run or should not will to serve God; rather, [Note: [Col. 1256C] We must first run by our own will—yet the Lord’s grace also works even the willing in us. Philippians II, 13. FABRICIUS.] we must first run by our own will, and then not with presumption and boastfulness, [Note: [Col. 1256D] “As though by our own strength . . . saved by mercy.” The word *ut* is superfluous both in the Hamburg and Basel editions; it is absent, and rightly so, in the Lyons edition. Moreover, the Corbie manuscript reads “and not Christ’s,” equally well. Above, ch. 127, the same Lyons edition reads “on account of everlasting duration,” and the Corbie manuscript agrees; but the Basel and Hamburg editions read “on account of eternity.” GALEARD.] as though by our own strength and worthy righteousness [Note: [Col. 1256C] Worthy, and not] we deserved to be saved by Christ’s mercy. For one who runs with pride and presumption does not hope for aid from God to the extent that, on the basis of his own conduct, he presumes righteousness for himself.

Thus the blessed Apostle teaches us both to run and to will, and teaches that it lies in our will to persevere in humility in the very course of good works; [Col. 1256B] and only then to hope that salvation can be obtained from the Lord himself, as the Lord says: “And when you have done everything, say, [Note: [Col. 1256D] ‘We are utterly worthless servants.’ Greek: *achreioi*, ‘unprofitable servants.’ Above, ch. 123. FABRICIUS.] ‘We are utterly worthless servants’” (Luke XVII, 10). And: “If the righteous is scarcely saved, where will the sinner [Note: [Col. 1256C] And the ungodly, where will he appear?] and ungodly appear?” (Prov. XI, 31).

Therefore, there are certain things in us in which we must run. But there are greater things which must be hoped and sought from God, as the Apostle says: “You do not know what you ask” (Luke XX, 22). For example, should someone say, “I can be a martyr; I can be an apostle,” and not say, “If God Christ should will it”—whereas the increase of this office and grace is bestowed by him, not acquired through vain human presumption and boasting—such a disposition is the will of a person testing and presuming; [Col. 1256C] it is not that of one seeking and supplicating, that he may deserve to attain so great a dignity.

## CXXIX. HERESY DENYING THAT DAVID WAS A PROPHET OF CHRIST

There are certain heretics, such as [Note: [Col. 1256D] Manichaeans. They rejected the Law and the Prophets, as is evident from Augustine’s book *Against the Adversary of Moses and the Prophets*. Alexander of Lycopolis says of the Manichaeans, *Tēn legomenēn palaian hapasan historian ekballousi*—“They reject the entire so-called ancient history” (p. 19). FABRICIUS.] the Manichaeans, [Note: [Col. 1256D] And Gnostics and Nicolaitans. Perhaps one should read “Gnostic Nicolaitans,” for Epiphanius XXVI, 1 testifies that the Gnostics were joined with Nicolaus (*tō Nikolaō synezeugmenous*). The same author, XXVI, 6, says that the Gnostics used both the Old and New Testaments, but rejected the one who spoke in the Old Testament. Accordingly, whenever they find something opposed to their doctrine, they allege that it proceeded from the spirit of this world: *hoti touto apo tou pneumatos tou kosmikou lelalētai*—“because this was spoken by the worldly spirit.” FABRICIUS.] Gnostics, [Col. 1257A] Nicolaitans, and others, who dare to say of blessed David [Note: [Col. 1257C] That he was not the prophet of Christ the Lord] [Note: [Col. 1257C] That he was not Christ’s prophet. Although the Psalms are distinguished from the Prophets and the Law in Luke XXIV, 19, 44, David is expressly called a prophet in Matthew XXVII, 35 and Acts II, 30. FABRICIUS.] that he was not Christ’s prophet, nor a teacher and interpreter [Note: [Col. 1257D] Of all the divine Scriptures. This refers to II Timothy III, 16, where the Apostle says that all Scripture—*pasa graphē*, and therefore David’s writings also—is divine and God-breathed (*theopneusta*). FABRICIUS.] of all the divine Scriptures, but was a writer of [Note: [Col. 1257D] Human song. Like any other poets. FABRICIUS.] human song and secular matter. Yet he was counted worthy, beyond many others, to proclaim to humankind the mysteries of the heavenly grace and saving secret of Christ the Lord.

For as Christ the Lord gave different grace to other saints, so he granted greater knowledge to this man, the Lord saying: “I will give you David’s faithful holy things” (Acts XIII, 14, from Isa. LV, 3). And: “I have found David son of Jesse, a man who will do all things that are in my heart,” says the Lord (Acts XIII, 22, from Ps. LXXXVIII, 21). They therefore do not know that this David, [Col. 1257B] king and prophet sent from the Lord, was a swift and mighty interpreter of the divine Scriptures; so that [Note: [Col. 1257D] “What was formerly said, was seen in the present, and was announced as future”: this is the reading of the Hamburg edition, with which the Basel and Lyons editions agree, but it is certainly wrong. For the Corbie manuscript adds after *videbatur*, “and was announced as future,” a fuller and better reading. Thus what follows in the printed editions—“past, present, and future [things]”—must be corrected from the manuscript, where *stantium* is read in place of *instantium*: for Livy calls that which is present “standing.” Moreover, a little earlier the Lyons edition wrongly has *praedicerentur* (“were predicted”) for *praedicarentur* (“were proclaimed”); past and present things are not predicted, but only future ones, whereas Philastrius speaks there not only of future things but also of past and present ones. GALEARD.] what was formerly said, and what [Note: [Col. 1257C] Was seen and announced as future, all these things] was seen in the present, all these things might be briefly gathered and proclaimed to humankind by him. In three verses of the first psalm he expounded every power of truth concerning past, present, and future things, and announced all the errors of every people and their diverse deeds when he says: “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly,” that is, pagans; “nor stood in the way of sinners,” namely Jews; “nor sat in the seat of pestilence,” namely heretics (Ps. I, 1).

Then, as though from abundant fountains and materials, he taught what diverse seeds of iniquity were to [Note: [Col. 1257C] Be cast down . . . sacrifice not to God in] confront the human race, so that, these three evils—[Col. 1258A] paganism, Judaism, and every heresy—being despised and condemned, the one true faith, namely faith in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, might be believed and worshiped by all. For blessed David, moved by divine zeal in that time, saw people [Note: [Col. 1258C] Not to God. The word “God” is missing in the earlier editions, though the sense necessarily demands it. FABRICIUS.—“Sacrificing to demons, not to God.” Fabricius adds: “The word GOD is missing in the earlier editions, though the sense necessarily demands it.” Correctly; for the Corbie manuscript also supplies it. Likewise in heresy 135, where the editions have *sequentes suum fraternum* (“following their brotherly . . .”), while Fabricius thought that *sponsum fraternum* (“brotherly bridegroom”) should be read, the Corbie manuscript has, somewhat better, *suum fratrem* (“their own brother”). GALEARD.] sacrificing to demons, not to God; and in the city of Jerusalem he established [Note: [Col. 1258C] Four choirs. I Chronicles XXV, 7. Their total number is given as 288, which results from four times seventy-two; for there were that many in each choir. FABRICIUS.] four choirs, according to the [Note: [Col. 1257C] Entrances of the world] entrances of the world, [Note: [Col. 1258D] Seventy-two apiece. *Ana obʹ*, as in Luke IX, 3 and X, 1, *ana dyo* (“two each”), or IX, 14, *ana pentēkonta* (“fifty each”). Or, if this seems unbelievable in a Latin writer, one should read “one [choir of] seventy-two.” For the whole system of sacred music established by David in the Temple, consult Salomo van Till, in the third part of his work on ancient music, particularly Hebrew music, first published in Dutch and then also in German. FABRICIUS.] seventy-two apiece. He also appointed four men from among the singers to guard the ark of God, while innumerable others stood outside on every side.

But in the middle, with the ark placed there, most blessed David the patriarch himself sang with the people. As so great a witness to and one predestined by the Lord for the incarnation of Christ the Lord, he offered in song the varied joys and praises of the psalms to none other than Christ the Lord himself. [Note: [Col. 1258D] Three times daily: in the morning and evening, and when the continual sacrifice was offered.
