FABRICIUS.] Three times daily, with prayers [Col. 1258B] and the sounding singer of the psalms, [Note: [Col. 1258C] With all things resounding in song] he rejoiced with all the people, announcing Christ’s divine presence and, concerning it, promising the world its future joys. [Note: [Col. 1258C] Promising . . . and from the Law] Of him the Lord also deigned to say that many [Note: [Col. 1258D] Prophets and wise men. Luke X, 24: *polloi prophētai kai basileis*—“many prophets and kings.” FABRICIUS.] prophets and wise men had desired to see and hear what the apostles were counted worthy to hear and see.

For it is [Note: [Col. 1258D] According to time. The poets and even the most ancient writers of the nations, such as Homer, Hesiod, and Herodotus, are much younger than Moses and David, as the ancient Doctors of the Church carefully observed in their apologies against the Gentiles. FABRICIUS.] manifest to all, according to chronology, [Note: [Col. 1258C] Manifest to all] that what seems to be the wisdom of the Greeks itself derives from the Law and the Prophets, and especially from David. Therefore poets and other wise men attempted to fabricate, by imitating him, what they wished to say in verse. [Note: [Col. 1258D] By imitating him. This may perhaps seem less credible to those who consider how ignorant Greeks [Col. 1259C] and Latins were of the Hebrew language and Jewish matters; not to mention that very different things sound in their poems from those with which David’s sacred page, inspired by the divine Spirit, resounds. FABRICIUS.] When they took their subjects from the Law [Col. 1259A] and the Prophets, they hastened, by changing names, to violate the laws of truth and sowed the diverse falsehoods of their own faithlessness in the world. [Note: [Col. 1259C] They sowed them in the world. Thus above, ch. 122: “When none other than those vain poets and philosophers sowed in human minds the seeds of pagan impiety—the names of gods and goddesses.” FABRICIUS.]

Thus many secular and unlearned people, ignorant of these things, prefer to worship and follow the pagan lies of [Note: [Col. 1259C] Pagan lies of temporality. Recent, and by no means ancient. So our author frequently above, chs. 110, 112, 121, 122. FABRICIUS.] recent origin rather than the ancient and true mysteries and firm foundations of the saving Christian law. From their own vanities, that is, from Greek historians, one may therefore recognize how recent the vain wisdom of the Greeks is; and when it gradually becomes known to its own adherents, it is beyond doubt [Note: [Col. 1259C] Is recognized, trampled upon, and] despised, trampled upon, and condemned daily.

## CXXX. HERESY CONCERNING THE UNEVEN ORDER OF THE PSALTER

[Col. 1259B] There are other heretics who suffer from no small error concerning the uneven order of the Psalter, supposing [Note: [Col. 1259C] The whole book . . . of blessed David, and when] [Note: [Col. 1259C] That the whole book is not David’s. Two things may be observed here. First, the learned man errs who, in the German *Lives of Biblical Writers*, part IX, p. 404, citing D. Brochmand as a witness, says that Philastrius counts among heretics anyone who affirms [Col. 1259D] that David is author of every psalm; for Philastrius attributes to heretics the view of those who persuade themselves that not all psalms were written by David. Second, the very view which Philastrius attributes to heretics is by no means heretical, but most true, and was approved even in Philastrius’s age by many Catholic and approved Doctors of the Church, such as Hilary and Jerome, to say nothing of countless others. FABRICIUS.] that the entire book of the Psalter is not by David. When they seek the history in chronological order, [Note: [Col. 1259D] They find unevenness. An *anomaly* (*anōmalian*) of disordered sequence, as he immediately explains it. Indeed, the most learned writers and interpreters of sacred literature, including ancient ones, acknowledge that Ezra arranged the book of Psalms not in the temporal order in which they were written, but in some other order. Eusebius, *On the Psalms*, p. 7: *Paratērēteon de hoti mē kata akolouthian tōn tēs historias chronōn hē tōn psalmōn synkeitai taxis*—“It must be observed that the order of the psalms is not arranged according to the sequence of historical times.” Add the same author, pp. 208, 214. Theodoret, in Garner’s supplement, p. 3: *Ou kathōs elechthēsan hoi psalmoi exetethēsan, alla kathōs heurēntai*—“The psalms were not set forth as they were spoken, but as they were found.” Huet’s view, p. 335 of the *Evangelical Demonstration*, that the psalms were placed in the order in which they were sung in the Second Temple, is conjecture, by no means a certain and established fact. FABRICIUS.] they find unevenness: that is, seeing that things which are latest are placed first and things which are first are placed latest, they suffer no small scandal.

For [Note: [Col. 1260C] In the third psalm. Its inscription: *Psalmos tō David, hopote apedidrasken apo prosōpou Abessalōm, tou huiou autou*—“A psalm of David, when he fled from the face of Absalom, his son.” Similar is the inscription of Psalm CXLIII: *Psalmos tō David, hote auton ho huios katediōken*—“A psalm of David, when his son pursued him.” FABRICIUS.] in the third psalm he suffers persecution from his son, while [Note: [Col. 1260C] And in the one-hundred-and-something [psalm]. That is, in Psalm CXLIV, which is beyond the hundredth: *tō David pros ton Goliad*. [Col. 1260D] Thus above, ch. 112, “three hundred and eighty-something years,” and ch. 106, “already more than four hundred years.” FABRICIUS.] in the one-hundred-and-something psalm he is described as fighting [Note: [Col. 1260D] Against the foreigner. A Philistine, as above, ch. 12. FABRICIUS.] against the foreigner. Yet we find that he first fought Goliath in his youth (I Sam. XVII), but later endured war from his son in old age (II Sam. XVIII). Although these things must be understood spiritually of Christ, those who diligently investigate the history of this prophet are nevertheless troubled by no small stumbling-block.

Since Scripture in the Psalms says that David’s hymns had [Col. 1260A] ceased after seventy-two psalms, [Note: [Col. 1260D] It says that they ceased. After Psalm LXXII is appended: *exelipon hoi hymnoi David tou huiou Iessai*—“The hymns of David son of Jesse have ended.” This appears to be the closing note of the second book, since the entire work of Psalms was formerly divided into five books. FABRICIUS.] and afterwards the heading [Note: [Col. 1259C] And afterwards that of the same man] of the same man is again announced in many psalms, [Note: [Col. 1260D] His heading. Even after Psalm LXXII, many psalms expressly bear David’s name in their heading—for example LXXXVI, XCI, XCIII, XCIV, XCV, and very many others. FABRICIUS.] they ask why it has been set down so, not knowing that the Lord rightly bestowed on the blessed king and prophet the various joys of the psalms. Therefore, even if headings of other persons are found in the psalms, nevertheless the highest praise in all things was granted by Christ to this author and founder, as prophet, king, and patriarch.

But concerning the unevenness of the psalms according to history, those who have investigated it [Note: [Col. 1259C] Most diligent authorities] most diligently have said this: because captivity often came upon the Jewish people from the Gentiles on account of idolatry—for Jews worshiped idols together with them—the divine Scriptures were then sought out and burned [Col. 1260B] by the Gentiles. If anyone had hidden something from the psalms, then later, when peace came, the same divine Scriptures were sought by a few holy persons. When they were found, those who were wise in that time—[Note: [Col. 1260C] They were not wise] for they were no longer prophets but priests, constrained by fear—arranged the text of the psalms according to what they received from certain persons, and ordered it to be expounded in that sequence.

[Note: [Col. 1260C] If, therefore . . . unevenness] Thus, according to history, this appears to be the cause of the unevenness, as many have said. But that in the very unevenness of the psalms there is a spiritual [Note: [Col. 1260C] Of the psalms, and that there is equality] equality—the knowledge of Christ—is manifest to careful students: what is at the beginning is likewise in the middle concerning Christ, and what was later to come is everywhere said beforehand concerning him. [Note: [Col. 1260D] Everywhere. Thus below, ch. 135. FABRICIUS.] Therefore the Apostle says: “Christ, yesterday and today, is himself also unto the ages of ages” (Heb. XIII, 8).

For there is no doubt that the psalms were spoken through spiritual power, so that what had formerly been done through the devil [Note: [Col. 1261B] Concerning the impiety of idols. Above, ch. 126, Philastrius noted from the opening words of Psalm I the heavenly and true faith opposed by David to Gentiles, Jews, and heretics; to these words he refers here also. FABRICIUS.] in the impiety of idols might also be shown as a crime committed among the Jews through his seduction; and the Catholic Church, which proclaims the faith, does not fail to know [Note: [Col. 1261C] Daily. Thus above, ch. 121. FABRICIUS.] that the perversity of heretics, springing up in the end, is his also, [Note: [Col. 1261B] The Catholic Church indeed, proclaiming] daily.

## CXXXI. HERESY CONCERNING CAIN’S SIN

There are heretics who think contrary to the book of Genesis, where the Lord said to Cain: [Note: [Col. 1261C] “Your turning.” Rather, “his turning” or “his return.” LXX: *Hēmartes, hēsychason; pros se apostrophē autou, kai sy arxeis autou*—“You have sinned; be still. His turning is toward you, and you shall rule him.” FABRICIUS.] “You have sinned; be at rest. Your turning is toward you, and you shall rule over him” (Gen. IV, 7). For when he says, “You shall rule over him,” they suppose he said to him: [Note: [Col. 1261C] “You shall be lord of your brother.” This interpretation, which Philastrius attributes to heretics, is defended by the most learned Bonaventure Cornelius Bertram, ch. 1 of the *Frankenthal Lucubrations*; John Lightfoot, *Posthumous Works*, p. 91; William van der Muylen, *Dissertation on the Birthday of the World and of All Things*; Ceneus, in his specimen of a French translation of the Bible; and others. Yet they do not make Cain Abel’s lord in such a way that he was therefore permitted to kill his younger brother; rather, through repentance, the prerogative of primogeniture, which he seemed to have lost through sinning, would be restored to him as by a right of return. FABRICIUS.] “You shall be lord of your brother.”

Even if anyone understood it in this way—because Cain was older than his brother Abel, and because [Col. 1261B] in the Law [Note: [Col. 1261C] In the Law, those older in age were also greater in honor. See interpreters on Genesis XXV, 31; XLIII, 33; Dan. Lundius, *Dissertation on the Firstborn among the Hebrews*, Uppsala, 1703; Outram, book I, *On Sacrifices*, ch. 4; Vitringa, *Sacred Observations*, II, 2 ff.; Witsius, *Sacred Miscellanies*, vol. I; and Salomo Deyling, part II of *Sacred Observations*, p. 48. FABRICIUS.—“In the Law those older in age were also greater in honor.” Thus the Hamburg edition; but certainly less fully than the Basel edition, which reads “those older in age were greater also in honor,” and the Corbie manuscript reads likewise. GALEARD.] those older in age were also greater in honor, that is, firstborn—nevertheless [Note: [Col. 1261B] Those older in age were greater also in honor] [Note: [Col. 1261B] This is not said . . . ‘you shall be’] Scripture does not here say, “You shall rule over him,” as though, “You shall be his lord”; for that is contrary to everything. For if that were so, how could the Lord have pronounced upon him a sentence of death, [Note: [Col. 1261D] He gives him a sentence of death. Not literally a death sentence; see Gen. IV, 15. Rather, he says: “You shall be cursed upon the earth.” FABRICIUS.] [Col. 1262A] because he had killed his own brother, as is written?

Scripture, therefore, does not say that he should rule his brother so as to kill him. Rather, “You shall rule” your own evil thought, which is in your power: [Note: [Col. 1261D] According to the choice and will of each person. See above, chs. 26 and 128. FABRICIUS.] by each person’s choice and will, either to cast from his heart the evil thought [Note: [Col. 1261D] Sent in by the devil. This is the common opinion of the Doctors of the ancient Church. See Eugubinus, VIII, 29, *On Perennial Philosophy*; interpreters on John XIII, 2; Acts V, 3; I Chron. XXI, 1; and D. John Fecht’s most blessed dissertation *On the Suggestions of Satan*. FABRICIUS.] instilled by the devil, or, by not casting it out, to incur everlasting guilt.

For Christ the Lord, as [Note: [Col. 1262B] Christ, the searcher of heart and mind. See interpreters on John II, 25; Matthew IX, 4; XII, 25; Luke V, 22; VI, 8; IX, 47. FABRICIUS.] searcher of the human heart and mind, seeing Cain’s hidden thoughts, rebuked what he had contemplated and warned him not to commit that crime, and thereby sow the path of fratricide [Note: [Col. 1262B] Sow it in the world. That is, scatter the seed of crime, as it were, through an evil example. Our author gladly uses *seminare* (“to sow”) in this sense, as above, ch. 129: “they sowed the diverse falsehoods of their faithlessness in the world.” FABRICIUS.] in the world.

This is also said in the Gospel: [Note: [Col. 1262C] “If you have anger against your brother.” Philastrius renders rather freely what is found in Matthew V, 23: “If you remember that your brother has anything against you”: *Ean mnēsthēs hoti ho adelphos sou echei ti kata sou . . . hypage . . . diallagēthi tō adelphō sou, kai tote elthōn prosphere to dōron sou*—“If you remember that your brother has something against you . . . go . . . be reconciled to your brother, and then, having come, offer your gift.” FABRICIUS.] “If you have anger against your brother, go and be reconciled, and afterwards you will offer your gift” (Matt. V, 23). David likewise says: [Note: [Col. 1262C] LXX: *Orgizesthe kai mē hamartanete*—“Be angry and do not sin.” FABRICIUS.] “Be angry, and do not sin” (Ps. IV, 4). And he himself then explains what is meant by “Be angry, and do not sin”: [Note: [Col. 1262C] LXX: *Ha legete en tais kardiais hymōn, epi tais koitais hymōn katanygēte*—“What you say in your hearts, be pierced with compunction for upon your beds.” FABRICIUS.] “What you say in your hearts, and upon your beds, be pierced with compunction” (ibid.). Solomon also says: [Note: [Col. 1262C] LXX: *Ean pneuma tou exousiazontos anabē epi se, topon sou mē aphēs*—“If the spirit of the ruler rises against you, do not leave your place.” FABRICIUS.] “If the spirit of the ruling enemy rises against you, do not give it a place to dwell in you” (Eccles. X, 4). [Note: [Col. 1262B] And the Lord says, ‘He shall be liable to judgment.’] And the Lord says: [Note: [Col. 1262C] LXX: *Pas ho orgizomenos tō adelphō autou eikē, enochos estai tē krisei*—“Everyone who is angry with his brother without cause shall be liable to judgment.” The phrase *eikē*, “without cause,” absent from many manuscripts, Jerome already found in certain Latin manuscripts in his own day. John Cassian, however, VIII, 20: “ ‘Without cause’ is superfluous and was added by those who thought that anger should not be cut off for just causes, though no one, however stirred without reason, says that he is angry without cause.” Irenaeus also appears to have read it, II, 56 and IV, 31, though he omits it at IV, 27. Cyprian read it as well, as did the author of the *Imperfect Work*, homily 11; Chrysostom, *Homilies on Matthew*, homily 16, p. 200, and homily 6 *On the Praises of the Apostle Paul*, vol. II, new edition, p. 511. It is also read in the *Apophthegmata of the Fathers*, in Cotelerius, vol. I of the *Monuments*, p. 622, and in the Syriac and Coptic translations. It is also defended by the distinguished John Henry Majus, book III of his *Sacred Observations*, p. 30; he observes that it agrees with Jewish rules which, in Maimonides’ ethical canons, forbid a disciple of wisdom to be angry except over a matter of great importance. FABRICIUS.] “Whoever is angry with his brother without cause [Col. 1263A] shall be liable to judgment” (Matt. V, 22).

Accordingly, the Lord at once taught that a thought arising from the enemy’s suggestion must be driven away, lest, after remaining long in a person, it make him more inclined to commit the deed.

## CXXXII. HERESY CONCERNING CAIN’S SIN: WHY GOD GRANTED HIM LIFE
There is a heresy which misunderstands Cain: after the fratricide he committed, he asks the Lord rather to die than to be spared, saying:

> [Col. 1263C] “My guilt is too great for me to be forgiven.” Μείζων ἡ αἰτία μου τοῦ ἀφεθῆναι με. The sense is: “My fault is greater than can be forgiven without punishment.” But those whom Philastrius reproves interpreted these words thus: “I suffer a greater punishment if I am spared,” as though they had read τῷ ἀφεθῆναι με instead of τοῦ ἀφεθῆναι. FABRIC.

“My guilt is too great if I am spared, and everyone who finds me will kill me” (Gen. IV, 4). But through this one man the Lord, as though teaching the whole human race a general rule, was granting through patience an abundant pardon of his goodness, so that, once crime had ceased, the fruitfulness of good works might follow; and so that all might know that they ought to embrace that saying of him:

> [Col. 1263C] “The Lord saying.” Above, chapter 89. FABRIC.

“I do not will the death of the sinner so much as that the sinner should turn back and live” (Ezek. XXXIII, 11). Thus, through Cain, repentance for so great a crime might be opened to all, and in it likewise abundant pardon; and the good fruitfulness of those who repent might be shown to human beings by God’s exhortation, so that, seeing it clearly, they might desire to acquire salvation for themselves rather than death.

Hence Cain, as it were his own accuser and judge, is produced in part when he says that he committed fratricide; and he deserved to hear from the Lord that, if thereafter the fruit of good works followed him, he would without doubt receive remission of so great a crime and would no longer suppose that any fear of an inflicted death threatened him

> [Col. 1263C] “from anyone, even with these words.” FABRIC.

from anyone. Moreover, he had also received a sign that he should not be killed

> [Col. 1263D] “He had received a sign that he should not be killed.” This itself may be taken as the sign: that God gave Cain assurance that he was not to be killed. Compare what I noted in the Pseudepigraphic Code of the Old Testament, pp. 115–16, and Johann Christoph Ortlob’s dissertation *On the Mark of Cain*, published at Leipzig in 1701. FABRIC.

by anyone; and it was determined by the heavenly sentence that he should also suffer seven punishments if any person dared to lay hands upon him:

> [Col. 1263D] “And that he should suffer seven punishments for this as well.” Targum of Uziel, Gen. IV, 15: “Whoever kills Cain, vengeance shall be exacted from him through seven generations.” Suidas, under Κάϊν, following Epiphanius, *On the Mysteries of Numbers*, vol. II, p. 307 ff., explains the seven punishments differently, as corresponding to Cain’s seven sins. FABRIC.—“And that he should suffer seven punishments for this as well.” The word *his* [“for these”] is altogether unsuitable in place of *huic* [“for him”], and, although it somehow crept into the Basel edition too, it ought certainly to have been removed from the Hamburg edition. It is correctly absent from the Cologne and Lyons editions. GALEARD.

It was determined. For this repentance was found to be feigned rather than genuine when he heard from the Lord: “Everyone who kills Cain shall pay sevenfold vengeance” (Gen. IV, 15). Therefore he deserved to receive the sign because of repentance, provided that worthy fruitfulness of good works should thereafter follow him.

> [Col. 1263D] “He deserved to receive.” That is, “he received.” Ancient writers frequently use *mereri* (“to deserve”) and ἀξιοῦσθαι in this sense, as Grotius on Matt. VI, 1 and Isaac Vossius on Ignatius, p. 293, observed. So below in this chapter: “those who deserved, alone, to escape the storm of so great a danger”; and above: “he deserved to hear from the Lord.” FABRIC.

But we do not find that the fruit of repentance’s good works continued in him; rather, all impiety sprouted from his race after him:

> [Col. 1264C] “sprouted after him.” FABRIC.

his descendants being heirs of paternal impiety and of the savagery of so great a crime. Since they were unwilling to repent of their evils, when blessed Noah proclaimed to them,

> [Col. 1264C] “with blessed Noah announcing to them.” Hence he is called “a herald of righteousness” in II Pet. II, 5. FABRIC.

they persisted in wickedness and perished by the dreadful destruction of death in the Flood, except only eight souls at that time, born from the line of the saints,

> [Col. 1264C] “Except eight souls.” I Pet. III, 20. Lyons: *exceptis* [“with eight excepted”]. FABRIC.—“Except eight souls.” This expression seems to have been written in accordance with an Italian idiom, *eccetto otto anime*. Fabricius notes that the Lyons edition has *exceptis*, perhaps arising from an ill-considered itch to emend; but the Basel edition of Sichard retains *excepto octo animis*. Compare Baluzius’s notes on Regino, p. 591; on Gratian, p. 514; and on the *Capitularies of the Kings of France*, vol. II, p. 1229. I recall discovering a similar trace of Italian idiom in Gaudentius, from the word *Brodium*, treatise 2, p. 44, Padua edition, though the editors of the *Leipzig Acts* showed little favor to my conjecture. Yet those men are possessed by an incurable vice of carping at another’s labor, as scholars well know. GALEARD.

who alone deserved to escape the storm of so great a danger.

## CXXXIII. HERESY CONCERNING STARS FIXED IN THE HEAVEN

There is a heresy which supposes that the stars are fixed

> [Col. 1264D] “Stars fixed”: that is, immovable. Chrysostom also refutes this in his homily on Gen. I, 17: “When we hear, ‘God placed the stars in the firmament,’ far be it from us to think that God fastened the heavenly bodies to heaven; for we see them move, and each one completes its course by passing from place to place.” See Sixtus of Siena, book V of the *Sacred Library*, annotation 14. FABRIC.

in heaven,

> [Col. 1264C] “in heaven.” FABRIC.

rather than emerging suddenly at God’s command in the evening from treasuries and hidden places arranged by God,

> [Col. 1264D] “From treasuries and hidden places.” As Ps. CXXXV, 7: Ὁ ἐξάγων ἀνέμους ἐκ τῶν θησαυρῶν αὐτοῦ, “Who brings forth winds from his treasuries.” See Suidas under θησαυροί. FABRIC.

and, at appointed times, performing their prescribed course and service by their own light.

> [Col. 1264C] “by their own light.” FABRIC.

If anyone thinks thus, it is found to be contrary and foreign to the Catholic Faith; he will be shown to share in pagan emptiness and the vain opinion of philosophers rather than in Christian knowledge. For Scripture teaches God’s omnipotence in such a way that it declares the stars to come together and move apart from different treasuries in a short time; and it declares that they have been furnished and granted by God as an ornament of heaven and night, in part for the sake of light, and that at different intervals of the hours they are appointed, as it were, to return again to their own places. Thus, from the places whence they are commanded daily to come forth, they cannot in any way fail, with an angel presiding and impelling them,

> [Col. 1265C] “with an angel presiding.” Not a few Jews of old taught that angels govern the remarkable motions of the heavenly spheres. Maimonides, *Guide of the Perplexed* II, 4, and Abarbanel on Isaiah VI agree with them. The same was the opinion of many Christians, for example Cosmas Indicopleustes, book II, pp. 150, 155 and many other places; also Theodore of Mopsuestia, whom John Philoponus rebukes on this account in book I, chapter 12 of *On Creation*. FABRIC.

to complete their due course. And thereby Christ’s poured-out mercy might be made manifest to the whole human race,

> [Col. 1265C] “and thereby to the human race.” FABRIC.

he who, declaring an equal grace of goodness in this world to the just and unjust, granted that “he makes his sun rise upon the just and unjust, and rains upon the good and evil” (Matt. V, 45).

> [Col. 1265C] “Who makes his sun rise.” Τὸν ἥλιον αὐτοῦ ἀνατέλλει ἐπὶ πονηροὺς καὶ ἀγαθοὺς, καὶ Βρέχει ἐπὶ δικαίους καὶ ἀδίκους: “He makes his sun rise on evil and good, and rains on just and unjust.” FABRIC.

“And,” he says, “the stars know their treasuries and their appointed daily course” (Baruch III, 33–34).

> [Col. 1265C] “And the stars, he says, know their treasuries.” I do not recall finding these words in precisely this form in Holy Scripture. But Wisdom VII, 15 mentions an ἀνεκλιποῦς θησαυροῦ, “an unfailing treasure”; and then verse 19 celebrates τροπῶν ἀλλαγαί, μεταβολαὶ καιρῶν, ἐνιαυτῶν κύκλοι καὶ ἀστέρων θέσεις, “the changes of the sun’s turnings, the changes of seasons, the cycles of years, and the positions of the stars.” FABRIC.

## CXXXIV. HERESY REJECTING MANY THINGS IN THE OLD TESTAMENT

There are certain heretics who reject many things in the Old Testament, namely Solomon’s Ecclesiastes,

> [Col. 1265C] “Solomon’s Ecclesiastes.” Huet in the *Evangelical Demonstration*, Frassenius in his *Biblical Disquisitions*, Natalis Alexander in the *History of the Old Testament*, fifth age, dissertation 4, Gottfried Wegner, *On the Canonical Authority of Ecclesiastes*, and above all Johann Heinrich Michaelis in his carefully prepared dissertation *On Solomon’s Ecclesiastes*, Halle in Saxony, 1716, refute Jews and certain Christians who, together with Theodore of Mopsuestia, detract from the divine authority of Ecclesiastes. FABRIC.

a book written indeed in few maxims, yet containing for seekers the whole treasury of heavenly knowledge. For the Savior himself testified that Solomon was wiser than all who had preceded him.

> [Col. 1265D] “The Savior himself testified.” In Matt. XII, 42 and Luke XI, 31 the most good Savior bears outstanding witness to Solomon’s wisdom. Yet Philastrius’s assertion that he explicitly testifies that Solomon was wiser than all his predecessors is nowhere made in express words. FABRIC.

When, then, they read, “All is vanity of vanities under heaven” (Eccles. I, 14),

> [Col. 1266C] “which are under heaven.” The Septuagint: ὑπὸ τὸν ἥλιον, “under the sun.” FABRIC.

and, “I desired to possess, as has been said, diverse things” (Eccles. II, 3), and, “God gave me [these],” he says, “and behold, all is vanity of vanities” (ibid., 11), he nonetheless adds afterward that this alone is from God: that one should eat, drink, and do good to one’s soul (ibid., 24). If he said that this food alone, or this drink, belongs to this age and is useful only in the flesh,

> [Col. 1266C] “useful, because it is carnal; nothing …” FABRIC.

and proclaimed nothing else of the immortal life to come,

> [Col. 1266C] “He proclaimed.” I have written *nuntiavit* [“he proclaimed”] in place of *nuntiabit* [“he will proclaim”]. Our author gladly uses the word *nuntiare*. So below in this chapter: “he proclaimed the carnal life of human beings, granted by God in abundant riches”; again, “he proclaimed a different food and the glory of holy human beings”; and again, “he proclaimed the perishing life.” FABRIC.—Fabricius adds that our author gladly uses the word *nuntiare*. To the instances he adduces may be joined chapter 110, “the Word of the Father and omnipotent knowledge was proclaimed”; chapter 75, “he proclaimed this by teaching”; chapter 80, “at the end he both proclaims and prophesies”; and elsewhere. GALEARD.

human labor is expended in vain.

Therefore, when the Apostle says of certain people, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die,”

> [Col. 1266C] Greek: Φάγωμεν καὶ πίωμεν, αὔριον γὰρ ἀποθνήσκομεν, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.” In an old manuscript of the Roman Library of the monks of St. Basil, cited by the celebrated Montfaucon, p. 212 of the *Italian Diary*, this is identified as a concise and ancient Laconian proverb. FABRIC.

such a heresy is surely that of pagans and Epicureans, and is comparable to the life of beasts. Therefore “man, though in honor, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts” (Ps. XLVIII, 11, 21).

> [Col. 1266C–D] Septuagint: Ἄνθρωπος ἐν τιμῇ ὢν οὐ συνῆκε, παρασυνεβλήθη τοῖς κτήνεσι τοῖς ἀνοήτοις καὶ ὡμοιώθη αὐτοῖς, “A human being in honor did not understand; he was likened to irrational beasts and became like them.” FABRIC.

Solomon, then, proclaimed both the carnal life of human beings, granted by God amid many riches, and likewise the future glory of angels as existing in the earnest few who desire and believe. For if a rich person has acted well in this age, he must also attain there a share in the life to come. For just as this earthly food was given by God, so that heavenly food from the Law must be desired more abundantly.

Indeed, the glorious faith of Christ the Lord, coming from the Law and Prophets to those who desire it,

> [Col. 1266C] “The faith of Christ.” FABRIC.

is that which Mary chose rather than Martha, the Lord saying: “Mary has chosen the greater portion, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke X, 42).

> [Col. 1266D] “The greater portion.” Τὴν ἀγαθὴν μερίδα, “the good portion.” FABRIC.

Therefore, if he said that the things in this age are vanity of vanities, he declared those things to be passing away, in view of that exalted and everlasting glory to come; as the Apostle says, “For the form of this world and its glory pass away” (I Cor. VII, 31).

> [Col. 1266D] Greek text: Παράγει γὰρ τὸ σχῆμα τοῦ κόσμου τούτου, “For the form of this world passes away.” Philastrius added the words “and its glory” for purposes of explanation. FABRIC.

But if the form, life, honor, and dignity of this world will cease and be destroyed, then that heavenly and angelic dignity must be desired,

> [Col. 1266D] “Angelic dignity.” See chapters 126, 134, and 137. FABRIC.

which through Christ’s incarnation,

> [Col. 1266D] “Incarnation.” Ἐνανθρωπήσει. This ought to be read as one word, a term our author frequently uses, as twice below in chapter 138, rather than the two words *in corporatione* (“in incorporation”), as printed in the editions. FABRIC.

passion, and resurrection is to come to believers. It will not be temporal, carnal, and perishable, as that of Jews according to the letter and of others such as these, who expect nothing hereafter.

Therefore the Lord says: “Work for the food which does not perish,” that is, “believe in me, whom my Father has sent” (John VI, 27, 29). Solomon therefore did not speak only of this carnal food and omit the other; rather, he proclaimed another food and the glory of holy human beings: first, the carnal life of human beings in the present age, and after death, for the just and faithful, that heavenly and angelic dignity to come. He proclaimed this carnal life, as it were, vain and temporal—the justification, that is, of Jews and of others such as these—and a life destined to perish,

> [Col. 1267C] “A life destined to perish.” He says this in place of *peritura* [“which will perish”], as above in chapter 80. FABRIC.

so that they might recognize it to be a shadow and might not fail to understand that the bodily life is temporary and will fall away before long, in comparison with that heavenly and everlasting dignity. Of this food the Prophet says: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. XXXIII, 9).

## CXXXV. HERESY CONCERNING THE BOOK OF THE SONG OF SONGS

There is a heresy which doubts the Song of Songs,

> [Col. 1267C] “Concerning the Song of Songs.” Theodore of Mopsuestia professed that Solomon had flattered the Ethiopian queen through this book; Theodoret rebukes him for this. See what I noted in vol. IX of the *Greek Library*, p. 161 ff. FABRIC.

likewise judging that it was proclaimed by the same author not through the divine Spirit but because of human affairs and pleasures. Yet the truth of heavenly things has taught the human race by comparison with human likeness, as is written in the Gospels

> [Col. 1267C] “In the Gospels.” For example, Matt. XXII, 2, where the kingdom of heaven is compared to a king preparing a wedding for his son. FABRIC.

and everywhere.

> [Col. 1267D] “And everywhere.” Also in prophetic and apostolic writings, for example Ezek. XVI and Eph. V, 32. FABRIC.

Thus Christ’s divine presence in the flesh taught everyone so as to summon them by divine love, soothe them by admonition, move them by mercy, and bend them by goodness. For as God he revealed [the Father];

> [Col. 1267D] “As God, he revealed.” The Father, whom no one had previously seen: John I, 18. FABRIC.

as a father he admonished; as a shepherd he showed pastures;

> [Col. 1267C] “pastures.” FABRIC.

as a king, by conquering the enemy, he showed them to follow his footsteps, so that, following their brother,

> [Col. 1267D] “Following their brotherly …” I think one should read *sponsum fraternum*, “brotherly bridegroom.” But some words seem to have fallen out here. FABRIC.

that is, the Lord Christ coming in the flesh,

> [Col. 1267C] “their brother.” FABRIC.

we may rejoice together with him in the triumph of immortal glory and heavenly reward.

For this reason they are called the Song of Songs:

> [Col. 1267D–1268D] “Song of Songs.” Paschasius Radbertus similarly called Jeremiah’s Lamentations “lamentation of lamentations.” Eleazar is called “prince of the princes of the Levites” (Num. III, 32). Artaxerxes, ruling Persia, is “king of kings.” Theology is “art of arts and science of sciences” for Gregory Nazianzen: τέχνη τεχνῶν καὶ ἐπιστήμη ἐπιστημῶν. Thales is “wise man of wise men,” σοφὸς σοφῶν, in Timon, as cited by Laertius I, 34; Syracuse is “city of cities” for Florus; the Mysians are “barbarians of barbarians.” Κύριος τῶν κυριευόντων, “Lord of lords,” I Tim. VI, 15 and Rev. XIX, 16; Βασιλεὺς βασιλέων, “King of kings,” Rev. XVII, 14. God is ἡλίου ἥλιος, “sun of the sun,” for Philo, p. 658, *On Sacrificers*; heaven is νοητὸς οὐρανὸς οὐρανοῦ, “intelligible heaven of heaven,” p. 660. The Day of Atonement is σάββατα σαββάτων, “Sabbath of Sabbaths,” Lev. XVI, 31; XXIII, 32. Chrysostom, vol. VI of the new edition, p. 330: “bishop of bishops.” See Baluzius, p. 107, on Cyprian: “pope, father of fathers”; likewise vol. V of the *Miscellanies*, pp. 338, 340–41; likewise “servant of the servants of God,” p. 434 and frequently elsewhere. The abbot of Monte Cassino is “abbot of abbots”; see the Chronicle of Leo of Ostia IV, 60. The archbishop of Lyons is “primate of primates,” Salmasius, *Eucharistica* to Sirmond, p. 597. Mind is ψυχὴ ψυχῆς, “soul of soul,” for Philo. Easter is ἑορτὴ ἑορτῶν, “feast of feasts,” for Nazianzen. The holy Eucharist is τελετὴ τελετῶν, “rite of rites,” for Dionysius. FABRIC.

so that what had formerly been said partly and shadowily in the Law might now, with Christ present and the mystery brought to fulfillment through the passion, be opened as a supplement to believers,

> [Col. 1267C] “might be opened as a supplement to believers.” FABRIC.

and, the shadow having ceased, the truth of heavenly light might shine upon every age,

> [Col. 1268C] “the truth of heavenly light now shines upon every age.” FABRIC.

kindling both the body and soul of humankind and awakening the human mind with heavenly love. Those vain persons, then, who serve the desires of the flesh imagine that they cannot perceive this,

> [Col. 1268C] “or be able to perceive.” FABRIC.

or, if it is explained to them, they despise learning it.

> [Col. 1268D] “Unable to perceive.” Unable to grasp or understand that mystical sense in the Song. FABRIC.

Since they are unwilling to acknowledge the Law’s power, they must be judged no less Jews or pagans.

## CXXXVI. HERESY CONCERNING THE COMMAND GIVEN TO ADAM

There is another heresy which says that the Command received by Adam our father should not be accepted,

> [Col. 1268D] “The Command should not be accepted.” By “Command” Philastrius means the time before the Law of Moses, when the first-created humans and the patriarchs lived under the unwritten law of nature and the command received in Paradise. See above, chapter 110. Eusebius also finely observes in chapter 6 of book I of the *Evangelical Demonstration* that this approved commandment for the patriarchs preceded Moses’ Law and that it was built upon it; and that Christ, having abolished the Mosaic ceremonial Law, came to restore and renew that life of the patriarchs and manner of worshipping God. FABRIC.

and they suppose it to have no virtue or usefulness. Yet without that Command neither the Law of Moses can be accepted nor the everlasting, poured-out, and abundant Grace of Christ recognized.

For every human being, constituted in a body, is to be taught or admonished from the divine Law through a threefold dispensation:

> [Col. 1268C] “or admonished.” FABRIC.

in the first age, under the Command; in the second, under the Law; in the third, under the Grace of the Savior. The Law is therefore an admonition because of forgetfulness of the original Command which our father Adam first received from God in Paradise. For it is thus written in the Law: “Lest, having forgotten the command of the Lord your God, you depart from him and perish” (Deut. VIII, 11, 19). The Law, then, is an admonition and confirmation of that first Command.

Again, the Command and the Law proclaim the full goodness of Christ’s Grace and his saving presence. Therefore the Lord says: “Behold, I who spoke in the Prophets am present” (Isa. LII, 6).

> [Col. 1269C–D] “Therefore the Lord says.” Isaiah LII, 6 is now read: Ὅτι ἐγώ εἰμι αὐτὸς ὁ λαλῶν, πάρειμι, “For I am he who speaks: I am present.” Epiphanius, vol. I, p. 301, cites it thus: Ὁ λαλῶν ἐν τοῖς προφήταις, ἰδοὺ πάρειμι, “He who spoke in the prophets, behold, I am present.” Our author cited the same passage above, chapter 109. FABRIC.

Greater therefore are those ancient people who lived under the Command, because, not forgetting Christ their Savior,

> [Col. 1269C] “ancient, who did not …” FABRIC.

they also proclaimed his mystery to their descendants.

> [Col. 1269C] “Christ their Savior to their descendants.” FABRIC.

When forgetfulness of him arose among the Jews, the admonition of the letter followed again,

> [Col. 1269D] “The admonition again of the letter”: of the Mosaic Law. FABRIC.

so that even in the letter the spiritual knowledge of Christ and his carnal presence, illuminating the world, might be hoped for. Thus the Law of Moses, containing one thing in the sound of the voice and another, the saving mystery of Christ, in what is hidden,

> [Col. 1269D] “In what is hidden”: in the typological and mystical sense. FABRIC.

proclaimed it. Therefore neither the Command without the Law, nor the Law without the Command, nor the Grace of Christ without Law and Command, ought to be received or believed by anyone.

## CXXXVII. HERESY CONCERNING THE IMAGE AND LIKENESS OF GOD IN HUMANITY

There are certain heretics who, when they read Scripture saying, “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (Gen. I, 26), fall into no slight madness, being ignorant first what the image and likeness of God are. Since they do not know what the image of God is by the nature of property, nor what likeness is by the grace of bestowed status,

> [Col. 1269D] “And what likeness is by the grace of bestowed status.” So shortly below: “begotten properly, not created from nothing by a bestowed status of servitude.” Gaudentius uses the same term in Sermon 1: “God by nature, not by bestowed status.” See, if desired, our notes on that passage. GALEARD.

they arrogate to themselves no slight pride of dignity.

For the image of God—that is, every human soul—was made from nothing.

> [Col. 1269D] “The image of God, that is, every human soul.” This persuaded many ancient Doctors of the Church. See Petavius, *Dogmatic Theology*, book II, *On the Work of the Six Days*, chapter 2; and the Benedictines’ prolegomena to the works of St. Hilary, pp. 78 and 112. FABRIC.

But likeness, unless it is known by God in faith and life, cannot be called an image like God. When someone considers himself more than he is, he incurs the fault of presumption rather than acquires for himself the merit of dignity.

For when the soul is found sinning and is known to be subject to condemnation and to be held for judgment,

> [Col. 1269C] “For when this sinning soul is found and is known to be liable to being held for judgment …” FABRIC.

how can this be the natural image of God, when it is known to serve diverse sins? For there can be no other divine and natural image of God, proper to the Father—not angel or human being—except Christ, the Son of God. He is the image, properly begotten by the undivided nature of the Father’s own substance and eternity,

> [Col. 1269D] “Image of the Father’s substance.” Heb. I, 3: χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ, “the impress of his substance.” FABRIC.

not created from nothing in a servile status, as human beings and angels are.

Accordingly Scripture declared that the image—that is, the souls of pagans, Jews, heretics, and all persons—may be so called in their common generation and as a substance of one nature and quality.

> [Col. 1269D] “A substance of one nature and quality.” Thus above, chapter 93: “one substance of quality.” FABRIC.

But it declared likeness to belong not to all but only to saints and Christians,

> [Col. 1269D–1270D] “Likeness belongs not to all, but only to saints.” St. Paulinus, Epistle 2 to Severus, similarly teaches that in Adam only the image remained to us, but that we are reformed to the original glory if we receive the divine likeness through imitation of Christ. Even for Plato in the *Theaetetus*, human ὁμοίωσις (“likeness”) to God is to become δίκαιον καὶ ὅσιον μετὰ φρονήσεως, “just and holy with understanding.” FABRIC.

who, continuing in faith, life, and good work, are promised that in the future they shall attain the heavenly merits of angels.

> [Col. 1270D] “The heavenly merits of angels.” That is, they will be ἰσάγγελοι, “equal to angels,” Luke XX, 36. Some ancient writers hence came to the opinion that the number of fallen angels would be restored from among human beings. See Anselm of Canterbury, book I, *Why God Became Man*, chapter 16, p. 81. FABRIC.

Such are the patriarchs, prophets, priests, judges, apostles, evangelists, and martyrs, who believe in the Trinity and remain in an excellent life, and who are proclaimed by the Lord to be joined to angelic glory.

For likeness is recognized as true from the teaching of the Law, faith, life, earnest striving, and work, so that the soul made by God, agreeing with the precepts of his divine Law by fulfilling its established commands, may hope to attain from him a share in the kingdom of heaven. As the Apostle says: “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III, 20). And again the Lord says: “Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke X, 20).

> [Col. 1270D] Greek text: Χαίρετε δὲ μᾶλλον ὅτι τὰ ὀνόματα ὑμῶν ἐγράφη ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς, “Rather rejoice because your names have been written in heaven.” FABRIC.

And, showing that they will be like angels on the day of judgment (Luke XX, 36), the Lord says of the kingdom of heaven: “Come, receive the Kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV, 34).

> [Col. 1270D] Greek: Δεῦτε οἱ εὐλογημένοι τοῦ Πατρός μου, κληρονομήσατε τὴν ἡτοιμασμένην ὑμῖν Βασιλείαν ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου: “Come, blessed of my Father; inherit the Kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.” FABRIC.

Likeness, therefore, is shown to exist through faith in the holy Trinity, good life, and the ensuing work, so that, when they depart, they may receive the promised share in angelic dignity; as John says: “Then we shall be like him” (I John III, 2).

> [Col. 1270D] Greek: Οἴδαμεν δὲ ὅτι ἐὰν φανερωθῇ, ὅμοιοι αὐτῷ ἐσόμεθα, “We know that when he appears, we shall be like him.” FABRIC.

And the Lord says: “Be like your Father.”

> [Col. 1270D] “Be like …” This refers to Matt. V, 48 and Luke VI, 36, although the exact words cited by Philastrius occur in neither passage. FABRIC.

## CXXXVIII. HERESY REPROACHING GOD FOR HAVING SPOKEN TO HUMAN BEINGS IN DIVERSE LANGUAGES AND WAYS

There are certain heretics who ask why God did not always speak in one way, but proclaimed himself to the human race in diverse ways and languages.

> [Col. 1271C] “In diverse ways and languages.” Πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως, “in many portions and in many ways,” Heb. I, 1. Clement of Alexandria, *Protrepticus*, p. 7: Πολύφωνός γε ὁ Σωτὴρ καὶ πολύτροπος εἰς ἀνθρώπων σωτηρίαν, “The Savior indeed has many voices and many modes for human salvation.” FABRIC.

But he spoke and appeared to human beings according to the capacity of those seeing and desiring to see and hear.

> [Col. 1271C] “and desiring.” FABRIC.

After human beings were cast out of Paradise and clothed with death,

> [Col. 1271C] “clothed with death.” The ancients interpreted the garments of skin put upon the first-created humans in Gen. I, 21 as a symbol of mortality contracted through sin. Conversely Paul says in I Cor. XV, 53–54, ἐνδύσασθαι ἀφθαρσίαν, “to put on incorruptibility.” FABRIC.

he no longer appeared as before, but spoke from heaven, his own voice being heard and preserved.

> [Col. 1271C] “His voice heard from heaven.” Philastrius thinks this is the sense when “God said” occurs at Gen. IV, 6, 15; VI, 3, 7, 13. FABRIC.

As time advanced, however, he deigned also to appear to the most blessed patriarch Abraham

> [Col. 1271C] “To Abraham.” Ἐν ὁράματι, “in a vision”: Gen. XV, 1; XVII, 1; XVIII, 1; XXII, 1, 14–15. FABRIC.

and to others in succession.

> [Col. 1271C] “And to others in succession”: Isaac, Gen. XXVI, 24; and Jacob, Gen. XXVIII, 12–13; XXXI, 3; XXXII, 1, 24, 30; XXXV, 1, 9; XLVI, 2. FABRIC.

Under Moses, appearing through diverse things,

> [Col. 1271D] “Appearing through diverse things”: through dream, vision, admonition, manifestation, and revelation. See commentators on Num. XII, 8 and what I noted on Chalcidius, chapter 254. FABRIC.

he displayed upon Mount Sinai what belonged to fear and terror,

> [Col. 1271D] “Of fear and terror.” Earlier editions wrongly have *erroris*, “of error.” FABRIC.

and afterward, in the figure of an angel (Exod. XIV, 19) and in the form of a human being (Gen. XXXII, 24), with preceding signs of his future incarnation,

> [Col. 1272C] “of his incarnation to come … in the incarnation.” FABRIC.

he proclaimed the universal vision of mercy, in which the Lord now showed himself to the righteous through dreams, as it is written (Num. XII, 6).

Afterward, appearing in the incarnation,

> [Col. 1271D] “Afterward, appearing in the incarnation.” Heb. I, 1: Ἐπ’ ἐσχάτων τῶν ἡμερῶν τούτων ἐλάλησεν ἡμῖν ἐν υἱῷ, “In these last days he spoke to us in a Son.” Our author uses *incorporatio* for ἐνανθρώπησις (“incarnation”) elsewhere too, as in chapter 134. FABRIC.

he bore witness to the Jews, declaring what he had formerly said through the prophets.

Therefore, because capacities for seeing the Lord differed, he, like a good physician, bestowed different remedies for the infirmities of human beings, as their weakness required. Thus, at the end he brought more healing to a sickly age,

> [Col. 1271D–1272C] “At the end he brought more healing to a sickly age.” Philastrius joins those who held that the Son of God was incarnate only when human corruption had reached its height. Gregory of Nyssa similarly praises this view in his sermon on Christ’s Nativity, vol. III of his works, p. 341. Johann Friedrich Mayer, “the blessed,” praises these passages in his dissertation *Why God Was Not Incarnate Immediately after Adam’s Fall, but Awaited the World’s Old Age*, Kiel, 1695. To these may be added Cyril of Alexandria, *Against the Anthropomorphites*, chapter 24 and elsewhere; Isidore of Pelusium; and John Zonaras, whose passages Bonaventure Vulcanius noted on Cyril. FABRIC.

so that the surpassing virtue of those first people might be displayed and the dangerous weakness of our race recognized. The Lord says: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick do” (Matt. XI, 12).

> [Col. 1272C] Greek text: Οὐ χρείαν ἔχουσιν οἱ ἰσχύοντες ἰατροῦ, ἀλλ’ οἱ κακῶς ἔχοντες, “Those who are strong have no need of a physician, but those who are ill.” FABRIC.

Greater, then, are those earlier people, who believed on hearing,

> [Col. 1272C] Helmstedt: *qua*, wrongly. FABRIC.

such as Seth, Enoch, Noah, and the rest, than we who, even while hearing and reading of the mercy and abundant goodness of Christ the Lord, despise it. For he also spoke in other languages and lips because of the Jews,

> [Col. 1272C] Septuagint: Διὰ φαυλισμὸν χειλέων, διὰ γλώσσης ἑτέρας ὅτι λαλήσουσι τῷ λαῷ τούτῳ, “Because of contemptuous lips, because with another tongue they will speak to this people.” But Aquila, whom Philastrius more closely follows: Ἐν ἑτερογλώσσοις καὶ χείλεσιν ἑτέροις λαλήσω τῷ λαῷ τούτῳ, “With speakers of another language and with other lips I will speak to this people.” FABRIC.

so that it might be fulfilled: “In other languages and lips I shall speak to this people” (Isa. XXVIII, 11); and even so they will not believe, says the Lord. For through Isaiah he says: “I shall send my word into Achaia.”

> [Col. 1272C] “I shall send my word into Achaia.” I do not find these words in Isaiah. FABRIC.

## CXXXIX. AN EXCEEDINGLY GROSS HERESY CONCERNING THE FOUR LIVING CREATURES IN THE PROPHETS

There is another heresy which, when it reads of the four living creatures in the prophets,

> [Col. 1272D] “In the prophets”: Ezek. I, 5; Rev. IV, 6. Compare, if you please, what was said above on chapter 56. FABRIC.

falls into no small error, supposing that creatures endowed with diverse forms praised God. Such people do not understand that irrational creatures, that is, beings incapable of reason, cannot render praise to God as human beings can. For God does not seek the praise of beasts, because beasts were not made in God’s image; rational human beings, rather, were created and appointed by God for this purpose.

But because it is a vision proclaimed to the prophets by the divine Spirit, there were here foretold the four diverse virtues of holy peoples

> [Col. 1272D] “The four virtues of holy peoples.” By “peoples” he means the multitude of patriarchs, prophets, priests, and apostles, whose virtues he shortly explains. There were also some who interpreted these living creatures as the final group of the four cardinal virtues: the Lion as fortitude, the Calf as justice, the Eagle as temperance, and the Human as prudence. See Arethas on Revelation. Other ancients preferred to refer the creatures to the four Evangelists; for their passages see what I noted in the *Apocryphal Code of the New Testament*, vol. I, p. 383, and vol. II, p. 559. See also the blessed Jacob Thomasius’s dissertation *On the Emblems of the Evangelists*, published at Leipzig in 1667. FABRIC.

and their diverse struggles, which would come into the world in diverse teachings and virtues and in diverse heights of eminence: those of the Lion, Calf, Human, and Eagle, whose diverse teachings and brilliant merits ran beforehand.

First, in the patriarchs royal authority would be seen; then, in the prophets, the fruitfulness of heavenly knowledge; in the priests, strong labor and persistent struggle; in the apostles, a lofty flight into heaven and an eminent dignity. As, therefore, the former diversity of forms foretold, so the heavenly merits of diverse virtues would be manifested in the world through Christ’s presence,

> [Col. 1273C] “In Christ’s presence.” In Arethas on Revelation, Christ is Lion because he is King; he is likewise Calf as Priest, or rather sacrifice and victim; Human because he became human for us; and Eagle because he imparts to us the heavenly Spirit: Διὰ τοῦ λέοντος ὡς Βασιλεύς, διὰ τοῦ μόσχου ὡς ἱερεὺς, μᾶλλον δὲ καὶ ἱερεῖον· διὰ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ὡς δι’ ἡμᾶς ἀνδρωθείς· διὰ τοῦ ἀετοῦ, ὡς χορηγὸς τοῦ ζωοποιοῦ Πνεύματος, καὶ ἐπὶ πάντας καταπτάντος: “Through the lion, as King; through the calf, as Priest—indeed, rather, as sacrifice and victim; through the human, as having become human for our sake; through the eagle, as giver of the life-giving Spirit, which flies down upon all.” FABRIC.

granted by him, the Lord and Savior. For in the Lion royal strength is recognized; in the Calf, abundant labor; in the Human, unceasing suffering; in the Eagle, lofty flight—namely, of those who struggle and shine forth in eminent dignity.

> [Col. 1273C] “And shine forth.” That is, in the eminent dignity which he above attributed to Christ’s disciples. Cotelerius restored this passage excellently in *Monuments*, vol. III, p. 543; the printed editions had *mirantium* (“marveling”). FABRIC.

As the Apostle says: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III, 20), and, “We shall be caught up into heaven and shall always be with Christ” (I Thess. IV, 17). And the Lord deigned to say: “Father, where I am, I will that these also may be.”

> [Col. 1273C] “that these also may be with me.” FABRIC.

CXL.

[Col. 1273B]

[Note: [Col. 1274C] From the cited Sangermanensis manuscript this heresy is added, which is absent from the printed editions.]

There are certain heretics who doubt concerning the day of the Epiphany of the Lord and Savior, celebrated on the eighth day before the Ides of January [6 January]. They say that they ought to celebrate only the Nativity of the Lord on the eighth day before the Kalends of January [25 December], but not the day of the Epiphany, being ignorant that, under the Law and according to it, the Savior fulfilled all things bodily in himself and from himself: that he was born on 25 December and appeared on 6 January. He appeared to the Magi twelve days afterward in the Temple. Therefore, lest that which was true should be brought forth as a shadow [reading uncertain] and thus be worshipped by the Magi, these greater annual feast-days were appointed in sequence for our salvation: first, that on which he was born; then [Col. 1274A] that on which he appeared, that is, twelve days afterward; then that on which he suffered at Passover; and finally that on which he ascended into heaven, about Pentecost. For the completion belongs to the conqueror. Whoever, therefore, does not know one of these neglects it.

You may also be doubtful concerning other days, not possessing the fullness of truth: namely, that in the four seasons of each year these distinct joys sprang forth for us from Christ the Lord—first, that on which he was born; next, that on which he appeared; third, that on which he suffered, rose again, and was seen; fourth, that on which he ascended into heaven. Let us celebrate these throughout the year without interruption, rejoicing together; and let us preserve and retain them whole and inviolate.

But some hold that the day of the Epiphany was that of the baptism; others, that of the transfiguration on the mountain.

CXLI. ERROR CONCERNING THE LEVITICUS OF MOSES.

[Col. 1274B]

There are other heretics who, being ignorant that the precepts of the Law spoken through Moses in Leviticus to the Jews in a bodily sense have in our own time been spiritually revealed, disregard the supreme festal order of realities and the number expressing their heavenly benefit. They do not know what they celebrate, supposing that Moses commanded only concerning Sabbaths, Passover, and Unleavened Bread, and not concerning the eight festivals which the Catholic Church knows and observes.

For Moses says thus to the people of the Jews (Leviticus 23; Numbers 28–29; Deuteronomy 16): first, concerning the New Moon and Sabbaths; second, [Col. 1274D] concerning Passover; third, concerning Unleavened Bread; fourth, concerning the Sheaves; [Col. 1275A] fifth, concerning the Trumpet-blast, which is called *salpinx* [σάλπιγξ, “trumpet”] in Greek, and which the Jews solemnly celebrate each year; sixth, concerning the Fast; seventh, the construction of Tabernacles; eighth, the fullness of fruits and the grape harvest of October, the final gathering and completion of all things.

This eightfold diversity according to the months is celebrated by the Jews according to the letter; and according to spiritual knowledge, beginning in March and completed in the eighth month, that is, October, all things are bestowed in order through Christ the Lord. These are full pledges of eternal salvation, to be brought to completion and proved in the faith and practice of Christianity.

For although at that time the Jews were commanded to offer God the various gifts of these months, so that, withdrawing from idols, they might recognize that all these things were to be offered to God, nevertheless they contained indications of a spiritual offering. In the eighth perfection of the virtues—that is, on the Lord’s Day—through the full grace of fruits in faith in the Lord’s resurrection, angelic human beings will attain the immortal reward and pledge of assuming divinity; no longer offering gifts of earthly oblation, that is, sacrifices belonging to the carnal life, but hoping rather to obtain from Christ the Lord and Savior a share in heavenly glory.

For, by offering annual gifts eight times and recognizing the fullness of the eighth day, [Col. 1276A] being equipped with the strength of the divine Spirit—that is, endowed with the supreme perfection of realities—they do not despair, when leaving this world, that they can attain the promised glory of the resurrection there and be joined to the fellowship of heavenly dignity. For the Lord deigned to say: “Then you shall be like angels.” He proclaimed this to all the righteous and perfect, as David also declared “for the Eighth.”

[Note: [Col. 1273C] “You are doubtful.” Perhaps read: “You may be doubtful.” FABRICIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 1273C] “Season.” Read: “seasons.” FABRICIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 1273C] “Spiritually revealed.” Manifestly fulfilled. FABRICIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 1273C–D] “The supreme festal order of realities.” Some read “of days,” but “of realities” is far preferable. For the festal order of realities is the true and real *antitype* [ἀντίτυπον] of the grace of the New Testament, corresponding, as Philastrius observes, to the shadowy festal order of days in the Mosaic Law. FABRICIUS.—“The supreme festal order of realities.” Fabricius adds: “Some read DAYS, but REALITIES is far preferable.” Fabricius does not say which manuscripts read “days”; but the Basel edition of Sichard reads “realities.” The Corbie manuscript, as also the Lyons edition, has “realities.” GALEARD.]

[Note: [Col. 1273D] “And the number expressing their heavenly benefit.” By the number eight, the pious ancients believed that blessed resurrection and the eternal joys of heavenly life were signified. Their passages are cited by Hugo Menard in his notes on the Sacramentary of Gregory the Great, pp. 33 ff., and Cotelerius on the Epistle of Barnabas, ch. 15, p. 47. FABRICIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 1273D–1274D] “Concerning the eight festivals which the Catholic Church…” In Philastrius’s time these were the eight festivals: (1) the Sabbath; (2) the Lord’s Nativity; (3) the day of Epiphany; (4) the fast of Lent; (5) Wednesday; (6) Preparation Day; (7) the festival of Passover; and (8) the joy of Pentecost. All these are mentioned in the Apostolic Constitutions 5.13 ff. and in Jerome, Epistle 289, to Caesaria, concerning the four fasts, below, ch. 149. (Of the eight feasts listed here by Fabricius, the rest are common and obvious. On Wednesday, see Apostolic Constitutions 7.23 and Cotelerius there, p. 369; one may add Amalarius the deacon, *On the Ecclesiastical Offices* 3.27, and Jerome, *Commentary on Galatians* 2.4, on “You observe days,” etc., cited by John Fronto in his prefatory notes to the Old Calendar, §5, p. 134. Augustine too, Epistle 86: “The reason why the Church fasts especially on Wednesday and Friday seems to be that, as the Gospel is considered, the Jews are found to have made their plot to kill the Lord on that Wednesday which is commonly called the fourth feria.” Compare Baronius on the year 57, nos. 199 ff.; Beveridge, book 3 of the *Codex of Canons of the Primitive Church*, ch. 10. GALEARD.) Seven festivals occur in the homily falsely ascribed to Chrysostom, beginning: “Every festival is splendid” [Φαιδρὰ μὲν πᾶσα ἑορτή]: (1) Nativity; (2) Epiphany; (3) Passion; (4) Resurrection; (5) Ascension; (6) Holy Spirit; (7) “the seventh festival, the expected day of the resurrection of the dead” [Ἑβδόμη ἑορτὴ ἡ προσδοκωμένη ἡμέρα τῆς ἀναστάσεως τῶν νεκρῶν]. Likewise in Proclus’s homily *On the Nativity*, *Bibliotheca Graeca* 8, p. 602. FABRICIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 1274D] “Concerning Passover.” On the fourteenth day of the month Nisan [March]. FABRICIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 1274D] “Concerning the Sheaves.” In the month Sivan [May], on the fiftieth day after Passover. FABRICIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 1275C] “Concerning the Trumpet-blast.” On the first day of the month Tishri [September], the festival of the new year. FABRICIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 1275C] “The Fast.” On the tenth day of the month Tishri, the great feast of atonement, which is called “the Fast” in Acts 27:9. FABRICIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 1275C] “The construction of Tabernacles.” On the fifteenth day of the month Tishri. FABRICIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 1275C] “The fullness of fruits.” For seven days from that same fifteenth day of the month Tishri. FABRICIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 1275B] “Vintage … consolation and completion.”]

[Note: [Col. 1275C] “The eightfold diversity according to the months.” Various festivals in the different months. FABRICIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 1275B] “By the Jews according to…”]

[Note: [Col. 1275B] “In the eighth month, that is, October, all things completed…”]

[Note: [Col. 1275B] “Which in the eighth … the full grace of fruits…”]

[Note: [Col. 1275C] “The immortal reward and pledge of assuming divinity.” I have written this in place of “now mortal,” which appeared in the printed editions. He says *subeundae* (“to be assumed”) for *subiturae* (“about to assume”), as *pereundae* for *periturae* in chs. 80 and 134. FABRICIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 1275C] “Angelic human beings.” Those who will be equal to angels [ἰσάγγελοι]. Above, ch. 137. FABRICIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 1276B] “Gifts and the fullness of the eighth day, namely the Lord’s Day…”]

[Note: [Col. 1276B] “And concerning this … they should not despair…”]

[Note: [Col. 1275C] “The Lord deigned to say.” Matthew 22:30: “In the resurrection … they are like the angels of God in heaven” [ἐν τῇ ἀναστάσει … ὡς ἄγγελοι τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐν οὐρανῷ εἰσι]. FABRICIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 1275D–1276C] “For the Eighth.” The superscription of Psalms 6 and 12: “concerning the Eighth” [ὑπὲρ τῆς Ὀγδόης]. Caesarius, Question 54, observes that David has in view the day of blessed eternity, without evening or succession, “the day without evening and without succession” [ἀνέσπερον καὶ ἀδιάδοχον ἡμέραν]. And Jerome—or whoever the author may be—*On the Celebration of Passover*, vol. 5 of the Marcianaeus edition, p. 170: “The mystery of the Eighth, by which the resurrection is signified. For a psalm is inscribed ‘for the Eighth,’ and infants were circumcised on the eighth day; and in Ecclesiastes [11:2], for the signification of the two Testaments, it is said: ‘To these seven and to those eight is reserved.’” Rufinus on Psalm 6: “By the Eighth the day of judgment is understood, because all times roll on by the repetition of seven days, and what occurs in one can be changed in another. But that eighth is to be understood as that which will not have this variation.” So also other ancients cited by Stephen le Moyne, notes on various sacred writings, p. 876. FABRICIUS.]

CXLII. HERESY REJECTING THE TRANSLATION OF THE SEVENTY-TWO.

There are heretics who, like the Jews, reject the translation of the seventy-two holy and most learned men and adopt the edition of a certain Aquila, [Col. 1276B] a single man from Pontus, who translated many years afterward. Since the seventy-two had been compelled by pressing necessity at that time to omit certain things, they are thought to have rendered discordant translations.

Aquila, however, is praised by certain persons—especially Jews—as though he had understood more, because he rendered differently from those earlier translators concerning the Father and the Son. For the seventy-two said (Psalm 2:2): “Against the Lord and against his Christ”; but Aquila: “Against the Lord and against his anointed one.” And again: [Col. 1277A] “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a Son” (Isaiah 7:14). The seventy-two said, “and his name [shall be called] God-with-us”; but Aquila said: “Behold, a young woman shall conceive and bear a Son, and his name [shall be] ‘powerful with men.’”

Indeed, if these things are received in a pious sense of reading—so that no one is strong and mighty except Christ, who is God, the Son of God—he understands correctly. But if he doubts this, such an edition must be rejected and despised. Therefore the Jews do not possess the translations of the seventy-two, who, thinking rightly concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, proclaimed one substance, divinity, and majesty; rather, they possess that of Aquila, who does not think so rightly concerning the Son of God, but speaks of him as though he were a prophet.

For this reason his translations are never placed in the middle of the books, [Col. 1277B] but are assigned to the right and left; and they are read by very many as contrary to and lacking the fullness of truth. But the Catholic Church always possesses and observes without hesitation the determinations and judgments of the seventy-two when reading them; Aquila’s work, however, it considers and judges as virtually superfluous.

For this translation, namely that of the seventy-two, was published under Ptolemy, king of the Egyptians, after Alexander of Macedon, and was given to all and to the Jewish people in Jerusalem, [Col. 1278A] when not many Jews were living there, being as it were already under the authority of the king of Egypt. At Ptolemy’s request, interpreters were sent to Alexandria. When the seventy-two wise and prudent men, interpreters, had arrived, they translated the Hebrew language into Greek speech at the king’s command and published it in Greek letters, as indeed happened.

And when Ptolemy king of Egypt had received them, wishing to test whether the divine Scripture read by the Jews was theirs, he ordered each one separately to be shut in a chamber, unable to see any other, except only the recorder who took down the interpreter’s dictation. Later, receiving the translation of all of them daily, and finding it in agreement as one, he ordered all their edition to be written down and placed in [Col. 1278B] the temple, so that philosophers, poets, and historians coming from Achaia and other provinces, who wished to read it, might not be denied access.

From it philosophers, poets, orators, and historians in particular drew arguments and, as they wished, transferred them to the lies of their paganism. Instructing the untaught minds of boys under other names, they hastened to make the divine Law of God void in the world; and they strengthened seeds of impiety in the sound of words and in dangerous opinions. On account of them the Lord also said that they were thieves and robbers (John 10:8), to be recognized in all things and by all persons.

[Note: [Col. 1276C] “Like the Jews.” Also the Judaizing Nazoraeans and Ebionites, whom Irenaeus, 3.24, notes to have preferred Aquila’s version. Testimony concerning the Jews is given by Trypho in Justin Martyr, Origen, Anastasius Sinaita, and others, whose passages Humphrey Hody cites in *On the Original Texts of the Bible*, p. 236. FABRICIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 1276C] “A single man from Pontus.” He implies that it is unworthy for the version of a single man to be preferred to that of the seventy-two elders. Epiphanius and others relate that Aquila was native to Sinope, a city of Pontus. Concerning him, as also concerning the seventy-two interpreters, I shall not repeat what I said in book 3 of the *Bibliotheca Graeca*, ch. 12. FABRICIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 1276C] “Many years afterward.” Around A.D. 130, after the twelfth year of Hadrian. FABRICIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 1276C–D] “Had omitted certain things.” Talmudists and other ancient rabbis say that the seventy-two interpreters altered thirteen passages in their translation, fearing that they might offend Ptolemy. See Jean Morin, *Biblical Exercises*, p. 354, and Humphrey Hody, pp. 139, 170. FABRICIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 1276B] “Rendered, and as it were…”]

[Note: [Col. 1276B] “Is praised … should have rendered…”]

[Note: [Col. 1276D] “Not as those earlier translators rendered concerning the Law.” Thus the Hamburg and Basel editions; but Paris and Lyons have *dictaverit* (“rendered”), supported by the Corbie manuscript. This reading seems truer, for Philastrius there speaks of Aquila, whom he says differs from the seventy interpreters. Thus on the following page, in the same chapter, the Hamburg edition reads *quo fortis* (“whereby [he is] strong”), and the Basel agrees; the Lyons edition has the somewhat better *quod fortis* (“that [he is] strong”), and this is also found in the Corbie manuscript. Again, a little later Hamburg and Basel have *contraria et non plena* (“contrary and not full”); Paris and Lyons, *contrariae et non plenae* (“contrary and not full”), which is a more suitable and easier reading and is retained by the Corbie manuscript. GALEARD.]

[Note: [Col. 1276D–1277C] The Seventy: “Against the Lord and against his Christ” [Κατὰ τοῦ Κυρίου καὶ κατὰ τοῦ Χριστοῦ αὐτοῦ]. Aquila: “Against his anointed one” [Κατὰ τοῦ ἠλειμμένου αὐτοῦ]. Aquila likewise rendered “anointed” [ἠλειμμένον] instead of “Christ” [Χριστῷ] in Daniel 9:26, as Eusebius testifies in *Evangelical Demonstration* 8, p. 397. This passage from the Psalm should be added to the fragments of Aquila collected by those most distinguished men John Drusius and Bernard de Montfaucon. FABRICIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 1277C] The Seventy: “Behold, the virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel” [Ἰδοὺ ἡ παρθένος ἐν γαστρὶ λήψεται, καὶ τέξεται υἱὸν, καὶ καλέσεις τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ Ἐμμανουήλ]; in its place Justin Martyr, in the longer *Apology*, p. 74, has: “and they shall say concerning his name, ‘God with us’” [καὶ ἐροῦσιν ἐπὶ τῷ ὀνόματι αὐτοῦ, Μεθ’ ἡμῶν Θεός]. FABRICIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 1277C–D] “Behold, a young woman.” Trypho in Justin Martyr, p. 226: “The Scripture does not have, ‘Behold, the virgin shall conceive in the womb,’ but, ‘Behold, the young woman…’” [Ἡ γραφὴ οὐκ ἔχει, Ἰδοὺ ἡ παρθένος ἐν γαστρὶ λήψεται, ἀλλ’ Ἰδοὺ ἡ νεανίς]. Irenaeus 3.24, in Eusebius, *History* 5.8, and Nicephorus 4.14: “Therefore the translation of some persons is not true, who dare to translate Scripture thus: ‘Behold, a young girl shall have in her womb and shall bear a son,’ as Theodotion of Ephesus and Aquila of Pontus translated it, both Jewish proselytes, followed by the Ebionites.” Eusebius, *Demonstration* 7, p. 316: “Aquila was a proselyte, not a Jew by birth; nevertheless, according to him also, it is spoken in this way … ‘Behold, the young woman conceives in the womb and bears a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel’” [Προσήλυτος δ’ Ἀκύλας ἦν, οὐ φύσει Ἰουδαῖος, ὅμως δ’ οὖν καὶ κατ’ αὐτὸν, τοῦτον εἴρηται τὸν τρόπον … Ἰδοὺ ἡ νεανὶς ἐν γαστρὶ συλλαμβάνει καὶ τίκτει υἱὸν, καὶ καλέσεις ὄνομα αὐτοῦ Ἐμμανουήλ]. FABRICIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 1277D] “Powerful with men.” “The powerful one with men” [Ὁ δυνατὸς μετ’ ἀνθρώπων]. It is uncertain whence Philastrius drew this, since Eusebius, in the passage already cited, testifies that Aquila retained the Hebrew name *Emmanuel* [Ἐμμανοήλ] in his version. FABRICIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 1277C] “God is … proclaimed substance, divinity, and majesty.”]

[Note: [Col. 1277D] “His translations are never placed in the middle of the books.” Origen placed the Greek versions in his Tetrapla and Hexapla in the following order, as is evident from an ancient fragment in the Barberini manuscript of the Twelve Prophets:

Aquila. Symmachus. The Seventy. Theodotion.]

[Note: [Col. 1277C] “But assigned to the right and left…”]

[Note: [Col. 1277D–1278C] “Under Ptolemy.” Philadelphus, concerning whom Aristeas (in Epiphanius, vol. 2, p. 166: Ἀρισταῖος), Josephus 12.2 drawing from him, and others speak. FABRICIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 1278C] “When they…”]

[Note: [Col. 1278C] “Each one separately.” Justin Martyr, *Exhortation to the Greeks*, p. 14, testifies that when he was at Alexandria, traces of those cells—or little houses [οἰκίσκων]—were shown to him on the nearby island of Pharos. Irenaeus 3.25, Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* 1.1, p. 342, Cyril of Jerusalem, and others also mention them. Humphrey Hody cites their passages and rejects the tale, long ago dismissed even by Jerome, in the work cited, pp. 138 ff. FABRICIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 1278C–D] “Except only the recorder.” The editions have: “except only him”; but the Corbie manuscript has: “except only the recorder who,” perhaps better. I have explained who the *exceptores* [official shorthand writers] were in my edition of Gaudentius, Padua, p. 7. The ancient glosses of Master Ison on Prudentius, *Weitz’s Hymn* 14, line 709, under “Scribes,” p. 821: “*Exceptores* were those who took down the words of the judge and the replies of the martyr.” Ennodius, *Life of Saint Epiphanius, Bishop of Pavia*: “Having acquired the abbreviations of shorthand writing and the various signs which compress a multitude of words into brevity, he shone forth when enrolled among the *exceptores*; and he began already to take down dictation in such a manner as enabled him to dictate without detraction from good men.” And *Life of the Blessed Monk of Lérins*: “Joined to the service of Constantius, a most eminent bishop of that period, he consecrated the beginnings of his life to glorious works; Constantius ordered him to enter upon the heavenly warfare among the ecclesiastical *exceptores*.” The office of *exceptor* is mentioned in the Martyrology, 25 August. GALEARD.]

[Note: [Col. 1278D] “Placed in the temple.” The Serapeum, in which that remarkable library of Alexandria was burned under Caesar: seven hundred thousand volumes, if we believe Ammianus Marcellinus, book 22, ch. 16. See there Valesius’s notes and Lipsius, *Syntagma on Libraries*, ch. 2. FABRICIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 1278C] “From Achaia.” Earlier editions: “from Achaia, from Greece.” But I think it evident that the words “from Greece” are a gloss here. FABRICIUS.]

CXLIII. [Note: [Col. 1279B] This heresy is absent from the Sangermanensis manuscript.] HERESY CONCERNING THE SEVENTY INTERPRETERS.

There is a heresy which, after Aquila, adopts the translation of thirty men rather than that of the most blessed seventy-two, who, thinking wholly and inviolately concerning the Trinity, handed down the surest foundations of the Catholic Church in their interpretation of the Scriptures. These thirty followed Aquila in many matters; therefore the Catholic Church does not receive their translation either, although it is contained in authoritative books.

[Note: [Col. 1279B–C] “Thirty men.” Lambda [Λ], as in the manuscript of the Prophets in the library of the Jesuit College at Paris. See Richard Simon, *Critical History of the Bible*, vol. 1, p. 181. This mark, however, does not designate Lucian, but “the others” [οἱ λοιποί], the remaining interpreters. See the most learned Montfaucon, preface to Origen’s *Hexapla*, p. 66. The opinion of the most learned Humphrey Hody seems to me highly probable: in p. 632 of his work *On the Original Bibles*, he acutely conjectures that Philastrius’s “translation of thirty men” refers to the edition of the Greek biblical version once revised by Lucian, presbyter of Antioch, and marked in the margins of Greek biblical manuscripts by the Greek letter lambda [Λ]. Since this letter is the initial of Lucian’s name, it is also among the Greeks the sign of the number thirty. On Lucian’s edition, whose use spread far and wide, see, if you please, what I noted in book 3 of the *Bibliotheca Graeca*, ch. 13, §14, and book 5, ch. 1, p. 278. FABRICIUS.]

CXLIV. ANOTHER HERESY ON THE SAME SUBJECT.

[Col. 1279B]

There is a heresy which again wishes to follow the translation of six men, published later, not that of the earlier holy seventy-two. Those who desire to interpret otherwise than the determinations and judgments of the seventy-two fall into no small error, likewise holding divergent views concerning the Catholic faith.

[Note: [Col. 1279C–D] “The translation of six men.” By a similar confusion Philastrius calls “the translation of six men” that version which in the margins of Origen’s Hexapla, or of the common text [κοινή] revised by Origen, was marked by the letter stigma [ς]. It means the Sixth Version, found by Origen at Nicopolis on the Actian coast, cited by Eusebius on the Psalms, p. 521. Others call it the Fifth, for they regard as the Sixth the one found by the same Origen in jars at Jericho. But this version—of which Philastrius speaks below in ch. 146—is the Fifth according to Epiphanius, Athanasius in the *Synopsis*, Josephus the author of the *Hypomnesticon*, and Euthymius. Eusebius cites passages from the Fifth in his work on the Psalms, pp. 73, 92, 94, 106, 139, 148, and in very many other places; and at p. 597 he observes that it agrees with the seventy interpreters in the place where Aquila and Symmachus had translated more closely to the Jewish sense. Saint Ambrose also cites the Fifth edition on Micah in Epistle 70, vol. 2 of the new edition, p. 1065. FABRICIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 1279B–1280B] “Not that of the earlier holy seventy-two, and those who desire to interpret the determinations and judgments of the seventy-two otherwise…” This passage has a gap through scribal fault in the editions; its sense cannot be grasped unless it is supplied from the Corbie manuscript thus: “not that of the earlier holy seventy-two; and those who desire to interpret the determinations and judgments of the seventy-two otherwise…” The repetition of “seventy-two” deceived, I know not whether the dictating author or the scribe. This at least I know: errors of this kind cannot be removed by those who lack the aid of manuscripts. GALEARD.]

CXLV. A THIRD HERESY ON THE SAME SUBJECT.

There are other heretics [Note: [Col. 1280B] This heresy also is absent from the cited Sangermanensis manuscript.] who follow the differently presented translations of Theodotion and Symmachus, not that of the most blessed earlier interpreters, which the Catholic Church honors and proclaims.

[Note: [Col. 1280C] “The most blessed earlier interpreters.” The seventy-two interpreters. FABRICIUS.]

CXLVI. HERESY CONCERNING THE BOOKS OF THE OLD TESTAMENT FOUND IN A JAR.
