There is another heresy which wishes to follow books found in a jar after the captivity and after the burning, and which do not agree with the first translation of the holy men; whereas the Catholic Church reads, honors, and proclaims the translation of the seventy-two, while it despises and rejects other versions as superfluous and contrary to so great an edition.

[Note: [Col. 1280C] “Books found in a jar.” He means the Fifth Greek edition of the Bible, found by Origen “in bronze jars” [ἐν πίθοις χαλκοῖς] at Jericho. See the note above on ch. 144. FABRICIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 1280B] “Reads, honors, and proclaims.”]

CXLVII. HERESY THAT ONE MUST NOT SPEAK EVIL OF FOREIGN GODS.

[Col. 1280B]

There are certain heretics who do not understand what Scripture says: “You shall not speak evil of foreign gods.” They observe this command, [Col. 1281A] thinking that it was spoken concerning the vanity of pagans, and by holding this view they suffer no small injury to their salvation.

For Moses says: “You shall destroy their temples and break their idols” (Exodus 24:13); and the blessed Abraham was justified by breaking idols; and Gideon, burning and breaking idols by night (Judges 6:28), merited from God so great a power that with a few men he conquered innumerable enemies; as did all the righteous, Elijah (5 Kingdoms 18:40), and others likewise. How, then, does an imprudent person judge that this was said concerning the vanity of idols, and that they must not be spoken against, when David says: “Let those who worship them become like them”?

Accordingly, when Scripture says that foreign gods are not to be spoken against, it means that angels and other saints dedicated to the true faith, who from the beginning of the world have cultivated true piety, are not to be cursed. For all the righteous cursed idols and broke them, and thereby deserved grace, as Moses did when descending from the mountain (Exodus 32:20). Moreover, the messengers of Christ are gods, as Moses was to Pharaoh and the Egyptians, when Scripture cries: “I said, ‘You are gods’” (Psalm 81:7).

Certainly, those who, worshipping the holy and adorable Trinity, preach it with strong faith—who are all truly blessed and holy righteous persons—are recognized as gods of unbelievers, because the Lord says: “Those to whom the word of God came”; and since it was preached through them, they themselves have been called gods of unbelievers, as Paul and Barnabas (Acts 14:12), and Moses to Pharaoh (Exodus 32:20). They are not to be cursed but in every way praised, [Col. 1282A] honored, and glorified, as David said: “But he glorified those who fear the Lord” (Psalm 14:4). And the Lord: “Those who glorify me I shall glorify” (1 Kingdoms 2:30).

Therefore, not understanding the force of the Scriptures, these persons agree with paganism according to the letter and are found alien to Christianity. Since the Jews did not believe the righteous prophets and others such as these, they too, like the pagans, were judged alien by the Lord through Scripture; and thus it was proclaimed that they should not curse their own teachers, prophets, and other righteous persons.

[Note: [Col. 1280C–1281D] “You shall not speak evil of foreign gods.” “You shall not speak evil of gods” [Θεοὺς οὐ κακολογήσεις], Exodus 22:28. Julian cites this passage in Cyril, book 7, p. 238; Cyril replies, pp. 240 ff., that by “gods” Moses means magistrates and rulers. Yet this was not so understood of old by the Jews. (See Bernard’s notes, p. 230, Amsterdam edition. Chrysostom also holds Cyril’s view in the *Synopsis of Sacred Scripture*, vol. 6, new edition, p. 329. Compare Schudt, *Compendium of Jewish History*, pp. 248, 251 ff.; Surenhusius, book *Katallagē*, p. 88; Lightfoot on Matthew 12:24; Grotius on Acts 19:37. Against this, see Morin, *Biblical Exercises*, p. 590; Bernard on Josephus, p. 288; Origen, *Against Celsus* 8, p. 404. The same, p. 402: “In the divine legislation this too is commanded: ‘You shall not speak evil of gods,’ so that our mouth may not become accustomed to speak evil of anyone whatsoever” [Ἐν τῇ θείᾳ νομοθεσίᾳ προστέτακται καὶ τὸ, Θεοὺς οὐ κακολογήσεις, ἵνα μὴ ἐθίζηται ἡμῶν τὸ στόμα ὁντιναοῦν κακολογεῖν]. Add p. 413.) Josephus, *Antiquities* 4.8, Origen’s edition: “Let no one blaspheme the gods whom other cities recognize” [Βλασφημείτω δὲ μηδεὶς θεοὺς οὓς πόλεις ἄλλαι νομίζουσι]; and *Against Apion* 2, p. 1077: “And concerning neither mocking nor blaspheming the gods recognized by others, our lawgiver expressly forbade it to us, for the sake of the very name of God” [Καὶ περί γε τοῦ μήτε χλευάζειν μήτε βλασφημεῖν τοὺς νομιζομένους θεοὺς παρ’ ἑτέροις ἄντικρυς ἡμῖν ὁ νομοθέτης ἀπείρηκεν, αὐτῆς ἕνεκα προσηγορίας τοῦ Θεοῦ]. Philo, book 3, *On the Life of Moses*: “It is necessary to refrain from blasphemy, so that none of Moses’ disciples may become accustomed wholly to disregard the designation ‘God’” [τῆς βλασφημίας ἀνέχειν ἀναγκαῖον, ἵνα μηδεὶς ἐθίζηται τῶν Μωϋσέως γνωρίμων συνόλως Θεοῦ προσρήσεως ἀλογεῖν]. Compare commentators on Exodus 23:13 and Leviticus 24:15; John Selden, *On Natural Law*, book 2, ch. 13. Rabbi Judah in *Hasidim*, no. 24: “Beware lest it ever enter your mind to insult any idol,” in John Wulfer, p. 136, *Theriaca*. Simon Luzzatto expresses the same view, *Discourse on the Condition of the Jews*, Consideration 13. Photius, Epistle 162, p. 217: “One ought not insult even a person devoted to Greek forms of worship in what he reveres” [Οὐ δεῖ οὐδὲ τὸν Ἑλληνικαῖς θρησκείαις προσανακείμενον ἐξυβρίζειν ὅπερ σέβεται]. Niphon, who pronounced an anathema upon the God of the Hebrews (see Cange on Cinnamus, p. 438), is condemned in the decree against the Bogomils, A.D. 1145, in Allatius, book 2, *On Consensus*, ch. 12, p. 682. Emperor Manuel Comnenus disapproved the anathema against the God of Muhammad found in Sylburg’s *Saracenica*, p. 86, according to Nicetas Choniates, book 7, ch. 6, pp. 235 ff. I do not doubt that one of the gravest obstacles to the conversion of Jews is that from childhood they are taught by their parents to blaspheme Jesus. In his own time Jerome, on Isaiah 5, 49, and 52, testified that the Savior was blasphemed by Jews three times daily in the synagogues, by day and by night. FABRICIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 1281C] “Thinking that it concerned divinity…”]

[Note: [Col. 1281D] The Seventy: “You shall destroy their altars, cut down their pillars, and burn in the fire the carved images of their gods” [Τοὺς βωμοὺς αὐτῶν καθελεῖτε καὶ τὰς στήλας αὐτῶν ἐκκόψετε, καὶ τὰ γλυπτὰ τῶν θεῶν αὐτῶν κατακαύσετε ἐν πυρί]. FABRICIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 1281D] “The blessed Abraham.” An ancient tradition holds that Abraham broke the idols of his father; it is reported in *Bereshit Rabbah*, ch. 38. See Dionysius Vossius on Maimonides, *On Idolatry*, ch. 1, §7; and Gottfried Wagner’s learned dissertation, *On Ur of the Chaldeans*, Leipzig, 1681, quarto. FABRICIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 1281C] “He merited from the Lord Christ alone so much … the righteous and Elijah…”]

[Note: [Col. 1281D] The Seventy: “Let those who make them, and all who trust in them, become like them” [Ὅμοιοι αὐτοῖς γένοιντο οἱ ποιοῦντες αὐτὰ καὶ πάντες οἱ πεποιθότες αὐτοῖς]. FABRICIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 1281C–1282C] “When he says … from the righteous.”]

[Note: [Col. 1281D–1282C] “Angels and other saints.” Philastrius will scarcely persuade anyone that by the foreign gods whom one must not curse Moses meant angels or holy men. FABRICIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 1281C] “For all the righteous cursed … and broke them.”]

[Note: [Col. 1282C] “Descending, and apart from the fact that…”]

[Note: [Col. 1282C] “Apart from the fact that.” Besides the example of Moses which he has cited, another argument occurs to Philastrius: Christ’s apostles and, after their example, the teachers of the Gospel can rightly be called gods, as Moses is called a god in Exodus 7:1. FABRICIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 1282C] “Messengers.”]

[Note: [Col. 1282C] “I said, ‘You are gods.’” The printed editions incorrectly had “therefore you are gods.” The familiar passage is Psalm 82:7: “I said, ‘You are gods’” [Ἐγὼ εἶπα, Θεοὶ ἐστε].]

[Note: [Col. 1282C] “Adorable.”]

[Note: [Col. 1282C] “Those to whom the word of God came.” John 10:35: “If he called those gods to whom the word of God came” [Εἰ ἐκείνους εἶπε θεοὺς πρὸς οὓς ὁ λόγος Θεοῦ ἐγένετο]. FABRICIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 1282C] “And to be prayed for … shall glorify.”]

[Note: [Col. 1282C–D] “Were judged.” The printed editions less well read “will be judged.” FABRICIUS.]

CXLVIII. HERESY CONCERNING MELCHIZEDEK THE PRIEST.

There are certain heretics who, reading in Genesis concerning Melchizedek, priest and king, who was in the city of Salem—so named at that time—under the most blessed patriarch Abraham, and of whom Scripture says that he was begotten without father and without mother, hold this view although it is contrary to reason. For Scripture did not deny that he was produced by a fleshly generation, but declared that he was not begotten of righteous parents. By his natural zeal, through the former Commandment, he deserved to attain such knowledge of Christ that, although he had not heard from his parents the things which were to be offered, nevertheless by his own study he might recognize through the Commandment the greater mysteries of Christ that were to be offered. For the Lord says through the prophets: “Behold, I make new things” (Isa. 43:19); and: “Before they come to pass, they have been announced to you” (Isa. 48:5–6); and: “Do not remember the former things,” which were spoken carnally in the Law (Isa. 43:18). And the Savior says: “What is born of flesh is flesh, and what is born of Spirit is spirit” (John 3:6).

[Note: [Col. 1282D] In Genesis 14:18: “And Melchizedek, king of Salem” (Καὶ Μελχισεδὲκ βασιλεὺς Σαλήμ). Louis Borghesius argues, by various arguments, in chapter 7 of his *Critical History of Melchizedek*, that this Salem, Melchizedek’s royal city, was identical with Jerusalem. Jerome, however, denies this in his Letter to Evagrius, as does in our own age the most learned Hadrian Reland in his *Palestine*, pp. 833 and 976; I would prefer to agree with him. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1282D] “Without father . . .” Ἀπάτωρ, ἀμήτωρ, ἀγενεαλόγητος: that is, one whose parents are not commemorated, as are those of the Levitical priests by Moses. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1282D] “By the former Commandment.” Philastrius is accustomed to call “Commandment” that divine light by whose guidance the patriarchs worshipped God before the Mosaic Law. See chapters 110, 136, 150, 153, 156. FABRIC.]

When, therefore, it says of him that he was produced without father and without mother, Scripture declares that he was an inquirer without the tradition and instruction of his parents, and that by nature he was capable and able to receive the bread of heavenly wisdom—that is, the mystery of Christ—through the Commandment, as those who attend carefully may perceive. The Apostle, knowing this, proclaimed that human nature is capable in all persons of heavenly knowledge and piety, thus:

“For when Gentiles, who do not have the Law, do naturally the things of the Law, these, though not having the Law, are a law unto themselves; they show the work of the Law written in their hearts,” and so forth (Rom. 2:14 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 1283B] “An inquirer” (συζητητήν): one who searches out divine matters and reflects upon the duty owed by him to God. Below in this chapter: “Being capable of the divine and heavenly Law, and, as the image of God, having sought out God’s mystery by his own study, despising his impious parents.” FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1283B–C] “Able and capable of heavenly [wisdom].” The Hamburg, Basle, and Lyons editions read very badly here; but the Corbie manuscript corrects it: “able and capable of heavenly wisdom.” So shortly afterward: “human nature is capable of heavenly knowledge and piety”; and below: “being capable of the divine and heavenly Law.” GALEARD.]

[Note: [Col. 1283C] “Through the Commandment”: without the Mosaic Law, through natural light kindled by God, as he immediately explains from Paul. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1283C] “Capable in all persons”: not by natural powers alone, but with God’s grace added, as the appended passages from Paul, Matthew, and John finely demonstrate. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1283C–D] “For when Gentiles . . .”: “For whenever Gentiles who do not have the Law naturally do the things of the Law, they show the work of the Law written in their hearts” (Ὅταν γὰρ ἔθνη τὰ μὴ νόμον ἔχοντα, φύσει τὰ τοῦ νόμου ποιεῖ, οἵτινες ἐνδείκνυνται τὸ ἔργον τοῦ νόμου γραπτὸν ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις αὐτῶν). Valerius Maximus, 5.4, external example 5: “Nature is the best teacher of filial devotion; needing neither the service of speech nor the use of letters, she instills love for parents into the hearts of children by her own silent powers.” FABRIC.]

The Lord likewise said to Peter: “For flesh and blood did not reveal it to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 16:17), thereby showing the faith of the Lord Savior. Therefore the Lord himself again says: “Unless someone is reborn of water and Spirit, he shall not enter,” he says, “into the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:3). And again in the Law: “Those who said to father and mother, ‘We do not know you,’ these kept my commandment,” says the Lord (Deut. 33:9).

[Note: [Col. 1283D] “For flesh . . .”: “For flesh and blood did not reveal it to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Ὅτι σὰρξ καὶ αἷμα οὐκ ἀπεκάλυψέ σοι, ἀλλ᾿ ὁ Πατήρ μου ὁ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς). FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1283D] “Unless someone is reborn . . .”: “Unless someone is born of water and Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (Ἐὰν μή τις γεννηθῇ ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ πνεύματος, οὐ δύναται εἰσελθεῖν εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ Θεοῦ). For γεννηθῇ, Philastrius may seem to have read ἀναγεννηθῇ, as in the Clementines: “Amen, I say to you, unless you are reborn in living water into the name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, you shall by no means enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν, ἐὰν μὴ ἀναγεννηθῆτε ὕδατι ζῶντι εἰς ὄνομα Πατρὸς, Υἱοῦ, καὶ ἁγίου Πνεύματος, οὐ μὴ εἰσέλθητε εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν οὐρανῶν). But Philastrius, when citing scriptural passages from memory, is accustomed to substitute one word for another. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1283D] “Those who said . . .”: “He who says to his father and mother, ‘I have not seen you’ . . . kept your ordinances” (Ὁ λέγων τῷ πατρὶ καὶ τῇ μητρί, Οὐχ ἑώρακά σε . . . ἐφύλαξε τὰ λόγιά σου). FABRIC.]

He did not, of course, praise hatred of one’s birth from parents, but rather contempt for and condemnation in every way of their pagan impiety, when he says: “Unless anyone renounces all that is his, he shall not be worthy of the kingdom of heaven” (Luke 14:23).

[Note: [Col. 1283D–1284B] “One’s birth from parents [is not] to be hated”: τὴν γέννησιν, “birth from parents.” He used *odiendam* from the old verb *odio*, whence Petronius and Apuleius have *odientes*. In *On Interpretation*: “The varieties of speech are those of commanding, narrating, becoming angry, wishing, warning, being enraged, and hating.” See Vossius, *On the Art of Grammar*, book 5, chapter 39. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1284B–C] “He shall not be worthy of the kingdom of heaven.” In Luke 14:33 one reads: “He cannot be my disciple”: Πᾶς ἐξ ὑμῶν ὃς οὐκ ἀποτάσσεται πᾶσι τοῖς ἑαυτοῦ ὑπάρχουσιν, οὐ δύναταί μου εἶναι μαθητής. But the eminent John Mill rightly observed in the prolegomena to his New Testament, §831, that Philastrius cited quite a few passages of Scripture in sense and from memory. FABRIC.]

This blessed Melchizedek, then, though he had been produced from foreign peoples, that is, impious Canaanites, despised the impiety of his parents. Being capable of the divine and heavenly Law, and by his own study, as God’s image, having sought God’s mystery and despised his impious parents, he deserved not only to know Christ the Lord before the Commandment, but also, seeing and understanding, to celebrate his heavenly mystery.

[Note: [Col. 1284C–D] “Being capable of the divine and heavenly Law, and by his own study.” The conjunction *and*, which considerably harms the sense, is absent in the Corbie manuscript. Then, for “God’s mystery,” it reads “Christ’s mystery,” which is better; for shortly afterward he says “his heavenly mystery also,” that is, Christ’s. Yet on the following page, p. 317 of the Hamburg edition, the editions display a notable error: where they have “the fitting meaning of the commandments and circumcision,” the Corbie manuscript rightly has “the fitting meaning of uncircumcision and circumcision.” For “commandments” has no place here, where he discusses the type of the Gentiles and the Jews. Both readings are also commended by a parchment nine hundred years old, sewn into manuscript no. 279 of the Library of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme at Rome. The most learned Joseph Blanchinus, formerly a canon of the Church of Verona and now a priest of the Roman Congregation of the Oratory, distinguished alike for piety and learning, kindly communicated knowledge of it to us in a letter sent to His Eminence Cardinal Quirinus, dated 21 September 1737. GALEARD.]

[Note: [Col. 1283B; 1284D] “Heavenly . . . Christ’s mystery.” FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1284D] “Before the Commandment”: in the state of natural light. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1284D] “He deserved”: this befell him. See above, chapter 132. FABRIC.]

Therefore the Apostle said to the baptized: “But you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit” (Rom. 8:9). Thus at that time Melchizedek and Abraham represented the union in one fellowship of two peoples. The fitting meaning of uncircumcision and circumcision was that Melchizedek should indeed bear the person of Christians, so that we may live and celebrate in all things; while Abraham’s circumcision bore the figure of the Jews, subject to Christ’s faith and serving his heavenly saving mystery, as the blessed Abraham was subject to Melchizedek, the great priest (Gen. 14:18; Ps. 109:4; Heb. 7:1, 21), to whom he did not hesitate to offer tithes from his possessions, as to king and priest of God (Gen. 14:20; Heb. 7:9).

[Note: [Col. 1284D] “But you . . .”: “But you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit” (Ὑμεῖς δὲ οὔκ ἐστε ἐν σαρκὶ, ἀλλ᾿ ἐν πνεύματι). FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1283B; 1284B] “Uncircumcision indeed . . . the fitting meaning . . . to bear.” FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1284B–1285B] “So that we may live and celebrate in all things.” The Lyons edition wrongly has “so that we may not live,” and other editions, “that we may celebrate.” FABRIC.—“So that we may live and celebrate in all things.” Although Fabricius admits that *celebremus* occurs in other editions, including Sichard’s Basle edition, he substituted *celebremur* by his own conjecture; I cannot see how this better suits the passage. The reading of the Corbie manuscript deserves especial consideration here. Although Fabricius acted cautiously in his other notes, this emendation seems quite suspect to me because it removes the Eucharistic type. The undoubtedly true and superior Corbie reading is “so that we may know and celebrate”; the nine-hundred-year-old parchment mentioned above confirms it, reading: “so that we may live and celebrate.” GALEARD.]

[Note: [Col. 1285B] “Tithes.” On royal tithes see the interpreters on 1 Samuel 8:15, 17, and D. Carpzovius, “the blessed one” (τὸν μακαρίτην), on Schickard’s *Royal Law*, p. 269. On priestly tithes, Numbers 18:21; Deuteronomy 18:2; and the writers on tithes cited by me in *Antiquarian Bibliography*, chapter 16, §2. FABRIC.]

This now is the teachability of the Jews: it is subject to us when it is willing to learn, gradually to recognize from us, from the Law and the Prophets, the mysteries of Christ, and in his Passion to hope for heavenly knowledge alike from the Law and the Prophets.

[Note: [Col. 1285B–C] “The Jews’ teachability is now subject to us when it is willing.” The earlier editions wrongly put a stop after “is subject to us,” for the words must be connected with what follows. “The Jews’ teachability” is to be understood of those Jews who do not disdain to bear Christ’s name and embrace Christian rites, or to acknowledge through Christians, from the Law and Prophets, Christ’s mysteries. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1285B] “Unteachability.”]

## CXLIX. HERESY CONCERNING ZECHARIAH THE PROPHET, ON FASTING

There are some who read in Zechariah, where he says: “The fast of the fourth, the fast of the fifth, the fast of the seventh, and the fast of the tenth shall be to the house of Israel for exultation and joy” (Zech. 8:9). What then? If someone wishes to fast the whole week, or many months, will he incur condemnation? Far from it. Rather, he will have greater praise, as many prophets did and as very many righteous persons do daily. But when he speaks of four fasts, he ordains, as it were, four days to be fasted. He has not, however, told us of any particular month or year; rather, he proclaimed it absolutely, so that we might recognize the mysteries of Christianity announced in these four fasts.

[Note: [Col. 1285C] “The fast of the fourth”: compare, besides St. Jerome, John Selden, chapter 8 of *On the Civil Year of the Jews*.—The fast of the fourth: on the seventeenth day of the fourth month, Tammuz (July), because Moses broke the tablets and the city was captured by Nebuchadnezzar. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1285C] “The fast of the fifth”: on the ninth day of the fifth month, Ab (August), because of the burning of the Temple. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1285C] “The fast of the seventh”: on the third of Tishri, the seventh month (October), because Gedaliah was murdered by the Ishmaelites, as Josephus relates in the unpublished *Hypomnesticon*, chapter 127. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1285D] “The fast of the tenth”: on the tenth day of the tenth month, Tebeth (January), because news reached the Jews dwelling in Babylon of the calamities that had befallen Jerusalem. FABRIC.]

For four fasts are celebrated in the Church through the year: first at the Nativity, then at Easter, third at Epiphany, fourth at Pentecost. At the Nativity of the Lord Savior one must fast; then in the Lenten fast of Easter; and likewise at the Ascension into heaven, after Easter on the fortieth day, and then for ten days up to Pentecost. This is what the blessed Apostles afterward did after the Ascension, persevering in fasts and prayers, as it is written; and they deserved at Pentecost to receive the fullness of the divine Spirit and the perfection of power. Thus, when the outpouring of the divine Spirit flowed upon them and they were already equipped with heavenly weapons, having put aside all the doubt in which they had formerly been, they hastened daily thereafter to become invincible teachers and glorious martyrs of the Lord himself, teaching Jews and pagans and everywhere proving to them from the Law and the Prophets, by the testimonies of the prophets, that Christ the Lord is eternal with the Father; and proclaiming to the world his most saving bodily presence.

[Note: [Col. 1285D–1286B] “Four fasts in the Church.” Although it is quite clear that these four fasts did not prevail widely throughout the whole Church not only in earlier times nearer the apostolic age, but not even in Philastrius’ time, as John Dallaeus shows in book 4, chapter 7 of *On Fasts*, this passage of Philastrius shows that Blondel is mistaken in observing, on the letter of Pseudo-Calixtus, p. 256, that Leo the Great was the first distinctly to mention the fast of the consecrated four seasons. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1286B] “First at the Nativity”: this is what Leo calls the winter fast, and others the fast of the Lord’s Advent; see Theophilus Raynaudus, vol. 11 of his works, p. 479. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1286B] “At Easter.” Jerome alone admits this, in Letter 54 to Marcellus: “We fast one Lent throughout the year, according to apostolic tradition, at a season suitable to us; they”—the followers of Montanus—“observe three Lents in the year, as though there had been three Saviors who suffered. This is not because it is impermissible to fast throughout the whole year except at Pentecost, but because it is one thing to offer a gift out of necessity and another by free choice.” FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1286B–1287C] “Third at Epiphany.” Since Philastrius mentions this fast after the pre-Easter fast and before Pentecost, and himself below explains it as the fast of the Ascension, Epiphany here must mean Ascension. On the fast, or Rogations, before the feast of the Ascension, introduced in Gaul only around A.D. 500 by Claudianus Mamertus, see Gregory of Tours, *History* 2.31; Alcimus Avitus’ homily on Rogations; and John Savaron’s notes on Sidonius Apollinaris, book 5, letter 14. Dallaeus, indeed, judging on p. 761, says that Philastrius writes so obscurely and confusedly about fasts here that he seems rather to squeak than to speak, and confesses that he cannot understand his words: “He consistently omits the fast of the seventh month. What he places at Epiphany is, if I am not mistaken, unheard-of. What he locates at the Nativity, unless ‘Nativity’ is taken for the days preceding it, or for what we commonly call Advent, is likewise utterly absurd. Finally, what does this man mean—or certainly say?—that one must fast at the Ascension and for the following ten days down to Pentecost? No one but this man has philosophized about fasts in this way; so far were the others from following such practices that they all thought fasting throughout Pentecost sinful.” FABRIC.—Here Philastrius uses “Epiphany” to mean the Ascension, as Fabricius rightly observed, although elsewhere this name commonly denotes the adoration of the Magi, as Cotelerius indicates on *Apostolic Constitutions* 5.13, p. 312. Philastrius himself is adequate witness that the fast “at Epiphany,” that is, at the Ascension, was one of the four fasts then celebrated in the Church, although Dallaeus, cited by Fabricius, criticizes Philastrius on this account and calls it an unheard-of thing. Moreover, somewhat below Philastrius also mentions a fast according to the four seasons of the year, observed by some, of which there is clear mention in Leo the Great, Sermon 18. I append Philastrius’ words from p. 321: “Others think that Scripture spoke according to each year’s four seasons.” The Lyons edition reads: “Others think that Scripture spoke according to each year’s four fasts”; it omits *seasons* and adds *fasts*. Compare Irenaeus, fragment of the Letter to Pope Victor, ed. Massuet, p. 340, where he says that diversity of fasts commends unity of faith. Elmenhorst cites this passage of Philastrius in his note on Minucius Felix, p. 19, Leiden edition of 1652. GALEARD.]

[Note: [Col. 1287C–D] “Fourth at Pentecost.” Other writers place this fast in the week after Pentecost, or after Pentecost’s octave. See Cotelerius on book 5 of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, chapter 20, p. 326. Conversely, most people even in Philastrius’ age considered it sinful to fast during Pentecost itself—that is, throughout the whole fifty days from Easter—as I have already noted from Jerome; add the striking testimony of St. Athanasius published by the celebrated Montfaucon in the *Coislinian Library*, p. 112. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1287D] “Persevering in fasts and prayers.” There is no explicit mention of fasts in Acts 1:14: προσευχῇ καὶ δεήσει προσκαρτεροῦντες, “persevering in prayer and supplication.” Yet fasts and prayers are joined in Acts 14:23: προσευξάμενοι μετὰ νηστειῶν, “having prayed with fasts.” FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1287D] “All doubt put aside, in which they had previously been.” This refers to Peter’s doubt—or rather, denial—in Matthew 26:70 ff., and to the denial of the other disciples; likewise verse 56. FABRIC.]

Others think that Scripture spoke according to the four seasons of each year.

[Note: [Col. 1287D] “According to the four seasons of the year.” Leo the Great, Sermon 18: “We celebrate the spring fast in Lent, the summer fast at Pentecost, the autumn fast in the seventh month, and the winter fast in this tenth month,” December. FABRIC.]

Others spoke of Noah: when he heard and believed (Gen. 6:13 ff.; 7:5, 7; 8:18); then when he made the ark; afterward when he entered it; and fourth, when he came out of the ark. Others think that Scripture spoke of the Israelites: because when the people first heard through Moses in Egypt and believed (Exod. 5 ff.), they were delivered from Pharaoh and the Egyptians; then because they went out of Egypt (Exod. 12 ff.); third, because they went up the mountain (Exod. 19 ff.) and received the Law from the Lord Savior; fourth, because they entered the land of promise (Josh. 1 ff.). But not all entered, as it is written (Num. 14:30; 32:12), but only two, Joshua and Caleb, as Scripture says.

[Note: [Col. 1287C] “In Exodus, because every . . . comes out”: every person who believes in Christ God comes out, liberated from darkness. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1288C] “Third, because in . . . all the things which are there”: in Leviticus he offers various sacrifices, all of which are mysteries of Christianity. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1287D–1288C] “Scripture spoke of Israel.” Others of the Jews think that the passage cited from Zechariah concerning the four fasts corresponds to the four events that Philastrius immediately recalls from Moses as having happened to Israel. FABRIC.]

Others said: These are the Church’s four fasts in the four books of Moses. For first, in Genesis, God made all things and man, as it is written. Second, in Exodus, every person who believes in Christ God comes out, liberated from darkness. Third, in Leviticus, he offers various sacrifices, which are all mysteries of Christianity. Fourth, after the offering of spiritual gifts, in the book of Numbers every faithful person deserves to be enrolled, as the Lord too says: “Rejoice, because your names are written in the book of heaven” (Luke 10:20). Therefore David also says concerning the Jews: “Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not be written with the righteous” (Ps. 68:29). And again: “Those who believe in you shall be enrolled in your book” (Ps. 138:16).

[Note: [Col. 1288C] “Rejoice . . . in the book of heaven”: “Rejoice because your names have been written in the heavens” (Χαίρετε ὅτι τὰ ὀνόματα ὑμῶν ἐγράφη ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς), “in heaven,” which Philastrius renders “in the book of heaven.” FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1288C] “Let them be blotted out . . .”: “Let them be wiped out from the book of the living, and let them not be written with the righteous” (ἐξαλειφθήτωσαν ἐκ βιβλίου ζώντων, καὶ μετὰ δικαίων μὴ γραφήτωσαν). FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1288C] “And in [your] book . . .”: “And all shall be written in your book” (Καὶ ἐπὶ τὸ βιβλίον σου πάντες γραφήσονται). FABRIC.]

We must also understand these fasts in relation to the four Gospels: patriarchs, prophets, priests, and apostles, which must be fulfilled in us. For first the faith of the patriarchs is proclaimed; then the strength of the prophets; third, the labor of the priests; fourth, the perfection of the apostles’ unconquered contest. These various virtues, joined together in their respective periods, grow strong mutually and furnish to people who desire and receive them various joys of delight.

[Note: [Col. 1288C–D] “In the four Gospels.” So that Philastrius may seek support and rationale everywhere for his own number four, he invokes the Gospels also. The ancients frequently commend their fourfold number by similar mystical and allegorical arguments, as I have shown by citing their own words in the *Apocryphal Code of the New Testament*, p. 382, and vol. 2, pp. 555, 735. I add one passage from Rabanus Maurus, *On the Universe*, book 4, chapter 1, vol. 1 of his works, p. 83: “The four soldiers who made for themselves four parts of Jesus’ garments prefigured the four parts of the world which divided among themselves Christ’s sayings, as it is written in Psalm 119: ‘I shall rejoice over your sayings as one who finds spoils.’” Rabanus gathers much more to this effect at the beginning of that book, p. 77; see Hardouin, *Councils*, vol. 3, p. 1983 ff. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1288D] “Patriarchs, prophets, priests, and apostles.” On this fourfold division see chapter 139, and below chapters 155 and 156. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1288D] “Various joys of delight for those desiring and receiving them.” This should be read instead of *cupientibus*, “desiring.” Below, in the following chapter: “The various gifts of grace, bestowed by the same one in various periods according to human willingness and the capacity of those who desire”; where there is more to this effect. Immediately below in the same chapter: “the diverse outpoured grace bestowed on those receiving and seeking.” FABRIC.]

## CL. HERESY CONCERNING SOLOMON’S WIVES AND CONCUBINES

[Col. 1289A]

There are heretics who, when they read concerning Solomon, “sixty queens, eighty concubines, and maidens without number” (Song 6:8), think that he set forth this number of women, maidens, and concubines on account of actual women. Thinking thus, they are judged barren—or rather, as impious pagans and unlearned, untaught Jews—because they do not know that these are rational and intelligible things declared by the same author: diverse gifts of grace which were to be shown as coming to humankind in Christ’s majesty and power, bestowed by him in different times according to the willing disposition of persons and the capacity of those who desire. He does not deny equal grace; rather, according to what human willingness could receive, it is made known, the Lord himself granting and bestowing it on those who seek diligently. For the blessed Apostle Peter says: “In truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons” (Acts 10:34). Likewise the Apostle Paul: “God,” he says, “does not accept a man’s person” (Rom. 2:11). Therefore, according to what each person desires, so it is granted and bestowed to him daily by Christ God.

[Note: [Col. 1289C] “Sixty.” The number was later increased: for in 1 Kings 11:3 there are seven hundred queens and three hundred concubines. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1289C] “Maidens”: innumerable virgins. Compare Wagenseil, pp. 397 ff., on *The Fiery Darts of Satan*. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1289C] “Rational and intelligible”: νοητά, things to be referred from sensible matters to a higher understanding. Below in chapter 149 he calls reason “intelligible.” FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1289C] “According to human willingness and capacity.” At the end of the preceding chapter: “They furnish various joys of delight to those desiring and receiving.” FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1289C] “In truth”: “Truly I understand that God is not a respecter of persons” (Ἐπ᾿ ἀληθείας καταλαμβάνομαι ὅτι οὐκ ἔστι προσωπολήπτης ὁ Θεός), from Deuteronomy 10:17 and 2 Chronicles 19:7. See also 1 Peter 1:17. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1289C] “God does not accept a person”: Οὐ γάρ ἐστι προσωποληψία παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ. Add Galatians 2:6. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1289B–D] “According to what each person receives and desires; thus it is granted to him by Christ God.” The Helmstedt edition wrongly reads *tribuetur*, “will be granted.” FABRIC.—Here again Fabricius criticizes the Helmstedt edition for wrongly reading *tribuetur*, although the Basle edition of Sichard, 1528, has the same reading; in other places too we find that Fabricius did not inspect it closely enough. The same is entirely true below at heresy 153, where he blames the Helmstedt edition for wrongly having *praedicentes* instead of *praedicantes*; but there too the Basle edition has the same reading as Helmstedt. Conversely, at heresy 155 he replaces *monstraret* with *monstraretur*, without mentioning the Basle edition, which has not *monstraret* but *monstraretur*. At the present passage, which Fabricius rightly corrected, the Corbie manuscript likewise has, omitting the conjunction: “thus it is granted to him by Christ God.” GALEARD.]

Thus diverse ranks and diverse glories are announced to us by Solomon. In the Commandment, the Law, and Christ’s grace, all the gifts of rank bestowed upon peoples in the first, second, and final periods according to differing merits—that is, upon the earlier people, then upon the Jews, and thirdly upon Christians—are, when we are taught by those earlier people who existed before the Jews, seen by us daily in Christ’s presence as diverse outpoured grace bestowed upon those who receive and seek it.

[Note: [Col. 1289D] “In the Commandment, Law, and Christ’s grace.” This is Philastrius’ familiar division; by “Commandment” he understands natural light before the Mosaic Law. See above, chapters 110, 136, 148, 150, 153. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1289D–1290A] “When we are taught.” The sense of this obscure passage seems to me to be this: when we are taught what diverse gifts were bestowed in those three different periods, we perceive that all these are poured out daily in Christ’s presence—that is, among Christians—upon different persons according to each one’s desire and capacity. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1290C] “Likewise in Christ’s presence.” Earlier editions nonsensically have *et de* instead of *itidem*. FABRIC.—Fabricius notes that earlier editions have the meaningless *et de* for *itidem*. The Basle edition indeed has this; the Lyons edition, omitting the conjunction, reads *in Christi praesentia de*; the Corbie manuscript, *in Christi praesentiam et de Christi*. Perhaps one should read *in Christi praesentiam, et de Christi praesentia*; but Fabricius’ correction still seems preferable. By “Christ’s presence” Philastrius means the Gospel age, as Fabricius rightly notes below in note o; this is evident also from other passages: chapter 149, “the unbelief of the Jews in the future age of Christ’s presence”; chapter 109, “that in Christ’s presence what had been foretold by them above the Law might be recognized”; chapter 75, “what was to be greater and better in the Lord’s presence”; chapter 136, “that heavenly merits might be manifested in Christ’s presence.” GALEARD.]

For it is clear that some souls are called to rule, others to union, others to union at the growth of a more perfect age in the faith of Christ the Lord, as the Apostle says: “He who is joined to Christ the Lord is one body” (1 Cor. 6:7). Where the title “queen” is used, the eminent loftiness of nobility in the heavenly kingdom is revealed; and the Lord too, preaching the calling of many, announces that the election of few is to come. In them a threefold rank of virtue shines out also in the Gospel, when the Lord says to the man: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor; come, follow me, and you will have treasure in heaven.” “But he went away sorrowful,” it says, as is written (Matt. 19:21–22).

[Note: [Col. 1290C–D] “To rule, to union, to union at the growth of a more perfect age.” These correspond to Solomon’s queens, concubines, and maidens. Below he calls the three grades the perfect, those following, and those who will follow, and assigns to them kingdom, paradise, and life. Earlier editions have *perfectionis*, “of perfection,” for *perfectioris*, “more perfect.” FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1290D] “One body”: “He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (Ὁ κολλώμενος Κυρίῳ ἓν πνεῦμά ἐστιν). As in chapter 26, Philastrius, citing the passage from memory, put “one body” for “one spirit.” FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1290D] “If you wish to be . . .”: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell your possessions and give to the poor; come, follow me, and you will have treasure in heaven” (Εἰ θέλεις τέλειος εἶναι, ὕπαγε, πώλησόν σου τὰ ὑπάρχοντα καὶ δὸς πτωχοῖς, καὶ δεῦρο ἀκολούθει μοι, καὶ ἕξεις θησαυρὸν ἐν οὐρανῷ). Philastrius has again changed the order of the words while citing the passage from memory. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1290D] “But he went away sorrowful”: Ἀπῆλθε λυπούμενος. The Gospel of the Hebrews in Origen, Homily 8 on Matthew: “But the rich man began to scratch his head, and it did not please him.” FABRIC.]

Therefore, although this occurred previously in a general way according to the division of times and peoples, nevertheless in Christ’s presence a threefold grace and rank shines forth, so that some may be shown perfect, others following, others yet to follow. They will not find the heavenly kingdom by one and the same rank of dignity, but according to their faith, labor, and varied struggles, will obtain a fitting reward, as the Lord says: “There are many dwelling places in my Father’s house” (John 14:2). Therefore David praises in every way the soul called to rule, teaching: “The queen stood at your right hand” (Ps. 44:9). He exhorts another also to follow: “Hear, daughter, and see; forget your father’s house, and the king shall desire your beauty” (ibid., 10). It is therefore reasonable to recognize that some in the future will be assigned to the kingdom (Matt. 25:34), others to paradise (Luke 23:43), others to life (Matt. 19:17), and to forgiveness of sins (Luke 24:47). These things are not denied to those now running and willing as they ought; but to those who are negligent and do not run rightly, they will not be granted by the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 1290D] “Many dwelling places.” Our author also cited this passage above in chapter 82 concerning differences of degrees of glory in eternal life, just as in chapter 125 he affirms differences of punishments and stripes. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1291C] “To rule.” FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1291C] “The queen stood”: “The queen stands at your right hand” (Παρέστιν ἡ βασίλισσα ἐκ δεξιῶν σου). FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1291C] “Hear, daughter . . .”: “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house” (Ἄκουσον, θύγατερ, καὶ ἴδε, καὶ κλίνον τὸ οὖς σου, καὶ ἐπιλάθου τοῦ λαοῦ σου, καὶ τοῦ οἴκου τοῦ πατρός σου). FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1291C] “As is reasonable.” So in heresy 98, “therefore it is of no reason,” and 106, “how will this be reasonable?” FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1291D] “It is not denied to those running and willing.” This alludes to Romans 9:16, on which see above at chapter 128. FABRIC.]

[Note: [Col. 1291D] “Those negligent.” See the note on chapter 124. FABRIC.]

## CLI

[Note: [Col. 1291C] This heresy, absent from the printed editions, is found in the Sangermanensis manuscript. We have printed it and the preceding remaining heresies as they stand in the cited manuscript, not free from errors.]

There is a heresy which thinks that Joshua son of Nun circumcised the Jewish people with stone knives. Neither the nature of things nor force or reason supports this; for the Jews could more easily have been endangered than cured. Although nothing is impossible according to God’s power, nevertheless the nature of things does not admit, nor reason persuade, certain things.

Therefore, lest they say that the Jews were circumcised with stone knives, let them refer this to the exceedingly hard and stony minds of pagans, which had formerly been devoted to impiety but afterward, believing in the Lord and having lost their stony mind, deserved—now capable of heavenly doctrine—to be circumcised in mind by the word of God and to circumcise the Jews; that is, to instill in them Christ’s saving knowledge from the Law and Prophets, announcing and proving it everywhere. For although the Jews are daily circumcised by those who were previously Gentiles—that is, they are taught from the Law and Prophets concerning faith in Christ the Lord, the Savior—yet if they too believe, they shall receive the remedy of salvation. But if they persist in the hardness of their stony mind, they shall be held under eternal judgment.

Therefore the Lord, in answer to their stubborn contradiction, said that their sons—that is, pagans—would themselves be their judges and teachers: namely, the people of the Gentiles, formerly occupied with a stony mind, but afterward through faith in Christ deserving to attain saving knowledge. But Israel, running according to the Law, as it is written, could not attain the power of the Law, because it hastened to run not from faith but from works. For Jacob says that he himself will be the hope of the Gentiles, not of the Jews. Therefore all the Gentiles must first believe; then at last the Jews must learn from those Gentiles and hear the doctrine of Christ the Lord from the Law and Prophets, and thus acquiesce, so that it may be fulfilled: “until the fullness of the Gentiles enters, and thus all Israel shall be saved,” as it is written. And another prophet says: “Take away from them the heart of stone, Lord, and give them a heart of flesh.” And the Lord says: “If these keep silent, the stones will cry out.”

[Note: [Col. 1291D] “Of the Jews”: it seems one should read “the Jews.” FABRIC.]

## CLII. HERESY CONCERNING THE BREATH WHICH ADAM RECEIVED
Another heresy holds that the breath which Adam received (Gen. 2:7) was exactly the same as that granted by Christ to the Apostles after the Resurrection. It fails to understand that the breath is a grace of some slight power, belonging first of all to many in hearing the Law of God; whereas the Spirit is the fullness of perfection.

> [Note: Col. 1291D. “And he breathed into his face the breath of life.” FABRIC.]

The breath is therefore given from infancy and to catechumens; but the Spirit, in the increase of doctrine and faith, and in the full grace of God of saving baptism, is given so that one may understand and may now be able to attain greater knowledge.

> [Note: Col. 1291D. “Granted”: John 20:22, ἐνεφύσησε, “he breathed upon”; Cicero’s word *inhalavit*, “he breathed into,” would render it correctly. FABRIC.]  
> [Note: Col. 1292C. “It is a breathing” (*spiramentum est*).]

Therefore, after baptism the person baptized in the Trinity receives not the Spirit as did the Apostles, but the breath. For the breath is common to all; whereas the Spirit belongs to the few who are faithful, believing, and learning—those who, as it were, advance from honour to honour and from glory to greater glory, toward heavenly knowledge and grace. As the Apostle says, we proceed “from faith to faith” (Rom. 1:17), and hasten to go forth “from glory to glory” (2 Cor. 3:18).

> [Note: Col. 1291D. “From faith to faith”: Ἐκ πίστεως εἰς πίστιν. FABRIC.]  
> [Note: Col. 1291D. “From glory to glory”: Ἀπὸ δόξης εἰς δόξαν. FABRIC.]  
> [Note: Col. 1291D. “Therefore after baptism.” As before baptism he grants catechumens, so in baptism he bestows upon all the baptized that common grace, reserving a more exalted rank thereafter for the holy Apostles and devout believers. FABRIC.]  
> [Note: Col. 1292C. “After baptism, he receives the Spirit as did the Apostles, no longer the breath.”]

Therefore he himself says: “The first man was earthly, from the earth; the second man was heavenly, from heaven” (1 Cor. 15:47), so that nature may not be found wholly alien and deprived of Christ’s gift—that is, not even the catechumen—and so that faith, doctrine, earnest endeavour, and an excellent life may be recognized as abounding in the will of the few faithful and desirous persons. For the Lord says: “To him who has, it shall be given, and more shall be added to him; but from him who does not have, even what he seems to have shall be taken away” (Matt. 13:12; 25:29). This happened to the Jew, and likewise to many others.

> [Note: Col. 1292C. “The first man”: Ὁ πρῶτος ἄνθρωπος ἐκ γῆς κοϊκὸς, ὁ δεύτερος ἄνθρωπος ὁ Κύριος ἐξ οὐρανοῦ, “The first man is from earth, earthy; the second man, the Lord, is from heaven.” Likewise “heavenly from heaven,” as Philastrius has it, is found in Ambrose, Jerome, and others; and a very large number omit Κύριος, “the Lord.” On this, besides John Mill, see what the late Dr Kortholt noted in his book *On Various Editions of Scripture*, p. 75 ff. FABRIC.]  
> [Note: Col. 1292D. “Nature.” As in the preceding chapter he had made three grades—of the perfect, those following, and those about to follow—so here he places first nature, succeeded in the second grade by faith and doctrine, and finally, in the third, by zeal and an outstanding life abounding in the will of a few faithful persons and those who desire—or perhaps “receive,” *capientium*, as in chapters 149 and 150. FABRIC.]  
> [Note: Col. 1292D. “To him who has, it shall be given”: Ὅστις ἔχει, δοθήσεται αὐτῷ, καὶ περισσευθήσεται, “Whoever has, to him it shall be given, and he shall abound.” FABRIC.]  
> [Note: Col. 1292D. “Even what he seems to have”: from Luke 8:18, καὶ ὃ δοκεῖ ἔχειν, ἀρθήσεται ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ, “even what he seems to have shall be taken from him.” FABRIC.]

## CLIII. HERESY CONCERNING THE MEASURING LINE IN THE PROPHET ZECHARIAH

[Col. 1292C]

There is a heresy which, when it hears in the prophet Zechariah of the surveyor’s measuring line—of which David also spoke—namely, that an angel holding it went to measure Jerusalem, supposes that Scripture said this literally. Yet it was not Jerusalem, which was to be handed over to enemies, that was to be measured; rather, through the angel there was announced the coming election of believers rightly, and of the few perfectly. As it is said: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20:16; 22:14).

> [Note: Col. 1292D. “Of which David also [spoke].” Villalpandus, vol. II, p. 179, thinks that Philastrius lapsed in memory and intended to name Ezekiel instead of David, looking to Ezek. 40:3. But perhaps Ps. 60:6 [LXX] and 108:7 was in his mind: τὴν κοιλάδα τῶν σκηνῶν διαμετρήσω, “I shall measure the valley of tents.” FABRIC.]  
> [Note: Col. 1292C. “And blessed David the prophet had also declared.”]  
> [Note: Col. 1292D. “That an angel, holding it, went.” Zech. 2:1: ἰδοὺ ἀνὴρ καὶ ἐν τῇ χειρὶ αὐτοῦ σχοινίον γεωμετρικόν … διαμετρῆσαι τὴν Ἱερουσαλήμ, “Behold, a man, and in his hand a surveyor’s line … to measure Jerusalem.” FABRIC.]  
> [Note: Col. 1293C. “The election of believers rightly, and of the few perfectly.” Villalpandus and Cotelerius, *Monumenta*, III, p. 524, print *electio*, “election,” in place of Philastrius’ *lectio*, “reading,” although it is well known that *lectio* for *electio*, *lectus* for *electus*, and *legere* for *eligere* were common among the best writers. Suetonius, *Augustus*, ch. 35: “He restored the excessive number of senators to its former measure and distinction by two selections”; and ch. 54: “Antistius Labeo, at the selection of the senate, when one man chose another man.” Yet below our author also writes *electio*, and a copyist could easily have omitted the letter *e* in *lectio* after *perfecte*. FABRIC.]  
> [Note: Col. 1293D. “Many are called”: Πολλοὶ εἰσι κλητοί, ὀλίγοι δὲ ἐκλεκτοί, “Many are called, but few are chosen.” FABRIC.]

Jerusalem, therefore, was measured by the surveyor’s line: that is, election was proclaimed in the world—first, before Christ, under the few; and after the faith of Christ, through the begetting of the few for the catholic faith and truth. The Apostle also says: “There must be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest” (1 Cor. 11:19).

> [Note: Col. 1293D. “And after the faith of Christ, the election of the few, begetting [persons] for the catholic faith.” The Corbie manuscript reads *catholicae fidei gignendae*, “to be begotten for the catholic faith”; but I would prefer *catholicae fidei gignendorum*, “of those to be begotten for the catholic faith,” for this final syllable, written in abbreviation, could easily have been omitted by an unskilled copyist. Thus, at the beginning of the following page, where he has: “For before by the prophet that which was then among the few,” unless the preposition is added and one reads “For before **by** the prophet,” the sense cannot stand at all. Philastrius means that what was then among the few was thus announced by the prophet; this will readily persuade anyone who examines the passage, since shortly before he had said: “the election of the few perfectly was announced through the angel as to come.” GALEARD.]  
> [Note: Col. 1293C. “For the catholic faith and truth.”]  
> [Note: Col. 1294C. “There must be …”: Δεῖ γὰρ αἱρέσεις ἐν ὑμῖν εἶναι, ἵνα οἱ δόκιμοι φανεροὶ γένωνται ἐν ὑμῖν, “For there must also be heresies among you, so that those approved may become manifest among you.” FABRIC.]

Since the hereditary cord is joined together by a threefold power—that is, of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—this conjunction is received in one and the same faith and belief. When the unity, which is to be joined and worshipped, of equality and power, is known by the Catholic Church, it is not proclaimed as a substance differing in majesty or quality, as certain heretics suppose.

The Lord also deigned to say: “Do you think that, when the Son of Man comes, he will find faith on the earth?” (Luke 18:8). For both what was then among the few had previously been foretold by the Prophet, and it was likewise announced that after Christ’s presence, passion, and resurrection, and his divine pronouncement, they would become transgressors. Thus there are heretics today who, departing from the Holy Spirit or from the Son, err daily by proclaiming an unequal diversity of majesty and power.

> [Note: Col. 1294C. “A cord joined with threefold power”: τὸ σπαρτίον ἔντριτον, “the threefold cord,” Eccles. 4:12. FABRIC.]  
> [Note: Col. 1294C. “Do you think [that] the Son of Man?” Πλὴν ὁ Υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐλθὼν ἄρα εὑρήσει πίστιν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς; “Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will he indeed find faith upon the earth?” FABRIC.]

In this, therefore, we must acknowledge that the cord, as Solomon says (Eccles. 4:12), “threefold is not broken”; and this too must be believed by us: that the Son and likewise the Holy Spirit are of divine and proper substance, joined to the Father in all things, and that they must be known and worshipped by all.

In this conjunction of baptism the Saviour also deigned to strengthen us, commanding: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” By joining the Son to the Father, and the Spirit with the Son and the Father, we recognize that we shall attain this salvation, because we know that no remedy of salvation will come to humankind from any other source than this faith.

> [Note: Col. 1294D. “Go, baptize”: Πορευθέντες μαθητεύσατε πάντα τὰ ἔθνη βαπτίζοντες αὐτοὺς εἰς τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ Πατρὸς καὶ τοῦ Υἱοῦ, καὶ τοῦ ἁγίου Πνεύματος, “Go, make disciples of all nations, baptizing them into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” Philastrius, as usual, omits certain words. FABRIC.]

Therefore we rejoice in this conjunction of the holy and adorable Trinity, in which our father Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, the prophets, priests, judges, Apostles alike, and evangelists preaching deserved to attain angelic dignity. In it the Catholic Church also exults, preaching and teaching this every day, and, by the same proclamation, destroying every pagan impiety and Jewish iniquity, exults daily with every joy.

> [Note: Col. 1294D. “Preaching.” The Helmstedt manuscript corruptly has *praedicentes*, “foretelling.” FABRIC.]  
> [Note: Col. 1294D. “Angelic dignity.” Above, ch. 137. FABRIC.]

For although the threefold cord should first be understood as the Commandment, then the Law in the intervening period, and then the grace of the Saviour, it is also of no small benefit if someone wishes to understand it as faith, hope, and charity, as the blessed Apostle said (1 Cor. 13:13). In this also there is understanding of no small importance for the wiser and for many who desire spiritual things.

> [Note: Col. 1294D. “Of the Commandment, the Law, and the Saviour’s Grace.” The three economies: pre-Mosaic, Jewish, and Christian; on these see chapters 110, 136, 148, 150, and 156. FABRIC.]

## CLIV

> [Note: Col. 1293C. This heresy also, absent from the printed editions, is found in the manuscript codex of Saint-Germain; and, like the others, is strewn with errors. FABRIC.]

There are certain heretics who hold concerning blessed Elijah that ravens brought him meat for food in the evening and bread in the morning. They do not consider that the holy and most blessed prophet never ate flesh, he who had despised every such food by voluntary abstinence; and for this reason he deserved to obtain from God the honour of so great a dignity, that he was taken aloft into Paradise, where he was placed with all the saints.

Now if someone should speak of bread, there is sometimes a reasonable explanation for the ravens’ bringing it to him; but concerning flesh it is found incongruous. For in this the beastly cruelty of the men pursuing the most blessed prophet was displayed; but in the birds—that is, the ravens—only gentleness and mildness were shown. These birds lacked human reason; they were not rational images of God, but birds created merely as sentient creatures like beasts. Yet in those birds, to the reproach of the Jewish people and of the king who, by their most wicked will, pursued the prophet, there was shown an awareness and gentleness of feeling implanted in the operation of so great a ministry which they displayed daily to the blessed prophet. Thus in those birds there was found, as it were, a certain rationality granted through an impulse of gentleness.

For all such creatures made by the Lord are subject to humankind, as to a king and rational lord, over beasts, birds, and serpents, as is shown written in the book of Genesis. The transmitted wording, *urbium versitatis*, is corrupt or otherwise materially uncertain.

## CLV. HERESY DRAWN FROM THE PROPHET ISAIAH CONCERNING THE CHERUBIM AND SERAPHIM

[Col. 1294C]

There is also a heresy which, when it reads in the prophet Isaiah that the Cherubim and Seraphim, two living creatures endowed with six wings, covered the face of God with two, his feet with two, and with two cried aloud in lofty voice, praising God, is greatly troubled. Now seeking the historical sense, now investigating the intelligible meaning, it is wearied by various uncertainty.

> [Note: Col. 1294C. “There is a heresy.”]  
> [Note: Col. 1294D. “Cherubim and Seraphim, two living creatures.” In Isaiah 6:2 there is mention only of two Seraphim: καὶ Σεραφὶμ εἱστήκεισαν κύκλῳ αὐτοῦ, ἓξ πτέρυγες τῷ ἑνί, “And Seraphim stood around him; each had six wings.” FABRIC.]  
> [Note: Col. 1294D. “With two [they covered] the face of God.” Rather, “their faces,” as “their feet.” Yet our author also says below: “they covered the face and feet of the Lord”; and again: “lest, when he says the face and feet of the Lord are covered …” FABRIC.]  
> [Note: Col. 1295C. “They are greatly troubled … seeking.”]  
> [Note: Col. 1295C. “Investigating the intelligible sense … they are wearied.”]

Yet even according to the letter there is no small benefit, and according to the intelligible meaning the heavenly knowledge of Christ resounds. For, according to the letter first, Scripture teaches that God is invisible, condemning everywhere pagan impiety, since their impious scriptures proclaim him visible and composite. It further taught this also lest the Jews themselves, veiled in equal blindness like the impious Gentiles, should perish through corrupted understandings.

> [Note: Col. 1296C. “The intelligible meaning.”]  
> [Note: Col. 1296C. “The heavenly knowledge [of Christ].”]

But here also the unbelief of the Jews in the future time of Christ’s presence, and the veiling of the mystery, had to be announced: veiled in excessive blindness, they were thereafter to believe neither the prophet nor the Lord himself, when he was sent and openly preached to the people: “You shall hear with hearing, and shall not understand; and seeing you shall see, and shall not perceive” (Isa. 6:9; Matt. 13:14).

> [Note: Col. 1295C. “And you shall not understand”: Ἀκοῇ ἀκούσετε, καὶ οὐ μὴ συνῆτε· καὶ βλέποντες βλέψετε, καὶ οὐ μὴ ἴδητε. Philastrius, in his customary fashion, omits, alters, and transposes some words of sacred Scripture. *Intendere*, “to attend,” is used for “to understand,” according to declining Latin usage; hence Italian *intendere* and French *entendre*. FABRIC. The character of the Italian language is also discernible in Philastrius elsewhere above, chapters 132 and 93, where he used *condescensio* for what we Italians call *condescendenza* or *condescensione*, Latin *indulgentia*, “forbearance.” GALEARD.]

For, covered in darkness, they were not to recognize the light of eternal salvation—that is, the bodily presence of Christ—as indeed came to pass. Teaching this, the Apostle affirmed that a veil remains placed upon their hearts to this day (2 Cor. 3:15), and that it will not be removed until they believe Christ to be the Saviour. But when they are converted—that is, when they believe in Christ the Lord—the veil will be taken away from their hearts.

> [Note: Col. 1295C. “A veil …”: Ἀλλ’ ἕως σήμερον … κάλυμμα ἐπὶ τὴν καρδίαν αὐτῶν κεῖται, “But until today … a veil lies upon their heart.” FABRIC.]  
> [Note: Col. 1295C. “But when they are converted.” Philastrius does not seem to have been remote from the opinion of those who, with Tertullian, Origen, Hilary, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, Gregory of Nyssa, Basil, Chrysostom, Cyril of Alexandria, Theophylact, Oecumenius, Peter Chrysologus, Primasius, and others, persuaded themselves that a great conversion of the Jews was still to be expected. Their passages were collected by Dr Christian Dreier in his dissertation *On the Conversion of the Jews*, and by the late Dr John Gunther in German sermons published on the Epistle to the Romans. FABRIC.]

That the two living creatures announced are the Cherubim and Seraphim—that is, the Law and the Prophets, witnesses of Christ and teachers of the world—is not doubtful. They covered the face and feet of the Lord, either because the mystery was taught in parables, likenesses, and riddles, as it is written: “I shall open my mouth in parables” (Ps. 77:2; Matt. 13:35). And David says: “Unveil my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders of your law” (Ps. 118:18). And the Apostle says: “The Father revealed his Son to me” (Gal. 1:16), that is, showing him from the Law and the Prophets.

> [Note: Col. 1295D. “The face and feet of the Lord.” Contrary to the sense of Isaiah, as I have already noted above. FABRIC.]  
> [Note: Col. 1295D. “I shall open my mouth”: Ἀνοίξω ἐν παραβολαῖς τὸ στόμα μου, “I shall open my mouth in parables.” FABRIC.]  
> [Note: Col. 1295D. “Unveil my eyes”: Ἀποκάλυψον τοὺς ὀφθαλμούς μου, καὶ κατανοήσω τὰ θαυμάσια ἐκ τοῦ νόμου σου, “Unveil my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders from your law.” FABRIC.]  
> [Note: Col. 1295D. “His Son”: Ἀποκαλύψαι τὸν υἱὸν αὐτοῦ ἐν ἐμοί, “to reveal his Son in me.” FABRIC.]  
> [Note: Col. 1296C. “Revealed.” Earlier editions corruptly read *revelabit*, “will reveal.” FABRIC.]

They had six wings: with two they covered the face, and with two the feet; with two they cried aloud, lest, when the face and feet of the Lord are said to be covered, what is above and below—and the length and breadth—should be shown concerning God: that neither his height (Job 11:8–9), nor depth, nor breadth, nor length can be known or discovered worthily by any creature, and least of all comprehended by human beings or by the thoughts of any humans. He who, in creating, perfected so great a nature and immeasurable magnitude of the elements—how much more does he who is known to have made such things surpass all things in every way!

> [Note: Col. 1296C. “Cried aloud.” Do not emend this to *volabant*, “flew.” For although the matter itself and the passage in Isaiah require this, Philastrius undoubtedly wrote *clamabant*, “they cried aloud”; hence below he also mentions the crying of the two wings. FABRIC.]  
> [Note: Col. 1296C. “Should be shown.” The sense requires *monstraretur*, “should be shown,” rather than *monstraret*. FABRIC. “*Monstraretur*.” Fabricius advises that *monstraretur* should be written here instead of *monstraret*; he could, however, have added that *monstraretur* is also read in the Basel edition. Philastrius uses this construction similarly in this same chapter 155: “No less a glory of faith and struggle should be shown in the union of diverse virtue”; in ch. 130: “this crime committed under the Jews through his seduction should be shown”; in ch. 132: “so that good fruitfulness of repentance should be shown to humankind by God’s exhortation”; in ch. 138: “so that the surpassing virtue of those first persons should be shown”; and elsewhere. GALEARD.]

He is known by faith alone: for “My power,” he says, “is perfected in weakness,” in likenesses and riddles, and is found thus (2 Cor. 12:9). When such immensity of God is spoken and proclaimed, it is sung and preached by two wings—that is, by the Cherubim and Seraphim, the Law and the Prophets.

> [Note: Col. 1296C. “For power, he says”: Ἡ δύναμίς μου ἐν ἀσθενείᾳ τελειοῦται, “My power is perfected in weakness.” FABRIC.]

The cry of the two wings, day and night—that is, both here and in the future—is the unceasing resonance every day of human belief in the heart and confession by the mouth. It was then sung by angels and preached by human beings in the world, so that, what they could not see in the height, depth, breadth, and length, they might rejoice at all times by believing in their hearts, confessing with their mouths, and singing with an unceasing voice.

For the Law and the Prophets show that the nature and substance of the divine quality are invisible and incapable of containment. As John says: “No one has ever seen God” (John 1:18). He did not say, “No one has believed,” but “No one has seen.” Therefore the Lord granted only the power of believing and the confidence of confessing, so that his power might be recognized as manifest when proclaimed by bodily frailty. Thus the Lord everywhere sets his faith before human beings—a faith which he had himself given earlier and later confirmed by his presence.

> [Note: Col. 1296D. “Incapable of containment.” That which can be contained in no place and comprehended by no human mind: ἀχώρητος. FABRIC. “For [the divine nature] is invisible and incapable of containment.” This word is frequently used by the ancient Fathers of the Church. Examples are available from Du Cange’s *Glossary*, under *Capabilis*; to these I add two from the old translator of Irenaeus. I, ch. 2: “As he was without beginning, incapable of containment, and incomprehensible”; Irenaeus: Ὡς ἧν ἀναρχός τε καὶ ἀχώρητος, “As he was without beginning and incapable of containment.” Likewise IV.20, or 37: “For the Father is incapable of containment”; and shortly afterward: “And therefore, although incapable of containment and incomprehensible, he makes himself visible, comprehensible, and capable of being received by human beings.” GALEARD.]

But the fourfold Cherubim and Seraphim—that is, lion, calf, human being, and eagle—are the diverse and stronger contests of the saints and virtues, joined to the varied and surpassing dignity of patriarchs, prophets, priests, Apostles, and likewise martyrs. Among those in whom abundant faith and love of Christ had formerly been recognized, doctrine was later proclaimed unequally in some, compelled by the circumstances of the time; nevertheless, a glory of faith and struggle no less great was shown, in the union of diverse virtue granted and bestowed by Christ and recognized among the whole Christian people.

> [Note: Col. 1296D. “Fourfold.” Above, ch. 139. FABRIC.]  
> [Note: Col. 1296D. “Patriarchs, prophets, priests, Apostles.” On this sacred tetractys, see above, chapters 139, 149, and 153. FABRIC.]  
> [Note: Col. 1297C. “Abundant faith and love of Christ.” Above, ch. 152: “and faith, doctrine, earnest endeavour, and an excellent life were recognized as abounding in the will of the few faithful persons and those who receive.” FABRIC.]  
> [Note: Col. 1297C. “Doctrine unequal.” Because of persecutors, during the first three centuries it was not permitted to preach Christian doctrine publicly everywhere in the manner subsequently permitted. Yet the glory of faith and struggle was not less, but rather greater, in the martyrs, especially in that period. FABRIC.]

Thus, what we cannot see or adequately define by human understanding, let us, believing in the heart and confessing with the mouth, not cease to preach with these powers of the two wings to Jews and Gentiles as a matter of joy, and let us fly upward by these exalted virtues, hoping for “the things above, where Christ the Lord is,” as the Apostle says (Col. 3:1). Let us not doubt that in this conviction we can attain perpetual salvation, as the same Apostle teaches: “If you believe in your heart and confess that Christ the Lord, the Saviour crucified in the body, has risen, you shall be saved. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:9).

> [Note: Col. 1297C. “The things above, where Christ the Lord is”: Τὰ ἄνω, οὗ ὁ Χριστός ἐστιν ἐν δεξιᾷ τοῦ θεοῦ καθήμενος, “the things above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God.” FABRIC.]  
> [Note: Col. 1297C. “If you believe”: Ὅτι ἐὰν ὁμολογήσῃς τῷ στόματί σου Κύριον Ἰησοῦν, καὶ πιστεύσῃς ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ σου ὅτι ὁ Θεὸς αὐτὸν ἤγειρεν ἐκ νεκρῶν, σωθήσῃ. Καρδίᾳ γὰρ πιστεύεται εἰς δικαιοσύνην, στόματι δὲ ὁμολογεῖται εἰς σωτηρίαν: “If you confess with your mouth Jesus as Lord, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you shall be saved. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth one confesses unto salvation.” Philastrius reverses the order of the first words and adds, of his own, “Christ the Saviour crucified in the body.” FABRIC.]

Accordingly he says of Christ the Lord that the substance of his divine quality does not consist in vision, measurement, or any composition, but is consummated abundantly in the power of our faith and confession. “What the breadth and length, height and depth are,” he says (Eph. 3:18–19), and the surpassing and incomprehensible grace and power of Christ God cannot be expressed powerfully by human frailty; but he taught that it may readily be attained in faith and through faith, though the human mind cannot prevail in setting it forth.

> [Note: Col. 1297D. “What the breadth and length [are]”: Ἵνα ἐξισχύσητε καταλαβέσθαι σὺν πᾶσι τοῖς ἁγίοις τί τὸ πλάτος καὶ μῆκος, καὶ βάθος, καὶ ὕψος, “That you may be strong enough to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and depth and height.” FABRIC.]  
> [Note: Col. 1297D. “The surpassing and incomprehensible grace of Christ God.” Γνῶναί τε τὴν ὑπερβάλλουσαν τῆς γνώσεως ἀγάπην τοῦ Χριστοῦ, “and to know the love of Christ which surpasses knowledge.” FABRIC. “The grace and [power] of Christ God, and it is not …” Thus the Hamburg edition, certainly incorrectly; the Basel and Cologne editions correctly read: “the grace and power of Christ God cannot …” GALEARD.]

## CLVI. HERESY CONCERNING THE PROPHET ISAIAH: LIPS TOUCHED BY A COAL
Some hold that, after Isaiah’s confession on behalf of the sinful people and the prayer which he had humbly poured out to God, one of the Cherubim (Isa. 6:6) was sent by God to the prophet, took a coal with tongs, touched his lips, and said to him: “Behold, now you have been cleansed” (ibid., 7).

[Note: [Col. 1297C] That the blessed Isaiah afterward.]  
[Note: [Col. 1297D] One of the Cherubim. “One of the Seraphim.” Our author below: “For when he says here that one creature is from among the Cherubim or Seraphim.” FABRICIUS.—One of the Cherubim. On these words Fabricius says: “Our author below: ‘For when he says here that [one creature is] from among the Cherubim or Seraphim.’” From this it appears that Fabricius wished *cum* to be changed to *nam* [“for”], where the editions read *cum hic de Cherubim aut Seraphim* [“when here he says [one creature is] from among the Cherubim or Seraphim”]; and certainly the latter is better, although the Hamburg edition still retains *cum* for *nam*, even against Fabricius’s wish. What follows in the text a little later, *edixerint* [“have proclaimed”], for which, Fabricius says, someone prefers *eluxerunt* [“have shone forth”], perhaps pleases more; although he himself adds that nothing should be altered—and rightly so, since both the Corbie manuscript and the Basel edition have *edixerint*. Likewise, a little later: *virtus ignea peragrans* [“a fiery power pervading”], although Cotelerius, cited by Fabricius, preferred *flagrans* [“burning”] to *peragrans*. GALEARD.]

[Note: [Col. 1297C] By the Lord.]  
[Note: [Col. 1298C] “Behold, now you have been cleansed.” “Behold, this has touched your lips, and it will take away your lawless deeds and cleanse away your sins.” FABRICIUS.]

But they suppose that one of the angels, or one of the living creatures, came to him, or that he took fire from the tongs and cleansed the prophet. This is not especially conducive to saving knowledge. For when he says here that one creature is from among the Cherubim or Seraphim, he speaks of the two Testaments. Hence the patriarchs, prophets, and priests proclaimed, and the apostles, who showed to the whole world the grace that was to come, ministering radiant gifts of fourfold power to those entering heavenly contests.

[Note: [Col. 1298C] But they suppose. The earlier editions have *aut* [“or”], and shortly afterward: *cum hic de Cherubim, aut Seraphim* [“when here [he speaks] of the Cherubim or Seraphim”]. FABRICIUS.]  
[Note: [Col. 1298C] They have proclaimed. Someone prefers “have shone forth,” but nothing should be changed. FABRICIUS.]  
[Note: [Col. 1298D] With fourfold power. See chapter 155. FABRICIUS.]

For Cherubim is said to mean “fullness of knowledge,” and Seraphim is called a fiery power pervading. Thus, possessing the fullness of spiritual knowledge and holding the riches of Christ’s mystery, they send and bear down to us diverse doctrines at the Lord’s command, announcing them likewise to every age without any interruption. From among them one was sent to the prophet Isaiah, proclaiming this teaching of Christ: that the Savior was to come in the flesh and bring abundant grace of the divine Spirit to believers.

[Note: [Col. 1298D] Cherubim is said to mean fullness of knowledge. In Philo, p. 668: “abundant recognition and knowledge,” and “a multitude of knowledge”; in Anastasius Sinaita, *Twelfth Anagogical Contemplation on the Hexaemeron*, p. 13; in Dionysius, *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, “an outpouring of wisdom”; and in Chrysostom, Homily 3 against the Anomoeans, “knowledge filled to overflowing.” For Origen, Jerome, Augustine, and others: “a multitude of knowledge.” See Petavius, *Dogmatic Theology*, On Angels, II.3. FABRICIUS.]  
[Note: [Col. 1298D] Seraphim: a fiery power pervading. The name *Seraphim* had wrongly dropped out in the printed editions; Cotelerius rightly observed that it should be restored, *Monumenta*, III, p. 559. He reads *flagrans* [“burning”] for *peragrans* [“pervading”]. For Jerome, Seraphim means “kindling” or “burning”; for Dionysius, “fire-kindlers”; for Cyril of Alexandria, “those who make warm”; for Chrysostom, “fiery mouths”; for Eusebius, *Demonstration of the Gospel*, VII.1, “the beginning of their mouth.” Others call them “spirits rising up.” See Jerome, Martianay edition, vol. II, p. 266. FABRICIUS.]

Isaiah, therefore, had received from the patriarchs, the Law, and his earlier prophets a stronger grace—that is, a fuller power of the divine Spirit—from those who came before, in order that he might proclaim to the age the mystery of Christ, namely his incarnation. Therefore the Lord also said to certain persons: “O dull of heart and slow in understanding” (Luke 24:25), why do you not perceive that everything which the Law and the prophets foretold concerning the Son of Man as yet to come had necessarily to be fulfilled? For it was fitting that blessed Isaiah should receive from the patriarchs and the Law, so that, taught by them, he might preach with courageous mind Christ’s bodily coming.

[Note: [Col. 1298C] That he might proclaim the holy mystery.]  
[Note: [Col. 1298D] The Lord to certain persons: to his disciples. “O foolish ones, and slow of heart.” FABRICIUS.]

Moreover, when he says that the angel received fire and cleansed Isaiah’s lips, he was undoubtedly showing that grace of the divine Spirit had been granted to him by the Lord, who says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I will, if it has already been kindled?” (Luke 12:49).

[Note: [Col. 1299C] “I came to cast fire.” “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I will if it has already been kindled?” Cotelerius’s note on *Recognitions of Clement*, VI.4, p. 549, should be compared with this passage. FABRICIUS.]

By the tongs, that is, by iron, he spoke of Christ’s unconquered nature and divine power: Christ’s body was created and completed in the womb of the holy Virgin by the divine Spirit and divine power, as it is written: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of God shall overshadow you” (Luke 1:35).

[Note: [Col. 1299C] “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you.” “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.” Philastrius has written “the power of God,” as he commonly renders one word by another. FABRICIUS.]

In that body, appearing, he would conquer all things, while himself being conquered by none. For just as all things are subdued and subjected by iron, from which the sword is produced, as has been said: “The word of the Lord [is] a two-edged sword” (Heb. 4:12), which can subdue all testimonies but cannot be subdued by anyone. After his Passion, in the resurrection, he was to give the blessed apostles the unconquered power of the divine Spirit, as it is written: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me,” and so forth (Isa. 61:1). And Peter, having received the promise from the Father, said to the Jews that he had poured out this grace “which you see and hear today.”

[Note: [Col. 1299B] And appearing in it.]  
[Note: [Col. 1299C] “The word of the Lord.” The Apostle says that the word of God is sharper than every two-edged sword: “sharper than any two-edged sword.” FABRICIUS.]  
[Note: [Col. 1300B] It can subdue all things.]  
[Note: [Col. 1299C] “The Spirit of the Lord.” “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me.” FABRICIUS.]  
[Note: [Col. 1299C] And so forth. Thus above, chapter 144. FABRICIUS.]  
[Note: [Col. 1299C] Saying to the Jews. Philastrius briefly indicates the force and meaning of that passage; he does not quote the words themselves. FABRICIUS.]

And just as we know tongs are fashioned for fire, so too we know that the Lord’s body was completed by the divine Spirit (Luke 1:35). Thus he gave his own, in the body, that promised grace and unconquered power, as he says: “Behold, I give you authority to tread upon every power of the enemy” (Luke 10:19); and the Apostle says: “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?” (Rom. 8:35). Through these things, to all who then believed in this age, as has been said, the divine Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands to those believing in Christ the Lord and Savior (Acts 6:6; 8:17; 9:17; 13:3; 28:8).

[Note: [Col. 1299B] The tongs and the fire.]  
[Note: [Col. 1299C] “I gave you …” “Behold, I give you authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy.” FABRICIUS.]  
[Note: [Col. 1299C] “Who shall separate us?” “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?” FABRICIUS.]
