And just as these two living creatures are understood as the two Testaments—the Law and the prophets—standing beside the Lord, as the apostles saw on the mountain, so it is reasonable to understand the two creatures also as: first, the Commandment which was given, which can likewise be understood spiritually, as it is written, and which the Savior did not abolish but rather confirmed. The second creature contained the teaching of Christ, namely faith in him, the grace of incarnation, the mystery of his Testament, Passion, and resurrection.

[Note: [Col. 1299D] As the apostles saw on the mountain. The apostles Peter, James, and John saw Moses and Elijah standing with Christ on Mount Tabor (Matt. 17:3); from this Philastrius infers this anagoge concerning the twofold Testament of the Law and the Prophets. FABRICIUS.]  
[Note: [Col. 1299D] It will be reasonable. Thus above, chapter 146: “therefore it is reasonable.” FABRICIUS.]  
[Note: [Col. 1299D] The first Commandment which was given. Our author frequently calls the pre-Mosaic dispensation “the Commandment”; I recall having noted this at chapters 110, 136, 148, 150, and 153. FABRICIUS.]  
[Note: [Col. 1299D] Which is also spiritual. Rom. 7:14: “the law is spiritual.” FABRICIUS.]  
[Note: [Col. 1299D] He did not abolish, but rather confirmed. Matt. 5:17: “not to abolish, but to fulfill.” FABRICIUS.]

Thus the law of the letter stands in the middle between the Commandment and Grace. If it is understood with reference to Christ, it is suitably accepted in many respects; but if anyone supposes that salvation lies in carnal justification, it is judged to be rejected. For before the Law—that is, before three thousand seven hundred years—the earlier righteous persons lived under the Commandment, worshipping the blessed Trinity, handing it down to their children and kinsfolk, and preaching it to the age; and the mystery of Christ the Lord was proclaimed from that most ancient Commandment itself.

[Note: [Col. 1299D] The law of the letter. The written, Mosaic Law. St. Augustine also distinguishes three periods, Sermon 110: one before the Law, another under the Law, and a third under Grace. So too the author of the books *On the Promises*, among the works of St. Prosper. Pelagius, preface to the Epistles of Paul, distinguishes the law of nature, the law of the letter, and the third law of the Old and New Testament, given last through the Holy Spirit by Jesus Christ our Lord, through whom “we have access into this grace wherein we stand and glory.” Pelagius frequently uses “the law of the letter” for the Mosaic law, Commentary on Romans 2.3. FABRICIUS.]  
[Note: [Col. 1300C] Before three thousand seven hundred years. According to Philastrius’s calculation, so many years elapsed from the creation of the world to the giving of the Law to Moses. See the notes above on chapters 110 and 112. FABRICIUS.]  
[Note: [Col. 1300B] Was proclaimed from the most ancient Commandment.]

The Law, therefore, is a reminder of the Commandment; it is also joined, according to faith, to the worship of the Trinity. Yet certain parts of it are again separated because of Jewish and carnal justification, since the prophets had previously overthrown those matters, the Savior rejected them, and the apostles forbade men to be circumcised (Gal. 5:2). The Law descended for a time because a carnal cause compelled it.

[Note: [Col. 1300C] The Law is a reminder of the Commandment. The Law repeats and recalls those things which God had indicated, through natural light, as to be observed by human beings before the Law. FABRICIUS.]  
[Note: [Col. 1300C] Which is also joined according to faith. The part of the Mosaic Law which concerns piety and innocence of conduct is to be kept devoutly even by Christians. FABRICIUS.]  
[Note: [Col. 1300D] A carnal cause compelling. These words should be joined as follows. The meaning is that, because of a carnal cause—the hardness of the Jews’ hearts—certain things were added by Moses to the natural law; they were by no means perpetual, however, but were again to be abrogated by Christ. FABRICIUS.]

But the grace of Christ—that is, the mystery of incarnation, Passion, resurrection, faith in him, and ascension into heaven—was known before the Law by all the righteous, and was not concealed from those who sought and received it: Enoch, Noah, Melchizedek, Jacob, and the other righteous and most blessed patriarchs, and the rest who lived before the Law of Moses, being established under the Commandment and justified in all things by the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 1300D] To those seeking and receiving. You will scarcely doubt that this should be read instead of *cupientibus* [“those desiring”], if you compare chapters 145 and 146 and my notes on them. FABRICIUS.—To those seeking and receiving. An excellent emendation by Fabricius, who adds: “You will scarcely doubt that this should be read instead of *cupientibus*, if you compare chapters 145 and 146 and my notes there.” The Basel and Lyons editions read *cupientibus*, but the Corbie manuscript rightly reads *capientibus*; from this chapter 150 should likewise be supplied: “according to what each one desires,” where the Corbie manuscript more fully reads, “according to what each receives and desires.” Thus Philastrius himself, chapter 156: “ministering radiant gifts to those receiving them for heavenly contests.” Therefore in chapter 153 also, *capientium* [“those receiving”] should undoubtedly be written instead of *cupientium* [“those desiring”], concerning which Fabricius had hesitated. GALEARD.]

The Law is also called Christ’s faith, as the Apostle says: “through the law of faith” (Rom. 3:27). The carnal Law is the justification of the Jews. Although the Commandment is not considered to be Law, nevertheless what is said and decreed by the Lord to his servant has the character of Law, so that he may choose either to keep it as a friend and faithful person, or to despise it as a servant subject under Law. Thus the Savior gave the apostles a commandment as to friends and faithful persons; and he had similarly given it to our father Adam before he sinned.

[Note: [Col. 1301A] Through the law of faith. “Through a law of faith.” FABRICIUS.]  
[Note: [Col. 1301A] But although the Commandment.]  
[Note: [Col. 1301A] As a friend and faithful person. See John 15:14–15; Matt. 24:45; 25:21 ff. FABRICIUS.]  
[Note: [Col. 1301A] He gave a commandment. Concerning loving one another: John 13:34; 15:12, 17. FABRICIUS.]

After sin, however, there was no longer a commandment of fellowship, kinship, love, and brotherhood; rather, a judgment of fearsome severity was decreed for despising the ordinances of the Law, as Moses also says: “Cursed is everyone who does not remain in the lawful provisions of this book.”

[Note: [Col. 1301A] Of fearsome severity. I think it should be read: “a judgment of servitude was decreed.” For above it says: “what is said and decreed by the Lord to his servant”; and shortly afterward: “either to keep [it] as a friend and faithful person, or to despise [it] as a servant subject under Law.” FABRICIUS.]  
[Note: [Col. 1302A] “Cursed is everyone.” “Cursed is every person who does not continue in all the words of this Law to do them.” FABRICIUS.]

Therefore the Savior reminded them of what had been said in the Law, and confirmed what had been given before the Law under those most blessed persons, so that he might join his teaching with that of the earlier righteous; unite many who thus believed, both the circumcised and likewise those natural persons—that is, believing Gentiles; and condemn the combined unbelief and ignorance of the Jews who refused, and of the others likewise.

[Col. 1301]

## SYLLABUS OF EXOTIC WORDS OCCURRING IN PHILASTRIUS

*Alligaturae*, 1132. Gaudentius, Sermon 4: *suballigaturae*.  
*Ana septuaginta duo*, 1258. It appears in Du Cange’s Glossary, which cites Philastrius.  
*Apocrypha*, 1199, 1240.  
*Beluinus*, 1250. Gellius, XIX.2, and Ambrose, *Hexaemeron*, VI.9, use this word.  
*Biothanati*, 1198.  
*Capaciter*, 1185. It is absent from Du Cange’s Glossary.  
*Carra*, 1225.  
*Christianitas*, 1228 ff., 1249.  
*Clima*, 1248.  
*Condescensio*, 1208. Du Cange has it, but in another sense.  
*Continentia*, for the act of containing, 1167.  
*Fructuositas*, 1263. It is absent from Du Cange’s Glossary. Gaudentius, Sermon 18: *infructuositas*.  
*Historiographi*, 1244, 1247, 1259, 1278.  
*Immensibilis*, for *immensus*, 1205.  
*Impassibilis*, 1204, 1205. It is absent from Du Cange’s Glossary.  
*Incapabilis*, 1296.  
*Incapacitas*, 1185. It is absent from Du Cange’s Glossary.  
*Inconvertibilis*, 1185. It is absent from Du Cange’s Glossary.  
*Incorporatio*, 1183.  
*Indocilitas*, 1231. Apuleius, *On Philosophy*. It is absent from Du Cange’s Glossary.  
*Intendere*, for *intelligere*, 1296, and there Fabricius in the Notes.  
*Numeralis*, 1174. It is absent from Du Cange’s Glossary. See Passerat’s *Lexicon*.  
*Numerositas*, 1155, and there Fabricius in the notes. It is absent from Du Cange’s Glossary. See *Thesaurus Eruditionis Scholasticae*, p. 1617.  
*Paganitas*, 1247, 1249, 1278. See also several other passages noted in the index of the Hamburg edition, where these had been omitted.  
*Passibilis*, 1204. It is absent from Du Cange’s Glossary, where *passibilitas* occurs.  
*Pecudialis*, 1176, and there Fabricius in the Notes.  
*Poenitudo*, 1201, 1251, 1263.

# INDEX OF MATTERS CONTAINED IN THIS VOLUME

## FIRMICUS MATERNUS

Prolegomena, ibid.—**TREATISE ON THE ERROR OF PROFANE RELIGIONS**, 981.—Preface, ibid.—**CHAPTER I.** He maintains that the elements are the principles of things; but since they are diverse and opposed in power, none of them is the supreme deity—although here he speaks only of fire, with the worship of the rest refuted in what follows—but that all have God as their maker and governor, 983.—**CHAPTER II.** He refutes the worship of water among the Egyptians, 984.—**CHAPTER III.** [The worship] of earth among the Phrygians, 987.—**CHAPTER IV.** [The worship] of air among the Assyrians and certain African peoples, 989.—**CHAPTER V.** [The worship] of fire among the Persians. He exposes their mysteries and fables, denounces their lascivious and mournful rites, often adding sacred Christian exhortations; and, at the end of the chapter, after the second lacuna, where he speaks of the human soul, he also offers a philosophical argument concerning the indissoluble nature of the mind, 992.—**CHAPTER VI.** From the worship of the elements he passes to other superstitions and reveals their secrets; first he recounts the history of the two Libers, the Cretan and the Theban, 995.—**CHAPTER VII.** He sets forth the story of Libera or Proserpina and asserts that Liber is worshipped as the sun and Libera as the moon, 999.—**CHAPTER VIII.** It contains a prosopopoeia in which the sun is imagined as refuting and detesting, in an address made to human beings, the divine worship which they themselves rendered to it, 1002.—**CHAPTER IX.** He briefly treats the mourning over the death of Adonis, struck by Mars transformed into a boar, and briefly recalls the Gospel narrative concerning the expulsion of a demon, 1004.—**CHAPTER X.** Obscenities in the cult of Paphian Venus, 1005.—**CHAPTER XI.** [Those] of Jupiter Sabazius, ibid.—**CHAPTER XII.** And he rejects the Corybants and their foul rites, 1006.—**CHAPTER XIII.** He teaches that every kind of wickedness is commended to humankind by narratives of the gods’ crimes, and that the deities are depicted as inferior and worse than human beings, 1006.—**CHAPTER XIV.** He contends that Serapis, his name, and his rites are a fiction borrowed from the history of the patriarch Joseph; and that demons gather in statues through continual sacrifices and are fed by the blood of victims. From Porphyry he proves that Serapis obeyed human commands and was forced to speak unwillingly; and he maintains the same of all the other pagan gods, who are subject to Christian command, 1011.—**CHAPTER XV.** He discusses the Penates, deriving their name from *penus* (“provisions”), and Vesta, merely the domestic fire: things therefore freely granted and useful to human beings, which they made into gods, 1015.—**CHAPTER XVI.** He explains the origin of the Palladium and maintains that neither Troy nor Rome was protected from fire by its divinity, nor will its worshippers be safe hereafter, 1016.—**CHAPTER XVII.** He discusses five Minervas. He says that the Palladium was dedicated to the fifth, daughter of Pallas; he exhorts that its image be burned and its temples destroyed, while at the same time inveighing against the shameful and bloody rites in which people are taught to sin, and demanding their abolition, 1018.—**CHAPTER XVIII.** He explains the etymologies, or origins, of the names attributed to the gods. He then expounds the symbols and signs of the worship of the gods, adducing many biblical passages wherever occasion seemed to permit, according to the character of the age and the method of interpreting sacred Scripture; and he is especially occupied in explaining five symbols, 1020.—**CHAPTER XIX.** 1. In the Eleusinian [mysteries]: “I have eaten from the drum” (*ἐκ τυμπάνου βέβρωκα*), etc.; here he says much concerning heavenly bread, perhaps Eucharistic, 1022.—**CHAPTER XX.** 2. Perhaps in the Mithraic [mysteries]: “Hail, bridegroom; hail, new light” (*χαῖρε νύμφιε, χαῖρε νέον φῶς*), on which occasion he says much concerning Christ as bridegroom and light of the world, 1025.

[Col. 1311]

**CHAPTER XXI.** 3. In another, certainly Mithraic [formula]: “God from the rock” (*θεὸς ἐκ πέτρας*), where he gathers many passages from Holy Scripture concerning Christ the rock, 1026.—**CHAPTER XXII.** 4. In a Bacchic [formula]: *ἐλιλικερος δέμορφοι*, more correctly *ἑλιξικέρως δίμορφε*, “spiral-horned, two-formed”; this he understands of the Devil as dragon, whose horns he relates to Christ’s cross, 1030.—**CHAPTER XXIII.** 5. In the Isiac [mysteries], concerning Osiris restored to life: “Take courage, initiates” (*Θαρρεῖτε μύσται*); here, on the occasion of the ointment with which the throats of the initiates were anointed, 1031.—**CHAPTER XXIV.** He discusses the ointment which the Father handed on to the Son and which the Son bestows on believers, 1033.—**CHAPTER XXV.** He gives a solemn warning concerning this wretched error of profane people, teaches that by this anointing the kingdom given to Christ is indicated, adducing many passages of Holy Scripture; and he also touches upon Christ’s descent into hell, 1034.—**CHAPTER XXVI.** He briefly expounds the Church’s doctrine concerning Christ compared with Adam: whatever Adam had lost, Christ, born of the Virgin Mary, found, 1037.—**CHAPTER XXVII.** 6. He returns to the subject and explains the final symbol of Mithraic initiation: “the bull [is] of the dragon, and the dragon [is] father of the bull” (*ταῦρος δράκοντος, καὶ δράκων ταύρου πατήρ*). He recalls the serpent, seducer of the first-formed humans, and its deadly worship, and says that the dragon was struck on the day when Christ appeared, 1038.—**CHAPTER XXVIII.** He calls the dragon the author of false deities and says that it always procured the restoration of its rites through wood. From this he notes, by a few examples drawn from the Phrygian rites and those of Osiris and Proserpina, the abuse of wood in idolatrous cults; then, intending to expound the order of the Cross, he adduces passages of the New Testament which the ancient Church and that age interpreted concerning the cross. Thus, having expounded and refuted the principal symbols and signs then prevailing in idol worship, so that the emperors to whom he wrote might proceed more confidently to the utter destruction of idols and their rites, 1040.—**CHAPTER XXIX.** He gathers judgments from the sacred book testifying to the vanity of idols; he speaks of the prosperous and flourishing state of the commonwealth under their rule and of the very near impending punishment of pagan impiety, 1043.—**CHAPTER XXX.** He presses upon the emperors the divine command concerning the extirpation of idolaters (Deuteronomy 13), promising them both a prosperous outcome and a happy future reign if they obey it, 1048.
